## Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed throughout the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume and every author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, and also with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; enlarged by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers wrote on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily learn which Fathers commented on the individual texts of each biblical book and in what places of their works they did so. An exceptionally accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and above all this collection, unique, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but for the first time gathered in our library from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. # In the year of the Lord 875. Saint Ado, archbishop of Vienne in Gaul

[Col. 0009]

# Historical encomium of Saint Ado

(From Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. VI.)

[Col. 0009A] **1.** All learned men know Ado, archbishop of Vienne, to have been famous not less for his dignity than for his writings. But who and what he was before his episcopate, no one, so far as I know, has hitherto explained. Some may perhaps wonder that I count him among the Benedictine family, since Trithemius, Wion, Menard, Bucelinus, and others did not enter him in our calendars; but they will cease to wonder when I explain the basis of my action.

**2.** I found a summary of Ado’s Life in the Breviary of the collegiate church of Romans among the Allobroges, where Ado’s memory is celebrated. In that Breviary, printed in 1612, the acts of the saints are reported word for word, not from recent writers but from the ancient authors who wrote them. The same was done in the case of Ado, whose feast day is marked in the said Breviary on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January: “Saint Ado, bishop and confessor.” Say everything from the Common except the Legend; and below: “Here begins the Life of Saint Ado, archbishop of Vienne.” These words sufficiently suggest that the summary of his Life [Col. 0009B] which I shall soon reproduce from the Breviary itself was excerpted word for word from an ancient author who long ago committed the deeds of Saint Ado to writing.

**3.** In addition, the church of Vienne, in its Breviary, which was printed 120 years ago, uses almost the same words as the church of Romans, up to Ado’s election as archbishop. From that point onward the Viennese Breviary gives another account of the deeds performed by Ado after becoming bishop. The very courteous man Peter Louvet, physician and historian of the Dombes, sent us a copy of it. It is useful here to present in turn the nine readings of the two Breviaries.

## From the Viennese Breviary

**I.** In the time of King Charles, who was reigning in France after his father, the emperor Louis, this holy man, born of noble lineage, was still a little child when his parents entrusted him to the monastery which from ancient times they call Ferrières.

[Col. 0009C] **II.** From there, with God as his companion, he visited for the sake of prayer the most renowned house of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and the other holy places established in the city of Rome; there he remained for nearly five years. Setting out on the return journey, he came to Ravenna, where he stayed for some time and also copied a certain little book lent to him by a religious brother. He testifies that this book greatly assisted him in describing the passions of the holy martyrs.

**III.** Moving on from there, he reached the famous city of Lyon. At that time its bishop was the distinguished Remigius, greatly beloved by kings. He piously received God’s servant Ado in the clothing of a poor man and supplied him with whatever he needed. But when, through mutual conversation, he was able, as Ado possessed a prudent mind, to recognize fully the marks of learning and integrity hidden within him, he tried with every effort to retain him with himself.

**IV.** After sending a petitioning embassy to Ado’s abbot, he obtained a letter of permission to retain him in his own service and that of his Church for as long as he judged useful. From then a considerable time had passed when, behold, the bishop, having learned with certainty of the death of the bishop of Vienne, resolved to act more urgently so that a bishop might be ordained for the church of Vienne. Accordingly, with the consent of both clergy and people, and with the counsel and presence of the bishops of the ecclesiastical province, this same servant of God was consecrated bishop of Vienne.

[Col. 0009D; Col. 0010A] **V.** For he was not, as happens with most people, immediately lifted into pride after receiving the degree of honor; rather, persevering even more in the humility with which he had begun, he continually urged all his subjects to become, according to their ability, imitators of the Truth, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart.”

**VI.** Because of this wholesome and holy zeal, at the entrance of the holy mother church built in honor of the Savior, he had a small house constructed in the form of the Lord’s tomb. Before its little doorway he also solemnly consecrated an altar, hollowed out of stones, in the name of Mary the sinner, Peter the denier, and the confessing thief. When many sick people came there, they customarily returned home rejoicing through the intercession of those persons.

[Col. 0010B] **VII.** It is unnecessary to commit to writing how great his care and constancy were in hospitality and in mercy toward the poor, since the door of his house was never closed—not even at mealtime. Thus he could rightly say with blessed Job: “My door was open to the traveler, and I was a father to the poor.”

**VIII.** Yet, though he was an indefatigable worker and occupied during the day with such exercises of good works, at night he did not give himself entirely to sleep as though exhausted by the day’s labor. After allowing himself a little rest to satisfy nature, he devoted what remained of the night to prayer and compelled the brothers to rise early for the night vigils. He himself was also present as usual, and had the lessons and responsories sung at length until, as daylight approached, the morning praises were performed.

[Col. 0010C] **IX.** When the time had come for the Lord, King of kings, to let his soldier rest from labor, after spending approximately sixteen years in the episcopate he passed from the present life to the future in a blessed end. His body was carried according to custom by the clergy and the whole people and buried in the church of the holy apostles among his predecessors, the bishops.

## From the Roman Breviary

**I.** In the time of King Charles, who was reigning in France after his father, the emperor Louis, this holy man, born of noble lineage, was still a little child when his parents entrusted him to the monastery which from ancient times they call Ferrières.

**II.** While he lived under regular discipline and was at that time regarded in that monastery as stricter than the others [or: “was held to be stricter”], inspired and chosen by God, he began to surpass all his contemporaries in literary studies. Avoiding everywhere the wantonness congenial to that age and all other childish pursuits, he earnestly strove to follow the serious conduct of old men and of the perfect.

[Col. 0010D; Col. 0011A] **III.** But when strengthened by the vigor of youth, he was kindled by an irresistible fire of desire to visit, for the sake of prayer, the house of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and the other holy places established in and outside the city of Rome. Therefore, taking on the dress of a pilgrim, he undertook the journey he desired.

**IV.** Humbly dressed and devout in heart, he entered the apostolic house, remaining constantly awake in prayer. He frequently rejoiced to spend the night in nocturnal vigils until morning. Since he was known to nearly everyone in the city of Rome, after nearly five years had passed he came to Ravenna, where he copied a certain little book lent to him by a religious man for the purpose of describing the passions of the holy martyrs.

**V.** From there he reached Lyon. At that time, as it happened, its bishop was the distinguished Remigius, worthy of honorable memory and greatly beloved by kings. He piously received God’s servant Ado and treated him kindly. When he was able to discern the marks of learning and integrity in him, he entrusted to him the church of Saint Romanus together with its adjoining possessions, so that he might devote himself to prayer in greater seclusion.

[Col. 0011B] **VI.** When the death of the bishop of Vienne had become known, the sons of that Church, moved by divine inspiration in this matter, all together, with one counsel and equal will, requested that Lord Ado be placed over them as bishop. Accordingly, with the consent of clergy and people and with the counsel of the bishops of the province, this same servant of God was consecrated bishop of Vienne.

**VII.** Seeing, however, that religious observance had partly fallen away from its proper practice because of adverse circumstances, he exerted himself in every way so that through his own zeal it might gradually be restored to the former standard of rectitude. Many enduring proofs of his institution remain. For he also beautifully established a rule for the singing of the offices, both nocturnal and diurnal.

[Col. 0011C] **VIII.** Moreover, although there may be no testimony of a human being to the zeal with which he undertook the restoration and adornment of churches, the buildings themselves are not lacking. It is unnecessary to commit to writing how great his care and constancy were in hospitality toward the poor, especially since the door of his house was not closed—I will not say at any other time, but not even at mealtime.

**IX.** When the time had come for the Lord to reward his soldier with blessed recompense, after spending approximately sixteen years in the episcopate he passed from the present life to the future in a blessed end. His body was buried with the greatest devotion in the church of the holy apostles. He lived approximately seventy-six years.

**4.** When I first read these things in the Roman Breviary—for I received the Viennese copy much later—I was greatly rejoiced that I had some material with which to illuminate the history of so important a man. But this tempered my pleasure: I lacked ancient and reliable monuments with which to prove the account. While I was thinking about this and rereading the letters of Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, his 122nd letter came to mind, and it satisfies my wishes. For in this letter, addressed to Gerard, duke or count of the province, and to Berta, his wife, I discovered most certain evidence that agrees entirely with what has been set out above concerning Ado and his deeds. Since this matter is of no small importance, it will be worthwhile to reproduce the entire letter here, so that no one may suspect my reliability.

> “To the most excellent Duke G. and his most illustrious wife B., Lupus sends present and future salvation.
>
> “The distinguished reputation of your integrity has always gladdened all good people; but now it has blossomed more abundantly into everyone’s knowledge, since God has confirmed that same integrity of yours by an outcome beneficial to all Christians. When you have granted what at first you deigned to promise and afterward to undertake, we shall endeavor to heap up our thanks.
>
> “As for the matter you diligently investigate, know that the monk and my disciple Ad. never fled from our monastery. Rather, at the request of Marcward, abbot of Prüm, we honorably sent him from Prüm—or, as the reading is corrected, to Pronea—and he lived there with him for some time, avoiding the plots of certain envious men. From there, out of a desire for learning and love of quiet, he settled in the city of Lyon.
>
> “When the most reverend men Remigius and H. of Grenoble earnestly requested him and praised the conduct of the brother mentioned above, although he had once received my permission verbally, he also received a regular letter of permission. When it is produced, it will faithfully declare what I think of him. I know with certainty that he also possesses ecclesiastical letters from our venerable bishop Guenilo. Nothing hinders him, if God calls him, by which his election could rightly be invalidated.
>
> “He conducted himself well among us. He is capable of teaching what the Church greatly needs; he is supported by regular and episcopal letters; he is adorned by the nobility of his ancestors; and, in the holy purpose, according to the judgment of the aforementioned bishops among whom he dwelt, he perseveres devoutly. What remains except that what God inspires in the holy bishops should be done?
>
> “What wonder, then, if I once spoke somewhat harshly about him? That was the fault of his enemies, who shamelessly spread falsehoods. What I now attach to this letter [or: “present”] is my judgment: a steadfast account of what I had first seen and afterward learned. I wish you prosperous health.”

**5.** From this letter of Lupus we learn that a certain noble and learned monk of Ferrières, whose name began with the letters *Ad.*, lived in the province of Lyon, was approved by the bishops Remigius and Hebo, and was elected to episcopal dignity. All these details agree with the Viennese and Roman Breviaries and cannot legitimately be applied to anyone other than Ado. They must be explained more distinctly, point by point.

But before I do so, it is right to remind the reader how much the literary commonwealth owes to the diligence of the most learned Stephen Baluzius. In the new edition of the works of Lupus the abbot, he brought light to the memory of our Ado by correcting a single word—or rather only two letters. For where the Massonian edition had previously read *monachum meum nonnunquam* (“my monk sometimes”), he restored from a collation of ancient codices *monachum meum Ad. nunquam* (“my monk Ad. never”), although, as he modestly admits, he could not guess who this man was whom we see represented by the two letters *Ad.* I now turn to the sequence of events in Ado’s life.

**6.** When Ado is said to have been born in the time of King Charles, surnamed the Bald, interpret this as I have often explained similar passages: he became famous during that period. For it is established that he came into the world while Charlemagne was reigning, around the year 800. Indeed, he died at approximately seventy-six years of age in the year of Christ 875, as we shall see below.

In both Breviaries he is said to have been born of noble lineage; Lupus says that he was adorned by the nobility of his ancestors. I conjecture that his homeland was the district of Wastin or Sens.

**7.** While still a little child, he was entrusted by his parents to the monastery which from ancient times they call Ferrières, in accordance with the custom prescribed in chapter 59 of the Rule of Saint Benedict concerning the offering and reception of children. From this I conjecture that Ado was born in a place near the monastery of Ferrières, which was mentioned above in connection with the Life of Saint Aldric, archbishop of Sens.

There he appears to have been received as a boy by Abbot Sigulf. He conducted himself well there and, according to Lupus, surpassed all his contemporaries in literary studies, as the Roman Breviary says. Lupus supplies testimony to his learning when he writes that Ado was capable of teaching what the Church greatly needs.

**8.** After remaining for some time in the monastery of Ferrières, he was honorably sent, at the request of Marcward, abbot of Prüm or Pronea—who governed that place from 829 to 853—to Pronea. Ausonius praises in his *Mosella* by that name a stream flowing past the place; hence the monastery was sometimes called Pronea and commonly Prüm, with a slight alteration of the word.

Nevertheless, I would prefer to read: “At the request of Abbot Marcward, Ado was sent to Prüm on the Pronea,” so that the location of Prüm beside the river Pronea may be indicated.

There was easy movement of monks back and forth between the two monasteries, Ferrières and Prüm, both because Marcward had been taken from the monastery of Ferrières and because he was closely connected with Lupus. Indeed, the monks of Ferrières were sent to Prüm chiefly to learn the German language, the necessity of which at that time Lupus attests in letters 70 and 91.

Moreover, although at that time the monasteries were connected by no bond of common governance, they were nevertheless readily open to monks traveling back and forth because of the unity of their religion, as Marcward says in Lupus’s letter 72 to Dido, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter at Sens, a man highly skilled in the medical art, to whom he sent his monks for healing.

Hence Lupus writes in letter 116 to the monks of the monastery of Saint-Germain near Auxerre:

> “True charity has always flourished among the inhabitants of our monasteries; but never has it displayed its greatness by such certain signs as in our own time.”

**9.** After Ado had remained for some time at Prüm, he was, according to Lupus, attacked by the plots of certain envious men. To avoid them, he went to Rome to visit, for the sake of prayer, the house of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles.

Lupus does not mention this journey. He himself admits that he lent too credulous an ear to Ado’s rivals, although elsewhere he records the Roman pilgrimages of his monks in letters 101, 102, and 103, written on behalf of Aldulf and Acaricus, and in letters 106 and 107, written on behalf of Dolivold, both in his own name and in that of Guenilo, archbishop of Sens, to commend the pilgrims.

After spending nearly five years in Rome, the holy man came to Ravenna, where he copied a certain little book lent to him by a religious brother, for the purpose of describing the passions of the holy martyrs—that is, the Martyrology, to which we shall return later.

This little book was the ancient Martyrology that Ado used in composing his own and that was edited by Rosweyde. Prefixed to it is a letter of Ado, declaring how much he benefited from that ancient Martyrology. He says:

> “For this work”—that is, for Ado’s Martyrology—“so that the days of the martyrs might be marked with complete accuracy, since they are usually found confused in the Kalends, there assisted me a venerable and very ancient Martyrology, sent from the city of Rome to Aquileia to a certain holy bishop by the Roman pontiff, and afterward lent to me for several days by a religious brother. I carefully transcribed it while staying at Ravenna and judged that it ought to be placed at the beginning of this work.”

This is what Ado says in the preface to his Martyrology; from it the preceding words of the Viennese Breviary are derived.

**10.** Leaving Ravenna, Ado proceeded to Lyon, where the distinguished Remigius, worthy of honorable memory, was then bishop. He piously received God’s servant Ado and kindly supplied him with everything necessary. When, through mutual conversation, he was able to recognize the marks of learning and integrity hidden within him, he tried with every effort to retain him with himself.

After sending a petitioning embassy to Ado’s abbot, he obtained letters of permission to retain him in his own service and that of his Church for as long as he judged useful.

The Viennese Breviary agrees with Lupus on this point, for Lupus testifies that Ado settled in the city of Lyon out of a desire for learning and love of quiet. “When the most reverend men Remigius and Hebo of Grenoble earnestly requested him and praised the conduct of the brother mentioned above,” Lupus says, “although he had once received my permission, he also received a regular letter”—they call such letters obediential letters—and “also ecclesiastical or dismissal letters from the venerable Guenilo, bishop of Sens.”

That literary studies flourished at Lyon at that time, if ever they did, is proved by the learned men Leidrad, Agobard, Amulo, and Remigius, bishops of that Church, as well as by the deacon Florus.

The Roman Breviary adds that Remigius entrusted to Ado the church of Saint Romanus, together with its adjoining possessions, so that he might devote himself to prayer in greater seclusion.

I would not dare to state with certainty which church this was. Perhaps it was the church of Saint Romanus situated in the eastern part of the city of Vienne. Ado himself testifies to this in his Martyrology on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, where he writes that the bodies of Saints Severinus, Exsuperius, and Felix were transferred to that church. In the little book on the Life of Saint Theuderius the abbot, he mentions the basilica of Saint Romanus the martyr in the suburb of the city, in the village of Brenniacus. This basilica still survives and is entrusted to the Knights [Col. 0014B] of the Order of Malta.

**11.** When the death of the bishop of Vienne had become known, the sons of that Church, moved by divine inspiration in this matter, all together, with one counsel and equal will, requested that Lord Ado be placed over them as bishop. Accordingly, with the consent of clergy and people and with the counsel of the bishops of the province, this same servant of God was consecrated bishop of Vienne.

The letter of Lupus quoted above teaches us that some resisted this election, among them Gerard, count of those regions, because he believed that Ado had escaped by flight from his monastery. Lupus absolves him from every stain of defection and infamy, declaring that nothing prevented his election from being valid if God called him.

This occurred after the death of Agilmar, bishop of Vienne and successor of Saint Barnard. This election, I say, took place in the year 860, as is established both by the acts of the council of Langres, held around the Kalends of July in the preceding year, which Agilmar attended; by the council of Tusiacum, to which Ado subscribed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November in the year 860; and finally by the Synod of Vienne mentioned below, which Ado held in the year of Christ 870, in the third indiction, in the tenth year of his episcopate.

Therefore Agilmar, his predecessor, must be said to have held the see for nineteen years, not merely nine, as John a Bosco maintained, since it has been demonstrated that Barnard, Agilmar’s predecessor, died in the year 842.

Agilmar indeed departed this life on the day before the Nones of July, and in the year 860, according to volume I of the *Analecta*, page 103. In his place Remigius of the holy church of Lyon and Hebo, bishop of Grenoble, with the clergy and people, elected Saint Ado.

In John a Bosco’s *Appendix to the Floriacensis Library*, where the Antiquities of Vienne are discussed, there is a letter of Pope Nicholas I sent to Ado with the pallium at the beginning of his pontificate. In that letter he warns Ado that he is saddened because, in the profession of faith he sent to the pontiff, Ado approved only four general councils, omitting the fifth and sixth. He orders him to explain his position on this matter; meanwhile he sends the pallium and the chapters of the Roman synod recently held.

He afterward sent him another letter confirming the privileges of the church of Vienne. Whether Ado approved the seventh synod is uncertain. Indeed, in the *Chronicle*, which he seems to have composed after receiving episcopal dignity, he rejects this synod—a position that was then held by the Gallican Church.

In the short Chronicle of the bishops of Vienne, composed in 1139 at the command of Burno, Saint Ado is said to have received the pallium and confirmation of the privileges from Pope Nicholas in 861, together with the decrees of the Lateran—that is, the Roman—council.

**12.** Nor was he, as happens with most people, immediately lifted into pride after receiving the degree of honor. Rather, persevering even more in the humility with which he had begun, he continually urged all his subjects to become, according to their ability, imitators of the Truth, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). These words are read in the Viennese Breviary.

**13.** In the year 866, according to the Bertinian Annals, King Charles, surnamed the Bald, and King Lothair jointly arranged a mission at Attigny concerning the affair of Teutberga, Lothair’s concubine. Charles communicated privately to Pope Nicholas what seemed appropriate to him through Egilo, archbishop of Sens; Lothair did so through Ado, archbishop of Vienne, and through his chamberlain Walter.

Ado carried this out by a letter written to Nicholas. The pope’s reply on this matter survives incomplete. In it the pontiff praises his most holy brother Ado, archbishop, because he watched zealously over the condition of God’s holy Church and, aroused by zeal for rectitude, stood against the conduct and actions of offenders, transgressors, and violators of the holy laws.

**14.** Four other letters of Nicholas written to Ado are extant in the second appendix to the letters of Nicholas, in volume VIII of Labbe’s edition of the Councils.

In the first, the pontiff replies to Ado’s consultations about King Lothair’s divorce and about the cleric Alvicus. In the second, he says that the lower churches ought not to depart from Roman customs. In the third, he explains the reason for the delayed synod and rebukes Ado because he had called Count Gerard’s presbyter a priest; he also responds to various consultations. In the fourth, he confirms the privilege of the metropolitan church of Vienne.

A fifth letter is added, from Anastasius the librarian to Ado, concerning the death of Pope Nicholas. I have learned that this letter was also sent to other bishops of Gaul from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Marianus at Auxerre, in which it is inscribed as follows:

> “To the venerable and greatly beloved Ill. archbishop, Ill. [sends] abundant greetings. Sad news to you, etc.”

There is also another fragment of a letter sent to Ado by Pope Nicholas, in which the pontiff rebukes Ado because, relying on his authority, the subdeacon Albericus had taken a wife contrary to the prescriptions of the canons.

Two letters of Pope Adrian II were also printed in Labbe’s edition of the Councils. In the first, the pontiff, having been warned by Ado why he had departed from the decrees of Pope Nicholas, excuses himself while praising Ado’s zeal. In the other, which is mutilated, he testifies that he received the letters Ado had sent to Nicholas, his predecessor.

**15.** In the same year 866, Pope Nicholas, in letters given to Hincmar, bishop of Reims, ordered Remigius of Lyon, Ado of Vienne, Wenilo of Rouen, together with the other archbishops and bishops of Gaul and Neustria, to assemble jointly at the city of Soissons in order to examine the case of Wulfad and the other clerics of Reims, whom Hincmar had restored to clerical rank after they had been ordained by Ebbo.

This synod was convened on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, but Ado did not attend it. The reason is uncertain.

**16.** Hincmar himself, in his own name and in the name of Ado and the other bishops of Gaul, wrote to Louis, king of Germany, on behalf of Bertulf, archbishop of Trier, against Walton, a monk of the monastery of Saint Maximin and, as Hincmar says, an invader of the see of Trier.

Hincmar also wrote to Ado, archbishop of Vienne, among other matters concerning a letter of blessed Avitus written to Saint Remigius, which a certain monk named Rotfrid had told him he had read in Ado’s possession. If Ado could discover anything further about Saint Remigius, Hincmar asked him to send it, more precious than gold and topaz.

The author Frodoardus, in book III, chapter 21 of his *History of Reims*, also testifies elsewhere that this Rotfrid was a monk of the monastery of Remigius at Reims.

**17.** I add, from the *Chronicle* of Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, that Remigius, bishop of Lyon, sent letters to Ado, bishop of Vienne—whom he calls vicar, that is legate, of the Roman Church—and to Pope Nicholas on behalf of the deposed bishops of Trier and Cologne, namely Teutgaud and Gunthar.

Finally, Remigius himself and Ado wrote to Pope John concerning simony and the fact that unworthy men were being promoted to the episcopate by lay hands.

**18.** In the year 869, after the death of Hebo, bishop of Grenoble, King Lothair obtained from his brother, the emperor Louis II, that the bishopric of Grenoble be granted to one of his clerics named Bernarius.

Ado received a letter from Louis concerning this matter on the day before the Ides of July, instructing him to ordain Bernarius bishop as soon as possible.

At the Kalends of August he also received other letters: one from King Lothair, who informed him of his prosperous journey to Rome and ordered him to come to meet him on his return at Saint Maurice; and another from King Charles, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September. Charles calls Ado “most dear to us” and explains that he had granted the bishopric of Grenoble to a certain cleric who had formerly been deacon of the venerable archbishop Remigius and afterward of his nephew Lothair, on the condition, he says, that “if you approve him canonically in your judgment, he be ordained bishop there by your holiness.”

These letters are extant in Sirmond’s third volume of the Councils of Gaul.

**19.** Ado, seeing that religious observance had partly fallen away from its proper practice because of adverse circumstances, exerted himself in every way so that through his own zeal it might gradually be restored to the former standard of rectitude, as we read in the Roman Breviary.

Many enduring proofs of his institution remain. For he also beautifully established a rule for the singing of the offices, both nocturnal and diurnal.

**20.** Among the synods held on his authority, one comes to mind which the learned Peter Louvet, mentioned above, copied from the Chartulary of Vienne and sent to our Acherius. It runs as follows:

In the year 870 of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, a synod was convened at Vienne, the metropolitan church, with the lord and venerable Archbishop Ado presiding. He investigated with the most vigilant care the affairs of the churches and the needs of his sons, and settled them according to ecclesiastical custom.

The reverend Manno, provost of the monastery of Saint Augendus, arrived and, explaining the reason for his coming, brought forward a certain church belonging to the aforesaid monastery and situated within the diocese of Vienne, in the village of Velnis. It was endowed in honor of Saint Peter by a privilege granted to him by the predecessors of the most holy archbishop just mentioned, and preserved until that time by the same pontiff [probably “by the same bishop”]. The rector of the village of Saint Alban asserted that the church had been left desolate.

The same venerable provost also produced a written record of an inquiry conducted in the time of the lord Agilmar, of pious memory, since even then there had been a dispute between the rectors of the churches concerned. But because that holy synod judged the inquiry invalid, since it did not see it supported by the canons [lacuna: *canonicorum …*], it pleased the holy pontiff that the whole matter should be reopened from the beginning by the most holy priests, so that, once the truth had been established, the dispute—which had long been debated—might be confirmed [or: brought to an end].

When these men had testified and stated the order of events, it seemed good to the lord pontiff, with the consent of the most holy synod, that just as the holy congregation of the monastery of the most blessed Augendus had been honored in the days of his holy pontifical predecessors, so also, in this petition and in its other necessities, the holy metropolitan Church of Vienne should offer it honor and assistance to the extent of its powers. In order that the complaint, once silenced, might possess its privilege more securely in the future concerning the matter of the Church of Vienne [of Saint Augendus], it should also be strengthened by written letters.

Accordingly, in this manner, I, Ado, archbishop of Vienne, consenting and agreeing to the pious counsel of my sons, have confirmed this below with my own hand, and have asked my holy sons to confirm it according to ecclesiastical custom. Done publicly at Vienne in the month of April, in the tenth year of the episcopate of the lord Ado, in the third indiction.

### 21

There are also several other documents made during Ado’s pontificate in the same Chartary. One records the litigation of Witfred, advocate of the Church of Saint Maurice, who came publicly into the city of Vienne, in the presence of the lord Ado, venerable archbishop of that same church, and of Erlulf, viscount and envoy of the illustrious Count Boso, Constantius, fellow bishop, and others. He complained against a certain Sigifred because he had violated the immunity of the Church of Saint Maurice in the villages subject to it.

Another document in the same codex concerns Rodstagnius and his wife Bertildis, who transferred their property in the estate of Saint Ferreolus to Ado and the Church of Vienne. From Ado himself they received five books from the treasury of the Church of Vienne, together with a chalice and paten of refined gold, each weighing one pound according to Spanish measures. Rodstagnius transferred the property belonging to him in that village to Ado and his clergy, receiving a doorway, a sod, and an *andelanc*; after some time, when parchment had been supplied, he asked Ado, Constantius the chorepiscopus, Erlenus the provost, Leutbertus the dean, Teutelmus the abbot and deacon, and other clerics to draw up a written instrument concerning it.

Done on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the fourth year in which the lord King Charles succeeded to the kingdom of his nephew Lothair, that is, in the year of Christ 869.

The third document is by the same Ado. He grants the usufruct of certain estates to Amalgaudus, his wife Volfolda, and their son Hadrian, because they had donated their property to the episcopal Church of Saint Stephen. It is useful to excerpt certain passages from this kind of grant, which they called a *praestaria*:

> It is the custom and justice of the Church that, when someone has transferred his property and resources to God and his servants, the Church should in return grant him from its possessions something that he has reasonably requested. Therefore I, Ado, archbishop of the Church of Vienne, together with the priests and clerics of that same holy mother Church, grant to you, Amalgaudus, and to your wife Volfolda and your son Hadrian, the property which you have transferred from your authority and right into the authority of our church by written charters. And in return for this so pious a donation, we also grant to you, your wife, and your aforesaid son, by way of a benefice, the village of Alausium belonging to our church, to be served by you for as long as you live, and the tenant-holdings which, by this *praestaria*, we have already granted to you together with the churches in Valle-Aurea. [lacuna]
>
> In return for the vesting, each year, on the feast of the most blessed Maccabees, on the Kalends of August, you shall provide one meal for the canonical brothers residing in the monastery at Vienne, and on that same day the aforesaid church shall offer “general” prayers for you and your relatives.

This document bears no date.

In a letter of Raganfridus, archbishop of Vienne, written at the prompting of Berilo, viscount, the property belonging to the Church of Saint Peter outside the walls of the city of Vienne is confirmed. This property had formerly been restored by a royal order of Lothair, the former king, at the urging of the holy bishops Remigius of Lyon and Ado of Vienne.

### 22

In the aforesaid year 870, Ado adorned the Acts of Saint Desiderius, bishop and martyr of Vienne, in a more polished style for the benefit of the people of Vienne. He sent them to the monks of the monastery of Saint Gall in Alamannia together with some relics of that same saint. More on this and on his other literary labors below.

### 23

He subscribed to two synods of Chalon: the first, convened in the year 873 in the church of Saint Lawrence, which was restored to the canons of the Church of Saint Marcellus; the second, in the year 875, in the basilica of Saint Marcellus itself, where he subscribed letters issued on behalf of the monastery of Tournus, published by Peter Francis Chifflet in the *Probations of the History of that Monastery*.

### 24

The Vienne Breviary briefly recounts the remaining deeds of the holy man: his devotion to adorning the churches, his hospitality and charity toward the poor, and his assiduity in the divine offices, as may be seen above in lessons 6, 7, and 8 of that same Breviary.

### 25

When the time had come for the Lord to reward his soldier with blessed recompense, after spending approximately his sixteenth year in the episcopate, he passed from the present life to the future by a happy death. His body was reverently buried in the church of the holy Apostles. Thus says the Breviary of Romans, with which the Vienne Breviary agrees. The Breviary of Romans adds:

> He lived approximately seventy-six years.

I am convinced that Ado died in the year 875, both because he held the episcopate for sixteen years from the year of Christ 860, and because Ortramnus, his successor, subscribed to the Council of Pontion in the year 876.

The Breviary and Martyrologies of Romans and the Gallican Breviary and Martyrology assign the day of his death to the sixteenth day of December. The Vienne manuscript also gives the year; our Claudius Stephanotius received a copy of it from the learned Nicholas Chorier. Here are its words:

> On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January: Saint Ado, bishop of Vienne, a man of extraordinary holiness, in the year 875 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the eighth indiction. He governed his church for sixteen years and was buried in the Church of the Apostles at Vienne, that is, in the basilica outside the walls belonging to the monastery of Saint Peter, where it was customary for the bishops of Vienne to be buried.

The monastery of Saint Peter passed from the Order of Saint Benedict to secular canons, as did many other institutions which, as a little book on the Life of Saint Clarus the abbot in the second century teaches us, once existed at Vienne.

From this one may conclude that Ado was born around the year 800, since he died in 875 after living approximately seventy-six years.

This is what can be said about the deeds of Saint Ado, insofar as it has been possible to recover them from reliable records, especially from Lupus’s Letter 122 and from the Vienne and Romans Breviaries. The latter first gave me the opportunity and material for illuminating the life of Ado.

Andreas Sausseius had read the Vienne Breviary; in his Gallican Martyrology he writes that Ado spent his early years in the monastery of Ferrières under the discipline of Abbot Lupus. No one before him, if I am not mistaken, had noticed this.

The feast of Saint Ado is celebrated with a double rite in the Church of Vienne, and more solemnly in the Church of Saint Peter, where his relics are believed to be kept together with the bones of other holy archbishops beneath the altar, after the plundering of the sacred reliquaries by heretics within the memory of our fathers.

### 26

At the end, something must be said about Ado’s writings. The first place among them appears to belong to the *Martyrology*, for he composed his other works when he was already a bishop; but he undertook this one before his episcopate, as may be inferred from the fact that, after spending five years at Rome, he reached Ravenna. There he transcribed a certain book lent to him by a religious brother, for the purpose of recording the passions of the holy martyrs—that is, a *Martyrology*—which some have wrongly attributed to Ado, bishop of Trier.

It was first published in print by Jacobus Mosander, a Carthusian, and then by Heribert Rosweyde, who found Ado’s name prefixed in the Everbodius Codex in the following form:

> Ado, archbishop of Vienne, compiled it as a kind of epilogue, beginning with the feasts of the apostles, or of their disciples, or of their successors; and at the end there follows in his work the Prayer of Ado, composed in verse.

Both editors relegated to an appendix the names of certain saints whom they believed had been inserted by others. Whether this was rightly and properly done, we shall soon see.

### 27

In many handwritten copies of this *Martyrology* that I have seen, Ado’s name does not appear. This was doubtless because the letter bearing Ado’s name was prefixed not to the beginning of Ado’s own *Martyrology*, but to the old Roman *Martyrology*—as Rosweyde believed—the one Ado used in composing his work and which is absent from most manuscript codices. For this reason, the copyists of Ado’s *Martyrology* omitted it.

Nevertheless, its author sufficiently reveals himself in many passages of his *Martyrology*. For, when discussing the translation of the body of Saint Augustine, doctor of the Church, to Ticinum in the year 822 by Liutprand, king of the Lombards, he says that it had recently taken place on the fifth day before the Kalends of September.

Then, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, he mentions the translation of the relics of Saint Cyprian: first from Africa to Gaul during the reign of Charlemagne, and then from Arles to Lyon by Bishop Leidradus. The account added in printed editions concerning a translation to Compiègne by Charles the Bald appears to have been inserted after Ado’s death; it does not occur in our copy, which was transcribed by hand six hundred years ago.

Later, when discussing the institution of the feast of All Saints on the Kalends of November, the author says:

> But in Gaul, at the admonition of Gregory, of holy memory, the most pious Emperor Louis, with all the bishops of his kingdom and empire consenting, established that the feast of All Saints should solemnly be celebrated annually and perpetually on the aforesaid day.

Furthermore, in our manuscript codex the dedication of the church of the monastery of Celle, carried out in the year 850, is described accurately on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, in precisely the manner reported above under the year 873, where we discussed the translation of Saint Frodobertus the abbot.

What moves me to reject the idea that this was added by an interpolator is that a person of a later age would not have known the individual circumstances—so to speak—with such precision, whereas the anonymous author who composed the book on the Life of Saint Frodobertus, abbot of Celle, published in the second century, appears to have been ignorant of them.

From this it may be inferred that this martyrologist lived during the reign of Charles the Bald.

### 28

The place where he spent much of his time is sufficiently indicated: Burgundy, clearly, whose native saints he commends more carefully than others. Above all, he seems wholly occupied with recording matters relating to the city of Auxerre and the monastery of Saint Germanus. For this reason I once conjectured that he had been a pupil of that monastery.

In our codex, the dedications of each of its churches, altars, and crypts are recorded. Saint Germanus, bishop of that city, is mentioned wherever an occasion arises—for example, on the fourth day before the Ides of July, where, discussing Saint Sabinus, the author says:

> He was one of the disciples of the great Father Germanus.

And on the Nones of August, where he discusses Saint Cassianus, at whose tomb, he says, Saint Germanus the bishop arrived:

> Astonishing to relate! After the customary prayer had been offered, he called to him from the tomb and said: “What are you doing here, brother Cassianus?”

Finally, in addition to the other feasts of Saint Germanus, he records his vigil on the day before the Kalends of October. All these details sufficiently indicate that the man at some time lived not far from Auxerre.

### 29

I know that Mosander and Rosweyde either did not read these and many other passages in the manuscript codices they used, or relegated them to an appendix as though they had been inserted by others. Certainly some things were added by more recent writers in our codex, such as the commemoration of Saint Maiolus the abbot on the fifth day before the Ides of May, and the reception at the monastery of Vézelay, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, of the body of Saint Ragnobertus, bishop of Bayeux, together with a few other items.

But I believe that the material concerning Auxerre and the monastery of Saint Germanus was written by the original author, since precisely the same material occurs in several copies of his *Martyrology* that I have read, both complete and abridged.

The same judgment should be made concerning nearly all the names that Mosander and Rosweyde relegated to a separate section. The fact that different parchment codices lack different items arises from two causes.

First, when this *Martyrology* was read during the divine offices in various churches, some people abridged it, while others removed certain saints unknown to their own province or church. Second, the author himself enlarged his *Martyrology* on many occasions, adding various saints who were not present in the first version.

Thus it happened that those who copied the primary exemplar do not have as many entries as those who used secondary exemplars.

Certainly, the commemoration of Saints Florentinus and Hilarius, which is absent from Rosweyde’s Ado, is cited from Ado’s *Martyrology* by Peter de Natalibus in book VIII, chapter 124.

Finally, it is clear that Ado was the author of this *Martyrology*, both from the letter prefixed to the old *Martyrology* that he used and from Notker’s *Martyrology*, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June. There Notker explains why Ado makes no mention in his own work of Saint Desiderius, although he was archbishop and martyr of Vienne. In fact, no commemoration of him appears in the commonly circulated *Martyrology* of Ado, which Peter de Natalibus repeatedly cites under Ado’s name.

### 30

From this we understand that Ado wrote this *Martyrology* before his episcopate and that, when he later reread his work, he overlooked Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, and Theuderius, abbot in the same city.

He was an old man when he appended to this work the prayer which begins in Rosweyde with these verses:

> Christ, I beg you, in your gentleness grant pardon to your sluggish pupil;  
> I am slow, yet no one comes too late to you.  
> Long has error held us through the years that have passed;  
> Let this punishment, I beg, suffice for my merits.  
> Brief life remains, and old age is more inclined toward death;  
> Now, an old man, I can no longer sin, nor do I wish to—I am yours.

Yet one may doubt whether these verses are Ado’s, since they are attributed to Florus in volume I of the *Ancient Analecta*, page 407. But since the space for the title is blank in the Petavian manuscript, these verses cannot legitimately be taken away from Ado.

These are the reflections that occurred to me concerning the aforesaid *Martyrology*. The commemoration of Saint Maurus the abbot, Saint Scholastica, and nearly all the other saints whom Mosander and Rosweyde removed ought to be restored to it.

As for whether the old *Martyrology* that Ado used was Roman, I have discussed that matter in the preface to this volume.

### 31

Ado also recorded, with as much brevity as he could, a summary of past times from the beginning of the world down to the beginning of the reign of the emperors Lothair and Louis and of the kings Louis and Charles, as he himself states in his *Chronicle*. Its final section in the printed editions belongs to another author, beginning, if my conjecture does not deceive me, at the point where it discusses the division of the kingdom which King Louis of Noricum made among his sons.

Nevertheless, the Thuanus copy, which is more than five hundred years old, ends in the same way as the printed books, that is, in the year 879.

### 32

He also polished the Acts of Saint Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, for the benefit of his fellow citizens of Vienne, as is confirmed by the preface of Ado, bishop of the Church of Vienne, written in the year 870 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third indiction, and sent with the Passion of Saint Desiderius the bishop to that same church. It contains these words:

> Ado, sinful and humble bishop of the Church of Vienne, to the most beloved brothers and sons of that same church: Since the life and martyrdom of your most blessed Father Desiderius have been commended in ancient writings, I have undertaken to review them and commit them to writing for you, so that, through his exhortations and zeal, I might inflame you more fervently to love eternal life.

This *Life* was first published in print by Henry Canisius in volume VI of the *Ancient Readings*. At the end of the *Life* there is added the following short work by Ison, a monk of Saint Gall.

The aforesaid Ado, archbishop, took care in the year mentioned above to send this Passion to us brothers serving God in the monastery of Saint Gall under Abbot Grimald, when we had requested relics of Saint Desiderius from him, together with the relics of that saint and of other saints, as well as the deeds and passions described below. He sent them through sufficiently trustworthy messengers, especially through Beroldus the priest, as Notker testifies in his *Martyrology* on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, where he writes concerning Saint Desiderius:

> Since the venerable Father Ado, in our own time bishop of that same church, judged it superfluous to say anything about him, since he was present and therefore thoroughly known in every respect to his own people, we have thought it appropriate to communicate a brief summary to those ignorant of these matters, following the written account which that apostolic man sent to us in the year 870 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the third indiction, through the most holy priest Beroldus, a native of those regions but now devoted to the service of Christ in the fortress of Zurich, together with the relics of that holy martyr Desiderius and the remains and sufferings of other saints, while we were established in the monastery of Saint Gall.

### 33

Both testimonies mention the deeds and passions, or sufferings, of the saints which Ado gave in handwritten form as a gift to the monks of Saint Gall. From these words it is clear that the *Martyrology* was composed by Ado himself.

This is openly declared by Notker’s testimony, in which he explains why Ado does not mention Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, in his *Martyrology*:

> Concerning him, the venerable Father Ado, since he was present and therefore thoroughly known in every respect to his own people, judged it superfluous to say anything.

For it was observed above that the mention of Desiderius is omitted from copies of Ado’s *Martyrology*, both printed and handwritten.

### 34

Moreover, the same holy pontiff committed to writing a little book on the Life of Saint Theuderius, abbot of Vienne, and dedicated it to the monks of that monastery with this prologue:

> Ado, bishop of Vienne, sends eternal salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ to the brothers residing in the monastery of Saint Theuderius. I have decided to commend the life of your father, the blessed Theuderius, to your holiness in writing, so that through his example I might invite you more fervently to the love of eternal life, and so forth.

This *Life* was published in the appendix to the first century.

Before we take leave of Ado, it is useful to make a few observations concerning the succession of the bishops of Vienne who existed in the ninth century. In addition to the index in both editions of *Gallia Christiana* and a third by John de Bosco, our Claudius Stephanotius supplied me with one taken from a Vienne manuscript. This index was compiled at the command of Bishop Burno in the year 1239.

You also have another index of the bishops of the ninth and tenth centuries in volume I of the *Analecta*. All these indexes should be compared with the Vienne manuscript Calendar.

The *Chronographer* of Burno of Urso, from whom I begin, writes as follows about Urso and his successors:

> Saint Urso, a good and simple man, weighed down by old age, chose an assistant for himself to act in his place. He was buried in the Church of Saint Stephen on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

> Saint Ultraja, a Christian descended from a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, highly learned, assistant and successor to the aforesaid Bishop Urso, and greatly loved by Charlemagne, ended his life on the Ides of March and was buried with his predecessor in the Church of Saint Stephen.

In the commonly circulated indexes and likewise in the manuscript Calendar of the Church of Vienne he is commemorated in these words:

> Commemoration of Ultraja, bishop of Vienne, who, in the time of the Emperor Charles, while the aged Urso was still living and since he was a man of Benjaminite descent, assumed the episcopate of Vienne. In his time, through the action of the pious prince Charles, the Church of Vienne recovered part of its property. He governed the church for eleven years and was buried in the Church of Saint Severus [read: Saint Stephen], where his predecessor Urso lies buried.

The *Chronographer* of Burno, the manuscript Calendar, and consequently also John de Bosco place Wlferius before Urso or Ursio, whose presence at the Council of Frankfurt in 794 is established by canon 8, and distinguish Wlferius from Ultraja.

But our Ado, whose testimony deserves greater credence, places Wlferius after Urso. He says that Wlferius was of Bavarian nationality, had two names, and bore Ultreja as his native name.

> Saint Barnardus, who was appointed in about the year 810 in succession to Ultraja or Wlferius, died in 842, as was established in the preceding volume in his Life.

Here the *Chronographer* of Burno must be corrected, for it places Barnardus’s ordination in 817 and his death in 862.

> Saint Agilmarus obtained from the Emperor Lothair a confirmation of the foundation of the monastery of Roman, founded by Saint Barnardus, says the *Chronographer*. According to the foregoing evidence, he died in the year 860, not 800, as the *Chronographer* mistakenly states, on the day before the Nones of July, and was solemnly buried at the feet of Naamatius in the Church of Saint Peter.

> Saint Ado lost the light of this life on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January in the year 873, according to the foregoing evidence, not in 876, as in the *Analecta*, nor in 879, as in the *Chronographer*.

After Ado, the clergy and people elected Othtrannus archbishop of Vienne. Bernerius, bishop of Grenoble, attended his consecration, according to the *Analecta*. The *Chronographer* says:

> Saint Othrannus lies in the Church of Saint Peter. He died on September 16 in the year 888.

After Othrannus, Barnoinus was elected and consecrated. He died in the year 899 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eleventh indiction, according to the *Analecta*. There is an error in the year of the Incarnation, as I later discovered from the autograph, and likewise in the following entry.

For in the same year of the Incarnation, 899, in the eleventh indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, a Sunday, Raganfridus was consecrated archbishop. Isaac, bishop of the holy Church of Grenoble, attended his consecration, during the reign of Louis, son of Boso.

Here again the *Chronographer* must be corrected: it places Barnoinus’s death in the year 901 and says that he attended the council held at Vienne by a legate of the Apostolic See in the year 892.

Let this suffice concerning the bishops of Vienne and concerning Ado.

[Col. 0023]

# The Chronicle of Saint Ado of Vienne Divided into Six Ages

[Note: Ado, archbishop of Vienne, renowned for his life, morals, and learning, wrote a commentary on the six ages of the world, or a *Chronicle* from the origin of the world down to his own times, that is, to the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, surnamed the Stammerer. The same Ado is said to have died in the year 874; therefore, what is added in the same *Chronicle* down to the year 879 appears to have been appended by someone else. It is unfortunate that this *Chronicle* is riddled with many errors which could not be corrected because of the lack of manuscript codices.]

Namely:

1. From the origin of the world to the Flood.  
2. From the Flood to the birth of Abraham.  
3. From Abraham to David.  
4. From the reign of David to the migration of the Hebrews to Babylon.  
5. From that migration to Christ our Savior.  
6. From Christ to the end of the world.

*(From the* Bibliotheca Patrum Maxima, *volume XVI.)*

# The First Age: From the Origin of the World to the Flood

[Col. 0023A]

Julius Africanus, during the reign of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, was the first among our writers to extract brief chronological accounts arranged by generations and kingdoms in the plain style of historical writing. Then Eusebius of Caesarea and Jerome the priest, of holy memory, published histories of many chronological canons, arranged simultaneously according to kingdoms and times.

After them came various other writers, among whom Victor, bishop of the Church of Tours, after reviewing the histories mentioned above, completed the deeds of the succeeding ages down to the consulship of Justin the Younger.

We have recorded a summary of these times, from the beginning of the world down to the reigns of the emperors Lothair and his brother Louis and of the kings Louis and Charles, with as much brevity as we could manage. We have added alongside it a descending line of chronological notices [Note: We have placed these chronological notices, enclosed in parentheses, before the text. EDITOR.], by which the general outline of the past age may be known.

We have also added notes from the divine books wherever we thought it appropriate for the instruction of readers, so that the reader may gather much from a little.

God formed the creation of all things in six days. On the first day he created light. On the second, he suspended the firmament of heaven in the midst of the waters, while the waters themselves, the earth, and the heaven above, together with the powers that would praise the Creator in it, had been created before the beginning of these six days.

On the third day, after gathering into their proper place the waters that had covered everything, he commanded the dry land to appear.

On the fourth, he placed the stars in the firmament of heaven. This day is now called, as is inferred from the conjunction of the equinox, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

On the fifth day he created the swimming and flying creatures.

On the sixth, he formed the terrestrial animals and the man Adam himself. From the side of Adam, while he slept, he brought forth Eve, the mother of all living beings. This day is now called, as seems credible, the tenth day before the Kalends of April.

Hence it is rightly believed—unless a more probable opinion prevails—that on that same tenth day before the Kalends of April the Lord was crucified. For it was said that on one and the same day, not only of the week but also of the month, the second Adam, having been put to sleep by a life-giving death for the salvation of the human race, sanctified for himself the Church as his bride through the heavenly sacraments brought forth from his side. It was, of course, on that day that he himself had first created Adam, the father of the human race, and, taking a rib from his side, had fashioned the woman, through whose assistance the human race would be propagated.

[A. M. 130] Adam, at the age of 130, begot Seth, and lived 800 years after him. But the Seventy Interpreters placed 230 years before the birth of Seth and 700 afterward.

Seth is interpreted as “resurrection,” because in him the righteous seed was restored to life—that is, the stock of the sons of God—and because he signified the resurrection of Christ from the dead. Abel, whose death was inflicted by the Jews, signified Christ’s death; Abel’s name is said to mean “mourning,” and he was killed by his brother Cain.

[235] Seth, at the age of 105, begot Enos, and lived 807 years after him. The Seventy, however, placed 205 years before the birth of Enos and 707 afterward.

Enos is interpreted as “man,” concerning whom blessing is spoken. He began to call upon the name of the Lord, because it is proper to human beings, mindful of their condition, to invoke the help of the Creator, so that they may rejoice in being sons of the resurrection.

[Col. 0025A] [325] Enos, in his ninetieth year, begot Cainan, and lived 815 years after him. The Seventy placed 190 years before the birth of Cainan and 705 afterward.

His name is interpreted as “the nature of God.”

[395] Cainan, at the age of 70, begot Malaleel, and lived 840 years after his birth. The Seventy said that there were 170 years before the birth of Malaleel and 740 afterward.

Malaleel is interpreted as “Who is the Lord God?” or “God from life.”

[460] Malaleel, in his sixty-fifth year, begot Jared, and lived 830 years after him. The Seventy placed 165 years before the birth of Jared and 630 afterward.

Jared is interpreted as “descending” or “strengthening.”

[622] Jared, at the age of 162, begot Enoch, and lived 800 years after him. In this generation the two textual traditions nowhere differ.

Enoch was taken up by God. He is also said to have written certain things, as the Apostle Jude testifies. But because of their antiquity, the writings attributed to him were rejected by the Fathers as suspect, such as the stories about giants put forward under his name [Note: On the writings of Enoch, see Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca*, book II.], according to which they had no human fathers.

[684] Enoch, at the age of 65, begot Methuselah, and after his birth walked with God for 300 years. The Seventy placed 155 years before the birth of Methuselah and 200 afterward.

Enoch is interpreted as “dedication.” Taken up in the seventh generation, he signifies the city of the elect, which, laboring for God in the sixth age of this world, awaits the glory of dedication in the seventh, the Sabbath of the future.

But because the reprobate are content with faithfulness to the present alone, Cain consecrated the city he founded not in the seventh generation but in his firstborn son Enoch.

[874] Methuselah, at the age of 187, begot Lamech, and lived 782 years after him, that is, until the Flood. The Seventy place 167 years before the birth of Lamech and 802 afterward.

As the reader will easily see, this number extends beyond the time of the Flood by twenty years according to the Hebrew truth, but by fourteen years according to the authority of the Seventy. How, then, is it true that only eight persons were saved in the ark?

But in the books of the Hebrews and Samaritans it is written as follows:

> And Methuselah lived 187 years and begot Lamech. And Methuselah lived, after he begot Lamech, 782 years, and begot sons and daughters. And all the days of Methuselah were 969 years, and he died. And Lamech lived 182 years and begot Noah.

Thus, from the day of Methuselah’s birth to the day of Noah’s birth there are 369 years. Add to these the 600 years of Noah, because the Flood occurred in the six hundredth year of his life, and it follows that Methuselah died in the 969th year of his life, in the year when the Flood began.

Methuselah, at the age of 187, begot Lamech. In this generation giants were born; and in this age Jubal, from the line of Cain, discovered the art of music. His brother Tubal-cain was also the inventor of bronze and iron.

[1056] Lamech, at the age of 182, begot Noah, and lived 705 years after him. The Seventy place 189 years before the birth of Noah and 565 afterward.

In this one generation alone the total differs, because Lamech is found to have lived thirty-four years longer in the Hebrew texts than in the books of the translators of the Seventy. Since this could have happened through a scribal error, greater credence is given to the language from which the translation into the other language was made by interpreters.

[1556] At the command of a divine oracle, Noah began to build the ark in the five-hundredth year of his life. At this time, as Josephus reports (*Antiquities*, book I), those men, knowing that they might perish either by water or by fire, recorded their discoveries on two pillars, one made of brick and the other of stone, so that the things they had wisely discovered would not be erased from memory.

The stone pillar is said to have survived the Flood and to remain to this day in Syria.

In Noah’s six-hundredth year the Flood came, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month. Josephus reports that his ark came to rest on the mountains of Armenia called Ararat.

This first age of the world contains 1,656 years according to the Hebrew translation, and 2,242 according to the edition of the Seventy.

*(Orosius, book I, chapter 3.)*

In this first age, the sacred writings contain, in addition to historical truth and the condition of every creature, the following teaching: through the power of the Holy Spirit, creation, defiled by the stain of sin through disobedience, was to be washed by sanctified waters for perpetual grace; and thus the light of piety was to be separated from the night of impiety by a merciful and just division.

In the formation of Adam and of the woman Eve from the rib of his side, they contain the sacrament of Christ and the Church.

In the despised commandment, they contain the teaching that perpetual death is inflicted by a just judgment upon all who transgress God’s commands.

They also contain the sentence pronounced against the serpent, the devil, which remains upon those who do his will; and, in the woman’s curse, the continuation of original sin; and the birth of the children of transgressors under sin; and the aforesaid punishment of sin in the labor of sweat and pain, which Adam, the root of the human race, transmitted by propagation to the branches growing from the condemned root.

In Cain and Abel, the figure of two peoples—the Jews and the Christians—is set forth: the sacrifice of the elder is rejected, while that of the younger is accepted; the multitude of the elect is to be transferred to true and eternal dedication, whereas the sons of the murderer, corrupting the order of their way, are to be cut off by the just and manifest judgment of almighty God.

## THE SECOND AGE, FROM THE FLOOD TO THE BIRTH OF ABRAHAM

[Col. 0027]

[Col. 0027A] [1657] In the second age of the world, on the first day of this age, which is the twenty-seventh day of the second month, Noah came out of the ark, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water. Blessed Peter the apostle, recalling this in his Epistle, immediately took care to explain it: “Which baptism, in a similar form, now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience to God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who is at the right hand of God.” He teaches that, in the water of the flood, baptism was prefigured; in the ark and the things it contained, the Church and her faithful; and in the number eight of the souls, the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, in whose faith we are baptized.

Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, from whom there are seventy-two languages: that is, [Col. 0027B] twenty-eight from Shem, thirty from Ham, and fifteen from Japheth.

[1658] In his hundredth year, Shem fathered Arphaxad, two years after the flood; from him came the Chaldeans. After the birth of Arphaxad, Shem lived on for five hundred years—that is, until the fiftieth year of Jacob’s birth.

[1694] In his hundred and thirty-fifth year, Arphaxad fathered Shelah. Here the Seventy translators inserted one generation more than the Hebrew text, saying that Arphaxad, when he was one hundred and thirty-five years old, fathered Cainan, who, when he was one hundred and thirty years old, himself fathered Shelah. The evangelist Luke appears to have followed their translation at this point. After Shelah’s birth, Arphaxad lived four hundred and three years; the Seventy, however, assign him [Col. 0027C] four hundred and thirty years after the birth of Cainan, and Cainan three hundred and thirty-eight years after the birth of Shelah. From Arphaxad came the Samaritans or Indians.

[1724] When Shelah was thirty years old, he fathered Eber, after whose birth he lived on for four hundred and three years. Before Eber’s birth, the Seventy placed one hundred and thirty years, and afterward three hundred and thirty. From this Eber the name and lineage of the Hebrews arise.

[1785] When Eber was thirty-four years old, he fathered Peleg, after whose birth he lived on for four hundred and thirty years. The Seventy placed one hundred and thirty-four years before Peleg’s birth and two hundred and seventy afterward. Peleg is interpreted as “division.” His parents therefore gave him this name because, at the time of his birth, the earth was divided through the confusion of languages. [Col. 0027D] The rhetorician Arnobius thus recalls this division (ARNOBIUS, on Psalm 104): “To Shem, Noah’s firstborn, a portion was assigned from Persia and Bactria as far as distant India, and as far as Rhinocorura. These regions of the earth contain twenty-seven languages, in barbarian speech [Note: [Col. 0027] Philastrius, *On Heresies*, chapter 106; he asserts that people used several languages before Babel.]. In these languages there are peoples of forty-six homelands—not of different languages, but of different homelands: just as, although there is one Latin language, under that one language there are different homelands, those of the Bruttians, Lucanians, Apulians, Calabrians, Picenians, Tuscans, and so forth, if we mention these and similar examples.

“Ham, however, Noah’s second son, [extended] from Rhinocorura as far as Gaddila. He had languages in Punic speech in the region of the Garamantes; in Latin, toward the north; and in barbarian speech, toward the south, among the Ethiopians, Egyptians, and inner barbarians, with varied speech in twenty-two languages, in three hundred and ninety-four homelands. Japheth, the third, [extended] from Media northward as far as Gaddila. Japheth has the river Tigris, which divides Media and Babylonia; in two hundred homelands he has twenty-four languages with varied speech.

“Thus all the languages together number seventy-two; the homelands of the peoples, however, number one thousand, situated in the three-part world—Asia, Africa, and Europe. As we have said, Japheth has the river Tigris, which divides Media and Babylonia; Shem has the Euphrates; and Ham has the Geon, which is called the Nile.”

When Peleg was thirty years old, he fathered Reu, after whose birth he lived on for two hundred and nine years. The Seventy placed one hundred and thirty years before Reu’s birth and two hundred and eight afterward. In Peleg’s time the tower was built and the division of languages took place. The height of this tower is said to have been 5,174 paces, narrowing into increasingly constricted levels so that the weight above could be supported more easily. They describe there marble temples adorned with precious stones and gold, along with many other things that seem incredible. [Col. 0028C] The author of this tower was the giant Nimrod. After the confusion of languages, he migrated from there to the Persians and taught them to worship fire. From that point the errors of the nations increased; temples were built, and certain rulers of the nations were worshiped as gods.

[1820] When Reu was thirty-two years old, he fathered Serug, after whose birth he lived on for two hundred and seven years. The Seventy placed one hundred and thirty-two years before Serug’s birth and two hundred and eight afterward. The kingdom of the Scythians arose; its first king was Tanaus.

[1858] When Serug was thirty years old, he fathered Nahor, after whose birth he lived on for two hundred years. The Seventy placed one hundred and thirty years before Nahor’s birth and two hundred afterward. The kingdom of the Egyptians began; its first king was Zos.

[Col. 0028D] [1878] When Nahor was twenty-eight years old, he fathered Terah, after whose birth he lived on for one hundred and nineteen years. The Seventy placed seventy-nine years before Terah’s birth and one hundred and thirty-nine afterward. The kingdoms of the Assyrians and Sicyonians arose. The first king among the Assyrians was Belus, whom some consider to have been Saturn. Among the Sicyonians, it was Aegialeus, after whom Aegialea was named; it is now called [Col. 0029A] the Peloponnese. Ninus, the first king of the Assyrians, driven by a desire to extend his rule, carried warfare abroad and passed his bloody life amid great wars throughout Asia.

[1948] When Terah was seventy years old, he fathered Abraham, after whose birth he lived on for one hundred and thirty-five years. Under him Zoroaster, the inventor of magic, was killed by King Ninus. Ninus himself, while attacking a city that was defecting from him, was struck by an arrow and died; and the walls of Babylon were built by Semiramis, queen of the Assyrians (BEROSUS, book V). Thus far the second age of the world extends, and the years from the flood to Abraham amount to 1,072 according to the Vulgate edition, that is, the edition of the Seventy translators; according to the Hebrew books, however, they are found to be far fewer, [Col. 0029B] namely 292.

In this second age, the sacred Scriptures contain, besides historical truth, the faith and obedience of the Fathers, full of mysteries. In this age Noah, obeying the mystical command and construction, built the ark according to symbolic numbers and measurements, and, fulfilling the command given to him, filled it with clean and unclean animals. Thus he fashioned for us the holy Church, overflowing with wondrous mysteries: bearing the wood of the passion and cross; displaying, through Christ’s death, the grace of baptism; and, as it were, pouring forth our price through the door in its side. Through that door the dove—which is itself the Church, endowed with so great a gift—went forth. But the heretical raven, going out and being unworthy of such great mysteries, lured by the blackness of sin from the one who had sheltered it, flies across the waters, shipwrecked by its desire for a human corpse, and refuses to return. Noah built the ark from incorruptible wood; Christ builds the Church from human beings who will live forever, and she now floats upon the waves of this world.

That the ark was commanded to be made from squared timbers signifies the stable life of the saints, prepared on every side for every good work: for whichever way a square is turned, it stands firmly.

That the timbers of the ark are joined with pitch inside and outside signifies, in the bond of unity, the endurance of charity, so that when scandals assail the Church—whether from those within or from those outside—the fraternal bond may not yield and break the bond of peace. Pitch is an extremely hot and powerful adhesive, signifying the ardor of love, [Col. 0029D] which, with great strength, endures all things in order to preserve spiritual fellowship.

That the ark is three hundred cubits long, so that six times fifty are completed, signifies that the whole duration of this world is extended through six ages, in all of which Christ never ceased to be preached. But in the three hundred cubits the sign of the wood of the passion is displayed: the numerical value of the letter itself indicates the sign of the cross, through which, made companions in Christ’s passion by baptism, we attain the length of eternal life. That its breadth is expanded to fifty cubits signifies that the hearts of believers are enlarged by the gift of the Holy Spirit in charity. Thus, on the fiftieth day after his resurrection, Christ sent the Holy Spirit to believers. That its height rises to thirty cubits—the number which its length, three hundred cubits, contains ten times—signifies that Christ is our height. At thirty years of age he consecrated evangelical teaching, testifying that he had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it. That the ark is six times as long as its breadth and ten times as long as its height displays the form of the human body in which Christ appeared. For the length of the body from crown to foot is six times the breadth from one side to the other, from right to left or from left to right; and it is ten times as long as it is high from the ground. Thus the ark was made three hundred cubits in length, fifty in breadth, and thirty in height.

[Col. 0030B] The same ark, gathered into a single cubit, is completed above; so the Church, the body of Christ, gathered into unity, is raised up and perfected. That it has an entrance at the side signifies that no one enters the Church except through the sacrament of the redemption of sins, which flowed from Christ’s opened side.

That the lower parts of the ark are constructed with two and three chambers signifies that the Church gathers from all nations either a twofold multitude, on account of circumcision and uncircumcision, or a threefold multitude, on account of Noah’s three sons, whose descendants filled the world.
