The lower parts of the ark are so called because in this earthly life there is a diversity of nations. But at the summit we are all perfected into one, and there is no diversity, [Col. 0030C] because Christ is all and in all.

That animals of every kind are enclosed in the ark signifies that people from all nations and peoples are gathered into the Church. The sheet shown to Peter also signifies this, showing that clean and unclean animals are there (Acts 11), just as in the Church’s sacraments both good and evil people are found (Acts 2).

That the clean animals are in sevens and the unclean in pairs is because the good preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, while Holy Scripture commends the Holy Spirit in a sevenfold operation. The evil, however, are shown by the number two to be prone to schism and, in a certain sense, divisible.

That Noah himself is counted as the eighth with his family is because the hope of our resurrection appeared in Christ, who rose from the dead on the eighth day, that is, after the seventh day, the Sabbath.

That the flood occurred seven days after Noah entered the ark is because we are baptized in the hope of the future rest, which was signified by the seventh day.

That, apart from the ark, all flesh sustained by the earth was consumed by the flood signifies that, apart from fellowship with the Church, the water of baptism, although it is the same water, not only does not bring salvation but rather brings destruction.

That it rained for forty days and forty nights is because every guilt of sins is admitted through the ten commandments of the Law throughout the whole world, which is contained in four parts. Whether that guilt pertains to the days and is contracted through prosperity, [Col. 0031A] or pertains to the nights and is contracted through adversity, it is washed away through the sacrament of baptism.

That Noah was five hundred years old when the Lord spoke to him and commanded him to make an ark, and that he was six hundred years old when he entered it, signifies that in the sixth age, through the manifestation of the Gospel, the Church was to be built. The second month of his six-hundredth year, in which Noah enters the ark, signifies the same. For two months are concluded by the number six: from the number six come the names sixty, six hundred, six thousand, sixty thousand, six hundred thousand, and whatever thereafter rises indefinitely into greater sums according to the same numerical progression. That the twenty-seventh day of the month is mentioned pertains to the symbolism of the square, which has already been explained in connection with the squared timbers. Here, however, it is more evident, because the Trinity perfects us, prepared for every good work—that is, squared, in a certain sense—in the memory by which we remember God, in the understanding by which we know him, and in the will by which we love him. For three times three, and that again three times, make twenty-seven, which is the square of the number three.

That the ark came to rest—literally, rested—in the seventh month refers to that seventh rest in which the perfected rest. There too the number of the square is repeated: on the twenty-seventh day of the second month this sacrament was commended, and again on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month the same commendation was confirmed when the ark came to rest. For what is promised in hope is exhibited in reality.

[Col. 0031C] Moreover, because that seventh rest is joined to the eighth resurrection, there is in the sacrament of our regeneration—that is, in baptism—a profound and lofty mystery: the water rose fifteen cubits above the mountains. Thus eight and seven make fifteen; but eight signifies resurrection, and seven signifies rest. This sacrament of resurrection and rest surpasses all the wisdom of the proud, so that by their knowledge they can in no way investigate the height of resurrection and rest. And because seventy is counted from seven and eighty from eight, the two numbers being joined together make the one hundred and fifty days during which the water was raised up. These days commend and confirm to us the same height of baptism in consecrating [Col. 0031D] the new human being to maintain the faith of rest and consecration.

That the raven, sent out after forty days, did not return—whether it was intercepted by the waters or lured by some floating corpse—signifies people rendered most foul by the impurity of desire, and therefore inclined to go after the things outside, in this world; or to be rebaptized, as though baptism outside the ark—that is, outside the Church—were of benefit, so that they may kill and lead astray, teach and hold fast.

That the dove, having been sent out and finding no place of rest, returned shows that, through the New Testament, rest is not promised to the saints in this world. For it was sent out after forty days, and that number signifies the life lived in this world. Finally, after seven days it was sent out again, on account of the sevenfold spiritual operation, and it brought back a fruitful olive branch. This signified that some who have been baptized even outside the Church, if the richness of charity has not been lacking in them, may at a later time be brought, in the mouth of the dove as in a kiss of peace, into the unity of fellowship. That, after another seven days, when it was sent out again, the dove did not return signifies the end of the world, when there will be rest for the saints—not still in the sacrament of hope by which they are joined together in this age, as long as they drink what flowed from Christ’s side, but already in the perfection itself of eternal salvation, when the kingdom will be handed over to God and the Father, so that, in the clear contemplation of unchangeable truth, we will need no bodily ministries.

[Col. 0032B] That in the six hundred and first year of Noah’s life the roof of the ark was opened signifies that, when the sixth age of the world has ended, the hidden mystery and promise will be revealed.

That on the twenty-seventh day of the second month the earth is said to have been dry signifies that the necessity of baptism had already ended, in the number of fifty-seven days. For this is the twenty-seventh day of the second month, a number which, from the conjunction of spirit and body, contains seven times eight, with one added on account of the bond of unity.

That those who had entered separately came out of the ark joined together signifies that in this present age the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Galatians 5); afterward, however—that is, at the end of the world, in the resurrection of the saints—the spirit will cling to the body in complete and perfect peace, with no necessity or desire of mortality resisting.

All the animals are given to them for food, but they are forbidden to eat the blood, so that the former life may not remain in the conscience as though suffocated, but may have, as it were, an outpouring through confession.

But when God established a covenant between himself and human beings, and every living soul, so that he would not destroy it by a flood, he established the rainbow that appears in the clouds, which never shines except from the sun. This signifies that those do not perish in the flood who recognize Christ in the prophets and in all the divine [Col. 0032D] Scriptures, as in the clouds of God.

In this second age, after the flood, Noah planted a vineyard and became drunk and lay naked in his house. He bore the figure of Christ, who became drunk when he suffered and was stripped naked when he was crucified—in his own house, among his own people and the members of his own bloodline. Seeing this nakedness—that is, Christ’s passion—Ham mocked him; and the Jews, seeing Christ’s death, jeered. Shem and Japheth, however, as two peoples, from circumcision and uncircumcision, believed and in a certain way covered Christ’s passion with a veil—that is, honored it as a sacrament. For clothing signifies the sacrament which they placed upon his back, [Col. 0033A] as though in remembrance of past events, because the Church celebrates Christ’s passion as something accomplished, not as something still expected in the future.

Ham, the middle brother—that is, the impious Jewish people, who neither held the primacy of the apostles nor believed last among the nations—saw the nakedness of his father because he consented to the death of the Lord and Savior. He reported it outside to his brothers because through him what had been hidden in the prophets was made manifest. Therefore he became the servant of his brothers, that nation itself becoming, in a certain sense, the archivist of the Christians, carrying the Law and the Prophets as testimony in support of the Church’s affirmation, so that we may honor through the sacrament what they enumerate according to the letter. When Ham sinned, his descendants were condemned, because the Jewish people, which crucified the Lord, [Col. 0034A] also transmitted the punishment of its condemnation to its children. Likewise, the reprobate who sin here receive the sentence of condemnation in the age to come, that is, in the future.

Nimrod, the son of Cush, was the first to seize a new tyranny out of desire for empire. He is compared with the devil, who, swelling with pride, wished to exalt himself above the stars. As a hunter and deceiver of human beings, he is rightly said to have ruled at Babel—that is, in confusion—where the languages of all who build the tower of proud impiety are confused, namely, all who, as though through a discord of language, have acted against one another by departing from the unity of faith and the integrity of confession.

## THE THIRD AGE, FROM ABRAHAM TO DAVID

[Col. 0033]

[Col. 0033B] [2185] The third age of the world began with the birth of the patriarch Abraham. When he was seventy-five years old, he left his people and homeland and, at God’s command, went into the land of Canaan, receiving the promise of the Savior who was to be born from his offspring, in whom all nations would be blessed, and also the promise that he himself would become a great nation (Genesis 12): one promise spiritual, the other carnal (Romans 4; Galatians 3–4). At this time Ninus and Semiramis were still reigning in Assyria.

[2271] When Abraham was eighty-six years old, he fathered Ishmael, from whom came the Ishmaelites, later called Hagarenes and finally Saracens. Ishmael lived one hundred and thirty-seven years. Ishmael is interpreted as “hearing of God,” signifying the Jewish people, because at the end of the world it will believe and be heard by the Lord. Hagar is interpreted as “stranger” or “convert,” and represents the Synagogue.

[2285] When Abraham was one hundred years old, he fathered Isaac, who is the first and only person in the sequence of the Old Testament recorded as having been circumcised on the eighth day. This privilege was granted to the son of promise for no small mystery. Abram is interpreted as “exalted father,” referring to the earlier Jewish people; Abraham, however, means “father of many,” that is, of nations, as the Apostle says: “He believed against hope in hope, so that he might become the father of many nations” (Romans 4:18). He lived one hundred and seventy-five years.

[2350] When Isaac was seventy years old, he fathered Esau and [Col. 0033D] Jacob, the patriarchs of the Idumean and Israelite peoples. After their birth he lived one hundred and twenty years, making all his years one hundred and eighty. At this time Inachus first reigned at Argos for fifty years. His son was Phoroneus, who first wrote down laws and judicial rules in Greece; [and] Io, whom the Egyptians worshiped under the changed name Isis. Isaac is interpreted as “laughter,” and in the type of the Savior he was offered by his father as a sacrifice.

[2440] When Jacob was ninety years old, he fathered Joseph. At this time Serapis, said by some to have been the son of Jupiter, died as king of the Egyptians and, through a false delusion, was transferred among the gods. The city of Memphis in Egypt was founded by Apis, king of the Argives; Sparta likewise was founded by Sparto, son of Phoroneus, king of the Argives.

[2480] When Jacob was one hundred and thirty years old, he went down into Egypt with seventy persons. He lived seventeen years in Egypt, making all the days of his life one hundred and forty-seven years. Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter”; he is also called Israel, “seeing God,” or, better, “a prince with God,” presenting the image of all the saints who, through faith and purity of heart, always see God. Joseph died at the age of one hundred and ten. Moses and the children of Israel carried his bones, together with the bones of his brothers, Jacob’s sons, and brought them into the land of Canaan. At this time, while Argo reigned in Greece, Greece began to have grain crops, seeds having been brought from elsewhere.

[2546] The Hebrews were enslaved in Egypt for one hundred and forty-four years. As the Book of Exodus testifies, the residence of the children of Israel who remained in Egypt lasted four hundred and thirty years. When these were completed, the entire army of the Lord went out of the land of Egypt on that very day. Chronographers, however, calculate this total of years from the seventy-fifth year of Abraham’s birth, when he entered [Col. 0034D] the promised land, following the edition of the Seventy translators, which says: “The residence of the children of Israel, during which they dwelt in Egypt and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers, was three hundred and thirty years.” The Hebrew text itself also shows that this must necessarily be followed. It relates that Kohath, the son of Levi, who is known to have been born in the land of Canaan, lived one hundred and thirty-three years; Amram, the son and father of Moses, one hundred and thirty-seven years; and Moses himself was eighty years old at the time of the exodus from Egypt. For it is clear that the sum of these years cannot possibly amount to four hundred and thirty.

The Apostle also agrees with this translation when he says: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. He does not say, ‘And to offspring,’ as though referring to many, but as referring to one: ‘And to your offspring,’ who is Christ. This is what I mean: the Law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not annul a covenant previously confirmed by God, so as to abolish the promise” (Galatians 4:16–17). At this time, namely during Israel’s enslavement in Egypt, Prometheus is said to have lived, whom the myths depict as having fashioned human beings from clay. At that time his brother Atlas was regarded as a great astrologer, and Mercury, Atlas’s grandson, was skilled in many arts; for this reason, after his death, he too was transferred among the gods through a vain delusion.

[2645] Also in this age Procidus first yoked a chariot. At the same time Cecrops founded Athens and, after the name of Minerva, called the people of Attica Athenians. He also sacrificed an ox and was the first to command that Jupiter be worshiped in sacrifice. At that time the Corybantes, the first of the Chorites, invented a rhythmic dance in armor accompanied by music. At that time too a flood is said to have occurred in Thessaly under Deucalion, along with the fabled conflagration of Phaethon.

[2649] Moses ruled the people of Israel for forty years after bringing them out of Egypt and freeing them from Egyptian slavery. In the first year he built the tabernacle for the Lord, and, completing the work in seven months, erected it on the first day of the first month of the second year. Through this same Moses the Jews began to possess letters along with the Law. The five books of Moses, according to the translation of the Seventy elders, contain events covering 3,730 years. But how many years the Hebrew text contains for this period Joseph records in the first book of his work *Against Apion the Grammarian*:

“Among us, therefore, there are not countless volumes disagreeing with one another, but only twenty-two books, which contain the record of all time and are rightly believed to be divinely inspired. Of these, five belong to Moses, containing the laws of life and the genealogy of the human race, and extending to the end of Moses himself; their content falls just short of three thousand years.”

In the time of Moses, the temple at Delphi was built, and Lacedaemon was founded. Moses died at the age of one hundred and twenty. The vine was discovered in Greece. At this time such an immense and oppressive heat blazed up that the sun, passing beyond its accustomed paths, is said not merely to have affected the whole world with heat but to have scorched it with fire. From this arose the ridiculous tale of Phaethon.

Joshua ruled the people of Israel for twenty-six years, as Josephus teaches, for Sacred Scripture does not state how many years his leadership lasted. Eusebius assigned twenty-seven years in his *Chronicle*. In the first year of his leadership, on the tenth day of the first month, Joshua brought the people into the promised land after the bed of the Jordan had been exposed. In that year, as we find in the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, began the fifty-first jubilee according to the Hebrews. It can easily be established that 2,500 years had been completed from the beginning of the world, with each sequence of jubilees assigned fifty years.

But our investigation finds this total of time smaller. It is clear that 1,656 years elapsed up to the flood; from then to Abraham, 292 years, and Abraham was seventy years old when he received God’s promise; the years of the promise, 430; and the leadership of Moses, sixty years. This total amounts not to 2,500 years but to seven fewer—that is, 2,493 years. In Joshua’s time, Erichthonius, the first ruler of the Athenians, first yoked a chariot in Greece. Joshua died at the age of one hundred and ten.

[2757] Othoniel, from the tribe of Judah, was appointed the first judge of Israel by God’s command and served for forty years. He prefigured the one who, in the third age of the world, came from the tribe of Judah with grace to save the peoples. At the beginning of his leadership, the children of Israel first served Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, for eight years. Cadmus reigned at Thebes, and was the first to devise the Greek letters. During the same period Linus and Amphion first became famous among the Greeks for musical skill, and the Idaean Dactyls discovered iron.

[2797] Ehud, in the eightieth year, son of Gera, son of Gemini, used both hands as though they were his right hand. During his leadership Israel served Eglon, king of Moab, for eighteen years, until Ehud struck down Eglon and liberated Israel. At this time the city of Cyrene was founded in Libya. At this time myths were also invented about Triptolemus, who, at Ceres’ command, was carried on the wings of serpents and distributed grain to the needy as he flew; about the Hippocentaurs, who were of mixed human and equine nature; about Cerberus, the three-headed dog of the underworld; about Phrixus and his sister Helle, who, riding on a ram, flew through the air; about the prostitute Gorgon, whose hair consisted of snakes and who turned those looking at her into stones; about Bellerophon, who rode a winged flying horse; and about Amphion, who moved stones and rocks by the song of his lyre.

[Col. 0036D] [2877] Deborah, a prophetess from the tribe of Ephraim, together with Barak from the tribe of Naphtali, for forty years. At the beginning of her leadership, Jabin, king of Canaan, oppressed the children of Israel. He reigned at Hazor for twenty years, but, after Sisera, commander of his army, had been killed by Israel and Jael, the wife of Abercineus, he was finally humbled and destroyed. At this time Miletus was founded. During the same period Apollo discovered the art of medicine. A myth was also invented at that time about the craftsman Daedalus and his son Icarus, who are said to have flown after fastening wings to themselves. In this age Picus first reigned over the Latins; he is said to have been the son of Saturn.

[2918] Gideon, from the tribe of Manasseh, for forty years. Under him Israel served the Midianites and Amalekites for seven years, but was liberated when Gideon fought. The city of Tyre was founded 240 years before the temple of Jerusalem. Orpheus of Thrace and Linus, the teacher of Hercules, were renowned as inventors of the musical art. The voyage of the Argonauts is recorded.

[2955] Abimelech reigned at Shechem for three years. He killed the seventy brothers, the sons of Gideon. Hercules destroyed Ilium.

[2958] Tola, son of Puah, the uncle of Abimelech, a man from Issachar who lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim, for twenty-four years. Priam reigned in Troy for thirteen years after Laomedon. The myth was invented of the Minotaur, the beast enclosed in the labyrinth. There was also the war of the Lapiths and Centaurs, whom Palaephatus, in the first book of *On Incredible Things*, writes to have been noble horsemen of the Thessalians.

[2981] Jair, from the tribe of Manasseh, for thirty-two years. During this period Hercules established the Olympic contest and killed Antaeus in Libya. From that event 430 years are reckoned to the first Olympiad.

[3004] Jephthah the Gileadite, for six years. The Philistines and Ammonites oppressed Israel; Jephthah defeated the Ammonites. In the Book of Judges he says that from the age of Moses to his own time 300 years were to be reckoned—or, as some manuscripts read, 325 years. In his time Hercules, in his fifty-second year, cast himself into flames because of the pain of an illness. During the same period Alexander carried off Helen, and the ten-year Trojan War began.

[3010] Abesa of Bethlehem, for seven years. Agamemnon ruled at Mycenae for twenty-five years. In his fifteenth year Troy was captured. The Amazons took up arms.

[3017] Ajalon the Zebulunite, for ten years. His ten years are not found in the Seventy translators, and, in order to make up for this omission, Eusebius assigned more years to Joshua son of Nun and to Samuel and Saul—whose years Scripture does not state—than he had read in Josephus, so that the total of 480 years proclaimed by Scripture from Israel’s exodus from Egypt to the building of the temple might be preserved.

[Col. 0037D] [3025] Abdon, or Labdon, from the tribe of Ephraim, for eight years. In his third year Troy was captured, and Aeneas came to Italy. From the first year of Cecrops, who first reigned in Attica, 335 years were completed. From the forty-third year of the reign of Ninus, king of the Assyrians, 825 years are reckoned. After Labdon’s death Israel served the Philistines for forty years. In this age the nymph Carmentis discovered the Latin letters.

[2025] Samson, from the tribe of Dan, for twenty years. Ascanius, the son of Aeneas, founded Alba. The story of Ulysses was also invented. Thus far the Book of Judges records the periods, containing 299 years and twelve judges. After them Latin priests were appointed; they were later called Romans, three years after the capture of Troy. After Aeneas had reigned eight years, as some write, Ascanius reigned for thirty-eight years. Before Aeneas, Janus, Saturn, Picus, and Faunus reigned over the Latins in Italy for approximately 150 years.

[3046] Heli the priest, for forty years. In the books of the Hebrews, forty years are found; in the Seventy, twenty years. The Ark of the Covenant was captured by the foreigners. The kingdom of the Sicyonians came to an end; from Aegialeus to Zeuxippus they had ruled for 962 years. The sons of Hector recovered Ilium, having expelled the descendants of Antenor, with Helenus assisting them. Silvius, the third of the Latins and the son of Aeneas, reigned for twenty-nine years. Because he was born after his father’s death and had been raised in the countryside, he received the names Silvius and Posthumus; from him all the kings of Alba were called Silvii.

[3085] Samuel and Saul, forty years. How many years Samuel’s leadership lasted is not at all clear in Sacred Scripture; Josephus nevertheless states that his rule flourished for thirteen years. The Chronicon, however, records that Samuel and Saul ruled together for forty years. In the Acts of the Apostles the Apostle Paul preached to the people as follows: “The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and exalted the people when they were sojourners in the land of Egypt, and with an uplifted arm he led them out from it; and for a period of forty years he endured their ways in the wilderness. And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he distributed their land to them by lot, for about four hundred and fifty years. And after this he gave them judges, until Samuel the prophet. And thereafter they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul, son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.” From this point the period of the prophets begins. The kingdom of the Lacedaemonians arises; Homer is also thought to have lived.

In this third age of the world, without prejudice to historical truth, the calling of Abraham prefigures the land of the living that was to belong to Christ’s people, and that we should not fear the long termination of our sojourn, but should always hope in Christ the Lord, through whose grace, by living rightly, we shall possess an everlasting inheritance. In Abraham’s seed it prefigures the Christian people being multiplied like the stars of heaven; in his offering and priesthood, the royal priesthood of the Church; and in the meaning of his name, that he would be in Christ “the father of many nations” through faith, although by physical descent he had been the father of only one nation. In the circumcision of the flesh it signifies that the Christian was to be circumcised in the heart.

In the birth of Isaac, whose name means “laughter,” it signifies that the people of the nations who would believe in Christ, coming in the flesh from that lineage, would be mocked by the Jews, and would recognize his shameful Passion as their true liberation.

In Sodom and Gomorrah, through the overthrow of the impious cities, it signifies the day of the future judgment and that it is impossible to escape the punishments decreed, for those who, through guilty curiosity, despise the purpose of holy conduct and look back while living wickedly; only those will be liberated whom the grace of Christ has liberated.

In the sacrifice of the ram in place of Isaac, Christ’s Passion is represented. In God’s oath, that Abraham’s seed would be extended in Christ beyond counting, it signifies that the children of Abraham would be called to an infinite number, not only from physical descent but also through faith.

From Abraham’s thigh it signifies the flesh of Christ that was to come. When that same Abraham commands his servant, “Place your hand beneath my thigh and swear to me by the God of heaven,” he shows that Christ, who is the God of heaven, would come in the flesh through the Virgin Mary from his own thigh.

In Rebecca’s twins, the two peoples—Christians and Jews—are represented. Their younger son Jacob, the gentle one, already in childhood supplanting his hairy elder brother Esau through the cooking of the red lentil stew, signifies the gentle and meek Christian people. Through the red cooking—that is, Christ’s Passion, reddened with blood—it received the dignity of primacy from the voracious and savage Jewish people, whose concern Esau represented, when Esau sold it. Esau lost through desire what he had by birth; the Christian acquired through grace what he did not possess by nature.

His mother fitted the skins of goats onto his arms and bare neck and clothed him in the garment of his firstborn brother, as though already showing us the Christ prefigured in him: Christ received not sinful flesh, but the likeness of sinful flesh, and, accepting the law of the Old Testament as the garment of the firstborn, did not abolish it but fulfilled it. After the fragrance of the blessed one, all the nations run—those who through grace took from the Jews both primacy and blessing.

Jacob too, son of Isaac and grandson of Abraham, fleeing his brother’s plots, raised upright in a sacred sign the stone that he had placed beneath his head while sleeping at a distance, and anointed it with oil; thus he consecrated for us Christ, the cornerstone. The same Jacob, made lame in the breadth of his thigh, signifies the Hebrew people that would limp.

Judah, Jacob’s son, slept with his daughter-in-law Tamar. She signifies the Jewish people, to whom kings from the tribe of Judah were assigned as husbands. Hence her name is interpreted as “bitterness,” because she gave the Lord a cup of gall.

In Judah’s two sons are signified two kinds of rulers who did not act rightly among the people: one who goes astray and another who was of no benefit. There are, after all, no more than two kinds of useless people in the human race: those who do harm, and those unwilling to provide benefit, who, if they possess anything good, lose it in this earthly life, as though pouring it onto the ground.

Hence the elder, Er, is interpreted as “entangled,” such as were the tunics with which the first human beings were clothed when, as punishment for their condemnation, they were expelled from paradise. The next, Onan, is interpreted as “their sorrow”—that is, those who are of no benefit although they have the means to benefit.

In Judah’s third son, Shelah, whose name is interpreted as “his dismissal,” the period is signified from which kings over the Jewish people began no longer to come from the tribe of Judah. The tribe of Judah still existed, but no one from the Jewish people ruled. For this reason Tamar did not receive a husband from Judah’s son. At that time all Jewish authority, and the mystical anointing from which they were called “christs” (anointed ones), had failed.

Nor does Herod, a foreigner, belong to the mystical anointing. When the royal ruler from the tribe of Judah had failed, he received the kingship in Judaea from the Romans. During his reign Christ was born, anointed as the Holy of Holies with the oil of gladness above his companions. Coming to the sheep that had perished, the house of Israel, he used water, as John testified; Judas himself prefigured him when he went to shear the sheep at Tamna, which is interpreted as “failing.” For the ruler from Judah had already failed, as had the mystical anointing of the Jews.

He came with his shepherd from Adullam, whose name was Hira. “Adullamite” is interpreted as “testimony in water.” Although the Lord had a greater testimony than John, he used this testimony in water on account of the weak sheep. For Hira, the name of that shepherd, is interpreted as “the vision of my brother.” He clearly saw his brother Jesus according to the seed of Abraham, according to the kinship of Mary and Elizabeth, his mother; and he recognized as Lord and God the one whom he had already greeted from the womb, more perfectly through the dove. Therefore, as an Adullamite, he truly bears witness in water.

The Lord came to shear the sheep—that is, to unload the burdens of sins. Then Tamar changes her appearance; for her name is also interpreted as “changing.” She changes her name as well, and from the Synagogue becomes the Church. Yet the name of bitterness remains entirely within her—not the bitterness in which she served the Lord gall, but that in which Peter wept bitterly. For “Judah” also signifies confession; therefore bitterness must be mingled with confession, so that true repentance may be prefigured.

This repentance makes the Church fruitful among all nations. Even the appearance of a prostitute signifies confession of sins. Tamar, called from the nations, bears the type of the Church. She sits in this attire at the gate of Enaim, which is interpreted as “springs”; for she runs like a deer to reach the springs of water, to arrive at the seed of Abraham. There she conceives from one who does not recognize her, because this was foretold of her: “A people whom I did not know served me.”

In secret she receives a ring, a necklace, and a staff. By the ring calling is signified; by the necklace she is adorned through justification; by the staff she is exalted through glorification. Yet these things remain hidden for the present, where the conception of holy abundance takes place.

The promised kid is sent to the prostitute—namely, the reproach of sin—through that same Adullamite, as though he were rebuking her and saying, “Brood of vipers.” But the reproach of sin did not find her, because the bitterness of confession had changed her.

Afterward, through the public signs of the ring, necklace, and staff, she rebukes the Jews who judge rashly—Judas himself already bearing their person—when she produces the most certain proofs of her calling, justification, and glorification. She shows the staff, the sign of the Passion; the necklace, the lawful teaching; and the ring, the pledge of immortality, when she is accused by the Jews as an adulteress against the law.

In the deeds of Joseph and Benjamin, Christ and his Church are also represented. Joseph, sent by his father, signifies Christ sent by the Father to visit the sheep. His brothers stripped him of his tunic in the Passion and threw him into a pit; then they sent his garment to his father, dyed in the blood of a kid, under false testimony. They sold and sent the Savior to the nations. To him were to be subjected the sun, star, and moon in heaven; the earth in the sheaves; and the underworld in the prison, so that every knee might bow to him—of those in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth.

Together with Joseph, for the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, two officers of Pharaoh were thrust into prison, so that the number of the three crucified might be completed. Of these, the true Joseph, Christ, by revealing the mysteries, would punish one with the punishment he deserved and liberate the other by undeserved grace.

That same Joseph, after two years had passed and the third was beginning, is brought out of prison. Christ rises from the dead on the third day. He is presented to Pharaoh; the resurrection is proclaimed to the world. Joseph is given authority in Egypt; Christ is given all authority in heaven and on earth.

Joseph gathered much grain through his agents; Christ gathered the number of believers beyond counting. Joseph established storehouses throughout Egypt; Christ consecrated churches throughout the whole world. Joseph opened the storehouses in time of famine and distributed grain to the peoples; Christ opened his storehouses to provide enduring nourishment from his body to those hungering and thirsting for righteousness.

Joseph acquired all Egypt for Pharaoh; Christ acquired the world, fed and reconciled to the Father. Joseph’s brothers, who had sold him, came to him compelled by famine; the Jews who had crucified Christ also came to him, so that, refreshed by his food, they might be freed from the famine of the soul. They worship, and these worship as well. Thus, through wondrous mysteries, the apostolic action is prefigured for us in the action of the brothers.

In Benjamin, Joseph’s younger brother, Paul is also prefigured as the teacher and master of the nations in faith and truth. Figuratively, a silver cup is hidden in his sack, and three hundred pieces of silver together with five splendid garments are given to him.

In Jacob’s descent into Egypt, Christ’s descent into the world is signified; and in the multiplication of his seed in Egypt, the multiplication of the nations throughout the whole world through faith in Christ.

In Moses the figure of the Mediator is expressed. He brought peace to the world, just as Moses hid the Egyptian in the sand; Christ, by expelling and restraining the power of the devil from those he possessed, did the same. Moses’ taking as wife the daughter of the priest of Midian, though she was a foreigner, signifies that the Mediator would take a wife from the nations—that is, the Church.

Because Moses was a shepherd of sheep, he signified the Mediator as the good shepherd who was to come in the flesh. Gathering his sheep from this world as from Egypt, he would bring them together into one fold, the Church.

The tricks of the magicians are overcome, and Moses’ serpent devours the serpents of those magicians: the rod of Christ is his teaching, by which all the doctrines of pagans and heretics are consumed.

In Egypt the world is struck by ten plagues. In the slaughter of the lamb, Christ’s sacrifice is signified; in the figure of Passover, Christ’s passage to the Father. In the Red Sea, baptism reddened by Christ’s blood. In the manna, the heavenly bread. Christ is expressed in the extension of Moses’ hands, by which enemies are conquered through the sign of the cross. In the laws given on the mountain, Christ’s commandments are kept in spiritual exaltation; in the tabernacle, Christ’s Church is signified.

In Aaron’s priesthood, the new priesthood in Christ is represented. In all the sacrifices, Christ is prefigured. In the varieties of leprosy, the varieties of heresies or errors. In clean and unclean foods, the teaching that all things are made clean through almsgiving. In the desired foods of Egypt, the meaning that they loathed Christ, the manna, and indulged desires for illicit pleasures.

In Aaron’s budding rod, the confirmation of Christ’s priesthood. In the bronze serpent, Christ’s death, sounding everywhere in the mouths of the faithful; the venom of men is to be destroyed, and those struck by the devil are healed as they behold Christ’s death in faith.

In the twice-struck rock, the mysteries of Christ’s Passion are distinguished through a wondrous work. In the red heifer, whose ashes are cast into the waters of purification, the mystery of our redemption and salvation is expressed most fully.

In the hidden burial of Moses, the letter of the law is signified, and the carnal observances are to be concealed.

In the succeeding leadership of Joshua son of Nun, the Lord Christ is signified as the true leader and ruler who was to come in the New Testament. He would destroy the cities of the world, defeat the powers of the air, utterly wash away all idolatry, and conquer vices of every kind.

Deborah, in the type of the Church, overcame the enemy. Gideon commended the abundant grace of Christ and indicates through his deeds that the enemies of the Trinity were to be overcome by faith and that martyrdoms were to be sought.

In Abimelech, the son of the concubine, heretics are represented. In Jephthah’s virgin daughter, the sacrifice of Christ’s flesh from a virgin, and in the resurrection the swallowing up of all corruption, are signified.

In Samson the Nazirite, Christ the Lord, strong in his head, is represented. In his being bound by a prostitute, Christ the Lord is signified as the one who would in power break all the bonds of the Jews.

In Ruth, the Church from the nations, mocking the Jews. In Samuel, Christ the Lord as leader, priest, and prophet, rebuking the priests and exchanging the old Synagogue for the new priesthood of Christ in the grace of the New Testament.

This third age, venerably marked by the deeds of the Patriarchs, the mysteries of the law, and figures of judgment, closes with Saul’s rejection and casting away. It contains nine hundred and forty years.

## THE FOURTH AGE, FROM THE REIGN OF DAVID TO THE BABYLONIAN TRANSMIGRATION OF THE HEBREWS

[Col. 0043]

[Col. 0043A] [3125] The fourth age of the world. David, the first king from the tribe of Judah, forty years. The fifth of the Latins, Silvius, fifty years. Codrus, offering himself voluntarily to the enemy, is killed. Ephesus is founded by Andronicus. Carthage is founded by Dido, daughter of Carchedon the Tyrian, in the one hundred and forty-third year after the destruction of Troy; Gath, Nathan, and Asaph are prophesying in Judaea.

[3165] Solomon, son of David, forty years. In the fourth year of his reign, in the second month, he began to build the temple for the Lord in Jerusalem, four hundred and eighty years after the departure of Israel from Egypt. This prefigures the entire period during which Christ’s Church is built in this age and perfected in the future. He dedicated it after seven years, in the seventh month of the eighth year. The sixth of the Latins, Alba Silvius, son of Aeneas, reigned eighty-eight years. The Queen of Sheba came to hear Solomon’s wisdom.

[3205] Rehoboam, son of Solomon, sixteen years. Under him Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim separated ten tribes from the house of David and from the Lord, prefiguring heretics who separate their followers from Christ and the Church. In his fifth year Shishak, king of Egypt, came to Jerusalem and plundered the temple. The seventh of the Latins, Aegyptus Silvius, son of Alba, the preceding king, reigned twenty-three years. Samos was founded, and Smyrna enlarged in the form of a city. The Erythraean Sibyl is held in high repute.

[3882] Abijah, son of Rehoboam, three years. He defeated Jeroboam fighting against him, killing five hundred thousand of his army, because he had hoped in the Lord. Under him Abimelech, high priest of the Hebrew nation, was regarded as distinguished.

[3885] Asa, son of Abijah, forty-one years. Ben-Hadad, king of Syria of Damascus, was hired by him against Israel and struck the whole land of Naphtali. Ahijah, Elihu, Amos, Joel, and Azariah prophesied in Judaea. The eighth of the Latins, Capys Silvius, son of Aegyptus, the preceding king, reigned twenty-seven years.

Asa destroyed the idols and cleansed the temple. He defeated Zerah the Ethiopian, who came against him, together with his army. Omri, king of Israel, bought the mountain of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and built it. Hiel of Bethel restored Jericho.

[3926] Jehoshaphat, twenty-five years. Elijah, Elisha, Obadiah, Azariah, and Micah prophesied. Elijah the Tishbite withheld rain for three and a half years on account of the sins of Ahab and the people of Israel. Among his other great deeds, he anointed Elisha son of Shaphat, who was from Abel-meholah, as prophet in his place.

The ninth of the Latins, Carpentus Silvius, son of the preceding king Capys, reigned thirteen years. After him his son Tiberius, the tenth, reigned eight years. Jehoshaphat did what was right before the Lord.

[Col. 0044A] [3951] Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, eight years. Elijah is carried away in a chariot of fire, as though up to heaven; and Elisha, left as heir of the prophecy, heals the waters of Jericho in his first miracle. In the days of Joram, Edom withdrew from under Judah and appointed a king for itself. Joram walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his wife was a daughter of Ahab.

[3959] Ahaziah, or Azariah, one year. Jonadab son of Rechab is held in high repute. Because of the enormity of their crimes, and because none of them possessed either father or son who was good, the evangelist Matthew excludes Azariah, his son Joash, and his grandson Amaziah from the genealogy of the Lord Savior.

[3960] Athaliah, mother of Azariah, seven years. When she saw that her son Azariah had been killed by Jehu, king of Israel, she killed the entire royal offspring of the house of Joram, except for Joash, son of Azariah. Jehosheba, wife of Jehoiada the high priest, stole him from among the king’s sons while they were being killed. Jehoiada the high priest is said to have been the only person after Moses to live for one hundred and thirty years.

[3967] Joash, son of Azariah, forty years. He began well but ended very badly. At the beginning of his reign he renewed the temple. At the end, among his other crimes, he ordered Zechariah, son of Jehoiada, once his guardian and the one who had established him as king, to be stoned between the temple and the altar. Because of his merits, the Lord calls him in the Gospel “the son of Zechariah,” that is, “of the blessed Lord.”

Lycurgus the lawgiver is held in high repute through the oracle of Apollo. The twelfth of the Latins, Aremulus Silvius, son of the preceding king Agrippa, reigned eighteen years. He established a settlement of the Albans between the mountains where Rome now stands. His son was Julius, great-grandfather of Julius Proculus, who, migrating with his people to Rome, founded the Julian people.

Amaziah, son of Joash, twenty-nine years. The prophet Elisha died and was buried in Samaria. Hazael, king of the Syrians, afflicted Israel.

[4047] The thirteenth of the Latins, Aventinus Silvius, the elder son of Aremulus, the preceding king, reigned thirty-seven years. He died and was buried on the same mountain that is now part of the City, and gave the place its everlasting name.

The city of Vienna was founded by Venerius, an exile from Africa, and was named from him, as Livy writes in the Annals, because it was completed in two years. It was first called Bienna; afterward, with the removal of b and the addition of v, it was called Vienna. Later the Romans wished to call it Senatorial, after establishing a Senate there to administer the Gallic provinces. After some time, having stationed five legions there, they distinguished it with five camps around it and established there the public granaries and storehouses of the entire army.

From the names of the tribunes of Julius Caesar they gave names to the camps: Crappus, Eumedium, Sospolus, Quiriacum, and Pompetiacum.

[4076] Azariah, also called Uzziah, son of Amaziah, fifty-one years. The thirty-sixth of the Assyrians was Tonosconleros, who is called Sardanapalus in Greek. He founded Tarsus and Anchiale, and, defeated in battle by Arbaces the Mede, burned himself to death. Histories report that there had been Assyrian kings up to that time, and the years from the first year of Ninus, king of the Assyrians, amount altogether to one thousand one hundred and sixty-four.

Arbaces the Mede, after destroying the Assyrian empire, transferred the kingdom to the Medes. Then, as many battles broke out everywhere, through various turns of fortune it passed to the Scythians and Chaldaeans, and again returned to the Medes by an equal course.

The fourteenth of the Latins, Procas Silvius, son of the preceding king Aventinus, reigned. After him came Amulius Silvius. The poet Hesiod flourished, and Pheidon of Argos discovered measures and weights. During the same period the first Olympiad was established. The kingdom of the Macedonians began, with Cananus as its first king. The kings of the Lacedaemonians came to an end; those of the Lydians began. Hosea, Amos, Isaiah, and Jonah prophesied in Judaea.

Jotham, son of Uzziah, sixteen years. The first Olympiad was established by the Eleans. Remus and Romulus were born to their mother Ilia. Among his other good and virtuous works, Jotham built the highest gate of the house of the Lord, which in the Acts of the Apostles is called the Beautiful Gate.

[Col. 0045C] [4103] Ahaz, son of Jotham, sixteen years. Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians, was hired by him; he killed Rezin, king of Syria, and transported the inhabitants of Damascus to Cyrene.

Rome was founded on the Latin Hill on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May by the twins Remus and Romulus, sons of Rhea Silvia, who was the daughter of Numitor, brother of King Amulius, a Vestal virgin, though she had been violated. In the third year from the founding of the City, the Sabine women were carried off during the Consualia games. Remus was killed by Fabius, Romulus’ commander.

[4119] Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, twenty-eight years. In his sixth year, Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, captured Samaria, transported Israel to Assyria, and sent Samaritan settlers into Judaea. The kingdom of Israel had stood from the first Jeroboam for three hundred and sixty years.

At this time Romulus first took soldiers from the people and selected one hundred of the most distinguished men from the people. On account of their age they were called senators; on account of their care and concern for the state, they were called fathers. When Romulus died, after reigning thirty-seven years, the senators governed the state for five days each, and one full year was completed.

After them Numa Pompilius reigned forty-one years. He built the Capitol from its foundations.

[4147] Manasseh, fifty-six years. Because of his crimes he was bound and fettered and led to Babylon; but because of his repentance and prayers he was restored to the kingdom.

Numa Pompilius first established the Vestal virgins and added two months, January and February, to the ten months of the year. The Samian Sibyl flourished.

The third of the Romans, Tullus Hostilius, reigned thirty-two years. He was the first of the Roman kings to use the purple and the fasces. He added the Caelian Hill and enlarged the city.

[4203] Amon, son of Manasseh, two years according to the Hebrew truth; in the Septuagint he is read to have reigned twelve years. The city of Histria was founded in Pontus. Amon was killed by his servants.

[4205] Josiah, son of Amon, thirty-one years. After Judaea had been cleansed and Jerusalem and the temple renewed, and after the filth of idolatry had been cast away, he celebrated a most famous Passover to the Lord in the eighteenth year of his reign. When he engaged Necho, king of the Egyptians, in battle, he was killed in the plain of Megiddo, which is now called Maximianopolis.

Thales of Miletus is held to have been the first distinguished natural philosopher. Jeremiah, Huldah, and Zephaniah prophesied in Judaea.

The fourth of the Romans, Ancus Marcius, grandson of Numa through his daughter, reigned twenty-three years. He added the Aventine and Janiculum hills to the City and founded Ostia by the sea, at the fifteenth milestone from the City. After him Tarquinius Priscus reigned thirty-seven years. He built the Circus around Rome, increased the number of senators, established the Roman games, and built the walls and sewers. He built the Capitol.

In the Hebrew text Josiah is said to have reigned twenty-one years; in the Septuagint interpreters he is read to have reigned thirty-three. Eusebius also inserts an additional year of his own between the reigns of Josiah and Joachim, on account of the six months during which Jehoahaz, or Joachim, reigned.

But what the truth is, Jeremiah makes clear. He states that he prophesied from the thirteenth year of Josiah to the fourth year of Joachim, for twenty-three years; that Nebuchadnezzar began to reign in the fourth year of Joachim; and that Jerusalem was destroyed in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign.

[4259] Joachim, son of Josiah, eleven years. After Josiah, Jehoahaz reigned for three months. Necho took him bound to Egypt and appointed Joachim king. In Joachim’s third year, Nebuchadnezzar captured Jerusalem and, taking many captives—including Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael—transported part of the temple vessels to Babylon.

Scripture reckons Nebuchadnezzar’s reign from the fourth year of Joachim, because from that point he began to reign not only over the Chaldaeans and Jews but also over the Assyrians, Egyptians, Moabites, and countless other nations.

Joachim, also called Jeconiah, son of Joachim, three months and ten days. When Jerusalem was surrounded by the Chaldaeans, he went out to the king of Babylon, together with his mother, and was taken to Babylon with his people in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign.

[4347] Zedekiah, eleven years, also called Mattaniah, son of Josiah. In his eleventh year, in the ninth year of the king of Babylon, Judaea was taken captive to Babylon and the temple of God was burned, in the four hundred and thirtieth year from its construction. The Jews who remained fled to Egypt; five years later, when Egypt was struck by the Chaldaeans, they too were transported to Babylon.

According to the Septuagint interpreters, four hundred and fifty-four years are reckoned from the construction of the temple. During the same period the woman Sappho flourished in various kinds of poetry; Solon gave laws to the Athenians.

In this fourth age, the mysteries of our King Christ are represented in David’s strong hand: he was small among his brothers and anointed as king. A shepherd of sheep, anointed by God the Father, he rescued both Peter who denied him and the thief who confessed him from the mouth of the lion, the devil.

If you consider his sounding harp, fitted to the wood of the cross with the cords of his flesh and limbs, when he touched it with the plectrum of the Holy Spirit, it filled every living creature with blessing and drove the devil from the hearts of the wicked, for whom he prayed on the cross.

When he was about to fight the great enemy, the true Goliath, he rejected the wisdom of this world, as though it were Saul’s armor, and chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong. For from the five books of Moses’ law, one stone placed in the sling of flesh and propelled by the strong hand struck down all the devil’s pride and killed him with his own sword, when he killed death by death. From this victory the hostile Jews conceived envy and repaid love with hatred.

That David ran through mountain hiding places, caves, and deserts while pursued by his enemy expressed the persecutions suffered by his members and martyrs.

That he spared his enemy, cutting off a corner of his cloak, signifies that, when he cuts away the great vice of pride from his enemies, he spares them so that they are not handed over to eternal death.

That he avoided the persecutor’s ambush and fled to Gath signifies that Christ, withdrawing from the Jews who raged against him, gave himself to the nations.

When David pretended to be possessed and his saliva ran down his beard, he conveyed to us, through a mystery, Christ’s firmness seasoned with wisdom and his most sacred body carried in consecrated bread by the hands of the priest.

That same David grieves over Saul, his enemy, when he is killed, because Christ also loved his enemies very greatly.

All Israel gathers to David the anointed; as was promised, the whole world gathers to Christ.

[Col. 0047D] In David, Christ—the one desired by all nations—is represented as walking about for their consolation, because he placed his tabernacle in the sun. He loved the Church washing herself on the roof—that is, cleansing herself from the filth of the world, transcending and trampling down the earthly house through spiritual contemplation. Having begun with her the knowledge of the first covenant, he afterward killed the devil, who had been completely separated from her, and joined her to himself in an everlasting marriage.

When David was worn out in old age, the virgin Abishag was brought to him to warm him. As old age presses upon the world, the true David, Christ, takes the virgin Church, warmed by faith, to himself.

In Solomon, our peace, who is Christ, is represented. In him Christ is wisdom, coming to cast a sword upon the earth, removing the deceit of heretics, and restoring the living and undivided child to its true mother, the Catholic Church. He does not wish, because of the quarrel among heretics, to cut and divide the son who, building a house from living stones, made one temple from all the faithful.

The Queen of Sheba—that is, the Church—came from the ends of the earth to see him and hear his wisdom. Therefore everything that is rightly recorded about Solomon or prophetically enacted by him is attributed to Christ the Lord.

But so that no one might suppose that everything spoken prophetically about Christ was fulfilled in Solomon, Solomon was corrupted in old age and lost his wisdom by divine judgment, so that all those things that had been signified might be preserved in Christ the Lord.

Otherwise, because he fornicated in mind and body, with the Lord abandoning him, he appears to have died badly, leaving a fearful example for later generations: lest, disturbed by the prosperity of this life, they abandon Christ, who is the eternal felicity of his own.

In the division of the kingdom, and of almost the whole Israelite people from the house of David, the figure of heretics and schismatics is shown.

In Elijah, Christ is represented. In the figure of the evening of the age, he was sacrificed like a calf and destroyed all the priests of idolatry together with their error, filling the earth with the rain of grace, by which the famine of the faithful soul might be driven away.

When ravens bring bread in the morning and meat in the evening to Elijah living in the wilderness, the figure of the whole body of the Lord is shown. First, in the commandments, the Jews supplied bread to the nations; afterward, they supplied the flesh of the Lord’s Passion, cooked from the wood of the cross, darkened in color.

For three periods and a half—that is, three years and six months—the heavenly rain is denied by God’s high judgment to those who, not eating his flesh or drinking his blood, are found to have been redeemed yet alienated from his body.

Elijah is fed by a widow. Christ receives works of mercy and repays them in the Church, which, still a widow in the field of the Sacred Scriptures, gathers two pieces of wood—the two commandments of the cross—so that she may provide for herself and her children in a time of famine.

In Elisha also is represented the twofold spirit of Elijah; in the chorus of Christ’s disciples, the reception of the Holy Spirit with a double gift.

In the raising of the dead man, the human race is represented as raised by Christ through the breath of grace, whom the law was wholly unable to raise.

Elisha crosses the Jordan through the operation of the same Spirit by which our Lord Jesus consecrated that river in his Baptism.

The boys insult Elisha and are torn apart by wild beasts; the Jews insult Christ and are possessed by Romans or evil spirits.

Elisha commands Naaman to wash seven times so that he may be cleansed of leprosy. This signifies that the soul is cleansed from vices by the sevenfold Spirit of grace, by which the inner and outer person are polluted. This is also shown by the water in which the consecrated are baptized, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Gehazi, the prophet’s servant, receives gifts from Naaman and is thereby sprinkled with the spots of leprosy. He represents heretics who sell what they present as expiations of sins and are themselves filled with the spots with which they had been stained.

In the sign given to King Hezekiah, the descent of Christ, who is the Sun of righteousness, and also his merciful penetration of the underworld, are prefigured. He also teaches us, even when doing good, never to become elated by prosperity.

[Col. 0050A] In the deeds of Josiah, Christ is openly represented as having become the true Passover for us, cleansing and purifying his Church, for which he died. His sons, led into captivity on account of the merit of their guilt, signify those who render Christ’s grace fruitless. Despising Christ’s commandments as though they were Jeremiah’s, they are handed over captive to vices by the devil, as by Nebuchadnezzar.

This fourth age of the world, from David to the transmigration to Babylon, concludes with four hundred and seventy years.

## THE FIFTH AGE, FROM THAT SAME TRANSMIGRATION TO CHRIST OUR SAVIOR

[Col. 0049]

[Col. 0049B] [4271] The fifth age of the world began with the final destruction of the Jewish kingdom, which, according to the prophecy of Jeremiah, lasted seventy years. This occurred in the fourteenth year after the city had been struck down—that is, in the twenty-fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin, with whom Ezekiel was taken captive. Ezekiel himself, brought in divine visions into the land of Israel, saw the renewal of the city and its temple, together with its ceremonies. When Judaea had been devastated, the Chaldaeans, unlike the Assyrians in Samaria, did not send other settlers there but left the land deserted, until the Jews returned to it after seventy years. The fire taken by the priests from the altar of burnt offering and hidden in a well was recovered after the seventieth year of the return, still alive.

The sixth Roman king, Servius, reigned forty-four years, [Col. 0049C] adding three hills to the city—the Quirinal, Esquiline, and Viminal—and digging ditches around the walls. After Nebuchadnezzar, who, according to sacred Scripture, lived twenty-five years after overthrowing Jerusalem, his son Evil-merodach reigned eighteen years; after him his son Egesar reigned forty years. His brother Laborsodach succeeded him and reigned nine months. When he died, the empire passed to Belshazzar, who is called Naboan. When he had already reigned seventeen years, Babylon was captured by Cyrus, king of the Persians, and Darius, king of the Medes, while Arbaces, the governor through whom Babylon had first been disgraced, withdrew to the Medes.

The Chaldaeans retained part of the kingdom and claimed Babylon for themselves against the Medes. Consequently, Nebuchadnezzar and the other kings after him down to Cyrus, although powerful through Chaldaean strength and renowned under the name of Babylon, are nevertheless not counted among the illustrious kings in the reckoning and succession of rulers. Darius, son of Astyages, who destroyed Babylon, was in his sixty-second year with his kinsman Cyrus when Babylon was invaded. He took the prophet Daniel with him to Media and honored him with every distinction. Daniel himself thus recalls this Darius, saying:

> “In the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus, of Median descent, who ruled over the kingdom of the Chaldaeans—[Col. 0049D] I, Daniel, understood from the books the number of years concerning which the word of the Lord had come to Jeremiah the prophet, that the seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolations should be completed.”

Eusebius, in his *Chronological Books*, counts thirty years from the overthrow of Jerusalem to the beginning of the reign of Cyrus, king of the Persians; Julius Africanus, however, counts seventy. Jerome, in his *Commentary on the Prophet Daniel*, says the following:

> “The Hebrews relate a story of this kind. Until the seventieth year, in which Jeremiah had said that the captivity of the Jews would be released—a matter of which Zechariah also speaks at the beginning of his book—Belshazzar, considering God’s promise void and the pledge false, turned to rejoicing and held a great banquet, mocking, in a sense, the hope of the Jews and the vessels of the temple. But punishment immediately followed.”

Although Daniel’s entire prophecy is full of mysteries, one part of it shines with such clarity that it even indicates the time when the Savior and Lord himself would come. The angel Gabriel revealed to Daniel, among his people, that the seventy weeks had been shortened, so that everlasting righteousness might be brought in, prophecy fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies anointed. Blessed Jerome, through great labor and ingenuity in calculating the years of the kings of Babylon, extended the seventy weeks to the birth of our Redeemer, making them 490 years. He separated seven weeks for the restoration of the temple, fifty-seven weeks up to the Lord’s birth and his passion, and one week for the devastation carried out by the commander Vespasian with his son Titus. [Col. 0050A] Daniel’s prophetic visions are indeed twelve in number, but only ten are found in the Hebrew text. Pythagoras, a philosopher and renowned inventor of arithmetic, is said to have lived at the same time.

[4292] Cyrus, the first of the Persians, reigned thirty years. In the first year of his reign, so that the word of the Lord spoken through Jeremiah might be fulfilled, he released the Hebrews from captivity and caused nearly fifty thousand people to return to Judaea, restoring to them 5,400 gold and silver vessels of the Lord’s temple. After gathering in Jerusalem, they built an altar in the seventh month and began offering burnt offerings to the Lord from the first day of that month. In the second year after their arrival, in the second month, they laid the foundations of the temple; according to Africanus, in the seventy-second year from its burning; according to the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, in the thirty-second. But because of the opposition of the Samaritans, the work was suspended until the second year of Darius, when they also wrote an accusation against the Jews during the reigns of Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes; and Artaxerxes replied that Jerusalem should not be built.

The seventh Roman king, Tarquin, reigned thirty-five years. He was expelled from the kingdom because of his younger son Tarquin, who had violated Lucretia.

[4322] Cambyses, son of Cyrus, reigned eight years. After conquering Egypt, he detested all its religion, abolished its ceremonies and temples, and built Babylon in Egypt. The Hebrews say that he was called a second Nebuchadnezzar, under whom the story of Judith is written.

The Magian brothers reigned seven months. Jesus was high priest and leader of the nation. Zerubbabel, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi are regarded as eminent prophets.

[4330] Darius reigned thirty-six years. In the books of the *Chronicles* we find that two Magian brothers reigned between Darius and Cambyses. But Blessed Jerome writes in his commentary on Daniel that after Cambyses the Magian Smerdis reigned, and married Pantaptes, the daughter of Cambyses. When he was killed by seven Magi and Darius assumed the empire in his place, that same Pantaptes married Darius and bore him a son, Xerxes.

In the second year of Darius, according to Eusebius, the seventieth year of Jerusalem’s captivity was completed. He adduces the prophet Zechariah as a witness, for in the second year of Darius the angel says:

> “Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry?”

“This is the seventieth year” (Zechariah 1:12).

In the sixth year of Darius, the construction of the temple was completed, on the third day of the month Adar. This was the forty-sixth year since its foundations had been laid under Cyrus; hence the Jews say in the Gospel:

> “This temple has been under construction for forty-six years” (John 2:20).

They began building in the second year of Darius, in the sixth month, on the twenty-fourth day; and in the sixth year, as stated, in the twelfth month, they completed it on the third day. From this it is clear that the temple’s work had already been substantially carried out earlier, but that the seventy years are to be counted from its destruction until full permission to restore it.

After the kings who had ruled for 244 years were driven from the city, Rome’s power extended scarcely to the twelfth milestone. After the expulsion of the kings, Rome was first governed by consuls beginning with Brutus; then by tribunes of the plebs and dictators; and again by consuls. This continued for approximately 464 years, until Julius Caesar, who first seized sole power, in the 184th Olympiad.

[4360] Xerxes, son of Darius, reigned twenty years. He captured Egypt, which had revolted from Darius. When he was preparing to fight against Greece, he is said to have had 700,000 armed men, 300,000 auxiliaries, 1,200 warships with beaks, and 3,000 cargo vessels. Nevertheless, he was defeated and fled back to his homeland. Pindar, Sophocles, and Euripides are celebrated as eminent writers of tragedies. Among learned writers of history, Herodotus is recognized, as is Zeuxis the painter. Arrabanus reigned seven months. Socrates was born.

Artaxerxes, also called Longimanus, reigned forty years. In his seventh year, on the first day of the first month, Ezra the priest and scribe of the law of God went up from Babylon with a letter from the king; on the first day of the fifth month he arrived in Jerusalem with 1,700 men. Among other vigorous actions, he disciplined the descendants of the exile concerning their foreign wives. In the twentieth year of the same king, Nehemiah, the cupbearer, came from the fortress of Susa, restored the wall of Jerusalem in fifty-two days, and provided leadership to the people for twelve years.

Up to this point, sacred Scripture contains the sequence of the ages. What was subsequently done among the Jews is presented from the books of the Maccabees, from Josephus, and from the writings of Africanus, who thereafter followed the whole history down to Roman times. Africanus, in the fifth book of his *Chronology*, speaks of this period as follows:

> “The work therefore remained unfinished until Nehemiah and the twenty-fifth year of King Artaxerxes. At that time 115 years of the Persian kingdom had elapsed. It was the 155th year of the captivity of Jerusalem. Then for the first time Artaxerxes ordered the walls of Jerusalem to be built; Nehemiah directed the work, and the street was built and the walls enclosed it. From that time, if you wish to count, you can find the seventy weeks of years extending to Christ.”

Xerxes reigned two months; after him Sogdianus reigned seven months. Hippocrates is regarded as a distinguished physician, and Democritus is recognized. At that time the Senonian Gauls and the people of Vienne established a temple of Mars and Victory to the east of the city of Vienne.

[4428] Darius, surnamed Nothus, reigned twenty-eight years. Egypt withdrew from the Persians. After the Jews returned from captivity, they were governed not by kings but by high priests, until Aristobulus, who began to assume for himself the title of king as well as the dignity of high priest. Plato was born.

[4446] Artaxerxes, surnamed Mnemon, son of Darius and Parysatis, reigned forty years. Under this king the story of Esther appears to have been completed. He is the one whom the Hebrews call Ahasuerus and the Seventy translators call Artaxerxes.

The Athenians began to use twenty-four letters; previously they had only sixteen. The Senonian Gauls, under Brennus, invaded Rome with a large army and ravaged the city after setting it on fire for six months. They enclosed the entire young population—said to have numbered scarcely a thousand at that time—who were hiding in the citadel of the Capitoline Hill, holding the unfortunate survivors in a siege and terrifying, subduing, and selling them through hunger, plague, despair, and fear. For they agreed upon 1,000 pounds of gold as the price of their departure.

Military tribunes began to serve in place of consuls. The terrifying war with Carthage began under the consul Livius. A naval battle was fought with the elder Hannibal. Thirty-one of Hannibal’s ships were captured, twenty sunk, 3,000 men killed, and 7,000 captured. Hannibal escaped by withdrawing in a small boat.

When Gaius Aquilinus Florus and Lucius Cornelius Scipio were consuls, Hanno was appointed commander in Hannibal’s place. Defeated in a naval battle and having lost his army, Hanno himself plunged into the thickest enemy ranks and was killed there. The elder Hannibal was again made commander by the Carthaginians. After engaging the Romans unsuccessfully in a naval battle and being defeated, he perished when his own men covered him with stones.

Under Carpeno as commander and Hanno as admiral, the Carthaginians again joined battle with the Romans and lost sixty-four ships. More than 300 forts were devastated. When Manlius was consul, 27,000 captives, together with immense spoils, were sent from Africa to Rome. A serpent of astonishing size, 120 feet long, was killed in Africa by the consul Regulus not far from the river Bagradas.

Under the commanders Hasdrubal and Hamilcar, with Regulus as consul, a savage war was fought. Seventeen thousand Carthaginians were killed and 5,000 captured. Eighteen elephants were led away. Eighty-two towns surrendered. The Carthaginians, having secured the aid of Spaniards, Gauls, and Greeks as well, summoned Xanthippus of Lacedaemon with auxiliaries and joined battle with the Romans. Thirty thousand Roman soldiers were struck down. Regulus, that distinguished commander, was captured with 500 men and thrown into chains.

In the tenth year of the Punic War, Xanthippus, fearing a change in unstable circumstances after becoming involved in so audacious an act, departed from Africa for Greece. When Aemilius Paullus and Fulvius were consuls, the Romans with a fleet of 300 ships met the Carthaginians, who had an equal fleet. One hundred and four Carthaginian ships were sunk; thirty were captured with their fighting men; 35,000 soldiers were killed. Nine Roman ships were sunk and 1,100 soldiers lost.

Under Hanno, commander of the Carthaginians, and with Aemilius again consul, they lost 9,000 soldiers in battle. The Roman fleet, returning to Italy laden with booty, was overturned in an unspeakable shipwreck. For out of 300 ships, 220 perished; scarcely eighty were freed after casting off their cargoes.

Hamilcar, king of the Carthaginians, condemned Numidia to pay 1,000 talents of silver and 20,000 cattle. He crucified the leaders of all the peoples. Servilius and Sempronius crossed into Africa with 260 ships and ravaged the coast around the Syrtes. When they returned from there to Italy, they struck the rocks and lost 150 cargo vessels.

The commander Hasdrubal, with 120 elephants and more than 30,000 cavalry and infantry, joined battle with Metellus. Twenty thousand Carthaginians were killed in that battle. Twenty-six elephants were also killed and 104 captured. Hasdrubal fled with a few men to Lilybaeum.

Regulus, who had been held captive for five years, was sent to Rome to seek peace. Having failed to obtain it, he returned. The Carthaginians cut off his eyelids, bound him to a machine, and killed him by keeping him awake.

The consuls Attilus Regulus and Manlius were defeated by Hannibal, son of Hamilcar. After losing part of their army, they barely escaped. The consul Claudius, overcome by the Carthaginian fleet, fled with thirty ships into the camp at Lilybaeum. Eight thousand soldiers were killed and thirty captured, as reported.

The consul Lutatius, fighting Hanno with his fleet, captured sixty-four Punic ships and sank 130. Thirty-two thousand men were captured, and 4,000 killed. Hanno, steering his ship ahead, escaped. Lutatius killed 2,000 Carthaginians in a pitched battle near the city of Eryx.

The Carthaginians agreed on the condition that they withdraw from Sicily and Sardinia and pay 3,000 talents of refined silver in equal installments over twenty years. After twenty-three years, the First Punic War, from the time it had begun, was ended. Aristotle, in the eighteenth year of his life, became a pupil of Plato.

Artaxerxes, also called Ochus, reigned twenty-six years. Through envoys he ordered all Greece to withdraw from arms and rest in peace, declaring that anyone who opposed peace would be attacked by war.

A civil war, and more than a civil war, was fought among the Persians, when Artaxerxes and Cyrus, sons of Darius, disputed the kingdom. In the battle, when the two brothers, rushing against each other from opposite sides, had both fallen by a mutual accident, Artaxerxes was wounded first by his brother but escaped death through the speed of his horse. Cyrus, however, was soon overwhelmed by the royal cohort and brought the conflict to an end. Thus Artaxerxes secured the power of the kingdom through fratricide.

The Lacedaemonians declared war on the entire East and appointed Hircylides as commander for this campaign. When he saw that he had to fight against two very powerful prefects of the Persian king, Pharnabazus and Tissaphernes, he devised a timely plan to avoid the burden of fighting both at once: he attacked one after declaring war, while suspending the other through a negotiated peace.

Pharnabazus accused Tissaphernes before Artaxerxes of treason. Conon the Athenian exile was appointed in his place to command the naval battle. He attacked the Lacedaemonian fleet, stormed hostile fields, towers, forts, and other strongholds; and, like a storm unleashed, he overthrew everything wherever it settled.

The Thebans, greatly encouraged by the assistance of the Athenians and by confidence in the courage and ability of their commander Epaminondas, joined battle on land. Lysander, the distinguished Lacedaemonian commander, was killed. Pausanias, another commander, was accused of treason and driven into exile. Agesilaus, king of the Lacedaemonians, attacked the Thebans, who were elated by the success of two victories, and defeated them. Agesilaus himself was severely wounded.

Conon the Athenian commander rebuilt Athens. The Lacedaemonians secretly broke into an Arcadian fort in a sudden attack. The Arcadians, joining themselves to the Thebans for assistance, recovered what they had lost through the surprise attack. Archedamus, the Lacedaemonian commander, was wounded there. The Thebans gave the signal for mercy and ended the battle.

While the Lacedaemonians were occupied with other wars, the Thebans came silently to Lacedaemon in the dead of night. When the enemy’s arrival had been discovered, armed old men, worn out by age, scarcely one hundred in number, placed themselves in the narrow entrances of the gates against 15,000 soldiers. When the youth of Lacedaemon arrived, Epaminondas, commander of the Thebans, fought incautiously in open battle and was wounded. When he learned of his men’s victory, he kissed his shield, removed the hand with which he had closed his wound, and revealed the escape of his blood and the entrance of death.

Again a terrifying inundation of Gauls settled near the river Anio, at the fourth milestone from the city. There Manlius Torquatus began an especially savage battle in single combat. Titus Quintus, as dictator, brought the bloodiest encounter to an end. Again the Gauls rushed into war and were defeated by the dictator Gaius Sulpicius. Again the Gauls spread through the coastal regions and were severely slaughtered by Marcus Valerius Corvinus after he killed their champion.

Artaxerxes, also called Ochus, after completing a great and prolonged war in Egypt, led many Jews into exile and ordered them to live in Hyrcania by the Caspian Sea. In the course of that war he also destroyed Sillodam, the wealthiest city of the province of Phoenicia, and, although previously defeated, then subdued Egypt and crushed it with the sword, subjecting it to Persian rule. Demosthenes is recognized as an orator. Aristotle is acclaimed as a philosopher. Plato died.

[4512] Arses, son of Ochus, reigned three years. Jaddus, the high priest of the Jews, is regarded as eminent; his brother Manasseh established a temple on Mount Gerizim. Speusippus died, and Xenocrates succeeded him. In these days Alexander the Great, the most savage storm of the entire East, was born.

In the 402nd year from the founding of the City, Alexander, king of the Epirotes and uncle of Alexander the Great, crossed into Italy, was defeated in a great battle in Lucania, and killed. In the 400th year from the founding of the City, Philip, son of Amyntas and father of Alexander, acquired the kingdom of the Macedonians and held it for twenty-five years. During these years he accumulated every heap of bitterness and constructed every mass of evil.

First given by his father as a hostage to the Thebans, he was educated for three years under the commander and philosopher Epaminondas.
