This holy king waged war against Athens and won; he captured the famous city of Larisa; he invaded Thessaly out of a desire to possess cavalry and incorporated it into his army. Having made an agreement with Arrybas, king of the Molossians, he married his sister Olympias.

Arrybas, thinking that he would extend his own power through an alliance with the Macedonians, was deceived by this and lost his power; deprived of it, he grew old in exile. At the city of Methone, Philip lost an eye to an arrow and, having outmaneuvered almost all Greece by his plans, subdued it by force. After capturing its king through a deception, he subjected Cappadocia to Macedonian rule.

Philip attempted to kill his brothers, who had been born to his father by a stepmother. He filled the flourishing city of Olynthus with blood, emptied it of its wealth and inhabitants, and carried away his brothers from there to punishment and death. He seized gold mines in Thessaly and silver mines in Thrace.

Philip entered the pass of Thermopylae with his forces drawn up and fortified it with garrisons. He subdued the Athenians, Phocians, and Thessalians. He besieged Byzantium, founded by Pausanias, king of the Spartans. He attacked the Scythian war with all his strength. Twenty thousand boys and women of the Scythian people were captured. A great quantity of livestock was carried away, but no gold or silver was found. Twenty thousand noble horses were sent to Macedonia to replenish the breed.

In the Triballic War, Philip was wounded in the thigh so severely that the horse beneath him was killed through his body. Later, on the wedding day of his daughter Cleopatra, while he was standing between two Alexanders—his son and his son-in-law—he was surrounded without guards in a narrow passage and killed by Pausanias, a noble Macedonian youth.

The Romans made war on the Latins when they rebelled, with Manlius Torquatus and Decius Mus as consuls. Decius fell in that war; Manlius killed his victorious young son. The Vestal virgin Minucia was buried alive in the field now called the Wicked Field because of the incest she had committed. Three hundred and seventy matrons were condemned after being found to have given poison to their husbands and to have been accomplices in the crime.

[4525] Darius, son of Arsames, reigned six years. Alexander, son of Philip and Olympias, began to reign over the Macedonians when he was twenty years old.

When Fabius, master of the cavalry, joined battle, 20,000 Samnites fell. Under the consuls Veturius and Posthumius, the Samnites gained victory at the Caudine Forks and disgracefully captured the entire Roman army. They stripped it even of its weapons and clothing and sent it under the yoke, accepting 600 Roman cavalrymen as hostages.

Under the consul Papirius, the Samnites were defeated. Among all the commanders who were then regarded as the best in their republic, the Romans selected this Papirius to withstand Alexander’s attack.

The orator Demosthenes, corrupted by Persian gold, became the instigator of the Greeks’ revolt from Macedonian rule. Alexander released the Athenians from the fear of punishment; he destroyed the Thebans along with their ruined city; he sold the rest under the crown; he made the other cities of Achaia and Thessaly tributary; and he subdued the Illyrians and Thracians by war.

Before departing for the Persian war, he killed all his relatives and close associates. His army contained 32,000 infantry, 4,000 cavalry, and 180 ships. With so small a force he dared to attack the whole world.

At his first encounter with King Darius, 600,000 Persians were present in the battle line. At Darius’s second approach, Alexander, fearing the narrowness of the terrain, crossed Mount Taurus with astonishing speed and, covering 500 stades in a single day’s march, reached Tarsus. There, when he descended sweating into the very cold river Cydnus, he became stiff; because his muscles contracted, he came near death.

Darius entered the battle line with 300,000 infantry and 100,000 cavalry. The battle was joined with immense courage on both sides. In it both kings, Alexander and Darius, were wounded. Eighty thousand Persian soldiers and 10,000 cavalry were killed; 40,000 were captured. Of the Macedonians, 130 infantry and 140 cavalry fell.

Much gold and other wealth was found in the Persian camp. Among the camp’s captives were Darius’s mother and wife, his sister, and his two daughters. Darius could not obtain their release even when he offered half his kingdom.

Having abandoned hope of peace, Darius opposed Alexander at Tarsus with 44,000 infantry and 100,000 cavalry. The Macedonians rushed into the sword, and rarely in any battle was so much blood shed. Darius was defeated and, persuaded by his men, compelled to flee; the whole East passed under Macedonian rule.

For thirty-four continuous days Alexander inspected the plunder of the camp. He invaded Persepolis, the densely wealthy capital of the Persian kingdom and of the whole world. When he discovered that Darius was being held in chains with golden fetters by his kinsmen, he decided to pursue him with 6,000 cavalry. Finding him on the way pierced by many wounds and dead, he ordered him to be buried in the tombs of his ancestors.

Across three battles and an equal number of years, 1,500,000 infantry and cavalry were consumed. Alexander also entered Judaea and was received favorably; he sacrificed to God and honored Jaddus, the high priest of the temple, with the greatest distinctions, leaving Andromachus as governor of the region.

Under the Persian kings the high priests were: Jeshua, Joiakim, Eliashib, Joiada, Jonathan, and Jaddus. The Persian kingdom, which was destroyed after Darius was killed, lasted 231 years.

Alexander reigned five years after Darius’s death. Entering India, he approached the city of Nisa. He killed the philosopher Callisthenes, who had been his fellow student under Aristotle, along with many other leading men, because Callisthenes would not worship him as a god after the customary manner of greeting had been set aside.

He fought a very bloody war with Porus, king of the Indians. Porus, pierced by many wounds and captured, was restored to his kingdom in memory of his valor. Many peoples were subdued in extremely dangerous battles.

Entering the Indus River, he returned quickly to Babylon, where an embassy from the provinces terrified throughout the whole world awaited him: from the Carthaginians, all the cities of Africa, the Spaniards, the Gauls, Sicily, and Sardinia, as well as many parts of Italy. There, in the thirty-second year of his life and the twelfth year of his reign, he died after drinking poison through the treachery of his attendants.

After him, the empire was divided among many rulers. Ptolemy, son of Lagus, held Egypt; Philip, also called Aridaeus, Alexander’s brother, held Macedonia; Seleucus Nicator held Syria, Babylon, and all the kingdoms of the East; Antigonus ruled Asia. These are signified in Daniel by the four horns of the goat that crushes the ram.

[4537] Ptolemy, son of Lagus, reigned forty years.

The Greeks, judging that the exiles, once granted freedom as Alexander had ordered by letter, would be plotting revenge, revolted from the Macedonian kingdom and provoked war against Antipater, to whom Greece had fallen by lot.

A very serious war arose between Antigonus and Perdiccas, to whom Lesser Media had fallen by lot. Ptolemy attacked Perdiccas with the forces of Egypt in a bitter war and killed him.

Olympias, Alexander’s mother, was captured and killed by Cassander, commander of Caria. Ptolemy and Cassander, having formed an alliance with Lysimachus and Seleucus, prepared a war by land and sea against Antigonus, who pretended that he wanted to free Hercules, the son of Alexander, while actually hoping to rule.

In that war Antigonus was defeated together with his son Demetrius. Cassander, sharing the victory with Ptolemy, arranged for Hercules, Alexander’s son, now fourteen years old, to be killed with his mother.

Ptolemy fought Demetrius in a naval battle, was defeated, and fled to Egypt. Elated by this victory, Antigonus ordered Demetrius, his son, to be called king together with him.

All the others followed this example and assumed for themselves the name and dignity of kings. Ptolemy, Cassander, and the other commanders of the opposing faction, as well as Seleucus from Greater Asia, strengthened one another by letters and prepared a war against Antigonus with their combined forces.

In that war Antigonus was killed. When the victors could not agree about the spoils, they divided into two factions: Seleucus joined Demetrius, while Ptolemy joined Lysimachus and Cassander.

When Cassander died, his son Philip succeeded him. Antipater stabbed his mother, Thessalonice, the wife of Cassander, with his own hand. His brother Alexander prepared war against him to avenge their mother, but Demetrius, whose assistance he had sought, entrapped and killed him.

Ptolemy, Seleucus, and Lysimachus again formed an alliance and transferred the war against Demetrius. Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, joined them as a companion and ally in the war. After Demetrius had been expelled from Macedonia, Pyrrhus seized the Macedonian kingdom.

Lysimachus killed his son-in-law Antipater, who was plotting against him, and, hating his own son Agathocles, killed him. In the thirteenth year of Ptolemy, Seleucus began to reign over Syria. He conquered Babylon, subdued the Bactrians who were rising in new revolts, and crossed into India, which after Alexander’s death had shaken the yoke from its shoulders and killed his prefects.

He fought many serious battles with the commander Andragathus. After strengthening the terms, he departed when peace had been agreed. From that time the Hebrew history of the Maccabees reckons the reign of the Greeks. The Edessenes also calculate their chronology from this point.

Seleucus founded the cities of Antioch, Laodicea, Seleucia, Apamea, Edessa, Beroea, and Pella. Into the cities he had built he transferred Jews, granting them the rights of citizens and municipal status, with equal honor alongside the Greeks.

After thirty-four of Alexander’s commanders had already died, Lysimachus, seventy-four years old, and Seleucus, seventy-seven years old, went to war against one another. This was the final war of Alexander’s comrades-in-arms. Lysimachus, after fifteen children had either died or been killed before him, was the last to be killed.

Afterward Seleucus, pursued by Ptolemy, whose sister Lysimachus had married, was surrounded by a plot and killed. Ptolemy brought Jerusalem and Judaea under his power by deceit and transferred many captives to Egypt.

Onias, son of Jaddus, is regarded as an eminent high priest of the Jews. After him came Simon, son of Onias, a deeply religious and devout high priest.

After him came Eleazar, his brother, leaving Onias, his son, still very young. At this time Zeno the Stoic, Menander the comic poet, and Theophrastus the philosopher were distinguished.

Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes, allied with the people of Tarentum, whose forces had attacked a Roman fleet passing by, joined battle with the Roman army under the consul Laevinus. He was the first to bring into Italy twenty elephants, previously unknown to the Romans.

[4570] Ptolemy Philadelphus, for thirty-eight years. Sostratus built the lighthouse at Alexandria. Ptolemy allowed the Jews who were in Egypt to be free, and, restoring the sacred vessels to Eleazar the high priest, sent many gifts to the temple at Jerusalem. He requested the seventy interpreters to translate Holy Scripture into the Greek language. He was of such great power that he defeated his father Ptolemy. For he had countless thousands of infantry, twenty thousand cavalry, two thousand chariots, and four hundred elephants, which he was the first to bring from Ethiopia. After Eleazar, his uncle Manasses assumed the high priesthood of the Jews. [Col. 0059C] Aratus is recognized as an astrologer; and silver coins were first established at Rome. Hamilcar, commander of the Carthaginians, was killed by the Spaniards in battle. A most savage war was waged with the Romans in Illyricum. Cisalpine Gaul revolted from the Romans. When battle had been joined at Arretium, the consul Atilius was killed. In that same year dreadful portents terrified the wretched City. For blood flowed from a river in Picenum; among the Etruscans the sky was seen to burn; at Ariminum, during the night, a great bright light was said to have shone forth, and three moons appeared to have risen in different regions of the sky. The consul Flaminius, disregarding the auspices, both engaged the Gauls and defeated them. Hannibal, commander of the Carthaginians, when he was nine years old, swore to his father Hamilcar that he would never be a friend to the Romans. [Col. 0059D] Crossing the Pyrenees, he opened a way by the sword among the fiercest peoples of Gaul; and only on the ninth day did he reach the Alps from the Pyrenees. He cut through impassable cliffs with fire and iron, and on the fifth day, with the greatest exertion, reached the level ground. He engaged in battle with the consul Scipio. Scipio himself was severely wounded there, but, through his son Scipio—still wearing the *praetexta*, later called Africanus—escaped death itself. The consul Sempronius likewise engaged him and barely escaped alone. Hannibal lost an eye through the violence of the cold, sleeplessness, and toil. At Lake Trasimene, after the consul Flaminius had been killed, the Roman army was utterly slaughtered. At Cannae, a village of Apulia, the consuls Lucius Aemilius Paulus and Publius Terentius Varro, sent against Hannibal, lost nearly all the strength on which Roman hopes rested: forty-four thousand Romans were killed. The consul Aemilius Paulus was killed; the consul Varro fled with fifty cavalrymen; twenty consular and praetorian men were killed; thirty senators were captured or killed; three hundred noblemen, forty thousand infantrymen, and three thousand five hundred cavalrymen were killed.

So great was the final despair of the Republic among the Romans who remained that the senators thought the City should be abandoned, unless Cornelius Scipio, then a military tribune—the same man who was later Africanus—had deterred them with drawn sword and compelled them instead to swear allegiance to him for the defense of their country. Claudius Marcellus routed Hannibal’s army [Col. 0060B] in battle. Centenius Penula, a centurion, was killed by Hannibal with eight thousand men. The praetor Gnaeus Fulvius was defeated. Hannibal, about to engage in battle at the Anio River, three miles from the City, with the consuls Gnaeus Fulvius and Sulpicius, was suddenly frightened when a rain mixed with hail poured down from the clouds and fled back to his camp. He is said then to have remarked that he was denied only the will, not the power, to take Rome.

The two Scipio brothers crushed Hasdrubal, the Carthaginian commander, in Spain in a very serious war. Both Scipios were then killed in Spain by Hasdrubal’s brother. Capua was captured by Quintus Fulvius. Scipio, twenty-four years old, received proconsular command in Spain in place of his father and uncle, who had been killed there. He sent to Rome Magon, Hannibal’s brother, captured along with the others. Scipio defeated Hasdrubal, commander of the Carthaginians, and stripped him of his camp. He reduced all Spain, from the Pyrenees to the Ocean, to the status of a province. Elected consul with Licinius Crassus, he crossed into Africa.

He killed Hanno, son of Hamilcar, commander of the Carthaginians. Hasdrubal, the commander, fled to Carthage. In Italy Hannibal killed the proconsul Flavius together with eleven tribunes. The consul Marcellus fought Hannibal continuously for three days. On the first day they withdrew after an evenly matched battle; on the next, the consul was defeated; on the third, Hannibal was victorious and forced Marcellus to flee to his camp. The consul Fabius Maximus captured Tarentum, which had defected from the Romans; there he destroyed Hannibal’s immense forces, together with his commander Carthalo. The consul Claudius [Col. 0060D] Marcellus was killed by Hannibal along with his army. Hannibal ambushed and killed both consuls, Marcellus and Crispus. Hasdrubal, Hannibal’s brother, was intercepted and killed in Italy with his entire army by the consuls Marcus Livius and Claudius Nero. Hannibal’s brother Hasdrubal’s head was thrown before his camp.

The consul Sempronius engaged Hannibal, was defeated, and fled to Rome. After thirteen years Hannibal was ordered to return to Africa to aid the Carthaginians, who were under siege. Weeping, he left Italy, after killing all the soldiers of Italian origin who did not wish to follow him, and arrived at Carthage. He requested a conference with Scipio. When they had gazed at one another for a long time in astonishment and mutual admiration, the negotiations for peace having failed, battle was joined. From there Hannibal, slipping away amid the confusion with a few men, fled to Hadrumetum. Peace was granted to the Carthaginians through Scipio, and more than five hundred ships were burned. Scipio entered the City in triumph. Terence the comic poet, wearing the cap that signified the liberty granted to him, followed behind the triumphal chariot; he had been one of the noble Carthaginian captives. [Note: We have taught that this should be understood of Terentius Culeo, chapter 19, book IV of Orosius, section 3.] The Second Punic War ended; it had lasted sixteen years.

[4588] Ptolemy Euergetes, brother of the preceding king, for twenty-six years. He was thereafter called Euergetes by the Egyptians because, after capturing Syria, Cilicia, and almost all Asia, he brought back, amid countless weights of silver and precious vessels, even the gods whom Cambyses had carried off to Persia after capturing Egypt. [Col. 0061B] Onias, high priest of the Jews, son of Simon the Just, is held in renown. His son Simon likewise shines with no lesser glory. Under him Jesus son of Sirach composed the Book of Wisdom, which he calls *Panaretus*; in it he also mentioned Simon. The proconsul Flaminius subdued in war King Philip, together with the Thracians, Macedonians, Illyrians, and many other peoples who had come to his aid. Antiochus, king of Syria, preparing war against the Roman people, crossed from Asia into Europe. Hannibal, ordered by the senate to be handed over to Rome, secretly departed from Africa and went over to Antiochus. Finding him hesitating at Ephesus, he soon drove him into war. Scipio Africanus, sent with the other ambassadors to Antiochus, also held a private conversation with Hannibal; but, when the negotiations for peace had failed, he departed from Antiochus. When war had been joined, Antiochus was defeated by the consul Glabrio and barely escaped from the battle with a few men. Again Scipio Africanus, aided by Eumenes, son of Attalus, waged a naval battle against Hannibal, who at that time commanded Antiochus’ fleet. Antiochus, after Hannibal had been defeated and put to flight and his entire army had likewise been lost, asked for peace and voluntarily sent back Africanus’ son [the time when he had captured him is uncertain]. Hannibal, when the Romans demanded him from Prusias, king of Bithynia, killed himself with poison.

King Philip, who had killed ambassadors of the Roman people, earned pardon because of the most respectful pleas of his son Demetrius, whom he had sent as ambassador; yet he immediately killed that same Demetrius with poison, as though he were a friend of the Romans and his own brother. Scipio Africanus, long an exile from the City that had shown him no gratitude, died of illness at the town of Amiternum. During the consulship of Lepidus and Mucius, the fiercest tribe of the Bastarnae, stirred up by Perseus, son of Philip, with the hope of plunder and enabled to cross the Danube, was destroyed without any battle or enemy. For at that time the Danube, also called the Hister, happened to be covered by thick ice and allowed an easy crossing on foot; but because of the enormous weight and the resounding impact of marching feet, the frozen surface broke apart and, defeated and shattered, left everyone in the midst of the deep waters. An island of Vulcan, which had not existed before, suddenly rose from the sea.

[Col. 0062A] Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, near the city of Vienna in Gaul, while passing into Further Spain, built Platoma [place-name uncertain] with remarkable workmanship and constructed a bridge over the Rhône, having established camps with remarkable workmanship on both banks and extending the bridge across. During the consulship of Publius Licinius Crassus and Gaius Cassius Longinus the Macedonian War was waged. At first all Italy, then King Ptolemy of Egypt, Ariarathes of Cappadocia, Eumenes of Asia, and Massinissa of Numidia came to the aid of the Romans. Perseus, described as the son of Demetrius and Philip [the transmitted wording is uncertain], and the Macedonians followed; when battle was joined, the Romans were defeated and fled, while the Thracians were with their king Cheses and all the Illyrians with King Gentius. In the following engagement, after nearly equal losses, they withdrew into winter quarters. Then, after Perseus had routed the Roman army in many battles, he crossed into Illyricum. He stormed a Roman garrison, where he killed a great multitude of Romans—some by the sword, some he sold under the crown, and some he led with him into Macedonia. But later he was defeated and captured by Lucius Aemilius Paulus, driven in triumph before the chariot with his sons, and died in custody at Alba. His younger son learned metalworking at Rome in order to endure poverty, and was consumed there.

[4614] Ptolemy Philopator, son of Euergetes, for seventeen years. After defeating sixty thousand armed Jews in battle, he undertook war against Antiochus, king of Syria; and, after Philopator had been defeated, [Antiochus] annexed Judaea to himself. Onias, son of Simon, is held in distinction as high priest of the Jews; to him Arrius, king of the Lacedaemonians, sent ambassadors. Claudius Marcellus captured Syracuse, the most flourishing city of Sicily. The younger Scipio Africanus voluntarily offered himself for military service in Spain, and after setting out inflicted great slaughter upon the peoples. The Third Punic War began. The proconsuls set out for Africa. Although the senate had already voted that Carthage should be destroyed, the Carthaginians, when ordered to do so, surrendered their weapons and ships. Later, settling far from the sea, they turned their grief into desperation and appointed two commanders named Hasdrubal. Because they lacked iron, they undertook to make weapons and supplied themselves from mines of gold and silver.

The site of Carthage is said to have been as follows: it enclosed twenty-two thousand paces within its wall and was almost entirely surrounded by the sea, except for an entrance three thousand paces wide. The place had a wall twenty feet wide and forty cubits high, built of squared stone. The citadel was called Byrsa; it occupied somewhat more than two thousand paces. On one side the wall shared by the city and Byrsa overlooked the sea. At first the consuls were driven back from this position; later, Scipio drove the enemy within the walls. Hasdrubal the commander, grandson of Massinissa, king of Numidia, was killed in the senate-house by his own men with fragments of benches, because of suspicion of treachery. Scipio, determined by the final decree of fate to destroy Carthage, fought continuously for six days and nights. At last the Carthaginians were reduced to despair, and the other King Hasdrubal voluntarily surrendered. The deserters who had occupied the temple of Aesculapius threw themselves down voluntarily and were consumed by fire. [Col. 0063A] Hasdrubal’s wife threw herself and her two sons into the midst of the flames, choosing for herself the same end in death that the first queen of Carthage had chosen. The city itself burned continuously for seventeen days, every piece of wall-stone being crushed into dust, in the seven hundredth year after its foundation.

[4631] Ptolemy Epiphanes, son of Philopator, for twenty-four years. In his time the events contained in the history of the Second Book of Maccabees took place. Onias the priest, taking with him many Jews, fled to Egypt. He was honorably received by Ptolemy, received the region called Heliopolis, and, with the king’s permission, built in Egypt a temple like the temple of the Jews. It remained until the reign of Vespasian, for two hundred and fifty years. Thus, under the pretext of Onias the high priest, innumerable throngs of Jews fled to Egypt. At that time Cyrene too was filled with their multitude. While the great Antiochus and the commanders of Ptolemy were fighting against one another, Judaea, placed between them, was divided into opposing factions, some favoring Antiochus and others Ptolemy. This was the reason either for Onias or for the others to seek Egypt.

During the consulship of Mummius, Corinth, the wealthiest city—since it had been like a workshop of every craftsman and craft and the common marketplace of Asia and Europe—was stormed and destroyed. A very large part of the population was consumed by sword and flames; the remainder of the city was sold under the crown. The city was burned, its walls utterly demolished, the wall-stones reduced to dust, and immense booty carried away. Since, because of the number and variety of the statues and images in that conflagration of the city, all the gold, silver, bronze, and every kind of metal had melted together into one mass, a new kind of metal was produced. Hence, whether made from it or in imitation of it, bronze and vessels are called Corinthian bronze and Corinthian vessels down to the present day.

Viriathus in Spain, a Lusitanian by birth, a shepherd and brigand, first became a great terror to the Romans by attacking the roads and ravaging the provinces. He put to flight the praetor Ventidius with his entire army; he likewise shattered Gaius in many battles and drove out Claudius with a great military force. He hung the Roman standards, fasces, and other insignia as trophies in his mountains. Thus, after overthrowing Roman commanders and armies for fourteen years, he was killed by a treacherous plot of his own men. An androgyne was seen at Rome and, by order of the soothsayers, was thrown into the sea. So great a pestilence arose that at first the undertakers were insufficient, and afterward there were none; great houses, empty of the living, remained full of the dead, with extensive inheritances within and no heirs at all. At Rome a child born to a slave-woman was four-footed, four-handed, had four eyes and as many ears, and possessed a double male nature.

During the consulship of Scipio Africanus, Numantia in Hither Spain, and all the Numantines as well, were alike destroyed by sword, poison, and fire. Scipio consulted a certain Celtic leader named Tiresus about the means by which Numantia, previously unconquered, might be overcome or afterward destroyed. Tiresus replied: “Invincible through concord, it was brought to ruin through discord.”

Ptolemy had sexual relations with his sister and afterward took her in marriage; finally he cast her away in a manner even more disgraceful than the way in which he had taken her. He took his stepdaughter—that is, the daughter of his sister and wife—as his wife. He killed his son born from his sister, and also his brother’s son. Therefore, detestable for such incest and parricides, he was driven from the kingdom by the Alexandrians.

Antiochus, not content with Babylonia, Ecbatana, and the whole realm of Media, engaged Phraates, king of the Parthians, and was defeated. For he had in his army one hundred thousand armed men and more than two hundred thousand camp-followers and sutlers, mixed together with prostitutes and actors. Thus he perished, overcome by the power of the Parthians.

[Col. 0064B] [4655] Ptolemy Philometor, for thirty-five years. Aristobulus, a Peripatetic philosopher by nationality a Jew, is known. He also wrote commentaries explaining Moses for Ptolemy Philometor. Attalus, son of Eumenes, dying, ordered by his will that the Roman people should succeed him as heir to the empire of Asia. The consul Licinius Crassus was sent with a very well-equipped army against Aristonicus, brother of Attalus, who had invaded Asia bequeathed to the Romans. He was also aided by great kings—that is, Nicomedes of Bithynia, Mithridates of Pontus and Armenia, Ariarathes of Cappadocia, Philemenus of Paphlagonia—and by their enormous forces. Battle was joined, and he was defeated. Surrounded by the enemy, he would almost have been captured had he not struck a Thracian in the eye with the staff he had been using for his horse. [Col. 0064C] The barbarian, inflamed with anger and pain, therefore pierced Crassus’ side with his sword. Thus, by devising this kind of death, Crassus escaped both dishonor and slavery.

The consul Perpenna, finding Aristonicus resting after his recent victory, unexpectedly turned him to flight and forced him to surrender the city to which he had fled after surrounding it with a siege. Aristonicus was strangled at Rome by order of the senate. Seleucus, surnamed Philometor, reigned eleven years in Syria. During the time of Seleucus, Heliodorus, sent by the king to plunder the temple treasury, was scourged by divine power and driven away. He was succeeded by Antiochus, who was called Soter; then by Antiochus, who was called Theos, that is, “God”; then by Antiochus Epiphanes. He entered Egypt and prepared war against Ptolemy, king of Egypt. He attacked the law of the Jews, filling everything with the filth of idols, and placed in the temple of God an image of Jupiter Olympius. He also built on the summit of Mount Garizim in Samaria a shrine of Jupiter the Stranger, at the request of the Samaritans themselves that he do so. But the priest Mattathias defended the ancestral laws and took up arms against the commanders of Antiochus. From this arose the exceedingly venerable martyrdom of the seven holy Maccabean brothers, in whose honor the Church of Vienne was founded.

Onias is held to have been the high priest. His brother Jason, seizing the high priesthood with Antiochus’ permission and abolishing the lawful rights of the citizens, established a gymnasium beneath the citadel and an *ephebeion* at Jerusalem. After he had been expelled, three years later, into the region of the Ammonites, Menelaus, brother of Simon, from the tribe of Benjamin, obtained control of the priesthood. Through his impious faction the pious high priest Onias was killed by Andronicus. For this reason King Antiochus ordered Andronicus to be stripped of his purple and put to death in the same place where he had committed his impiety against Onias. Antiochus Eupator, later the son of Antiochus, ordered Menelaus to be thrown down from a tower fifty cubits high; by such a death he was most justly condemned.

After the priest Mattathias died, Judas Maccabaeus assumed command of the Jews, in the one hundred and forty-sixth year of the Greek kingdom. He soon expelled the commanders of Antiochus from Judaea and cleansed the temple of the images of idols; after three years he restored the ancestral laws to his fellow citizens. Antiochus, wishing to plunder Persipolis, a most noble and wealthy city, was put to flight when a multitude rushed to arms. As heavenly judgment pressed him onward, while he hastened his journey to make Jerusalem a heap of Jewish tombs, he was struck by an incurable wound and died a miserable death as a murderer and blasphemer. He was succeeded by his son Antiochus Eupator; and after two years, that is, in the one hundred and fifty-first year of the Greek kingdom, Demetrius, son of Seleucus, reigned. He appointed the impious Alcimus to the priesthood, while Judas Maccabaeus was killed fighting for the ancestral laws and the people of God. In the one hundred and fifty-fourth year, after Alcimus died miserably, the leadership and priesthood were awarded to Jonathan with the approval of all.

[4690] Ptolemy Euergetes, for twenty-eight years. Jonathan, leader and high priest of the Jews, made alliances of friendship with the Romans and the Spartans. After administering the priesthood with the greatest diligence for eighteen years, he was killed by Tryphon, and his brother Simon was appointed to the priesthood, in the seventh year of Euergetes’ reign.

Scipio Africanus was found lifeless in his bedroom, killed by the treachery of his wife Sempronia, sister of the Gracchi. His courage and moderation had such influence in the Roman state that while he lived it was thought that neither a social nor a civil war could arise. During the consulship of Lucius Caecilius Metellus and Quintus Titius Flaminius, Carthage in Africa was ordered to be restored. Only in the twelfth year after it had been destroyed was it restored and repopulated, with families of Roman citizens brought in to inhabit it, during the consulship of Fabius.

When Bitoitus, king of the Arverni, a Gallic people, was preparing for war with a very great force, a small Roman army confronted him, so that Bitoitus boasted that it could scarcely be enough food for the dogs he had in his column. Realizing that one bridge was insufficient for transferring his forces across the Rhône, he built another by joining boats together with chains and laying and fastening planks across them. Battle was joined; the Gauls were defeated and turned to flight. Because the men were crowded together carelessly, their excessively hasty crossing broke the bridge’s fastenings, and soon they were submerged together with the boats.

The consul Quintus Martius attacked in war a Gallic people settled at the foot of the Alps. When they saw themselves surrounded by Roman forces, they killed their wives and children and threw themselves into the flames. Those whom the Romans anticipated and thus prevented from carrying out their intended death consumed themselves by various means: some by the sword, some by hanging, and some by refusing food. Absolutely no one, not even a small child, survived to endure the condition of slavery.

Jugurtha, the adopted son of Micipsa, king of Numidia, and made co-heir with his natural sons, killed his co-heir Hiempsal and expelled Adherbal from Africa after defeating him in war. He corrupted the consul Calpurnius, sent against him, with money and brought him to shameful peace terms. When Jugurtha himself came to Rome, after corrupting or attempting to corrupt everyone with money, he stirred up seditions and disputes. As he entered it, he marked the City with a sufficiently infamous saying: “A city for sale, and doomed to perish quickly if it finds a buyer.”

At last Jugurtha was defeated by the Romans in bloody wars and allied himself with Bocchus, king of the Moors. When battle was joined, Bocchus and Jugurtha fled together from the Romans under the consul Marius; thereafter ninety thousand armed men were slaughtered to the point of annihilation by the victorious Romans. As the price of peace, Bocchus treacherously captured Jugurtha, bound him in chains, and sent him through the legate Sulla to Marius. Jugurtha was led in triumph before the chariot with his two sons and was soon strangled in prison.

Mithridates, king of the Parthians, sixth in succession from Arsaces, after defeating the commander of Demetrius, victoriously invaded the city of Babylon and all its territories. He also subdued all the peoples who live between the Hydaspes and Indus rivers and extended his bloody rule as far as India. He defeated and captured Demetrius himself when Demetrius met him in battle for the second time. After Demetrius was captured, a certain Deodatus usurped his kingdom and royal title with his son Alexander. Later he killed that same son Alexander, whom he had made his partner in the danger of seizing the kingdom, so that he would not have him as a partner in possessing it.

The consul Lucius pursued the Tiburtians in Gaul as far as the Ocean and was killed after being surrounded by an ambush. The consul Scipio captured the Gallic city of Toulouse and received from the temple of Apollo one hundred thousand pounds of gold and one hundred ten thousand pounds of silver. When he had sent these, together with garrisons, to Massilia, a city friendly to the Roman people, it is said that, after the guards had secretly been killed, everything was stolen by criminal means.

During the consulship of Manlius and Quintus Caepio, they were sent against the Cimbri, Teutones, Teugurini, and Ambrones, peoples of Gaul and Germany. They divided the provinces between themselves along the Rhône River. There, while contending with one another in the fiercest jealousy and rivalry, they were defeated, to the great disgrace and danger of the Roman name. It is reported that of the entire army only ten men survived to bring back the miserable news. The enemy, having obtained enormous booty, destroyed everything they had captured by a certain novel and unprecedented execration.

When the consul Marius, in his fourth consulship, had set up camp in the province of Vienna near the Isère and Rhône rivers, where they flow together, the Teutones, Cimbri, Teugurini, and Ambrones had decided to make for Italy in three columns. They were defeated by the Romans in a most dangerous battle. [Col. 0067A] At Rome, Publius Malleolus, with the assistance of slaves, killed his mother. Condemned for parricide, he was sewn into a sack and thrown into the sea; in response to such a crime the Romans established this distinctive punishment.

In the sixth consulship of Gaius Marius, the condition of the Roman empire was so shaken that it almost collapsed through internal disaster right up to the end. Metellus Numidicus, an outstanding man, was unjustly condemned through the faction of Marius by Glaucia the praetor and Saturninus the tribune, and departed into exile amid the grief of the entire City. Later Saturninus, Saufeius, and Labienus, after they had already begun battle in the Forum, fled at Marius’ command into the senate-house. There they were killed by Roman cavalry, who broke down the doors. Glaucia and Dolabella, Saturninus’ brother, were killed.

Rutilius too, a man of perfect integrity, who had displayed such constancy of faith and innocence that, on the day assigned to him by his accusers, he neither cut his hair or beard before the hearing, nor sought supporters by means of dirty clothing or humble appearance, nor softened his enemies or influenced the judges, was condemned through the perjury of the judges, although he was attacked by evident calumny. He moved to Smyrna and, devoted to literary studies, grew old there.

During the consulship of Sextus Julius Caesar and Lucius Martius, the Social War, arising from internal causes, stirred up all Italy. After Simon, Jonathan’s brother, John his son was appointed to the high priesthood. While waging war against the Hyrcani, he took the name Hyrcanus. Requesting from the Romans the right of friendship, he was enrolled among their friends by decree of the senate.

He captured Samaria—which in our time is called Sebaste—and leveled it to the ground. Ptolemy, who had treacherously killed John’s father and bound his mother in chains, had fled there for refuge. Later Herod restored the city and wished it to be called Sebaste in honor of Augustus.

Ptolemy Phiscon, also called Soter, for seventeen years. Cicero was born at Arpinum, to his mother Helvia and his father, a man of equestrian rank from the royal Volscian stock. Dreadful portents, appearing during the Social War, terrified the sorrowful Roman City. For at sunrise a globe of fire shot forth from the northern region with an enormous crash of the sky. Among the Attatines, while loaves were being broken, blood flowed from the middle of the loaves as though from wounds. For seven continuous days hailstones, mixed also with fragments of tiles, beat the earth over a very wide area. From a fissure in the earth a flame burst forth, which seemed to extend to the sky.

The praetor Gnaeus Pompeius waged war against the Picentes by order of the senate and was defeated. Likewise Julius Caesar, defeated in battle by the Samnites, fled after his army had been killed. Later, after gathering forces from every direction, he killed many thousands of the enemy, Samnites and Lucanians. When he was hailed as commander by the army, the senate laid aside the *saga*—that is, the garment of mourning which it had assumed when the Social War arose—and, with hope smiling again, recovered the ancient dignity of the toga.

Gnaeus Pompeius routed the Picentes in a severe battle. Through this victory the senate recovered its broad-striped robes and the other insignia of rank. Before the Social War had ended, civil war first broke out at Rome. In that same year, the six hundred and sixty-second from the founding of the City, the Mithridatic War began. It lasted thirty years, or, as some writers record, forty.

Mithridates, king of Pontus and Armenia, was defeated by the Romans in many battles. Finally, when his prefect Castor, who was in command at Phanagoria, had killed the king’s friends, seized the citadel, and sent four of his sons to the Roman garrisons, Mithridates, inflamed with anger, at last erupted into crimes and killed several of his other friends, as well as his son Exipodras and another son, Macares.

Pharnaces, terrified by the example of his brothers, won over the army that had been sent to pursue him and soon led it against his father. Mithridates long pleaded with his son from the top of a very high wall, but when he saw him unmoved, he is said to have cried out as he was about to die: “Since Pharnaces orders me to die, I pray you, ancestral gods, if you exist, that he too may one day hear this voice from his own children.”

He then immediately descended to his wives, concubines, and daughters and gave poison to them all. When he himself had drunk last of all, yet could not be killed by the poison because of the antidotes with which he had often fortified his vital organs against harmful substances, he wandered about in vain, hoping that somehow the infused poison might be driven through his veins by movement of the body. He invited a certain Gallic soldier, who was already running about after the wall had been breached, and offered him his throat. At the age of seventy-two he met this end of life.

During the consulship of Tullius Cicero and Gaius Antonius, after receiving news of Mithridates’ death, Pompey attacked Coele-Syria and Phoenicia in war, subdued the Ituraeans and Arabs, and captured their city, which they call Petra. From there he sent Gabinius with an army to the Jews and their city Jerusalem. At that time Aristobulus ruled them as king, the first priest to do so, after expelling his brother Hyrcanus, for one year.

In the four hundred and eighty-third year of the Babylonian captivity, after Janeus, surnamed Alexander, had reigned for thirty-seven years, he also administered the high priesthood and ruled his fellow citizens with the greatest cruelty. Pompey himself, following Gabinius immediately, was received by the leading men of the City but repulsed by the common people from the temple wall. He set about storming it. It was fortified not only by the nature of the site but also by enormous walls and a very large ditch. Since he had to compel different legions to take turns succeeding one another day and night without rest, he captured it only with difficulty in the third month. Thirteen thousand Jews are said to have been killed there. The rest of the multitude submitted.

Pompey ordered the walls of the city to be destroyed and leveled to the ground, and struck several Jewish leaders with the axe. He restored the high priesthood to Hyrcanus and led Aristobulus, as a captive, to Rome. Hyrcanus remained in the high priesthood after the death of his mother Alexandra, who had reigned over the Jews after her husband Alexander, for approximately thirty-four years. For Aristobulus succeeded Hyrcanus in the high priesthood for one year, after which came Janeus, surnamed Alexander. When Alexander died, his wife Alexandra reigned. After her death, her sons Aristobulus and Hyrcanus, fighting one another over the rule, gave the Romans an opportunity to invade Judaea.

As we have said, after capturing Jerusalem and opening the temple, Pompey advanced as far as the Holy of Holies. He took the defeated Aristobulus away with him and confirmed the high priesthood to Hyrcanus, who held it, as we have said, for thirty-four years. Pompey appointed Antipater, son of Herod the Ascalonite, procurator of Palestine. Pompey declared publicly that he had waged war in the East against twenty-two kings.

In those days the conspiracy of Catiline against his country was formed and exposed at Rome. Sallust described this history in a work dealing with Cicero. Virgil Maro was born in the village called Andes, not far from Mantua. The poet Lucretius was also born; he later killed himself in a fit of erotic madness.

[4735] Ptolemy, also called Alexander, for ten years. In his seventh year Syria passed into Roman control, after Philip had been captured by Gabinius.

[4745] Ptolemy Phiscon, expelled from the kingdom by his mother Cleopatra, withdrew to Cyprus. Returning from exile, he regained the kingdom and held it for nine years, because the citizens had expelled Alexander, who had preceded him, for killing his mother.

[4745] Ptolemy Dionysius, for thirty years. Apollodorus, later the tutor of Augustus, was held in renown. By the Vatinian Law, three provinces with seven legions were assigned to Julius Caesar for five years: Transalpine Gaul, Cisalpine Gaul, and Illyricum. The Senate later added Comata Gaul.

Orgetorix, king and chief of the Helvetii, the bravest of all the Gallic peoples—especially because they were almost continually at war with the Germans, from whom they are separated only by the Rhine River—had inflamed their spirits to arms in the hope of invading all Gaul. When the other nobles seized him and forced him to his death, the Helvetii, having formed a conspiracy and burned their villages and houses so that no desire to return might remain, set out. When the entire population of the Helvetii, Tulingi, Latobici, Rauraci, and Boii, of both sexes, first advanced, their number was 157,000 people. When Caesar encountered them near the Rhône River, he defeated them twice in a great and difficult war. Of these, 47,000 fell in battle; he compelled the rest to surrender.

Again Caesar defeated near the Sequani the incredible forces of the Germans, commanded by King Ariovistus. In Ariovistus’s army were the Harudes, Marcomanni, Triboci, Vangiones, Nemetes, Sedusii, and Suebi.

Again the nation of the Belgae, which is a third part of Gaul, rose up against Caesar. Their forces were distributed as follows: the Bellovaci, who seemed to surpass the others in number and valor, had 60,000 picked armed men; the Suessiones, from twelve towns, 50,000; the Nervii, whose savagery was so untamed that up to that time they had never allowed merchants to bring them wine or other things for sale, lest the pleasure introduced by these should bring torpor upon their courage, likewise had 50,000.

The Atrebates and Ambiani had 10,000; the Morini, 25,000; the Menapii, 9,000; the Caleti, 10,000; the Velocasses and Veromandui, likewise 10,000; the Aduatuci, 18,000; the Condrusi, Eburones, Cerosi, and Caemani, who are called Germans by one name, 40,000. Thus, they are reported to have had 272,000 picked armed men.

When these suddenly burst out of the forest, Caesar’s army attacked them and, encouraged by its commander, stood firm; it defeated them and nearly annihilated them. Caesar sent Galba with the Twelfth Legion against the Veragri and Seduni. When Galba had settled in a village of the Veragri called Octodurus for the purpose of wintering, he was surrounded by the Gauls. Pouring down from the mountains, they overwhelmed the unfinished camp with stones and weapons. But when the Romans burst through the gates, more than 30,000 barbarians were slain.

The Veneti and the other peoples bordering on the Sefes enlisted the Osismii, Lexovii, Namnetes, Ambibariti, Morini, Diablintes, and Menapii for war; they also summoned auxiliaries from Britain. Against them Caesar ordered long ships to be built on the Loire River, by which it flows into the Ocean. When a naval battle was joined, the enemy ships were burned, and after the Gauls who had fought were killed, all the rest surrendered. But Caesar, chiefly on account of the wrongs done to his envoys, had all the leaders killed under torture and sold the rest under the auctioneer’s crown.

Titus Sabinus likewise destroyed the Aulerci, Eburonices, and Lexovii in an extraordinary slaughter, after making a sortie; they had killed their own leaders because those leaders refused to be authors of a renewal of the war. The town of Sauciatum in Aquitania was captured. Fifty thousand from the Aquitani and Cantabri were killed. The Germans who had crossed the Rhine with immense forces were destroyed to the last man. Their number was about 440,000.

Then Caesar crossed into Germany over a bridge. He freed the Sugambri and Ubii from siege. He terrified the Suebi, the greatest and fiercest people, of whom many have reported that there were one hundred districts and peoples, and by his arrival he terrified all Germany. Soon he cut down the bridge and withdrew into Gaul.

From there he came to the Morini, from whom the nearest and shortest passage to Britain lies. After preparing about eighty cargo ships and fast ships, he crossed into Britain, where he was worn down by a fierce battle. Then, caught by an adverse storm, he lost most of his fleet.

Returning to Gaul, he ordered six hundred ships of both types to be built. With these he crossed again into Britain in early spring. He finally captured Tridentum, a very strong town, after receiving forty hostages, and Cassobellaunus, a town situated between two marshes, in a hard-fought battle. Accepting the Britons’ surrender, he returned to Gaul.

A multitude of Treveri, Eburones, Aduatuci, and Nervii conspired to take up arms. Their numbers can be judged to have been very great because, although they had no agricultural tools, they cut the earth with swords and carried it away in their cloaks; scarcely within three hours they completed, around a circuit of fifteen miles, a rampart ten feet high and a ditch fifteen feet deep. In addition, they built 120 towers of astonishing height.

Caesar destroyed them in a vast slaughter. Labienus, who commanded the legions, killed all the forces of the Treveri and immediately captured the city itself. When Caesar learned that the Eburones had taken refuge in the Ardennes Forest—which is the greatest forest in all Gaul, extending from the banks of the Rhine and the territory of the Treveri as far as the Nervii and stretching for more than fifty miles in length—he invited all Gaul by messengers to seek out and plunder, each according to his own preference, the spoils hidden in the Ardennes Forest. By this action, while Gauls died on both sides, he avenged the greatest wrongs done to the Romans without endangering a single Roman.

Caesar subdued Gaul through many battles. When Lucullus had subdued Asia, Pompey Spain, and Caesar Gaul, the Roman Empire was extended almost to the farthest limits of the earth.

When Caesar was returning victorious from Gaul, the Senate decreed that he should not enter the City unless he had dismissed his army. Caesar therefore withdrew to Ravenna. Pompey and all the senators, alarmed by Caesar’s increasing power, crossed into Greece as though expelled from Italy and chose Dyrrachium as the headquarters for conducting the war.

Caesar came to Rome and, when money from the treasury was refused him, forced its doors and brought out from it 4,135 pounds of gold and nearly 80,000 pounds of silver. Soon, having crossed the Alps with his legions, he came to Massilia. After subduing it by siege and granting it freedom, he stripped it of everything else.

At Dyrrachium many kings of the East had assembled with auxiliaries on Pompey’s side. When battle was joined, Caesar’s soldiers fled, and 4,000 of his army were killed. From there Caesar marched rapidly through Epirus into Thessaly. Pompey followed him with large forces.

Pompey had eighty cohorts arranged in three lines, 40,000 infantry, 600 cavalry on the left wing, and 500 on the right; in addition, there were many kings. Caesar likewise had eighty cohorts arranged in three lines, fewer than 30,000 infantry, and 1,000 cavalry.

When battle was joined and for a long time the outcome was uncertain as men were cut down on both sides, at last Pompey’s entire army fled and the camp was scattered. Pompey, fleeing, obtained a transport ship and crossed into Asia. From there he went through Cyprus to Egypt, and as soon as he reached the shore, he was killed on the order of the young Ptolemy, who wished to curry favor with the victorious Caesar.

Pompey’s wife and sons fled, and Pompey’s fleet was plundered. After settling affairs among the Thessalians, Caesar came to Alexandria. When Pompey’s head and ring were brought to him and he saw them, he wept.

[4755] Achillas, the royal commander, once stained with Pompey’s blood, was also plotting Caesar’s death. For when he was ordered to dismiss the army under his command—20,000 armed men—he not only disregarded the order but also drew up his battle line.

During the battle itself, the royal fleet, which had accidentally been hauled ashore, was ordered to be burned. When the fire also seized part of the city, it burned 40,000 books stored by chance in nearby buildings.

When battle was joined again with Achillas, Caesar, pressed by the force of the enemy’s assault, boarded a small boat. When it was soon weighed down and sunk by those following him, he reached a ship by swimming for 200 paces, holding his papers aloft in one hand.

Soon, in a naval battle, he himself either sank or captured the royal fleet. When the Alexandrians demanded their king, he returned the child Ptolemy to them. As soon as the boy was free, he made war, but he himself was immediately destroyed together with his entire army. In that war 20,000 men were killed, while 12,000 surrendered with seventy long ships. The young king himself, taken aboard a small boat as he attempted to flee, was drowned and killed when many men leapt into it.

«[4784] Caesar gave the kingdom of Egypt to Cleopatra, the sister of Ptolemy; she held it for twenty-two years. Caesar, after traversing Syria, defeated Pharnaces in Pontus. Created dictator and consul at Rome, he crossed into Africa. At Thapsus he fought against Juba and Scipio and defeated them.

Cato killed himself at Utica. Juba offered his throat to the executioner after giving him a price. Petreius pierced himself with the same sword. Scipio, boarding the ship in which he intended to flee to Spain, was driven back to Africa by the wind and killed himself. Titus Torquatus was also killed on the same ship.

Caesar ordered the grandsons of Pompey the Great and his daughter Pompeia to be killed. The final battle was fought at the river Munda against the two Pompeys, Labienus, and Attius Varus.

When Caesar returned to Rome, while he was restoring the condition of the Republic with clemency, contrary to the examples of wicked men, he was stabbed in the senate house by twenty-three wounds, with Brutus, Cassius, and a very large part of the Senate as the instigators, and died. They say that more than forty accomplices were involved in the conspiracy.

The people, driven by grief, carried away his body and burned it in the Forum with fragments of platforms and benches, three years and six months after they had begun to reign. For for four years after the death of Gnaeus Pompey the Great, civil war thundered without interruption throughout the world.

While Cleopatra was reigning among the Alexandrians, when her fourth year had ended, Julius Caesar became the first of the Romans to obtain sole power. From him the Caesars also received their name. Meanwhile Cassius, after Judaea had been captured, plundered the Temple. From this point onward comes the name of the emperors.

Octavian Caesar Augustus, the second of the Romans, reigned fifty-six years and six months; from him Roman kings were called Augusti. Of these years, he lived fifteen while Cleopatra was still alive and forty-one thereafter.

In the eleventh year of Augustus, when the rule of the high priests in Judaea had come to an end, the seventy weeks written in Daniel were completed.

In the 710th year from the founding of the City, after Julius Caesar had been killed, Octavian—who by the will of his uncle Julius Caesar had assumed both his inheritance and his name—came to Rome as a very young man and overcame his natural disposition through civil wars.

To explain briefly the civil wars that he himself waged: the Mutinensian, Philippian, Perusian, Sicilian, and Actian. Of these, two—the first and the last—were against Mark Antony; the second, against Brutus and Cassius; the third, against Lucius Antony; the fourth, against Sextus Pompey, the son of Gnaeus Pompey, whom he destroyed.

To secure the loyalty arising from the favor he had shown Antony by receiving him back, Caesar took Antony’s daughter in marriage.

Herod, when the kingdom and priesthood of the Jews had come to an end, although he had no connection with that people—being the son of Antipater the Ascalonite and of his Arabian mother Cypros—received from the Romans the rulership of the Jews, which he held for thirty-six years.

So that he might not perhaps be accused of being ignoble and foreign to the seed of the Jews, he burned all the books in which the nobility of the Jewish people was recorded and preserved in the Temple, so that, when the proofs had been destroyed, he too might be thought to belong to that people.

Moreover, so that he might mingle his offspring with their royal lineage, he cast aside Dossida, a woman of Jerusalem whom he had married as a private citizen, and, after she had borne him a son, Antipater, he joined himself in marriage to Mariamne, the daughter of Alexander and granddaughter of Aristobulus, the brother of Hyrcanus, who had ruled the Jewish people before him.

She bore him five sons, two of whom, Alexander and Aristobulus, he himself killed in Samaria. Soon afterward he also killed their mother, whom he had known to be dearer to him than anything, in a similar crime.

Aristobulus among them had a son by Berenice, whom we read in the Acts of the Apostles was struck down by an angel.

Antony captured Artabanus, king of Armenia, through treachery and deceit. Having bound him with a silver chain, he forced him to reveal the royal treasures. After storming the town where Artabanus had said they were stored, Antony carried away a great quantity of gold and silver.

Elated by this wealth, he declared war against Caesar and announced the repudiation of Octavia, Caesar’s sister and his own wife. He ordered Cleopatra to come to him from Alexandria and married her.

He himself set out for Actium, where he had stationed his fleet. When he found that nearly a third of the rowers had been consumed by hunger, he was not disturbed. “Only the oars,” he said, “are safe; for rowers will not be lacking as long as Greece has people.”

Caesar had 230 ships with rams and thirty without rams. The triremes equaled the Liburnians in speed; eight legions were stationed aboard the fleet, apart from five praetorian cohorts.

Antony’s fleet consisted of 170 ships. Although it was inferior in number, it surpassed Caesar’s in size; for its ships rose ten feet above the sea.

The battle, begun at the fifth hour and continuing until the seventh with uncertain hope of victory, produced very heavy slaughter on both sides. During the remainder of the day and the following night, the advantage turned toward Caesar’s victory.

Queen Cleopatra fled first with sixty of the fastest ships. Antony soon followed his fleeing wife.

Twelve thousand of the defeated are reported to have fallen, and 6,000 were wounded; of these, 1,000 died while under treatment. Caesar, acclaimed emperor for the sixth time, and himself consul for the fourth time together with Marcus Licinius Crassus, came to Brundisium. There he arranged the defenses of the world by distributing the legions.

Finally, when Antony was preparing to fight a naval battle, all the ships on Antony’s side suddenly went over to Caesar. Alarmed, Antony withdrew with a few men into the royal palace.

Then, as Caesar approached and the city was thrown into confusion, Antony pierced himself with a sword. When Cleopatra realized that she was being reserved for the triumph, she sought voluntary death. She was found lifeless, apparently from the bite of a serpent on her left arm, even though Caesar uselessly brought in Psylli, who are accustomed to draw out and suck back serpent poisons from human wounds.

Caesar took possession as victor of Alexandria, by far the richest and greatest of all cities. Until this point, those called the Lagids (Lagidae), after Ptolemy the First, son of Lagus, had ruled in Egypt for 295 years.

Caesar, returning victorious from the East, entered the City in a triple triumph on the eighth day before the Ides of January. On that day he was first hailed as Augustus, and from that same day supreme authority and power began to belong to one man and remained so—what the Greeks call a monarchy.

Moreover, no one among believers, or even among those who contradict the faith, is unaware that this is the same day—the eighth day before the Ides of January—on which we observe the Epiphany, that is, the appearance or manifestation of the Lord’s sacrament.

Thus, in every respect, Caesar’s empire is shown to have been prepared for the grace of the coming Christ. For when, after his uncle Gaius Caesar had been killed, he was returning from Apollonia and entering the City, at about the third hour, suddenly, in a clear and perfectly calm sky, a circle resembling a rainbow surrounded the disk of the sun, as though to show that he alone was supreme in this world and the only one brilliant throughout the world: the one in whose time he would come who had both made and ruled the sun itself and the whole world.

Then, when on the second occasion, after receiving the legions of Pompey and Lepidus in Sicily, he had restored 30,000 slaves to their masters, crucified 6,000 whose masters could not be found, honorably discharged 20,000 soldiers with great courage, and distributed forty-four legions under his sole command for the protection of the world, and, entering the City in an ovation, had decreed that all the debts owed to the Roman people should be forgiven, with even the written records erased, during those very days an exceedingly abundant fountain of oil flowed all day from a hired lodging-house (taberna meritoria).

What sign could be clearer than that, under Caesar’s rule and the Roman Empire, throughout the entire day—that is, throughout the whole period of the Roman imperial power—Christ, and from him Christians, that is, the Anointed One and those anointed from him, would flow abundantly and unceasingly from the hired lodging-house (taberna meritoria), that is, from the hospitable and generous Church; that all slaves who nevertheless recognized their master would be restored through Caesar, while the others who were found without a master would be handed over to death and punishment; and that under Caesar the debts of sins would be remitted in that city in which oil had flowed spontaneously?

But on the third occasion, when he entered the City in triumph as consul for the fifth time, namely on the eighth day before the Ides of January, he both closed the Temple of Janus for the first time in 200 years and assumed that famous name, Augustus.

What can be believed more faithfully and truly than that Caesar, through the hidden order of events, had been predestined to serve as a preparation for him who, a little later on that same day, was to be manifested, while Caesar bore the sign of peace and assumed the name of power? Thus, in the 763rd year from the founding of the City, after the gates of Janus had been closed, when Caesar Augustus, after completing the Cantabrian war and pacifying all peoples, had entered the City from east to west, from north to south, and around the entire circuit of the Ocean, while he was watching the games a line was spoken in a mime: “O fair and good master!” Everyone approved it as though it had been said about him. He immediately restrained the unbecoming flatteries with hand and expression, and on the following day censured them in a most severe edict. From then on he did not allow himself to be called “master,” not even by his children or grandchildren, whether seriously or in jest.

## THE SIXTH AGE, FROM CHRIST TO THE END OF THE WORLD

[Col. 0075]

[Col. 0075B] [4832] Therefore, at that time—namely, in the forty-second year of Caesar Augustus, but the twenty-seventh year from the death of Cleopatra and Antony, when Egypt was also converted into a province, in the third year of the 103rd Olympiad, and in the 752nd year from the founding of the City—that is, in the year when, after all the disturbances of the nations of the world had been subdued, Caesar established the firmest and truest peace through God’s arrangement—Jesus Christ, the Son of God, consecrated the sixth age of the world by his coming.

In the forty-eighth year of Augustus’s reign, Herod, perpetrator of crimes and killer of the innocent children slain for Christ, died miserably and deservedly from dropsy and worms teeming throughout his body.

His son Archelaus, appointed in his place by Augustus, reigned nine years, that is, until the end of Augustus himself. For then, when the Jews could no longer endure his savagery and accused him before Augustus, he was exiled to Vienna, the most distinguished city of Gaul. To diminish the power of the Jewish kingdom and tame its insolence, four of his brothers were appointed tetrarchs in his place: Herod, Antipater, Lysias, and Philip. Philip and Herod, who had previously been called Antipas, had already been appointed tetrarchs while Archelaus was still alive.

Thus Christ, born as the true Lord of the entire human race, was immediately enrolled among human beings for the Roman census, in that first and most illustrious registration by which Caesar marked himself as ruler of all and the Romans as masters of everything, by the enrollment of each individual.

(Orosius, book VII.)

Christ was born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, when all the growth of the green year first begins. Caesar sent his grandson Gaius to organize the provinces of Egypt and Syria. Passing from Egypt, he refused to worship within the territory of Palestine, at Jerusalem, in the Temple of God, which was then holy and renowned, as Suetonius Tranquillus relates. When Augustus learned of this, he praised him for having acted prudently, although he had used faulty judgment.

[17] Tiberius, Augustus’s stepson—that is, the son of his wife Livia—reigned thirty-two years. He himself waged no wars. Indeed, in the fourth year of his reign, Germanicus, son of Drusus and father of Caligula, triumphed over the Germans to whom he had been sent by the aged Augustus.

Tiberius himself governed the state through most of his reign with great and serious restraint, so much so that when certain governors advised increasing the taxes of the provinces, he wrote to them that it was the duty of a good shepherd to shear the flock, not to flay it.

In his twelfth year, Pilate was sent by him as procurator of Judaea. Herod the tetrarch, who held the rulership of the Jews for twenty-four years, founded Tiberias and Livia in honor of Tiberius and his mother Livia.

In the fifteenth year of Tiberius’s reign, after his baptism, which John preached, the Lord announced the kingdom of heaven to the world. According to the Hebrews, 4,000 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world, as Eusebius also records in his Chronicles, noting that the sixteenth year of Tiberius was the beginning of the eighty-first Jubilee according to the Hebrews. Our reckoning, however, considers that nineteen fewer years should be counted.

According to those same Chronicles, which Eusebius himself composed, as it seemed to him, from both versions, the years are reckoned as 5,228.

John the Baptist was imprisoned by Herod and beheaded for the sake of truth.

In the eighteenth year of Tiberius’s reign, the Lord redeemed the world by his passion. The apostles, preaching throughout the regions of Judaea, appointed James, the brother of the Lord, bishop at Jerusalem. They also appointed seven deacons. When one of them, Stephen, was stoned by the Jews, the Church was scattered throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria.

The governor appointed over the province of Palestine reported to the emperor Tiberius and to the Senate concerning Christ’s passion and resurrection, the miracles that had openly been performed through him or were being performed by his disciples in his name, and the fact that, as the faith of many was rapidly increasing, God was being believed in.

With the support of great favor, Tiberius brought before the Senate a proposal that Christ should be regarded as God. The Senate, angered that the matter had not first been brought before it according to custom so that it might decide whether this worship should be accepted, refused to consecrate Christ. By an edict it decreed that the Christians should be driven from the City, especially since Sejanus, Tiberius’s prefect, stubbornly opposed the adoption of this religion.

Nevertheless, Tiberius threatened the accusers of Christians with death by edict. Thus that highly praised restraint of Caesar Tiberius was gradually altered, as punishment for the Senate’s opposition. For he proscribed very many senators and forced them to their deaths.

He had selected twenty patrician men as his council; scarcely two of them did he leave unharmed, while he killed the others on various pretexts. He killed his prefect Sejanus, who was plotting revolution. He destroyed his own sons Drusus and Germanicus, Drusus being his natural son and Germanicus his adopted son, with clear signs of poison; and he killed the sons of Germanicus, his own son.

Agrippa, surnamed Herod, son of Aristobulus, son of King Herod, and accuser of Herod the tetrarch, went to Rome. He was thrown into chains by Tiberius, and there he first cultivated friendships, especially with Gaius, the son of Germanicus.

[40] Gaius, surnamed Caligula, reigned three years, ten months, and eight days. He was the most depraved man of all who had preceded him and seemed truly worthy to have been appointed as a punishment for blasphemous Romans and persecuting Jews.

He is said to have exclaimed: “Would that the Roman people had a single neck!”

After a revolt had arisen at Alexandria, the Jews were defeated, expelled from their settlement, and driven out of the city. To present their complaints, they sent to Caesar as an envoy a certain Philo, a man especially learned. But Caligula, exceedingly hostile to the Jews, rejected Philo’s embassy and ordered all the sacred buildings of the Jews, including the ancient sanctuary at Jerusalem, to be profaned with sacrifices to the Gentiles and filled with statues and images. After a statue of Jupiter had been set up, he ordered himself to be worshiped there as a god.

He freed his friend Herod Agrippa from imprisonment and made him king of Judaea. Agrippa remained in the kingdom for seven years, that is, until the fourth year of Claudius. After he was struck down by an angel, his son Agrippa succeeded him in the kingdom and continued until the extermination of the Jews, for twenty-four years.

Herod the tetrarch, himself seeking the friendship of Gaius, came to Rome at the urging of Herodias. But after being accused by Agrippa, he also lost his tetrarchy. Exiled after Gaius’s death, he fled from Vienna, a city of Gaul, to Spain with Herodias and died of grief.

Pilate, who had pronounced the sentence of condemnation against Christ, was himself confined at Vienna in perpetual exile. There, afflicted by such great sufferings inflicted by Gaius, he sought a shortened end to his miseries by piercing himself with his own hand.

Matthew, preaching the Gospel in Judaea, wrote it in Hebrew letters.

Gaius Caligula was killed by his own guards. Two little books were found among his private papers. On one was drawn a dagger and on the other a sword as a sign of its title; they contained the names and marks of the most distinguished men destined for death. An immense chest of various poisons was also found there. By order of Caesar Claudius, these were soon sunk into the sea, and the waters were infected, not without great destruction of fish.

[45] Claudius reigned fourteen years.

At the beginning of his reign, Peter came to Rome to overcome Simon the Great, after first founding the Church at Antioch. He taught the saving faith to all believers with faithful speech and confirmed it with most powerful miracles. There he held the episcopal chair for twenty-five years, that is, until the final year of Nero.

Mark the Evangelist first preached at Aquileia the Gospel that he had written at Rome at Peter’s direction. After appointing his disciple Hermagoras there, he reached Egypt. Having established and strengthened Churches throughout Libya, Marmarica, Ammoniaca, Pentapolis, Alexandria, and all Egypt, he finally completed his martyrdom among the pagans of Alexandria.

Furius Camillus Scribonianus, governor of Dalmatia, plotting civil war, had enticed many very strong legions to change their oath of allegiance. Accordingly, when a day had been set for everyone to gather from all directions to the new emperor, neither could the eagles be arranged nor could the military standards be moved, shifted, or stirred in any way.

Moved by confidence in so great and unfamiliar a miracle, the soldiers turned to repentance, killed Scribonianus after he had been abandoned on the fifth day, and remained faithful to the oath of their former military service. Without doubt, this civil war was divinely suppressed because of the arrival of the apostle Peter and the tender shoots of the Christians.

Tiberius Claudius went to Britain, which seemed to have been stirred into revolt and which no one had dared to approach either before Julius Caesar or after him. Without any battle or bloodshed, within only a few days he received a very large part of the island into surrender. He also added the Orkney Islands to the Roman Empire and returned to Rome in the sixth month after his departure.

In that year, namely the fourth of his reign, a very severe famine occurred throughout Syria, which Luke also mentions. But Helena, queen of the Agabeni, converted to faith in Christ, provided most generously for the needs of the Christians by transporting grain from Egypt to Jerusalem.

In the fifth year of his reign, between Thera and Therasia, an island emerged from the depths, extending for a distance of thirty stadia.

In the seventh year of his reign, under the procurator of Judaea, Cumanus, such a great riot arose in Jerusalem during the days of Unleavened Bread that, when the people were compressed at the exits of the gates, 30,000 Jews are reported to have been struck down by slaughter and suffocation.

In the ninth year of his reign, Claudius expelled the Jews who were causing disturbances from Rome. Suetonius reports the matter in these words: “Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because, instigated by Christ, they were constantly causing disturbances.” Luke also records this expulsion in the Acts of the Apostles.

Nevertheless, in the following year there was such a great famine at Rome that, when the emperor was seized by the people in the middle of the Forum and disgracefully assailed with insults and fragments of bread, he barely escaped through the Pseudotyrum to the palace.

Claudius died from unmistakable poisons.

[59] Nero, thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days; in all vices and crimes he followed, indeed surpassed, his uncle Gaius Caligula.

After all his attempted crimes, he was the first to inflict punishments and deaths upon the Christians at Rome and ordered them to be tortured throughout all the provinces with a similar persecution.

In his second year, Festus succeeded Felix as procurator of Judaea. From there Paul was sent to Rome in chains. After remaining for two years in free custody, he was afterward released for preaching, before Nero erupted into the degree of persecution against the Christians that histories report of him.

At that time Paul is believed to have reached Spain, and to have left his disciples Trophimus at Arles and Crescens at Vienna to preach.

James, the brother of the Lord, after having governed the Church of Jerusalem for thirty years, was killed by the Jews in Nero’s seventh year, who took vengeance on him for what they had been unable to do to Paul.

Festus was succeeded in the administration by Albinus, and Albinus by Florus. Unable to bear his extravagance, greed, and other crimes, the Jews rebelled against the Romans. Against them Vespasian was sent as commander of the army and captured many cities of Judaea, having his elder son Titus among his commanders.

Nero dared nothing at all in military matters and nearly lost Britain. Attempting to eradicate even the name of Christianity, he killed the blessed apostles of Christ: Peter by crucifixion and Paul by the sword.

Soon, disasters arising from every direction overwhelmed his miserable life in heaps. At this time the poet Persius arose. Lucan and Seneca were also killed at Nero’s command.

When Nero learned that Galba had been proclaimed emperor by the army in Spain, he collapsed entirely in spirit and hope. Later, while he was contriving unbelievable evils against the collapsing Republic, he was declared an enemy by the Senate. Fleeing in the most disgraceful manner to the fourth milestone from the City, he killed himself; and with him the entire family of the Caesars was extinguished.

After Nero’s death, Galba came to Rome and adopted into his family and for the kingdom Piso, a noble and energetic young man. In the seventh month of his reign he was killed by Otho.

As soon as Otho learned that Vitellius had been created emperor in Gaul by the Germanic legions, he began a civil war. He first engaged the Vitellian commanders in three minor battles—one near the Alps, another around Placentia, and a third near a place called the Castores—and emerged victorious.

But in the fourth battle, at Vetriacum, realizing that his men were being defeated, in the third month after he had become emperor he killed himself.

Vitellius entered Rome as victor. There, after acting cruelly and wickedly in many matters, when he learned about Vespasian, he first attempted to lay down the imperial power. Later, encouraged by certain men, he killed Sabinus, Vespasian’s brother, and set fire to the Temple. With fire and ruin mingled together, he gave them all equally to a single destruction and tomb.
