After his army began to fail in favor of Vespasian, Vitellius, already abandoned and frightened, hid himself in a small room near the palace. Dragged out most disgracefully, he was led into the Forum. In the eighth month after he had seized the kingdom, he was tortured at the Gemonian Steps by repeated stabbings with the smallest blows and then, in a single pull, thrown into the Tiber; thus he was denied even ordinary burial.

Vespasian, therefore, after capturing many Jewish towns and especially besieging the Jews gathered in Jerusalem for the festival, learned of Nero’s death. At the urging of many kings and commanders, he obtained the imperial power. Leaving his son Titus in the camp to direct the siege of Jerusalem, and having also learned of Vitellius’s death, he paused for a short time at Alexandria.

Titus, however, pressing the Jews with a great and prolonged siege and employing engines and every kind of military device, not without much bloodshed among his own men, at last broke through the city walls.

But to storm the inner fortification of the Temple, which the gathered multitude of priests and leaders defended, required greater force and delay. Therefore Titus, proclaimed emperor by the army, burned and destroyed the Temple at Jerusalem. From the day of its first foundation until the day of its final overthrow, it had stood for 1,089 years—or, as many reckon, 1,102.

He leveled all the walls of the city to the ground. Cornelius and Suetonius report that 600,000 Jews were killed in that war. Josephus the Jew, who commanded there in that war and had earned pardon and favor from Vespasian on account of the imperial power foretold above, writes that 1,100,000 perished by the sword and famine; besides these, 100,000 were publicly sold and scattered throughout the whole world.

The war was brought to an end in four years: two while Nero was still alive, and two afterward. Vespasian, among other great deeds while still a private citizen, was sent by Claudius to Germany and then to Britain, and fought the enemy thirty-two times. He added two very powerful peoples, twenty towns, and the Isle of Wight, lying near Britain, to the Roman Empire. The Colossus was erected at Rome, measuring 109 feet in height. Vespasian died at his own villa near the Sabines, in the ninth year of his reign, from a flux of the bowels.

[82] Titus: eleven years and eleven months. A man admirable in every kind of virtue, so much so that he was called “the love and delight of the human race.” He built an amphitheater at Rome, and at its dedication killed five thousand wild beasts. He was so eloquent that he pleaded cases in Latin verse and composed tragedies in Greek. He was also so warlike that, while serving under his father in the assault on Jerusalem, he pierced forty-one defenders with twelve arrow-strikes. In his rule he was of such great goodness that he punished no one at all, but released those convicted of conspiring against him and retained them in the same intimacy in which he had previously held them. Among all his sayings, this one was especially famous: “I have lost a day,” whenever he had done nothing good. Amid the immense mourning of all, he was carried off by illness in the same villa in which his father had died.

[84] Domitian, the younger brother of Titus: fifteen years and five months. He fell into such great arrogance that he ordered himself to be called, written of, and worshiped as a god and lord. He was the second after Nero to persecute the Christians. By issuing edicts of the most savage persecution, he attempted to overthrow the Church of Christ, which had been firmly established throughout the world. Under him the apostle John was banished to the island of Patmos, and Flavia Domitilla, the niece of the consul Flavius Clemens through his sister, was exiled to the island of Pontia on account of her testimony to the faith. It is also said that Domitian himself had the blessed John placed in a cauldron of boiling oil. From it he emerged as unharmed by punishment as he had always remained untouched by corruption of the flesh. Domitian also ordered the Jews to be killed with every severity of torture, together with the family of David, as though someone destined to acquire the kingdom were still to arise from that seed. He was cruelly killed in the palace by his own attendants. His corpse was carried out in a common bier by undertakers and buried dishonorably.

[99] Nerva, already very old, was made emperor by the prefect Petronius and the eunuch Parthenius, Domitian’s assassin. He ruled for one year, four months, and eight days, and adopted Trajan as his successor. In his first edict he recalled all the exiles whom Domitian had banished. Consequently the apostle John, freed by this general act of clemency, returned to Ephesus. Because he saw that, in his absence, the faith of the Church had been shaken by heretics, he immediately strengthened it by setting down in his Gospel the eternity of the Word of God. After completing somewhat more than a year of his reign, Nerva died from illness.

[101] Trajan, a Spaniard by origin, received the reins of government when Nerva handed them over to him. He ruled for nineteen years, six months, and fifteen days. At Agrippina, a city of Gaul, he received the insignia of imperial power. Soon afterward he restored Germany beyond the Rhine to its former condition. Beyond the Danube he subdued many peoples; he made the regions lying beyond the Euphrates and Tigris into provinces; he occupied Seleucia, Ctesiphon, and Babylon; and, following Alexander, he advanced as far as the borders of India. In his fourth year, Clement, a disciple of the apostle Peter and bishop of the Roman Church, was crowned with martyrdom, and Flavia Domitilla, together with many others, was deported into exile on the island of Pontia for Christ’s sake. The apostle John, in the sixty-eighth year after Christ’s Passion and in the ninety-eighth year of his own life, peacefully rested at Ephesus. When Trajan initiated a persecution against the Christians, Simeon, also called Simon, son of Clopas and bishop of Jerusalem, was crucified; and Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was brought to Rome and handed over to the beasts. Alexander also, bishop of the Roman Church, was crowned with martyrdom and buried seven miles from the City on the Nomentan Way, where he had been beheaded. Under the same emperor, the most venerable old man Zacharias, bishop of the Church of Vienne, was also crowned with martyrdom.

For Crescens, the first disciple of the apostle, had remained at Vienne for several years. When he had returned to Galatia, Martin, the third bishop and a disciple of the apostles, remained at Vienne. Later, however, prompted by the report of Pliny the Younger, an orator and historian who was said to have been a persecutor among the other judges, Trajan learned that these people did nothing contrary to Roman laws apart from confessing Christ and holding respectable assemblies. Since no one seemed to regard death as grievous or frightening when supported by the confidence of an innocent confession, he immediately softened his edict by milder rescripts.

The Golden House at Rome, founded by Nero, was suddenly consumed in a conflagration. The Pantheon at Rome, which Domitian had built, was burned by lightning. An earthquake almost completely destroyed the city of Antioch, and also other cities in different parts of the world—an incredible thing to relate. At the same time, the Jews, driven almost to madness, broke out in various parts of the earth and waged the most savage wars, until they were laid low in a fitting slaughter by order of the emperor. Trajan, as some report, died from a flux of the bowels at Seleucia, a city of Isauria. Verus, bishop of Vienne, one of the disciples and hearers of the apostles, flourished in doctrine and confession of the faith during Trajan’s reign. At that time, in the city of Sinope in Pontus, the bishop Phocas gloriously endured martyrdom. His most holy relics were transferred to Gaul, to the city of Vienne, and were placed there in the church of the holy apostles.

[120] Hadrian, the son of Trajan’s cousin, ruled for twenty-one years. Instructed and educated through Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles; Aristides of Athens, a man full of faith and wisdom; and Serenus Granius, the legate, who supplied him with books composed on the Christian religion, he ordered, in a letter sent to Minicius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, that no one should be permitted to condemn Christians without an accusation or proof of a crime. Hadrian ordered the state according to the most just laws. He was also called “Father of his Country” in the senate, beyond the custom of his ancestors, and his wife was called Augusta. Being highly educated in both languages, he built at Athens a library of remarkable workmanship.

He finally subdued the rebellious Jews, who were devastating the province of Palestine, once their own, and took revenge for the Christians whom they had tortured under their leader Bar Kokhba because they would not join them against the Romans. He ordered that no Jew should have permission to enter Jerusalem, while the city was permitted only to Christians. He himself restored it to excellent condition by rebuilding its walls and ordered that it be called Aelia, from his own praenomen. Marcus was appointed the first bishop of Jerusalem from the Gentiles, after the fifteen bishops who had been Jews ceased to hold office; they had presided from the Lord’s Passion for almost 107 years.

At the same time, Aquila, the second interpreter from Pontus after the Septuagint, arose, and Basilides was recognized as a heresiarch. At this same time, Justus, bishop of the Church of Vienne, also distinguished himself greatly in his confession of the faith. Quadratus, whom we mentioned above, was appointed in the place of Publius, bishop of Athens and a disciple of the apostles, who had been crowned with martyrdom for Christ. By his faith and diligence Quadratus gathered together the Church, which had been scattered by great terror.

[141] Antoninus, surnamed Pius, was made emperor and governed the state with his sons Aurelius and Lucius for twenty years and almost three full years, together with three months. During his reign, by burning the bonds, he released the debts of everyone throughout the Roman Empire. He lived so peacefully that he was deservedly called Pius and Father of his Country. Justin the philosopher presented Antoninus with a book composed on the Christian religion and made him kindly disposed toward Christians. Not long afterward, when persecution had been stirred up through the denunciation of Crescens the Cynic, Justin shed his blood for Christ.

Valentinian and Marcion were exposed as heresiarchs, and Galen, the physician born at Pergamum, was famous at Rome. Pius was bishop of Rome. Under him Hermes wrote the book called *The Shepherd*, which contains an angel’s command that Easter should always be celebrated on Sunday. Polycarp, a hearer of the blessed John, came to Rome and corrected many who had recently been corrupted by the teaching of Valentinus and Cerdo. Justus was still renowned as bishop of Vienne, and Photinus as bishop of Lyons. Antoninus died of illness at the twelfth milestone from the City. Anicetus was bishop of Rome.

[161] Marcus Antoninus Verus held the empire for nineteen years and one month together with his brother Lucius Aurelius Commodus Antoninus. These were the first to protect the state under equal authority, since up to that time there had always been individual Augusti. They then waged war against the Parthians with remarkable courage and success. During the Parthian war, the fourth persecution of Christians after Nero’s arose severely in Asia and Gaul. Polycarp and Pionius suffered martyrdom in Asia, and in Gaul also many shed their blood gloriously for Christ. Justus, bishop of Vienne, worn down by a long exile, became a glorious martyr. At that time the venerable old man Photinus, after an interval, completed his martyrdom together with forty-eight people from Lyons and Vienne.

Not long afterward, as an avenger of crimes, a plague devastated many provinces far and wide, especially Italy and Rome. Severinus, Exuperius, and Felicianus had shortly before been crowned with martyrdom at Vienne. While Commodus was sitting in a vehicle with his brother, he was suffocated and died from an attack of illness that the Greeks call *apoplexia*, “apoplexy.” After his death, Marcus Antoninus ruled the state alone for a short time and then took his son Commodus into the government.

Under the emperor Antoninus, Melito of Asia, bishop of Sardis, presented an apology on behalf of the Christians. Lucius, king of the Britons, sent a letter to Eleutherus, bishop of Rome, asking to become a Christian. Apollinaris Appianus of Hieropolis and Dionysius of Corinth were renowned bishops. Montanus of Ardabau and Tatian also flourished; from Tatian the heresiarchs called Encratites arose.

Antoninus forgave the tribute owed throughout all the provinces from earlier times. He ordered all the deceitful records accumulated in fiscal affairs to be burned together in the Forum, and he moderated the harsher laws by new constitutions. After the Marcomannic War, in which barbarian peoples—the Vandals, Sarmatians, and almost all Germany—had surrounded the Roman army, certain soldiers, at the invocation of the name of Christ, suddenly poured themselves out in prayer with great steadfastness of faith. They obtained such a great force of rain that it most abundantly refreshed the Romans without harming them, while the barbarians, terrified by repeated strikes of lightning, were forced to flee. The emperor Antoninus himself acknowledges in his letters that, through the invocation of the Christian name by Christian soldiers, the thirst caused by the lack of water in the Roman camp was driven away and victory was granted to him.

Antoninus, stationed in Pannonia, died suddenly of illness. Theophilus flourished as the sixth bishop of the Church of Antioch, and Pinitus as bishop of the Cretan city of Gnosus. Tatian, the heresiarch of the Encratites, flourished in the Church for as long as he remained at the side of the martyr Justin. Severianus increased his error, and from him came the Severians.

[181] Lucius Antoninus Commodus ruled for thirteen years after his father’s death. He successfully waged war against the Germans. In every other respect, however, he was corrupted by the disgrace of luxury and obscenity. He very often fought with gladiatorial weapons in the arena and frequently exposed himself to wild beasts in the amphitheater. He also killed many senators, especially those whom he noticed to excel in nobility and ability.

The Capitol of the city was struck by lightning. The resulting fire consumed the library assembled through the care and diligence of the ancestors, as well as other buildings standing nearby, in a destructive whirlwind of flame. Irenaeus was bishop of Lyons. Dionysius also, a hearer of the disciples of Christ, governed the Church of Vienne at that time. Theodotion of Ephesus, the third interpreter, appeared. The emperor Commodus ordered the head of the Colossus to be removed and the head of his own image to be placed upon it. Since he was thus an affliction to everyone, he is said to have been strangled in the Vestalian house and to have died.

[194] Aelius Pertinax, already an old man, was made emperor by the senate and ruled for six months. He was killed in the palace through the crime of Julianus the jurist, in the sixth month after he had begun to reign. Severus later defeated Julianus in the civil war at the Milvian Bridge and killed him.

Victor, the thirteenth bishop of Rome, established through widely circulated letters that Easter should be celebrated on Sunday, as had also been decreed by his predecessor Eleutherus, from the fourteenth day of the first month until the twenty-first. Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, supported these decrees and, together with the other bishops who had sat in the same council, wrote a synodical and very useful letter against those who celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon.

When the senate urged Aelius Pertinax to make his wife Augusta and his daughter Caesar, he refused, saying: “It ought to be enough for me that I myself rule unwillingly.” During the reigns of Aelius, Julianus, and Severus, Dionysius, as we have said, flourished as a most learned bishop of Vienne. Apollonius, a most eloquent man, wrote against Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, and declared that Montanus and his insane prophetesses had died by hanging. Serapion flourished as bishop of Antioch, and Apollonius the senator became a martyr.

[195] Severus Pertinax, an African from Tripolitania, from the town of Lepcis, wished to be called Pertinax after the name of the emperor whom he had avenged by killing. He ruled for seventeen years. Naturally savage and often challenged by many wars, he governed the state with great courage but with extreme difficulty. He defeated and killed Pescennius Niger, who had aspired to tyranny in Egypt and Syria, at Cyzicus. He restrained the rebellious Jews and Samaritans by the sword, and overcame the Parthians, Arabs, and Adiabenians.

In the fifth persecution after Nero, he tortured Christians, and very many saints throughout the provinces were crowned with martyrdom. Among them were Leonides, the father of Origen, and Clement of the Church of Alexandria. At that time Irenaeus of Lyons also completed his martyrdom with a very great multitude. Paracodes, bishop of Vienne, distinguished in the teaching of the faith and steadfast in his confession, remained in the episcopate until the time of Maximinus. In his time Zacharias flourished as bishop of Lyons.

After Claudius Albinus, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul, was killed at Lyons, Severus transferred the war to Britain. After many great and severe battles, he judged that the recovered part of the island should be separated from the remaining untamed peoples by a rampart. He therefore built a great ditch and a very strong wall, fortified above by frequent towers, for a distance of 132,000 paces from sea to sea. There, at the town of Eboracum, he died of illness.

He left two sons, Basilianus and Geta. Geta died as a public enemy; Basilianus, having assumed the surname Antoninus, obtained the kingdom. Perpetua and Felicitas were assigned to the beasts at Carthage in Africa and, for Christ, were crowned on the Nones of March. Symmachus is recognized as the fourth interpreter. Origen was educated through study at Alexandria. Victor governed the Roman Church for thirteen years. Pantaenus, a philosopher of the Stoic school, who had first been sent to India by Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, to teach, instructed the Church of Christ by word of mouth and by example.

[212] Aurelius Antoninus Bassianus, also called Caracalla, obtained the principate and remained in it for not quite seven years. He was harsher than his father Severus and more uncontrolled in lust than all other men; he even took his stepmother Julia as his wife. At Jericho the fifth edition of the divine Scriptures was discovered, though its author is unknown.

When Alexander, bishop of Cappadocia, came to Jerusalem out of a desire to visit the holy places, while Narcissus was still alive, the Lord, through a revelation, instructed him to do this very thing. Alexander was appointed bishop in Narcissus’s place, although Narcissus was extremely old. Tertullian the African, son of the proconsular centurion, was celebrated in the speech of all the Churches. Aurelius Antoninus, preparing to wage war against the Parthians, was surrounded and killed by the enemy between Edessa and Carrhae.

[219] Macrinus, prefect of the praetorian guard, seized the empire together with his son Diadumenian. After completing a year, he was killed in a military revolt at Archelais. Tertullian, whom we mentioned above, was a presbyter. Until middle age he belonged to the Church; afterward, through the envy and insults of the clergy of the Roman Church, he fell into the doctrine of Montanus and composed books against the Church.

[220] Marcus Aurelius Antoninus obtained the empire and held it for four years. He had been a priest of the temple of Heliogabalus and left no memory of himself except one infamous for sexual crimes, disgrace, and every kind of obscenity. When a military revolt arose, he was killed at Rome together with his mother.

In Palestine the city of Nicopolis was founded, formerly called Emmaus. This is the Emmaus that the Lord deigned to sanctify by entering it after his resurrection, while the historian Julius Africanus undertook the task of advocating its claim. The sixth edition was discovered at Nicopolis. Sabellius arose as a heresiarch. The bishop Hippolytus, author of many short works, composed a canon of the eras and brought it down to this point.

[224] Aurelius Alexander, made emperor by the will of the senate and the army, governed for thirteen years, deserving praise for his equity. His mother, Mammaea, arranged to hear the presbyter Origen and received him with the highest honor after summoning him from Antioch. After undertaking an expedition against Persia, Alexander defeated and crushed Xerxes, their king. But he was killed in a military revolt at Mainz.

Urbanus, bishop of Rome, led many nobles to faith in Christ and to martyrdom. At that time the virgin Cecilia, Valerianus, Tiburtius, and Maximus completed their martyrdom.

[234] Maximinus, without the will of the senate, was made emperor by the army after successfully waging war in Germany. He held power for three years. He persecuted the priests and clergy of the Churches, especially because of the Christian household of Alexander, whom he had succeeded, and of his mother Mammaea. Pupienus killed him at Aquileia. Pontianus and Anteros, bishops of the city of Rome, were crowned with martyrdom and buried in the cemetery of Callistus.

[241] Gordian was made emperor and remained in power for seven years. Pupienus, the slayer of Maximinus, and his brother Albinus, who had usurped the empire, were soon killed in the palace. Julius Africanus was renowned among ecclesiastical writers. In his *Chronicles* he reports that he came to Alexandria, summoned by the exceedingly famous reputation of Heraclas, whom popular report described as highly instructed in both divine and philosophical studies and in every branch of Greek learning.

At Caesarea in Palestine, Origen instructed Theodorus, surnamed Gregory, and Athenodorus, adolescent brothers who later became highly distinguished bishops of Pontus, in divine philosophy. Fabianus was ordained bishop of Rome when, according to the testimony of the Holy Spirit, a dove descended upon his head, although some maintain that this happened more truly to Zephyrinus. Florentinus, bishop of Vienne, also distinguished himself in life and teaching. He remained until the reigns of Gallienus and Volusianus and, after being exiled, completed his martyrdom. Gordian, still a very young man, set out for the East for the Parthian war and was killed through the treachery of his own men not far from Circesium, above the Euphrates.

[248] Philippus, making his son Philippus his associate in the kingdom, remained in power for seven years. He was the first of all the emperors to be a Christian. After the third year of his reign, the thousandth year from the founding of Rome was completed. Accordingly, this anniversary was celebrated by a Christian emperor with magnificent games, more splendid than all those of the past.

Origen replied in eight books to a certain Epicurean philosopher named Celsus, who had written books against us. To put the matter briefly, he was so diligent in writing that Jerome recalls in one passage having read five thousand of his books. Philippus the father and Philippus the son, although in different places, were both killed in a military revolt through the treachery of Decius.

[254] Decius, instigator of civil war: one year and three months. After he had killed Philippus the father and son, he issued deadly edicts for the persecution and killing of Christians out of hatred for the two Philips. He also appointed his own son Caesar, and the two were immediately killed together in the midst of the barbarians.

During the persecution of Decius, Fabianus was crowned with martyrdom in the city of Rome and left the seat of his bishopric to Cornelius. After Cornelius too had been crowned with martyrdom, Lucius held the pontificate. Stephen succeeded him; when Stephen passed through martyrdom, Xystus took his place and likewise received the palm of martyrdom through his confession of the faith. Cyprian, the most illustrious light among teachers, was renowned as bishop of Carthage. At that time the archdeacon Laurentius and many others also adorned the glory of martyrdom.

[255] Gallus Hostilianus held the kingdom for two years and four months together with his son Volusianus. During his reign a great plague spread through almost all the provinces of the Roman Empire, doubtless as vengeance for the violated name of Christ. Novatian, a presbyter of Cyprian the bishop, came to Rome and founded a new heresy.

Origen died before fully completing his seventieth year and was buried in the city of Tyre. Cornelius, bishop of Rome, at the request of a certain matron named Lucina, secretly removed the bodies of the holy apostles from the Catacombs and placed them: Paul’s on the Ostian Way, where he had been beheaded; Peter’s not far from the place where he had been crucified, among the bodies of holy bishops, in a temple once belonging to Apollo, on the Golden Mount, in Nero’s Vatican palace.

Gallus and Volusianus were killed while preparing a civil war against Aemilianus, who was attempting a revolution. Aemilianus himself, however, was killed in the third month after seizing the tyranny. Ammonius, learned in philosophy and the author of the Gospel canons, was renowned at Alexandria.

[257] Valerian together with his faithful colleague Gallienus: fifteen years. Valerian was proclaimed Augustus by the army in Greece, while at Rome Gallienus was made Caesar by the senate. When Valerian began a persecution against the Christians, he was immediately captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, and, after being deprived of his sight, grew old in the most shameful servitude among the Persians. As long as he lived, he suffered this continual sentence: stooping toward the ground himself, he had always to raise the king, mounting his horse, not with his own hand but upon his back.

Gallienus, terrified by so clear a judgment of God and seemingly moved by the example of his wretched colleague, restored peace to the Churches with a fearful act of submission. In this stormy period Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, was crowned with martyrdom. Pontius, his deacon, left an outstanding book about his life and passion; he had endured exile together with him until the day of his passion.

The Germans, having penetrated the Alps, all of Raetia, and Italy, reached Ravenna. The Alamanni, roaming through Gaul, also crossed into Italy. Greece, Macedonia, Pontus, and Asia were destroyed by the inundation of the Goths. Publius Ingenuus, who had assumed the imperial purple, was killed at Mursa.

Postumus seized the tyranny in Gaul and, after exercising great courage and moderation for ten years, drove out the ruling enemies. He was nevertheless killed in a military mutiny. Victorinus, spontaneously chosen emperor by the Gauls, was killed shortly afterward at Vienne. Theodorus, surnamed Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, was renowned for his many virtues. One of these was that, to provide sufficient space for a church to be built, he moved a mountain by his prayers.

At that time Lupicinus flourished as a distinguished bishop of the Church of Vienne. After Gallienus had abandoned the state and devoted himself to pleasures at Milan, he was killed. When Cornelius, who had governed the Roman Church for two years, was crowned with martyrdom for Christ, Lucius succeeded him. The blessed Cyprian suffered in the eighth persecution on the same day, but not in the same year, as Cornelius at Rome.

[272] Claudius, having received the empire by the will of the senate: two years. He attacked the Goths, who for fifteen years had been devastating Illyricum and Macedonia, and destroyed them in an incredible slaughter. The senate decreed for him a golden shield in the senate-house and an equally golden statue in the Capitol. Soon afterward, however, he was seized by illness at Sirmium and died.

[273] Soon his brother Quintilius, a man of good moderation, was chosen emperor by the army but was killed on the seventeenth day of his reign. Malchion, the most eloquent presbyter of the Church of Antioch, who had taught rhetoric in that city, disputed against Paul of Samosata, who was teaching as bishop of Antioch that Christ had been merely a man of common nature. Notaries recorded the disputation.

[274] Aurelian obtained the empire and held it for five years and six months. A man outstanding in military ability, he undertook an expedition to the Danube and routed the Goths in great battles.

He surrounded the city of Rome with stronger walls. Finally, when he decided that persecution should be undertaken against the Christians, a thunderbolt fell before him, greatly terrifying those standing nearby, and not long afterward he was killed while traveling. Eutychianus, bishop of Rome, was crowned with martyrdom and buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He himself had also buried 313 martyrs with his own hands.

Tacitus ruled for six months. After he was killed in Pontus, Florianus held the empire for eighty-nine days. He too was killed at Tarsus. Anatolius, an Alexandrian by birth and bishop of Laodicea in Syria, was an educated disciple of the philosophers and was widely celebrated for his learning. The greatness of his intellect can be most clearly recognized from the book he composed on Easter and from his ten books of *Arithmetic*. At that time the madness of the Manichaean heresy arose. At the same time Simplides, bishop of Vienne, flourished in remarkable holiness. He continued until the time of the emperor Carus.

[279] Probus, emperor: six years and four months. He finally freed Gaul, which had long been occupied by barbarians, after many difficult battles and the destruction of the enemies. He then fought two civil wars, both with much bloodshed. In the first, in the East, he subdued, crushed, and captured the tyrant Saturninus. In the second, he defeated Proculus and Bonosus in great battles and killed them at Agrippina. Probus himself was killed at Sirmium in a military revolt in an iron-clad tower.

In the second year of his reign, as we read in the *Chronicles* of Eusebius, the year-count was, according to the Antiochenes, 326; according to the Tyrians, 403; according to the Lacedaemonians, 324; according to the Edessenes, 588; according to the people of Ascalon, 380; and according to the Hebrews, the beginning of the eighty-seventh jubilee, which contains 4,250 years.

Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia, composed in the Syriac language a book of the disputation he had held against the Manichaean who had come from Persia. Translated from Syriac, it is held by many in Greek.

Carus, together with his son Carinus and Numerianus: three years. After Carus had captured the two most distinguished Parthian cities, Caelen and Ctesiphon, and triumphed over the Persians in the Parthian war, he was struck by lightning in the camp above the Tigris and died.

[285] Caius was a distinguished bishop of the Roman Church; afterward he suffered martyrdom under Diocletian. Phierius, a presbyter of Alexandria, taught the people with great distinction under the bishop Theonas and composed books of sermons and various treatises. He achieved such elegance of composition that he was called a lesser Origen. A man of remarkable frugality and voluntary poverty, he spent the whole period of his life after the persecution at Rome.

Numerianus, who had taken part with his father Carus in the Parthian war, was killed on the return journey through the treachery of his father-in-law Aper.

[288] Diocletian, chosen emperor by the army in the 1041st year from the founding of the City, ruled for thirty years. As soon as he had acquired full power, he killed with his own hand Aper, the murderer of Numerianus.

He then defeated Carinus, whom Carus had left as Caesar in Dalmatia, in a very difficult war and with the greatest exertion. After Anolus and Helianus had raised dangerous disturbances in Gaul with a gathered band of peasants whom they called Bagaudae, he made Maximian, surnamed Herculius, Caesar and sent him to Gaul. Maximian easily organized the confused band of country people through military skill.

Thus, throughout every boundary of the Roman Empire, the crash of sudden disturbances resounded: Carausius was in revolt in Britain. He had originally been placed there to watch the shores of the Ocean, which the Franks and Saxons were then harassing. Since he was acting more to the destruction than to the advantage of the state, Maximian ordered him killed, whereupon he seized the imperial purple. Achilleus was in revolt in Egypt, while the Quinquegentians were also ravaging Africa; and Narseus, king of the Persians, was pressing the East with war.

Moved by this danger, Diocletian elevated Maximian Herculius from Caesar to Augustus, and appointed Constantius, Maximinus, and Maximian Valerius as Caesars. Constantius took Theodora, the stepdaughter of Herculius Maximian, as his wife, and by her fathered six sons, the brothers of Constantine.

After Carausius had vigorously secured Britain for himself for six years, he was finally killed through the treachery of his associate Allectus. Allectus then held the island for three years, until Asclepiodotus, prefect of the praetorium, overthrew him and recovered Britain after ten years.

Constantius Caesar, in Gaul, was almost himself captured when his army was routed by the Alamanni in the first battle. In the second, however, a sufficiently favorable victory followed, so that 40,000 Alamanni were killed within a few hours. Maximian Augustus, meanwhile, subdued the Quinquegentians in Africa. Diocletian besieged Achilleus for eight months, captured him at Alexandria, and killed him.

Moreover, Valerius Maximianus, after fighting Narseus in two battles, engaged him for a third time between Gallinicum and Carrhae and was defeated. Having lost his forces, he fled to Diocletian, who received him with extreme arrogance, so that he had to walk in purple before Diocletian’s chariot for several miles.

This Diocletian was the first to order gems to be inserted into clothing and footwear, whereas earlier emperors had used only purple. In the eighteenth year of Diocletian, he himself in the East and Maximian Herculius in the West ordered the Churches to be devastated and Christians to be afflicted and killed, while the divine books were burned.

At this time the martyrdom of the Theban saints, Maurice and his companions, numbering 6,666, was completed. There was also the passion of Victor and Ursus at Castrum Solodorum; the passion of the blessed Faith and her companions at the city of Agen, whose relics were later transferred to Conques; and the martyrdom of Gereon and his 328 companions at Cologne in Agrippina.

This persecution burned so cruelly and continuously that within one month 18,000 martyrs were found to have suffered for Christ. Crossing even the boundary of the Ocean, it also condemned Alban, Aaron, and Julius of Britain, together with many other men and women, to a blessed death by bloodshed.

At that time the presbyter Pamphilus also suffered martyrdom. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, set forth his life in three books. In the second year of the persecution, Diocletian laid down the purple at Nicomedia, and Maximian Herculius at Milan. Nevertheless, the persecution once begun did not cease raging until the seventh year of the emperor Constantine.

Constantine, a man of the greatest gentleness and civility, died at Eboracum in Britain in the sixteenth year of his reign. In the third year of the persecution, in which Constantius also died, Maximinus and Severus were made Caesars by Valerius Maximianus. Of these, Maximian added his crimes and sexual outrages to the persecutions of the Christians.

At that time Peter, bishop of Alexandria, suffered martyrdom. He had first condemned the presbyter Arius. Many Egyptian bishops suffered martyrdom with him.

Lucian also suffered martyrdom. He was a man distinguished in character, self-restraint, and learning, and a presbyter of the Church of Antioch. Timothy suffered at Rome on the tenth day before the Kalends of July. At that time Melchiades flourished as pontiff of the Roman Church. At the same time the most eloquent man Paschasius flourished as bishop of the Church of Vienne.

Phileas, a bishop noble by birth from an Egyptian city called Thebaid, composed a most elegant book in praise of the martyrs and was beheaded for Christ. Arnobius taught rhetoric with great distinction in Africa and composed books against the nations, which are commonly available.

[306] Constantine, son of Constantius by his concubine Helena, was proclaimed emperor in Britain and reigned thirty years and ten months, beginning in the fourth year of the persecution. Maxentius, son of Herculius Maximianus, was styled Augustus at Rome. Licinius was proclaimed emperor at Carnuntum, as the brother-in-law of Constantine through Constantine’s sister Constantia. The emperor Constantine, having become a Christian from a persecutor, granted Christians permission to assemble freely and to build churches everywhere in Christ’s honor. Throughout nearly the entire Roman Empire he granted individual cities privileges, so that the Christian people might live freely under the authority and regulation of bishops and might freely establish structures of honor for God’s temples.

In his time the Arian heresy arose, and the Council of Nicaea was assembled from throughout the world for the condemnation of Arius and the confirmation of the integral faith, in the year 322 after the Lord’s incarnation, on the twenty-ninth day of the month called Desius by the Greeks—that is, the tenth day before the Kalends of July—during the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus. At one and the same time that most sacred Council at Arles was also convened, with six hundred bishops, while Martin was bishop of that city; at Vienne, Claudius was the bishop, most distinguished in Catholic doctrine.

At the same time the schism of the Donatists arose in Africa. For Donatus, claiming that the Scriptures had been handed over by our people to the enemies during the persecution, deceived many throughout Africa, and especially in Numidia, by his persuasion. During the same period the Lord’s cross was discovered at Jerusalem by Helena, Constantine’s mother.

Constantine, instructed in the faith by the blessed Pope Sylvester, constructed at Rome a baptistery of marvelous workmanship, where he was baptized beside the basilica of the blessed John the Baptist, which is called Constantinian. He also built a basilica for the blessed Peter in the temple of Apollo, and likewise one for the blessed Paul, surrounding the bodies of both with Cyprian bronze five feet thick. He also built a basilica in the Soranus palace, called Jerusalem, where he deposited a portion of the wood of the Lord’s cross. He built another basilica for the blessed martyr Agnes at the request of his daughter Constantia. He also built a baptistery at the same place, where his sister Constantia and her daughter Augusta were baptized. He built another basilica for the blessed martyr Lawrence on the Tiburtine Way, in the Veranus estate, where that glorious martyr was buried. He also built a basilica on the Lavican Way, between the two laurels, for the blessed martyrs Peter and Marcellinus, together with a mausoleum where he placed his mother in a purple sarcophagus.

He also built a basilica in the city of Ostia, beside the harbor of the city of Rome, for the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and for the blessed John the Baptist. He built another basilica in the Alban city for Saint John the Baptist. In the city of Naples he magnificently adorned another basilica in honor of the apostles and martyrs.

The same emperor restored the city of Deprana in Bithynia in honor of the martyr Lucian, who was buried there, and, taking its name from his mother, called it Helenopolis. Establishing a city bearing his own name in Thrace, he desired it to be the seat of the Roman Empire and the capital of the whole East. He entrusted Rome, the head of the whole Empire, by testament to the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, settling in the second or new Rome, Constantinople, the more distinguished Romans, including consular men and nearly the entire senatorial order with their wives and children.

He himself decreed that, without any killing of people, the temples of the pagans should be closed and the altars of the gods broken. Rheticius, bishop of Autun, was held in the highest renown. So too was Juvencus, a Spanish presbyter who composed four books of the Gospel in hexameter verse. Firmianus, also called Lactantius and a disciple of Arnobius, taught rhetoric at Nicomedia; because of the scarcity of students—since it was a Greek city—he withdrew, judging that he should be assigned elsewhere. In extreme old age he was tutor in Gaul to Crispus, Caesar and son of Constantine, who was later killed by his father.

Jacob, bishop of Nisibis, one of the confessors under the persecution of Maximinus and among those who at the Nicene synod condemned the Arian perversity by opposing it with the term *homoousios*, and the author of many short works, died.

[337] Constantius, together with his brothers Constantine and Constans, reigned eighteen years, five months, and fourteen days. Jacob, bishop of Nisibis, was recognized; at his prayers the city was often delivered from danger. With the support of the emperor Constantius, Arian impiety persecuted first Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and then all bishops who did not belong to its party, through exiles, prisons, and various forms of affliction.

Maximinus, bishop of Trier, was held in renown. When Athanasius was being sought by Constantius for punishment, Maximinus received him honorably. At that time Nectarius, bishop of Vienne, also flourished, an exceptional teacher of the faith. He was the first to participate in that venerable synod at Vaison, and publicly preached and taught in the Church that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one nature, power, divinity, and virtue.

Antony the monk died in the desert in the 105th year of his life. The relics of the apostle Timothy were brought to Constantinople. Relying on the favor of Constantius, the presbyter Arius was on his way to the church at Constantinople, where the aged bishop Alexander then presided, intending to fight against our people concerning the faith. Turning aside beyond the Forum of Constantine to attend to a necessary matter, his entrails suddenly poured out together with his life.

When Constantius entered Rome, the Constantinopolitans received with extraordinary devotion the bones of the blessed apostle Andrew and of Luke the evangelist. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, who had been driven into exile in Phrygia by the Arians, returned to Gaul after presenting a book on his behalf to Constantius at Constantinople.

The heresy of the Anthropomorphites arose in Syria and Macedonia, and also at Constantinople. Donatus, a writer on grammar and teacher of Jerome, was held in renown at Rome. Eusebius of Caesarea in Palestine, most diligent in the divine Scriptures and a most careful investigator of the divine library together with the martyr Pamphilus, died. After first falling into the Arian heresy, he returned, corrected, to Catholic doctrine.

Eustathius, first bishop of Coelesyria and later of Antioch, composed much against Arian doctrine, was driven into exile, and was buried at Trajanopolis, a city of Thrace. Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra, was accused of Sabellian heresy because he wrote against the Arians; the blessed Hilary also mentions him as though he were a heretic in his seventh book against the Arians. But Marcellus defended himself, saying that he did not share the doctrine of which he was accused, as attested by Julius and Athanasius, bishops of Rome and Alexandria. Basil, bishop of Ancyra, was a leader of the Macedonian party together with Eustathius of Sebaste; he was also skilled in the art of medicine.

[361] Julian, two years and eight months. Having become emperor from the clergy, he turned to the worship of idols, inflicted martyrdoms upon Christians, and persecuted them through cunning stratagems and hatred. At that time, among others who suffered for Christ throughout the world, John and Paul underwent a distinguished martyrdom at Rome.

The pagans at Sebaste, a city of Palestine, invaded the tomb of the blessed John the Baptist, scattered his bones, then gathered them up again and burned them, scattering them more widely through the fields. But by God’s providence certain monks from Jerusalem arrived. Joining those who were gathering the bones, they carried whatever they could recover to their father Philip. He immediately sent them to the chief bishop Athanasius through his deacon Julian—for he said that so great a treasure should be preserved by his own vigilance above all else. Athanasius received them and, with only a few witnesses, stored them beneath a hollowed-out wall of the sanctuary, preserving them for the benefit of a future generation. His prediction was fulfilled under the emperor Theodosius through Theophilus, bishop of that same city. After destroying the temple of Serapis, Theophilus consecrated a church there to Saint John.

Out of hatred for Christ, Julian permitted the Jews to rebuild the temple at Jerusalem. When they had gathered from all the provinces and were laying new foundations, an earthquake suddenly arose during the night; stones were torn from the bottom of the foundations and scattered far and wide. A ball of fire also emerged from within the temple building and struck many of them down with its flames. Terrified by this, the survivors confessed Christ against their will. And lest they believe that this had happened by chance, the sign of the cross appeared the following night on the clothing of all of them.

Julian ordered the bones of the venerable Jacob, bishop of Nisibis, to be carried outside the city, envying his miracles. Not long afterward the city was subjected to Persian rule.

When Julian was arranging his army in battle formation against the Persians, he was killed—whether by whom is uncertain—and, throwing his entrails into the air and blaspheming the Lord Christ with a deranged voice, he lost his life and kingdom, crying: “You have conquered, Galilean, you have conquered.” Many throughout the Church immediately learned of his death through revelation.

Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, had been exiled to Palestine by Constantius because he refused to condemn the Nicene faith; he returned from exile, and from him the Luciferian schism later arose. Eusebius, a Sardinian by nation and bishop of Vercelli, was likewise exiled by Constantius for confessing the faith, first to Scythopolis and then to Cappadocia. After returning from exile, he was killed by an Arian faction.

Fornacius, bishop of the Church of Aquileia, was especially detestable because he was the first to pressure Liberius, bishop of Rome, when the latter was going into exile for the faith; he broke him and compelled him to sign the heresy. Acacius the One-Eyed, bishop of Caesarea, became so prominent under Constantius that he consecrated Felix at Rome as bishop in place of Liberius.

[363] Jovian, for one year—or, more accurately, eight months. When he saw that the army was making him emperor, and, declaring himself a Christian, asserted that he could not rule over pagans, the whole army said: “We too, who under Julian abandoned the name of Christ, wish to be Christians with you.” On hearing this, he accepted the scepter of empire.

A synod was held at Antioch by Meletius and his associates, at which the Macedonian doctrine was wrongly confirmed. Warned by the lapse of his predecessor Constantius, Jovian summoned Athanasius by an honorable and most respectful letter. From him he received the rule of faith and the method for organizing the churches; but premature death seized these pious and joyful beginnings.

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers in Aquitaine, was exiled to Phrygia under Constantius by the faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles, because of the synod of Béziers. There he composed twelve books against the Arians and wrote a book on synods to the bishops of Gaul. After returning from exile, he produced other Catholic and highly distinguished works.

Serapion, bishop of Thmuis, a man of elegant intellect and renowned under Constantius for confessing the faith, died.

[364] Valentinian and his brother Valens, twelve years. Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea, composed writings of many kinds concerning our religion. Later, however, unwary and deviating from the faith, he established the heresy named after him. Photinus and Eunomius were also recognized as heretics at that time.

The Goths on the Danube were divided into two factions, between Frigidernus and Ataricus. Frigidernus overcame Ataricus with the aid of Valens; in gratitude for this favor, he and the whole Gothic people were turned from Catholicism to Arianism.

Then their bishop Vulfila devised Gothic letters and translated both Testaments into their own language. Damasus, bishop of Rome, built a basilica beside the atrium of Saint Lawrence and another in the catacombs, where the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul had lain. At that place he adorned the very *platomum*—the pavement or burial platform on which the holy bodies had lain—with verses.

Baptized by Eudoxius, the Arian bishop, Valens persecuted our people. In the third year of Valentinian, his son Gratian was made emperor at Amiens. At Constantinople the martyrs’ shrine of the apostles was dedicated.

After the prolonged death of Auxentius, bishop of Milan, Ambrose was made bishop there, and all Italy was converted to the right faith. Nectarius, bishop of Vienne, and Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, died.

Valens, with Gratian and Valentinian, the sons of his brother Valentinian, reigned four years. When Valens issued a law that monks should serve in the army, those unwilling to do so were ordered to be killed with clubs.

The nation of the Huns, long shut away behind inaccessible mountains, suddenly burst forth in frenzied violence against the Goths and, scattering them in confusion, drove them from their ancient settlements. The Goths, fleeing across the Danube, were received by Valens without laying down their weapons, through the greed of the commander Maximus. Compelled by hunger to revolt, they defeated the army of Valens and, spreading through Thrace, filled everything alike with slaughter, fires, and plunder.

During the time of Valentinian and Valens, the Franks, joined to the Romans between the Danube and the Maeotian marshes, defeated the rebelling Alamanni. The emperor Valentinian was the first to wish the Franks to be called by the Attic word for their ferocity, harshness, and boldness.

A little later, when they refused to pay tribute to the Romans and could not withstand the Roman attack, they departed from Sicambria and reached the farthest regions of the Rhine, among the settlements of the Germans. There they remained for several years with their leaders Marcomer and Sunno. Later they first established Pharamund as their king and submitted themselves to laws discovered by their ancestors Wisovast, Wisogast, Artogast, and Salegast.

Victorinus, an African by birth, taught rhetoric under the emperor Constantine and, in extreme old age, surrendered himself to the faith of Christ. Titus, bishop of Bostra, a vigorous disputant against the Manichaeans, died.

Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, after enduring many plots by the Arians, fled to Constans, ruler of Gaul. He returned from there with letters, but after Constans’s death was again driven into flight and remained concealed until the reign of Jovian. Under Valens, when the Church was restored by Jovian, Athanasius died.

Ephrem, deacon of the Church of Edessa, a man most learned in his own language, that is, Syriac, died. Basil of Caesarea in Cappadocia, formerly Mazaca, under Gratian. Gregory of Nazianzus, also an exceedingly eloquent man and Jerome’s teacher, died when Theodosius was already emperor.

[379] Gratian, with his brother Valentinian, seven years. Theodosius, an energetic man, was made emperor by Gratian. In great and numerous battles he defeated the largest Scythian peoples, namely the Alans, Huns, and Goths. The Arians, unable to endure his zeal for the faith, abandoned after forty years the churches they had held by force.

At that time Nicetas, bishop of Vienne, most distinguished in the doctrine of the faith, governed the Viennese Church. Just, bishop of Lyon, was also a man of remarkable holiness. Later, having abandoned the seat of his bishopric, he hid himself with great humility among the holiest anchorite fathers and died in Egypt. The people of Lyon, devoted to him with pious affection, brought his bones back to their city, together with the bones of his most holy fellow minister Viator.

It is established that this venerable bishop Just was educated under Paschasius, bishop of Vienne, and was deacon to Claudius, bishop of that same city, before being transferred to govern the holy Church of Lyon.

A synod of 150 fathers was convened in the royal city of Constantinople against Macedonius. Under Damasus, bishop of Rome, Ambrose, bishop of the Church of Milan, became renowned in Catholic doctrine.

The emperor Theodosius made his son Arcadius his partner in the Empire. In the second year of the emperor Gratian, when Gratian was consul for the sixth time together with Theodosius, Theophilus wrote a calculation of the date of Easter.

Maximus was an energetic and upright man, worthy of the title Augustus, had he not arisen as a tyrant against the sacraments of the faith. In Britain he was almost against his will proclaimed emperor by the army, crossed into Gaul, and there, after Gratian Augustus had been ensnared by deceit at Lyon, killed him. He drove his brother Valentinian from Italy and first forced him to hide at Vienne, where he paid a most just penalty together with his mother Justina, who had polluted him with the Arian heresy.

He also harassed Ambrose, the bishop and most eminent bulwark of the Catholic faith, with a treacherous siege, nor did he abandon his wicked undertaking until the relics of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius had been brought forth. The blessed bishop had discovered them incorrupt through the Lord’s revelation.

Theodosius kindly received Valentinian, who had been expelled from Italy. The Priscillianist heresy arose. Priscillian himself, accused by Ithacius, was struck down with the sword by the tyrant Maximus.

Martin, bishop of Tours, shone forth as distinguished by miracles. After Pharamund, the Franks established Clodio, his son, as their king. From then onward, the Franks living in the territory of the Thuringians began to have long-haired kings.

At that time the Romans held Gaul. On this side of the Loire, the Goths—and also the Burgundians, infected with Arian doctrine—lived on both sides of the Rhône. Clodio, the first king of the Franks, set out from Dispargum, a fortress of the Thuringians, crossed the Rhine, defeated the Roman population, took possession of the Carbonarian Forest, and reached Cambrai. There he killed the Romans and established his seat.

[385] Theodosius held the East for six years while Gratian was still alive; after Gratian’s death he ruled for eleven years. He and Valentinian, whom he had kindly received after his expulsion from Italy, killed the tyrant Maximus at the third milestone from Aquileia.

Maximus stripped Britain of nearly all its armed youth and military forces. These followed him into Gaul and never returned home. Seeing the island deprived of soldiers and defenders, the savage overseas peoples—the Scots from the northwest and the Picts from the north—arrived, and for many years oppressed it after ravaging and plundering it.

Jerome the presbyter was held in renown throughout the world at Bethlehem. His book, which he wrote on the illustrious men of the Church, extends to the fourteenth year of the entire reign of Theodosius.

At Theodosius’s command, the temples of the nations were overthrown throughout the world, and in their place Christ’s temples shone everywhere. During the same period the distinguished anchorite John flourished. When Theodosius consulted him about the tyrant Eugenius, John foretold victory to him.

Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, possessed an elegant talent for composing verse and died at nearly eighty years of age. Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, was not unlearned in the Scriptures; the Apollinarists are said to have been named after him.

Patianus, bishop of Barcelona in the Pyrenees, died in an excellent old age. He was distinguished both in life and speech by restrained eloquence. Photinus of Gallograecia, a disciple of Marcellus and bishop of Syrini, was expelled from the Church by Valentinian and attempted to restore the heresy of Ebion.

Didymus of Alexandria was blind and, for that reason, also ignorant of the elements. Yet he provided everyone with such a remarkable demonstration of his abilities that he learned even dialectic and geometry—which especially require sight—to perfection.

[396] Arcadius, son of Theodosius, with his brother Honorius, fourteen years. The bodies of the holy prophets Habakkuk and Micah were revealed by divine revelation.

Innocent, bishop of Rome, dedicated a basilica to the most blessed martyrs Protasius and Gervasius, in fulfillment of the devotion expressed in the testament of a most illustrious woman, Vestina.

Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, was held in the highest renown. Among his other miracles, because of an impending disaster he instituted solemn litanies before the Lord’s Ascension.

Martin, bishop of Tours, died. Donatus, bishop of Epirus, was regarded as distinguished for his miracles. He killed a huge dragon by spitting into its mouth; eight yokes of oxen could scarcely drag it to the place where it was burned, lest its corruption pollute the air.

When King Clodio died, after ruling the Franks for twenty years, Meroveus succeeded him. From him the kings of the Franks were called Merovingians. Metz was set ablaze by the Franks and Trier was destroyed; the Franks reached as far as Orléans.

After Meroveus, Childeric obtained the kingdom and reigned twenty-four years. Chlodoveus succeeded him. He was the first Christian king of the Franks, instructed and baptized with his people by the blessed Remigius, bishop of Rheims.

The Goths attacked Italy, and the Vandals and Alans attacked Gaul. Augustine, bishop of Hippo, was held in renown for knowledge and teaching. John of Constantinople and Theophilus of Alexandria were also proclaimed illustrious bishops. Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis, wrote, among other works, books against all heresies.

Eunomius, bishop of Cyzicus and a member of the Arian party, broke out into blasphemy and publicly confessed what the Arians had concealed. Tiberianus of Baetica, a follower of Priscillian, overcome by weariness of exile after the killing of his associates, returned like a dog to his vomit and joined his daughter, a virgin devoted to Christ, in marriage.

[410] Honorius, with Theodosius the Younger, the son of his brother, fifteen years. The emperor Honorius, seeing that nothing could be accomplished against the barbarians while tyrants opposed him, ordered the tyrants themselves to be destroyed first.

The supreme command of this war was entrusted to the count Constantius. He first marched into Gaul with an army, shut up Constantine the emperor in the city of Arles, captured him, and killed him. Constans, the son of Constantine, was killed at Vienne by his own count Gerontius, a man more wicked than upright; Gerontius replaced him with a certain Maximus. Gerontius himself was then killed by his own soldiers.

Maximus, stripped of the purple and abandoned by the Gallic soldiers, lived as a destitute exile among the barbarians in Spain. Jovinus, a most noble man of Gaul, rose into tyranny and soon fell. His brother Sebastian was killed immediately after being proclaimed.

When Alaric had made Attalus emperor, then corrupted him, restored him, and finally deposed him—almost more quickly than these things can be said—he awaited the outcome of the Empire like an actor expecting laughter and entertainment. Attalus was its shadowy consul. Tertullus dared to say in the senate: “I shall speak to you, consul and pontiff, one of whom I already possess and the other I hope for.”

Thus Attalus, like an empty image of empire, was carried with the Goths as far as Spain. From there, while descending from a ship, he was captured at sea and brought to the count Constantius. Then he was presented to the emperor Honorius, who had one of his hands cut off but left him alive.

Heraclianus, count of Africa, swollen with pride, adopted Sabinus, his domestic officer, an energetic and clever man, as his son-in-law. After holding back the African grain supply for some time, he eventually sailed toward Rome with an immense and, one might scarcely believe it, vast fleet. He is said to have had 3,700 ships; history records that neither Xerxes, nor Alexander the Great, nor any other king possessed that number.

But after disembarking on the shore, terrified by the arrival of the count Marinus, he seized a ship and returned alone to Carthage. There he was immediately killed by a military force. His son-in-law Sabinus fled to Constantinople. After some time he was brought back from there and condemned to exile. Thus, with Christ’s help, peace and unity were restored throughout the Catholic Church in Africa.

At Carthage the count Marinus, stimulated either by zeal for his undertaking or corrupted by gold, killed Marcellinus the tribune, a man of exceptional prudence and energy. Marinus was immediately recalled from Africa, reduced to private status, and released either for punishment or for the repentance of his conscience.

Alaric, king of the Goths, invaded Rome and burned part of it on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, in the 1,164th year from its foundation and the sixty-fourth year of Honorius’s reign. Thus, on the third day after entering the plundered city, he departed.

The Goths then attempted to cross into Sicily, but in the sight of their own people they were miserably seized and drowned. Atavulfus succeeded Alaric as king of the Goths and took Placidia, the emperor’s captive sister, as his wife. He was a most devoted seeker of peace and preferred to serve the emperor Honorius faithfully in military matters.

Persuaded and guided by Placidia, his wife—a woman of exceptionally sharp intelligence and sufficiently upright religious character—he was restrained in all good and orderly undertakings. He was reportedly killed through a plot by his own people at Barcelona, a city of Spain.

After him the Goths made Segeric king. Although he too was inclined toward peace by God’s judgment, he was nevertheless killed by his own people. The count Constantius, stationed at Arles and distinguished by his ability to accomplish great things, expelled from Narbonne the Goths whom Atavulfus, Placidia’s husband, then ruled, and forced them to depart into Spain.

Vallia succeeded Segeric in the Gothic kingdom. The Goths appointed him to break the peace; God appointed him to confirm it. He was especially terrified by God’s judgment, because when a great multitude of Goths, equipped with arms and ships, was preparing to cross into Africa, it was caught by a storm twelve miles from the Strait of Cádiz and perished in a pitiable disaster.

Vallia made an excellent peace with the emperor, giving Honorius distinguished hostages, and honorably and decently returned the emperor’s sister Placidia, who had been staying with him, to her brother.

At this time Pelagius preached the doctrines of his error against Christ’s grace. For his condemnation, a council of 214 bishops was convened at Carthage. Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, was held in renown.

Lucian the presbyter wrote the revelation of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, which God revealed to him in the seventh year of Honorius’s reign, and of Gamaliel and Nicodemus, who are mentioned in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles. He wrote it in Greek for all the churches. Avitus, a Spanish presbyter, translated this revelation into Latin and, adding his own letter, gave it to the West through Orosius the presbyter. Orosius had been sent by the blessed Augustine to Saint Jerome to learn about the soul and had reached the holy places. He was the first to return to his homeland and bring the relics of the blessed Stephen to the West.

As we have said, after Meroveus Childeric ruled the Franks. At this time Anianus, bishop of Orléans, was held in renown. Through his prayers he freed the people of Orléans from the attack of the Huns, when Aetius was then the Roman patrician.

The Britons, unable to endure the attacks of the Scots and Picts, sent to Rome and, after offering their submission, begged for aid. A legion was immediately sent to them; it slaughtered a great multitude of barbarians and drove the rest from the borders of Britain.

To keep the enemy at bay, they built a wall across the island between the two seas. Constructed without a skilled master, more from turf than stone, it benefited the Britons nothing. For as soon as the Romans departed, the former enemies arrived by ship and cut down, ravaged, and overthrew everything in their path.

The Britons again requested aid from the Romans. When the Romans arrived, they drove the enemies beyond the seas and, joining the Britons to themselves, built a solid stone wall between the cities that had formerly been established out of fear of the enemy, carrying it from sea to sea.

Along the shore of the southern sea they also erected, at intervals, numerous towers facing the sea, so that an enemy invasion might not occur from that direction. Bidding farewell to their allies as though they would never return, Boniface, bishop of Rome, built an oratory in the cemetery of Saint Felicitas and adorned her tomb. He also built an oratory for Saint John the Apostle, of sufficiently honorable workmanship.

Jerome the presbyter died in the twelfth year of Honorius, on the day before the Kalends of October, in the ninetieth year of his life. Macarius, that Egyptian monk, shone forth through signs and miracles.

The presbyter Severus, surnamed Sulpicius, of the province of Aquitaine, a man noble by birth and learning and distinguished by his love of poverty, and dear to the holy bishops Martin of Tours and Paulinus of Nola, died. In his old age he had been deceived by the Pelagians; recognizing the fault of his loquacity, he maintained silence until death, so that he might completely correct by silence the sin he had contracted by speaking.

Severianus, bishop of Gabala, was learned in the divine Scriptures and a remarkable orator. For this reason he was frequently summoned to Constantinople by Bishop John and the emperor Arcadius to deliver a sermon. He received the younger Theodosius from the sacred font and died during his reign.

[425] Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius, twenty-four years. Valentinian the Younger, son of Constantius, was made emperor at Ravenna. His mother Placidia was called Augusta.

During the same period Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, devised the heresy of his own impiety. Against him the First Synod of Ephesus was convened and condemned his wicked doctrine.

In his time the devil appeared to the Jews in Crete in the form of Moses. While promising to lead them across the sea on dry feet to the promised land, he killed many of them; the survivors immediately converted to Christ’s grace.

The savage nation of Vandals, Alans, and Goths, crossing from Spain into Africa, defiled everything with sword, fire, and plunder, as well as with Arian impiety (Paul the Deacon, book XIV).

But the blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo and outstanding teacher of all the churches, so as not to see the ruin of his city, departed to the Lord in the third month of its siege, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the seventy-sixth year of his life. He had remained in the clergy or episcopate for forty years.

At that time, after the Vandals captured Carthage, they also devastated Sicily. Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, mentions this captivity in the letter he wrote to Pope Leo concerning the calculation of Easter.

Chlodoveus, still a pagan, ruled the Franks. During his reign Gondoveus, king of the Burgundians, who is said to have been descended from Alaric, lived. He had four sons: Gundobald, Godegisel, Chilperic, and Gothmarus.

Gundobald killed his brother Chilperic and drowned his wife in a river with a stone tied around her neck. He sent her daughters into exile, one of whom was called Chrona; but he kept the other, Chlotild, with him. King Chlodoveus later took her as his wife. Through her diligence, prayers, and admonitions, and by God’s inspiration, Chlodoveus himself became a Christian with his people.

Since the Scots were believing in Christ, Palladius was ordained by Pope Celestine and sent as their first bishop.

In the eighth year of the emperor Theodosius, when the Roman army withdrew from Britain, the Scots and Picts returned and seized nearly the entire island from the north, which had been left almost empty of its native inhabitants, as far as the wall. Without delay, after killing, capturing, and routing the guards and breaking through the wall itself, the cruel marauder ravaged even within the fortification.

A letter filled with tears and distress was sent to the ruler of Roman power, requesting aid, but none was obtained. Meanwhile dreadful hunger afflicted the refugees. Some, compelled by necessity, surrendered to the enemy; others bravely resisted from mountain caves and forests and inflicted slaughter upon the enemy.

The Scots turned back home, while the Picts remained to inhabit the farthest part of the island. The aforesaid famine was followed by great abundance of crops, prosperity, luxury, and negligence; negligence was followed by a most severe plague, and soon by the still more severe attack of new enemies, namely the English.

The Britons chose these people by unanimous decision, together with their king Vortigern, as though they were defenders of the homeland, inviting them to come to their aid. But they soon found them to be conquerors.

Xistus restored with marvelous workmanship at Rome the basilica of Saint Mary, the Mother of the Lord, which had formerly been a shrine of Liber Pater.

Eudoxia, wife of the emperor Theodosius, returned from Jerusalem bringing with her the relics of the most blessed protomartyr Stephen. They were placed in the basilica of Saint Lawrence and are devoutly venerated by the faithful.

Bleda and Attila, brothers and kings of many peoples, ravaged Illyricum and Thrace. Maximus, bishop of Turin, a man sufficiently devoted to the divine Scriptures, was held in renown.

Petronius, bishop of Bologna in Italy, a man trained from adolescence in holiness of life and the practices of monks, died. His father Petronius, prefect of the praetorium and learned in secular literature, also died.

Julian, bishop, and Celestine were recognized as followers of Pelagius. The presbyter Leporius, while still a layman, also followed Pelagian doctrine, presumptuously believing that he had attained the truth of his life by his own judgment and effort alone, not through God’s help.

But after being cleansed of this error by the blessed Augustine and returning to the Catholic Church, he composed a book of his satisfaction in the true faith.

Victor, a rhetorician of Massilia, who composed commentaries on Genesis in the person of his son Etherius, died without being fully trained in the divine Scriptures.

Cassianus, a Scythian by nation, who had been ordained deacon at Constantinople by John, died a presbyter at Massilia. Among other works he wrote the book of the *Institutes*. His works must be read with the utmost caution by Catholics, especially those concerning free will and grace; he also showed excessive and unwary favor toward the heresy of the Encratites.

Cassiodorus, senator of Ravenna, wishing to purge his errors, was not able to do so completely in every respect. Vincentius, also a Gaul by birth, died a presbyter on the island of Lérins, sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures.

Marcian and Valentinian reigned for six years. At the beginning of their reign, through the industry of the most blessed Pope Leo, the Council of Chalcedon was held, where Eutyches was condemned together with Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria. In the sixth year of these emperors, King Theodoric of the Goths entered Spain with a vast army. The people of the Angles, or Saxons, were brought to Britain in three long ships. When news of their successful expedition was carried home, a stronger army was sent, which indeed drove back the enemies; but, turning its weapons against its allies, it subdued nearly the whole island from east to west with fire and sword, inventing the pretext that the Britons had paid too little tribute. [Col. 0102B]

Under the patrician Aegidius, the Franks captured Agrippa in Gaul on the Rhine, and called it Cologne because colonists had lived there. Syagrius, the son of Aegidius, succeeded him. After the death of Childeric, king of the Franks, Syagrius engaged in battle with Chlodoveus at Soissons; when Chlodoveus was victorious, Syagrius fled to the king of the Goths. Soon, however, Chlodoveus demanded his return; he was immediately handed over and killed. Thus the power of the Romans fell within Gaul. Aetius the patrician was later appointed in his place; he fought great battles against the Vandals and other peoples.

Chlodoveus was established as king of the Franks, and Chlotildis, the granddaughter of Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, was betrothed through Aurelianus. She was later brought to King Chlodoveus by that same Aurelianus and married to him. After his victory over the Alamanni, Chlodoveus, in the fifteenth year of his reign, was baptized in faith. Thereafter he subdued Burgundy and compelled Gundobad and his brother Gundesilus to pay tribute.

At this time the most blessed Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, removed an impending disaster from the city of Vienne through his tears and prayers. For frequent fires, continual earthquakes, and certain nocturnal noises, threatening the entire city with something portentous and deadly, were observed; and amid large gatherings of people, the appearance of wild beasts was observed. Wolves, bears, and naturally timid deer entered through the narrow gates and reached the broad spaces of the forum.

What more need be said? As the solemnity of the vigils approached, on which annual custom required the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection to be celebrated, the public building that the lofty height of the city of Vienne had raised to an immense elevation on the city’s summit began at dusk to burn with terrible flames. The joy of the height was interrupted by reports of danger, and the church was emptied of a people filled with fear. For all feared a disaster similar to their own possessions or houses, as though from a citadel threatened by the approaching fire.

Yet the unconquered bishop, the holy Mamertus, remained before the festal altars. Kindling the fire of his faith, he restrained the power that had been granted to the flames: the fire departed and was quelled by a flood of tears. Once despair had been laid aside, the people returned to the church; and on that night of the Paschal vigil he conceived the Rogations in his mind and there, silently with God, determined what the world now proclaims with psalms and prayers. [Col. 0102C–D; 0103A]

John the Baptist revealed his head to two Eastern monks who had come to Jerusalem for prayer, near what had once been Herod’s dwelling. It was later carried to Emesa, a city of Phoenicia, and honored with due reverence.

The Pelagian heresy disturbed the faith of the Britons. Seeking assistance from the Gallican bishops, they received Germanus, bishop of the Church of Auxerre, and Lupus, bishop of Troyes—both prelates endowed with apostolic grace—as defenders of the faith. The bishops confirmed the faith both by the word of truth and by signs of miracles.

The same blessed Germanus, together with the holy bishop Severus, also went a second time to Britain, moved by the prayers of the Gallican bishops to safeguard the integrity of the faith. With divine grace accompanying them, they utterly confounded the renewers of error. The holy bishops also repelled by divine power the war undertaken by the Saxons and Picts against the Britons with united forces. Germanus himself became commander of the battle and, not by the blast of a trumpet but by the cry of “Alleluia,” raised by the voice of the entire army to the stars, put the savage enemy to flight. [Col. 0103B]

Later reaching Ravenna and received with the highest reverence by Valentinian and Placidia, he departed to Christ. Accompanied by a solemn procession and by works of power, his body was carried to Auxerre.

At that time Severus, a presbyter of Indian origin, a man renowned for miracles, destroyed a temple of idols where pagan error, in its insane worship, adored a hundred gods. He was preparing, at the gates of Vienne, a church of the most blessed Stephen, the first martyr, to be consecrated. But he waited for a long time for the return of the most blessed Germanus, since Germanus had said that he would come to the dedication of the church. It happened that on the very day of the dedication, before the services began, the most blessed bishop Germanus’s body, being carried through Vienne, was brought into that same new church for its repose. Thus the man of God’s promise was fulfilled.

At that time Isicius governed the Church of Vienne, the sixth after the blessed Paschasius. During his episcopate the aforementioned and glorious presbyter Severus came from India to Vienne. Isicius flourished until the time of the emperor Zeno.

Aetius the patrician, the great salvation of the Western Roman state and once the terror of King Attila, was killed by Valentinian; and with him the empire of the West nearly fell. Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures, died. Among his other works, he compressed certain of Cassian’s writings, extended in expansive eloquence, into a single volume of narrower compass. Philip, a presbyter and a disciple of the blessed Jerome, who published books on Job in simple language, died.

Leo the Elder and Leo the Younger reigned for sixteen years. Alexandria and Egypt, languishing under the error of the heretic Dioscorus and filled with an unclean spirit, barked with canine fury.
