At the same time the heresy of the Acephali appeared, attacking the Council of Chalcedon. They are called Acephali—that is, “headless”—because it is not known who first introduced this heresy. Many of the Eastern peoples languished under the plague of this heresy. [Col. 0103D; 0104A]

The emperor Leo, on behalf of the Tome of Chalcedon, sent throughout nearly the whole world individual letters to individual orthodox bishops, written in the same terms, asking them to write back what they thought about that Tome. He received such agreement in their replies concerning the true incarnation of Christ that all their responses seemed to have been written at one time and by a single dictation.

Theodorus, bishop of a city founded by Cyrus, king of the Persians, which bears the name Cyria, writes about the true incarnation of the Lord and Savior against Eutyches and Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, who deny that Christ had human flesh. He also wrote an ecclesiastical history from the end of Eusebius’s books up to his own time—that is, up to the reign of this Leo, under whom he also died. [Col. 0104A–B]

At the command of Pope Hilary, Victorius wrote a paschal cycle of six hundred and thirty-two years.

Chlodoveus, king of the Franks, engaged in battle with Alaric, king of the Goths, ten miles from the city of Poitiers, and, being victorious there, killed Alaric. Amalaric, the son of Alaric, escaped and fled into Spain. Chlodoveus, king of the Franks, subdued Toulouse, Saintes, and the remaining cities, together with the whole land of Aquitaine, driving the Arian Goths from it and establishing Catholic Franks there as inhabitants.

Salvianus, a presbyter at Massilia, trained in human and divine literature, wrote, among other works, one book of exposition on the final part of Ecclesiastes for Claudianus, a presbyter of Vienne. [Col. 0104B–C]

Hilary, bishop of the Church of Arles, a man learned in the holy Scriptures, a lover of poverty, and concerned for the provision of the needy not only through the compassion of his mind but also through the labor of his body, shone forth.

Leo, the most blessed bishop of the city of Rome, was renowned for his teaching of the faith. Claudianus, likewise a presbyter of the Church of Vienne, a man skilled in speaking and subtle in disputation, flourished. Prosper of Aquitaine also flourished, the secretary of the blessed Leo, who is believed to have dictated the letters against Eutyches concerning the true incarnation of Christ and against those who held erroneous views about free will.

[475] The emperor Zeno reigned for seventeen years. When he sought to kill his son Leo, the boy’s mother presented another child resembling him in appearance in his place and secretly made Leo a cleric. He lived in the clerical state until the time of Justinian. [Col. 0104C–D]

At this time the body of the apostle Barnabas and the Gospel of Matthew, written in Matthew’s own hand, were found, he himself revealing their location.

King Odoacer of the Goths took possession of Rome, which from that time their kings held for a long period. After Theodoric, son of Triarius, died, another Theodoric, surnamed Valamer, assumed the kingship of the Goths. He devastated both Macedonias and Thessaly, set many places in the royal city on fire, and seized Italy as an enemy.

Huneric, the Arian king of the Vandals, exiled and dispersed more than three hundred and thirty-four Catholic bishops in Africa and closed their churches. He subjected the people to various punishments, killed an innumerable multitude of Catholics for their confession of the truth, cut off the hands of countless others, and, to remove the speech of the Catholic confession, also cut out their tongues. He made nearly the whole of Africa, which had been thoroughly established in Catholic truth, in a certain sense one martyr.

The Britons, under Ambrosius Aurelianus, a modest man who alone, perhaps, had survived the slaughter of the Roman people by the Saxons, challenged the victorious Saxon people to battle and defeated them. From that time, now one side and now the other held the palm of victory, until the immigrant Saxons, growing stronger, possessed the entire island for a long period.

King Chlodoveus engaged in battle with his kinsman Ragnacarius. Ragnacarius and his brother were captured and presented to the king with their hands bound behind them. King Chlodoveus said to Ragnacarius: “Why did you disgrace our people by allowing yourself to be bound?” He drove a battle-axe into his head, and thus Ragnacarius died. He said likewise to his brother: “If you had given assistance to your brother, he would not have been bound and fettered.” Then he swung a battle-axe into his head and killed him.

When their betrayers discovered that the gold they had received for the brothers had been debased, they returned it to King Chlodoveus. He replied to them: “He who betrayed his lord to death rightly receives such corrupted gold. Let it be enough for you that you are alive.” Hearing this, they valued their lives more highly than their immense payment.

Timothy, after Protherius had been killed by the Alexandrians, either wished or permitted himself to be ordained by one bishop in the place of the murdered bishop. To win the favor of the people, who had hated Protherius, and to prevent the charge that his ordination had been contrary to law, he declared all those with whom Protherius had communicated to be Nestorians. Rejecting the Council of Chalcedon, he was refuted by everyone and driven into exile as the founder of a heresy. There he died under Zeno. [Col. 0105B–C]

[492] Anastasius reigned for twenty-eight years. Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, closed the Catholic churches and exiled two hundred and twenty bishops to Sardinia. Fulgentius, bishop of the Church of Ruspe, became renowned for knowledge and learning.

Avitus, bishop of Vienne, was also preeminent in eloquence and holiness. His brother Apollinaris, bishop of Valence, was distinguished for miracles. These two most illustrious sons were the chief lights of Isicius the senator, later bishop of Vienne.

The blessed Avitus contended with great effort against the Arian heresy, which at that time had occupied not only Africa but also much of Gaul and Italy. His celebrated works bear witness to this. He wrote a dialogue attacking that heresy, addressed to Gundobad, king of the Burgundians and son of Gundoveus, with the most faithful, learned, and immortal genius. He also wrote two other books against Nestorius and Eutyches, the authors of error, in an exceedingly lucid and sufficiently polished style. He produced many other outstanding works, highly approved in the Church of Christ. [Col. 0105C–106A]

He instructed King Sigismund in the faith and devotion; later, at Avitus’s urging, Sigismund built the monastery of the holy martyrs of Agaunum, Mauritius and his companions. Avitus afterward grieved most bitterly when Sigismund was captured and killed by the Franks.

Whoever wishes to know fully how great Avitus was during his life in the Church of Christ should, after considering his countless labors in divine matters, read his epitaph. There he will be able to see what he was, where, among other things, the following verses were composed as a truthful poetic tribute:

> He alone was in the citadel, and in every form of speech  
> No orator was his equal, and no poet;  
> The books scattered through countless volumes proclaim  
> That he who lived still lives, and will live through all the ages.

Pope Symmachus, among his many works for the churches—some founded from their foundations, others restored from antiquity—built dwellings for the poor at Saint Peter’s, Saint Paul’s, and Saint Lawrence’s. Every year he also supplied money and clothing throughout Africa and Sardinia to the bishops who were in exile.

The emperor Anastasius, because he favored heresy and persecuted Catholics, perished by a divine thunderbolt. [Col. 0106A–B]

This Anastasius sent King Chlodoveus letters patent for the consulship. From that day Chlodoveus was called both consul and Augustus, and he established the seat of his kingdom at Paris. He reigned over the Franks for thirty years.

From the passing of Saint Martin until the passing of King Chlodoveus there were one hundred and twelve years. From the passing of Saint Martin, the third bishop of Vienne—for the first was Crescens and the next was Zacharias the martyr—until the passing of Martin, bishop of Tours, there were two hundred and ninety years. Until the passing of Saint Mamertus, bishop of the Church of Vienne, three hundred and twenty-eight years are reckoned. [Col. 0106B–C]

After Chlodoveus died, Queen Chlotildis held the kingdom of the Franks with Chlodoveus’s four sons: Theodoric, Chlodomer, Childebert, and Chlotarius.

The Danes crossed into Gaul with many ships under their leader Cochilaicus. Theutbert, the son of Theodoric, fought them and defeated them together with their king.

Chlodomer, Childebert, and Chlotarius, the brothers, led an army against Sigismund and Godomar. When they had come together in battle and the Burgundians were fleeing, Sigismund fled to the monastery of the holy martyrs of Agaunum. He was captured by Chlodomer with his wife and sons, killed, and thrown into a well, where he was hidden.

Later, however, through a revelation, the abbot of the holy martyrs raised him from there. He was honorably buried not far from their church, in the monastery that he himself had built, where their bodies—namely, those of Mauritius and his six thousand six hundred and sixty-six companions—had been honorably placed. There he later also became renowned for miracles.

At that time the distinguished presbyter Avitus was also held in esteem at Orléans.

Chlodomer was killed in the province of Vienne, at a place called Vézeronce, while fighting the Burgundians. The Franks, indignant, pursued and killed Godomar. (Deacon, Book XV; Sigismund, year 503.) [Col. 0106C–D]

At the same time, at Carthage, a certain Arian named Olympius blasphemed the Holy Trinity in a bath and was visibly burned by a bolt of fire. A certain Arian bishop named Barbas, while baptizing someone contrary to the rule of faith, said: “Barbas baptizes you in the name of the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit.” Immediately the water that had been brought for the baptism disappeared completely. When the person who was to be baptized saw this, he promptly went to the Catholic church and received Christ’s baptism according to the custom of the faith. (Nicephorus, Book XVI, chapter 35.)

Faustus, formerly abbot of the monastery of Lérins and later made bishop of Riez in Gaul, attempted to destroy the Pelagian doctrine but fell into error. Therefore those who proclaim that his views in this matter were Catholic—such as Gennadius in his account of illustrious men—are altogether mistaken. For both Augustine and the other Catholics in the Church of God teach free will in such a way that its illumination, strength, and salvation come to it from Christ, through Christ, and with Christ. But this Faustus attempts to teach Christian free will in such a way that its illumination, strength, and salvation come not from Christ but from nature. [Col. 0107A–B]

Against him the most blessed Avitus, bishop of Vienne, wrote with the clearest faith, refuting his error. Likewise John, a learned man and presbyter of Antioch, wrote against him.

[519] Justin, the emperor, reigned for eight years. John, pontiff of the Roman Church, came to Constantinople and reached the gate called the Golden Gate. When crowds of people came out to meet him, he restored sight to a blind man who asked him for light in the presence of everyone.

When John returned and reached Ravenna, Theodoric, driven by envy because Justin had received him honorably as a defender of Catholic devotion, killed him in prison together with his companions. At that time the same Theodoric also killed Symmachus and Boethius, men of consular rank, for their Catholic devotion. Theodoric died a sudden death the following year, and his nephew Athalaric succeeded him in the kingdom.

After Thrasamund, Childeric, born of a captive daughter of the emperor Valentinian, assumed the kingdom among the Vandals. Bound by an oath to Thrasamund, by which he had promised before assuming the kingdom that he would not assist the Catholics, he nevertheless ordered the bishops to return from exile and commanded them to restore the churches, after seventy-four years of heretical profanation. [Col. 0107C–D]

Julian, bishop of the Church of Vienne, flourished.

The kings Theodoric, Childebert, and Chlotarius raised an army against Hermenefrid, king of the Thuringians, and, victorious, drove Hermenefrid into flight. Later, after Theodoric had received him under pledge of faith, Hermenefrid was speaking with him on the wall of the city when Theodoric threw him down and killed his children.

Childebert also went to war in Spain on behalf of his sister, the wife of King Amalaric. There Amalaric was killed, his treasures were plundered, and the city of Toledo was devastated. Childebert returned with his sister, who nevertheless died on the journey. Among the remaining treasure Childebert brought sixty extremely precious chalices, fifteen patens engraved with marvelous workmanship, and twenty Gospel cases of purest gold set with gems. He distributed all these things among the churches. [Col. 0107D–0108A]

Childebert and Chlotarius killed the sons of Chlodomer, their nephews, whom Chlotildis was raising, so that they would not reign in their father’s place. One of them, Chlodoald, escaped. Later, abandoning his earthly kingdom, he became a cleric and was then ordained presbyter. Rich in good works and full of virtues, he departed to the Lord and was buried at Nogent, in the suburb of the city of Paris.

Eugenius, bishop of the African city of Carthage, was publicly regarded as a confessor.

[527] The emperor Justinian reigned for thirty-nine years. He was Justin’s nephew through his sister. Benedict the abbot became renowned for the glory of his virtues. The blessed Pope Gregory wrote his life in the books of the Dialogues.

The patrician Belisarius triumphed wonderfully over the Persians. Justinian then sent him to Africa, where he destroyed the Vandal people. Carthage too, after ninety-four years of devastation, was recovered: the Vandals were defeated and expelled, their king Gelimer was captured and sent to Constantinople.

Dominus, bishop of Vienne, flourished. He was distinguished both in divine and secular arts, a lover of the poor, a redeemer of captives, and a man of thoroughly approved life.

At this time the body of Saint Antony the monk, found through divine revelation, was brought to Alexandria and buried in the church of Saint John the Baptist.

Dionysius wrote paschal cycles, beginning with the year 232 of the Lord’s Incarnation. This was the 248th year of Diocletian after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes. In that year the Justinianic Code was promulgated to the world. [Col. 0108B–C]

Victor, bishop of Capua, also wrote a book on Easter and criticized the errors of Victorius.

Theodoric, king of the Franks, died, and his son Theutbert succeeded him.

Childebert and Chlotarius, kings of the Franks, ravaged Spain. They surrounded and besieged Caesaraugusta. But the citizens carried about the tunic of the blessed martyr Vincent and prayed for the Lord’s mercy. The kings Childeric and Chlotarius, moved by this, made peace and received from the people of Caesaraugusta, as a gift, the stole of the most blessed martyr Vincent. When Childebert returned to Paris, he built a church there in honor of the blessed martyr Vincent and placed that same stole in the same church. [Col. 0108C–D]

Theutbert entered Italy, defeated the Lombards, and reduced them to tribute. He returned and died in the fourteenth year of his reign.

Chlothildis, full of good works, also departed to the Lord at the city of Tours. Her sons carried away her body and buried her at Paris beside her husband Chlodoveus in the church of Saint Genovefa.

King Chlotarius ordered his son Chramnus, who had rebelled against him and resisted him in open battle, to be burned in the fire with his wife and children, after Chramnus himself had first been captured and bound.

At this time the blessed bishop Medard, full of virtues, departed to the Lord. King Chlotarius buried him gloriously in the city of Soissons, surrendering many possessions and gifts for his burial. The king himself died not long afterward and was buried by his sons in that same church of the blessed Medard. He had reigned for fifty-one years. [Col. 0108D–0109A]

[564] Justin the Younger reigned for eleven years. The patrician Narses defeated and killed Totila, king of the Goths, in Italy. Later, terrified by the threats of Sophia Augusta, the wife of Justin, he invited the Lombards from Pannonia and brought them into Italy.

John, pontiff of the Roman Church, completed and dedicated the church of the apostles Philip and James.

Pantagathus, bishop of the Church of Vienne, flourished. First elevated by consular office, but foremost in the humility of Christ, he afterward governed the episcopal see with complete faithfulness for five years. He died during the consulship of Paulinus the Younger and Basil. Isicius succeeded him in the episcopate and likewise flourished under Justinian. [Col. 0109A–B]

The four brothers, sons of Chlotarius, divided the kingdom among themselves. Charibert received Childebert’s kingdom and established his seat at Paris. Gunthchramn received Chlodomer’s kingdom and established his seat at Orléans. Chilperic received the kingdom of his father Chlotarius and made the city of Soissons his seat. Sigebert received Theodoric’s kingdom and established his seat at Rheims.

In the eighth year of his reign, the Huns engaged in battle with Sigebert in Gaul. Defeated, they sought friendship and thus withdrew to their own land.

Sigebert and Chilperic, the brothers, fought against each other. Chilperic first seized the city of Rheims. Sigebert then occupied Soissons and captured Theutbert, the son of Chilperic. Later, however, after exchanging oaths with one another, they remained at a certain peace for several years.

King Charibert died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Romanus at Blavia Castle.

King Sigebert took Brunichild, the daughter of King Athanagild, as his wife. Since she had been baptized by the Arians, he ordered her to be rebaptized in the name of the undivided Trinity.

King Chilperic sent her sister to their father in Spain and sought Chilsuinta. Although he already had other wives, he took her in addition. Later, however, following the advice of Fredegund, he strangled her by night in her bed. [Col. 0109B–C]

At that time Chilperic had three sons by his wife Audovera: Theutbert, Meroveus, and Chlodoveus.

While Chilperic was absent, Fredegund deceived Queen Audovera by such a trick that Audovera herself, rather than someone else, received from the sacred font the daughter whom she had borne to Chilperic. Audovera, thoroughly misled, did so; for this reason she was later dismissed by her husband Chilperic, and Fredegund entered into marriage with him.

Audovera, veiled and secluded, received only estates and properties sufficient for her support. The bishop who had baptized the daughter and had not forbidden the mother to hold her was condemned to exile.

King Leovigild of the Goths brought certain rebellious regions of Spain back under the power of his kingdom by conquering them.

At this time Namatus, bishop of the Church of Vienne, flourished—noble in birth but nobler in life and eloquence.

The Franks who were under Chilperic’s rule went over to Sigebert. Thus Sigebert besieged Tournai, where Chilperic resided.

At that time Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, sent word to King Sigebert that he should by no means go against his brother or think of killing him. Sigebert scorned this warning. But, with the Franks agreeing, he was lifted onto a shield according to the custom of the nation and proclaimed king; thus he obtained the kingdom of his brother Chilperic, who was soon afterward treacherously killed by two young men through the plotting of Fredegund.

For they pretended that they had something secret to tell him and pierced his side. Chilperic was buried by his brother in the village of Lambres. From there he was transferred to the basilica of Saint Medard and placed beside his father Chlotarius. He had reigned for thirteen years. [Col. 0109C–D; 0110A]

Meroveus, the son of Chilperic, married Brunichild, the wife of his uncle. For this reason he was captured by one faction, tonsured, ordained a presbyter, and sent to a monastery in the district of Le Mans.

Childebert the Younger, the son of Brunichild, was established as king in Austrasia. He entered Italy, devastated it, and made it tributary.

King Gunthchramn, of good memory, died and was buried in the Basilica of Saint Marcellus the martyr at Chalon. He had reigned for thirty-one years.

Leovigild, king of the Goths, took as his wife Rinchild, the daughter of Chilperic and Fredegund.

Fredegund, committing adultery with Landeric, the mayor of the palace, arranged for King Chilperic, returning from the hunt, to be killed by deceit through assassins. Pretending to be unaware of the crime, she had him carried with the army to Paris and buried in the church of the blessed martyr Vincent. Thus she remained in the kingdom with Landeric and her young son Chlotarius. [Col. 0110A–B]

Against her Childebert, king of the Austrasians, who had succeeded his kinsman Gunthchramn in the kingdom of Burgundy, raised an army.

Fredegund, however, gave her men this advice: they should go out at night with lamps, carry branches before them in their hands, and hang bells around the horses’ necks, so that they would not be recognized by the guards on watch. At that time the Austrasians used to send their horses out to pasture with bells ringing.

They did everything as instructed and deceived the Austrasians and Burgundians by this trick. The guards thought that the horses were grazing near the forest and that the bells they heard were those of their own horses. Thus Childebert’s army was cut down, while the survivors and their commanders were put to flight.

After some time Fredegund died and was buried in the church of the blessed Vincent at Paris.

Theodebert and Theodoric, the sons of Childebert, were sent with their grandmother Brunichild into Burgundy, into the kingdom of the glorious King Gunthchramn. Theodoric engaged in battle with Chlotarius, his cousin, and put him and his army to flight. Thereafter, on the advice of his mother Brunichild, Theodoric joined battle with his brother Theodebert.

His brother entered Cologne and was treacherously killed there. His head was brought to his brother Theodoric, as he himself had ordered, and Theodoric killed Theodebert’s sons. He wished to take his daughter in marriage but was prevented by his mother. Later his mother Brunichild, fearing that he might kill her, gave him poison, and he died such a death after reigning for forty years. Brunichild killed his sons. [Col. 0110C–0111A]

Namatus, bishop of Vienne, died in the seventieth year of his life.

The emperor Justin became insane and died. Tiberius assumed the empire in his place.

The Burgundians and Austrasians, together with the remaining Franks, made peace and raised Chlotarius as king over all three kingdoms.

[575] Tiberius Constantine reigned for seven years. Gregory, still apocrisarius of the Roman Church at Constantinople, composed books of exposition on Job. In the presence of Tiberius he proved that Eutychius, the bishop of that city, had erred concerning our resurrection, to such an extent that the emperor ordered Eutychius’s book, which he had written about the resurrection, to be burned in the flames.

For Eutychius taught that our body in the resurrection would be intangible, more subtle than the winds, and destined for repose. [Col. 0111A–B]

The people of the Lombards, accompanied by famine and pestilence, invaded all Italy and besieged the city of Rome. At that time Alboin was their king.

The Goths, divided into two factions under Hermenegild, the son of King Leovigild, devastated one another in mutual slaughter.

Philip, bishop of Vienne, a distinguished man, flourished. During his episcopate the monastery of Saint Andrew below Vienne was founded by Remilla Eugenia, daughter of the duke Ansemundus, and was transferred by testament to the mother Church. For another, upper monastery of Saint Andrew, situated on the city hill, already existed. The most blessed Leonianus had founded it during the time of Saint Avitus, bishop of that city, and the same Remilla had been raised there under regular discipline. [Col. 0111B–C]

After Philip, the holy man Evantius was raised to the episcopate of Vienne. Together with Saint Priscus and Artemius of Sens, Remigius of Bourges, and other holy bishops, he firmly confirmed twenty ecclesiastical chapters. Syagrius, bishop of Autun, a man of supreme holiness, also took part in their deliberations.

The Suevi were conquered by King Leovigild and subjected to the Goths.

[583] The emperor Maurice reigned for twenty-one years. Hermenegild, the son of Leovigild, king of the Goths, was stripped by his Arian father of the insignia of kingship because of his steadfast confession of the Catholic faith. He was also thrown into prison and finally, on the holy night of the Lord’s Resurrection, struck on the head with an axe. Thus, as king and martyr, he entered the heavenly kingdom in place of an earthly one.

As soon as his brother Reccared received the kingdom after their father, he converted the entire Gothic people over whom he ruled to the Catholic faith, at the urging of Leander, bishop of Seville, who had also instructed Hermenegild.

The Anari, fighting against the Romans, were driven back more by gold than by iron.

Verus, bishop of Vienne, became renowned. During his episcopate Desiderius of Autun, by birth a nobleman, served in the order of deacons of the Church of Vienne.

Gregory, bishop and outstanding teacher of the Roman Church, became renowned.

After Bishop Verus, Saint Desiderius succeeded him. This most blessed man reproved Queen Brunichild for her impieties. At her command he was killed by her attendants in the territory of Lyons, over the river Chalaron, and as a glorious martyr entered the heavenly kingdom.

Pope Gregory gathered a synod of twenty-four bishops at the body of the blessed apostle Peter and decreed what was necessary for the Church. He also sent Augustine, Mellitus, and John, together with many others who feared God, to Britain; through them he converted the Angles to Christ.

Indeed, King Æthelberht of Kent was converted to Christ together with the people over whom he ruled, and he granted residences both to Augustine, his teacher, and to the other bishops.

Queen Brunichild, on account of her many crimes, was judged by the Franks in the presence of King Chlotarius. Tied by her arms and legs to untamed horses, she was torn limb from limb, and her bones were burned in the fire.

Phocas reigned for eight years. Gregory appointed metropolitans for the English people and gave the pallium to the bishops of Lindona and Eboracum. In the second year of Phocas’s reign [Col. 0112B], in the eighth indiction, he departed to the Lord. Phocas, at the request of Pope Boniface, decreed that the Roman See should be the head of all the Churches, because the Church of Constantinople was styling itself first of all.

At that time Domnolus, bishop of Vienne, was flourishing—a vigorous man and most devoted in ransoming captives. At the request of another Boniface, Roman pontiff, Phocas ordered that, in the ancient temple called the Pantheon, after the filth of idolatry had been removed, a church of the Blessed Ever-Virgin Mary and of all the martyrs should be dedicated, so that where once the worship had been conducted not of gods but of demons, there might thereafter be the commemoration of all the saints.

The Patasini and the Venetians waged civil war throughout the East and Egypt, overthrowing one another in mutual slaughter. The Persians, waging the most grievous wars against the Roman state, captured many Roman provinces and Jerusalem itself [Col. 0112C]. Destroying the churches and profaning the holy places, they also carried away the standard of the Lord’s Cross.

Heraclius, emperor, for twenty-six years. Anastasius the Persian, a monk, suffered noble martyrdom for Christ. Born in Persia, he learned magical arts from his father as a boy; but when he learned the name of Christ from Christian captives, he was immediately converted in mind. Leaving Persia, he went to Chalcedon and Hierapolis in search of Christ, and then proceeded to Jerusalem, where he received the grace of baptism. Four miles from there he entered the monastery of Abbot Anastasius. After living there according to the rule for seven years, when he had come to Caesarea of Palestine for the sake of prayer, he was captured by the Persians and endured many beatings for a long time amid prisons and chains under the judge Marcebana [Col. 0112D]. At last he was sent to Persia, to their king Chosroes. The king had him beaten three times at intervals; finally, after he had been suspended by one hand for three hours, he was beheaded with seventy others and completed his martyrdom. Soon afterward, a demoniac who put on his tunic was healed.

Sisebut, king of the Goths in Spain, subdued many cities by war and converted to the faith of Christ the Jews subject to his kingdom, except those who, having escaped by flight, secretly migrated to the Franks.

The Persians reached as far as Chalcedon. The Aeunni, breaking through the long wall and approaching the fortifications of Constantinople, conversed with the emperor Heraclius, who was standing on the wall opposite them. Having received from him a payment for peace, they withdrew for a time [Col. 0113A].

Aetherius of Vienne, a man outstanding in every respect, was held in high renown. King Chlothar ravaged the land of the Saxons so thoroughly that, as is reported, he left no living man there taller than his own sword. Not long afterward, in the forty-fourth year of his reign, he died. His son Dagobert succeeded him, a vigorous man and severe in judgments. He had two sons, Sigebert and Chlodoveus. He sent one of them, Sigebert, to Austrasia with Duke Pippin, while he kept the younger, Chlodoveus, with himself.

Gundoland, mayor of the palace, died, and Dagobert appointed Herthenold in his place. The emperor Heraclius, arriving with an army, defeated the Persians, brought back the Christians who were held captive there, and triumphantly carried the standard of the Lord’s Cross back to Jerusalem [Col. 0113B]. The relics of the blessed martyr Anastasius were also brought first to his monastery and then to Rome. They are venerated in the monastery of the blessed apostle Paul, called “at the Salvian Waters.”

In the eighteenth year of the emperor Heraclius, in the fifth indiction, Edwin, most excellent king of the English, in Britain north of the Humber, received the word of salvation with his people through the preaching of Bishop Paulinus, whom the venerable archbishop Justus had sent from Kent. This occurred in the eleventh year of Edwin’s reign; the arrival of the English in Britain had taken place approximately one hundred and eighty years earlier. Edwin gave Paulinus an episcopal see at York.

At that time a great error arose among the Scots concerning the observance of the fourteenth day of the paschal moon. Pope Honorius rebuked their error in a letter [Col. 0113C]. John also, who succeeded his predecessor Severinus in the pontificate, wrote while he had already been elected to the pontificate, both concerning the same error about the fourteenth day of the moon and concerning the Pelagian heresy, which was reviving among them.

### [639]

Heracleonas, with his mother Martina, for three years. Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria, and Sergius and Pyrrhus, bishops of the imperial city, revived the heresy of the Acephali and taught as doctrine that there was one operation in Christ, of divinity and humanity, and likewise one will.

Among them, Pyrrhus came from Africa to Rome under Pope Theodore. With a repentance that later proved to be feigned, he presented the pope, in the presence of the clergy and people, with a written declaration bearing his signature. In it, everything written or done by his predecessors against the catholic faith was condemned [Col. 0113D]. He was therefore kindly received by the pope as though he were the pontiff of the imperial city. But when he returned and repeated the same error, the aforesaid Pope Theodore summoned a synod of priests in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter and condemned Pyrrhus under the bond of anathema.

### [642]

Constantine, son of Heraclius, for six months. Paul, the successor of Pyrrhus, afflicted the Catholics not only with doctrine as deadly as that of his predecessor but also through open persecution. He harassed the representatives of the holy Roman Church who had been sent to correct him, subjecting some to imprisonment, others to exile, and others to beatings. He also overturned and plundered their altar, consecrated in the house of Placidia in the venerable sanctuary, forbidding them to celebrate Mass there [Col. 0114A]. For this reason he too, like his predecessors, was justly condemned by the Apostolic See.

Dagobert reigned over the Franks; his son Sigebert over the Austrasians.

### [641]

Constantine, son of Constantine, emperor for twenty-eight years. Deceived by Paul, just as his grandfather Heraclius had been by Sergius, bishop of that same city, Constantine promulgated the *Typos* against the catholic faith, declaring that neither one nor two wills or operations in Christ were to be confessed—as though Christ were to be regarded as willing nothing and performing nothing.

Therefore Pope Martin, having convened at Rome a synod of one hundred and five bishops, condemned under anathema the aforementioned heretics Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul. After this, Theodorus the exarch, sent by the emperor Constantine [Col. 0114B], removed Pope Martin from the Constantinian Church and brought him to Constantinople. There, because he acted apostolically in defense of the catholic truth, he was exiled to Cherson, where he ended his life. To this day he shines there through many signs of miraculous power.

The aforesaid synod took place in the ninth year of Constantine’s reign, in October, in the eighth indiction. Clarentius, a sufficiently learned man and bishop of Vienne, was renowned.

Pope Vitalian was ordained at Rome. Under him the emperor Constantine sent to the blessed apostle Peter golden Gospels adorned around the edges with white gems of marvelous size. Some years later, when the emperor himself came to Rome in the sixth indiction, he offered upon the apostles’ altar a pallium woven with gold, while his entire army entered the church with candles.

In the following year [Col. 0114C] there was an eclipse of the sun, on the fifth day before the Nones of May, at about the tenth hour of the day. Pope Vitalian sent Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Adrian, a holy and most learned man, to Britain. They enriched many of the English Churches with ecclesiastical learning.

After committing many acts of plunder in the provinces, the emperor Constantine was killed and died in a bath, in the twelfth indiction. Not long afterward Pope Vitalian also died.

### [669]

Constantine, son of the preceding Constantine, for seventeen years. The Saracens invaded Sicily and, after carrying away an enormous amount of booty, soon returned to Alexandria.

Agatho was appointed pontiff of the Roman Church. At the request of Constantine, Tiberius, and Heraclius, most devout rulers, he sent his legates to the imperial city [Col. 0114D] to bring about the union of God’s Churches. Among them was John, still a deacon and not long afterward a bishop. They were received with the greatest kindness by Constantine, defender of the catholic faith, and were ordered to set aside philosophical disputations and seek the truth of the faith through peaceful discussion. They were supplied from the Constantinopolitan library with the writings of the catholic Fathers that they had requested.

One hundred and fifty bishops were also present, with Gregory, patriarch of the imperial city, presiding, and Macarius of Antioch. Those who asserted one will and one operation in Christ were therefore convicted of having falsified a great many statements of the catholic Fathers.

When the conflict had ended, Georgius was corrected. Macarius, however, together with his followers and his predecessors Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, was anathematized [Col. 0115A]. In his place Theophanes, an abbot from Sicily, was made bishop of Antioch.

Such grace accompanied the legates of catholic peace that John, bishop of Porto, one of their number, celebrated Mass publicly in Latin in the Church of Holy Sophia before the emperor and patriarch on the Lord’s Octave of Easter.

This is the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, celebrated at Constantinople and written in the Greek language during the pontificate of Pope Agatho. The most devout emperor Constantine conducted and presided over it within his palace, together with the legates of the Apostolic See and one hundred and fifty bishops in attendance.

The First Ecumenical Synod was assembled at Nicaea against Arius, with three hundred and eighteen Fathers [Col. 0115B], during the time of Pope Julius and the emperor Constantine.

The Second was held at Constantinople, with one hundred and fifty Fathers, against Macedonius and Eudoxius, during the time of Pope Damasus and the emperor Gratian, when Nectarius of that city was ordained bishop.

The Third was held at Ephesus, with two hundred Fathers, against Nestorius, bishop of the imperial city, who preached two persons in the Lord Jesus Christ, under the great emperor Theodosius and Pope Celestine.

The Fourth was held at Chalcedon, with one thousand one hundred and thirty Fathers, under Pope Leo and during the reign of the emperor Marcian, against Eutyches, the most impious leader of the monks.

The Fifth was held at Constantinople, during the time of Pope Vigilius and under the emperor Justinian, against Theodore and all the heretics.

This is the Sixth [Col. 0115C], of which we have spoken in the present place.

Sindulfus was held in high renown as bishop of the Church of Vienne. The holy virgin of Christ, Æthelthryth, daughter of Anna, king of the English, was first given in marriage to another man and afterward to King Ecgfrith. After preserving her marital bed undefiled for twelve years, she took the veil and became a nun. Soon afterward she also became a mother and nurse of virgins. Her merits are attested even by her dead flesh: after sixteen years of burial, she was found incorrupt, together with the garment in which she had been wrapped, and had remained as undefiled as a virgin.

King Dagobert enriched the churches of the saints and gave them many gifts; he ruled the Frankish kingdom peacefully and quietly. After Bishop Sindulfus died, Hecdicus, a man of great religious devotion, assumed the episcopate of the Church of Vienne. He remained renowned until the final period [Col. 0115D] of the emperor Justinian, and died during that emperor’s time.

### [686]

Justinian the Younger, son of Constantine, became emperor and reigned for ten years. He established peace with the Saracens by land and sea for a decade. The province of Africa, which had been held by the Saracens, was also subjected to the Roman Empire after Carthage had been captured and destroyed.

King Dagobert, sick with a severe fever, died at the estate of Spino­gilo in the Parisian district and was buried in the church of the blessed martyr Dionysius. The Franks mourned him for many days. He had reigned forty-four years.

In his place the Franks appointed his son Chlodoveus king; Chlodoveus’s wife was Baltildis, of Saxon descent. After Pippin’s death, Sigebert, king of Austrasia, appointed his son Grimoald mayor of the palace [Col. 0116A].

Not long afterward, when King Sigebert had died, Grimoald tonsured Sigebert’s young son, named Dagobert, and sent him into the custody of Doddo, bishop of Poitiers. The Franks were greatly angered by this and handed the captured Grimoald over to King Chlodoveus. Chlodoveus placed him in custody at Paris; there, after suffering prolonged torment, he died.

King Chlodoveus, acting rashly, cut off the arm of the blessed martyr Dionysius. From that time, as the Franks maintained, their kingdom began to decline, afflicted by various misfortunes.

King Chlodoveus, enticed by many vices, eventually had three sons by Queen Baltildis: Chlothar, Childeric, and Theodoric.

Justinian, of blessed memory, ordered Pope Sergius of the Roman Church to be taken to Constantinople by his protospatharius Zacharias, because Sergius had refused to approve and subscribe to the synod concerning heresy that Justinian had held at Constantinople [Col. 0116B]. But the army of the city of Ravenna and the neighboring regions forestalled the emperor’s impious orders and drove the same Zacharias from the city of Rome with insults and injuries.

King Chlodoveus, excessively dissolute, died after reigning sixteen years. The Franks appointed his son Chlothar king. After Herchinold, mayor of the palace, died, the Franks, proceeding without a clear decision, appointed Ebroin to that dignity, so that he might be chief in the royal court.

Chlothar died after reigning four years. In his place the Franks elevated his brother Theodoric. They sent his other brother Childeric to rule in Austrasia together with Duke Ulfeldus.

Pope Sergius ordained the venerable man Wilibrord, also called Clement, bishop for the Frisian people. Bishop Chaldeoldus governed the Church of Vienne until the time of King Theodoric. The emperor Justinian, deprived of the glory of the kingdom because of his treachery, withdrew into exile in Pontus.

### [696]

The emperor Leo, for two years. Pope Sergius found, by divine revelation, in the shrine of the blessed Peter, a silver chest that had long lain in a very dark corner. In it was a cross decorated with various precious stones. When he drew out four petals in which gems had been enclosed, he saw inside a portion of the life-giving wood of the Lord’s Cross.

From that time onward, every year on the day of its Exaltation, the whole people kisses and adores it in the basilica of the Savior called the Constantinian Basilica [Col. 0116D].

Dodolenus was regarded as bishop of Vienne. The Franks, plotting against Ebroin, expelled Theodoric from the kingdom and tonsured Ebroin at the monastery of Luxeuil. They raised Childeric as king over themselves and made Ulfuoldus mayor of the palace.

Not long afterward, because of his fickleness of mind, Childeric was killed by the Franks. Ulfuoldus escaped by flight. The Franks appointed Leodosius, son of Archenoldus, mayor of the palace, and recalled Theodoric to the kingdom. It is said that Leodegarius, the venerable bishop of Autun, and his brother Gerinus were involved in this plan.

Ebroin, a man of great impiety, therefore abandoned his clerical tonsure and left the monastery of Luxeuil. Without doubt he had been led astray by the spirit of falsehood, which had told him that he would live for eighteen years. He returned to Francia, gathered forces from everywhere, and marched against Audoenus, bishop of Rouen. Soon, having received an answer from him, he raged tyrannically against his enemies and killed Levidesius, whom he had captured through treachery.

Thus he seized the government by force under King Theodoric. Immediately afterward he struck the holy Leodegarius with the sword after subjecting him to various tortures. He also killed his brother Gerinus after long torment. He forced many into exile and confiscated their property; among those who succumbed under many injuries were the illustrious men Vulbaldus and Ragnebertus, venerable for their virtue.

After Ulfuoldus died, Martin and Pippin, the younger son of Ansegisel, ruled in Austrasia while the kings were dying. When battle was joined against King Theodoric and Ebroin, Martin escaped and shut himself in a sewer at Lyon [Col. 0117B]. Pippin also escaped from the flank.

Ebroin, having given sworn assurances, persuaded Martin to come to King Theodoric. Trusting him, Martin soon came with his men and was killed. Ebroin, raging with excessive cruelty, was killed by a Frank named Hermenfrid. Hermenfrid fled to Pippin in the kingdom of the Austrasians and escaped.

At that time there was a blind man on an island in the province of Lyon called Barbara, one of those whose eyes Ebroin had gouged out. One night, while sitting on the bank of the river Saône to pray, he heard the rush of voyagers and the great force of their arms struggling against the current. When he asked where that vessel was heading, a voice rang in his ears: “It is Ebroin, whom we are carrying to Vulcan’s cauldron [Col. 0117C]. There he will pay the penalty for his deed.” The same man heard this for his consolation, so that he might know what punishment the persecutors of the righteous would suffer.

The most reverend Cuthbert, bishop of Lindisfarne in Britain, formerly an anchorite, led a life renowned for signs of miracles from childhood to its end. His venerable body, buried for eleven years, was found incorrupt, as though he had died that very hour, together with the garment that covered him.

The Franks made Waratto mayor of the palace in place of Ebroin. He made peace with Pippin. Pippin waged civil war against Giselmar, Waratto’s son, who was acting against his father’s wishes. But Giselmar was struck by God and died. His father Waratto recovered the government.

Saint Audoenus, bishop, renowned for his miracles, departed to the Lord [Col. 0117D].

After Waratto, the Franks appointed Bertharius mayor of the palace, a man small in stature and wisdom. Pippin went to war against Theodoric and Bertharius and was victorious.

### [699]

The emperor Tiberius, for seven years. A synod was held at Aquileia. Because of ignorance concerning the faith, it hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, it agreed to assent to that council together with the other Churches of Christ.

John, who had succeeded Sergius, was regarded as Roman pontiff. Bobolinus, bishop of the Church of Vienne, was renowned. After him Georgius, a bishop of great virtue, was appointed in the same city.

Gisulphus, duke of the Lombards, ravaged Campania around Benevento with fire, sword, and captivity. Since there was no one able to resist him, Pope John sent many gifts and legates, ransomed all the captives, and compelled the enemies to return home. Another John succeeded him; he constructed, with marvelous workmanship, an oratory of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, in the Church of the blessed Peter.

Aripert, king of the Lombards, restored to the jurisdiction of the Apostolic See many estates and patrimonies of the Cottian Alps that had been taken away by the Lombards. He sent this restoration to Rome written in letters of gold.

Pippin, duke of the Austrasians, captured King Theodoric. After receiving his treasures, he appointed one of his own men, Norbert, mayor of the palace under that same king. He himself returned to Austrasia. By his noble wife he had two sons, Drogo and Grimoald. Drogo received the duchy in Campania [Col. 0118B].

### [706]

Justinian II, with his son Tiberius, for seven years. With the aid of Terbellius, king of the Bulgars, he recovered the kingdom and killed those who had expelled him—the patricians and Leo, who had usurped in his place—as well as his successor Tiberius, who had held him in custody in the same city throughout the whole period of his reign after he had been expelled from the kingdom.

He sent Callinicus, the patriarch, to Rome after having his eyes torn out, and gave the episcopate to Cyrus, who had been an abbot in Pontus and had supported him in exile. He ordered Pope Constantine to come to him, received him honorably, and sent him back. When he ordered Mass to be celebrated for him on Sunday, he received Communion from the pope’s hand. Prostrate on the ground, he asked the pope to intercede for his sins [Col. 0118C] and renewed all the privileges of the Church.

When Justinian sent an army to Pontus to seize Philippicus, whom he had exiled there, the entire army went over to Philippicus’s side and made him emperor. Returning with him to Constantinople, it fought against Justinian twelve miles from the city, defeated and killed him. Philippicus then reigned in Justinian’s place.

Theodoric still reigned among the Franks. Deodatus, bishop of Vienne, a man of great frugality, was flourishing.

### [712]

Philippicus, emperor, for one year and six months. He expelled Cyrus from the pontificate and ordered him to return to govern his monastery. Philippicus sent letters containing a corrupt doctrine to Pope Constantine. The pope rejected them with the counsel of the Apostolic See, and for this reason caused paintings to be made in the portico of Saint Peter, containing the acts of the six Ecumenical Synods [Col. 0118D].

For Philippicus had also ordered such paintings, which existed in the imperial city, to be brought to him. The Roman people therefore decreed that the name of the heretical emperor should not be accepted either in documents or on solid coins. Consequently neither was his image brought into the church nor was his name proclaimed during the solemnities of Mass.

Philippicus was captured and blinded by Anastasius, but was not killed. King Theodoric of the Franks died; he had reigned nineteen years.

### [714]

The emperor Anastasius, for three years. He sent letters to Pope Constantine at Rome through Scholasticus, patrician and exarch of Italy, in which he declared himself a supporter of the catholic faith and a proclaimer of the holy Sixth Council [Col. 0119A].

Chlothar, son of Theodoric, reigned over the Franks as a child for three years. His brother Childebert, an illustrious man, succeeded him. When Norbert, mayor of the palace, died, Grimoald, son of Pippin, was appointed.

Pippin waged many wars against Rittod, the pagan duke of the Frisians, and likewise against the Suebi and many other peoples. Blidrannus was bishop of the Church of Vienne.

Leutprand, king of the Lombards, confirmed, at the admonition of the venerable Pope Gregory, the donation of the Cottian Alps patrimony that King Aripert had made but that Leutprand had reclaimed.

Drogo, son of Pippin, died in winter, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 708. Bishop Anepo, a man of secular conduct, led the Frankish army against Williarius among the Suebi, where a very great slaughter took place, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 712 [Col. 0119B].

Childebert, king of blessed memory, died after reigning thirteen years. He was buried at the monastery of Clichy, in the basilica of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. His son Dagobert, still a child, assumed the kingdom.

Grimoald, mayor of the palace, was a modest and just man. He had taken Theudesinda, daughter of Duke Ratbod, as his wife; by another woman he had had Theudoald.

When Pippin, his father, was ill and Grimoald had come to visit him, he was killed by the pagan Frisian Rangar in the basilica of Saint Lambert. His father appointed Theudoald to the dignity held by his deceased father, at Leodidicum, in April of the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 714 [Col. 0119C].

Not long afterward Pippin, his father, died in the same year, in mid-December. He had held the chief power under the kings named above for twenty-seven years.

Hechbert, a holy man of the English nation, a pilgrim for the heavenly homeland and adorning Christ’s priesthood, converted by pious preaching many provinces of the Scottish people to the canonical observance of Easter, from which they had long strayed. This occurred in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 715.

### [717]

The emperor Theodosius, for one year. Having been elected emperor, he defeated Anastasius in a serious battle near the city of Nicaea. After Anastasius had given him an oath, Theodosius had him ordained a presbyter.

Once he had received the kingdom, since he was a catholic, he restored to its former place in the imperial city the venerable image depicting the six holy synods, which Philippicus had cast down [Col. 0119D].

The river Tiber left its channel and rose so high that it overflowed the public road to a depth of one and a half men’s heights, causing much destruction in the city of Rome. Finally, from the gate of Saint Peter to the Milvian Bridge, the descending waters joined together. The flood remained for seven days. While the citizens were conducting frequent litanies, it receded on the eighth day.

At that time many of the English people from Britain, inflamed by divine love, were especially eager to come to Rome and there receive the clerical tonsure as a sign of their religious devotion.

At that time also the reverend Abbot Geolfrid, aged seventy-eight, who had been a priest for forty-eight years and an abbot for twenty-five, died when he reached Langres and was buried in the church of the blessed twin martyrs [Col. 0120A].

Charles, son of Pippin by another wife, had been captured by Plectrude, Pippin’s former wife, and was being held in custody, but escaped with the Lord’s help. The Saxons devastated the land of the Matuarii. Eoldus was already regarded as bishop of Vienne.

### [718]

The emperor Leo, for nine years. The Saracens came to Constantinople with an immense army and besieged the city for three years. At last, while the citizens cried out to God with great persistence, many of the Saracens perished from hunger, cold, and pestilence, and the rest, weary of the siege, withdrew.

After returning from there, they attacked in war the Bulgarian people who live beyond the Danube [Col. 0120B]. They were defeated by them as well, fled, and returned to their ships. As they were heading out to sea, a sudden storm arose, and many were killed when their ships sank or were smashed along the shores.

When King Leutprand heard that the Saracens, after devastating Sardinia, had also profaned the place where the bones of the blessed bishop Augustine had once been transferred and honorably buried because of the devastation of the barbarians, he sent men, paid for them, obtained them, and transferred them to Pavia. There he reburied them with fitting honor in the monastery called the Golden Cell, which he himself had built.

At that time Saint Bishop Eoldus increased the resources of the Church of Vienne. He was related to the Frankish kings, and within the city he also constructed a small crypt—so the text reads, *crypatim*—in honor of the blessed Theban martyrs, Maurice and his companions [Col. 0120C]. There he deposited a considerable portion of the relics, both of those martyrs and of others.

From that time the property of the Church was assigned to the name of Saint Maurice, whereas from ancient times both the principal building was associated with the honor of the seven Maccabean martyrs and the resources of that same church were offered and remained consecrated by the faithful under their name.

King Dagobert died after reigning five years. In those days, shortly beforehand, the Franks had fallen upon one another in mutual slaughter and, by fiercely pursuing Theudoald, son of the just Grimoald, driven him into flight. They elected Raganfrid as mayor of the palace.

The Franks established in the kingdom a certain cleric named Daniel, after objecting to his tonsure, and called him Chilperic. They mobilized an army against Charles as far as the river Meuse [Col. 0120D]. From the other side Duke Ratbod rose against that same Charles with the Frisians. A fierce battle was fought with the Frisians, and Charles, afflicted by heavy losses, fled.

Ratbod reached Cologne, devastating everything along the way, in July of the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 715. Chilperic, together with Raganfrid, entered the forest of the Ardennes with a large army and reached the Rhine and the city of Cologne. They received much treasure from Plectrude, ravaged the land, and returned to Amblève. But Charles suddenly fell upon them, and their forces suffered enormous losses.

Again Charles marched with an army against Chilperic and Raganfrid [Col. 0121A]. They, for their part, prepared for battle and hastened to meet him at a place called Vinchy, on Sunday at daybreak during Lent, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 717.

Chilperic and Raganfrid were put to flight, and victory belonged to Charles. Charles came to Cologne, recovered his father’s treasures from Plectrude, and appointed Chlothar as king.

Chilperic and Raganfrid sought the aid of Duke Eudo against him. Charles marched fearlessly against them. Eudo fled to Paris. Chilperic, taking the royal treasures, escaped beyond the Loire into Aquitaine. King Chlothar died that year.

After Bishop Eoldus, Eobolinus succeeded as bishop of Vienne. Ostrebertus, a vigorous and noble man, succeeded him as bishop [Col. 0121B]. He was buried at a certain estate of his own called Julidiac, not far from the river Seine.

Charles sent an embassy to Eudo and established friendly relations with him. Eudo returned King Chilperic to him with many gifts. But Chilperic did not remain long in the kingdom. He died and was buried in the city of Noyon. He had reigned for more than five years.

The Franks established Theodoric, son of the younger Dagobert, as king over themselves.

Charles, mayor of the palace and prince of the Austrasians, ravaged everything and plundered the fields of the Saxons, reaching the Weser. Duke Ratbod of the Frisians died, and Charles went to war against the Saxons. There was a very great slaughter of men on both sides.

After several years Charles set out for Bavaria and, with the greatest difficulty, compelled the Bavarians to submit [Col. 0121C]. When they resisted again, he confronted them once more and subdued them a second time through the strength of his army.

Again he went into Saxony, and then to the Suebi against Lantfrid, whom he restrained from excessive aggression. From there he mobilized an army against Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, and, having put Eudo to flight, pursued him as far as Gascony.

The Saracens, with many forces and a great number of ships, devastated far and wide many cities both of Septimania and of the province of Vienne. Charles led an expedition against them and, after heavily defeating them, drove them back into Spain. The engagement took place in October. After fighting other battles in various regions, he again marched several years later as far as Gascony and ravaged Aquitaine.

After Eudo died, he took up arms against Eudo’s sons and afflicted them severely. But as the fighting shifted from side to side, with many being killed on both sides, they eventually made a treaty that would not last long.

The Saracens devastated almost all Aquitaine and, overcoming other provinces far and wide with fire and sword, plundered Burgundy with the most savage violence. They burned almost everything in flames, profaned monasteries and sacred places, drove away an innumerable population, and transported them into Spain [Col. 0121D].

Charles again undertook an expedition against them. Resisting them with a strong hand, he killed a great multitude and forced the survivors to flee; only a few of them escaped.

Wilicarius succeeded the venerable Bishop Ostrebertus at Vienne [Col. 0122A]. Because of the devastation caused by the Saracens—the very splendid house of the martyrs beyond the Rhône having already been burned by them—he transferred the bones of the blessed Ferreolus and the head of the martyr Julian within the city. He built a church for them with rapid workmanship and at little expense, and reverently placed the relics of those same martyrs there.

When the Franks, with a sufficiently furious and insane policy, began diverting the sacred property of the churches to their own uses, Wilicarius saw his Church of Vienne being dishonorably humbled. He abandoned the episcopate and entered the monastery of the holy martyrs of Agaunum, where he led a venerable life.

After the provinces of Vienne and Lyon had been ravaged and laid waste, both Churches remained for several years without bishops, while laymen sacrilegiously and barbarously took possession of the sacred property of the churches [Col. 0122B].

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 751, Charles, son of Pippin and duke of the Franks, died. His authority was held by Carloman and his brother Pippin. Childeric was installed in the Frankish kingdom.

[727] Constantine the emperor, for twenty-six years. Carloman and Pippin led an army against Hunald, duke of Aquitaine, and captured a fortress called Lucas. On that very march, at a place called Vetus Pictavus, they divided the kingdom of the Franks between themselves. In the same year Carloman devastated Alamannia. Carloman and Pippin engaged in battle with Odilo, duke of Bavaria. In the same year Carloman fought with the Saxons and captured the fortress called Hocseoburg; by negotiation he won over the Saxon Theotecnus, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 743.

Again Pippin and Carloman undertook a campaign in Saxony, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 744, and the Saxon Theoderic was captured. The following year they undertook no campaign, because Carloman had resolved to abandon secular military service; in that same year he prepared for his journey, and his brother Pippin prepared himself honorably to serve him, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 746.

Carloman went to Rome according to his vow, was tonsured there, and built a monastery on Mount Sarepta in honor of Saint Sylvester. There he lived for some time in the monastic habit [Note: Regino, book II, says that he patiently endured frequent slaps and beatings from the cook.]. From there, coming to Saint Benedict on Monte Cassino, he joined the monks.

Grifo fled from before Duke Pippin into Saxony. Pippin set out through Thuringia, entered Saxony, and reached the River Missaha at a place called Scaamgi. Grifo gathered a multitude of Saxons around him on the River Oacrus, at a place called Horahim; Pippin pursued him there as well. But Grifo took flight and reached Bavaria, bringing the duchy itself under his control; he captured and subdued Tassilo and Iltrude. Swidger came to his aid.

When Pippin heard this, he set out after him, captured Grifo, and brought him back with Lanfrid and Swidger. He placed Tassilo in the duchy of Bavaria and entrusted Bavaria to him as a benefice. To Grifo he also gave twelve counties in the region of Austria. Thereafter Grifo fled and joined Waifarius, son of Hunald and duke of Aquitaine; together they began a rebellion against Pippin.

Meanwhile, while forces were being assembled, Pippin sent Utgard, bishop of Würzburg, and his chaplain Fulrad to Zacharias, then pope of Rome, to ask him whether the kings of the Franks ought to remain in office when they possessed almost no power and were content with the royal title alone. Pope Zacharias replied that the one who governed the state ought rather to be called king.

When the envoys returned, and Childeric—who then held the royal title—had been deposed, the Franks, on the advice of the envoys and by the decision of Pope Zacharias, established Pippin as their king. Childeric was tonsured and sent to a monastery.

Soon afterward Pippin, having become king of the Franks, undertook war against Saxony. In this campaign Bishop Childegarius was killed by the Saxons in a fortress called Witbergh. Victorious, Pippin reached a place called Rhime. On his return he was informed that his brother Grifo, while attempting to enter Italy, had been killed near Morivennum. Although he was a traitor to his homeland, he grieved deeply over his death.

After Pope Zacharias died, Stephen succeeded him. At that time Saint Boniface, archbishop, governed the Church of Mainz. This venerable preacher converted a very great multitude of Frisians to Christ. Wilicarius, having left the see of Vienne, first went to Rome, where he became known to Pope Stephen; after not much time had passed, he took charge of the monastery of Agaunum.

Aistulf, king of the Lombards, in great treachery violated the charters of gifts previously granted to blessed Peter and gave the possessions of the Roman Church to his soldiers. Under this pressing necessity, Pope Stephen came to Pippin in Francia to seek aid. Carloman, Pippin’s brother, also came to Francia, reportedly agreeing with Aistulf’s plan and with the counsel of his abbot that Stephen’s petition should be rejected.

Pope Stephen anointed Pippin king and likewise anointed both his sons, Charles and Carloman. Blessed Boniface, archbishop, while preaching the word of God in Frisia, completed his martyrdom.

After his apostolic anointing, King Pippin hurried into Italy with an army. Passing through the city of Vienne, he sent his brother Carloman, now a monk, there together with Queen Bertruda. Carloman fell ill and died there.

When Aistulf heard of King Pippin’s arrival, he closed and blocked the passes and came with the Lombards to meet Pippin. But King Pippin pressed forward in battle and, with the assistance of blessed Peter, entered Italy. He sent Pope Stephen back to his own see through Fulrad and other officers, while he himself besieged Pavia, where Aistulf had shut himself in.

Seeing that he could not escape, Aistulf promised to restore everything to blessed Peter and the Roman Church. He therefore gave forty hostages together with an oath and was released from the siege. King Pippin returned to Francia. But Aistulf, being treacherous, lied about everything.

For this reason King Pippin entered Italy again and besieged Pavia, shutting Aistulf inside. Aistulf, compelled once more by an oath, pledged firmly that he would return everything. In addition, King Pippin handed over Ravenna and the whole Pentapolis to the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

After King Pippin had returned, Aistulf suddenly died, struck down by divine judgment in his veins [Note: Something appears to be missing.]. After some time, Desiderius succeeded to the Lombard kingdom.

The Emperor Constantine sent gifts to King Pippin, including a musical organ, and established peace with the Franks.

While King Pippin was holding an assembly at Compiègne, Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, came to him there and commended himself to him as a vassal. He swore over the bodies of the holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, and likewise over the bodies of the holy confessors Martin and Germanus, that throughout all the days of his life he would preserve complete faith and submission toward the king and his sons.

This took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 758. All the leading men of Bavaria, together with Tassilo, were bound by the oaths they had sworn.

Berteric, a simple man, undertook the governance of the Church of Vienne. After him came Bishop Proculus, likewise innocent and of simple character.

King Pippin entered Saxony again, gained control of all the Saxon strongholds, and subdued the Saxon people with a great slaughter, to such an extent that he imposed upon them an annual tribute of three thousand horses to be brought each year to the Franks.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 759, a son was born to King Pippin, and the father ordered that he too be called Pippin. He died in the third year after his birth.

Waifarius, duke of Aquitaine, invaded in Aquitaine all the possessions of the churches that belonged by right to the Franks. For this reason King Pippin set out and reached a place called Todoat. There Waifarius, through his envoys, promised that he would restore everything. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 760, after receiving hostages, the king returned. Waifarius made the promise but did not fulfill it at all.

King Pippin returned again, and his son Charles accompanied him. He captured many fortresses of the Aquitanians—Burbontis, Cantela, and Clarimontis, the last of which he burned. He reached as far as Limoges, devastating the land and pursuing Waifarius.

On his third journey into Aquitaine he captured the city of Bourges and the fortress of Toartis. On his fourth journey into Aquitaine he held his assembly at Nevers. From there Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, abandoning his oaths and setting aside his kinship—for he was the king’s nephew—withdrew from that expedition and returned to Bavaria. King Pippin nevertheless traversed Aquitaine as far as Cahors.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 765 he undertook his fifth journey into Aquitaine and held his assembly at Orléans. He rebuilt the fortress of Argenton, which Waifarius had shortly before destroyed, placing Franks there for its defense. Likewise, at the city of Bourges, he stationed an army for its defense.

At that time, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 767, a synod was held, and a dispute was debated between the Greeks and the Romans concerning the Trinity: whether, just as the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, it also proceeds from the Son; and concerning the holy images, whether they ought to be fashioned or painted in churches.

On his sixth journey into Aquitaine he captured many extremely well-fortified places and reached the Garonne. Returning to Bourges, he received envoys announcing the death of Paul, the Roman pontiff.

On his seventh journey into Aquitaine, passing through Vienne, where after several years he then gave the bishopric of Vienne to a certain Berteric, a member of the Church’s household, he reached Saintes. Waifarius’s mother, sisters, and nieces were captured. Thus the king plundered everything as far as the Garonne.

After some time had passed, he again crossed into Aquitaine with Queen Bertruda and killed Waifarius, duke of Aquitaine, near Périgueux. After the victory he returned to Saintes, where he had left the queen, and began to fall ill. From there he went for the sake of prayer to Saint Martin.

He also reached Saint-Denis and died there on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 768. He had reigned a little more than eighteen years from the day of his anointing.

His illustrious sons, Charles and Carloman, were raised to the kingship of the Franks: Charles at the city of Noyon, and Carloman at Soissons.

King Charles entered Aquitaine against the rebellious Hunold. He sent his envoys to Lupus, duke of the Gascons, and the aforesaid Hunold was brought from there. Together with his wife Bertha, he proceeded through Bavaria into Italy.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 771, Carloman died at a villa called Salmontiacus, on the day before the Nones of December. His wife, however, entered Italy with some Franks. The more distinguished Franks, together with the bishops and counts, commended themselves to the illustrious King Charles.

The illustrious King Charles completely destroyed the Saxon temple of Ardurmensul. When the army was suffering from severe thirst there, at midday an immense quantity of water suddenly flowed from a certain stream, enough for the entire army and their animals.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 774, Peter, an envoy of the Roman Church, came from Pope Adrian to the illustrious Charles. Since the land routes had been closed by the Lombards, he came by sea as far as the port of Marseilles, requesting aid against Desiderius, king of the Lombards.

The pious King Charles reached Genoa. There he divided his army and sent part of it through the Cottian Alps and across the Ghibennian passes—that is, over the mountain which the inhabitants call Cenis—and whose slopes open onto the fields of Turin.

King Desiderius had then drawn up his army near the Lombard passes. But, unable to withstand the attack of the Franks, Desiderius himself fled to Pavia. The pious King Charles followed Desiderius through the open passes and besieged the city itself.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 774, the pious King Charles went to Rome. Returning from there, he captured Pavia and took for himself and his people King Desiderius, his wife, his daughter, and his treasure. He subdued all the Lombards, capturing their cities and plundering everything throughout Italy.

Adalgis, the son of Desiderius, escaped by flight and reached Constantinople by ship. After organizing Italy, King Charles returned to Francia.

Meanwhile, while the king was in Italy, the Saxons came out with an army against the Frankish garrisons and besieged a certain fortress, Buriaburg. They attempted from outside the fortress to burn a church which blessed Boniface the martyr had consecrated. Suddenly, however, two youths of wondrous brightness and radiance appeared, seen by both Christians and pagans, who seemed to be defending the church. Terrified by their dreadful appearance, the Saxons turned to flight, and thus that fortress was freed from the siege.

When King Charles reached a place called Ingilinham, he sent four divisions into Saxony, and by God’s help they were victorious. The glorious King Charles captured the fortress of Sigiburg in Saxony and rebuilt Eresburg above the River Weser, at a place called Brunisberg. Thus the Franks gained possession of both banks, after the Saxons had been put to flight and partly killed.

The glorious King Charles traversed Saxony and other peoples as far as the River Oboacrus, received hostages, and returned to Francia.

When he learned that the Lombard Rothgaud had turned traitor, he returned to Italy in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 776. After killing Rothgaud, he took possession of Friuli, Treviso, and other cities and entrusted them to the Franks for defense.

The Saxons attacked and destroyed the fortress of Heresburg. But when they were preparing siege engines, stone-throwers, and wicker screens in order to seize another fortress, two flaming spheres appeared above the church within that fortress, in the form of a shield, in full view of the enemy. Terrified by this vision, the Saxons abandoned all their preparations and fled so wildly that they cut one another down with their swords.

The glorious King Charles attacked the Saxons again, gained possession of all their strongholds, traversed the whole region where the Lippe rises, and recovered all Saxony. After rebuilding the fortress of Heresburg on the Lippe, he joined the Saxons, together with their wives and children, to himself through baptism in the faith. He held a general assembly at Paderborn, attended by both Franks and Saxons.

Witiching, with some Saxons, fled as a rebel into Northmannia, requesting their aid against the glorious King Charles. For the baptized Saxons, freedom and allodial property strengthened the security of their faith, should they again lose Christianity and relapse into treachery.

After celebrating Easter in Aquitaine, at a villa called Canssinogilo, the glorious King Charles entered Spain in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 778.

Earlier, while he was still in Saxony, he had received an embassy from the Saracens. It included Ibinalaribi and the son of Devisfexi, who is called Joseph in Latin.

After destroying Pamplona, he joined together at Zaragoza an army from Burgundy, Bavaria, Septimania, and Lombardy. Having received hostages from Ibinilaram and Abutaurus, and having subdued other Saracens, the Navarrians, and the Gascons, he returned to Francia [Note: Turpin, archbishop, wrote that the walls of Pamplona collapsed at Charles’s arrival, chapter 3 of *The Life of Charlemagne and Roland*.].

After several years he entered Rome for the sake of prayer. There Pope Adrian received Charles’s son Pippin from the sacred font, and Charles’s two sons were inaugurated as kings.

At Milan, his daughter Gissa was baptized and received by Bishop Thomas, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 783.

Queen Hildegard died on the day before the Kalends of May, on the vigil of the Ascension of the Lord, at a villa called Theudone.

The war against the Saxons therefore continued over a period of years, since they frequently relapsed into treachery, while the most valiant king, together with the Franks, repeatedly crushed them almost to extermination (Regino, book II of the *Annals*).

Witiching and Albi, with their companions, who had long incited the Saxons to rebellion, were received upon the giving of hostages. The pious king most generously pardoned their treachery, and, having been baptized at Attigny, they brought great peace to the region.

When King Charles was staying near Rome, Arichis, duke of Benevento, sent his son Romold with rich gifts, requesting that he not enter the duchy of Benevento. But since Arichis was suspected of disloyalty, the glorious King Charles set out for Benevento.

At his arrival Duke Arichis abandoned Benevento and shut himself up at Salerno, fearing to see the king’s face. He gave two sons as hostages, Romold and Grimold, whom he had still kept with him, together with very rich gifts.

After receiving the hostages, the pious King Charles returned, having bound the Beneventans by an oath. After celebrating Easter with the holy Roman pontiff, he also received the envoys sent by Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, whose treachery was widely reported.

After some time, Tassilo, surrounded on every side by royal armies, came—willingly or unwillingly—to the public assembly of the Franks and of the other peoples already placed under their authority, at a villa called Ingilena. He was brought into the midst of the assembly, and when criminal charges were brought against him, he himself publicly confessed his perjuries. He was condemned to death, together with his son Theudo.

But the most merciful king granted him his life. They were tonsured and confined in a monastery to do penance, while he sent several Bavarians into exile on account of their treachery.

The Greeks fought with the Lombards, and likewise with the Avars and the Franks who lived in Italy; there was also fighting between the Bavarians and the Taurians. In all these conflicts victory belonged to the Franks.

Again, when the Avars, together with the Bavarians who were subject to the Franks, were preparing to fight, they were cut down in a very great slaughter. Most of them were swept away by the River Danube and killed there.

The most excellent King Charles established bridges over the River Elbe and built fortresses at the head of the bridge on both sides. He subdued the Slavs whose name is Wlizi. He already possessed other Slavs called the Surbi, as well as the Abodrites; their prince was Wtizam.

The fierce nation of the Avars, extremely hostile to the borders of Bavaria, had savagely plundered and devastated churches and towns near its own frontier. Fearing the pious and glorious king and dreading his army, they abandoned their strongholds and garrisons and escaped by flight, leaving their former territory.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 792, Felix, bishop of Orléans, was detected teaching that our Lord Jesus Christ was the adoptive, not the proper, Son of God. He was brought before Adrian, the Roman pontiff, and verbally renounced the heresy alone.
