A synod was again held against the aforesaid heresy at Frankfurt, with the legates of the Apostolic See presiding, the bishops Theophylact and Stephen. By the authority of the holy Fathers, Felix was again convicted and condemned together with his error, and was banished into perpetual exile at Lyon. It is said that he died in that very error of his.

But the pseudo-synod which the Greeks call the Seventh Synod was utterly rejected because it supported the adoration of images.

Tudun, prince of the Avars, came to the pious King Charles. Believing with his people, he was baptized, received royal gifts, and returned faithful.

Likewise Herric, duke of Friuli, after the Avars had been defeated and killed in civil war among themselves, sent Wonomir to plunder Clavobringum of the Avar people, long previously at peace. He carried away the treasures that had been collected there over a long period and later sent them to the pious King Charles.

The king gave thanks to God and sent part of the treasure to the memorial shrine of the holy apostles; he distributed another part among the royal officials and the churches.

Pope Adrian died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 796. As soon as Leo succeeded him, he sent envoys to the pious King Charles and dispatched the keys of the confession of Saint Peter together with the banner of the city of Rome.

King Pippin, whom his father had established in Italy, set out with an army into Pannonia and, returning victorious, brought his father part of the treasure that remained.

The city of Barcelona, which had defected from the Franks, was restored to them through the Saracen Zatus. For he came to the pious king and surrendered the city of Semeth together with it.

Louis, son of the great prince Charles, was sent into Spain, and with him went the Saracen Abdella, son of Zathibinmauge, king, because his brother, expelled from Mauretania, had commended himself to the pious King Charles.

Another son, Pippin, was appointed to organize Italy.

The Nortluidi, who lived beyond the Elbe, seized the royal envoys who were then staying among them to administer justice. They killed some of them and held others for ransom.

Afterward they drew up their battle line against Trassuc, duke of the Abodrites, and Heburis, the Frankish envoy. Four thousand of the Nortluidi were killed in that place; the rest, requesting peace, surrendered themselves.

At that time Ursus governed the Church of Vienne, while Ado governed the Church of Lyon. After Ado, his nephew Ilduin held the Church of Lyon for a short time, though not as bishop; then, withdrawing, he adopted the monastic way of life in the monastery on the island of Lérins.

After Ursus, a bishop of excessive simplicity, Wlferi—whom the Bavarians called Wltreia by his native name—assumed the bishopric of Vienne.

[799]

Leidradus, a man deeply devoted to secular dignity and useful to the honor of the state, governed the Church of Lyon. Wlferi governed the Church of Vienne for eleven years.

The Emperor Constantine was captured and blinded by his own people. His mother Irene, residing at Constantinople, ruled as empress for eight years afterward. She sent an embassy to the excellent King Charles to preserve peace.

The star called Mars could not be seen that year from the month of July until the following July.

The Balearic Islands were plundered by the Moors and Saracens.

King Alfonso of Galicia and Asturias, after plundering Lisbon, the farthest city of Spain, sent the glorious King Charles, through envoys, the insignia of victory, many coats of mail, mules, and Moorish captives.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 799, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, during the greater litany, the Romans captured and blinded Pope Leo and, as is reported, cut out his tongue. He was then placed under guard, but at night escaped over a wall to the church of blessed Peter, where Frankish envoys happened to be present.

From there he was first taken to Spoleto and then to the glorious King Charles in Saxony, at a place called Paderborn. He was received there with honor and sent back to Rome with the same honor.

The Avar nation, having fallen back into treachery, ambushed and killed Herric, duke of Friuli, near Tarsatica, a city of Liburnia.

Gerald, prefect of Bavaria, was also killed after engaging the Avars in battle.

But the Balearic Islands, which had been plundered by the Moors and Saracens, received aid from the Franks and likewise surrendered themselves.

The standards and weapons of the Britons, inscribed with the names of their commanders, were brought to the glorious King Charles by Wido the Margrave, who had traversed the whole of Britain and received its submission. Thus the whole of Britain was then subjected to the Franks for the first time.

The glorious King Charles received from the patriarch of Jerusalem a blessing of relics from the Lord’s tomb and sent very great gifts through the priest Zacharias from Jerusalem to the holy places.

Queen Leutgardis died at Tours on the day before the Nones of June and was buried there.

After this the distinguished King Charles entered Italy and went to Rome for the sake of prayer. Pope Leo met him twelve miles from the city and received him with the greatest honor on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December.

For seven days, therefore, he worked to expose the things that had been wrongly done there. Pope Leo also spent a long time addressing the accusations brought against him. After he had refuted his accusers, he mounted the ambo and, placing his hands upon the holy Gospel in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, in the presence of the people, invoked the name of the Holy Trinity by oath and satisfied everyone, in their sight and hearing, that he was not conscious of the crime with which he had been falsely charged.

On the same day the envoy Zacharias, returning from Jerusalem, was received, together with the patriarch’s envoys. They carried the keys of the Lord’s tomb, as well as those of the city and Mount Olivet, and also the banner of the city.

On the holy day of the Lord’s Nativity, before the confession of the apostle Peter, when the glorious King Charles had risen from prayer, Pope Leo placed a crown upon his head. Thus the whole Roman people acclaimed him:

“Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor of the Romans, life and victory.”

When the acclamations had been completed, the pope worshiped him according to the custom of the ancient rulers. The title of patrician, which he had first received in that city, having been removed, he was called Emperor and Augustus. The pontiff then entered for Mass with his clergy.

[800]

Charles the emperor, first of the Frankish nation, for forty-five years.

After he had entered Rome and assumed the title of emperor and Augustus, he ordered those who had insulted Pope Leo by deposing and humiliating him in such a dishonorable and indecent manner to be brought before him. After an inquiry had been held, they were condemned to death under Roman law as guilty of treason against the majesty of the state.

Nevertheless, the pope and pontiff most graciously interceded for their lives. At his request the emperor pardoned their lives and limbs, but they were driven into exile on account of the enormity of their crime. The leader of this faction was Paschalis the Nomenclator.

After arranging both private and public affairs, he left Rome on the seventh day before the Kalends of May and came to Spoleto.

An earthquake occurred on the day before the Kalends of May, at the second hour of the night. It shook almost the whole of Italy, so violently that the roof of the blessed apostle Paul, with its beams, fell for the most part, and cities and mountains collapsed in certain regions. This earthquake also shook many places in Gaul and Germany.

A terrible pestilence also arose because of the mildness of the winter.

An elephant, together with other gifts, was sent by the Persian king Aaron Amiralinus to the emperor through envoys.

The city of Barcelona in Spain, after being besieged for two years, was captured, together with its prefect Zatus and many other Saracens. In Italy, the city of Theare was likewise captured and taken by assault, and its prefect Roselmus was also seized.

On the same day Zatus and Roselmus were brought before the emperor and sent into exile.

The Empress Irene again sent an embassy to Emperor Charles to establish peace between the Franks and the Greeks.

The city of Hortona in Italy surrendered. Luceria, too, worn down by a frequent siege, surrendered.

Winusus, who was in command of the garrison at Spoleto, was captured after being weakened by illness and besieged by Grimoald, duke of Benevento. Grimoald nevertheless treated him honorably and later returned him to the emperor.

[803]

Around the palace at Aachen, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 803, an earthquake occurred, followed by a deadly pestilence.

Irene was deposed from the empire, and Nicephorus was made emperor at Constantinople. He sent back his envoys together with the envoys of Emperor Charles. For Emperor Charles had sent Jesse, bishop of Amiens, and Count Elingaud to Constantinople.

The envoys received a letter from Emperor Nicephorus entitled “Concerning a Peace Treaty,” and they returned to Constantinople under such an agreement.

Godefrid, king of the Danes, promised that he would first come to meet the emperor. But, frightened by the counsel of his own men, he sent the emperor, through envoys, whatever message he wished to convey.

The emperor transferred to Francia all the Saxons who lived beyond the Elbe and in Wihmodia, together with their women and children.

[804] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 804, Pope Leo of Rome came to Francia and was received in the city of Rheims. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord with him at the estate of Carisiacum; afterward, at Aachen, he had him escorted as far as Ravenna, wishing to proceed through Bavaria and having bestowed great gifts upon him. The reason for his arrival was that the emperor had sent to him to investigate the truth of the matter—whether, as was being reported, the blood of Christ had been found in the city of Mantua. The pontiff therefore took the opportunity and went into Lombardy, ostensibly for the investigation; from there he proceeded as far as the emperor.

Theodorus, prince of Capua and leader of the Huns, because of the attacks of the Slavs—for he himself was a Christian—asked the emperor to grant him a place to settle between Savaria and Carnuntum. The emperor received him kindly and, granting his request, allowed him to return after presenting him with gifts.

The emperor divided the kingdoms among his sons, so that each might know, if he survived, which portion he ought to defend and govern. A testament was then drawn up and confirmed by oath by the leading men of the Franks, and it was sent to Pope Leo for him to sign with his own hand.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 806, a fleet commanded by the patrician Nicetas was sent by the emperor Nicephorus to recover Dalmatia. There was an eclipse of the moon on the fourth day before the Nones of September, with the sun standing in the sixteenth degree of Virgo and the moon in the sixteenth degree of Pisces. In that same year, on the day before the Ides of February, when the moon was in its seventeenth day, the star called Jupiter was seen to pass across it. On the third day before the Ides of February there was an eclipse of the sun at midday, with both heavenly bodies standing in the twenty-fifth degree of Aquarius. In that same year the moon was darkened three times and the sun once, and formations of extraordinary size were seen.

Ratbert, the emperor’s envoy, who was returning from the East, died together with the envoys of the king of the Persians. The gifts that the envoys brought to the emperor were as follows: a pavilion and awnings for the courtyard, made of fine linen and of varied colors, together with ropes arranged in an equal order; many silken and costly cloaks; balsam, perfumes, and ointments (Regino, *Annals*). There was also a clock wonderfully constructed of bronze by mechanical art, in which the course of the twelve hours was regulated by a water-clock, with an equal number of bronze balls that fell when the hours were completed and, by their fall, caused a cymbal placed beneath them to ring. In the same clock there were also riders of the same number, who emerged through twelve windows when the hours were complete and, by the force of their exit, closed the same number of windows that had previously been open. Many other marvelous features were also present in that clock.

At that time the bones of the blessed Cyprian were brought from Carthage, together with the relics of the blessed Scillitan martyrs, Speratus and his companions, and were placed in the church of the blessed John the Baptist in the city of Lyon.

The Saracens, driven from Sardinia, first engaged the Sardinians in battle; after losing three thousand of their men, they reached Corsica by a direct course. There they fought against the fleet commanded by Count Burgarius and were either defeated or put to flight, losing thirteen of their ships and having many of their men killed.

Godefrid, king of the Danes, also crossed into the territory of the Abodrites with an army. Although he had driven their duke Brasco from his position and had treacherously captured and hanged another duke, he nevertheless returned with great loss to his forces. For there he lost his brother’s son Raginold, who was killed, together with many leading Danes, while attacking a certain town.

The emperor Charles’s son crossed over, with the army under his command and with all possible speed, against the Linones and Smeldingi, who had defected to Godefrid. After ravaging their fields all around, he crossed the Elbe again and withdrew safely with his army into Saxony.

But Godefrid, having destroyed the trading settlement established on the coast of the Ocean, which in the Danish language was called Relic, and having transferred the merchants from there, set sail and came with his entire army to the harbor called Liesthorp. After remaining there for several days, he decided to fortify with a rampart the frontier of his kingdom facing Saxony, so that he could protect with a defensive wall the entire northern bank of the river Egidora, from the eastern inlet of the sea, which they call Hostharsaltia, to the western Ocean. Only one gate was left open, through which wagons and horsemen could be sent out and brought back in.

Eardof, king of the Northumbrians, driven from his kingdom in Britain, came to the emperor at Nijmegen. From there he proceeded to Rome and was later restored to his kingdom with the envoys of the emperor and the pontiff.

As the envoys were returning, Adulphus, a Saxon by nation and a deacon of Pope Leo, was captured by pirates. The others crossed without danger. Adulphus was taken back to Britain, ransomed by someone, and returned to Rome.

Trasco, duke of the Abodrites, gathered a strong force and, having also received assistance from the Saxons, attacked his neighbors the Scavi, who are called Wltzi (Wilzi); he devastated them with sword and fire. He captured their greatest city, Senelding, and by these successes compelled all who had defected from him to return to his alliance.

[809] A great synod was convened at Grainiacum in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 809. At this synod the question was discussed whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son in the same way as he proceeds from the Father. John, a monk of Jerusalem, had raised this question, although ecclesiastical rule and faith affirm that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, is neither created nor begotten, but is coeternal and consubstantial with the Father and the Son.

The name of the procession from the Father and the Son is stated so clearly in the Apocalypse: “And he showed me”—there is no doubt that the angel did so—“a river of the water of life, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb.”

At the same synod the state of the churches and the order of each one was also examined and debated, including the manner of life that the clergy of each ought to follow.

Trasco, duke of the Abodrites, was treacherously killed in the trading settlement of Relic by the companions of Godefrid. Aureolus, who resided at Nicomarcia in Spain and in Gaul beyond the Pyrenees, opposite Osca, near Zaragoza, also died. Amoroz invaded his office and stationed garrisons in his fortress. He wished to cross over to the emperor with his followers, but because of intervening circumstances the undertaking remained unfinished.

Pippin, king of Italy, prompted by the treachery of the Venetian dukes, ordered Venice to be attacked by land and sea. After Venice had been subjected and its dukes had submitted, he sent the same fleet to ravage the coast of Dalmatia. But when Paul, prefect of Cephalonia, arrived with the eastern fleet to bring aid to the Dalmatians, the royal fleet returned to its own territory.

Godefrid, king of the Danes, was killed by one of his own retainers, and Erming, his brother’s son, succeeded him in the kingdom. Pippin, king of Italy, died on the eighth day before the Ides of July, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 810.

Charles, emperor of the Franks, made peace with Nicephorus, emperor of Constantinople, and recovered Venice. Ambulaz, king of Córdoba in Spain, made a treaty with the emperor, while Abduram, his son, expelled Amoroz from Zaragoza and compelled him to enter Osca.

There were two eclipses of the sun and two of the moon that year: eclipses of the sun on the seventh day before the Ides of July and on the day before the Kalends of December; eclipses of the moon on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July and on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January.

The island of Corsica was ravaged by the Saracens. In the following year peace was arranged between the emperor and Herming, king of the Danes.

The great lighthouse that had been built for the guidance of sailors not far from the maritime city of Boulogne was restored, and a nighttime fire was lit there.

Charles, the emperor’s eldest son, died on the day before the Nones of December, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 811. Not long afterward Herming, king of the Danes, also died. In his place the Danes appointed Heriold and Ragamfrid as kings.

Nicephorus, emperor of Constantinople, after many notable victories, died in battle against the Bulgarians in the province of Moesia. His son-in-law Michael was made emperor in his place. His envoys, sent to Aachen to the emperor Charles, delivered the customary praises, calling him emperor and “Basileus.” Having received a document of peace from the emperor and again from Pope Leo at Rome, they returned.

Grimald, duke of Benevento, made an agreement on these terms: twenty-five thousand gold solidi were to be paid annually by the Beneventans to the Franks.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 813, after a general assembly had been summoned at Aachen, the emperor placed the imperial crown upon his son Louis, king of Aquitaine, and made him his associate in the imperial title. He also appointed his nephew Bernard, the son of Pippin of Italy, and ordered that he be called king.

He likewise decreed that councils should be held in five parts of his kingdom, to correct whatever required correction: at Mainz, Rheims, Tours, Chalon, and Arles. What was decreed can be found in the archives of the churches or of the palace.

The emperor Charles, a man energetic in every aspect of imperial administration, having enlarged the empire and established peace everywhere among the Franks, died at Aachen in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 814 and was buried there. He died in the forty-fifth year and more of his reign, in the thirteenth year after he had been acclaimed emperor.

Bernard was bishop of Vienne, and Leidrad was bishop of Lyon. At the beginning of the reign of the emperor Louis, Leidrad sought the position at the monastery of Soissons, and Agobard, chorepiscopus of the same church, was appointed bishop in his place, with the consent of the emperor and of the entire synod of the bishops of Gaul.

Some who wished to defend this action said that the same venerable Agobard had been ordained in the see of Lyon by three bishops at the command of Leidrad. But canonical authority declares that there must not be two bishops in one city and that, while a bishop is alive, he ought not to choose a successor for himself. Therefore, whatever the reason, the rules of the Church, established in so important an order, ought not to be disregarded.

[815] The emperor Louis, son of the emperor Charles, reigned for a little less than twenty-eight years. He was a lover of every form of piety and religion and adorned the entire ecclesiastical order throughout his realm with devout zeal. At the beginning of his imperial rule he enjoyed a second and peaceful tranquility; but its end was wearied by many troubles and adversities.

Among his other remarkable and most honorable works throughout his empire—in Gaul, Germany, and Italy alike—he appointed envoys to seek diligently the rights of the poor and oppressed and to hear fully the needs of each person. He also decreed that episcopal synods should be held everywhere to restore the statutes of the holy Fathers and to ensure observance of Christian rules.

Yet the plots of the wicked often sought to obstruct his pious efforts. For prolonged peace gives rise to treachery, treachery to rebellion, and rebellion to danger for the empire.

This most pious emperor had three sons by Queen Hermengarde. He enrolled the eldest, Chlothar, first as Caesar and then as his associate in the empire; he entrusted Italy to him for governance. He made Pippin king of Aquitaine and appointed the third, Louis, king in Bavaria.

When the entire power of the Franks was enjoying moderate leisure and imposing its rule upon neighboring peoples, certain men who could not endure so great a hope of good seized, through their faction, the emperor’s beloved wife Judith. They transferred her from her husband’s side to Aquitaine under guard.

Although she returned to her husband’s bed, the malice of certain men, boiling over, did not cease. It grew to such a degree that, together with the Roman pontiff, it stirred not only the nobles of the kingdom but also his sons against the emperor.

For the whole people defected from him and went over to his sons. He himself was held under guard, dishonorably confined, and deprived of his weapons; his wife was entrusted to be kept in Italy.

But by divine will, after so many adversities, better circumstances followed. The people turned to repentance, changed their course for the better, restored the same emperor to his former honor, and reinstated him in his former dignity. His sons also sought pardon for their offense. Chlothar, already emperor, was instructed not to proceed outside Italy under any circumstances except at the command of his most pious father.

But changing times threaten now adversity, now prosperity. After Pippin had finally died in those days, the emperor entered Aquitaine with the army, together with the wife whom he had already taken back and by whom he had fathered his illustrious son Charles, in order to settle Aquitaine. For against his will the Aquitanians had made Pippin, the son of Pippin, king for themselves.

While the emperor Louis was there, Louis, his third son by his first marriage, again turned against his father and compelled the leading men of Germany to swear loyalty to him.

When the emperor received news of this, he entrusted the kingdom of Aquitaine to the leading Franks, appointed his illustrious son Charles king of the Aquitanians, left his beloved wife there, and quickly went into Germany, transferring the forces of his army to meet his son.

There he arranged peace in the kingdom for several days. Then, worn down by ill health, he ended his last day in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 840.

His body was carried by Bishop Drogo, his brother by another mother, together with the leading men of the Franks, to Metz and was buried in the church of the blessed confessor Arnulf.

In the time of this emperor, part of the body of the blessed martyr Sebastian was brought to the city of Soissons; there many remarkable kinds of healing were bestowed upon the sick to the praise of almighty God.

The bones of the blessed martyrs Hippolytus and Tiburtius were also brought from Rome and buried with due honor in the church of the blessed martyr Dionysius in the territory of Paris.

Bernard and Agobard still governed the churches of Vienne and Lyon. Both were denounced before the emperor and, having abandoned their churches, went to Italy to join the emperor’s son Chlothar. Later, through the efforts of the pious emperors, Agobard recovered the see of Lyon and Bernard that of Vienne. After a few years Agobard died at Saintes while stationed there on a royal expedition.

[841] The emperor Lothar, son of the most pious emperor Louis, reigned for fifteen years. His father had designated the empire for him after his death. But because he followed evil counselors and seriously wounded his father’s spirit, he scarcely deserved to retain a portion of the kingdom intact.

Indeed, the pious father, remembering the wound inflicted upon him, divided the empire again and assigned the greater part to the younger Charles, after having the leading men confirm the arrangement by oath.

Thus, after the burial of his glorious father, Lothar left Italy in the following year and attempted to seize the empire. For this reason he stirred his brothers to battle against him at Fontenay.

Two joined against one, alas! and brought upon all Christians a lamentable war, both fraternal and civil. They were not distinguished by different weapons or by the dress of their peoples; they faced one another only in opposing camps.

An innumerable multitude of Franks was struck down by the sword, and the people once feared by other nations raged in its own wound. Yet the bloody victory was credited to the two brothers. The third escaped and finally withdrew to the royal residence at Aachen.

Thereafter the glorious king and illustrious young Charles, not long afterward, vigorously hastened the enterprise he had begun together with his brother Louis, and drove his brother Lothar, the emperor, from Aachen.

Lothar, with excessive speed, advanced with his wife and sons as far as Lyon and Vienne. There he gathered his forces and halted for a short time.

As envoys traveled back and forth for a conference, the three brothers came to an island in the Seine. There they decided, under a certain agreement, to divide the empire among themselves.

Thus the emperor Lothar returned to Upper Francia. Afterward, when the empire had been divided, each of them proceeded to govern and administer his own portion.

Not long afterward Lothar sent his son Louis, whom he had made king in Italy, to Rome through his uncle Drogo, so that he might receive the imperial title. Pope Sergius, then pontiff, placed the crown upon him, and, with the whole people acclaiming him, he was hailed as emperor and Augustus.

When the emperor Lothar perceived that he was becoming ill, he divided the kingdom among his sons. He ordered that Charles, the younger, receive Provence and part of Burgundy; that Lothar, his middle son, receive his own seat; and that Louis, the emperor, receive Italy.

He himself entered the monastery of Prüm, relinquishing the temporal kingdom, having been tonsured and made a monk. After several days had passed, he died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 865, in the twenty-third year of his empire, and was reverently buried there by the brothers in the basilica of the holy Savior.

In the time of this emperor, the bones of the most blessed martyr Andeolus were found, through his own revelation, in a place called in ancient times Gentibus, situated in the parish of Viviers.

Bernard, bishop of Vienne, died during this emperor’s reign, and Aglimatus succeeded him in the bishopric of Vienne. Amulo also became bishop of Lyon.

Pope Gregory died, and Sergius was ordained in his place. After Sergius’s death, Leo succeeded him. When Leo died, Benedict was appointed to the apostolic see, though by then the emperor Lothar had already died.

During the reign of this emperor, Segar, duke of Benevento, was killed by his own men. The murderers received within the city of Benevento the Saracens whom the Beneventans had summoned.

## The Emperor Louis in Italy

After his father’s death, in the eighth year, when his younger brother Charles had died and been buried at Lyon in the monastery of Saint Peter, in the church of Saint Mary ever-virgin, Louis divided his dead brother’s kingdom with his brother Lothar.

He received part of Transjurane Burgundy together with Provence; King Lothar retained the remaining part for himself.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 851, at his father’s command, the emperor Louis moved an army into the duchy of the Beneventans against the Saracen garrisons. After killing the Saracen duke, Amalmater recovered Benevento.

But Lothar, his brother, deceived by evil counselors, wavered for a long time over the marriage of two women and nearly stirred the whole Church against himself. For this reason the two metropolitan bishops, Theutgaud of Trier and Gunthar of Cologne, were condemned by apostolic judgment. Synodal assemblies were subsequently summoned.

His distinguished uncle, King Charles, always wished to advise him with sound counsel; nevertheless, his youthful mind, rushing headlong toward pleasure, resisted. At last, wishing to prevail and acting without counsel, he entered Italy to go to his imperial brother and attacked Benevento.

The most pious King Charles consented to this journey, in the hope that, perhaps overcome at last by the counsel of the Roman pontiff, he would desist from his unlawful undertaking. Many bishops of Gaul, however, opposed him, fearing, touched by the Spirit of God, that a general danger would arise in the Church of God—lest the Roman pontiff, swayed by favoritism and departing from definitions of piety, inflict upon the Roman Church the wound of error.

He proceeded according to his own desire and did at the Roman Church what seemed right to him at the time. But on his return, stirred by false hopes and weakened by divine judgment, he reached the city of Piacenza, where he died and was buried in the church of the blessed martyr Antoninus.

In the year 862, they divided his kingdom and that of his glorious uncle among themselves.

But when the emperor Louis entered Benevento in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 868, he brought under his authority nearly all the castles and towns of the Beneventans that had withdrawn from the Franks and joined the Saracens. With God’s help, he cleansed and restored the holy places that the impious Saracens and treacherous Christians had polluted.

Pope Nicholas, a man distinguished in religion, died. He was buried in the courtyard before the doors of Saint Peter’s, not far from the remains of his predecessor Benedict. During his time the remains of the saints Eusebius and Pontianus were transferred to Vienne and reverently placed in the basilica of the apostles. Adrian succeeded him in the episcopal office.

The pious and illustrious King Charles fought against the Danes and Northmen for several years with varying results. He ordered a bridge of extraordinary strength to be built across the Seine against their attacks, with castles most skillfully founded at both ends, in which he stationed garrisons to guard the kingdom.

The zeal of this pious king for the administration of ecclesiastical affairs remained strong until this time. By Queen Ermentrude he had four sons: Louis, Charles, Carloman, and Lothar. Of these he offered two to God in clerical dress: Carloman and Lothar. But Lothar, a boy of good character, was carried off by premature death. Charles, also, a young man of sufficiently honorable appearance, already established as king of Aquitaine, died after first being troubled and dishonored by an unjust injury.

Thus, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 866, while that Charles, son of Louis, was reigning, two of his sons, as has been said, died: Lothar, the abbot, and Charles, king of the Aquitanians. His uncle Rodulf, his chief counselor and first man of the palace, also died, as did Rodulf, archbishop of the Aquitanians.

Two Aquitanian princes, Landric and Muno, fighting one another, killed each other. Robert and Ranulph, men of extraordinary power and courage in arms and themselves among the foremost leaders of the Northmen, were also killed by the sword.

Finally, Lothar, before the death of his father, the emperor Louis, was anointed by the emperor in his eighteenth year. By Ermengarde, the daughter of Hugh, he had three sons. When he divided his father’s kingdom with his brothers, he received the kingdom of the Romans, all Italy, the eastern part of Francia, and the whole of Provence.

Louis, apart from Noricum, which he already possessed, retained the kingdoms his father had given him: Alamannia, Thuringia, Austrasia, Saxony, and the kingdom of the Avars, that is, of the Huns.

Charles received half of western Francia, all Neustria, Brittany, and most of Burgundy; Gothia, Vasconia, and Aquitaine, after Pippin, the son of Pippin, had been removed from them and tonsured at the monastery of Saint Medard.

Pippin later escaped from there by flight, returned to Aquitaine, and remained hidden for a long time while fleeing. Again he was deceived by the faithlessness of the aforementioned Ranulph and brought to Charles; he was condemned to perpetual exile at Senlis.

Louis, king of Noricum, that is, of Bavaria, son of the emperor Louis, divided the kingdom among his sons in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 878—namely, Carloman, Louis, and Charles—while himself retaining authority over his sons.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 879 he departed this life. Since his son Charles had already died, his remaining sons divided his kingdom among themselves by equal allotment in the following year near the city of Amiens.

One of them, Louis, died three years later. But Charles, brother of that Louis and son of the emperor Louis, died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 877, leaving a son Louis, who received his paternal kingdom in that same year.

At that time Pope John came to Gaul. He stayed for a long time at the city of Troyes and held a synod of bishops. At it Immaurus, bishop of Laon (the printed name Davitti is uncertain), was granted the bishopric after his eyes had been torn out.

Louis, son of Charles, also left as heir to the kingdom the boy Charles who was called “the Simple.” Before he was captured, this Charles fathered Louis by Eadgifu, daughter of the king of the English.

# Martyrology of Saint Ado, Archbishop of Vienne, Revised from Manuscript Copies

By the work and study of Heribert Rosweyde of Utrecht, theologian of the Society of Jesus. Preceded by the Old Roman Martyrology, placed before his own work by Ado.

*(From the* Bibliotheca Patrum Maxima*.)*

[Col. 0139]

## Dedicatory Epistle

To His Holiness Our Lord Pope Paul V, Supreme Pontiff: blessings.

[Col. 0139] The Old Martyrology—that is, the Roman Martyrology—returns to Rome, most holy Father: the work once conceived at Rome, sent forth from Rome, and longing to return to Rome, its place of origin. Your predecessors collected it with the greatest care in the City, wrote it down with singular fidelity, and sent it, as a supreme benefaction, throughout the dioceses of the Roman world.

Indeed, a ray returns to the sun, a stream to its spring, a branch to its trunk, a star to the sky. It returns to Rome, where the hinge and head of the apostolic see turns; where the origin of truth and the head of faith are preserved, together with the teaching of the heavenly Master; where the school of piety flourishes; where the metropolis of the apostles shines; where the world’s brightest lamps, Peter and Paul, give light (Anacletus I, epistle 3; Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*; Sozomen, book III, chapter 7; Chrysostom, homily 31 on Romans VII).

It returns to him whose predecessors once gave it its origin, at the very beginning of the nascent Church: I mean Clement I, Roman pontiff, who first distributed notaries by regions, so that each might diligently and carefully investigate the deeds of the martyrs in his own district.

Thereafter Anterus faithfully placed the results of the investigation in the ecclesiastical archives. Fabian afterward took even greater care that nothing based on feigned faith should creep in, joining the discerning and trustworthy eyes of deacons to the notaries.

Just as no duty was more ancient among the prelates of the holy Roman Church than to gather the mighty deeds of the saints, so none could have been undertaken more gloriously than to commend to posterity the memory of those whose souls, received into heaven and blessed by the enjoyment of God, are proclaimed by miracles and attested by votive tablets. These accounts possess—I scarcely know what power—for arousing or increasing in the minds of the faithful the inward fervor of religion, as the holy Leo once wrote with distinction (Leo, sermon on Saint Lawrence; Ambrose, sermon 39, on Nazarius and Celsus).

For the instruction of God’s people, no form is more useful than the eloquence of the martyrs: its method is easy for exhortation and effective for persuasion, yet examples are stronger than words, and teaching by deeds is fuller than teaching by voice.

They also possess the greatest strength for implanting the faith of our forefathers in hearts from the beginning or for asserting it more firmly. “It is a matter of great danger,” says the great Ambrose, “if, after the oracles of the prophets, after the testimonies of the apostles, after the wounds of the martyrs, you presume to examine the ancient faith as though it were new; and, after such manifest leaders, remain in error; and, after the sweat of the dying, contend in idle disputation.”

If, then, the illustrious champion of the faith Athanasius once considered it a great gain and benefit that he remembered one Antony, what flames of faith, what sparks of virtue, will the many ranks of martyrs—arrayed in robes, clad in purple, and clothed in scarlet—arouse in human hearts as they serve beneath the radiant banner of one faith and are marked with diverse crowns of victory? What of the adorned ranks of so many confessors and virgins, divided into different cohorts and joyfully carrying different companies of virtues?

It therefore came about that, when the Acts of the martyrs, investigated with such care and diligence, written down by the notaries of the holy Roman Church, examined by the deacons, finally approved by the Roman pontiffs themselves, and stored in the archives of the Church, had grown to immense size, a brief Martyrology was compiled from them. In it, as Saint Gregory says, only the day and place of the passion were recorded, so that their memory might more easily be inserted into the sacred diptychs and commemoration of them might be made in the solemn celebrations of the Mass.

The archbishop of Vienne, Ado, when he was staying at Ravenna, occupied, as I believe, with ecclesiastical affairs, obtained this Martyrology from a certain holy bishop who had received it from the Roman pontiff. He judged that it should be placed before his own Martyrology, remembering what had once been written by Innocent I: “so that the other churches might draw from it, just as all waters proceed from their native spring, and so that they might remain pure and undefiled as they flowed through the various regions of the whole world” (Innocent I, epistle 25 to the Council of Chalcedon, in Augustine, epistles).

I now bring to Your Holiness this Old Roman Martyrology, which Pope Gregory the Great, writing to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, both desired and believed to be dispersed throughout the whole world.

I bring what Ado, eight hundred years ago, valued so highly that he considered it venerable and extremely ancient and proposed it to himself as though it were the first outline of his own work, which he would afterward paint in his own colors and illuminate with the splendor of light.

I bring what has remained hidden until this day—the object of such ardent desire to Cardinal Baronius that he wished records to remain as witnesses to his mind, by which he might encourage an editor and offer thanks in advance for the benefit.

I therefore bring this Martyrology to Your Holiness with greater confidence because it comes accompanied by the patronage of so many most distinguished men.

I have added the Martyrology of Ado himself, archbishop of Vienne, revised with such fidelity and care that I do not fear to assert that it differs little from the author’s pen and mind.

It was certainly in the interest of the Christian commonwealth that nothing should be read under the title of so great a man that was not his own; that nothing corrupted and sewn on by another hand should be circulated under his name; that posterity, following the authority of the man, should not weave cords of error; and that nothing should be taken away from Ado for which the unanimous testimony of the manuscripts provided the surest evidence.

Aloysius Lippomanus of Verona—first bishop of Verona, afterward of Bergamo, a most distinguished man and, together with his colleagues, president of the Council of Trent—once valued this matter so highly that he considered it dearer than gold.

All these things, therefore, I bring to the Roman See, most holy Father, to the one who once occupied it, Pope Theodore, to whom the African Fathers brought their own writings. They were entirely convinced that at the apostolic see there stood a great and inexhaustible spring, overflowing with streams for all Christians.

From it streams issue, abundantly watering the entire Christian world. In honor of the most blessed Peter, the Fathers also decreed for it every special reverence in investigating the matters of God. Such matters ought always and diligently—and especially, and with justice, by the apostolic summit itself—to be examined, since it is the ancient concern of that summit both to condemn what is evil and to approve what is worthy of praise.

Receive, therefore, most holy Father, these first fruits of the saints. Just as once, through the benefaction of Paul I, the sacred relics of the saints, when the cemeteries had collapsed through age, were distributed among titular churches, deaconries, and monasteries, so that they might be honored at altars and adorned with memorials, so may posterity speak of the benefaction of Paul V: that the hidden lives of the saints have been brought into the open and brought to light.

Thus I vow:

Your Holiness’s devoted son,  
**Heribert Rosweyde, S.J.**

[Col. 0141]

## Greetings to the Reader

[Col. 0141] I have reproduced this Old Roman Martyrology from the manuscript codex of Saint Pantaleon, the celebrated abbey at Cologne belonging to the family of Saint Benedict, which the Carthusian house of Cologne most graciously sent to me.

This had been prefixed to Ado’s Martyrology, to which Ado himself had once prefixed it, as his preface testifies. From that codex Jacobus Mosander, a religious of the Carthusian house of Cologne, reproduced Ado’s Martyrology some years ago, omitting this Old Roman Martyrology, though he left a great desire for it in the minds of learned men.

[Col. 0142] Although I possessed two manuscript codices of Ado’s Martyrology—of which I shall speak in the section on Ado himself—this Old Roman Martyrology appeared only in this third codex, that of Saint Pantaleon.

Therefore, if some error has crept in anywhere, remember how difficult it is to reproduce everything with complete fidelity from the authority of a single codex, whose text occasionally wavers. Certainly I took care that you should have everything with the greatest possible fidelity.

For this reason I marked with a small stroke the few things that appear to have been inserted by the copyist and that are absent from Ado, who always follows the traces of this Old Martyrology; in the margin I noted that they are absent from Ado. Those insertions generally concern Cologne, where this book was written, and neighboring places. You will find an account of them here in the notes.

Indeed, anyone who has even glanced lightly at this Old Roman Martyrology will not hesitate to assert that it is the source of all the other Martyrologies. Certainly Ado drew his waters from this spring.

Just as the water of a spring, leaving its source, gradually increases and becomes a stream as waters flow into it from every direction, so this Martyrology developed: now through Bede, now through Usuard, now through Ado, now through others, it gradually grew.

It will now be possible always to point a finger toward the spring. For this purpose I have brought into the open the head of the spring, which until now lay hidden.

## Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 13

“The common people too are crowned, now in the celebration of imperial distinctions, now in that of civic solemnities; and every public rejoicing is a captivating extravagance.

But you are a stranger in this world, a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem. ‘Our citizenship,’ he says, ‘is in heaven’ (Philippians III). You have your own census and your own calendar; you have nothing to do with the joys of this age.”

## Cyprian, epistle 37

“Record the days on which they depart, so that we may celebrate their commemorations among the memorials of the martyrs.”

## Augustine, book XX against Faustus, chapter 31
The Christian people celebrate the memorials of the martyrs together with religious solemnity, both to awaken imitation and to be united with their merits and assisted by their prayers.

[Col. 0143]

## Eulogies concerning this ancient Roman Martyrology

[Col. 0143B] Pope Gregory to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, Letter 29, Book VII, indiction 1.

“We possess in a single codex the names of nearly all the martyrs, with their passions distinguished according to individual days, and on each day we celebrate the solemn rites of Mass in their honor. Yet in that same volume it is not indicated who suffered in what manner; only the place and day of their passion are given. Hence it happens that many, from different lands and provinces, are recognized as crowned with martyrdom on each day, as I said. We believe that you possess these things in the highest degree of blessedness.”

Baronius, in the Prolegomena to the Roman Martyrology, chapter 8.

“This same simple and very brief Roman Martyrology, without any other addition, in which only the names of the martyrs, the place, and the day of their passion were set down, is the very one of which Ado makes mention.”

[Col. 0144B] Ado, archbishop of Vienne, in the preface to his Martyrology.

“To this work, so that the days of the martyrs might be recorded with the greatest accuracy—for they are usually found sufficiently confused in the Kalends—there assisted a venerable and very ancient Martyrology, sent from the city of Rome to Aquileia to a certain holy bishop by the Roman pontiff, and afterward lent to me for several days by a certain religious brother. I carefully transcribed it and, while staying at Ravenna, thought that it ought to be placed at the beginning of this work.”

Baronius, in the place cited above.

“Moreover, in all the printed Martyrologies of Ado that I have seen, that very text received from Rome is missing. Mosander would certainly have performed an excellent service, worthy of learned men and much to be desired, if he had published such a distinguished monument of antiquity, which he testifies was contained in his manuscript Ado, together with Ado’s Martyrology itself, which, after Surius, he added to the seventh volume of the Lives of the Saints.”

[Col. 0143]

## The Ancient Roman Martyrology

### Ado the Sinner to the Reader: Greetings

[Col. 0143C] “Lest you think that I have labored at this work in vain and undertaken something unnecessary, I shall briefly explain the reason for what I have done. First, there was the command and injunction of holy men that the days which had been marked in the Martyrology without the names of martyrs should be supplied—this Martyrology had been increased through the labor of the venerable Florus upon the work of Bede. Then the codices of the passions, collected from every source, so greatly stirred my mind that I described not only the festivals of days already past but also those of others which had been set down there, day by day, throughout the year, at greater length and somewhat more clearly, serving weaker brothers and those less able to read, to the praise of almighty God. Thus, in the memorials of the martyrs, they might have a concise reading and, in a little book, what others seek out with much labor through many codices.

[Col. 0144C] “To this work, so that the days of the martyrs might be recorded with the greatest accuracy—for they are usually found sufficiently confused in the Kalends—there assisted a venerable and very ancient Martyrology, sent from the city of Rome to Aquileia to a certain holy bishop by the Roman pontiff, and afterward lent to me for several days by a certain religious brother. I carefully transcribed it and, while staying at Ravenna, thought that it ought to be placed at the beginning of this work.

“Do not be surprised that the passions of the saints have been inserted into this Martyrology at somewhat greater length, especially toward the end, since the explanation given above, when the work was undertaken, should suffice for you. Only pray—I most earnestly beg you—that I may be joined to the merits of those whose triumphs I wished to celebrate, even if less than I ought. Greeted in Christ, farewell.”

## The month of January has thirty days; the moon, thirty.

[Col. 0145A]

### Rosweidus to the Reader

“Do not expect, reader, extensive notes here. You have them in the work of Cardinal Baronius, the most accomplished investigator of every aspect of ecclesiastical antiquity. And what can a swift vessel carry after a cargo ship? For now it will be enough for me to touch upon certain places passed over, corrupted, or insufficiently understood by others. I have changed or transposed nothing without the authority of the ancient books. Remember that I corrected many other things in Ado’s text, for which I give no explanation here. That would be a lengthy undertaking and perhaps less welcome. I have merely sampled a few rarer matters.

“If I learn that these things have not been unwelcome, and if at some time I am granted equal success in obtaining Bede, Usuard, and the other ancient Martyrologists from an ancient and incorrupt hand—for I have now received part of such a source, and greater hope shines forth from friends who love inviolate antiquity—it may perhaps happen that I shall one day set all the ancient Martyrologies, together with the Greek Menologion, before a single view, illustrated with brief notes. [Col. 0145B] Thus, when their connections are struck together—that is, when the deeds of the saints are compared with one another—the immortal brilliance of spiritual jewels, reflecting one another’s borrowed light, will suffer no loss, but will shine more and more brightly through the friendly convergence of their rays.

“If certain less familiar turns of expression, not always conforming to the rule of Priscian, occasionally occur in these Martyrologies, you will attribute them to the age. I thought it best to leave them untouched, so that they might reveal the author of their own age. In the names of cities, however, which manuscripts generally put in the accusative case, I have mostly followed the usage of our own age, lest you interpret as affected barbarism in the text what was merely an editorial choice, or reproach me for scrupulous superstition. Nevertheless, I now provide evidence of this matter for confirmation.

“Indeed, after applying every diligence, I fear that I have not sufficiently guarded against something foreign to Ado’s Martyrology finding its way into it. If some such names of saints have perhaps slipped in, they are generally those of several bishops of Vienne and certain other saints not much later in age than Ado, which were not always represented in all three manuscript codices. For some of these were absent from Scriverius’s book, which was the oldest of them all. I have no doubt that what happens to water also happens to books. The farther water recedes from its spring, the more impure it becomes, continually drawing something from the less pure places through which it flows; so a book is the more ancient, the nearer it approaches the author’s age, and the more complete and less mixed with additions made by the hands of scribes succeeding one another through the ages. Antiquarians to whom the manuscripts of books have been available for inspection know this. For my part, having handled several thousand such books, I have never found otherwise.

“The following is the notation of the manuscript codices that I have now used.

“E. denotes the Everbode codex.

“P. denotes the codex of St. Pantaleon.

“S. denotes the codex of Peter Scriverius.”

[Col. 0145]

1. AA, Kalends of January. The Octave of the Lord and the Circumcision. At Rome, the beheading of St. Almachius under Alippius, prefect of the city. And St. Martina, virgin. And at Spoleto, St. Concordius, martyr. And in the church at Ruspe, St. Fulgentius, bishop.

2. II B, fourth day before the Nones. Blessed Macarius.

[Note: “Blessed Macarius.” After 15 January: “and Macarius the abbot, the disciple of Antony.” These are the two celebrated Macariuses, formerly monks in Egypt and fathers of monks. It is generally thought that the Egyptian and the Alexandrian are meant. But which is which, and on what day, is not equally certain. I fear that the matter has hitherto been recorded incorrectly. The Alexandrians wish the feast of the Alexandrian to be celebrated on 11 January, and that of the Egyptian on the 15th; but I do not know on what authorities this can be established. Certainly this Martyrology, and with it Bede, Usuard, and Ado, distinguish these Macariuses in no other way than by calling the one whose feast is on 15 January the disciple of Antony. Yet Antony’s disciple was not the Egyptian but the Alexandrian, as may be gathered from Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, chapter 20—or else a third person. See our notes on the *Lives of the Fathers*.]

And at Tomi, the martyrs Argeus, Narcissus, and Marcellinus.

3. III BC, third day before the Nones. At Rome, Anterus, pope and martyr.

4. IV D, second day before the Nones. In Crete, Titus, a disciple of the apostles. At Rome, the martyrs Priscus, presbyter, Priscillianus, and Benedicta. And Daphrosa.

5. V CE, Nones. At Rome, St. Telesphorus, pope and martyr. At Antioch, St. Simeon the monk.

6. VI F, eighth day before the Ides. St. Macra, virgin, under the governor Rictiovarus. The Epiphany of the Lord, that is, the manifestation or appearance of the Lord.

7. VII DG, seventh day before the Ides. The return of the child Jesus from Egypt. And St. Lucian, martyr of Antioch. And Cletus, martyr.

8. I H, sixth day before the Ides. At Naples, Severinus the confessor, brother of Victorinus.

[Note: “At Naples, Severinus the confessor, brother of Victorinus.” After 5 September: “At Rome, Victorinus, martyr, brother of Severinus, who after remarkable repentance became bishop and martyr of the city of Amiternum.” Therefore it was not so much Ado—as Baronius thought on 8 June, making this Victorinus the brother of Severinus of Naples—as the Ancient Roman Martyrology that Ado followed, expressing the matter here as it actually was.]

9. II EI, fifth day before the Ides. In Caesarean Mauretania, Macra [Ado: Martiana], virgin and martyr. And Saints Julian and Basilissa, his wife, and Celsus and Martionilla, with twenty soldiers.

[Col. 0147]

10. III K, fourth day before the Ides. In the Thebaid, St. Paul the hermit. And in Cyprus, Nicanor, one of the seven deacons.

11. IV FL, third day before the Ides. At Alexandria, the confessors Peter, Severus, and Lucius. In Africa, Salvius, martyr.

12. V M, second day before the Ides. At Antioch [Ado: in Achaea], Satyrus, martyr. Arcadius, martyr.

13. VI GN, Ides. At Rome, on the Via Labicana, forty soldiers under the emperor Gallienus. At Poitiers, St. Hilary.

14. VII O, nineteenth day before the Kalends of February. At Nola, Felix the presbyter, buried at Pincus.

15. I HP, eighteenth day before the Kalends. The prophets Habakkuk and Micah. And Macarius the abbot, the disciple of Antony.

16. II Q, seventeenth day before the Kalends. And Isidore.

17. III IR, sixteenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, on the Via Salaria in the cemetery of Priscilla, St. Marcellus, pope. In the Thebaid, Antony the monk.

18. IV S, fifteenth day before the Kalends. The Chair of St. Peter, on which he first sat at Rome. And St. Prisca, martyr.

19. V KT, fourteenth day before the Kalends. At Smyrna, St. Germanicus, martyr, condemned to the beasts. And at Spoleto, Pontianus, martyr, who suffered on the nineteenth day before the Kalends, was buried on the fifteenth, and was transferred to the tomb on the sixteenth, on which his feast is more widely celebrated.

20. VI V, thirteenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Fabian, pope and martyr. And Marius, Martha, Audifax, and Habakkuk. And Sebastian, buried in the footsteps of the apostles.

21. VII LA, twelfth day before the Kalends. St. Agnes, virgin. At Athens, St. Publius, bishop, to whom Militenus was ordained bishop by Paul [the syntax/name is uncertain in the source].

22. I B, eleventh day before the Kalends. St. Vincent, deacon and martyr, in Spain. At the Waters of Silvius, St. Anastasius the monk.

[Note: “At the Waters of Silvius, St. Anastasius the monk.” The manuscript book clearly has *Silvias* here. So also in the Life of St. Gordianus, 10 May: “He ordered his wife Marina to be taken into the service of the peasants in a certain district called the Waters of Silvius.” Yet the copies transmitted under Ado display *Salvias*. Whether one reads *Silvias* with the manuscript or *Salvias* with the common text, I think the same place is meant. See Baronius on 23 January and 9 July.]

[Ado: Salvias], St. Anastasius the monk.

23. II MC, tenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, St. Emerentiana, virgin. In Caesarean Mauretania, Severianus and Aquila. At Philippi, Parmenas, one of the seven deacons.

24. III D, ninth day before the Kalends. At Ephesus, Timothy, apostle. At Antioch, St. Babylas, bishop.

25. IV NE, eighth day before the Kalends. The Conversion of St. Paul the Apostle. Near Damascus, St. Ananias, who baptized Paul himself.

26. V F, seventh day before the Kalends. St. Polycarp, disciple of St. John the Apostle, who suffered at Smyrna. And Theogenes with thirty-six others.

27. VI OG, sixth day before the Kalends. At Constantinople, John Chrysostom. And the death of St. Paula.

28. VII H, fifth day before the Kalends. St. Agnes, a second time. In the city of Apollonia, Leucius and Thyrsus, martyrs.

29. I AI, fourth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Papius and Maurus, soldiers under the emperor Diocletian.

30. II K, third day before the Kalends. At Antioch, the passion of St. Hippolytus. At Jerusalem, Matthias, bishop, who was eighth after James. Blessed Alexander, who suffered in the persecution of Decius.

31. III BL, second day before the Kalends. At Alexandria, St. Mettanus, martyr. At Trent, St. Vigilius, bishop and martyr.

## The month of February has twenty-eight days.

[Col. 0147]

1. IV CM, Kalends. At Antioch, Ignatius, bishop and martyr. At Smyrna, Pionius, martyr, and fifteen others.

[Col. 0149]

2. V N, fourth day before the Nones. The Hypapante of the Lord. At Caesarea, Cornelius the centurion, bishop of that city. And Apronianus, martyr, at Rome.

3. VI DO, third day before the Nones. Blessed Celerinus the deacon, and Celerina his grandmother, and Laurentinus, and Ignatius.

4. VII P, second day before the Nones. In the Egyptian city of Thmuis, blessed Phileas, bishop of that city, and Philoromus the tribune, and countless martyrs.

5. I EQ, Nones. St. Agatha, virgin, at the city of the Catanenses.

6. II R, eighth day before the Ides. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, St. Dorothy, virgin, and Theophilus the scholasticus.

7. III FS, seventh day before the Ides. St. Moses, who, at the request of Mauvia, queen of the Saracens, was made bishop of that people.

8. IV T, sixth day before the Ides. Saints Dionysius, Aemilianus, and Sebastian. At Alexandria, St. Cointa, martyr.

9. V GV, fifth day before the Ides. At Alexandria, Apollonia, virgin.

10. VI A, fourth day before the Ides. At Rome, Zotichus, Irenaeus, Hyacinthus, and Amantius. And Soteris, virgin. On the Via Labicana, ten soldiers.

11. VII HB, third day before the Ides. At Alexandria, St. Euphrasia, virgin.

12. I C, second day before the Ides. At Barcelona, Eulalia, virgin and martyr. At Alexandria, Molestus and Ammonius.

13. II ID, Ides. Agabus the prophet of the New Testament, at Antioch. In Militana of Armenia, St. Polyuctus, martyr.

14. III E, sixteenth day before the Kalends of March. At Rome, Valentine the presbyter. And St. Valentine, bishop of Interamna.

15. IV KF, fifteenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, St. Brato, martyr. At Sebaste, the passion of St. Blaesius [also Blasius], bishop.

16. V G, fourteenth day before the Kalends. St. Onesimus, apostle. And at Cumae, St. Juliana, virgin.

17. VI LH, thirteenth day before the Kalends. In Persia, blessed Polychronius, bishop and martyr.

18. VII I, twelfth day before the Kalends. At Jerusalem, Simeon, bishop and martyr. And at Rome, the martyrs Claudius, Praepedigna, Alexander, Cutia, and Maximus.

19. I MK, eleventh day before the Kalends. At Rome, Gabinus, presbyter and martyr.

20. II L, tenth day before the Kalends. At Tyre, martyrs whose number only God’s knowledge can reckon; Veturius, commander of the army, killed them with various tortures at the command of Diocletian.

21. III NM, ninth day before the Kalends. In Sicily, seventy-nine martyrs who suffered various tortures under Diocletian.

22. IV N, eighth day before the Kalends. At Antioch, the Chair of St. Peter. At Alexandria, Abilius, bishop.

23. V OO, seventh day before the Kalends. At Sirmium, Sinerius [Ado: Syrenus], the monk. And forty-two [Ado: sixty-two] martyrs. At Rome, Polycarp the presbyter.

24. VI P, sixth day before the Kalends. St. Matthias, apostle. And the Finding of the head of the Forerunner. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Sergius, martyr.

25. VII Q, fifth day before the Kalends. In Egypt, Victorinus, Victor, Nicophorus, Claudianus, Dioscorus, Serapion, and Papius.

26. I R, fourth day before the Kalends. At Perge in Pamphylia, blessed Nestor, bishop. At Alexandria, Alexander, the glorious old bishop.

27. II S, third day before the Kalends. At Alexandria, Julian, martyr, and Eunius, who persevered with the old man in his confession.

28. III T, second day before the Kalends.

## The month of March has thirty-one days; the moon, thirty.

[Col. 0151]

1. IV A, Kalends of March. Two hundred and sixty holy martyrs in the time of Claudius, who had been condemned while digging sand on the Via Salaria.

2. V B, sixth day before the Nones. At Rome, Jovinus and Basileus. And very many martyrs condemned to death under Alexander.

3. VI C, fifth day before the Nones. Saints Hemitherius and Cheledonius, crowned with martyrdom at Calagurris. At Caesarea, Marinus the soldier and Asterius the senator.

4. VII D, fourth day before the Nones. Lucius, pope and martyr. And nine hundred martyrs who are placed in the cemetery at St. Cecilia.

5. I E, third day before the Nones. At Antioch, St. Phocas, martyr. And St. Eusebius of the Palatium, and eight other martyrs [Ado: nine].

6. II F, second day before the Nones. At Nicomedia, Victor and Victorinus, who completed the course of their life in prison.

7. III G, Nones. In the Mauretanian city of the Tuburbitani, Saints Perpetua and Felicitas, martyrs.

8. IV H, eighth day before the Ides. At Carthage, St. Pontianus the deacon, blessed Cyprian, who, always glorifying the Lord in his sufferings, earned the crown of life.

9. V I, seventh day before the Ides. In the city of Nyssa, St. Gregory, bishop, brother of Basil. At Barcelona, Pacianus, bishop.

10. VI K, sixth day before the Ides. At Apamea, Alexander and Caius of Eumenia. In Persia, forty-two martyrs.

11. VII L, fifth day before the Ides. At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, forty soldiers in the time of King Licinius.

12. I M, fourth day before the Ides. Saints Gregory and Innocent, pontiffs. At Nicomedia, Peter the martyr, companion of Dorotheus and Gorgonius, martyrs.

13. II N, third day before the Ides. At Nicomedia, Macedonius the presbyter, Patricia his wife, and their daughter Medesta.

14. III O, second day before the Ides. At Rome, forty-eight martyrs who were baptized by blessed Peter the Apostle while he was held in custody; all were consumed by Nero’s sword.

15. IV P, Ides. At Thessalonica, Matrona, maidservant and martyr.

16. V Q, seventeenth day before the Kalends of April. At Rome, Cyriacus the martyr, Largus, Smaragdus, Crescentianus the martyr, and twenty others.

17. VI R, sixteenth day before the Kalends. St. Patrick, bishop, who first preached among the Scots.

18. VII S, fifteenth day before the Kalends. St. Alexander, bishop, who with Narcissus assumed the governance of the Church of Jerusalem.

19. I T, fourteenth day before the Kalends. In the city of Penarense [reading uncertain], blessed John, a man of great holiness. At Sorrento, Quintus, Quintilla, Quartilla, and Martia [Ado: Marcus], with eight others [Ado: nine].

20. II V, thirteenth day before the Kalends. Archippus, fellow soldier of the Apostle Paul.

21. III A, twelfth day before the Kalends. At the fortress of Cassino, Benedict, abbot. And Serapion the anchorite.

22. IV B, eleventh day before the Kalends. At Narbonne, St. Paul, bishop, disciple of the apostles.

23. V C, tenth day before the Kalends. In Africa, the martyrs Victorianus, Frumentius, another Frumentius, and two brothers, who suffered under King Hunneric in the Vandal persecution.

24. VI D, ninth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Pigmenius, presbyter and martyr, buried in the cemetery of Pontianus.

25. VII E, eighth day before the Kalends. The Annunciation of the Lord, and the Crucifixion. At Rome, Cyrinus, martyr. [Col. 0153] At Nicomedia, Dula, martyr. At Sirmium, Irenaeus, bishop and martyr.

26. I F, seventh day before the Kalends. At Rome, St. Castulus, keeper of the imperial palace. In the Pentapolis of Libya, Theodore, bishop.

27. II G, sixth day before the Kalends. In Egypt, John the Hermit, a man of prophetic spirit.

28. III H, fifth day before the Kalends. At Caesarea in Palestine, the martyrs Priscus, Malchus, and Alexander, who were given to the beasts in the persecution of Valerian.

29. IV I, fourth day before the Kalends. In Africa, the confessors Armogastes, Archinimus, and Saturus, in the time of the Vandal persecution.

30. V K, third day before the Kalends. At Rome, Quirinus, tribune and martyr, father of St. Balbina.

31. VI L, second day before the Kalends. At Rome, St. Balbina, virgin, buried in the cemetery of Praetextatus beside her father Quirinus.

## The month of April has thirty days; the moon, twenty-nine.

[Col. 0153]

1. VII M, Kalends of April. At Rome, Theodota, sister of Hermes the martyr, who suffered martyrdom under Aurelian and was buried on the Via Salaria.

2. I N, fourth day before the Nones. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, St. Theodosia, virgin and martyr, beheaded.

3. II O, third day before the Nones. At Thessalonica, the virgins Agape and Chionia. At Tomi, Evagrius and Benignus. At Tauromenium, St. Pancratius.

4. III P, second day before the Nones. At Milan, blessed Ambrose, bishop and confessor.

5. IV Q, Nones. At Thessalonica, St. Irene, virgin. In Egypt, Marciana, Nicanor, and Apollonius.

6. V R, eighth day before the Ides. Sixtus, pope and martyr, who suffered in the time of Hadrian.

7. VI S, seventh day before the Ides. Hegesippus, who lived near the apostolic age.

8. VII T, sixth day before the Ides. At Tours, Perpetuus, bishop.

9. I V, fifth day before the Ides. At Antioch, Prochorus the deacon, who is one of the seven. At Sirmium, seven virgins, crowned together.

10. II A, fourth day before the Ides. Ezekiel the Prophet. At Rome, very many martyrs who were baptized by Pope Alexander.

11. III B, third day before the Ides. At Gortyna, Philip, bishop, who flourished in the time of Antoninus Verus and Lucius.

12. IV C, second day before the Ides. On the Via Aurelia, Julius, pope and confessor, under Constantius the Arian.

13. V D, Ides. At Pergamum in Asia, Carpus, bishop, and Papyrius, Agathonica, and many others.

14. VI E, eighteenth day before the Kalends of May. At Rome, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, the martyrs Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus.

15. VII F, seventeenth day before the Kalends. Cordula, Olympias, and Maximus. In Italy, Maro, Eutyches, and Victorinus.

16. I G, sixteenth day before the Kalends. At Corinth, Callistus and Carisius, drowned at sea with seven others.

17. II H, fifteenth day before the Kalends. In Africa, St. Mappalicus. At Antioch, Peter the deacon and Hermogenes.

18. III I, fourteenth day before the Kalends. At Messina in Apulia, Eleutherius, bishop, and Anthia his mother. At Rome, Apollonius the senator.

19. IV K, thirteenth day before the Kalends. At Corinth, Timon, one of the seven deacons. In Militana, Hermogenes, Caius, Expeditius, Aristonicus, and Rufus the Galatian.

20. V L, twelfth day before the Kalends. The Finding of many holy relics at Instabe.

[Note: “The Finding of many holy relics at Instabel.” Here I was, and still am, considerably perplexed. Nothing concerning this appears in Ado or in any other Martyrology. I suspect that this was added by a copyist, and that the famous monastery among the Eburones, Stavelot or Stablot, is meant. The basis of my suspicion is that later, on 17 November, we find: “The Dedication of St. Peter at Malfidar”; and there we shall establish that this is Malmedy, a monastery near Stavelot. But what are these many relics, and when were they found at Stavelot? I would say more confidently when they were hidden and concealed.

“Sigebert, in his *Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 882, writes: ‘In that year Godefrid and Sigifrid, kings of the Northmen, settling with an immeasurable multitude beside the Meuse at a place called Haflon, burned Liège, Utrecht, Tongeren, Cologne, Bonn, and the neighboring castles. At Aachen, while stabling their horses in the palace, they burned the town and palace. Moreover, at the monasteries of Stavelot, Malmedy, Inda, and Prüm, the ministers of the sacred Order of both sexes hid wherever they could most suitably; and they concealed the bodies and relics of the saints in safer places.’ Anselm, canon of Liège, has the same account in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*, chapter 37, where he says that they ascended at Halos beside the Meuse. This Northmen’s devastation continued for several years. Hence it could have happened that relics hidden several years earlier were later found, and that the memory of their discovery was introduced into the sacred calendar.

“Hariger, abbot of Lobbes, explains the etymology of the name in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*, chapter 52: ‘At last Remaclus found a place suitable for the future work; because wild animals from every direction converged there for drinking or feeding, as to a stable, it had anciently been given the name Stavelot.’ Thus Hariger pursues the etymology through the similarity of the word. Everelmus, abbot of Hautmont, is no less fanciful in the Life of St. Poppo, abbot of Stavelot, 25 January, chapter 21: ‘Stavelot, where stable praise is continually sung by the faithful.’ It is therefore clear that the name was not originally given for any of these reasons, but that afterward an etymology was adapted to suit each person’s understanding. This monastery was founded in 651 by King Sigebert, according to Sigebert’s testimony in the *Chronicle*. See below, 17 November, where Malmedy is discussed.”]

[Col. 0155] At Rome, Victor, bishop and martyr. Sulpitius and Servilianus.

21. VI M, eleventh day before the Kalends. In Persia, St. Simeon, bishop, and one hundred others, and Ustazades, Abdella, Ananias, and Pusicius.

22. VII N, tenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, in the cemetery of Callistus, Caius, pope. In Persia, very many martyrs under Sapor, king of the Persians. Cordula, Parmenius, Helimenas, and Chrysotelus, presbyters; and Lucas and Mucius, deacons.

23. I O, ninth day before the Kalends. In the Persian city of Diospolis, George, martyr.

24. II P, eighth day before the Kalends.

25. III Q, seventh day before the Kalends. At Alexandria, Mark the Evangelist. Erminus the confessor.

[Note: “Erminus the confessor.” He is absent here from Ado, and does not occur in any Martyrology with this particular ending. I think St. Erminus is meant, bishop and abbot of Lobbes, whom I find on this day in the expanded Martyrology of Usuard made by the Carthusian house of Cologne in 1521. Molanus writes of him in his additions to Usuard, 25 April, from the local Martyrology: “At Lobbes, the passing of St. Erminus, bishop and confessor.” Baronius incorporated this into the Roman Martyrology expanded by him.

“Thus the ancient memory of Erminus occurs in this Ancient Roman Martyrology. Yet, since Erminus is absent from Ado, who records all the saints of the Ancient Roman Martyrology, it appears that in Ado’s time Erminus was not yet in the Ancient Roman Martyrology, but was added later, perhaps by a religious of St. Pantaleon at Cologne, where this book was written.

“Moyerus, Book I of the *Annals of Flanders*, notes that he succeeded St. Ursmar in governing the bishopric and abbey in the year 713. My manuscript *Florarium of the Saints* places his death in the year of Christ 737. Trithemius mentions him in *On Illustrious Men of the Order of St. Benedict*, Book III, chapter 160, and Book IV, chapter 180, in both places giving ‘Herwinus’ for ‘Erminus.’ Molanus also mentions him in his *Index* and in the *Birthdays of the Saints of Belgium*. His Acts are found written at Lobbes, in the monastery near Binche, by a contemporary.

“It is not surprising that this Erminus is called Ermino by others. Thus the man now commonly called Servatius was formerly also called Servatio, as appears in Sulpicius Severus, Book III of the *Sacred History*.”]

And at Rome, the Greater Litany at St. Peter.

26. IV R, sixth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Anacletus, pope and martyr. And Marcellinus, pope and martyr.

27. V S, fifth day before the Kalends. St. Anastasius, pope. At Nicomedia, Anthimus, bishop, with an innumerable multitude of martyrs.

28. VI T, fourth day before the Kalends. At Ravenna, St. Vitalis, martyr, father of Saints Gervasius and Protasius. At Alexandria, Theodora, virgin, and Didymus.

29. VII A, third day before the Kalends. At Paphos, Tychicus, a disciple of the apostles. At the colony of Cirta, Agapius and Secundinus.

30. I B, second day before the Kalends. The martyrs Marianus and James, beheaded at Lambesis with many others. Quirinus, martyr.

[Note: “Quirinus, martyr.” He is absent here from Ado and from the other Martyrologies. I think Quirinus the martyr is meant, whose feast you have above on 30 March. At this place he was inserted again by the copyist of this Martyrology because of the translation of his body. The Carthusian house of Cologne writes of this in its additions to Usuard, 30 April: “In the diocese of Cologne, in the town of Neuss, the translation of St. Quirinus, tribune and martyr. His sacred body, obtained from the pope by the noble lady Gepa, abbess, was transferred from the city of Rome to Neuss and reverently placed in her monastery.” Hence I think Molanus derived his notice in Usuard.]

And the Vigil of the apostles.

## The month of May has thirty-one days; the moon, thirty.

[Col. 0157]

1. II C, Kalends of May. Jeremiah the Prophet. And the apostles Philip and James, the brother of the Lord.

2. III D, sixth day before the Nones. Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. And Saturninus and Neopolis, who rested in prison.

3. IV E, fifth day before the Nones. At Jerusalem, the Finding of the Holy Cross. At Rome, on the Via Nomentana, Alexander the pope, and Eventius and Theodulus, presbyters.

4. V F, fourth day before the Nones. In the city of Gaza, Silvanus the bishop, crowned with a great many of his clergy.

5. VI G, third day before the Nones. At Alexandria, St. Euthymius the deacon, resting in prison. At Thessalonica, Irene and Peregrinus.

6. VII H, second day before the Nones. Blessed Evodius, bishop, who was first ordained by the apostles at Antioch. And St. Lucius of Cyrene, who was ordained bishop of Cyrene by the apostles. And St. John the Apostle, when he was thrown before the Latin Gate into a cauldron of boiling oil.

7. I I, Nones. Juvenalis, martyr. And Flavia Domitilla. At Nicomedia, Augustus and Augustinus.

8. II K, eighth day before the Ides. At Milan, St. Victor, martyr.

9. III L, seventh day before the Ides. In Persia, 310 martyrs. At the town of Nazianzus, Gregory the theological bishop.

10. IV M, sixth day before the Ides. Job the prophet. On the Via Latina, Gordianus and Epimachus. And Calepodius, an old presbyter.

11. V N, fifth day before the Ides. At Rome, on the Via Salaria, St. Anthimus.

12. VI O, fourth day before the Ides. In the cemetery of Praetextatus, Nereus and Achilleus, brothers. On the Via Aurelia, St. Pancratius, martyr. And Dionysius.

13. VII P, third day before the Ides. Servatius, bishop. The day of the dedication of St. Mary’s at the Martyrs is celebrated, established by Pope Boniface.

14. I Q, second day before the Ides. In Syria, Victor and Corona, martyrs.

15. II R, Ides. Torquatus, Ctesiphon, Secundus, Indalecius, Caecilius, Hesychius, and Euphrasius, who were ordained at Rome by the apostles.

16. III S, seventeenth day before the Kalends of June. In Isauria, Aquilinus and Victorianus.

17. IV T, sixteenth day before the Kalends. In Tuscany, Torpetes, martyr, under Nero.

18. V V, fifteenth day before the Kalends. In Egypt, Dioscorus the lector.

19. VI A, fourteenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Potentiana, virgin. And Prudens, a disciple of Paul. And the eunuchs Calocerus and Parthenius.

20. VII B, thirteenth day before the Kalends. On the Via Salaria, St. Basilia, virgin and martyr.

21. I C, twelfth day before the Kalends. In Caesarean Mauretania, Timothy and Pollius.

22. II D, eleventh day before the Kalends. In Africa, Castus and Aemilius.

23. III E, tenth day before the Kalends.

24. IV F, ninth day before the Kalends. St. Vincent, martyr. In Istria, Zoellus and Silvanus.

25. V G, eighth day before the Kalends. In the cemetery of Praetextatus, St. Urban, bishop and martyr.

26. VI H, seventh day before the Kalends. At Athens, Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles.

27. VII I, sixth day before the Kalends. In the Moesian city of Durostorum, Julian, martyr.
