28. I K, fifth day before the Kalends. John, pope. In Sardinia, Aemilius and Felix.

[Col. 0159]

29. II L, fourth day before the Kalends. On the Via Aurelia, Restitutus. On the Via Tiburtina, the seven brothers. At Trier, St. Maximinus, bishop and confessor.

30. III M, third day before the Kalends. On the Via Aurelia, in the cemetery, Felix, pope. At the Towers of Sardinia, Crispulus and Gabinius.

31. IV N, second day before the Kalends. At Rome, Petronilla, virgin. At Aquileia, Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla.

## The month of June has thirty days; the moon, twenty-nine.

[Col. 0159]

1. V O, Kalends of June. The dedication of St. Nicomedes, martyr. And St. Pamphilus, martyr.

2. VI P, fourth day before the Nones. At Rome, Marcellinus the presbyter and Peter the exorcist.

3. VII Q, third day before the Nones. At Arezzo in Tuscany, the martyrs Pergentinus and Laurentinus. In Campania, Erasmus, bishop and martyr.

4. I R, second day before the Nones. In Illyricum, in the city of Siscia, St. Quirinus, bishop and martyr.

5. II S, Nones. Boniface, martyr, who suffered at Tarsus on the fourteenth day of the month of May and was buried at Rome on the Nones of June.

6. III T, eighth day before the Ides. Philip, one of the seven deacons, at Caesarea. At Rome, Artemius, Candida, and their daughter Paulina. At Tarsus, twenty martyrs.

7. IV V, seventh day before the Ides. At Constantinople, Paul, bishop. In Cappadocia, Lucian, martyr.

8. V A, sixth day before the Ides.

9. VI B, fifth day before the Ides. At Rome, on the Caelian Hill, the martyrs Primus and Felicianus.

10. VII C, fourth day before the Ides. At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, Basilides, Tripodis, Mandalis, and twenty others. And Getulius, martyr, and Cerealis. Barnabas, apostle.

[Note: “And St. Maurinus, martyr.” He is absent here from Ado. I did not express him in the text because the name had been added by a later hand, doubtless by the religious of St. Pantaleon who copied this book. For at Cologne, in the church of St. Pantaleon, the body of St. Maurinus is held in veneration. He was crowned with martyrdom there on 10 June, and his tomb remained hidden until the year 965. For how it was discovered, after the death of Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, under his successor, Bishop Folcmar, see Stephen, the author of the account of this discovery, written around the year of the Lord 990 to Christian, the abbot; the memory of the discovery is commemorated on 13 October. That he suffered on this day is attested by the inscription of the sarcophagus, which is preserved by the same author:

“Here rest the bones of good-memory Maurinus,

who suffered martyrdom in the atrium of the church.”]

On the fourth day before the Ides of June. In what year he suffered martyrdom here, I do not find stated. For I fear that Baronius, under 10 June, and Erhard Winheim in *The Sacrarium of Agrippina*, are mistaken in assigning the year 670 from Trithemius, *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, Book III, chapter 134. Trithemius is not speaking of our Maurinus, but of another, formerly abbot of Claroangium in Auvergne and companion of Saint Praejectus, bishop. Their feast day appears in Baronius’s Roman Martyrology on 25 January; this Maurinus is called at different times Maurinus, Marinus, Marianus, or Amarinus.

The occasion for the error was that our Maurinus is said to have suffered martyrdom in the atrium of a church. Trithemius writes similarly of the other Maurinus, although in the martyrdom of Praejectus and Maurinus on 25 January there is no mention of a church atrium; they are said to have been killed in a place called Volonicum. Thus Trithemius may have attributed to the martyr Maurinus of Auvergne what is read on the sarcophagus concerning Maurinus of Cologne.

11. I D, third day before the Ides. At Corinth, Sosthenes, Paul’s disciple.

[Note: “At Corinth, Sosthenes, Paul’s disciple.” Below, on 28 November: “Sosthenes, disciple of the apostles.” Thus this Martyrology seems to make two Sostheneses and to distinguish one from the other. There is a double remembrance of Sosthenes in sacred Scripture: Acts 18, “But having seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue,” and 1 Corinthians 1, “Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes, a brother.” The interpreters identify them as one and the same man. If that opinion is correct, his memory could have been celebrated on different days for different reasons.]

At Aquileia, Felix and Fortunatus.

12. II E, second day before the Ides. At Milan, Nazarius and Celsus, whose discovery is commemorated on the second day before the Ides of June and whose martyrdom is commemorated on the fifth day before the Kalends of August.

13. III F, the Ides. At Rome, Saint Felicula, virgin and martyr.

14. IV G, eighteenth day before the Kalends of July. The prophet Elisha. In Cappadocia, Saint Basil, brother of Gregory and Peter.

[Col. 0161]

15. V H, seventeenth day before the Kalends. In Sicily, Modestus, Vitus, and Crescentia, martyrs; at Dorostorum, Hesychius, a soldier.

16. VI I, sixteenth day before the Kalends. At Antioch, Cyricus and Julitta, his mother, and 401 others.

17. VII K, fifteenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, 262 martyrs.

18. I L, fourteenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, on the Via Ardeatina, the martyrs Mark and Marcellian.

19. II M, thirteenth day before the Kalends. At Milan, Gervasius and Protasius.

+ And the commemoration of Nazarius and Celsus.

[Note: “And the commemoration of Nazarius and Celsus.” Their commemoration is indeed absent here from Ado, both in the common printed text and in the manuscript. Yet on 12 June, when he is discussing the discovery of Nazarius and Celsus, he adds: “Their public and celebrated commemoration is also attended and reverently observed by the faithful on the feast of Saints Gervasius and Protasius”; this is the very day in question. The manuscript *Florarium of the Saints* agrees: under 12 June, the day of the discovery of Saints Nazarius and Celsus, it says: “Among some people, their festive commemoration—that of Nazarius and Celsus—is held on the feast of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.” Thus you see that this ancient Roman Martyrology did not join the commemoration of Nazarius [Col. 0162] and Celsus to this day, on which Gervasius and Protasius are commemorated, without reason.]

At Ravenna, the martyr Ursinus.

20. III N, twelfth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Novatus, brother of Timothy the presbyter, who were instructed by the apostles.

21. IV O, eleventh day before the Kalends. At Syracuse, the martyrs Rufinus and Martia. At Rome, Demetria, virgin.

22. V P, tenth day before the Kalends. The martyr Albanus.

[Note: “The martyr Albanus.” It had been corrected to Albinus, as it is also in Ado. I think this correction was made in later copies written after the year 991. For in that year Theophano, wife of Otto II, transferring the body of Saint Alban from Rome to Cologne, presented it to this church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, formerly called the Six, now dedicated to Saint Pantaleon. Coming from Rome by way of Mainz, and wishing to distinguish this Alban from the Alban of Mainz, she called him Albinus, who suffered under Diocletian on 22 June in the year 286. So Erhard Winheim records in his *Sacrarium of Agrippina*, p. 141. See our *Sacrarium of Mainz*, Book II, chapter 28.]

At Nola in Campania, Paulinus, bishop.

23. VI Q, ninth day before the Kalends. Saint John the presbyter, buried on the old Via Salaria.

24. VII R, eighth day before the Kalends. The Nativity of the Lord’s Forerunner.

25. I S, seventh day before the Kalends. At Pyrriberoea, Sosipater, Paul’s disciple. At Alexandria, Gallicanus, martyr. At Rome, Lucia, virgin, with twelve others.

26. II T, sixth day before the Kalends. At Rome, John and Paul, brothers.

27. III A, fifth day before the Kalends. In Galatia, Crescentius, disciple of the apostle Paul. In the Tiburtine region of Italy, Symphorosa with her seven sons.

28. IV B, fourth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Pope Leo. At Alexandria, Plutarch, Serenus, Heraclides, Heron, Potamioena, Marcella, and others.

29. V C, third day before the Kalends. At Rome, the apostles Peter and Paul.

30. VI D, second day before the Kalends. The commemoration of Lucina, a disciple of the apostles.

## The month of July has thirty-one days; the moon, thirty.

[Col. 0161]

1. VII E, the Kalends of July. On Mount Hor, Aaron, the first priest.

2. I F, the sixth day before the Nones. In the cemetery of Damasus, Processus and Martinianus, baptized by the apostles Peter and Paul. Also three soldiers who suffered with the apostle Paul. And the martyrs Ariston, Crescentianus, Eutychianus, Urbanus, and others.

3. II G, the fifth day before the Nones. The translation of the apostle Thomas. At Constantinople, Eulogius. At Laodicea, Anatolius, bishop. And Gregory, martyr.

4. III H, the fourth day before the Nones. Hosea and Haggai. Jocundinianus, martyr. At Sirmium, Innocentius and Sabbatius, with thirty others.

5. IV I, the third day before the Nones. In Syria, Saint Domitius, martyr. At Rome, the feast of Zoe, wife of Nicostratus.

6. V K, the second day before the Nones. The prophets Isaiah and Joel.

[Col. 0163]

And the octave of the apostles. And the apostle Paul’s first entrance into the city of Rome. And the martyr Tranquillinus. And the feast of Saint Goar, confessor.

7. VI L, the Nones. At Alexandria, Saint Pantaenus. At Rome, the martyr Nicostratus, chief secretary. Claudius, Castorius, Victorinus, and Symphronianus.

8. VII M, the eighth day before the Ides. In Asia Minor, Aquila and Priscilla, his wife. In Palestine, Procopius, martyr.

+ At the city of Maralana, Brictius, bishop.

9. I N, the seventh day before the Ides. At Rome, at the ever-flowing Gutta, Zeno and 10,203 others. In the city of Tyre, Anatolia and Audax; Cyril, bishop and martyr.

10. II O, the sixth day before the Ides. At Rome, the Seven Brothers. In Africa, Januarius, Marinus, Nabor, and Felix. At Rome, Rufina and Secunda.

11. III P, the fifth day before the Ides. In Lesser Armenia, the martyr Januarius.

12. IV Q, the fourth day before the Ides. At Aquileia, Hermagoras, bishop, disciple of Saint Mark. In Cyprus, Nason, an ancient disciple of Christ.

13. V R, the third day before the Ides. Ezra and Joel, prophets. And the holy confessors: Eugenius, bishop, and the entire clergy of the Church.

14. VI S, the second day before the Ides. In Pontus, Phocas, bishop of the city of Sinope.

15. VII T, the Ides. At Nisibis, Jacob, bishop. At Rome, in the Portus district, Eutropius, Zosima, and Bonosa, sisters.

16. I V, seventeenth day before the Kalends of August. At Ostia, Saint Hilarinus, martyr. At Antioch in Syria, Eustathius, bishop.

17. II A, sixteenth day before the Kalends. At Carthage, the martyrs of Scillium: Speratus, Narthalus, Cythinus, Bethurius, Felix, and seven others.

18. III B, fifteenth day before the Kalends. At Carthage, Saint Guddena, virgin and martyr.

19. IV C, fourteenth day before the Kalends. At Seville, Saints Justa and Rufina.

20. V D, thirteenth day before the Kalends. Joseph, who was surnamed Justus, who suffered much from the Jews for Christ and died victorious in Judea.

21. VI E, twelfth day before the Kalends. The prophet Daniel. At Rome, Praxedis, virgin. At Marseille, Victor, martyr.

22. VII F, eleventh day before the Kalends. Saint Mary Magdalene. And Syntyche, who sleeps at Philippi. At Ancyra, Plato, martyr.

23. I G, tenth day before the Kalends. At Ravenna, Apollinaris, bishop and martyr.

24. II H, ninth day before the Kalends. At Rome, on the Via Tiburtina, Vincentius. At Emerita in Spain, Victor, a soldier. Near Lake Bolsena in Italy, Christina, virgin.

25. III I, eighth day before the Kalends. James, apostle, son of Zebedee. At the city of Samos, Christopher, martyr.

26. IV K, seventh day before the Kalends. At Rome, in the Portus district, Saint Hyacinth, martyr.

27. V L, sixth day before the Kalends. In Sicily, Simeon, monk. At Nicomedia, Harmolaus, presbyter.

28. VI M, fifth day before the Kalends. At Nicomedia, Saint Pantaleon, martyr.

[Note: “At Nicomedia, Saint Pantaleon, martyr.” This was written in large illuminated letters, because this saint is the patron of the church and monastery of Saint Pantaleon at Cologne, where this Martyrology was copied. They possess there the head of Saint Pantaleon, which was brought from Constantinople by the knight Henry van Ulmen in the year of Christ 1208. The memory of this translation is celebrated at Cologne on 18 January, as the Martyrology of Father Canisius records.

There was therefore another Pantaneon, whose head was brought to Lyon, as Sigebert records in his Chronicle under the year 802. The envoys of the Emperor Charlemagne, coming from Aaron the Emir, brought among other gifts to France the bones of Cyprian, martyr of Carthage, and of Speratus, the first of the Scillitan martyrs, and the head of the martyr Pantaleon.

Perhaps this Pantaneon was one of Speratus’ companions and one of the other Scillitan martyrs, even though the name Pantaleon is not expressly given among them in the Martyrologies. One might infer this from Ado’s Chronicle under the year 806: “At that time the bones of Blessed Cyprian were brought from Carthage with the remaining blessed Scillitan martyrs, companions of Speratus, and were placed in the church of Saint John the Baptist in the city of Lyon.” Ado does not mention Pantaleon, perhaps including him among Speratus’ companions. Yet in his Martyrology, under 17 July, he does mention the head of Pantaleon and distinguishes it from the relics of the Scillitan martyrs.

Agobard, bishop of Lyon, also names Pantaleon in a poem about the arrival of these relics. There were therefore several Pantaleons. Certainly in the Roman Martyrology under 27 July one finds both Pantaleon, the physician of Nicomedia, and Pantaleomon of Vigilia in Apulia. Pantaleon and Pantaleemon are the same name according to some authorities: the one called Pantaleon in the Roman Martyrology is called Pantaleemon in the Menologion, where another Pantaleon also appears on 17 September as a companion of the martyr Charalampus.]

[Col. 0165]

29. VII N, fourth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Felix, pope and martyr under Constantius. And Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrix.

30. I O, third day before the Kalends. At Rome, Abdon and Sennen. At Tuburbo Lucernaria, Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda, virgins.

31. II P, second day before the Kalends. At Caesarea, Fabius, martyr.

## The month of August has thirty-one days; the moon, twenty-nine.

[Col. 0165]

1. III Q, the Kalends of August. At Rome, at Saint Peter ad Vincula. At Antioch, the holy Maccabees. At Philadelphia, the martyrs Cyril, Aquila, Peter, and others. At Vercelli, Eusebius, bishop.

2. IV R, the fourth day before the Nones. At Rome, Stephen, pope and martyr. In Bithynia, Theodota with her three sons.

3. V S, the third day before the Nones. At Jerusalem, the discovery of the body of Blessed Stephen, Gamaliel, Nicodemus, and Abibon. At Constantinople, Hermellus, martyr.

4. VI T, the second day before the Nones. Aristarchus, a disciple of the apostles. In the Arenarian crypt, Tertullinus, martyr, at Rome.

5. VII V, the Nones. In the city of Augusta in Raetia, Saint Afra, martyr.

6. I A, the eighth day before the Ides. At Rome, on the Via Appia, Pope Sixtus, martyr, and the deacons Felicissimus and Agapitus, in the cemetery of Praetextatus.

7. II B, the seventh day before the Ides. At Arezzo, Donatus, bishop and martyr. At Rome, Peter and Juliana, with eighteen others. At Milan, Faustus, martyr.

8. III C, the sixth day before the Ides. At Rome, on the Via Ostiensis, Cyriacus, martyr, with twenty-one others, whose bodies were buried on 8 August.

9. IV D, the fifth day before the Ides. At Rome, Romanus, soldier. The vigil of Saint Lawrence.

10. V E, the fourth day before the Ides. At Rome, Lawrence, archdeacon and martyr. And 165 soldiers.

11. VI F, the third day before the Ides. At Rome, between the two laurel trees, Tiburtius, martyr. And Susanna, virgin and martyr.

12. VII G, the second day before the Ides. At Catana, Euplus, deacon and martyr. In Syria, Macarius and Julian.

13. I II, the Ides. At Rome, Hippolytus, martyr, with his household, and Saint Concordia, his nurse. In the Forum of Sulla, Cassianus.

14. II I, the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September. At Rome, Eusebius, presbyter and confessor, buried in the cemetery of Callistus under Constantius the Arian.

15. III K, the eighteenth day before the Kalends. The Dormition of Saint Mary. Saint Tharsicius, acolyte and martyr.

16. IV L, the seventeenth day before the Kalends. At Nicaea in Bithynia, Ursacius, confessor under Licinius. At Rome, Serena, wife of the Emperor Diocletian.

17. V M, the sixteenth day before the Kalends. In Africa, the martyrs Liberatus, abbot; Boniface, deacon; Servus and Rusticus; and others, under the Vandal persecution. At Caesarea, Mammeas, martyr.

18. VI N, the fifteenth day before the Kalends. In the city of Praeneste, Agapitus, martyr. At Rome, John and Crispus, presbyters.

19. VII O, the fourteenth day before the Kalends. Saint Magnus, or Andrew, martyr, with 2,597 companions. At Rome, Julius, senator and martyr.

20. I P, the thirteenth day before the Kalends. The prophet Samuel.

[Col. 0167]

And Porphyrius, a man of God.

21. II Q, the twelfth day before the Kalends. At Salona, Anastasius, martyr.

22. III R, the eleventh day before the Kalends. At Rome, on the Via Ostiensis, Timothy, martyr. And Anthony, martyr. And the pilgrim martyrs Martial, Epictetus, and Saturninus with their companions.

23. IV S, the tenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Hippolytus, Quiriacus, and Archilaus. Zacchaeus, bishop. Theonas, bishop.

24. V T, the ninth day before the Kalends. Bartholomew, apostle and martyr. At Massa Candida, in Carthage.

25. VI A, the eighth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Genesius, martyr and mime. He was a teacher of the theatrical art. And Saint Genesius of Arles. At Rome, the four martyrs Eusebius, Pontianus, Peregrinus, and Vincentius.

26. VII B, the seventh day before the Kalends. Pope Zephyrinus. Irenaeus and Abundius. At Bergamo, Alexander. At Victimilium, Secundus, martyr.

27. I C, the sixth day before the Kalends. At Capua, Rufus, martyr, a disciple of Apollinaris. At Tomis, Marcellinus and Mannea.

28. II D, the fifth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Hermes, martyr. In Africa, Augustine, bishop. At Constantinople, Saint Alexander, bishop.

29. III E, the fourth day before the Kalends. At Rome, at the Arch of Faustinus, Sabina, martyr. On this day the beheading of Saint John the Baptist is venerated.

30. IV F, the third day before the Kalends. On the Via Ostiensis, Felix and + Audax, martyrs.

31. V G, the second day before the Kalends. At Athens, Aristides, who presented books concerning the Christian religion to the Emperor Hadrian.

## The month of September has thirty days; the moon, thirty.

[Col. 0167]

1. VI H, the Kalends of September. Joshua son of Nun and Gideon, prophets. At Capua, Priscus, martyr, one of those ancient disciples of Christ. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Longinus, soldier and martyr, who opened the Lord’s side on the cross.

2. VII I, the fourth day before the Nones. At Apamea, Antoninus, martyr.

3. I K, the third day before the Nones. At Rome, Seraphia, virgin, who suffered on the fourth day before the Kalends of August and was buried on the second day before the Kalends; on the third day before the Nones of September, the memory of her passion is more solemnly celebrated.

4. II L, the second day before the Nones. Moses, prophet. At Ancyra, the three child-martyrs Rufinus, Silvanus, and Vitalica.

5. III M, the Nones. At Rome, Victorinus, martyr, brother of Severinus, who, after remarkable repentance, became bishop and martyr of the city of Amiternum. At Rome, Hercon.

6. IV N, the eighth day before the Ides. Zachariah, prophet. And Onesiphorus, Paul’s disciple. And the confessors Donatianus and the others.

7. V O, the seventh day before the Ides. John, martyr, who at Nicomedia under Diocletian tore the book of the wicked law into pieces.

8. VI P, the sixth day before the Ides. The Nativity of Mary, Mother of God. And Adrian, martyr, with twenty-three martyrs. And Natalia.

9. VII Q, the fifth day before the Ides. At Nicomedia, Dorotheus and Gorgonius, martyrs; one of them, Gorgonius, was transferred to Rome. In the Sabine region, Hyacinthus, Alexander, and Tiburtius.

[Col. 0169]

10. I R, the fourth day before the Ides. In Africa, the bishops Nemesianus and Felix, and seven others. At Chalcedon, Sosthenes and Victor.

11. II S, the third day before the Ides. At Rome, Hyacinthus and Protus, eunuchs.

12. III T, the second day before the Ides. At Ticinum, the confessor Syrus, and Eventius, disciples of Hermagoras, first bishop of Aquileia.

13. IV V, the Ides. At Alexandria, Philip, bishop and martyr, who had first been prefect.

14. V A, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October. At Rome, Cornelius, bishop and martyr. At Carthage, Cyprian, bishop and martyr. The Exaltation of the Holy Cross, brought back from the Persians to Jerusalem by the Emperor Heraclius; on the same day at Rome the life-giving wood of the Cross, discovered by Pope Sergius, is venerated by the entire people.

15. VI B, the seventeenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Nicomedes, martyr.

16. VII C, the sixteenth day before the Kalends. At Chalcedon, Euphemia, virgin. At Rome, Lucia and Germinianus, martyrs.

17. I D, the fifteenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Justinus, presbyter, to whom Blessed Lawrence came by night in the district called the Vicus Patricius. Also Narcissus and Crescentianus.

18. II E, the fourteenth day before the Kalends. Methodius, of Olympus in Lycia and later bishop of Tyre, who was crowned with martyrdom under Diocletian.

19. III F, the thirteenth day before the Kalends. At Naples, Januarius, Socius, Festus, Desiderius, Proculus, Eutyches, and Acutius. And Peleus and Nilus.

20. IV G, the twelfth day before the Kalends. At Cyzicus, Fausta, virgin, and Evilasius.

21. V II, the eleventh day before the Kalends. Matthew, apostle.

22. VI I, the tenth day before the Kalends. Mauritius with his companions, who are said to have been Thebans and to have suffered under Maximian.

23. VII K, the ninth day before the Kalends. Mesenathes; Sosius, deacon, a martyr of thirty years; and Thecla, virgin, resting at Seleucia.

24. I L, the eighth day before the Kalends. The conception of John the Baptist.

25. II M, the seventh day before the Kalends. Cleopas, to whom the Lord appeared on the road after the resurrection.

26. III N, the sixth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Cyprian, bishop of Antioch, who suffered martyrdom and was transferred to Rome with the martyr Justina.

27. IV O, the fifth day before the Kalends. In the city of Aegeae, Cosmas and Damian, Anthimus, Leontius, and Euprepius.

28. V P, the fourth day before the Kalends. At Córdoba, Faustus, Januarius, and Martial, martyrs.

29. VI Q, the third day before the Kalends. On Mount Gargano, the venerable memory of the archangel Michael. And at Rome, the dedication of a church of that same archangel, built by Blessed Pope Boniface in the Circus, a place called Internubes.

30. VII R, the second day before the Kalends. At Bethlehem, Jerome, presbyter.

## The month of October has thirty-one days; the moon, thirty.

[Col. 0169]

1. I S, the Kalends of October. At the city of Tomis, Priscus, Crescentius, and Evagrius. And at the city of Reims, Saint Remigius, bishop.

2. II T, the sixth day before the Nones. At Nicomedia, Eleutherius, martyr under Diocletian, and innumerable others whom the enraged Diocletian killed with various tortures, out of hatred for the Christian name, because the palace had been burned.

3. III V, the fifth day before the Nones. At Athens, Dionysius the Areopagite, who suffered various tortures under Hadrian, as Aristides testifies in the work he composed concerning the Christian religion. This work is held among the Athenians as one of the most renowned records of antiquity.

[Note: “At Athens, Dionysius the Areopagite, who suffered various tortures under Hadrian,” etc. Shortly afterward, under 9 October: “At Paris, Dionysius, bishop, with his companions, executed by the sword of Fescenninus.” You see that on the authority of this Martyrology two Dionysiuses are distinguished by day and place. The ancient Martyrologies, Bede, Usuard, Ado, and Notker likewise distinguish them. It cannot be suspected that something was later added among these writers, since they faithfully transmitted what they found in this ancient Roman Martyrology. I hear that a learned man is presently undertaking a careful investigation of this matter; I shall therefore say no more.]

4. IV A, the fourth day before the Nones. At Corinth, Crispus and Caius. In Egypt, Mark and Martianus, brothers, and with them an innumerable multitude.

5. V B, the third day before the Nones. At Eumenia, Thraseas, bishop, crowned at Smyrna, one of the ancients.

6. VI C, the second day before the Nones. Sagaris, bishop of Laodicea, one of the ancient disciples of the apostle Paul.

7. VII D, the Nones. At Rome, Mark, pope. And Julia, Sergius, and Bacchus; Marcellus and Apuleius, who first adhered to Simon Magus and afterward to the apostle Peter; they were crowned with martyrdom under Aurelian, a man of consular rank.

8. I E, the eighth day before the Ides. At Gortyna, Philip, bishop. At Thessalonica, Demetrius, martyr.

9. II F, the seventh day before the Ides. Abraham, patriarch. At Paris, Dionysius, bishop, with his companions, executed by the sword of Fescenninus.

10. III G, the sixth day before the Ides. Lot, prophet. In Crete, Pinytus, one of the most distinguished among the bishops.

11. IV H, the fifth day before the Ides. At Tarsus, the martyrs Tharacus, Probus, and Andronicus.

12. V I, the fourth day before the Ides. At Ravenna, Edistius. In Africa, 4,976 holy confessors who suffered under the Vandal persecution.

13. VI K, the third day before the Ides. At Troas, Carpus, a disciple of the apostle Paul. At Antioch, Theophilus, bishop, who was sixth from the apostles.

14. VII L, the second day before the Ides. At Rome, Callistus, pope and martyr, and Privatus, soldier.

15. I M, the Ides.

16. II N, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November. The holy martyrs Martianus and Satyrianus, with their two brothers and 270 others, crowned together under the Vandal persecution.

17. III O, the sixteenth day before the Kalends. Martha, sister of Lazarus. And Aristion, who was one of the seventy disciples of Christ.

18. IV P, the fifteenth day before the Kalends. Luke, evangelist. And Asclepiades, bishop of Antioch. At Rome, Tryphonia, formerly wife of Caesar Decius.

19. V Q, the fourteenth day before the Kalends. At Antioch, Beronicus, Pelagia, and 49 others. And Ptolemy, who was handed over to the judge by a certain centurion, Urbicius, together with Lucius and Tertius, all of whom were beheaded and buried at Alexandria.

20. VI R, the thirteenth day before the Kalends.

[Note: In the manuscript the saints of the following day were written here; on the 21st, Mark and Salome; and the 22nd was left blank. But Ado and all the others have it as printed here.]

21. VII S, the twelfth day before the Kalends. At Nicomedia, Dasius, Zoticus, Caius, with twelve soldiers. And Saint Hilarion, monk.

22. I T, the eleventh day before the Kalends. At Jerusalem, Mark, who was the first of the Gentiles to be made bishop there. And Salome, who is mentioned in the Gospel.

23. II V, the tenth day before the Kalends. At Antioch, Theodoretus, presbyter. In Spain, Servandus and Germanus.

24. III A, the ninth day before the Kalends. At Venusia, Felix, bishop of Tubzoca, and Audactus and Januarius, presbyters, and Fortunatianus and Septimus, lectors.

[Note: “The dedication of Saint Pantaleon.” This was added in the margin after the saints assigned to that day. For this reason I have not included it in the text. It was certainly added later by a religious of Saint Pantaleon, the copyist of this Martyrology, who wished the solemnity of his own church to appear here also. It is absent from Ado, who is older than that dedication: he lived around the year of the Lord 779 and received the Roman Martyrology, whereas the church of Saint Pantaleon was first founded in the year of Christ 954 by Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, as recorded in the *Sacrarium of Agrippina*, edited by Father Erhard Winheim, p. 141.]

25. IV B, the eighth day before the Kalends. At Rome, on the Via Salaria, 46 soldiers who, having been baptized at the command of Pope Dionysius, were beheaded by order of Claudius.

26. V C, the seventh day before the Kalends. In Africa, Rogatianus, presbyter, and Felicissimus, martyr.

27. VI D, the sixth day before the Kalends. At the city of Abila, Vincentius, Sabina, and Christetes, martyrs.

28. VII E, the fifth day before the Kalends. Simon and Thaddeus, apostles. At Rome, Cyrilla, daughter of Caesar Decius.

[Col. 0173]

29. I F, the fourth day before the Kalends. Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, a man praiseworthy for holiness, endurance, and faith. At Sidon, Zenobius, presbyter and martyr.

30. II G, the third day before the Kalends. In Tingitana, Marcellus, centurion and martyr. In Africa, 220 martyrs.

31. III H, the second day before the Kalends. Nemesius, deacon, and Lucilla, his daughter, who suffered on the eighth day before the Kalends of September but were buried by Pope Sixtus on the day before the Kalends of November.

## The month of November has thirty days; the moon, thirty.

[Col. 0173]

1. IV I, the Kalends of November. The feast of the Saints, celebrated at Rome as a solemn and universal observance. Caesarius, deacon and martyr, and Julianus, presbyter. And Severinus, monk, of the Tiburtine city.

2. V K, the fourth day before the Nones. At Laodicea, Theodotus, bishop, who had been a physician by profession.

3. VI L, the third day before the Nones. Quartus, disciple of the apostles. In Cappadocia, the martyrs Germanus, Theophilus, Caesarius, and Vitalis, under the persecution of Decius.

4. VII M, the second day before the Nones. At Alexandria, Hierius, presbyter, of exceptionally pure life and nobly learned in the Scriptures.

5. I N, the Nones. Zachariah, prophet, father of John the Baptist. At Terracina, Felix, presbyter, and Eusebius, monk.

6. II O, the eighth day before the Ides. At Toniza in Africa, Saint Felix, martyr. In the city of Theopolis, forty martyrs.

7. III P, the seventh day before the Ides. At Alexandria, Achillas, bishop. In the region of Perugia, Herculanus, bishop and martyr.

8. IV Q, the sixth day before the Ides. At Rome, the martyrs Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphronianus, Castorius, and Simplicius, highly distinguished craftsmen. And on the same day, the Four Crowned Martyrs: Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus. Pope Melchiades ordered their feast to be celebrated under the names of five martyrs, because their names could not be found; but as the years passed, they were revealed to a certain holy man.

9. V R, the fifth day before the Ides. At Euchaita, Saint Theodore, martyr.

10. VI S, the fourth day before the Ides. At Cherson in Lycia, Martin, pope, who, having been exiled there for the Catholic faith, ended his life.

11. VII T, the third day before the Ides. At Tours, Martin, bishop and worker of miracles. In Scythia, Menas, martyr, transferred to Constantinople.

12. I V, the second day before the Ides. In Africa, Arcadius, Paschasius, Probus, and Eutychianus, martyrs under the Vandal persecution.

13. II A, the Ides. At Ravenna, the martyrs Valentinus, Solutor, and Victor.

14. III B, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December. At Alexandria, Serapion, who was thrown from a height under Decius and thus became a martyr.

15. IV C, the seventeenth day before the Kalends. Felix, bishop, who from his fifteenth year was distinguished by the glory of miracles and completed his martyrdom with thirty others under Martianus; he was buried in the church at Nola.

16. V D, the sixteenth day before the Kalends.

17. VI E, the fifteenth day before the Kalends. The dedication of Saint Peter at Malmundarium.

[Note: “The dedication of Saint Peter at Malmundarium.” No mention of this appears in Ado, and I have no doubt that this too is an addition. The Cologne copyist wished to insert here two very ancient and famous monasteries in the Ardennes forest, in the territory of the Eburones. Above, on 20 April, we had Sabuletum, commonly called Stavelot; here we have Malmundarium, commonly called Malmedy.

Sigebert writes of both in his Chronicle under the year 651: “King Sigebert, despairing of offspring, built twelve monasteries for God here and there, among which Stavelot and Malmundarium were prominent, with the assistance of Grimoald, mayor of the palace, and Remaclus, bishop of Tongeren. Remaclus, not long afterward, weary of worldly disturbances, assumed the habit of monastic life at Stavelot itself.”

That Malmundarium was dedicated to Saint Peter is recorded by Notger in the *Life of Saint Remaclus*, 3 September, chapter 20, where he gives this charter of King Sigebert, its founder: “The holy and venerable monasteries called Stavelot and Malmundarium, where the venerable Remaclus, bishop and abbot, appears by Christ’s favor to preside, which the illustrious Grimoald, mayor of the palace, built by his own work in the vast and deserted forest of the Ardennes in honor of Saint Peter, Saint Paul, Saint Martin, and the other saints; just as we granted the places themselves from our forest for the construction of those monasteries by our command,” and so forth.

I do not know whether this passage of the Martyrology should be understood of that first dedication of the monastery and church. Neither Sigebert nor Notger gives a definite day. Therefore the Martyrology more probably refers to the second dedication of the monastery and church of Malmundarium. The manuscript *Acts of the Abbots of Malmundarium* says:

“Absalon, the fifteenth abbot, in the year 801. In the year 817, in the tenth indiction, he caused the monastery of Malmundarium to be restored, in the time of Louis, the most pious king, by whose assistance and at whose expense it was restored. It was dedicated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December by Willibert, archbishop of Cologne.”

I owe this information from the *Acts* to the Reverend Father Aegidius Bouchier, a diligent investigator of chronology.

Concerning the etymology of the name, Harigerus, abbot of Lobbes, writes in chapter 55 of his *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*, where he is speaking of Saint Remaclus: “And because he cleansed that place from the pollution of superstitions, it pleased him to call it Malmundarium, as though ‘cleansed from evil.’” Thus, evidently, they then took pleasure in hunting for an etymology based on the syllables.]

[Col. 0175]

At Alexandria, Dionysius, bishop, often distinguished by many confessions, in the times of Valerian and Gallienus.

18. VII F, the fourteenth day before the Kalends. At Antioch, Romanus, monk and martyr. And Saint Hesychius, a palace official and martyr.

19. I G, the thirteenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Maximus, presbyter and martyr. And Faustus, deacon, and Eusebius, his colleague, martyrs who were visitors.

20. II H, the twelfth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Pontianus, pope and martyr. At Messina, Ampelus and Caius.

21. III I, the eleventh day before the Kalends. Rufus, whom the Apostle greets in his Letter to the Romans.

22. IV K, the tenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Cecilia, virgin and martyr.

23. V L, the ninth day before the Kalends. Saint Clement, bishop. And Felicitas, mother of seven sons.

24. VI M, the eighth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Chrysogonus, martyr, and Zoilus.

25. VII N, the seventh day before the Kalends. Saint Peter of Alexandria, bishop, with 660 others.

26. I O, the sixth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Linus, pope. And Blessed Alexander, bishop and martyr, who suffered on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October and was transferred on the sixth day before the Kalends of December by Pope Damasus, who dedicated a feast to him on that day.

27. II P, the fifth day before the Kalends. At Bologna, Vitalis and Agricola, martyrs.

28. III Q, the fourth day before the Kalends. Sosthenes, disciple of the apostles. And Saint Rufus, martyr, with his entire household, won for Christ by Chrysogonus. In Africa, Papinius and Mansuetus, bishops.

29. IV R, the third day before the Kalends. At Rome, Saturninus, martyr, and Sennen and Sisinnius, deacons.

30. V S, the second day before the Kalends. Andrew, apostle.

## The month of December has thirty-one days; the moon, twenty-nine.

[Col. 0175]

1. VI T, the Kalends of December. At Rome, the martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria, and Diodorus and Marianus, with an innumerable multitude of martyrs.

2. VII V, the fourth day before the Nones. At Rome, Viviana [variant: Bibiana], martyr. Faustus, martyr, and Daphrosa, a daughter.

3. I A, the third day before the Nones. At Rome, Claudius, tribune, and Hilaria, his wife, and Jason and Maurus, seventy soldiers, under Numerianus.

4. II B, the second day before the Nones. At Rome, Symphronius and Olympius, Exsuperia and Theodulus, who suffered on the seventh day before the Kalends of August and were transferred by Blessed Sixtus on the Via Latina on the second day before the Nones of December; their feast is celebrated more solemnly on that day.

5. III C, the Nones. Crispina, martyr. And Dalmatius, martyr.

6. IV D, the eighth day before the Ides. Nicholas, bishop of Myra in Lycia. In Africa, Dionysia, Dativa, Leontius, and Aemilianus the physician, and others.

7. V E, the seventh day before the Ides. At Alexandria, Agatho, martyr and soldier under Decius.

8. VI F, the sixth day before the Ides. At Rome, Eutychianus, pope and martyr, who personally buried 342 martyrs. At Alexandria, Macarius, martyr, of Libyan descent.

[Col. 0177]

9. VII G, the fifth day before the Ides. Leocadia, virgin.

10. I H, the fourth day before the Ides. Eulalia, virgin and martyr. At Spoleto, Carpophorus, presbyter, and Abundius, deacon.

11. II I, the third day before the Ides. Daniel, prophet. At Rome, Damasus, pope. And the martyrs Pontianus, Praetextatus, and Thrason, who ministered to the martyrs from his own means.

12. III K, the second day before the Ides. At Alexandria, Epimachus and Alexander. And the four holy women Ammonaria, Mercuria, Dionysia, and Ammonaria.

13. IV L, the Ides. At Syracuse, Lucia, virgin and martyr.

14. V M, the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January. At Antioch, Drusus, Zosimus, and Theodore. At Alexandria, Heron, Arsenius, Isidore, and Dioscorus. In Cyprus, Spyridon, bishop.

15. VI N, the eighteenth day before the Kalends. In Africa, Valerianus, bishop and confessor, under the Vandal persecution.

16. VII O, the seventeenth day before the Kalends. The martyrdom of the holy Ananias, Azariah, and Misael. In Tuscany, Barbara, virgin and martyr.

17. I P, the sixteenth day before the Kalends. The translation of Ignatius, bishop and martyr of Antioch. And Lazarus, whom Christ raised, and Martha, his sister, at Bethany.

18. II Q, the fifteenth day before the Kalends. Rufus and Zosimus, among the first disciples of Christ, through whom the primitive Church was founded among Jews and Greeks.

19. III R, the fourteenth day before the Kalends. In Egypt, Nemesius, martyr, who through false accusation was handed over to the judge as though he were a thief.

20. IV S, the thirteenth day before the Kalends. At Alexandria, Ammon, Zeno, Ptolemy, Ingenus, and Theophilus.

21. V T, the twelfth day before the Kalends. Thomas, apostle. In Tuscany, John and Festus.

22. VI V, the eleventh day before the Kalends. At Rome, thirty martyrs under Diocletian, buried on the Via Labicana between the two laurel trees. At Alexandria, Ischyrion, martyr. And very many others, among them the aged Chaeremon.

23. VII A, the tenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, Victoria, martyr. At Nicomedia, twenty martyrs. At Rome, Servulus, worn down by illness, buried in the church of Blessed Clement, where the Lord deigns to perform miracles through him.

24. I B, the ninth day before the Kalends. The vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. At Spoleto, Gregory, presbyter and martyr.

25. II C, the eighth day before the Kalends. THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD ACCORDING TO THE FLESH. At Rome, Anastasia. And Eugenia.

26. III D, the seventh day before the Kalends. Stephen, protomartyr.

27. IV E, the sixth day before the Kalends. John, apostle and evangelist, at Ephesus.

28. V F, the fifth day before the Kalends. At Bethlehem, the holy Innocents.

29. VI G, the fourth day before the Kalends. David, king. And Trophimus, bishop, a disciple of the apostles.

30. VII H, the third day before the Kalends. At Spoleto, Sabinus, bishop; Exsuperantius and Marcellus; and Venustianus with his wife and sons. They suffered on the seventh day before the Ides of December, but celebrate the feast of their burial on the third day before the Kalends of January.

31. I I, the second day before the Kalends. At Rome, Sylvester, pope and confessor. And Saint Columba, virgin.

[Col. 0179]

## In what manner the holy martyrs are to be venerated

From the books of Blessed Augustine, bishop (*Against Faustus*, Book XX, chapter 21)

[Col. 0179A] The Christian people solemnly celebrates the memorials of the martyrs, both to stir up imitation and to be associated with their merits and aided by their prayers; yet in such a way that, although we set up altars in the memorials of the martyrs, we set them up for no martyr, but for the God of the martyrs himself. For which bishop, standing in the places of the holy bodies, has ever said at the altar, “We offer to you, Peter, or Paul, or Cyprian”? Rather, what is offered is offered to God, who crowned the martyrs, at the memorials of those whom he crowned; so that, through the reminder provided by those places, a greater affection may arise, increasing our charity both toward those whom we can imitate and toward him by whose help we can do so.

We therefore honor the martyrs with that worship of love and fellowship with which the holy men of God are honored in this life also—men whose hearts we perceive to have been prepared for such suffering on behalf of the truth of the Gospel—but we honor the martyrs with greater devotion, because they have more securely overcome every uncertainty, and because we proclaim them with more confident praise as victors already in the happier life, rather than as men still fighting in this one.

But with that worship which in Greek is called λατρεία (*latreia*), and which cannot be expressed in Latin by a single word, since it is a certain service properly owed to the divinity, we neither worship nor teach that anything should be worshiped except the one God. Since the offering of sacrifice belongs to this worship—for which reason those who offer this even to idols are called idolaters—we in no way offer or command that anything of this kind be offered either to any martyr, to any holy soul, or to any angel. Whoever falls into this error is corrected by sound doctrine, whether so that he may be corrected [Col. 0179B] or so that others may be warned.

The saints themselves, whether human beings or angels, do not wish anything to be offered to them that they know is owed to the one Lord. This was evident in Paul and Barnabas (Acts 14), when the Lycaonians, moved by the miracles performed through them, wished to sacrifice to them as gods. For they tore their garments, declaring and persuading the people that they were not gods, and forbade this to be done to them. It was also evident in the angels, as we read in the Apocalypse (chapters 19 and 22), where an angel forbids himself to be worshiped and says to the one who would worship him: “I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers; worship the Lord.”

The proud spirits plainly demand these things for themselves—the devil and his angels—as is seen throughout all the temples [Col. 0180A] and sacred rites of the pagans. Their likeness has also been displayed in certain proud human beings, as we remember having been recorded concerning certain kings of Babylon. Thus the holy Daniel endured accusers and persecutors because, when a royal decree had been issued that nothing should be asked of any god except the king alone, he was discovered worshiping and praying to his own God, that is, the one true God.

How, then, can those who make themselves drunk at the memorials of the martyrs be approved by us, when sound doctrine condemns them even if they do this in their own homes? But one thing is what we teach, another what we tolerate; one thing is what we are commanded to prescribe, another what we are commanded to correct—and until we correct it, are compelled to tolerate. The discipline of Christians is one thing; the indulgence of drunkards, or the error of the weak, is another. Nevertheless, even in this matter there is a very great difference between the guilt of drunkards and that of sacrilegious persons. For it is a far lesser sin to return drunk from the martyrs than either to sacrifice while fasting to the martyrs.

I said “to sacrifice to the martyrs”; I did not say “to sacrifice to God in the memorials of the martyrs.” This we do very frequently, but only with that rite by which, through the revelation of the New Testament, he commanded sacrifice to be offered to himself; this belongs to the worship called λατρεία (*latreia*) and is owed to God alone.

[Therefore, the true sacrifice, which is owed to the one true God, whose altar Christ alone has filled, the demons arrogantly demand for themselves in imitation of the sacrifices of animals. Hence the Apostle says: “What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God” (1 Cor. 10)—not blaming what was offered, but because it was offered to them. [Col. 0180C] The Hebrews, however, in the animal victims that they offered to God, celebrated in many different ways, as was fitting for so great a matter, a prophecy of the future victim whom Christ offered. Hence Christians now celebrate the memorial of that sacrifice, once accomplished, through the most holy offering and participation in the body and blood of Christ.]

The flesh and blood of this sacrifice were promised before Christ’s coming through the likeness represented by the victims; in Christ’s passion they were given in the reality itself; after Christ’s ascension the memorial is celebrated through the sacrament.

[Col. 0179]

## Rosweidus to the Benevolent Reader

[Col. 0179D] Aloysius Lipomanus, bishop of Verona and an illustrious ornament of Italy, took not a little from the manuscript Martyrology of Ado in the fourth volume of his *Lives of the Saints*, published at Venice in the year 1554. He valued it so highly that he himself writes: “I considered all gold as nothing in comparison with it.” Then Jacobus Mosander, a distinguished alumnus of the Carthusian house of Cologne, in the year 1581, in the seventh volume of his *Lives of the Saints*, gave Surius a substitute and published this Martyrology of Ado in a fuller form.

But since he both changed its order, inserted certain things from another hand, removed a few passages, and failed to obtain some others, it seemed worthwhile to examine Ado once again, restore him to his former purity, and append him to the old Roman Martyrology, as he himself once did. [Col. 0181A] To carry this out faithfully, I had the assistance of three ancient codices, very kindly supplied by various supporters of ecclesiastical antiquity. The first was from Saint Pantaleon of Cologne, supplied by the Carthusian house of Cologne, from which Ado had emerged under Mosander’s care. I obtained the second from the abbey of Everbode near Sichem; the third from Petrus Scriverius. Although each of them demonstrated its antiquity, the third nevertheless stood out—except that it lacked everything at the beginning, through March, as well as part of June and July. The others represented Ado complete, in the order and manner in which I now present him. The letters prefixed to the individual days of the Martyrology were found only in the Everbode codex.

Therefore, reader, do not be surprised that here, at the beginning of Ado’s Martyrology, there appears a little book on the festivals of the holy apostles and of the others who were their disciples or their immediate successors and successors in office. For I have added nothing on the authority of authors or books, even the most ancient; nor have I changed anything in the commonly circulated Ado except with the support of these same authorities. Indeed, Ado himself supports the authority of this little book in his Martyrology on 2 July, where, after briefly mentioning the holy martyrs Processus and Martinianus, he adds: “Their passion is recorded above in the little book of the apostles.” These words are lacking in the commonly circulated Ado, as are certain other passages. This happened because Mosander inserted this little book of the apostles throughout Ado’s Martyrology, each passage in its proper place, after removing what had been recorded about those same saints only in brief form. But Ado himself had adopted a different plan. He wished the apostles and their apostolic successors to appear at the front as leaders of a noble army, and to lead the glorious soldiers out as if into battle; he also wished them to appear again at the beginnings and after the beginnings—as capable commanders customarily do. Why should we alter this?

That the author of this little book, like the author of the Martyrology, was Ado, archbishop of Vienne, not of Trier—as Aloysius and Mosander believed—is demonstrated by the Everbode codex, which bears this title: “Ado, archbishop of Vienne, compiled this as a kind of epitome, beginning with the festivals of the apostles, or of their disciples, or of their successors.” The title I placed before it, however, comes from the codex of Saint Pantaleon, in which Ado prefaces the old Roman Martyrology, as stated above, without any distinction being added concerning the episcopal see.

This Ado of Vienne is much earlier than the Ado of Trier. The latter lived in the time of John VIII, around the year 879; for he brought his *Chronicle* down to that year. The other, whether called Ado or Udo, lived in the time of Gregory VII, around the year 1076. Ado of Vienne’s feast is listed among the saints on 16 December: “At Vienne, the blessed Ado, bishop and confessor.” [Col. 0182B]

You should know that here Ado’s Martyrology begins not with the Kalends of January, as it has hitherto been published, but with the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. This was done according to the rite of the Roman Church, which formerly had the Nativity of Christ as the epoch of the year and began the year from the Vespers of the Vigil of that Nativity. The three manuscript copies that I used consistently displayed it in this way. See also the learned Paulus Petavius’s *Syntagma on the Epoch of Years*.

[Col. 0181]

## Little Book on the Festivals of the Holy Apostles and of the Others Who Were Their Disciples or Immediate Successors and Successors in Office

### E. III Kalends of July (29 June)

[Col. 0181C]

(Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 1.) At Rome, the feast of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, who suffered under the consuls Bassus and Tuscus.

Peter, in the second year of Claudius, after his episcopate of the Church of Antioch and the preaching of the dispersion of those who had believed from the circumcision throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, was sent to Rome to overthrow Simon Magus. There he held the priestly chair for twenty-five years, until the final year of Nero. By Nero he was fastened to a cross and crowned with martyrdom, with his head turned toward the earth and his feet raised upward, declaring himself unworthy to be crucified like his Lord. Buried in that same city, in the Vatican near the Triumphal Way, he is honored by the veneration of the whole world.

He wrote two letters called Catholic; the second is denied by many on account of its difference in style from the first. The Gospel according to Mark, who was his hearer and interpreter, is also said to be his. But the books of which one is called his *Acts*, another his *Gospel*, a third his *Preaching*, a fourth his *Apocalypse* (Ἀποκάλυψις), and a fifth his *Judgment*, are rejected among the apocryphal writings.

(Ibid., chapter 2.) Paul also, in the twenty-fifth year after the Lord’s passion—that is, the second year of Nero—after he had filled with the Gospel of Christ the region from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, was sent to Rome in chains. As he himself writes in the Second Letter to Timothy, he was delivered from the mouth of the lion (2 Tim. 4), namely, from Nero, the most savage persecutor, and preached the Gospel of Christ also in the regions of the West.

He too, therefore, in the fourteenth year of Nero, on the same day on which Peter was beheaded for Christ at Rome, was buried on the Ostian Way, in the thirty-seventh year after the Lord’s passion. He wrote nine letters to seven churches: one to the Romans; two to the Corinthians; one to the Galatians; one to the Ephesians; one to the Philippians; one to the Colossians; and two to the Thessalonians.

In addition, he wrote to his disciples: two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon. The letter said to be addressed to the Hebrews is not believed to be his, because of its difference in style and language. It is attributed either to Barnabas, according to Tertullian; or to Luke the evangelist, according to some; or to Clement, afterwards bishop of the Church at Rome, who, they say, arranged and adorned Paul’s thoughts in his own language; or certainly—because Paul was writing to Hebrews and, on account of the envy aroused among them by his name, had cut off the title at the beginning of the greeting, while he had written as a Hebrew in Hebrew, that is, most eloquently in his own language—because someone translated into Greek, even more eloquently, what had been written eloquently in Hebrew, and this is why it appears to differ from Paul’s other letters. [Col. 0183A] Nevertheless, the whole Church now holds with the greatest firmness that it is Paul’s, not another’s.

Some also read a letter to the Laodiceans, but it is rejected by everyone. He was of the tribe of Benjamin and from the Judean town of Gischala [another reading: Gischalis]. When it was captured by the Romans, he migrated with his parents to Tarsus in Cilicia. From there, on account of his zeal for the Law, he was sent to Jerusalem and instructed by Gamaliel, a most learned man (Acts 7 and 9). When he had taken part in the killing of the martyr Stephen and, having received letters from the chief priest of the Temple, was going to Damascus to persecute those who believed in Christ, he was compelled by a revelation to embrace the faith and was transformed from a persecutor into a vessel of election. When Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Cyprus, first believed through his preaching, he received his name from him, because he had subjected him to the faith of Christ.

### F. II Kalends of December (30 November)

[Col. 0183B]

At the city of Patras in the province of Achaia, the feast of the blessed apostle Andrew, who also preached in Scythia.

This most blessed apostle was arrested by Aegeas, proconsul of Achaia. Since he remained steadfast in the faith of Christ and in the ministry of the Gospel, and proved unconquerable, he was first shut in prison; then, before the proconsul, he was beaten most severely; finally, with hands and feet bound to a cross and his whole body stretched with ropes so that he might suffer longer, he survived there for two days, never ceasing to teach the people the things that belong to Christ.

When those who had believed in Christ the Lord through him did everything possible to have him taken down and forced Aegeas, who was unwilling, to carry this out, the apostle of the Lord—while the people stood around and the proconsul Aegeas was working to have him released—after words of prayer was almost for an hour surrounded from above by heavenly radiance. When the light withdrew, he breathed out his spirit and went to the Lord in a blessed end.

(Eusebius, *Chronicle*.) His most holy body was reverently taken down and buried by Maximilla, the most powerful of women. But as the years passed, his most sacred bones were transferred from Achaia to Constantinople in the twentieth year of the emperor Constantius.

### C. VIII Kalends of August (25 July)

The feast of the blessed apostle James, brother of John the evangelist, who was beheaded by King Herod at Jerusalem, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles teaches (chapter 12). [Col. 0183D] The sacred bones of this most blessed apostle were transferred to Spain and buried at its farthest limits, namely opposite the British Sea; they are honored with the most celebrated veneration of those peoples.

### D. VI Kalends of January (27 December)

(Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 9.) The feast of the blessed apostle and evangelist John, whom Jesus loved exceedingly. When Domitian began the second persecution after Nero, John was plunged into boiling oil but suffered no harm; afterward he was exiled to the island of Patmos, where he saw the Apocalypse.

After Domitian was killed and his acts were rescinded by the Senate because of his excessive cruelty, John returned to Ephesus under Pertinax. When he saw that, in his absence, the faith of the Church had been shaken by heretics, he immediately set it down in his Gospel and established it upon the eternity of the Lord’s Word.

Indeed, when the bishops of Asia asked him to oppose Cerinthus and the other heretics, and especially the doctrine of the Ebionites that was then arising—those who asserted that Christ had not existed before Mary—he was compelled to undertake the holy work of writing the Gospel.

They report another reason for this writing: that when John had read the volumes of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, he approved the substance of their history and affirmed that they had spoken the truth, but that they had confined their history to only one year, in which Christ also suffered, after the imprisonment of John. Passing over that year, whose events had been set forth by the three, he narrated what had taken place in the earlier period, before John was shut in prison. [Col. 0184B] This will be evident to those who carefully read the four volumes of the Gospels. This also removes the *diaphōnia* (διαφωνία), that is, the disagreement that seemed to exist between John and the others.

John himself continued until the reign of Trajan and founded and governed all the churches of Asia. Worn out by old age, he died in the sixty-eighth year after the Lord’s passion and was buried near that same city. He also wrote one letter, whose opening is: “What was from the beginning.” It is approved by all ecclesiastical and learned men.

The other two letters, whose beginnings are “The elder to the chosen lady and her children” and “The elder to the beloved Gaius,” are thought by some to be by John the presbyter. But now the general consensus of the Church holds that the apostle John wrote these letters as well.

### B. Kalends of May (1 May)

The feast of the blessed apostles Philip and James.

Of these, Philip, after converting almost all Scythia to the faith of Christ and establishing deacons, priests, and bishops there, returned to Asia. There he devoted himself to continuous preaching for several years and, always serving Christ through pious labors, won a multitude of peoples. He fell asleep at Hierapolis, a city of Asia, and was buried with his fathers in a blessed end.

(Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 2.) James, who is also read of as the brother of the Lord, called the Just, was immediately after the Lord’s passion appointed bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles. He was holy from his mother’s womb; he drank no wine or strong drink, ate no flesh, was never shorn, never anointed with oil, and never used a bath. To him alone it was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies. He did not wear woolen garments, but linen ones; and he alone entered the Temple and prayed for the people on bended knees, so much so that it was believed his knees had acquired the hardness of camels.

When the Jews publicly compelled him in the council to deny that Christ was the Son of God, he protested to the people in a very loud voice, saying: “Why do you question me about the Son of Man? Behold, he sits at the right hand of the power of God, and he will come with the clouds of heaven.” Then he was thrown down from the pinnacle of the Temple. Though his legs were broken, though half-dead he still raised his hands toward heaven and said: “Lord, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” He died after being struck on the head with a fuller’s club.

He is the one of whom the apostle Paul writes to the Galatians: “I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord” (Gal. 1). The Acts of the Apostles also repeatedly testify to this.

The Gospel called “According to the Hebrews,” which was translated into Greek and Latin by the blessed Jerome, reports this about him after the Savior’s resurrection:

“But when the Lord had given the linen cloth to the servant of the priest, he came to James the Just and appeared to him. James had sworn that he would not eat bread from the hour at which he had drunk the Lord’s cup until he saw him risen from the dead.”

And again, a little later:

“Bring a table and bread,” said the Lord.

Immediately it is added:

“He took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to James the Just, saying to him: ‘My brother, eat your bread, for the Son of Man has risen from the dead.’”

He governed the Church at Jerusalem for thirty years, that is, until the seventh year of Nero, and was buried beside the Temple, where he had been thrown down. Some think that he was buried on the Mount of Olives, but their opinion is false. He wrote only one letter, which is one of the seven canonical letters.

### E. IX Kalends of September (24 August)

The feast of the blessed apostle Bartholomew, who, preaching the Gospel of Christ in India, completed his martyrdom by beheading. His most sacred body was first transferred to the island of Lipara, which lies near Sicily, and then to Beneventum, where it is honored by the pious veneration of the faithful.

### E. XII Kalends of January (21 December)

The feast of the blessed apostle Thomas, who, preaching the Gospel among the Parthians and Medes, suffered in India. His body was transferred to the city which the Syrians call Edessa, and there buried with due honor.

### F. II Kalends of October (21 September)

(Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 3.) The feast of the blessed apostle and evangelist Matthew, who first wrote the Gospel of Christ in Judea in the Hebrew language (Matt. 2; Luke 5); afterward, while preaching in Ethiopia, he suffered martyrdom. His Gospel, written in his own style, was discovered during the reign of the emperor Zeno through his own revelation. This same Matthew is called Levi in the Gospel.

### G. V Kalends of November (28 October)

(Isidore, *On the Lives and Deaths of the Saints*, chapter 81.) The feast of the blessed apostles Simon the Cananaean, who is also called the Zealot, and Thaddaeus, who is also called Judas of James and elsewhere Lebbaeus, which is interpreted as “little heart.”

Thaddaeus is reported to have preached in Mesopotamia, while Simon preached in Egypt. From there they entered Persia together, and after subjecting an innumerable multitude of that nation to the faith of Christ and seeing that the Lord’s Church had already been widely established, they completed their martyrdom there, finishing the course of their lives in a blessed contest. They were honorably buried by the Christian peoples whom they themselves had begotten for the Lord.

Some think that the apostle Simon was the one of the Twelve who suffered crucifixion under Trajan, but this is entirely false. For the holy presbyter Bede, who holds this view in his work on the Acts of the Apostles, later, following Isidore, reproached himself in his book of *Revisions* for having judged incorrectly on this matter. Moreover, the *Ecclesiastical History* relates events concerning not the apostle but another Simon. (Eusebius, book 3, chapter 16.)

### K. VI Nones of May (2 May)

The feast of the blessed bishop and martyr Simeon [Note: In Ado’s Martyrology, it is 18 February], who was related to the Savior according to the flesh and was appointed bishop of Jerusalem after James, the brother of the Lord. During the persecution of Trajan, after being subjected to punishments for a long time, he was brought to martyrdom. All who were present, including the judge himself, marveled that an old man of one hundred and twenty years had endured the punishment of the cross. (Eusebius, book 2, chapter 26.)

### F. VI Kalends of March (24 February)

The feast of the holy apostle Matthias, who, after the Lord’s ascension, was chosen by lot by the blessed apostles (Acts 1) and appointed in the place of Judas, the Lord’s betrayer. He preached the Gospel of Christ in Judea.

### A. III Ides of June (11 June)

(Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 6.) The feast of the holy apostle Barnabas, who, being a Cypriot, was appointed with Paul as an apostle to the Gentiles (Acts 11). Later, because of John, who was also called Mark, he separated from Paul; nevertheless, he carried out the work of evangelical preaching entrusted to him. His body was discovered during the reign of the emperor Zeno through his own revelation. He composed one letter pertaining to the edification of the Church, but it is nevertheless read among the apocryphal writings.

### D. XV Kalends of November (18 October)

(Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 7; Eusebius, *Chronicle*.) The feast of the holy evangelist Luke, who was by nationality a Syrian of Antioch, by profession a physician, and a disciple of the apostles. He followed Paul, serving the Lord without reproach until Paul’s confession; he never had a wife or children. He died at the age of seventy-three in Bithynia, full of the Holy Spirit.

He is now buried at Constantinople; to that city his bones were transferred in the twentieth year of Constantius, together with the relics of the apostle Andrew. He wrote the Gospel, which he learned not only from the apostle Paul—who had not been with the Lord in the flesh—but also from the other apostles. He himself declares this at the beginning of his volume, saying: “Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word delivered them to us” (Luke 1).

He also published another distinguished volume, entitled *The Acts of the Apostles* (Πράξεις). Its history extends to the two years Paul spent at Rome, that is, to the fourth year of Nero. From this we understand that the book was composed in that same city.

### C. VII Kalends of May (25 April)

[Col. 0187A]

(Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 8.) The feast of the holy evangelist Mark.

He was the disciple and interpreter of the apostle Peter. When the brothers at Rome asked him, he wrote the Gospel. Although he began it later than the others, he extended it over a longer period in writing. For, beginning with the start of the evangelical preaching that took place through John, he continued his narrative up to the time when the apostles, by preaching, had scattered the word of the Gospel throughout the whole world.

When Peter heard this, he approved it and published it on his authority for reading in the churches. After taking it up, Mark went to Egypt and, as the first to announce Christ at Alexandria, established a church there. His doctrine and self-discipline of life were so great that he compelled all the followers of Christ to conform to his example.

Peter also mentions this Mark in his First Letter, figuratively signifying Rome under the name Babylon: “She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, greets you, and so does Mark, my son” (1 Pet. 5).

After establishing and strengthening churches throughout Libya, Marmarica, Ammoniaca, Pentapolis, Alexandria, and all Egypt, he was finally seized by the pagans who remained at Alexandria. When they saw him celebrating Mass on the holy day of Easter, they cast a rope around his neck and dragged him to the districts of Bucolia, which lay beside the sea beneath cliffs, where a church had been built. His flesh fell onto the ground, and the rocks were stained with blood.

When evening came, they put him in prison. There, around midnight, he was first comforted by an angelic visitation; then the Lord himself appeared to him and called him to the heavenly kingdoms. In the morning, while he was being dragged to the districts of Bucolia, he gave thanks and said: “Lord, into your hands I commend my spirit.” He died and was buried by devout men with glory in a place of hewn stone. He had appointed Anianus bishop of Alexandria in his place. He died in the eighth year of Nero.

### C. VII Kalends of January (26 December)

The feast of the most blessed Stephen, the first martyr. Not long after Christ’s ascension, the apostles ordained him deacon, since he was full of faith and the Holy Spirit.

Performing great signs and wonders among the people, and full of grace and power in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, he was opposed by certain men from the synagogue called that of the Libertines, Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and by others from Cilicia and Asia. They disputed with him, raised objections, and quarreled, but could not withstand the wisdom and the Holy Spirit by which he spoke.

They stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes against him. He was seized and brought before the council. When he was accused of having spoken against the holy place and the Law, he, full of the Holy Spirit, showed how Jesus Christ was demonstrated by the Law and the prophets.

But they gnashed their teeth at him, were enraged in their hearts, and stopped their ears. Then they rushed upon him, drove him outside the city, and stoned him. The martyr fell asleep (Acts 5, 6, 7). Devout men carried away his most blessed body and made great lamentation over him. The blessed evangelist Luke records his most blessed passion in the Acts of the Apostles.

### C. VIII Ides of June (6 June)

(Eusebius, book 2, chapter 1, and book 3, chapter 25.) The feast of Philip, one of the seven deacons whom the apostles ordained together with the blessed Stephen immediately after Christ’s ascension.

The blessed Luke reports of him in the Acts of the Apostles (chapters 8 and 21) that, performing signs and wonders, he converted the Samaritans to the faith of Christ by his preaching. He baptized, in the spring at the village of Bethsoro, in the tribe of Judah, on the road from Aelia to Hebron at the twentieth milestone, the Ethiopian queen Candace’s eunuch, a man devoted to the Scriptures.

He afterward rested at Caesarea. Beside him lie buried his three virgin daughters, who were prophetesses; for his fourth daughter, full of the Holy Spirit, died at Ephesus. Some nevertheless think that they were buried at Hierapolis, where the apostle Philip, one of the Twelve, rests. Some writers have thought that they were his daughters.

### A. V Ides of April (9 April)

The blessed deacon Prochorus, a man outstanding in faith and miracles, who completed his martyrdom at Antioch and rests there.

### C. IV Ides of January (10 January)

The blessed deacon Nicanor, admirable for the grace of his faith and his virtue, who was gloriously crowned in Cyprus and reverently buried there.

### D. XIII Kalends of May (19 April)

The holy deacon Timon, at Beroea. He first served as a teacher; then, spreading the word of the Lord, he came to Corinth. There he was handed over, as they say, by zealous Jews and Greeks persecuting the name of Christ. First he was thrown into the flames but suffered no harm; then he was fastened to a cross and completed his martyrdom. He was gloriously buried at Corinth.

### B. X Kalends of February (23 January)

The holy deacon Parmenas, who, having been entrusted by the brothers to the grace of God, faithfully completed the preaching duty assigned to him, attained the glory of martyrdom, and rested at Philippi.

### C. IX Kalends of February (24 January)

The feast of the holy Timothy, disciple of the blessed apostle Paul. The blessed apostle ordained him bishop at Ephesus. After many struggles for Christ, he fell asleep. His body was transferred to Constantinople in the twentieth year of Constantius, together with the relics of the blessed Andrew and Luke.

### D. II Nones of January (4 January)

The feast of the blessed Titus, disciple of the apostles. The apostle Paul ordained him bishop of the Cretans and sent him the letter celebrated throughout the whole Church of God. After faithfully completing the duty of preaching, he attained a blessed end and was buried in the church where the blessed Apostle had appointed him a worthy minister.

### C. VII Ides of May (9 May)

The feast of the holy Hermas, whom the apostle Paul mentions in writing to the Romans: “Greet Phlegonthas, Hermas, Patrobas, Herman, and the brothers who are with them” (Rom. 16).

He is said to be the author of the book called *The Shepherd*, which is also publicly read in certain churches of Greece. It is truly a useful book, and many ancient writers have drawn testimonies from it; but among the Latins it is almost unknown.

Having worthily sacrificed himself to God and become an acceptable offering to God, firmly established in virtues, he sought the kingdoms of heaven. He was buried near the city of Rome. A shrine bearing his name, beside which a baptistery was constructed from the resources of the holy Praxedes and consecrated through the zealous work of the blessed Pius, a disciple of the apostles, was reverently established for him.

### E. XIV Kalends of March (16 February)

The feast of the holy Onesimus, to whom the blessed Apostle sends a personal letter to Philemon:

“I appeal to you concerning my son, whom I begot in chains, Onesimus, who was once useless to you but now is useful both to me and to you; I am sending him back. You, therefore—my very heart—receive him” (Philem. 1).

The same blessed Apostle ordained him bishop, entrusting to him the word of preaching, and left him at the city of Ephesus, where he himself served as bishop after the blessed Timothy. Concerning him, the blessed Ignatius also says in his letter to the Ephesians (Ignatius, Letter 14 to the Ephesians):

“Since, therefore, I have received your whole community in the name of the Lord in Onesimus, our beloved teacher and your bishop, I entreat him, in accordance with Jesus Christ, to love you, and all of you to be in harmony with him; for blessed is the Lord, who has granted you to have such a bishop in Christ.”

He was brought to Rome and there stoned for the faith of Christ. As Christ’s martyr he was first buried there; afterward his body was carried back to the places where he had been ordained bishop.

### E. IX Kalends of December (23 November)

(Hieronymus, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 15; *Pontifical Book*, ch. 4.)

The feast of Saint Clement, concerning whom the Apostle Paul says: “With Clement and my other fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life” (Phil. 4). He was the fourth bishop of Rome after Peter—for Linus was second and Anacletus third—and during the persecution of Trajan he was banished across the Pontic Sea into a desert adjoining the city of Cherson.

[Note: [Col. 0189B] Across the Pontic Sea into the desert adjoining the city of Cherson. This is word for word from the *Acts* in Mombritius, vol. I, with which my manuscripts agree. So also Bede and Rabanus. The *Menaea*, 24 November: “In a deserted city adjoining Cherson”—*Ἐν ἐρήμω πόλει παρακειμένη τῇ Χερσῶνι*—“in a deserted city adjoining Cherson.” Metaphrastes, on the same day as the *Menaea*: “Beyond the Pontus, into a deserted city situated near Cherson.” Thus you see that some join *πόλιν* (“city”) with *ἐρήμῳ* (“desert”), so that a deserted city—*ἐρημόπολις*—is indicated, while others join it with *Χερσῶνι* (“Cherson”), so that a desert adjoining the city of Cherson is meant.

But where Saint Clement’s place of exile was, I do not yet see clearly explained. Before its most recent correction, the Roman Breviary read: “He was banished by the emperor Trajan to an island of Lycia”; now, instead of “to an island of Lycia,” it reads “across the Pontic Sea.” You find both versions in the *Acts of Clement* apud Mombritius. As for what Baronius says on 23 November—that the *Acts of Clement* contain no mention of Lycia—this is correct if he means the *Acts* of Metaphrastes. For in Mombritius, vol. I, at the end of the *Acts*, we read:

“Now the venerable holy man of God, Clement, bishop of the city of Rome, suffered under the emperor Trajan and the commander Aufidianus in the city of Cherson in Lycia, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December.”

Although these words are absent at the end of the *Acts* in the manuscripts.

Whatever the case may be, Clement was formerly believed to have suffered in Cherson of Lycia, or on an island of Lycia, as the Breviary once stated. But what is this Cherson or island of Lycia? Baronius, referring to the Roman Martyrology on 23 November, and, I think, to the wording of the Roman Breviary before its last correction, says:

“That Lycia should be called a Chersonesus is not at all on account of its being in the province of Lycia in Asia, where no Chersonesus is found named; rather, I think an error has crept in, so that *Bycia* was written as *Lycia*. For a marsh washes against Bycia, so called from the river Bycus; and from its upper part it is a Chersonesus, as Ptolemy teaches in table VIII of Europe.”

Thus far Baronius. The conjecture is certainly plausible if one considers the similarity of the letters. But Clement did not suffer in the Chersonesus near the marsh of Bycia, but on another island near Cherson or Chersonesus.

The *Acts of the Discovery of His Body*, clearly, are found in Peter of Natalibus’ *Catalogue*, book X, chapter 98; Baronius himself also cites them in volume X of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 867:

“Leo,” he says, “bishop of Ostia, reports that in the time of Michael, emperor of Constantinople, a certain priest named Philip, coming from Cherson, questioned the inhabitants about the things narrated in the history of Saint Clement concerning the opening of the sea. They professed that they knew nothing of this, because they were more newcomers than natives. For that miracle had long since ceased on account of the inhabitants’ guilt, and the temple had been destroyed by the incursions of the barbarians, while the chest containing the body had been overwhelmed by the waves of the sea.

“Then, taking with him the bishop of the city of Georgia, together with the clergy and the people, they approached the island where they thought the martyr’s body was located. There, digging by divine revelation, they found the body and the anchor with which he had been cast into the sea.”
