Therefore another island near Cherson must be sought.

I hope I shall be forgiven if I attempt to identify the certain place of exile to which Pope Clement was banished, and to do so not so much by conjectures as by a sure indication. I therefore think that he was banished to the island of Leuce, called the island of Achilles, which lies near Cherson.

If anyone wishes the name *Leuce* to have later been changed into *Lycia*, I shall not strongly object. But I maintain that Pope Clement was sent to the island of Leuce:

First, because Anastasius the Librarian, in the *Lives of the Pontiffs*, chapter 4, says of Clement: “He was also buried in Greece.” Baronius considered this passage corrupt in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for 23 November. Yet that it is sound is evident from the fact that Marius Niger, a man highly skilled in geography, asserts that even today the island is called Leuce, commonly *Graeciaria*; and how little does this differ from Anastasius’ “Greece”? Perhaps someone might conjecture that *Graeciaria* should even be read there.

Perhaps that island was called Greece or Graeciaria because Tauric Chersonesus, in which the island lies, is full of Greek colonies, as Ammianus Marcellinus says in book XXII.

Second, because this island is extremely suitable for exiles, since it is deserted. Arrian says in his *Periplus of the Euxine*:

*Ἡ δέ νῆσις ἀνθρώπων μὲν ἐρήμη ἐστιν.*

“This island is deserted of human beings.”

Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXII:

“In this island of Tauric Chersonesus, Leuce, without any habitations, is dedicated to Achilles. If anyone should happen to be carried there, after seeing the ancient remains, and the temple and offerings consecrated to that hero, they return to their ships in the evening. For they say that no one can spend the night there without danger to his life.”

Now in the *Acts of Clement* the place of his exile is called *ἔρημος*, that is, deserted.

Third, because the island is entirely rocky. Hence Festus Avienus, in his description of the world:

> “Where the hollow rock yields into vast  
> caves in its curving recess; where the rocks gape apart,  
> worn away into massive crags, and hang beneath a curved vault.”

Now in the *Acts of Clement* we read:

“They found there more than two thousand Christians engaged in cutting stone, condemned to prolonged banishment.”

Let this, then, be what has been argued about the island to which Pope Clement was banished: both in the light of the old Breviary and for establishing and explaining the reading of Anastasius. I submit all this to the judgment of the learned, prepared not so much to teach as to learn.]

He was exiled across the Pontic Sea into a desert adjoining the city of Cherson. When, through his teaching, many were converted to the Lord, an envious report spread among the pagans and reached the emperor Trajan, alleging that the Christian population there had increased through Clement. Trajan sent the commander Aufidianus. When Aufidianus saw that many Christians were being killed, but that blessed Clement remained steadfast in everything and could not be changed at all, he ordered him to be thrown into the middle of the sea with an anchor fastened around his neck. By such a martyrdom the disciple of Peter was crowned, and a church built at Rome preserves the memory of his name to this day.

### D. Kalends of February (1 February)

(Hieronymus, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 16.)

The feast of Saint Ignatius, bishop and martyr, who governed the Church of Antioch as the third after the Apostle Peter. Condemned under the persecution of Trajan to the beasts, he was sent bound to Rome. There, while Trajan was present and the senate was seated around him in the amphitheatre, his shoulders were first crushed with leaden rods; then his sides were torn with hooks and scraped with rough stones. Afterward his hands were stretched out, filled with fire, and his sides were burned with papyrus soaked in oil and incense. Next he stood with his holy feet upon coals scattered across the floor. Then came a flaming bed; his back was torn open and lacerated with hooks; his wounds were drenched with vinegar and salt; his blessed limbs were bound with iron fetters; and his feet were fastened in a wooden stock at the bottom of the prison. There he remained for three days and nights without eating bread or drinking water, while Trajan sat in judgment before the tribunal in the amphitheatre and the entire crowd of Romans gathered.

Bound, he was exposed to two lions. When, having already been thrown down, he heard the roaring beasts, he said in the ardor of his desire to suffer:

“Romans, who watch this contest, I have not labored without cause. I suffer these things not for wickedness but for devotion. I am Christ’s grain; I am ground by the teeth of beasts, so that I may be found pure bread.”

As he said this, the lions rushed upon him. Falling upon him from both sides, they suffocated him only, and did not touch his flesh, so that his relics might be a protection for the Romans and for the great City in which Peter was crucified, Paul beheaded, and Onesimus stoned.

He suffered in the eleventh year of Trajan, during the consulship of Atticus and Marcellus, on the Kalends of February. His bodily relics were brought back to Antioch by the brothers who had accompanied him to his martyrdom. They lie outside the Daphne Gate in the cemetery of the Church; they were transferred there on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January.

### G. Day before the Nones of May (6 May)

The feast of Saint Evodius, who was ordained bishop of Antioch by the apostles. Concerning him blessed Ignatius writes to the Church of Antioch (Epistle 12):

“You became disciples of Paul and Peter. Do not lose the deposit that they entrusted to you. Worthily remember the most blessed Evodius, your shepherd, who was first ordained your bishop by the apostles. Let us not dishonor our father, but let us become true sons and not illegitimate ones.”

He was martyred and buried at the city of Antioch, over which he had presided.

### A. Tenth day before the Kalends of August (23 July)

The feast of Saint Apollinaris, bishop [Note: [Col. 0192D] See the fuller account of him in the Martyrology of Ado.], who, ordained at Rome by the Apostle Peter, was sent to Ravenna. He also preached in Aemilia, in the regions of Corinth, in Moesia, on the bank of the Danube, and in the regions of Thrace. In those places he was sent into exile; wherever he arrived, he performed innumerable miracles and endured sufferings.

For he was nearly slaughtered in an excessive beating, beaten for a long time with clubs, placed barefoot upon burning coals, beaten again and suspended on the rack, tortured, and struck in the mouth with a stone. Then he was confined in an honorable prison with a very heavy iron weight and stretched upon a wooden frame. There, neglected by human beings but publicly fed by an angel, he was afterward chained and sent into exile. In exile he was again beaten for a long time with clubs; again, after being bound in Ravenna, he was beaten and wounded by pagans; again he was thrown into prison and beaten. Thus he completed his martyrdom under Caesar Vespasian and the patrician Demosthenes.

He governed the Church for twenty-eight years, four days, and one month.

### E. Seventh day before the Kalends of February (26 January)

The feast of Saint Polycarp [Note: [Col. 0192D] See there.], who was a disciple of blessed John and was ordained bishop of Smyrna by him. He was the leading man of all Asia. Later, during the reign of Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, in the fourth persecution after Nero, while the proconsul was seated at Smyrna and the entire people were shouting against him in the amphitheatre, he was handed over to the fire.

Together with him, twelve others who had come from Philadelphia completed their martyrdom in the aforesaid city.

At that time Germanicus also, a distinguished athlete of Christ, was translated through the glorious contest of martyrdom. For when the judge had condemned him to the beasts, he voluntarily challenged the beast prepared for him, despising temporal death, evidently desiring to attain the crown of eternal life by a swift end.

That same blessed Polycarp wrote a very useful letter to the Philippians, which is read in the assembly of Asia to this day.

### E. Third day before the Ides of July (13 July)

The feast of Saint Sileas [also Sila], the apostle, who, being one of the first brethren and having been sent by the apostles to the churches of the Gentiles, was afterward taken up by the Apostle Paul together with Barnabas and Judas (Acts 15–18). Full of the Lord’s grace, he diligently completed the work of preaching and later rested in Macedonia, glorifying Christ through his sufferings.

### D. Fourteenth day before the Kalends of August (19 July)

The feast of blessed Epaphras, who was ordained bishop of Colossae by blessed Paul (Col. 1 and 4; Phil. 2). Renowned for his virtues, he won the palm of martyrdom in manly combat for the sheep entrusted to him. He was buried in the same city.

### D. Seventh day before the Kalends of August (26 July)

The feast of Erastus, who was left by blessed Paul as bishop at Philippi (Acts 19; Rom. 16). There he rested, crowned by martyrdom.

### B. Fifteenth day before the Kalends of January (18 September)

The feast of the blessed Rufus and Zosimus. Saint Polycarp writes of their happy struggle in his letter to the Philippians, saying:

“But I urge you all to practice obedience and to meditate upon the endurance that you saw in the most blessed men Ignatius, Rufus, and Zosimus. Know that they did not run in vain, but in faith and righteousness, until they came to the place prepared for them by the Lord; for they became participants in his sufferings and did not love the present age, but him who died and rose again for them and for all.”

### F. Second day before the Nones of August (4 August)

[Col. 0193C]

The feast of blessed Aristarchus, concerning whom the Apostle Paul writes to the Colossians: “Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you” (Col. 4). He remained the Apostle’s constant companion until the latter’s confession. Having been appointed bishop of the Thessalonians (Acts 19, 20, 27), he rested, crowned by Christ after long and most blessed struggles.

### D. Eighth day before the Ides of September (6 September)

The feast of Saint Onesiphorus, concerning whom the Apostle writes to Timothy:

“May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain; but when he came to Rome, he diligently sought me and found me. May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day. And how much he ministered at Ephesus, you know better” (III Tim. I).

### B. Seventh day before the Kalends of October (25 September)

The feast of Cleophas, who was one of the seventy disciples of Christ (Luke 4). After the resurrection, as he was going with another fellow disciple to a village named Emmaus, now called Nicopolis, the Lord appeared to him. Tradition says that he was killed by the Jews in that same city and in the same house where he had prepared a meal for the Lord as though for a stranger, in testimony to the one whom he himself had recognized there; and that he was buried there with glorious remembrance.

### D. Fourth day before the Nones of October (4 October)

The feast of the saints Crispus and Gaius, whom the blessed Apostle says he baptized among the Corinthians (1 Cor. 1). The same Apostle mentions this Gaius in his letter to the Romans: “Gaius, my host and host of the whole Church, greets you” (Rom. 16). Blessed John also mentions him when writing him a letter: “The elder to the most beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth” (3 John).

### F. Fourth day before the Kalends of January (29 December)

The feast of Saint Trophimus, concerning whom the Apostle writes to Timothy: “I left Trophimus sick at Miletus” (2 Tim. 4). He was ordained bishop at Rome by the apostles and was the first sent to the city of Arles in Gaul to preach Christ’s Gospel. From his source, as blessed Pope Zosimus writes, all Gaul received streams of faith. He rested in peace in that same city.

### D. Eleventh day before the Kalends of April (22 March)

[Col. 0194B]

The feast of Saint Paul, whom the blessed apostles sent, after ordaining him bishop, to the city of Narbonne. Tradition says that he was the very same Sergius Paulus, the proconsul, a prudent man, from whom Paul himself took his name because he had brought him under the faith of Christ. When that holy apostle was traveling to Spain to preach, he left him at the aforesaid city of Narbonne. Having diligently fulfilled the work of preaching, he was renowned for miracles, crowned, and buried.

### D. Twelfth day before the Kalends of February (21 January)

The feast of Saint Publius, bishop of Athens, who was chief magistrate of the island of Melite or Militene. When the blessed Apostle Paul was sailing to Rome under guard (Acts 28), Publius received him hospitably for three days and treated him humanely, as blessed Luke reports. Publius’ father happened to be lying ill with fever and dysentery.

When the blessed Apostle entered to him, laid his hands upon him, and prayed, he healed him. Later the blessed Apostle took Publius as his companion, ordained him bishop, and sent him to preach. Publius subsequently governed the Church of the Athenians nobly; distinguished for virtues and shining with doctrine, he was gloriously crowned by martyrdom for Christ. First Dionysius presided at Athens, then Publius, and then this man.

### F. Seventh day before the Kalends of June (26 May)

(Hieronymus, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 19.)

The feast of Saint Quadratus, bishop and disciple of the apostles, who was appointed in place of blessed Publius of Athens [Col. 0194D] and gathered together by his faith and diligence the Church, which had been scattered in great terror.

When Hadrian had departed from Athens in winter, visiting Eleusis and having been initiated into almost all the sacred rites of Greece, he gave an opportunity to those who hated Christians to harass believers without the emperor’s command. Quadratus presented him with a book composed on behalf of our religion, very useful and full of reason and faith, worthy of apostolic teaching. In it, displaying the antiquity of his own age, he said that he had seen many who, after being afflicted by various calamities in Judaea, had been healed by the Lord, and many who had risen from the dead; for he was also famous in prophetic grace together with the daughters of Philip (Acts 21). [This is absent from Hieronymus.]

### C. Fifth day before the Nones of October (3 October)

[Col. 0195A]

The feast of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, who, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles indicates (Acts 17), was converted to the faith of Christ at Athens through the preaching of the blessed Apostle Paul and was appointed by him as the first bishop of that city.

### G. Eleventh day before the Kalends of August (22 July)

The feast of Saint Mary Magdalene, from whom, as the Gospel reports, the Lord cast out seven demons. Among her other outstanding gifts, she also deserved to be the first to see Christ risen from the dead.

### G. Ninth day before the Kalends of October (23 September)

The feast of Saint Thecla, a virgin from the city of Iconium in the East, who, instructed by the Apostle Paul, conquered fires and beasts in her confession of Christ and, after many struggles, came to Seleucia for the instruction of many and rested in peace.

### A. Third day before the Nones of September (3 September)

The feast of Saint Phoebe, concerning whom the blessed Apostle writes to the Romans:

“I commend to you our sister Phoebe, who is in the ministry at Cenchreae, so that you may receive her in the Lord worthily, as is fitting for the saints, and assist her in whatever matter she may need from you; for she herself has assisted many, including me” (Rom. 16).

### A. Sixth day before the Nones of July (2 July)

The feast of the saints Processus and Martinianus, who, when they were *magistriani melloprincipi* [Note: [Col. 0195C] This passage has hitherto been strangely corrupted. The commonly published text of Ado reads: *Magistri Animelli principis*. Surius, in the *Acts* of these martyrs for 11 July, reads: *Magistriani melloprincipis*, and notes in the margin: *Animelli*. Thus they considered either *Mellum* or *Animellum* to be the proper name of some prince.

Mombritius, vol. XI, in the *Acts* of these martyrs, has: *Magistri principes*. I think he omitted *Mello* or *Animello* as though it were not a word. The true reading is the one I have presented, and it must now be explained.

*Magistriani*, or *magisteriani*, are, by office, members of the palace military service, also called *agentes in rebus*. The Latin-Greek glosses give *agens in rebus*, *Μαγιστεριανὸς*. The glosses to the Basilics identify these same men with the *Castrenses* or *Castrensiani*, in which one reads: *Μαγιστεριανὸς ὁ Καστρήνσιος*—“the magistrian is the castrensian.”

The Code of Justinian, book XII, distinguishes *agentes in rebus* from *castrensiani* under a different title. Nevertheless, the castrensiani were also subordinate to the master of offices, as were the magistriani, according to title XXVI.

Suidas mentions other *magisteriani*, also called *Κανστρίσιοι*, from *κανστρήω*, “basket”; this is an ecclesiastical office. See Meursius, *Glossarium Graeco-Barbarum*.

In the glosses to the Basilics, *Μαγιθριανὸς* is also called *Μαιδάτωρ*. Magisteriani occur in the *Acts of Saint Abercius*, bishop of Hierapolis, on 22 October, apud Metaphrastes, where the emperor Antoninus says: “We have sent Valerius and Bassianus, magistriani of our divine offices.” They also occur in Evagrius, book III, chapter 16: *Οὐ παρὰ τοὺς Μαγιστριανοὺς ἀπεστάλησαν*—“They were sent not to the magistriani.”

Malchus, in his *Byzantine History*, writes: *Ἀδεμαντοῖς δὲ ταῦτα πυθύμενος, προπέμπει τῶν ἱππέων τῶν βασιλικῶν τινὰ, οὗς Μαγιστριανοὺς καλοῦσι*—“When Adementus learned these things, he sent ahead one of the imperial cavalrymen, whom they call magistriani.”

*Melloprinceps* is one who is next to the principate, one who will soon become prince. Thus the Greek *μέλλων* (“future,” “about to be”) is compounded both with Greek and with Latin words. The Greek compound is common enough not to require examples; the Latin is rarer. Among the jurists one finds *melloproximi*. In the Code of Justinian, book XII, title 19, laws 5, 7, and 14, this means those who are next in rank to the *proximatus*, or those who are destined to become the next officials of the bureaux.

But who was this prince to whom the *melloprinceps* was next? The various manuscript readings disturb the matter. If one reads “who were magistriani of the future prince” or “of the future prince’s [household],” it seems to suggest that Processus and Martinianus served some future prince. But no one was next in succession to the principate under Nero, since he had neither offspring who could be *princeps iuventutis* nor anyone else adopted.

Therefore I judge the following reading, found in certain manuscripts, to be more genuine: “who were magistriani, future princes.” Among the magistriani, or *agentes in rebus*, some were *principes*. Hence the Code of Justinian, book XII, title 22: “Concerning the principes of the agentes in rebus,” where law 1 says: “We reward the agentes in rebus, after the palm of their completed labor, with the honor of the principate.”

Thus those who were next to this principate were called *melloprincipes*. Such were Processus and Martinianus: not merely magistriani, but also melloprincipes.

The formula of the magisterial dignity to which the magistriani were subordinate, together with an account of its excellence, is found in Cassiodorus, book VI, formula 6, where its duties are set out and it is finally said: “Thus, having discharged the office with the gravity of his name, he adorns the principate by his acts.” And afterward: “His office is adorned by so great a distinction of genius that, having discharged the duties of military service, he is honored with the name of principate.”]

They were magistriani of Mello, the prince, and when they saw the wonders that the Lord Jesus Christ performed through his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, they began to marvel.

[Col. 0195C]

At that time the most blessed apostles had been handed over to Paulinus to be held under guard in the Mamertine prison on the Tarpeian Hill. There, by their prayers, they caused water to flow from the mountain.

Then Processus and Martinianus were baptized by the blessed Apostle Peter, together with twenty-three others of both sexes [sic].

When this was reported to Paulinus—that Processus and Martinianus had become magistriani—he sent soldiers, seized them, and ordered them to be thrown back into custody. On the following day they were brought out, and when they steadfastly confessed Christ, Paulinus ordered their mouths to be crushed with stones. But they gave glory to God in the highest.

A tripod was also brought, and upon it a golden image of Jupiter. When they saw it, they laughed and spat upon Jupiter and upon the tripod. Then they were ordered to be suspended on the rack, stretched with sinews, and beaten with clubs. It was also ordered that flames be placed around their sides.

A most noble matron named Lucina was there, encouraging them and saying:

“Soldiers of Christ, stand firm, and do not fear punishments that last only for a time.”

Again they were hung on the rack and beaten by the soldiers with scourges; again they were thrown into custody, where the venerable woman Lucina ministered to them.

After three days Paulinus was seized by a demon and died. The prefect Caesareus reported this to Nero, and Nero ordered him, saying: “Let them not be delayed; let them be destroyed as quickly as possible.”

Then they were led outside the walls of the city of Rome, onto the road now called the Aurelia, and were killed with the sword. Their most blessed bodies were collected by Lucina, who buried them with precious spices on her own estate at the Arenarium, near the place where they had been beheaded, on the sixth day before the Nones of July.

### F. Second day before the Kalends of July (30 June)

[Note: [Col. 0196D] See the deeds of Saints Processus and Martinianus, 2 July.]

The feast of the most blessed Lucina, who was baptized and instructed by the blessed apostles. Sharing from her resources to meet the needs of the saints, she always strove to lighten their chains and imprisonments and to serve reverently at their burials.

Associated with them through her merits, she too attained a precious death by confessing Christ and deserved to enter the courts of Jerusalem while fulfilling her vows to the Lord. At Rome she was honorably buried in the revered crypt that she herself had built for burying the bodies of the martyrs.

### G. Twelfth day before the Kalends of February (21 January)

The feast of the most blessed Agnes, virgin and martyr, who suffered in the city of Rome in the thirteenth year of her age.

As she was returning from school, the prefect’s son fell in love with her. When he had inquired about her parents, he began offering many things and promising still more. Finally, he brought with him the most precious ornaments, which blessed Agnes rejected as though they were mere dung.

As a result, the young man was driven on by an even greater goad. Thinking that she wished to receive finer ornaments, he brought every precious stone with him and began, both personally and through acquaintances and relatives, to appeal to the virgin with promises of riches, houses, estates, servants, and all the wealth of the world, if she would not refuse her consent to marry him.

But when he could not incline the most blessed virgin by any gifts or promises, the mad young man was corrupted by blind love and, amid anguish of mind and body, was tormented by breathless distress. In the midst of this he was thrown upon his bed, and his love was disclosed to the physicians through his deep sighs.

What the physicians had discovered was reported to his father, and the very words that had already been spoken by the son were repeated by the father in requesting the virgin. Most blessed Agnes refused and declared that she would in no way violate the covenant with her first Bridegroom.

Then the prefect began to inquire vehemently who this person was whose power Agnes boasted. Someone came forward and said that she had been a Christian from infancy and was so possessed by magical arts that she called Christ her bridegroom.

When the prefect Symphronius heard this, he became glad. Sending an official with great pomp, he ordered her to be brought before his tribunal. When he could move her neither by blandishments nor by threats from the position she had taken, he ordered her to be stripped and led naked to a brothel, while the herald proclaimed:

“Agnes, a sacrilegious virgin who blasphemes the gods, delivered as a prostitute to the brothels!”

As soon as she had been stripped, divine grace gave such thickness to her loosened hair that she appeared better covered by its locks than by clothing.

When she entered the place of shame, she found an angel of the Lord prepared there, so that he surrounded her with immense light. As she prostrated herself in prayer before the Lord, a dazzling white robe appeared before her eyes. She took it and clothed herself in it; the garment was conspicuous for its extraordinary whiteness and fit the measure of her little body.

Meanwhile the prefect’s son came to the place, believing that he would indulge in mockery. Entering boldly, he saw such a great light around her. But because he did not honor the Lord, he fell on his face and died, suffocated by the devil.

The virgin, however, shortly afterward raised him again by prayer. When he went outside, he began to cry:

“There is one God in heaven, on earth, and in the sea—the God of the Christians. For all the temples are vain; the gods who are worshiped are vain, and they are wholly unable to benefit either themselves or others.”

When the prefect saw such great miracles, he was astonished. But, fearing proscription if he acted against the priests of the temples, who had stirred up popular revolt, he abandoned Agnes to his deputy as judge, to preserve himself from the people’s uprising. He himself departed sadly because he had been unable to free her after the resurrection of his son.

The deputy, named Aspasius, ordered a great fire to be kindled in the sight of everyone and commanded her to be thrown into the middle of the flames. When this had been done, the flames immediately parted into two, and on either side they burned the rebellious crowd.

But blessed Agnes stretched out her hands and poured out a prayer to the Lord in the midst of the fire. When the prayer was complete, all the fire was extinguished so completely that not even the warmth of the blaze remained.

Then Aspasius, unable to bear the people’s revolt—for they attributed this not to divine power but to magic—ordered a sword to be thrust into her throat. By this outpouring of blood, Christ consecrated her as his bride and martyr.

Her parents joyfully took away her body and placed it on their estate not far from the city, on the Nomentan Way, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February. Several years later, at the request of his daughter Constantia, Constantine Augustus built a basilica there. For that same queen and virgin had been healed of wounds that covered her body at Agnes’ tomb, and there she established a mausoleum for herself.

Blessed Agnes suffered under the prefect of the city, Symphronius, and his deputy, Aspasius.

### A. Nones of February (5 February)

Saint Agatha, virgin and martyr, suffered in the Sicilian city of Catania under the proconsul Quinctianus, during the reign of the emperor Decius.

Quinctianus, a consular man, desired by various means to obtain her because she was born of a most noble family. He had her confined and handed over to a certain matron named Aphrodosia, who had nine most depraved daughters, so that they might change her mind.

When Aphrodosia saw that Agatha’s mind was immovable, after thirty days she went to Quinctianus and said to him:

“Stones could sooner be softened and iron changed into the softness of lead than this girl’s Christian mind could be turned away from its purpose.”

Quinctianus therefore ordered her to be brought to his secretariat. Sitting before the tribunal, he questioned the most blessed Agatha:

“What is your condition?”

Agatha replied:

“Not only am I freeborn, but I am also distinguished by my lineage, as all my family bears witness.”

Quinctianus said to her:

“If you are shown to be freeborn and noble, why do you demonstrate by your behavior that you have a servile character?”

Blessed Agatha replied:

“I am Christ’s servant; therefore I demonstrate that I have a servile character.”

When she continued with the greatest courage in confessing Christ and proclaiming the things that belong to faith, Quinctianus ordered her to be struck on the face. Then he ordered Constantius, who was preaching Christ, to be dragged to prison.

Agatha entered the prison most joyfully and with exultation. As though invited to a banquet, she commended her contest to the Lord with prayers.

On the following day she was again brought before the judge, who ordered her to be suspended and tortured on a great rack. Then Agatha answered the judge:

“Just as one rejoices when he sees the one whom he has long desired, or as one who has found many treasures, so I rejoice when placed in these bodily punishments. For wheat cannot be stored in the granary unless its husk has been thoroughly crushed and reduced to straw. In the same way, my soul cannot enter the paradise of God with the palm of martyrdom unless you have carefully caused my body to be handled by the executioners.”

She was then ordered to be tortured in the breast, and the impious judge had the breast that had been tortured for so long cut away.

The blessed virgin was returned to prison, where not even water was given her. At about midnight, behold, a certain old man came, saying that he was a physician and carrying various medicines. A boy carrying a light went before him. Among other things, the old man said to the virgin:

“I have examined you and have seen that your breast can receive healing.”

But she did not assent to the old man’s words, thinking that he wished to apply a bodily medicine to her. Among other things she said to the old man:

“I have the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who heals all things by his word, and whose speech alone restores everything.”

The old man smiled and said:

“He himself sent me to you; for I too am his apostle. Know that you have been healed in his name.”

With this, he vanished from her sight.

After four days she was brought again before Quinctianus. He ordered sharp potsherds and burning coals to be scattered and commanded her to be rolled naked over them. Suddenly the whole place was shaken, and part of the wall fell, crushing two men, the judge’s counselors and his friend.

Quinctianus therefore fled, fearing on one side the earthquake and on the other the people’s uprising. He again ordered her to be taken back into prison.

When she entered, she stretched out her hands to the Lord and said:

“Lord, who created me and guarded me from my infancy, who enabled me to act courageously in my youth, who took from me love of the world, who separated my body from pollution, who made me conquer the tortures of the executioner, iron, fire, and chains, who granted me the power of endurance amid torments: I beseech you now to receive my spirit, because the time has come. Command me to leave this age and come to your mercy.”

Saying this, she sent her blessed spirit to heaven.

The Christian people took away her sacred body and placed it, embalmed with spices, in a new tomb. As it was being laid there, a certain young man dressed in silk garments arrived, followed by more than one hundred boys, white-robed and beautiful. He entered the place where the body of the holy virgin was being buried and placed there a short marble tablet on which was written:

“A holy and willing mind, the honor of God, and the liberation of the homeland.”

The young man remained there until the tomb had been carefully closed. Then he departed and was never again seen throughout the whole province of the Sicilians. There is no doubt, therefore, that he was an angel.

Blessed Agatha suffered on the Nones of February. Afterward Quinctianus set out to investigate the possessions of blessed Agatha and to seize all her relatives, but by God’s judgment he perished in the middle of a river.

### G. Eighth day before the Kalends of July (24 June)

The Nativity of blessed John the Baptist, the Lord’s precursor, son of Zechariah and Elizabeth. Filled with the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb, and sanctified before he came forth from it, he lived strengthened by the Spirit in the wilderness until the day of his manifestation to Israel, clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist; his food was locusts and wild honey (Mark 1). In the thirtieth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor in Judaea and the kingdom of the Jews had already been divided into four principalities, he came into the whole region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins [Col. 0200B] (Luke 1 and 3).

### C. IV KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER (29 August)

The passion and beheading—or rather, the discovery of the head—of that same most blessed John the Baptist. As the Evangelists relate, Herod the tetrarch seized and bound him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, whom he had married; for John said to him: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6; Luke 3; Matthew 14). For this reason Herodias plotted against him and sought to kill him, but could not. Herod, however, feared John, knowing him to be a righteous and holy man.

But when Herod himself was celebrating his birthday, and Herodias’s daughter was dancing in the midst of the guests, while her mother raged and the banqueters indulged in pleasures and wantonness, Herod rashly made an oath, and what he had impiously sworn was fulfilled in the prophet’s death [Col. 0200C]. For severity could not endure with an even temper what the man of God admonished, because lust had conquered the king.

The holy Baptist was imprisoned in Arabia, in the fortress of Machaerus. A guard was sent, and he was beheaded in the prison; his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl. When his disciples heard this, they came, took his body, and placed it in a tomb at Sebaste, a city of Palestine formerly called Samaria. There it lay for several years, until the time of Julian, the most impious Caesar.

Since Julian was extremely hostile to Christians, the pagans at Sebaste invaded the tomb of that same John the Baptist, scattered the bones, then gathered them again, burned them, and scattered them more widely. But by God’s providence certain monks from Jerusalem arrived [Col. 0200D]. They joined those who were gathering the remains, collected what they themselves could, and carried what they had taken to their father Philip. He immediately sent these relics—for he regarded such a great treasure as something to be preserved by his own vigilance—to Athanasius, then supreme pontiff, through his deacon Julian. Athanasius received them and, with only a few witnesses present, enclosed them beneath a hollowed-out wall of the sacristy; in prophetic insight he preserved them for the benefit of a later generation.

His prophecy was fulfilled under the emperor Theodosius through Theophilus, bishop of that same city. After destroying the shrine of Serapis, he consecrated a church there to Saint John. Moreover, that blessed John himself revealed his head to two Eastern monks who had come to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer, near [Col. 0201A] the former residence of King Herod:

[Note: [Col. 0201C] “It was afterward brought to Emesa,” etc. In place of this clause, the Everbodiensis codex substitutes the following, in a later hand:

“It was discovered, but negligently preserved, and was lost. Later, having been found by others, it was carried to the city of Edessa in Phoenicia and ignobly stored away, where it remained hidden until Jurioramus, bishop of that city, informed by Abbot Marcellus—to whom John himself had shown both the head and himself—found it again and placed it honorably. From that day the feast of his beheading was celebrated.”

See the fuller account of this matter in Ado’s Martyrology, 24 February. Sigebert, in his Chronicle under the year of Christ 761, according to the Aquicinctine and Ortelian codices, writes: “The head of John the Baptist is transferred to the city of Emesa.” There, from the Lipsian codex, a more extensive history is appended:

“The head of John the Baptist was transferred from Alexandria to Aquitaine in the following manner. A monk of commendable life named Felicianus came from the regions of Gaul to Jerusalem with a few companions for the sake of prayer. After completing the duties of pious devotion, he was warned by an angelic message to go to Alexandria. The same angel revealed the place where the head of John the Baptist had once been hidden by Theophilus, bishop of that city. Felicianus took it up and carried it to Aquitaine, into the territory of Angoulême.

At that time King Pippin was staying there in a palace called Angiriacum. Seeing the daily benefits that came through the relic for the inhabitants, and the frequent victories that came to him over the Aquitanian enemies, he built a basilica of royal workmanship not far from the bank of the Vulturnus River. In it he constructed a ciborium of marvelous workmanship and honorably placed the richly adorned head of the Precursor.

He also established there a monastery of monks and magnificently endowed it with royal estates. The same king made a reservoir, from which water flowed underground for nearly two thousand units through cemetery buildings and aqueducts into his palace. Dividing this water, he brought it by iron and bronze into the basilica of Saint John the Baptist, so that it bubbled up beneath the ciborium through a hollow marble column; there the washing of sacred baptism was performed in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and Saint John the Baptist, after which the water returned again to the reservoir. This monastery is called Anglisz.”

Thus far in Sigebert, as edited by our friend Miraeus.]

It was afterward carried to Emesa, a city of Phoenicia, and venerated with due honor.

### A. VIII IDES OF OCTOBER (8 October)

The feast of the most blessed old man Simeon, concerning whom blessed Luke the Evangelist reports:

“And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; and this man was righteous and devout, awaiting the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. He had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord. And he came in the Spirit into the temple. And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, he also took him in his arms, blessed God, and said: ‘Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace’” (Luke 2).

### F. KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER (1 September)

The feast of the most blessed Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, whose holiness the Gospel account reveals:

“She had advanced in age and had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity; and she was a widow until eighty-four years of age. She did not depart from the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day” (Luke 2).

### F. VI IDES OF SEPTEMBER (8 September)

The feast of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, ever-Virgin, whom the Holy Spirit guarded and sanctified as the chosen one, so that from her womb the most high God might be born as man [Col. 0202A].

To her the angel Gabriel was sent by the Lord into a city of Galilee named Nazareth, when she was betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house of David. The angel entered and announced the good news to her, saying: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke 1).

When she saw him, she was disturbed by his entrance and considered what sort of blessing this might be. The angel said to her: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (ibid.).

Glorified by so great a message and made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, she remains eternally, reverently blessed, exalted above human beings by him who deigned to take flesh from her. Her Dormition is celebrated by the whole Church on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September. Her sacred body is not found upon the earth, just as the tomb of blessed Moses is not found, whom Holy Scripture says was buried by the Lord.

Nevertheless, the devout mother Church, established upon unblemished faith in her observances, celebrates her venerable memory as a feast, without doubting that she departed according to the condition of the flesh. But where that venerable temple of the Holy Spirit—that is, the most blessed Virgin Mary’s body—has been hidden by divine will and counsel, the sobriety of the Church, together with piety, prefers not to know rather than to teach something frivolous or apocryphal by holding to it.

For the testimonies of the Evangelists suffice for commending the holiness and life of the Virgin and Mother of the Lord, and the Church does not consider it necessary to inquire further about her.

[Col. 0201]

## THE MARTYROLOGY BEGINS

### THE MONTH OF DECEMBER

### A. IX KALENDS OF JANUARY — Eve of the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 0201D]

[Col. 0202D] On the same day at Antioch in Syria, the feast of forty holy virgins, who completed their martyrdom through various torments during the persecution of Decius [Col. 0203A].

On the same day, at Spoletum, a city of Tuscia, the feast of Saint Gregory, martyr and priest, in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, under the judge Flaccus. When Gregory was brought before him, Flaccus addressed him thus:

“Are you a rebel against the gods and a despiser of the rulers?”

Blessed Gregory replied: “If you truly wish to know, from my infancy I have never departed from my God, who formed me from the clay of the earth.”

When he remained steadfast in his confession of faith, his back was beaten and torn with knotted clubs, and his belly was ripped open and disemboweled. Then, bound by his hands and feet, he was placed upon a grating with wood beneath it. Immediately an earthquake struck, and one district of the city of Spoletum collapsed, crushing more than three hundred [Col. 0203B] people who served idols.

Afterward he was bound with iron and thrust into prison under military guard, where he was comforted by an angelic visitation. Brought out of prison, he was struck on the knees with iron hinges. His sides were also burned with flaming lamps. The blessed martyr said to the impious judge:

“If you destroy my entire body, the Lord Jesus Christ, my physician, is at hand; he heals and strengthens me.”

Then Flaccus ordered a certain Tyrcanus to drag blessed Gregory into the amphitheater and behead him. After this was done, Tyrcanus ordered terrifying wild beasts to be released so that they might devour the holy martyr’s body; but none of them touched the sacred body.

A woman named Abundantia requested the martyr’s body. Since she could not obtain it otherwise, she gave Tyrcanus thirty-five gold pieces, received the body, and buried the martyr as was fitting beside the stone bridge and the stream called Sanguinarius, by the walls of the city, on the ninth day before the Kalends of January.

### B. VIII KALENDS OF JANUARY (25 December)

Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is born at Bethlehem in Judaea, in the forty-second year of Caesar Augustus, in the one hundred ninety-third Olympiad, and in the 752nd year from the founding of the City. The disturbances of all the nations throughout the world being quelled, and the firmest and truest peace having been established throughout the ordering of God by Caesar Augustus, Quirinus was sent by decree of the Senate to Judaea to record a census of the people and their possessions. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ, by his most holy coming, consecrated the sixth age of the world [Col. 0203D].

On the same day, the feast of Saint Anastasia, who in the time of Diocletian first endured a harsh and merciless confinement from her husband Publius. In it, however, she was greatly comforted and strengthened by Chrysogonus, Christ’s confessor.

Afterward she was tormented by the prefect of Illyricum in an equally severe and prolonged imprisonment. During it she was restored by heavenly food through Saint Theodota, who had previously suffered martyrdom.

Then she was placed on a ship with two hundred men and five hundred women and carried to the Palmaria Islands to be drowned in the sea [Col. 0204A]. There she was stretched out by her hands and feet, bound to stakes, and a fire was lit around her at the middle of her body; in it she completed her martyrdom. All who had come with her also celebrated martyrdom through various forms of execution.

Among them was a man named Eutychianus, of entirely innocent character. Although he was wealthy, after all his possessions had been taken from him he remained silent, thinking of and fearing nothing except that he might lose his possessions and riches of faith. Whenever he was brought to trial, whenever he was questioned, he said nothing else: “Even he who cuts off my head will not take Christ from me.”

Then Apollonia, a Christian matron, took the body of blessed Anastasia, kissed it, embalmed it with spices, wrapped it in worthy linen, and buried it as befitted a martyr in a basilica built within the garden of her house [Col. 0204B].

On the same day at Rome, in the cemetery of Apronianus, the passion of Saint Eugenia, virgin. In the time of the emperor Gallienus, after many outstanding deeds of virtue and sacred choirs of virgins whom she had joined to the Lord Christ, she was bound to a stone under Nicetius, prefect of the city, and thrown into the Tiber; but she could not be drowned. Then she was shut up in heated baths and found unharmed. Finally she was slaughtered with a sword in prison. Her Christian relatives took up her body and placed it not far from the City, on the Latin Way, in her own estate, where she herself had buried the bodies of many.

### C. VII KALENDS OF JANUARY (26 December)

[Col. 0204C] [Note: [Col. 0203D] See the booklet *On the Feasts of the Apostles*; *Pontifical*, chapter 42.]

The feast of Saint Stephen, the protomartyr, who suffered not long after the Lord’s Ascension, namely in the same year as Christ’s Passion.

On the same day, Pope Zosimus, who sat at Rome for one year. He established that deacons should cover the left side with cloaks, and decreed that no cleric should offer a cup publicly except in the cells of the faithful and of clerics.

### D. VI KALENDS OF JANUARY (27 December)

[Note: [Col. 0204D] See the same work.]

The feast of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist, beloved of the Lord, who died at Ephesus sixty-eight years after the Lord’s Ascension, at the age of ninety-nine.

At Rome, Saint Dionysius, pope, who held the episcopate for six years and was buried on the Appian Way in the cemetery of Callistus. He gave churches to presbyters and assigned and established the parishes of the diocese.

### E. V KALENDS OF JANUARY (28 December)

(Eusebius, book 1, chapter 8.) At Bethlehem, the feast of the Holy Innocents, whom Herod ordered killed in the thirty-fifth year of his reign after learning of Christ’s birth through the report of the Magi (Matthew 2). In the thirty-sixth year he died miserably and deservedly from an internal-water disease, with worms swarming throughout his body.

### F. IV KALENDS OF JANUARY (29 December)

[Col. 0205A]

[Note: [Col. 0205D] See the same work.]

Of King David.

Also at Arles, the feast of Saint Trophimus, bishop and confessor, a disciple of the apostles Peter and Paul.

On the same day, Saint Crescent, a disciple of the Apostle Paul and the first teacher of the Church of Vienne (2 Timothy 4).

### G. III KALENDS OF JANUARY (30 December)

At Spoletum, the passion of Saint Sabinus, bishop; Exuperantius and Marcellus, deacons; and Venustianus with his wife and sons, under Maximian Augustus.

Blessed Sabinus, distinguished in every form of divine instruction and most eloquent in speech, was seized by Venustianus, prefect of Tuscia, together with the two deacons Exuperantius and Marcellus and many clerics.

Venustianus offered him his god Jupiter for worship. It stood in his bedroom, wonderfully fashioned from coral stone and clothed in golden garments. Blessed Sabinus took it in his hands, prayed, and immediately dashed it against the pavement and shattered it.

When Venustianus saw this, he ordered in fury that Sabinus’s hands be cut off, and that Marcellus and Exuperantius be suspended on the rack in his presence, tormented with clubs, their sides scraped with claws, and fire placed beneath them. After this was done, they gave up their spirits in confession of the Lord.

He ordered their bodies thrown into the river, but Saint Sabinus the bishop was thrust into prison. A certain fisherman and priest heard this, collected the saints’ bodies [Col. 0205C], and buried them beside the road on the day before the Kalends of January.

Serena, a most Christian widow who cared for Saint Sabinus the bishop, brought her nephew Priscianus, who was blind, to him in prison. Then Saint Sabinus placed his severed stumps upon the boy’s eyes and, after praying in faith in Christ, restored his sight.

Those who were under guard saw this, threw themselves at his feet, and were baptized that day, eleven in number.

When this was reported to the prefect Venustianus—for his eyes had become diseased and, because of the pain, he could take neither food nor sleep—he sent his wife and two sons to bring blessed Sabinus from prison to his house.

When Sabinus had been brought there, Venustianus prostrated himself at his feet in tears, together with his wife and sons. They repented and asked to be baptized. As soon as Venustianus had been baptized and raised from the baptismal basin, he felt no pain in his eyes.

This was reported to Maximian, who, enraged, ordered Sabinus condemned and Venustianus himself beheaded. The tribune Lucius came and, without a hearing, killed blessed Venustianus with his wife and sons in the city of Assisium. He brought Saint Sabinus to the city of Spoletum and ordered him beaten until he collapsed.

The venerable Serena collected his body—she had already placed his hands in a glass vessel with spices and set it beneath her house—and buried him approximately one mile from the city of Spoletum, on the seventh day before the Ides of December. Nevertheless, his feast and that of the martyrs named above are celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of January.

### A. THE DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JANUARY (31 December)

(Pontifical, chapter 34.) At Rome, the feast of Saint Silvester, bishop and confessor, who, after blessed Peter, was the thirty-fourth to occupy the see, for twenty-three years, ten months, and eleven days.

Through his efforts, the most illustrious synod of 318 Fathers was celebrated throughout the world at the city of Nicaea in Bithynia, under the consulship of Constantine Augustus and Licinius, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July; nevertheless, it was completed in the time of Pope Julius.

In the month of December he performed six ordinations: forty-two priests, twenty-five deacons, and sixty-five bishops in various places. He sat from the day of the Kalends of February until the day of the Kalends of January.

He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, three miles from the city of Rome, on the day before the Kalends of January; his episcopate then remained vacant for fifteen days.

He established that chrism should be prepared by the bishop, that a presbyter should anoint the baptized, that no layman should dare bring a charge against a cleric, that dalmatics should be used in the church, and that the left side of deacons should be covered with a linen cloak.

At Sens, Saint Columba, virgin, who, after overcoming fire, was struck with a sword.

Also at Sens, the feast of the blessed Sabinian and Potentian, who, sent by the holy apostles to preach, made the aforesaid city illustrious by their confession of martyrdom.

[Note: [Col. 0205D] Litanies to be proclaimed. In three manuscripts this is placed before each month. It therefore appears that formerly Litanies were proclaimed at the beginning of every month; but I cannot affirm which Litanies they were or on what day they were celebrated.

Apart from the two most solemn Litanies observed throughout the whole Church—namely, the Greater Litany, said to have been instituted by Gregory the Great, celebrated on 25 April, the fixed and perpetual sacred day of Saint Mark, and the Lesser Litany, instituted by Mamertus, archbishop of Vienne, to which the three days of Rogation before the Lord’s Ascension are devoted—many other Litanies were customarily celebrated during the year, according to the diversity of the Churches.

Gregory the Great, book 7 of the letters, letter 76, indiction 2, writing to Castorius, notary of Ravenna, mentions four or five solemn Litanies [Col. 0207C] [Col. 0207D], at which the bishop of Ravenna used the pallium; he does not wish its use to be granted to him at other common or non-solemn Litanies.

Anastasius the Librarian, in the *Lives of the Pontiffs*, under Sergius I, around the year of the Lord 687, mentions several monthly Litanies celebrated on a fixed solemn day:

“He established that on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Nativity and Dormition of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin, and of Saint Simeon, which the Greeks call Hypapante, a Litany should always go forth from Saint Hadrian’s, and the people should meet at Saint Mary’s.”

Here 2 February is the day of Hypapante, 25 March that of the Annunciation, the Sunday 15 August that of the Dormition of the holy Mother of God, and 25 December that of the Nativity of the Lord.

A weekly Litany, and specifically one held on a fixed Saturday, is mentioned by the same Anastasius under Honorius I, around the year of the Lord 626:

“He established an ordinance in the Church and decreed that every Saturday a Litany should go forth from Saint Apollinaris, and that the entire people should proceed with hymns and songs to Saint Peter the Apostle” [Col. 0208C].

Under Stephen III, around the year of Christ 722, the same writer says:

“This most blessed man established that, for the salvation of the province and of all Christians, a Litany should be held every Saturday, with every form of neglect put aside: on one Saturday to Saint Mary, Mother of God, at the Crib; on another to blessed Peter the Apostle; and on another to blessed Paul the Apostle” [Col. 0208D].

A memory of the proclamation of a Litany for the following day is found in Pope Gregory I, book 11 of the *Registrum*, chapter 11:

“Tomorrow, at first light, let us come with devout minds and tears to the sevenfold Litany, according to the arrangement set out below.”

That Litany proceeded on 30 August. On this, see Baronius, volume 8 of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 590, and the little golden Liturgical books of our Serarius.

Walafrid Strabo traces the origin of the Litany of the saints in his commentary on the Martyrology. He writes in his book *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 28:

“The Litany of the saints is believed to have been adopted into use later than the time when Jerome, following Eusebius of Caesarea, compiled the Martyrology through the cycle of the year.”]

LITANIES TO BE PROCLAIMED. THE MONTH OF JANUARY HAS THIRTY-ONE DAYS, BUT THE MOON HAS THIRTY.

[Col. 0205]

### B. KALENDS OF JANUARY — The Octave of the Lord

[Col. 0205D]

[Col. 0206D] At Rome, the feast of Saint Almachius the martyr, who, when ordered by Alippius, prefect of the City, said, “Today is the octave of the Lord’s day; cease from the superstitions of idols and polluted sacrifices,” was killed by gladiators for this reason.

Also at Rome, the feast of Saint Martina, virgin and martyr. She was of noble birth, born to a consul, and extremely wealthy in possessions, which she generously distributed to those in need. Seized by the emperor Alexander, she was ordered to sacrifice to Apollo.

But as soon as the blessed virgin poured out a prayer, a great earthquake occurred, shaking the city. Part of Apollo’s temple was destroyed, the statue shattered, and a great multitude, together with the priests of the shrine, was crushed.

The emperor Alexander, greatly enraged, ordered her face struck with blows and her eyelids torn apart with hooks. The executioners assigned to beat her, however, became exhausted and began to cry out that they saw four splendid men strengthening her and instead inflicting punishment upon them.

Then she was beaten with fragments of pottery. When she had endured steadfastly, those to whom this impious task had been assigned—eight in number—were finally surrounded by divine light. They immediately abhorred their cruel service, believed, and confessed the true Lord Christ Jesus.

The emperor, greatly inflamed against them, had their flesh torn with swords while they were suspended. Then their heads were cut off, and they ended their life in this world on the seventeenth day of November; having become martyrs of Christ, they sought the blessed kingdoms.

Martina was again subjected to punishment. Stripped of her clothing, she was cut over her entire body and then stretched out on four stakes; two centurions beat her with clubs. When she persevered in her confession, the seven centurions who took turns beating her were converted. But she laughed at the punishments inflicted upon her with a courageous spirit.

Then she was taken back to prison. There she was smeared with fat and grease, brought again before the emperor, and, at his command, taken into the shrine of the gods. But immediately after she had prayed, fire fell from heaven, reduced the idol to ashes, burned the priests of the temple [Col. 0208A], and killed a multitude of the people.

The emperor, struck with terror, handed her over to a certain prefect named Justin to compel her to sacrifice. Justin immediately ordered her stretched upon a pole, her limbs cut with swords, and her breasts touched with claws, until the hooks had made one hundred and eighteen incisions.

When she still had not died as he expected, she was taken down from the pole and returned to prison. Then, presented again by the prefect Justin to the emperor in the amphitheater, she was thrown to the beasts.

A most savage lion was released from its cage. Roaring, it came as far as the feet of the holy martyr, where it immediately laid aside its ferocity and did not touch her in any way. But when it was led back into the cage, it killed Eumenius, a relative of the emperor.

She was again returned to prison at the emperor’s command [Col. 0208B]. Two days later, when the emperor was going to sacrifice, the martyr was brought before him. Since she remained steadfast in the Lord, she was again suspended and scraped with claws. Her hair was cut off, in which they believed magical power resided. Seeing that she could not be overcome, they confined her in the temple of Diana for three days and three nights.

When by her prayers she had reduced the statue to dust, she was brought out of the shrine and finally condemned by the emperor to be struck with a sword. By such an end the venerable martyr earned the kingdom of heaven.

On the same day at Spoletum, a city of Tuscia, the feast of Saint Concordius the martyr, in the time of the emperor Antoninus.

He was born at Rome. His father was called Gordianus. He was a priest of most holy conduct and, from the pastoral title, was ordained subdeacon by Saint Pius, bishop of the city of Rome [Col. 0208C]. He devoted himself day and night to nothing but fasts and prayers with his father, always serving the poor through almsgiving.

It happened that, with his father’s advice, he lived with blessed Eutyches, who was then staying on his small estate beside the Salarian Way near the city. The count Torquatus of Tuscia, who was residing in the city of Spoletum, heard their reputation and sent for Saint Concordius.

He said to him: “What is your name?”

Saint Concordius replied: “I am a Christian.”

The count said: “I ask your name, not about your Christ.”

Saint Concordius replied: “I am a Christian, and I confess Christ.”

When he was being forced to sacrifice and steadfastly persisted in the faith of Christ, he was ordered to be beaten with clubs.

The following night blessed Eutyches came to him with Bishop Anthimus, and they asked the count to allow him to remain with them for several days. Anthimus was the count’s friend, and during those days he made the blessed man Concordius a priest.

After several days had passed, blessed Concordius was summoned again and came to the count. The count said to him: “What have you considered concerning your salvation?”

The holy man replied: “My salvation is Christ, to whom I sacrifice daily the sacrifice of praise.”

The count, enraged, ordered him suspended on the rack. After long torment, he was brought back, bound in iron, to prison, where he merited angelic consolation.

After three nights, men were sent to him either to release him if he sacrificed or to punish him if he refused. The envoys came and said to him: “Either sacrifice to Jupiter or receive the sentence of death.”

They were carrying a small statue of Jupiter. Blessed Concordius said: “Thanks be to you, Lord Jesus Christ,” and spat in Jupiter’s face.

Then one of the attendants drew his sword and cut off his head. Thus, in confession of the Lord, he gave up his spirit.

Two clerics then came with religious men, took his body, and buried him not far from Spoletum, in a place where many waters flow forth [Col. 0209C].

Also at Rome, on the Appian Way, thirty soldiers received crowns; under Diocletian they were deemed worthy to receive them for confessing the true faith.

In Africa, the feast of Saint Fulgentius, bishop and confessor of the Church of Ruspe. During the Vandal persecution, he suffered much from the Arians on account of the Catholic faith and his outstanding teaching, and was long banished into exile in Sardinia. At last he was permitted to return to his Church, and, renowned both in life and triumph, he rested in a holy death, completing the twenty-fifth year of his episcopate and the sixty-fifth year of his entire life.

At Alexandria, Saint Euphrosyne, virgin, born of a barren mother through the prayers of her father Paphnutius. When she had reached childhood, she secretly had her hair cut and sought the monastic life, taking for herself the name Smaragdus. She then persevered in complete holiness for twenty-eight years in seclusion. When afflicted by illness and recognizing that death was approaching, she revealed herself to her devout father, who had repeatedly sought her with tears.

In the territory of Lyon, at the monastery of the Jurenses, Saint Eugendus, abbot, who shone forth full of virtues and miracles.

### D. IV NONES OF JANUARY (2 January)

The feast of blessed Macarius, abbot.

And in the Pontic city of Tomis, the feast of three brothers, Argaeus, [Col. 0210A] Narcissus, and Marcellinus. Marcellinus, a boy, was seized among the recruits under Licinius. When he refused military service, he was beaten to death and long tormented in prison; then he was drowned in the sea and completed his martyrdom. His body was carried to the shore and deposited by religious men, and it shone forth with great virtues.

### C. III NONES OF JANUARY (3 January)

(Pontifical, chapter 20.) At Rome, the feast of Saint Anterus, pope and martyr, who was twentieth after blessed Peter. After governing the Church for twelve years, one month, and twelve days, he suffered under Maximinus and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way. He diligently sought out the deeds of the martyrs from the notaries and deposited them in the church.

[Col. 0210B] At Paris, Saint Genevieve, virgin, who, dedicated to Christ by blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, became widely renowned for astonishing virtues and miracles and grew old in the service of Christ until the age of eighty.

On the same day, Saint Florentius, bishop and martyr of Vienne, the eighth bishop of that city.

### D. II NONES OF JANUARY (4 January)

(Ado, *Chronicle*, year 241; above, see the booklet *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.) The feast of Saint Titus, a disciple of the apostles.

In Africa, the feast of the holy martyrs Aquilinus, Geminius, Eugenius, Martianus, Quintus, Theodetus, and Tryphon, most illustrious men, whose acts are preserved [Col. 0210C].

On the same day at Rome, the holy martyrs Priscus, priest, Priscillianus, cleric, and Benedicta, a most devout woman, under the most impious Augustus Julian. They completed their martyrdom by the sword.

Also at Rome, blessed Daphrosa, wife of the martyr Fabian. After her husband’s condemnation, she was first banished into exile and then ordered by the impious Julian to be beheaded.

### E. NONES OF JANUARY (5 January)

(Pontifical, chapter 9.) At Rome, the feast of Saint Telesphorus, who was ordained the seventh pontiff after the Apostle Peter. He sat for eleven years, three months, and twenty-one days, and endured a glorious martyrdom.

He established that a fast should be observed for six weeks before Easter, that Masses should be celebrated on the night of the Nativity of the Lord Jesus Christ, and that the angelic hymn—that is, “Glory to God in the highest”—should be sung at the hour of the Mass sacrifice.

Also at Antioch, the burial of Saint Simeon, a monk of admirable virtue. At the age of thirteen he renounced this world and sought the enclosure of a monastery. There, practicing remarkable abstinence and allowing himself food scarcely on the seventh day, he learned the Psalter in four months.

Afterward, through excessive zeal in subduing his body, he bound his loins tightly with a palm rope and was severely lacerated [Col. 0211A]. Then he shut himself in a certain well; the brothers forcibly brought him from it back to the monastery. He secretly fled and sought the desert.

After remaining there for a long time, he shut himself up on a lofty column, burning with an even greater holiness. He allowed no strange woman, not even his own mother, to see him. To this day no woman enters the basilica of that column. For a certain woman, dressed in male clothing, wished to enter, and as soon as she touched the threshold she fell backward, dead.

### F. VIII IDES OF JANUARY (6 January)

The Epiphany of the Lord.

On the same day, the passion of Saint Macra, virgin. When the governor Rictiovarus ordered her to be tortured and thrown into the fire, she remained unharmed. Then, after her breasts had been cut off and she had been afflicted by the squalor of prison, she rolled upon extremely sharp potsherds and embers and, while praying, departed to the Lord.

### G. VII IDES OF JANUARY (7 January)

The return of the child Jesus from Egypt.

Also the feast of Saint Lucian, priest and martyr of the Church of Antioch, a most learned and eloquent man. He suffered at Nicomedia for confessing Christ during the persecution of Maximinus and was buried at Helenopolis in Bithynia. When that city had previously been called Drepanum, the emperor Constantine rebuilt it in honor of that glorious martyr and, after his mother, named it Helenopolis.

[Col. 0211C] Also at Antioch, blessed Clerus the deacon, who, because of his confession of Christ, was tortured seven times and long tormented in prison; finally he was beheaded and completed his martyrdom.

### A. VI IDES OF JANUARY (8 January)

At Naples in Campania, Saint Severinus the confessor [Note: [Col. 0211D] See more about him on 5 September], brother of the most blessed Victorinus, a man distinguished by miracles. He too, an imitator of his brother, after performing many virtues, rested full of holiness. He was buried in the place where he had first lived a life of great abstinence, before he was called to the episcopate.

At Beauvais, Saints Lucian and Messianus.

### B. V IDES OF JANUARY (9 January)

[Col. 0211D]

In Caesarean Mauritania, the feast of Saint Martiana, virgin and martyr.

Item, on this day at Antioch, the feast of Saint Julian the martyr and of Basilissa, his wife. These chaste spouses, therefore, bound by a most holy vow, lived together for several years, preserving their flesh virgin for Christ. Since they were of illustrious parentage and lineage, they founded monasteries from their possessions, so that the blessed Julian became father to ten thousand monks, while Basilissa became mother to many virgins. After she had already sent their multitude, victorious, before her to the Lord, she herself, most distinguished by the conduct of her life and devotion to learning, serenely surrendered her spirit to the Lord amid words of prayer and the sweetest sighs, and was joined in heaven to the company of the angels.

Julian, however, was later sought by the governor Martianus, at the time when the rage of cruelty against the saints of God had flared up under Diocletian and Maximian. A multitude of priests and ministers of Christ had fled to him because of the savagery of the persecution. Julian was arrested with this immense crowd and reserved for the governor’s hearing; the other servants of God, by order of the cruel judge, were consumed in a great fire that had been kindled and placed before them, at the spot where they stood. There, to commend the precious death of the saints, choirs are said to have been heard singing at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, and they also sang evening and morning hymns to God.

When the blessed Julian was first brought before the tribunal, he was beaten with extremely hard cudgels. While he was being beaten, one of the attendants needed by the governor lost an eye. He immediately recovered it when the blessed Julian prayed, and, believing in Christ, was at once beheaded by the mad judge.

Then the blessed Julian was led to a temple of demons. The crystal and amber images, and those made from various kinds of metal, were so thoroughly shattered and reduced to powder that it was impossible to recognize what they had been. Next the holy martyr was tightly bound with iron chains and led around the city at the herald’s proclamation.

When he reached the place where the governor’s son was being educated at school, the boy, named Celsus, saw a multitude of men in white garments around the holy martyr and a crown shining with the most precious stones above his head. When he related what he had seen to his schoolmates, suddenly inspired by God, he threw down his teachers’ books and the clothes he was wearing and quickly reached the feet of the bound martyr.

Almost the entire city, astonished by this deed, hurried there; the governor and the boy’s mother arrived with the others, lamenting. But when they could not separate the boy from the blessed company, he was committed with the blessed Julian to the depths of the prison. There they were comforted by divine light and covered with a wondrous fragrance, so that about twenty soldiers guarding them were moved and struck with amazement and believed in Christ the Lord.

Seven brothers, together with the presbyter Antoninus, therefore came to the prison to visit them. Through the ministry of the presbyter Saint Antoninus, both the boy and the twenty soldiers were baptized. When the governor heard this, he ordered the seven brothers, after they had long been tormented in custody, finally to be handed over to the fire, and the soldiers to be slaughtered with the sword. Thus, victorious, they completed their martyrdom.

As for Saint Julian, the boy Celsus, Saint Antoninus the presbyter, and Anastasius—whom the blessed Julian had raised from the dead and made a participant in Christ’s grace—the governor had them brought before him and threw them into cauldrons boiling with pitch and fat, ordering a quantity of wood and brushwood to be piled beneath them. But the blessed men, unharmed by the fire, remained unconquered in their confession. They were therefore led back into custody.

With the boy, his mother Martionilla was confined there as well, wishing to convert him. But while she desired to make her son a prey for the devil, she herself was taken as prey by Christ, became his faithful servant, and received the grace of baptism. When her impious husband heard this, he thrust the devout handmaid of Christ into the lowest part of the prison and joined her to the martyrs.

He had them brought before him once again and sent them to the temple of the demons, where the temple’s priests were waiting inside, so that they might sacrifice. But as soon as the saints prayed, the temple was thrown down to its foundations, and about a thousand priests, together with a multitude of pagans, were killed.

Again the saints were thrust back into prison by the enraged and impious governor. There they were wonderfully strengthened during the night by divine consolation. At daybreak they were brought out of custody.

[Note: After oil had been poured over them, their hands and feet are tied with licinia. Thus I have restored the reading from the manuscripts. The common text wrongly has lignis, “with pieces of wood,” instead of liciniis; because the latter word is rare and less understood, it was judged to be an error and replaced with lignis. But who ties feet and hands with pieces of wood? They were therefore tied with licinia—that is, with cords made of hemp or cotton, from which candle wicks are made; they were plainly a material suitable for receiving oil. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XX, chapter 10: “A lamp is called *lucerna* from *licinium*, and therefore its light is brief, as Persius says:

“‘The lamps, set out, vomited forth thick smoke.’

“If it were derived from *lux*, ‘light,’ the verse would not scan. *Licinius*, however, is as though from *lucinius*, for it is the glow-worm of a lamp.” See the same author, book XIX, chapter 19, and book XVII, chapter 6. The manuscript *Glossary of Camberon*: “*Licinium* is what is extinguished in the smoke from the *licinium* of a burning candle.” I omit the other passages from more recent glossographers.]

After oil had been poured over them, their hands and feet are tied with licinia, and fire is placed beneath them. But when they continued steadfast and unconquered, he ordered the skin of Julian’s and Celsus’s heads to be flayed, the eyes of Antoninus and Anastasius to be gouged out, and a rack to be prepared for Martionilla.

When they had endured these torments with the greatest courage, the martyrs were thrown into the amphitheater, with wild beasts let in to devour them. But the beasts licked the saints’ feet. When they had endured everything, he ordered the soldiers to strike them. Having won the palm through such a contest, they received kingdoms that shall endure.

## C. IV IDUS JANUARII. (10 Jan.)

In the Thebaid, the feast of Saint Paul, the first hermit, who remained alone in the desert from the sixteenth year of his age until his hundred and thirteenth year. Saint Antony saw his soul being carried by angels into heaven among the choirs of the apostles and prophets.

[Note: *Pontificale*, chapter 10. See the little book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.]

Saint Hyginus, pope, who sat in Rome for four years. He established the clergy and assigned the ranks. He was buried in the Vatican on 10 January.

In Cyprus, the blessed Nicanor, who was one of the first seven deacons.

[Note: “And the arrival of Saint Hermes the martyr.” The common text incorrectly has *inventio*, “discovery.” It means the translation of Saint Hermes from Rome to Gaul. Here belongs what Molanus, the most exact investigator of the history of the saints, notes in the *Feasts of the Saints of Belgium* under 28 August: that he observed the following entry in an ancient Martyrology: “17 January, the arrival of Saint Hermes the martyr at Inda.” This concerns the day of the first translation. Sigebertus gives the year in his chronicle, 851: “The relics of Saint Hermes the martyr were sent into Gaul by Emperor Lothair and honorably deposited at the monastery of Inda.” Inda is a place near Aachen, where there is the monastery of Saint Cornelius, to which these relics were first brought. From there they were taken to Rothnacum, a village in Brabant, in the year 860, on 6 July, as recorded in the Martyrology of that church: “On this day, the translation of the body of Saint Hermes the martyr at Rothnacum.” Later, when the Danes were ravaging Belgium, they were brought back to Inda under Emperor Otto. After peace had been restored, they returned to Rothnacum.]

And the arrival of Saint Hermes the martyr.

## D. III IDUS JANUARII. (11 Jan.)

At Alexandria, the feast of the holy confessors Peter, Severus, and Lucius, whose acts are preserved.

(Possidius, *Index*, chapters 3 and 9.) In Africa, the feast of Saint Salvius. On his feast day Saint Augustine delivered a sermon to the people of Carthage.

## E. PRIDIE IDUS JANUARII. (12 Jan.)

In Achaia, the feast of Saint Satyrus the martyr, a citizen of Arabia. As he passed before a certain idol, he blew upon it and made the sign of the cross on his forehead; it immediately collapsed. For this reason he was beheaded.

(Zeno of Verona, *Proper Sermons*.) On the same day, the feast of Saint Arcadius the martyr, distinguished by lineage and miracles.

## F. IDIBUS JANUARII. (13 Jan.)

At Rome, on the Lavican Way, the crown of forty soldiers under the emperor Gallienus.

At Poitiers, Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor, who was exiled to Phrygia for four years on account of the Catholic faith. Among his other virtues, he is said to have raised a dead man.

At Vienne, Saint Verus, bishop, who presided over the church after Saint Evantius.

## G. XIX KAL. FEBRUARII. (14 Jan.)

At Nola in Campania, the feast of the blessed Felix the presbyter. He had been invested with the honor of the priesthood by Maximus, bishop of the city of Nola. When the emperors’ decrees ordered Christians to be persecuted, the supreme pontiff, already weighed down by old age and thinking himself unable to endure the punishments, went into the forested hills. As he wandered through them in distress because of the persecution, afflicted by hunger and worn down by frost, he collapsed on the ground half alive.

But the blessed Felix the presbyter was arrested, bound in chains, and brought before the governor Draccus. As he argued at length that the wonders of the gods were nothing, and the prefect urged him to sacrifice, he replied: “You are enemies of your gods. For whatever temples of your gods you lead me to, the same thing will happen to them as happened to those to which you regretted leading my brother Felix.
