But if you wish to test the power of my Lord Jesus Christ, order me to go to the Capitol, so that I may make Jupiter himself, the prince of your demons, collapse.”

At once the impious judge covered his ears and ordered him beaten with cudgels; then he had him subjected to the tortures of the rack. After that he was shut in prison, where, bound with no ordinary chains, he was stretched out with screws and potsherds placed beneath him.

And behold, at midnight an angel of the Lord, having broken his chains and split the beam in which his feet had been confined, said to him: “Rise and go out, seek your priest, bring him back when you have found him, and hide him so that he does not perish from want and hunger until the persecution ends.”

While the blessed Felix went out and searched for his priest and bishop, he found him lying on the ground, his eyes closed and his teeth clenched, scarcely breathing. As he anxiously considered what food he could offer the weakened old man, he suddenly marvelled to see a bunch of grapes hanging from a thornbush. When he squeezed several of its grapes into the confessor of Christ’s mouth, the old man revived a little and rose.

Felix carried him to the city on his shoulders, entrusted him to the care of a certain widow under a thatched shelter, and fed him. Then the blessed martyr was arrested and deported into exile to a mountain called Circeii, where stones were quarried, so that he might serve as a stonecutter together with the condemned.

There he freed the daughter of a certain tribune, Probus, from a demon and cured his wife of dropsy. He baptized Probus himself, with his wife and daughter and many others, into Christ.

Later, when he had returned, as the persecution intensified, a persecutor from among the attendants was sent again to seize the blessed Felix. While he diligently searched for him, he asked Felix whether he knew where Felix the presbyter was hiding. “He went away in this direction,” Felix replied.

When the persecutor departed, Felix sought a hiding place. But the persecutor himself soon followed. The martyr was concealed among ruined walls; at the very entrance of the house, spider webs hanging across it gave evidence that no one had entered inside at that time. Deceived by this sight, the enemy withdrew.

Thus the martyr moved to another place, where he was fed for three months by a certain woman, whose face, while he was concealed in the same hiding place, he never saw in any way.

Later, at Nola, he converted the priest of the demons to Christ. After first driving out the demon that gave oracles, he cast down the temple of Apollo by divine power.

So illustrious in miracles, when the entire people of Nola wished him to be made bishop, he did not consent. Instead, choosing another for the episcopal throne, he himself, after spending twelve years at Nola while the persecution had ceased, celebrated the mysteries on the Lord’s Day, gave peace to everyone, and threw himself down on the pavement to pray. Immediately the blessed man’s soul departed from the prison of the flesh and, after the grievous torments he had patiently endured for Christ, he—truly Felix—ascended to the blessed kingdoms.

He was buried near the city in a place called Pincis, where he continually shines with glorious miracles, by Helpidius, a venerable and holy presbyter. This most blessed martyr and confessor also resisted the heretics with unconquerable strength.

At Vienne, Saint Caelus, bishop. (Ado, *Chronicle*, year 686.)

## A. XVIII KAL. FEBRUARII. (15 Jan.)

The prophets Habakkuk and Micah, whose bodies were discovered by divine revelation under the emperor Arcadius.

Also the blessed Macarius, abbot, disciple of the blessed Antoninus, renowned for his life and miracles.

Also the blessed Isidore, distinguished by holiness of life, faith, and miracles.

At Bourges, the translation of Sulpitius, bishop and confessor. From childhood he was educated in sacred letters and conspicuous for the radiance of a holy way of life; even as a layman he was renowned for his virtues. Later, after laying aside the crown, he became father of monks; then, advanced to the episcopal chair, he rested illustrious in life and glorious in miracles.

## B. XVII KAL. FEBRUARII. (16 Jan.)

At Rome, on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla, the feast of Saint Marcellus, pope. By order of the emperor Maximinus, he was first beaten with cudgels and expelled from the presence of the man whom he had rebuked.

Afterward, when the emperor heard that Marcellus was turning the house of Saint Lucina—which he himself had condemned to confiscation because she had given her property to Christians—into a church and celebrating Mass there, he ordered that planks be laid in the middle of the city in that same church for the animals of the public stable, and he assigned the bishop of that stable to serve the animals under public guard. After serving there for many years, dressed in a cilicium, he died. John the presbyter and the blessed Lucina embalmed him with spices, and he was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla.

At Arles, Saint Honoratus, bishop, whose life, teaching, and miracles shone forth with distinction.

## C. XVI KAL. FEBRUARII. (17 Jan.)

In Egypt, in the Thebaid, the blessed Antony the monk, who, although entirely uneducated in letters, is said to have retained the divine Scriptures in memory by hearing them and to have understood them through prudent reflection. Father of many monks, he lived most distinguished for his life and miracles. His body, discovered by divine revelation under the emperor Justinian, was brought to Alexandria and buried in the church of Saint John the Baptist.

At Langres, the feast of the holy twin martyrs Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Meleusippus. When they were twenty-five years old, they were crowned with martyrdom together with their grandmother Leonilla, and with Ionilla and Neone, in the time of the emperor Aurelian.

The twins were hung from one tree, their hands tied upward and their feet downward, stretched so tightly that they seemed almost to be separated from the joints of their limbs. After this they were thrown into the fire, yet were not harmed, and together they departed to the Lord amid words of prayer.

[Note: “Their hands tied upward and their feet *inusum*.” Thus the manuscripts consistently read *iusum* or *iosum* for *iursum* or *iorsum*, in place of which the common text has *deorsum*, “downward.” So also below, 14 May: “Then he ordered him to be hung head *iusum* for three days”; where the common text is incorrect: “then he ordered him to be hung by the head.” The preceding *jussit*, “he ordered,” is repeated in the corresponding clause. Thus Sebastian, duke of Alexandria, ordered Victor to be hung head *iusum*, that is, downward. I have no doubt that this is an ancient adverb, in the form of *susum*. Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, and Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 57, use it for *sursum*, “upward.” Thus *susum*, *iusum*, or *iosum* was formerly said for what later became *sursum*, *iorsum*, or *deorsum*. Scaliger, too, in his commentary on book V of Manilius, cites from a very ancient Martyrology, under the day before the Ides of May, *capite iorsum suspendi*: “to be hung head downward.” This is precisely the passage I have cited for 14 May.]

When Ionilla saw this, she confessed that she too was a Christian. Afterward she was seized by the mob, hung by her hair, and afflicted with many punishments. Since she refused to deny Christ, she was killed with Leonilla by the sword.

Neon, the recorder of the proceedings, also confessed the name of Christ and was crowned with martyrdom. Benignus the presbyter taught and baptized these twins; Saint Polycarp, a hearer of the apostle John, had sent Benignus from the East into Gaul, together with Andochius the presbyter and Thyrsus the deacon.

The twins were buried two miles from the city of the Lingones. Turbon, who wrote of the victories of those confessing the Lord, also suffered martyrdom not long afterward.

At Bourges, Sepultius, bishop.

## D. XV KAL. FEBRUARII. (18 Jan.)

The Chair of Saint Peter the apostle, on which he first sat at Rome.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Prisca, virgin and martyr.

And in Pontus, the feast of the holy martyrs Mosaeus and Ammonius. Since they were soldiers, they were first assigned to the mines and finally handed over to the fire.

## E. XIV KAL. FEBRUARII. (19 Jan.)

[Note: Eusebius, book IV, chapter 4. See the little book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*, under Polycarp.]

At Smyrna, the feast of Saint Germanicus the martyr. While he flourished in the beauty of early youth, by the grace of God’s power he cast out fear of bodily weakness. Condemned by the judge, he voluntarily challenged the beast prepared for him. Torn to pieces by its teeth, he deserved to be incorporated into the true bread, that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, by dying for him.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Pontianus the martyr at Spoleto, in the time of the emperor Antoninus, under the judge Fabianus. When he was brought before him and asked what his name was, he replied: “My parents gave me the name Pontianus; but my greater name is Christian.”

Then Fabianus, enraged, ordered him stripped and beaten with rods until his blood appeared to flow onto the ground. Again he ordered him to walk barefoot over coals. The blessed Pontianus said to him: “I walk over burning coals in the name of my Lord Jesus Christ. You, if you can, put your hand into hot water in the name of Jupiter.”

Fabianus, enraged, ordered a rack prepared and iron hooks made, and had him suspended there. But when the impious attendants failed, God’s martyr was thrust into the depths of the prison, where religious men encouraged him for the struggle of martyrdom.

He was brought out again for the contest, while the people watched in the amphitheater, and two lions were released against him. They were tamed and did not touch the blessed Pontianus at all. When the people saw this, they cried out: “Truly the God of the Christians is great!”—so that a riot arose.

Again the blessed martyr was thrust into prison for twelve days, so that he might waste away from hunger. There he was strengthened by an angel and nourished with heavenly food. After twelve days, the attendants, thinking that he had died, came to remove his body and found him singing psalms and giving praise to God.

He was brought out of prison again and, by order of the impious judge, stretched out on an iron bed; molten lead was poured over his back. But when the martyr remained unconquered, making light of such things, Fabianus, confounded, dictated the sentence that he should be beheaded. Struck by the executioner, he rested in peace.

He completed his martyrdom on 14 January. His body was taken up by Christians and buried on 18 January. His feast day, however, is celebrated on 19 January, when his sacred body was translated again.

## F. XIII KAL. FEBRUARII. (20 Jan.)

(Pontifical Book, chapter 21.) At Rome, Saint Fabian, bishop. After presiding over the Church for fourteen years, eleven months, and twelve days, he suffered martyrdom in the time of Decius and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Sebastian the martyr, who was so dear to the emperors Diocletian and Maximian that they entrusted him with command of the first cohort. When Diocletian learned that he was a Christian and could not be recalled from the faith, he ordered him bound in the middle of the field, like a target for arrows, and shot by the soldiers.

When he stood full of arrows like a hedgehog, they thought him dead and went away. During the night a certain woman named Irene came to take away the body and found him alive. She brought him into her house and cared for him. When he recovered, he strengthened many in the faith.

Soon afterward he appeared before the emperors themselves and rebuked them as they deserved. Then Diocletian ordered him taken to the palace hippodrome and beaten until he died. His body was thrown into a great sewer.

But he appeared in a dream to the holy matron Lucina and said: “Near the circus you will find my body hanging on a hook; the filth has not touched it. When you lift it down, carry it to the Catacombs and bury me in a crypt near the tombs of the apostles.” That same night she came with servants and fulfilled everything accordingly.

On the same day at Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Marius and Martha, with their sons Audifax and Abacuc, noblemen from Persia, who had come to Rome to pray in the time of the emperor Claudius. After enduring cudgels, the rack, fires, claws, and the cutting off of hands, Martha was killed at the Nympha, while the others were beheaded; all their remaining bodies were burned and scattered.

## G. XII KAL. FEBRUARII. (21 Jan.)

[Note: See the little book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*. Prudentius, hymn 6.]

At Rome, the feast of Saint Agnes, virgin and martyr, who, under Symphronius, prefect of the city, was thrown into the fire; but when the fire was extinguished through her prayer, she was struck with the sword.

Also at Athens, the blessed Publius, bishop, crowned on account of martyrdom for Christ.

In Spain, at the city of Tarragona, the feast of the holy martyrs Fructuosus the bishop and Augurius and Eulogius the deacons. In the time of Gallienus, under the governor Aemilianus, they were first thrown into prison and then cast into the flames. When their bonds had burned away, they stretched out their hands in the form of a cross and prayed that they might be burned, and obtained their desire. Immediately one of the brothers and the governor’s daughter, who was standing nearby, saw the souls of the saints ascend to heaven crowned.

At Troyes, the passion of Saint Patroclus the martyr.

## A. XI KAL. FEBRUARII. (22 Jan.)

In Spain, the feast of Saint Vincent the deacon and martyr. Together with his bishop Saint Valerius, he was led from the city of Zaragoza to Valencia in heavy chains by order of Dacianus.

There he was long tormented by hunger and the filth of prison, afflicted with the tortures of the rack and the dreadful tearing of claws, and for a very long time burned on an iron bed. He was sprinkled with drops of fat and crackling salt.

After this he was sent into a most dreadful prison. His legs were spread apart in a wooden stock, and he was thrown upon extremely sharp fragments of pottery. There a great light appeared during the night, and the martyr, freed by God’s power, sang a hymn among the angels, by whom he was deemed worthy to be visited, so that the jailer himself believed in Christ.

When morning came, Dacianus ordered him laid on a very soft bed, so that, having recovered somewhat, he might be tortured more severely again. But he gave his tireless spirit back to Christ.

Then Dacianus ordered his body thrown into a field and exposed to wild beasts and birds. But immediately a raven, divinely assigned to guard it, not only kept away the other birds but also drove a savage wolf away from the holy body.

When this was reported to Dacianus, he ordered the body sewn into a sack and sunk into the depths of the sea with the enormous weight of a stone. But before the rowers could touch the harbor, by God’s power it floated upon the waves, was carried to shore, and buried in the sand.

Later, when the holy martyr revealed himself to a certain faithful old woman, after the fury of the persecution had ceased, Christians reverently took up his body and buried it in a basilica.

At the Waters of Salvia, the feast of Saint Anastasius the martyr and monk from Persia. After enduring many torments of imprisonment, blows, and chains in Caesarea of Palestine, he finally suffered great punishment at the hands of the Persians in Persia and was at last beheaded by their king Chosroes, together with seventy others.

His bodily relics were first brought to Jerusalem, to his monastery, and afterward to Rome. They are venerated in the monastery of the blessed apostle Paul, called “at the Waters of Salvia.”

## B. X KAL. FEBRUARII. (23 Jan.)

At Rome, the feast of Saint Emerentiana, virgin of Christ and martyr, who was the foster-sister of Saint Agnes. While she was praying at Agnes’s tomb and defending those praying with her from the violence of the pagans, she was stoned by them.

In Mauritania, at the city of Neocaesarea, the feast of Saint Severinus and Aquila, his wife, who were burned with fire.

[Note: See the book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.]

At Philippi, the blessed Parmenas the deacon, who was one of the seven deacons.

## C. IX KAL. FEBRUARII. (24 Jan.)

[Note: See the book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*. Eusebius, book X, chapter 35, from Rufinus’s translation.]

At Ephesus, the feast of Saint Timothy the apostle.

At Antioch, Saint Babylas, bishop, who, after glorifying the Lord frequently through his sufferings and torments during the persecution of Decius, received the end of a glorious life in chains.

A great miracle concerning him is narrated in the tenth book of Ecclesiastical History. When the emperor Julian, having turned to the worship of idols, was at one time sacrificing to Apollo at Daphne, a suburb of Antioch, beside the Castalian spring, he received none of the responses he sought. When he asked the priests the reason for the silence, the demons replied that the tomb of the martyr Babylas stood nearby and that for this reason no responses were being given.

Then he ordered the “Galileans”—for this was the name he customarily used for our people—to come and remove the martyr’s tomb. The Christians immediately assembled and, girded with great joy, carried away the martyr’s coffin, singing in the ears of the profane ruler, for six miles, in loud voices and with rejoicing:

“Let all who worship carved images and glory in their idols be put to shame” (Psalm 96).

Also in the city of Neocaesarea, the feast of the holy martyrs Mardonius, Musonius, Eugenius, and Metellus. They were all handed over to the fire, and their relics were scattered in the river Axum.

## D. VIII KAL. FEBRUARII. (25 Jan.)

The Conversion of Saint Paul (Acts 9:22).

On the same day, the feast of Saint Ananias at Damascus, who baptized the blessed Paul.

At the city of Gabala, Saint Severianus, a man of extraordinary holiness and learning.

Also the feast of Saint Praejectus, bishop of Auvergne.

## E. VII KAL. FEBRUARII. (26 Jan.)

[Note: See the little book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.]

At Smyrna, the feast of Saint Polycarp, bishop. A disciple of the blessed apostle John, and ordained bishop of Smyrna by him, he was the chief man of all Asia.

Later, under Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, in the fourth persecution after Nero, while the proconsul was seated at Smyrna and the whole people were rousing themselves against him with acclamations, his own people first urged and pleaded with him to withdraw once and again to a nearby place.

Then, when he was arrested by the investigators, he ordered a table to be set before them and lavish food served to them. Having obtained one hour for prayer, as the appointed time approached he went forth.

When the proconsul asked whether he was Polycarp, he confessed that he was. “Therefore,” he said, “respect your age, and spare your extreme old age. Swear by the fortune of Caesar, repent of your former conduct, and shout that the Christians are sacrilegious.”

Then Polycarp, looking with a stern expression at the people seated in the stadium, raised his right hand to heaven and cried out with a groan: “Take away the sacrilegious.”

But the proconsul persisted, saying: “Swear by the fortune of Caesar, curse Christ, and I will release you.”

Polycarp replied: “For eighty-six years I have served him, and he has never harmed me. How can I blaspheme my King, who has given me salvation?”

When he was again pressed more forcefully to swear by the fortune of Caesar, he said: “If you are seeking this boast, that I should swear by the fortune of Caesar, and you pretend not to know who I am, hear me freely: I am a Christian.”

He was therefore filled with confidence and joy, so that the proconsul marvelled greatly at the brightness of his countenance and the steadfastness of his answers.

The proconsul sent a herald to the people and ordered him to proclaim in a loud voice that Polycarp had confessed a third time that he was a Christian. When they heard this, the entire multitude of Smyrna—pagans and Jews alike—cried out with immense fury:

“This is the teacher of all Asia and the father of the Christians, but the destroyer of our gods. He is the one who teaches many not to sacrifice or worship the gods.”

They all cried out together that Polycarp should be burned alive. For his vision had to be fulfilled: he had seen in a vision that the pillow beneath his head would be consumed by flames.

As these things happened more quickly than words could say, the people themselves gathered wood from the baths and from every public place, as well as brushwood. The Jews in particular, according to their custom, were especially fervent in this matter. With all speed the pyre was constructed.

Then the old man removed his garments and loosened his belt; he also tried to take off his sandals, which had never been removed except by religious men who outdid one another in faith and devotion. For throughout the rest of his life he had been held in reverence by everyone.

When everything concerning the fire had been prepared and they wished to place him upon the pyre and fasten him with nails, he said: “Leave me. He who has granted me to endure the punishment of fire will grant me also to bear the flames steadfastly without being fastened with nails.”

They therefore omitted the nails and used only bonds. With his hands bound behind his back, he was offered to God like a chosen ram taken from a great flock, an acceptable holocaust to the Almighty.

When he had finished his prayer, the men set fire to him—the fire of eternal fire. When the great flame blazed up, all those to whom God granted the sight witnessed miracles. For the flame curved itself into the form of a chamber and stood above the martyr’s body like a ship’s sail billowing in the wind.

The body in the middle did not look like burning flesh, but like gold or silver glowing in a furnace. Moreover, those standing nearby perceived a fragrance, as though of incense or the most precious perfume.

Finally, when the agents of wickedness saw that the body could not be consumed by the fire—

[Note: “They ordered the *confectores* to come closer.” Eusebius, book IV, chapter 14, uses this very Latin word *confectores* in the same account of Polycarp: “Πέρας οὖν ἰδόντες οἱ ἄνομοι μὴ δυναμένον τὸ σῶμα ὑπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς δαπανηθῆναι, ἐκέλευσαν προσελθόντα αὐτῷ κομφέκτορα παραβύσαι τὸ ξίφος”—“Finally, when the lawless men saw that the body could not be consumed by the fire, they ordered an executioner who had approached him to thrust in the sword”; Christophorsonus renders κομφέκτωρα as *carnifex*, “executioner.” Thus, when the wicked and impious men finally saw that his body could not at all be consumed by the fire, they ordered the executioner to advance nearer to the pyre and pierce him with a drawn sword.

Properly speaking, however, *confectores* are slayers of wild beasts, as in Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 43: “In the circus he brought forward charioteers, runners, and slayers of wild beasts, and sometimes young men from the noblest families.” I shall say no more about this, since the matter is already known. The *κομφάκτωρ, κατασκευαστὴς*—“maker, builder”—in the Glosses of the *Basilica* is not *confector*, as Meursius explains in his *Glossary of Barbarous Greek*, but *compactor*, “assembler,” and is irrelevant here.]

—they ordered the *confectores* to come closer and pierce with a sword the body from which the fire had recoiled. When this had been done, so great a quantity of blood poured forth that it extinguished the pyre.

The people departed in astonishment at the miracle. But the enemy of all goodness began to take sufficient measures that no one should carry his relics away for burial, with the Jews pressing this point especially strongly.

When the centurion saw the Jews’ obstinate contention, he burned the body itself, which had been placed in their midst. Later, however, the brothers gathered the bones, which, having been burned by the fire, were more precious than the most precious gems and more excellent than all gold, and buried them according to custom.

At that place, by the Lord’s favor, solemn and celebrated gatherings are held. Along with him, twelve others who came from Philadelphia also completed their martyrdom in the aforesaid city.

On the same day, the holy martyrs Theogenes and thirty-six others, who despised temporal death and obtained the crown of eternal life.

## F. VI KAL. FEBRUARII. (27 Jan.)

The feast of Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, who is called Chrysostom.

Also the blessed Marius, abbot of the monastery of Badon, whose life, full of virtues, was written by the illustrious patrician Dynamius.

And at Bethlehem of Judea, the dormition of Saint Paula, mother of Eustochium, virgin of Christ. Although she belonged to a most noble senatorial family, she renounced the world and distributed her wealth among the poor. She attained the poverty of Christ and, at the aforementioned little town glorified by the Lord’s Nativity, became mother of a monastery of virgins.

Writing her life, admirable for its virtues, Saint Jerome testifies that she was crowned by a long martyrdom. (Epistle 27, to Eustochium.)

## G. V KAL. FEBRUARII. (28 Jan.)

[Col. 0223B]

The second feast of Saint Agnes.

And in the city of Apollonia, the martyrdom of Leucius, Thyrsus, and Galenicus, who, in the time of the emperor Decius, under the governors Combricius, Silvanus, and Baudo, were tortured with various kinds of torments. The first and the last completed their martyrdom by beheading; the one in the middle, summoned by a heavenly voice, gave up his spirit. They suffered in Greece.

On the same day, at Alexandria, the blessed Cyril, bishop, who proved himself a most renowned champion of the catholic faith.

Likewise, in the monastery of Reoma, Saint John, [Col. 0223C] a priest and man of God.

### A. IV Kalends of February (29 January)

At Rome, the feast of Papias and Maurus, soldiers, in the time of Diocletian. When they saw the steadfastness of the martyrs Saturninus and Sisinnius, they were converted to the faith. Immediately Laodicius, prefect of the City, ordered that the mouths with which they confessed Christ should be crushed with stones, and that they should be shut up in prison, where they were baptized by the blessed Pope Marcellus. After twelve [Col. 0224A] days he ordered them to be brought out, laid on the ground, and beaten with clubs; then, lifted from the ground, they were struck with leaden weights until they expired. The priest John gathered their bodies by night and buried them on the Nomentan Way, at the Nymphs of Saint Peter, where he himself baptized. This is recorded in the acts of the blessed Pope Marcellus.

On the same day at Trier, the deposition of the blessed Valerius, bishop and disciple of the holy apostle Peter.

### B. III Kalends of February (30 January)

At Antioch, the martyrdom of Saint Hippolytus, who, having been somewhat deceived by the schism of Novatian, was corrected through the working of Christ’s grace and returned to the Church’s charity. For this charity, and within it, he later completed a glorious martyrdom.

[Col. 0224B] *(Eusebius, book IV, chapter 5.)* At Jerusalem, the most blessed Matthias, bishop, concerning whom marvelous deeds, full of faith, are related. After enduring many things for Christ, he finally ended his life in peace. He governed the Church as the eighth after James.

Likewise, the blessed Alexander. During the Decian persecution, he was brought before the courts for his confession of the faith and handed over to prison bonds. As he shone with the venerable gray hair of an advanced age, after repeatedly glorifying the Lord through his sufferings and tortures, he was taken from his bonds to the tribunals and from the tribunals returned to his bonds. Amid the torments that followed one another in turn, he rested with a good end.

### C. The day before the Kalends of February (31 January)

[Col. 0224C]

At Alexandria, the feast of Saint Metranus the martyr, whom the pagans seized and ordered to utter impious words. When he refused, they battered his entire body with clubs, pierced his face and eyes with sharp reeds, and drove him outside the city amid tortures; there they expelled what remained of his spirit by stoning him.

Likewise, Saints Saturninus, Thyrsus, and Victor.

On the same day, at the city of Trent, the blessed Virgil, bishop and martyr.

**Litanies are to be proclaimed. The month of February has twenty-eight days, but in a leap year twenty-nine; the lunar month, twenty-nine.**

[Col. 0223]

### D. Kalends of February (1 February)

[Col. 0223D]

At Smyrna, the feast of Saint Pionius the martyr, who, during the persecution of Antoninus Verus, after unconquerable steadfastness in his answers and the misery of imprisonment—where he strengthened many of the brethren by his exhortations to endure martyrdom—was finally harassed by many tortures, fastened with nails, and placed upon a blazing pyre. Thus he obtained a blessed end of life for Christ. [Col. 0224D] Fifteen others suffered with him.

On the same day, the blessed Ephraem, deacon of the Church of Edessa.

[Note: [Col. 0223D] See the booklet on the Feasts of the Apostles.]

On the same day at Antioch, the blessed Ignatius, bishop and martyr.

Likewise, in Scotland, Saint Brigid the virgin, whose life was renowned for miracles. When she touched the altar’s wood as a testimony to her virginity, it became green.

On the same day, Saint Paul, bishop of the city of Troyes, whose life was renowned for virtues and whose precious death was commended by miracles.

### E. IV Nones of February (2 February)

The Meeting of the Lord (Hypapante).

At Caesarea, the most blessed Cornelius the centurion, whom the blessed Peter baptized; after being raised to the honor of bishop in the aforementioned city, he rested there.

On the same day at Rome, Saint Apronianus [Note: [Col. 0225D] Concerning him, in the Life of Saint Marcellinus, 16 January], the martyr. During the persecution of the emperor Maximian, when he had brought before the eyes of Laodicius the prefect the blessed deacon Sisinnius, led out of prison—for he was the prison official—and had suddenly seen a light appear from heaven and heard a voice at the same time, he fell trembling at Sisinnius’s feet and said: “I adjure you by Christ, whom you confess: do not delay to baptize me, and make me attain the crown with you.” The blessed Sisinnius, after baptizing him, presented him to Pope Marcellus to receive the sacramental chrism. When the governor learned of this, he ordered him to undergo the sentence of death. Accordingly, he was led out along the Salarian Way, at the second milestone, and, beheaded, departed as both martyr and victor.

### F. III Nones of February (3 February)

In Africa, the blessed Celerinus, deacon and confessor; and Saints Celerina, his grandmother, and Laurentinus [Col. 0225C] and Ignatius. The first was his paternal uncle, and the next his maternal uncle. Concerning the glorious praises of all of them, there exists a letter of the blessed Cyprian, which says among other things: “His grandmother Celerina was crowned by martyrdom. Likewise his paternal and maternal uncles, Laurentinus and Ignatius, once serving in the military camps, though secular soldiers, were true and spiritual soldiers of God. While overthrowing the devil by confessing Christ, they earned the Lord’s palms and crowns through a glorious passion. We always offer sacrifices for them, as you remember, whenever we commemorate the sufferings and anniversaries of the martyrs,” and so forth. “I do not know whom I should call more blessed: whether them, because of so illustrious a descendant, or him, because of so glorious an origin.”

### G. The day before the Nones of February (4 February)

[Col. 0225D]

In the Egyptian city called Thmuis, the martyrdom of the blessed Phileas, bishop of that city, and Philoromus, a tribune of the Roman soldiers. With them also an innumerable multitude of the faithful from the same city, following the footsteps of their shepherd during the persecution of Diocletian, was crowned with martyrdom.

[Note: [Col. 0225D] Eusebius, book VIII, chapters 9–10, from the translation of Rufinus, who inserted very much.]

For when the most savage governor was seated at the tribunal, countless crowds of the faithful were brought before him. He ordered each of them, after confessing in turn that they were Christians, to be put to death. Since they vied with one another in presenting themselves willingly, after first making their confession, to the sword, that inhuman and cruel man—moved neither by the sight of such a multitude nor by the greatness of their courage—nevertheless ordered them all to be led away and beheaded. But these steadfastly and bravely, with joy and exultation, seized the death immediately before them as the beginning of eternal life.

At last, while the first were being slaughtered, the others did not surrender their minds to idleness or sluggishness. Rather, singing psalms and hymns to God, each awaited the place of his martyrdom, so that while doing these things they might breathe out even their final spirits in the praises of God. O truly wondrous flock, worthy of all veneration—the band of blessed men, the crown of the splendor of Christ’s glory! This crown was adorned by the most precious of all stones and the noblest gem; this band was led by a more illustrious leader; this flock was honored by a nobler shepherd: his name was Phileas, who was bishop of that city.

He derived the nobility of his first lineage from heaven, in accordance with the virtue of his soul; in earthly matters, insofar as they pertain to this age, he had enjoyed the highest honors in the Roman state. He was also exceptionally learned in the liberal arts and in all disciplines pertaining to virtue of soul.

Although he had many noble relatives and kinsmen in the same city, he was frequently brought before the governor. He was urged to yield to his admonitions, to show consideration for so many and such important relatives, and to heed his wife and take thought for his children, rather than persist in the undertaking he had rashly begun. But he, as if a motionless rock were being struck by a wave, rejected the words of these chatterers, directed his mind toward heaven, kept God before his eyes, and regarded his parents and relatives as holy martyrs and apostles.

At that time there was a certain man commanding a troop of Roman soldiers, named Philoromus. When he saw Phileas surrounded by the tears of his relatives and wearied by the governor’s cunning, yet in no way able to be bent or broken, he exclaimed: “Why do you test the man’s steadfastness vainly and needlessly? Why do you wish to make faithless the man who keeps faith with God? Why do you compel him to deny God so that he may yield to human beings? Do you not see that his ears do not hear your words, that his eyes do not see your tears? How can he be swayed by earthly tears, whose eyes behold heavenly glory?”

After these words, everyone’s anger turned against Philoromus. They demanded that he undergo the same sentence together with Phileas. The judge willingly assenting, ordered both to be beheaded. These blessed martyrs suffered under the persecution of Diocletian.

[Note: [Col. 0226D] The manuscript incorrectly had “Decian.”]

### A. Nones of February (5 February)

[Note: [Col. 0226D] See the booklet on the Feasts of the Apostles.]

In Sicily, in the city of Catania, the martyrdom of Saint Agatha the virgin, under the emperor Decius and the proconsul Quintianus. After slaps and imprisonment, after the rack and tortures, after the cutting off of her breasts—but also after healing by the Lord—and after being rolled over potsherds [Col. 0227A] and coals, she finally completed her course in prison.

At Vienne, the blessed Avitus, bishop, through whose faith, diligence, and admirable teaching, in the time of King Gundobad, Gaul was defended from the infestation of the Arian heresy.

### B. VIII Ides of February (6 February)

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Dorothea the virgin, who, under Apricius [alternative: Sapricius], governor of that province, was first tortured by being stretched on the rack, then beaten for a very long time with blows, and finally punished by sentence of death. As she was being led out of the governor’s residence to her death, a certain rhetorician named Theophilus said to her: “Come now, bride of Christ, send me apples from the paradise of your bridegroom.” She immediately promised that she would send them.

When they had reached the place where she was to be slaughtered, she prayed for a little while, brought out her handkerchief, and, calling to her a certain little boy of six years, sent him to Theophilus, saying: “Tell him: Dorothea, the handmaid of God, sends you apples from the paradise of her bridegroom Christ.” He received them and gave thanks that she had fulfilled his request. He began to wipe his face, and suddenly he was suffused with such sweetness that, completely changed in mind, with great exultation and a clear voice he repeatedly exclaimed: “Blessed is the name of my Lord Jesus Christ.” Because of this confession he himself was immediately seized, hung upon the rack, and tortured with such cruelty that all who stood around were horrified. Finally, his head was cut off, and he completed his martyrdom.

[Col. 0227C] On the same day, the feast of Saint Antholianus, who was crowned with martyrdom at the city of Clermont.

### C. VII Ides of February (7 February)

In Britain, in the city of Augusta, the feast of Saint Augulus, bishop and martyr.

Likewise, Saint Moyses, a venerable bishop, who at first led a solitary life in the wilderness and became greatly known through his merits, virtues, and the miracles God performed through him. Later, at the request of Mauvia, queen of the Saracens, he became bishop of that people. He preserved the fellowship of the catholic faith undefiled and converted a large part of the people to whom he had been given as bishop to the faith of Christ. Thus perfected in virtues, he rested in peace.

### D. VI Ides of February (8 February)

[Col. 0227D]

[Note: [Col. 0227D] Eusebius, book VI, chapter 34, or 31, from the translation of Rufinus.]

In Lesser Armenia, the feast of Saints Dionysius, Aemilianus, and Sebastian.

On the same day at Alexandria, the feast of Saint Cointha the martyr. The pagans seized her, led her to the idols, and compelled her to worship. When she rejected them with abhorrence, they fastened fetters to her feet, dragged her through the streets of the entire city, and tore her apart in a dreadful punishment.

### E. V Ides of February (9 February)

[Note: [Col. 0228D] Eusebius, book VI, chapter 34, or 31, from the translation of Rufinus.]

At Alexandria, Saint Apollonia the virgin. The persecutors first knocked out all her teeth. Then, when they threatened that they would build and set fire to a pyre and burn her alive unless she uttered impious words with them, she deliberated within herself for a little while about what she should do, suddenly broke free from the hands of the wicked, and willingly leapt into the fire with which they had threatened her.

### F. IV Ides of February (10 February)

At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Zoticus, Irene, Hyacinthus, and Amantius.

On the same day in the East, Saint Soteris the virgin, who, after being struck severely and for a very long time with slaps and after overcoming other kinds of punishments as well, completed her martyrdom by the sword.

[Col. 0228B] Likewise at Rome, on the Lavican Way, ten soldiers.

### G. III Ides of February (11 February)

At Vienne, Saint Symphlidus, bishop and confessor.

Likewise at Alexandria, the deposition of Saint Euphrasia the virgin, who shone in the monastery through extraordinary virtue of abstinence and through miracles.

### A. The day before the Ides of February (12 February)

In Spain, in the city of Barcelona, the feast of Saint Eulalia the virgin and martyr, who suffered in the time of the emperor Diocletian, under Dacianus, governor of Spain. Under the same governor, Saint Cucuphas at Barcelona and Saint Felix at Girona are also known to have received glorious crowns of martyrdom. Recorded in the Passion of Saint Leocadia (9 December).

In Africa, the martyrdom of Saint Damianus the soldier.

And at Alexandria, that of Modestus and Ammonius, children.

### B. Ides of February (13 February)

The feast of Saint Agabus, a prophet of the New Testament, at Antioch. Concerning him, the blessed Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “While we were staying at Antioch, one of the prophets, named Agabus, stood up and signified through the Spirit that a great famine was about to come upon the whole world, which occurred under Claudius Caesar” (Acts 11). Again, when the blessed Paul was going to Jerusalem to celebrate Pentecost and had already come to Caesarea: “While we were staying,” he says, “in Caesarea for several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. He came to us, took Paul’s belt, bound his own hands and feet, and said: ‘Thus says the Holy Spirit: The Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man to whom this belt belongs in this way and deliver him into the hands of the nations.’”

Likewise, in the Armenian city of Melitene, the feast of Saint Polyeuctus the martyr, whose name is interpreted in Latin as “one who prays much.”

### C. XVI Kalends of March (14 February)

At Rome, the feast of Saint Valentine the priest, who, after many notable acts of healing and teaching, was beaten with clubs and then beheaded under Claudius Caesar.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Valentine, bishop of Interamna, who was seized by pagans, beaten with rods, and, after a prolonged beating, committed to custody. When he could not be overcome, he was taken from prison in the silence of midnight and beheaded by order of the enraged Placidus, prefect of the City. Then his disciples Proculus, Ephibus, and Apollonius transferred his body to their church in the city of Interamna and buried it by night. While they were keeping constant vigils there, they were seized by the gentiles and handed over to custody under the consulship of Leontius. He ordered them to be brought before his tribunal in the middle of the night. When they could be recalled from the faith neither by blandishments nor by threats, he ordered them to be beheaded. They were buried not far from the body [Col. 0229B] of Saint Valentine.

Likewise at Alexandria, the feast of the holy martyrs Bassus, Antonius, and Protolichus, who were drowned in the sea.

Likewise, Cyrionus the priest, Moyses, Bassianus the lector, and Agatho the exorcist, all of whom were burned in fire.

Likewise Dionysius and Ammonius, who were beheaded.

On the same day at Rome, Saints Vitalis, Felicula, and Zeno, martyrs.

### D. XV Kalends of March (15 February)

At Rome, Saint Crato the martyr [Note: [Col. 0229D] Concerning him, in the Acts of Valentine of Interamna, 14 February]. He had a son named Chaeremon, a rhetorician, who had fallen into a very serious illness. He brought him to the blessed Valentine, bishop, to be healed, on the condition that, if the boy were healed, he himself and his entire household would become Christians. When the boy was healed, he fulfilled his promise and was baptized with his wife and whole household. Not many days afterward, he completed his martyrdom.

And at the city of Sebaste, the passion of Saint Blaise [manuscript: Blavius], bishop. A performer of many miracles, under the governor Agricolaus, after a long beating, imprisonment, and suspension on a wooden frame, where his flesh was torn with iron combs; after another, most dreadful imprisonment; and after being thrown into a lake, from which he came out safely by walking upon the water, he was finally beheaded by order of the most wicked judge together with two boys, and thus entered with them into the blessed kingdom.

[Col. 0229D] While he was still engaged in the struggle, seven most blessed women who were discovered gathering drops of his blood as they flowed from the most blessed wounds of his body were found to be Christians. After the furnace of fire, where they were covered with molten lead; after iron combs, by which their flesh was torn; and after red-hot bronze tunics, they were finally sentenced, struck with the sword, and, paying the price of their blood, purchased eternal life.

In Gaul, in the city of Vaison [alternative: Wangionensis], the deposition of Saint Quinidius, bishop, whose death is testified to have been precious in the sight of the Lord by frequent miracles.

### E. XIV Kalends of March (16 February)

[Note: [Col. 0229D] See the book on the Feasts of the Apostles.]

The feast of Saint Onesimus the apostle.

And at Cumae, the feast of Saint Juliana the virgin, who in the time of the emperor Maximian was first beaten and severely tortured by her father Africanus; then, by the prefect Eleusius [Eolasius], to whom she had been betrothed, she was beaten naked with rods, suspended by her hair, and drenched from head to foot with molten lead. She was then taken back to prison, where she openly contended with the devil. Summoned again, she overcame the torments of wheels, flames, and a boiling cauldron, and completed her martyrdom by beheading. She suffered at Nicomedia [Col. 0230B], but after a short time, by God’s providence, was transferred to Campania.

On the same day in Egypt, Julianus with five thousand others.

### F. XIII Kalends of March (17 February)

In Persia, the feast of the blessed Polychronius, bishop of Babylon and Ctesiphon. In the presence of the persecutor Decius, his mouth was beaten with stones. With his hands extended and his eyes raised to heaven, he gave up his spirit. Recorded in the Passion of Saint Laurence (10 August).

### G. XII Kalends of March (18 February)

[Note: [Col. 0229D] See the booklet on the Feasts of the Apostles, where he is listed on 2 May. Concerning them, in the Acts of Susanna, 11 August.]

At Jerusalem, the blessed Simeon, bishop and martyr, [Col. 0230C] who is said to have been related to the Savior according to the flesh.

On the same day, Saints Claudius and his wife Praepedigna, their sons Alexander and Cutia, and Claudius’s brother, the blessed Maximus, martyrs. Since they were of distinguished birth, they were baptized through the agency of their brother Gabinius the priest by the blessed Caius, Roman pontiff. Later, by order of Diocletian, they were seized by the impious judge Julius. Claudius, with his wife and children, was deported into exile. Finally, after being burned in a fire, they offered God the fragrant sacrifice of martyrdom; afterward they were cast into the stream at Ostia. Christians searched for their remains and buried them near the city.

### A. XI Kalends of March (19 February)

[Col. 0230D]

At Rome, Saint Gabinius [Note: [Col. 0230D] Concerning him, in the Life of Susanna, 11 August], priest and father of the most blessed Susanna. After being afflicted for a long time by imprisonment and chains under Diocletian, he obtained the joys of heaven through a precious death.

### B. X Kalends of March (20 February)

At Tyre, which is the greatest city of Phoenicia, the blessed martyrs whose number is known to God alone. At the command of Diocletian, Veturius, master of the soldiers, killed them with various kinds of torture following one another.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 7, from the translation of Rufinus.]

First, the martyrs of God were mangled with scourges over their entire bodies. After this they were handed over to beasts: lions, bears, leopards, and every kind of wild animal were brought against them; also boars and bulls, whose ferocity was increased with iron and fire. Finally, God’s worshipers, their limbs stripped bare, were placed in the middle of the arena. The beasts, driven on inside their cages and becoming more savage among themselves, rushed from their enclosures, suddenly filled the stadium, surrounded the church of the martyrs situated in the middle, and repeatedly went around it and glared at it. Sensing that the protection of divine power was present with them, they withdrew far from the bodies of the martyrs.

But immediately the fury that had been restrained in the beasts passed into human beings. Thus, with swords, they accomplished what the beasts had been unable to do; and, to show in every way that they were more savage than the beasts, they even prevented the corpses from being buried and ordered them to be given to the waves.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Eusebius, book VIII, chapters 22 and 25.]

The blessed bishops Tyrannio and Silvanus led this most glorious multitude, this army of heaven, and urged it on to victory. After a short interval, Silvanus completed his martyrdom through the bites of beasts; and the bishops Peleus and Nilus, who were burned with many clergy, likewise suffered; and the venerable priest Zenobius was beheaded.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] The manuscripts read *complevit* (“he completed”). The common text incorrectly has *compleverunt* (“they completed”). For Tyrannio and Silvanus, the bishops, did not obtain the palm of martyrdom by the same kind of death. Tyrannio was not exposed to beasts but drowned in the sea. Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 25: “The bishop, delivered to the depths of the sea,” Tyrannio the bishop was plunged into the deep whirlpools of the sea. Concerning Silvanus and the others with him: “But this man, having become food for beasts together with others in Emesa itself, was received into the choirs of the martyrs.” Here Silvanus, having become prey to beasts with others in the same city of Emesa, was received into the choir of the martyrs.]

Likewise in Alemannia, the blessed Gallus, abbot, a man of marvelous holiness and a disciple of Saint Columbanus, abbot.

### C. IX Kalends of March (21 February)

In Sicily, the seventy-nine holy martyrs who, under Diocletian, through various torments, deserved to receive from Christ the crown of their confession prepared for them.

### D. VIII Kalends of March (22 February)

At Antioch, the Chair of Saint Peter.

On the same day at Alexandria, Saint Abilius, bishop, who, after the blessed Mark, served as the second bishop for thirteen years.

At Hierapolis, Saint Papias, bishop and hearer of Saint John the apostle.

Likewise, the blessed Aristion, who was one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ.

At Vienne, Saint Paschasius, confessor and pontiff, of admirable holiness.

### E. VII Kalends of March (23 February)

At Sirmium, the blessed Syrenus [alternative: Synerus], a monk. In the time of the emperor Maximian, he had rebuked and driven away the wife of one of the emperor’s household officials, who was walking at an unsuitable hour in the garden that he himself cultivated. At Maximian’s command he was seized; after confessing that he was a Christian, he was beheaded.

Likewise, sixty-two others who suffered there.

On the same day, Saint Polycarp [Note: [Col. 0232D] Concerning him, in the Acts of Saint Sebastian, 20 January], a priest and confessor, who together with the blessed Sebastian converted many to the faith of Christ and, by exhorting them, led them to the glory of martyrdom.

### F. VI Kalends of March (24 February)

[Note: [Col. 0232D] See the booklet on the Feasts of the Apostles. See below.]

The feast of Saint Matthias the apostle.

And the discovery of the head of the Forerunner, in the time of the emperor Marcian, when the same Forerunner revealed to two monks where his head lay concealed. It is established that he was beheaded when the feast of Easter was approaching, as appears in the Gospel; and that in the following year, when the Easter season had returned, the mystery of the Lord’s Passion was accomplished. Therefore, because in the Sacramentary his feast is recorded on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, and in the Martyrology bearing the names of Eusebius and Jerome it is read: “On the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the city of Emesa in the province of Phoenicia, the feast of Saint John the Baptist, on which day he was beheaded,” it designates not specifically the day of his beheading but rather the day on which his head was found in the same city of Emesa and laid to rest in the church.

[Note: [Col. 0232D] In the Sacramentary. I think he means the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory, in which, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, one finds: “On the same day, the beheading or passion of Saint John the Baptist.” The learned Pamelius attributes this book to Saint Gregory in the Prolegomena to volume II of the Liturgica.]

For two Eastern monks had come to Jerusalem to worship and to see the holy places. The same Forerunner of the Lord, appearing to them in a revelation, instructed them to go to the former dwelling of King Herod, search for his head there, and, when it was found, rebury it with due honor. They found and took it, but not long afterward it was lost through their careless negligence. They carried it to Emesa and unworthily concealed it for a considerable time in a subterranean urn in a certain cave, until it again revealed itself and its own presence to a certain religious priest named Marcellus, while he was living in the same cave. From that time onward, in that city, the beheading of the blessed Forerunner began to be celebrated on the day on which his head had been found or raised.

Likewise, at Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of the blessed Sergius the martyr, whose acts are held in high renown.

### G. V Kalends of March (25 February)

In Egypt, the feast of Saints Victorinus, Victor, Nicophorus, Claudianus, Dioscorus, Serapion, and Papias, under the emperor Numerianus, while Sabinus was serving as commander.

The first was placed in a hollow wooden ball pierced all around, and for a very long time was pierced through each of its openings. When an excessive amount of blood flowed out, he was taken from the ball and beheaded.

The second, after his hands and feet had been cut off, was placed in the same ball and endured the torments of the first; finally he was struck with the sword.

The third, after entering the ball of his own accord, aroused the judge’s anger. The judge ordered him to be brought out and roasted for a while on a grate laid over burning coals, and turned over. Since he persisted in his confession, he was taken from there, cut to pieces with the sword, and gave up his spirit.

Of the remaining four, Claudianus and Dioscorus were burned in flames; Serapion and Papias completed their martyrdom by the sword.

### A. IV Kalends of March (26 February)

In the city of Perge in Pamphylia, the feast of the blessed Nestor, bishop. During the persecution of Decius, he devoted himself day and night to prayer, asking that Christ’s flock be guarded. He was seized by a certain Irenarchus, who was chief of the city council, and offered to the governor Pollio like a harmless ram.

When he confessed the name of Christ with marvelous freedom and joy, and declared that the gods of the gentiles were utterly wicked demons, the same governor ordered him to be suspended on the rack and tortured most cruelly. He sang joyfully, saying: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33).

The governor, astonished at such endurance and wishing to recall him from the faith with gentle words, said to him: “Do you wish to be with us, or with your Christ?” Saint Nestor replied with great joy: “With my Christ I was, with him I am, and with him I shall be.”

Then the governor, enraged, pronounced sentence against him: because he confessed Jesus crucified under Pontius Pilate, he should, as one devoted to his God, undergo that sentence and be released from life by crucifixion on the wood.

He gave thanks to God. Once he had been fastened to the cross, he instructed the Christian people standing nearby to persevere in the faith and love of Christ and most willingly to suffer with him, so that they too might be glorified together. After this, he asked the entire crowd of the faithful standing there [Col. 0234A] to bend their knees and pray with him. When he had completed the prayer and everyone had said “Amen,” he gave up his spirit. He completed his martyrdom on Thursday, at the third hour.

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Eusebius, book X, chapter 1, and Rufinus, book I, chapter 1.]

On the same day, the blessed Alexander, bishop of the city of Alexandria, a glorious old man. After the blessed Peter, he expelled his own presbyter Arius from the Church, when Arius had been corrupted by heretical impiety and convicted by divine truth; afterward, among the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, he condemned him at the Council of Nicaea.

### B. III Kalends of March (27 February)

In Spain, in the city of Seville, Saint Leander [Note: [Col. 0233D] Concerning him, Gregory, in the preface to the *Moralia*], bishop and confessor. To him the blessed Gregory wrote the books of the *Moralia*. Through Leander’s preaching and diligence, the entire Gothic people were converted from Arian impiety to the catholic faith by King Reccared. He also corrected his brother, King Hermenegild, while their heretical father was still alive, bringing him from the same Arian heresy to the catholic faith; and through his exhortations he led him onward to the glorious suffering of martyrdom.

[Note: [Col. 0234C] Eusebius, book VI, chapter 34.]

Likewise, on the same day at Alexandria, the feast of Saint Julian the martyr. He was so afflicted with gout that he could neither walk nor stand, yet he was brought before the judge with those who carried him in a small chair. One of these immediately denied the faith; the other, named Eunus, persevered with the aged Julian in confessing the Lord. They were ordered to be placed on camels and led around the entire city, and to be mangled with scourges on every side before the watching people, until they met their end beneath the blows.

Likewise at Lyons, Saint Baldomerus, a man of God, whose tomb is made illustrious by frequent miracles.

### C. The day before the Kalends of March (28 February)

In the territory of Lyons, in the Jura region, the blessed Romanus, abbot, who was the first there to lead an eremitical life and, renowned for many virtues and miracles, afterward became the father of many monks. His venerable body lies in the territory of Besançon.

**Litanies are to be proclaimed. The month of March has thirty-one days; the lunar month, thirty.**

[Col. 0233]

### D. Kalends of March (1 March)

[Col. 0233D] [Note: [Col. 0233D] Concerning these, in the Life of Saint Valentine the priest.]

At Rome, two hundred and sixty holy martyrs, in the time of Claudius, who had been condemned for the name of Christ while digging sand on the Salarian Way [Col. 0234D] (14 February). Claudius ordered them to be placed in a pottery kiln outside the walls at the Salarian Gate; enclosed in that place, they were killed by the arrows of soldiers in the city amphitheater.

### E. VI Nones of March (2 March)

[Col. 0235A]

At Rome, on the Latin Way, the holy martyrs Jovinus and Basileus, who suffered under the emperors Gallienus and Valerian.

On the same day, many martyrs who suffered under the emperor Alexander, whom the impious Alexander, after long tortures, finally condemned to death.

### F. V Nones of March (3 March)

The feast of the holy martyrs Emeterius and Chelidonius. They were soldiers at first in the Galician city of León. When the storm of persecution arose, they suffered many torments for confessing the name of Christ, were led as far as Calahorra, and there were crowned with martyrdom. When the executioner was cutting off their heads, a great miracle appeared to the people. For the ring of one and the handkerchief of the other were received by a cloud and carried up into the heavens. (Prudentius, hymn 1.) All who were present saw these things, and for as long as their eyes could follow, they watched in astonishment the gleam of the gold and the whiteness of the linen. Aurelius Clemens records this in the book of the *Crowns*.

At Caesarea in Palestine, the holy martyrs Marinus the soldier and Asterius the senator, under the persecution of Valerian. When the former had been accused by his fellow soldiers of being a Christian and, questioned by the judge, had testified in a very clear voice that he was a Christian, three hours were granted him for deliberation. After he had left the tribunal, he was greatly strengthened in the faith by the blessed Theotecnus, bishop of the same city. Returning immediately to the judge’s tribunal, he replied with complete confidence: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5). At once he received the crown of martyrdom by the cutting off of his head.

When the aforementioned Asterius received the martyr’s beheaded body upon his shoulders and on the garment he was wearing, he immediately received the honor that he had rendered to the martyr. Recorded in the *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 14.

### G. IV Nones of March (4 March)

[Note: [Col. 0235D] The *Pontifical*, chapter 23.]

The feast of Saint Lucius, pope and martyr, who during the persecution of Valerian and Gallienus was banished into exile for the faith of Christ, and afterward, by divine command, was permitted to return to his own church. He completed his martyrdom by beheading. He was buried on the Appian Way at Saint Sixtus. He ordered that in every place two priests and three deacons should not abandon the bishop, for the sake of ecclesiastical testimony. He sat in the episcopate for three years, three months, and three days.

Likewise at Rome, on the Appian Way, nine hundred holy martyrs who were placed in the cemetery at Saint Cecilia.

[Col. 0236A] On the same day, Saint Caius Palatinus, who was drowned in the sea.

### A. III Nones of March (5 March)

[Note: [Col. 0235D] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, ch. 99.] At Antioch, the passion of Saint Phocas the martyr: after suffering many injuries for the name of the Redeemer, how he triumphed over that ancient serpent is proclaimed to the peoples even today. Indeed, if in these regions a snake should fasten upon someone with a bite and pour in its venom, the person who has been bitten is healed as soon as, trusting in the example, he touches the door of the martyr’s basilica, the power of the poison having been dispelled.

Also on this day, Saint Eusebius Palatinus and nine other martyrs.

### B. The day before the Nones of March (6 March)

[Col. 0236B] At Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Victor and Victorinus, who for three years were afflicted with Claudianus and his wife Bassa by tortures and confinement in prison, and there completed the course of their lives.

### C. The Nones of March (7 March)

In the city of Tuburbitanorum in Mauretania, the passion of the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicity, and with them of Revocatus, Saturninus, and Secundulus. The last of these rested in prison; all the others were handed over to the beasts under the emperor Severus, on his birthday. While they were still being held in prison and Felicity was in labor, it was obtained through the prayers of all their holy fellow soldiers that she should give birth in the eighth month. Moreover, among other things, Perpetua was granted that her mind should somehow be turned away from her body, in which she endured the charge of a cow, so that she still awaited what was to happen, unaware that it had already happened to her.

### D. The eighth day before the Ides of March (8 March)

[Note: [Col. 0235D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men of the Church*, ch. 68.] At Carthage, Saint Pontius, deacon of the blessed Cyprian, bishop, who endured exile with him until the day of his passion, left behind an excellent volume of his *Life and Passion*, and, always glorifying the Lord in his own sufferings, earned the crown of life.

### E. The seventh day before the Ides of March (9 March)

[Col. 0236D] [Note: [Col. 0236D] Jerome, above, ch. 128.] At the city of Nyssa, Saint Gregory, bishop, brother of the blessed Basil of Caesarea, a most learned man and highly distinguished for eloquence.

At Barcelona, Saint Pacianus, bishop, distinguished both in life and in speech, who died in an excellent old age, in peace, in the time of the emperor Theodosius.

### F. The sixth day before the Ides of March (10 March)

[Note: [Col. 0236D] Eusebius, book V, ch. 15.] The feast of the holy martyrs Alexander and Caius of Eumenia, who were crowned with martyrdom at Apamea during the persecution of Antoninus Verus. Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis, writes this in his book *Against the Cataphrygians*.

[Col. 0237A] In Persia, the feast of forty-two holy martyrs.

### G. The fifth day before the Ides of March (11 March)

[Note: [Col. 0237D] Basil, Homily 20.] At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, the feast of forty soldiers, in the time of King Licinius and under the governor Agricolaus. After repeated imprisonment and chains, and after their faces had been beaten with stones, they were sent into a pond, where their bodies, stiffened by the ice, were being broken apart during the night. One of the forty, however, having become faint-hearted, fled to the bathhouse; and as soon as he touched the warmth, he immediately dissolved and gave up his spirit. Seeing this, [Col. 0237B] the others, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, broke forth in praise of almighty God. Around the third hour of the night, a fervent light shone over them like the sun, and the ice melted. Those guarding them were weighed down by sleep; only the jailer remained awake. Hearing them praying and seeing so great a light and the ice melted, he looked to see from where the light itself arose and saw crowns descending over the saints, thirty-nine in number. He began to think to himself, saying, “There are forty of them; where is the crown of the one?” Then, awakening the rest of the guards, he threw his clothing in their faces and leapt into the pond, crying out and saying, “I am a Christian! I am a Christian!”

When morning came, the agents of the most impious tyrant found the jailer himself numbered among the martyrs, in the place from which one had fallen. When they discovered [Col. 0237C] that he was truly faithful, they dragged them all to the shore, broke their legs with clubs, and thus completed their martyrdom by the breaking of their legs.

The names of these martyrs are as follows: Domitianus, Eunoicus, Sisinnius, Heraclius, Alexander, John, Claudius, Athanasius, Valens, Helian, Meliton, Hecditius, Achatius, Vibianus, Helius, Theodulus, Cyrillus, Flavius, Severianus, Cyrion, Valerius, Chudion, Sacerdon, Priscus, Eutychius, Smaragdus, Philoctimon, Aetius, Micallius, Lisimachus, Domnus, Theophilus, Euthycius, Xantius, Aggius, Leontius, Ysitus, Caius, Gorgonius, and Candidus.

One of them, named Meliton, was the youngest of all in age and was still alive although his legs had been broken. His most blessed mother, who was standing beside the martyrs, fearing that he might fail amid the torments, encouraged him with a manly spirit, saying: “Son, endure a little longer. Behold, Christ stands at the door, helping you.”

When the bodies of the saints, placed upon *birotae*, that is, carts, were being carried by the ministers of the devil to be burned, the pious mother saw that her only son had been left behind. The ministers had left him for this reason: they hoped that, if he lived, his spirit might be induced to [Col. 0238A] incline toward the worship of demons. She lifted him upon her shoulders and followed the vehicles with manly stride. As the boy was being carried, he gave back his spirit to heaven amid his mother’s embraces.

When the woman reached the place where the bodies of the saints were being burned, she placed his bones upon the bones of the martyrs, so that in death and burial alike he might share their company. Their bodies were therefore burned and thrown into the river. But by divine providence their relics were found intact and buried with due honor.

[Note: [Col. 0237D] The bodies of the saints were placed upon *birotae*, that is, carts. This explanation of *birotae*, which was lacking in the Vulgate, was thus found in the manuscripts. *Birota*, a type of vehicle, derives its name from its two wheels. It also occurs below, on 13 June, where it is not *birota* but *birotis*: “And during the night he brought him in a *birota* to his little house.” It is mentioned in the Theodosian Code, under *On the Public Cursus*: “We decree that only one thousand pounds be placed upon a four-wheeled carriage, two hundred upon a *birota*, and thirty upon a *veredus*.”]

### A. The fourth day before the Ides of March (12 March)

[Note: [Col. 0238D] *Pontificale*, ch. 65. This is Gregory I.] At Rome, the blessed pontiff Gregory, teacher and apostle of the English, who sat there for thirteen years, six months, and ten days.

[Col. 0238B] [Note: [Col. 0238D] *Pontificale*, ch. 41. This is Innocent I.] And Innocent, who governed the Church for fifteen years, two months, and twenty-one days.

[Note: [Col. 0238D] Eusebius, book VIII, ch. 6.] At Nicomedia, the blessed martyr Peter, who was one of the companions of the martyrs Dorotheus and Gorgonius, who were in the king’s bedchamber. At the command of Diocletian, because he had spoken too freely against the immense punishments inflicted in the name of the holy martyr, he was brought before the court and compelled to sacrifice. When he refused, the order was given that he be hung up and his whole body mangled with lashes, so that under the necessity of pain he might do unwillingly what was commanded.

But when he remained immovable, with his entrails already exposed by the stripping of his skin, the order was given that he be sprinkled with vinegar and salt. When he had also endured this kind of torture steadfastly and courageously, a grate spread over burning coals beneath it was ordered to be placed in the middle, and what remained of his body, already consumed by the beatings [Col. 0238C], was laid upon it. He was not to be burned suddenly, but gradually and little by little, so that the punishment might be prolonged.

As the ministers of wickedness, turning his body now this way and now that, began to inflict punishments upon each of his limbs and renew the tortures, hoping that they could draw consent from him, he remained firm in faith. As though his flesh had already been consumed and dissolved by the fire, he joyfully breathed out his final spirit in faith. Thus Peter—for that was also his name—adorned with such martyrdom, truly proved heir both to Peter’s faith and to his name.

Also at Nicomedia, the feast of the holy priest Egdunus and seven others, who were strangled on successive days in order to instill fear in the rest.

[Col. 0238D] On the same day, the passion of Saint Maximilian the martyr.

### B. The third day before the Ides of March (13 March)

At Nicomedia, the feast of the holy priest Macedonius, his wife Patritia, and their daughter Modesta.

At the city of Nicaea, the holy martyrs Theuseta and her son Horris, Theodora, Nymphodota, Marcus, and Arabia, all of whom were handed over to the fire.

### C. The day before the Ides of March (14 March)

[Col. 0239A] At Rome, the passion of forty-seven holy martyrs [Note: [Col. 0239D] Concerning them, in the *Passion of Processus and Martinianus*, 2 July.] who were baptized by the blessed apostle Peter while that apostle was being held in the Mamertine prison with his fellow apostle Paul, where they were detained for nine months. All of them, with the most devout confession of faith, were consumed by Nero’s sword.

### D. The Ides of March (15 March)

[Note: [Col. 0240D] *Pontificale*, ch. 92.] At Rome, the pontiff Zacharias, who sat at Rome for ten years.

At the city of Thessalonica, the feast of Saint Matrona. She was the maidservant of a certain widow named Plautilla and secretly worshiped Christ, attending the church daily in stolen [Col. 0239B] hours of prayer. Discovered by her mistress, she was stretched out and bound upon a bench, flogged almost to death, and then left bound upon the bench for the night, the doors having been most carefully sealed. On the following day she was found divinely released and praying, with great grace in her countenance.

Again she was fastened with raw sinews to the same bench and beaten with straps until she became speechless, and there she was left for three days with the doors sealed. When the third day came, she was again divinely released and found praying. Then she was beaten with heavy clubs until death and gave up her undefiled spirit in confession of Christ.

### E. The seventeenth day before the Kalends of April (16 March)

[Col. 0239C] At Rome, the feast of Saint Cyriacus. After the long torment of imprisonment which he endured under Maximian, he performed many miracles with his fellow deacon Sisinnius, and with Smaragdus and Largus. Among these miracles, at the request of Diocletian himself, he healed and baptized Artemia, Diocletian’s daughter, who was possessed by a demon. He also healed and baptized Jobia, the daughter of Sapor, king of the Persians, having been sent there for this purpose by Diocletian, and baptized her together with the king himself and four hundred others.

Thirty days after Diocletian’s death, he returned to Rome and was seized among other Christians by his son Maximinus and sent into custody because he had made his sister a Christian. Then Maximinus ordered that, on the day of his procession, Cyriacus should be dragged naked and bound in chains before his chariot. After this, he was brought out of prison with his companions Largus, Smaragdus, and [Col. 0239D] Crescentianus. By the vicar Carpasianus, his head was drenched with liquefied pitch. Four days later he was brought out of prison again, stretched upon the rack, pulled with sinews, and beaten with clubs. Then, by order of Maximian, he was beheaded together with Largus, Smaragdus, and twenty others.

This is written in the *Acts of Pope Marcellus* (16 January). At that same time Maximinus killed his sister Artemia.

Also at Vienne, Saint Isicius, bishop.

### F. The sixteenth day before the Kalends of April (17 March)

In Scotland, the feast of Saint Patrick, bishop and confessor, [Col. 0240A] who first preached Christ there.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Gertrude, virgin.

### G. The fifteenth day before the Kalends of April (18 March)

[Note: [Col. 0240D] Eusebius, book VI, chs. 7, 9, 16, and 29, from Rufinus’s translation.] The feast of Saint Alexander, bishop, who came from his city in Cappadocia and was traveling to Jerusalem with a desire to visit the holy places. Narcissus, bishop of that city, was already governing the Church in extreme old age. It was revealed both to Narcissus and to many of his clergy that on the following morning a bishop should enter who was to be an assistant to the priestly chair.

When everything had thus been accomplished as foretold, all the people of Palestine having gathered together, Alexander, with Narcissus especially taking the initiative, assumed with him the governance of the Jerusalem Church. During the persecution of Decius, when he was already distinguished by the venerable gray hair of advanced [Col. 0240B] age, he was led to Caesarea and shut up in prison; there he was crowned with martyrdom for his confession of Christ.

### A. The fourteenth day before the Kalends of April (19 March)

At the city of Penara, the feast of the blessed John, a man of great holiness, who was born in Syria and came to Italy. As he sought a place for his dwelling, he poured out a prayer to the Lord:

“I beseech you, Lord, who are the true light: if you make my journey prosperous, let this be a sign for me—that wherever I walk, if I give away my psalter and it is returned to me on that same day, there shall be the place of my dwelling.”

It happened. A certain matron [Col. 0240C] received him as a guest; the man of God gave her his psalter, asked for it back, and it was immediately returned to him by the woman. By this sign he was confirmed in establishing his station there. Then, after proceeding not far from that place, about the distance of two arrows, he encountered an angel of God, who said to him: “Servant of God, here the Lord will prepare a place of dwelling for you.”

It was winter, and the man of God was sitting beneath a tree. Hunters, passing through the area, saw him sitting there and the tree beside him clothed with leaves. When they asked who the man was, he replied that he had come from overseas regions for the service of the Lord and wished to remain there.

When they reported this, and fame spread the holy man’s life farther and farther, so great a crowd of God’s people came there from every direction that [Col. 0240D], once a monastery had been established, a large community of servants of God living together was formed there. The blessed John, distinguished by many virtues, presided over it for forty-four years and then rested in peace. He was buried on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the place where God’s benefits are bestowed to this day.

On the same day at Surrentum, Saints Quintus, Quintillus, Quartilla, and Marcus, with nine others.

### B. The thirteenth day before the Kalends of April (20 March)

In Britain, Saint Cuthbert, who, from being a hermit to becoming bishop of the Church of Lindisfarne, led from childhood [Col. 0241A] to old age a life made famous by signs of miracles. When his body had remained buried for eleven years, it was later found incorrupt, as though he had died at that very hour, together with the clothing in which it had been covered. The priest Bede wrote about his life.

### C. The twelfth day before the Kalends of April (21 March)

At the fortress of Cassinum, the feast of Saint Benedict, abbot, whose life, glorious for virtues and miracles, the blessed Pope Gregory records in the books of the *Dialogues* [Note: [Col. 0241D] Book II of Gregory’s *Dialogues*; Gregory of Tours, *On the Lives of the Fathers*, ch. 1.].

On the same day, Blessed Serapion the hermit.

And in the territory of Lyon, Saint Lupicinus, abbot of the Jura, whose life was distinguished by holiness and the glory of miracles. His body is venerated in the territory of Besançon [Col. 0241B], at the monastery of Laocona.

### D. The eleventh day before the Kalends of April (22 March)

[Note: [Col. 0241D] See the booklet *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.] In Gaul, at the city of Narbonne, the feast of Saint Paul, bishop and confessor, a disciple of the apostles.

### E. The tenth day before the Kalends of April (23 March)

[Note: [Col. 0241D] Victor of Africa, book III.] In Africa, the holy martyrs Victorianus, Frumentius, another Frumentius, and two brothers, all of whom, during the Vandal persecution, under the Arian king Hunneric in Africa, were tortured with monstrous punishments for the constancy of their Catholic confession and were gloriously crowned.

### F. The ninth day before the Kalends of April (24 March)

[Col. 0241C]
