At Rome, the feast of Saint Pigmenius, priest. He had raised the apostate and impious Julian from childhood and instructed him also in sacred letters. But after becoming emperor, Julian abandoned the worship of piety. When he heard that Pigmenius was burying the bodies of the holy martyrs whom he was killing, he ordered him: “Go wherever you wish; for here your life will not be bought. Nevertheless, I repay your services with a reward—not to you.”

Then Saint Pigmenius went to Persia, where he remained for four years and became blind. From there he was warned in a dream by the Lord to return to Rome. When he returned after four months and was climbing the slope of the Sacred Way, begging alms with a certain boy, he encountered the emperor Julian, sitting in a golden chariot.

When Julian saw Pigmenius from a distance, he ordered him to be summoned and said to him: “Glory to my gods and goddesses, because I see you.” The man of God Pigmenius immediately replied: “Glory to my Lord Jesus Christ the Nazarene, who was crucified, because I do not see you.”

At these words Julian became angry and ordered him to be thrown from the bridge into the Tiber. His body was found and gathered up and was buried in the cemetery of Pontianus, not far from Saints Abdon and Sennes.

### G. The eighth day before the Kalends of April (25 March)

[Col. 0242A]

At the city of Nazareth in Galilee, the Annunciation of the Lord.

And at Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Dula, a soldier’s maidservant, who was killed for her chastity.

At Rome, Saint Cyrinus, who was killed by Claudius and thrown into the Tiber, found on the island of Lycaonia, and buried in the cemetery of Pontianus. It is written in the passion of Saint Valentine (14 February).

And at Sirmium, the feast of Saint Irenaeus, bishop, who in the time of the emperor Maximian, under the governor Probus, was first tormented with exceedingly severe tortures, then afflicted for many days in prison, and finally brought to completion by the cutting off of his head.

### A. The seventh day before the Kalends of April (26 March)

[Col. 0242B]

At Rome, on the Lavican Way, in its cemetery, the feast of Saint Castulus, who, being a *zaetarius* of the palace and a host of the saints—as is read in the *Acts of the Blessed Sebastian* (20 January)—was seized by the persecutors, hung up and questioned a third time, and, persevering in confession of the Lord, was thrown into a pit. A mass of sand was poured down upon him, and thus, with the palm of martyrdom, he departed to Christ.

On the same day, in Pentapolis of Libya, Theodorus, bishop, Irenaeus, deacon, and Serapion and Ammonius, readers.

And at Sirmium, the feast of Saint Montanus, priest, who was seized with his wife Maxima and thrown into a river. Their bodies were found and buried at the ninth milestone from the city.

### B. The sixth day before the Kalends of April (27 March)

At Egypt, the blessed John the Hermit, a man of admirable holiness, who, filled also with the prophetic spirit, foretold to the most Christian emperor Theodosius great victories over tyrants [Note: [Col. 0242D] Rufinus, book II, ch. 19.].

### C. The fifth day before the Kalends of April (28 March)

At Caesarea of Palestine, the holy martyrs Priscus, Malchus, and Alexander. During the persecution of Valerian, while they lived on a suburban estate of the aforesaid city and the crowns of heavenly martyrdom were being offered [Col. 0242D] in it, they were kindled by divine fervor of faith and went voluntarily to the judge, rebuking him for raging so fiercely against the blood of the godly. He immediately handed them over to the beasts to be devoured for the name of Christ.

And at the city of the people of Chalon, the burial of Guntram, king of the Franks, a religious man who devoted himself so completely to spiritual works that, abandoning the pomp of the world, he distributed his treasures to churches and the poor.

[Note: [Col. 0242D] *Pontificale*, ch. 45. This is Sixtus III.] Also, Pope Sixtus, who sat at Rome for eight years. When his accuser, named Bassus, died by divine will [Col. 0243A], Sixtus himself handled him with linen cloths and spices and buried him beside blessed Peter.

### D. The fourth day before the Kalends of April (29 March)

The burial of Abbot Eustasius, a disciple of Saint Columbanus, who became the father of nearly six hundred monks and, distinguished by the holiness of his life, also shone forth through miracles.

[Note: [Col. 0243C] Victor of Africa, near the end of book I.] On the same day in Africa, the holy confessors Armogastes, Archinimus, and Satyrus. During the Vandal persecution, under the Arian king Geiseric, they were most radiant members of Christ’s Church. They frequently rebuked the Arian depravity with Catholic freedom and, for their confession of the truth, endured many severe punishments [Col. 0243B] and insults, completing the course of their glorious struggle.

### E. The third day before the Kalends of April (30 March)

At Rome, the feast of Saint Quirinus [Note: [Col. 0244C] Concerning him, in the *Acts of Pope Alexander*.], tribune and martyr, under the emperor Trajan. At Trajan’s command he had put the blessed Pope Alexander (3 May) and Hermes the prefect in chains. He had a daughter whose neck was encircled by a scrofulous swelling. After hearing the blessed Hermes’s exhortations concerning the faith of Christ and seeing the signs that God worked through his martyrs Alexander and Hermes, Quirinus offered this daughter of his to be healed.

The blessed Alexander said to him: “Take the *boia* from my neck and place it upon her.” When her father obediently did this, she was suddenly healed by divine will. [Col. 0243C] She was called Balbina. Thus her father Quirinus, she herself, all those who were being held in custody, and his entire household were baptized.

When the prison administrator reported this to the judge Aurelianus, he became angry and ordered Quirinus to be brought before him. He said to him: “I loved you as a son; but you have mocked me and been deceived [Col. 0244A] by Alexander.” Quirinus said to him: “I have become a Christian. Do you wish to kill me, beat me with clubs, or burn me? I shall be nothing else. For I caused all who were in the prison to become Christians, and I released them, but they refused to go anywhere.”

Angry, Aurelianus had his tongue cut out and then had him hung upon the rack. When he did not yield to Aurelianus’s abuses, Aurelianus ordered his hands and feet to be cut off, then ordered him to be beheaded and thrown to the dogs. But the Christians seized his body and buried it on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Praetextatus.

### F. The day before the Kalends of April (31 March)

At Rome, the feast of Saint Balbina, daughter of the martyr Quirinus. This blessed martyr, taking the *boia* from the neck of Pope Alexander [Col. 0244B] according to his command, was going to place it upon the neck of his daughter, who had the scrofulous swelling, when suddenly a boy appeared with a torch. It is certain that he was an angel of God. He came to the girl, saying: “Be healed, and remain in your virginity, and I shall make you see your bridegroom, who shed his blood for love of you.”

When her father arrived to carry out what had been commanded concerning the *boia*, he suddenly saw his daughter healthy. She was afterward baptized by Saint Alexander and, instructed in virginity, remained rich in good works.

Because she often kissed that *boia*, Saint Alexander said to her: “Stop kissing this *boia*, but rather seek the chains of my Lord Peter and kiss them.” She then set about this task and, after great desire and with the utmost diligence [Col. 0244C], finally reached them and handed them over to Saint Theodora, a most devout woman, sister of Saint Hermes the prefect and martyr.

The virgin Balbina, after overcoming the course of this present world, was buried beside her father, the martyr Quirinus, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, on the second day before the Kalends of April.

## Litanies to be proclaimed

April has thirty days; the moon, however, has twenty-nine.

### G. The Kalends of April (1 April)

[Col. 0243]

[Col. 0243D]

At Rome, the most blessed Theodora [Note: [Col. 0243D] Concerning her, in the *Acts of Pope Alexander*.], sister of the illustrious martyr Hermes, whom the blessed Alexander, pope and martyr, instructed, baptized, and taught in the faith of Christ. She suffered martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian. She was buried beside her brother, the martyr, on the Salarian Way, not far from the city of Rome.

On the same day, Saint Venantius, bishop and martyr.

And in the district of Wimno, Saint Walaricus, confessor, whose tomb is glorified by frequent miracles.

### A. The fourth day before the Nones of April (2 April)

[Col. 0244D]

The feast of Saint Nicetius, bishop of Lyon, whose life was distinguished by miracles and whose precious death was likewise commended by miracles.

[Note: [Col. 0244D] Eusebius, book VIII, ch. 17.] And at Caesarea in Cappadocia, the passion of Saint Theodosia, virgin. In the time of Diocletian, when she was eighteen years old, she voluntarily joined herself to the holy confessors in prison. Seized by the prefect Urbanus and tortured upon the rack, she was then loaded with chains and thrust into prison. There, by the power of God, all her bonds were broken [Col. 0245A]. After this she was tied to a stone and plunged into the sea; but soon returned unharmed to the shore. She was thrown to the beasts in the amphitheater, but remained untouched by them, and worthily completed her martyrdom by the cutting off of her head.

### B. The third day before the Nones of April (3 April)

At Thessalonica, the feast of the holy virgins Agape and Chionia, under Diocletian. First tormented in prison, they were afterward thrown into the fire; but, untouched by the flames, they gave up their souls after pouring out a prayer to the Lord.

At Scythia, in the city of Tomis, the feast of the holy Evagrius and Benignus.

At Tauromenium in Sicily, Saint Pancratius.

### C. The day before the Nones of April (4 April)

[Col. 0245B]

At Milan, the burial of the blessed Ambrose, bishop and confessor. Through his diligence, among his other distinctions in doctrine and miracles, the whole of Italy was converted to the Catholic faith during the time of the Arian perfidy.

### D. The Nones of April (5 April)

At Thessalonica, the feast of Saint Irene, virgin, who, after enduring imprisonment, was struck by an arrow by the count Sisinnius, under whom her sisters Agape and Chionia likewise suffered martyrdom.

Also in Egypt, the feast of Saints Martiana, Nicanor, and Apollonius.

[Col. 0245C] At Caesarea in Lycia, the feast of Saint Amphianus.

### E. The eighth day before the Ides of April (6 April)

[Note: [Col. 0245D] *Pontificale*, ch. 8. This is Sixtus.] At Rome, Saint Sixtus, pope and martyr, who governed the Church for ten years, two months, and one day. He suffered in the time of the emperor Hadrian.

### F. The seventh day before the Ides of April (7 April)

Hegesippus, a most holy man, who lived near the times of the apostles and, weaving histories of ecclesiastical events from the passion of the Lord up to his own age and gathering many things here and there for the benefit of readers, composed five books. He wrote in simple speech, so that he might also reproduce in his manner of speaking the character of those whose life he followed.

He states that he came to Rome under Anicetus, who was the tenth bishop after Peter, and remained until Eleutherius, bishop of that same city, who had once been Anicetus’s deacon. This same Hegesippus also relates in his books the change in his way of life, from pagan philosophy [Note: [Col. 0245D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men of the Church*, ch. 22; Eusebius, book IV, chs. 8, 10, and 12.].

“For I myself,” he says, “having been educated in the Platonic schools, when I heard Christians being defamed and saw them undaunted in accepting death and enduring every punishment, considered that it was impossible for them to live in wickedness and lust.”

### G. The sixth day before the Ides of April (8 April)

[Col. 0246A]

At Tours, Saint Perpetuus, bishop, a man of admirable holiness. Through his work, a temple was completed over the venerable bones of the blessed bishop Martin; his sacred body was also transferred and reburied from the place where it had first been entombed to the place where it is now worthily venerated.

### A. The fifth day before the Ides of April (9 April)

At Sirmium, the feast of seven virgins, who together merited to be crowned on the fifth day before the Ides of April.

At Antioch, Saint Prochorus, deacon [Note: [Col. 0246D] See the booklet *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.], who was one of the first seven.

### B. The fourth day before the Ides of April (10 April)

[Col. 0246B]

Ezekiel the prophet.

And at Rome, the blessed multitude of many martyrs whom the blessed Pope Alexander, pope and martyr, baptized while he was being held in prison, and who were exiled together with him. The emperor Aurelian had all of them placed upon an old ship, taken out into the open sea, and there drowned in the depths of the sea with stones tied around their necks, on the fourth day before the Ides of April.

### C. The third day before the Ides of April (11 April)

At Crete, in the city of Cortyna, the blessed Philip, bishop, who was distinguished in life and teaching in the times of the emperors Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

### D. The day before the Ides of April (12 April)

[Col. 0246C]

(*Pontificale*, ch. 36.) At Rome, on the Aurelia Way at the third milestone, in the cemetery of Calepodius, the feast of Saint Julius, bishop and confessor. Under Constantius, the Arian son of Constantine, he endured ten months of tribulations and exiles; after Constantius’s death, he returned to his own see with great glory.

### E. The Ides of April (13 April)

(*Eusebius*, book IV, ch. 14.) At Pergamum, a city of Asia, the feast of the holy bishop Carpus, the deacon Papyrus, and Agathonica, an excellent woman, together with many others who were crowned with martyrdom through proven confessions [Col. 0246D]. With them was the remarkable man Justin, the philosopher, who also wore the dress of philosophers and labored greatly for the religion of Christ, to the extent that he presented to Antoninus Pius, his sons, and the Senate a book written against the pagans, and was not ashamed of the dishonor of the Cross.

When he had already presented a second book to the successors of the aforementioned emperor, namely Antoninus Verus and Aurelius Commodus, in defense of our religion, he received the reward of a faithful tongue, the gift of martyrdom.

(The same source, in the same place, chs. 8 and 11.) In Spain, the feast of Saint Herminigildus, whom his father, the Arian Leovigildus [Col. 0247A], king of the Goths, seeing him unshakable in his confession of the Catholic faith, threw into prison and chains. There, on the holy night of the Lord’s Resurrection, by order of his impious father, he was struck on the head with an ax and entered the heavenly kingdom, king and martyr, in place of an earthly kingdom. The blessed Pope Gregory writes this (*Dialogues*, book III, ch. 31).

### F. The eighteenth day before the Kalends of May (14 April)

At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, the feast of the holy martyrs Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus [Note: [Col. 0247D] Concerning them, in the *Acts of Cecilia*.], under the prefect Almachius. The first two were beaten with clubs and struck with the sword (22 November); the last was beaten with leaded whips until he gave up his spirit.

[Col. 0247B] At Terni, Saint Proculus the martyr.

Also Saint Domna, virgin, crowned with her companions, the virgins.

At Alexandria, Saint Fronto, abbot, whose life was glorious in holiness and miracles.

### G. The seventeenth day before the Kalends of May (15 April)

At the city of Cordula, the feast of the holy nobles Olympias and Maximus [Note: [Col. 0247D] Concerning them, in the *Life of Saint Laurence*.], who, by order of Decius, were beaten with clubs and then with leaded whips; finally their heads were hewn with axes until they gave up their spirits.

Also in Spain, at the city of Caesaraugusta (10 August), the feast of the eighteen holy martyrs Optatus, Lupercus, Successus, Martialis, Urbanus, Julius, Quintilianus, [Col. 0247C] Publius Fronto, Felix, Caecilianus, Evotus, Primitivus, Apodemus, and the remaining four, all of whom are reported to have been called Saturninus.

In Italy, the feast of the holy martyrs Maro, Eutyches, and Victorinus [Note: [Col. 0247D] Concerning them, in the *Life of Nereus and Achilleus*.]. They lived in prolonged exile with the blessed Flavia Domitilla on the island of Pontia and supported her in the confession of Christ with devoted consolation. Because of the envy and persecution of Aurelian, her betrothed and persecutor, whom she had rejected for Christ, they were later handed over by the emperor Nerva to that same Aurelian as slaves.

He first divided them individually among his estates as slaves and ordered them to dig the earth throughout the day, but in the evening to eat *cantabrum*. Then, when they converted very many to the faith of Christ and increased the people of believers [Col. 0247D], he was filled with anger by the devil and sent men to kill them by various kinds of punishment.

He ordered Eutyches to be beaten in the middle of the road until he breathed out his spirit. The Christian people seized his body. Victorinus he ordered to be suspended head downward for three hours at a place called Cotilia, where foul and sulfurous waters flow. After suffering this for three days in the name of Christ, he departed to the Lord.

When, by order of Aurelian, his body had lain unburied for one day, the Christian people of Amiternum came [Col. 0248A], seized it, and carried it into their own territory.

As for Maro, that same Aurelian sent his friend named Turgius to have him led away and crushed beneath a huge stone. But because the Lord protected him, they could harm him in no way. The governor, after receiving an order from Aurelian, killed him, and the Christian people seized his body and buried it with due honor.

### A. The sixteenth day before the Kalends of May (16 April)

At Corinth, Callistus and Carisius with seven others, all drowned in the sea.

### B. The fifteenth day before the Kalends of May (17 April)

At Africa, the feast of Saint Mappalicus, who was crowned with martyrdom together with many [Col. 0248B] others. The blessed Cyprian writes about him in his letter to the martyrs and confessors as follows [Note: [Col. 0248D] Cyprian, Letter 9; likewise the letter of Lucian, Letter 22, concerning his companions, in the same author]:

“A voice full of the Holy Spirit burst from the martyr’s mouth when the most blessed Mappalicus said to the proconsul amid his torments: ‘You will see the contest tomorrow.’ What he said with the testimony of courage and faith, the Lord fulfilled. The heavenly contest was displayed, and God’s servant was crowned in the struggle of the contest he had promised.

“And shortly afterward: ‘This contest, foretold beforehand through the prophets, ordained by the Lord, and carried out through the apostles, Mappalicus promised to the proconsul in his own name and that of his companions. The faithful voice did not fail in its promise: it displayed the battle it had pledged and received the palm it had earned.

“‘I both desire and exhort you all to follow this most blessed martyr and the others who shared and [Col. 0248C] accompanied him in the same struggle: steadfast in faith, patient in suffering, victorious in questioning; so that those whom the bond of confession and the lodging of prison joined together may also be joined by the completion of virtue and the heavenly crown.’”

At Antioch, the feast of Saints Peter the deacon and Hermogenes.

At Vienne, Saint Pantagathus, bishop.

### C. The fourteenth day before the Kalends of May (18 April)

At Messana [another reading: Misenam], a city of Apulia, the feast of the holy martyrs Eleutherius, bishop, and Anthia [another reading: Evanthia], his mother. This blessed bishop, illustrious both for the holiness of his life and for the power of his miracles, under the emperor Hadrian, by the grace of Christ, overcame an ignited iron bed, a grating, and a frying-pan boiling with oil, pitch, and resin; he was also thrown to lions but remained unharmed by them. Finally, together with his mother, he was beheaded with the sword.

(Eusebius, Book V, chapters 20–21, in Rufinus.) Also on this day at Rome, Saint Apollonius the senator, who, having been betrayed by a slave under the emperor Commodus because he was a Christian and ordered to give an account of his faith, composed an impressive volume, which he read in the senate. Nevertheless, by the sentence of the senate, he was beheaded for Christ [Col. 0249A], since among them the ancient law remained in force that Christians who had once been brought before their tribunal were not to be released without a denial of their faith.

At the monastery of Laubac, the passing of Saint Ursmar, bishop and confessor.

## D. Thirteenth day before the Kalends of May (19 April)

In Armenia, in the city of Melitene, the feast of the holy Hermogenes, Caius, Expeditius, Aristonices, Rufus, and Galata, crowned on one and the same day.

At Caucoliberis in Spain, the feast of Saint Vincent the martyr.

At Corinth, Saint Timo, one of those first seven deacons (Acts 6).

## E. Twelfth day before the Kalends of May (20 April)

[Col. 0249B]

At Rome, Saint Victor, bishop, who, the thirteenth after blessed Peter [Note: [Col. 0249D] See the booklet on the Feasts of the Apostles], governed the Church for ten years and was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Severus.

Also at Rome, the holy martyrs Sulpitius and Servilianus [Note: [Col. 0249D] Concerning them, see the Acts of Nereus and Achilleus], who were converted to the faith of Christ through the preaching and miracles of the blessed Flavia Domitilla. She had also won their brides, Theodora and Euphrosyna, to the hope of eternal life and perseverance in holy virginity. During the persecution of Taiadi, because they refused to sacrifice to idols, they were beheaded by Anianus, prefect of the City. Christians seized their bodies and placed them on their estate, on the Latin Way, at the second milestone [Col. 0249C].

(Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 69.) On the same day in Gaul, in the city of Ebredunum, Saint Marcellinus, the first bishop and confessor of that city. By divine command, he came from Africa with his holy companions Vincent and Domninus and converted a great part of the Maritime Alps to the faith of Christ through wondrous signs, which still shine today. Thus the baptistery that he established near the aforesaid city is flooded each year, by divine power, with sudden waters during the sacred vigils of the Paschal feast, and remains overflowing with grace throughout the seven days of that solemnity. His venerable companions, buried at the city of Digne, are likewise commended for their glorious miracles.

## F. Eleventh day before the Kalends of May (21 April)

[Col. 0249D]

(Cassiodorus, Book II of the Tripartite History.) In Persia, the feast of Saint Simeon, bishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon, royal cities. During the persecution of Sapor, king of the Persians, he was arrested at the command of that same tyrant and loaded with chains. When brought before unjust tribunals, he bore witness to the Lord Jesus Christ with a free and utterly steadfast voice. First, he was tormented for a long time in a prison confinement with a hundred others, some of whom were bishops, others priests, and others clerics of various orders. Finally, when he remained immovable in his testimony to Christ [Col. 0250A], he was ordered to be beheaded together with them all. Thus, while the others were slaughtered, he stood by and was himself killed last. As they were all struck down before his eyes, he courageously encouraged each one with paternal exhortations; at the final blow of the executioner, he too fell and received the palm of martyrdom. It was Friday of Holy Week, during which the annual remembrance of Christ’s Passion is celebrated before the feast of the Resurrection.

Ustazades the eunuch, the king’s foster-father and chief official of the royal household, also suffered with him, as did Abdella and Ananias, venerable old men; and Pusitius, chief of the royal craftsmen. The latter, seeing the aforesaid old man Ananias trembling under the sword, had confidently cried out: “A little longer, old man; close your eyes and be without fear. Soon you will see the face of Christ.” Pusitius’s daughter, a consecrated virgin, was also killed at the same time.

At Alexandria, the feast of the holy Fortunatus, Arator the priest, Felix, Silvius, and Vitalis, who rested in prison.

## G. Tenth day before the Kalends of May (22 April)

At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus [Note: [Col. 0250D] Concerning this, see the Acts of Sebastian and Susanna, August 11; the Pontifical Book, chapter 29], Saint Caius, pope, who, after governing the Church for eleven years, four months, and twelve days, was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Diocletian. His brother, blessed Gabinius the priest, had already completed the triumph of his victory in many illustrious sufferings under the same impious emperor, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March [Col. 0250C].

(Cassiodorus, Book III of the Tripartite History, chapter 2.) In Persia, a great number of holy martyrs who, at the command of Sapor, king of the Persians, were slaughtered by the sword throughout the entire region of Persia on the annual day when the Passion of the Lord is commemorated. In this struggle of faith suffered Melisius, a bishop distinguished for holiness and the glory of miracles; also the bishop Acepsimas with his priest James; and likewise the bishops Mareas and Bicor, together with nearly two hundred clerics, fifty monks, and many consecrated virgins. Among them was Tarbua, sister of Bishop Simeon, with her attendant. They bound them to stakes, split them with a saw, and killed them with the utmost cruelty [Col. 0250D].

On the same day, in the city of Cordula, the feast of the holy Parmenias, Helimenas, and Chrysotelus, priests, and Luke and Mucius, deacons from Babylonia. The first of these continued to speak even after his tongue had been cut out. They were all first suspended on the rack and stretched by cords; then they were burned with glowing plates applied to their sides, torn with claws, and finally killed with the sword, in the presence of the persecutor Decius. This is written in the Passion of Saint Laurence (10 August).

(Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 64.) Also at Lyons in Gaul, the feast of Saint Epipodius the martyr. During the persecution of Antoninus Verus, after the glorious sufferings of the forty-eight martyrs who suffered in that same city, he was arrested with Alexander, his most beloved companion. While Alexander was meanwhile thrown into prison, Epipodius’s mouth was first beaten with terrible blows of the fists; then he was tortured by being stretched on the rack; finally he completed his martyrdom by beheading [Col. 0251A].

At Vienne, Saint Julian, bishop and confessor.

## A. Ninth day before the Kalends of May (23 April)

(Distinction 15, chapter “The Holy Roman Church.”) In Persia, in the city of Diospolis, the Passion of Saint George the martyr. Although the account of his Passion is counted among the apocryphal writings, the Church of God nevertheless venerates his most illustrious martyrdom among the crowns of the martyrs.

[Col. 0251B] In Gaul, in the city of Valence, the feast of the holy Felix the priest, Fortunatus and Achilleus the deacons. Sent by the blessed Irenaeus, bishop and martyr of Lyons, to preach the word of God, they converted a great part of the aforesaid city to the faith of Christ. They were thrown into prison by the commander Cornelius; then beaten for a very long time with the harshest scourging of sinews. Afterward, with their hands bound behind their backs and their legs broken, they were fastened around the circumference of wheels; bitter smoke was placed beneath them, and they were suspended on the rack through day and night without interruption. Finally, they were put to death with the sword.

At the monastery of Fontenelle, Saint Wulfran, bishop, a man renowned for miracles and learning.

## B. Eighth day before the Kalends of May (24 April)

[Col. 0251C]

At Lyons in Gaul, the feast of Saint Alexander, who, brought out of prison on the third day after the Passion of Epipodius, was first so mangled by the cruelty of those beating him that, when the lattice of his ribs had been broken and his entrails exposed, the hidden places of his soul were laid open. Then, fastened to the cross-shaped gibbet, he breathed out his blessed spirit. Thirty-four others also suffered with him. Both were buried on opposite sides of the altar, in a crypt constructed with beautiful and ancient workmanship on the hill above the city.

(Bede, Book I of the Ecclesiastical History of the English, chapters 20 and 30, and Book III, chapters 2 and following.) On the same day, the deposition of Mellitus, bishop in Britain, who, third after Augustine, bishop of Canterbury, assumed charge of the Canterbury church and governed it for five years. He was buried in the monastery, in the church of blessed Peter, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, in the year 624 from the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0251D].

## C. Seventh day before the Kalends of May (25 April)

At Alexandria, the feast of Saint Mark the evangelist [Note: [Col. 0251D] See the booklet on the Feasts of the Apostles], who died a martyr and was buried gloriously in a place of hewn stone. He had appointed Anianus bishop of Alexandria in his own place, and had likewise appointed bishops, priests, and deacons for other churches far and wide.

[Col. 0252A] On the same day at Rome, the greater litany, at Saint Peter’s.

At Vienne, Saint Clarentius, bishop and confessor.

## D. Sixth day before the Kalends of May (26 April)

(Pontifical Book, chapter 3.) At Rome, the feast of Saint Anacletus, pope, who, second after blessed Peter, governed the Church for twelve years and was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Domitian.

(Pontifical Book, chapter 30.) On the same day, Saint Marcellinus, pope, who, after governing the Church for nine years and four months, was beheaded under Diocletian and Maximian, by that same Diocletian, for confessing the true faith, together with Claudius, Cyrinus, and Antoninus [Col. 0252B]. Thirty-five days later he was buried on the Salarian Way, in a chamber, by the priest Marcellus and the deacons, with hymns. At that time there was a great persecution, so that within one month seventeen thousand were crowned with martyrdom.

## E. Fifth day before the Kalends of May (27 April)

(Pontifical Book, chapter 40.) At Rome, Saint Anastasius, pope, who sat for three years and ten days.

At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Anthimus, bishop and martyr, shining in the memories of the faithful in the kingdom of Christ. During the persecution of Diocletian, because of his confession of Christ, he received the glory of martyrdom by beheading. Almost the entire multitude of his flock followed him as a good shepherd going before them on the way of martyrdom. The aforementioned tyrant, who at that time resided in the same city, ordered some of them to be beheaded with the sword, others to be burned in the fire, and others to be placed in small boats and drowned in the sea. The crowds of believers were so inflamed by the fire of faith through God’s grace that they would not even allow themselves to be interrogated, but rushed voluntarily into the flames or offered their necks to the blows of the swords. This is written in the Ecclesiastical History, Book VIII (Eusebius VIII, chapter 6).

## F. Fourth day before the Kalends of May (28 April)

At Ravenna, the feast of Saint Vitalis the martyr, father of the holy Gervasius and Protasius. He entered Ravenna while serving under the judge Paulinus. When he saw before his judge a Christian named Ursicinus, a physician by profession and a Ligurian by birth, receive a death sentence after excessive torments, and then approach the palm of martyrdom and grow afraid, he cried out: “Do not, do not, Ursicinus the physician, who have been accustomed to cure others, wound yourself with the dart of eternal death! After coming through such great sufferings to the palm, do you wish to lose the crown prepared for you by the Lord?” When Ursicinus had completed his martyrdom, blessed Vitalis immediately seized his body and buried it within the city of Ravenna, refusing to come again before the judge. Therefore, because he had strengthened the aforesaid Ursicinus with his exhortations while he was engaged in the struggle of his Passion, he was arrested by the consul Paulinus and, after the tortures of the rack, ordered to be led to the Palms [Col. 0253A].

The place where Christians were beheaded had this name because palm trees grew there. A pit was dug until water was found; there he was laid on his back and buried under earth and stones. His wife Valeria, while returning to the city of Milan, came upon people sacrificing to Silvanus. When they took her down from the pack animal and urged her to eat food sacrificed to idols, she declared that she could not lawfully do so because she was a Christian. They slaughtered her with such excessive blows that her own people could scarcely carry her, half-dead, to the city of Milan. Within two days she departed to the Lord.

[Col. 0253B] At Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0253C] Ambrose, Book II On Virgins, has Antioch instead], the feast of Saint Theodora the virgin. Because she refused to sacrifice, she was handed over to a brothel but was rescued by God’s wondrous favor. A crowd of shameless young men was already standing at the door of her cell when suddenly one of the brothers, named Didymus, full of faith and divinely inspired, put on military clothing and was the first to enter the brothel. Explaining to the holy virgin why he had come, he clothed her in military garments and himself put on virginal clothing. Thus the virgin escaped, leaving the brothel and fleeing toward the city without being recognized by anyone. Didymus was brought before the governor; he steadfastly explained everything and confessed that he was a Christian. His head was cut off and his body was given to the fire. The blessed virgin, who had fled from the brothel to preserve her virginity, returned at once to the arena out of love for the crown. She was struck down together with Didymus and was crowned together with him [Col. 0253C].

On the same day, Aphrodisius, Charillus, Agapius, and Eusebius, martyrs.

Also in Pannonia, Saint Pollio the martyr.

## G. Third day before the Kalends of May (29 April)

At Paphos, Tychicus, a disciple of the apostles (Ephesians 6; 2 Timothy 4).

In Numidia, at the colony of Cirta, the feast of the holy martyrs Agapius and Secundinus, bishops. During the persecution of Valerian, after a long exile in the aforesaid city, where at that time the rage of the devil’s persecution was especially intent on testing the faith of the just through the blind fury and military duties of the pagans, they were made glorious martyrs, though they had come from illustrious priestly office. Their companions in suffering were Aemilianus the soldier, Tertulla and Antonia, consecrated virgins, and a certain woman with her twins.

## A. The day before the Kalends of May (30 April)

The feast of the holy martyrs Marianus and James [Note: [Col. 0254C] Concerning them, see the Acts of Saints Marianus and James], the former a lector and the latter a deacon. Marianus had already previously overcome the attacks of the Decian persecution by his confession of Christ, but he was arrested again with his beloved companion at the colony of Cirta. There, after dreadful and elaborate tortures—for Marianus was suspended by the tips of his thumbs, with a heavy weight attached to his feet, and was tortured most cruelly—they were tormented for a long time in prison [Col. 0254B]. Strengthened wondrously by divine revelations, they were then sent to the city of Lambesis before the governor and again confined for a long time in a prison cell. But once more they were raised up by divine revelations, and finally, together with many others, they were put to death with the sword.

(Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 56.) On the same day, at the city of Saintes, the feast of Saint Eutropius the martyr. He was sent into Gaul by the blessed Clement, bishop, and was also consecrated by him with the grace of the episcopal order. Having fulfilled the duties of that office and preached among unbelievers, he was attacked by pagans whom the author of envy did not permit to believe. His head was smashed, and he fell as a victor [Col. 0254C].

After many years had passed, Palladius, bishop of that city, together with other men of God, transferred his body into a new basilica in order to give it the honor due to it. When they opened the sarcophagus, they saw the scar on his head where the edge of the axe had struck. The following night, when the priests had laid their limbs down to rest, he appeared to them in a vision and said: “Know that I completed my martyrdom through the scar that you saw on my head.”

In Asia, the Passion of Saint Maximus the martyr, whose Acts are preserved.

# Litany to be proclaimed

The month of May has thirty-one days; the moon, thirty.

## B. Kalends of May (1 May)

[Col. 0253]

The prophet Jeremiah.

And the feast of the apostles Philip and James [Note: [Col. 0253C] See the booklet on the Feasts of the Apostles], James being the son of Mary, who was the sister of the Lord’s mother; hence they were called the Lord’s brothers [Col. 0254C].

In Gaul, in the territory of Viviers, at a place anciently called by the pagans, Saint Aneolus the subdeacon [Col. 0255A]. Saint Polycarp sent him from the East with the blessed Benignus and Andochius, priests, and Thyrsus, a deacon, to preach the word of God in Gaul. When Caesar Severus learned of his preaching, he ordered him to be scourged most cruelly with thorny clubs and thrown into prison. On another day, when he saw that he could not be overcome, he ordered a sword to be made in the likeness of a sword from extremely hard wood and Aneolus’s head to be split in the form of a cross. When this had been done, his brain struck against the ground, and he was translated by a glorious death.

Also in the city of Sion, at Agaunum, the Passion of Sigismund, son of Gundobad, king of the Burgundians. When he saw that he could not resist the Franks, he fled alone, cut off his hair, and adopted the religious habit. Occupying himself day and night with fasts, vigils, and prayers, he was captured by the Franks with his wife and children and perished after being thrown into a well. Later revealed to an abbot and reverently buried by him, he also became renowned for miracles.

## C. Sixth day before the Nones of May (2 May)

(Jerome, On Illustrious Men, chapter 15; Rufinus, Book I, chapter 14.) The feast of our holy father Athanasius, bishop and confessor of the city of Alexandria. After suffering many plots by the Arians, in the forty-sixth year of his priesthood, following many struggles and many crowns of endurance, he rested in peace.

He was a man of keen intelligence and exceptionally vigilant in ecclesiastical affairs. His origin and formation from childhood are related in the following manner. At the time when Bishop Alexander was celebrating the feast of Peter the martyr at Alexandria, he was waiting for the clergy to come to his banquet after the solemn rites had ended. Nearby, on the seashore, he saw from a distance boys playing and imitating—as is customary—a bishop and the things usually done in churches. But as he watched the boys attentively for a long time, he saw them also performing certain more secret and mystical acts. Disturbed, he immediately ordered the clergy to be summoned and showed them what he himself had seen from a distance. Then he ordered them to depart and bring all the boys to him after apprehending them.

When they arrived, he asked what their game was, what they had done, and how they had done it. At first they were frightened and denied it, as children of that age do. Then they disclosed the whole matter in order and confessed that they had baptized certain catechumens [Col. 0255D] through Athanasius, who had played the bishop in that childish game. He then carefully inquired of those said to have been baptized what they had been asked and what they had answered, and likewise questioned the one who had asked them. When he saw that everything conformed to the rite of our religion, he is said to have conferred with the council of clergy and determined that those over whom water had been poured with complete questions and answers should not be baptized again, but should receive whatever the priests’ custom required to complete the rite.

As for Athanasius and those whom this game had represented as priests or ministers, he summoned their parents and, under the solemn charge of God, entrusted them to the Church to be raised. After a short time, when Athanasius had been thoroughly instructed by a notary and adequately taught by a grammarian [Col. 0256A], his parents immediately returned him to the priest as one entrusted to the Lord as a faithful servant. He was raised by him like another Samuel in the temple of the Lord, and, when the priest departed to his fathers in a good old age, Athanasius was chosen to bear the priestly ephod after him.

His struggles in the Church for the integrity of the faith were so great that this saying also seems to have been spoken concerning him: “For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (1 Samuel 1; Acts 9). Indeed, the whole world conspired against him in his persecution, and the rulers of the earth were stirred up. Peoples, kingdoms, and armies united against him. After suffering many plots by the Arians, he was driven about as an exile throughout the world; no safe place remained for him to hide. Tribunes, prefects, counts, and even armies were mobilized to search for him. (Rufinus, Book I, chapters 18 and 19.) By imperial edicts, rewards were offered to informers if anyone brought Athanasius alive—or, if that was impossible, certainly his head [Col. 0256B]. Thus, with all the forces of the kingdom, they struggled in vain against him, for God was with him.

Meanwhile, he is said to have hidden for six continuous years in a cistern that had no water, so that he never saw the sun. But when he saw that no safe place remained for him—for he had been betrayed by a maidservant who alone knew of the assistance of the householders who had provided him a hiding place—he fled to Constans, ruler of Gaul. He was received by him with sufficient honor and religious respect. After learning more carefully about his case, which rumor had made known, Constans wrote to his brother, saying that he had discovered with certainty that Athanasius, priest of the Most High God, had been unjustly driven into exile and was suffering banishment. Thus Athanasius returned to Constantius with the letter and was permitted to go back to his church.

Again driven into exile after Constantius’s death, he remained hidden until the reign of Jovian. Jovian, who summoned him with honor and highly dutiful letters to arrange the churches, restored him to his seat and granted him authority. He died during the reign of the emperors Valentinian and Valens.

On the same day, the feast of the holy Saturninus and Neopolis, who rested in prison.

## D. Fifth day before the Nones of May (3 May)

At Jerusalem, the discovery of the holy cross by Queen Helena under the emperor Constantine, whose mother she also was.

The history of the discovery of the precious wood, worthy of being known, is as follows. Hadrian, who was the eleventh Caesar and emperor at Rome, thinking that he would destroy the Christian faith by profaning its places, consecrated an image of Jupiter at the place of the Passion. Bethlehem was also polluted by a shrine of Adonis, so that the root and foundation of the Church might be removed, if idols were worshiped in those places where Christ was born to suffer, suffered to rise again, rose to reign, and would judge as judge or king.

At Bethlehem, too, where the ox had recognized its owner and the donkey the manger of its lord (Isaiah 1), the leaders of men, having denied the Lord’s Savior, cultivated infamous human loves and customs. Where the Chaldaeans, having been told by a new star of the eternal King, had worshiped the cradle with reverence and with their treasures [Col. 0257A], there the Romans consecrated barbarous lusts (Ezekiel 7). Where shepherds, as the army of angels sang together, had greeted the newborn Savior with heavenly joy in the illuminated night, there prostitutes mingled with eunuchs mourned Venus’s lover. Alas! What human piety could compensate for this impiety? Where the sacred infancy of the newborn Savior had wailed, there an infamous rite howled the laments of Venus amid lascivious mourning; and where the Virgin had given birth, adulterers were worshiped.

This crime of the earlier age continued until the time of Constantine, who, as the first among Christian rulers, deserved his position no less through his own faith than through that of his mother Helena. Inspired by divine counsel, as the outcome showed, she asked her son to give her the means to cleanse all the places marked by the Lord’s footprints and stamped with memorials of his divine works toward us, demolishing the temples and idols, removing every taint of profane impiety, and restoring them to their religion, so that at last the Church might be celebrated in the land of its origin.

Accordingly, with the emperor son’s willing consent, the Augusta mother opened the treasuries for the holy works and exhausted the entire treasury. With whatever expense and splendor a queen could provide and religion demand, she built basilicas, covered and adorned all the places in which the Lord our Redeemer had completed for us the saving mysteries of his goodness, incarnation, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension.

Among these things, it is remarkable that in the basilica of the Ascension the place alone from which he was received into the cloud and ascended, leading our captivity captive in his flesh (Ephesians 4), is said to have been so consecrated by the divine footprints that it has never permitted itself to be covered with marble or paved [manuscript reading: paveri]. Whatever hands have attempted to place there in their desire to adorn it has always been shaken off, rejected by the ground (Psalm 131). Thus, throughout the entire space of the basilica, it alone remains green in the form of its own turf, and the sand, both visible and accessible to those who venerate it, preserves the imprint of the divine feet and the dust trodden by God, so that it may truly be said: “We worshiped in the place where his feet stood.”

When that venerable queen came to Jerusalem, she carefully and devoutly examined the places there and throughout the surrounding region, eager to absorb with her eyes every sign of divine things and to grasp the faith that she had received through pious ears and writings. She began most earnestly to seek the Lord’s cross.

But what means or method of finding it could exist, since no reliable judge could be found, and the memory and care of religious conscience or observance had been erased by the antiquity of time and the long duration of impious superstition? Yet, with the Lord himself knowing and witnessing all things covered in the earth and in human hearts, the faithful woman deserved the Holy Spirit through her pious devotion. Under his inspiration, when she had diligently but unsuccessfully sought the matter, which had been removed from human knowledge by divine providence, she sought only to be informed of the place of the Passion.

Accordingly, she sought out not only men full of Christian learning and holiness but also the most learned of the Jews, as interpreters of their own impiety—which they, in their misery, took pride in—and summoned and gathered them at Jerusalem. Then the testimony of all was confirmed by a single account of the place [Col. 0258A].

Without delay, doubtless moved by the impulse of the revelation she had conceived, she ordered excavation to begin at the very spot. With the citizens and soldiers soon assembled for the work, she quickly completed the labor of this undertaking, and, contrary to everyone’s expectation but in accordance with the faith of the queen alone, the deep excavation opened the hidden secrets of the buried cross.

But when three crosses were found together, as formerly the Lord and the thieves had lain fixed upon them, the joy of the discovery began to be confused by anxious doubt. The pious were rightly afraid that they might either mistake the thief’s gibbet for the Lord’s cross or reject the saving wood while treating the thief’s stake with reverence.

The title, written by Pilate in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters, was indeed also present, but it did not itself reveal clearly enough which gibbet belonged to the Lord [Col. 0258B]. The Lord looked faithfully upon the pious concerns of those who were stirred with anxiety and, above all, infused the light of this counsel into the woman who was the chief of such pious solicitude: she ordered that someone recently dead be sought and brought in.

Macarius, bishop of that church, was present at the time. There was no delay: the word was carried out, and a corpse was brought in. One of the crosses was placed upon the dead man, and then another was brought near; but death rejected the wood of both. Finally, the Lord’s cross was revealed by resurrection. At the touch of the saving wood, death fled, the funeral trappings were cast off, and the body was raised. While the living trembled, the dead man stood; freed from his funeral bonds, like Lazarus once, he immediately walked alive among the spectators [Col. 0258C].

Therefore, was not the Lord’s cross, hidden for so many ages and concealed from the Jews at the time of the Passion, and likewise not revealed to the pagans when they built the shrine—undoubtedly carrying away earth for the very construction—hidden by the divine hand so that it might now be found when it was sought religiously? Just as was fitting for Christ’s cross, it was discovered and proved by the evidence of resurrection. A basilica was soon built at the place of the Passion and consecrated with worthy magnificence. Gleaming with gilded ceilings and rich in golden altars, it preserves in a hidden sanctuary a portion of the cross, which the incomparable queen deposited there, enclosed in silver cases. She also carried a portion of the saving wood to her son; every year, when the Lord’s Passover is celebrated, the bishop of that city brings it forth for the people to venerate, himself foremost among those who venerate it [Col. 0258D].

Nor, apart from this day on which the mystery of the cross itself is celebrated, is it brought forth as a kind of emblem of the sacred solemnity—for it is the cause of the sacraments—unless exceptionally the most devout request it, especially those who have traveled there for this sole purpose, so that its unveiling may be offered to them as the reward of their distant pilgrimage. They say that this can be obtained only through the bishop’s favor.

Although the cross is made of insensible material, it possesses living power. From that time onward it has lent its wood almost daily to the countless petitions of men, without suffering any loss and remaining as though untouched: divided among those who receive portions, yet always whole to those who venerate it. But this incorruptible power and indestructible solidity it surely draws from the blood of that flesh which, having suffered death, did not see corruption [Col. 0259A].

The same venerable queen also carried to her son the nails with which the Lord’s body had been fastened. From some of these he fashioned a bridle for use in war, and from others a helmet, likewise suited to military use.

(Rufinus, Book I, chapter 8; Pontifical Book, chapter 7.) On the same day at Rome, on the Nomentan Way, at the seventh milestone, Saint Alexander [Note: [Col. 0259D] Rufinus, Book I, chapter 8; Pontifical Book, chapter 7. This is Alexander I], pope, with Eventius and Theodulus, priests, under the emperor Trajan and the judge Aurelianus. He held the episcopate of the Roman Church, fifth after Peter, for ten years, two months, and ten days. Incomparable in holiness and illustrious in faith, he converted a great part of the city’s senators to the Lord.

Later, at the command of the emperor Trajan, he was imprisoned by Aurelianus, commander of both military forces. After astonishing and divine miracles, he was led out of prison in the silence of night through a window by a boy carrying a burning torch and brought to the house of the tribune Quirinus, where the blessed Hermes the prefect was being held under guard. After Quirinus’s daughter, named Balbina, had been healed, Quirinus himself was converted and desired the grace of baptism. After the release and baptism of those whom Quirinus himself had held bound in prison—including the two most holy priests Eventius and Theodulus, who had come from the East, whom he had confined among the prisoners—after all these things, and whatever else he had reverently accomplished, Alexander was again brought before the commander Aurelianus, while Trajan was still emperor, for Hadrian was not yet reigning, together with the same two blessed priests [Col. 0259C].

He was first raised onto the rack, tortured with claws, and most grievously burned with lamps. When he made no sound, Aurelianus said to him: “Why are you silent?” Saint Alexander replied: “Because during prayer a Christian speaks with God.”

When Alexander had been taken down, the impious judge ordered Eventius and Theodulus to be brought forward and asked blessed Alexander: “Who are these men?” Blessed Alexander said: “Both are holy men; both are priests.”

Then the judge turned to blessed Eventius and asked him: “When did you become a Christian?” Blessed Eventius answered: “I was baptized seventy years and eleven years ago, and I was ordained a priest at the age of twenty. I am now eighty-one years old, which I have completed in prison and chains” [Col. 0259D].

After he had also interrogated Theodulus and found him steadfast in his confession, he ordered a furnace to be heated intensely and commanded that blessed Alexander and Eventius, bound, be thrown into the middle of it. Blessed Theodulus voluntarily leaped into the flames with them, singing and giving thanks together with them: “You have tested us by fire, and no iniquity has been found in us” (Psalm 16).

When this was reported to the impious Aurelianus, he ordered the most blessed Alexander to be pierced with countless punctures throughout all his limbs [Col. 0260A] until he died. In this manner the holy man completed his martyrdom. The two holy priests were put to death with the sword. A religious woman named Severa gathered their bodies and placed blessed Alexander and Eventius in one tomb, and Saint Theodulus separately in another, on the Nomentan Way, on her estate, on the fifth day before the Nones of May.

## E. Fourth day before the Nones of May (4 May)

(Eusebius, Book VIII, chapter 14, and Book IX, chapter 6; Rufinus.) In Palestine, in the city of Gaza, the feast of Saint Silvanus, bishop of that city. During the persecution of Diocletian, he was crowned with martyrdom together with many of his clergy.

Also at the Fanum mine, the forty holy martyrs who were beheaded together [Col. 0260B].

At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Antonia. After being excessively tortured and afflicted with various torments, she was suspended by one arm for three days and thrown into prison for two years; finally she was burned in the flames by the governor Priscillianus.

On the same day, in Noricum Ripense, at the place called Lauriacum, the feast of Saint Florian. At the governor’s command, he was thrown into the river Enns with a stone tied around his neck. Immediately, in the sight of all who stood around, the eyes of the one who threw him burst.

On the same day, blessed Quiriacus, glorious bishop and martyr, under the emperor Julian.

## F. Third day before the Nones of May (5 May)

[Col. 0260C]

[Note: [Col. 0259D] Gennadius, On Illustrious Men, chapter 69.] At Alexandria, Saint Euthymius the deacon, resting in prison.

At Thessalonica, the feast of the holy Irenaeus, Peregrinus, and Irene, burned in the flames.

In Gaul, in the city of Arles, [the feast of] Saint Hilary, bishop, a great, learned, and most distinguished man. He was a lover of poverty and concerned for the provision of the needy not only through the compassion of his mind but also through the labor of his body. For, in order to refresh the poor, he even undertook agricultural work beyond his strength, although he was a man of distinguished birth and had been brought up in a very different manner. Nor was he negligent in spiritual matters: he possessed grace in teaching and imposed correction upon everyone without respect of persons. Among his other works, with immortal talent and through a work necessarily undertaken for the benefit of many, he composed the Life of Saint Honoratus, his predecessor. He died under the emperors Valentinian and Marcian.

Likewise at Vienne, blessed Nicetius, bishop, a man of venerable holiness.

At Auxerre, the passion of Saint Jovinian, lector and martyr.

### G. THE DAY BEFORE THE NONES OF MAY (6 May)

[Note: Jerome, book 1 *Against Jovinian*, chapter 14, and on Matthew 20; from Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 36.]

The feast of Saint John the apostle at the Latin Gate in Rome. From Ephesus, by order of Domitian, the brother of Titus, during the second persecution—which he himself carried out after Nero—John was brought to the city of Rome and, in the presence of the Senate, placed before the Latin Gate in a vessel of boiling oil. This was done by that impious ruler, who was the most hostile persecutor of Christians. But the blessed apostle emerged from it as free from harm as he had been free from the corruption of the flesh. Then he was exiled to the island of Patmos, where he saw the Apocalypse. Therefore, to honor his worthy memory and his apostolic steadfastness in the faith, the Christians built at the aforesaid place, before the Latin Gate, a church bearing his veneration, with splendid and marvelous workmanship. There, down to the present day, they hold a festive gathering on the eleventh day before the Nones of May.

On the same day, blessed Evodius, bishop of Antioch, who was the first bishop ordained there by the apostles.

[Note: See the little book on the Feasts of the Apostles, Acts 19.]

Likewise, blessed Lucius of Cyrene, who was established by the holy apostles as the first bishop at Cyrene; Saint Luke mentions him in the Acts of the Apostles.

### A. THE NONES OF MAY (7 May)

The feast of Saint Juvenal the martyr.

And of the most blessed and illustrious servant of God, Flavia Domitilla.

[Note: Gregory, Homily 27. Concerning these saints, see the Acts of Nereus and Achilleus, 12 May.]

She was the niece, through his sister, of the consul Flavius Clemens, and Saint Clement consecrated her with the sacred veil so that she might persevere in purity. During the persecution of Domitian, in the fifteenth year of his rule, because of the testimony she bore to Christ, she was deported with many others into exile on the island of Pontia and there endured a prolonged martyrdom. Finally, after she had been transferred to the city of Terracina in Campania by Aurelian, her fiancé—whom she had rejected for Christ and through whose accusation she had been sent into exile—and after she had first converted to the faith of Christ by her teaching and miracles Euphrosyna and Theodora, her foster-sisters and fellow virgins, and then also others, Aurelian himself, her exceedingly hostile persecutor, was killed by divine power amid these great deeds. Her brother Luxorius then set fire to the room in which she was confined together with the aforesaid virgins, and she completed the course of her glorious martyrdom under the persecution of Trajan. For, when the holy deacon named Caesarius came the following day, he found the bodies of the holy virgins unharmed: they had fallen upon their faces and departed while praying to the Lord. The same holy deacon placed their bodies together in a new sarcophagus, buried them deep in the earth, and interred them.

On the same day at Nicomedia, the passion of the holy martyrs Flavius, Augustine, and Augustine, brothers.

### B. THE EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF MAY (8 May)

[Note: Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 45.]

At Milan, Saint Victor the martyr. He was a Moor by birth and a Christian from earliest youth. While serving as a soldier in the imperial camp, and already honored by the whiteness of his hair, he was compelled by Maximian to sacrifice to idols. Remaining most steadfast in his confession of the Lord, he was first beaten severely with clubs; but, protected by God, he felt no pain. Then he was drenched with molten lead, yet was entirely unharmed. Finally, he completed the course of his glorious martyrdom by the cutting off of his head. He was a fellow citizen of the holy martyrs Nabor and Felix, who were beheaded in Africa and transferred to Milan together with Januarius and Marinus.

### C. THE SEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF MAY (9 May)

[Note: Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 117; Rufinus, book 1, chapter 9.]

In Persia, the three hundred and ten holy martyrs.

On the same day, at the town of Nazianzus, blessed Gregory, bishop, who is called the Theologian. He was noble and educated at Athens and a companion of blessed Basil, later bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. After he had devoted himself entirely to God’s service, he presumed so greatly upon his love for his companion that he removed Basil, who was seated in the teacher’s chair, and led him away with his own hand to the monastery. There they devoted themselves for thirteen years to the books of the divine Scriptures alone, setting aside all the books of the secular Greeks. Accordingly, when he was appointed bishop in place of his father at the town of Nazianzus, he faithfully endured the storm of the heretics. When peace had been restored, he was entreated to come to Constantinople to teach the Church, and he did not refuse. There, in a short time, he made such progress in reforming the people, who had been infected with the ancient poisons of the heretics, that the Christians then seemed for the first time to become Christians to themselves and to behold the new light of truth. But when envy followed upon his glory, some began to resist and employ unsound legal objections, so that, when he returned to his own place, another might be ordained bishop. When he sensed that this was being whispered and turned over under the breath, he himself brought it forward, since no one dared tell him. “God forbid,” he said, “that any hostility should arise among the priests of God on my account. If this storm is because of me, remove me and cast me into the sea, and the turbulence will cease for you.” Then he returned and spent the rest of his life in his own church. Since he was already exhausted by age and weak in body, he himself chose a successor, so that, while that man governed the church, Gregory might enjoy the leisure of weakness and old age.

At Constantinople, the feast of Saint Timothy.

[Note: See the little book on the Feasts of the Apostles.]

This was when his sacred bones were brought from Ephesus.

### D. THE SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF MAY (10 May)

The prophet Job.

At Rome, on the Latin Way, in the cemetery on that same road, the feast of the holy Gordian and Epimachus. Julian, the apostate emperor, committed them to public custody along with many Christians. But he had the blessed Januarius, an elderly presbyter who had been arrested, handed over to a certain Vicar, Gordian, for examination. Gordian patiently listened to the blessed Januarius and, enlightened by the Spirit of God, began to believe. The blessed presbyter immediately baptized him, together with his wife Marina and fifty-three members of his household of both sexes, and even more. When Julian heard what had happened, he was filled with anger and condemned the holy presbyter Januarius by written sentence. He likewise condemned Saint Gordian and placed him in public custody, handing him over to a certain Clementianus, whom he had appointed vicar in his place. He ordered Gordian’s wife to remain at the Waters of Salvias [also read: Silmas], serving the agricultural laborers.

Clementianus, seated on the tribunal, had the blessed Gordian, bound in chains, brought before him. Firm in his confession of Christ, Gordian was beaten for a long time with leaded scourges; finally, his head was cut off. The wicked judge ordered his body to be thrown before the temple of Apollo at Tellude, so that it might be gnawed by dogs.

[Note: At Tellude. The same expression occurs below, on 30 July and 6 August. The manuscript Acts of Pope Cornelius, 24 September: “He was brought before him at night, and at Tellude, with the prefect of the City also present, he was examined.” The Acts of Hippolytus, Eusebius, and their companions, 2 December: “He had a tribunal prepared for himself at Tellude.” It was a temple in which the people were often accustomed to be assembled, as appears from Cicero, Dio, and others. Where this place was is explained by the Acts of Abundius and his companions: “Diocletian ordered the saints Abundius and Abundantius to be brought out of custody and presented at Tellude, in the forum, before the temple.” It seems altogether to be a compound term, so that *Telludis* is something like “the temple of Tellus.”]

But Christians carried it away at night and placed it in a crypt approximately one Roman mile from the city, where the body of the blessed martyr Epimachus had long before been buried. This Epimachus, at Alexandria, had been tortured for a long time with his companion Alexander in chains and the sufferings of prison. When, amid frequent and various punishments, he had been worn down but had persevered in the faith, he was finally consumed by fire. His remains were then transferred to Rome.

Likewise at Rome, the feast of Saint Calepodius, an elderly presbyter, under the emperor Alexander. Alexander had him killed by Laodicius, his body dragged through the city, and thrown away on the first day of May. Fishermen found it, lifted it up, and reported this to Bishop Callistus. Callistus therefore received it, embalmed it with spices and linen cloths, and buried it in his cemetery, three miles from the City, in a crypt, on the sixth day before the Ides of May.

Then Palmatius, consul, was beheaded by Alexander, together with his wife and children and forty-two members of his household of both sexes. With them were Simplicius, a senator, with his wife, children, and household—about sixty-eight people of both sexes—and Felix likewise with his wife Blanda. They had recently been baptized through the teaching of Pope Callistus and the presbyter Calepodius.

This Palmatius, consul, was so dear to the emperor Alexander that he had received from him authority to compel Christians to sacrifice. A multitude of Christians had gathered at a certain place across the Tiber, among them the blessed Callistus, bishop of the City, with his clergy, and the blessed Calepodius, an elderly presbyter. Palmatius sent soldiers to seize them. When the soldiers entered the place where the multitude of saints was gathered, they suddenly became blind.

Seeing this, Palmatius was terrified with fear, reported it to Alexander, and presented the soldiers before him. Then Alexander began to shout: “O excellent citizens, do you see magical art?” Palmatius replied: “If this happened through magic, where are the powers of our gods? Therefore let your piety command offerings and sacrifices to be made to the gods, lest the state perish through their incantations.”

A day was therefore appointed, and by the herald’s voice all those in the city of Rome were ordered to sacrifice to Mercury. While the blood of pigs and calves was being poured out and the priests and maidens were raging through the demon’s temple, one of them, named Juliana, was seized and began to cry out: “The God of Callistus, he is the living and true God; he is angered by the pollutions of your state, and he will crush your mortal king, because you do not worship the truth.”

When Palmatius heard this, he ran across the Tiber to the blessed Callistus, where the multitude of Christians was gathered, and fell at his feet. “I have recognized,” he said, “that the Lord Christ is the true God, whom the demons confessed today. By him I adjure you: free me from the worship of demons and baptize me, as you preach.”

The blessed Callistus imposed a fast upon him, instructed him, and baptized him with water that had been brought. After his baptism Palmatius began to cry out: “Truly I have seen the Lord Jesus Christ, the true light, who has enlightened me.” His entire household was also baptized.

From that day he began to distribute all his wealth to poor Christians wherever they were found, supplying them with food and clothing. After thirty days, Alexander summoned him, for it had been reported to him that Palmatius was a Christian. He was therefore seized by a certain tribune, Torquatus, confined for three days in the Mamertine prison [also read: Mamurtine], and brought in chains before Alexander.

When Alexander saw him, he ordered him to be released and said to him: “Are you so mad, Palmatius, that you abandon the gods and seek a dead man?” Among other things Palmatius replied: “I acted as an unfortunate man; but now I have recognized what is true.”

Then Alexander handed him over to a certain senator, Simplicius, to bring him back to the worship of the gods with gentle words. But Palmatius, devoting himself to fasting, prayers, and vigils, did not cease to beseech God the almighty Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, with tears.

A certain man named Felix came to him and pleaded with him on behalf of his wife, who had lain bedridden for four years. In the presence of Simplicius’s wife and the entire household, the blessed Palmatius fell to the ground and began to pray with tears: “Lord God, who enlightened your servant and gave me the eternal light, the Lord Jesus Christ, save your servant Blanda and raise her from her bed of suffering, so that all may know that you are the Creator of all things.”

Immediately she rose healed. When Simplicius and Felix, and the others who were in Simplicius’s house, saw this, they began urgently asking the blessed Palmatius to baptize them. He sent for the holy Callistus, and they were all baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.

Likewise at Rome, on the Latin Way, at the Hundred-Hall, the feast of the holy Quartus and Quintus.

### E. THE FIFTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF MAY (11 May)

At Rome, on the Salarian Way, at the twenty-second milestone, the feast of Saint Anthimus.

At Vienne, blessed Mamertus, bishop, who, because of an impending calamity, instituted the solemn litanies before the Ascension of the Lord.

### F. THE FOURTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF MAY (12 May)

At Rome, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, the feast of the holy martyrs Nereus and Achilleus, brothers. They were eunuchs of the blessed Flavia Domitilla and, together with her, endured a long exile for Christ on the island of Pontia. Later, Aurelian, Domitilla’s fiancé—whom she had rejected for the love of Christ—first subjected them to extremely severe scourging and then handed them over to the consular judge Mommio [also read: Mummius and Memmius] Rufus. When he tried to compel them to sacrifice with the rack and flames, they said that they had been baptized by the blessed apostle Peter and could in no way sacrifice to idols. They were beheaded.

Auspicius, their disciple and the foster-father of the holy virgin Domitilla, seized their bodies, placed them in a small boat, brought them away, and buried them in a sandy crypt on Domitilla’s estate, on the Ardeatine Way, one and a half miles from the wall of the City.

Likewise on the Aurelian Way, at the second milestone, the feast of Saint Pancratius the martyr. When he was twenty-four years old, he completed his martyrdom by beheading under Diocletian. Octavilla, an illustrious woman, secretly took away his venerable body during the night, embalmed it with spices, and buried it on the fourth day before the Ides of May.

On the same day, the blessed Dionysius, uncle of blessed Pancratius.

[Note: Concerning him, see the Acts of that same Pancratius.]

Through Dionysius’s efforts Pancratius had been baptized, strengthened in the fear of the Lord, and encouraged toward martyrdom. Dionysius himself, dear and worthy to God, closed the day of this life in peace, having received the rewards of heaven.

At that time also the most sacred virgin Soteris suffered; she was of noble birth and suffered under the emperor Diocletian Augustus.

On the same day at Cyprus, Saint Epiphanius, our holy father, at Salamis.

### G. THE THIRD DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF MAY (13 May)

The feast of Saint Mary at the Martyrs. Under the emperor Phocas, blessed Pope Boniface, having removed the filth of idolatry from the ancient shrine called the Pantheon, dedicated it as a church of blessed Mary ever-virgin and of all the martyrs. The most sacred anniversary of this dedication is celebrated at Rome on the third day before the Ides of May.

On the same day, Saint Servatius, bishop of the Church of Tongeren. When the Huns were ravaging Germany, he was warned by a revelation of the Lord and crossed over to the settlement of the Trajectenses, so that he would not see the destruction of his city and church. He died there and was buried in the middle of the public road. To make his merit manifest to human beings, although winter snow filled everything around it, it never covered his tomb, until the citizens’ industry built a basilica over it.

### A. THE DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF MAY (14 May)

Saint Pachomius, our holy father.

[Note: Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 7.]

He was distinguished by works of apostolic grace. After founding monasteries in Egypt, he wrote rules for monks, which he had learned with an angel dictating them, and also wrote concerning the season of Easter.

On the same day in Syria, the feast of Victor and Corona, under the emperor Antoninus, with Sebastian as governor of Alexandria. Victor was a soldier from Cilicia. Because of his confession of the faith, Sebastian ordered his fingers to be crushed and his nails torn from the flesh; then he ordered him to be thrown into a furnace. He remained there for three days and was not harmed. Next he was ordered to drink poison, but he did not die; rather, he converted the poisoner to the faith. Afterward it was ordered that the sinews of his body be removed; then that boiling oil be poured upon his private parts. After this, Sebastian ordered burning lamps to be applied to his sides while he was suspended. Then he ordered vinegar and lime to be mixed together and given to him in his mouth; afterward, his eyes were torn out. Then he ordered him to be hung head downward for three days; and while he was still breathing, he ordered him to be flayed.

Corona, who was the wife of a certain soldier, then began to proclaim the blessed Victor in honor of his martyrdom. As she did so, she saw two crowns fall from heaven, one sent for Victor and the other for herself. When she declared this openly before all who were listening, she was seized by the governor. It was ordered that two palm trees be bent toward one another and tied together with hempen ropes, and that Corona be bound by her hands and feet to the two trees. Then the trees were released. As this was done, Corona was torn into two parts, and so she received the crown of eternal life. She was sixteen years old. Victor too was then beheaded and earned the triumph of everlasting victory.

### B. THE IDES OF MAY (15 May)

The feast of the holy confessors Torquatus, Ctesiphon, Secundus, Indalecius, Caecilius, Hesychius, and Euphrasius. They were ordained bishops at Rome by the holy apostles and sent to preach the word of God to the Spaniards, who at that time were still entangled in pagan error. When they had come to the city of Acci and were resting briefly because of the fatigue of the journey, they sent their disciples into the city to purchase food. Immediately a multitude of pagans, who happened at that time to be celebrating festivals for their gods, pursued them as far as a river. A bridge of extraordinary size and strength had been built there; as the saints crossed it, by God’s will it collapsed completely together with the entire multitude of their pursuers.

At this miracle the others were terrified and, following the example of a certain great senator-woman named Ludaria—who, divinely inspired, received them kindly and believed—abandoned their idols and believed in Christ the Lord. After this, preaching the Gospel in various cities and bringing innumerable multitudes under the faith of Christ, Torquatus rested at Acci; Ctesiphon at Vergium; Secundus at Ávila; Indalecius at Urci; Caecilius at Eliberi; Hesychius at Carteia [also read: Carcera]; and Euphrasius at Iliturgi.

A famous miracle remains to this day as a testimony to their precious death. For each year on this same solemnity, at the aforesaid city of Acci, an olive tree at the tomb of Saint Torquatus miraculously blossoms and becomes laden with ripe fruit.

On the island of Chios, the feast of Saint Isidore the martyr. In his basilica there is a well into which he is said to have been thrown. Demoniacs, fever sufferers, and other sick people are often healed after drinking its water.

At Lamosacus, the passion of the holy Peter and Andrea, Paul and Dionysia.

[Note: Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 102.]

### C. THE SEVENTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (16 May)

In Isauria, the feast of the holy Aquilinus and Victorianus, whose Acts are extant.

At Auxerre, the passion of Saint Peregrinus, the first bishop of that city.

And in the district of Fréjus, at a village called Calidianus, Saint Maxima the virgin, who, renowned for many virtues, rested in peace.

### D. THE SIXTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (17 May)

In Tuscany, the feast of Saint Torpes the martyr under Nero the ruler. He held a high office in the household of Caesar Nero. He was baptized by the blessed presbyter Antoninus and instructed in the faith of Christ. When Nero learned that he was a Christian, he handed him over to a certain kinsman of his, Satellicus, to compel him to sacrifice.
