But when the blessed man, strengthened by the Spirit of God and firmly grounded in the faith, remained immovable, Satellicus had him struck in the face, beaten, and tied to a column. He was scourged until blood dripped from his body. Suddenly, while the martyr was being beaten, the column fell and crushed the judge and fifty men with him.

Then he was seized by the attendants and placed on a wheel. Afterward he was exposed to wild beasts by Satellicus’s son, named Sylvius, but was not harmed by them. A certain adviser of Nero, named Evellius, witnessed his steadfastness and courage and believed in Christ. Shortly afterward he was baptized and beheaded in the city of Rome on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

The blessed Torpes, however, was led outside the city of Pisa by order of Sylvius and completed his martyrdom by beheading on the third day before the Kalends of May. The servants of wickedness placed his body on a nearly broken and worm-eaten ship and threw it into the course of the river, together with a dog and a rooster.

An angel of the Lord appeared to a venerable woman named Celerina and instructed her to seek the martyr’s body and bury it. She promptly fulfilled this command, found the body, and buried it with every mark of reverence. After the persecution had ceased, she built a church of marvelous workmanship over it from her own resources. The martyr’s feast and the gathering of the citizens are celebrated on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June.

### E. THE FIFTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (18 May)

In Egypt, the feast of Saint Dioscorus the lector. The governor inflicted many and various tortures upon him, even digging out his nails and setting his sides aflame with torches. But the attendants were terrified by the radiance of heavenly light and fell down. Finally, he was burned with heated plates and completed his martyrdom.

### F. THE FOURTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (19 May)

At Rome, the feast of Saint Pudentiana, or Potentiana, the virgin. She was of very distinguished birth and was the daughter of Pudens, a disciple of the holy apostle Paul. Her mother was Sabinella, and her sister Praxedis. Their most devout father Pudens instructed them in every aspect of the religion of Christ and left them as virgins to Christ.

After the death of their holy father, they grew so greatly in every exercise of piety that, night and day, they served the Lord continually with hymns and prayers, together with their female household, while the most blessed Pius, bishop of the City, joined them in praising God. Thus, about to receive a reward for their most devout labors, which they had fruitfully completed through the grace of Christ, after countless struggles, after reverently providing burial for many martyrs, and after placing all their possessions in the bosoms of the poor and commending them faithfully to Christ, they finally departed from earth to Christ.

Potentiana, the venerable virgin, departed on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June and was placed in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way. Praxedis, likewise a most holy virgin, departed on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August and was herself placed with her sister beside their holy father Pudens.

On that same day, the feast of the most blessed Pudens, the father of the aforesaid virgins. The apostles clothed him with Christ in baptism, and he guarded and preserved his innocent tunic undefiled until the crown of life.

Likewise at Rome, the feast of the holy eunuchs Calocerus and Parthenius, servants of the wife of the emperor Decius. One was chief of the bedchamber and the other chief secretary. Because they refused to sacrifice to idols, they were killed by Decius. Their bodies were placed beside the Appian Way on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June.

### G. THE THIRTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (20 May)

At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the feast of Saint Basilla, virgin and martyr.

[Note: Concerning her, see the Acts of Saint Eugenia, 25 December.]

She was of royal descent and had an illustrious fiancé named Pompeius. Through the blessed Eugenia and the holy men of God Protus [also read: Protum] and Hyacinthus, she was converted to the faith. Her fiancé accused her of being a Christian. Gallienus Augustus, who was then persecuting the Church of Christ, immediately decreed that she must either accept her fiancé or die by the sword. When questioned about this, she replied that she had as her bridegroom the King of kings, who is Christ, the Son of God. After saying this, she was pierced through with a sword.

[Note: Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 78.]

On the same day in Gaul, in the city of Nîmes, the feast of Baudelus the martyr. He was seized by pagans who were celebrating sacrifices to their gods because he refused to sacrifice. Remaining steadfast in the faith of Christ amid blows and tortures, he received the palm of martyrdom through a precious death.

### A. THE TWELFTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (21 May)

In Caesarean Mauritania, the feast of the holy deacons Timothy, Polius, and Eutychius. While spreading the word of the Lord throughout that region, they were all found worthy to receive the crown together.

Likewise at Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of the holy Polyeuctus, Victorius, and Donatus.

### B. THE ELEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (22 May)

In Africa, the holy Castus and Aemilius, who completed their martyrdom through the fire of their passion. Cyprian writes about them in his book *On the Lapsed*, chapter 6.

On the same day in Corsica, Saint Julia, who suffered the punishment of the cross.

### C. THE TENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (23 May)

At Langres, the passion of Saint Desiderius, bishop. When he saw his people being ravaged by the army of the Vandals, he went out to their king to plead on their behalf. The king immediately ordered him to be slaughtered. For the sheep entrusted to him, Desiderius willingly offered his neck, and, struck by the sword, he departed to Christ. His executioner soon died, seized by madness.

The blessed martyr was buried there in a basilica beside the city walls. The faithful people entrusted to him by Christ, because of their exceptional love for him and their pious devotion, arranged for it to be built as a protection for the citizens. Many others from his flock also suffered with him and were buried in the same city.

### D. THE NINTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (24 May)

The feast of Saint Manaen, foster-brother of Herod the tetrarch, a teacher and prophet under the grace of the New Testament, resting in Christ at Antioch.

[The reference “Acts 13” is supplied in the source.]

Likewise, the feast of blessed Joanna, wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward, whom the evangelists mention.

[The source cites Luke 8 and 24.]

Likewise at the Roman Port, the feast of Saint Vincent the martyr.

[Note: Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 6.]

In Gaul, in the city of Nantes, the feast of the holy martyrs Donatian and Rogatian, brothers.

In Istria, the feast of the holy Joël, Sirvilius, Silvanus, and Diocles.

### E. THE EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (25 May)

[Note: Concerning him, see the Acts of Saint Cecilia, 22 November.]

At Rome, on the Nomentan Way, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, the feast of Saint Urban, bishop and martyr. Through his teaching, during the persecution of Alexander, many were crowned with martyrdom.

At Milan, Saint Dionysius, bishop and confessor. He was condemned to exile in Cappadocia by the Arian emperor Constantius on account of the Catholic faith, and there he rested. The blessed Ambrose received his bodily relics from Saint Basil, bishop of that city, and honorably interred them.

[Note: Ambrose, Letter 82 to the Bishop of Vercelli, chapter 14.]

On the same day in Moesia, in the city of Dorostorum, the feast of the holy martyrs Passicrates, Valention, and two other crowned martyrs.

At Rome, Pope Eleutherius. He received letters from Lucius, king of the Britons, requesting that he become a Christian through his command. He was buried beside the body of the blessed apostle Peter.

### F. THE SEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (26 May)

[Note: See the little book on the Feasts of the Apostles.]

At Athens, the feast of Saint Quadratus, bishop and disciple of the apostles.

Likewise, the feast of Saint Quadratus the martyr, on whose solemnity sermons of Saint Augustine are found.

[Note: Possidonius mentions only one of them.]

At Rome, the blessed martyrs Symmetrius, presbyter, and twenty-two others, whom the emperor Antonius ordered to be punished by the sword for Christ. The blessed Praxedis gathered their bodies by night and buried them in the cemetery of Priscilla on the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

At Todi in Tuscany, the feast of the holy Felicissimus, Heraclius, and Paulinus.

In the territory of Auxerre, the passion of Saint Priscus the martyr with a great multitude.

In Britain, Saint Augustine, bishop and confessor. Sent by the blessed Pope Gregory, he was the first to preach the Gospel of Christ to the English people, and he rested in Christ there, glorious for his virtues and miracles.

### G. THE SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (27 May)

In Moesia, in the city of Dorostorum, the feast of Saint Julius. During the persecution, he was a veteran who had completed his military service. He was arrested by officials and brought before the governor Maximus. Refusing to sacrifice to idols and confessing the name of the Lord Jesus Christ with the greatest steadfastness, he was condemned to death.

As he was being led to the place where the execution was to be carried out, a certain soldier named Hesychius, who himself had been arrested and detained on account of the faith of Christ, pleaded with him, saying: “Remember me, for I too am following you. Give my warmest greetings also to Passicrates and Valention, servants of God, who through their good confession have already gone before us to the Lord.”

Julius kissed Hesychius and said: “Brother, hasten to come; those whom you greeted have already heard your message.” Then, taking a headcloth, he bound it over his eyes and received the palm of martyrdom as the sword struck him.

In Gaul, in the city of Orange, Saint Eutropius, bishop, whose life, illustrious for virtues and miracles, Bishop Verus describes in eloquent speech.

### A. THE FIFTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (28 May)

[Note: Pontifical Book, chapter 54; Gregory, *Dialogues*, book 3, chapter 2, and book 4, chapter 30.]

The feast of Saint John, pope. Because he was orthodox and had been gloriously received by the orthodox emperor Justin when he came to Constantinople, the Arian king Theodoric, as John was returning to Ravenna, kept him in custody until his death, together with other men who were equally Catholic. Saint Gregory mentions him in his book of the *Dialogues*. His body was transferred from Ravenna and buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the fifth day before the Kalends of January, during the consulship of Olybrius.

On the same day at Paris, the feast of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor.

Likewise in Sardinia, the feast of Aemilius, Felix, Priamus, and Lucian.

### B. THE FOURTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (29 May)

At Rome, on the Aurelian Way, Saint Restitutus.

On the Tiburtine Way, the seven brothers.

At Trier, blessed Maximinus, bishop, by whom Athanasius, fleeing the persecution of Constantius, was honorably received.

Likewise, the passion of Saint Conon the martyr and his son under the emperor Aurelian, at Iconium, a city of the province of Isauria, before the judge Domitianus. Conon was distinguished in faith. Brought before the judge with his twelve-year-old son, they manifested by a true confession that the Holy Spirit dwelt within them.

First, they were placed upon heated iron. Then they steadfastly endured a grate with burning coals beneath it and oil poured over it. Next they endured a frying pan. Then they were suspended, and a powerful fire was applied beneath them. Finally, their hands were crushed with a wooden mallet, and they gave up their spirit in praise of almighty God.

On the same day, the feast of the holy Sisinnius, Martyrius, and Alexander. While pagan men were persecuting them in the region of Anaunia, they obtained the crown of martyrdom. Vigilius, bishop and martyr of the city of Trent, sent them to that neighboring region, called Anaunia, to preach. One of them, the venerable elder Sisinnius, was a Greek by birth, from the province of Cappadocia.

After they had preached the word of God for some time, a crowd of pagans, indignant at this, rose up to fight against the saints of God. It happened that, according to pagan custom, for five years they went around their cultivated fields, seeds in hand, with a diabolical procession, crowned with mournful ornaments and intending to sacrifice victims to Saturn. At that time the saints too were seized by the crowd of pagans and ordered to sacrifice. When they resisted, they were slaughtered with such violence that they could scarcely draw their final breath.

After a night’s delay, they soon reached the crown of martyrdom. Saint Sisinnius had been struck on the head with a bronze trumpet and pierced with axes, and lay beside the threshold of the church itself. Saint Martyrius, however, was seized and stood immovable, giving thanks to God. Wounded in the head with axes and pierced through beneath them, he was being led to the idol; on the way he gave up his spirit.

The crowd of pagans then seized the bodies of the saints, hung a little bell around the neck of Saint Sisinnius, and mocked them, saying: “Now let Christ avenge you.”

Then the living Alexander was placed between the bodies of Saint Sisinnius and Martyrius and dragged along, so that, over the rough road, the bodies and limbs might be torn apart. When they reached the altar of Saturn, they built a great fire and threw the bodies of the saints into it. They scourged Saint Alexander and asked him whether he wished to escape the flames by sacrificing to Saturn. But he rejected their impious words and received the palm of glorious suffering.

These things happened on a Friday, the day on which the Savior had been crucified. A certain black shadow close to the earth immediately covered the entire region, while frequent flashes of lightning darted about, so that even the impious, struck with terror, confessed that this was happening on account of the saints.

Later, when the people of Milan received their relics with the greatest devotion, a certain blind man who came from the Dalmatian shore recovered his sight after touching the reliquary, as Saint Paulinus writes in the Life of Saint Ambrose.

### C. THE THIRD DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE (4 April, 30 May)

[Note: *Pontificale*, chapter 27.]

At Rome, on the Aurelian Way, in the cemetery, the feast of Saint Felix, pope. After governing the Church for five years, he was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Claudius.

At Turribus in Sardinia, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Gabinius and Crispulus.

**D. The day before the Kalends of June (31 May).**

[Note: [Col. 0272D] Concerning her, in the Acts of Nereus.] At Rome, Saint Petronilla, virgin. She was the daughter of the most blessed apostle Peter. After many miracles of healing, when the count Flaccus wished to marry her, she asked for a delay of three days. During that time she devoted herself to continual fasting and prayer with the holy virgin Felicula, her companion. On the third day, after the mysteries of the Lord’s offering had been celebrated, as soon as she had received Christ’s sacrament, she reclined on her little bed and gave up her spirit.

On the same day at Aquileia, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla, brothers and sister.

At Turribus in Sardinia, the commemoration of Saint Crescentianus.

**LITANIES TO BE ANNOUNCED. JUNE HAS THIRTY DAYS; THE MOON, TWENTY-NINE.**

[Col. 0273]

**E. The Kalends of June (1 June).**

[Col. 0273A]

[Note: [Col. 0273D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men of the Church*, chapter 75.] The dedication of Saint Nicomedes, martyr and presbyter, near the city of Rome; his martyrdom is celebrated on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.

At Caesarea in Palestine, the commemoration of Saint Pamphilus, presbyter, a man of admirable faith and holiness, who was crowned with martyrdom under the persecution of Maximinus. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, set down his life in three books. Blessed Jerome also writes that he found several volumes written in Pamphilus’s own hand. “I embrace and preserve them,” he says, “with such joy that I believe I possess the wealth of Croesus. For if it is a joy to possess one letter of a martyr, how much more so to possess so many thousands as his own, which seem to me to have been marked by the traces of his blood?”

On the same day, Saint Caprasius, abbot of the monastery of Lérins.

At Vienne, Saint Claudius II, bishop.

**F. The fourth day before the Nones of June (2 June).**

At Rome, Marcellinus, presbyter, and Peter, exorcist, under Diocletian and the judge Serenus.

It happened that blessed Peter was being held in a very dark prison, bound with iron chains. The prison guard, named Artemius, had a daughter possessed by a demon, whom he loved dearly. The man of God Peter said to him:

“Hear my advice, Artemius, and believe in the only-begotten Son of the living God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the liberator of all who believe in him. If you believe, your daughter will be saved.”

Artemius replied: “I marvel at the foolishness of your advice. Your God cannot free you, although you believe in him and daily endure blows and chains for his name. How will he be able to free my daughter if I believe in him? If you want me to believe in your God, behold, I shall double the chains upon you and secure every door of the prison. I shall shut you alone in its deepest darkness. If your God frees you from all these things, I shall believe in him.”

Blessed Peter agreed, promising that he would come to his house. “I shall do this,” he said, “not to satisfy the desire of your testing, but to manifest the divinity of my Lord Jesus Christ.”

Artemius shook his head and said: “This man, exhausted by excessive sufferings, is speaking irrationally.” Saying this, he departed and related the deeds and words to his wife Candida.

And suddenly, at the beginning of the night, the man of God Peter appeared to Artemius and Candida, dressed in white garments and holding in his hand the triumph of the cross. Falling at his feet, they cried out: “Truly there is one God, and our Lord Jesus Christ is the true Lord.”

Immediately their daughter, Paulina by name and a virgin in body, who had been tormented by an unclean spirit, was healed. When this happened, everyone in Artemius’s household believed. A crowd of more than three hundred neighbors gathered, and an even greater number of women, crying out: “There is no other God besides Christ.”

Since all desired to become Christians, the man of God Peter brought the presbyter Marcellinus, who baptized them all unanimously. Artemius released everyone who was in chains, and all of them also received the grace of baptism.

When the judge Serenus heard this, he ordered the presbyter Marcellinus and Peter the exorcist to be brought before him. After hearing blessed Marcellinus, he ordered that he be beaten with fists on both arteries [possibly “both sides”]. When the beaters had grown weary, Serenus had Peter separated from him and ordered that Peter, naked, be laid upon fragments of glass in custody, and that food and light be denied him.

Peter turned to Serenus and said: “Although your name is Serenus, by your deeds you show yourself wholly clouded and dark.”

Then Serenus ordered that Peter himself be taken into chains and that his feet be fastened in a very tight stock.

While they were separated, an angel of the Lord appeared to the presbyter Marcellinus as he prayed naked, clothed him in his own garments, and brought him to where blessed Peter was in the stocks and irons. The angel also released Peter, and led them both to the house where those newly baptized were praying.

Not long afterward, when blessed Artemius, his wife, and his daughter had received a capital sentence, they too were seized by those who were to punish the holy martyrs. Their hands were bound behind them to a tree until word of them was brought to the judge Serenus.

He ordered them to be taken to the Black Forest, which today is called Candida Forest in honor of the saints, and there to be beheaded together. When they had reached the middle of the forest, they cleared a place of thorns with their own hands. There they prayed together, gave one another the kiss of peace, knelt, and were beheaded.

The man who beheaded them saw their souls, splendidly adorned by angels, being carried to heaven. He repented and, under Pope Julius, was baptized in his old age under the name Dorotheus.

After the blessed martyrs revealed the place, the most Christian women Lucilla and Firmina later took their bodies and buried them beside Saint Tiburtius, in the lower part of the crypt, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September.

[Col. 0274D] [Note: [Col. 0274D] Eusebius, book V, chapters 2–3; Rufinus.] On the same day at Lyon, Saint Blandina with forty-eight martyrs, in the time of Marcus Aurelius Verus, Antoninus, and Lucius, his sons. At that time, through the acclamation and sedition of the crowd, extremely severe persecutions against Christians were stirred up throughout many provinces of the Roman world, so that many thousands of martyrs were made in each place.

At that time, at Lyon and Vienne, cities of Gaul, a degree of punishments and tortures was inflicted upon the servants of God beyond all description. First, they were forbidden to live in their homes; then the use of baths was forbidden; afterward, their appearance in public; finally, they were not to be seen anywhere at all, whether at home or outside, in public or in private.

At last, while a tribune and the leading citizens were present, the Christians were seized merely because of the people’s outcries and thrust into prison until the governor’s arrival; and whenever he came, they were brought before him. He treated them with such cruelty that no one could describe the individual forms of his savagery.

Then Epagathus, one of the brothers, full of divine zeal and spiritual fervor, saw cruel punishments being inflicted upon God’s servants and so many penalties devised against human bodies contrary to right and justice. Unable to endure the outrage any longer, he requested that he be heard. He was the most noble and learned among his people.

But since the judge’s obstinacy would not admit his defense, the judge asked him only whether he too was a Christian. When he clearly and freely testified that he was a Christian, the judge said: “Let him be associated with the Christians as their advocate and included among the prisoners himself.”

But because he had within him Jesus, the advocate for us, he deserved to be honored by this name. He followed the example of the holy presbyter Zacharias, who had shown the fullness of charity toward the saints. While attending his brothers, Zacharias also carried out the defense of the freedom that belongs to our religion. Following the Lord’s example, he laid down his life for his sheep and for his friends.

Blessed Photinus, bishop of Lyon, was more than ninety years old. His body, weak as was natural at such an age, was almost entirely dead; he lived only through his love of martyrdom. He was led—or rather carried—to the tribunal, undone by old age and weakness.

The impious crowd raised an outcry from every side, shouting that he himself was Christ. The governor then asked him who the God of the Christians was. He replied: “If you are worthy, you shall know.”

At this, a kind of immense madness seized everyone, so that those standing nearby subdued the old man with their fists, while those farther away threw at him from a distance whatever weapons their fury placed in their hands. They believed that by this they were avenging their gods.

After they had thrown him into prison half-dead, he gave up his undefiled spirit shortly afterward.

There was also a deacon named Sanctus. He endured new kinds of punishment, with the servants of the demons pressing upon him more fiercely than can be said or human nature rightly bear. But that man, full of God, laughed at their cruelties and at the savage brutality of the interrogation to such an extent that he never deigned to tell them his lineage, his home, his homeland, or even his name.

Asked these individual questions, amid all the tortures he answered nothing except that he was a Christian. “This is my name; this is my lineage and homeland. I am nothing at all,” he said, “except a Christian.”

Finally, glowing plates of bronze and iron were applied around his groin and all the more delicate parts of his body, with fires renewed beneath them. His flesh, burned by the fire, fell away, but he himself remained motionless, unshaken, and fearless. Every limb of his was a martyr, and his whole body bristled as a single wound.

Recognition of human form perished in him. The cruelty of the tortures had taken away not only the ability to recognize who he was, but even what he was. Yet Christ alone was recognized in him through the glory of martyrdom.

The craftsmen of wickedness were not ashamed of the martyr’s courage. After a few days they inflicted tortures again, and his already rotting limbs began once more to be tormented. But—something scarcely credible—his body was restored to its original appearance through the second tortures, so that the repeated punishments brought him not suffering but healing.

Attalus, a citizen of Pergamum, was also demanded by the cries of the people. He was very noble, and—something nobler than all else—a man of excellent conscience, always a martyr in every exercise of faith in Christ.

When he had been led around the amphitheater, preceded by a placard on which was written, “Attalus the Christian,” the fury of the raging crowd began to roar against him more violently. But when it was reported to the governor that he was a Roman citizen, the governor ordered him to be taken into prison with the others. He also reported the matter to Caesar and awaited Caesar’s decision about what should be ordered concerning him.

From both churches, namely Lyon and Vienne, all who appeared zealous and prominent, and by whose labor and industry the churches were governed, were held together.

Thus the devil prepared to attack the servants of God with such devices: that, consumed by the affliction of prison and its penal squalor, and their feet stretched in the innermost place of darkness by the seventh point, as they say, upon the nerve [the wording is uncertain], they might perish amid every kind of punishment that the fury of maddened men could devise.

Very many were thus consumed in the prisons, while the Lord received such an end for them.

A certain Alcibiades was among those who were held captive for Christ. He led a very arduous and austere life, refusing to take any food and using only salt and bread with water.

When, even after being placed in prison, he wished to maintain this strictness of life, it was revealed to Attalus—after Attalus’s first confession, which he had made in the amphitheater—that Alcibiades was not acting rightly by refusing himself God’s creatures and leaving others an example of scandal. Once this was understood, Alcibiades began to accept everything with thanksgiving.

Then, when a rescript from Caesar had arrived ordering that those who persisted should be punished, but those who denied their faith should be released, the judge ascended the tribunal on a certain solemn day and ordered the Christians to be brought before him, so that the spectacle of their punishments might be displayed to all who were present.

Thus crosses, punishments, and tortures were prepared again. The most blessed martyrs were brought from their punishments joyfully, displaying on their faces something divine, I know not what, and regarding their chains as precious necklaces.

Through the prison’s squalor they had become the good fragrance of Christ (2 Corinthians 2), so that they seemed not to be confined in a prison but in a perfumery.

Great glory was given to Christ by all on account of those who had earlier denied him and could not be released without denying him again. There had been nearly ten of these, who by their lapse had left the others mourning and in great sadness. But now, since pardon was not granted to those who denied, they persisted in confession and, recalled from the flock of perdition, were joined to the number of the martyrs.

Therefore the judge decreed that if any Roman citizens were found, they should be put to death; the others were to be given to the beasts.

While the inquiry concerning the persons mentioned above was being conducted, Alexander—by birth a Phrygian, a physician by profession, [possibly “a religious man”] and prudent, esteemed and welcome to all for the integrity of his life and character—was stirred by love of God. As he stood near the tribunal, he encouraged by gestures those whose case was being tried to confess their faith, so that it became clear to everyone standing nearby what he had in mind.

When the people noticed this, they shouted indignantly against Alexander. Ordered by the governor to be placed in the midst and asked who he was, he freely testified that he was a Christian.

The governor immediately condemned him to be prepared for the beasts, and on the following day he was brought out together with Attalus. Wishing to please the crowds, and contrary to Caesar’s command, the governor ordered that Alexander too be handed over to the beasts.

But when none of the wild animals touched the bodies of the saints, he ordered them to be tortured with every punishment of blows and other torments. Throughout all the sufferings he endured, blessed Alexander did not utter even a single word.

Attalus, however, was roasted on an iron chair with burning coals placed beneath it. When the smell of the burned flesh reached the noses and mouths of the watching crowd, he cried out in a loud voice to the people:

“Behold, this is what it means to eat human beings, as you do. We neither eat human beings nor do any other evil. For when their servants were seized and feared the tortures, they, at the instigation of demons, devised this accusation against their masters.”

When he was asked what name God had, he replied: “Those who are many are distinguished by names; the one who is one has no need of a name.”

With these excellent and faithful leaders, the entire remaining chorus of the saints laid down their souls, ready and eager, for the freedom of the faith.

Among them the most blessed woman Blandina was crowned most gloriously. Through her Christ showed that those things which are despised and held in contempt among human beings are counted in great glory before the Lord.

From first light until evening the torturers continually renewed her torments; at last they confessed themselves defeated. On the second day she was again subjected to tortures but was not overcome.

On the third day she was tied to a stake, stretched out in the form of a cross, and prepared as food for the beasts. Since none of the beasts dared touch her, she was taken back to prison.

On the fourth day she was driven onward by blows, burned on grates, and subjected to many other sufferings. Finally she was killed by the sword.

Then the boy Ponticus, fifteen years old, was subjected together with her to every kind of torture. Strengthened by her encouragement, he completed his martyrdom before her.

But Mathurus, Sanctus, and Attalus were placed in the middle of the arena on the days of the public games, with countless thousands of people of various nations gathered for the spectacle.

Mathurus, though a neophyte, was strongest in faith and endurance. Together with the holy deacon, he was subjected anew to every kind of torture, as though they had suffered nothing before.

Their adversaries competed in every way to break their endurance and, so to speak, tear their crowns from the very top of their heads. But hope of the approaching glory strengthened their souls all the more, and they seemed already to touch and grasp it with their hands.

When nearly all the kinds of punishments and spectacles had been employed, and they could not in any way be moved from their resolve, they were placed upon iron chairs. Fire applied beneath burned the flesh already consumed by blows. At last, their spirits untiring, the martyrs escaped through the sword that struck their necks.

Then, in an unheard-of act of savagery, the bodies of those who had been killed in prison were ordered to be exposed to dogs. A guard was stationed there day and night so that no one, moved by human compassion, might take the collected remains for burial.

Whatever might have remained of the martyrs’ bodies after the beasts or fire, together with the heads of those punished and their trunks, was kept unburied under military guard.

There was no possibility of persuading the guards by gifts, prayers, or any other means. They watched so attentively and carefully to prevent burial from being given to the final bones.

These things are written in the *Ecclesiastical History*, book five.

[Note: [Col. 0277D] Eusebius, book I, chapter 2, from Rufinus’s translation.] The names of the forty-eight martyrs are these:

Photinus, bishop; Zacharias, presbyter; Epagathus; Macarius; Alcibiades; Silvius; Primus; Ulpius; Vitalis; Cominus; Octuber; Philuminus; Geminus; Julia; Albina; Grata; Rogata; Aemilia; Potamia; Pompeia; Rhodana; Biblis; Quartia; Materna; Helpes, also called Amnas.

Those who were handed over to the beasts were: Sanctus, Mathurus, Attalus, Alexander, Ponticus, and Blandina.

Those who gave up their spirit in prison were: Aristaeus, Cornelius, Zosimus, Titus, Julius, Zoticus, Apollonius, Germinianus, Julia, Ausonia, Aemilia, Jamnica, Pompeia, Domna, Justa, Trophima, and Antonia.

All these servants of Christ were crowned together under the emperors mentioned above.

Their remains were burned by the persecutors and scattered into the river Rhône. But when the Christians were in great sorrow, as though the sacred relics had perished, the saints appeared by night to faithful men, standing whole and unharmed in the place where they had been handed over to the fire.

Turning toward the men, they said to them: “Let our remains be gathered from this place, for none of us has perished. From here we have been transferred to the rest that Christ, the King of heaven, promised us, for whose name we suffered.”

When those men reported this, they gave thanks to God and were strengthened in faith. They gathered the sacred ashes and buried them with fitting honor beneath a holy altar, where they continually reveal by evident miracles that they dwell with God.

The citizens of the city of Lyon celebrate their feast, together with all who joyfully come from every direction, as they descend along the river with hymns and songs of thanksgiving. They solemnly offer the rites of the Mass to the Lord in the church of the apostles, where their holy ashes are preserved in burial. Following the tradition of the ancients, they call that day itself the day of miracles.

The place where they suffered is called Athanacus; therefore they are called the Athanacian martyrs.

**G. The third day before the Nones of June (3 June).**

At Arezzo, a city of Tuscany, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Pergentinus and Laurentinus, brothers. During the persecution of Decius, under the judge Turtus, although they were boys, they endured harsh punishments, displayed great miracles, and were struck down by the sword. They were buried at the same city.

In Campania, the commemoration of blessed Erasmus, bishop and martyr, under Diocletian and Maximian. At the command of the impious emperor Diocletian, he was first cruelly beaten with leaded clubs, then tormented for a very long time with cudgels. Afterward, he was covered with melted resin, sulfur, lead, pitch, wax, and oil; by an immense miracle he appeared unharmed.

When many saw this, they rejected the idols and accepted the faith of Christ. He was then bound with an immense weight of iron and confined in prison under severe guard. He was released and rescued from this confinement through an angelic visitation.

Later, when the fame of his most remarkable miracles had spread, he was seized by the other emperor, Maximian, by whom he was tortured with various punishments, even to the point of being clothed in a heated bronze tunic.

Again he was placed in a cauldron heated with lead, pitch, wax, resin, and oil. By the Lord’s power he overcame everything and emerged unharmed.

Thus, preserved by the Lord to strengthen the others, he reached Campania fortified by angelic assistance. There, after strengthening many in the faith or converting them to the faith of Christ, he was called by the Lord and, illustrious through martyrdom, rested in a holy death.

**A. The day before the Nones of June (4 June).**

[Note: [Col. 0279D] Prudentius, hymn 7.] At Siscia, a city of Illyricum, the commemoration of Saint Quirinus, bishop. During the persecution of Maximian, he was thrown into a river with a millstone tied to his hand because of his faith in Christ.

After speaking at length with those standing around, so that they would not be frightened by his example, he scarcely obtained through his prayers that he be drowned. His relics were transferred to Rome and placed in the Catacombs.

**B. The Nones of June (5 June).**

In Egypt, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Marianus, Nicander, and Apollonius, whose deeds are recorded.

On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Boniface, martyr, who suffered at Tarsus under Diocletian and Maximian and was buried at Rome on the road called the Latina.

He was the administrator of the affairs of a certain noble matron named Aglahes, and he was involved with her in fornication. At last, both of them were moved by divine prompting and, struck with remorse, took counsel that Boniface should be sent to seek the bodies of martyrs, so that by serving and obeying them in some way they might deserve to be saved through their prayers.

After several days he reached the city of Tarsus and said to those who were with him: “Men, go and find lodging for us; I shall go to see those whom I greatly desire to see—the martyrs who are contending.”

Hurrying to the place, he saw the most blessed martyrs: one hanging by his feet with a fire placed beneath him; another stretched upon four pieces of wood and afflicted for a very long time; another lacerated with hooks; another with his hands cut off; another with a stake fixed in his neck and raised from the ground. Thus the impious executioner had arranged their martyrdoms through various punishments.

Watching them from a distance, burning with love of Christ, he began to cry out: “Great is the God of the holy martyrs!”

He ran up, sat at their feet, kissed their bonds, and said: “Contend, martyrs of Christ; trample down the devil; persevere for a little while. The labor is small, but the rest is great, and afterward there is unutterable satisfaction.”

The judge Simplicius saw him and ordered him brought before the tribunal. He said to him: “Who are you?”

Saint Boniface replied: “I am a Christian, and I am called Boniface.”

Then the angry judge ordered him to be suspended and his body scraped with hooks until his bones appeared. He then ordered sharp reeds to be driven beneath the nails of his hands.

As the holy martyr of God looked toward heaven and endured the pains cheerfully, the impious judge ordered his mouth to be opened and boiling lead to be poured in.

The holy martyr said: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God.”

Then the judge ordered a cauldron to be brought and filled with pitch, and the holy martyr to be thrown headfirst into the boiling pitch. But when he was unharmed, the impious judge ordered that his head be cut off with a sword.

When this had been done, a great earthquake occurred, so that many unbelievers, seeing Christ’s power in the martyr, believed.

Boniface’s fellow servants went everywhere searching for him. Not finding him, they said to one another: “He is probably now feasting in adultery or in a tavern.”

As they were speaking among themselves, one of the officials happened to meet them. They asked him: “Have you seen a foreign Roman man?”

He replied: “Yesterday a foreign man was beheaded in the stadium.”

They asked again: “What did he look like?”

He said: “He was square-built and stout, with strong hair, and dressed in a scarlet *armelausia*.”

He told them: “The man you are seeking finished his martyrdom among us yesterday.”

They replied: “The man we are seeking is an adulterer and a drunkard.”

He said to them: “Come and see him.”

When he had shown them the body and its precious head, they said to him: “This is the man we are seeking. We ask you to give him to us.”

He replied: “I cannot give you his body for nothing.”

They gave him five hundred solidi, received the body of the holy martyr, anointed it with spices, wrapped it in costly linen, placed it in a *basterna*, and returned joyfully, glorifying God.

An angel of the Lord appeared to his former mistress and informed her of what had happened to the blessed martyr. She immediately went out with every mark of reverence to meet the holy body. She built a worthy house for it and placed it there, five stadia from the city of Rome.

The holy martyr Boniface was martyred on the fourteenth day of May at Tarsus, the metropolis of Cilicia, and was buried at Rome on the Nones of June.

Blessed Aglahes renounced the world and its pomp, distributing everything she possessed to the needy and to monasteries. She released her entire household from the yoke of slavery and earned such grace from the Lord that she became renowned through signs of miracles performed in his name.

She lived thirteen additional years in the habit of a religious woman and, perfected in good works, was buried beside the aforementioned martyr.

On the same day, Saint Boniface, who came from Britain and preached the faith of Christ to the nations, after bringing a very great multitude in Frisia under the Christian religion, was finally killed by the remaining pagans with the sword. He completed his martyrdom with Eoban, his fellow bishop, and other servants of God.

**C. The eighth day before the Ides of June (6 June).**

[Col. 0281D] [Note: [Col. 0281] See the booklet *On Festivals*; Augustine, *City of God*, book XXII, chapter 8. Concerning these matters, in the Acts of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, 2 June.] Saint Philip the deacon, who was one of the Seven.

On the same day at Tarsus in Cilicia, twenty martyrs under the judge Simplicius, in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. Through various punishments they glorified the Lord in their bodies.

On the same day at Rome, the commemoration of Saint Artemius, with his wife Candida and his daughter Paulina.

When Artemius was the prison guard and kept blessed Peter the exorcist confined in custody, his only daughter was tormented by a demon. As soon as she was healed through the prayers of blessed Peter, Artemius believed in Christ together with his wife and the same daughter. He was baptized by the presbyter blessed Marcellinus, and his entire household and many others were baptized as well, so that, excluding the women, they numbered three hundred men.

When the judge Serenus heard what had happened, he ordered Artemius, Candida, and their daughter Paulina, who had been brought before him, to be buried beneath an immense mass of rubble.

Thus the saints of God were led to the place of their passion: blessed Artemius was struck with the sword, while Saints Candida and Paulina were thrown down through the entrance of a crypt and buried beneath stones.

**D. The seventh day before the Ides of June (7 June).**

At Constantinople, the commemoration of Saint Paul, bishop of that city. During the time of the Arian perfidy, he was driven into exile by the emperor Constantine to a certain small city of Cappadocia called Cucusa because of the Catholic faith. He was cruelly strangled through the plots of the Arians and migrated to the heavenly kingdoms.

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the commemoration of Saint Lucian, martyr.

**E. The sixth day before the Ides of June (8 June).**

In Gaul, at the city of Soissons, the commemoration of Saint Medard, bishop and confessor.

At Angers, Saint Licinius, bishop and confessor.

Likewise on the same day, Saint Carilefus, confessor.

**F. The fifth day before the Ides of June (9 June).**

At Rome, on Mount Caelius, the commemoration of the holy Primus and Felicianus under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian.

These most glorious martyrs, ever living in the Lord, were accused and denounced by the priests of the temples before the emperors because they were Christians. They were Roman citizens, and they were brought before the emperors, who ordered them bound with iron and confined in prison. There the angel of the Lord appeared to them and consoled them.

After several days, the emperors ordered them brought before them and commanded the soldiers to lead them to the temple of Hercules. If they refused to sacrifice, the soldiers were to afflict them with severe punishments.

When they could not move them in any way, and the martyrs preferred to die for Christ’s name, the soldiers stretched them out and beat them severely with rods.

When the soldiers reported to the emperors what had happened, the emperors became very angry and ordered them handed over to Promotus, governor of the city of Nomentum, so that he might kill them through various punishments.

The soldiers took them, led them along the road called the Nomentana to the thirteenth milestone, bound them with iron, and placed them in prison beside the city forum. There they were again relieved by an angelic visitation.

After a long time, Governor Promotus ordered a tribunal prepared for him in the city forum. When Primus and Felicianus had been brought in, and, at the governor’s command, had been separated from each other after their answers, the governor first ordered blessed Felicianus to be beaten with leaded clubs. He said to him:

“Why do you not put aside this madness of your heart, choose good and pleasant days, and cease tormenting your body with various punishments?”

Blessed Felicianus said: “I am eighty years old, and it is thirty years since I came to know the truth of God. Thinking nothing of the enticements of this world, I chose to serve my Creator, the eternal and almighty God.”

Then the governor ordered him tied to a stake, with spikes driven into his hands and feet, and tortured for a long time. For three days he was given neither bread nor water nor any kind of food.

When he had remained continuously praising God for three days, the governor ordered him beaten with whips, taken down from the stake, and confined in custody. He then ordered blessed Primus to be brought before him.

After Primus had been beaten with very heavy cudgels and then raised upon the rack, the governor ordered torches placed around his sides. When he had been taken down from the rack, he ordered lead to be melted over the blessed martyr as he lay stretched out and boiling lead to be poured into his mouth.

Then he ordered blessed Felicianus to be brought before him. But when the unconquerable holy martyrs continued firm, the distressed governor ordered them led to the amphitheater and two lions released against them.

When the lions rushed to the saints’ feet, the most savage bears were also released. But through the martyrs’ power they too lost their ferocity.

When those who had come to the spectacle saw this, nearly fifteen hundred men, struck by the miracles, believed in the Lord Jesus Christ.

But when the governor saw that they could not be overcome, he ordered them executed with the sword.

Their bodies were secretly taken by faithful Christians and buried at the Nomentan Arches, inside the sand-pit, on the fifth day before the Ides of June, at the fourteenth milestone from the city of Rome.

In Gaul, at the city of Agen, in the place called Pompeianum, the passion of Saint Vincent, levite and martyr.

**G. The fourth day before the Ides of June (10 June).**

At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, at the thirteenth milestone, the commemoration of the holy Basilides, Tripodus, and Mandalis, under the emperor Aurelian and the governor Plato, together with twenty other martyrs.

On the same day, the feast of the blessed martyr Getulius, during the reign of the emperors Hadrian and under the judge Licinius. He was exceedingly learned in every aspect of divine law, and through his teaching many were instructed in the faith of Christ. When the emperor Hadrian heard of his reputation, he sent Cerealis, his deputy, to seize him. Cerealis came upon the holy Getulius sitting and teaching many people. Now Cerealis himself had previously been received into Hadrian’s presence together with the blessed Getulius’s brother Amantius; but Amantius, a tribune, was hiding in concealment out of fear of Hadrian. The blessed Getulius disclosed him to Cerealis. When Cerealis saw him, he rejoiced greatly. Having been carefully instructed by them concerning the Lord Jesus, and now believing faithfully, they came to the city of Rome. They summoned the blessed Bishop Sixtus and showed him the place where Cerealis was to be baptized. The blessed Sixtus baptized him, for he truly loved the Christian faith.

At that time a certain Vincentius, an officer of the treasury, learned that the deputy Cerealis was a Christian and, becoming extremely angry, reported this to Hadrian. Hadrian immediately sent Licinius, the consul-governor, to arrest Cerealis, ordering that, if he refused to sacrifice, he should be burned alive. The blessed Getulius, Amantius, and Primitivus were arrested with him.

Licinius the consul-governor said to Cerealis, his deputy: “Have you become so desperate for life that you appear to scorn the commands of the rulers who dominate the whole world?”

The blessed Cerealis replied: “I have duly returned the public treasuries to the public, and I promise to serve the Lord Jesus Christ; I believe that I shall enjoy the eternal way.”

Licinius said: “Tell me whether you wish to live or to die.”

The blessed Cerealis replied: “If I did not wish to live, I would not confess Christ.”

Then Licinius turned to the holy Getulius and said: “Sacrifice to the god Jupiter and to Mars.” The blessed martyr laughed at his words. Licinius, inflamed with anger, ordered them to be stripped and beaten, and then shut up in prison for twenty-seven days. He came to Rome and again informed Hadrian about them; Hadrian ordered them to be handed over to the fire.

But when the holy Getulius survived the fire, his martyrdom was completed by blows that crushed his head. The blessed martyrs were put to death at the estate of Capreoli, on the Salarian Way, about thirteen miles, more or less, from the city of Rome, above the river Tiber, in the region of the Avinienses [another reading: in the region of the Sabines]. Their bodies were gathered by the blessed Symphorosa, wife of the blessed martyr Getulius. Not long afterward she was martyred with her seven sons, namely on the twenty-seventh day of June. She was buried in her own battle-place, in the Arenarium, at the place and settlement mentioned above.

## A. III IDES OF JUNE (11 June)

[Col. 0284C]

[Note: See the booklet *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.]

The feast of Saint Barnabas the apostle, whose body was found in the time of the emperor Zeno, when he himself revealed it.

On the same day at Corinth, Saint Sosthenes, disciple of Saint Paul the apostle.

At Aquileia, the feast of the holy martyrs Felix and Fortunatus, under the persecution of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, with Euphemius as governor. Since they were brothers by birth, ardent in the faith of Christ, they were denounced by Apamius, who was one of the governor’s officials; bound in irons, they were brought to Aquileia before the judge Euphemius.

There, when they steadfastly confessed Christ, the enraged judge first had them suspended on the rack, with burning lamps placed around their sides. But the lamps were extinguished as the martyrs sang psalms. They were then drenched over the belly with boiling oil. Finally, because they remained firm in the confession of Christ, they were led outside the city to the river adjoining it and beheaded.

That night religious men of the same city, Aquileia, wrapped them in spices and linen cloths, carried them away, and buried them. But citizens of Vicetia arrived afterward intending to bring their bodies to their own city. When the Aquileians refused permission and strongly resisted, the pious dispute was finally settled by divine providence in this way: the people of Vicetia were to have Felix, and the Aquileians Fortunatus; yet Aquileia was to receive the head of the blessed Felix, while Vicetia received the head of Fortunatus. This arrangement remains in force to this day, to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ.

## B. THE DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF JUNE (12 June)

At Milan, the feast of the holy martyrs Nazarius and the boy Celsus. The blessed Nazarius’s father was Africanus and his mother Perpetua; they were baptized by the blessed apostle Peter. Saint Nazarius himself was instructed and baptized by Saint Clement. During the violent persecution stirred up by Nero, Anolinus had him long tormented and afflicted in prison, together with the most blessed boy Celsus, whom Nazarius himself had raised; then he ordered them to be struck with the sword.

Christians secretly took away their bodies and buried them on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, outside the gate called the Roman Gate, in their own gardens. The most blessed martyrs revealed themselves to a certain man named Ceratius, whose wife was Fortunata, and in a vision they warned him that they were to remain hidden because of the fury of the persecution that the impious Nero had raised.

They remained concealed until the time of the emperors Honorius and Arcadius. The blessed Ambrose found them when the Lord revealed them. When the tomb in which the body of Saint Nazarius lay was opened—although, as Saint Paulinus writes, it had previously been unknown when he had suffered—those present saw the martyr’s blood so fresh that it seemed to have been shed that very day. His head also, which had been cut off by the impious, was so whole and incorrupt, with the hair of his head and beard, that it appeared to have been washed and arranged in the tomb at the very time it was being lifted. They were also filled with such a great fragrance that it surpassed the sweetness of every spice.

After the body had been lifted and placed on a bier, the holy bishop immediately went to pray at the tomb of Saint Celsus the martyr, who had been laid in the same garden, and transferred him to the Basilica of the Apostles, which is at the Roman Gate. They were found and transferred on the day before the Ides of June; their martyrdom, however, is celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. Their public and solemn commemoration is also observed and reverently celebrated by the faithful on the feast of the holy Gervasius and Protasius.

Also, the blessed Basilides, Quirinus, and Nabor.

Likewise Nazarius and Celsus, whom antiquity celebrates in its traditions as having suffered near the city of Ebredunum.

## C. THE IDES OF JUNE (13 June)

At Rome, the feast of Saint Felicula, virgin and martyr.

[Note: Concerning her, see the Acts of Nereus and Achilleus, 22 May.]

When Count Flaccus wished to marry her after Petronilla’s death, he tried to frighten her by saying: “Choose one of these two things: either be my wife or sacrifice to the gods.” She replied: “I shall neither be your wife, because I have been consecrated to Christ, nor shall I sacrifice to your gods, because I am a Christian.”

Then Flaccus handed her over to his deputy, who had her shut in a dark room without food for seven days. When she continued steadfast in the confession of Christ, they brought her out and led her to the virgins of Vesta. There she remained for another seven days without food, because she would in no way accept food from their hands.

After this she was lifted onto the rack and cried out: “Now I have begun to see my beloved, in whom my love is fixed.” When her torturers said to her, “Deny that you are a Christian and you will be released,” she cried out: “I shall not deny my beloved Christ, who for my sake was fed with gall and given vinegar to drink, crowned with thorns, and crucified.”

Afterward she was taken down and thrown into a sewer. The holy presbyter Nicomedes, who had stationed himself nearby as a watchman, secretly lifted her out and during the night carried her in a two-wheeled cart to his little estate, seven miles from the city on the Ardeatine Way. There he buried her.

## D. XVIII DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (14 June)

The prophet Elisha, who is buried at Samaria in Palestine—a city later called Sebaste, that is, Augusta, by Herod in honor of Augustus. The prophet Obadiah also rests there, as does John the Baptist, than whom no one born of woman was greater.

At the tombs of the saints there, miracles of such terror occur that demons are heard roaring there amid various tortures, and people possessed by them are heard howling like wolves, barking like dogs, roaring like lions, hissing like snakes, and bellowing like bulls. Some are seen rolling over the ground, with their heads touching the earth behind them; and women, with their feet suspended upward, are seen with their garments not falling over their faces.

On the nearby mountain two caves are also visible, in which, during the time of persecution and famine, Obadiah fed one hundred prophets with bread and water (1 Kings 18). The blessed Jerome records this in his book *The Life of Saint Paula*.

At the city of Soissons, the passion of the holy martyrs Valerius and Rufinus.

[Note: Jerome, Letter 27 to Eustochium.]

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Basil, bishop, brother of Gregory and Peter. Established in every virtue, he was at one time forced into exile by the emperor Valens on account of the faith. Brought before the prefect’s tribunal, he began to be assailed—with the threats and intimidation customary to that authority—and was told that, unless he obeyed the emperor’s command, death and punishment awaited him.

Then, fearless and without any disturbance of mind, he is said to have replied to the prefect who threatened him: “Would that I had some worthy gift to offer him who would release Basil more quickly from the knot of this sack.”

When he was granted the night, which was then at hand, as time for deliberation, he is reported to have replied again: “Tomorrow I shall be the same man I am now; would that you did not change.”

That very night the emperor’s wife was tortured as though handed over to executioners. Their only son, however, having died, paid the penalty for his father’s impiety. Thus, before dawn, messengers were sent to ask Basil to intercede for them by his prayers, lest they too—and with far greater justice—should perish.

And so it happened that although Valens expelled all the Catholics, Basil remained in the Church until the end of his life, preserving the sacrament of communion undefiled.

At Vienne, Saint Etherius, bishop.

## E. XVII DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (15 June)

In Sicily, the feast of the holy martyrs Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia. The blessed Vitus, mature in virtue despite his youth, was first tested by his sacrilegious father Hila, who tried to turn him away from the worship of God. Then, by the judge Valerian, he was beaten *catomis* and remained steadfast in his confession.

[Note: *Catomis caedi*: to be beaten *catomis*. Below, 18 November: to be suspended *catomo*. I think *catomis* and *catomo* are used adverbially. The expression means nothing other than to be suspended or beaten head downward. This was done especially to boys, when they were suspended from another person’s shoulders with their feet raised upward; it was sometimes done to men and women as a mark of disgrace. In the Acts of Saint Afra, 5 August: “I shall order you, naked, to be beaten *catomis*,” which Scaliger, improperly, interprets in connection with Book V of Manilius as “to be beaten on the neck with leaden weights after being stripped.” Victor, *The Vandal Persecution*, book I: “At one time they beat an aged and venerable man *catomis* in public.” Aristophanes, in *Peace* and *The Acharnians*, has κατωκάρα. Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book V, chapter 10, has κατομαδόν.]

He was then returned to his father. When his father was planning to afflict him with punishments, he boarded a ship at an angel’s warning and, accompanied by Modestus and Crescentia, his foster-parents, arrived in the territory of Tanagritum.

Because the daughter of the emperor Diocletian was afflicted by a demon, Vitus was sought out and brought before Diocletian; by his prayer he healed the emperor’s daughter. But when the impious emperor tried, by promising many gifts, to persuade him to worship the gods, and could not turn his mind from his good purpose, he ordered him bound tightly with iron chains and taken into a most dreadful prison, together with Modestus and Crescentia.

Then, with the people standing around, they were placed in the amphitheater. Diocletian ordered them thrown into a cauldron heated with resin and pitch and brought to a boil with molten lead. There the holy martyrs sang psalms and offered a hymn to God like the Three Youths (Daniel 3). They emerged from the cauldron with their faces unharmed, and a ferocious lion was released against them. It immediately fell at their feet and began to lick the martyrs’ feet with its tongue.

At last, the sacrilegious emperor, defeated in every respect, and seeing at the same time that the multitude of people had been struck by the miracle and converted to Christ the true God, ordered a torture-frame to be prepared and the servants of God stretched upon it. When God’s martyrs were being beaten and their bones split apart, a great thunderclap occurred, with flashes of lightning and so great an earthquake that the temples of the gods collapsed and crushed many people.

Florentia, a woman of illustrious rank, gathered the bodies of the saints and buried them at the place called Marianus, having embalmed them with spices.

On the same day, at Dorostorum in the province of Moesia, Saint Esychius, a soldier, who was arrested together with the blessed Julius under the governor Maximian and later crowned with martyrdom.

## F. XVI DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (16 June)

At Antioch, the feast of the holy martyrs Cyricus and his mother Julitta. The former, after dreadful beatings, also received a cup containing vinegar and mustard into his mouth; then both were nailed through, had their eyes torn out, and were thrust into prison. After this their heads were shaved and their skin flayed; they were roasted on coals in a bronze bed. Finally, after being rasped with saws and having their tongues cut out, they completed the course of their martyrdom by beheading. Four hundred and four others suffered with them.

Near the city of Besançon, the holy martyrs Ferreolus, presbyter, and Ferrution, deacon. Sent by the blessed Irenaeus, bishop and martyr of Lyon, to preach the word of God, they were stretched on pulleys and flogged under the judge Claudius, then shut in prison. In the morning, with their tongues cut out, they preached the word of God. After this, thirty awls were driven into the hands, feet, and chest of each of them. Finally, they were struck with the sword.

At the city of Nantes, Saint Similianus, bishop and confessor.

At Lyon, the deposition of Saint Aurelianus, bishop of Arles.

## G. XV DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (17 June)

At Rome, the holy two hundred and sixty-two martyrs who were laid on the old Salarian Way, at the slope of Cucumer.

On the same day, Saint Wulthmar, confessor, a man of admirable holiness and religious devotion.

## A. XIV DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (18 June)

At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, the feast of the holy martyrs Mark and Marcellian, of most noble birth.

[Note: Concerning them, see the Acts of Saint Sebastian, 20 January.]

They were the sons of Tranquillinus and Marcia. They first endured imprisonment for the faith; afterward, when arrested by the commander Fabianus, they were tied to a stake and had sharp nails driven into their feet.

When the mad judge said to them, “Unhappy and wretched men, put away your madness and free yourselves from the tortures that threaten you,” they replied: “Never have we feasted so well; only now have we begun to be fixed in the love of Christ. Would that you permit us to remain as we are for as long as we are governed by the clothing of this body.”

When one day and one night had passed, and they continued praising Christ in psalms and hymns, they were pierced through the sides with spears and went with the glory of martyrdom to the heavenly realms.

## B. XIII DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (19 June)

At Milan, the feast of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. These most blessed men had spent ten years shut up in a single upper room, devoted to readings, prayers, and fasts; in the eleventh year they attained the palm of martyrdom.

They were arrested by Count Astasius, who first ordered Gervasius beaten with leaded clubs until he breathed out his spirit; then he ordered the second, Protasius, beaten with clubs and beheaded. A religious man named Philip secretly carried away their bodies with his son and buried them in his house in a marble sarcophagus.

Long afterward, during the reign of Theodosius, the blessed Ambrose found their tombs when the Lord revealed them. Their bodies were so incorrupt that it was as though the martyrs had been killed that very day. When they were being brought into the city, a man who had been blind for a long time received his sight by touching the bier.

At Ravenna, Saint Ursicinus the martyr.

[Note: Ambrose, Sermon 71 and Book X, Letter 85.]

Under the judge Paulinus, after excessive tortures, he remained immovable in his confession of the Lord and completed his martyrdom by decapitation. He was buried in the same city by the blessed Vitalis, father of the saints Gervasius and Protasius.

## C. XII DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (20 June)

[Col. 0289B]

At Rome, the feast of Saint Novatus, brother of the presbyter Timothy; both had been instructed by the blessed apostles. Concerning this Novatus, Pastor writes in the Acts of the virgins Pudentiana and Praxedis, addressed to the aforementioned Timothy, his brother:

“The venerable virgin Praxedis was greatly afflicted after the death of her sister Potentiana. Many Christian nobles came to console her, together with Saint Pius the bishop. Among them was your brother Novatus, who is our brother in the Lord, and who refreshed many poor Christians with his gifts; he also frequently commemorated you with the most blessed Bishop Pius at the Lord’s altar.

“After a year and twenty-eight days, the same Novatus was seized by illness and was absent from the presence of the virgin Praxedis. While Bishop Pius was thinking of all the Christians together with the virgin, Novatus, the man of God, was sought. When it became known that he was ill, we were all saddened. The blessed Praxedis said to our father, Saint Pius: ‘Let your holiness order that we go to him; by our visit together with your prayers, he will be saved.’

“After the decision had been made, we went at night with Bishop Pius and the Lord’s virgin to the man of God Novatus. When the man of God Novatus heard that everyone had gathered and come to him, he began to give thanks to God because he had been deemed worthy to be visited by Saint Pius the bishop and the Lord’s virgin, together with our devotion. We remained in his house for eight days and nights. And it happened that on the thirteenth day Novatus, the man of God, departed to the Lord, to receive the glory of the heavenly kingdom.”

## D. XI DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (21 June)

In Sicily, at the city of Syracuse, the feast of the holy martyrs Rufinus and Marcia.

At Rome, Saint Demetria, virgin, who was the daughter of the blessed Faustus. When she was brought before the impious Julian on account of the faith of Christ, she gave up her spirit in confession. She was buried by the blessed presbyter John beside her mother, Saint Daphrosa, and her sister Joviana, near the Lucian Palace.

## E. X DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (22 June)

[Col. 0290A]

In Britain, the feast of Saint Alban, martyr, who in the time of Diocletian was beheaded in the city of Verulamium after beatings and bitter tortures. When he fell to the ground, the eyes of the man who struck him also fell to the ground.

One of the soldiers also suffered with him because, although ordered to strike him, he refused, terrified by the divine miracle: he had seen the blessed martyr, as he hastened toward the crown of martyrdom, make the bed of the intervening river passable by prayer.

At that time, a cruel persecution crossing beyond the shores of the Ocean also condemned Aaron and Julius of Britain, together with many other men and women, to a blessed death.

[Col. 0290B] Likewise, at the city of Nola in Campania, the feast of Saint Paulinus, bishop and confessor.

[Note: Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 22.]

He handed himself into slavery during the time of the Vandals in place of the son of a certain widow. When the king of the Vandals learned who he was through a terrifying vision, Paulinus was released together with all the captives from his city. After loading ships with grain, he returned from Africa to his own see with immense glory. He became distinguished not only for learning and abundant holiness of life, but also for power against demons.

On the same day, the deposition of the blessed Niceas, bishop of the city of Romatiana.

## F. IX DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (23 June)

The vigil of Saint John the Baptist.

On the same day, Saint John the presbyter, whom the impious Julian ordered to be beheaded on the old Salarian Way before an image of the Sun. His body was gathered by the blessed presbyter Concordius and buried near the memorials of the martyrs.

In Britain, Saint Edeltrudis, virgin and queen, whose body, after having been buried for eleven years, was found incorrupt.

## G. VIII DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (24 June)

The Nativity of the Lord’s Forerunner.

[Note: See the book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.]

## A. VII DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (25 June)

At Pyrrhiberoea, Saint Sosipater, disciple of Saint Paul the apostle.

[Note: Acts 20; Romans 16. Concerning him, see the Acts of John and Paul, 26 June.]

[Col. 0294D] Likewise at Alexandria, the feast of Saint Gallicanus the martyr. Having been elevated and received with triumphal honors, he was a favorite of Augustus Constantine and extremely dear to him. He asked to marry his daughter, the most holy virgin Constantia.

Constantine Augustus began to grieve, knowing that his daughter, established in a holy purpose, could more easily be killed than overcome. But she tried to remove her father’s anxiety by her devotion to holiness. Confident in God, she said to her father: “Set aside all your anxiety and promise that you will give him a bride, so that, if he conquers the Scythian nation, he may receive me as both victor and wife.””

Everything happened as the virgin had arranged. As a pledge of the engagement, two eunuch brothers, John and Paul, were assigned to Gallicanus from the household of Augusta Constantia, and two sisters, Attica and Artemia, daughters of Gallicanus, were entrusted to the Augusta. The virgin converted them to the Lord.

Gallicanus was then shut up by the Scythian people in the Thracian city of Philippopolis. Fearing to engage them because he had only a small band of soldiers while the enemy possessed an innumerable multitude, he persisted in sacrifices and offered victims to Mars.

What more is there to say? At last the siege grew stronger, and all his tribunes and soldiers surrendered themselves to the enemy. When he wanted to find a way of escape, Paul and John—one of whom was chief officer and the other chief secretary of Augusta Constantia—said to him: “Make a vow to the God of heaven that, if he frees you, you will become a Christian, and you will be a better victor than you were before.”

As soon as the vow had been spoken aloud, a tall young man appeared to him, carrying a cross on his shoulders, and said: “Take your sword and follow me.” As he followed him, armed soldiers appeared on either side, strengthening him and saying: “We shall serve as your attendants. Enter the enemy camp, holding your drawn sword in your right and left hands, and continue until you reach their king.”

When he reached the king, the king, together with his men, fell at his feet and begged that none of his people be killed by the sword. Gallicanus neither did this himself nor ordered it done. Thus all Thrace was freed, and the Scythian nation became tributary.

He himself devoted himself so completely to God that he also promised to abstain from marriage. Returning, therefore, Gallicanus did not enter Rome before going to the sacred threshold of the blessed apostle Peter.

When Emperor Constantine learned everything that had been accomplished around him through Christ’s mercy, he embraced Gallicanus. Constantine reported to him everything that had happened concerning Gallicanus’s daughters and how they had been profitably consecrated as virgins to Christ.

When Gallicanus entered the palace with Augustus, Helena came forward with her daughter Constantia and Gallicanus’s daughters. Tears filled with joy were shed.

When Gallicanus wished to depart as a private citizen, Augustus asked him to continue as consul, and he entered upon the office. He freed five thousand slaves and made them free citizens and Roman citizens. He gave them estates and houses, and ordered all his possessions, except the legal rights of his daughters, to be sold and given to the poor.

He joined himself to a holy man named Hilarinus, who was living in the city of Ostia. Gallicanus enlarged Hilarinus’s dwelling to receive pilgrims, a service that he himself provided for many. Many of his former slaves, whom he had freed, joined him.

His fame spread throughout the whole world, so that people coming from East and West saw a man who had been a patrician, a consul, and a close friend of Augustus washing feet, setting the table, pouring water over people’s hands, carefully ministering to the sick, and performing the other duties of holy service.

He was the first to build a church in the city of Ostia and to endow the clerical offices. The holy deacon Lawrence revealed himself to him and urged him to build a church in his name at the gate that is still called the Laurentian Gate.

When he was asked to be ordained bishop there, he refused. He himself chose six men according to his own judgment, who were to be ordained. God granted him such great grace that those possessed by demons were immediately cleansed as soon as they came into his sight; and he possessed many distinguished marks of holiness.

But when Julian had been made Caesar by Constantius, he issued a law that Christians were to possess nothing in this world. Gallicanus then had four houses in the district of Ostia, whose rents he distributed for the works mentioned above. He merited God as his defender to such a degree that whoever entered them maliciously, either to affix the marks of the treasury or to collect the rents, was immediately seized by the devil. Whoever acted as a collector of his revenues became a leper.

When the demons were questioned, they answered that, unless Gallicanus had been forced to sacrifice, the collectors of his revenues would not escape these dangers.

Since no one dared to summon Gallicanus to account for this alleged crime, Caesar Julian sent him a message: “Either sacrifice to the gods or leave the borders of Italy.” He immediately abandoned everything and went to Alexandria, where for an entire year he joined the confessors of Christ.

Afterward he withdrew into the desert. There, when the count of the temples, Raucianus, compelled him to sacrifice and Gallicanus refused, Raucianus struck him with a sword in the body and made him a martyr of Christ. Thus he went rejoicing and triumphing to the Lord.

His followers immediately built a basilica in his name. In it, the martyr’s benefits abound from that time onward and continue to this age.

[Col. 0292C] Likewise at Rome, Saint Lucia, virgin, with thirty-two others.

## B. VI DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (26 June)

At Rome, the feast of Saints John and Paul, brothers. The first was chief officer and the second chief secretary of Constantia the virgin, daughter of Constantine. Every day they refreshed companies of Christians from the resources that the most holy virgin Constantia had left them.

This came to Julian’s attention. He sent people to summon them, saying that they ought to attach themselves to him. Among other things, they replied: “Because of your wickedness we have ceased to salute you and have completely withdrawn ourselves from fellowship with your empire. We are not false Christians but true Christians.”

Julian sent them a message: “You ought to consider that, since you were raised in the royal palace, you should not be absent from my side, so that I may have you as the foremost men in my palace. But if I am despised by you, I shall have to act so that I cannot be despised.”

Paul and John said: “We do not do you this injury, that we should place some person or other above you; we place God above you, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them. And we want you to know that we shall never come to greet you, never to worship you, and never to come to your palace.”

Julian said to them: “I grant you ten days’ reprieve. When the tenth day has passed, come to me of your own accord, and I shall regard you as friends; if you do not come, I shall punish you as public enemies.”

The holy men John and Paul invited Christians to come to them. During all ten days they arranged everything they could leave behind and devoted themselves continually, day and night, to almsgiving.

On the eleventh day they were confined inside their own house. Terentianus, a *compiductor* [an uncertain official title], was sent to them with soldiers at the hour of supper. When he entered, he found them praying and said: “Our lord Julian has sent you a little golden image of Jupiter, so that you may worship it and burn incense. If you do not do so, both of you will immediately be struck with the sword. It is not fitting that you, who were raised in the palace, should be publicly killed.”
