John and Paul said: “If Julian is your lord, share his portion. We have no other Lord except the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whom he was not afraid to deny. And because he has once been cast from the face of God, he wants others also to descend with him into destruction.”

Then Terentianus had a pit dug inside their house so that they might be punished without causing public disturbance. He ordered them beheaded, immediately wrapped up, and placed in the pit, while spreading the report that they had been sent into exile by order of the Caesar.

As soon as Julian was killed in the Persian war and the most Christian emperor Jovian had been made emperor, the churches were opened and the Christian religion began to rejoice.

Demons were driven from possessed bodies inside the house of John and Paul, confessing the holy passion of the saints. Thus the only son of Terentianus, who had beheaded them, came into the saints’ house, and the demon cried out through his mouth that Paul and John were burning him.

Then Terentianus came, prostrated himself on his face, and cried out that, being a thoroughly pagan man who did not know what he was doing, he had fulfilled the Caesar’s order. As a result, after he gave his name, he received the grace of Christ on the following Easter day.

Praying and weeping continually, he remained at the place where the bodies of the saints rested, until the saints of God cleansed his son. Terentianus himself wrote down the passion of these martyrs. They suffered on the sixth day before the Kalends of July.

## C. V DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (27 June)

[Note: Ado, *Chronicle*, year 110.]

In Galatia, the blessed Crescentius, disciple of Saint Paul the apostle (2 Timothy 4). Passing into Gaul, he converted many to the faith of Christ by the word of preaching. He settled for several years in the city of Vienne in Gaul and there ordained Zacharias as bishop in his place. Returning to the people to whom he had been specially appointed bishop—the Galatians—he strengthened them in the work of the Lord until the blessed end of his life.

At the Italian city of Tibur, the feast of Saint Symphorosa, wife of the blessed martyr Getulius, with her seven sons: Crescens, Julian, Nemesius, Primitivus, Justinus, Stacteus, and Eugenius. She suffered together with them under the emperor Hadrian.

Hadrian ordered Symphorosa beaten with slaps and then suspended by her hair. When she could not in any way be overcome, he ordered her bound to a stone and thrown into the river. Her brother Eugenius, a chief member of the Tiburtine council, gathered her body and buried it.

When morning came, the emperor ordered seven stakes to be fixed and her sons stretched upon racks there. Crescens was pierced through the throat, Julian through the chest, Nemesius through the heart, and Primitivus through the navel. Justinus was stretched out by his limbs and cut apart at each joint and articulation of the body. Stacteus was fixed to the ground with innumerable spears until he died. Eugenius was split open from the chest down to the lower parts.

On the following day Hadrian ordered their bodies all to be taken away together and thrown into a deep pit. The priests of the sacred rites gave that place the name:

“Of the Seven Violent Dead.”

[Note: *Ad septem biothanatos*. Christians were formerly called *Biothanati* by the pagans as an insult because they exposed themselves so readily to death and departed from life by violent rather than natural death. Below, 3 September: *Biothanata* and *malefica*. Among writers on magical superstition this word is common, as Tertullian shows in *On the Soul*, chapter 57: “Either it is best to be kept here, according to the *Ahoroi*, or worst, according to the *Biothanatoi*, to use the very terms in which the magical author of these opinions speaks.” It is also used among natural philosophers. Servius, on *Aeneid* 4: “Natural philosophers say that the souls of the violently dead are not received into their origin.” The word is frequent among astrologers. Lampridius, in *Heliogabalus*: “It had also been foretold to him by the Syrian priests that he would become a *biothanatos*.” Thus in Julius Firmicus a violent death is called in Greek βιοθάνατος (*biothanatos*) and βιαιοθάνατος (*biaiothanatos*), and βιοθανὴς (*biothanēs*), from βία (*bia*, violence) and θάνατος (*thanatos*, death)—not, as Isidore has it in Book X of the *Etymologies*, letter B: “*Biothanatus*, that is, twice dead.” Rather, it derives from a violent death, whether one inflicts it upon oneself—such a person otherwise being called αὐτοθάνατος (*autothanatos*)—or whether one voluntarily encounters it. Cassian, *Conferences* II, *On Discernment*, chapter 5, concerning the old man Heron, who, deceived by the devil, threw himself into a well: “Therefore, on account of the merits of such great labors and the many years he had endured in the desert, and through the greatest compassion and kindness, those who mourned his death could scarcely obtain from the presbyter and abbot Paphnutius that he should not, being counted among the *biothanatoi*, be judged unworthy even of the memory and offering made for those who rest.”]

The feast of the holy martyrs themselves is on the fifth day before the Kalends of July. Their bodies rest on the Tiburtine Way, at the ninth mile.

On the same day, at Córdoba in Spain, the feast of the holy Zolius and nineteen others.

On that day, the Acts of the Seven Sleepers.

## D. IV DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY (28 June)

[Col. 0294C]

The vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul.

On that day, the feast of Saint Leo the pope.

[Note: [Col. 0294D] *Pontifical*, chapter 81. Leo II. Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 45; and Eusebius, book V, chapters 3, 4, 7, 8, 20, 26. Rufinus, Eusebius, book VI, chapters 4, 5. Rufinus.]

At Lyons in Gaul, the commemoration of Saint Irenaeus, bishop. After Blessed Photinus, nearly ninety years old, had been crowned with martyrdom for Christ, Irenaeus succeeded him. He is also known to have been a disciple of the most blessed priest and martyr Polycarp, and a contemporary of the apostolic age. Later, during the persecution under Severus, he was gloriously crowned with martyrdom together with almost the entire population of his city. He was buried by the presbyter Zacharias in the crypt of the basilica of Saint John the Baptist, beneath the altar. On one side of him Epipodius was buried, and on the other Alexander the martyr. The radiance of this crypt is so venerable that it is believed to signify the merit of martyrdom.

On the same day at Alexandria, the holy martyrs Plutarch, Serenus, Heraclides, Hero, another Serenus, Potamioena, Marcella, and the catechumen Herais [Rhais.], who attained the baptism of martyrdom. Among them Potamioena the virgin shone forth especially. First she endured immense and countless struggles on behalf of her virginity; then, also for martyrdom, she suffered tortures of an extraordinary and unheard-of kind; finally, together with her venerable mother Marcella, consumed by the punishment of fire, she departed from earth for heaven.

**E. III KAL. JULII. (29 June)**

[Col. 0296A]

[Note: [Col. 0295A] See the book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.]

At Rome, the commemoration of Saints Peter and Paul.

**F. PRIDIE KAL. JULII. (30 June)**

[Note: [Col. 0296A] See the book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.]

The commemoration and celebration, once again, of Saint Paul the Apostle.

Likewise, the commemoration of the most blessed Lucina, a disciple of the apostles.

Likewise at the city of Limoges, Saint Martial, bishop and confessor.

**LITANIES TO BE PROCLAIMED. THE MONTH OF JULY HAS THIRTY DAYS; THE MOON ALSO HAS THIRTY.**

[Col. 0295]

**G. KAL. JULII. (1 July)**

[Col. 0295B]

On Mount Hor, the burial of Aaron, the first priest.

On the same day, Saint Monegundis the virgin.

And in the territory of Lyons, at a place now called Vebronna Valley, the burial of the man of God, the most blessed Domitian, abbot. He was the first to practice the eremitical life there; gathering many to himself in the service of God, he founded a monastery. Very renowned for great virtues and glorious miracles, he was gathered to his ancestors in a good old age.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] Ado, in the *Chronicle*, year 101.]

At Vienne, Blessed Martin, the third bishop of that city, sent by the apostles to the aforesaid city.

**A. VI NONAS JULII. (2 July)**

[Col. 0295C] [Note: [Col. 0295D] See the book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.]

At Rome, in the cemetery of Damasus, the commemoration of the holy Processus and Martinianus, who were baptized and instructed by the blessed apostles Peter and Paul; their passion is recorded above in the little book of the apostles.

On the same day, the three holy soldiers who suffered with the blessed apostle Paul.

Likewise on that day, the holy martyrs Aristo, Crescentianus, Eutychianus, Urbanus, Vitalis, Justus, Felicissimus, Felix, Martia, and Symphorosa, all of whom were crowned with glorious martyrdom in Campania.

**B. V NONAS JULII. (3 July)**

[Note: [Col. 0296D] See the book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*. Eusebius, book VII, chapter 28. Rufinus. Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*.]

At Edessa in Mesopotamia, the translation of the body of Saint Thomas the Apostle.

[Col. 0295D] Likewise on that day at Constantinople, the commemoration of Saint Eulogius.

At Laodicea in Syria, Blessed Anatolius, bishop.

Likewise at Neocaesarea in Pontus, the commemoration of Saint Gregory, bishop and martyr, brother of Blessed Athenodorus, bishop. This Gregory the bishop was renowned for his teaching and miracles. At last, there was a certain pond situated in the regions of Pontus, rich in fish, whose catch provided very great revenues to its owners. This property had fallen by lot as an inheritance to two brothers; but greed for money, which overcomes almost all human hearts, violated even their fraternal relationship. Slaughters and wars were set in motion, and human blood was shed for fish.

But God’s providence eventually intervened. Gregory saw the battles and deaths of men, and the brothers raging against one another. When both sides had fallen somewhat silent out of respect for his arrival, he said:

“Do not, my little sons, violate rational souls for the sake of mute creatures; do not dissolve fraternal peace through greed for profit; do not at the same time violate the laws of God and the rights of nature. Come with me to the shore of the deadly pond, and I shall now, by the power of the Lord, release you from every bloody conflict of strife.”

When he had said this, in the sight of everyone he planted the staff he held in his hand into the first waves along the shore. Then, kneeling, he stretched out his hands toward heaven and entreated the Lord. As soon as he had finished praying, the water immediately withdrew and, fleeing in a swifter course—as though ordered by the heavenly presence to depart—returned to its depths, leaving a dry field to the brothers, now reconciled. It is said to remain fertile for crops even to this day.

Again, in a certain narrow place in the countryside, when circumstances required a church to be built, a cliff projecting from the neighboring mountain on the eastern side, and a river flowing past on the other, denied sufficient space for a church. Since there was absolutely no other place in which to build it, he is said to have spent the night in prayer, full of faith. When he earnestly and devoutly petitioned the Lord, at dawn, as the people gathered, the obstructing cliff was found to have withdrawn by precisely as much space as was sought for establishing the church.

Many other deeds of this blessed man are also related, greatly commending his faith and holiness. Among other works that he wrote with great clarity, he also left behind a brief exposition of the Catholic faith:

“One God, the Father of the living Word, of subsisting Wisdom, and of his own Power and Form; the perfect Father of the Perfect, the Father of the only-begotten Son.

“One Lord alone from the one God, the Form and Image of the Godhead, the Word penetrating all things, the Wisdom comprehending all things, and the Power through which the whole creation was able to come into being.

“The true Son of the True, and the Invisible from the Invisible, the Incorruptible from the Incorruptible, the Immortal from the Immortal, the Eternal from the Eternal.

“One Holy Spirit, having his substance from God. He who appeared through the Son is the perfect Image of the perfect Son, the cause of living things, holiness, and the giver of sanctification; through him the one God is known above all and in all, and the Son through all.

“The Trinity is perfect; in majesty, eternity, and kingdom it is neither divided nor separated. Therefore there is in the Trinity neither anything made nor anything serving, nor anything introduced—as though previously it had not subsisted and afterward had entered in. Nor was the Son ever lacking to the Father, nor the Holy Spirit to the Son; rather, the same Trinity always remains unalterable and immutable.”

**C. IV NONAS JULII. (4 July)**

[Col. 0297C]

Of the prophets Hosea and Haggai.

[Note: [Col. 0297D] Gregory of Tours, book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 14.]

At Tours, the translation of Saint Martin, bishop; the establishment of his episcopate; and the dedication of his basilica.

On the same day in Africa, the commemoration of Saint Jucundianus, a martyr drowned in the sea.

And in the territory of the city of Bourges, in the village of Justina, the commemoration of Saint Laurianus, martyr, whose head was carried to Seville in Spain.

At Sirmium, the holy martyrs Innocent and Sabbatia, with thirty others.

**D. III NONAS JULII. (5 July)**

[Col. 0297D]

In Syria, the commemoration of Saint Domitius, martyr, who by his virtues grants many benefits to the inhabitants.

[Note: [Col. 0297D] Concerning her, in the acts of Saint Sebastian, 20 January.]

Likewise at Rome, the commemoration of Saint Zoa, wife of the blessed Nicostratus the martyr. While she was praying at the confession of the blessed apostle Peter, she was seized by the pagans and taken to Naumachia, the patron of the district. He first thrust her into a very dark prison, deprived her for six days of every comfort of light and food; then, on the seventh day, he suspended her by the neck and hair, hanging her body, and, with a dreadful smoke applied beneath her, she surrendered her spirit while confessing the Lord.

**E. PRIDIE NONAS JULII. (6 July)**

[Col. 0298A]

The commemoration of the prophets Isaiah and Joel.

And the Octave of the apostles.

And the first arrival of the blessed apostle Paul in the city of Rome, in the second year of Nero’s reign. After he had already traversed these places and provinces preaching, he was sent forth from Antioch with Barnabas by the Holy Spirit. Having already proclaimed the word of God in Arabia and Cilicia, and in other provinces, he reached Seleucia, Cyprus, Salamis, Paphos, Perga in Pamphylia, Antioch in Pisidia, Iconium, and from there the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra, Derbe, and the entire surrounding region. Returning from there to Antioch in Pisidia, they came to Perga in Pamphylia. [Col. 0298B] From there they returned to Antioch, from which they had been sent. Then, because of the question of circumcision among the Gentiles, they departed for Jerusalem. Afterward they returned again to Antioch.

When disagreement arose between them concerning John, who was surnamed Mark, Paul alone, taking Silas, was commended by the brethren to the grace of God. He traveled through these regions and islands preaching: Syria, Cilicia, Derbe, Lystra, Phrygia and the region of Galatia, Mysia, Troas, Macedonia, Samothrace, Neapolis, Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia, Thessalonica, Beroea, Athens, and Corinth. From there he sailed to Syria, came to Ephesus, and from there to Caesarea and Antioch, and to the region of Galatia and Phrygia.

When he wished to go to Jerusalem from there, the Holy Spirit told him to return to Asia. After traversing the upper regions, he came to Ephesus. From there he departed for Macedonia and visited Philippi, Troas, Assos, Mitylene, and opposite Chios, Samos, Trogylion [Note: It is present in the Greek; it is absent from the Latin text.], Miletus, Cos, Rhodes, and Patara. From there, after seeing Cyprus and leaving it on his left, he crossed over to Syria. From there he came to Tyre, Ptolemais, Caesarea, and Jerusalem. There he was bound by the Jews and handed over to the Gentiles. From there he was sent to Felix, the governor of Caesarea [Note: Concerning him, in the acts of Saint Sebastian, 20 January]. When he appealed to Caesar, he was sent to Rome to that same Caesar to whom he had appealed. He sailed past Sidon, Cyprus—with the city of Thalassa nearby on the island of Mitylene—Syracuse, Rhegium, Puteoli, and Rome. After remaining for two years in free custody, he was released to preach. At that time it is credible that he went on to Spain, since Nero had not yet erupted into the extent of crimes that history relates about him.

At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Tranquillinus, father of the martyrs Mark and Marcellianus. Having believed in the Lord Jesus Christ through the preaching of the blessed Sebastian, on the day of the Octave of the apostles, while he was praying at the confession of Blessed Paul, he was seized by the pagans, stoned, and completed his martyrdom.

On the same day, the burial of the most blessed Goar, confessor.

**F. NONIS JULII. (7 July)**

[Col. 0299A]

[Note: [Col. 0299D] Eusebius, book V, chapter 10; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 36.]

At Alexandria, the commemoration of Saint Pantaenus, an apostolic man adorned with every wisdom. Such was his zeal and love for the word of God that he went forth, fired by faith and devotion, to preach the Gospel of Christ to all the nations hidden in the remotest recesses of the East, and reached even Further India by preaching. There he found Bartholomew, one of the twelve apostles, who had preached the coming of the Lord Jesus according to the Gospel of Matthew. Written in Hebrew letters, this Gospel he brought back with him to Alexandria, where he brought his distinguished life to a blessed end.

[Note: [Col. 0300D] Concerning these, in the acts of Saint Sebastian, 20 January.]

At Rome, the commemoration of the blessed martyrs Nicostratus [Col. 0299B] the First Secretary, Claudius the Records Officer, Castorius, Victorinus, and Symphronianus, whom Blessed Sebastian taught to believe in Christ and whom the presbyter Saint Polycarp baptized. While they were recovering the bodies of the saints along the banks of the Tiber, they were seized and brought before the prefect of the city. The judge was Fabianus, who urged them to sacrifice, dealing with them for ten days through threats and blandishments, but he could not move any of them at all. Then he reported them to the emperors, who ordered them to be tortured a third time. Since they yielded under no compulsion, they ordered them to be thrown headlong into the sea. Thus, bound with enormous weights, they were cast into the waves of the sea, so that in a pure place among the waters they might celebrate the crown of martyrdom.

At Vienne, Bishop Evoldus, through whose efforts the relics of the holy Theban martyrs were brought to the city of Vienne.

**G. VIII IDUS JULII. (8 July)**

In Asia Minor, Saint Aquila and his wife Priscilla, concerning whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles. The blessed apostle Paul stayed and worked with them because they were of the same trade as the Apostle, namely tentmaking, after they had come from the city of Rome to Achaia (Romans 16; 1 Corinthians 16; Acts 18).

In Palestine, the commemoration of Saint Procopius the martyr, who was led from Scythopolis to Caesarea and, at the first confident answer he gave, was beheaded by the enraged judge Fabianus.

**A. VII IDUS JULII. (9 July)**

At Rome, at the ever-flowing Gutta, Saint Zeno and 10,203 others.

In the city of Tyre, the commemoration of the holy Anatolia and Audax, under the emperor Decius. After Anatolia had healed many sick, epileptic, and possessed persons in Picenum, she was taken, at the command of Faustinianus, to the city of Tyre and afflicted with various kinds of blows. Then she was shut up all night with a serpent and remained unharmed. Indeed, she rescued from being devoured by his own serpent the very Marsian, named Audax, who had released it, and converted him to Christ’s martyrdom. After this he was himself placed in custody because of his confession of the truth.

The virgin of Christ herself was also pierced through while standing in prayer with outstretched hands, so that a sword entering through her right side came out through her left. She suffered on the seventh day before the Ides of July; she was buried in the morning by the citizens of Tyre. Audax, however, because he was from the East, was carried there by his wife and children.

On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Cyril, bishop, who, after being thrown into flames, escaped unharmed; the judge, astonished by so great a miracle, released him. When he again preached the word of God eagerly and converted many more effectively to the faith of Christ, the judge, moved by regret, ordered him to be beheaded, and he completed the desired end of martyrdom.

In the city of Martula, Saint Brictius, bishop and confessor. Under the judge Martianus, his mouth was bruised with a stone and he was cruelly tortured on the rack. Remaining steadfast in confessing the Lord, he was thrust into prison. During the night, the city was shaken by a severe earthquake, which killed, among many others, Martianus as well. The confessor of Christ was visited by a holy angel and by the blessed apostle Peter, and strengthened to preach the Gospel. Having won great multitudes of believing peoples for almighty God, he rested in peace. Those standing by saw his soul received into heaven in the form of a snow-white dove.

Likewise in Egypt, Saint Serapion, bishop and confessor.

**B. VI IDUS JULII. (10 July)**

At Rome, the seven brothers, sons of Saint Felicity: Januarius, Felix, Philip, Silvanus, Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis, under Publius, prefect of the city, during the reign of the emperor Antoninus. First they were heard, then sent before various judges to be torn apart by various punishments. Januarius, after being beaten with rods and imprisoned, was killed with leaded clubs. Felix and Philip were slaughtered with cudgels; Silvanus was killed by being thrown from a height. Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis were punished by sentence of death.

On the same day in Africa, the commemoration of Saints Januarius, Marinus, Nabor, and Felix, who were beheaded; their bodies [Col. 0300D] were transferred to Milan.

At Rome, at the tenth milestone, the commemoration of Rufina and Secunda, sisters born to the most illustrious father Asterius and the most illustrious mother Aurelia, under the persecution of Valerian and Gallienus, with Junius Donatus as prefect and Archesilaus as count. Their fiancés, Armentarius and Verinus, abandoned the Christian faith. Therefore, wishing to avoid the mad persuasion of these men, the blessed virgins traveled by wagon to their small estate, which they appeared to possess in the regions of Tuscany.

When Armentarius and Verinus heard this, they informed the count Archesilaus of the reason why [Col. 0301A] they were fleeing the city. Then the most wicked Archesilaus, traveling on horseback with his soldiers, seized the holy virgins on the Flaminian Way at the fourteenth milestone, brought them back to the city of Rome, and presented them to Junius Donatus, the prefect. He ordered them to be placed in custody, separated from one another, and on the third day brought into the tribunal.

Ordering Rufina to enter, he said to her: “Since you were born noble, why have you fallen into lowliness and desire to be a captive in chains rather than enjoy freedom with a husband?”

Rufina replied: “This temporary captivity excludes eternal captivity, and temporary chains dissolve the everlasting bonds of fetters.”

The prefect said: “Cast away these empty and old-womanish tales, and sacrifice to the immortal gods, so that you may enjoy your bridegroom with happiness and reach old age amid the joy of pleasures.”

Rufina replied: “You are persuading me of two useless things and promising one uncertain thing. You say that I ought to sacrifice to idols so that I may perish forever, and afterward take a husband so that I may lose the glory of virginity. After these two utterly contradictory things, you promise that I shall reach old age amid the joy of pleasures, although you yourself are uncertain whether you will reach tomorrow.”

The governor ordered Secunda to be brought in, so that her sister Rufina might be beaten with whips in her sight. When she saw her sister being beaten with whips, she began to cry out to the judge:

“What are you doing, most wicked man and hater of the kingdom of heaven? Why do you glorify my sister and dishonor me?”

The prefect said to her: “As I see it, you are more insane than your sister.”

Secunda replied: “Neither is my sister insane, nor am I mad; rather, we are both Christians, and it is right that together we confess Christ the Lord.”

When they openly professed the faith of the truth, the prefect ordered them to be shut up in a dark place and caused a smoke of dung to be made. When this had been done, that smoke exhaled like incense, and the darkness was overcome as though it were midday.

Again they were ordered to be taken from there and shut up in their baths, and to be thrown into a burning and untempered bath. When, after two hours, those who were to remove their bodies entered, they found the bath inside cold and steaming.

When the prefect heard this, he was astonished and ordered them to be taken and thrown into the middle of the Tiber, with a single stone fastened around the neck of both. They were submerged for nearly half an hour. Then those who had been cast in naked appeared upstream, clothed in dry garments and singing the glory of Christ.

When this was reported to the judge, the prefect said to the count Archesilaus: “These women whom you handed over to me either overcome us by magical art, or holiness truly reigns in them. Therefore, just as you handed them over to me, I return them to you, so that according to your judgment they may either receive sentence or escape.”

Then Archesilaus ordered them to be taken to a forest on the Cornelian Way, at the tenth milestone from the city of Rome, on an estate called Buxus, and there to be struck on the head. Thus he left their unburied [Col. 0302A] bodies.

But the grace of the Lord was not absent from those who believed in Christ, even after their death. For the matron Plautilla, on whose estate this occurred, saw them in a vision seated, adorned with jewels, in a bridal chamber, and saying to her:

“Plautilla, cease from the crimes of idols and abandon impious unbelief; believe in Christ and come into your true inheritance, and, finding our bodies, bury them there.”

Plautilla rose, came to the place, and, finding the bodies of the holy virgins, worshiped and believed. She built a tomb for the virgins to the praise of the Lord Jesus Christ.

**C. V IDUS JULII. (11 July)**

The translation of Saint Benedict, abbot. After his monastery had been devastated by the Gentiles—as he himself had foretold while alive—the body was found by the Lord’s revelation and transferred to Gaul. It was honorably buried in the territory of Orléans, in the monastery called Fleury. The body of his sister, the blessed virgin Scholastica, was likewise transferred and, through the devotion of the faithful, buried in the region of Le Mans. The man of God had seen her soul leaving the body and entering the hidden places of heaven in the form of a dove; and he ordered her body to be placed with his own in a single tomb, so that, since their minds had always been one in God, their bodies too might not be separated by burial [Note: [Col. 0301D] This translation is mentioned in the *Life of Saint Aigulf*, 3 September; *Pontifical*, chapter 12].

On the same day in Lesser Armenia, in the city of Nicopolis, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Januarius and Pelagia, who, tortured for four days on the rack with claws and fragments of pottery, completed their martyrdom.

At Rome, in the Vatican, Saint Pius, pope, who sat in the episcopate for eighteen years. During his time Hermes wrote the book called *The Shepherd*, because an angel appeared to him in the guise of a shepherd.

**D. IV IDUS JULII. (12 July)**

At Aquileia, the commemoration of Saint Hermagoras, the first bishop of that city and a disciple of the blessed Mark the Evangelist (Acts 21).

[Note: [Col. 0302D] *Pontifical*, chapter 3.]

At Cyprus, the commemoration of Blessed Nason [also Jason or Mnason], an ancient disciple of Christ.

At Caesarea, Saint Dii.

At Milan, the translation of the holy martyrs Nabor and [Col. 0302D] Felix.

Likewise on the same day, Saint Cletus, pope, who sat at Rome for twelve years. At the command of the blessed apostle Peter, he ordained twenty-five presbyters in the city of Rome; he was buried beside the body of Blessed Peter.

**E. III IDUS JULII. (13 July)**

Of the prophets Ezra and Joel.

Likewise, the commemoration of Saint Sila [also Silae], the apostle.

[Note: [Col. 0302D] See the book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.]

In Africa, the commemoration of the holy confessors: Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, glorious in faith, virtues, and miracles, and the entire clergy of the same church. Tortured by slaughter and hunger, nearly five hundred of them, or even more—among whom were very many child-lectors—were driven joyfully in the Lord into a cruel exile. Among them were the most distinguished men, the archdeacon named Salutaris and Muritta, second in the ministry. After enduring many punishments for the Catholic confession and becoming confessors a third time, they were ennobled by the title of glorious perseverance in Christ.

**F. PRIDIE IDUS JULII. (14 July)**

[Note: [Col. 0303D] Ado, in the *Chronicle*, year 101.]

At Pontus, the commemoration of Saint Phocas, bishop of the city of Sinope, who under the emperor Trajan and the prefect Africanus overcame prison, chains, iron, and even fire for Christ. His relics are kept in the basilica of the apostles in the Gallic city of Vienne.

**G. IDIBUS JULII. (15 July)**

[Note: [Col. 0303D] Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 1.]

At Nisibis, the commemoration of Saint James, bishop, a man of great virtue, so that through his prayers the city was often delivered from danger. He was one of the confessors under the persecution of Maximian and one of those who at the Council of Nicaea condemned Arius’s perversity by opposing it with the *homoousion*. By order of the emperor Constantine he was buried within the walls of his city for its protection and defense; later, through the zeal of Julian the Apostate, he was taken outside the city and reburied. But soon the same city, deprived of the relics of so great a patron, succumbed to Persian rule.

[Col. 0303C] At Rome, in the Portus district, Eutropius, Zosima, and Bonosa, sisters.

At Alexandria, the commemoration of the holy Philip, Zeno, Marseus, and ten children.

At Carthage, Catulinus the deacon, Januarius, Florentius, Julia, and Justa, who are buried in the basilica of Faustus.

**A. XVII KAL. AUGUSTI. (16 July)**

[Note: [Col. 0303D] Concerning him, in the acts of John and Paul.]

At Ostia, the commemoration of Saint Hilarinus, who, under the persecution of Julian, refused to sacrifice, was beaten with clubs, and suffered martyrdom.

At Antioch in Syria, the commemoration of Saint Eustachius, bishop and confessor, who under the emperor Constantius was exiled to the city of Trajanopolis in Thrace on account of the Catholic faith and there rested.

**B. XVI KAL. AUGUSTI. (17 July)**

At Carthage, the commemoration of the holy martyrs of Scillium: Speratus, Narthalus, Cythinus, Bethurius, Felix, Aquilinus, Lethatius, Januaria, Generosa, Bessia, Donata, and Secunda, under Saturninus the prefect. After their first confession of Christ, they were sent to prison and fastened to a wooden frame; in the morning they were beheaded with the sword. Their relics, together with the bones of Blessed Cyprian and the head of Saint Pantaleon the martyr, were transferred from Africa to Gaul and are venerated at Lyons in the basilica of the most blessed John the Baptist.

**C. XV KAL. AUGUSTI. (18 July)**

At Carthage, the commemoration of Saint Guddena the virgin, who, during the consulship of Plautianus and Geta, at the command of Rufinus the proconsul, was tortured four times at different intervals by being stretched on the rack, tormented by the dreadful tearing of claws, and afflicted for a very long time by the filth of prison; finally she was struck with the sword.

At the city of Metz, Saint Arnulf, bishop, illustrious in holiness and the grace of miracles. Loving the eremitical life, he rested in a blessed end.

**I. XIV KAL. AUGUSTI. (19 July)**

[Col. 0304B] [Note: [Col. 0304D] See the book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.]

The commemoration of Blessed Epaphras.

Likewise on the same day, Saint Arsenius, our father, of whom it is related in the *Sayings of the Elders* that, because of the abundance of his tears, he always kept a handkerchief in his bosom or in his hand for wiping them.

On the same day at Seville in Spain, the commemoration of Saints Justa and Rufina. Seized by the governor Diogenianus, they were tortured by being stretched on the rack and torn by claws; afterward they were thrust into prison and afflicted by hunger and pains. After this the governor ordered them to follow him barefoot wherever he went. At last Justa breathed out her spirit in prison. Her body was thrown into a well and raised by Bishop Gabrinus; it was buried in the cemetery of Seville. Rufina’s [Col. 0304C] neck was broken, and her body was handed over to the fire. Her relics were cared for by the faithful.

**E. XIII KAL. AUGUSTI. (20 July)**

The commemoration of Blessed Joseph, who was surnamed Justus (Acts 1). Together with the blessed Matthias, he was appointed by the apostles to complete the number twelve. But when Matthias filled the place of Judas the betrayer, Blessed Joseph nevertheless continued to serve through preaching and holiness, enduring much persecution from the Jews for the faith of Christ, and rested in Judaea in a most victorious end. It is related of him that he drank poison and suffered no harm from it, because of his faith in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0304D] Eusebius, book III, final chapter.]

At Damascus, the commemoration of the holy Sabinus, [Col. 0304D] Maximinus, Julianus, Macrobius, Cassius, Paula, and ten others.

**F. XII KAL. AUGUSTI. (21 July)**

Of the prophet Daniel.

At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Praxedes the virgin. Together with her sister Potentiana, she was instructed in every chastity and in divine law by their most holy father Pudens, who had been taught the faith by the apostle Paul. After the death of their parents, she devoted herself continually to vigils, prayers, and fasts, and, together with the sister mentioned above, distributed all her patrimony for the support of the poor and the saints of Christ.

At the title which their father Pudens had dedicated in the name of Blessed Pastor, she and her sister worked, together with the council of Blessed Pius, bishop of the apostolic see, to construct a baptismal font, so that their household might be baptized on the holy day of Easter. Blessed Pius washed ninety-six freed persons in the saving waters.

After countless works of piety and the burial of many martyrs—among them the presbyter Blessed Symmetrius with twenty-two others, whom she buried with her own hands at the aforesaid title, after they had passed through the palm of martyrdom to the kingdoms of heaven—the same most blessed virgin departed to the Lord to receive the crown of righteousness, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August. She was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, placed beside her sister and their holy father Pudens.

On the same day in Gaul, in the city of Marseilles, the commemoration of Saint Victor. During the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, although he was a soldier, he refused either to serve as a soldier or to sacrifice to idols. First he was thrust into prison by his tribune, Asterius; but every night an angel led him out to console and visit the sick.

Then, at the command of the prefect Eutychius, his arms were twisted behind him, he was bound with thin straps, and his feet were fastened with a rope; he was dragged through the middle of the city. Afterward he was cruelly beaten with clubs, suspended, and tortured with thongs. When they brought forward an altar on which he was to sacrifice, he could not even look at it, and kicked it from the priest’s hand. The governor ordered his foot to be cut off.

At last, remaining steadfast in his confession, he was put into a millstone of the kind in which scattered grain is crushed by the revolving motion of an animal; thus pulverized, he completed his martyrdom.

Three soldiers suffered with him: Alexander, Felicianus, and Longinus. While they were guarding him in prison during the silence of night, holy angels visited him. Struck dumbfounded by so great a brilliance, they fell at his knees, believed in Christ, and were baptized that same night in the sea. On the following day, before the blessed martyr’s death, they were slaughtered by the sword.

The boy Deutherius too gave up his spirit while praying at his tomb.

**G. XI KAL. AUGUSTI. (22 July)**

[Note: [Col. 0305D] See the book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*.]

The commemoration of Saint Mary Magdalene.

[Col. 0305D] And of the blessed Syntyche, who lies buried at Philippi, concerning whom the blessed apostle Paul writes to the Philippians: “I urge Euodia, and I entreat Syntyche, to be of the same mind in the Lord” (Philippians 4).

At Ancyra in Galatia, the commemoration of Saint Plato the martyr, whose acts are preserved.

**A. X KAL. AUGUSTI. (23 July)**
[Note: [Col. 0306D] See the book on the Feasts of the Apostles.]

At Ravenna, the commemoration of Saint Apollinaris, bishop. He was ordained at Rome by the blessed apostle Peter and sent to Ravenna. When he arrived there, he stayed not far from the city of Ravenna with a certain soldier named Irenaeus, whose son was blind. Brought to him, the boy was given sight when Apollinaris made the sign of the cross; afterward he baptized the boy’s parents. A matron named Thecla, the wife of a military tribune, had been afflicted for many years by a very serious illness. Apollinaris took her hand in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, raised her from her bed healed, and baptized the tribune, his wife, their children, and their household, after they had believed in Christ.

Later, within the city of Ravenna, he celebrated Masses and baptisms for twelve years in the house of the tribune, together with his disciples. He ordained two priests, Adheretus and Calocerus; he appointed Martianus, a most noble man, and Leucadius, a philosopher, as deacons; and he established six clerics. With them he sang psalms day and night. This was reported to the governor Saturninus. He brought Apollinaris forward and set him before the priests of the Capitol at Ravenna. They beat him savagely and, after casting him out toward the sea, left him half alive. His disciples gathered him up and cared for him.

Six months later, he went to the house of Boniface, a most noble man who had lost the power of speech, intending to heal him. First he healed a girl who had an unclean spirit, and then he healed Boniface by releasing his tongue. Five hundred people believed in Christ there. Not many days afterward Apollinaris was seized by pagans, beaten for a very long time with clubs, placed barefoot upon burning coals, and then driven from the city. The Christians had a small hut not far from the wall, where he celebrated Mass; in the sea he baptized people. There, those who feared God supplied him with provisions from their own resources.

After many years he also went to Aemilia to preach the word of the Lord, performing many miracles in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. When he returned, he raised from bodily death the daughter of Rufus the Patrician and consecrated her to Christ as a virgin. Her mother and 304 members of the household, of both sexes, were baptized. The matter concerning the holy man reached Caesar, as did the report that the household of Rufus the Patrician obeyed Christ. Caesar sent Rufus a successor and wrote to the prefect’s deputy of the praetorian prefecture, Massalinus, ordering him either to make Apollinaris submit to the gods or to send him into distant exile.

The deputy summoned him, interrogated him, stripped him, and had him beaten with rods. He ordered boiling water to be poured over his wounds, had him suspended on the rack and tortured, and had his mouth crushed with a stone. Then he ordered him shut in a dreadful prison, weighed down with a very heavy iron burden, and stretched upon a wooden frame. There he was neglected by men but publicly fed by an angel.

On the fourth day the judge had him brought out of prison, chained, placed in a ship, and sent into exile. Three men from his clergy followed him and ministered to him. When all the others perished in a storm and shipwreck, Apollinaris escaped with the clerics and two soldiers, whom he immediately consecrated to Christ after washing them in saving water. Passing beyond Corinth through Mysia, he washed a leper and cleansed his skin in Christ. Then, reaching the bank of the Danube, he joined many people to himself through faith.

When unbelievers sought to kill him, he went down into the regions of Thrace. After spending several days there, he entered a temple of Serapis. In his presence the demon became silent. At last, when questioned, the spirit replied:

“Because a disciple of Peter, the apostle of Jesus Christ, has come here and bound me. Unless he is driven from these regions, I cannot give you answers.”

The blessed Apollinaris was sought and found. After a very long interrogation, he was beaten with clubs and led as far as the sea by the governor of the province. He was placed with his companions aboard a ship bound for Italy. Thus, after three years, he entered Ravenna. A few days later, when a sudden riot arose in the city and pagans attacked, he was bound and brought to the forum. There he was beaten and wounded.

Then the priests of the Capitol arranged for him to be taken to the temple of Apollo. When he arrived there and prayed, the idol fell apart and the temple was destroyed. Seeing this, the pagans shouted, “Let the impious old man be killed!” They handed him over to a judge named Taurus, who had a son born naturally blind. The holy Apollinaris gave the boy sight in the name of Christ, to the amazement of many, who were converted to the Lord.

Apollinaris remained for four years on the estate of the governor Taurus. It was six miles from the city, and Christians gathered there to be taught by him. Whoever was afflicted by any illness was brought to him and healed.

Accordingly, an envious report from the priests of the Capitol against the blessed Apollinaris reached Caesar. Caesar immediately decreed that if anyone insulted the gods with presumptuous speech, he must either make satisfaction or be deprived of the city. This order quickly reached the patrician Demosthenes. He sent out a search party and ordered the holy Apollinaris to be brought before him. After hearing him, Demosthenes placed him secretly in the custody of a centurion who was a Christian, while considering by what tortures he might destroy him. The centurion released him at midnight so that he could escape.

When the pagans learned of this, they pursued him and seized him not far from the gate. He was beaten until he was thought to be dead. His disciples then gathered him up and carried him to a village where lepers lived. He survived there for seven days, continually warning the Church not to depart from the faith of Christ.

Thus the most glorious martyr Apollinaris died in praise of Christ. He was buried outside the wall, and his body was placed underground, sealed in a stone coffin. He had followed the apostle Peter from Antioch and had been sent by that same apostle from Rome to Ravenna. He governed the Church for twenty-eight years, one month, and four days. He suffered his final martyrdom under Caesar Vespasian and the patrician Demosthenes, on the tenth day before the Kalends of August.

**B. Ninth day before the Kalends of August (24 July).**

On the same day, in Italy, at Tyre, which is near Lake Vulsini, the commemoration of Saint Christina, virgin. Believing in Christ, she smashed the golden gods of her father Urbanus, the prefect, and distributed them to the poor. Because of this, at her father’s command, she was struck in the face, torn by scourging, loaded with iron, and thrown into prison. After she had been torn apart for a very long time and with extreme cruelty, she threw pieces of her own flesh into her father’s face.

When she was tied to a wheel, with fire placed beneath it and oil poured over her from above, the escaping flames killed a thousand pagans. She was again handed over to prison, but an angel visited her, healed her, and restored her strength. Then she was thrown into the sea—that is, Lake Vulsini—with a great stone weight, but angelic protection rescued her.

Dion, her father’s successor, again afflicted her with many punishments. But as she prayed, the statue of Apollo, which she had been ordered to worship, was suddenly reduced to ashes. Through this miracle three thousand people were converted to the faith of Christ.

Finally, Julian, the successor of the aforementioned Dion, ordered her to be shot with arrows after she had remained unharmed for five days in a blazing furnace and after serpents sent by a magician had been overcome by faith in Christ. He had first ordered her tongue to be cut out. Thus she completed the course of her martyrdom in the eleventh year of her age.

At Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, at the nineteenth milestone, the commemoration of Saint Vincent.

At Emerita, a city of Spain, the commemoration of Saint Victor, a soldier, who completed his martyrdom after undergoing various tortures together with his two brothers, Stercatius and Antinogenus.

[Note: [Col. 0307D] Concerning these, see the Life of Saint Christopher.]

On the same day, the commemoration of the holy virgins Niceta and Aquila. Converted to Christ through the preaching of Saint Christopher the martyr, they received the palm of martyrdom by decapitation.

And at the city of Amiternum, the commemoration of eighty-three soldiers.

**C. Eighth day before the Kalends of August (25 July).**

[Note: [Col. 0308D] See the book on the Feasts of the Apostles; Prudentius, Hymn 4.]

The commemoration of the blessed apostle James, son of Zebedee.

On the same day, in Lycia, at the city of Samos, Saint Christopher. After being crushed with iron rods and saved by the power of Christ from the flames of a raging fire, he was finally pierced by blows from arrows and completed his martyrdom by decapitation.

In Spain, at the city of Barcelona, Saint Cucufas the martyr. He was originally from the city of Scillium and suffered at Barcelona under the proconsul Galerius, together with Maximian and Rufinus. First he was tortured and beaten most severely; then he was bound with chains, stretched out upon a gridiron, sprinkled with vinegar and mustard, and ordered to be roasted.

When he appeared unharmed by the fire and the balls of flame, the impious judge ordered him led outside the city and thrown again into a great fire. When this fire was extinguished by divine command, he was again bound in iron and returned to custody, where he was comforted by divine radiance.

Again he was cruelly beaten with iron hooks and bullwhips. Finally, after the sentence had been dictated, the judge ordered Cucufas, a rebel against the rulers who refused to sacrifice to the gods, to be struck with the sword. He was led eight miles from Barcelona and put to death with the sword, completing his martyrdom. Christians buried his body with reverence. Later it was transferred and honorably buried not far from the city of Paris, in the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius.

[Note: [Col. 0309D] Concerning him, in the Life of Saint Pantaleon, 28 July.]

On the same day, at Paris, the burial of Saint Germanus, bishop.

At Metz, the commemoration of Saint Glodesindis, virgin.

**D. Seventh day before the Kalends of August (26 July).**

At Rome, at Portus, the commemoration of Saint Hyacinth, under Leontius, a consular official, with Luxurius, chief official of the city of Tarracina, acting as accuser. He was thrown into a fire but could not be harmed in any way. Then he was hurled into a very powerful torrent and was cast out unharmed upon the shore. This was reported to the consul Leontius, who sent an executioner with soldiers to seize him and strike him with the sword.

Then a devout matron named Julia came at night with her servants, gathered his body, and buried it with honor on her estate near Rome, on the seventh day before the Kalends of August.

**E. Sixth day before the Kalends of August (27 July).**

[Note: [Col. 0309D] Concerning him, in the Life of Saint Pantaleon, 28 July.]

At Nicomedia, the commemoration of Saint Hermolaus, priest. Through his teaching, the blessed Pantaleon was converted to the faith. Hermolaus was seized by Maximian and punished with a capital sentence because of his confession of Christ.

On the same day, in Sicily, Saint Simeon the monk.

**F. Fifth day before the Kalends of August (28 July).**

At Nicomedia, the passion of Saint Pantaleon. While studying medicine at the command of Maximian, he was converted to the faith of Christ by the priest Hermolaus. He performed many miracles and brought his father, the senator Eustorgius, under the faith of Christ. For this reason he was seized by Maximian himself and tortured on the rack and by the burning of lamps; but during these torments the Lord appeared to him and refreshed him. At last he completed his martyrdom by a stroke of the sword.

On the same day, at Lyons, Saint Peregrinus, priest, whose holiness is attested by the glory of his miracles.

**G. Fourth day before the Kalends of August (29 July).**

[Note: [Col. 0309D] + This is Felix II, pope. Chapter 37.]

At Rome, on the Aurelian Way, the blessed + Felix, bishop, under Constantius, son of Constantine. The emperor Constantius, approving the counsel of the heretics and of the Arians Valens and Ursacius—for he too was an Arian—was rebaptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia and expelled the holy Felix, bishop of the City, from his episcopal see. A great persecution then arose against the clergy, so that many priests and clerics were killed and crowned with martyrdom.

The holy and most blessed pope Felix, deposed, lived on his small estate on the Portuensis Way. Later, when the heretics took action, he was brought from there to the city and crowned with martyrdom by decapitation on the fourth day before the Ides of November. His body was then taken by priests and clerics and buried in the basilica that he himself had built on the Aurelian Way, at the second milestone, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December. His commemoration is celebrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of August. He sat in the episcopate for one year, three months, and two days.

[Note: [Col. 0309D] Concerning these, see the Acts of Saint Anshimus, 11 May.]

Also on the same day, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrix, during the reigns of Diocletian and Maximian. After many and various tortures, they were ordered to undergo the death sentence. A stone was tied around each of their necks, and they were thrown from the bridge called the Stone Bridge into the waters of the Tiber.

By God’s providence their bodies were found by their blessed sister Beatrix and by the blessed priests Crispus and John. They were buried at a place called the Sixth of Philip, on the Portuensis Way, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

Beatrix, the martyrs’ sister, was staying with the venerable Lucina. A certain neighboring landowner named Lucretius coveted her small property. He therefore had the holy Beatrix seized and brought to sacrifice. Then the blessed Beatrix cried out, “I am a Christian; I do not sacrifice to demons.” She was taken away and handed over to prison custody.

While she freely lived in the name of God, the covetous Lucretius had Beatrix strangled at night. The venerable Lucina buried her beside her holy martyr brothers on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

Afterward Lucretius entered the estate of the saints. While he was dining there, a certain woman was nursing an infant. In the presence of everyone at the feast, the infant cried out: “Hear, Lucretius! You have killed and seized; behold, you have been handed over to the possession of the enemy.” At these words, an evil spirit took possession of Lucretius there at the feast. After being tormented for three hours, he gave up his spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0310D] Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors, chapters 67–68.]

On the same day, the burial of Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes. He came to Britain with Germanus and served in the priesthood for fifty-two years. When King Attila was ravaging Gaul—as is sung in his hymn, “While wars were destroying everything”—Lupus fortified Troyes by his prayers.

**A. Third day before the Kalends of August (30 July).**

[Note: [Col. 0310D] Concerning these, see the Passion of Saint Lawrence, 10 August.]

At Rome, the commemoration of Abdon and Sennen, subordinate kings, under the emperor Decius. Decius ordered them brought before him in the city of Cordula in Persia. He said to them:

“Have you become so foolish that you do not remember that, because you did not worship the gods, you were handed over into the hands of the Romans and into ours?”

The blessed Abdon replied: “Rather, with God’s favor, we have become victors, through the Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns forever.”

At Decius’s command they were bound in chains and shut up in a narrow prison. Then Abdon said to Sennen: “Behold the glory for which we have always hoped.”

After four months Decius came to Rome, bringing the blessed Abdon and Sennen with him in chains. He ordered the entire senate to be summoned and held an assembly in Tellus with the prefect Valerian on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. He ordered Abdon and Sennen, weakened by various punishments, to be brought before him. He said to the senate:

“The gods and goddesses have delivered the fiercest enemies into our hands. Behold the enemies of the state and of the Roman Empire.”

They were brought in adorned with gold and precious stones and bound in chains. The entire senate began to marvel at their appearance. When they steadfastly confessed Christ in the presence of all, Decius, enraged, ordered the prefect Valerian that, if they did not worship the sun-god, they should perish by the bites of wild beasts.

Valerian stripped them and led them before the statue of the Sun beside the amphitheater so that they might sacrifice. But they despised it and spat upon the statue of the Sun. Then Valerian ordered them to be beaten with leaded clubs.

Next they were brought into the amphitheater, and two lions and four bears were released against them. Roaring, the animals came to the saints’ feet, and, without withdrawing, guarded them. Valerian, however, filled with fury, ordered gladiators to enter, kill the blessed subordinate kings, tie their feet, and throw them before the statue of the Sun. Their bodies lay there for three days.

After three days a Christian subdeacon named Quirinus, who lived near the amphitheater, came at night, gathered their bodies, and concealed them in a leaden chest in his house on the third day before the Kalends of August. They remained hidden there until the time of Constantine. Then the blessed martyrs revealed themselves; they were taken up and transferred to the cemetery of Pontianus.

On the same day in Africa, in the city of Tuburbo Lucernaria, the commemoration of the holy virgins Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda. They suffered during the persecution of Gallienus under the judge Anolinus.

After conducting an interrogation, Anolinus postponed the hearing and ordered the blessed virgins and sisters Maxima and Donatilla to be led to the city of Tuburbum. He ordered that neither bread nor water be given them, but that they be made to drink vinegar and gall.

Seeing the confidence of the most blessed women, he burned with anger and ordered them to be forced to walk. There was a girl named Secunda, twelve years old, who was staying in the upper part of her house. Although many marriage proposals were offered to her, she rejected them all and loved the one God.

Inflamed by the Spirit of God, she saw her fellow martyrs Maxima and Donatilla passing by. A balcony was situated in the upper part of her house, where she was standing. Considering the beauty of the holy virgins with the eyes of faith, she reflected and resolved to attain a similar grace.

To ensure that no one would prevent her from descending honorably and to avoid every impediment, she gave no thought to wealth or family and paid no attention to her earthly father. Leaving everything behind, she sought the one God, author of chastity, whom she possessed and held forever.

As the blessed martyrs were leaving and proceeding onward, Secunda hurried after them, crying out: “Do not leave me behind; I will come with you.” She entered the city of Tuburbum together with them.

On the following day, at the third hour, the proconsul Anolinus took his seat on the tribunal. He ordered Maxima and Donatilla brought before him and thrown into the tortures. While they were being beaten, he ordered lime to be scattered over their wounds and rubbed in. Then he ordered them stretched and tortured on the rack.

[Note: [Col. 0311D] And “stativa” was offered to them for drinking. Thus all the manuscripts read. The printed edition up to this point has: “and a statue was offered for libation,” which is spurious and contrived. It means *aqua stativa* (“standing water”), called *stagnans* by Pliny and *reses* by Varro.]

He then ordered standing water to be offered them for drinking; afterward they were laid upon a gridiron and burning coals, and glowing embers were heaped upon their heads. Later they were placed in the theater before the shrine and trampled by everyone.

It was then reported officially that another girl named Secunda was with them. The proconsul Anolinus ordered her brought before his tribunal. When she appeared, he said: “Are you a Christian or a pagan?”

Secunda replied: “I am a Christian.”

Immediately Anolinus condemned her, together with Maxima and Donatilla, to the beasts and ordered the three women, bound in chains, brought before the people for the spectacle. As they were being led in, they kissed one another in the middle of the arena so that they might complete their martyrdom in peace.

A very fierce and savage bear was immediately released upon them, but it became gentle and licked their feet rather than biting them. Anolinus was angry because, while he was raging, he saw the beasts become tame. He conferred with the council and read the sentence from the tablet:

“It is our decision that Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda, persisting in their superstition, who have endured various punishments, been exposed to beasts, and refused to sacrifice to our gods, be put to death by the sword.”

Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda said: “Thanks be to God.”

And they were brought to completion on the third day before the Kalends of August.

**B. Eve of the Kalends of August (31 July).**

At Caesarea, the passion of Saint Fabius the martyr. When he refused to carry the standards of the governor, he was first thrust into prison for several days. Then he was brought out and made to stand before the tribunal. Questioned once and again, he persevered in the confession of Christ, and at once the furious judge condemned him to death.

Afterward the judge ordered his unburied body to be guarded. After three days it was sewn into a net and submerged in the depths of the sea, with the head in one place and the corpse in another. But by the Lord’s power the net was torn apart, the limbs were reunited with the head, and the neck was joined to the shoulders, bearing the marks of his passion.

Thus restored to wholeness, the body was carried by a gentler wave to the shore of Cartenarium [or Cartemianum, commonly Cartenitanum], where the faithful buried it with fitting honor.

At Auxerre, Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor.

**LITANIES TO BE ANNOUNCED. AUGUST HAS THIRTY-ONE DAYS; THE MOON, TWENTY-NINE.**

[Col. 0313]

**C. Kalends of August (1 August).**

[Col. 0313A]

[Note: [Col. 0313D] 2 Maccabees 7; Jerome, On Illustrious Men, chapter 96.]

At Rome, at Saint Peter in Chains.

At Antioch, the commemoration of the holy Maccabees.

In Italy, at the city of Vercelli, the blessed Eusebius, bishop and confessor. Because of his confession of the faith, he was exiled by the emperor Constantius to Scythopolis and from there to Cappadocia. Under the emperor Julian he returned to his own church. Finally, when the Arians were persecuting him, he suffered martyrdom.

In Arabia, at the city of Philadelphia, the holy martyrs Cyril, Aquila, Peter, Domianus, Rufus, and Menander, crowned on one day.

[Note: [Col. 0313D] Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 92.]

In Spain, at the city of Gerona, the commemoration of Saint Felix the martyr. He was originally from the city of Scillium. When persecution began to be carried out against Christians in Spain, he boarded a merchant ship and hurried there out of love for martyrdom.

After preaching the word of God for some time at Barcelona, Emporiae, and Gerona, strengthening many in the faith, and as his fame spread far and wide, he was suddenly seized by Rufinus, an official, at the command of Dacianus.

When he confessed the name of Christ with complete confidence, he was first beaten with clubs and thrown into the lowest part of the prison. Then, with his hands and feet bound, deprived of food and drink, he was thrown into a filthy place. Afterward he was bound with even heavier chains, dragged through all the streets by untamed mules, and almost torn to pieces.

Then he was sent to prison. During the night an angel visited and healed him, and at daybreak he was recalled to the contests. His skin was torn with hooks, and he was hung upside down from the third hour until evening. He felt no pain at all.

Then Rufinus ordered him thrust into prison, where a great radiance shone throughout the night. The voices of angels singing psalms were also heard. When the guards reported this to Rufinus, he ordered Felix’s hands tied behind his back and had him sunk into the depths of the sea.

Immediately his bonds broke. With angels holding his hands, he walked across the waves and reached the shore. Rufinus then ordered his skin torn away again with hooks and afterward his flesh lacerated to the bone. The wounds were reopened with further wounds until he gave his unconquered spirit back to Christ.

His body was placed at Gerona in the tomb that he had prepared for himself, on the Nones of August.

**D. Fourth day before the Nones of August (2 August).**

[Col. 0313D]

[Note: [Col. 0314D] Pontifical Book, chapter 24.]

At Rome, in the cemetery of Callistus, the commemoration of Saint Stephen, [Col. 0314A] pope and martyr, under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus.

When a savage persecution was raging, the blessed Stephen gathered all his clergy and urged them to receive the crown of martyrdom eagerly for Christ. He had ordained three priests, seven deacons, and sixteen clerics, with whom he continually taught about the kingdom of God.

Through the provision of divine grace, many honorable men from among the pagans came to him to be baptized. Among them were the tribune Nemesius with his entire household and his daughter Lucilla, who had been given sight through the blessed Stephen; another tribune, Olympius, with his wife Exuperia and his son Theodulus; and all those in Olympius’s household who believed. They later earned martyrdom through a glorious confession.

Stephen celebrated Masses and held assemblies in the crypts of the martyrs. It happened that Valerian and Gallienus, persecutors of the name of Christ, sought the blessed Stephen with the utmost diligence so that they might afflict him and his clerics with various punishments.

They therefore sent a multitude of soldiers and seized him together with a multitude of priests, deacons, and clerics. When he came before Valerian’s tribunal, he entered alone.

Valerian said to him: “Are you Stephen, who is trying to overturn the state and, through evil persuasion and exhortation, urging the people to abandon the worship of the gods?”

The blessed Stephen replied: “I do not overturn the state. Rather, I urge people, abandoning the demons worshiped in idols, to return to the living and true God, the creator of heaven and earth, and to recognize that Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is God. Together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he alone is eternal, so that they may not perish with the devil in everlasting destruction.”

Then Valerian ordered Stephen taken to the temple of Mars and, if he did not consent to worship the abominable statue of Mars, sentenced and beheaded there.

The blessed Stephen was led by the soldiers outside the walls, through the Appian Gate, to the temple. Raising his eyes to heaven, he said:

“Lord God, Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, who destroyed the tower of Babylon’s confusion, destroy now also this place, where through devilish superstition and the worship of idols the souls of peoples are perishing.”

Immediately, with a thunderous crash and terrifying flashes of lightning, the greater part of the temple collapsed, and the frightened soldiers fled.

The blessed Stephen went with all the Christians to the cemetery of Saint Lucina. After consoling them with many words, he offered sacrifice to almighty God on their behalf.

When Valerian heard what had happened, he sent many soldiers to punish the blessed Stephen. They came and found him offering sacrifice to God. He was fearless and steadfast before the solemn rites of the altar and was completing what he had begun. In that same place, in his own seat, they beheaded him on the fourth day before the Nones of August.

The Christian people buried his body in the same crypt together with the seat where he had been standing when his blood was poured out, at the place now called the cemetery of Callistus. He sat in the episcopate for seven years, five months, and two days.

On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Theodota with her three sons in the province of Bithynia, at the city of Nicaea, during the reign of Diocletian, under the consular official Nicetius and Count Leocadius.

For many days the latter tried, through persuasion and threats, to compel Theodota to marry him. But when the holy woman refused in every way, he sent her, bound in iron with her sons, to Nicetius, the consular official of Bithynia.

Nicetius had her firstborn son, Evodius, beaten with clubs in his mother’s presence because he confessed Christ with confidence. His devout mother cried out to him: “Do not fear these blows, my son; through them you will reach the eternal joys of Christ.”

Then the consular official Nicetius ordered a certain Hirtacus to seize the blessed Theodota, first to violate her and afterward to place her among the public prostitutes. When Hirtacus tried to hold her, blood began to flow violently from his nostrils. Crying out, he said to Nicetius: “A handsome young man, dressed in golden garments, is standing beside her; from his hand I received a blow upon my nose.”

Therefore the consular official Nicetius ordered a great fire to be kindled and the blessed Theodota and her three sons to be thrown into it. Giving thanks to God, she said:

“Blessed is the name of your mercy, Lord, who have neither separated me from my sons in this world, nor allowed us to be divided in the confession of your name, nor permitted us to be separated in martyrdom.”

Thus Saint Theodota was brought to completion together with her three sons, on the fourth day before the Nones of August.

**E. Third day before the Nones of August (3 August).**

[Note: [Col. 0315D] Gennadius, On Illustrious Men, chapter 46.]

At Jerusalem, the discovery of the body of the most blessed Stephen, the protomartyr, and of the saints Gamaliel, Nicodemus, and Abibon, as it was revealed by the Lord to the blessed priest Lucian in the seventh year of the emperor Honorius.

While Lucian was resting on his bed in the basilica of the baptistery, at dawn on Friday, around the third hour of the night, while he was still awake, he seemed to fall into an ecstasy of mind. He saw an elderly man, tall in stature and handsome in appearance, with a long beard, dressed in white and wrapped in a cloak whose edges were woven as though with golden crosses. He wore boots gilded on the surface and held in his hand a golden staff. Touching Lucian with it, he said that he was Gamaliel, who had educated the apostle Paul.

Among other things he said to him: “With the utmost care, uncover our tombs, because we have been buried improperly in a despised place.”

When Lucian asked who the others were who were with him, Gamaliel replied:

“One is the lord Stephen, overwhelmed with stones by the Jews at Jerusalem for the faith of Christ. By order of the priests he was left outside the gate, on the road leading to Cedron, to be devoured by beasts and birds. But the one to whom that martyr preserved an unbroken faith completely prevented this.

“When the unbelief of the Jews began to dissipate, I summoned a crowd of religious men and called together an assembly of the faithful. Addressing them with gentleness and persuasion, I said: ‘I beseech you, dearest brothers, fear no one. Gather the holy relic of the blessed Stephen, carry it to our little village, called Caphargamala, situated at the twenty-second milestone from the city of Jerusalem, and bury it according to custom with a solemn funeral.’ And this was done.

“The one who lies in the tomb adjoining this one is my nephew Nicodemus. He heard from the Savior that he must be born again of water and the Holy Spirit, and was soon baptized by Peter and John. Later, the leaders of the priests became angry with him and, stripping him of the honor of his office, tried to hand him over to death. But restrained by our favor and the right of kinship, they did not do so.

“Nevertheless, after expelling him from the city, they plundered all his possessions and, inflicting many blows upon him, left him half alive. I gathered him too and ordered that he be cared for. He survived for a short time, then departed into the rest he desired. After the funeral rites had been performed, I ordered him buried at the feet of the protomartyr.

“The third man, who shares with me this place of rest, is my son Abibas. At the age of twenty, he believed together with me in Christ Jesus and was washed by the water of the eternal fountain by the apostles mentioned above. Since he was thoroughly educated in the teaching of the Law, he devoted himself diligently to the temple of God with Paul, meditating on divine commands. By the protection of heaven he was freed from that vice to which the human race is especially prone, and he rested in peace in this resolve of chastity. I lie here with them.

“My wife Ethna and our firstborn son Selemias, unwilling to believe in Christ and disparaging the unity of religion and faith, were buried on the estate of Capharselemia. Nevertheless, when you begin to dig where we have been laid, you will find their tombs empty, because they were not worthy to be buried with us.”

When the venerable priest asked the man, “Where shall we find you, lord?” he replied:

“In our little field, which in Syriac is called Delamgabrica and also Debatthalia, that is, ‘the possession of the men of God’ or ‘of the blessed.’”

This same vision appeared to him again and again.

The venerable priest arose and went into the city to the bishop John, about whom he had been warned in the vision. When he had recounted the sequence of the vision to John and his clergy in detail, John shed tears of joy and blessed the Lord. Since everything had truly been verified, the blessed bishop immediately sent word to the brothers and fellow bishops of the neighboring cities.

When they arrived and began to dig at the designated place, an earthquake immediately occurred. A sweetness of immense fragrance spread from the earth, greater than any generation of human beings remembered having sensed at that time, so that they thought themselves present amid the delights of paradise. At that very hour, seventy-three souls were healed of various illnesses through the sweetness of the fragrance.

At that time witnesses to the miracles were present with the blessed John: Eustominus of Sebaste and Eleutherius of Jericho, bishops, together with a most holy company of clerics. They kissed the relic of the blessed Stephen, closed the place, and returned joyfully to their own homes.

After a few days they carried the body of the protomartyr Stephen to Zion, to the holy church where he had been ordained archdeacon, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, with psalms and hymns.

At that time there was an immense and prolonged drought. A sufficient rain of heavenly mercy descended, moistening and abundantly irrigating the thirsty earth. No one doubts that this was granted to the endangered people through the merits of the blessed martyr Stephen.

The priest Lucian wrote this revelation in Greek for all the churches. The priest Avitus, a Spaniard, translated it into Latin and delivered it through the priest Orosius to the churches of the West. Orosius also first brought the relics of the blessed Stephen to the West, where innumerable miracles were performed at the memorials of the holy martyr. The blessed Augustine records many of them in his books *On the City of God*.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] It is extant in volume 10 of Saint Augustine. Sigebert, *Chronicle*, year 418. Augustine, *On the City of God*, book XXII, chapter 8.]

At Constantinople, the commemoration of Saint Hermellus the martyr.

**F. Eve of the Nones of August (4 August).**

[Col. 0317C]

The commemoration of the blessed Aristarchus, disciple of the holy apostle Paul.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] See the book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*. Concerning this, see the *Life of Stephen* [Col. 0318D] of the pope. 2 August.]

Also at Rome, in the Arenarian crypt, the feast of the martyr Tertullinus, whom the blessed pontiff Stephen baptized and ordained a presbyter *in albis*. Among other admonitions he particularly commended this to him: “Brother,” he said, “make it your care to seek out the bodies of various holy martyrs.” Two days after his ordination, he was arrested by the prefect Marcus and brought before the emperor Valerian. The emperor ordered him stretched out and beaten with clubs. While he was being impiously beaten, he cried out: “I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus Christ, who have not separated me from my lord Olympius, your servant, who went before me, having completed his martyrdom.” While he was saying this amid the blows, Valerian ordered that fire be placed beneath his sides. Since he continued joyfully and steadfastly, saying, “Do quickly, wretch, what you are doing, so that from this fire you may offer me, though a sinner, as a sacrifice to Christ for his name’s sake,” Valerian ordered him lifted up and handed over to the prefect Sapricius. Sapricius first ordered his mouth to be battered with stones; then he ordered him stretched on the rack and tortured for a long time with cords; thereafter he ordered him burned with fire. Since, strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he steadfastly confessed Christ the Lord, this deed was reported to the tyrant Valerian. Valerian [Col. 0318A] sent back word that, after sentence had been pronounced, his head should be cut off. Then Sapricius ordered him taken down from the rack and led along the Latin Way to the second milestone, where he was beheaded. The pontiff Saint Stephen gathered his body with the clergy, buried it in the same place, and gave praise to God with hymns, in the Arenarian crypt, on the second day before the Kalends of August. A solemn gathering is held there on the eleventh day before the Nones of August.

At Lyons, the arrival of the body of Saint Justus, bishop, from the wilderness. After he had lived for several years in the wilderness a life close to that of the angels, and a worthy end had come to such labors, he ascended to the kingdom of heaven and gained a blessed reward. The venerable citizens of the city of Lyons sought out his holy body and brought it back with joy and reverence from distant parts of the earth; they buried it in the city of his priestly office.

G. THE NONES OF AUGUST. (5 August)

[Col. 0318B]

[Note: [Col. 0318D] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapters 7 and 9.]

In the province of Rhaetia, in the city of Augsburg, the feast of Saint Afra, martyr. Although she had been a pagan and a prostitute, she was converted to the faith through the teaching of Saint Narcissus, bishop, and was baptized with her entire household; for her confession of the Lord she was handed over to the fire.

At Autun, the feast of Saint Cassian, bishop.

A. THE EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF AUGUST. (6 August)

[Note: [Col. 0318D] Concerning these matters, see the *Life of Saint Laurence*, 10 August.]

At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus, the feast of Saint Sixtus, bishop and martyr; and in the cemetery of Praetextatus, that of the holy deacons Felicissimus and Agapitus, his companions, under the emperor Decius and the prefect Valerian. Valerian seized the most blessed old man Sixtus, bishop of Rome, together with all his clergy, and shut them in public custody, where they remained confined for many days.

It happened that Caesar Decius and the prefect Valerian ordered the blessed bishop Sixtus, together with his clergy, to be brought before them at night inside the city, at Tellus. Caesar Decius said to him: “Do you know why you have been arrested and brought before us in a public hearing?” Sixtus replied: “I know, and I know it well.” Decius said: “Then, if you know, make sure that everyone knows, and you will live, and your clergy will increase.” The blessed Sixtus replied: “Indeed, I have done and am doing what will cause my clergy to increase.” Decius said to him: “Then sacrifice to the immortal gods and become chief of the priests.” To this the holy bishop replied: “I have always sacrificed, and I sacrifice, to God the almighty Father, [Col. 0318D] and to the Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, and to the Holy Spirit, a pure and spotless offering.”
