Then, by Decius’s command, soldiers led him to the temple of Mars, so that he might be defiled by sacrifices. But because he refused to sacrifice, they shut him in private custody with the two deacons Felicissimus and Agapitus.

As he was being led away, the blessed archdeacon Laurence began to address him in these words: “Where are you going without your son, Father? Where are you hurrying, holy priest, without your deacon? You have never been accustomed to offer sacrifice without a minister. What have I done to displease you, Father? Have you judged me degenerate? At least test whether you have chosen a suitable minister. To the one to whom you entrusted the consecration of the Lord’s blood, to the one to whom you entrusted participation in the completion of the sacraments, do you deny participation in your blood? Beware lest your judgment be endangered while courage is being praised. The rejection of a disciple is the loss of a teacher. What is more, illustrious men often conquer more gloriously through the contests of their disciples than through their own. Abraham offered his son (Genesis 22); Peter sent Stephen ahead. And you, Father, show your strength in your son; offer the one whom you have instructed, so that, secure in the noble company of your judgment, you may reach the crown.”

Then the blessed Sixtus said: “I am not abandoning you, my son, nor am I deserting you, but greater contests are owed to you. We, like old men, are undertaking the course of a lighter combat; you, like a young man, have a more glorious triumph over the tyrant awaiting you. As soon as you come, stop weeping; after three days you will follow me. Between priest and Levite, this intervening number is fitting. It was not yours to conquer under your teacher, as though you were seeking an assistant. Why do you seek a share in my suffering? I leave you the whole inheritance. Why do you seek my presence? Elijah left Elisha (2 Kings 2), but he did not take away his power.”

The blessed Sixtus also said to the blessed Laurence: “Take the resources or treasures of the Church and distribute them among the poor, wherever you think fit.”

Having received this authority, the blessed Laurence began carefully searching through the districts for wherever holy clerics or poor people were hidden. Carrying the treasures, he ministered to each according to his need.

After this, therefore, the blessed Sixtus [Col. 0319C] was brought back to Tellus, so that the deacons Felicissimus and Agapitus might hear the proceedings with him. When Decius and Valerian were seated, the blessed Sixtus was presented before them. Decius, filled with anger, said to him: “We are consulting for your old age. Obey our commands and sacrifice.” The blessed Sixtus replied: “Wretch, look after yourself, and do not blaspheme; rather, repent of the blood of the saints that you have shed.”

Then, at Valerian’s urging, Decius ordered them taken to the temple of Mars and, if they refused to sacrifice, beheaded in that same place. When they had been led outside the wall at the Appian Gate, the blessed Sixtus said to the temple of Mars: “May Christ, the Son of the living God, destroy you.” When all the Christians had replied, “Amen,” part of the temple suddenly fell and was shattered.

Then the blessed Laurence [Col. 0319D] began to cry out: “Do not abandon me, holy Father, for I have already spent your treasures, which you entrusted to me.” When the soldiers heard about the treasures, they seized the blessed archdeacon Laurence. But they led the holy Sixtus, Felicissimus, and Agapitus to the slope of Mars, before the temple, and there they were beheaded on the eighth day before the Ides of August.

At night the clergy and a very large number of Christians came, gathered the bodies of the saints, and buried the blessed Sixtus in a crypt in the cemetery of Callistus on the same road. They buried the holy martyrs Felicissimus and Agapitus in the cemetery of Praetextatus. Four others were also beheaded with them, as is read in the *Pontifical Acts*: the subdeacons Januarius, Vincentius, and Stephanus. The blessed Quartus also suffered with them, as the blessed Cyprian writes (*Letter* 82).

This blessed Sixtus was born at Athens and was educated there. At first he was a philosopher; afterward he became a disciple of Christ. He held the episcopate for one year, ten months, and twenty-three days.

[Note: [Col. 0319D] Eulogius, book II, chapter 11.]

On the same day in Spain, in the city of Complutum, the feast of the holy brothers Justus and Pastor. While they were still boys being instructed in letters, they threw down their school tablets and voluntarily ran to martyrdom. Soon ordered to be held by a deacon, they strengthened each other with the firmest mutual exhortations; they were led outside the city and slaughtered by executioners in the Field of Praise. There they also rest in the basilica bearing their name.

B. THE SEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF AUGUST. (7 August)

[Col. 0320B]

[Note: [Col. 0320D] Gregory, *Dialogues*, book I, chapters 6–7.]

In Tuscany, in the city of Arezzo, the feast of Saint Donatus, bishop and martyr. He was brought up by the priest Saint Pigmeneus and instructed, in the church of the blessed Shepherd, most thoroughly not only in divine learning but also in secular letters. Julian grew up with him and was ordained a subdeacon; afterward, having been rejected from that rank and rendered useless, he aspired to imperial power. At that time he imprisoned the blessed Pigmeneus at Rome and killed Donatus’s holy father and mother with the sword.

Donatus, who was a lector, fled to the city of Arezzo and lived with Hilarinus, a most illustrious monk, serving God continually with prayers and fasts.

It happened that a gentile and pagan woman named Surana, blind in her eyes and truly blind in heart, came with her only son, named Herculeus, seeking the cell of the blessed Hilarinus, with whom the holy man lived. Hilarinus and Donatus instructed her in the faith of Christ and brought her to the blessed bishop Satyrus. When he accepted her faith, he gave thanks to God and imposed a fast upon her, so that she might humble herself in sackcloth and ashes. Then he catechized and baptized both her and her son.

Immediately Surana’s eyes were opened, and she began to cry out: “Truly Christ is God, who has illuminated my eyes.”

When Apronianus heard of this, not long afterward he brought his demon-possessed son to the blessed Donatus. When Donatus prayed together with Bishop Satyrus and Hilarinus, the demon was expelled and left the boy healthy.

Not long afterward, a certain man named Eustasius, governor of Tuscany and collector of the treasury, was detained elsewhere on business. When enemies arrived, his wife Euphrosina hid the treasury money; a few days later, while her husband was still absent, she died. When her husband later returned, he found his wife dead and the treasury money concealed from him. He was greatly distressed by this; and since the authorities were also planning punishments for him because of the missing money, Eustasius fled and came to the blessed Satyrus and Donatus, to whom he disclosed his anguish.

Then Donatus stood over his wife’s tomb and cried out in a loud voice: “Euphrosina, by Christ crucified I adjure you to tell us what happened to the treasury money, because your husband is being severely harassed by the collectors on its account.”

She immediately answered from the tomb: “The money you seek lies buried at the entrance of the house.”

The money was recovered, and Eustasius was freed from the charge brought against him.

After the blessed Satyrus had been gathered to his fathers, the blessed Donatus assumed the priesthood in his place. One day, after he had celebrated Mass for the people, and the people had reverently refreshed themselves with Christ’s body and blood, a deacon named Antimus was distributing the sacred blood of Christ. Suddenly, pushed by pagans, he fell and shattered the holy chalice. Both he and the people of Christ became very sorrowful.

The Lord immediately revealed this sorrow through the blessed Donatus. The fragments of the Lord’s chalice were collected and brought to the holy man. Weeping, he received them; after prayer, he restored the vessel to its original form.

Struck by this sign, the pagans confessed Christ’s divinity together with the Christians, and about seventy-nine souls, believing in Christ, were saved through baptism.

After glorifying his saint with many signs, the Lord led him onward to the crown of martyrdom. Finally, during the reign of the emperor Julian, he was arrested by Quadratianus, the Augustal prefect, together with Hilarinus, the man of God, and was ordered to sacrifice to idols.

When Donatus faithfully resisted, Quadratianus ordered his mouth battered with stones. He ordered the monk Hilarinus to be beaten with clubs in Donatus’s presence until he gave up his spirit; then he ordered the blessed Donatus shut in prison.

While Donatus was there and the Lord was performing innumerable miracles through his servant, Quadratianus sent for him and struck him with the sword, on the seventh day before the Ides of August. Christians buried his body with veneration near the city. The bones of the martyr Hilarinus are preserved, buried in the city of Ostia.

At Rome, the holy martyrs Peter and Juliana, with eighteen others.

At Milan, Saint Faustinus [another reading: Faustus], martyred in the time of Aurelius Commodus.

C. THE SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF AUGUST. (8 August)

At Rome, on the Ostian Way, at the seventh milestone [Note: [Col. 0321D] The translation concerning Cyriacus and his companions is found in the *Acts of Pope Marcellus*, 16 January], the feast of Saint Cyriacus, martyr.

After Augustus Maximinus ordered that all who were in custody, together with the deacon Cyriacus, should be beheaded, and after twenty-one persons of both sexes had been beheaded indiscriminately on the Salarian Way, outside the walls, within the Baths of Sallust, the priest John gathered their bodies at night and buried them on the same road, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April.

Eight days later, the blessed bishop Marcellus came with the very Christian matron Lucina. They embalmed the bodies of the saints with spices and linen cloths; then they lifted them up and transferred them to his estate on the Ostian Way, seven miles from the city of Rome. With his own hand he placed them in stone sarcophagi, together with the blessed Cyriacus, on the eighth day of the month of August.

Carpasius, the vicar, then requested the house of the blessed Cyriacus, which Augustus Diocletian had given him, and Augustus Maximinus immediately granted it to him. When Carpasius entered it, he found the place where Saint Cyriacus had built a fountain, which Saint Marcellus the bishop had consecrated, where Saint Cyriacus baptized those who came to the faith.

At that place Carpasius built a bath for himself. While Carpasius and nineteen others were bathing and being served a meal, and were mocking the Christian faith, they suddenly fell down and died.

The sufferings of the blessed martyrs—Cyriacus, Largus, and Smaragdus—are recorded in their proper places in the present Calendar, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, under Augustus Maximinus and the vicar Carpasius.

[Col. 0322B]

At Vienne, a city of Gaul, the feast of Saint Severus, priest and confessor. As his acts testify, he was an Indian by nationality, fervent in the faith of Christ. Having undertaken a most arduous pilgrimage for the purpose of preaching the Gospel, he eventually reached the aforementioned city and converted an immense multitude of pagans to the faith of Christ by word and miracles. When he had rested in peace, he was buried in the basilica of Saint Stephen. Famous for his signs, he is honored with wondrous veneration by the faithful.

D. THE FIFTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF AUGUST. (9 August)

[Note: [Col. 0322D] Concerning him, see the *Life of Saint Laurence*.]

The vigil of Saint Laurence.

On the same day, at Rome, Saint Romanus, a soldier. Moved to repentance by the confession of Saint Laurence, he asked Laurence to baptize him; and soon, by Decius’s order, he was beaten with clubs and beheaded.

E. THE FOURTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF AUGUST. (10 August)

At Rome, the feast of Saint Laurence, archdeacon and martyr, under Decius. As he proceeded toward the crown of martyrdom, the blessed Sixtus entrusted him with all the resources and treasures of the Church.

Laurence came to the Caelian Hill, where there was a certain widow who had lived in widowhood for thirty-two years. Many Christians, priests, and clerics were concealed in her house. He took the garments and treasures of the Church, began distributing them, and washed the feet of all the Christians.

The widow Cyriaca fell at his feet and said: “By Christ I adjure you to place your hands upon my head, because I suffer from many ailments of the head.”

The blessed Laurence made the sign of the cross, placed his hands upon the widow’s head, and laid upon it the linen cloth with which he had wiped the feet of the saints.

As he passed through a district called Canarius, he found many Christians gathered in the house of the Christian Narcissus. He washed everyone’s feet and gave them some of the treasure.

In the same house there was a blind man named Crescentius, who began to ask the blessed deacon to place his hand upon his eyes. Then the blessed Laurence said with tears: “May our Lord Jesus Christ, who opened the eyes of the man born blind, himself illuminate you.” After he had made the sign of the cross, the man’s eyes were opened.

When the blessed Sixtus was already being led away with the two deacons to complete his martyrdom, and the blessed Laurence came crying out, “Do not abandon me, holy Father” (John 17:24), because he had already spent the treasures that Sixtus had entrusted to him, the soldiers seized him and handed him over to the tribune Parthenius.

Parthenius reported to Decius that Laurence, the archdeacon of Sixtus, who possessed hidden treasures, was being held in custody. Decius rejoiced, had him brought before him, and after hearing him, handed him over to the prefect Valerian. Valerian in turn entrusted him to a certain Hippolytus, who shut him up with many others.

There was there a blind man named Lucillus. Saint Laurence said to him: “Believe in the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and be baptized, and he will illuminate you.”

Lucillus replied: “I have always desired to be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.”

The blessed Laurence catechized him, took water, and baptized him; his eyes were illuminated.

When many blind people heard of this, they came to the blessed Laurence. He placed his hand upon their eyes, and they were illuminated.

When Hippolytus saw this, he believed. After being catechized, he too was baptized.

By order, therefore, the blessed Laurence was brought before Valerian. Valerian said to him: “Now put aside your stubbornness and hand over the treasures that we know are hidden with you.”

Saint Laurence replied: “Give me two or three days’ delay, and I will bring the treasures before you.”

From that day he began gathering the blind, the lame, the weak, and the poor, and hiding them in Hippolytus’s house.

Valerian had reported to Decius that Laurence had promised to produce the treasures if he were granted a delay.

When the three days had been completed, Laurence presented himself at the Sallustian palace. Decius said to him: “Where are the treasures that you promised to present?”

The blessed Laurence brought the gathered multitude of poor people into the palace and said in a loud voice: “These are the eternal treasures, which never diminish or decline; it is distributed among individuals and found in all.”

The prefect Valerian said: “Why do you evade the matter with many words? Sacrifice to the gods and abandon the magical arts in which you trust.”

When the blessed Laurence said to him, “Why does the devil compel you to say to Christians, ‘Sacrifice to demons’?” Decius became angry and ordered him stripped and beaten with scorpions.

As he was beaten, Laurence said: “I give thanks to my God, who has deemed me worthy to join his servants; but you, wretch, are tormented by your madness and your fury.”

Then Decius said: “Lift him up and subject him to every kind of torture.”

Iron plates, beds, leaded clubs, and hooks were brought.

Afterward the blessed Laurence was bound in chains and led to the palace of Tiberius, so that he might be heard there according to the legal proceedings. Decius sat on the tribunal in the basilica of Jupiter. When Laurence had been presented, Decius said: “Sacrifice to the gods, [Col. 0324A] and do not trust in the treasures that you have hidden.”

The blessed Laurence answered freely: “Indeed, I trust in my treasures and am secure concerning them.”

Therefore Decius, filled with anger, ordered him stripped naked and beaten with clubs. As he was beaten, he cried out to Caesar: “See, wretch, now at least recognize that I triumph through the treasures of Christ and do not feel your torments.”

Decius then ordered the clubs increased and burning iron plates applied to his sides.

The blessed Laurence said: “Lord Jesus Christ, God from God, have mercy on me your servant, for when accused I did not deny you, and when questioned I confessed you as the Lord Jesus Christ.”

When he had been beaten for a very long time with leaded clubs, he said: “Lord Jesus Christ, who for our salvation deigned to take the form of a servant, so that you might free us from slavery to demons, receive my spirit.”

A voice was heard: “Many more contests are still owed to you.”

Then he was stretched out on the frame and beaten most severely with scorpions. Smiling and giving thanks, he said: “Blessed are you, Lord God, Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, who have granted us a mercy that we have not deserved. But you, Lord, because of your compassion, give us grace, so that all who stand around may know that you console your servants.”

Then one of the soldiers, named Romanus, believed in the Lord Jesus Christ and said to the blessed Laurence: “I see a most beautiful man standing before you with a linen cloth and wiping your limbs. I adjure you by Christ, who sent his angel to you, not to abandon me.”

The blessed martyr was lifted from the frame and released, but was kept only in the palace under Hippolytus’s charge.

Romanus came carrying water and threw himself at the feet of the blessed Laurence, asking to be baptized. Laurence blessed the water and baptized him.

When Decius heard of this, he ordered Romanus brought before him with clubs. Without being questioned, Romanus began to cry out: “I am a Christian.”

By Decius’s order, he was led outside the walls at the Salarian Gate and beheaded on the fifth day before the Ides of August.

The priest Justin gathered his body at night and buried it in a crypt in the Veran field.

Caesar Decius then went by night to the baths near the palace of Sallust. Saint Laurence was brought before him again, and every kind of torture was brought out: leaded clubs, iron plates, claws, beds, [Note: [Col. 0323D] *Batuli*. These are certainly what others call *batilli* or *batilla*. Pliny, book XXXIII, chapter 8: “There are two kinds of silver: it is tested with glowing iron *batilli*, with powder placed upon it so that it remains white”; and book XXXIV, chapter 11: “The test is made in an iron *batillum*.” Trebellius Pollio, in *Claudius*: “Four *batilla* for daily cooking.” Horace, *Satires* 5: “and the *batillum* of the embers.” Abdias, book IX of the *Apostolic History*: “Others with *vatilla* and incense burners.” Perhaps the smaller vessels used with fire were called *batilli*; hence the Glossary gives *vatillum*, πυράμμη or πυράμης; the larger ones, *batuli*, as you have twice here, upon which the saints are placed.] *batuli*.

He said to the blessed martyr: “Now abandon the unbelief of magical art and tell us your lineage.”

The blessed Laurence replied: “As for my lineage, I am a Spaniard; I was educated and brought up at Rome, and from the cradle I have been a Christian, instructed in the whole holy and divine law.”

Decius said: “Sacrifice to the gods, for this night will be spent upon you in punishments.”

Laurence replied: “My night has no darkness; rather, everything shines in the light.”

When stones were striking his mouth, he laughed and was strengthened, saying: “I give you thanks, Christ, because you are the God of all things.”

A bed with three ribs was brought. The blessed Laurence was stripped of his garments [Col. 0325A] and stretched upon an iron grating. *Batuli* with burning coals were brought and placed beneath the iron grating.

When he was being pressed from above with iron forks, he said to Decius: “I have offered myself as a sacrifice to God for a pleasing fragrance, because a sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit.”

The executioners continued their work, throwing coals beneath the grating and pressing him from above with iron forks.

Saint Laurence said: “Learn, wretch, how great is the power of my God. Your coals provide refreshment for me but eternal punishment for you, because the Lord himself knows that when accused I did not deny him, when questioned I confessed Christ, and, when roasted, I give thanks.”

With a most beautiful countenance he said: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, who have deemed me worthy to be strengthened.”

Raising his eyes toward Decius, he said: “See, wretch, you have roasted one side; turn the other and eat.”

Then, giving thanks and glorifying God, he said: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, because I have been deemed worthy to enter your gates.” And he gave up his spirit.

At first light, while it was still twilight, Hippolytus seized his body, wrapped it in linen cloths and spices, and entrusted the matter to the priest Justin.

Then the blessed Justin and Hippolytus, weeping and greatly sorrowful, carried the body of the blessed martyr. They came by the Tiburtine Way to the estate of the widow Cyriaca in the Veran field. The martyr himself had visited her there at night and had given her the linen cloth with which he had wiped the saints’ feet. There, at the evening hour, they buried him on the fourth day before the Ides of August.

They fasted and kept night vigils for three days, together with a multitude of Christians. The blessed priest Justin offered the sacrifice of praise, and all partook.

On the same day at Rome, one hundred and sixty-five soldiers. At that time Claudius, Severus, Crescentius, and Romanus suffered, on the very day on which the blessed Laurence suffered, three days after the passion of Saint Sixtus.

F. THE THIRD DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF AUGUST. (11 August)

[Note: [Col. 0325D] Concerning these matters, see the *Acts of Sebastian*, 20 January.]

At Rome, between the two laurel trees, the feast of Saint Tiburtius, martyr, son of Chromatius, prefect of the city. He was instructed in the faith by the blessed Sebastian, Saint Tranquillinus, and the glorious priest Polycarp, who renewed him in the sacred baptismal font. Together with him, Polycarp baptized his household, numbering fourteen hundred persons of both sexes.

When his father and a great multitude of Christians, because of the ferocity of the persecution, had gone to Campania on the advice of the pontiff Caius, Tiburtius, burning with love for martyrdom, remained in the city of Rome.

While he was occupied there with the blessed Pope Caius in fasts and prayers, one day as he was passing by he encountered a man who had fallen from a height and had so shattered his head and all his limbs that only his burial seemed possible. Tiburtius approached him and began slowly reciting over his wounds the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed. The man immediately became whole, his limbs restored, as though nothing harmful had happened to him.

Then Tiburtius took hold of the man’s parents, separated them from the crowds, and revealed to them the power of Christ’s name. Seeing that their minds were firmly established in the fear of the Lord, he led them to Pope Caius. Caius baptized the young man, who had been healed and was giving thanks to God, and baptized his parents as well.

Meanwhile, while the storm of persecution was raging violently, someone joined himself to the blessed Caius while pretending to have faith. This man had in fact become an apostate; he was deceitful in every word and cunning in every undertaking.

The blessed Tiburtius, a most learned, noble, and holy man, frequently reproved him because he arranged the hair upon the top of his forehead in a barber’s fashion; because he was constantly eating and took his meals in play; because he willingly exposed himself to women’s looks; because he withdrew from fasting and prayer; and because, being devoted to sleep, he was not continually watchful in God’s hymns.

Although the blessed Tiburtius reproved him sharply for these things, the man pretended to accept the admonition calmly and contrived by his craft that the pagans should seize the praying Tiburtius. In the course of this arrest he had himself seized as well, and both were led to the judge’s courtroom.

When they had been brought in, Fabianus said to the man who had handed himself over by this trick: “What is your name?”

He replied: “Torquatus.”

“What do you profess?”

“I am a Christian,” he said.

Fabianus said: “Do you not know that the invincible emperors have ordered that those who refuse to sacrifice to the gods be tormented with various punishments?”

Torquatus replied: “This man is my teacher, and he has always instructed me. Whatever I see him do, I must do.”

Fabianus turned to Tiburtius and said: “Have you heard what Torquatus claims?”

Saint Tiburtius replied: “Torquatus has long pretended to be a Christian. The very dignity of the holy name bears heavily and painfully that he should use his name without embodying it in his conduct.

“Indeed, most illustrious sir, the title ‘Christian’ belongs to divine virtue: it belongs to the followers of Christ, who truly practiced philosophy, who were truly called Christians, who fought bravely to crush lusts.

“Do not believe that this man is a Christian—he who, in self-indulgent effeminacy, lets the locks of his hair fall loose [another reading: *vibras committit*, ‘arranges the locks’; commonly, *fimbrias admittit*, ‘allows the fringes’]; he who loves the barber; who minces softly with his shoulders; who distends his loose gait with shameful effort; who treats men carelessly and gazes more attentively at women.

“Christ never deigned to have such plagues as his servants. Since this man claims that he will imitate me, you will now prove him a liar in your presence. Here he will clearly show what he has always been.”

Fabianus said: “You will act more wisely if, looking after your safety, you do not despise the emperors’ decrees.”

Tiburtius replied: “I cannot better look after my safety than by despising gods and goddesses and confessing the one God, Jesus Christ.”

Torquatus added: “Not only is this Christian himself cruel, but he also persuades and deceives many others; together with his companions, with whom he practices magical arts, he is occupied day and night with enchantments.”

Saint Tiburtius said: “A false witness will not go unpunished (Proverbs 19). This man whom you see, most illustrious sir, burning with the anxieties of his wickedness, has joined himself to the Christians for no other reason than to devise how he might display himself to us as a Christian and falsely represent himself to others as most faithful.

“Yet I reproved in him Cyclopean gluttony, the stench of wine rising from him, and the holiness of the divine name buried in him. Drunk, he suffered thirst; vomiting hunger, he ate, drank, and vomited—not as a Christian, but as that banqueter of old, Antonianus. And now he accuses Christians, denounces Christians, incites a lenient judge against us, puts the sword into the hand of an unwilling judge, and urges us to bow our necks to demons.

“We see your desire; we see your bloody designs; by your wicked art of speech we discern the poisons of your heart.

“Gird yourself now, most wicked man; perform the executioner’s office. Claim for yourself even the judge’s voice. Apply the racks, hang the Christians, condemn, strike, burn—we welcome it. If you threaten exile, the whole world belongs to those who practice philosophy. If punishment, we escape the prison of the world. If fires, we overcome greater fires in our desires. Decide whatever you please. Every punishment is worthless to us when a pure conscience is our companion.”

After this, when the most holy young man was confessing Christ with complete truth, Fabianus ordered burning coals poured before his feet and said to him: “Choose one of two things: either sprinkle incense upon these coals, or walk upon them barefoot.”

Making the sign of the cross, Tiburtius firmly walked upon them with bare feet and began to say: “Lay aside unbelief and learn that this alone is God, whom we confess to rule over all creatures. For, in the name of my Lord Jesus Christ, it seems to me that I am walking upon rose-filled flowers, because creation itself serves the command of its Creator.”

Fabianus said to him: “Who does not know that you taught your Christ magical art?”

“Be silent, wretch!” Tiburtius exclaimed. “Do not do me the outrage of making me hear you, with your rabid mouth, barking out the sweet and holy name.”

Fabianus, enraged, dictated the sentence that he should be executed by the sword. He was led along the Lavican Way, three miles from the city, and departed this life from a single blow of the sword. At that same place he was buried by a certain Christian relative on the third day before the Ides of August.

[Col. 0327D] On the same day at Rome, the feast of Saint Susanna, virgin and martyr, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, with Macedonius as judge. She was the daughter of the glorious presbyter and martyr Gabinius, brother of Gaius, bishop and martyr. Born of a sufficiently noble family, she had been raised and instructed in the divine writings by her father.

When Diocletian heard that the girl excelled in beauty and wisdom, he sent to Gabinius a certain Claudius, his kinsman and cousin, and sought her in marriage for his son, the Augustus Maximinus. At length Gabinius came to his daughter Susanna, summoned Gaius, bishop of the city and her uncle, to be present, and told them how the Augustus Diocletian had sent Claudius, their cousin, to ask Susanna in marriage for his son Maximinus. Strengthened by the Holy Spirit, she rejected such a marriage. Answering her father and uncle, she said:

“Father, I know that I have been instructed by your teaching to strive to preserve chastity and to offer purity to the Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, already established in his fear, I shall never be defiled by intercourse with a man. Rather, I serve him to whom you once entrusted me, and in him I trust; for he knows my conscience.”

Accordingly, Claudius himself answered her and disclosed Diocletian’s request. When he could in no way incline her mind to unite with his son Maximinus, but instead, instructed and taught in the way of God by the blessed Gaius and Gabinius, he sought repentance for the blood of the saints that he had shed, he was baptized [Col. 0328B] together with his wife, Praepedigna, and their children, Alexander and Cutia. He grew so strong in the faith that he sold all his possessions and distributed them to poor Christians. Whoever he could reach who was being held in custody, he relieved with food and clothing, throwing himself at the feet of each one and asking from them only the grace of their prayers.

Meanwhile, after one month and sixteen days, Diocletian inquired about him. When he was told that Claudius was ill, he sent his brother Maximus, count of the private estate, to visit him and discuss the girl Susanna with him. Maximus came and found Claudius praying in sackcloth and was astonished. When he had related in order the matter for which he had come, Claudius led him to the house [Col. 0328C] of the blessed Gabinius, and the blessed Gabinius and Saint Gaius carefully explained to him the way of the Lord. Struck with compunction, Maximus believed and was baptized.

From that same day Maximus began selling his property through a certain friend of his named Thrason, a most Christian man who was secretly a Christian and whom the blessed Gaius had baptized many years earlier. Going around the streets and prisons during the night, Thrason supplied poor Christians with necessities and collected accounts of their deeds, adorning their memorials.

After fifteen days, everything became known to Diocletian, and he sent Julius to punish Claudius, Maximus, Praepedigna, Alexander, and Curia, but to bind Gabinius and Susanna in chains. After fifty-five days [Col. 0328D], Diocletian ordered that blessed Susanna be brought to his wife Serena, who was secretly a Christian.

While Susanna was spending time with Serena in hymns and prayers and singing psalms in praise of God day and night, this was reported to Diocletian. Then he ordered his son Maximinus to have Susanna brought back to the house of her father Gabinius and there to abuse her as he pleased.

That very night, after she had been brought back, Maximinus entered the house where Susanna was praying. He saw an extraordinary brightness above her, became frightened, and hurried back to the palace. Diocletian, however, attributing this to magic, sent Macedonius to confine her inside her house and compel her to sacrifice.

When he wished to force her to sacrifice to the gods, he stripped [Col. 0329A] her and began to beat her with clubs. But blessed Susanna said: “Glory to you, Lord.” Thus the blessed virgin remained in her confession of the Lord, was struck with a sword inside her own house, and gave her undefiled spirit back to God.

The Augusta Serena collected her body by night, adorned it with her own hands with linen cloths and spices, and placed it beside the bodies of the saints in the cemetery of Alexander, in the sand quarry, in a crypt beside Saint Alexander, on the third day before the Ides of August. She wiped away the martyr’s blood, which had been poured out at the place of her house, with a cloth, and placed it in a silver box in her palace, where day and night she poured herself out to the Lord in secret prayers. She suffered on the third day before the Ides of August.

### G. THE DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF AUGUST. (12 Aug.)

[Col. 0329B]

In Sicily, in the city of Catania, the feast of Saint Euplus, deacon, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. When the blessed Euplus was outside the curtain of the secretarial office, he confessed himself a Christian and, by order of Calvisianus, the consular governor, was brought inside to the tribunal. When he there professed his faith, Calvisianus said:

“Let Euplus be tortured until he confesses the true, almighty gods: Mars, Apollo, and Asclepius.”

The blessed Euplus replied:

“You have spoken well, Calvisianus, that I should worship the inseparable Trinity, the one God.”

Hearing this, Calvisianus thought that he had spoken of his gods and, filled with joy, said: “Then sacrifice.”

The blessed martyr answered him: “I sacrifice and offer myself to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.”

Hearing this, the impious judge, moved by anger, ordered him to be tortured further. Finally he pronounced sentence, saying: “We order Euplus to be killed by the sword according to our just judgment.”

But the blessed Euplus gave thanks to our Lord Jesus Christ. As he was being led away, filled with the Holy Spirit, he sang:

“Great is your glory, Lord, in your servants, whom you have deemed worthy to call to yourself.”

Then, bending his knees, he finished his prayer, prepared his neck, and was beheaded on the fourth day before the Ides of August. His body, embalmed with spices, was buried in a venerable place in the city of Catania on the second day before the Ides of August.

On the same day, Saint Hilaria, mother of Saint Afra [Note: [Col. 0329D] Concerning them in the Life of Saint Afra, 5 Aug.], martyr. While she was keeping vigil at Afra’s tomb, she was handed over to the persecutors there and burned for the faith of Christ, together with Digna, Eumenia, and Euprepia, who had been maidens of Saint Afra.

In Syria, the feast of Saints Macarius and Julian.

### A. ON THE IDES OF AUGUST. (13 Aug.)

At Rome, Saint Hippolytus [Note: [Col. 0330D] Concerning him in the Acts of Saint Lawrence, 10 Aug.], martyr, under the emperor Decius, with Valerian as prefect. While Saint Lawrence was being held in his custody, he baptized this blessed Hippolytus.

After the sacred burial of the martyr, Hippolytus returned home on the third day, gave peace to all his male and female servants, and partook of the sacrifice of the altar of the blessed martyr Lawrence. After the table had been set, but before he took food, soldiers arrived, seized him, and brought him before Decius.

When Decius saw him, he smiled and said: “Have you also become a magician, because you are said to have carried away Lawrence’s body?”

Saint Hippolytus replied: “I did this not as a magician, but as a Christian.”

Decius, filled with rage, ordered that his mouth be crushed with stones. He stripped him of the garment he wore in Christian fashion and said to him: “Sacrifice and you will live; otherwise you will perish through torments like Lawrence.”

Saint Hippolytus said: “May I deserve to become an example of the blessed martyr Lawrence, whom you, wretched man, dared to name with your polluted mouth.”

He was then stretched out and beaten for a long time with clubs and iron combs, until those beating him grew weary. He was lifted from the ground, and Decius ordered him to be dressed in the military clothing that he had worn as a pagan [Col. 0330B]. He said to him: “Recall your military service, become our friend, and in our presence resume the former service that you always held.”

When the blessed martyr said, “This is my military service: to serve as a steadfast Christian. From it I desire to come swiftly to the palm of victory with its fruit,” Decius, full of anger, said to Valerian:

“Take all his possessions and kill him by a cruel death.”

Valerian therefore searched out all his property and found in Hippolytus’s house an entire Christian household, which he had brought before him. He ordered the blessed Hippolytus to be led outside the walls at the Tiburtine Gate with his household.

The blessed Hippolytus encouraged them all, saying: “Brothers, do not be afraid, because you and I have one God.”

Nineteen people of both sexes were beheaded indiscriminately [Col. 0330C]. The blessed Hippolytus, however, had his feet tied to the necks of untamed horses and, dragged in this way through thistles and thorn bushes, gave up his spirit.

At night the blessed Justin, a presbyter, came, collected the bodies, and buried them in the same field beside Nympha, alongside the field of Veranus, on the Ides of August.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Concordia, nurse of the same blessed Hippolytus. When Valerian said to the household of the blessed Hippolytus, who had been brought before him, “Consider your ages, lest you perish together with Hippolytus, our master,” blessed Concordia replied:

“We desire rather to die chastely with our master than to live immodestly.”

Valerian answered: “The race of slaves is corrected only by punishments.” He ordered blessed Concordia to be beaten with leaded scourges [Col. 0330D]. While she was being beaten, she gave up her spirit, and her body was thrown into a sewer.

When Saint Justin searched for it for a long time without finding it, he became so sad that his eyes did not cease to weep. On the thirteenth day after the passion of Saint Hippolytus, a certain soldier named Porphyrius came to a sewer-worker named Irenaeus, who was secretly a Christian, and said to him:

“If you can keep a secret, I will disclose something to your trade that will bring considerable profit. A few days ago, the prefect Valerian ordered a certain creditor of Hippolytus to be beaten with leaden scourges in his presence, and her body thrown into a sewer. I hope that she has pearls or gold hidden in her garments.”

Hearing this, Irenaeus secretly informed the blessed presbyter Justin. Justin bent his knees and gave thanks to God. Porphyrius came by night with Irenaeus and found the holy body. But they found nothing in the garments.

The blessed Irenaeus then called to him a certain Christian named Abundius. They took the body and brought it to the blessed Justin. Giving thanks to God, Justin received it and buried it beside the bodies of the martyrs Hippolytus and the others, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September.

On the same day, at the Forum of Sulla, the feast of Saint Cassian. When he refused to worship idols, the persecutor asked him what trade he practiced. He replied that he taught children their letters.

Immediately, after his clothes had been stripped off and his hands bound behind his back, he was placed in the midst of them. The children whom he had made himself hated by teaching were summoned, and permission was given them to kill him. They had suffered as learners, and now rejoiced in taking revenge: some struck him with tablets and writing boards, others wounded him with styluses. The weaker their hands were, the more grievous was the punishment of his martyrdom, prolonged by his delayed death.

The poet Prudentius wrote about this (Hymn 9).

### B. THE NINETEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (14 Aug.)

The vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Eusebius, presbyter and confessor. In the presence of Constantius, he steadfastly defended the Catholic faith and grieved that Pope Liberius had consented to the Arian treachery. Therefore the angry Arian emperor Constantius confined him in a certain room of his house, four feet in width, where he persevered steadfastly in prayer for many days.

On the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, after seven months, while still confined, he received his rest. The presbyters Gregory and Orosius collected his body and buried it in a crypt beside the body of the blessed Sixtus, martyr and bishop, on the Appian Way in the cemetery of Callistus. There, writing his epitaph, they set it up as follows:

“To Eusebius, a man of God.”

When Constantius heard that Gregory and Orosius had buried the body of the blessed Eusebius, he ordered Gregory to be shut alive in the same crypt where they had buried Eusebius. The presbyter Orosius removed him from there by night while he was half alive. Shortly afterward, when Gregory had died, Orosius buried him beside [Col. 0331D] the body of Saint Eusebius the presbyter.

A most severe persecution was then carried out against the Catholic Church by the Arians, while Liberius held the apostolic see.

### C. THE EIGHTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (15 Aug.)

The dormition of Saint Mary [Note: [Col. 0331D] See the booklet On the Feasts of the Apostles, 8 Sept., under her feast day.]

On the same day, Saint Tharsicius, acolyte and martyr. When pagans found him carrying the sacrament of Christ’s body, they began to question him about what he was carrying. Judging it unworthy to cast pearls before swine, he was beaten with clubs and stones until he breathed out his spirit [Col. 0332A].

After his body had been searched and turned over, those who had investigated him sacrilegiously were unable to find any of Christ’s sacraments in his hands or garments [Note: [Col. 0332D] Concerning him in the Acts of Pope Stephen, 20 Aug.]. Christians collected the martyr’s body and buried it in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.

### D. THE SEVENTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (16 Aug.)

At Nicaea in Bithynia, the feast of Saint Ursatius, confessor, under Licinius the persecutor. Abandoning military service, he led a solitary life in a tower of the aforementioned city. He became so renowned for his virtues that it is recorded that he drove out demons and killed an enormous dragon by prayer.

This is written in Book Five of the Ecclesiastical History in Three Parts (chapter 33).

[Col. 0332B] At Rome, Saint Serena, formerly the wife of the emperor Diocletian.

### E. THE SIXTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (17 Aug.)

In Africa, the feast of the holy martyrs Liberatus, abbot; Boniface, deacon; Servus and Rusticus, subdeacons; Rogatus and Septimius, monks; and Maximus, a boy.

During the Vandal persecution, by order of the most cruel and impious king Huneric, they were taken from the territory of the city of Capsa, from their monastery dwelling, and brought to the city of Carthage. There, for their confession of the Catholic faith and their defense of the one baptism, they were first handed over to prison custody, bound with cruel weights of iron, and assigned to dark places.

There, after strengthening the Christian people day and night in steadfastness of faith [Col. 0332C], the tyrant, inflamed with rage, ordered a ship to be filled with bundles of wood and all of them to be bound together on the sea and burned after fire had been placed beneath them.

When, at the will of the infamous king or of the cruel ministers, their hands had been stretched out and their feet raised, and wood had been thrown onto the fire, it was immediately extinguished by divine command before everyone’s eyes. Whenever the balls of flame were renewed, they were again and again extinguished.

Thus the tyrant, filled still more with rage and shame, ordered them to be killed with the shafts of oars, and so each one was slain like a dog, with his brains crushed. In this way, with the Lord crowning them, they completed the noble course of their contest.

Their bodies [Col. 0332D], thrown into the sea, were returned unharmed to the shores at that very hour. The Christian people reverently lifted them up, and, with the clergy leading the way and hymns being sung, buried them in the monastery adjoining the basilica called Celerina.

The blessed Victor, African bishop, writes about this in his history of that same Vandal persecution (Book 3), which he himself endured together with the others and arranged in a faithful and distinguished style.

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Mammes, martyr, who suffered under the emperor Aurelian, with Alexander as governor.

### F. THE FIFTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (18 Aug.)

[Col. 0333A]

At the city of Praeneste, thirty-three miles from the city, the feast of Saint Agapitus, martyr, under the emperor Aurelian, with Antiochus as governor.

When he was fifteen years old and burned with love for Christ and martyrdom, he was seized by order of the emperor and first beaten for a long time with raw sinews. Then he was handed over to the governor to be compelled to sacrifice. The governor shut him in a very harsh and dark prison and denied him all food for four days.

After this he was brought out of prison before the governor, who ordered burning coals to be placed upon his head. While the martyr was giving thanks to God, he was beaten with scourges and hung naked with his head turned downward, while a sharp smoke was made beneath him.

When he said to the governor, “Your wisdom and your vanity are laboring in smoke,” he was again beaten with scourges by four men who took turns. Then the ministers of the devil poured boiling water over his belly and shattered his jaws.

Meanwhile, the judge fell from his tribunal, was gathered up by his attendants, and laid back on a bed. Sensing God’s power in the martyr, he shortly afterward gave up his troubled soul.

The emperor was informed about the blessed Agapitus and ordered that the holy man be thrown to lions. But the beasts became gentle and bent down at the martyr’s feet to lick them.

Seeing this, the ministers of wickedness removed the holy martyr from their midst and went toward the city of Praeneste, where there are two columns. There they struck him with a sword, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September.

His body was taken away by Christians during the night [Col. 0333C] and placed one mile from the city in the countryside, in a new sarcophagus found there by divine command.

On the same day at Rome, in the Sixth District of Philip, the feast of the blessed presbyters John and Crispus. During the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, they most devotedly buried many bodies of saints. Later joined to them through their merits, they also deserved the joys of life.

### G. THE FOURTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (19 Aug.)

The feast of Saint Magnus, or Saint Andrew the martyr, with his companions, two thousand five hundred and ninety-seven.

In Gaul, in the district of Sigistericum, on a mountain called Jura, the feast of Saint Donatus, presbyter. Endowed with the marvelous grace of God from the beginnings of childhood, he came from the city of Orléans to the aforementioned place so that he might devote himself to Christ alone. There he led an anchoritic life for many years and became renowned for such glory of miracles that, among his other magnificent deeds, he even drove away and destroyed a huge and terrifying dragon through his prayers.

When the day of his calling drew near, the blessed abbot Marius arrived, to whom this had been revealed. Donatus departed to Christ amid words of prayer, and the same father buried him in his place.

At Rome, the feast of the blessed Julius, senator and martyr, under the emperor Commodus, with Vitellius as judge. The blessed martyrs Eusebius and Vincentius, Peregrinus [Col. 0334A], and Pontianus [Note: [Col. 0333D] Concerning them in the Life of Saint Eusebius, 25 Aug.] instructed him. Through their hands he also distributed his possessions to the poor and received the grace of baptism from the blessed presbyter Rufinus.

When Commodus heard this, he became angry and ordered Julius to be seized and handed over to a certain Vitellius, commander of the infantry, to search out all his possessions and compel him to sacrifice. Vitellius threw him into prison and, after three days, had him brought before him in chains.

He ordered him to be beaten with clubs for so long that he gave up his spirit. The blessed Eusebius, Pontianus, Peregrinus, and Innocentius collected his body by night and buried it in the cemetery of Calepodius, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September.

### A. THE THIRTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (20 Aug.)

[Col. 0334B] The feast of the prophet Samuel. The emperor Arcadius transferred his sacred bones from Judea to Thrace, with bishops carrying them and the peoples of all the churches coming to meet them with such joy, as though they were seeing and receiving Samuel alive and present, that crowds of people extended from Palestine to Chalcedon and resounded with one voice in the praises of Christ.

Saint Jerome writes this in his book Against Vigilantius (chapter 2).

On the same day, the blessed Porphyrius, a man of God, who instructed the holy martyr Agapitus in the faith and teaching of Christ.

### B. THE TWELFTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (21 Aug.)

In the territory of the city of Gavalitana, in the village of Minatensis [Col. 0334C], the feast of Saint Privatus, bishop and martyr, who suffered under the persecution of Valerian and Gallienus.

On the same day, the feast of the holy martyrs Bonosus and Maximian, whose acts are available.

And in the city of Salona, the feast of Anastasius [Note: [Col. 0334D] Gregory of Tours, Book 1 of the History of the Franks, chapter 34], martyr. When he saw Saint Agapitus confessing Christ more boldly amid the torments, he cried out: “Great is God, and there is none besides him.”

He was a soldier serving as a cornicularius. The governor said to him: “As I see it, you have been led astray.” The governor reported him to the emperor Aurelian, who immediately ordered him to be put to death. Thus he became a martyr and departed to the Lord.

### C. THE ELEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (22 Aug.)

[Col. 0334D] At Rome, on the Ostian Way, in the cemetery on that same way, the feast of Saint Timothy. Coming from Antioch to Rome, he was received under Pope Melchiades. After preaching there for an entire year and several months and converting many to the faith of Christ, he was seized by Tarquinius, prefect of the city, and worn down by a long imprisonment.

When he refused to sacrifice to idols, he was beaten three times, subjected to the gravest punishments, and finally beheaded and buried beside the blessed apostle Paul. This is found written in the history of Saint Sylvester.

On the same day at Autun, the feast of Saint Symphorian (31 Dec.). In the time of the emperor Aurelian, under Heraclius the consul, he refused to sacrifice to idols. First afflicted with beatings, then handed over to prison, he finally completed his martyrdom by having his head cut off [Col. 0335A].

At Roman Port, the feast of the holy pilgrim martyrs Martial, Epictetus, Saturninus, Aprilis, and Felix, with their companions [Note: [Col. 0335D] Concerning them in the Life of Saint Eusebius].

Likewise at Rome, the feast of the blessed martyr Antonius. He was an executioner and saw a young man standing with a sponge, wiping the sides of the holy martyrs Eusebius, Pontianus, Peregrinus, and Vincentius while they were being suspended on the rack and beaten.

Immediately Antonius began to cry out: “Truly Christ is God, whom these men proclaim.” He secretly fled and was baptized by the presbyter Rufinus. When he returned to Vitellius and openly confessed that he was a Christian, he was condemned to death by beheading and buried on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September [Col. 0335B], on the Aurelian Way beside the Trajan aqueduct.

### D. THE TENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (23 Aug.)

The feast of the holy martyrs Donatus, Restitutus, Valerian, and Fructuosa, with twelve others, who were crowned at Antioch with the most illustrious honor of confession.

On the same day, the blessed Theonas [Note: [Col. 0335D] Eusebius, 23 Aug., Book 7 of Ecclesiastical History, final chapter], at Alexandria, a venerable man and truly worthy of God, who raised the blessed Peter—later bishop and martyr—and was renowned in every purity and virtue of spirit.

On the same day, the blessed Zacchaeus, bishop, who was the fourth after James to rule the Church of Jerusalem with great distinction.

At Lyon in Gaul, the feast of the holy martyrs Minervius and Eleazar with eight sons, whose bodies [Col. 0335C] are said to be buried in a crypt overlooking the city from the west.

At the Port of the city of Rome, the feast of Saints Hippolytus, Quiriacus, and Archillaus.

On the same day, the feast of the holy martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris [Note: [Col. 0335D] Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 55], who, having completed their martyrdom near the city of Rheims, deserved the heavenly kingdoms.

### E. THE NINTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (24 Aug.)

In India, the feast of the blessed apostle Bartholomew.

On the same day at Carthage, the feast of the holy martyrs of the White Mass, who suffered in the time of Valerian and Gallienus.

For they say that, among the other punishments then inflicted by the governor, a lime kiln was heated, and burning coals with incense were presented at its mouth [Col. 0335D]. The governor said to the Christians:

“Choose one of these two: either offer incense to Jupiter upon these coals, or be plunged into the lime.”

Then three hundred men, armed with faith, confessed with the swiftest leap that Christ, the Son of God, is God, and threw themselves into the fire, where they were submerged amid the vaporous lime dust. From this, that white army of the blessed also deserved to be called the White Mass [Note: [Col. 0336D] See the booklet On the Feasts of the Apostles; Prudentius, Hymn 13].

### F. THE EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (25 Aug.)

At Rome, the feast of Saint Genesius, martyr, who had previously [Col. 0336A] been a mime and master of the theatrical art in the city [Note: [Col. 0336D] Incorrectly in the manuscript: *mimithemelae*].

One day, wishing to perform a farce about the mysteries of Christian observance before the emperor Diocletian, who hated Christians as an especially savage man, he arranged that, with the emperor and all the people watching, he would lie in the middle of the theater as if ill and ask to be baptized.

He began the mime with these words:

“Come, my people, I feel myself burdened; I want to become light.”

They answered: “How can we make you light if you are burdened? Are we perhaps craftsmen, and are we going to send you to the lathe?”

These words made the people laugh.

Genesius continued: “Fools, I desire to die a Christian.”

“Why?” they asked.

Genesius answered them: “So that on that day I may be found in God like a fugitive.”

A presbyter and an exorcist were summoned. Suddenly inspired by God [Col. 0336B], Genesius believed. For when they had sat beside his bed as though he were ill, they said to him:

“Little son, why have you sent for us?”

Genesius answered not as a pretender or actor, but from a pure heart:

“Because I desire to receive the grace of Christ, through which, being reborn, I may be freed from the ruin of my sins.”

When they had completed the mysteries of the sacraments and he had been clothed in white garments, soldiers seized him as though in a game and brought him before the emperor as though he were to be examined concerning the name of Christ, like the holy martyrs.

Standing in a higher place, he addressed the assembly:

“Hear me, emperor, and all the army, the wise men, and the people of this city. Whenever I heard a Christian or the name ‘Christian’ mentioned, I shuddered and mocked those who persevered in their confession. I also cursed my parents and relatives because of the Christian name [Col. 0336C], and I held Christians in such derision that I investigated their mysteries with careful examination, wishing to present a performance for you from their sanctification.

“But when the water touched me naked, and, being questioned, I answered that I believed, I saw a hand descending from heaven above me. I saw angels of God shining beside me. They recited all the sins I had committed from infancy from a book, and then washed them in that very water with which I had been drenched before you. Afterward they showed me whiter than snow.

“Now therefore, illustrious emperor, and all you peoples who know nothing of these mysteries, believe with me that Christ is the true God; that he is the light, he is the truth, he is piety; and that through him you can attain forgiveness.”

At this, the emperor Diocletian was extremely indignant. He immediately had Genesius beaten most cruelly with clubs and handed over to the prefect Plutianus to compel him to sacrifice. Plutianus suspended him on the rack, subjected him to prolonged tearing with hooks, and also burned him with torches.

Since Genesius persevered in the faith, he said:

“There is no king except the one whom I have seen, adore, and worship. For his worship, even if I am killed a thousand times, I shall remain as I have begun. Torments cannot remove Christ from my mouth or Christ from my heart. For I deeply repent that previously I shuddered before the holy name and before holy men, and that, a proud soldier, I came so late to worship the true King.”

He deserved the crown of martyrdom by beheading on the eighth day before the Kalends of September.

On that same day, the feast of Saint Genesius [Note: [Col. 0337D] Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 68], of Arles. While serving before the judge as a court secretary, he refused to record the impious edicts by which Christians were ordered to be punished. Throwing the tablets down in public, he testified that he was a Christian and withdrew.

After a short interval he was discovered by the attendants, beheaded on the bank of the river Rhône, and received the glory of martyrdom, baptized in his own blood.

On the same day at Rome, the feast of the four holy martyrs Eusebius, Pontianus, Peregrinus, and Vincentius, under the emperor Commodus, with Vitellius as judge.

First they distributed all their possessions to the poor. Then, through their preaching, they converted the senator Julius and his entire household to the faith of Christ, and brought them to the grace of baptism through the presbyter Rufinus [Col. 0337B]. Julius became a martyr not long afterward and was also buried by them.

Because of this especially, Vitellius seized the four men, lifted them onto the rack, stretched them with sinews, and then beat them with clubs. Flames were subsequently placed at their sides. But since they persevered most faithfully in the praise of Christ, they were finally removed from the rack.

When they nevertheless continued in their confession of Christ, Vitellius, enraged, ordered Eusebius’s tongue to be cut out by the roots. The blessed Faustus collected it, hid it in his bosom, and fled.

With his tongue cut out, Eusebius cried:

“Glory to you, Lord Jesus Christ, who have deemed me worthy to number me with your servants for glory.”

They were shut in prison, where they resounded with hymns to God day and night. A certain priest of the Capitol named Lupulus, who had been blind for four years, came to them. He believed, was given sight, and received the grace of baptism.

When the prison guard, named Simplicius, saw this deed, he too rejected the idols and was baptized.

When Vitellius reported these events to Commodus, the emperor ordered them to be punished. After three days they were brought out of prison and killed at the Accursed Stone, beaten with leaded scourges until they gave up their spirits.

The blessed presbyter Ruffinus collected their bodies and buried them six miles from the city of Rome, between the Aurelian and Triumphal Ways, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September.

Much later [Note: [Col. 0337D] Sigibertus, in the Chronicle, under the year 865], the remains of the blessed martyrs Eusebius and Pontianus, through the generosity of Pope Nicholas [Col. 0337D], were transferred to Gaul and reverently buried in monasteries dedicated by a religious vow to the holy apostle Peter.

### G. THE SEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (26 Aug.)

At Rome, Saint Zephyrinus, pope [Note: [Col. 0337D] The Pontifical Book, chapter 16], who ruled the Church for eight years, seven months, and ten days.

Likewise at Rome, the feast of the holy men Irenaeus and Abundius [Note: [Col. 0338D] Concerning them in the Acts of Saint Lawrence, 10 Aug.]. During the Decian persecution, Valerian ordered them to be thrown into the sewer because they had removed the body of blessed Concordia after it had been thrown into the sewer.

The presbyter Justin also recovered their bodies [Col. 0338A] and buried them in a crypt beside the blessed Lawrence.

At Victimilium, a fortress of Italy, the feast of the blessed martyr Secundus, a distinguished man and commander from the legion of the holy Thebans. Before the blessed Maurice and the others, after imprisonment and confinement, he completed his martyrdom by beheading.

At the Italian city called Bergamo, the feast of Saint Alexander, martyr, under Caesar Maximian. He was a soldier, one of the Theban legion, and became a Christian.

After fifteen days Maximian heard of this, sent for him, and said:

“I summoned you for no other reason than that you should sacrifice. For I have learned that, having abandoned our gods, you have become a Christian.”

As he said this, he asked for a table. When it had been brought and covered with a cloth, he began to urge the blessed Alexander to sacrifice.

Saint Alexander, looking toward heaven, said:

“If only God would grant me such grace—for he grants all things through Jesus Christ to those who ask—that I might turn your will toward knowledge of God and turn you away from this most vain unbelief! But you have an incurable evil: clinging through long habit to this vanity, you refuse to believe.

“He has called me, the one who long ago promised to call the nations to his grace. Abandon your devilish counsels, grieve, recognize your evil deeds, and believe in the living God who made all things.”

Then Maximian, moved by such confidence, ordered those standing by to force upon him the sacrifice that had been set out, while armed men were stationed opposite [Col. 0338C]. But the most blessed man, shaming the wickedness of the emperor and despising his commands, armed with faith, struck the table with his foot and overturned it with everything placed upon it.

Filled with anger, Maximian ordered him to be handed over to one of the attendants. The man drew his sword but stood stupefied, not daring to strike.

Maximian said to him: “Are you still standing there, bad soldier?”

He replied: “His head is like a mountain before me, and I tremble all over.”

Then Maximian handed him over to others to be killed.

The martyr, filled with joy, asked for water and washed his hands. Bending his knees and lowering his neck to the ground, he poured out a prayer to the Lord and was put to death.

After several days, a most chaste matron named Gratia collected his body and placed it on her small estate, not far from the wall of the city of Bergamo [Col. 0338D]. His passion was completed on the seventh day before the Kalends of September.

### A. THE SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (27 Aug.)

At Capua, the feast of Saint Rufus [Note: [Col. 0338D] Concerning him in the Life of Apollinaris, 23 Jul.], whom the blessed Apollinaris, disciple of the apostle Peter, taught and baptized when Rufus himself held patrician rank.

At Tomis, the feast of the holy martyrs Marcellinus, tribune; his wife Mannea; his son John; Serapion, a cleric; and Peter, a soldier [Note: [Col. 0338D] Gennadius, On Illustrious Men, chapter 86].

[Col. 0339A] In Gaul, in the city of Arles, Saint Caesarius, bishop and confessor, a man of remarkable holiness, piety, and zeal.

At Autun, Saint Syagrius, bishop and confessor.

### B. THE FIFTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER. (28 Aug.)

At Rome, the feast of the most blessed martyr Hermes [Note: [Col. 0339D] Concerning him, see the Life of Saint Alexander.]. The blessed Alexander, bishop and martyr (3 May), baptized this most illustrious man, who was prefect of the city of Rome, together with his wife, his sons, and his sister Theodora; along with him he also baptized 1,250 of his slaves, together with their wives and children, first granting them their freedom.

Not long afterward, Hermes was thrust into prison by the emperor Aurelian, while the blessed Alexander was likewise held in custody, and Hermes was commended to the tribune Quirinus. Quirinus said to the blessed Hermes: “What reason is there, illustrious man, that, while you exercise a sacred office of judgment, you should wish not only to be reduced to this injury, but also, stripped of the honor of the prefecture, calmly endure being thrust into chains like a private citizen?”

Saint Hermes replied: “I have not lost the prefecture, but changed it. For earthly dignity is removed from the earth and altered; heavenly dignity, however, endures in eternal sublimity.”

Quirinus said to him: “I am amazed that you, a prudent man, have fallen into such great folly as to believe that you will possess anything beyond this life, once the ashes of the human body have been reduced to nothing, so that not even the bones themselves remain.”

The blessed Hermes replied: “I too, before these years, used to mock that belief and say that this carnal life was useful.”

Quirinus said: “Make me test this, so that, if it is as you have believed, I too may believe.”

The blessed Hermes said: “Saint Alexander, who is held in chains, taught me these things.”

When Quirinus heard this, he began to curse Alexander and said to Hermes: “I asked you, saying, ‘Make me test whether you have believed rightly’; and you have named for me a great man whom I hold in chains and have shut away in the depths of the prison. If what you say is true, then I myself shall go to him and triple his chains and guards. If he can come to you at supper time, I shall believe what he has taught.”

He went, tripled the chains, and added guards. At the very beginning of the night, a boy appeared who seemed to be no more than five years old, carrying a burning torch into the prison. Kneeling with the blessed Alexander, he prayed, reciting the Lord’s Prayer; then, taking Alexander by the hand, he led him out through the window and brought him to the blessed Hermes in Quirinus’s house.

When Quirinus saw this, he was terrified. Afterward the blessed Hermes said to him: “Behold, you see us together, whom you had delivered to custody. The reason why I believed Saint Alexander is this: I had an only son, lying in extreme illness, who was still attending the study of letters. When I had taken him with his mother to the Capitol, sacrificed to the gods, and given gifts to the priests, he died.

“Then his nurse began to rebuke me, saying: ‘If you had taken him to the threshold of Saint Peter and believed in Christ, you would have your son safe and sound.’

“I answered her: ‘While you yourself have become blind and have not been healed, how will he restore my son to health?’

“She replied: ‘If I had believed in Christ five years ago, my eyes would have been restored to me.’

“I said to her: ‘Go and believe; and if Alexander opens your eyes, I shall believe that he can restore my son to me as well.’

“She went to him blind, and behold, she returned to me healed. She placed my dead son upon her shoulders, ran, and cast him before the feet of the blessed Alexander. After praying, he raised him from the dead.

“I immediately threw myself at Alexander’s feet and begged to become a Christian. I bestowed on him his mother’s patrimony and added some of my own property. The rest I either distributed to the poor or gave to my slaves who had become Christians with me.”

When the blessed Hermes had done these and similar things for Quirinus, Quirinus believed with all his household and was baptized. When Aurelian heard all this, he issued a final sentence that the blessed Hermes should be punished with the sword. After he had been beheaded, his blessed sister Theodora gathered him up and buried him on the old Salarian Way, not far from the city of Rome, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September.

On the same day in Africa, the burial of Saint Augustine, bishop. [Col. 0340A] He was born in the African province, in the city of Thagaste, of respectable and Christian parents among the members of the municipal council. He was brought up and educated through their care and diligence, and was thoroughly instructed at secular expense in all the disciplines called liberal arts. He first taught Grammar in his own city, then Rhetoric in Carthage, the capital of Africa; afterward, he taught across the sea at Rome and at Milan.

At that time, the episcopate of that city was administered by Ambrose, a priest most pleasing to God and most distinguished among excellent men. Augustine stood among the people at the frequent disputations in the church of this preacher of the word of God, listening intently, as though suspended and fastened to his words. Through divine assistance it came to pass that, through such a great bishop as Ambrose, he received both the saving teaching of the Catholic Church and the divine Sacraments.

Soon, from the innermost depths of his heart, he abandoned every hope that he had placed in the world. Now seeking neither wife nor children, nor the riches of the flesh, nor worldly honors, he resolved to serve God with his companions. Thus, with those who clung to the same God, he lived for God in fasts, prayers, and good works, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord. What God revealed to him as he pondered and prayed, he taught both those present and those absent through sermons and books.

It came to pass that he was ordained a priest in the Church of Hippo, when everyone with one accord and desire requested and urged that this be done, pressing the matter with great zeal and clamor. Soon he established a monastery within the church and began to live with God’s servants according to the manner and rule established under the holy apostles: above all, no one in that fellowship was to possess anything as his own, but everything was to be held in common and distributed to each person according to need.

After some time, when the holy bishop Valerius arranged it, and everyone rejoiced and clamored with immense desire that it should happen, Augustine was compelled to accept the episcopate while his bishop was still living. Thus it came about that, as bishop, he preached the word of eternal salvation to the Lord’s flourishing and growing Church with far greater urgency and fervor and with greater authority.

He lived in the clerical or episcopal state for approximately forty years, and his total age was seventy-six years. Until his final illness he preached the word of God without interruption, joyfully and steadfastly, with sound mind and sound judgment, in the Church. With all the members of his body unharmed, his sight and hearing intact, and with the brothers standing by, watching, and praying, he fell asleep with his fathers, nourished in a good old age.

He made no will, because the poor man of God had nothing from which to make one. In the third month of the siege—for his city was enclosed and besieged for fourteen months by the Vandals, Alans, and other peoples joined with them—he took to his bed with fevers and was worn down by that final illness.

This blessed bishop, touched by the divine Spirit, composed in the holy Catholic Church, for the instruction of souls, 1,030 books, treatises, and letters, apart from those that cannot be counted because he did not specify their number. His venerable body was first transferred from his own city, because of the barbarians, to Sardinia; recently, King Liutprand of the Lombards, after paying a great price, brought it back to Ticinum and honorably buried it.

At Brioude, the feast of Saint Julian, martyr [Note: [Col. 0341D] Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Martyrs, book II, throughout.]. During the persecution, at the urging of the blessed Ferreolus, whose companion he was in military service, Julian secretly departed from the city of Vienne and moved to the aforementioned territory of the city of Clermont. There he was seized by the pursuing persecutors, had his throat cut, and was killed by a horrible death.

At Constantinople, Saint Alexander, bishop and confessor [Note: [Col. 0341D] Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 58.], a glorious old man. Through the power of his prayer, Arius was condemned by divine judgment, burst open in the middle, and his entrails poured out. The blessed pontiff fell asleep in the ninety-eighth year of his life and the thirty-third year of his episcopate.

On the same day at Saintes, Saint Bibianus [or Viviana], bishop and confessor.

## C. Fourth day before the Kalends of September (29 August)

[Col. 0341D]

At Rome, on the Aventine, in the town of Vindinum, at the Arch of Faustinus, the feast of the most blessed and illustrious martyr Sabina. She was the wife of the once-famous Valentinus and the daughter of Herod the Metalworker. She suffered under the emperor Hadrian, under the prefect Helpidius.

The blessed virgin Seraphia, while living in her household, persuaded Sabina to embrace the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ. Later Sabina followed that same virgin even to the place of her passion. When the governor Berillus said to her:

“Why do you yourself degrade your dignity? Why do you make yourself contemptible? Why do you not consider who you are or whose daughter you are? You have joined yourself to Christians and forgotten your birth and the memory of the great man whose wife you were. You have also forgotten the gods, whose anger I fear you may incur. Return instead to your home and abandon this wicked woman, who by her magic has turned you and many others away from the worship of the gods.”

Blessed Sabina replied: “Would that you too were persuaded by the magic of that holy girl of whom you speak, just as I was persuaded, so that you might withdraw from unclean idols and acknowledge the true and absolutely certain God, who calls the good to eternal life and leaves the wicked to everlasting punishment.”

When the governor heard this, he respected her and dismissed her. After the blessed Seraphia had been crowned with a glorious martyrdom, the illustrious Sabina gathered her relics, celebrated the venerable funeral rites, and placed this everlasting treasure, this precious pearl, in her own tomb, which she herself had prepared with the greatest care and adornment.

Then, after several days had passed, Sabina was arrested and brought before the judge Helpidius. When he saw her, he said: “Are you Sabina, the illustrious wife of the once-famous Valentinus and daughter of Herod?”

The holy matron replied: “I am, and I give thanks to my Lord Jesus Christ, who through his holy servant Seraphia has deigned to free me, a sinner, from many impurities and from the power of demons.”

Afterward the prefect was moved to anger when he saw her steadfastness in confessing Christ. He issued this sentence: “We decree that Sabina, disobedient to the gods and also blaspheming our masters and Augusti, be struck with the sword, and that all her possessions be marked by public notices.”

The blessed servant of Christ Sabina suffered on the fourth day before the Kalends of September. Christians took up her body and buried it in the tomb where she had reverently placed Seraphia, the virgin and teacher of her faith, at the Arch of Faustinus, beside the estate of Vindicianus, in the town of Vindinum.

On the same day, the beheading of Saint John the Baptist is venerated [Note: [Col. 0342D] See the booklet On the Feasts of the Apostles. Also, here before 24 February.]. He was first buried in Samaria, but is now in Alexandria. His head, moreover, was carried from Jerusalem to Emesa, a city of Phoenicia.

## D. Third day before the Kalends of September (30 August)

At Rome, on the Ostian Way, two miles from the city, the feast of the most blessed martyrs Felix and Adauctus, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, with Draco as prefect and judge.

There were two brothers, both named Felix and both priests in name and deed. The elder Felix, by order of the emperors, was brought to the judge’s secretariat beside the temple of Serapis. When he was compelled to sacrifice, he blew in the face of the bronze statue, and it immediately fell. Then he was led to a statue of Mercury in another shrine; in the same manner he blew upon it, and it soon fell. Then he was brought to the image of Diana, which he likewise threw down.

Returned to the prefect, he was placed on the rack and questioned about the magic by which he had done these things. Blessed Felix replied: “I did this not by the magic of the devil, but by the benefits of almighty God.”
