The prefect, inflamed with rage, ordered him to be taken outside the city along the Ostian Way, because there stood an exceedingly tall tree consecrated to demons, beside which was a temple, so that Felix might be compelled there to sacrifice. When he had been brought there, he prayed and then said to the tree:

“I command you, in the name of my Lord Jesus Christ, to fall from your roots and utterly shatter the temple, the image, and its altar, so that souls may no longer be deceived by your worship.”

At his words it immediately fell so completely that it crushed the temple and image, and nothing remained of what had stood there. When this was reported to the prefect, he immediately ordered Felix to be beheaded and his body to be left unburied for dogs and wolves.

After the sentence had been issued, a certain Christian man met him, hidden from men but manifest to God. When he learned that the blessed Felix had been ordered to execution, he began to cry out:

“I too belong to the same law, and I worship the Lord Jesus Christ whom this holy priest confesses.”

He too was immediately seized by the prefect’s officials. After exchanging a kiss with the blessed Felix, he was beheaded together with him. Because the Christians did not reveal his name, they later called him Adauctus, meaning that he had been added to the holy martyr Felix for the crown, and that the crown of martyrdom had been increased for him through his confession of faith.

The Christians therefore came by night and buried them in the same place where the tree had stood, whose fall had opened an enormous depth in the earth. When the pagans afterward wished to dig up their bodies, all who laid hands upon the task were struck by the devil. Later, in a time of peace, a basilica was built there and the martyrs’ memory was worthily honored. They completed their martyrdom on the third day before the Kalends of September.

## E. The day before the Kalends of September (31 August)

At Trier, the feast of Saint Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0343] Concerning him, see the Life of Saint Maximus, bishop of Mainz, 18 November; Jerome, On Illustrious Men of the Church, chapter 20.], bishop and confessor. During the Arian persecution, he was banished into exile by the emperor Constantius on account of the Catholic faith. Even until death, he was worn down by changing places of exile beyond the bounds of Christendom; at last he died in Phrygia and received from the Lord the crown of a blessed passion.

On the same day at Athens, the blessed Aristides, most renowned for faith and wisdom. He presented books concerning the Christian religion to the emperor Hadrian and, in the emperor’s presence, argued with brilliant eloquence that Christ Jesus alone was God.

LITANIES TO BE ANNOUNCED. SEPTEMBER HAS THIRTY DAYS; THE MOON, TWENTY-NINE.

## F. Kalends of September (1 September)

[Col. 0343C]

Jesus son of Nave (Joshua), and Gideon, prophets.

At Capua, on the Aquarian Way, the feast of Saint Priscus, martyr, who was one of those ancient disciples of Christ.

On the same day, the feast of Anna the prophetess.

Likewise on the same holy day at Sens, the blessed Lupus, bishop, illustrious for holiness and signs of miracles.

Likewise at Caesarea in Cappadocia, the blessed Longinus [Note: [Col. 0343C] See the booklet On the Feasts of the Apostles.], soldier and martyr. He is said to have been the man who opened the side of the Lord Jesus Christ, hanging on the cross, with a spear (John 19). Later baptized by the apostles, he lived in Cappadocia, distinguished by holiness. At last he was arrested by the governor Octavius; after confessing the faith, his tongue was cut out, his teeth were knocked out, and he was beheaded.

Aphrodisius the Commentariensis was crowned together with him. The governor had likewise ordered Aphrodisius’s tongue to be cut out; yet after it had been cut out, he spoke of Christ clearly and easily in a loud voice.

## G. Fourth day before the Nones of September (2 September)

The feast of Saint Justus, bishop of Lyons, a man of extraordinary holiness and prophetic spirit. Secretly abandoning his episcopate, he boarded a ship accompanied by only one boy, Viator by name, who served as a lector in the church, and reached Egypt.

There he lived for several years among holy monks whose only concern was contemplation of heaven, incomparable in humility and holiness of life. When the course of time had been completed, he too, perfected in virtues, departed to the Lord on the day before the Ides of October, to receive the crown of righteousness prepared for him.

His body was brought back to Lyons by devout citizens, together with the bones of his servant Viator, and was buried with fitting honor in the basilica of the glorious holy seven Maccabean brothers, martyrs, on the fourth day before the Nones of September.

On the same day, the venerable burial of the blessed Helpidius, bishop, at the aforementioned city. His sacred body, honorably buried in that same church where the most sacred members of Saint Justus the confessor were entombed, rests there.

At Apamea, the blessed Antoninus, martyr.

## A. Third day before the Nones of September (3 September)

The feast of Saint Phoebe.

[Col. 0345A] At Rome, the passion and feast of the blessed Seraphia [Note: [Col. 0345D] See the booklet On the Feasts of the Apostles.], virgin, under the emperor Hadrian and the judge Berillus.

She was of Antiochene origin and was living in the household of the most illustrious woman Sabina near the city when she was seized by the prefect’s officials and brought before him. He said to her:

“Sacrifice to the immortal gods, to whom our imperial masters sacrifice.”

Blessed Seraphia replied: “I fear and worship almighty God, who made heaven and earth and all that is in them. For the gods whom you command me to worship are not gods but demons; therefore I may not worship them, because I am a Christian.”

Since she continued most steadfastly to defend the faith of truth, the governor ordered her to be handed over to two lustful young men, so that they might assault her by night. When they had taken her into a very dark chamber and were about to touch her, suddenly a great earthquake occurred, and they fell lifeless to the ground, all their limbs loosened.

At dawn, men sent by the governor came to inquire either about the young men or about the virgin. When they entered, they found the holy woman praying, while the shameless young men lay on the ground like dead men. When many people therefore gathered because of what had happened, the governor again ordered her to be brought before his tribunal.

At the governor’s command, the same young men were brought and placed before him. The blessed virgin approached them after praying, touched them, and said: “In the name of my Lord Jesus Christ, rise and stand upright.” At her word they stood upon their feet.

The governor asked them: “What did this woman do to make you insane and leave you helpless?”

They replied: “A certain handsome young man of extraordinary stature entered. He shone all over like the sun, and, standing between us and this girl, struck us with trembling and weakness by his radiance.”

The governor turned to the blessed Seraphia and said: “Sacrifice to the gods, or you will be punished with death.”

The virgin replied: “I will not do the will of your father Satan, because I am a Christian.”

Then the governor ordered burning lamps to be placed against her sides, but immediately those holding them fell backward. The governor again said to the blessed virgin:

“Biothanata (self-destroyer) and sorceress, hear the imperial command: sacrifice to the immortal gods and free yourself from torture and death.”

Blessed Seraphia answered him: “You are the biothanatoi (self-destroyers) and sorcerers, you who deny the living and true God and worship demons; with them you shall likewise die. But to the immortal God I offer myself as a sacrifice, if he deigns to accept me, though I am a sinner, yet a Christian.”

Then she was beaten with clubs. Suddenly a great earthquake occurred. A splinter shaken from the club with which the virgin was being beaten sprang into the governor’s eye and made him one-eyed after the pain.

In anger he issued this sentence: “We order Seraphia, who has despised the imperial command and has been detected in such great sorceries, to be struck with the sword.”

She suffered on the fourth day before the Kalends of August and was buried beside the estate of Vindicianus in the tomb of the illustrious martyr Sabina, on the second day before the Kalends of August. The venerable sarcophagus of both women was arranged and adorned, and a place of prayer was suitably dedicated on the third day before the Nones of September, when the memory of her passion is also celebrated with greater solemnity.

At Capua, the feast of the holy martyrs Antoninus, a boy of twenty years, and Aristeus, bishop, whose acts are preserved.

On the same day, the burial of Saint Remaclus, bishop and confessor, and of the most blessed Mansuetus, confessor and pontiff of Toul.

## B. The day before the Nones of September (4 September)

Moses, prophet.

And at Ancyra in Galatia, the feast of the holy three child-martyrs Rufinus, Sylvanus, and Vitalica [Note: [Col. 0346D] Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 53.].

At Chalon, the feast of Saint Marcellus. In the time of Antoninus Verus, he was one of the fifty martyrs who had been thrust into confinement at Lyons. When the prison doors were divinely opened, he escaped from the custody to which he had been committed together with Valerianus.

After converting to the faith of Christ a certain Latin who had given him hospitality, together with his entire household, Marcellus set out for the city of Chalon. There he encountered a certain Priscus, governor, sacrificing to his gods. When Priscus invited him to a profane banquet, Marcellus condemned such banquets and openly rebuked all who were present, asking why they served idols.

The governor ordered him, in an unheard-of form of cruelty, to be buried upright to the waist. Thus the holy martyr of God, persevering in praises out of love for God for three days, gave up his undefiled spirit on the second mile from the town of Chalon.

## C. Nones of September (5 September)

[Col. 0346C]

In the suburb of Rome, the feast of the blessed martyr Victorinus.

There were two brothers, Victorinus and Severinus. After the death of both their parents, they educated one another; each rivaled the other in mutual service, and by their fraternal bond they proved themselves worthy. They offered themselves to God as a living sacrifice.

When they had grown so far in virtue that, for the sake of perfection, they abandoned everything they possessed and sold their property, distributing its value to the poor so that they might serve God more freely, they remained stripped of every possession. Each, in turn, served the other with mutual and emulous charity. Authority and freedom were theirs. Nothing was lacking to them, though they had nothing.

Victorinus, however, breathing more deeply after perfection and judging even what they had achieved to be incomplete, considered it insufficient if one were permitted to serve the other or if either brother performed service for the other. He entered the wilderness and sat in a cave in a lofty cliff, which the waters flowing beneath had hollowed out into a double cleft. It offered room for only one man to sit and sleep, or, if it received another, to pray standing.

He covered the entrance with wickerwork and remained constantly at reading and prayer. Meanwhile the enemy of every good work, unable to endure the man’s progress, pretended to be a girl and repeated mournful words before the man’s door:

“Alas, miserable me, wandering through the woods and straying in the darkness! The place is unknown; I seek a path. Whoever you are, inhabitant of this place, the heavens on every side and the forests proclaim the fame of your virtues and your work. Rescue me from the bristling boars, rescue me from the raging wolves and the jaws of bears. While I live, I shall be yours; if I die, I shall be yours. Let it be more than enough for me to be sheltered at your threshold. I do not seek a long dwelling; I shall be your guest for only one night.”

Victorinus opened his cell and, moved by pity, let the enemy in with him. Barely an hour had passed when, amid struggles and constant movement of the body, the intruder touched the man of God with an outstretched foot and, as though pricking him with a poisonous wound, inflamed him with a destructive heat. The sweetness of speech added a spark; solitude pressed on the deed.

Why delay? The column of a tall tree, long rooted and standing firmly, fell. Secret desire completed the crime. The devil, now victorious over Victorinus, cried out:

“What are you doing, most perfect man, to whom even your brother was a burden? Now you are joining yourself to another, though you withdrew from your own brother. What are you doing, establishing a new doctrine in the forests and commending chastity to the rocks?”

As he uttered these words, he vanished from the deceived man’s eyes like smoke. The one who had fallen lay as though drained of blood.

After some time he returned to himself, left the forests, and went back to his brother Severinus. For a long while he suppressed his voice out of shame; at last he explained what he had done, imposing the punishment upon himself. He split a tree, thrust his hands into the cleft, and, fastening it shut with wedges and bolts, closed the tree’s wound around them.

Soon Severinus reported his brother’s deed and punishment to his bishop. The bishop came and first tried to release him; but when he saw that Victorinus resisted, he prayed, blessed, and consoled him, then departed.

The man of God, who had condemned himself to the most severe penance, was compelled by his brother to receive only a little bread and water on the Lord’s Day. His brother likewise disciplined himself with similar food and fasting.

Thus three years passed in this condition. When his humility, worthy of imitation in Christ, had moved nearly everyone, the bishop of the city returned and could scarcely bring him to permit himself to be released from the punishment to which, mindful of the terrible judgment, he had condemned himself, his flesh having almost been consumed.

What great holiness he afterward possessed and how powerful he was in miracles cannot easily be expressed by anyone’s tongue. Later, chosen by the entire people, he obtained the priesthood of the city of Amiternum.

Afterward, under the emperor Nerva, together with the other servants of God Eutyches and Maro, he was first banished by the judge Aurelianus to the sixtieth milestone from the city on the Salarian Way. Then, at a place called Cotilia, where foul and sulphurous waters flow, the impious judge ordered him to be hung upside down by the head for three hours.

After suffering this for three days in Christ’s name, he was gloriously crowned and departed to the Lord. When, by order of Aurelianus, his body had lain unburied for one day, the Christian people of Amiternum came, seized it, carried it into their territory, and buried it with honor on the Nones of September.

Likewise at Rome, in the port, the feast of Saint Herculanus.

At Capua, the feast of the holy martyrs Quintus, Arcontius, and Donatus.

## D. Eighth day before the Ides of September (6 September)

Zechariah, prophet.

Likewise, the feast of Saint Onesiphorus, a disciple of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0347D] See the book On the Feasts of the Apostles; Victor of Africa, book II.].

And in Africa, the most blessed confessors and bishops Donatianus, Praesidius, Mansuetus, Germanus, and Fusculus. During the Vandal persecution, by order of Hunneric, the Arian king, they were savagely beaten with clubs in Africa and condemned to exile for asserting the Catholic truth.

Among them was also a bishop named Laetus, an energetic and highly learned man. After enduring the squalor of prolonged imprisonment, Hunneric burned him alive. Then, by public decree, he sent executioners through the various provinces and, while the bishops were gathered as though for a council at Carthage, closed all the churches of Africa in a single day and granted all the property of the bishops and churches to his own bishops.

## E. Seventh day before the Ides of September (7 September)

The feast of the blessed John at Nicomedia under the emperor Diocletian [Note: [Col. 0347D] Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 5.].

Born of noble parents and illustrious in honor and rank, when he saw cruel edicts hanging in the forum against the worshipers of God, he was inflamed by the fervor of faith. In public, while the people watched, he laid hands on the book of the impious law, pulled it down, and tore it to pieces. At that time the Augustus Diocletian was residing in the same city together with Maximian as Caesar.

When the deed of this religious and illustrious man was reported to them, they immediately raged against him with every kind of cruelty. Yet they could not even bring about this much: that anyone should see him saddened amid his punishments. Rather, although his entrails had already failed under the tortures, his spirit rejoiced in his happy and cheerful face.

For this reason his torturers were tormented more severely: they exhausted every kind of punishment upon a man whom they could not even make sorrowful by them.

## F. Sixth day before the Ides of September (8 September)

The Nativity of the Holy Mother of God [Note: [Col. 0348D] See the booklet On the Feasts of the Apostles.].

On the same day at Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Adrian the martyr, together with twenty-three others. When Maximian was violently persecuting the Christians, certain Christians of outstanding faith and piety were brought before him at Antioch. After they had confessed the truth, he ordered them stretched out on wooden frames and beaten with raw sinews; then their faces were crushed with stones and their tongues cut out.

Seeing all this, Adrian, who was chief officer, said to them: “I adjure you by your God, for whom you suffer these things: tell me truthfully, what reward is yours, which you await in return for these torments? For it seems to me to be great and marvelous.” The twenty-three martyrs said to him: “We await what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not entered the human heart: the indescribable good that God has prepared for those who love him” (Isaiah 64; 1 Corinthians 2).

Hearing this, Adrian immediately leaped up and stood among them. He said to those who were performing the duties of the recorder: “Record my confession together with these holy athletes of God, for I too am a Christian.”

After a short time, when Maximian heard his name being recited among the names of the holy martyrs, he summoned him and said: “Are you mad, Adrian? Do you too wish to perish so miserably?” Adrian replied: “I am not mad; rather, I am returning from great madness to sound understanding.”

When he continued steadfastly to proclaim the things belonging to faith and truth, Maximian, filled with fury, ordered him, bound in irons, to be dragged with the other holy martyrs to prison. He was twenty-eight years old.

When news quickly spread, his wife Natalia learned everything that had happened to Adrian, her husband. Full of joy—for she was a most devout Christian—she ran to the prison and, falling at her husband’s feet, kissed his bonds, saying to him:

“You are blessed, my lord Adrian, because you have found riches that your parents did not leave you. Truly, you now go securely to Christ, wisely storing up in him the riches that you will find in the time of necessity, when no one will free anyone from the punishments of the condemned: neither a father his son, nor a mother her daughter, neither passing riches, nor any ambition among servants or greatness of inheritance; finally, not even a friend will free his friend. For then each person will be accompanied by his own burden.

“But you, my lord, having Christ with you—in whom you have placed all that is yours—go confidently; go without fear, so that you may receive his promises. Let no sight of things that pass like a shadow call you back; neither relatives, nor the groaning of parents, nor the very beauty of your body. Abhor the flatteries of deceptive friends; do not let the appearance of torments terrify you. Look upon the steadfastness and patience of these martyrs who are with you; attend to them alone.”

After the most glorious woman had spoken these words, kissing the bonds of each of the martyrs, she said: “I ask you, servants of Christ, strengthen this Adrian with your most blessed admonitions and win his soul for Christ. Be fathers to him; through you may he be born to eternal life.”

Blessed Adrian said to her: “Go now, my sister, to your house, and when I learn that our interrogation is to take place, I will summon you, so that you may see the outcome of the matter.”

After several days, when the examination was imminent, blessed Adrian, having paid the guards and provided guarantors, went to his house to summon blessed Natalia. As he was going, a man who knew him well saw him and ran ahead to the house, announcing that he was coming.

When his wife heard this, she did not believe it at first. “Who,” she said, “could have released him from those bonds? May it not happen to me that he has been released, lest he should at some time be separated from those saints?” When a household boy arrived and affirmed that he had been released, she suspected that Adrian had fled from martyrdom. Grieved, she wept most bitterly.

When she began to see Adrian, she threw down what was in her hands, ran forward, shut the door of the house, and cried out: “Let this man who has fallen and lied to the Lord his God be far from me. Let him not speak to me, nor may I hear the tongue that has acted deceitfully in the presence of its Maker.”

Then she turned toward him and said: “O godless man above all others, who compelled you to undertake a task that you could not complete? Who separated you from the saints, or who deceived you so that you withdrew from the fellowship of peace and rest? Tell me: why did you turn to flight before the battle began? Why did you throw down your weapons before seeing the enemy opposing you? How were you wounded before an arrow had even been shot? What shall I do, most wretched woman that I am, joined to an impious man? It has not been granted to me to be called the wife of a martyr, but to be called the consort of a transgressor. My rejoicing lasted for an hour, and behold, my disgrace will last through the ages.”

Blessed Adrian, standing outside the door, said to her: “Open to me, my sister Natalia, because I did not flee from martyrdom as you suppose. I have come because the time of our examination is at hand, so that, as I promised, you may be present.”

But she did not believe him. “See,” she said, “how the transgressor deceives me! Behold how another Judas lies! Go away from me, man; for I will kill myself before I join myself to you.”

The most blessed martyr, rejoicing in the zeal of his pious wife, satisfied her with his words and declared that, unless she opened quickly, he could not delay. At last she opened to him and fell at his feet.

Then they went out quickly and hastened to the confession, so that Adrian might be found among the crowned martyrs.

While they were still on the way, blessed Adrian said: “My sister, tell me: how have you arranged your property?”

She replied: “Do not, my lord, do not recall the things of this world, lest they draw your mind away. Let all corruptible things be removed from your thoughts; hasten only to see those things that have been stored up for you and for the saints with whom you walk on the way of God.”

When the appointed day had come for him to be brought forth, the most blessed martyrs were presented before Maximian. Their flesh had already become so putrefied from the severity of their torments that worms poured from their wounds.

Natalia, drawing close to blessed Adrian, said: “See, my lord, that your mind be directed solely toward God, and let your heart tremble at nothing when you see the torments prepared for you. The labor is brief now, but the rest is eternal throughout the ages of ages.”

Maximian looked at Adrian and said: “Do you still persist in madness?”

The blessed martyr replied: “For this very folly and madness I am prepared to end this life.”

After his pious confession, the tyrant became angry and ordered him beaten with such cruelty by successive executioners that, when his ribs had been opened, his entrails were exposed. Then he was again bound in irons and sent to prison.

After he had remained there for several days with the other holy servants of God, he was finally brought back, together with the others, whom the immense severity of their punishments had nearly consumed, and was set before Maximian. Seeing that they were now unshakable, Maximian ordered their shins to be broken with a great iron bar.

After their legs had been broken and their feet cut, and after the hand of blessed Adrian had also been cut off, they gave up their spirits while praying and giving thanks to the Lord.

The tyrant ordered their bodies to be burned. But suddenly flashes of lightning, thunder, and rains occurred, and the fire was extinguished. Many of the attendants were struck by lightning, and only a few barely escaped by flight.

Meanwhile, Christians came running, seized the martyrs’ relics from the already extinguished fire, boarded ships, and fled. They reached Byzantium and buried them there with reverent honor.

Not long afterward, the body of blessed Adrian was also transferred to Rome, where it was honored with a splendid church.

Natalia herself, sailing from Nicomedia to Byzantium out of love for the holy martyrs, received her repose in the Lord a few days after her arrival and was buried beside the bodies of the saints on the Kalends of December.

The passion of these martyrs is celebrated on the sixth day before the Ides of September.

## G. V IDUS SEPTEMBRIS. (9 Sept.)

[Note: [Col. 0351D] Eusebius, Book VIII, chapter 6.]

The passion of the blessed martyrs Dorotheus and Gorgonius at Nicomedia, under the emperor Diocletian.

The former, Dorotheus, was a master in the offices carried out within the palace and was superintendent of the royal chamber. With him was Gorgonius, equal to him in office, faith, and greatness of spirit. Through their excellent instruction, nearly all the attendants of the chamber persevered vigilantly and freely in faith in God.

When these men saw a certain martyr being tortured with cruel and savage punishments, they boldly and freely said: “Why, emperor, do you punish in this one man the conviction that lives in all of us? Why is he charged with the crime that we all confess? This is our faith, this is our worship, and this is our unanimous and identical judgment.”

Although he nevertheless ordered them to come forward, he commanded that they be hung up and their entire bodies torn by scourges. When their entrails had been stripped bare of skin, they were ordered to be drenched with vinegar and salt.

When they had endured this kind of torture steadfastly and courageously, a grating spread over burning coals was ordered to be placed in the midst. What remained of their bodies, already consumed by the beatings, was laid upon it and kindled—not suddenly, but slowly and little by little.

Finally, he ordered them to be killed while hanging by the noose.

After some time, blessed Gorgonius was transferred to Rome and reverently placed on the Via Latina between the two laurel trees. They completed their martyrdom on the fifth day before the Ides of September.

At the thirtieth milestone from the city, in the Sabine territory: the feast of the holy Hyacinthus, Alexander, and Tiburtius.

## A. IV IDUS SEPTEMBRIS. (10 Sept.)

In Africa, the feast of the holy bishops Nemesianus, Felix, and Lucius; likewise of Felix, Liteus, Polianus, Victor, Jader, and Dativus. When the fury of persecution arose under Decius and Valerian, they were severely beaten with clubs at the first steadfast confession of Christ. Then, bound in fetters and assigned to the mines, they completed the struggle of their glorious confession.

A large portion of the people followed their example and, confessing together with them, was likewise crowned. A letter of blessed Cyprian to them exists (Letter 77), and writings concerning them also survive.

[Note: [Col. 0351D] Concerning these men, in the Life of Saint Euphemia, 16 September.]

On the same day at Chalcedon, the feast of the holy Sosthenes and Victor. When blessed Euphemia was contending for the name of Christ under the consul Priscus, their eyes were divinely opened, and they saw angelic defenses surrounding her and a choir of holy virgins.

At this sight they turned to Christ. Because of their unshakable confession of faith, they were thrust into prison and then brought out and bound to stakes. First bears and then a most savage lion were released upon them, but when the animals did them no harm, the proconsul ordered a vat to be brought in which he could burn them together.

Meanwhile they devoted themselves to prayer. Called from heaven, they gave one another the kiss of peace and gave up their spirit.

## B. III IDUS SEPTEMBRIS. (11 Sept.)

[Note: [Col. 0352D] Concerning these men, in the Acts of Saint Euphemia, 25 December.]

At Rome, on the old Via Salaria, in the cemetery of Basilla, the feast of the holy Prothus and Hyacinthus. They were eunuchs of the blessed virgin Eugenia. Baptized with her by Bishop Helenus, they devoted themselves for some time solely to divine instruction, persevered in their holy purpose, and lived with remarkable humility in a monastery of the servants of God; this was in Egypt.

From there they returned to Rome with the most blessed virgin. Under the emperor Gallienus, because they were Christians, they were arrested and compelled to sacrifice. When they refused to consent, they were beaten with extreme cruelty. While rejoicing because they kept faith with God, they were beheaded together on the third day before the Ides of September.

After this, Saint Eugenia was detained, and the prefect of the city, Nicetius, ordered her to offer sacrifices to Diana. Standing before the temple, she poured out a prayer with outstretched hands. As she prayed, the statue of Diana was shattered so completely that only traces of its dust remained.

But they attributed this to magical arts. They bound a huge stone around her shoulders and threw her headlong into the Tiber. How she completed the struggle of her passion has been briefly recorded above, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

## C. PRIDIE IDUS SEPTEMBRIS. (12 Sept.)

[Col. 0352D]

At the city of Ticinum, also called Pavia, the feast of the holy Syrius and Evantius. Sent to that city by blessed Hermagoras, bishop of Aquileia and disciple of Saint Mark the Evangelist, they were the first there to preach the Gospel of Christ. Shining forth through great powers and miracles, they also enlightened the neighboring cities—Verona, namely, Brixia, and Lodi—through divine works.

Thus, after the faith of the believing peoples had been founded and strengthened, they rested in peace with a glorious end in the dignity of bishops.

## D. IDIBUS SEPTEMBRIS. (13 Sept.)

[Col. 0353A]

[Note: [Col. 0353D] Concerning these men, in the passion of Saint Eugenia, 25 December.]

In Egypt, in the city of Alexandria, the feast of Blessed Philip, bishop and martyr. He was first a prefect; then, sanctified by the grace of baptism, he attained the dignity of bishop with the support of the Christian people.

Under the emperors Volusian and Gallienus, the prefect Perennius was sent to Alexandria and ordered to kill Philip. But he could not accomplish this, because the whole population of the city appeared to be bound to Philip as though by certain bonds of love. Therefore he sent some men into the church who pretended to be Christians. When they entered, they struck Philip while he was engaged in prayer.

He was buried in Nitria, where a basilica worthy of the martyr was built over his body. He held the episcopate for one year and three months. He suffered on the Ides of September.

Likewise, Saint Amatus, priest and abbot of the monastery of Saint Romaricus. A follower of remarkable abstinence and an anchoritic life, he led a distinguished way of life through virtue and miracles.

## E. XVIII KAL. OCTOBRIS. (14 Sept.)

[Note: [Col. 0354D] Pontifical Book, chapter 22; Cyprian, Letter 34.]

At Rome, on the Via Appia, in the cemetery of Callistus, the feast of Saint Cornelius, bishop. During the persecution of Decius, he was sent into exile at Centumcellae together with priests and deacons. Many Christians came to encourage him.

At that time blessed Cyprian wrote to him concerning the lector Celerinus and all that he had suffered for the faith and confession of Christ.

When Caesar Decius heard that many people were writing to Cornelius concerning blessed Cyprian, he ordered Cornelius brought before him. When Cornelius was brought before Decius and asked why he had received letters from Cyprian against the commonwealth, he replied: “I received letters concerning the crown of the Lord, not against the commonwealth.”

Angry, Decius ordered his mouth to be beaten with leaded clubs, and then ordered him taken to the temple of Mars to sacrifice. If he refused, he was to be executed there.

As he was being led away, one of the soldiers, named Cerealis, began to beg the blessed pope to visit his wife, who had lain paralyzed for five years. Entering his house, Cornelius took Salustia by the hand and raised her, saying: “In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, arise and stand upon your feet.”

She immediately rose and cried out: “Truly Christ is the Son of God.” Then she said to blessed Cornelius: “Baptize me; I adjure you by Christ.” She ran, filled a vessel with water, and brought it to him.

Then all the soldiers threw themselves at his feet and asked to be baptized. When he had baptized them, he offered a sacrifice of praise for them, and they all partook of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

When Decius heard this, he sent men to seize them all and ordered them to be led with blessed Cornelius to sacrifice. If they refused to obey, they were to be beheaded.

They were led outside the walls at the Appian Gate. After spitting upon that temple, they were beheaded together with the most blessed pope, twenty-one in number.

Cerealis and his wife Salustia were also martyred on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.

That same night blessed Lucina came with her clergy and household, seized the bodies of the martyrs, and buried them on her estate in a crypt in the cemetery of Callistus.

At the request of this blessed Lucina, the same blessed Cornelius also secretly removed the bodies of the apostles from the catacombs and placed Paul on the Ostian Way, where he had been beheaded, and Peter beside the place where he had been crucified, among the bodies of the holy bishops, in the temple of Apollo on the Golden Mount, in the Vatican, at Nero’s palace, on the third day before the Kalends of July.

Likewise in Africa, the feast of blessed Cyprian, bishop, under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, with Galerius Maximus as proconsul.

He was arrested at the command of the consul Aspasius Paternus, through the efforts and exertions of the pagans, and sent into exile in the city of Curubis. There he lived with his mind suspended toward heaven, animated solely by love of Christ to trample underfoot the sufferings of the present age.

Many distinguished men of illustrious rank and lineage came to him, men also renowned for their worldly nobility. Because of their long-standing friendship with him, they repeatedly urged him to withdraw, and, so that their persuasion would not be merely verbal, they even offered him places to which he might retire.

After many days he returned from exile and lived in his gardens. While he was staying there, two officials from the office of the consul Galerius Maximus, who had succeeded Aspasius Paternus, came to him. They lifted him into a carriage and brought him to the proconsul at the estate of Sextus, where he was staying to recover his health.

There, received by an officer of the staff, Cyprian withdrew into his lodging in the Saturnian quarter. All the people of the brethren gathered around him.

When the blessed martyr learned this, he ordered the girls who had come to hear the word of God to be kept under guard, since they were remaining before the officer’s door out of love for the glorious martyr.

The next day, the morning of the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, Galerius Maximus ordered Saint Cyprian the bishop to be brought before him in the small courtyard.

Among other things, the proconsul said to him: “The most sacred emperors have ordered you to perform the rites.”

Saint Cyprian said: “I will not.”

The proconsul Maximus said: “Take counsel for yourself.”

Saint Cyprian said: “Do what has been commanded you, for in so just a matter there is no deliberation.”

The proconsul Maximus said: “For a long time you have lived with a sacrilegious mind, and you have gathered around you wicked men of your conspiracy. You have made yourself an enemy of the Roman gods and sacred religious observances, and the pious emperors have not been able to summon you to the practice of their rites. Since you have been caught as the author and standard-bearer of the most wicked crime, you yourself will serve as an example, together with those whom you have gathered to yourself through your crime; by your blood their discipline shall be confirmed.”

After saying this, he read the decree from the tablet: “It is decided that Thascius Cyprian is to be punished by the sword.”

When Saint Cyprian heard this, he said: “Thanks be to God.”

As he was being led away, the crowd of the brethren wept and said: “Let us too be beheaded with him.”

Thus the glorious martyr was led behind the praetorium into the estate of Sextus. He removed his short military cloak and folded it beneath his knees. Then he took off his dalmatic tunic and handed it to the deacons. Standing in his linen garment, he awaited the executioner, to whom he ordered that twenty-five gold pieces be given.

The brethren, weeping, laid linen cloths and napkins before him, so that the holy blood flowing forth would not be absorbed by the earth. When he could not tie the strips of cloth around himself with his own hands, the presbyter Julius and the subdeacon Julian tied them for him.

He himself covered his eyes with his own hand, placed his knees upon the ground, and poured out a prayer to the Lord. Then he was struck by the sword and departed this life.

Because of the curiosity of the pagans, his body was placed nearby. But, lest it be taken by the pagans, when night came it was removed from the place where it had been laid.

From there, with candles and scolaces, it was buried with great triumph in the courtyard of a certain Candidus, a procurator, on the Mappalian Way near the fishponds.

[Note: [Col. 0355D] “With candles and scolaces.” This is the genuine reading, and it is found in the very ancient manuscript books of the Life of Saint Cyprian. In all printed books up to now, the reading has commonly been scholaribus, which gave Baronius, in his Notes for 6 February, the occasion to interpret scholares as clerics of various classes. But the true reading is the one I have given; it must now be explained, since it has so far occurred to me in only a few authors.

Isidore, Etymologies, Book XX, chapter 10: “Funalia are what are within wax; they are called from funes, ‘cords,’ because before the use of papyrus our ancestors enclosed cords in wax; hence they are also called funera. The Greeks call funalia scolaces, because they are scoliciae, that is, of death.” Read instead: “because they are σκολιοί, that is, twisted.” The Glosses of Isidore open the way to this reading: “Scolaces, which we call funalia, because they are scoliae, that is, twisted. The Romans called these cords and funalia.”

Peter Damian, Book VI, Letter 17: “For who lights a lamp in order to see the sun? Who uses scolaces in order to see the brightness of shining stars?”

Thus Cyprian’s funeral was honored with both candles and scolaces. Among the ancients, candles and torches were very often joined in funerals, just as here candles and scolaces.]

After many years had passed, while the most glorious Charles ruled the Franks, it happened that illustrious and prudent ambassadors, bearing a mission from the Franks, traveled through Africa.

When returning from King Aaron of the Persians—who, except for India, held almost the whole East—they saw Carthage in ruins and the venerable places of the holy martyrs. Having easily won the favor of the ruler, who showed goodwill in such a matter, they asked him as a great gift to allow them to carry away the bones of Blessed Cyprian.

He, considering the request of little importance, immediately granted what they asked. He willingly agreed that they should carry them to the pious emperor, whose favor he valued above the friendship of all the kings and rulers throughout the world.

When the venerable ambassadors returned bearing immense gifts—namely, relics of martyrs, for they also had with them the remains of blessed Speratus, one of the twelve most illustrious Scillitan martyrs, and the head of the glorious martyr Pantaleon, together with the blessed bones of Cyprian—they sailed with favorable winds and eventually reached Arles.

There they temporarily left the sacred remains of the martyrs under seal and hurried to report their mission to the glorious emperor. In order to win the king’s favor still more through their successful embassy, they also increased his enthusiasm by telling him, among other things, about the relics of the saints brought from Africa.

He was exceedingly pleased and ordered that they be kept at Arles with fitting reverence until he himself should build a church in his kingdom through some great undertaking, where he could place so precious a pledge with immense devotion and adornment.

But while the work was being delayed because of intervening circumstances, Leidradus, the venerable bishop of Lyon, seized the opportunity and asked the glorious emperor for permission to bring the blessed bones of the martyrs to his own city.

The emperor agreed. The pious bishop promptly fulfilled his desire. They were carried with honor into the city of Lyon and kept for some time in the principal church of blessed John the Baptist and Saint Stephen the martyr.

Since God mercifully brought this about for the defense of the citizens, and since the emperor had now transferred his plan for building the church elsewhere, the holy bishop placed the most blessed relics of the glorious martyrs in the aforementioned church, behind the venerable and sacred altar, in a most suitable burial place, and honorably entrusted them to his future citizens for their benefit.

Later, after some time had passed, while the glorious King Charles, son of the emperor Louis, was reigning, the relics of Blessed Cyprian were again transferred, at his command, to the new monastery that the same king had built in imperial fashion at Compiègne, his palace.

Crescentianus, Victor, Rosula, and Generalis are reported to have suffered together with blessed Cyprian.

On the same day: the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, which was found by Helena, the mother of Constantine, and divided through the middle, so that one part of the cross was carried to Constantinople, while the other part was preserved in silver cases at Jerusalem.

After many years had passed, while Phocas ruled the Romans, the Persians, waging extremely fierce wars against the commonwealth under their king Chosroes, invaded many Roman provinces and Jerusalem itself. Destroying the churches and profaning the holy places, they also carried away, among the sacred ornaments they seized, the standard of the Lord’s cross.

For King Chosroes had made a silver tower in which, amid gleaming gems, he had constructed a golden throne. There he placed the sun’s four-horse chariot and an image of the moon or the stars. Through hidden pipes he had brought in channels of water, so that he might appear, as though he were God, to pour down rain from above.

While the tower, constructed in an underground chamber and seemingly set in motion by horses drawing it around in a circle, was made to revolve, it imitated, as far as the craftsman’s ability allowed, something like the roar of thunder.

In this place he had prepared a seat for himself, and beside it he placed the Lord’s cross as though he were God’s colleague. After handing the kingdom over to his son, he himself remained seated in such a shrine.

After Phocas died, Heraclius was made emperor, a vigorous man trained in warfare. He began war against the Persians, killed Chosroes—whom he found seated in the aforementioned tower—and received the Persians into submission.

Then, returning from there, he carried with him the wood of the most glorious cross and restored it with great veneration to Jerusalem, from which it had been taken.

As God renewed the ancient miracles, among the many wonders then displayed from heaven, on that same day one dead man received life, four paralytics were healed, ten lepers were cleansed, fifteen blind people received sight, many were rescued from demons, and many others were freed from various illnesses.

The emperor therefore offered many gifts to the churches of God and had them repaired at royal expense. At the same time, with all the bishops agreeing, he decreed that the day of the restoration and exaltation of the holy and venerable cross of the Lord should be solemnly celebrated every year throughout his entire empire by all faithful peoples.

As the years passed, while Leo ruled the Romans, at the city of Rome Sergius found in the sacristy of blessed Peter the Apostle, in an exceedingly dark corner, a silver chest that had lain there for a very long time. In it, by the Lord’s revelation, he discovered a cross adorned with various precious stones.

After removing four panels in which gems had been set, he saw inside a portion of the life-giving wood of the Lord’s cross, of marvelous size.

From that time onward, every year on the day of its exaltation, this portion is kissed and worshiped by the entire people in the Basilica of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana.

## F. XVII KAL. OCTOBRIS. (15 Sept.)

[Note: [Col. 0357D] Concerning him, in the Life of the Saints Nereus and Achilleus, 12 May.]

The feast of Saint Nicomedes the martyr. When Count Flaccus was informed that Nicomedes had buried the body of the holy virgin Felicula, whom Flaccus himself had punished for Christ, he ordered Nicomedes seized and led away to sacrifice.

When Nicomedes said, “I sacrifice only to the almighty God who reigns in heaven, not to these stones cut from rock, which are shut up and guarded in temples as though in prisons,” he was beaten for a very long time with leaded clubs and departed to the Lord.

His body was thrown into the Tiber. A cleric named Justus, both by name and deed, recovered it, carried it to his own little garden, and buried it beside the walls on the Nomentan Way.

[Note: [Col. 0358D] Concerning him, in the Life of Saint Marcellus, 4 September.]

On the same day, in the territory of the people of Chalon, at the fortress of Trenortius, the feast of Saint Valerian the martyr. He was one of the fifty saints who, in the time of Antoninus Verus, had been thrust into prison at Lyon and who, together with Blessed Marcellus, escaped when the divinely opened barriers of the prison in which they were detained were opened.

When he reached the aforementioned fortress and preached the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, converting many to his faith through the Lord’s inspiration, he was denounced to the governor Priscus as he was returning from the city of Chalon, where Priscus had killed Blessed Marcellus the martyr for the name of Christ.

Priscus had him brought before him and first tried to break him by threats and intimidation. Then he had him hung up and tortured with severe tearing by claws. When he saw that Valerian remained immovable in his confession of Christ and continued joyfully in Christ’s praises, he immediately ordered him executed by the sword at the place where his sacred body is now honored with due veneration.

On the same day, the burial of the most blessed Aprus, bishop and confessor of Toul.

## G. XVI KAL. OCTOBRIS. (16 Sept.)

The feast of Saint Euphemia the virgin, who was martyred under the emperor Diocletian, with Priscus as proconsul, in the city of Chalcedon.

When the most wicked Apellian denounced her, she was handed over to the proconsul Priscus together with forty-nine others.

Priscus said to her: “Honor yourself and do not lose the dignity of your family; sacrifice to the god Mars.”

Blessed Euphemia, rejecting his wicked persuasion, fortified her breast with the sign of the cross and stood undaunted.

Priscus, enraged and wishing to overcome her, used against her, after tortures and prisons, beatings and the devices of wheels, fires and the weights of massive stones, beasts and blows of rods, axes and fiery frying pans. Finally, he ordered her taken into the theater and lions and beasts released upon her.

Then the blessed virgin poured out a prayer to the Lord and said:

“You, Lord, known to all who call upon you with pure and whole faith, receive the soul of your handmaid. And just as you received the sacrifice of our father Abraham, so may you deign to receive the sacrifice of my humility, which is offered to you for the confession of your praise.”

Then only one of the beasts rushed forward, fastened its teeth into her holy body, and the virgin gave her immaculate spirit to the Lord.

Her mother Theodora and her father Philosophron came and buried her body, after it had been attended to, about a thousand paces from the city of Chalcedon.

Her martyrdom was completed on the sixteenth day of the month of September.

On the same day, at Rome, the birthday [martyrdom] of the holy Lucia and Geminianus, under the emperor Diocletian and the judges Apofrasius and Megasius.

The blessed Lucia had remained a widow for thirty-six years. The whole span of her life was seventy-five years. When she was accused by her son Euprepius of being a Christian, the emperor Diocletian ordered her to be brought before him and said to her:

“I hear that you confess the one who was crucified as guilty, and that you mock our gods. Now, therefore, if you are prepared to live, the almighty gods are ready for you to offer incense to them, so that they may be propitious to you and you may live.”

Saint Lucia replied:

“They are propitious neither to themselves nor to their worshipers; [Col. 0358D] but my Lord Jesus Christ will be propitious to me, for whose love I am prepared to endure fire, chains, and whatever punishments you wish.”

When Diocletian heard the steadfastness of her faith, he ordered her to be dragged to prison, where she earned divine consolation. Then she was brought again before Diocletian, seated on the tribunal; the glorious woman was stretched out and beaten with clubs for a very long time. And suddenly an earthquake occurred, and the temple of Jupiter was so thoroughly destroyed that not one stone of its structure remained upon another.

Diocletian then had a bronze cauldron brought and ordered it to be filled with pitch and lead, wood to be piled around it and set alight [Col. 0359A], and Saint Lucia to be plunged beneath the cauldron. There, while singing psalms to God, the holy woman lived for three days. Diocletian sent someone to report whether she had by then been reduced entirely to ashes. The man who had been sent returned and informed the emperor that she was living unharmed and healthy, without any injury.

Then the impious man, not in the least moved to believe in Christ by so great a miracle, ordered her to be loaded with iron and lead and dragged through the streets of the city. She came before the house of a powerful man named Geminianus, whose house contained countless images of demons. When Saint Lucia had passed through the house itself, suddenly a white dove, like snow, descended from heaven and, forming the sign of the cross three times above Geminianus’s head, settled upon it. Looking up, Geminianus saw that heaven was open to him, and immediately set out at a run, arriving [Col. 0359B] at the place where the holy woman was already being tortured.

Throwing himself at her feet, he began to relate what he had seen and to ask for the bath of baptism. Thus the blessed Lucia was returned to prison. There was a certain priest named Protasius. One night an angel of the Lord appeared to him and instructed him to go to the prison and baptize Geminianus, who was seeking the fountain of salvation. When he awoke, he went there at once and washed the blessed man with saving water.

On the third day Saint Lucia was brought before Diocletian, and Geminianus with her, of whom the emperor had already heard. After inflicting the most severe punishments upon them and torturing them for a long time, he handed them over to a most wicked judge, so that he himself might supply whatever punishments were still lacking. The judge first ordered their necks to be battered with clubs. Then, when an earthquake occurred, the roof of the judicial building collapsed [Col. 0359C] and crushed the impious judge.

Afterward the holy martyrs were brought before Apofrasius. Under him seventy-five martyrs also completed their martyrdom, having believed when they saw the miracles that the Lord worked around his saints. After the death of these holy martyrs, this most impious judge was thrown from the Stone Bridge into the river by the devil, who spurred on his horse. His body was afterward found nowhere.

Then the blessed Lucia and Saint Geminianus, seized by Megasius, a consular official, were put to death by the sword after their praiseworthy victory of martyrdom, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October. A Christian woman named Maxima took away their bodies and buried the martyrs as was fitting.

**A. Fifteen days before the Kalends of October (17 September).**

[Col. 0359D]

[Note: [Col. 0359D] Concerning this, see the Acts of Saint Laurence.]

In Britain, Saints Socrates and Stephen.

At Nividunum, the birthday of the holy martyrs Valerian, Macrinus, and Cordianus.

Likewise at Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, at Saint Laurence’s, the birthday of the blessed Justin, a priest whom the blessed Sixtus ordained. The blessed Laurence came to him at night in the district of Patricius, in the Nepotian crypt, in order to distribute to the poor the treasures entrusted to him by Saint Sixtus. He said to him [Col. 0360A]:

“Fulfill my vow, so that the feet of the saints and your feet may be washed by my hands.”

The blessed Justin replied:

“This is the Lord’s commandment; let the will of our Lord Jesus Christ be done.”

He then set down a basin, poured in water, and washed the feet of all the men. When he came to the blessed Justin, he first began to kiss and wash his feet. After washing everyone’s feet, he commended himself to the blessed Justin.

This Justin honorably buried the body of the same martyr in the estate of the widow Cyriaca. By making the sign of Christ and placing upon her head the linen cloth with which he had wiped the feet of the saints, he healed her from illnesses of the head.

He also buried Saint Hippolytus and Concordia, Irenaeus, Abendius, Cyrilla, the daughter of Caesar Decius, and many other martyrs. During the persecution of Decius, Gallus, and Volusianus [Col. 0360B], he was renowned above all for the glory of his confession.

At Rome, in the sand quarry, the holy martyrs Narcissus and Crescens.

[Note: [Col. 0359D] Concerning these, see the Acts of Saint Laurence, 30 August.]

In the diocese of Tongeren, at Liège [manuscript: Leogium], a public estate, the birthday of Saint Lambert, bishop. When he had rebuked the royal household, inflamed by zeal for religion, and afterward returned to devote himself to prayer, he was unexpectedly shut up inside the church building by most wicked men sent from the royal palace and was killed. His tomb is illuminated by very frequent miracles, and his death is nevertheless commended as precious in the sight of the Lord.

**B. Fourteen days before the Kalends of October (18 September).**

[Note: [Col. 0359D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 83.]

The birthday of Saint Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia and afterward [Col. 0360C] of Tyre, who was crowned with martyrdom at Chalcis in Greece under Diocletian.

At Vienne, the birthday of Saint Ferreolus. During a persecution, while he held the office of tribune, he was seized by order of the most impious governor, first beaten with extreme cruelty, then loaded with the heavy weight of chains, and thrust into a most dreadful prison. From there, when God’s will released his bonds and the prison doors were opened, he entered the public road and reached as far as the River Jare. There he was seized again, his hands bound behind his back, and he was led as far as the territory of Brioude. There he received the palm of martyrdom by the cutting off of his head.

His body, together with the head of the blessed Julian, was brought back to the city of Vienne and buried with fitting honor in the basilica which Castulus, a man of distinguished reputation [Col. 0360D] among the leading citizens of Vienne, had built in honor of the same martyr while still a catechumen, with as much workmanship as faith, on the farther bank of the Rhône [Note: [Col. 0360D] Sidonius Apollinaris 1.7, chapter 1].

**C. Thirteen days before the Kalends of October (19 September).**

[Note: [Col. 0360D] Concerning him, see the Passion of Sosius, 23 September.]

At Naples in Campania, the birthday of the holy Januarius, bishop of the city of Benevento, together with Sosius, deacon of the city of Misenum, and his own deacon Festus and lector Desiderius. After chains and imprisonments, they were beheaded [Col. 0361A] in the city of Pozzuoli under the emperor Diocletian and the judge Dracontius.

When they were being led to death, they saw among the others Proculus, deacon of the city of Pozzuoli, and two laymen, Eutyches and Acutus, who asked why just men were being ordered to be killed. When the judge saw that these men were Christians, he ordered them to be beheaded with the others. Thus all seven were beheaded together.

Christians took away their bodies. The Neapolitans placed Januarius in a basilica beside the city; the people of Misenum likewise placed Sosius in a basilica; the people of Pozzuoli placed Proculus, Eutyches, and Acutus beside the basilica of Saint Stephen; and the people of Benevento gathered Festus and Desiderius.

[Note: [Col. 0361D] Eusebius, book VIII, chapters 22 and 25.]

On the same day in Palestine, the birthday of the holy martyrs Peleus and Nilus, bishops, who during the persecution of Diocletian were consumed by fire for Christ together with many clerics [Col. 0361B].

At Nocera, the birthday of the holy martyrs Felix and Constantia, who suffered under Nero.

In the territory of the city of Langres, Saint Sigo, a priest.

**D. Twelve days before the Kalends of October (20 September).**

At Cyzicus, the birthday of Saint Fausta, a virgin, and Evilasius, under the emperor Maximian. When Evilasius was chief official of the palace, he ordered Fausta’s head to be shaved and her hair cut off to shame her; afterward he ordered her to be suspended and tortured. At that time a flash from heaven struck many of the attendants.

Then he ordered boxes or coffins (*loculos*) to be brought, and, after she had been placed in and fixed there, ordered her to be sawn through the middle like wood [Col. 0361C]. But the executioners were unable to injure her with their saws. Evilasius, astonished at this, began to believe in Christ.

When this was reported to the emperor, he sent a prefect to have Evilasius suspended and severely tortured. He also ordered Fausta to be led naked from the prison, without a mantle, and to have her head pierced and nails driven into it. Later, not only her head and face but also her breast and entire body, down to her shins, were filled with nails.

After this he ordered a frying pan to be heated, but while she sang psalms it grew cold. Then a voice came from heaven and called them; thus they gave up their spirits. Fausta was twenty-three years old, and Evilasius eighty.

**E. Eleven days before the Kalends of October (21 September).**

[Col. 0361D] [Note: [Col. 0362D] See the book on the Feasts of the Apostles. Concerning him, below, 26 November.]

The birthday of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist.

On the same day, the passion of Saint Alexander, bishop, under the emperor Antoninus.

**F. Ten days before the Kalends of October (22 September).**

In Gaul, in the city of Sion, at Agaunum, the birthday of the holy Theban martyrs Maurice, Exuperius, Candidus, Victor, Innocentius, Vitalis, and their companions, who suffered for Christ under Maximian and were crowned most gloriously.

To speak briefly, then, about the cause of their most blessed passion: under Maximian, who held the empire together with Diocletian as colleague of the Roman state, peoples of martyrs were torn apart and killed throughout almost every province [Col. 0362A]. For this same Maximian had armed his profane impiety against the Lord of heaven in order to extinguish the name of Christianity. If anyone at that time dared to profess the worship of the true God, bands of soldiers were scattered everywhere, and such people were dragged either to punishment or to death.

At that same time there was in the army a legion of soldiers called Thebans. A legion was the name given to a force that then had six thousand six hundred armed men. These men had been summoned from the eastern regions to assist Maximian. They were vigorous in military affairs and noble in courage, but nobler still in faith; toward the emperor they competed in courage, and toward Christ in devotion.

When they, like the other soldiers, were assigned to tear apart the multitude of Christians, they alone dared to refuse the service of cruelty and declared that they would not obey commands of this kind [Col. 0362B]. Maximian was not far away, for he had halted near Octodurum, wearied by the journey. When he learned the response of the Thebans, burning with sudden anger, he ordered every tenth man of that same legion to be struck down with the sword for neglecting his commands, so that the others, terrified by this definite example, might more easily yield through fear.

His orders having been renewed, he announced that the rest were to be compelled to persecute the Christians. When the repeated order reached the Thebans, and they learned that profane executions were once again being imposed upon them, shouting and tumult arose throughout the camp. They declared that they would never yield to anyone in such utterly sacrilegious services.

When this became known, Maximian, more bloodthirsty than any beast [Col. 0362C], returned again to the savagery of his nature and ordered a second tenth of them to be put to death; the others were nevertheless to be compelled to perform what they despised. When these commands had again been brought to the camp, the man who by lot had fallen as the tenth was separated and struck down.

The remaining multitude of soldiers encouraged one another in conversation to persist in so glorious an order. The greatest stimulus to their faith, however, came from Saint Maurice, the first officer of that legion. Together with Exuperius, called in the army the camp commander, and Candidus, the soldiers’ senator, he went among them, exhorting and admonishing each one and placing before the faithful comrades the examples of their fellow soldiers, who had also become martyrs.

Thus encouraged by these leaders and authors of their resolve, the most blessed men sent Maximian, still seething with madness, a message [Col. 0362D] both devout and courageous:

“We are your soldiers, emperor; but we are also, as we freely confess, servants of God. To you we owe military service; to him, innocence. From you we receive the pay for our labor; from him we received the beginning of life. We cannot in this matter follow the emperor and deny God, who is our author and, whether you wish it or not, your author as well.

“If we are not compelled to such deadly acts that we offend him, we shall continue to obey you as we have done until now; but if it is otherwise, we shall obey him rather than you. We offer our hands against any enemy, but we consider it unlawful to stain them with the blood of the innocent. These right hands [Col. 0363A] know how to fight against the impious and against enemies; they do not know how to tear apart the devout and their fellow citizens.

“We remember that we took up arms for our fellow citizens rather than against our fellow citizens. We have always fought for justice, for piety, and for the safety of the innocent; these have until now been the rewards of our dangers. We have fought for the faith. How can we preserve it for you in any way if we do not present it to our God?

“We first swore the divine oath; thereafter we swore the royal oath. Believe us: we need nothing from the second if we break the first. You command that Christians be sought out for punishment by our hands; from now on you need seek no others. Here you have us confessing God the Father, author of all things, and believing in his Son, Jesus Christ the Lord.

“We see our companions in labors and dangers being slaughtered by the sword, while we too are sprinkled with their blood [Col. 0363B]. We have not wept over or grieved at the deaths of our holy comrades and the funerals of our brothers; rather, we have praised them and accompanied them with joy, because they were considered worthy to suffer for the Lord their God.

“Not even the necessity of this final life drives us into rebellion. Not even despair itself—which is at least the strongest force in dangers—has armed us against you, emperor. Behold, we hold weapons, yet we do not resist, because we prefer to die rather than to kill, and we prefer the innocent to perish rather than the guilty to live.

“If you decide anything further against us, if you give any further order, if you apply anything else—fire, torture, or iron—we are prepared to endure it. We confess that we are Christians; we cannot persecute Christians.”

When Maximian heard these things and saw that the men’s minds were obstinate in the faith of Christ [Col. 0363C], he despaired of being able to turn back their glorious steadfastness. He therefore decreed in a single sentence that they should all be killed and ordered the deed to be carried out by surrounding them with ranks of soldiers.

When the soldiers sent for this purpose came to the most blessed legion, they drew their impious swords against the saints, who did not refuse to die for the love of life. They were struck down everywhere with swords, not even crying out or resisting, but laying aside their arms, offering their necks to the persecutors, and presenting their throats—or their uncovered bodies—to those who persecuted them.

The martyr Victor, however, had not belonged to this legion and was not a soldier, but a veteran who had already completed his military service. While traveling, he suddenly came upon these men, who were joyfully feasting everywhere on the spoils of the martyrs. Invited by them to join their meal, he learned from the revelers in due order the reason for their celebration [Col. 0363D]. He denounced the banqueters and, having denounced the banquet, withdrew. When they asked whether he too might perhaps be a Christian, he replied that he was a Christian and would always remain one.

He was immediately killed by those who attacked him and was joined to the other martyrs not only in death but also in honor.

It seems fitting to gather briefly what afterward befell the tyrant Maximian. When he was plotting the death of his son-in-law Constantine by arranging an ambush, his deception was discovered and he was captured near Massilia. Not long afterward he was strangled and subjected to a most dreadful punishment, ending his impious life by a death he deserved.

But after many years had passed since the passion of the most blessed martyrs, their bodies were revealed to Saint Theodore, the bishop, and a basilica was honorably built in their honor [Col. 0364A]. After a long passage of time, the Rhône also revealed the remains of the blessed martyr Innocentius. It did not bring them forth from the earth’s embrace in order to drown them in the violence of its whirlpool, but so that they might be joined honorably in burial to the other martyrs.

**G. Nine days before the Kalends of October (25 September).**

The birthday of Saint Sosius, deacon of the city of Misenum in Campania. When he was thirty years old, he received martyrdom by beheading together with the blessed Januarius, bishop of Benevento, in the time of the emperor Diocletian.

Once, while he was reading the Gospel in the church of the city of Misenum, with Bishop Januarius present—for Januarius frequently visited him because of his holiness and prudence [Col. 0364B]—the bishop suddenly saw a flame rising from Sosius’s head, which no one else saw. He declared that Sosius would become a martyr.

Not many days later the deacon was seized and sent to prison. When the bishop came to visit him, together with the deacon Festus and his lector Desiderius, he too was seized with them, and all were killed together with three others.

On the same day, the birthday of Saint Thecla, a virgin, who rests at Seleucia. She had been instructed in the city of Iconium by the blessed apostle Paul. When her mother saw that she was a Christian and that she rejected marriage, preferring to cling to Christ the bridegroom rather than submit to the corruption of the flesh, she went to the judge and accused her own virgin daughter of being a Christian. She said that the girl ought to be burned alive so that the other women would be frightened [Col. 0364C].

When the judge ordered her to be brought before him and learned of her resolve to preserve her chastity, he had a pyre prepared in order to burn her. When the attendants seized her to throw her into the fire, she climbed onto the pyre willingly, made the sign of the cross, and stood among the flames with manly courage. Suddenly there was a great inundation of rain, the fire was extinguished, and the blessed virgin was rescued unharmed by heavenly power.

Again, while she was devoting herself to fasts, vigils, and prayers, she was seized by a powerful man and brought before the governor because she called herself a Christian. When the proconsul asked her whether the accusation was true, she replied that she was indeed a Christian. The governor immediately condemned her to the beasts.

Meanwhile, so that she might be cared for [Col. 0364D; the printed reading *subrigeretur* is uncertain], she was entrusted to a noblewoman named Tryphaena, who was related to Caesar. On the following day the beasts were brought out from their cages. The blessed Thecla was placed in the middle of the arena, while the people marveled that the beasts did not touch her at all.

The blessed Thecla was returned to Tryphaena’s house so that she might once again be thrown to the wild animals on the following day. When the attendants came to take her from the house, Tryphaena, full of grief, followed her all the way to the spectacle, where there was an immense shouting and tumult from the crowd watching the blessed Thecla.

After the blessed virgin had been stripped, lions and bears were released against her together. But none of the beasts dared injure her. Then, when she was being driven by the raging crowds into a pit full of water, where snakes had been gathered and collected, she leapt in protected by the sign of the cross [Col. 0365A]; but she was not harmed by them in any way.

Again more savage beasts were prepared, but they were in no way permitted to touch her. Yet cruelty still did not put an end to itself. She was bound to two most ferocious bulls, goaded with red-hot iron, so that they might tear her apart. But the bulls broke their ropes, ran about wandering here and there, and left the martyr unharmed.

At last the proconsul summoned her and asked who she was and where she came from, since none of the beasts had been able to injure her. The blessed Thecla replied:

“I am only a servant of the living God.”

The proconsul, terrified at the magnitude of her power, clothed her in garments and pronounced the sentence:

“I release Thecla, the devout worshiper and servant of God.”

After she was released, she returned to Tryphaena’s house, where she rested for a few days, teaching Tryphaena and her household [Col. 0365B] the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ.

From there she departed and came to Seleucia. There, by the example and conduct of her life and also by her teaching, she instructed very many people. After many struggles for the double crown of virginity and martyrdom, she rested in peace.

**A. Eight days before the Kalends of October (24 September).**

The conception of Saint John the Baptist of the Lord.

At Augustodunum, the birthday of Saint Andochius, priest, Thyrsus, deacon, and Felix. Sent from the East by Saint Polycarp, bishop, to teach Gaul, they were crowned most gloriously under the emperor Aurelian.

They were beaten with whips and, finally, suspended all day with their hands inverted and thrown into the fire, but they were not burned. At last their necks were struck with bars, and thus they completed their martyrdom most gloriously, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [Col. 0365C].

**B. Seven days before the Kalends of October (25 September).**

[Note: [Col. 0365D] See the book on the Feasts of the Apostles.]

The birthday of the blessed Cleophas, to whom the Lord appeared on the road after the resurrection.

At Lyon, Saint Lupus, bishop, formerly an anchorite.

**C. Six days before the Kalends of October (26 September).**

The birthday of the holy martyrs Cyprian, bishop, and Justina, who suffered under the emperor Diocletian and the judge Eutolmius.

Justina’s father was Dusius, in the vicinity of the city of Antioch. Having heard the way of religion from a deacon named Prohelius, they were baptized by Saint Optatus, the bishop [Col. 0365D]. The virgin Justina, serving the Lord, regularly attended church.

When Agladius, a student, saw her, he burst into love for her. Since he could in no way reach her, he asked the magician Cyprian and promised him two talents of gold if he could arouse the virgin Justina’s love for him.

The magician Cyprian, having summoned demons, began to work so that they might bring Christ’s virgin to Agladius. They came to the blessed Justina once, twice, and a third time, but their deceptions achieved nothing with her. Driven back by the sign of the cross, they withdrew defeated.

When Cyprian saw that their power had in no way prevailed against the virgin, he said to the devil:

“Tell [Col. 0366A] me, how were you defeated by the virgin Justina?”

The devil replied:

“We cannot tell you unless you first swear to me.”

When Cyprian had sworn to him, the devil said:

“I saw the sign of the Crucified One, and I was afraid.”

Cyprian said:

“Then what? Is the Crucified One greater than you?”

The devil replied:

“Yes; for he is greater than all.”

When Cyprian heard this, he despised the devil’s power, ran to Bishop Anthimus, fell at his feet, and begged him to teach him and seal him with Christ’s baptism. The blessed bishop gave thanks to God and instructed him as a catechumen.

When Cyprian returned to his house, he broke all the idols. Then he returned to the church and began carefully to listen to the word of salvation.

Later, at the hour when the catechumens were sent out of the church, a deacon warned him to leave with the other catechumens [Col. 0366B]. Turning to the deacon, he said:

“I have become Christ’s servant, and you are sending me outside?”

The deacon said to him:

“Have you become a perfect servant of God?”

Cyprian replied:

“Christ lives for me—he who confounded the demons and had mercy on me. I will not leave here until I have become a perfect servant of Christ.”

The deacon reported these words to Bishop Anthimus. The bishop baptized him according to the established order, and not long afterward ordained him a deacon as well. Growing beyond what can be expressed in teaching and conduct, he flourished most brilliantly through the grace of miracles.

After not much time had passed, he became a bishop and appointed the holy Justina mother of the virgins. The devil, unable to tolerate their power, worked through his agents upon the governor Eutolmius, the count of the East [Col. 0366C], so that Bishop Cyprian and Christ’s virgin Justina would be arrested.

When they had been brought before him in chains, the count said to the blessed Cyprian:

“Are you Cyprian, the teacher of the Christians, who by your sorceries have led many astray?”

The blessed Cyprian replied:

“Once, while I was given over to the destruction wrought by demons, I led many into lust. But God saved me through the virgin Justina, when I tried to tempt her through demons; armed with the faith of Christ, she utterly despised them.”

After this the wicked count ordered the holy bishop to be suspended and his flesh torn with hooks; after slapping the blessed Justina, he ordered her to be savagely beaten with raw sinews. He then ordered the holy bishop to be shut up in prison and the holy virgin to be guarded in the house of a certain matron.

After several days he had them brought again before him and ordered them to be roasted on an iron frying pan while his attendants poured pitch, fat, and wax over them [Col. 0366D]. While they were praising almighty God there, Athanasius, a priest of the idols, appealed to the count, saying:

“Let Your Excellency command it, and in the name of the gods I shall overcome the power of the Christians.”

When he approached the frying pan, a flame burst out and consumed him.

The count, having witnessed so many miracles that Christ performed in his servants, wrote to the emperor asking what should be ordered concerning them. The emperor replied that they should be sent to Nicomedia and struck down there with the sword.

They were therefore brought to the place of execution. A certain Christian named Theognitus [Theognidus] saw them and ran up [Col. 0367A] and kissed Cyprian. When Servius, a kinsman of the king, saw this, he was angered and arranged for Theognitus to be beheaded with the saints Cyprian and Justina.

The bodies of the saints lay abandoned to wild beasts and unburied for six days. Some Christian sailors secretly took them away by night and transported them by ship to the city of Rome. A venerable matron named Rufina received them reverently and buried them on her estate.

They suffered on the sixth day before the Kalends of October.

**D. Five days before the Kalends of October (27 September).**

[Note: [Col. 0367D] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 98.]
