At the city of Aegae, the birthday of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian, during the persecution of Diocletian and under the governor Lysias.

Born of a venerable mother and educated in the sacred [Col. 0367B] writings, they practiced the medical profession and were renowned for their virtues. When the governor Lysias heard of their religion, he sent attendants to bring them before him. Looking at them, he asked from which province they came and what their names were.

The blessed Cosmas and Damian replied:

“We are from Arabia. Our names are Cosmas and Damian. We are Christians. We also have other brothers: Anthimus, Leontius, and Eutropius.”

The governor sent an official and ordered these men to be brought before him immediately. He began to urge them to sacrifice. Since he could not in any way move their minds, founded upon Christ the rock, he ordered them, bound hand and foot, to be tortured severely and then, still chained together, to be thrown into the sea.

At once an angel of the Lord came to them, broke their bonds, and rescued them from the sea. When the soldiers saw this [Col. 0367C], they reported it to the governor.

He had them brought back before him and said:

“Teach me your magic, and I will follow you, sharing in your works.”

The saints replied:

“We are Christians; we know nothing of magic, and in the name of Christ we despise the power of magic.”

By order of the governor they were returned to prison. On the following day the proconsul, seated on the tribunal, had a great fire prepared and the blessed martyrs brought out of prison and thrown into its midst. But while the saints prayed, the fire lost its power.

The governor was overcome and attributed what had happened to God’s martyrs to magical arts. He therefore again ordered them to be suspended and tortured. But when they remained above the tortures with a grateful and joyful face, the impious proconsul had crosses prepared and ordered the glorious martyrs to be suspended and stretched out upon them, and then to be attacked with stones while raised on the crosses [Col. 0367D].

But when the blows of the stones rebounded against those who threw them, the governor, inflamed with rage, ordered them to be attacked with arrows, so that at least iron might be driven into them by a lighter flight. Yet when the arrows did not injure the saints in any way, many of those who shot them and those standing nearby collapsed from wounds inflicted by the arrows.

Seeing that his wickedness was overcome by divine power, the governor ordered them to be put to death with the sword. The blessed Cosmas and Damian, Anthimus, Leontius, and Eutropius were martyred on the twenty-seventh day of September.

Religious men buried their bodies in a venerable place not far from the city of Aegae. Rome also solemnly celebrates the memory of the two brothers Cosmas and Damian, having built a splendid church in their name [Col. 0368A].

**E. Four days before the Kalends of October (28 September).**

In Spain, in the city of Córdoba, the birthday of the holy Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis. At first they were tortured on the rack; afterward they were disfigured by having their eyebrows shaved, their ears and noses cut off, and their upper teeth pulled out. Finally, they completed their martyrdom by suffering in the fire.

**F. Three days before the Kalends of October (29 September).**

On Mount Garganus, the venerable memory of the blessed archangel Michael, where there is a church consecrated to his name, poor in appearance but endowed with heavenly power [Col. 0368B]. It is situated at the summit of a lofty mountain and is displayed as though the body of the rock itself had been hollowed out in the form of a cave.

The place lies within the boundaries of Campania, where the city of Sipontus [Note: [Col. 0368D] Manuscript: always *Sepontus*] is situated between the Adriatic Gulf and Mount Garganus. The mountain rises twelve miles from the city walls and bears upon its highest summit this church, venerated throughout the world.

It became known to mortals in the following way. A very wealthy man named Garganus, who gave the mountain its name after his arrival, possessed an immense multitude of sheep and cattle. It happened that a bull, rejecting the company of the herd and accustomed to wander alone, failed to return home when the herd came back.

Its master searched for it along every byway and finally found it [Col. 0368C] standing at the summit of the mountain before the entrance to a certain cave. When he shot an arrow at it, the arrow, twisted back as if by a gust of wind, returned and struck the man who had shot it.

The citizens were disturbed and astonished at how this had happened—for they did not dare approach more closely—and consulted the bishop about what should be done. The bishop ordered a three-day fast and instructed them to seek an answer from God.

When it had been completed, the holy angel Michael appeared to the bishop in a vision and said:

“I am Michael the archangel, who always stands in the presence of God. By this sign I wished to demonstrate that I am the guardian of this place and the observer of everything that happens there.”

When the citizens learned this revelation, they made it their custom to pray to God there and to seek Saint Michael as their intercessor.

They saw two doors there [Col. 0368D]. The southern one, which was larger, could be approached by several steps descending toward the west. They did not dare enter farther than the crypt, but prayed every day before the entrance.

Meanwhile, the Neapolitans attempted to provoke the people of Benevento into war. Instructed by the exhortations of their bishop, the Beneventans observed a three-day fast. And behold, on the very night preceding the day of battle, the same Saint Michael appeared in a vision to the bishop and said that their prayers had been heard, promised them victory, and assured them that he would be with them.

The truth of this was soon demonstrated by the outcome. Returning home as victors, they hastened to the church to offer vows of thanksgiving to the Lord. In the morning they saw near the northern door, like a small postern gate, what seemed to be the imprint of human footsteps pressed deeply into the marble [Col. 0369A]. They recognized that the blessed Michael had wished to display this as a sign of his presence.

Later, after a roof had been added and an altar installed, the place was called Appodonia because of the signs of the footprints. Subsequently, after consultation, the people of Sipontus built a church to the east of that place in the name of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

Again, when the Roman pontiff and the bishop of Sipontus were seeking guidance about the consecration of the place and were therefore celebrating a three-day fast with their citizens, on the final night of the fast Saint Michael appeared in a vision to the bishop of Sipontus and instructed him to enter the church that he himself had dedicated and celebrate Masses there according to custom.

“It will be my task,” he said, “to show how I myself consecrated the place.”

In the morning they arrived with offerings and entered [Col. 0369B] the southern entrance with great persistence in prayer. Behold, a long portico extended northward and reached the little postern gate outside which, as we have said, the footprints were impressed in the marble.

Before they reached this point, a very large basilica appeared to the east, approached by steps. Together with its portico, it seemed able to hold nearly five hundred people. Near the middle of the southern wall it displayed a venerable altar covered with a red cloth.

The building itself was angular, not raised with walls in the manner of human workmanship, but rough like a cave, with precipitous and frequently projecting rocks. Its rocky roof was of varying height: in one place it could be touched with the head, while elsewhere it could scarcely be reached by hand. I believe that, through the teaching of the archangel, the Lord seeks and loves not the adornment of stones but purity of heart [Col. 0369C].

No one dared enter there at night. After dawn had passed, they sang the morning hymns there. From the rock itself with which the sacred building is covered, on the north side of the altar, sweet and exceedingly clear water flows drop by drop. The inhabitants call it the “Drop.” For this reason a glass vessel was prepared to collect it.

Finally, some people, after enduring the flames of prolonged fevers, drank this drop and immediately received the swift refreshment of health. The sick are frequently healed there in countless other ways as well, and it is demonstrated that many miracles are performed there solely by angelic power.

Not long afterward, the venerable pontiff Boniface also dedicated at Rome a church built in the name of Saint Michael, rising very high at the summit of the Circus in a cryptlike structure of marvelous workmanship [Col. 0369D]. Hence that place, containing a church at its summit, is called “Situated Among the Clouds.”

**G. The day before the Kalends of October (30 September).**
In Gaul, at Solodorum, which is situated above the [Aurula] Arula River, the passion of the holy martyrs Victor and Ursus, from the glorious Theban Legion. When they had withdrawn there to escape the fury of the tyrant Maximian, they were arrested by his order by the executioner Hyrtacus. At first they were tortured with dreadful punishments; but when a heavenly light flashed over them and the attendants fell to the ground, they were rescued. Then they were thrown into the fire. Soon, however, a violent rain came, extinguished the pyre, and left them entirely unharmed; finally, they were put to death by the sword. Of these, Saint Victor was transferred to the city of the [Note: [Col. 0369D] Jenavenses, commonly called Januenses.] Jenavenses, where he is celebrated for the glory of his miracles and the devotion of the faithful.

Likewise at Bethlehem in Judea, the deposition of Saint Jerome the presbyter. He was born in the town of Strido, once situated on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia. His father was Eusebius. As a boy in Rome he put on the garment of Christ, and there he was educated from childhood in Greek and Latin literature. After acquiring the entire course of secular literary studies, he also imitated the way of life and conduct of the most approved monks, and was later ordained presbyter of the Roman Church.

[Col. 0370B] For three continuous years he was honored as dear and welcome to the people, and by everyone’s judgment was considered worthy of the highest priesthood. But certain men from the ranks of the clergy and the monks, roaming about in wantonness and gluttony, plotted to drive Jerome from the city, because in his writings he had exposed both their vices. He, however, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, left Rome and abandoned his house, parents, sister, and relatives. Going to Jerusalem to serve God, he first approached Gregory Nazianzenus, then bishop of Constantinople, as an obedient and teachable disciple, so that he might be instructed in the study of the Holy Scriptures.

From there he went to Syria and stayed for a while at the estate of the presbyter Evagrius. Then he proceeded to the deserted places so eagerly and resolutely that you would have thought he had flown there rather than traveled. Thus he spent four years in that vast solitude, which, scorched by the sun’s heat, provides the monks with a terrifying dwelling. From there he returned to the town of Bethlehem, where, like a prudent animal, he offered himself to remain at the Lord’s manger.

He had himself carefully prepared a library, and, rereading it and the discourses of all the books—which he retained almost entirely by heart—he passed the day in fasting until evening. Many religious men, who had learned of his way of life by report, immediately flocked to him, and, while he still lived under a small shelter, good disciples attended upon the good teacher.

Not long afterward, because of the number of his disciples and the continual arrival of visitors, he built small cells there beside the Bethlehem gate, which faces west and is seen by those going out toward the north. By what efforts and with how many labors he learned the Hebrew and Chaldaean languages and the Hebrew letters, I shall state in his own words:

“When I was young,” he says, “and the deserts of solitude enclosed me, I could not endure the incentives of vice and the heat of nature. Though I broke this by frequent fasts, my mind nevertheless seethed with thoughts. To subdue them, I placed myself under the discipline of a certain brother who had come to believe from among the Hebrews, so that, after the refinements of Quintilian, the flowing eloquence of Cicero, the gravity of Fronto, and the gentleness of Pliny, I might learn the alphabet and practice harsh, breathy words. My conscience bears witness to what labor I undertook there, what difficulty I endured, how often I despaired, and how, through the struggle to learn, I began again.”

Armed, therefore, with faith and having obtained the grace of Christ, he translated the Hebrew volumes contained in the Canon from Hebrew into Latin, and commented on nearly all of them.

To recall briefly the works he completed with great usefulness: he wrote the Life of the Monk Paul; one book of Letters to Various Persons; an exhortation to Heliodorus; The Debate between a Luciferian and an Orthodox Christian; a Chronicle of Universal History; and twenty-eight Homilies on Jeremiah and Ezekiel, which he translated from Greek into Latin. He also wrote homilies on the Seraphim, on “Hosanna,” on the frugal and profligate son, and two homilies on the Song of Songs; Against Helvidius on the Perpetual Virginity of Mary; To Eustochium on the Preservation of Virginity; one book of Letters to Marcella; a Consolation to Paula on the Death of Her Daughter; three books of commentaries on Paul’s Letter to the Galatians; one book on the Letter to Titus; one book on the Letter to Philemon; commentaries on Ecclesiastes; one book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis; one book On Places; and one book of Hebrew Names.

One book on Didymus’s On the Holy Spirit, which he translated into Latin; thirty-eight homilies on Luke; seven treatises on the Psalms from the tenth through the sixteenth; The Captive Monk; the Life of Blessed Hilarion; and he rendered the New Testament according to the Greek text. The number of his letters to Paula and Eustochium is uncertain.

He commented on the sixteen volumes of the prophets in seventy-four books. In the midst of these numerous pages of his work, he arranged in order the names of one hundred and thirty-five distinguished ecclesiastical writers, from the passion of Christ to the fourteenth year of the emperor Theodosius. He also wrote two books Against Jovinianus; an Apology to Pammachius; four books of commentaries on Matthew; and a Handbook on the Psalter. Against Vigilantius and against Pelagius he published brilliant volumes. He also composed, with pious concern for the edification of the Catholic Church, a work on the stations of the children of Israel and many other writings.

Finally, he was so exhausted by his labors that even when lying on his bed he had to be raised upright by grasping a rope suspended from a beam, so that he might perform, as best he could, the duties of the monastery. At last, after a life perfectly and pleasingly devoted to God, in the ninety-eighth year of his age, he rested in peace at Bethlehem on the day before the Kalends of October, in the twelfth year of the emperor Honorius. He completed his books over fifty-six years.

## LITANIES TO BE ANNOUNCED

October has thirty-one days; the moon, however, has twenty-nine.

## A. KALENDS OF OCTOBER (1 October)

[Col. 0371C]

At Auxerre, the feast of Saint Germanus, bishop, who was distinguished by many virtues, learning, and continence. To strengthen the faith by heavenly grace, he was compelled, by the judgment of all the Gallic bishops, to come to Britain, with Blessed Lupus, bishop of the city of Troyes, accompanying him. For the Pelagian heresy had stained the faith of the Britons with a loathsome plague.

As he was carried across the gulf stretching from Gaul to Britain by favorable winds, suddenly a hostile force of winds stirred up storms. The sky and the day were withdrawn into the night of clouds, and the bishop himself, overcome in body and weakened by weariness and sleep, lay in the ship. Then Blessed Lupus [Col. 0371D] and all the others, thrown into confusion, awakened the elder. He immediately invoked Christ, took oil in the name of the Holy Trinity, and poured it into the sea. He subdued the raging waves and restored calm serenity.

When the stretches of sea had been traversed, the priests of God reached the desired shore in peace. Soon they filled the island of Britain with their reputation, preaching, and miracles, so that everywhere the Catholic faithful were strengthened and those who had been corrupted recognized the path of correction.

Meanwhile, someone presented to the priests a ten-year-old blind daughter of a man holding tribunician authority, asking that she be healed. Without delay, Blessed Germanus, after invoking the Lord, took in his hands a small reliquary hanging at his side containing relics of the saints, removed it from his neck, and applied it to the girl’s eyes before everyone. She immediately received her sight.

Moreover, while the blessed man was detained for some time in a nearby cottage by the necessity of illness, a fire broke out. But the flame, terrified of the lodging of the holy man, did not dare touch it; it leapt over it, and amid the balls of blazing fire the unharmed dwelling, in which its inhabitant was enclosed, emerged. And although he allowed no remedy to be applied to his weakness, one night he saw a figure clothed in shining white garments standing beside him. With hand outstretched, the figure seemed to raise him as he lay and commanded him to stand firmly on his feet. After an hour, therefore, when the pains had been driven away, he recovered his former health, so that when day returned he could undertake the labor of travel without fear.

A war also undertaken at that time by the Saxons and Picts, who had joined forces against the Britons, was repulsed by divine power. Germanus himself became commander of the army and, not by the blare of trumpets but by the cry of “Alleluia,” raised to the heavens by the voice of the entire army, turned the savage enemy to flight.

When the island had been set in order, the bishops prepared to return, and it happened that a fortunate vessel restored them to their own people’s desire in a peaceful voyage. Not long afterward, however, word was brought from [Col. 0373A] the same island that Pelagian perversity was again being spread by a few instigators. Once more the prayers of all the priests were conveyed to the blessed man, asking him to defend God’s cause, which he had previously secured.

He promptly granted their request. Taking with him Severus, a man of complete holiness—who had been a disciple of Blessed Lupus, bishop of Troyes, and who, having then been ordained bishop at Trier, was preaching the word to the peoples of First Germany—he boarded the ship. With the elements cooperating, he sailed in calm waters toward Britain. After expelling the instigators of wickedness and setting everything in order, the blessed priests returned with the same favorable fortune by which they had come.

After this Germanus came to Ravenna to plead for peace for the Armorican people. There he was received with the greatest reverence by Valentinian and his mother Placidia, [Col. 0373B] and after a few days departed to Christ. His body was carried to his own city in an honorable procession, accompanied by the works of his virtues.

At the city of Tomi, Saints Priscus, Crescentius, and Evagrius.

At the city of Rheims, Saint Remigius, bishop and confessor, a man of outstanding virtue and holiness. He converted the Frankish people, devoted to the worship of idols, to Christ, after their king had first been initiated into the sacred baptismal font and the sacraments of the faith. He completed more than seventy years in the episcopate. Among his other deeds, he raised a girl from bodily death.

## B. SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE NONES OF OCTOBER (2 October)

[Col. 0373C]

[Note: [Col. 0373D] Eusebius, Book VIII, chapters 5 and 6.] At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Eleutherius the martyr, under Diocletian. In his time, part of the palace happened to be consumed by fire. The emperor falsely presumed that this had been done by Christians. Inflamed by immeasurable fury, he ordered all the Christians to be gathered in heaps, some to be cut down by the sword, others to be consumed by fire.

The first of these, and the one who encouraged them all to lay down their lives bravely for Christ, was Eleutherius. Finally, when the attendants who stood by asked each person whether he wished to be released if he were willing to sacrifice, neither the men nor the women would even allow themselves to be questioned. Instead, they rushed forward of their own accord into the flames or eagerly presented their necks to the striking swords.

When even the spectators themselves were horrified by the excess of cruelty, the ministers of wickedness put part of the people into small boats, carried them into the open sea, and there threw them into the depths while they remained firm in their profession of faith.

Their rage became so violently inflamed that, after the royal boys had been made martyrs and buried according to the customary human rite, they dug them up again and threw their bodies into the sea, saying: “Perhaps they may become gods of the Christians.”

But Blessed Eleutherius, tortured for a long time by the most savage punishments, became stronger through each successive torture. Tested by the fires like gold, he completed the martyrdom of his victory. The Christians secretly carried away his relics and placed them in honorable burial at Nicomedia.

At Siricinium, a village in the territory of Atrebates, the passion of Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Autun. Ebroinus, mayor of the royal palace, killed him after afflicting him with various insults and different punishments for the sake of truth. His sacred body was transferred to the diocese of Poitiers and honorably buried in the monastery of Blessed Maxentius.

## C. FIFTH DAY BEFORE THE NONES OF OCTOBER (3 October)

[Note: [Col. 0373D] See the book On the Feasts of the Apostles.] The feast of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, who was instructed by the Apostle Paul and believed in Christ. He was ordained by that same apostle as the first bishop at Athens, and under the emperor Hadrian, after a most illustrious confession of faith and the heaviest forms of torture, he was crowned with glorious martyrdom. Aristides of Athens, a man remarkable for faith and wisdom, bears witness to this in the work he composed on the Christian religion. The work is held in the highest esteem among the Athenians and regarded as one of the most distinguished monuments of antiquity, as the more learned among the Greeks affirm.

Among the ancient Saxons, the feast of the two holy priests Ewald, who came into Germany with Saint Willibrord the bishop and crossed over to the Saxons. When they began preaching Christ there, they were seized and killed by the pagans. Over their bodies, a great light appeared for a long time during the night, revealing both where they were and what their merit was.

## D. FOURTH DAY BEFORE THE NONES OF OCTOBER (4 October)

[Col. 0374C]

[Note: [Col. 0373D] See the same work.] At Corinth, the feast of Saints Crispus and Gaius, whom the blessed Apostle Paul mentions in writing to the Corinthians.

[Note: [Col. 0374D] Eusebius, Book VIII, chapters 8 and 9.] In Egypt, the feast of the holy martyr brothers Mark and Marcian, together with innumerable others of no lesser glory, both men and women. Children and old men alike, despising the present life for the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, sought the blessedness of future glory.

Some of them, after beatings, hooks, scourges, and other horrible tortures of various kinds, were handed over to the flames; others were thrown into the sea; some were consumed by hunger; others were beheaded, so that they voluntarily offered their necks to the axes. Others were fastened to gallows. Some of these, in a perverse manner, were suspended with their heads pressed downward and their feet raised aloft, and thus earned the most blessed crown of passion.

## E. THIRD DAY BEFORE THE NONES OF OCTOBER (5 October)

[Note: [Col. 0374D] Eusebius, Book V, chapter 24; Rufinus.] In Sicily, the feast of Saints Placidus, Eutychius, and thirty others.

In Gaul, at the city of Valence, Saint Apollinaris the bishop, whose life was distinguished by virtues and whose death likewise was adorned with signs and wonders.

[Col. 0375A] At Eumenia, Blessed Thraseas, bishop of Smyrna, completed his martyrdom. He was one of the ancients and asserted that, through the tradition of those who came before, he had received the teaching that the Savior had commanded his apostles not to depart from Jerusalem before the twelfth year.

## F. DAY BEFORE THE NONES OF OCTOBER (6 October)

[Note: [Col. 0375D] Eusebius, Book V, chapter 24; Rufinus.] At Capua, the feast of Saints Marcellus, Castus, Aemilius, and Saturninus.

In Gaul, at the city of Agen, the feast of Saint Faith, virgin and martyr, whose example inspired Blessed Caprasius to enter the contest of martyrdom.

On the same day, Blessed Sagaris, martyr and bishop of Laodicea, who was one of the early disciples of Saint Paul the Apostle.

## G. NONES OF OCTOBER (7 October)

[Col. 0375B]

[Note: [Col. 0375D] Pontifical Book, chapter 35.] At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of Saint Mark, pope and confessor, who sat in the episcopate for two years, nine months, and twenty days. He was buried in the cemetery of Balbina on the Ardeatine Way, which he himself established and completed.

On the same day, the feast of the holy martyrs Julia, Sergius, and Bacchus, under the emperor Maximian. Raised to positions of honor, they were held in high esteem in his palace. Sergius was chief secretary, while Bacchus was second secretary of the school of the pagans.

Some people therefore accused them before the emperor of being Christians. They were summoned by the emperor so that, after sacrificing to Jupiter, they might taste with him of the sacrifices that had been offered. The emperor entered the temple, tasted the sacrifices, and, looking around, did not see Sergius and Bacchus; for they had not entered the temple. He therefore sent soldiers from those standing beside him and ordered them to be brought in.

He said to them: “As I see it, you have become enemies of the gods. Approach the altar of great Jupiter, sacrifice, and eat of his sacrifices as the others do.”

Blessed Sergius and Bacchus replied: “We have a true and eternal king in heaven, Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Every day we offer him a holy, living sacrifice and rational worship; but we do not adore stones and wood.”

Then the emperor, angered, ordered them stripped of their military cloaks, dressed in women’s tunics, and dragged through the middle of the city to the palace with chains placed around their necks.

When they had reached the palace, the emperor said to them: “Most wicked men, do you know that the Christ whom you worship was the son of a carpenter, and that before a lawful marriage had taken place his mother conceived him through adultery?”

The soldiers of Christ replied: “You are mistaken, emperor. The one whom we worship is the true God and eternal life, who made heaven and earth and everything in them.”

Maximian, now still more angered by their truthful declarations, ordered them to be handed over to Antiochus, who was to fasten them in the stocks. In the morning he sat in the tribunal, and Sergius and Bacchus were brought before him.

When he could bend them from their purpose neither by persuasion nor threats, he ordered Blessed Sergius [Col. 0376A] to be taken back into custody, but Bacchus to be stretched out and beaten with raw sinews until the executioners, exhausted, could beat him no longer. As executioners took turns succeeding one another, the glorious martyr, his whole body torn apart in his confession of Christ, gave up his spirit. Antiochus left his body to the birds and wild beasts.

But Christians came secretly, carried away the martyr’s body, and buried it in a certain cave. On the following day Blessed Sergius was brought out of custody and presented to Antiochus. When Antiochus could not bend him by words, he first had him shod in boots fixed with nails and made him run nine thousand paces before him. Later, seeing that he remained firm in his conviction, he ordered him beheaded. Christians then buried him in the same place.

After a short time, they also took Blessed Bacchus from the place where he had been buried and laid him in an honorable place among the martyrs beside Saint Sergius. There the virgin Julia also rests in burial with the martyrs; she completed her martyrdom under the governor Martianus.

On the same day, the holy martyrs Marcellus and Apuleius, who at first attached themselves to Simon Magus. But when they saw the wonders that the Lord performed through his apostle Peter, they abandoned Simon and devoted themselves to apostolic teaching. After the martyrdom of the apostles, they too, honored by their confession of Christ, received the crown of martyrdom when the consular official Aurelian pronounced sentence. They were buried not far from the city of Rome.

## A. EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF OCTOBER (8 October)

[Col. 0376C] [Note: [Col. 0376D] Concerning him above, 11 April; Jerome, On Illustrious Men of the Church, chapter 30. See the book On the Feasts of the Apostles.] In Crete, at the city of Gortyna, Blessed Philip the bishop, a man endowed with great virtues and excellent studies.

At Thessalonica, Saint Demetrius the martyr.

And the most blessed elder Simeon.

## B. SEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF OCTOBER (9 October)

Abraham the Patriarch.

At Paris, the feast of the holy martyrs Dionysius the bishop, Eleutherius the presbyter, and Rusticus the deacon. The blessed bishop had been sent by the Roman pontiff to Gaul to offer the service of preaching to peoples estranged from the faith of Christ. At last he reached the city of Paris and, after faithfully and zealously carrying out the holy work for several years, was seized by the prefect Fescenninus Sisinnius. Together with him, Saint Eleutherius the presbyter and Rusticus the deacon were condemned to the sword and completed their martyrdom.

## C. SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF OCTOBER (10 October)

At Cologne Agrippina, the feast of the holy martyr Gereon and three hundred eighteen others, who are said to have been Thebans. Together with that legion of Blessed Maurice, they had crossed into Gaul at the emperor Maximian’s command, settled near the banks of the Rhine, and, rejecting the tyrant’s deadly rule, patiently submitted their necks to the swords for true piety.

Lot the prophet.

At Crete, Blessed Pinytus, one of the most distinguished among the bishops, [Note: [Col. 0377D] Jerome, On Illustrious Men of the Church, chapter 28.] who left in his writings an image of himself as though in a certain mirror.

Likewise at the city of Agrippina, the feast of the holy martyrs Mallosus and Victor. The former, after the place where he had been buried had remained unknown for a long time, was revealed by God to the holy bishop of that place. When his body was raised from the hidden location, such sweetness of fragrance poured forth that the faithful standing by were filled as though with the scent of an immense quantity of spices.

Likewise in Britain, [Note: [Col. 0377D] Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People, Book II, chapters 9, 14, 16, 17, and 20; and Book III, chapter 14.] Saint Paulinus, bishop of York. He had been ordained bishop by Blessed Justus, who had been consecrated bishop by Saint Augustine, whom Blessed Gregory had sent to preach to the English people. Paulinus converted the nation of the Northumbrians—that is, the English people who lived north of the River Humber—together with their king Edwin, by preaching the word of faith. Distinguished in life, teaching, and miracles, he rested in peace on the sixth day before the Ides of October.

## D. FIFTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF OCTOBER (11 October)

At Tarsus, the metropolis of Cilicia, the feast of the most blessed martyrs Tharacus, Probus, and Andronicus. During the persecution of Diocletian, under the governor Maximus, they were afflicted for a long time by the filth of prison and examined three times by different tortures and punishments; in their confession of faith they gained the triumph of glory.

They were severely beaten with raw sinews and rubbed with the roughest tiles; they were also burned around the belly and sides with burning papyrus; their jaws were broken; their legs were tortured; vinegar and mustard were poured into their nostrils; burning spikes were applied; their fingers were pierced with extremely sharp nails; their eyes were stabbed; and their tongues were cut out. Finally, they were thrown to bears and lions in the amphitheater.

But when none of the beasts dared touch the bodies of the saints, Maximus, inflamed with anger, ordered them to be slaughtered with the sword and their bodies thrown among the corpses of the gladiators. At night the faithful came and begged the Lord to show them the relics of the saints. Suddenly they saw what seemed like a brilliant star sent from heaven resting over each of the saints’ bodies. Thus, seizing them with immense joy, and with the radiance of that same star going before them, they buried the glorious athletes of Christ in a most suitable place.

## E. FOURTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF OCTOBER (12 October)

At Ravenna, on the Laurentine Way, the feast of Saint Edistius.

In Africa, [Note: [Col. 0378D] Victor of Africa, Book II.] the holy confessors and martyrs, four thousand nine hundred seventy-six in number. During the Vandal persecution, when they were bishops, presbyters, and deacons of the churches of God in Africa, they were joined by crowds of faithful people and, by order of Hunneric, the Arian king, were driven into exile in a dreadful desert and assigned among the fiercest Moors, in defense of Catholic truth.

Among them were Cyprian and Felix, eminent priests of the Lord. Many of these men, after being cruelly threatened, beaten with the points of spears and stones, or dragged by their bound feet like corpses through hard and rugged places, were torn limb from limb by that dreadful punishment. While sharp stones crushed the head of one and split the sides of others, they breathed out their spirits into the hands of those dragging them.

Along the entire public embankment there remains a sight of the burial places of the saints, with tombs that speak.

## F. THIRD DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF OCTOBER (13 October)

The feast of Blessed Carpus, disciple of the Apostle Paul, at Troas.

[Col. 0378B] At Antioch, Blessed Theophilus, who held the episcopate of the Church as the sixth after the apostles, a man of exceptional learning. [Note: [Col. 0378D] Jerome, On Illustrious Men of the Church, chapter 25.]

## G. DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF OCTOBER (14 October)

The feast of Saint Callistus, pope, [Note: [Col. 0378D] Pontifical Book, chapter 17.] who sat in the episcopate for seven years, two months, and ten days, and obtained the glory of martyrdom under the persecution of the emperor Alexander.

After he had baptized the proconsul Palmachius and his entire household, as well as the senator Simplicius at Palmachius’s house, and Felix with his wife Blanda, whom he had healed of paralysis, all these were killed by Alexander and obtained the glory of martyrdom. After his presbyter Calepodius had also suffered martyrdom by the sword, Callistus was arrested by Alexander, tormented for a very long time by hunger, and beaten daily with clubs. It was forbidden for anyone to come to him; if anyone dared to come at night, they were to be arrested and killed.

When he had been in custody for many days, Blessed Calepodius appeared to him in a vision and consoled him, saying: “Be steadfast, father, for your crown is already complete.”

There was a certain soldier named Privatus, covered with ulcers and tormented by continual pains. He threw himself at the feet of Saint Callistus, asking him to heal him of his ulcers and pains. The holy pontiff immediately healed him, in the name of the most holy Trinity, both of the pain and foulness of the ulcers and of his unbelief, after baptizing him.

When Alexander heard this, he had the soldier beaten to death with leaded clubs. He ordered Blessed Callistus to be thrown from the window of a house, sunk into a well with a stone tied around his neck, and buried beneath rubble thrown into it.

After seventeen days, his presbyter Asterius came at night with the clerics, raised his body, and buried it in the cemetery of Calepodius on the Aurelian Way, on the day before the Ides of October.

On the same day, the passing of Saint Justus in the desert. After he had led an angelic life in the desert for several years and the worthy end had arrived, promising the kingdom of heaven in return for such great labors, while the holy soul of the one who was departing was already at its final moment, Viator stood there weeping and distraught, saying: “Why do you abandon me, Lord?”

He is said to have replied, so that Viator would not be troubled as though deprived of consolation, that he himself would soon follow him there as well. It is evident that this prophecy and revelation was fulfilled by the swift death of his most holy servant, who alone, moved by the ardor of faith, had followed the bishop who was fleeing the episcopate and wishing to remain hidden.

## A. IDES OF OCTOBER (15 October)

In Gaul, [Note: [Col. 0379D] Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 62.] at Cologne Agrippina, the holy Moors from the soldiers of Saint Gereon. They were fifty in number and belonged to the sacred Theban Legion. Completing their martyrdom at that city, they were buried in a basilica that shines with marvelous workmanship, almost gilded by a kind of mosaic. Hence the inhabitants customarily call them the golden saints.

On the same day at Lyon, the feast of Blessed Antiochus the bishop. While he was still a presbyter of Lyon, moved by devoted duty, he resolved to go to visit his bishop, Justus by name and truly just in name and conduct, who was already living in the desert. Antiochus was a man outstanding in strictness and, not undeservedly, after some time was raised to the height of that episcopal office. Having administered it energetically, he attained the heavenly kingdom. He was buried in the church of the Maccabean martyrs, where Saint Justus also lies buried.

## B. SEVENTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER (16 October)

[Col. 0379C] In Africa, [Note: [Col. 0379D] Victor of Africa, Book I.] the feast of two hundred seventy holy martyrs crowned together, and of the holy martyrs Martianus and Saturianus, together with their two brothers and the distinguished handmaid of Christ, the virgin Maxima.

During the Vandal persecution, under Geiseric the Arian king, they were first beaten with knotted clubs for the steadfastness of the Catholic faith and torn to the bone. Although they endured such treatment for a long time, they were restored unharmed every following day.

Later they were condemned to harsh imprisonment. When they had been bound in the stocks, the strength of the huge timbers was miraculously dissolved by God’s power. At this miracle Maxima, the servant of Christ, was released to freedom. She later became the mother of many virgins of God and grew old gloriously in the confession of the truth.

The others, banished into exile among the fiercest Moors, won a multitude of barbarians for Christ the Lord through their preaching. By order of the impious Geiseric, they were ordered to die together, their feet bound behind running chariots, as they were dragged through thorny woodland.

As the bodies of the innocent were torn by the spikes of the bushes and trees while the untamed horses ran nearby, they said farewell to one another in these words: “Brother, pray for me. God has fulfilled our desire. In this way one reaches the kingdom of heaven.”

Thus, praying and singing psalms, while the angels rejoiced, they gave up their holy souls. To this day Jesus Christ the Lord does not cease to perform great miracles there.

## C. SIXTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER (17 October)

Martha, the sister of Lazarus.

Likewise Blessed Aristion, who was one of the seventy disciples of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0379D] Eusebius, Book III, chapter 30; Ignatius, Letter 10.]

Likewise Blessed Heron, concerning whom it was revealed to the most blessed Ignatius as he went to his passion that Heron would govern the Church of Antioch after him. He was then the deacon of Blessed Ignatius the martyr. Having become bishop, he followed devoutly in the way of his teacher and, as a lover of Christ, died for the flock entrusted to him.

In Gaul, at the city of Orange, Saint Florentius the bishop, who, distinguished by many virtues, rested in peace.

## D. FIFTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER (18 October)

[Col. 0380B]

The feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist.

On the same day, [Note: [Col. 0380D] See the book On the Feasts of the Apostles; Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 9.] Saint Asclepiades, bishop of Antioch, who was one of the distinguished company of confessors who suffered gloriously under Decius.

Likewise at Rome, Saint Tryphonia, [Note: [Col. 0380D] Concerning her, in the Acts of Saint Lawrence, 10 August.] wife of Decius Caesar. After her husband had been divinely punished following the killing of the blessed Sixtus and Lawrence, she asked to be baptized with Decius’s daughter Cyrilla by the presbyter Justin. She died the following day and was buried in a crypt beside Saint Hippolytus, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November.

## E. FOURTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER (19 October)

[Col. 0380C] At Antioch in Syria, [Note: [Col. 0380D] Eusebius, Book IV, chapter 16; Rufinus, chapter 17.] the feast of the holy martyrs Beronicus, Pelagia, and forty-nine others.

Likewise on the same day, Blessed Ptolemy and Blessed Lucius, martyrs. Blessed Ptolemy was arrested by a certain centurion and asked whether he was a Christian. As a lover of truth, Ptolemy did not conceal the glory of his profession; when questioned, he confessed that he was a Christian.

The centurion immediately threw him into chains and, after he had been weakened for a long time by the filth of prison, finally brought him before the judge Urbicius. The judge likewise asked him only whether he was a Christian. Conscious again of possessing so great a good, Ptolemy openly professed the divine religion and bore public witness to the teaching of Christ and the institutions of every good thing. For whoever denies what is undoubtedly judges that what he denies is blameworthy.

Immediately after his confession, therefore, Urbicius ordered him to be led away. But a certain Christian named Lucius, seeing the sentence pronounced so recklessly, said to Urbicius: “What, I ask, is the reason that you have ordered a man to be led to death who is neither an adulterer, seducer, murderer, robber, kidnapper, nor guilty of any other crime, but only of the Christian name, because he confessed that he was called by this designation? What you are doing is not worthy of a devout emperor, his most wise young son, or the sacred senate, Urbicius.”

But Urbicius, making no further inquiry, said to Lucius: “You too seem to me to be a Christian.”

When Lucius replied, “That is precisely what I am,” Urbicius ordered him also to be led away to death. He said: “I give thanks that you are sending me, freed from wicked masters, to the good and excellent Father and King of all, the Lord.”

A third man likewise exercised the same freedom and was punished by the same sentence. These blessed martyrs suffered under Antoninus, surnamed Pius, and his son, and were buried at Alexandria, the metropolis of Egypt.

## F. THIRTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER (20 October)

In Gaul, at the city of Agen, Saint Caprasius the martyr. While he was hiding in a cave to avoid the fury of the persecution, he heard Blessed Faith, the virgin, courageously struggling for Christ. Inspired to endure suffering, he prayed to the Lord that, if the Lord truly judged him worthy of the glory of martyrdom, the clearest water might flow from the stone of that cave.

When the Lord immediately granted this, Caprasius went confidently to the arena of combat and, fighting bravely, earned the palm of martyrdom.

## G. TWELVE DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER (21 October)

At Nicomedia, the feast of the holy martyrs Dasius, Zoticus, and Caius, together with twelve soldiers.

On the same day, [the feast of] our holy father Hilarion, whose life Jerome describes as filled with virtues [Note: [Col. 0381D] Jerome, vol. I]. He was born in the village of Thabatha, situated about five miles south of the city of Gaza in Palestine. Although his parents were devoted to idols, a rose, as they say, blossomed from thorns. [Col. 0381C] Sent by them to Alexandria, he was entrusted to a grammarian, and there, as far as his age allowed, he displayed great promise of intellect and character. Soon he became dear to everyone and skilled in the art of speech; and what is greater than all these things, he believed in the Lord Jesus. His entire desire was directed toward the assemblies of the Church.

When he heard the celebrated name of Antony, which was being proclaimed throughout all the peoples of Egypt, he was inflamed with a desire to see him and went into the desert. As soon as he saw him, he changed his former clothing and remained beside him for two months, observing the order of his life and the gravity of his conduct: how frequent he was in prayer, how humble in receiving the brothers, severe in correcting them, cheerful in encouraging them, and how no illness ever broke his self-restraint or the austerity of his food.

Afterward he returned to his homeland with some monks. Since his parents were already dead, he distributed one part of his property to his brothers and another to the poor, keeping absolutely nothing for himself. He was then fifteen years old. Thus, naked and armed in Christ, he entered the solitude, covered only with a sackcloth garment and wearing a leather ependytes, and a *tenatte* (an uncertain garment-term) which blessed Antony had given him when he departed, together with a rustic cloak; he ate only fifteen figs after sunset.

Accordingly, from his sixteenth to his twentieth year, he sheltered himself from heat and rain in a little hut which he had covered with reeds and sedge. Later he constructed a small cell, which remains to this day: four feet wide, five feet high—that is, lower than his stature—and slightly longer than his little body required, so that you would think it a tomb rather than a house. He cut his hair once a year, on Easter Day. Until his death he slept on the bare ground, on a bed of reeds. He never washed the sackcloth garment which he had once put on, nor did he change his other tunic unless the former had been completely torn. He also retained the Holy Scripture in his memory and, after prayers and psalms, recited it as though God were present.

From his twenty-first year to his twenty-sixth [Col. 0382B], for three years he ate half a sextarius of lentils soaked in cold water; for another three years, dry bread with salt and water. From his twenty-seventh to his thirtieth year, he sustained himself on wild herbs and the raw roots of certain shrubs. From his thirty-first to his thirty-fifth year, his food consisted of six ounces of barley bread and a small amount of cooked vegetable without oil.

When he sensed that his eyes were growing dim and that his whole body was contracting under an eruption and a certain pumice-like roughness, he added oil to the foregoing diet. Until his sixty-third year he continued at this level of abstinence, tasting nothing else—neither fruit, nor legumes, nor anything whatsoever from outside.

Then, seeing that his body was exhausted and thinking that death was near [Col. 0382C], from his sixty-fourth to his eightieth year he abstained from bread, with an incredible fervor of mind, so that at that time he might approach the service of the Lord as though newly enlisted, when others ordinarily live more moderately. A little gruel was made for him from flour and finely chopped vegetables; the food and drink together scarcely weighed five ounces. Thus, completing the course of his life, he never broke his fast before sunset—not even on feast days or during the most serious illness.

Accordingly, powerful in miracles and incomparable in holiness, in the eightieth year of his life, while Hesychius was absent—he had always cherished Hilarion with the greatest intimacy—he wrote with his own hand a brief letter, almost as a kind of will, leaving him all his possessions: namely, the Gospel, a sackcloth tunic [Col. 0382D], a hood, and a little cloak.

Thus only a little warmth remained in his breast, and nothing of a living man remained beyond sensation; yet, with his eyes open, he was speaking: “Go forth! What are you afraid of? Go forth, soul! Why do you hesitate? For nearly seventy years you have served Christ, and do you fear death?” While he was saying these words, he breathed out his spirit. Immediately he was covered with earth, because he himself had adjured all who came to the sick man that his body should not be kept even for a single hour after his death.

When the holy man Hesychius of Palestine heard this, he went to Cyprus and, at the grave risk of his own life, stole his body after approximately ten months. Bringing it to Majuma in Palestine, with whole crowds of monks and townspeople accompanying him [Col. 0383A], he placed it in the ancient monastery. His tunic, hood, and cloak were undamaged, and his entire body was intact, as though he were still alive; it exuded such great fragrances that you would have thought it drenched in perfumes.

On the same day, the anniversary of Saint Asterius, priest of Callistus. When he had lifted Callistus’ body from the well and buried it, the emperor Alexander, hearing of this after six days, ordered him to be thrown from a bridge. His body was found and buried in the same city by certain Christians. Written in the Passion of Saint Callistus, pope (14 October).

And on the same day, the passing of Saint Viator [Note: [Col. 0383D] Concerning him, in the Life of Justus, 2 September; Eusebius, Book IV, chapter 7], lector and companion of Saint Justus in the desert.

## A. Eleventh day before the Kalends of November (22 October)

[Col. 0383B] At Jerusalem, the anniversary of blessed Mark, a most renowned and learned man, who was the first at Jerusalem, after the bishops from the circumcision, to receive the priesthood of that city from among the Gentiles, and who not long afterward was brought to completion through martyrdom.

Likewise, of blessed Salome, who is read about in the Gospel (Matthew XV, XVI) as being concerned, together with the other holy women, for the burial of the Lord.

At Adrianople in Thrace, the anniversary of Saints Philip the bishop, Eusebius, and Hermes.

## B. Tenth day before the Kalends of November (23 October)

At Antioch in Syria, the anniversary of Saint Theodoret [Note: [Col. 0384D] Sozomen, Book V, chapter 7], priest. During the persecution of the impious Julian, under Julian, his prefect and uncle, when the church of the Antiochenes had been stripped of its possessions by him and all the devout had been scattered by his terror, Theodoret remained fearlessly in the despoiled church. Ordered to be arrested, after the punishment of the rack and many harsh and severe tortures, he was also burned with lamps placed around his sides.

But when these were extinguished by divine power, and the soldiers holding them fell on their faces, terrified by the sight of angels, and, believing in Christ, refused the impious service, Julian ordered them to be plunged into the sea. Blessed Theodoret said to them: “Go ahead, brothers; I shall follow you, overtaking the enemy, to the Lord.” Thus remaining steadfast in his confession and filled with the prophetic spirit, he foretold the death of Julian the Apostate, whom divine vengeance overtook in Persia, and completed his martyrdom by the sword.

In Spain, the anniversary of Saints Servandus and Germanus [Col. 0383D]. After scourging, the filth of prison, the hardship of thirst and hunger, and the labor of a very long journey—which, loaded with irons, they endured at the command of the governor Viator—they finally completed the course of their martyrdom when their necks were struck with the sword. Germanus was buried at Mérida near blessed Eulalia; Servandus, however, was transferred to Seville and buried near the holy Justa and Rufina.

## C. Ninth day before the Kalends of November (24 October)

At Venusia in Apulia, the anniversary of Saints Felix, bishop of the city of Tubzoca, Audactus and Januarius, priests, and Fortunatianus and Septimus, lectors. In the time of Diocletian, they were arrested in their own city by the procurator Magnellianus, then tormented for a long time by many bonds and imprisonments, both in Africa and in Sicily, and finally brought to completion by death from the sword. They were honorably buried between Carthage and Utica. Felix died a virgin at the age of fifty-six.

## D. Eighth day before the Kalends of November (25 October)

In Gaul, at the city of Soissons, the anniversary of Saints Crispin and Crispinian. During the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, they were stretched upon the rack and beaten with clubs. After their fingers had been pierced with awls and strips had been cut from their backs, they were finally killed by the sword and received the crown of martyrdom.

[Col. 0384B] On the same day, at the city of Périgueux, the anniversary of Saint Fronto, bishop. He was ordained at Rome by blessed Peter and sent with the priest George to preach the Gospel. When George died on the third day of their journey, the grieving Fronto returned to the Apostle, received his staff, and, placing it upon the body of the dead man, brought his companion back from death. Thus coming to the aforesaid city, he converted a great multitude of that people to Christ and, renowned for many miracles, rested in peace.

On the same day at Rome, on the Salarian Way, the anniversary of forty-eight soldiers who were baptized together by blessed Pope Dionysius and soon afterward beheaded at the command of the emperor Claudius. Blessed Justin the priest and John gathered their bodies by night and buried them in a crypt [Col. 0384C] with a multitude of Christians on the Salarian Way, at the Cucumber Hill, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, where one hundred and twenty-one other martyrs were also placed. Among them were four soldiers of Christ: Theodosius, Lucius, Marcus, and Peter. When they saw armed men coming toward them, they asked to be beheaded first. Written in the Passion of the holy martyrs Sixtus, Laurence, and Hippolytus.

## E. Seventh day before the Kalends of November (26 October)

In Africa, the anniversary of the holy martyrs Rogatianus the priest and Felicissimus, who were crowned with glorious martyrdom during the persecution of Decius and Valerian. Blessed Cyprian also writes about them in his Letter to the Confessors, in these words:

“Follow,” he says, “in all things Rogatianus, the glorious aged priest, who by the religious virtue and divine favor of our own time is making the way to glory for you. Together with our brother Felicissimus, always calm and sober, he received the attack of the raging populace and first prepared lodging for you in prison; and, in a certain sense your guide, he now goes before you.”

On that same day the holy bishops Vedastus and Amandus are commemorated; their life and death are glorified by very many miracles.

## F. Sixth day before the Kalends of November (27 October)

In Spain, at the city of Ávila, the anniversary of Saints Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta [Col. 0385A]. First they were stretched upon the rack so severely that all the joints of their limbs were loosened. Then, with their heads placed upon stones, they were beaten with powerful bars until their brains were forced out. Thus they completed their martyrdom under the governor Dacian.

On the same day, at the fortress of Tyle, the anniversary of Saint Florentius the martyr.

At Rome, of Evaristus [Note: [Col. 0385D] Eusebius, Book III, chapter 34; the *Pontifical Book*, chapter 6], pope, who occupied the episcopal office for nine years, was crowned with martyrdom under Trajan, and was buried at the Vatican.

On the same day, the vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude.

## G. Fifth day before the Kalends of November (28 October)

The anniversary of Saints Simon and Jude [Note: [Col. 0385D] See the Book on the Feasts of the Apostles; concerning her, in the Passion of Saint Laurence, 20 August].

[Col. 0385B] At Rome, of Saint Cyrilla, daughter of Caesar Decius, who was strangled and killed with the sword under the emperor Claudius and buried by the priest Justin with her mother, near Saint Hippolytus.

## A. Fourth day before the Kalends of November (29 October)

The anniversary of blessed Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, a man praiseworthy for holiness, endurance, and faith.

It happened [Note: [Col. 0385D] Eusebius, Book VI, chapters 78 and 9; Rufinus] once, on the solemn day of the Easter vigil, that oil was lacking for the lamps. When this became known through the ministers, the people were overcome by the greatest sorrow. But Narcissus, trusting in faith, ordered the ministers to draw water and bring it to him. When they had brought it, he prayed, blessed the water, and ordered it to be poured into the lamps.

[Col. 0385C] Then suddenly, by a wondrous power unheard of through the ages, nature was transformed into the richness of oil, and the lamps gave a brilliance even greater than usual. As proof of the event, many of the devout brothers preserved some of the same oil that had been changed from water.

Since, among the other good qualities of his virtues, Narcissus was a man of very steadfast spirit and unwaveringly attached to what was just and right, certain wicked little men who were conscious of their own evil, fearing that if their crimes were exposed they would be unable to escape punishment, anticipated him with plots and prepared to ensnare the man whose judgment they feared. They therefore concocted against him a highly disgraceful and harmful accusation.

They assembled listeners and produced witnesses from among themselves, who, under oath, confirmed the charges that had been brought. One of these witnesses declared that he was speaking the truth so that he would not be consumed by fire; another, so that he would not be corrupted by jaundice; a third, so that he would not be deprived of his sight.

Although no faithful and God-fearing person believed these oaths, because Narcissus’ life, discipline, and chastity were known to everyone, he himself could not bear the disgrace and annoyance of what had been set in motion. At the same time, because he had always desired to lead a secluded and philosophical life, he withdrew from the multitude of the church and hid for many years in deserted places and more remote fields [Col. 0386A].

But that great eye of divine providence does not remain inactive for long. Through the very curses which they had invoked upon themselves in their perjuries, it devised vengeance against the impious.

The first witness, when a small spark of fire set his house alight during the night, was consumed by avenging flames together with his entire household and family. The second was suddenly filled and consumed, from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head, by the jaundice which he had invoked upon himself. The third, seeing the destruction of the former two and realizing that the divine eye had not overlooked their deeds, burst into the midst of the assembly and, before everyone, revealed in tardy repentance the entire sequence of the crime they had contrived.

He lamented the monstrous deed he had committed with such abundant tears and continued in weeping day and night to such an extent that he was finally deprived of his sight. Thus these men suffered penalties of this kind for their fabrication.

Narcissus, however, had withdrawn into the desert and concealed himself in secluded places so completely that no one knew where he lived. It therefore seemed necessary to the bishops to ordain another in his place. His name was Dius; after he had presided over the Church for a short time, Germanio succeeded him, and Cordius succeeded Germanio.

Then suddenly, as though restored to life and returned from heaven, Narcissus appeared unexpectedly. Once again the brothers asked him to preside over the church. But since he was now weakened by old age and unable to carry out the ministry of the episcopate, divine providence summoned Alexander, who was already bishop of another place, to assist the old man through very clear revelations.

After completing one hundred and sixteen years, he left the episcopal seat to Alexander and received from the Lord the reward of his labors.

On the same day, at the city of Sidon, the anniversary of Saint Zenobius [Note: [Col. 0386D] Eusebius, Book VIII, chapter 25], priest, who was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian.

In Gaul, at the city of Vienne, the deposition of the holy and most blessed Theodarius, abbot and confessor, and his translation to the place called Rupian Valley, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November.

## B. Third day before the Kalends of November (30 October)

At the city of Tingis, the Passion of Saint Marcellus the centurion, who completed his martyrdom by beheading [Col. 0386D], under Agricolaus, acting in place of the prefects of the praetorium.

In Africa, the anniversary of two hundred and twenty martyrs.

At Antioch, of blessed Serapion [Note: [Col. 0386D] Eusebius, Book V, chapters 18 and 21; Rufinus 19; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapters 41 and 31 October], bishop, a learned man and renowned for his faith.

## C. The day before the Kalends of November (31 October)

At Rome, the anniversary of blessed Nemesius the deacon and his daughter Lucilla [Note: [Col. 0386D] Concerning them, in the Life of Saint Stephen, pope, 2 August], whom the holy pontiff Stephen baptized [Col. 0387A]. He also appointed Nemesius deacon, in the time of Valerian and Gallienus. They decreed that wherever Nemesius might be found, he should be punished without a hearing.

Strengthened by the grace of Christ, Nemesius went around the crypts and the meeting places of the martyrs, so that wherever he found a Christian in need, he might minister to him from his own resources as far as he could.

When he came on the Appian Way in the silence of night, near the temple of Mars, he discovered Valerian and Maximus sacrificing in the temple of Mars. He therefore bent his knees and prayed to the Lord, saying:

“Lord, God, creator of heaven and earth, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, whom you sent into this world, shatter the schemes of the devil’s craft, so that these wretched men may recover from the devil’s snares.”

Immediately Maximus the consul was seized by the devil [Col. 0387B] and began to cry out in a loud voice: “The Christian Nemesius has set me on fire; his prayer torments me.”

Some men came out of the temple, seized Nemesius, and began to insult him. Suddenly Maximus expired. They took Nemesius and led him to Valerian.

Valerian said to him: “Nemesius, where is your wisdom, which we have always recognized both in counsel and in action? We urge you: consider the truth. Do not abandon the gods whom you have always worshiped from your very cradle.”

The deacon Nemesius replied with tears:

“I, wretched and sinful, always abandoned the truth, shed innocent blood, and, now heavily burdened and weighed down with sins, recognized my Creator only through belated repentance. Having obtained the mercy of Christ, the Son of God, I fear him, I worship him, and to him I offer the service of my devotion. For I reject all idols made of stone and bronze by human hands.”

Valerian became angry and ordered him to be confined in private custody. After the third day he was brought before Valerian and Gallienus, together with his daughter Lucilla, whom they punished before questioning her father, believing that in this way they might soften the spirit of blessed Nemesius.

But he, whose inmost being was possessed by the Holy Spirit, became more joyful at his daughter’s martyrdom and more ardent in confessing Christ. When they saw that they could in no way turn him away from the faith of Christ, they ordered him to be led [Col. 0388B] to execution.

He was beheaded on the Appian Way before the temple of Mars, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. Blessed Pope Stephen buried his body in the same place, but blessed Pope Sixtus afterward lifted it and gave it a more honored burial beside the same Appian Way, in a venerable crypt, on the day before the Kalends of November.

[Note: [Col. 0387D] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 73.] In Gaul, at the town of Vermand, the anniversary of Quintinus the martyr, who suffered martyrdom under the emperor Maximian. After fifty-five years, his body was discovered through an angel’s revelation and buried on the eighth day before the Kalends of July.

**Litanies are to be said. The month of November has thirty days; the moon likewise has thirty.**

## D. Kalends of November (1 November)

[Col. 0387C]

The feast of All the Saints.

At the request of Pope Boniface, the emperor Phocas ordered that the old shrine called the Pantheon, formerly built by Domitian, be cleansed of the filth of idolatry and made into a church of the ever-blessed Virgin Mary and all the martyrs. Thus, where once worship had been offered to all—not gods, but demons—thereafter the memory of all the saints might be celebrated. From that time, on the Kalends of November, it has been solemnly and universally observed in the city of Rome.

In Gaul also, at the urging of Gregory, a pontiff of holy memory, the most devout emperor Louis, with all the bishops of his kingdom and empire consenting, decreed that the feast of All the Saints should be solemnly celebrated annually and perpetually on the aforesaid day. The whole Church received this holy constitution with reverent love.

[Note: [Col. 0387D] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*.]

And at the fortress of Dijon, the anniversary of Saint Benignus the priest. He was sent into Gaul from the East by Saint Polycarp the bishop [Col. 0388C], together with Andochius, his fellow priest, and Thyrsus, the deacon.

When the count Terentius learned of his preaching, he ordered him to be bound, beaten, and brought before him. After again hearing the steadfastness of his words, he ordered him to be beaten with very harsh cords. Then, stretched upon the rack and beaten, he was again confined to prison. In the morning he destroyed the idols by prayer and was returned to prison.

They drove ten heated awls into his hands and fixed his feet with molten lead in a perforated stone. They also shut twelve savage dogs in with him for six days. An angel brought him heavenly bread, removed the awls, and rescued him from the lead and iron.

Finally, they ordered his neck to be beaten with an iron bar and his body to be pierced with a lance. When this had been done, a snow-white dove ascended from the prison to heaven before the eyes of the Christians, and a very sweet fragrance, as though from paradise, followed it [Col. 0388D]. Blessed Leonilla came and buried his body, embalmed with spices, not far from the prison.

On the same day, the anniversary of Saint Caesarius the deacon and Julian the priest.

Caesarius came from Africa to Tarracina, a city of Campania, in the time of Claudius. While he was publicly denouncing the idolaters, he was arrested by Firminus the pontiff and confined in custody. After being tormented there for many days, he was handed over to Leontius, the consul of Campania.

When Leontius could not overcome him with words, he ordered him to be led before his own chariot, bound by the hands and naked, as far as the temple of Apollo. When he arrived there, the temple collapsed at his prayer and killed Firminus the pontiff.

After this, he was confined in prison by Luxurius, the leading man of the city, and remained there for one year and one month. Then Luxurius brought him out into the forum. While Caesarius was praying, he was surrounded by heavenly light, so that Leontius himself believed, clothed the naked Caesarius in his own military cloak, was baptized by him, and received the body and blood of the Lord from the hand of Julian the priest.

Without delay, after a prayer had been spoken over him, Leontius gave up his spirit on the third day before the Kalends of November. Then Luxurius ordered Julian and Caesarius to be put into a sack and thrown into the sea. On that same day they were cast back onto the shore and buried by Eusebius, a servant of God, near the city of Terracina. The same Eusebius later suffered martyrdom with Felix the priest.

Likewise on the same day, the deposition of Saint Severinus the monk, from the city of Tibur.

Likewise, the anniversary of Saint Mary the virgin. Although she was a slave and was fasting on the birthday of her master’s son, she could in no way be persuaded to eat food sacrificed to idols. First afflicted with harsh beatings, then tormented by prolonged imprisonment, stretching on the rack, and tearing with hooks, she completed her martyrdom.

## E. Fourth day before the Nones of November (2 November)

[Col. 0389C]

[Note: [Col. 0389D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 74; Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 29; Rufinus.] The anniversary of Saint Victorinus, bishop of Pettau, who was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian.

At Laodicea, the anniversary of blessed Theodore, bishop, a man adorned not only with words but also with deeds and virtues. He had indeed been a physician by profession, but was transferred by the Lord to the medicine of souls. Truly incomparable, he excelled almost all men in faith, mercy, zeal, vigilance, and every excellent discipline. He also labored greatly in the divine Scriptures and rested in good old age.

On the same day, the anniversary of Saint Ambrose, abbot of the monastery of Agaunum. Previously he had been head of the monastery on the island of Barbara near Lyons, renowned for great virtues; when he was transferred there because of the excellence of his religious rule, he soon afterward rested in the Lord with a blessed end.

## F. Third day before the Nones of November (3 November)

The anniversary of Saint Quartus, disciple of the apostles.

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the anniversary of Saints Germanus, Theophilus, Caesarius, and Vitalis, who nobly completed their martyrdom during the persecution of Decius.

On the same day, the deposition of Saint Hubert, bishop.

## G. The day before the Nones of November (4 November)

[Col. 0390A]

[Note: [Col. 0389D] Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 29; Rufinus; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men* [Col. 0390D], chapter 76.] At Alexandria, of blessed Pierius the priest, a man of keen intellect, nobly learned in the divine Scriptures, most pure in life, and wholly stripped and free for Christian philosophy; an incomparable teacher of the Church, who disputed wonderfully both privately and publicly. He rested in the time of the emperor Philip.

In Gaul, at the city of Rodez, the anniversary of Saint Amantius, bishop, whose life was glorious in holiness and miracles.

## A. The Nones of November (5 November)

Of Zachariah the prophet, father of John the Baptist.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] Concerning these matters, in the Life of Saint Caesarius, 1 November.] At Terracina, a city of Campania, the anniversary of Saints [Col. 0390B] Felix the priest and Eusebius the monk, in the time of the emperor Claudius.

Eusebius had buried the holy martyrs Julian and Caesarius. As he converted many to the faith by praying and fasting at their graves, whom Felix the priest baptized, both men were arrested by Leontius, son of Leontius the consul, chiefly because Caesarius had made his father a Christian.

They were led before him into the forum. Since they could not be overcome, they were confined in prison and, on that same night, because they refused to sacrifice, they were beheaded and thrown into the river. Their bodies were carried as far as the sea, cast back onto the shore, and found by a certain priest from Capua named Quartus. He immediately placed them on a vehicle and took them to his house. Searching carefully, he also found their heads and, joining them to the bodies, buried them near Saint Caesarius.

## B. Eighth day before the Ides of November (6 November)

At Tonza in Africa, the anniversary of Saint Felix. On his solemnity, blessed Augustine appears to expound a certain psalm to the people (Psalm 127), where, among other things, he speaks of his passion, saying:

“Felix the martyr, truly fortunate both in name and in crown, whose day it is today. Know, brothers, that he did not suffer the death which the other martyrs suffered. For after confessing, he was delayed for torture; on another day his lifeless body was found. They had closed the prison on his body, not on his spirit. The executioners who were preparing to torture him found him absent; they lost the object of their savagery. He lay lifeless, without sensation, so that they could not torture him, but with sensation before the Lord, so that he might be crowned.”

In the East, at the city of Theophilus, the ten holy martyrs who are said to have suffered under the Saracens, as recorded in the Acts of the Forty Saints.

## C. Seventh day before the Ides of November (7 November)

[Note: [Col. 0390D] Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 29; Rufinus.] At Alexandria, of Achillas the bishop, distinguished in learning, faith, conduct, and character.

On the same day, the anniversary of Saint Amarantus the martyr, who, having completed the course of his faithful contest at the city of Albi, lies buried and lives in glory [Col. 0391A]. His sacred tomb is made illustrious by frequent miracles through the power of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] Gregory, Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 13.] At Perugia in Italy, the anniversary of Saint Herculanus, bishop and martyr.

## D. Sixth day before the Ides of November (8 November)

At Rome, the anniversary of the holy martyrs Claudius, Nicostratus, Simphronianus, Castorius, and Simplicius, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian.

They were exceptionally skilled craftsmen and highly accomplished cutters of marble, and became greatly favored by the emperor Diocletian. Once, while they were engaged in squaring blocks of marble and strengthening their work with the sign of the cross, so that their craftsmanship proceeded according to their wishes, one of them, Simplicius, who still remained in pagan error, said to the other four:

“I adjure you by the god Sol to tell me who this god is in whose name you work so well.”

Symphronianus replied: “If you can believe, we will tell you, and you will soon attain the craft; but you will also have eternal life.”

After they had joined him to the faith and entrusted him to blessed Cyril the bishop, that same bishop baptized him and instructed him to believe in Christ the Lord.

Not long afterward, philosophers accused them of being Christians and of refusing to make, as the emperor had ordered, a god Aesculapius from porphyry and proconnesian marble. Diocletian ordered a certain tribune named Lampadius to hear them, with measured words.

Lampadius said to them: “Worship the god Sol, so that you may destroy the philosophers’ accusation.”

They replied: “We never worship the work of our hands, but we worship the God of heaven and earth, who reigns forever, Jesus Christ, the Son of God.”

They were therefore confined in public custody. Since they could not be turned away from the faith of Christ, at Lampadius’ command they were stripped and beaten most severely with scorpions. Soon Lampadius was seized by a demon and expired.

When Diocletian heard what had happened, filled with extreme fury he ordered a certain toga-wearing man named Nicetius to have them enclosed alive in leaden coffins and thrown into the river. After forty-two days, a Christian named Nicodemus came, lifted the martyrs’ bodies together with the coffins, and placed them honorably in his own house. They suffered on the sixth day before the Ides of November.

[Col. 0391D] On the same day, the anniversary of the four holy Crowned Martyrs, namely Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus.

When they were being compelled to sacrifice, they resisted and, refusing to consent to the impious demand, remained steadfast in the faith. This was reported to the emperor Diocletian, who immediately ordered that they be beaten to death with leaded clubs before the image [Col. 0392A] of Aesculapius.

He ordered their bodies to be thrown into the street to the dogs, and they lay there for five days. Then devout Christians came, gathered the bodies, and buried them on the Lavican Way, the third milestone from the city, in a sand-pit, near the bodies of the holy martyrs Claudius, Nicostratus, Simphronianus, Castorius, and Simplicius.

They suffered on the sixth day before the Ides of November, but two years after the passion of those five martyrs. Since their names could not be found at all, blessed Melchiades the bishop decreed that the annual day of the four Crowned Martyrs should be commemorated under the names of the five holy martyrs.

In the intervening years, however, their names were also revealed to a certain holy man. The feast remained celebrated, as it had been established, within the feast of the other martyrs, and the place became distinguished by the name of the Four Crowned Martyrs.

## E. Fifth day before the Ides of November (9 November)

The anniversary of Saint Theodore the martyr, in the time of the emperors Maximian and Maximinus. He was a soldier and a true Christian. He was brought before Brinca, commander of the legion, who granted him a delay so that the sentence might remain irrevocable.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] He is presented to the judge Popilius. The Vulgate reads, “He is presented to the judge and the people.” Who, on reading the Vulgate, would have suspected that an error lay beneath it? The manuscripts rightly give the name of the judge as Popilius, whom Metaphrastes calls the judge and governor Publius. The manuscript Acts which I obtained from the library at Fulda read: “When Cronides the secretary learned of this event, terrified by fear, he seized blessed Theodore and brought him before Popilius the governor” [Col. 0392D]. The same reading occurs in the histories of many saints, printed at Louvain in 1485. In Membritius, vol.
