II, the reading is wrongly “before Populius the governor.” In Ado, Popilius is more correct than Populius in other authors. Popilia is a well-known Roman family.]

He was presented to the judge Popilius, who ordered him to be sent to prison and the door of the prison to be sealed. There he was comforted by a divine visitation.

After several days he was again brought before the governor, suspended on a wooden frame, and his sides scraped with iron hooks until his ribs were exposed. Then the governor dictated the sentence, saying:

“Theodore, who does not obey the commands of the most invincible emperors and the power of the gods, but believes in Jesus Christ crucified, I order to be handed over to the flames.”

Then the blessed martyr, fortified with the sign of the cross and with his hands bound behind his back, was driven into the fire. Looking ahead, he saw Cleonicus weeping in the crowd; Cleonicus had been brought with him as a recruit.

He cried out: “Cleonicus, I am waiting for you; hurry and follow me.”

When the blessed martyr was already surrounded on every side by masses of flame, he poured out a prayer, praising and glorifying the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Thus he gave his holy soul back to Christ on the fifth day before the Ides of November.

A certain woman named Eusebia collected his body, wrapped it in a clean shroud, and carried it to her estate, to a place called Euchaita.

[Col. 0392D] [Note: [Col. 0392D] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 80.] Likewise, on the same day at Bourges, Saint Ursicinus, who, having been ordained at Rome by the successors of the apostles, was sent as the first bishop to that city.

## F. Fourth day before the Ides of November (10 November)

In the territory of Agde, at Cessation, the anniversary of the holy martyrs Tiberius, Modestus, and Florentia [Col. 0393A]. In the time of Diocletian, they were tortured by various torments and completed their martyrdom.

Likewise on the same day, Saint Martin, pope, who, on account of the Catholic faith, was seized from the church by the heretical emperor Constantine through the exarch Theodore, taken to Constantinople, and banished to Cherson in the province of Lycia. There he ended his life, still shining to this day in that place through many signs of virtue.

## G. Third day before the Ides of November (11 November)

In Gaul, at the city of Tours, the anniversary of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor.

On the same day, in Scythia, in the metropolitan city of Salutary Phrygia, [Col. 0393B] the passion of Saint Menas the martyr. He was a soldier of noble birth, born in the province of Egypt. During the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, renouncing earthly military service, he first served the heavenly King in secret solitude in the desert. Then, on the birthdays of the aforesaid emperors, he came forth into public and openly declared before them that he was a Christian. He was handed over to the commander Pyrrhus to be tortured, and Pyrrhus ordered him confined in prison for as long as the emperors’ birthday celebrations continued.

When the festival had ended, and Pyrrhus was seated on the tribunal, he ordered Menas to be brought before him and said to him: “Yesterday, inauspiciously and rashly, you dared to enter the theatre and profane it with certain most vain speeches—I do not know what they were—especially since it is asserted that you belonged to our faction. [Col. 0393C] Sacrifice to the gods, so that everything you have done through ignorance may be forgiven you and you may be restored to your former rank.”

When blessed Menas replied, “I take no pleasure in this worldly honor, but desire to become a disciple of Christ the Lord,” the commander ordered him stretched out and his hands bound with ox-hide thongs. The soldiers beat him with rods for so long that the place in the street was filled with his blood. Then he was raked with claws on the torture-frame; lamps were applied and he was burned along the sides; the wounds were rubbed by the soldiers with sackcloth, and burning coals were placed upon them. He was dragged over thorns and iron stakes with his hands and feet bound, and was severely battered on the neck and jaws with lead-weighted scourges. Yet he remained steadfast in praise and confession of almighty God.

Finally, the commander Pyrrhus ordered the sentence to be read from a tablet: [Col. 0393D] “It is decided that Menas, an ex-soldier and ringleader of all Christians, unwilling to obey the emperors’ commands and refusing to sacrifice to the gods, shall be executed by the sword and his body burned with fire.”

The Christians therefore secretly rescued his body from the midst of the fire, prepared it with clean linens and spices, [Col. 0394A] and, with due veneration, laid it to rest in the cemetery on the third day before the Ides of November. His sacred body was later transferred to Constantinople and is venerated there in the royal city with fitting honor.

Likewise at Lyons, Saint Veranus, bishop, whose life was illustrious for faith and the merits of his virtues.

A. THE DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF NOVEMBER (12 November)

[Note: [Col. 0393D] Prosper, in the Chronicle, under the year 437.]

In Africa, the commemoration of Saints Arcadius, Probus, Paschasius, and Eutychianus. Born in Spain, they were held in high esteem and affection by Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, because of their wisdom and faithful service. They would not in any way turn toward the Arian perfidy to which he himself was devoted. Driving the barbarian into the most furious rage, he first proscribed them, then sent them into exile, afterwards tortured them with the most atrocious punishments, and finally killed them by various deaths. Thus they wonderfully met their end in a glorious martyrdom.

The boy Paulillus, brother of Eutychianus and Paschasius, could not be driven by any threats from his profession and love of the Catholic faith. He was beaten for a long time with clubs and condemned to the lowest form of slavery; evidently he was not killed so that even that age might glory in the defeat of the impious man’s savagery.

[Note: [Col. 0393D] “At Sigeric,” king of the Vandals. The manuscripts consistently read this; commonly they have Genseric, or, as others call him, Geiseric, perhaps more correctly. I have therefore also placed this form in the margin. I think the error arose from a transposition of letters, so that they wrote *Sigericum* instead of *Gisericum*. Certainly Geiseric was king of the Vandals, as you find in Prosper’s Chronicle under the year of Christ 437, in this very account of the martyrs, which Ado took from him. Sigeric, however, was king of the Goths, according to Isidore’s Chronicle [Col. 0394D] of the Goths, era 454, the seventh year of Theodosius the Younger. As for the fact that Victor of Africa does not mention these martyrs in his account of the Vandal persecution, Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 437, considers the reason to be that Victor did not take much trouble to record the Vandal disasters inflicted upon Numidia and the neighboring provinces, being concerned chiefly with the affairs of the Church of Carthage, where he lived.]

[Alternative reading: Geiseric.]

On the same day, Saint Melanius, bishop of the city of Rennes, who, after innumerable signs of virtue, continually intent upon heaven, departed from this world.

B. THE IDES OF NOVEMBER (13 November)

At Ravenna, the commemoration of Saints Valentinus, Solutor, [Col. 0394C] and Victor, martyrs.

At Tours, Saint Brictius, bishop.

In Provence, at the city of Aix, blessed Mitrius, most illustrious martyr.

C. THE EIGHTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF DECEMBER (14 November)

In Thrace, at the city of Heraclea, the feast of Saints Clementinus, Theoditus, and Philumenus, martyrs.

[Note: [Col. 0394D] Eusebius, book VI, chapter 34; Rufinus, chapter 31.]

At Alexandria, blessed Serapion. During the persecution under Decius, the persecutors found him in his house and subjected him to the cruelest punishments. First they dislocated all his joints; then they threw him down from an upper story, and thus he became a martyr of Christ. [Col. 0394D]

D. THE SEVENTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF DECEMBER (15 November)

The feast of Saint Felix, bishop, who from the fifteenth year of his life was distinguished by the glory of miracles and, under the governor Martianus, completed his martyrdom with thirty others. The presbyter Elpidius buried his body in the church at Nola. [Col. 0395A]

E. THE SIXTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF DECEMBER (16 November)

The feast of Saint Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, a man of admirable faith, life, and teaching. From the most noble senatorial order he had turned to a religious life and manner of living. For a long time, on his estate beside the river Druentia, he voluntarily shut himself within the enclosure of a cave and served Christ, devoting himself to fasts and prayers.

[Note: [Col. 0395D] Manuscript: Durentiam.]

When the bishop of Lyons died, the whole Church, following its ancient custom, sought from the Lord through three days of fasting and supplication that it might be revealed to them who should undertake the governance of that church. An angel of the Lord appeared in a vision to a certain boy and said: “There is a certain senator named Eucherius, shut up in a cave beside the river Druentia, who, having abandoned everything he possessed, has followed the Lord. Go and bring him, and appoint him your shepherd, for he has been chosen by God.”

When the boy reported this to the elders at dawn, they gave thanks to almighty God after summoning all the brothers. They sent the archdeacon, who at that time administered the church, with clergy to the place mentioned, and found Eucherius just as the Lord had revealed. When the archdeacon told him why he had come, Eucherius began to declare under oath that he would not willingly leave the cave and would not go with him unless he were led away bound.

[Col. 0395C] When he continued repeating this for a long time, the archdeacon broke through the wall of the cave, brought him out, and, in accordance with his oath, led him bound to Lyons. The clergy and people, choosing him with one mind and equal accord as their priest, solemnly installed him in the episcopal chair.

His wife Galla, serving God in the holy religious habit, entered his cave and spent all the rest of her life there in religious devotion. Their two daughters, one named Consortia and the other Tullia, became renowned for the glory of virginity and miracles.

F. THE FIFTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF DECEMBER (17 November)

[Note: [Col. 0395D] Eusebius, book VI, chapter 33; Rufinus, chapter 30 and following; Eusebius, book VII, chapter [reference incomplete].]

At Alexandria, blessed Dionysius, bishop, often sufficiently renowned for his many confessions and magnificent in the variety of his sufferings and tortures, in the time of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus.

It is related that, when his persecutors were harassing him and he stood before the judge, he answered: “Why do you weary yourselves by persecuting me? Take my head, for which you are laboring so greatly, severed from my neck, and carry this great gift to your tyrant and emperor.”

The governor was Aemilianus. When Dionysius confessed before him the one God who had made heaven and earth, saying that He alone must be worshiped and that the others were neither gods nor to be worshiped, he was driven into exile to a certain deserted fort called Cephro. It was chosen especially because its inhabitants were pagans and sufficiently devoted to the superstitions of idols.

At first they received the exile Dionysius with hostile and thoroughly antagonistic feelings. But afterwards, when by the grace of the Lord he gradually began to sow the word of God among them, the greater part of that fierce and barbarous people abandoned their idols, turned to the true God, and submitted to Christ.

When this became known, they transferred him again to another place, indeed near Alexandria, but deserted by its inhabitants and almost empty of dwellers. There too, because of the city’s proximity, our people frequently visited him, and, having received him as a shepherd, the flock became more joyful and more steadfast for the contests of faith.

[Col. 0396B] Again they sent military men with a centurion and dragged Dionysius, together with Gaius and Peter, bound in chains and afflicted with various torments, into a desert region of Libya. There they left them bound in a most desolate place, lacking every human convenience, extending into the desert three days’ journey from Paraetonium.

At that time the presbyter Maximus, and Dioscorus, Demetrius and Lucius, as well as Faustinus and Aquila, also became sufficiently renowned and distinguished by the title of confession.

Meanwhile blessed Dionysius returned to Alexandria and, weighed down by old age, rested in peace, having served as bishop for seventeen years.

On the same day, in the city of Córdoba in Spain, the passion of the holy martyrs Asisclus and Victoria. There, in honor of their precious death, roses are gathered on that same day, divinely sprung and blooming.

[Note: [Col. 0395D] 10. Rufinus. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, [Col. 0396D] chapter 7.]

At Orléans, Saint Anianus, bishop.

G. THE FOURTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF DECEMBER (18 November)

[Note: [Col. 0396D] Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 12.]

At Antioch, the feast of Saint Romanus. In the time of Diocletian, when the prefect Asclepiades attempted to break into the church and utterly destroy it, Romanus urged the other Christians to oppose him. Therefore the prefect immediately ordered him brought before him in chains. Because he confessed Christ with the utmost steadfastness, he was first stretched on the torture-frame, then severely beaten with weighted clubs and cudgels. After this, he also had his cheeks scraped with a very sharp razor.

[Col. 0396D] [Note: [Col. 0396D] Prudentius, hymn 10.]

At Romanus’s request, the prefect then ordered a small boy to be brought in. Invoking the name of Christ, Romanus asked him whether it was better to worship one god or several, so that the prefect might be confounded by the boy’s confession. When the boy said that one God alone must be believed in, Asclepiades, enraged, ordered him suspended from the *catomus* and beaten, and finally beheaded. The boy’s name was Baralas.

Romanus was again suspended on the torture-frame and raked with claws; then he was led to a blazing pyre into which he was to be thrown. But as he prayed, a sudden deluge of rain came and extinguished the fire. Afterwards the prefect ordered his tongue to be cut out. When, even after this, Romanus praised Christ in a very clear voice, he was shut in prison and finally strangled with a noose.

On the same day, in the same city, the feast of Saint Hesychius. Under the aforesaid emperor, he was a soldier, and when he heard the order that anyone who did not sacrifice to idols must lay aside his military belt, he immediately removed his belt. For this reason the emperor first had him dressed in a tunic and assigned to the women’s quarters; then, after a huge stone had been tied to his right hand, ordered him thrown into the river.

A. THE THIRTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF DECEMBER (19 November)

[Col. 0397B]

At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of Saint Maximus, presbyter and martyr, who suffered in the persecution of Maximinus and was placed beside Saint Sixtus.

At Vienne, Saints Severinus, Exuperius, and Felicianus, martyrs. After many years had passed, their bodies were found through revelations made by the saints themselves. The city’s bishop, clergy, and people honorably lifted them up and buried them with fitting honor in the basilica of Saint Romanus, situated in the eastern part of the aforesaid city.

[Note: [Col. 0397D] Eusebius, book VII, chapter 10.]

On the same day, the feast of the holy martyr Faustus. God’s grace gave him such confidence and greatness of spirit that, when no one at all was permitted to approach the brothers held in prison for purposes of humanitarian service and ministry, he, together with his companion Eusebius, visited them continually and supplied what they needed.

As the governor’s fury increased day by day—slaughtering some, afflicting others with punishments and various forms of torture, killing others through the prison’s squalor and the weight of their chains—and as he ordered above all that no one should approach them, so that hunger might be applied as another kind of torture, God nevertheless granted this deacon and his companion the grace that, despite everyone’s opposition, access to the confessors of Christ was not denied them.

Thus blessed Faustus, an aged confessor full of days, persevering to the end, completed his perfect martyrdom by decapitation.

B. THE TWELFTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF DECEMBER (20 November)

[Col. 0397D]

[Note: [Col. 0397D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 19.]

At Rome, the feast of Saint Pontianus, pope. When Maximinus stirred up persecution against the priests of the churches, Pontianus was deported to Sardinia together with the presbyter Hippolytus [alternative reading: Philip]. There he was killed with clubs and completed his martyrdom. His body was brought back by blessed Pope Fabian and buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He occupied the episcopal see for nine years, five months, and two days.

In Sicily, at the city of Messana, Saints Ampelus and Caius.

[Note: [Col. 0398D] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 85.]

At Chalon, the most blessed Sylvester, bishop [Col. 0398A] and confessor, who, full of days and virtues, departed to the Lord in the forty-second year of his priesthood.

C. THE ELEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF DECEMBER (21 November)

The feast of the most blessed Rufus, of whom the apostle Paul writes to the Romans: “Greet Rufus, the chosen one, and his mother and mine” (Romans 16).

In Italy, at the monastery of Bobbio, Saint Columbanus, abbot, who was the founder of many monasteries and became the father of countless monks. Renowned for many virtues, he rested in a good old age.

D. THE TENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF DECEMBER (22 November)

At Rome, the feast of Saint Cecilia, virgin. She thoroughly instructed her bridegroom Valerian and his brother Tiburtius to believe in Christ, and afterwards encouraged them to martyrdom.

After their martyrdom, Almachius had Cecilia arrested and ordered her compelled to offer incense to demons. But the officials, observing her exceptional beauty and prudence, begged her not to destroy such glory or give such beauty over to death.

She, however, sufficiently conveying a counsel of piety and instructing them concerning the grace of almighty God, saw that they were moved to believe in Christ and said to them: “Go and tell the wretched Almachius that I shall ask for a delay, so that I may bring here, within my house, one who will make you all sharers in eternal life.”

Then holy Pope Urban came and baptized more or less [Col. 0398C] four hundred men and women, among whom was a very distinguished man named Gordianus.

Again Almachius ordered blessed Cecilia brought before him. When he saw that she remained unshakable in her confession of faith, he ordered her taken to her house and burned there in the flames of the bathhouse. She was enclosed there for an entire day and night, yet remained in perfect health as though in a cool place, although the fires were continually fed with piles of wood.

When Almachius heard this, he sent someone to behead her. The executioner struck her three times but could not cut off her head. She survived for three days. Then Saint Urban took her body away by night and buried it among his fellow bishops.

Blessed Cecilia suffered in the time of the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus.

E. THE NINTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF DECEMBER (23 November)

[Col. 0398D]

[Note: [Col. 0398D] See the little book *On the Feast of the Apostles*.]

The feast of Saint Clement, who under the persecution of Trajan was crowned with martyrdom.

At that time also the most illustrious and most blessed servant of God Flavia Domitilla, who was the niece, through his sister, of the consul Flavius Clemens, and who, by Saint Clement, was consecrated and entrusted to the sacred veil for perseverance in chastity, was deported into exile on the island of Pontia with many others because of the testimony she bore to Christ. There she endured a long martyrdom.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Felicity, mother of seven martyr sons, who, by order of Antoninus, was beheaded for Christ.

That emperor had ordered the city prefect Publius to compel her and her sons to bow before the sacrifices of the gods. The prefect, inviting her to sacrifice with flattering words, threatened her with the punishment of death.

Blessed Felicity answered him: “I can be neither loosened by your flatteries nor broken by your threats. For I have the Holy Spirit, who will not permit me to be conquered by the devil. Therefore I am confident, because while alive I shall overcome you; and if I am killed, I shall overcome you more completely in death.”

The next day the prefect sat in the Forum of Mars and ordered her brought with her sons. He said to her: “Take pity on your sons, fine young men flourishing in the bloom of their first youth.”

Blessed Felicity replied: “Your mercy is impiety, and your exhortation is cruelty.” Then she turned to her sons and said: “Look upon heaven, my sons, and gaze upward, where Christ awaits you with his saints. Fight for your souls and show yourselves faithful in the love of Christ.”

When Publius heard this, he ordered her struck on the face. Then he summoned her sons and began urging them to sacrifice.

Januarius replied: “You give foolish advice, for the wisdom of the Lord preserves me and will make me overcome every torture.” Immediately the judge ordered him beaten with rods and taken into prison.

Felix said: “There is one God whom we worship, to whom we offer the sacrifice of dutiful devotion. Therefore do not suppose that either I or any of my brothers will depart from the love of the Lord Jesus Christ. Even if blows threaten us, our faith can neither be conquered nor changed.”

Philippus said: “Those beings of whom you speak are neither gods nor almighty. They are vain, wretched, and senseless images; and whoever wishes to sacrifice to them will perish forever.”

Sylvanus said: “If we fear transitory death, we shall incur eternal punishment. Since we truly know what rewards are prepared for the just and what punishment is appointed for sinners, we disregard Roman laws in order to keep the divine commands.”

Alexander said: “I am Christ’s servant. With my mouth I confess him, in my heart I hold him, and I worship him without ceasing. The weak age you see possesses the wisdom of old age.”

Vitalis said: “He lives better who worships the true God than he who desires to have demons favorable to him.”

Martialis said: “All who do not confess that the true God exists will be in eternal fire.”

The judge reported the whole proceedings in writing to Antoninus. He ordered them to die by various punishments, their mother being executed last.

F. THE EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF DECEMBER (24 November)

[Note: [Col. 0399D] On this subject, see the Acts of Anastasia the martyr, 26 December, and Anastasia’s letter.]

At Rome, the feast of Saint Chrysogonus the martyr, who by order of Diocletian was thrown into chains for two years. There he endured much suffering and was sustained by the provisions of Saint Anastasia.

When her husband Publius, jealous of blessed Anastasia, had confined her with guards so strictly that she could not even look toward the opening of any window, she sent the following letter to Chrysogonus the confessor, who had instructed her in Christ:

“To the holy confessor of Christ Chrysogonus, Anastasia.

“Although my father was a worshiper of idols, my mother Fausta is shown always to have lived as a most Christian and chaste woman. She had me made a Christian while I was still in the cradle. After her death, I took upon myself the yoke of a sacrilegious husband. By God’s mercy, avoiding his bed under the pretense of illness, I embrace day and night the footsteps of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Since this man exhausts my patrimony, by which he is distinguished, upon unworthy and shameful idolaters, he has also handed me over, as though I were a great sacrilegious woman, to such severe custody that I suspect I shall lose my bodily life. Nothing remains except that, having given up my spirit, I should succumb. Although in such a death I may glory in confessing our Lord Jesus Christ, my mind is nevertheless greatly crushed by the fact that my wealth, which I had wholly vowed to God, is serving those who are alien to God and shameful.

“Therefore I beg you, man of God, earnestly to pray to the Lord either that, if he foresees Publius will come to his faith, he may allow him to live; or, if he foresees that he will remain in this perversity of unbelief, that he may command him to make way for those who worship him. It is better for Publius to breathe out his spirit than to deny the Son of God and obstruct those who confess him.

“For Christ almighty is my witness that, if I am freed, I shall cling to the footsteps of the saints and diligently undertake the care of all, as I had begun. Farewell, man of God, and remember me.”

When Chrysogonus had read this letter, he prayed with many confessors and replied as follows:

“To you tossed amid the storms and whirlwinds of the world, Christ will soon come, walking upon the waves, and with one word of his command will restrain the spirit of the devil blowing against you.

“Patiently, and as though placed in the midst of the sea, believe that Christ will come to you. Turning inward to yourself, cry out with the prophet, saying: ‘Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet confess him: the salvation of my countenance and my God’ (Psalm 41).

“There is shown to be a twofold sign of divine generosity when both earthly things are restored to you and heavenly things are bestowed. For God prolongs his beneficence to the utmost extremity so that what he grants may not seem cheap to us.

“See that you are not troubled because adversity is inflicted upon you while you are living piously. You are not being deceived but tested. The defense you think can be secured through a human being is not safe. Hear Scripture saying: ‘Cursed is the man who places his hope in man; and blessed is the man who places his hope in God’ (Jeremiah 17).

“Guard yourself courageously, watchfully, and vigorously from every sin, and seek consolation from God alone, whose commands you preserve. Soon a peaceful time will turn toward you, and, as after the darkness of night, you will see the bright light of day; and after the icy cold of passing winter, golden and serene seasons will follow for you, so that you may offer temporal joy to all who are afflicted for the love of Christ, through which you will doubtless attain eternal joy.

“Farewell in the Lord, and pray for me.”

When Anastasia read this letter, she received stronger powers of faith and began to glory in the strength of patience as greatly as before she had complained that she was afflicted by the oppression of her utterly faithless husband.

Accordingly, when blessed Anastasia was so tightly confined that she was scarcely given water, she thought that she was failing amid that tribulation and wrote a letter:

“To the blessed martyr and confessor of Christ Chrysogonus, Anastasia.

“The end of the body has come. Remember me, so that he himself may receive my departing soul for whose love I endure these things, which you will learn from the mouth of this old woman.”

To this Saint Chrysogonus sent the following reply:

“Chrysogonus to Anastasia.

“It is always the case that darkness precedes light. Thus, after sickness, health also returns, and life is promised after death. The adversity and prosperity of this world are brought to one conclusion, so that neither despair may rule the sorrowful nor arrogance the joyful.

“There is one sea in which the little boats of our bodies sail, and under one helmsman of the body our souls perform the work of sailors. Some people’s ships, strengthened by the strongest bonds of their keels, pass unharmed through the turbulent waves of the dark sea. Others, however, because of the fragile joining of their timbers, complete a course near death even in calm waters. Those who do not consider how they may reach the harbor of salvation are close to perishing.

“But you, O blameless servant of Christ, rise in your whole mind to the trophy of Christ’s cross, and prepare yourself for the work of God. When you obey his desires, you will reach Christ with the palm of martyrdom.”

While Diocletian was stationed in the region of Aquileia and killing Christians, he ordered Chrysogonus brought before him. He said to him: “Accept the dignity of the prefecture; take also the consulship appropriate to your lineage—only worship the gods.”

Blessed Chrysogonus replied: “With my mind I worship one God, in my heart I revere him, and in sincere actions I honor him. But I curse and reject the images of these gods of yours, because I know them to be entirely demons—[text reads: *theno*, sic].”

Then, by Diocletian’s order, Chrysogonus was led to the Gradated Waters and beheaded there. His body was thrown into the sea and shortly afterwards found on the estate called Ad Saltus. The aged presbyter Zoilus collected it and placed it in an underground chest in his chamber. His head too was revealed to Zoilus, as fresh as though it had been cut off that same day, and he joined it to the body.

Blessed Chrysogonus suffered on the eighth day before the Kalends of December and was buried on the fifth day before the Kalends of the same month. Saint Zoilus, on the thirtieth day after Chrysogonus’s passion, when Saint Chrysogonus appeared to him, departed to the Lord.

G. THE SEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF DECEMBER (25 November)

[Note: [Col. 0401D] Eusebius, book VII, final chapter, and book IX, chapter 5; Rufinus, chapter 6.]

The feast of Saint Peter, bishop of Alexandria. He spent twelve years in that episcopate: three before the persecution and the remaining nine amid various kinds of trials.

Since, while constantly placed in every contest of persecution, he bound himself with the strictest restraints of self-control, and nobly devoted himself to the word of God for the benefit and instruction of the Church, laboring with great vigilance day and night over every duty of the priesthood, in the ninth year of the persecution and the twelfth of his episcopate he earned the crown of martyrdom by decapitation.

To arrest him, the tyrant Maximinus sent a certain tribune. When the tribune entered Alexandria, he found Peter celebrating the commemoration of the holy apostles with a crowd of people. He arrested him, bound him in chains, and placed him under guard in prison.

After several days, the tyrant Maximinus sent written orders to the tribune that he should punish Peter as quickly as possible. Meanwhile, while Peter was kept in prison and the entire people of the city of Alexandria watched the prison doors out of love for their shepherd, the wretched Arius—who was regarded as excommunicated and degraded by blessed Peter because of his erroneous doctrine—learned of Maximinus’s sentence against blessed Peter and hurried to the church. He begged the clergy and people to intercede for him with the bishop, thinking that after Peter’s departure he himself would be raised to the episcopate.

Those who had been asked therefore came and began to plead with the blessed bishop on Arius’s behalf. The holy bishop answered them with a deep sigh that Arius, dead to God, had already been cast away from the face of God, because he had blasphemed grievously against the essence of the Godhead by teaching that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not of one essence and nature.

Taking aside from the crowd two presbyters, Achillas and Alexander, he said to them secretly: “Although I am a sinner, I know that by a heavenly calling I have been summoned to this contest of martyrdom. It is therefore pious for you to confess the mystery of God that has been revealed to me, because after my martyrdom you will obtain my seat and episcopate. You, Achillas, will be first; Alexander will follow you.

“Finally, at this hour of the night, let me disclose everything concerning Arius to you. When I had completed the customary sacrifice of prayers to God, suddenly Christ my Lord appeared to me in the form of a boy. At his presence I was illumined by such immense brightness that I could not look upon his majestic face.

“He was clothed in a very white linen tunic, torn from top to bottom, and with both hands he held it together around his chest, in a way covering his nakedness. When I saw him, I was seized with great fear; at last, taking courage, I said to him: ‘What is this, Lord, that I see—your tunic torn from top to bottom?’

“He answered me: ‘Every day you discuss that matter, and you do not know how it was torn? Arius did this, for he has separated from me the people of my inheritance, purchased with my blood.

“‘I now command and warn you not to receive him into communion, nor, when those whom he has sent come to you, to grant him pardon at their request. Make known to the two presbyters what I have revealed to you, so that after you they may reject him by anathematizing him, lest the people be deceived by his error.’”

After exhorting them and commending them to the Lord in whom they believed, urging them to remain in the unity of the Catholic faith, he dismissed them in peace.

Because of their immense love for him, the people remained around the prison, and blessed Peter could not openly be led out of it. Therefore, in the middle of the night, the tribune, together with the soldiers, broke through the prison wall and had him led through a small opening to the place where he was to be beheaded.

Saint Peter prayed at the tomb of blessed Mark the evangelist and of his holy successors Anianus, Demetrius, Heraclius, and Theonas. Bending his knees and giving thanks to God who had joined him to his martyrs, he extended his neck to the executioner and was struck down, thus receiving the palm of martyrdom.

The Christians reverently took up his body and buried it at a place called Leucadius, in the cemetery that he himself had built, [Col. 0403B] east of the city of Alexandria.

Whenever he entered the *Thysiasterium* and climbed to the place of the upper pulpit, after praying and giving peace to the people, he saw the splendor of a fire as though coming forth from the seat. At its radiance his mind was carried away into an immense love of the contemplation of God. Considering the virtue of his predecessors, he then humbled himself with such great humility that he never sat upon the more elevated throne where they had sat, but beneath the footstool of their feet.

This most blessed bishop suffered in the time of the emperor Maximus, who carried out in the eastern regions the tenth persecution begun by Diocletian and Maximian. At the same time, many other bishops from Egypt were slaughtered, together with clergy and laity, numbering nearly six hundred and sixty.

A. THE SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF DECEMBER (26 November)

[Note: [Col. 0403D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 2.]

The feast of Saint Linus, pope, who after the apostle Peter was the first to govern the Roman Church, for twelve years, three months, and twelve days. Crowned with martyrdom, he was buried in the Vatican. Paul mentions this Linus in his Letter to Timothy (2 Timothy 4).

[Note: [Col. 0404D] Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 25; Rufinus, chapter 14.]

At Alexandria, Saints Faustus, presbyter, Dius, and Ammonius, martyrs. By order of Maximinus, they were slaughtered together with blessed Peter, bishop of that city.

On the same day, the feast of Blessed Alexander, bishop and martyr, under the emperor Antoninus.

When this blessed bishop was renowned throughout the world for his miracles, a dead man was brought to him one day. The man’s parents, when the holy man urged them to believe in Christ, promised that they would do so if the dead man were raised. Then, after praying, the holy man turned toward the body and said: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, arise.” He immediately rose and began to cry out:

“Listen, parents, and all the people. I was led by two Egyptians, most terrible in appearance and filled with anger, and placed in a very dark place where there was a well. Suddenly, when a certain young man came, flashing with extraordinary brilliance, the whole place trembled, and that most radiant young man exclaimed: ‘Release the boy, because he is being summoned by God’s servant Alexander.’ And behold, I was restored to my body. Now, Lord Alexander, baptize me in the name of your God, so that I may never again see what I saw today.”

His name was Luceius; together with him, 125 others were baptized.

When rumor spread Blessed Alexander’s name everywhere, Antoninus sent the governor Cornelianus to bring Bishop Alexander before him. Cornelianus found him on Sunday in the church, teaching and celebrating the Mass; and, as the emperor had ordered, he arrested him and brought him to Rome. Crescentianus the presbyter, Boniface, and Vitalio followed him.

The governor, with Alexander’s hands bound behind him, presented him to Antoninus. When questioned, Alexander spoke most steadfastly about Christ. Antoninus ordered him to be beaten with clubs and severely scourged, and then confined in prison.

As he was being led there by the soldiers, Antoninus shouted after him: “I grant you a reprieve of four days, so that, having laid aside your vain religion, you may come voluntarily to me.”

The holy martyr Alexander replied: “Consider the four days already past. Fulfill today what you desire.”

After he had been sent to prison, Blessed Crescentianus sat beneath a tree and began to weep; overcome by grief, he fell asleep. An angel of the Lord appeared to him and said:

“I have already been to Alexander, released his bonds, and strengthened him. Now do not sit beneath this tree, lest you be reported to the tyrant.”

Blessed Alexander was therefore brought out of prison and again placed before Antoninus. At the impious man’s command, he was suspended on the rack; burning lamps were placed against his sides, and his body was scraped with hooks.

Then he was taken down from the rack and led to the temple of Apollo. As soon as he entered and prayed, part of the temple, together with Apollo’s statue, collapsed.

Antoninus, however, attributing this event to magical arts, sat in judgment and condemned the holy bishop to the beasts. When none of the beasts touched him, he ordered a fiery furnace to be prepared and the blessed man to be thrown into it. But when the holy martyr, with his hands extended, prayed to the Lord in the middle of the furnace, the entire fire was extinguished so completely that not even a trace of heat remained.

Then Antoninus ordered the holy man to be taken from the furnace and beheaded.

As the soldiers were leading him away, a young man from Antoninus’s staff, named Herculanus, cried out:

“Antoninus, senseless tyrant, why do you persist, blind and deaf? Behold, God’s servant, after your rods, your racks, your lamps, and the touch of your hooks; after the destruction of your temple and idol; after the fury of lions and bears has been overcome; after the furnace fire has been extinguished—he now goes joyfully to be beheaded. Who would doubt that the true God exists, who so strengthens his servants?”

When Antoninus heard this, he said: “Unhappy young man, what has happened to you, that you speak such words?” In anger, he ordered the young man to be seized; after afflicting him with various tortures, he completed his martyrdom by the sword.

As blessed Alexander was being led away, a certain widow met him. The blessed martyr said to her: “Lend me your head-cloth.”

She handed it to him. The officials said to the woman: “You have lost your head-cloth.”

After making the sign of the cross, the blessed martyr stripped off his tunic. Standing in his linen garment, he covered his eyes with the head-cloth; then, kneeling, he received the sword on the Claudian Way, twenty miles from Rome.

An earthquake occurred, and a village and its baths collapsed.

Saint Crescentianus and those who were with him, after the martyr revealed the place to them, took his holy relics and buried them where, while praying, he had extinguished the furnace fire. They placed above him a marble inscription reading:

“Here rests the holy and venerable martyr Alexander, bishop.”

His burial was celebrated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. Later Pope Damasus built him a worthy crypt there and transferred him to it on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, when he also dedicated a feast to him.

The head-cloth that had been lent to him, with which the martyr had covered his eyes, was restored to the woman immediately after he had been beheaded by a certain little boy—undoubtedly an angel. She received it with great astonishment and, confessing that Alexander was truly a martyr, believed in Christ.

### B. Fifth day before the Kalends of December (27 November)

The feast of the holy martyrs Vitalis and Agricola, who, after other tortures, completed their martyrdom by being crucified at Bologna, a city of Italy. Later, when their bodies had been placed among Jewish tombs and were entirely unknown to the Christian people, blessed Ambrose—when the holy martyrs themselves revealed them—found them near the city of Bologna. He built a church there and placed the bodies beneath the altar, amid great rejoicing among the faithful and the punishment of demons, who confessed the merits of the martyrs.

In Gaul, at the city of Riez, the feast of Saint Maximus, bishop [Note: Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 83], who from his earliest age was endowed with the grace of every virtue. First father of the monastery of Lérins, and afterward bishop of the Church of Riez, he became renowned for signs and wonders. Finally, among his other magnificent deeds, while still alive he raised three dead men: one by touching the bier in which he was being carried to the tomb.

### C. Fourth day before the Kalends of December (28 November)

The feast of Saint Sosthenes, a disciple of the apostles (Acts 18; 1 Corinthians 1).

On the same day, Saint Rufus the martyr, whom our Lord Jesus Christ won, together with his entire household, through the martyr Chrysogonus; Diocletian punished Rufus and his whole household and made them martyrs for Christ.

On the same day in Africa, the feast of the holy martyrs Papinius and Mansuetus [Note: Victor of Africa, books II and III], bishops who, during the Vandal persecution under the Arian king Geiseric, were burned over their entire bodies on glowing iron plates for the defense of the Catholic faith and completed their glorious struggle. At that time other holy bishops also—namely Quodvultdeus of Carthage, Valerian, Urban, Crescens, the man called Habetdeum, Eustachius, Crescentianus, Crescenius, Felix, Hortolanus, and Florentianus—were condemned to the harshest exile for the same truth of their preaching and completed the course of their lives in the confession of piety.

### D. Third day before the Kalends of December (29 November)

The vigil of Saint Andrew the apostle.

And at Rome, the feast of Saint Saturninus the martyr, and of Sennis and Sisinnius [Note: Concerning them, see the deeds of Pope Marcellus, 16 January], deacons, under Maximian. He first condemned them, together with other servants of God, to dig sand and construct the Baths of Diocletian.

When one of them, Sisinnius, was brought before Maximian, the emperor asked him his name. He replied: “I, the sinner Sisinnius, servant of the servants of the Lord Jesus Christ.”

After other exchanges, Maximian said to him: “Either sacrifice to the god Hercules, or I shall burn your flesh with fire.”

Sisinnius replied: “I have always desired this—provided that I am worthy—that I may receive the crown I long for.”

He was therefore handed over to the prefect Laodicius and confined for seventeen days. Then Apronianus, the records officer, brought him from prison before Laodicius. Suddenly a light came from heaven, and a voice was heard together with the light:

“Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25).

Then Apronianus, terrified, fell at the feet of the deacon Sisinnius and said: “I adjure you by Christ whom you confess: do not delay in baptizing me, and enable me to reach the crown together with you.”

After he had been baptized, he immediately found the crown of martyrdom through beheading.

Sisinnius was again shut in prison, together with the elderly Saturninus. There they taught and baptized many pagans who came to them. After forty-two days, they were brought out again, bound in chains and barefoot, before the prefect. A tripod was brought so that they might sacrifice.

Then blessed Saturninus said: “May the Lord crush the gods of the nations.”

Immediately the bronze tripod dissolved like mud. Seeing this, two soldiers, Papias and Maurus, believed in Christ. They were seized by Laodicius and, not long afterward, received the crown of martyrdom.

Then Laodicius ordered blessed old Saturninus and Sisinnius to be raised upon the rack, stretched with cords, and beaten with clubs and scourges. Later he ordered burning torches to be applied to their sides; after they had been taken down from the rack, they were led two miles along the Nomentan Way and beheaded.

The most Christian man Thrason, who had supplied much from his own resources to martyrs condemned to prisons and mines, collected their bodies with the presbyter John and buried them on his own small estate along the Salarian Way, on the third day before the Kalends of December.

On the same day at Toulouse, the feast of Saint Saturninus [Note: Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 48], bishop. In the time of Decius, he was seized by pagans in the Capitol of that city because, whenever he appeared before their presence, all their gods became silent and could give no response, as was customary, to those offering sacrifice. A bull had been prepared for the sacrifice; Saturninus was tied to it with ropes. When the bull was goaded more violently, Saturninus was hurled from the summit of the Capitol through all the steps. His head was shattered, his brains scattered, and his entire body torn apart; thus he breathed out a soul worthy of Christ. His sacred body is now venerated with fitting honor in the Church.

### E. The day before the Kalends of December (30 November)

The feast of Saint Andrew the apostle [Note: See the book *On the Feasts of the Apostles*].

On the same day, the feast of Saint Trojan [Note: Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 59], bishop, at Saintes, a man of great virtue and holiness. Though buried in the earth, he shows by many virtues that he lives in heaven.

Litanies are to be proclaimed. December has thirty-one days, while the moon has twenty-nine.

### F. Kalends of December (1 December)

The feast of the holy martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria, who suffered at Rome in the time of Numerian, under the judge Celerinus.

Chrysanthus’s father, Polemius, was an illustrious man, Alexandrian by birth. He united his son to a virgin of elegant beauty, who is known to have come from one of the noblest Roman families. Chrysanthus, having been adequately and faithfully instructed in the divine Scriptures by the blessed presbyter Carpophorus, converted her to the faith of Christ, taught her by his preaching to preserve her virginity for God, and arranged that, although they bore the name of marriage, they should live chastely; he had her baptized.

It happened that through Chrysanthus a multitude of men, and through Daria—for that was her name—countless women flocked to the grace of Christ.

After some time, an uprising arose against them because they were Christians, while Celerinus was prefect of the city. He had both of them arrested and handed over to the tribune Claudius, so that he might kill them by various punishments.

The tribune Claudius gave Chrysanthus to seventy soldiers to torture. They bound him with raw cords, but immediately all the bonds came loose. Then they placed him in a very knotty wooden stock, tightening his leg at its third point; at once the entire wood of the stock dissolved into ashes.

Next they drenched him with the purest human urine, saying: “You will lose your magic by this.” But the stench was changed into a sweet fragrance.

Then they bound him naked in a fresh calfskin and exposed him to the burning sun; but by divine power the skin remained as soft as it had been.

Next, binding his neck, hands, and feet with iron chains, they shut him in a very dark place. Immediately the chains came loose, and such a great light shone there that they thought countless lamps were burning.

The soldiers reported all this to the tribune, who ordered Chrysanthus to be brought before him and beaten with clubs. But when the very stiff rods were brought, they immediately began to soften in the hands of those beating him.

When Claudius saw this, he ordered Chrysanthus to be raised and clothed. He fell at Chrysanthus’s knees and, together with all his soldiers, begged to become a Christian. Why delay? After being instructed, he received the grace of baptism; with him were baptized his wife Hilaria, his two sons Jason (3 December) and Maurus, his friends and household members, and seventy soldiers with all their families.

When the emperor heard of this, he ordered Chrysanthus and Daria to be shut in the Tullian prison, from which a horrible stench rose, since the filth of the houses and the city continually flowed there through the channels of the sewers.

Afterward Daria was placed in a public brothel. But Chrysanthus was given divine light and sweet fragrances. To Daria, however, the Lord’s power granted protection in the form of a lion that escaped from its cage. It entered the cell where God’s holy woman lay prostrate in prayer and lay down beside her, driving away by its strength those who came and wished to enter.

When many, struck by this miracle, began to venerate Christ’s power, the prefect Celerinus ordered a great fire to be lit at the entrance of the cell where blessed Daria was with the lion.

When the lion had already begun to pant and roar, blessed Daria said: “Go out safely, and farewell, because he whom you honored in me is himself setting you free.”

Chrysanthus and Daria were again brought before the prefect Celerinus at the emperor’s command. Chrysanthus was suspended on a huge rack; but immediately all the wood of the rack was shattered, the bonds were broken, and the lamps applied to his sides were extinguished.

The prefect Celerinus was greatly terrified and reported this to the emperor. Attributing it to magic, the emperor ordered them to be led along the Salarian Way to a sandpit, buried alive, and covered with earth and stones.

They suffered on the day of the Kalends of December.

Since God granted many benefits at their venerable memorial, it happened that on the day of their feast an infinite multitude of people gathered there. This was reported to the emperor, who ordered the wall at the entrance of the crypt to be raised. Thus it happened that, while all together received the sacraments of Christ, they celebrated the glory of the martyrs. Among them were the presbyter Diodorus, the deacon Maximianus, and many other clergy.

On the same day, blessed Eligius, bishop of Noyon, glorious for his miracles.

### G. Fourth day before the Nones of December (2 December)

The feast of Saint Viviana [also Biviana], martyr, daughter of the blessed martyrs Faustus and Dafrosa [Note: Concerning her, see the Life of Saint Pimenus, 24 March; concerning them, see the deeds of Chrysanthus and Daria, 25 October]. At the command of the sacrilegious emperor, she was beaten with leaded scourges for so long that she gave up her spirit. By the emperor’s order, her body lay in the forum for two days. At last it was carried away by the presbyter John and buried in the house where her mother and her sister Demetria had already been buried, beside the Licinian palace at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones of December.

### A. Third day before the Nones of December (3 December)

At Tingis, the capital of Mauretania Tingitana, the feast of the glorious martyr Saint Cassianus.

Likewise, the feast of the holy martyrs Claudius the tribune, his wife Hilaria, their sons Jason and Maurus, and seventy soldiers, all of whom believed in Christ through the preaching of blessed Chrysanthus.

When this was reported to the emperor Numerian, he ordered the tribune Claudius, tied to a huge stone, to be thrown into the middle of the sea. He ordered the seventy soldiers and Jason and Maurus, Claudius’s sons, to be punished by sentence of death.

At the place where they were beheaded there was an ancient underground passage. Christians secretly cleaned it out and buried all the bodies together, not far from the city of Rome, along the Salarian Way.

Saint Hilaria, the widow of the martyr Claudius, gathered the bodies of her sons Jason and Maurus. While she was praying continually in service at the confession of the saints, pagans seized her.

As they were dragging her away, she begged them, saying: “I ask you, allow me first to complete my prayer.”

When she had planted her feet, she received the sacrament of the Lord. Then, extending her hands, she threw herself into prayer; while praying, she gave up her spirit.

Those who had seized her, grieving over her sudden death, left her two maidservants who had been with her. They buried her with the greatest care in their gardens and built a very small church over her.

### B. The day before the Nones of December (4 December)

At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Symphronius and Olympius [Note: Concerning them, see the Acts of Pope Stephen, 2 August], in the time of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus.

Valerian had Symphronius, a creditor of blessed Nemesius, brought before him and ordered him handed over to the tribune Olympius, so that Olympius might demand Nemesius’s property from him under examination by torture.

When Symphronius was brought before Olympius and questioned, he replied:

“If you are seeking the property of Nemesius, my lord, I have already handed it over to Christ, since it was his and will remain his. But if you compel me to offer sacrifice, I do sacrifice—but to Christ Jesus, my Lord, I offer a sacrifice of praise and confession, to whom my lord Nemesius also offered himself.”

Then Olympius, filled with anger, had him stretched on the wooden frame and beaten with clubs. Next he ordered a golden statue of Mars, together with its tripod, to be brought. At Symphronius’s words it immediately dissolved.

When Olympius saw this, he began to marvel. He went to his wife Exuperia and told her how Symphronius had melted the statue of Mars in the name of his God.

That same night, Exuperia came with their only son, named Theodulus. They prostrated themselves at Symphronius’s feet, repented, and asked for saving baptism.

Blessed Pope Stephen was summoned and came by night to Olympius’s house. After catechizing him, he baptized Olympius, his wife Exuperia, his son Theodulus, and all who believed in Olympius’s household.

When Valerian and Gallienus heard this, they were inflamed with extreme fury and ordered Symphronius to be brought before them. They sent soldiers, who led him away loaded with iron chains, naked and bridled, together with Olympius, his wife, and his son Theodulus.

Gallienus said to Olympius:

“Until now I have postponed inflicting punishments upon you, though I have no doubt about your conscience: you will certainly not abandon the gods whom you have always worshiped and compelled others to worship. You also persecuted with many tortures, even to the shedding of blood, those who would not consent to sacrifice to our gods.”

Olympius replied:

“I did these things not as Olympius, but as an impious and cruel man. For these crimes I repent and shed bitter tears in the presence of him in whom I believe, the living and true God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, asking that he deign to forgive me the iniquity I committed against the blood of his saints, which I caused to be shed.”

Then sentence was given that they should be consumed by fire.

They were therefore led before the statue of the Sun beside the amphitheater. Stakes were fixed, their hands were bound, and they were tied to them; then fire was set beneath a heap of branches and thorns.

At the very beginning of the fire, they sang their thanks to Christ the Lord and gave up their spirits.

The soldiers left their bodies and departed. Then Saint Stephen the bishop arrived with clergy and religious persons. After the customary hymns had been offered, they took away the bodies of the martyrs Symphronius, Olympius, Exuperia, and Theodulus and buried them beside the Latin Way, one mile from the city, on the seventh day before the Kalends of August.

Later, the blessed bishop Sixtus transferred them and celebrated their solemn feast on the second day before the Nones of December.

### C. Nones of December (5 December)

In Africa, at the city of Thebeste, the feast of Saint Crispina [Note: Augustine, on Psalms 128 and 137; *On Virginity*, chapter 44; Sermon 55 *On the Word of the Lord*, and Sermon 39 *On Various Matters*]. In the time of Diocletian and Maximian, because she refused to sacrifice, she was beheaded at the command of the proconsul Anulinus.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Dalmatius the martyr.

Likewise on that day at Trier, Saint Nicetius, bishop, a man of complete holiness, who lies buried and rests in the basilica of blessed Maximinus the bishop.

### D. Eighth day before the Ides of November (6 December)

Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra in Lycia.

In Africa, the holy Dionysia, Dativa, Leontius, Aemilianus the physician, and the most religious man named Tertius, together with Boniface, Servilius, Victrix, and Majoricus the young man [Note: Victor of Africa, book III]. During the Vandal persecution under the Arian king Hunneric, all of them, for confessing the Catholic faith and refusing to be rebaptized by the Arians, were tortured with the most severe and innumerable punishments and were deemed worthy to be numbered among Christ’s confessors.

Among them, the aforementioned venerable young man Majoricus, strengthened by the exhortations of his mother Dionysia, gave up his spirit in the struggle of confession and completed his palm-bearing course.

### E. Seventh day before the Ides of December (7 December)

At Alexandria, the feast of blessed Agathon the martyr [Note: Eusebius, book VI, chapter 34; Rufinus, chapter 31], under the emperor Decius.

He was a soldier and was present where the most blessed martyrs were being tortured. Among them, Julianus and Eunus, persevering in confessing the Lord Jesus Christ, offered marvelous spectacles of their martyrdom to angels and human beings.

When Agathon prevented certain people from mocking even the dead bodies of the martyrs, the whole crowd suddenly raised a cry against him. The outstanding soldier, now the Lord’s soldier, was brought before the judge. He did not become inferior in any respect but persisted in his confession, and was condemned to death for his devotion.

He suffered on the seventh day before the Ides of December.

At Saintes, blessed Martin [Note: Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 57], abbot and disciple of Saint Martin, bishop of the city of Tours. He rests in peace in the monastery that he himself built. At his tomb, divine miracles occur with great frequency.

### F. Sixth day before the Ides of December (8 December)

At Rome, the feast of Saint Eutychianus [Note: *Pontifical Book*, chapter 28], pope, who ruled the Church for one year and, crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian, was buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He himself also buried 342 martyrs with his own hands in various places.

On the same day at Alexandria, Saint Macarius [Note: Eusebius, book VI, chapter 34; Rufinus, chapter 31], under Decius. He was of Libyan origin. Although the judge tried to persuade him with many words to deny the faith, he professed it with still greater steadfastness and was finally ordered to be burned alive.

### G. Fifth day before the Ides of December (9 December)

The feast of Saint Leocadia, virgin, who in the time of Diocletian and Maximian was subjected to harsh imprisonment at Toledo by Dacian, prefect of Spain. When she saw the severe tortures of blessed Eulalia and the other martyrs whom Dacian was killing, she placed her knees in prayer and gave her undefiled spirit to Christ.

Also on the same day, Cyprian [Note: Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 100], abbot of Périgueux, a man of magnificent holiness and renowned for miracles.

### A. Fourth day before the Ides of December (10 December)

At Emerita, a city of Spain, the feast of Saint Eulalia [Note: Prudentius, hymn 3], virgin.

When she was thirteen years old, she endured many tortures at the command of the governor Dacian. Finally she was suspended on the rack, scraped with hooks, and burning torches were placed against both sides of her. After drawing in the fire, she gave up her spirit; and, in the sight of the Christians, she went up to heaven in the form of a snow-white dove.

By order of the governor, her blessed body hung on the wood for three days. But although human honors had been denied her, heavenly gifts were granted: snow fell from above upon the girl’s body, so that what the fire placed on both sides had consumed in the blaze of its heat might be whitened by divine grace and covered with snowy brightness.

Thus her body was reverently taken away by Christians, placed beneath a sacred altar with due devotion, and made radiant by the glory of miracles.

On the same day, in the aforementioned city, the passion of Saint Julia, who was the virginal companion of Saint Eulalia and remained with her as an inseparable companion and associate when Eulalia hastened toward her passion.

Likewise, at the city of Hispona [also Spoletana], the holy martyrs Carpophorus the presbyter and Abundius the deacon. During the persecution of Diocletian, under the judge Martianus, they were first cruelly beaten in confession of Christ; then they were shut in prison without food or drink. From there they were led out by an angel. After preaching the word of God, they were seized again, and their faces were battered with stones. They were tortured once more on the rack, then tormented for a long time in prison, and finally struck down with the sword.

### B. Third day before the Ides of December (11 December)

Daniel the prophet.

At Rome, Saint Damasus [Note: *Pontifical Book*, chapter 38], pope, who ruled the Church for eighteen years, three months, and two days.

And the feast of the holy martyrs Pontianus, Praetextatus, and Thrason [Note: Concerning them, see the deeds of Pope Marcellus, 16]. Thrason, who was powerful, wealthy, and most Christian, supplied food from his resources to holy martyrs condemned to prisons and mines, through the blessed Sisinnius and Cyriacus, whom blessed Marcellus had ordained deacons for this work. Not long afterward, Thrason himself was seized by Maximinus and joined to the martyrs; with the two others named above, he was deemed worthy to receive the palm of martyrdom.

In Gaul, at the city of Amiens, the feast of the holy martyrs Victoricus and Fuscianus, who adorned their most glorious confession of faith with the blood of their passion.

In Spain, Saint Eutychius, whose deeds are preserved.

### C. The day before the Ides of December (12 December)

The feast of the holy martyrs Hermogenes, Donatus, and twenty-two others [Note: Eusebius, book VI, chapter 34; Rufinus, chapter 31].

At Alexandria, the blessed martyrs Epimachus and Alexander [Note: The same source, in the same place]. They had persevered in the faith for a long time while being tortured in chains and the torments of prison, and were often worn down by separate punishments. Finally they were ordered to be consumed by fire.

On the same day, the feast of the four holy women Ammonaria, Mercuria, Dionysia, and another Ammonaria [Note: Eusebius, book VI, chapter 33; Rufinus, chapter 31; 13 December].

Against the first virgin, Ammonaria, the judge exerted himself with the greatest determination and afflicted her with immense and carefully devised tortures, especially because he wished to overcome her resolve. She had declared in a praiseworthy voice that she would do absolutely none of the things that were unlawfully commanded her. Remaining faithful to her decision, she was finally punished by beheading.

The second, Mercuria, was a venerable old woman and extremely fruitful in children, but she preferred none of them to Christ.

The third, Saint Dionysia, and the fourth, the other Ammonaria, displayed such great steadfastness before the judge that he was ashamed to be defeated by women. They endured unheard-of forms of torture and, when the sword finally prevailed, met the end of all things. They were buried gloriously and reverently at Alexandria.

Blessed Dionysius records this in his book *On the Martyrs*.

### D. Ides of December (13 December)

At Syracuse, a city of Sicily, the feast of Saint Lucia, virgin and martyr, who suffered during the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, under the consular governor Paschasius.

She was a most noble Syracusan. After distributing to the poor, widows, orphans, strangers, and those serving God everything that had remained to her from her parents, she was denounced to the judge Paschasius by her fiancé because she was a Christian. She was compelled to sacrifice to demons on the charge that she lived contrary to the laws of the emperors.

Then blessed Lucia replied to Paschasius:

“The true and undefiled sacrifice before God and the Father is this: to visit widows and orphans in their tribulation” (James 1). “For these three years I have done nothing but sacrifice to the living God; and now, since nothing else remains, I offer myself as a sacrifice to God.”

After this, Paschasius said to her: “Words will cease when we come to blows.”

Lucia replied: “God’s words cannot cease. For he himself said: ‘When you stand before kings and governors, do not consider how or what you will speak’ (Matthew 10). ‘For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit who speaks in you’ (Mark 13).”

Paschasius said again: “Then the Holy Spirit is in you?”

Lucia replied: “The Apostle testifies that those who live chastely and piously are the temple of God, and that the Holy Spirit dwells in them.”

When Paschasius again said: “I shall have you taken to a brothel, so that, once you have been prostituted, the Holy Spirit may flee from you,” the blessed virgin replied:

“The body is never defiled without the consent of the mind (1 Corinthians 3). For even if you place incense in my hand and make me offer sacrifice through my hand, God observes these things and laughs; he judges thoughts and desires. He regards the violator of chastity like a robber, like a barbarian, like a serpent. For if you cause me to be violated against my will, my chastity will be doubled for my crown.”

After this, Paschasius handed her over to pimps, saying: “Invite the crowds to violate her chastity, and let her be abused until word is brought that she is dead.”

But the pimps could not move her at all, even when they came together and pushed her by force, nor when ropes were added [alternative reading: “nor entrances were added”], nor with many pairs of oxen.

Then Paschasius ordered his servants to kindle a great fire around her and throw pitch, resin, and boiling oil over her.

But she stood motionless in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and said:

“I asked my Lord Jesus Christ that this fire might not prevail over me, so that I might mock you, rejoicing in the Lord; and I obtained from him a reprieve in my martyrdom, so that it might remove fear of suffering from believers and take away the voice of mockery from unbelievers.”

At last she was struck with a sword thrust into her throat. She prayed as long as she wished and addressed the surrounding crowd as long as she wished. She did not die at all until priests came and she received Communion of the Lord’s body and blood.

She suffered on the Ides of December and was buried at the place where she was struck; afterward a basilica was built over her body.

Paschasius, however, was taken to Rome because the Sicilians had accused him of plundering the province. He was heard by the entire Senate and received the sentence of death.

### E. Nineteenth day before the Kalends of December (14 December)

At Antioch, the feast of the holy martyrs Drusus, Zosimus, and Theodore [Note: Eusebius, book VI, chapter 34; Rufinus, chapter 31].

At Alexandria, the feast of the holy martyrs Heron, Arsenius, Isidore, and Dioscorus.

After they had been brought before the judge, he first attacked the boy Dioscorus, thinking that because of his age he would be easy to bend—for he was fifteen years old—first with words and then with blows.

When he saw that Dioscorus yielded to him in nothing, he tried to torture him more savagely. Then, after tearing the others apart with various tortures and seeing that they were armed with equal steadfastness of faith, he ordered them to be handed over to the flames.

But the judge admired the boy Dioscorus because he had answered him in every matter with steadfastness and wisdom, and ordered that his punishment be postponed, hoping that at his age he would repent.

But he, illumined by the glory of his confession, was released by divine providence for the consolation of the faithful.

These acts belong to the persecution under Decius.

At Cyprus, the feast of Saint Spyridon [Note: Rufinus, book I, chapter 5], bishop, a man of wondrous blessedness. He was one of those confessors whom Maximian had condemned to the mines after having their right eyes torn out and their left knees cut through. He led a prophetic life and was also renowned for the glory of his signs.

### F. Eighteenth day before the Kalends of January (15 December)

At Africa, the feast of Saint Valerian, bishop and confessor [Note: Victor of Africa, book I].

During the Vandal persecution, when, by order of the Arian king Geiseric, all the priests of the Lord were compelled to surrender the sacred vessels and books, so that the impious Arians even made shirts and undergarments for themselves from the altar cloths, Valerian fought courageously so as not to surrender the divine sacraments. He was ordered to be expelled alone beyond the city, and the command was given that no one should allow him to live even in the countryside.

Although he was more than eighty years old, he lay naked on the public road under the open sky for a long time. Thus, in confessing the Catholic truth and defending holiness, he completed the course of his blessed life.

At Orléans, blessed Maximinus the presbyter, a man of venerable holiness.

### G. Seventeenth day before the Kalends of January (16 December)

The martyrdom of the three holy men Ananias, Azariah, and Misael (Daniel 3).

In Tuscany, the commemoration of Saint Barbara, virgin and martyr, under the emperor Maximian. [Note: [Col. 0415D] Concerning her, see also 4 December.] She was first long afflicted by her father Dioscorus under harsh confinement; then handed over to the governor Martianus, she was stripped, beaten severely with sinews and bullwhips, torn apart, and her wounds were rubbed with rough haircloth. Thereafter she was shut up in prison, where she was comforted by divine light. Soon burning lamps were applied to her sides, her head was beaten with hammers, and her breasts were cut off. Then she was led naked through the streets and tormented for a very long time with scourges. Finally, handed over to the sword, she completed her martyrdom on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January.

A. XVI Kalends of January (17 December)

The translation of Saint Ignatius, bishop and martyr, who, third after the blessed apostle Peter, governed the Church of Antioch. [Note: [Col. 0415D] A fuller account of him is given on 1 February.]

Likewise on the same day, of blessed Lazarus, whom the Lord Jesus is read in the Gospel (John XI) to have raised from the dead; likewise of blessed Martha, his sister. Their venerable memory is preserved by a church built not far from Bethany, where their house was nearby.

In the East, at the city of Eleutheropolis, fifty holy martyrs who suffered under the Saracens.

B. XV Kalends of January (18 December)

[Col. 0416A]

The commemoration of the blessed martyrs Rufus and Zosimus, who were among those first disciples through whom the primitive Church was founded among Jews and Greeks. [Note: [Col. 0415D] See the little book on the Feasts of the Apostles.] They rest at Philippi, the city of the Macedonians.

In Africa, the commemoration of Saint Moysetes, martyr.

At Tours, Saint Gratian, bishop, who was sent from the city of Rome as the first bishop to that city, was renowned for many miracles, and rests there in peace.

C. XIV Kalends of January (19 December)

In Egypt, the commemoration of blessed Nemesius, martyr. [Note: [Col. 0416D] Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 34; Rufinus, 31.] He was first brought before the judge Aemilianus by false accusation as though he were a robber. [Col. 0416B] Having been acquitted of that charge, he was afterward denounced as a Christian. In this matter the judge showed no moderation, but, after torturing him with doubled punishments, ordered him to be burned with the robbers, unaware that by his cruelty he had granted the excellent martyr a likeness to the Savior, who for the salvation of the human race endured the cross together with robbers (Isaiah LIII; John XIX).

At Orléans, Saint Avitus, abbot, who was illustrious in the spirit of prophecy and was honorably buried in that same city. [Note: [Col. 0416D] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 99, 20 December; Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 34; Rufinus, 31.]

D. XIII Kalends of January (20 December)

The commemoration of the most blessed martyrs Ammon, Zeno, Ptolemy, Ingenus, and Theophilus. [Col. 0416C] While they were standing before the tribunals at Alexandria, a certain Christian was being tortured by the judge and was already almost inclining toward denial. They were inwardly agitated and tried, by their faces, eyes, and gestures, as though to raise up the man who was trembling under the punishments. At times they even extended their hands; and, by the movements and posture of their whole bodies, inclining in different ways, they seemed eager to lift up the spirit of the one who was falling. When everyone turned toward them and recognized from their movements what they were professing about themselves, before the crowd could attack them with shouts, they themselves rushed into the midst and declared that they were Christians. In their victory Christ most gloriously triumphed over the ancient enemy of the human race; and, in turn, from their confidence he gave fear to the persecutors and steadfastness of spirit to his own. [Col. 0416D]

E. XII Kalends of January (21 December)

At Edessa, a city of Mesopotamia, the commemoration of Saint Thomas the Apostle. [Note: [Col. 0416D] Rufinus, 31. See the book on the Feasts of the Apostles; Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 66.]

At Châlons, Saint Memmius, the first bishop sent to that city from Rome. Among other miracles, he raised a dead man; his tomb is now glorified by very frequent miracles.

[Col. 0417A] Likewise in Tuscany, the commemoration of Saints John and Festus.

F. XI Kalends of January (22 December)

At Rome, on the Lavican Way between the Two Laurels, the commemoration of thirty martyrs, all of whom were crowned on one day during the persecution of Diocletian.

[Note: [Col. 0417D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 34; Rufinus, 31; Eusebius, same work.]

[Note: [Col. 0417D] “The Lavican Way between the Two Laurels.” This was the name of a place at Rome, the Lavican Way, made famous by the martyrdom of many saints. The Roman Martyrology also commemorates it on this day. Anastasius the Librarian, *Lives of the Popes*, chapter 34, under Sylvester, in *On Constantine’s Munificence*: “He built a basilica on the Lavican Way between the Two Laurels, to the blessed martyrs Peter and Marcellinus, and a mausoleum where he placed his most blessed mother in a porphyry sarcophagus.” Thus it appears in the Bertinian manuscript. Ado of Vienne, in his *Chronicle*, around the year of Christ 306: “He built a basilica on the Lavican Way between the Two Laurels to the blessed martyrs Peter [Col. 0418D] and Marcellinus, and a mausoleum where he placed his mother in a purple sarcophagus.” Meursius, in his Greek-Barbarian Glossary, changed *lauros* into *lauras* in these last two passages, but it will now easily be clear that nothing should be changed. There is also another place called the Latin Way, mentioned by Ado above under 9 September, to which Saint Gorgonius was transferred and placed on the Latin Way between the Two Laurels, unless the passage is corrupt and *Lavican* should be read, as the Roman Breviary has it on 9 September in the lesson on Saint Gorgonius. Nevertheless, Ado’s manuscripts agree with his published reading.]

At Alexandria, the commemoration of blessed Ischyrion, martyr. For while he was administering the property of a certain powerful man for payment, that man ordered him to sacrifice to idols. When he refused, he was compelled by insults to sacrifice to idols; when he persisted, he was again coaxed with blandishments. But when he despised both, he was pierced with great force through the middle of his entrails by a sharpened stake and handed over to death.

[Col. 0417B] On the same day, of very many other martyrs who, wandering through the deserts and mountains of Egypt, were consumed by hunger, thirst, cold, sickness, robbers, and wild beasts. All of them, imitating God’s chosen prophets, were crowned with the glory of martyrdom. Among them was the venerable old man Chaeremon—he was bishop of the Egyptian city called Nilopolis. When he withdrew to the Arabian mountain together with his very old wife, he was seen by no one thereafter.

G. X Kalends of January (23 December)

At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Victoria, virgin and martyr, during the persecution of the emperor Decius. She had been betrothed to a pagan man named Eugenius. At the request of Titus Aurelius, who had a virgin bride named Anatolia, she went to persuade Anatolia to marry him. She said to her:

“Listen to me, Lady Sister Anatolia. I too am a Christian, and I know that God does not condemn marriage. The prophets and patriarchs had wives, and their descendants were blessed by God.
