Therefore listen to me now, and accept a husband who will not betray the fact that you are a Christian; rather, through marital favor it will happen that he himself will consent to Christianity.”

When Victoria had said this, the virgin Anatolia replied:

“O Victoria, conquer the devil and be a true victory. When the whole earth was empty, God said to human beings: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.’ Now the earth is full. After the Son of God descended from heaven, he cries out daily: ‘Increase in faith, multiply in charity, and fill the heavens,’ because the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

Again, among other things and after other words, Saint Anatolia added:

“On the day when I distributed the value of my ornaments [Col. 0418A] among Christ’s poor, I saw in a vision a young man crowned with gold, splendid in purple and jewel-studded garments. Looking at me with a gracious face and joyful expression, he said: ‘O virginity, which is not conquered by death, which frees from everlasting death! O virginity, which is occupied not with works of darkness but always with light!’ Hearing this, I awoke and began to weep. Throwing myself upon the pavement, I begged the Lord that the one who had spoken such sweet words to me might continue them again.

“As I prayed and lay prostrate, the same one who had spoken before continued to say to me: ‘Virginity is royal purple; whoever puts it on becomes more eminent than the rest. Virginity is a precious jewel. Virginity is the king’s immeasurable treasure. Thieves lie in wait for it. When you awaken, guard it carefully; and the more you recognize that you possess it, guard it the more earnestly, lest you lose it.’”

Moved by these and similar words and deeds, Victoria herself sold all the value of her ornaments to the poor. Thus it happened that, through the efforts of their fiancés Aurelius and Eugenius, because Christ’s virgins refused to marry them, they were expelled from the city of Rome by the emperor Decius and taken to the estates of their fiancés. There they were so afflicted by hunger and starvation that scarcely a little coarse bread was given them toward evening. Their fiancés could in no way induce them either to incline toward marriage or to sacrifice.

Blessed Victoria, therefore, persisting invincibly in her purpose of virginity, after performing many miracles—including bringing many virgins to the Lord—was struck in the heart with a sword by the executioner Taliarchus. At the request of her fiancé Eugenius, Julian, chief priest of the Capitol and overseer of the temples, had sent him for this task. She suffered on the tenth day before the Kalends of January. Her body was treated with every reverence. Taliarchus, her executioner, however, became a leper and, consumed by worms within six days, died.

At Nicomedia, twenty holy martyrs whom the persecution of Diocletian, after subjecting them to the most grievous tortures, made martyrs for Christ and joined to the blessed number of the saints in heaven. [Note: [Col. 0418D] Concerning these, Eusebius, Book VIII, chapter 5; chapter 5 of the Fourth Dialogue, chapter 41; and Homily 15 on the Gospels.]

Likewise at Rome, blessed Servulus, concerning whom blessed Gregory writes. Poor in worldly goods but rich in merits, he had been weakened by a long illness; for from his earliest age until the end of his life he lay paralyzed. He was unable not only to stand, but even ever to rise from his bed or sit up. He could never bring his hand to his mouth or turn himself onto his other side. Whatever he was able to receive from alms he distributed to the poor. He did not know letters, but he bought copies of the sacred Scriptures for himself; and, receiving religious people as guests, he continually made them read these books before him. Thus it happened that, insofar as his capacity allowed, he learned the sacred Scriptures completely. He made it his practice, even amid pain, always to give thanks and to devote himself day and night to the hymns and praises of God. Glorified by a most blessed end, he was buried in the church of Saint Clement, bishop and martyr, where miracles very frequently occur at his tomb to commend his holiness.

For the remaining days of this month, see the beginning of Ado’s Martyrology.

[Col. 0419]

## ADO’S PRAYER

[Col. 0419A]

Christ, I beg you, in your gentleness grant pardon to your sluggish servant;

I am slow, but no one comes to you too late.

Long error has held us through the years that have passed;

Let this punishment, I beg, suffice for my merits.

[Col. 0419B]

A short life remains, and age is already more inclined toward death;

Now, as an old man, I cannot sin—and I do not wish to, since I am yours.

By the outstanding merits and blessed prayers of the saints,

[Col. 0420A]

Whose perpetual triumphs this book commemorates,

Grant, almighty Father, pardon; grant, Christ, healing,

To those who with supplicant vows and faithful mind

Entrust themselves through the ages to such great patrons,

[Col. 0420B]

Who, after conquering the devil, conspicuous beneath the stars with shining crowns,

Obtain from you whatever they ask.

[Col. 0419]

## APPENDIX TO THE MARTYROLOGY OF SAINT ADO

### FRIENDLY READER,

[Col. 0419C]

In this Appendix you have material that has hitherto been inserted into Ado’s Martyrology, although it comes from another hand. In particular, those items marked with asterisks were judged not to belong to Ado even by the judgment of Jacob Mosander, who was the first to publish Ado. He explains their status to the reader in these words:

“We transcribed this Martyrology in our own hand from four very ancient manuscript books that correspond with one another. The fourth, however, written by a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, contained the names of several saints not found in the other three. Since we were uncertain whether these belonged to Ado or had rather been added to his Martyrology by that monk, following the advice of learned men we marked those same saints beforehand with a star (*), in order to avoid every error and scruple.” Thus far Mosander.

But by collating three manuscript books older than Mosander’s copies—of which I spoke at the beginning of Ado’s “To the Reader”—I discovered that considerably more material does not belong to Ado. I have also placed these items in the Appendix, though without the sign of the asterisk, so that it may be clear which passages, by the agreement of our judgment and Mosander’s, should be removed from Ado, and which others are excluded by the evidence of the three manuscripts I have mentioned.

## THE MONTH OF JANUARY

[Col. 0419C]

[Col. 0419D]

Kalends of January (1 January).—* On the same day, of Saint Paragoda, most holy, seventh bishop of Vienne.

IV Nones of January (2 January).—* Likewise of Saint Isidore, bishop and martyr.

III Nones of January (3 January).—Likewise the octave of Saint John the Evangelist.

II Nones of January (4 January).—Likewise the octave of the Innocents.

Ides of January (13 January).—The octave of the Epiphany.

* At Trier, Saint Agritius, bishop and confessor.

* At Rheims, the burial of Saint Remigius, bishop.

XVIII Kalends of February (15 January).—* Likewise of Maurus, abbot and disciple of blessed Benedict.

XVII Kalends of February (16 January).—In the entry on Marcellus, after “Priscilla,” the published Ado adds:

“He made cemeteries on the Salarian Way and established twenty-five titular churches in the city of Rome, for the baptism and penance of many who were converted from paganism, and for the burials of martyrs.” [Note: [Col. 0419D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 31.]

[Col. 0420D]

XV Kalends of February (18 January).—And the passion of the holy martyrs Thyrsus, Leucius, and Galericus [read: Callinicus]. [Note: [Col. 0419D] Concerning these, Ado, 28 January.]

XIV Kalends of February (19 January).—At Jerusalem, Martha and Mary, sisters of Lazarus.

XIII Kalends of February (20 January).—In the entry on Fabian, after “was buried,” the published Ado adds:

“He divided the regions among deacons and made seven subdeacons to oversee the seven notaries, so that they might collect the acts of the martyrs in full. During his time Novatus arrived from Africa and separated Novatian from the Church, after Moses the Confessor had died in prison; he had been there eleven months.” [Note: [Col. 0420D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 21.]

XI Kalends of February (22 January).—On the same day in Gaul, at the city of Embrun, the holy martyrs Vincent, Orontius, and Victor. [Note: [Col. 0420D] Ado, in the little book on the Feasts of the Apostles, 22 March.]

[Col. 0421A]

* Likewise the commemoration of Saint Paul, whom the blessed Apostle ordained and sent as bishop to the city of Narbonne. They relate that he was the same Sergius Paulus, the prudent proconsul, who from the time when the Apostle had brought him under Christ’s faith received the name Paul. When he was sent by the same Apostle to Spain for the sake of preaching, he was left in the aforesaid city of Narbonne. Having diligently fulfilled his preaching ministry, he was buried, crowned with glory and miracles.

X Kalends of February (23 January).—* [Note: [Col. 0421D] Ado, in the same work.] Elsewhere, the passion of the holy martyrs Eugenius, Macarius, and Perulvius.

VII Kalends of February (26 January).—In the entry on Polycarp, after “they were brought to completion,” the published Ado added:

“Then Germanicus also, a distinguished athlete of Christ, was transferred through the glorious contest of martyrdom. For when the judge had condemned him to the beasts, he voluntarily challenged the beast prepared for him, plainly scorning temporal death and desiring to attain the crown of eternal life by a swift end. The same blessed Polycarp wrote to the Philippians a very useful letter, which is read to this day in the assembly of Asia.” [Col. 0421B]

[Note: [Col. 0421D] Ado in the Martyrology, 17 January.] Likewise at the city of Bourges, blessed Sulpitius, bishop and confessor, whose life and death are commended by glorious miracles.

III Kalends of February (30 January)

Likewise the commemoration of Saint Aldegund, virgin.

## THE MONTH OF FEBRUARY

IV Nones of February (2 February).—At Orléans, the burial of Saint Flosculus, bishop, and of Saint Sicharia, a virgin consecrated to God, in the same place.

III Nones of February (3 February).—* At Hamburg, Saint Ansgar, bishop and confessor, first bishop of Hamburg and archbishop of Bremen.

* At Vienne, Saint Eventius, bishop and confessor.

VIII Ides of February (6 February).—* Likewise on the same day, of Vedastus and Amandus, bishops and confessors.

[Col. 0421C]

VI Ides of February (8 February).—Likewise the burial of Saint Helena, queen.

IV Ides of February (10 February).—* Likewise of Scholastica, virgin, sister of Saint Benedict the abbot (21 March), who saw her soul enter heaven in the form of a dove. [Note: [Col. 0421D] Concerning her, in the Life of Saint Benedict.]

III Ides of February (11 February).—* At Lyon, the commemoration of Saint Desiderius, bishop and martyr. This blessed man did indeed suffer at Prisciniacum, a village in the territory of Lyon, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June; but he was transferred to Vienne, the city of his episcopate, on the third day before the Ides of February.

Ides of February (13 February).—The commemoration of Pope Gregory II. [Note: [Col. 0422D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 90.] He governed the Church for sixteen years, during the reign of Leo Constantine. This man was chaste and learned in the divine Scriptures. Through the bishop Boniface he preached the word of salvation in Germany. During Lent he established that on Thursday the fast and the celebration of Mass should take place, something that had not previously been done.

[Col. 0421D]

XV Kalends of March (15 February).—Likewise of blessed Severus, priest and confessor, whom blessed Gregory mentions in the *Dialogues* (last chapter).

At Brescia, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Faustinus and Jovita. They were born of noble stock in the city of Brescia; their parents had been heads of the senate in that city. By order of the emperor Hadrian, they were arrested in the aforesaid city by an Italian count of Rhaetia and thrown into prison.

Afterward, by Hadrian’s order, following many and various tortures, they were handed over to be torn apart by the most savage beasts—lions, leopards, bears, and exceedingly fierce bulls. But the beasts themselves, the Lord calming them, were changed into gentleness toward the saints of God like lambs, so that, prostrating themselves at their feet, they licked their footprints, while attacking and killing the enemies of God together with the Italian count.

Finally, they were bound to the rack and thrown into the fire, and placed over a bronze cauldron in which lead was melted here and there. But that fire did no harm to the saints of God; rather, it struck down all whom it could reach, together with Pompeius, Hadrian’s brother. When Saint Calocerus, who at that time was in charge of the palace, saw this, he believed, together with twelve thousand men. Therefore Hadrian, enraged against all of them except Calocerus, ordered their heads to be cut off.

Then, at the prompting of the holy angels, blessed Apollonius, bishop of the Church of Brescia, ordained Saint Faustinus a priest and blessed Jovita a deacon.

After this, by Hadrian’s order, blessed Faustinus and Jovita, together with Saint Calocerus, were bound in chains and taken to Milan. In that city Hadrian ordered boiling, molten lead to be poured through tubes into the mouths of all three [Col. 0422B]; but it did no harm to the saints of God. Moreover, he ordered the eyes of the blessed Faustinus and Jovita to be torn out; but on the following day the Lord deigned to restore their eyes to them.

Then the three were handed over to the fiercest beasts—tigers, bears, and exceedingly fierce bulls. But the beasts, as before, through the Lord’s working, were changed into gentleness toward the saints of God, while they killed a very great multitude of pagans.

After these and other tortures, Hadrian ordered a certain Sapricius, first officer of the school of candidates, to take blessed Calocerus to the city of Ambinganum and punish him there if he did not obey his commands. There, after many tortures, he became Christ’s martyr through the cutting off of his head and rested for a long time, although afterward Angilbert, archbishop of Milan, transferred him from there and took the greatest care to place him with honor in a monastery of his own diocese called Clavate.

As blessed Calocerus was being taken into custody to Ambinganum, he came to the city of Asti and there found a distinguished man of that city named Secundus. When he preached Christ to Secundus and told him much about the blessed Faustinus and Jovita—how they had suffered greatly at Milan for Christ’s name and were being held in chains—Secundus believed. With great haste he went to Milan, was baptized by Saints Faustinus and Jovita, and returned to his own city. There he was beheaded by the aforementioned Sapricius and became Christ’s martyr.

After this, the holy martyrs Faustinus and Jovita were taken to Rome in custody under a certain governor named Antiochus. There they were afflicted with various punishments and converted many to the faith, while the Lord performed very many miracles through them.

There they also found Saint Evaristus, bishop of the city of Rome, hiding among the tombs of the martyrs. They asked him to make blessed Calimerus—who, through their preaching, had believed together with many Romans—bishop in the city of Milan. After this had been done, they were again taken under the custody of the count Aurelianus to Naples [Col. 0422D]. There they endured many and varied tortures and, with the Lord’s help, converted many to the faith by displaying very many miracles.

Afterward, bound hand and foot, they were thrown into the sea, but were freed by God’s angels and brought to shore. Finally, by order of the emperor Hadrian, they were brought back to Brescia and there, after once again enduring many tortures, had their heads cut off by the aforesaid Aurelianus and became martyrs of Christ.

XII Kalends of March (18 February).— [Note: [Col. 0422D] Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book I, chapter 27.] In the entry on Simeon, after “was,” the published Ado adds:

“It is nevertheless established that Cleopas, whose son he was, was the brother of Joseph.”

XI Kalends of March (19 February).—Likewise Saint Theodore, martyr, brother of Saint George.

## THE MONTH OF MARCH

[Col. 0423A]

Kalends of March (1 March).—+ On the same day, Suvitbert, bishop and confessor.

VI Nones of March (2 March).—At Rome, Pope Simplicius, who sat for fifteen years. [Note: [Col. 0423D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 48.] He condemned Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, and Peter, bishop of Alexandria, as Eutychians.

IV Ides of March (12 March).—+ At Rome, the burial of Saint Gregory, pope. [Note: [Col. 0423D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 65.] He was born of noble family and educated in the liberal arts. After his parents had died, he built six monasteries in Sicily and established a seventh within the walls of the City. There, after putting aside secular dress and gathering many brothers under the authority of an abbot, he served vigorously and exalted the line of his nobility by his conduct and adorned it with upright deeds.

For the man who had previously been accustomed to go through the City in a senatorial robe, glittering with silken garments and shining jewels, afterward, covered with a cheap garment, served as a poor man among the poor. To these monasteries he assigned from the revenues of his estates only as much as could suffice for the daily sustenance of those living there; he sold the rest and distributed it to the poor.

Then, compelled and much resisting, he became supreme pontiff of the city of Rome. He converted the English people to the faith by sending monks from his monastery—Mellitus, Augustine, and John—and many other brothers with them.

He governed the Roman Church most gloriously for thirteen years, six months, and ten days. He also added to the prayer of the canon: “And dispose our days in your peace,” and so forth.

Likewise at Rome, Pope Innocent, who governed the Church for fifteen years, two months, and twenty-one days. [Note: [Col. 0423D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 42.] He issued a decree concerning the Church and condemned Pelagius and Caelestius as heretics. He established that whoever had been born should be reborn through baptism as a Christian, which Pelagius condemned.

+ In Africa, John and forty-four others.

[Col. 0423C]

+ At Rome, the burial of Saints Innocent and Rasi, bishops.

The day before the Ides of March (14 March).—On the same day, Pope Zacharias, who sat at Rome for ten years. [Note: [Col. 0423D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 93.] In the patriarchium of the blessed martyr George he found the head of Saint George hidden in a box. In it he also found a *pittacium* [Note: [Col. 0423D] In it he likewise found a *pittacium*. Because this was poorly understood by the editor, he substituted *epitaphium*; but the author wrote *pittacium*, as the manuscripts show. The glossaries give Greek *πιττάκιον*, *pittacium*, “a brief document.” Isidore’s Glossary: “*Pictatium*, a short and small letter. *Pictatiuncula*, a piece of parchment.” Lampridius uses the word in his *Alexander*: “He also made notes for himself concerning the promotion of soldiers and read through all the *pittacia*.” It also occurs in Cassiodorus, *Celsus*, Book III, chapter 10: “Then to have two *pittacia*, equal in breadth to the forehead and in length as well.” I do not accumulate more examples; these suffice to clarify the matter.] written in Greek letters. He was buried in the church of Saint Peter the Apostle.

XVII Kalends of April (16 March).—+ On the same day, Saint Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, glorious in life and miracles, resting in the monastery at Deutz.

XIV Kalends of April (19 March).—+ Likewise on the same day, Saint Joseph, foster-father of the Lord.

XIII Kalends of April (20 March).—+ Likewise the commemoration of Saint Archippus, fellow soldier of blessed Paul the Apostle.

XI Kalends of April (22 March).—Likewise the holy virgin sisters Herlinda and Relinda.

X Kalends of April (23 March).—At Antioch, Saint Theodore, priest and martyr.

VIII Kalends of April (25 March).—At Jerusalem, our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified.

And in the same city, the passion of Saint James the Apostle, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XIII).

[Col. 0424A]

On the same day, the sacrifice of Isaac and the passage of the children of Israel through the Red Sea.

And the victory of the archangel Michael over the dragon.

VII Kalends of April (26 March).—+ On the same day, the burial of Saint Liudger, bishop.

VI Kalends of April (27 March).—Likewise at Jerusalem, the Resurrection of the Lord.

III Kalends of April (30 March).—* At the city of Aurelia, the burial of Saint Pastor, bishop.

## THE MONTH OF APRIL

VIII Ides of April (6 April).—In the entry on Sixtus, after “of the emperor,” the published Ado adds:

“He established that the sacred mysteries should be handled only by sacred ministers; and that any bishop who had been summoned to the apostolic see, on returning to his parish, should not be received unless he brought the people letters of greeting—that is, *formatae*—from the apostolic see. He also established that during the celebration of Mass the words ‘Holy, holy, holy’ should be sung three times.” [Note: [Col. 0424D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 8.]

VII Ides of April (7 April).—Likewise Pope Celestine, who governed the Church for eight years. [Note: [Col. 0424D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 44, where it is said that he died on the eighth day before the Ides of April.] He established that the 150 psalms of David should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice; for previously only the Epistle and the holy Gospel were read.

V Ides of April (9 April).—+ Likewise the five virgins, whose names God knows.

And Mary of Egypt.

IV Ides of April (10 April).—+ Likewise at Antioch, Saint Theodore, priest.

III Ides of April (11 April).—+ On the same day at Rome, blessed Pope Leo. [Note: [Col. 0424D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 46.]

The day before the Ides of April (12 April).—In the entry on Julius, after “returned,” the published Ado adds:

“He established that no cleric should conduct any case in public except in the Church; that an account of the faith should be collected by notaries; and that securities, instruments, donations, exchanges, transfers, wills, pleadings, or manumissions should be carried out by clerics in the Church.” [Note: [Col. 0424D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 36.]

Ides of April (13 April).—+ Likewise Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr.

XVI Kalends of May (16 April).—* In Mauretania, the commemoration of Basilla.

Likewise Saint Anicetus, pope, who sat in the episcopate for eleven years and was crowned with martyrdom during the reigns of Severus and Marcus; he was buried in the cemetery of Callistus. [Note: [Col. 0424D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 11.] He established, according to the Apostle’s command (1 Corinthians XI), that the clergy should not grow their hair long.

+ On the same day, the dedication of the oratory of Saint Gangulphus, martyr.

XIII Kalends of May (19 April).—+ On the same day, the burial of Saint Baldric, bishop.

X Kalends of May (20 April).—In the entry on Victor, after “is crowned,” the editions hitherto add:

“He established that holy Easter should be celebrated on Sunday and observed from the fifteenth moon of the first month through the twenty-first; and he established that, when necessity required, whether in a river, in the sea, or in springs, any people coming from paganism should be baptized under the Christian confession.” [Note: [Col. 0424D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 15.]

[Col. 0425A]

XI Kalends of May (21 April).—+ At Rome, in the cemetery on the Appian Way: Saints Valerian, Maximus, and Tiburtius.

+ In Campania, the commemoration of Saint Amphelicus.

At Rome, Saint Soter, pope, who sat in the episcopate for nine years and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus. [Note: [Col. 0425D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 13.] He established that no nun should touch the sacred pallium in church or place incense.

X Kalends of May (22 April).—In the African city of Hierapolis, the commemoration of Saint Philip the Apostle.

In the entry on Caius, after “the March,” the published Ado adds:

“This Caius established that, if anyone deserved to become a bishop, he should first ascend through all the grades: he should be doorkeeper, lector, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, and priest.” [Note: [Col. 0425D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 29.]

On the same day at Rome, Saint Agapetus, pontiff, who sat for eleven months. [Note: [Col. 0425D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 58.] When he entered Constantinople to visit the emperor Justinian, he deposed Anthimus, bishop of Constantinople, who denied two natures in Christ, and consecrated the Catholic Mena in his place.

[Col. 0425B]

IX Kalends of May (23 April).—+ On the same day, the passion of Saint Adalbert, bishop and martyr.

+ Likewise on the same day, Saint Pysinna, virgin.

VIII Kalends of May (24 April).—In Babylonia, the great city, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—who, with their names changed, were also called Ananias, Azarias, and Misael—were delivered from the furnace of blazing fire.

VI Kalends of May (26 April).—+ Likewise at Rome, Saint Tindemialis, bishop and confessor.

V Kalends of May (27 April).—In the entry on Anastasius, after “ten,” the published Ado adds:

“He established that whenever the holy Gospels were read, priests should not sit but stand bowed forward; and he established that a man from overseas should not be admitted into the clergy unless he were designated by the votes of five bishops.” [Note: [Col. 0425D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 48.]

The day before the Kalends of May (30 April).—+ At Rome, Saint Quirinus, tribune and martyr, concerning whom see above, on the third day before the Kalends of April.

+ Likewise Saint Sophia, virgin.

## THE MONTH OF MAY

[Col. 0425C]

Kalends of May (1 May).—* At the city of Auxerre, the burial of Saint Amator, bishop.

+ At Toulouse, the commemoration of Saint Orientius, bishop.

Likewise the burial of Saint Justin, at the city of Begorra.

+ On the same day, Saint Walburga, virgin.

IV Nones of May (4 May).—+ On the same day, the memorial of the most blessed Justus, bishop of Vienne.

The day before the Nones of May (6 May).—+ In a city of Galatia, the commemoration of blessed Gerontius, confessor.

Nones of May (7 May).—+ Likewise Pope Benedict, who sat at Rome for ten months during the reign of Constantine. [Note: [Col. 0425D] *Pontifical Book*, chapter 82; this is Benedict II.] From his earliest age he served in the Church, always a lover of poverty; he was buried near Saint Peter.

VIII Ides of May (8 May).—On Mount Gargano, the apparition of Saint Michael the Archangel, when the arrow, as though twisted back by a gust of wind, struck the one who had shot it; and it was said to the bishop:

“I am Michael the archangel, who always stand in the presence of God.” [Note: [Col. 0425D] More fully in Ado’s Martyrology, 29 September.]

VII Ides of May (9 May).— [Note: [Col. 0426D] Added from manuscript E.] On the same day, Saint Dionysius, bishop of Vienne, a man most distinguished in doctrine.

V Ides of May (11 May).— [Note: [Col. 0426D] Added from manuscript E.] On the same day, blessed Gangulphus, martyr, whose deeds are preserved.

The day before the Ides of May (14 May).—+ At Milan, Victor, Camorus, Felix, and Rusticus, four hundred and four holy martyrs who suffered together with Saint Cyricus.

XVII Kalends of June (16 May).—+ At Troyes, the burial of Fidolius (*) the priest [others: bishop], and fellow brother of Brendan the abbot.

XIII Kalends of June (20 May).—Likewise the passion of Saint Saturnina, virgin.

XII Kalends of June (21 May).—+ At Auxerre, the burial of blessed Valis, priest and confessor, and Valens, martyr.

### 22 May — Eleventh day before the Kalends of June

The birthday of Saint Julia, who, when the city of Carthage had been captured, was led away as a captive and fell by lot into the slavery of a certain Euchius, a citizen of Syria Palestina. Serving him diligently, when her service was completed and she had obtained leisure, she devoted herself either to prayer or to reading; for she also afflicted her body with fasts. Hence, although her master was a pagan, he greatly admired her and often urged her not to torment herself in this way. But neither by blandishments nor even by admonitions could she be turned away from what she had begun, except on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection.

Then it happened that her master came with her to Corsica, and there, while the others were sacrificing, he himself also began to offer sacrifice to the gods. [Col. 0426B] But blessed Julia, seeing their error, grieved. When a certain prince, Felix by name and a Saxon, heard that she refused to sacrifice, he asked her of her master, promising to give him four maidservants in her place. But, because of the great value he placed on her service, he refused to surrender her.

Then the aforesaid Felix craftily prepared a banquet for her master, so that, when the man had been overcome by excessive drinking and was unaware of what was happening, Felix might take her from his ship. And so it was done. While her master knew nothing of it, blessed Julia was brought before Felix. When Felix could not persuade her by blandishments to sacrifice, he ordered her to be struck on the face, then to be twisted by the hair and scourged, and finally even to be crucified; and thus, on the very cross, she breathed forth her last breath. From her most holy mouth a dove came forth and rose toward heaven.

Then, by angels and through the dispensation of divine grace, this was announced to certain monks living on the island of Margarita, which is now commonly called Gorgona. When they heard it, they boarded ships and came with the greatest haste to [Col. 0426C] Corsica, and found everything just as it had been revealed to them by the angels. Then, with the greatest reverence, they took her body down from the cross and, with the Lord’s help, quickly returned to their own place. There, on the island of Margarita itself, they embalmed her body with spices and joyfully placed it in a tomb.

Later, Anza, queen and wife of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, ordered her body to be brought from that island and placed with the greatest magnificence in the monastery which she had built in her honor at Brescia.

At Rome, the birthday of Saints Faustinus and Timothy, and of others.

+ At Auxerre, the burial and translation of Saint Helena, virgin.

+ At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the birthday of Saint Polyeuctus.

### 23 May — Tenth day before the Kalends of June

At Vienne, the birthday of Saint Desiderius, bishop [Note: [Col. 0426D] Ado, in the *Chronicle*, year 583. It was in manuscript S., in the margin.], who suffered in the territory of Lyon, in the village of Prisciniacum, on the river Chalaron; his life shone forth, full of miracles, and he is honored by burial in the Church of Vienne.

At Rome, Saint Silverius, pope [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Pontifical*, chapter 6], who sat for one year. With the consent of the emperor Justinian, he was deposed by the patrician Belisarius, became a monk, and died in exile as a confessor.

### 28 June — Fourth day before the Kalends of July

In the entry for Leo, after “pope,” the commonly circulated text adds:

“He sat at Rome for ten months [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Pontifical*, chapter 81. He is Leo II. It was in the manuscript]. He was most eloquent, sufficiently instructed in the divine Scriptures, and learned in the Greek and Latin languages. He translated from Greek into Latin the holy sixth synod, which was held in the imperial city, where Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius [omitted in the commonly circulated text], Pyrrhus, Paul, Peter, Macarius, Stephen, and the new Simon Polychronius were condemned—those who preached one will and one operation in the Lord Jesus Christ. He decreed that whoever had been ordained archbishop should not, by any custom, be required to pay anything for the use of the pallium in the various offices. [Col. 0427C] [Note: [Col. 0427D] These words concern Leo I, from the *Pontifical*, chapter 46.] When he was expounding the Catholic faith with many bishops, he condemned the Eutychian and Nestorian heresies, and through his diligence caused the most holy Council of Chalcedon to be assembled. He decreed [the commonly circulated text adds: ‘that within the action the holy Sacrifice should be said, and that’] a nun should not receive from a bishop the blessed veil for her head unless her virginity had first been tested.”

+ At Rome, the birthday of Saint Novatian, with 977 others.

### 18 July — Fifteenth day before the Kalends of August

At Brescia, the burial of Saint Philastrius, bishop of that city. When he had been ordained a priest, moved by the love of God, he left everything and traveled through almost the whole world, so that, following the footsteps of the Apostle Paul, he might in every place free from everlasting destruction by his preaching souls deceived by the devil’s fraud. Therefore he fought not only against Gentiles and Jews, but also against almost all heresies, and especially against Arian perfidy, which at that time was prevailing with great force, with the strength of faith. For this reason he was punished with beatings and bore the marks of the Lord Jesus Christ on his body.

He was also a capable guardian of the Lord’s flock in the city of Milan, and, before blessed Ambrose was chosen, he resisted Auxentius, bishop of Arian perfidy, with great force, supported by divine grace. He also remained for no short time at Rome, and won many people to the faith both by public and private disputation.

And because he fiercely attacked the heretics, he wished to compose a book concerning each of their sects and their most abominable doctrines, so that, once the error of each heresy had been exposed, no one, however simple, who had been established in the Church might be ensnared by them. Concerning him blessed Augustine said as follows (*On Heresies*, to Quodvultdeus, heresy 41): “Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, in the very extensive book which he composed concerning heresies, judged that 120 heresies [Augustine: 128] were to be counted.”

### 15 August — Eighteenth day before the Kalends of September

[Note: [Col. 0429D] Added from manuscript E.]

On the same day [Note: [Col. 0429D] Dedication of an oratory. I inserted this from manuscript E, which alone contained it. There is no doubt that this was inserted into Ado by the person who wrote that codex, where this oratory had been dedicated, since it is absent elsewhere. The codex seems to me older than the foundation of the abbey of Everbode itself. Since this oratory is said to have been consecrated by Archbishop Willibert, it is very ancient. For Willibert, archbishop of Cologne, died around the year of Our Lord 890. I am entirely of the opinion that that book of Ado was brought to Everbode from some ancient abbey [Col. 0430D] or church of the diocese of Cologne, where Willibert consecrated this oratory], the dedication of the oratory of Saints James the Apostle, Lawrence, Valentine, and Scholastica, virgin, consecrated by Archbishop Willibert.

## The Passion of Saint Desiderius, Bishop of Vienne, by Saint Ado, Bishop of the Same See

*(In Canisius, Ancient Readings, volume II, part II.)*

### Ado’s Preface

Ado, bishop of the Church of Vienne, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 870, indiction 3, when sending the Passion of Saint Desiderius, bishop of the Church of Vienne [Note: [Col. 0435B] The large manuscript codex lacks the preface. Canisius].

[Col. 0435B] Ado, sinful and humble bishop of the Church of Vienne, to the beloved brothers and sons of that same Church, in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, the one true and substantial God: greetings.

I have undertaken to review and commit to writing for you the life and martyrdom of your most blessed Father Desiderius, as it is preserved in ancient writings, so that through his encouragements and endeavors I might inflame you more fervently to love eternal life. May he who was given to you as a shepherd by heavenly appointment obtain for you, through his intercession with the Lord, the pastures of true innocence and afterward eternal fellowship.

Nor will his [Col. 0436B] patronage be lacking to you if, following his example, you cleave to the Lord Jesus Christ with chaste love. He is the true and eternal beginning. You possess no small consolation when you see the true Church illumined by the most splendid radiance of confessors and martyrs, by whose brilliance, with the Lord our God as protector, you are able to escape with unhindered steps all the darkness of error.

I myself, the servant and least of them, entreat you: stand firm in the Lord, dearest ones, fortified by the teachings, examples, and intercessions of so many.

## Here Begins the Passion of Saint Desiderius, Bishop of Vienne

[Col. 0435C] Desiderius, the most illustrious pontiff of the Church of Vienne, was most devoutly instructed from childhood; pure in life and not a little learned in knowledge of the Scriptures, he advanced through diligent practice in the bosom of holy mother Church. From there he was raised to the pontifical office, and the honor of martyrdom revealed how great was the grace that had been given him.

[Note: [Col. 0435] The words “Fuit idem vir” (“This same man was”), up to the words “Cum longe lateque” (“When far and wide”), are missing from the large manuscript Codex CAN.]

This same man lived during the reign of King Chlothar, the elder son of Chlodovech, and during the reigns of Chlothar’s sons: Charibert, who ruled at Paris; Chilperic, who ruled at Soissons; Guntram, who ruled at Orléans; and Sigibert, who ruled in the city of Rheims. Sigibert married Brunhild, the daughter of King Atanagild of Spain, who was at first an Arian but later joined the Catholics by profession of the faith, though she was separated from them by her disgraceful deeds. From her Sigibert fathered Childebert. Chilperic first had her sister Galswintha, who was later strangled through Fredegund’s treachery.

At that time the emperors of the Roman state were Justinian the Elder, and after him Justinian the Younger. During the latter’s reign, the body of the blessed monk Antony was discovered by divine revelation and buried in the Church of Saint John the Baptist at Alexandria; and the most savage nation of the Vandals was driven out of Africa. Justin was his successor, under whom the nation of the Lombards invaded Italy. Then Tiberius ruled, and after him Maurice.

But to return to my subject: when the fame of the blessed man Desiderius was spreading far and wide, and his miracles were already being reported abroad, and the power of his spirit was shining forth through evident signs, the devil, envious of every good thing, stirred men of deranged minds to persecute so great a man. Because he saw that the glory of our Lord God Jesus Christ was being spread everywhere through the blessed man, he sought by whatever means he could to extinguish so great a work of piety. He began by attacking him and assailing him with insults, and then by driving him away through injuries, as the certain facts will show.

But Desiderius, one of the blessed poor in spirit, whose desire God heard and whose heart’s preparation his ear heard, was founded upon the rock of faith. He could be battered by adversities, but he could not be moved from his upright state.

Accordingly, after King Sigibert had been killed through the conspiracy of Queen Fredegund, Queen Brunhild obtained Burgundy together with the very young Theoderic, the son of King Childebert. She was a woman of incomparable lustfulness, since she did not fear to have incestuous relations with Merovech, Chilperic’s son and her husband’s nephew. After he had been tonsured and made a presbyter—for his father could scarcely restrain him in this way—she burned with desire for various young men, exposing herself as a most shameful brothel to the most shameful youths.

Bishop Desiderius, inflamed with zeal for the fear of God, wished to restrain and correct her unheard-of crimes. Both privately and publicly he urged her to undertake a better life and to repent of what she had done. But because “the one who reproves the wicked brings a blemish upon himself,” she began to detest the holy man with unprecedented hatred and to devise how she might take his life.

Since she could not do this openly, she had the man of God carried away and banished into a certain island. There, exhausted by various hardships for four years, he was nevertheless neither deprived of nor abandoned by the help of almighty God, through whom our God bestowed benefits there upon all who were infirm. For example, a certain leper was cleansed of the leprosy that had covered his entire body, in the sight of the people, by the touch of the most blessed man.

From the day on which he entered the island, a lamp filled with oil, which had been lit by his hand, remained, through divine power, unfailing: it always burned and displayed to everyone its inexhaustible fullness, proclaiming the favor shown to the man of God. More wonderfully still, whoever suffering from any illness was anointed by the holy bishop with some of that same liquid immediately departed healed.

It happened that a vessel full of wine was carefully kept by his servant for those who came and drew from it. But when, after several days, it was thought that the wine had been used up and the servant of the man of God reported to him that he had nothing further to offer those who asked—

[Note: [Col. 0437D] The large manuscript Codex G has “adnuntiasset illi” (“had announced to him”) instead.]

—he was encouraged by the man of God to trust in the generosity and goodness of the Creator. As soon as he returned, he found the little vessel full, although shortly before it had been empty. These things are yours, Lord, who always glorify those who suffer for you, and who adorn the leaders of your flock with crowns of virtue, so that your sheep may not fear to follow them.

Moreover, after a multitude of priests had assembled, although the impious woman had not poured forth the poisons of her malice, she was nevertheless overcome by prayers and ordered that the holy man be restored to his see and his city. Who could adequately describe the joys with which he was received, the number of arms with which the clergy and people embraced him in affection, and the tears with which he was drenched? Truly, he was a devout shepherd whom no kind of tribulation could tear away from the love of his sheep. Truly blessed was the people that deserved to receive such a leader.

[Note: [Col. 0437D] The large manuscript Codex G has “doctorem” (“teacher”) instead.]

[Col. 0438B] By this time he was wholly a martyr in body and a sacrifice pleasing to God, and the time was approaching when the crown of precious stone would be placed upon his head, so that the desire of his heart might be granted him. Again, through the hostility of Brunhild and of those who had violated her, the holy bishop was ordered to come to the palace where the young Theoderic then resided.

The man of God was therefore tested to see whether he would remain in his former judgment. He was asked whether it was better for one man to be joined to one woman than for a woman to dissipate her lust through the desires of various young men. He replied that each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband, and that God would judge fornicators and adulterers; that it was not lawful to defile the temple of the Holy Spirit, since our bodies were the temple of the Spirit of God; and that if anyone violated God’s temple, God would destroy him (1 Cor. VII; Heb. XIII; 1 Cor. III).

When the man, speaking by the Spirit of God, had proclaimed these and similar things, they were immediately reported to Brunhild. She began to rage and to attack the man of God with the weapons of her malice, seeking with her young men how she might take his life. Miserable to relate, the man of God was driven back and shut inside the doors of the church. To satisfy her fury, a popular outcry was raised by her supporters: “This man is a rebel and an enemy of the state and of the honor of his country!”

Knowing that he was now being called to the palm of victory, especially since this had been revealed to him by an angel, the man of God waited for the hour without fear or trembling, wholly fixed upon God. He was again dragged from the church, and the saint of the Lord was handled by unworthy hands. Through the agency of the counts Betto, Gasifred, and Aefanus, counselors in the most impious crime, he was committed to custody and led as far as the territory of Lyon, to the river Calaron.

Surrounded on every side by crowds of wicked men, when he saw that the enraged multitude was preparing to rise up for his death, chiefly at the urging of the aforementioned young men, he bent his knees to the ground and devoted himself to prayer. He prayed for his persecutors, saying:

“Lord, do not hold this sin against them, because they do not know what they are doing” (Acts VII; Luke XIII). “I commend to you the sheep whom, by your grace, I received to govern. May the rage of wolves not scatter them; but, gathered into the holy fold of your Church and bound together by the bond of charity, may they live in you through the Spirit of grace and be guarded in your eternal mercy, Jesus Christ, Son of God, who live and reign for ever and ever.”

The maddened multitude, unable in any way to restrain its fury, saw one of the raging men seize a stone and strike it violently against the brain of the praying man. Immediately, when his skull had been broken, blood poured forth in streams. Another drove a stake, sharply pointed at both ends, into his neck and head. Thus the holy bishop gained the palm of martyrdom and departed victorious to the Lord. Life was granted him, and length of days for ever and ever.

Although his persecutors did not say to him, “Sacrifice to demons,” they did say: “Consent to us who are sinning; be silent about the truth, so that we may enjoy the embraces we desire.” He was therefore truly a martyr, because he both held fast to the truth and displayed love in his correction. He was not afraid to die, so that he might teach those whom he had nourished for Christ to accept death steadfastly for the truth, since Christ is the truth; and because no adversity, not even death, should ultimately separate them from the love of Christ.

He truly loved those by whom he was unjustly killed, and by his punishment he showed them how perilously they themselves would be punished eternally, since they lived shamefully and criminally, whereas, rather than commit or lend his support to such acts, he was prepared to endure any bodily punishment.

[Col. 0439C] I shall briefly touch upon the vengeance that struck that impious woman in the present life, so that no one may think that sin can be committed with impunity. Under King Chlothar—[Clothar]—when the Franks were acting as judges, she was tied by the arms to untamed horses, her legs were spread apart, and she was torn limb from limb. Thus God repaid her a punishment worthy of her pleasures.

The body of the blessed man, cared for through the devotion of the faithful, was buried at the place of his passion. There it publicly revealed through miracles how great was his merit before the Lord.

It happened that a certain poor man, contracted in all his limbs and also afflicted by a severe illness that caused his limbs to tremble, was carried in a wicker litter to the martyr’s memorial. As soon as he sought the martyr’s help with faith, he returned safe and sound in perfect health.

A man named Claudius had a daughter who had been lame in the leg for a long time. He approached and entrusted his daughter to the martyr for healing. As soon as she had been anointed with the martyr’s oil, she became completely healthy and lost the affliction of lameness.

It cannot be said how many blind people received there a light previously unknown to them, how many possessed persons were cleansed, how many lame people were healed, and how many others suffering from different illnesses were cured. Moreover, if anyone carried with faith a splinter from the stake with which the holy man’s head had been pierced, whether suffering from toothache, a type of various fevers, or other illnesses, he was freed through the merits of the blessed martyr.

After some time had passed, it seemed good to the bishop of the Viennese and to the most holy clergy and the entire people to prevail upon Chlothar, then a devout king, by their prayers, so that he might deign to grant them the remains of the most blessed man. They had been buried, as they were, in the diocese of Lyon and preserved at the place of his passion.

The devout king granted this graciously. He saw that they were asking for something most worthy and most dear to God, and that the affection of pious children toward the reverence due to their father was overflowing. Who would refuse those seeking so great a work of piety?

Fathers ought to store up treasure for their children. This man plainly stored up for them a treasure that would not fail in heaven, covering them with the purple of his blood for the adornment of his children. Sons, too, ought to offer their fathers the affection of devoted charity and obedience, and refresh them with the desirable fruits of virtue, so that, refreshed and satisfied by their taste and fragrance, they may become one in Christ in the love that is the temple of beauty and the house of God. What greater grace can the devoted mother Church possess than to see her children walking worthily before God? That the head of humility, joined together in the structure of charity, should supply the members with strength, with fear, with piety, and with the good hope?

The clergy and people returned joyfully from the prince, having obtained the desire of their heart, the desire of their love. Blessed be God, who placed this in the king’s heart, so that he might glorify our city through the reception of our most blessed shepherd and his martyr.

The whole Church assembled. A solemn celebration of joy was proclaimed to everyone. Crosses were prepared, lights were prepared, and the bier was adorned with the most precious garments. All were clothed in festive attire, and a procession of such honorable magnificence was made to the martyrdom of the holy bishop.

I shall relate an event filled with the greatest devotion toward God. The peoples of both Vienne and Lyon came together. A pious dispute arose: the people of Lyon claimed to possess the martyr, while the Viennese wished to take back their shepherd. There was a most affectionate contest between them, since the former claimed what they had acquired, while the latter demanded the return of their patron. The former were those with whom the martyr lived in God; the latter were those among whom he had lived as a teacher in the flesh.

Why delay further? While both sides steadfastly remained in their positions out of love for the martyr—

[Note: [Col. 0439D] The manuscript Codex S. G. has “utrumque” (“both sides”) instead.]

—night fell. The Viennese, who had loved him more and whose cause was more just, adopted a subtler plan. They secretly removed the earth and opened the holy tomb. Having prepared a small boat with a fishing net, they concealed the body and sent it ahead by way of the Saône—

[Note: [Col. 0440D] A manuscript note in the margin says: “The Saône, a very foul river, enters the Rhône at the city of Lyon.”]

—and the Rhône. With its cheerful waters, the Rhône itself received so holy a body and was destined to serve its own citizens. Dawn returned, and the Viennese crowd walked back with the empty bier. The people of Lyon rejoiced, deceived by their vain hope; but this fortunate theft did not remain hidden from them for long, and so they lost their joy when victory was despaired of.

Those who were transporting the bishop’s remains by boat, when they came opposite the estate of Fasiana, landed on the shore, awaiting the holy company of people traveling on foot. At that time the Fasian estate had already been assigned as property to the poor of the holy martyrs in whose honor the Church of Vienne was founded. For, as the same martyr records in his testament—which he made for the holy martyrs the Maccabees and Saint Maurice, and for six thousand six hundred and sixty others—the estate had fallen to the blessed Desiderius by inheritance from both his mother and his father.

In that testament, which he composed in his own hand in the presence of the holy co-bishops, he established under oath before almighty God that no one should presume, out of respect for piety, to change the bequest he had made into anything other than what he had determined. [Note: [Col. 0441] The following words are missing from the large manuscript Codex S. G.] But if anyone, driven by a spirit of greed, should do so and fail to change his decision by repentance, he would be anathema for ever.

The bearers of the holy body therefore waited in this estate for those who were coming on foot by land, and meanwhile placed the sacred remains in a very clean place. I do not think I should remain silent about the miracle that then occurred.

A woman who had been tormented for many years by an unclean spirit was dragged there by her relatives. As soon as she reached the place of the holy martyr, she was immediately healed by divine power.

When the blessed Aetherius, then bishop of Vienne, arrived with the others who had remained in the city, the holy bier was carried upon the arms of the devout, and the choir of the blessed people raised high their voices in song and praise to our God. Who could have had a heart so hard and an interior so unfeeling as not either to utter a groan from the excess of joy in his heart or to wet his face with tears?

With such a heavenly procession going before and following after, the body of the blessed man was carried to the place of the tomb, which had been prepared with fitting reverence in the church of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul outside the city. There also the remains of many bishops of that same city of Vienne were buried and preserved.

When the body of the most holy martyr was being handled by the bishops’ hands to be wrapped in perfumes and precious linen—a fact that must not be concealed from the praise of almighty God—the wounds of his most holy head appeared so completely restored that no sign could be seen of where the skin had been broken. The rest of his body, too, remained joined by its joints and sinews and clothed in its healthy skin.

The choirs sang again, answering one another antiphonally in harmony.

When the saint of God had been placed in the tomb for the protection of the entire city, the glorious woman who had once been the wife of the blessed Aetherius in secular life, but who was then truly a nun, brought a man blind from birth [Col. 0442A] and placed him beside the tomb of Bishop and Martyr Desiderius. She urged him beforehand to have faith. Divine power was present, the power that always glorifies its own, and it manifested through evident signs how great before God was the merit of the one whose body was kept in that place. For in the sight of the entire Church, that blind man received a light previously unknown to him.

The Lord afterward worked many things there through his servant. If anyone wished to write them all down, he would complete a volume of great length.

The most blessed Desiderius, bishop of the Church of Vienne, suffered during the reign of Theoderic, king of the Burgundians, through the plotting of Brunhild, the most incestuous queen, with the counts Betto, Aefanus, and Gasifred consenting to and supporting her wickedness. His day of passion is celebrated on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns—he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God for ever and ever.

The day of his translation, when he was transferred from the Lyon territory, from the estate of Prisciniacum, to the Viennese suburb, is observed on the third day before the Ides of February in the church of blessed Peter.

## HERE BEGIN THE WORDS OF BISHOP ADO OF VIENNE

I have transferred these things for you, most blessed brothers and sons, in complete truth, just as I saw them inserted in older parchments, for your admonition. I beseech you, and in the devotion with which I love you I admonish your holiness, to strive with all your strength to rise to the merits of this and of your other patrons.

Let their fervent devotion toward God dwell in your hearts; pure charity; constant diligence in every form of goodness; patience persevering through changing circumstances; a modesty fitting to the good customs of Christians; bashful and chaste gentleness in every manner of life and continence; and a unanimity dear and pleasing to God. Thus, when you have completed the course of this life along the way of your fathers, may you deserve, through their intercession, to enjoy eternal joy together with them.

May the advancement of your life be the increase of their righteousness, and may your perpetual joy be the crown of your glorification.

## A SHORT ACCOUNT BY ISON

The aforementioned Bishop Ado took care to send this Passion to us brothers serving God in the monastery of Saint Gall under Abbot Grimald, who had requested from him the relics of Saint Desiderius, together with the relics of other saints, as well as the acts and passions described below, in the aforementioned year, through sufficiently trustworthy messengers.

[Col. 0443]

## THE PRIVILEGE OF ADO BY WHICH HE CONFIRMS THE CHURCH OF VELNIS TO THE ABBEY OF SAINT EUGENDUS OF THE JURA

*(From the Miscellanies of Baluze.)*

[Col. 0443A] In the year 870 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, a holy synod of the metropolitan Church of Vienne assembled, with Lord and venerable Archbishop Ado presiding. He investigated with vigilant care ecclesiastical causes and the needs of his sons, and settled them according to ecclesiastical custom.

The reverend man Manno, provost of the monastery of Saint Eugendus of the Jura, then appeared. Explaining the reason for his arrival, he brought forward a certain church belonging to the aforesaid monastery and situated within the diocese of Vienne, in the estate of Velnis. Endowed in honor of Saint Peter, it possessed a privilege granted to it by the predecessors of the most holy archbishop just mentioned, and preserved by that same co-bishop up to that time.

He declared that the church of the village of Saint Alban had been left desolate. The same venerable provost also produced a written inquiry made in the time of the pious memory of Lord Agilmar, since at that time as well there had been a dispute between the rectors of the churches in question.

But because the holy synod judged that document invalid, since it did not see it confirmed by the canonic—[lacuna]—the most holy bishop decided that the entire case should be reconsidered from the beginning by the most holy priests, so that, once the truth had been established, the long-contested dispute might be settled.

With these men therefore bearing witness and stating the order of the truth, it seemed good to the lord bishop, with the consent of the most holy synod, that just as the holy congregation of the monastery of the most blessed Eugendus had been honored in the days of his holy episcopal predecessors, so the holy metropolitan Church of Vienne should provide it with honor and assistance according to its ability in this petition and in its other necessities.

Moreover, so that, once the complaint had been quieted, it might possess its privilege more securely in the future concerning the matter at issue with the Church of Vienne, the privilege should also be strengthened by written letters.

Therefore, in this manner, I, Ado, Archbishop of Vienne, giving my consent and agreeing to the pious counsel of my sons, have confirmed this below with my own hand, and have asked my holy sons to confirm it according to ecclesiastical custom.

Done publicly at Vienne in the month of April, in the tenth year of Lord Ado’s episcopate, in the third indiction.

[Col. 0443]

# LIFE OF SAINT THEUDERIUS, ABBOT OF VIENNE IN GAUL

By Saint Ado, bishop of that same city.

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, vol. I, p. 678, from manuscript codices whose fragments Benedictus Gononus reported in the Appendix to the Lives of the Fathers of the West.)*

[Col. 0443C] **1.** Ado, bishop of Vienne, sends eternal salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ to the brothers residing in the monastery of Saint Theuderius.

[Note: [Col. 0443C] The Abbey of Saint Theuderius, called Sainct-Chef in the vernacular, formerly belonged to the Order of Saint Benedict. It has now been converted into a collegiate church and united to the archiepiscopal table of Vienne in Allobroges. [Col. 0444C]]

For this reason I have decided to commend to your holiness in my writings the Life of your father, that is, of the blessed Theuderius: so that through his examples I might invite you more strongly to love eternal life. For I desire you to become imitators and emulators of the man whose patronage I rejoice greatly to have acquired through God’s gift. The beginning and course of this man’s life are as follows.

## Theuderius Distributes His Property and Seeks Lérins

**2.** This blessed man was born in the province of Vienne. His parents were distinguished according to worldly rank, and he was honored through the wealth of the world. While he was still a boy, he began through devout endeavors to aspire to the love of eternal life.

Because, having been born to distinguished parents, he had acquired no small amount of money from his patrimonial income, he did not delay in giving it to the poor, so that he might receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life in the future, becoming a perfect disciple of Christ. Relieved, therefore, of his temporal burden and completely stripped of the garment of the world, he considered seeking the monastery of Lérins so that he might serve the Lord God more perfectly.

## Saint Caesarius Detains Him

**3.** Having left his parents and committed himself entirely to God with this desire, he sought the city of Arles, where Saint Caesarius was then bishop, so that, aided by the bishop’s support, he might more easily undertake the journey to the island of the monks.

But by the disposition of almighty God it came about that he was delayed for a while by the holy counsels of the holy bishop. For they say that when they first looked upon one another, they greeted one another by name, and that the power of almighty God inspired both of them together with such a gift of grace that, although they had not previously known one another, as soon as they saw each other bodily they revealed to outsiders, through their mutual address, that they were truly servants of God.

It was truly like that blessed state in which there will be full knowledge of the truth, in which one person will be known wholly and truly by another; when God will be seen not through a mirror or in an enigma but face to face, and will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts.

When the blessed Caesarius learned of the ardor of his desire, he rejoiced with him and gave thanks to almighty God. Then he addressed the blessed Theuderius:

“O servant of God, if you give assent to my words, the Lord will be with you and will strengthen the counsel of your heart. Remain with us for a while, subject to the ecclesiastical order. Humbly endure whatever we impose upon you by God’s gift, so that, as Scripture teaches, when you have completed your works with gentleness and humility, you may be directed toward every glory.”

The blessed Theuderius replied:

“I know, most blessed Father, that the Lord said concerning his own: ‘Whoever hates you hates me, and whoever despises you despises me’ (Luke X, 16). Therefore I shall not delay in obeying your admonitions as the commands of the Lord.”

The blessed Theuderius therefore remained there according to the will of the blessed Caesarius. Day and night he committed the voice of his spirit to God through fasts, vigils, and prayers, and he brought no small joy both to the bishop and to God.

## Theuderius Is Made a Priest and Returns to His Homeland

**4.** After some time had passed, the blessed Caesarius, thinking to bind him more fully to divine ministries, imposed upon him the office of deacon, although he resisted and protested for a long time. Not long afterward, with the whole clergy and people acclaiming him, he bestowed upon him the dignity of the priesthood.

Saint Theuderius embraced this office with such reverence that he surpassed the others in merits and grace, was extraordinary in his ministry, and in humility subjected himself even to those beneath him, remembering the saying of the Lord: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XVIII, 14), and the saying of Scripture: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. III, 20).

When the course of time had passed, the man of God considered revisiting his native province and consoling his parents. He therefore disclosed his intention to the holy bishop and asked him for a blessing to go and return. At first he caused him great sorrow. Then, seeing that he could not oppose the holy man’s resolve, the bishop gave his consent, although sadly. Theuderius departed with his blessing from the city of Arles, accompanied by the weeping clergy and people, who lamented that the man of God was leaving them. At last he permitted him to go.

## Description of Vienne

[Col. 0446A] **5.** When Saint Theuderius had come near the city of Vienne, he began earnestly to seek where he should establish his dwelling cell.

Here, therefore, let me briefly turn aside into a writer’s description of the city of Vienne. Vienne is the most noble city of Gaul, toward the west, and is fortified on its northern side by commanding forts, so that access to the walls of the city is not easy.

The first fort, extending toward the south, is Cappro. Near it is Eumenius, and next is Quiriacus. Joined to it by a wall extending through the valley are Propiciacus and Pompeiacus, once famous among worshipers of demons for its hundred gods. Not far away a fifth fort is attached, to which antiquity gave the name Suspoli.

The entire city, together with its forts, is enclosed by a wall extending from the river [the river Jaira is perhaps missing] to the Rhône itself, running over the hills to the plain. It is a most illustrious metropolis and one of the most distinguished cities of Gaul.

## Theuderius Builds a Cell After a Miracle

**6.** As the man of God sought a place for his dwelling, he finally came to a site suitable for his solitude, not far from the city. There he began to build a small house in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, under the veneration of the blessed Eusebius, bishop and martyr of Vercelli.

After the foundations had been laid, it happened that a hill, rising nearby, split with a great fissure and threatened to collapse upon the site. But through the prayer of the man of God, by him who said to his own, “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to the sea,’ and it would move” (Luke XVII, 6)—wondrous to relate!—the mass settled on the other side without harming the building in any way.

After the house had been built and the relics of the saints placed upon the altar, the man of God again walked about beside the river Jaira, considering secretly in his heart where he might establish a cell for the servants of God. For this reason he was seized by sleep, and in a vision he was instructed to build a basilica over that very water in honor of the blessed martyr Symphorianus.

And so it happened. After adorning the place, he chose monks to serve God there. The fame of the man of God grew and spread far and wide. For Christ our God did not permit a lamp to be hidden under a bushel.

## He Builds Various Cells

[Col. 0446D] **7.** As many people therefore hurried to learn about the man of God, his brother Arvus and other relatives came one day among the rest for the sake of visiting him. He embraced them kindly and like a father, and devoutly instructed them concerning the hope of eternal life and the reward of the saints.

Then, greatly inflamed and kindled by the ardor of the Holy Spirit, he came to the fort called Alarona. Wishing to establish a monastery of monks there, he built an oratory of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and remained there for some time, devoting himself to God in prayers and vigils.

Afterward he came to the village and estate of his parents, called Assicia, where his parents had built an oratory in honor of the blessed martyr Maurice. Prostrating himself in prayer, he asked day and night without ceasing that the mercy of almighty God deign to show him a suitable place for the habitation of the servants of God.

When he had surrendered himself to sleep, an angel of God appeared to him, marked out for him a secluded place on Mount Rupianus, and instructed him to build there the monastery that he was burning to build—that is, that he desired to build.

At that time the place was wooded and full of wild beasts and serpents. When the man of God awoke, he came to the place divinely shown to him and poured out a prayer to God there for some time.

But the devil, envious of every good thing, sought to draw the holy man of God back from the intention he had begun, just as through the serpent he had offered the poison of his faithlessness to our first parents. Entering a serpent again and stirring up the fury of wild beasts, he held him back from the undertaking.

Recognizing his tricks, the man of God stood fearless, armed with the weapons of prayer. The devil’s deceit was overcome and collapsed as it vanished.

With the consent of the bishop of Vienne, a basilica was therefore constructed with great speed in veneration of holy Mary, the Mother of God. A small monastery was endowed from the resources of both his parents and his relatives, and monks were established there according to the rule of the holy Fathers.

## He Is Chosen as the People’s Intercessor Before God

**8.** At that time the venerable Bishop Philip was regarded as the twenty-first bishop of Vienne.

It was customary in that city to choose one man from among several who lived the holier life and place him in a secluded location within the same city. There, devoting himself solely to the contemplative life, he would more familiarly present the people’s prayers before God.

When the bishop was seeking throughout the diocese a man full of virtue to whom the people might entrust their private matters, as far as these concerned their salvation, he rejoiced exceedingly that he possessed the blessed Theuderius, who was already the father of monks. He therefore ordered him to be summoned.

The blessed man knew in what capacity the bishop was seeking him. Committing himself entirely to the grace of God, he placed his monastery under the care of his prior, Severianus by name. He exhorted the brothers, bade them farewell, commended them to the Lord in whom he had placed his hope, and went to the bishop.

The bishop received him reverently. After assembling the clergy and the entire people, he assigned the holy man to the brothers, the children of the Church, through the mercy of God, so that through the blessed man’s prayer he himself might bring gain from the flock entrusted to him back to the Lord.

The blessed man chose for himself a place on Mount Quirinal and the basilica of the blessed martyr Lawrence, where he might devote himself to prayer before God day and night.

## His Virtues and Commendation

**9.** It would not easily be possible for any tongue to express how strict and how humble this man was. He overflowed with tears, was cautious in prayer, and was wholly fixed in the Lord in his heart. I do not see how I could adequately describe his scantiness of food and drink or the poverty of his clothing, since he lay down in a hair shirt and continued day and night without food or drink.

Because people therefore flocked to him from every direction, he concealed himself as much as he could in seclusion, opening a very small window through which he gave instructions to those who came.

The grace of Christ had bestowed upon him wisdom of heart and gracious eloquence of speech, so that he knew what salutary counsel to disclose to each person. Who came to him wounded by the devil and did not immediately depart healed and made sound? Who, saddened by the burden of his sins, did not at once return more secure and joyful, consoled by the mercy of God?

Whoever the oppression of the world had made sadder, at his exhortation immediately lifted his spirit toward the hope of everlasting joy. To conclude everything in the words of the Apostle: “He became all things to all people, that he might save all” (1 Cor. IX, 22).

The Lord also glorified his servant, who clung to him with such intimacy, through miracles, so that many afflicted by evil spirits and burdened by various illnesses were healed through his prayers.

[Col. 0448B] ## Near Death, He Devotes Himself to God More Fervently

**10.** The same holy man remained for twelve years in the place chosen for him and so dear to him. There he continually offered his entire self to God through the most ardent contrition of spirit and body.

When he saw that the time of his release was near, he remained more fervently in the lofty contemplation of his mind. As though he were nearer to the gates of heavenly life, he could scarcely bear to turn the eye of his mind toward other things.

He was present through love at the vision of his Creator. Choirs of heavenly spirits, the manifold triumphs of the apostles, and the indescribable joy of the holy martyrs in heaven were present to his desires. Nothing was sweet to him—no sound, no food—except Christ.

Amid such happy and blessed labors, when the man of God became somewhat weak in body, full and perfected in pious works, he departed to the Lord.

O blessed man, counted after so many labors among the company of the holy spirits and the fellowship of the saints, eternally consoled and happily gladdened by the vision of his Lord, whom he had always loved!

## He Is Buried. His Body Becomes Immovable.

11. After the death of the holy man had been announced to the city, the entire city went out to attend the funeral: the priests, the rest of the clergy, and an innumerable multitude of people. The body was prepared according to custom and covered in a bier. When the holy bier had been taken up by the priests standing around, after the customary offices had been performed, so that it might be carried to the tomb, it could not be moved from the spot. Everyone present was amazed and astonished [Col. 0448D], and anxiously asked what should be done. When, by decree of the holy bishop, it had been determined—although the people objected—that it should be carried to its monastery, it was immediately moved with such ease that it seemed to have no weight at all. They reached the basilica of Saint Romanus the martyr in the suburb of the city, in the village of Brenniacum, and rested there briefly. They spent what remained of the night in vigil. I do not think that the miracle that then occurred should be passed over.

### Wine is multiplied for the bearers of the sacred body

12. Through the charity and service of the holy women serving God in the monasteries of Vienne [Col. 0449A], provision was made so that the fatigue of the brothers who had gone before and those who followed might be somewhat relieved. The servant of God who presided over the upper monastery sent three vessels full of wine after the holy funeral, so that those who were thirsty might be refreshed and those keeping vigil restored. They drank until the vessels had been emptied. Severianus, formerly the holy man’s superior, was then present there with the brothers who had come to meet the saint. When some of them asked where they might obtain something to drink, they found nothing.

But what does divine power not accomplish through its saints? When the servants of God who had carried the vessels full of wine wished at dawn to return to the monastery and reclaim their vessels, they found them full, as though nothing had been taken from them. Truly, the same one worked then [Col. 0449B] to magnify his servant in the vessels who at Cana of Galilee changed the taste of water into wine. The drink produced by divine power was sufficient for those who drank, so that enough of it was even carried back to the city’s monasteries, and a public miracle was performed to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### A blind man receives sight. A cripple is straightened

13. The holy body was carried on the shoulders of tall men, who took turns succeeding one another in their pious desire. Since the sky was cloudy and the air damp, and everyone feared that a storm was approaching, clear weather was suddenly restored through the merits of the blessed man.

The holy body was carried to a place called Duodecimum, where divine power performed the following miracle. A certain man who had been blind from birth had endured for three days, awaiting the holy crowds that were to come with the funeral of the blessed man. As soon as he could, he touched [Col. 0449C] the covering of the bier, and immediately blood flowed from his eyes; at once he received light, something he had never experienced before.

When they reached the place of burial [Col. 0450A], some men full of faith brought there a man whose limbs were so contracted that his feet adhered to his buttocks. The merit of the holy man was present: for he returned from the sacred tomb sound in his feet. So that no one might regard the matter as fabricated and not truly accomplished, both men—the one who had been blind and the one who had recovered the ability to walk—remained devoted in the holy man’s monastery until death, and proclaimed aloud the miracles that God had performed in them.

### Wax increases

14. It was thought that wax had run out for dispelling the darkness of night. The brothers were distressed and had nowhere to turn; but the one who caused the five loaves in the mouths of those eating [Col. 0450B] in the wilderness to increase drove away their fear. For the wax increased in their hands in such a way that from a small quantity a great number of lights grew.

Thus the holy body was treated with fitting veneration and reverently concealed in the burial place that he himself had formerly prepared for himself. There he reveals, through frequent miracles to the praise of the Lord Jesus Christ, that he lives with God.

If you desire to have him as a patron before God, my sons and brothers, eagerly seek to imitate his life, which was full of love.
