For this holy man always desired the gains of his Lord, and he himself rejoiced in Christ over your crown. He will never be absent from you, if you do not distance your soul and life from the manner of life that he practiced. May the Lord, who freely granted him merit and an eternal reward [Col. 0450C], increase in you the desire for every good and grant you obedience pleasing to himself, a perfection full of righteousness.

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF SAINT ADŌ

[Col. 0449]

## TRANSLATION, OR ELEVATION, OF SAINT BARNARD, BISHOP OF VIENNE

Performed in the year 945, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May; written by an anonymous author of that period.

(From Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*)

[Col. 0449D]

1. Almighty God has been accustomed to grant such glory to the citizens of the heavenly kingdom that, flashing forth in miracles, they spread among peoples the fame of their praise. In our own times, visions concerning our magnificent father, the blessed bishop Barnard, were revealed to men with clear manifestation, though they differed in age and merit.

When no one was willing to accept them, he appeared to a certain man named Rainaldus, advanced in age and elevated by priestly dignity. His testimony rightly removed every doubt, for he was a noble man, distinguished by the gift of chastity. As he himself related, the saint appeared to him in this way.

While he was resting on his bed in the deep silence of night [Col. 0450D], a man of great authority appeared to him, dressed in a priestly stole and bearing an archiepiscopal pallium. He called him and said:

“Rainaldus, I wish you to know that I was the founder of this place, and that you should command your brothers to transfer my body, which is disgracefully enclosed in the mud of the waters.”

The same revelation then began to appear to many people, and the saint, with threatening words, commanded that it be carried out more quickly. Unless they obeyed his commands, he declared that the place he had founded would be laid waste.

2. Therefore, on the Tuesday within Easter Week—namely, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May—in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0451A] 914, his holy body was uncovered and raised from the earth with the greatest joy.

**Note:** The Roman Breviary gives this year as 844, and more correctly so: for in that year Easter fell on 14 April, and the Tuesday within Easter Week, on which the translation took place, fell on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, that is, 25 April.

When the limbs of the blessed bishop were being raised from the tomb, the elders thought that they should be washed with wine, a custom that I have elsewhere noted as ordinarily observed in the translations of saints. Many remedies were thereby provided for the sick. We saw possessed persons and lunatics drink from this liquid [Col. 0452A] and recover their strength, the demonic impulse having been calmed.

But after the blessed relics had been placed upon the bier, there arose a cry of joy from the rejoicing saints; and they were placed, amid the greatest joy of the people, to the left of the altar of the Apostles, which he himself had consecrated while alive.

**Note:** The relics of Saint Barnard no longer appear in that place, as Lievraeus thought; rather, they are believed to have been burned by the Calvinists.

# MIRACLES OF THE SAME

[Col. 0451]

By an anonymous bishop of Vienne, as is evident from no. 7; he lived in the tenth century.

(From Mabillon, *ibid.*)

[Col. 0451B]

1. Although my incompetence may later be accused of ignorance of letters, nevertheless the force of my love for my lord bishop and nourisher, my Barnard, compels me to write of the wonders recently accomplished.

When, therefore, the people of Aquitaine were holding an assembly with their bishops at the city called Vetula, in the territory of the Vellavi, the congregation of Romans was also present, carrying the body of the aforesaid bishop.

**Note:** [Col. 0451D] That is, an assembly of the faithful summoned for religious purposes; the word has the same meaning below in no. 4. Some believe that the old city in which the supplication was proclaimed was none other than the city of Anicium, or Podium, the capital of the Vellavi, Le Velay. The monk Franco, in the *Chronicle of Tournus* cited above, says that Abbot Erveus acquired extensive estates for his church in the county of Velay, including the church of Saint George in the suburb of the city of Vetula—that is, in the suburb of Anicium or Podium of the Vellavi—as Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius explains in his *History of Tournus*. I followed this opinion above, where the translation of Saint Philibert was discussed. Later, however [Col. 0452D], I discovered with certain arguments that by the name “city of Vetula” the town of Saint-Paulianus is meant; I shall present these arguments in the Appendix to this volume.

If anyone wishes to know the abundance of miracles performed there, he can obtain true evidence from this fact: the chest containing his most sacred body, decently adorned with gold and silver through the abundance of offerings brought to him by the devout hands of the faithful, is seen to have been fashioned by skilled workmanship. Golden crosses also bear witness to this, as do candlesticks adorned with gold and silver.

2. At a later time there was among the Romans a certain holy woman deprived of the use of her tongue. Remaining in the church, she prayed to God with deep contrition of heart. On the feast of the Apostles [Col. 0451C] Peter and Paul, when the boys had sung *Benedicamus Domino* according to custom after the evening hymns had been recited, she herself proclaimed thanksgiving to God together with the rest of the people.

3. At about the same time there was a certain tanner at Viventiacum. Since he practiced his trade on Sunday without observing the honor due to the day, the handle of his tool adhered so firmly to his hand that it could not be torn away. Moreover, he was deprived of the light of his eyes, and confessed his rashness to everyone. Someone appeared to him in a vision and instructed him to seek the aid of Saint Barnard at Romans. He went to Romans and recovered his health.

4. I shall not be silent about what happened in the Golden Valley, which lies in the territory of Vienne. The citizens of Vienne had decreed that an assembly should be held there every year.

A certain blind man had arrived there and was awaiting the arrival of the blessed Barnard on the steps of a small chapel constructed from interwoven wooden posts. When people told him that a crowd praising God [Col. 0452B] on account of Barnard’s arrival was present, he immediately went there and recovered his sight.

5. I learned the truth from those who testified to it and who had come to Romans for the festival of Palm Sunday: they spoke of the restoration of sight to a certain blind man.

A custom had grown up among the inhabitants that on that day they carried the limbs of the most sacred bishop with them in procession, together with leafy branches. When the people had gathered for such great joy, a certain blind man was also present, crying out loudly that he had deserved to see clearly. At his cries the entire stirred crowd resounded in song: “We praise you, O God.”

6. As the blessed Luke testifies, we have learned that our Savior led the Apostles out beyond Jerusalem on the day of his Ascension and entered the heights of heaven. In memory of this procession, when the congregation at Romans was arranging it [uncertain: the text reads *hanc uno annorum componerent*], one of the young men joyfully placed in the chest of the aforesaid bishop flowers of a plant commonly called gladiolus.

On the following day he took care to preserve the flowers he had gathered and placed there. From them the blessed bishop Barnard later [Col. 0452C] granted many benefits to the sick.

7. I now wish to insert that miracle which was continually displayed openly after I assumed, by God’s authority, the government of this Church of Vienne, which I serve.

The parents of a certain young man brought him to the Romans; he had never walked. When they placed him before the tomb of the blessed Barnard, he rose healthy, his legs and feet having been strengthened.

He carries his miracle around every year. Although this most blessed man is inferior to the Apostles, the event is recognized as resembling what Peter once did with John at the Beautiful Gate of the Temple: Peter commanded that man to rise, while divine power, through the merits of the bishop, willed to raise this one.

Let this one account of his written miracles suffice for those seeking the wonders of the blessed bishop. But I want them to know that there were—and continually are—many others, so numerous that they seem to exceed the capacity of the writer.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 877. USUARDUS, MONK OF SAINT-GERMAIN

## THE MARTYROLOGY OF USUARD

Compared with fourteen printed copies, seventeen complete manuscript codices, and nearly fifty others; purged of additions, corrected, and illustrated with daily observations.

The work and scholarly labor of Joannes Baptista Sollerius, theologian of the Society of Jesus.

[Col. 0453]

# TO THE MOST SERENE AND MOST POWERFUL LORD, LORD J. WILHELM

Count Palatine of the Rhine, Arch-Steward and Elector of the Holy Roman Empire; Duke of Bavaria, Jülich, Cleves, and Berg; Prince of Moers; Count of Veldenz, Sponheim, and Mark; Lord of Ravensberg and Ravenstein, etc.

Here, most serene Elector, I present your Bensberg, displayed for the whole world to behold and your magnificence to contemplate: Bensberg, begun not long ago, built with royal splendor, a compendium of architectural art, a residence worthy of the loftiness of your mind.

So speak the Rhine and the Düssel, subject to you; so your territories resound around it; so Cologne, Agrippina, set before the sight of your fortress, proclaims it; so, with one harmonious voice, testify all who have surveyed Bensberg with their eyes, even from afar.

But, most serene Prince, forgive what I say of your property: when I formerly contemplated that fortress more attentively, however august it might be, I thought it a spectacle less of your magnificence than of your generosity.

I imagined that fortress, the dwelling place of the liberal arts, set upon the most pleasant ridge of hills—not as the poets tell of the two-peaked mountain, but as the training ground of a truly Christian hero, in which the liberal arts, the sciences, and disciplines, indeed all the Christian virtues, might dwell.

This was my thought when, received with the greatest favor and with a benevolence worthy of you as prince, and invited with no less courtesy to visit Bensberg, I was able with my own eyes to examine everything more closely, investigate everything more attentively, and contemplate everything at leisure.

This thought, I say, then entered my mind: that splendid fortress seemed an Athenaeum in which there were either truly stored, or artistically engraved, or at least capable of being placed, the outstanding specimens of your lofty mind, born for every art, which I had encountered elsewhere in abundance.

Let me express my thought more openly. The massive building visible before us, with its august façade, divided into spacious chambers—this I imagined as an atrium devoted to your delight in the art of painting, in which the most elegant works of the most skillful brushes, collected from all Europe at your study and expense, might compete for the prize of art.

In imagination I saw Michelangelos, Raphaels, Paulos, Tintorettos, Rubenses, Van Dycks—and why should I enumerate them all?—arranged in order, gathering into the companionship of Apelles, with such ornament and abundance that, without envy, I scarcely think there is any prince in the whole world who has acquired such treasures of this art at so great a price.

Indeed, I seemed to behold in your single fortress all those paintings which I had once found scattered elsewhere throughout Germany, Italy, France, and Belgium.

In my imagination the right wing was adorned by another distinction of a prince who was not merely curious but industrious, learned, and literary: a most complete library of books purchased and selected by you from every quarter [Col. 0455]. There I reviewed the labors of the most learned men, writing, discussing, and disputing on every branch of knowledge, science, and art.

For nearly forty years, from the time when you were an adolescent prince, Belgium, France, England, Italy, and Germany—all the regions which you traversed on a two-year journey—ought to have admired your extraordinary diligence, illuminated, like the passing sun, not so much by the rays of your most serene birth as by those of your virtues and distinguished learning.

At that time, I believe, you were seized by the interest, then reviving among the learned, in excavating antiquity through coins and similar ancient treasures. I assigned one side of your palace to this collection.

Here I distributed your entire equipment of exceptionally rare coins into its proper series, beginning with consular coins arranged according to the Roman families; proceeding then to the emperors, struck and organized in gold, silver, and various kinds of bronze; here placing the venerable features of learned Greece, breathing something august even through the metal itself; there the fragments of Asiatic wealth wrested from the barbarians; here Hebrew, Syriac, and Syro-Macedonian pieces; and there the more certain traces of the history of every people.

These are indeed illustrious proofs of your practiced intelligence and disciplined judgment, but you did not wish them to be barren attractions or spectacles for the eyes alone.

Hence your discernment in selecting learned men, whom with a generous hand you encouraged to cultivate these and all other arts; hence, in your capital of Düsseldorf, philosophical and other disciplines summoned in addition to the customary Muses; hence—shall I say restored, or rebuilt from the foundations—the celebrated academy of Heidelberg in your Palatinate, which had collapsed and almost been extinguished in the fury of Mars; hence chairs founded at your expense for teaching and learning every art, so that men of the greatest learning and cultivation from every quarter might gather at your Bensberg Athenaeum.

I say nothing of artists of every kind, painters, sculptors, and engravers, endowed with prizes and royal stipends, whom you invited to this training ground of all learning and every art.

In a word, you magnificently and generously prepared in Bensberg a refuge for both the gentler and the severer Muses.

Thus, most serene Prince, I already divided up that fortress of yours when it was not yet complete in every respect. Thus, I say, when I judged all these things to be most worthy of your intellect, your loftiness of mind, and your learning, other things were observed by my mind that seized me with still greater admiration and brought all value and esteem to those other accomplishments.

I mean those outstanding qualities of your inner spirit that shine with the splendor of Christian virtues: your highest love for God, and that strong love which animates all your other qualities; your piety, faith, and zeal for propagating it, with which God has heaped you so richly with favors that your subjects marvel at and rejoice over the Catholic cause, wonderfully enlarged under your leadership.

Let the non-Catholics—both the inhabitants of your territories and those nearby or more distant—gnash their teeth. Although they have often attacked you with complaints and injuries, they have tried in vain to obstruct and divert that zeal of yours, so worthy of a Catholic prince.

Those who have freer access to you had told me of your established and constant manner of dealing with God; your religious daily routine; the refreshment of your spirit through prayers, devotions, and sacred reading; and the occupations, constantly succeeding one another amid the administration of your territories, that you undertook with the supreme God, crowned by the never-interrupted sacrifice of the holy Mass.

Others had praised your prudence in handling affairs; your courage in carrying them out; the inviolable rigor of justice joined to innate clemency; piety joined to dignity; majesty joined to religion; and the highest greatness combined with innocence of life and moderation of spirit.

All these qualities displayed not merely the chief prince of your court, but an example attracting your subjects to every virtue and to the perfection of Christian holiness—attracting them, admonishing them through that attraction, and leading them onward through admonition.

I knew with what zeal you labored to increase the worship of God and to adorn churches, some of which you had splendidly repaired or built from their foundations.

In more than one place throughout your territories I had seen outstanding monuments of your veneration for the saints. I especially remembered the equestrian order restored not long ago in honor of Saint Aubert, which Gerard of Jülich had begun nearly three centuries earlier, so that, I believe, you might transfer even the innocent pleasure of hunting to the glory of God and the saints.

I knew how much you had contributed to the adornment of sacred relics and how much you were planning in order to make the blessed native woman Christina of Stommeln, or of Jülich, more illustrious through more celebrated worship.

But above all these things I revolved in my mind that singular veneration of yours for the saint whom I had honored in my first effort to illustrate the *Acts of the Saints*.

I speak of Raymond Lull, a great example of divine and human love, great both in the immense labors he undertook for the Catholic faith and sealed with his spilled blood, and in the writing of books—a prodigy of both nature and grace.

Your most recent and exceptional benevolence toward me on this saint’s account was fresh in my memory; and I openly and everywhere profess, with the happiest recollection, how gratefully I preserve that memory.

Allow me, most serene Prince, to announce to the whole world what will cause the whole world to marvel: the edition, undertaken by you after nearly four centuries and worthy of you alone among princes, of all the works of that blessed and prodigious man.

What need is there for me here to proclaim your diligence in searching out, summoning, and collecting works from every quarter? What need to mention the learned men sent in every direction, who brought them forth from the half-buried chests of libraries? What need to mention the expenses made and still to be made for this enterprise, so glorious to your name, under the auspices of the thrice-good and greatest God and of the blessed martyr himself?

I shall say boldly, most serene Prince, that in this matter you have accomplished what no prince, neither king nor emperor, has yet dared to undertake: so that, by a singular providence, this most ample addition might accrue to your glory, already sufficiently spread in every direction [Col. 0457].

Since I knew that you had expended all these efforts, most serene Prince, to advance the glory of the saints, and above all so that you might shape your life most religiously according to their examples, I could not doubt that this little gift of ours, however modest, would be most welcome to your serenity. Through it, examples of the saints are supplied each day—not of one alone, but of many—so that every day, as Augustine says, you may celebrate the memories of the martyrs with religious solemnity, both to stir imitation and to be joined to their merits and aided by their prayers.

Thus my Usuard comes confidently to you, most serene Elector—your Usuard, dedicated to you at almost the same time as he began to be illustrated.

Those who describe heroes born from the ancestral blood of Caesars and kings will have reason to recount and celebrate the distinction of your illustrious lineage, ennobled by so many emperors, kings, and other princes throughout Europe. They will praise not you, but your ancestors; indeed, they will praise you in all of them, since they will display in them your image revived.

But the honors of those forefathers, great-grandfathers, and remoter ancestors have already been sung so many times and adorned with so many panegyrics, and have been presented to the world through symbols and emblems, that if I linger over recalling them again, I might seem merely to be collecting the sayings of others and reweaving speeches already pronounced and long made public in entire volumes.

Those who have written in praise of the warriors of your family tree, famous for courage of spirit and deeds performed for their homeland and liberty, will also be able to exalt those qualities in you. They will praise your inviolable observance of treaties, by which, in the recent wars, you preferred to expose your territories and fortunes to the fury of the enemy and to throw yourself into danger rather than depart even by the breadth of a fingernail from the faith pledged to the Emperor and his allies.

Our Belgium saw this from close at hand and marveled when, at the beginning of the last war, you received—or shall I say laughed at—the enemy threatening your capital with approaching sword and fire, and with fearless constancy of spirit encouraged and strengthened subjects who were either terrified or fleeing.

Those who take up the task of praising a prince adorned with clemency, justice, and peaceful arts will offer you an image of yourself sketched in another.

They will praise the highly ordered administration of your provinces, however far separated from one another; they will praise the civil arts and restored commerce; they will praise your capital, Düsseldorf, so enlarged and adorned with more elegant houses that those who once saw it no longer recognize Düsseldorf as Düsseldorf.

They will speak of that new city, of its many vast buildings, established for the use of the poor, the elderly, and the military garrison; of its churches, chapels, and other structures intended no less for the cultivation of souls than for the support of bodies.

Finally, they will expand upon those most deserved praises for which your rejoicing subjects wished a bronze equestrian statue to be placed in the middle of the forum, as to the Father of the Fatherland.

But I, who consider above all in your fortress the virtues of a Christian prince—and those virtues not in your ancestors but chiefly in you; I, who contemplate your inner spirit more than the proofs of your power and magnificence; I put forward examples of Christian strength, constancy in faith, and blood poured out for Christ. These, to use Tertullian’s words, like registers and calendars, may transfer the mind from the perishing joys of the age to those that endure, and kindle it with desire for eternal things.

This work of ours, redolent of nothing but holiness, is an ornament to be brought into your Bensberg fortress; these are the insignia of a Christian hero, to be hung in the place of honor—namely, in that sacred building erected more magnificently than the rest of the palace, in which no ornament shines that does not breathe the glory of God and the veneration of the saints.

Since my Usuard clearly presents these things to you, and most manifestly explains these things about you among that illustrious company of saints, you will pardon me, most gracious Prince, if, in the open court before the palace gates, among the chambers recently described for the arts and virtues, I erect for you a statue more lasting than every bronze and every metal, since it will be cast from material that no tempest of the air, no rust of age, and no duration of time can ever corrupt, corrode, or overthrow.

I shall use neither chisel nor casting art, nor hammer.

The very body of the whole structure, representing you as the most serene prince, will be that most fervent love with which the innumerable martyrs contained in our Martyrology burned for Christ, and with which, now united most fervently to the highest Good, they wish for you the same eternal happiness.

Its base will consist of those dreadful instruments of execution upon which those very men were cruelly tortured and crucified. They will be outstanding incentives, urging the sluggishness of spectators toward Christian strength through the example of those martyrs and of yourself, more eloquently than any tongue and more powerfully than any speech.

In place of the supporting columns, four chief virtues of the martyrs will sustain the structure: living faith, unshaken hope, heroic courage, and unconquered endurance.

Countless other ornaments, received from the saints, will adorn it—especially from those who, although occupied with governing and ruling great empires, avoided the reefs of the corrupt age and restored an undefiled spirit to the Creator.

The great Charles, among your ancestors, will place the scepter in your hand. Following in his footsteps, the Catholic world recognizes you as protector of the Catholic faith and of the Roman See.

Henry will place the crown upon your head, such as he himself submitted to the Chair of Saint Peter in Christian piety.

Ferdinand the Catholic may gird you with a belt dyed purple with the blood of the Muslims, whose many thousands the legions of your country and the flower of its nobility, serving in Hungary under the most august and most pious Leopold, defeated to the immortal increase of your glory.

From England there will come Edwards; from France, Louises; from Hungary, Stephens; from Denmark, Canutes; from Sweden, Erics; from Bohemia, Wenceslauses; from Poland, Casimirs; and from every kingdom other princely citizens of heaven. All will compete to adorn your likeness—indeed, their living image in you—with the appropriate trophies.

Nor will kings and princes alone do this. That entire army of saints, spread far and wide throughout my Usuard [Col. 0459], will rejoice in your patronage, which you graciously permit me to invoke. In this compendium, as it were, of our *Acts*, I place them today under your protection—if I may so speak—under your patronage.

This shrine, most gracious Prince, I dedicate to you in the court of Bensberg; to you I consecrate it; I desire it to be an eternal monument of the unwavering devotion of myself and my companions to you and to your most serene family.

It may not improperly bear the inscription that was once your motto when traveling:

**The Lord of hosts is with us.**

But the following inscription is more suited to the work dedicated to you and to the statue erected:

**HIS PRAISE IS IN THE CHURCH OF THE SAINTS.**

Most serene and most gracious Prince,  
the most devoted client of Your Electoral Serenity,

**Joannes Baptista Sollerius, of the Society of Jesus**

# DECLARATION OF THE REVEREND FATHER SOLLERIUS

What my masters and colleagues repeatedly declared before the individual volumes of the *Acts of the Saints*—that throughout the entire work on the *Acts of the Saints* they wished to observe the constitutions of Pope Urban VIII, and that their commentaries, or those of others referred to therein, should carry no greater authority than history written by men liable to error—I likewise declare before this Martyrology of Usuard, which I have revised and illustrated.

# PREFACE

## A BRIEF SURVEY OF THE WHOLE WORK

1. Among the ancient martyrologists, none is more famous than Usuard, none more commonly used in the Church, none copied more often, and none dispersed through more editions—German, French, Italian, and Belgian—throughout Catholic Europe. Indeed, within approximately one hundred years it was printed nearly twenty times, as we shall explain more fully in the third chapter of this preface.

The zeal for printing that Martyrology later ceased, after the Roman Catholic Church prescribed for its use not merely any Usuard, but one adapted, enlarged, and reformed for its purposes and appointed to be used in the canonical office. Consequently, under a changed name, it began to be called the truly Roman Martyrology.

Thus the practice of reading the Usuardine Martyrology ceased in choirs, chapters, and other religious communities. Nevertheless, among lovers of hagiography and students of ancient ecclesiastical monuments there has remained, and still remains, an intense desire to see that very Martyrology restored to its native simplicity after so many editions that have not yet been fully purified, and completely cleansed of all additions.

This was long requested and long awaited in vain from the Reverend Benedictine Fathers of Paris, who boast possession of the author’s autograph, since he was once their fellow monk. Whether they voluntarily yielded that undertaking to us, as though we had long ago occupied it, I do not know. Certainly—and something that the world of letters has often had reason to wonder at—among so many *Analecta* issued to the public by those most learned men, no place has yet been granted to this Usuard, whether genuinely or supposedly represented by the autograph.

2. When I suggest here that the task of publishing the Usuardine Martyrology has been occupied by us, I wish this to be understood as referring to the edition once promised by Bollandus, as I shall soon show clearly from his *General Preface*, chapter 4, section 7.

Nor was that the only project contemplated by the founder of our vast work on the *Acts of the Saints*. He also intended to publish Martyrologies of every kind, so that nothing occurring in the *Acts* might delay learned readers.

It will be useful to hear Bollandus himself speaking in section 3 of the chapter cited. There, after listing the aids, supports, and resources collected and received from every quarter, and then proceeding to other monuments, he enumerates the calendars and fasts of various churches, breviaries, and instruments of that sort, from which an indication and opportunity are provided for investigating the *Acts of the Saints*.

He then continues as follows:

“But above all these things, the Martyrologies were also of great assistance to me. I intend one day to publish, carefully revised, at least those among the many that I possess which will prove most trustworthy, comparing them with those that our friends will meanwhile provide. Since, however, I mention here certain items that are not yet publicly available, lest anyone hesitate for that reason about my treating a few of them here, I have thought it necessary to say a little about them.”

Thus our standard-bearer, intending in his mind an edition not only of Usuard but also of other Martyrologies, judged most correctly and wisely at the very beginning of the great work. Before him, the first designer and collector of the monuments, Rosweyd, had judged the same.

For before undertaking the work already conceived in his mind, Rosweyd had prepared for the press a collection of the ancient Martyrologies then known—namely, Bede’s Martyrology published by Plantin, those of Usuard, Rabanus, Adō, and Notker, together with the modern Roman Martyrology and the Greek Menologion.

He prudently and wisely recognized that, for understanding so great a work as the *Acts of the Saints*, it was absolutely necessary to place beforehand a clear knowledge of the Martyrologies from which the cult of the saints is derived.

### 3.

The collection of Rosweyde mentioned above remained unpublished, written out in two large volumes, because our predecessors considered those Martyrologies sufficiently well known at that time. Nevertheless, they never abandoned the plan of publishing other manuscripts subsequently brought to light, although, while applying themselves more eagerly to advancing the work, they postponed the entire undertaking for several years. In the meantime, however, the genuine Bede appeared, distinguished from Florus’s additions with whatever degree of probability was then possible. How it was discovered and by what method it was edited is explained fully and clearly in the Prologue preceding the second volume for March; I judge it superfluous to reproduce that account here.

The manuscripts of the Hieronymian Martyrology were collected, illustrated with notes and studies, and published in 1667 by the distinguished scholar Franciscus Maria Florentinius, a nobleman of Lucca—the very year in which the genuine Bede also saw the light. Usuard remained. The aforementioned Bollandus had already remarked, in chapter 4, § 7 of the work cited above:

> “Several copies are preserved in our Museum, but in them the eulogies of the saints have been expanded and the names of many others inserted—such as those of the churches of Prague and Brussels, and of many monasteries, which it is not necessary to enumerate here. I shall do so elsewhere, when I publish Usuard, but with the native simplicity of the text, the various appendices being kept separate.”

Here, in the clearest terms, is the edition of Usuard’s Martyrology which, as I stated above, Bollandus had been planning for more than seventy years; yet neither he himself nor any of his subsequent colleagues ever afterward applied himself to it.

### 4.

Bollandus was not, as we have said, merely contemplating the production of a printed edition of Usuard. Having become accustomed to sifting and examining the manuscript copies of that Martyrology—frequently expanded, frequently corrupted, and frequently interpolated—and having recognized the confusion between those manuscripts and other Martyrologies, as well as observing that the names of Jerome and Bede had often been incorrectly prefixed to Usuardine manuscripts, he was, unless I am mistaken, aiming at the following: having mastered Usuard’s phrasing and style, he would distinguish him from all the rest, recover the native purity of the text, arrange the various appendices into their proper classes, and at the same time provide readers of our Acts with as much information as could then be obtained about the manuscript codices.

This projected edition would certainly have been a work worthy of Henschenius’s zeal, study, and supreme expertise in handling Martyrologies. Yet Henschenius preferred to employ his private learning in advancing the work rather than to provide for the convenience of posterity. Nor did Papebrochius devote much attention to the undertaking. When Henschenius had carried the laborious task of examining Martyrologies as far as the end of June, Papebrochius rightly foresaw that Henschenius’s labors would undoubtedly have to end there. The other colleagues, themselves occupied with more pressing matters, had left the entire project untouched.

### 5.

In the meantime, at the command of my superiors—having been ordered to place my shoulders beneath the burden of the enterprise, or, as Bollandus once playfully put it, of carrying heaven or the heavenly inhabitants—I thought that I ought to begin from this point, so that I might acquire knowledge of the hinges, elements, and supports of the whole work.

And behold, almost every day brought long series of Martyrologies, especially Usuardine ones. Anyone might have been deterred from pursuing so vast an undertaking merely by the great diversity of their names and distinguishing features, if he carefully considered how many and how varied were the prerequisites that had to be known beforehand before one could penetrate to their innermost structure. I am not ashamed to admit that I had to labor for years before I could adequately recognize even the distinctive features of the individual codices.

The difficulty was indeed considerable. Since the codices themselves bore various names, especially those of Jerome, Bede, and Ado, and since Henschenius had not taken care to assign them distinctly to their individual classes—for his own knowledge was sufficient for him—and since, moreover, the names assigned to the codices, whether to other codices or to Usuardine ones, had been taken from monasteries, churches, libraries, or cities and thereby produced confusion, it was necessary to compare nearly every manuscript individually before I could determine with certainty whether it belonged to the proper classes of the Hieronymian, Bede, Ado, or Usuard.

While I was laboriously engaged in unfolding, examining, and investigating these materials, the fifth volume for June was brought to completion. Since its greater bulk left insufficient space for the Supplement to the entire month, the thought of finally publishing Usuard’s Martyrology was opportunely revived. Together with the aforesaid Supplement, it would form the sixth volume for June and the final volume of the sacred half-year, as was indicated for the time being at the end of the aforementioned fifth volume.

### 6.

The purpose and entire structure of this new edition of Usuard’s Martyrology gradually reveal themselves—its distinctive method, that is, by which we have set ourselves to establish, explain, and verify day by day, from their sources, the native simplicity of Usuard’s text with the greatest diligence we can command. Our principal aim is that, together with the text of our Martyrology in its integrity, readers may come to know the age, character, reliability, authority, and every other feature of the Usuardine codices, so various and distinguished by so many names, that contributes to a perfect understanding of our monuments.

There will also be a continual comparison with the other Martyrologies, whatever their names or titles, whether transmitted in manuscripts or published in print. This comparison will be especially useful for understanding the thread of our Acts—or at least of our commentaries. In addition, nearly all the manuscripts will be described with such precision that any reasonably competent reader will be taught, almost at a single glance, to which series of Martyrologies the numerous codices cited there each day are to be assigned. I therefore persuade myself that this method will not only relieve readers’ weariness but also bring them considerable pleasure by presenting with greater clarity matters that are otherwise extremely obscure.

### 7.

From this you can also see the two principal—and most pressing—reasons that moved me to undertake this arduous labor. One concerned ourselves and our successors; the other concerned other lovers of sacred history, especially the readers of our Acts.

It was our concern to prevent difficulties from arising, so that future assistants in the work would not become entangled in those same labyrinths of extremely difficult investigations and spend many months, indeed years, with great weariness and little result merely to acquire an adequate idea of our Martyrologies. For outsiders, this investigation was necessary so that, without sufficient knowledge of the foundations and supports of our work, they might not remain perpetually hesitant for that reason, as Bollandus had wisely observed.

I remembered that this had happened to me hundreds of times. What could be more tiresome for a reader than to be overwhelmed on almost every page of our preliminary commentaries by a long procession of Martyrologies concerning which he might wonder whether they had ever existed in reality? Or, if in good faith he judged that they ought to be accepted, what could be more reasonable than for him at least to demand reliable information about the kind, provenance, age, style, and authority of the codices themselves? Once these matters had been weighed, he could, according to his own learning and expertise in such things, judge and prudently decide for himself the truth of all our assertions and arguments.

These considerations encouraged me to swallow enormous weariness, while at the same time instilling in me the strongest hope that our labor would not be unwelcome to all lovers of sacred history, and that they would allow Usuard a place in the Acts themselves—Usuard, who would bring no small measure of light for understanding the saints, and indeed many of their Acts themselves.

### 8.

Here, learned reader, you have in brief the true, open, and sincere reason for our entire Usuardine edition; here you have its plan, purpose, and method. I repeat and affirm that my chief aim was to separate from all others every codex belonging to Usuard’s lineage—codices of which our Museum possesses, if anywhere, a numerous store—whether we possess them intact or only the excerpts or variant readings that have survived from the collations made by Henschenius and Papebrochius with the codices themselves and with Greven’s Usuard. This will be demonstrated expressly when, in the third chapter of this preface, we reach Usuard himself and his descendants.

I shall now summarize what has been said as briefly as possible. We present Usuard with all additions removed, insofar as humanly possible. This is the first point. Then, in the observations appended to each day, we provide an exact account of the origin of the text that occurs there, tracing it back to its earliest roots and showing whether the commemoration in question was taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, from Bede, or from the little Roman Martyrology through Ado; whether it belongs properly to Ado alone; and finally whether Usuard borrowed it from some source other than Ado or the more ancient Martyrologies.

We also indicate whether the same saint, or group of saints, has not been recorded by Rabanus in the words of Jerome or Bede. Notker is not omitted either: we sometimes specify briefly which passages he transferred from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, which from Rabanus, and which finally from Ado. Thus, each day, I shall open a scene in which the reader may be properly instructed, almost at a single glance, concerning the entire relationship among all the Martyrologies—what one might call their closeness of blood or affinity. Wandalbertus is not excluded either: his metrical eulogies are inserted or appended to our observations whenever they mention the saint or saints of that day.

### 9.

This is the image, compressed into a brief table, of the entire work, which extends very widely; I shall explain it more accurately when I reach the third chapter.

Now briefly learn what has been accomplished by this preface. We divide the whole into three chapters. In the first, all the Martyrologies older than Usuard and contemporary with him are reviewed. They have some affinity with Usuard, but not such a close connection of blood, if I may use the expression, that they can properly claim the title of parents or primordial sources. These include works that are related to the Hieronymian Martyrologies or to Bede augmented by Florus, as well as those that have some proximity to them, such as the commonly known Martyrologies of Wandalbertus, Rabanus, and Notker.

I shall endeavor to attach to all of these their distinctive characteristics in such a way that anyone may easily distinguish them. A new discussion of the genuine Martyrologies of Bede and Florus will also occur, providing learned lovers of sacred history with material for further investigations.

Moreover, in the series of Martyrologies, the Hieronymian copies will lead the procession by right of antiquity: first the larger ones, as we call them, published by Florentinius; then the smaller ones, preserved in manuscript among us or published by others. Concerning these and the others I shall place before the eyes of lovers of Martyrologies such a delineation that lovers of Martyrologies may themselves assign the copies cited in great numbers in our Acts to their proper class and form a judgment concerning the quality and reliability of each codex.

### 10.

This will be followed by the second chapter, in which we shall approach Usuard himself more closely, first demonstrating the principal ancestor of his family, or his forefather in the direct line—namely, that old Roman Martyrology first published by Heribert Rosweyde and prefixed to Ado.

Here disputes will arise. Since that Martyrology has had, and still has, so many opponents, this chapter will have to be conducted polemically, so that its true title, authenticity, antiquity, and its transcription at Ravenna by Ado may be defended against every adversary. It will follow from this that it is the very work by which the Viennese Martyrologist was assisted, indeed the work from which he extracted most of his saints day by day.

Since we shall subsequently prove that Usuard was throughout his work Ado’s abridger and epitomizer, it may be clearly concluded that the old or little Roman Martyrology was Usuard’s grandfather and Ado his father. This will be discussed in the third chapter. Thereafter, in due order, will follow the whole progeny of Usuard—that is, all those Usuardine codices from which we have extracted the genuine text of his Martyrology, together with the appendices collected separately.

At first sight this material may seem somewhat obscure because of the excessive variety of matters largely unknown to most people. Throughout the course of the preface, however, it will, as I trust, be unfolded clearly and distinctly.

## CHAPTER ONE  
### The Relationship and Connection of the Ancient Martyrologies with One Another and with Usuard

### 11.

Much has already been discussed with great distinction by Molanus, Baronius, Bollandus, Henschenius, Papebrochius, Florentinius, and other most learned men concerning the origin, beginnings, and development of the Martyrologies, as well as their diversity according to the manner in which they were first compiled by various writers.

Interest in investigating these matters more deeply increased as greater light gradually became available, after the more ancient Martyrologies had been brought out of the archives of libraries and, through the benefit of printing, had begun to circulate in everyone’s hands. It is not relevant here to repeat what those most distinguished and well-known writers—especially our Bollandus—have explained clearly, distinctly, and learnedly.

There is one matter in which I observe that all of them fell short—if I may be forgiven for saying so. I mean that, by describing only the authors, age, and certain characteristics of the individual Martyrologies, they failed to penetrate far enough to compare them with one another and thereby investigate which were the primordial heads of the Martyrologies; what kind of derivation or origin the others had from earlier works; and consequently what connection, relationship, proximity, affinity, or kinship existed among all the Martyrologists.

Permit me to use these terms in order to illuminate, with as much clarity as I can, a matter hitherto tangled and confused.

I have already called all the classical Martyrologies—that is, those enjoying the prerogative and authority of antiquity—by their proper names: the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, Florus, the little Roman Martyrology, Rabanus, Wandalbertus, Ado, Usuard, and Notker. The question here is what order—or, shall I say, what subordination—exists among them: who are the great-grandfathers, who the fathers, who the sons, who the relatives? In a word, by what degrees of relationship do they touch one another?

### 12.

I am of the opinion that all the Martyrologists—or rather, their Martyrologies—can be reduced principally to three heads, roots, trunks, or sources. Their shoots, branches, or streams should be understood to include all the works that have so far been published under at least some name, or that remain in manuscript in various libraries, from which copies have been sent to our Museum by friends or obtained by our predecessors through great labor and expense.

By “heads” I mean those Martyrologies that should be regarded as primary or autograph works, insofar as they were not transcribed from any other surviving work but were themselves sources from which other Martyrologists derived their streams.

The first, principal, and most ancient of these is the work circulated under the name of Eusebius—or rather of Jerome, or of both—whether it was truly composed by them or falsely attributed to them by later generations. This matter will be treated more fully shortly.

Next to it in place stands the celebrated work composed by the Venerable Bede—not the spurious one published by Plantin, but the genuine work itself. We shall later show that it was augmented by Florus, the famous subdeacon of the Church of Lyon, as Ado clearly and explicitly testifies.

Third, we identify that very work which the aforesaid Ado found at Ravenna and, having received it there from a religious brother, transcribed and judged worthy of placing at the head of his own Martyrology. It was first brought to light together with Ado through the care of our Rosweyde in 1613. Many subsequently praised it, but even more fiercely attacked it; we have undertaken to defend it in the entire following chapter.

### 13.

I call these the primary trunks or stocks, from which the entire lineage of the Martyrologies is distributed into three principal classes, tribes, or primordial families.

Of these, the Hieronymian Martyrology must again be proclaimed the primary and most widely extended root. As the most ancient of all, it is also the most fertile soil, in which trees were born that extended their branches in every direction. By this I mean that nearly all the other Martyrologists transferred something from that primary work into their own.

It seems possible to deduce from the words of Bede himself, which will be cited below, that he saw Jerome’s Martyrology; indeed, I would scarcely dare deny that some names of saints very probably passed from one work into the other.

Whether the same can equally be affirmed of the old or little Roman Martyrology, I confess that it is not yet clear to me in every respect, although I have tried most diligently to reach a conclusion through lengthy and careful investigation.

Nevertheless, we also regard Bede as a head of the Martyrologists, especially because he composed his own Martyrology in a distinctive order and style, although incomplete. It was first augmented by Florus and then by others—indeed, I would almost say disfigured—yet it always preserves certain traces by which it can be distinguished from the others. Henschenius and Papebrochius accurately observed this before me when they published it, either pure or very close to pure, before the second volume for March of the Acts of the Saints in 1668.

These remarks have been made only in passing and will be explained more fully in their proper places throughout this chapter.

### 14.

Our fundamental assertion, therefore, is that all the others descend by legitimate succession, in one way or another, from these three patriarchs of the Martyrologists. Such are Rabanus, Ado, Usuard, Notker, and all those who are found to have derived their material from these works as secondary trunks.

From which particular root that metrical Martyrologist Wandalbertus sprang, I have not established with certainty. Some have wished to derive him from Bede; he himself admits that he first received assistance from Florus. I regard him as a gatherer of flowers who plucked here and there various names of saints, perhaps those better suited to verse. I shall speak more fully about him in his proper place.

It is certain, however, that Rabanus was copied from Bede, augmented from Jerome, and completed by its author with certain additions and fuller developments.

Ado pointed to his progenitor with his finger when he prefixed the little Roman Martyrology to his own work and, on almost every day, most evidently drew his saints from it.

It is no less certain that the whole of Usuard’s Martyrology was abridged from Ado, combined with the Cordoban martyrs, some Hieronymian saints, some local saints, and a few others borrowed from elsewhere. Usuard himself testifies that he also followed Bede, and we carefully note this in our observations whenever he speaks of it.

Nevertheless, we declare Ado to be his father, or true source, and we consider it beyond doubt that nearly his entire Martyrology flowed from him.

Finally, Notker transferred most of his principal material from the praised Ado, made a considerable amount of Rabanus his own, and scraped together many passages from Jerome to complete the lists for individual days.

These, then, are the propositions that our preface will demonstrate distinctly and systematically, insofar as the subject requires or has not already been dealt with by our predecessors.

## ARTICLE I  
### On the Manuscripts of the Hieronymian Martyrology

### § 1. On the Larger Manuscripts Published by Acherius and Florentinius

### 15.

In the recently praised general preface, chapter 4, Bollandus devotes the entire fourth paragraph to elucidating the Martyrology that bears the name of Eusebius and Jerome. There he first admits that it has not been sufficiently proved that such a Martyrology was ever written by Eusebius, nor can this be clearly deduced from Gregory’s letter to Eulogius.

Again, it is not certain that a work of Eusebius—whether a Martyrology or a commentary on the martyrs—was translated by Jerome, or that some other such work was written by the holy Doctor, whatever certain people may think they can establish from the famous letter of the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus to Jerome, and from Jerome’s reply to them. Baronius has demonstrated with solid arguments that both letters are spurious. Consequently, if such a letter was ever truly cited by Cassiodorus, it must be admitted that it has perished.

This is the more common opinion today among learned men. Florentinius, however, attempts through laborious annotations, beginning on page 57, to show that it can be challenged and that the said letters can in some fashion be defended against the charge of forgery.

In any case, while that dispute is still pending, Cassiodorus’s testimony seems to establish conclusively that Jerome compiled some sort of list or Calendar—whether it was written in the form of a letter or under some other title—in which the names of those saints whose Acts appeared in Eusebius’s collection may perhaps have been recorded. Eusebius himself mentions this collection in book 4, chapter 14, and book 5, chapter 20, and Eulogius mentions it in his letter to Gregory. Jerome may have added others of his own. From this arose and gradually hardened the long-standing opinion that a Martyrology had been composed by the holy Jerome.

### 16.

The antiquity of this opinion, reaching back to the sixth century, is supported by Cassiodorus’s authority, in chapter 32 of his book On the Institution of Divine Readings, as quoted by Bollandus.

For the seventh century there is Bede’s well-known testimony in his Retractation on the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 1:

> “The book of the Martyrology also bears witness to this, being entitled with the name and preface of the blessed Jerome, although Jerome is said not to have been the author of that book but its translator, while Eusebius was its author.”

The aforesaid opinion then passed down to later generations, confirmed in the clearest terms by Walafrid Strabo and by most of the Martyrologists of the ninth century. It has endured to the present, although for many centuries afterward no one mentioned this Martyrology, and although Baronius, despite applying the greatest diligence, was nowhere able to find it complete.

At last our Rosweyde fortunately extracted it from the Carthusian monastery at Trier, written in a most ancient script. We possess almost half of it impressed on copper plates, while the autograph itself was finally returned in 1668 to the people of Echternach, who had reclaimed their codex.

One may add what Papebrochius discussed in his prologue to Bede. Here we follow Bollandus, whose words deserve to be transcribed.

### 17.

> “When Bartholomaeus Gavantus, provincial superior of the Congregation of Clerics Regular of Saint Paul and consultor of the Sacred Roman Congregation of Rites, saw several printed leaves sent to him by Moretus—for whose expense that codex had begun to be engraved on copper—he approved them enthusiastically. He wrote several letters about it to Moretus, which I have read. In some he expressed the opinion that the Martyrology would be ‘VERY PLEASING’ to the wisest men of the rest of that college or congregation; in others he said that ‘THE MORE EXPERIENCED MEN THINK IT WILL BE USEFUL TO THE CHRISTIAN COMMONWEALTH.’ Other learned men also praised it enthusiastically as a distinguished monument of sacred antiquity.”

See there the remainder of Bollandus’s fuller and polished commendation of the aforesaid codex.

All learned men subsequently adopted the opinion of Gavantus and Bollandus—at least all orthodox scholars, with only a few exceptions. These few, driven by a desire to contradict, did not dare altogether to reject the work itself but began to nibble at its title, perhaps because Bollandus acknowledged that no certain argument was available by which it could be sufficiently demonstrated that the Martyrology had truly been composed by Saint Jerome, and because he admitted—as is entirely true—that many passages had been added at a later date and could in no way be attributed to Jerome, as is made perfectly clear by the specimens appended there.

Yet what harm to the republic of letters or to the Catholic faith did those most learned men imagine would result from allowing the name of Jerome to remain attached to that Martyrology, when they could never prevent it from continuing to be called Hieronymian after Cassiodorus, Bede, Walafrid, Ado, Usuard, Notker, and others?

I touch on these matters only briefly and in passing. Anyone who wants a fuller discussion should consult Florentinius’s Preliminary Admonitions, especially admonitions 3, 5, and 6. I have neither the time nor any particular desire to reproduce or abridge them here, since that would involve a contentious dispute over a name.

### 18.

I know of one Catholic writer who deliberately dared to attack the Martyrology under discussion: Henricus Valesius, in a special dissertation appended to his observations on Eusebius, on page 315. There he calls it a spurious book falsely attributed to Jerome.

Relying on him, and eager—as usually happens—to find an opportunity for mocking orthodox writers, a certain Matthias Fredericus Beckius gathered much material in his commentary on some German Calendar—for he prefers to call it a Martyrology—beginning on page 11. By rashly criticizing our predecessors, he tries to demonstrate that the Martyrology should in no way be attributed to Jerome. He does so on the basis of certain quibbles, to which he adds a sharper and more biting flavor drawn here and there from the doubts sincerely put forward by Florentinius and others.

But this is not important enough for us either to examine or to overturn all his little arguments. It will be enough for us if, by the common agreement of Catholics, it may bear the name of Jerome and thus safely be called Hieronymian, even though the monuments by which we could certainly vindicate it for the most holy Doctor are lacking.

Our predecessors judged in this way; learned men everywhere speak in this way today; and throughout our entire work we have decided always to use the designation “Jerome’s” or “Hieronymian,” that is, “of the Hieronymians.”

### 19.

As I said, the entire matter is examined more deeply by the distinguished and repeatedly praiseworthy Franciscus Maria Florentinius, a nobleman of Lucca and, while he lived, a very close friend of our predecessors. After defending Eusebius’s collections and books or booklets of the martyrs—not only of Palestine but also of other regions—he rightly observes near the end of page 13:

> “It is sufficient for the present to affirm concerning the author of the properly so-called Martyrology … that the Martyrology attributed to Eusebius, or rather to Saint Jerome on the basis of Eusebius’s collections, is the older one in the memory of writers.”

On the following page, 14, he learnedly proves that the Martyrology of Jerome which he published corresponds exactly to the characteristics attributed by Saint Pope Gregory to his own codex.

Since Florentinius himself published the Martyrology so often mentioned, after collecting several copies of it in 1668, and since he illustrated it with extremely learned notes, observations, and studies, some matters must be explained for a fuller understanding of the whole question—both concerning his codices and concerning other materials belonging to the Hieronymian Martyrology.

Nor should I fail to indicate why, both here and throughout the work, I have preferred to use the term “Hieronymian” rather than “Jerome’s.” Since the nature of Saint Jerome’s own work is unknown, while the copies are numerous and have been augmented and abridged in very different ways, I thought that the more general term would cut off opportunities for quibbling by attributing to the codices themselves what must certainly be removed from the first author.

Here, then, is something of a portrait of Florentinius’s labor.

### 20.

Among the various Preliminary Admonitions, the sixth is devoted almost entirely to describing two Hieronymian codices found at Lucca or in its vicinity. They had either been brought there from Gaul or copied from some manuscript of the monastery of Fontenelle; in any case, they were so similar that they must either have been taken from the same exemplar or one copied from the other.

When Florentinius acquired them, he was, as a man most devoted to the study of ancient ecclesiastical matters, advised by the distinguished Luca Holstenius and other learned men. He subsequently obtained from our predecessors—who had at times lodged with him—a copy of that most ancient manuscript from Antwerp or Echternach, written at the beginning of the eighth century. He was further supplied with the manuscript fragments of the Corbie codex published by Acherius in volume 4 of the Spicilegium in 1661.

Equipped with these materials, he turned his attention to producing an edition of such precious treasures and to illustrating it, with whatever care and study his learning could provide.

When the work was almost ready for the press, the illustrious Baron de Blum happened to communicate another codex, from Weissenburg, to Henschenius and Papebrochius. They immediately arranged for it to be sent to Lucca, sufficiently in time for it to be compared with the other codices and for its variant readings to be appended to the end of Florentinius’s work.

This is a brief summary of the history. Anyone who wants a complete and fuller account should consult Florentinius himself, who explains the plan of his entire undertaking and the purpose of publishing the work in the first admonition. A letter from Holstenius is appended there; most of it was reproduced by Papebrochius in his Responses, in the appendix to article 18, beginning at number 49.

Florentinius discusses his own codex—or perhaps his two codices—in detail in the sixth admonition, while the Antwerp codex and the Corbie fragments are treated in the seventh, beginning on page 30. I prefer to leave all of these matters to be read there rather than tediously report them here, since they concern our present purpose only insofar as, in reviewing them, we sketch at least a rough idea of the Martyrologies that are generally the archetype, or original ancestor.

### 21.

Here I should insert a brief but useful observation concerning an opinion very commonly accepted by our predecessors and widely disseminated throughout the commentaries to our Acts. They were convinced that the Echternach codex, the principal one among the Hieronymian manuscripts, was English and had been brought from England to Belgium, or Gaul, by Saint Willibrord himself.

It was certainly easy to form such a conjecture, but it does not seem to me sufficiently well founded. All lovers of Martyrologies will agree with me if they observe that, on 22 June—the tenth day before the Kalends of July—the celebrated protomartyr of England, Alban, together with more than eight hundred companions, is omitted from the aforesaid Echternach manuscript, although he is clearly recorded in the other codices published by Florentinius.

Who would believe that such a saint would be omitted from an English codex?

Our aforementioned predecessors add that the codex was augmented in Gaul. This is true, but the same must plainly be admitted of all the other codices as well, unless we wish to say that Saint Jerome could have recorded the death of Saint Paulinus on 22 July.

These remarks about the Echternach codex are incidental. More is said about it and the other codices in the observations. I now return to the point from which I digressed.

### 22.

To repeat once more: I shall not return to the dispute concerning the true author of the Hieronymian Martyrology, whether he was ultimately someone other than Saint Jerome or Jerome himself, the first architect of the little calendar. Whoever he was, he must be considered older than the sixth century, or at least to have lived in that century.

It seems entirely certain to us that Saint Gregory the Great referred to such a Martyrology when he replied to Eulogius of Alexandria in book 7, letter 29:

> “For our part, we have the names of almost all the martyrs collected in one codex, with their passions distinguished according to the individual days, and each day we celebrate the solemnities of Mass in their honor. Yet in the same volume it is not indicated how each one suffered; only the name, place, and day of suffering are given. Thus it happens that, from different lands and provinces, many are recognized as crowned with martyrdom on the several days, as I have said. But we believe that you, most blessed men, possess these things.”

No great diligence, skill, or labor is required to detect clearly in the Hieronymian codices published by Florentinius, and in others of the same kind, all the characteristics expressed so plainly by Saint Gregory. In this way the frequent interpolations can be separated from the ancient text.

We do not claim, however, to possess bare, simple, and complete Hieronymian—or Gregorian—codices, since many saints frequently recur whose lives demonstrably belong to the period after Saint Gregory, or who at least had not yet been honored as saints in his time.

On these matters one may again consult Bollandus and the Florentinian admonitions cited above.

To put it in a single statement: this is what we seek, what we desire, and what we affirm—that the Martyrology which we call Hieronymian is the first and most ancient of all, indeed older than the times of Gregory the Great, since in the letter cited above he refers not to some newly composed list or catalogue of martyrs but to an ancient one, which he believed had been received and used throughout the entire Catholic world, when he concludes:

> “But we believe that you, most blessed men, possess these things.”

### 23

In such exceedingly ancient codices, copied so many times by careless and unlearned scribes, who could reasonably look for distinct series of saints, carefully separated lists, correctly written names, rules of good expression preserved according to the art, or exact details of events? It must be admitted outright that, on almost every day, there repeatedly occur immense confusion, barbarism, and useless repetitions of places and names, produced by syllables joined together or badly divided, and very often truncated and distorted. Florentinius labors everywhere to restore, explain, combine, and distinguish these as best he can, and the daily commentaries show how much work and study our predecessors devoted to excavating this material [Col. 0472A]. Those commentaries are entirely occupied with forming certainty from doubtful readings, clarity from confused ones, simplicity from badly arranged material, and complete names from dislocated fragments—both the names of the places of contest and those of the martyrs themselves.

Moreover, this is the common fate of all ancient codices, especially those intended for regular use, such as Martyrologies: through the carelessness or incompetence of their copyists they are gradually so disfigured that it is often extremely difficult to detect the traces of the first autograph in the transcripts. Thus I have been deeply astonished, with Castellanus, that in the *Romanum parvum*, or the old Martyrology of Rosweyde, everything could have been preserved for so many centuries so neatly, clearly, and orderly. In this respect, certainly, this Martyrology surpasses the Hieronymian Martyrologies by as much as the latter surpass them in antiquity. This will be demonstrated more fully in the following chapter, as we have already said more than once [Col. 0472B].

### 24

It remains for me to offer, as a sample of each, a few observations concerning our Hieronymian codices, which have not yet been published and are mostly abbreviated, in case it should someday prove worthwhile to make them public as well. I was frequently and most urgently urged to do this by a man whom I must often name here, though I can never praise him as he deserves: an indefatigable helper both in this work and in our larger undertaking, the distinguished Claudius Castellanus, canon of Paris at the Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary. To our profound grief, and with immense loss to the Martyrology, he was taken from this life at the beginning of 1711.

The illustrious man’s opinion was that not only would the Usuardian recension be most welcome to the literary world [Col. 0472C], but that all learned men had a kind of rightful claim upon us to publish our remaining Hieronymian copies, whether complete, abridged, or epitomized. I gave my dearest friend hope that this would one day happen, especially if the Martyrology enthusiasts themselves should approve by their votes our efforts in purging and illustrating Usuard, which I was then planning. In this way they would encourage us to provide a general account of all our manuscript codices, which, in relation to our commentaries, would—as I said above concerning the Usuardian manuscripts—bring readers the light they most eagerly desire.

Nor am I retreating from my promises. Accordingly, to gratify somewhat the taste of those who love such matters, I willingly append here a brief outline of our Hieronymian codices [Col. 0472D], intending, if circumstances permit, to provide more later, once I have tested the various tastes of the hagiophiles.

## § II — On the Minor Hieronymian Martyrologies, Both Manuscript and Printed

### 25

Near the end of the fourth section of the fourth chapter of the general preface cited above, Bollandus discusses a certain Irish Hieronymian exemplar. Several scraps or extracts from it, sent by the celebrated Father Colgan, had been inserted into our January volumes of the *Acts of the Saints* under the name of the Tamlacht Hieronymian Martyrology.

Whether Bollandus ever saw the membrane autograph itself is doubtful. He considers this Tamlacht Martyrology similar to the Echternach one, although in truth it can only be called a fragment of some Hieronymian Martyrology. I became fully convinced of this when, through the kindness of the Reverend Father Livinus de Meyer—an exceptionally distinguished benefactor of the literary republic and at that time rector of our Louvain college—I was able to examine and scrutinize the autograph itself, which had been obtained from the Irish Franciscan Fathers.

Castellanus’s curiosity had especially prompted me to do this. Finding the Tamlacht Martyrology cited, and even praised, several times in the *Acts*, he had become firmly persuaded that a great treasure lay hidden at Louvain. After a careful examination, however, I readily perceived that the codex had been raised and commended by our predecessors far above its merits. They had received only extracts from the Irish Friars Minor—or from Colgan—as Papebrochius often testified to me [Col. 0473B].

For, besides containing interspersed Irish material of its own, it is not without several more recent additions, such as the feast of Saint Joseph, the Revelation of Michael the Archangel, All Saints, and several similar entries. On the other hand, of the twelve months of the year it contains only April in its entirety. Here, briefly, is its complete analysis.

### 26

The aforesaid codex contains ten large-format parchment leaves, covered by another similar leaf. On the front, in a more recent hand, is written: “The Tamlacht Martyrology and the works of Saint Aengus the Culdee.” At the bottom margin of the first page one reads: “For the use of the Dungall convent”; and again, at the foot of the third page: “From the books of the Dungall convent.”

The Martyrology itself is neither well written nor sufficiently orderly in arrangement [Col. 0473C]. It occupies only ten pages and nearly half of another, filled everywhere with many names that are scarcely legible. It is lacking from the fourth day before the Kalends of February to the fourth day before the Ides of March; consequently neither January nor March is complete, and the whole of February is absent. As I have already said, only April is complete. May continues up to the twentieth day, that is, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June. June and July are absent. August begins with the fourth day before the Nones, and its remaining days are present. In September, the twelfth, eleventh, and tenth days before the Kalends of October are missing. October continues to the third day before the Kalends of November. The whole of November is absent, while December begins with the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January.

It is therefore clear that the manuscript is thoroughly defective and scarcely deserving of being counted among the Hieronymian codices. After this somewhat irregular Martyrology there follows, over three leaves, some sort of list of names—Irish names, I believe—and finally some works or fragments of works written in a language which I confess I do not understand at all [Col. 0473D]. Let this suffice concerning the Tamlacht Martyrology.

### 27

Bollandus next gives a specimen of a more abbreviated Hieronymian Martyrology which once belonged to the monastery of Rheinau, or Rhinow, near Basel. It was found among Rosweyde’s papers, and he had received it in 1623 from our Stephen Vitus, then abbot of the monastery of Rheinau, as the surviving letter testifies. The letter correctly calls this Martyrology a fragment, since leaves are missing from the eighth day before the Kalends of February to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, and from the twenty-seventh day of September to the twenty-fourth day of December.

It begins with the earthly birthday of Jesus Christ [Col. 0474A]. There are thirteen parchment leaves, in a larger octavo format, written in a good and ancient script, clearly displaying even the diphthongs. Vitus rightly judged that this fragment had been written after the days of Saint Gregory the Great and after the time of Charlemagne; for, he says, “in their proper places I read the feasts of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin and of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross.”

That it is genuinely Hieronymian, or extracted from a Hieronymian Martyrology, is clearly demonstrated by the specimens supplied by Bollandus and by the many other entries in the following days. I shall add one example from 1 July, which will subsequently recur throughout all our following manuscript copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology. Suppose, then, that I compare all the texts marked for 1 July in these codices with the complete Hieronymian text for the same day.

### 28

I shall first set out here the entire text for 1 July from the oldest of all the Hieronymian codices, the Antwerp or Echternach manuscript. The reader may later compare with it the shorter lists of the other codices cited below. It reads:

**The Kalends of July.** At Nicomedia, Zoilus. At Rome, the deposition of Gaius, bishop. The birthday of Lucia, virgin, and of Anceia, king, with eight others. Likewise at Rome, Isicius, Processus, Marina, Antoninus, Serenus, Victor, and Zelius with eight others. Orion and 262 others. At Antioch, Severianus, Zoelus, and Pasus. The deposition of Idoneus with his sons. At Augustodunum, the deposition of Leontius, bishop. In Persia, the holy apostles Simon the Cananaean and Jude, the brother of James.

The Lucensian and Corbeian manuscripts are somewhat fuller. The former insert the deposition of Aaron and add Egolisma and Eparchus. The latter further add the deposition of Karilefus. But we, together with Bollandus, shall follow our codex, older and more excellent than the others, as the archetype.

Now attend to the wording of the Rheinau fragment:

**The Kalends of July.** At Nicomedia, Zoelus. At Rome, Gaius the pope. Lucia, virgin. Processus and Marinus. Perhaps for Marina.

When the words of the two lists are compared, scarcely a syllable will be found that was not taken and copied from the larger list. Let us now proceed to our other codices, which are for the most part more expansive.

### 29

Among them, the most famous in our *Acts* is the Reichenau, or Augia the Rich, near Constance in Germany. We possess a carefully written copy of it in a small quarto format, and I find that we first received it in 1651. Nothing has been recorded concerning the format or age of the autograph codex. I seem to remember that Henschenius discussed these matters more fully somewhere; but I shall not investigate, since it is otherwise sufficiently clear that the codex is of excellent quality and, unless I am greatly mistaken, much purer and superior to the Gellone manuscript published by d’Achery in volume XIII of the *Spicilegium*, although it lacks the *Breviary of the Apostles* prefixed to the Gellone Martyrology.

Let us set out here the text of both for 1 July, to be compared with the larger Hieronymian text already transcribed. The Reichenau manuscript reads:

**The Kalends.** At Nicomedia, Zoelus. At Rome, Gaius the pope, Lucia, virgin, Processus, Marinus. At Antioch, Severianus. On Mount Hor, the deposition of Aaron the priest. At Augustodunum, Leontius, bishop.

It is again obvious that everything is Hieronymian [Col. 0475A] and extracted from the larger codex, into which the deposition of Aaron, mentioned above, had already been inserted.

Now hear the Gellone manuscript from d’Achery’s edition:

**The Kalends of July.** At Rome, Gaius, Lucia, and Isicius. Elsewhere, Orion, Crilifus the confessor, Zoelus, and Severianus. On Mount Or, the deposition of Aaron the priest. In Persia, the apostles Simon and Jude. At Augustodunum, Leontius. At Ingolisma, Eparchus, bishop.

Here you see Pope Gaius placed confusedly, while Karilefus has been absurdly mixed in with others, including martyrs. Eparchus has also been added at the end; neither this Eparchus nor Karilefus is mentioned by the Reichenau codex. Thus the latter is, in this respect, more worthy of the light than the other, as may perhaps be demonstrated elsewhere by fuller and continuous examples.

In any event, both Martyrologies, the Reichenau as well as the Gellone, begin the year with the Nativity of the Lord [Col. 0475B], unlike many others to be cited below, which take their beginning from the Kalends of January.

### 30

We possess two other Hieronymian copies which, as I learned from a more careful comparison, agree more closely with the Gellone manuscript.
