One, mostly transcribed by Papebrochius’s hand in a smaller format, is called the Augsburg Martyrology of Saint Ulrich; it is mutilated at the end, from 6 November through the end of the year. The other is complete: a gift from our Labbe, written in folio in a Belgian script.

Both begin with the Kalends of January. To avoid weariness, I shall once again give only 1 July as an example. The Augsburg manuscript reads:

**The Kalends of June.** At Rome, Gaius, Lucia, and Isicius. Elsewhere—abbreviated *alibi*—Urion, Arileffus the confessor, Zoelus, and Severianus. On Mount Hor, the deposition of Aaron the priest. In Persia, Simon the Cananaean and Jude the Zealot. At Augustodunum, Leontius and Eparchus, bishop.

I am mistaken if any greater conformity can be found between the Gellone and this Augsburg manuscript. The same conformity shines out everywhere on other days, despite a word being here inserted, there corrupted, elsewhere transposed or abbreviated.

Nor is the Labbe manuscript much different. It likewise reads the Kalends of July, although the order of the names has been somewhat disturbed by the scribe’s carelessness:

At Rome, Zoelus, Severianus, Usicius, and Arilesa. On Mount Or, the deposition of Anton the priest. In Persia, Simon and Jude the apostles. At Augustodunum, Leontius. At Eclisma, Eparchius, bishop. Gaius, Unon, and Lucia.

Correct the displaced names and restore the last three to their proper place after “At Rome,” and the same text emerges that we have already given from the Gellone and Augsburg manuscripts, disregarding the minor details that those who have devoted even a little effort to examining ancient manuscripts know to recur in them with extraordinary frequency [Col. 0475D]. Codices of this kind could perhaps be counted among those which d’Achery compared with the Gellone manuscript, supplying variant readings from them.

### 31

The two codices just mentioned are preceded in our collection of Hieronymian manuscripts by another copy, much shorter, written in an elegant French hand in folio. I read the following notes attached to it:

“An exceedingly ancient Martyrology, written at least eight hundred years ago, copied from the most ancient manuscript of the Corbie abbey, in December 1661.”

At the end Papebrochius added:

“Given by the Reverend Lord Luke d’Achery, from the most ancient Corbie manuscript, which we ourselves saw in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.”

Such an ancient monument deserved a place in the *Spicilegium*. Perhaps the learned man believed that we would someday publish it with the others from the copy, as we have already mentioned that the distinguished Castellanus desired with such ardent wishes.

This codex differs from those immediately preceding it in beginning the order of the Martyrology with the eighth day before the Kalends of January, that is, with the Nativity of the Lord the Savior. Its texts are always extremely brief and generally confined to a single announcement, often to a single saint; nevertheless, it is clear that everything was taken from some Hieronymian codex.

Let us again give a selected day as an example, one furnished here with a somewhat longer text:

**The Kalends of July.** At Rome, Gaius the pope, and the birthday of the holy Lucia, virgin, and Aucea, king. In Persia, the passion of the holy apostles Simon the Cananaean and Jude the Zealot—“Zealot” being used for *Zelotes* [Col. 0476B].

The same arrangement is followed on the subsequent days. Its great brevity, however, does not prevent it from occasionally inserting matters proper to the Corbie community, as is clear from the fifth day before the Kalends of August, that is, 28 July, where it reads:

“At the Corbie monastery, the dedication of the basilica of Saint Peter the apostle.”

### 32

Two Casinensian copies follow, written in an Italian hand. Papebrochius mentions them in the *Prologue to Bede*, section 3. Would that either he or Henschenius, who had them transcribed, had added some clearer explanation of them.

The first is shorter than the other and cannot be called a pure Hieronymian Martyrology, since it inserts saints taken from elsewhere. In its brevity it agrees sufficiently with other abbreviated Hieronymian Martyrologies [Col. 0476C], as well as in recording only the names of saints and places of contest. I shall present the entire matter by an example. It reads:

**The Kalends of July.** The octave of Saint John the Baptist. And the birthday of Saint Domitian, abbot.

The first announcement comes from some interpolated Hieronymian Martyrology, such as the Saint Gall manuscript appended by d’Achery to the Gellone manuscript; the second is plainly Adonian, as may be seen in our observation on that day in our commentary on Usuard.

The other Casinensian manuscript, somewhat fuller, comes closer to the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Papebrochius rightly says of it in the immediately cited section 3:

“There were also churches for which the bare text of the Hieronymian Martyrology, contracted to fewer saints, was sufficient. Such is the other Martyrology we found at Monte Cassino, likewise exceedingly ancient, and very similar to it, at Rome in the celebrated library of Duke Altemps.”

The comparison made between the two is indicated by the variations, even the smallest, carefully marked in Papebrochius’s own hand.

How much this larger Casinensian manuscript should be preferred to the smaller one may be judged from the customary example:

**The Kalends of July.** At Rome, Gaius the pope. And the holy Lucia, virgin, and Acecla, king, with eight others. And on Mount Hor, the deposition of Aaron, the first priest.

Everywhere you see scribal errors committed through the incompetence of the copyists, while the texts have been extended more or less according to the discretion of the various scribes. Both begin with the Kalends of January.

### 33

From the parchment codex of Cardinal Barberini, in quarto and marked number 1852, two further but incomplete copies were produced [Col. 0477A]. Papebrochius transcribed one of them; he began the second, but it was completed by the same hand that wrote the two Casinensian manuscripts mentioned above.

The first begins with the Kalends of January and is defective from the second day before the Nones, that is, 6 May. It is not uniform, for here and there it presents eulogies in its own distinctive clauses. For example, concerning Genovefa on 3 January:

“Whose relics we honor as is due, offering Masses and prayers.”

On 10 January, concerning Paul the hermit:

“For this is also how he is commemorated among us, and his relics are venerated.”

On 16 January, concerning Priscilla:

“Whose glorious struggle for Christ we worthily venerate together with her patronage, and whose daily office we perform, as the holy Fathers have decreed.”

Again, concerning Furseus:

“Whose life shines forth full of virtues, and whose venerable body the monastery at Péronne preserves.”

On the following day, 17 January, concerning Sulpicius of Bourges, bishop:

“Whose life we possess, and by whose patronage we are supported.”

I do not remember finding formulas for eulogies of this kind in any Martyrologies up to the present. It is therefore sufficiently clear that this compiler indulged his own inclination. In other respects, however, he is briefer and conforms more closely to the Hieronymian style.

### 34

The second Barberini manuscript is much larger and more extensive, but is mutilated through the first two and a half months, since its first complete day is marked as the Ides of March. Henschenius repeatedly called it an “illustrious Martyrology,” although I have not been able to discover that this distinctive honor is deserved in any significant sense—at least not in such a way that it should be preferred to the two others that immediately follow, namely the Vatican Hieronymian codex and the other codex of Saint Cyriacus used by Cardinal Baronius [Col. 0477C].

I do not see why it should be preferred to them, unless it is because here and there it inserts both saints and eulogies more freely and at greater length, as we shall understand from the *Prologue to Bede* in the following section. Certainly the two later manuscripts surpass it in being closer to the Hieronymian style. In this respect, however, they agree with the Barberini manuscript: they too were contracted from the same Hieronymian Martyrology, although they were subsequently enlarged with certain eulogies taken from Bede.

To these three manuscripts should be applied Papebrochius’s well-founded opinion, expressed in section 2 of his prologue to Bede. He confesses himself persuaded that:

“In most Roman basilicas, after the use of the Hieronymian Martyrology—namely, the larger one—had been abolished, and after the one which, as we mentioned above, had been sent by the pope to the bishop of Aquileia had perhaps been received only at the Lateran and in a few other churches, Bede was so approved by the rest that many thought they ought to use it after suitably enlarging it, until Usuard appeared more suited to ecclesiastical use.”

Henschenius and Papebrochius accordingly assigned these copies to Bede because they found his eulogies interspersed with the Hieronymian announcements. Nor should we omit what the aforementioned Papebrochius proposes in the immediately following section 12 concerning our subject, that is, the distinction among the three codices just mentioned. He continues as follows.

### 35

“These three,” the Hieronymian copies filled with Bede’s eulogies, “are as follows. The first is that of the Church of Saint Peter in the Vatican, which had until now been preserved in the archive there and which we had transcribed from that place.

“The second is that of the monastery of Saint Cyriacus at the Baths, the one which Baronius alone commended and used in revising and arranging the Roman Martyrology. It had previously been sent to us from the Vallicellian Library of the Fathers of the Oratory by the most sincere evaluator and supporter of our studies, His Eminence Cardinal Pietro Aloysius Carafa of the Holy Roman Church.

“The third we received from the extremely well-stocked manuscript library of His Eminence Cardinal Francesco Barberini. It is headless—that is, lacking its beginning—through the Ides of March and, as far as could be gathered from the entry for the translation of Saint Benedict on the fourth day before the Ides of September and from other indications, it was brought to Rome from some Benedictine monastery in Gaul. Nevertheless, it is of the best faith, and not so carelessly faulty or so meager as the first two; rather, it is more faithfully and fully supplemented, partly from the Hieronymian Martyrology and partly from the proper calendars of the Gallican dioceses.”

Thus Papebrochius speaks of this codex in relation to Bede. Yet he could have observed in it that other recent additions had been inserted, such as the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, its vigil and octave, and other entries here and there that bear neither the stamp of Jerome nor of Bede.

Let us now give specimens from the three codices mentioned above for the day already designated.

### 36

Beginning with the last, the Barberini manuscript, we read:

**The Kalends of July.** At Rome, the birthday of the holy Lucia, virgin, and Ancena, queen, with twenty-one others. At the Anisola monastery, the deposition of Saint Karilefus, priest. On Mount Or, the deposition of Aaron the priest. In Mesopotamia, Zelius with six others. Orion with nine others, and 274 others. At Augustodunum, the deposition of Leontius, bishop, and Saint Quinctianus.

The corruption of this list is sufficiently obvious, as are several alterations and a fairly liberal interpolation. These are absent from the purer Hieronymian codex, the Vatican manuscript, which forms its list as follows:

**The Kalends of July.** At Rome, Gaius the pope. The holy Lucia and Accega the king, with eight others. And on Mount Hor, the deposition of Aaron, the first priest.

The codex of Saint Cyriacus is of exactly the same character, indeed somewhat more corrected. It reads:

**The Kalends of July.** At Rome, Gaius the pope, and the holy Lucia, virgin, and Accega, king, with eight others. And on Mount Hor, the deposition of Aaron, the first priest.

No great perspicacity is required to perceive clearly that the two latter codices are more uniform with one another and with the Hieronymian manuscript than with the Barberini codex, although for Henschenius’s and Papebrochius’s purpose it would have been sufficient if the latter perhaps reproduced Bede’s eulogies more purely.

### 37

Together with the three codices mentioned above—the Barberini, Vatican, and Saint Cyriacus manuscripts—Papebrochius, in section 12 of the cited prologue, praises “the exceedingly ancient and distinguished manuscript of the Queen of Sweden. How highly the learned Lucas Holstenius valued it is shown by his *Observations on the Roman Martyrology*, taken largely from it and published in print after his death.

“‘In this manuscript,’ says Papebrochius, ‘we too recognized Bede, although his eulogies are often more abbreviated.’”

Whatever may be the case with Bede’s eulogies, it must be admitted without qualification that this Martyrology, once belonging to Saint Columba at Sens, can rightly be counted among the more distinguished abbreviated copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology.

Here is its text:

**The Kalends of July.** At Nicomedia, the birthday of Saint Zoilus. At Rome, the deposition of Gaius the pope. On Mount Hor, the deposition of Aaron the priest. At Augustodunum, the deposition of Leontius, bishop.

Compare it with the preceding texts, and you will decide for yourself that nothing comes closer to the Hieronymian Martyrologies. We regret that it was found only in mutilated form, since everything after the seventh day before the Ides—that is, after 7 September—is missing.

Castellanus gave the reader a very confused account of this manuscript and of the Martyrology of Saint Cyriacus, in the first bimonthly section—January and February—of his Martyrology, published with learned notes, pages 26–28 [Col. 0479B]. When I amicably warned him about these matters, he sincerely promised a correction in a very long and extremely grateful letter dated 9 January 1709.

Since I hope that all these points will be corrected in his next bimonthly section, which may perhaps soon be published, I shall refrain here from listing them individually.

### 38

It is not, however, possible to pass over in silence certain other errors of that most distinguished man, by which he improperly inserts several codices into the Hieronymian class. I set them out here in the same spirit in which he himself received them when they were presented to him, returning the most courteous and heartfelt thanks.

Thus, on page 17 of the preliminary notice to his first bimonthly volume, he counts among the shorter Hieronymian Martyrologies:

1. The Marchiennes manuscript in Flanders;
2. The Liessies manuscript in Hainaut;
3. The Saint Lambert and Saint Lawrence manuscripts of Liège;
4. The Saint Martin manuscript of Tournai;
5. The Saint Gudula manuscript of Brussels.

None of these belongs to the Hieronymian order [Col. 0479C].

To begin with the last, it is as far removed from the Hieronymian Martyrologies as Ado himself and Usuard, as will clearly appear in chapter 3 from the series of Usuardian manuscripts. The Saint Martin manuscript of Tournai agrees sufficiently with the Liessies manuscript, as Bollandus once preserved it on page XLIX of the general preface, comparing both with the Antwerp and Saint Lambert of Liège manuscripts; from these it may be inferred how far they diverge from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

The first two, namely the Liessies and Tournai manuscripts, have been assigned to Bede. The Lambert manuscript is almost to be assigned to the Adonian class. The Antwerp manuscript—which we shall call the larger one below—must plainly be assigned to the Usuardian class. The Saint Lawrence manuscript of Liège is farthest removed from the Hieronymian manuscripts, for it is a thick and extensive codex, almost surpassing Ado himself.

What he means by the Marchiennes Hieronymian manuscript is entirely unknown to me. We shall discuss in its proper place the Usuardian fragments received from that monastery. There we shall also restore to its true class the Centula codex, falsely entitled in Bede’s name and counted by Bollandus on page XLVIII among Bede’s Martyrologies.

But let us now review other Hieronymian codices, or at least codices related to them in some way.

### 39

We possess a highly abbreviated copy, prefixed by part of the *Breviary of the Apostles*, written by the Reverend Father Alexander Wiltheim, once a most devoted student of our work. It was copied from a manuscript of Saint Maximinus at Trier and sent by that same Father from Luxembourg to Bollandus [Col. 0480A]. Among the various days it is fullest on 1 July, where it reads:

**The Kalends of July.** On Mount Or, the deposition of Aaron. The passion of the holy apostles Simon the Cananaean and Jude the Zealot. At the city of Reims, the deposition of Saint Theuderic, priest.

This last entry unmistakably suggests Reims and the province of Reims, once broadly extended. I observe similar examples there with a casual glance, in places not far distant from one another. Thus, on the Ides of June:

“At the city of Reims, on the River Vetula, the dedication of Saint Genevieve, virgin.”

And on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September:

“At the city of Reims, the birthday of the holy Timothy and Apollinaris.”

I shall join to this a Martyrology transcribed in an Italian hand from volume XXI of the Vallicellian Library of the Fathers of the Oratory at Rome; nothing can be determined concerning its age. The author follows the Hieronymian style in its brevity, but has brought together several saints from elsewhere, including the prophets of the Old Testament, whom he took from the *Romanum parvum*, or from Ado, or perhaps from Usuard.

Papebrochius judged, I believe, that it had been brought to Rome from Gaul because he found in it, on the fifth day before the Ides, that is, 11 July, the translation of Saint Benedict, and on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, that is, 22 July:

“At the Fontenelle monastery, the deposition of Saint Guandresilus”—for *Wandregisilus*—“the confessor.

Let us add the customary specimen, the first day of the often-mentioned month:

**The Kalends of July.** On Mount Hor, the deposition of Aaron, the first priest. In the territory of Lyon, the deposition of Domitian, abbot.

### 40

After this comes the Martyrology which our authors call the Trier Martyrology of Saint Martin. It is written in a Belgian hand, with rubricated entries that now scarcely meet the eye.

Papebrochius correctly observed that it was compiled from various sources and that its compiler had Bede before his eyes. Nor do I find any words to which the statement reported in section 14 of the prologue applies better:

“Thus whoever composed the manuscript copy of the calendar of saints that we possess for the Church of Trier also used Bede’s Martyrology for the Trier Church.”

I would readily believe that it was originally arranged entirely for the use of some church, either in Trier or even in Belgium, since at its very beginning, on 4 January, it contains:

“At Ghent, Pharaildis, virgin.”

To make the conjecture most plausible from a single month, consider 10 July: Amelberga, virgin; 14 July: Marchelmus, companion of Saint Lebwin; 16 July: Minulphus and Gundulphus; 22 July: at Blandinium, Wandregisilus, abbot.

To pass over other entries not far removed, there are: 7 July, Willibald; 8 July, Kilian; 13 July, Mildrada; 14 July, Plechelm; 23 July, Liborius at Paderborn; 25 July, Clodesinda; and so forth.

For the rest, it frequently follows the brevity of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, and it was chiefly on that account that it was assigned to their class. If eulogies from Bede or elsewhere occur among the entries, they are confined to a few words. It agrees with the Vallicellian manuscript in mentioning prophets of the Old Testament.

No sufficiently certain indication can be drawn from 1 July. It reads:

**The Kalends of July.** At Rome, Gaius the pope and martyr, and Lucia, Faith, and Charity, virgins, and Sophia, their mother.

### 41

Almost no manuscript in our entire collection of Hieronymian Martyrologies is more clearly distinguished by its characteristic features than the one we call the Cologne Martyrology of Saint Mary at the Steps. Father Joannes Gamans, highly esteemed in our *Acts*, sent it to Bollandus in 1638 from a copy made by Father Marcus, a Carthusian of Cologne. With his own hand he added this note [Col. 0481A]:

“An exceedingly ancient Martyrology preserved at Saint Mary at the Steps in Cologne, by an unknown author, containing many things absent from Usuard.”

Father Marcus’s observation is correct, but he could have added that this Martyrology lacks many things found in Usuard and others.

The pattern of its announcements is plainly Hieronymian, expressing only the names of places and saints, except that very rarely it briefly mentions sufferings endured or burial. Thus it reads:

**The Kalends of July.** At Rome, the birthday of Saint Gaius the pope, Saint Karilefus the priest, and Saint Monegundis, virgin. At Vienne, Saint Martin, bishop. Domitian, abbot.

It is clear that certain saints have been added to the Hieronymian list [Col. 0481B]. That some local or neighboring saints have also been added may be inferred from 4 July, where it gives:

“Woltharicus, bishop,” abstaining from the title “saint” or “blessed.”

On 7 July it has:

“At Bongia, the birthday of Saint Goar, confessor.”

On 8 July, Kilian, and so forth; on 18 July, the translation of Saint Arnulf of Metz; on 23 July, Liborius, bishop.

The copy is incomplete, ending at 9 October, on which day it records Dionysius with his companions at Paris. The compiler of this Martyrology does not appear to have consulted or copied the *Romanum parvum* in any way.

### 42

The final place in our codex is occupied by a copy, written in a Belgian hand, of the most ancient Romano-Gallican Martyrology, which the aforementioned d’Achery shared with our predecessors in 1663.

Concerning this Martyrology and the one immediately preceding it [Col. 0481C], Papebrochius left the following statement in section 3 of his prologue to Bede:

“The same work”—he is speaking of Rosweyde’s *Romanum parvum*—“slightly enlarged, was sent to us by Lucas d’Achery, transcribed from exceedingly ancient parchment, under the title ‘Romano-Gallican.’ It was formerly also customarily read at Cologne in the Church of Saint Mary at the Steps. This can be demonstrated by its copy, sent from there by our Joannes Gamans, taken from the papers of some Carthusian—unless this should rather be called a new compilation made from the former work and another later one.”

Thus wrote Papebrochius before the stock, descent, nature, and individual properties of the Martyrologies had been sufficiently examined. I agree with my venerable teacher that both Martyrologies—the one of Saint Mary at the Steps and the Romano-Gallican—are mere compilations. But he seems mistaken in comparing them with the *Romanum parvum*, or in thinking that these were compounded from it.

The *Romanum parvum* certainly has its own distinctive characteristics, by which it can be plainly distinguished both from the one just cited and from this Acherian manuscript [Col. 0481D].

### 43

There is one respect in which a slight similarity may be observed between the Romano-Gallican Martyrology and the *Romanum parvum*: the former too contains prophets of the Old Testament, generally received together with the other entries from Ado or Usuard.

But how far it differs from the latter in every other respect may be inferred from the fact that the Acherian manuscript is fuller on almost every day. The phrasing of the *Romanum parvum* is sometimes more expansive; that of the Romano-Gallican is always contracted according to the Hieronymian pattern.

Here is an example for 1 July. On that day the *Romanum parvum* concludes its text in a single entry:

“On Mount Hor, Aaron, the first priest under the Law.”

Now compare the Romano-Gallican:

**The Kalends of July.** At Rome, on Mount Hor, the deposition of Aaron, the first priest. Likewise Saint Monegundis, virgin. At Lyon, Domitian, abbot.

After “At Rome,” “Gaius the pope” appears to be missing.

What affinity, I ask, is there here between the two? In one there are several entries; in the other there is a single announcement.

If I may disclose my opinion, I shall not hesitate to assert that both this Romano-Gallican Martyrology and the foregoing Martyrology of Saint Mary at the Steps are, for the most part, abridgements of Ado or Usuard, composed according to the varying taste of compilers who aimed at brevity.

I would therefore ask the opponents of the *Romanum parvum*, whom I shall confront in the following chapter, to occupy themselves instead with matters of this kind. Those who so confidently construct Ado’s calendar from that distinguished and most ancient Martyrology might more suitably devote their attention to these examples, to which the characteristic features of Adonian abridgements or extracts can, as we believe, be applied more appropriately [Col. 0482B].

44. To all these, at least in part, other codices may also be added, those which Henschenius and Papebrochius used in editing Bede. From their recension I observe that the Martyrology of Aachen, compiled for the use of that Church, comes quite close to the style of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, just as we said above concerning that of St Martin of Trier. I again cite the first day of July:

“At Rome, the deposition of Bishop Caius, and of the holy virgins Faith, Hope, and Charity.”

Here and there new entries are inserted, for example on July 4:

“The Nativity of St Hodelricus, bishop and confessor.”

This may perhaps be the same man whom the Cologne Martyrology above called Woltharicus. July 7 is the feast of Willebald; July 8, of Kilian and his companions; July 13, of Emperor Henry; July 15, of Gondulf and Monulf; July 16, the Dedication of St Mary at Aachen; July 27, the Translation of St Charles. And there are other entries of this kind, which I pass over.

Finally, another codex of the basilica of St Peter at Rome may also be included among the copies of Bede, although it appears to have been arbitrarily compiled and abridged, as will be clear from the first day of July, where the text is arranged as follows:

“On Mount Hor, the deposition of Aaron, the first priest. In the territory of Lyon, the deposition of Domitian, abbot. And of St Quincianus, martyr.”

The same may perhaps be said of the remaining codices cited among Bede’s Appendices. But enough has now been said about all these manuscripts of ours that pertain, wholly or partly, to the Hieronymian Martyrologies. I have done so solely so that those who take pleasure in reading our Acts and commentaries of the saints may more easily perceive what kinds of Martyrologies supplied the names of those saints.

## ARTICLE II. New Conjectures Concerning the Martyrologies of Bede and Florus

45. These Martyrologists—or rather, their two Martyrologies, or perhaps the single Martyrology belonging to both—must be discussed here only insofar as Bede is connected with Ado and consequently with Usuard by a considerable kinship of origin. Thus the order, succession, and, in a sense, genealogy may become clear which, as we said above, descends from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, and the Little Roman Martyrology to other works more or less closely related to them.

Bede’s own words at the end of his *Epitome* must first be cited. There he states that he wrote a Martyrology of the saints’ natal days, in which he carefully strove to record, for all whom he could discover, not only on what day they had conquered the world, but also by what kind of combat, or under what judge.

Bolland’s preface and Papebrochius’s prologue portrayed this Martyrology of Bede in such a way, and both of them discussed Florus so extensively, while others after them settled various matters concerning the two authors, that I might seem to be wasting my labor by reweaving this same fabric—unless constant comparison of these and other Martyrologies had brought to light certain points which, with the agreement and approval of my still-living teacher Papebrochius, are not unworthy of the judgment of learned men.

Bede’s date is now almost universally accepted: he was born in 672 and lived until 735. I likewise consider the characteristics of Florus to have been established with such probability that I have little doubt that he flourished at Lyon and wrote his Martyrology, better known by name than by actual acquaintance, around the year 830.

46. It will not be out of place to warn the learned reader once again—although he may already be well instructed—that the Martyrology published in 1564 by Christoph Plantin under Bede’s name was in no way written by Bede, but was compiled by I know not whom from Ado and other sources. This is as evident as anything can be, and is now beyond dispute, since it is commonly known by no other name than the spurious or pseudonymous Martyrology of Bede. To avoid the offensive term, I have preferred simply to call it Plantin’s Bede.

The later and far more accurate second edition, prepared in 1668 before volume II of the *March*, by Henschenius and Papebrochius, is more distinguished and was received with acclaim throughout the world, especially among men of letters. They did not hesitate to say that in it they had most carefully purged and distinguished the genuine text of Bede from the additions of Florus.

For nearly fifty years this judgment has been accepted by everyone so unhesitatingly and universally that, so far as I know, no one has yet appeared who either wished or was able solidly to contradict it. Some have judged that only the feast of All Saints should be removed as an addition.

47. I could not fail to add my own voice to the suffrages of my masters, whose experience in these matters was consummate, and of other very learned men. Accordingly, throughout this entire recension of Usuard, I have called Bede and Florus what they are called in the editions published, divided, and distinguished by those authors.

Nevertheless, having now spent a considerable time examining Martyrologies, I too bring forward a contribution. Although it somewhat undermines the foundations of Papebrochius’s work, he himself, as a most candid lover of truth, wished me to propose the arguments, so that a matter not yet fully elucidated might be further discussed and explained.

The entire investigation concerns Florus. His Martyrology, whatever its extent and character, has always seemed to me a genuinely obscure problem. Although, guided by the authority of my predecessors, I accepted their judgments, once I undertook the task of illuminating the Acts, I could never bring myself firmly to believe that the true and genuine work of Florus had been discovered by Henschenius and published by Papebrochius.

48. There are two principal difficulties concerning the Martyrology of Florus, which neither Papebrochius nor anyone else has hitherto either sufficiently perceived or resolved as they ought to have been. We reduce them here to two questions.

First: What, precisely, are—or may truly be called—the materials by which the Martyrology composed in Bede’s labor was enlarged through the efforts of Florus, as Ado puts it, and which that holy bishop of Vienne professes to have used in arranging his Martyrology? That is, what are those broader and so often celebrated traces of Florus in Bede?

Second: What is Florus’s second book, which Usuard expressly says that he used in addition to those broader traces?

If I remember correctly, Castellanus touched upon this last question somewhere, happily conjecturing that Florus’s second book could be nothing other than Ado’s Martyrology itself, in its pure form. We shall attempt to demonstrate this more fully in the third chapter of this preface. From this it will be necessary to correct the long-standing prejudice, repeated so often by our predecessors and by others after them, that the second additions of Florus—or, under another name, the second book or supplement of Florus to Bede—had not yet been discovered.

Thus only the first difficulty properly and exclusively concerns us here: the first and genuine work which we know to have been added to Bede’s labor through the efforts of Florus.

49. Someone, however, may immediately think that Papebrochius has fully resolved this difficulty by distinguishing those elogies of Florus which have been so carefully removed and separated from Bede’s texts.

I sincerely repeat that I have the highest regard for the work of my predecessors, and have often admired their fortunate discovery: as I said above, from such varied codices they so skillfully distinguished Bede himself, as genuine, from the additions of Florus, and the latter from Bede’s words and style.

Yet an uneasiness persists in me, arising from constant comparison of the Bede edited by Henschenius and Papebrochius with Rabanus, Ado, and Usuard. Here lies the crux of the matter: Ado asserts in his preface that he used that Martyrology of Bede which had been enlarged through the venerable efforts of Florus in Bede’s work.

From this it must most certainly be concluded that Ado possessed the completed and integral work of Florus himself, whom he could have known personally. He was attempting to supplement it from the Little Roman Martyrology and elsewhere. Thus he possessed not merely that first and very imperfect Martyrology of Bede, but at the same time everything that had been composed by Florus and Bede and had, so to speak, coalesced into a single body. He therefore transferred—or at least could have transferred—the saints, words, and elogies of both into his own new Martyrology without distinction.

50. Ado’s own words are exceptionally clear on this point. In his preface he testifies that he compiled his Martyrology at the command and instruction of holy men, so that the days which had been marked in the Martyrology without the names of martyrs might be supplied—“in that Martyrology which had been enlarged through the venerable efforts of Florus in the work of the lord Bede.”

A person would have to be blind not to see that Bede’s Martyrology is here portrayed by Ado as containing, joined and interwoven, whatever had been increased and expanded in it through the efforts of Florus.

Now nothing is clearer than that Ado constantly follows Bede’s traces, repeatedly adopts his saints, and transcribes nearly all his elogies in substance, sometimes word for word. He does this so clearly and explicitly that one unmistakably recognizes Bede in Ado.

If, therefore, the bishop of Vienne had before his eyes that work of Bede which had been enlarged through the efforts of Florus, it clearly follows that he also copied those elogies which had been added to Bede’s labor through the efforts of Florus.

Yet throughout Ado’s entire, however extensive, Martyrology, not a single elogium is found among those which our edition attributes to Florus. Hence it may be concluded that the Florus published by our predecessors is not the genuine Florus—not, I say, that work which had been added to Bede’s labor through the efforts of Florus. Accordingly, either Florus wrote nothing, or, if he wrote something, it must be sought elsewhere.

51. An argument no less compelling is drawn from Usuard’s Martyrology. We know that it was abridged from Ado, but in such a way that in various places it copied certain elogies from Bede. This shows that Usuard possessed Bede’s Martyrology, not as it had first been composed by Bede, but as it had been enlarged by Florus.

Usuard himself provides the clearest testimony to this when he writes in his preface about the older Martyrologies that had shown him the way to compose his own:

> “I was encouraged by the pious, though concise, descriptions of the venerable priests Jerome and Bede concerning this subject. The former, seeking brevity, and the latter leaving very many calendar days untouched, are found to have passed over many things necessary to this work. Nevertheless, following them, I judged that I should also follow the broader traces of the memorable man Florus, already engaged in this same task, especially in his second book.”

I said in the third chapter of this preface that this second book must be discussed. For the present argument, it is enough that this passage makes it clearer than daylight that Usuard followed “the broader traces of the memorable man Florus in this same task”—that is, the labor of the lord Bede which had been enlarged through the efforts of Florus; in other words, the very Martyrology of Bede expanded by Florus into a broader form.

52. Now take and examine Usuard’s entire Martyrology from beginning to end. You will have prevailed if you find even a single elogium among all those which the Papebrochian edition attributes to Florus, or which may in any genuine sense be attributed to him.

I admit that one or two are not dissimilar, but we have proved that these were copied from Usuard by the fabricator of that Florus and composed in Usuard’s own style and words.

Here is the knot, for which I have hitherto found no straightforward and secure way of untying it, unless all the elogies attributed by our predecessors to Florus are completely denied to him.

Again, as a fact I take for granted that Rabanus, Bede’s constant copyist, used a copy of Bede’s Martyrology which itself had passed through Florus’s hands. Yet throughout the whole course of Rabanus’s Martyrology there is nowhere a Florus of the kind published by Henschenius and Papebrochius.

Therefore either there is no Florus, or the materials by which Bede’s work was enlarged must be extracted from elsewhere.

I do not remember that anyone has hitherto observed this difficulty—not Bollandus or Henschenius, diligent investigators of Martyrologies, nor Papebrochius, the principal editor of Bede. I had long ago detected the knot by examining and pondering it, but I lacked the wedge. For a long time and over difficult and circuitous paths we searched for it; whether it has been found may be inferred from what follows.

53. From the words of Bede cited above, which Bollandus, Papebrochius, and others regularly quote, it is beyond doubt that a Martyrology was composed by that venerable and holy writer. It is no less certain that it was very incomplete; and it is further certain that no one has yet published it in its original wording, though its existence is altogether certain.

Our edition comes close to the truth, but since it announces the feast of All Saints—a feast not yet instituted for the universal Church in Bede’s time—we infer from this one indication alone, to say nothing of the others, that it cannot be called wholly pure and integral.

From Ado, moreover, we learn most plainly that Bede’s very Martyrology was enlarged through the efforts of Florus. Yet nowhere is it reported that Florus composed a separate work which he added to Bede, or that he separated or distinguished it from Bede’s work by a particular method, style, or order.

It therefore occurred to me that the conjecture would not be unfounded if someone supposed that the whole Martyrology of Bede—or rather, the elements of his Martyrology—had been transferred into the work of Florus, and that the efforts of both had been fused into one and the same work, so that Henschenius and Papebrochius labored in vain to separate the style of Florus from Bede’s wording, and Florus’s additions from Bede’s own texts.

54. It seems to me much more probable—indeed, more than merely probable—that Florus adapted his own diction to Bede’s language so closely that they cannot be distinguished by any sufficient industry or skill.

You can easily convince yourself that this is what happened by considering the following explanation. Those who know Bede’s Martyrology cannot possibly be unaware that in it the saints are either commemorated in the simplest manner or are sometimes given rather lengthy elogies.

What could have been easier for Florus than to imitate this method of writing?

In England, Bede had extracted here and there from the Acts or passions of martyrs some portion which we commonly call a brief panegyric, elogium, praise, or encomium. Following the same method in Gaul, Florus—who, as Wandalbert testifies, was sufficiently well supplied with ancient monuments—consulted other passions and other Acts, discovered other saints, and adorned them with elogies precisely similar to those of Bede. He preserved the true or doubtful narratives of the aforementioned passions and adopted their abridgments.

To summarize the whole matter briefly: I believe that Bede’s labor and Florus’s efforts coalesced to such an extent that the commemorations of one could not be recognized or separated from those of the other—whether by manner, order, or style—even by Ado himself. Consequently, he called it the Martyrology of Bede, enlarged through the efforts of Florus.

55. With this foundation securely established, another path had to be opened for determining how much work Bede and how much Florus had contributed to the compilation of the Martyrology.

Since I knew from elsewhere that a Martyrology bearing Bede’s name existed in verse, composed in hexameter—not that Wandalbertian work which some have falsely imagined to be Bede’s, since it runs through the Kalends of the entire year, but a much shorter work that leaves many calendar days untouched—I thought that comparison of it with the prose Martyrology edited by us might perhaps provide some light. It might thus be possible, with reasonable probability, to divide and separate Bede’s compilation of the saints from Florus’s additions.

And behold, Acheri’s *Spicilegium*, volume X, p. 120 onward, opportunely supplied me with this metrical work. In the preface, p. 14, the editor states that Mabillon transcribed it “from a copy of the monastery of St Remigius at Reims, written by the hand of Bertigarius the monk under Archbishop Ebbo; it bears the name of Bede and the title, as we present them in the text.”

He goes on at length to show that there is nothing preventing this metrical Martyrology from being genuinely attributed to Bede, although in the testimony cited above Bede seems to be speaking only of a prose work and does not list this metrical Martyrology among his writings.

That should not seem surprising, since the work itself shows that it was composed toward the end of his life: in April it even commemorates the younger Walfridus, who died in 722, only three years before Bede himself.

This is approximately Acheri’s view. If it is correct, and Bede truly transferred his Martyrology, whatever its character, from prose into verse during the final years of his life, perhaps adding a few more recent saints, then I have found a second point on which to stand. Unless I am greatly mistaken, I may thereby distinguish Florus’s labor from Bede’s earliest outline with as much probability as the matter allows.

Perhaps by now you understand my thought.

56. My position is this: after comparing the two Martyrologies of Bede—the prose Martyrology edited by Henschenius and Papebrochius and the metrical Martyrology of Acherius—I shall attribute to Bede all those saints and elogies whom he himself mentions in the metrical work; everything else I shall leave to Florus.

To make the matter clear by an example, I take the first month that I encounter when opening our Bede, namely August, and compare it with the verses for that month in his metrical Martyrology, as represented by Acherius:

> The Maccabees are crowned at the rising of August’s month;  
>
> And holy Xystus is held on the eighth day before the Ides.  
>
> Laurence, victorious, overcomes his enemies on the fourth day.  
>
> The holy Mother of God, the Virgin borne among angelic choirs,  
>
> Is known to enter them on the eighteenth day before the Kalends.  
>
> Then Timothy holds the eleventh day in due order,  
>
> And at the same time the martyr Symphorianus receives his day.  
>
> Holy Bartholomew receives the eighth day.  
>
> John the Baptist, having suffered, is honored on the fourth day.

Here you count eight saints, whom, on our hypothesis, we must say were truly indicated by Bede.

But in our Bede there are twenty-eight saints—or rather, twenty-eight announcements—recorded for that month. It will therefore be necessary to admit that about twenty commemorations were added to Bede by Florus in the month of August.

57. We are now dealing with another hypothesis: namely, that everything which Henschenius and Papebrochius presented as belonging to Bede’s genuine texts truly does belong to the Martyrology of Bede enlarged through the efforts of Florus.

A wholly different and more difficult question would be whether the work of Bede and Florus was subsequently interpolated or abridged. But that is foreign to the argument we are pursuing here.

That our Martyrology of Bede is pure, or very nearly pure, and precisely the one which Ado admits having used, is sufficiently and clearly proved—not only by the arguments of Papebrochius’s prologue, but by Ado himself, who transferred the entire Martyrology into his own.

I say “entire” in respect of its most important and principal part. For if anyone compares our Bede with Rabanus and Ado, he will find here and there certain passages by which our Bede could easily be reduced to a more exact form.

Yet I do not see why Bede should be examined with such scrupulousness, even if he has perhaps been enlarged by certain minor additions, when we so confidently call works “Hieronymian” which, as everyone admits, cannot in any way pertain to Jerome.

58. Nor will it be a valid objection that in this way the greater part of the celebrated Martyrology, vindicated for Bede by our predecessors with such praise, would be taken away from Bede month by month.

For since it has hitherto been scarcely less doubtful what in Bede’s Martyrology properly belongs to Bede than what in the Hieronymian Martyrologies belongs to Jerome—or to the person who first designated the Hieronymian Martyrology—I shall certainly not have labored in vain if I restore Bede’s pure work, however small it may ultimately prove to be, to its author on grounds that are not unfounded, leaving the rest to Florus or to other interpolators.

Indeed, after long and most diligent labor, undertaken with all the care and zeal of which I was capable, I have so far found nothing that approaches complete probability.

Nevertheless, I do not fear to submit these arguments—or, if you prefer, conjectures—to the criticism and judgment of learned men, in case some clearer light should shine from elsewhere, by which at last the pure and genuine source of Bede himself may be cleansed more safely, securely, and certainly of the streams flowing into it from elsewhere.

59. In the meantime, the reader must once again be warned that throughout almost the whole recension of Usuard I have consistently cited Bede and Florus as they were published by Henschenius and Papebrochius in distinct type. Likewise, I call “Hieronymian copies,” or “Hieronymian codices,” the manuscripts published by Florentius and Acherius, or those preserved in manuscript among us, although some are fuller than others and some are more or less interpolated.

If you ask to whom the elogies attributed to Florus in our edition should be assigned, I shall candidly confess that I have no idea.

Since, however, we are dealing here with conjectural scholarship, what prevents us from asserting with the greatest probability that the compilers of the individual codices from which these materials were taken imitated Bede and Florus and, each according to his own ability, added what they thought suitable to their texts, excerpted from passionaries or from elsewhere?

This must certainly be admitted in the Usuardine codices, into which the freedom of interpolators advanced so far that, if all the appendices and additions are joined together, they surpass the actual Usuardine text on almost every day by twofold, threefold, often fourfold, indeed fivefold or more.

So much for Bede and Florus. Let us now hasten to three other ancient, or classical, Martyrologists.

## ARTICLE III. On Three Other Martyrologies Related to Usuard

### § I. On Wandalbert’s Metrical Martyrology

Among the Gallic Martyrologists, Wandalbert follows the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, and Florus most closely in time. He was a monk of Prüm in the diocese of Trier and, as Bollandus shows on p. LII, wrote his Martyrology in the year 842.

It was wrongly inserted by the editors of Bede’s works in volume I under the title *Bede’s Ephemerides*. For Bede’s metrical Martyrology, which we discussed in the preceding article, is extremely brief; it would certainly be wrong to attribute this work to Bede unless it likewise left very many calendar days untouched. Our Wandalbertian Martyrology, by contrast, reports at least one saint for every day throughout the entire year.

But no one now doubts its true author. See Bollandus’s preface to Wandalbert himself, from which the following words are relevant to our subject:

> “In this work, because the most certain enumeration of solemn days was not easily or lightly available, owing to the variety of books, I relied especially upon the aid and assistance of the holy and most renowned Florus, subdeacon of the Church of Lyon. Just as in our time he is known to excel, through extraordinary diligence and assiduity, in knowledge of Sacred Scripture, so he is recognized as abounding in authentic books, both in considerable number and in reliability. From him, taking old and corrected codices, I composed in verse a book of the Martyrology, from the Kalends of January to the end of the year, with the festivals occurring on each day.”

Wandalbert seems to speak rhetorically here. For if we examine the matter more carefully, everything he is known to have taken from those authentic, ancient, and corrected books can very easily be reduced to the contents of the Kalendars, the Martyrologies of Jerome, Bede, and Florus, and perhaps a few passionaries.

Nor, even with the aid and assistance of Florus of Lyon, was his enumeration of the solemn days so certain that he did not often, contrary to the manifest judgment of the older Martyrologists, transpose several days according to his own decision.

61. What we add here to Bollandus’s preface and to the accounts of others concerning Wandalbert is chiefly intended to provide examples showing that Wandalbert arranged many things according to his own pleasure.

Let others inquire what those authentic books and ancient corrected codices were from which Wandalbert obtained the saints whom he was to bind into verse. I myself doubt whether these claims are proclaimed more elegantly than truthfully.

We readily grant that he had before his eyes Bede as he had been enlarged by the holy and most renowned Florus, although Wandalbert does not appear to have been particularly scrupulous in using him.

It is equally certain that he extracted some saints from the Hieronymian codices. But it can be clearly demonstrated that, on his own authority, he added to them other saints summoned from elsewhere. Here are a few examples among many.

Thus he writes:

**February 17**

> And the holy Martialis honors the twelfth day.

**February 21**

> Victorinus, the ninth day shines under your name.

**February 25**

> The fifth day is increased by the praise of blessed Crescentius.

**March 2**

> Soon, on the sixth day before the Nones, Heraclus and Paulus are honored.

**April 20**

> And the festivals of the holy martyr Synesius are celebrated,  
>
> A bishop, blessed in his tomb, teaching, and death.

**July 13**

> The third day presents Egypt’s Serapion,  
>
> And the martyr Attalus shines with heavenly glory.  
>
> And holy Philibert adorns the thirteenth day.

**July 24**

> Soon, on the ninth day . . . Aquila and Nicetas consecrated.

**July 28**

He has four verses concerning the consecration of an altar by Pope St Stephen and other matters relating to it, about which nothing is found elsewhere.

**August 6**

> On the eighth day before the Ides, the holy flesh,  
>
> The holy flesh of Christ, about to suffer death and the cross, beforehand displayed a heavenly form.

**August 23**

> Lucius and Ptolemy crown the tenth day by their virtue.

**August 28**

> On this day also Pelagius, renowned for his shed blood.

**September 1**

> On this day too the solemn rites of holy Venerea shine.

**September 11**

> Felix likewise consecrated these by a blessed death,  
>
> Together with the holy and blessed martyrdom of Regula.

**November 11**

> . . . is summoned by vows and by the festival on the same day;  
>
> Having endured exile, lashes, threats, tortures, and death  
>
> For Christ, Domitilla likewise triumphs.

Many saints of this kind occur in Wandalbert, whom you will seek in vain among other Martyrologists, at least in the locations where he places them.

Just as he freely recorded many saints unknown to others, so with no less freedom he either transposed calendar days or inserted material that he had not found in the older Martyrologists.

It is worth clarifying the matter again with a few examples. Thus he writes for April 21:

> On the eleventh day Caius and likewise Simeon are honored.

This Caius can be no one other than the pope who belongs to the following day. He is placed still farther from his proper day when Wandalbert sings on May 16 what belongs to January:

> On the seventh day Timothy shines with the tenth in name;  
>
> Blessed Paul taught him with truthful voice.

He placed this saint on June 6, although he belongs to June 7:

> On the eighth day before the Ides Bishop Ceratus adorns the day,  
>
> He who illumined the city named by the emperor Gratian.

Again, on June 20 he places Vitalis, as though he had suffered on the day after his sons Gervasius and Protasius, whereas others commemorate him on April 28. His verse runs:

> And father Vitalis follows his sons on the twelfth.

On July 1 he speaks of Ephrem, who is listed by others on February 1; in this he followed Bede or Florus.

But on September 14 he alone speaks of Eparchus, whereas others place him on July 1:

> Here too the merit of Bishop Eparchus is celebrated.

Other Martyrologists do not recognize Pope Martin on September 16. Wandalbert writes:

> Hence, on the sixteenth day, Pope Martin is blessed.

He anticipates to October 24 the feast of the forty-six soldiers, whom others explicitly designate on the following day:

> On the ninth day before the Kalends, forty-six shine in triumph,  
>
> Renowned at Rome for military service and holy combat.

Now it is clear from June 8 that, besides the names of saints, other material was inserted for which he himself may have been the first author among the Martyrologists. There he appears to adopt the famous synchronism of Medardus and Gildardus:

> Their noble lineage and pious merit, whom altar joins together:  
>
> Gildardus and likewise Medardus honor the sixth day.

See also October 9 and 21, and many other days indicated in their proper places in our Observations on Usuard. From all this you may conclude that Wandalbert composed his verses with a fairly free hand—unless we suspect that interpolators occasionally intervened, in which case it would be surprising if they had kept their hands off this Martyrology more than from all the others.

Whatever the truth may be, we have recorded these matters to show that the metrical Martyrology is indeed descended from the Martyrologies of Jerome and Bede, enlarged by Florus, but not in such a way that its author, as an independent founder of a new Martyrology, considered himself bound by their decisions.

It is commonly known that Ado probably spent some time in the monastery of Prüm with Wandalbert himself. Nevertheless, we are convinced that he either did not know the metrical Martyrology or certainly did not use it.

I once had doubts, and in my Observations on Usuard did not dare to decide with sufficient certainty, whether it came to Usuard’s knowledge. Nor would I now dare to assert that as an established fact.

The same saints recurring on several days in both works favored the affirmative view. But it could immediately be answered that this was not surprising, since the same sources, or at least similar ones, were available to both.

The stronger argument arose when I found saints designated by no Martyrologist older than Usuard except Wandalbert—precisely what occurs on March 14, where his verse reads:

> Euphrosius shines on the preceding day together with the martyr Peter.

62. This seemed to compel the admission that at least some acquaintance existed between these Martyrologists.

Again, when one or another saint from some class of the Hieronymian Martyrologies was found to be precisely the same as those placed by Usuard and woven into Wandalbert’s verses, it could seem sufficiently probable that Usuard had consulted not the Hieronymian source but Wandalbert’s stream.

This appeared more clearly on December 2 in the case of Verus and Secundus, who had been separated from eighteen or nineteen other companions:

> On the fourth day before the Nones, Africa offers sacrifice to Verus and Secundus.

Yet all these considerations were outweighed by Usuard’s silence. When he openly enumerates his guides, he omits Wandalbert’s name.

Moreover, in the example just cited of Verus and Secundus, Usuard calls them brothers, something he certainly did not find in Wandalbert. Peter and Euphrosius must therefore have become known to Usuard from elsewhere.

To understand more certainly that Wandalbert should not be assigned a place among Usuard’s forebears, consider December 4. Finding no saints there in Ado whom he could designate, Usuard did not turn to Wandalbert, who speaks of Victoria and Heracleus, but fled to Rufinus, from whom he formed his two announcements.

The same is proved by December 19, where Wandalbert writes:

> On the fourteenth day Zosimus and Darius crown the day.

But in Usuard we read only:

> At Nicaea, St Darius, martyr.

There is no mention whatever of Zosimus on that day.

Thus the entire kinship between Wandalbert and Usuard consists principally in the fact that both draw upon the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, and Florus.

63. Curious readers might also ask whether Wandalbert ought not to number among his predecessors the author of the Little Roman Martyrology.

The reason for doubt is that our Observations sometimes show Wandalbert celebrating the same saints whom, among earlier Martyrologists, only the Little Roman Martyrology is found to have recorded.

Examples are May 15:

> Seven pontiffs together adorn Hesperia on the Ides;

and June 7:

> Your Paul, bishop, seven times, in lofty Byzantium.

There are many similar examples, from which it might appear that Wandalbert was not ignorant of the Martyrology we call the Little Roman.

I confess that here I am perplexed, and have been perplexed more than once in the Observations.

I see no serious objection if we readily grant that the Little Roman Martyrology preceded Wandalbert as a guide, whatever Ado may appear to boast when he says that he was the first to dig up in Italy the treasure previously hidden there and carry it to Gaul.

Moreover, since, according to Usuard, various Martyrologies of the holy Fathers existed, it could easily have happened that the Roman author of the Little Roman Martyrology drew from some more ancient source at Rome, and Wandalbert from it in his own Gaul.

Whoever wishes to compare or investigate further will find, in Molanus’s first edition and in this edition of Usuard, the verses joined to the Usuardine text for nearly every day. In volume V of Acherius’s *Spicilegium*, the entire Wandalbertian Martyrology has been published continuously.

### § II. On the Martyrology of Rabanus
64. In order and in chronological sequence there follows the distinguished offshoot of Bede: the Martyrology composed by Blessed Rabanus Maurus, formerly a monk of Fulda and afterward archbishop of Mainz [Col. 0493A]. It might perhaps not improperly be called Bede’s Martyrology supplemented by the efforts of Florus and Rabanus. For Rabanus inserted into his compilation, faithfully and throughout, all the notices attributed to Bede in Papebrochius’s edition, so that from this Martyrology alone they could be catalogued and perhaps here and there corrected. Papebrochius believed in his Prologue, no. 11, that Rabanus supplemented Bede in Germany at the same time that Florus was doing so in France, and therefore around the year 830. But Castellani’s conjecture seems to us far more probable, in the preface to his First Bimestre, p. 20, where he supposes that Rabanus wrote the Martyrology around the year 845—namely, when, after relinquishing the administration of the abbey of Fulda in 842, he was living there as a private individual [Col. 0493B], before being raised to the archbishopric of Mainz in 847. With the chronology thus suitably divided, it is readily understood that Florus’s work of expanding Bede came into Rabanus’s hands, and that he completed it for the whole course of the year from some Hieronymian manuscript and from other materials acquired elsewhere—as was fitting for so learned a man—adding those items that concerned the monks of Fulda in particular, so that it would be a Martyrology adapted to the uses of that celebrated monastery. This is so, whatever Papebrochius asserts in no. 14: namely, that the monks of Fulda used not that Martyrology but another one, found in the manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden, which had been abridged from Ado. Yet perhaps those monks too preferred the Usuardine method, which was much better suited to the ecclesiastical Office.

[Col. 0493C] 65. Thus our Rabanus preceded Ado, who at about the same time was contemplating another Martyrology; more will have to be said about it in the following two chapters. Both suffer from the same defect: that enormous inequality by which on some days one or another saint is announced very meagerly, while others are furnished with long notices, almost excessively prolix. Bede had preceded both of them, and Florus had preceded them as well. But Usuard, by embracing the entries for each day in more concise little sections, so far surpassed all the earlier Martyrologists that, being received everywhere, he effaced the memory of the others.

To return to Rabanus, nothing distinctive occurs in him that has not been noted with sufficient accuracy in our Observations. We took special care of this: that, by placing before the reader’s eyes the continuous agreement, difference, or opposition among all the Martyrologies, the Hagiophile might at the same time recognize the particular characteristics of each. Among other matters, it had to be pointed out that Rabanus’s Martyrology did not pass beyond the boundaries of Germany, since Ado and Usuard plainly knew nothing of it; whereas Notker, of whom we shall speak shortly, copied it in its entirety, enlarged it, or abridged it.

66. To continue the genealogy of the Martyrologies while adhering to the metaphor of generation adopted above, Rabanus—or rather their Martyrologies—touches Ado at such a degree of kinship that they may in a certain sense be called brothers, since both were begotten, to a greater or lesser extent, from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, and Florus [Col. 0494A]. Their most notable difference is that Ado was an exceedingly fertile parent of other Martyrologies, whereas Rabanus died almost ἄπαις—“childless”—having scarcely any follower except Notker. From Notker, perhaps more than from Rabanus himself, a few items passed into the fuller Usuardine manuscripts, as we have sometimes had occasion to indicate in our Supplements.

Anyone willing to devote a little time to comparing all these Martyrologies more carefully with one another will very easily observe with me that, if the material Rabanus took from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, and Florus is separated from the rest, little will remain that ought to be called Rabanus’s own. Likewise, if Notker is stripped of what he took from the Hieronymian, Rabanian, and Adonian Martyrologies, almost nothing will remain of what comes from his Martyrology—apart from the fact that in several places it is mutilated, as we shall explain somewhat more fully shortly.

§ III.—On Notker’s Martyrology

67. Papebrochius sketched this Martyrology in its native form in his Prologue to Bede, no. 14, in these words:

“Blessed Notker, a monk of the monastery of Saint Gall, was a contemporary of the aforementioned Ado in the year of Christ 870, when Ado sent that monastery relics of Saint Desiderius, bishop and martyr of Vienne, to be commemorated on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, as he himself testifies for that day in his Martyrology. Notker seems to have written it after the example of Ado, often taking entire notices from him word for word. He died in 912, as we shall clearly demonstrate in April, under his feast day. Besides Ado’s Martyrology—of which it is credible that Ado himself sent a copy to the monks of Saint Gall—Notker also had before his eyes Rabanus’s Martyrology, discussed above, and made very extensive use of it, so that he may seem to have wished to compose one work out of the two.”

Anyone who takes the trouble to examine and consider those three Martyrologists more attentively will see that this is entirely true. We did not fail to record the matter in our Usuardine Observations, where we represented, almost day by day, the genealogy of the classical Martyrologies. The last of these is the one under discussion here, Notker [Col. 0494D] Balbulus. If the curious reader wishes to know him thoroughly, let him consult Papebrochius’s commentary for 6 April, beginning on p. 576, where he carefully distinguishes this Notker from several others of the same name. Castellani collected everything in summary form in the frequently mentioned preface, p. 25.

68. The Martyrology of Notker, already mentioned, was first recovered from the library of Saint Gall and published in print among the Ancient Readings by Henricus Canisius. It was mutilated in several places: from 12 June to 19 June, from 11 July to 7 August, and from 18 August to 27 August; and it was incomplete from 26 October to the end of the year. In that Canisian edition it bears this title:

“In the name of the Lord, here begins the Martyrology for the course of the year of our holy father Notker, surnamed Balbulus, monk of Saint Gall.”

Both this Martyrology and that of Rabanus prove that in Notker’s time the ecclesiastical year had not yet become so generally established as beginning at the Nativity of the Lord or on its vigil, since both begin with the Kalends of January. Nothing is more familiar to Florentinius in his annotations on the Hieronymian Martyrologies than repeatedly to call Notker to witness, without consulting the source from which he clearly derived all his material. He seems to have noticed this only rather late, when, on 15 October, p. 920, he finally admits that Notker took a great deal from Ado.

69. But we have spoken of these matters in several places in our Observations. In any case, from what has been said it is clear how closely Notker is joined to Rabanus and Ado by the bonds of martyrological kinship.

So much, then, for the Martyrologists who are not so near to Usuard in the direct or immediate line, although Usuard himself is sometimes found to have consulted the Hieronymian Martyrologies and Bede supplemented by Florus.

Now we descend to the principal trunk of that family, or genealogical tree. We identify it as the old Roman Martyrology, formerly edited by our Rosweyd, discovered by Ado at Ravenna, copied there by him, placed at the head of his Martyrology, and transferred almost entirely into it. From this one may see that the old Roman Martyrology—which we call the Little Roman Martyrology—can be called the father of Ado, together with Bede enlarged by Florus, while one might not improperly call the Hieronymian Martyrologies their grandfather. It will then be demonstrated in chapter 3 that Usuard proceeded most immediately from Ado.

Here we must first introduce the serious controversy among scholars concerning this Little Roman Martyrology. A few have hitherto defended it as genuine and ancient Roman; many others have vigorously argued the contrary, claiming that it is neither old, nor Roman, nor truly a Martyrology, but rather a Calendar or an abridged summary drawn from Ado; while others, finally, like spectators at a theatrical performance, have declined to pronounce judgment in either direction. We undertake in the next chapter to take up these matters from the beginning and examine them more carefully.

# CHAPTER TWO

On the Martyrology which Heribert Rosweyd first called the OLD ROMAN, and which we think may for the time being be called the LITTLE ROMAN

70. The most eminent author of the Ecclesiastical Annals, Cardinal Baronius, is wholly occupied, in the Prolegomena to his edition of the Roman Martyrology with Notes, especially chapter 8, in seeking the ancient Roman Martyrology. He had found its traces by no means obscure in the celebrated letter of Gregory the Great to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, quoted above.

Since the earlier copies of the larger Hieronymian Martyrologies that we mentioned in the preceding chapter had not come to his notice—or to that of anyone else appointed to reform the Roman Martyrology—and since he had therefore seen no Martyrology to which the features described by Gregory could entirely correspond, he read Ado’s preface, in which that holy bishop of Vienne declares, in preparing his Martyrology, that he had “been assisted by a venerable and very ancient Martyrology, sent from the city of Rome to Aquileia to a certain holy bishop by the Roman pontiff.” From this, the same Eminent Cardinal did not hesitate to infer in the cited chapter 8:

“This very simple Roman Martyrology, without any other addition, and also very brief, in which only the names of the martyrs, the place, and the day of their passion were set down, is the very one mentioned by Ado.”

Thus Baronius.

71. But, with due respect to him, I shall say this: what Gregory praises in his letter to Eulogius concerning his little book of martyrs does not sufficiently agree with the characteristics Ado describes of the Martyrology found at Ravenna, as will be evident to anyone who compares their words. For Ado nowhere suggests that a Martyrology was sent by the Roman pontiff to Aquileia to a certain holy bishop, that it was very brief, that it contained only the names of martyrs, or that it set down only the place and day of their passion. Gregory asserts all these things about his own work, and does so in terms both clear and precise.

In any case, adhering to his preconceived opinion, Baronius makes sufficiently clear in the same place the intensity of his desire for that very Martyrology, when he says:

“Moreover, in all the printed Martyrologies of Ado that I have seen—I do not know whether any other editions then existed besides Lipomanus’s incomplete one and another by Mosander—that very Martyrology received from Rome is missing. Mosander would certainly have performed an outstanding service, worthy of learned men and greatly to be desired, if he had published, together with Ado’s Martyrology, which he appended after Surius to the seventh volume of the Lives of the Saints, that distinguished monument of antiquity which he testifies to be present in his manuscript of Ado.”

72. Wishing to satisfy so illustrious a cardinal’s desire, our Heribert Rosweyd, while preparing a new and more accurate edition of Ado’s Martyrology than the earlier ones, immediately devoted all his efforts to obtaining the actual manuscript of Saint Pantaleon, from which Mosander had printed his edition of Ado. When it was very courteously sent from the Cologne Charterhouse, he published together with Ado, in 1613, that same old Roman Martyrology—which he himself so called—with great applause from learned men [Col. 0496D], without doubting that he had found the very Martyrology praised by Gregory the Great in his letter to Eulogius.

It is pleasant to hear Rosweyd himself speaking, in his dedicatory letter to Pope Paul V:

“Now I bring before Your Holiness,” he says, “this old Roman Martyrology, which Gregory, the supreme pontiff, writing to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, both desired and believed to be dispersed throughout the whole world. I bring what Ado, eight hundred years ago, valued so highly that he considered it venerable and very ancient, and set it before himself as though it were the first outline of his work, which he would then paint again in his own colors and illuminate with the splendor of light [Col. 0497A]. I bring what remained hidden until this very day, and for whose discovery Cardinal Baronius burned with such desire that he wished to leave behind written witnesses to his mind, by which he might urge on the editor and offer gratitude in advance for the benefit. I therefore bring this Martyrology to Your Holiness with all the more confidence because it comes accompanied by the patronage of many most distinguished men.”

73. Thus Rosweyd did not hesitate to adorn his gift—or, so to speak, his offspring—to the common Father of the faithful with splendid and elegant language, and to display it reverently, not boastfully, as Beckius chatters, but, I insist, modestly. Nor did the most serious and learned men whose patronage accompanied it then doubt that he was truly presenting to the Roman pontiff the Martyrology commended by Saint Gregory.

Yet I believe Rosweyd himself subsequently recognized that these claims had been made prematurely. When he wrote this, he had not yet fortunately recovered from the Trier Charterhouse that illustrious Epternacensian Hieronymian Martyrology which we discussed with Bollandus in the preceding chapter. For, by comparing the two—namely, the Hieronymian Martyrology and the Little Roman—this most discerning man would easily have recognized that Gregory the Great’s description could be applied more properly to the former than to the latter. It plainly indicates a Martyrology in which only the names of the martyrs, the place, and the day of their passion were set down.

Baronius’s desire that it be very brief is not in accordance with Gregory’s meaning, since in Gregory’s little book many people from different lands and provinces are recognized, on each successive day, as having been crowned with martyrdom. That is a characteristic proper to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but not to the Little Roman, as will become clearer shortly. If Rosweyd had been able to observe all these things, there is no doubt that he would have thought his old Martyrology entirely distinct from Gregory’s. Nor did that Martyrology need to have splendor gratuitously borrowed for it from elsewhere, since it possesses other praises that are true and properly its own; we shall vindicate them throughout this chapter as deserved and due to it.

74. As for Rosweyd’s recent statement that his old Martyrology was coming to Rome accompanied by the patronage of many most distinguished men, I consider that statement entirely credible, although I am not at present able to collect the endorsements of those men. Let Andreas Saussayus stand here for all of them, at least in this matter an encomiast of Rosweyd who is by no means suspect.

He had praised, in more than one place in the apparatus to his Gallican Martyrology, the publication undertaken of that old Martyrology. But in chapter 19, gathering together its scattered rays, he says among other things of Rosweyd:

“The old Roman Martyrology, hidden for so many centuries and desired by Baronius with such ardor and sought out by him with such great labor, he at last found by divine gift and, having found it, first brought it to light, furnished with annotations worthy of his learning. He dedicated it to Pope Paul V in a most elegant letter, so that, as he says, the ray might return to the sun, the stream to the spring, the branch to the trunk, and the star to heaven, and so forth. Thus Heribert prefaced his address to the supreme pontiff, rejoicing over the treasure he had discovered and returned to its rightful Lord—Heribert, himself certainly an outstanding ray of the sun of wisdom, a stream from the living spring of faith, a branch of the flourishing trunk of justice, and now a beautiful and eternal star of heaven.”

75. What would you say—had Saussayus here bestowed something close to an apotheosis upon Rosweyd? Yet I shall soon make you understand the turned-about lyre.

The very man who here raises Rosweyd and his offering to the pontiff so magnificently to the stars, elsewhere observes that the Martyrology in question conflicts with his preconceived opinions about the Areopagite, opinions derived from Hilduin; then, as though seized by a fit of frenzy, he spews something like curses upon the Martyrology itself and its editor, shamefully retracting what he had sung so gloriously in praise of both. Florentinius records this at greater length in his preliminary admonitions, p. 17, and we shall show it more fully a little below.

So that I do not waste time seeking out more of Rosweyd’s eulogists, or of those who praised his edition of the old Roman Martyrology, and so that I do not weary the reader, I shall produce one man of outstanding learning and great reputation among scholars: Henricus Valesius. In the brief dissertation that we shall discuss, he gives this testimony concerning the writers of his own time:

“Rosweyd had persuaded learned men—so that this Martyrology should be accepted by men of every communion, even those differing from one another, as the old Roman Martyrology, and so that all should everywhere use its authority and testimony in their books.”

76. A more emphatic exaggeration is not unusual with Valesius. For learned men did not follow Rosweyd so completely that before Valesius there was no opponent of that Martyrology. He could have known the very liberal critic, the distinguished scholar Joannes Fronto, editor of the Roman Calendar, than whom no one rose up more briefly or perhaps more sharply against it. I shall confront him below in his proper place.

Nor, I suppose, was Valesius unaware of Bollandus’s very prudent judgment concerning the same Martyrology. Before proceeding further, we shall summarize it here from the General Preface, chapter 4, § 5. I find there several matters that in this work of ours have either been restored or explained more clearly. But regarding the Martyrology so often mentioned, Bollandus plainly states there “that the Martyrology published by Rosweyd is not the one that existed in the age of Saint Gregory” [Col. 0498D].

Again, after several other observations—some matters that even Bollandus, otherwise so clear-sighted, had not at that time adequately understood—he declares:
