“Nevertheless, I consider it plainly certain that the work described by Saint Gregory is not the one published by Rosweyd. Yet,” he adds, “whatever its nature may be, we do not reject it. Would that more similar monuments of antiquity might be brought to light, as far as possible.”

I pass over the scruple with which Bollandus struggles there: namely, lest he be reluctant to call the Martyrology published by Rosweyd Roman, “because it was published under the title ‘Old Roman’ by a most learned man, and that designation became established among scholars.” No one will take offense at my changing the word “old,” which is not quite suitable, to “little,” so as to distinguish it from the greater Hieronymian Martyrology. I am entirely convinced that Rosweyd himself would have done the same if, when he brought his lesser Roman Martyrology into common print, he had already seen the much older Hieronymian manuscript.

77. The true opinion of Bollandus and of us, therefore, is that the characteristics displayed by Saint Gregory in his celebrated and frequently praised letter to Eulogius cannot possibly fit the Martyrology published by Rosweyd. Gregory describes a little register in which the names of almost all the martyrs were collected, with their passions distinguished according to individual days. This certainly does not agree with Rosweyd’s Martyrology, just as it is certain that several days are found empty in it, while on many others only a single saint is recorded.

Furthermore, Gregory’s testimony makes clear that the same volume did not indicate how each person had suffered, but merely set down the name, place, and day of the passion. The author of the Little Roman, by contrast, added more and more distinct information, through which it far surpasses Gregory’s work—not in age, certainly, but in polish, clarity, and the exact ordering of its contents.

Finally, our Roman Martyrology marks in several places matters later than Gregory, such as the feast of Saint Mary ad Martyres on 13 May; on 14 September, the life-giving wood of the Cross, discovered by Pope Sergius; on 1 November, the feast of All Saints instituted at Rome; and other matters that a learned reader will readily observe. These relegate Rosweyd’s manuscript to the eighth century. Let these points suffice for a complete confirmation of Bollandus’s judgment.

78. There is one matter that our venerable master did not sufficiently perceive, when he left it uncertain whether Saint Ado had possessed Rosweyd’s lesser Martyrology or the greater one, namely, the Hieronymian. To me it seems absolutely certain that Ado speaks in such a way that his entire account plainly designates the Little Roman and cannot designate any other Martyrology.

But Bollandus says:

“Ado has many more saints in his Martyrology than are contained in the lesser Roman Martyrology; indeed, he could have drawn very little assistance from it, especially since he possessed Usuard’s Martyrology, which indicated the feast days of individuals and also of groups . . .”

Bollandus rightly admits that he finds himself unable to resolve this difficulty. It would have required the labor of many years and the most diligent comparison of many Martyrologies with one another to untie such a knot. Its latter part was only finally observed by Papebrochius more than fifty years after the work on the Acts of the Saints had begun, in volume 5 of the June volume, p. 250, col. 1 at the end.

Our predecessors, namely, had always cited Usuard and Ado in the wrong order, always assuming that Usuard was older than Ado, and therefore that Ado had received his material from Usuard, or at least could have received it from him. Alternatively, as the said Papebrochius argued in the Prologue to Bede, no. 11, and in volume 4 of the June volume, p. 482, below letter B, neither had known anything about the other. Similar statements recur in innumerable places throughout the twenty-three volumes of the Acts of the Saints.

But our Observations, appended day by day to the Usuardine text, will demonstrate all these matters with the clarity of the midday sun to be incompatible with the truth.

79. The first part of the difficulty—that Ado has many more saints in his Martyrology than are contained in the lesser Roman, and therefore could have drawn very little assistance from it—I shall say, with due respect to Bollandus, is very easily resolved. For Ado nowhere suggests that he took all his saints from the venerable and very ancient Martyrology. He merely admits that he was assisted by it so that the days of the martyrs, which were usually found confused in the Calendars, might be recorded with complete accuracy.

Unless I am greatly mistaken, what the holy Martyrologist means is that he found in that Martyrology a distinct series of days, or Calendar days, which is still represented in the Hieronymian Martyrology—whose order has been disturbed, dislocated, and confused—even after the painstaking work of many learned men. I refer to this the phrase “might be recorded with complete accuracy,” that is, distinctly. For whoever the author of that Martyrology may have been, he seems to have cared least of all about restoring the saints to their true days of death or martyrdom. He thought he had done enough if he attached to fixed days, almost at his own discretion, the saints whom he collected here and there from the Old Testament as well as from the New, but especially from Rufinus.

This is our second observation, extending through almost every day, which had hitherto escaped our predecessors and which could be brought to light, arranged, and confirmed only through the tireless and continuous investigation of our Martyrologies.

I reduce the whole matter to two propositions. The first is this: in arranging his Martyrology, Ado used Rosweyd’s Little Roman as a kind of framework, if one may speak in that way, and copied almost the whole of it word for word. The second is this: Usuard followed Ado—whom he called the second book of Florus—in everything so closely that he may rightly be called an abridgment of Ado. But, as we have already noted above, this second proposition must be treated more fully in chapter 3.

80. With these matters in some sense presupposed and established in advance for the following dissertation, we undertake here the defense of the Little Roman and of its editor Rosweyd. Although we agree with Bollandus that Rosweyd was entirely mistaken in thinking that his Martyrology was the one Gregory mentions in his letter to Eulogius of Alexandria, we nevertheless defend it against its many detractors as a true, venerable, and very ancient Martyrology, sent from the city of Rome to Aquileia to a certain holy bishop by the Roman pontiff, and later lent to Ado for several days by a certain religious brother. Ado, having carefully copied it while staying at Ravenna, thought it should be placed at the head of his work. We do not deny, however, that some interpolations were added, and we have not yet been able to find any Martyrology entirely free of them.

These points must be defended against Saussayus, Fronto, Florentinius, and all other opponents of the Little Roman.

We have another matter to settle with Henricus Valesius. He attacked the title rather than the substance of the Martyrology itself and hurried through the cited dissertation, appended to the end of his edition of Eusebius on p. 315. We shall first examine it here, so that, once the head has been secured, we may more easily defend the rest of the body.

# ARTICLE I

It is maintained, against Valesius and Florentinius, that Rosweyd’s Little Martyrology may not inappropriately be called Roman

81. Henricus Valesius, mentioned above, in that singular dissertation in which he attacks Rosweyd’s Martyrology and, together with it, the Hieronymian Martyrology, first argues that before Sixtus V there was no distinct Martyrology belonging to the Roman Church. Let us hear him himself:

“I, for my part, affirm the contrary,” he says, “namely, that there never was any proper and distinctive Martyrology of the Roman Church before the one published by order of Pope Sixtus V under that title and illuminated by Baronius’s notes.”

He then gives the reasons that led him to think so, but most of them reduce to a purely verbal question about the name, as Florentinius rightly demonstrates in his fifth admonition, successfully overturning Valesius’s entire construction. These works are in everyone’s hands, so there is no need to weave the fabric again here.

Florentinius proves, and rightly, that the Hieronymian Martyrology published by him, which he entitled the oldest Martyrology of the Western Church, may entirely properly be called Roman, or the Martyrology of the Roman Church, even though neither Saint Gregory nor Bede, Ado, or Usuard designated it by that name.

It certainly seems strange that Valesius should acknowledge that all the characteristics specified by Saint Gregory fit the Hieronymian Martyrology perfectly—in fact, that he should say that Gregory the Great possessed a Martyrology in which the names of many martyrs were gathered together—while nevertheless persistently denying that Gregory the Great called it a Roman Martyrology, or that it was a proper and distinctive Martyrology of the Roman Church. It is as though the Roman Martyrology today were something other than the one it shares with the other Western churches.

82. That such a Martyrology must have existed a thousand years ago—as Valesius himself concedes in the very terms—is established by the most lucid testimony of the Council of Clovesho, held in 747 under Cuthbert, archbishop of Canterbury, canon 13, in Spelman, volume 1, p. 249, and in Labbe, volume 6, col. 1577, where these precise words are explicitly expressed:

“Likewise, throughout the whole course of the year, let the feasts of the saints be venerated on one and the same day, according to the Martyrology of that same Roman Church, with the psalmody or chant appropriate to it.”

Nor could it have been any other Martyrology than this one that the abbots of France prescribed to be recited in choir at the council of Aachen in 817, canon 69, in Labbe, volume 7, col. 1511, in these words:

“Let the Martyrology first be read at the chapter.”

Since these statements absolutely cannot be understood of Bede’s incomplete work [Col. 0502A], and even less can they refer to the later Martyrologists, there can be no doubt that they refer to the Roman Martyrology—whether the greater or Hieronymian, or the old Roman and Little Roman of Rosweyd. Refer the matter wherever you wish: Valesius is compelled to admit that a ROMAN MARTYROLOGY truly existed before the time of Sixtus V. Let him now agree with Florentinius that this designation should be assigned to the Hieronymian Martyrologies; I turn to our Little Roman and insist that it too must be granted the designation of Roman Martyrology, though in the lesser or little sense.

83. Here we must contend with both of these distinguished men. Both deny that Rosweyd’s Martyrology can be called Roman, but they do so for entirely different reasons.

Florentinius, as will become clearer below, believes that the Martyrology published by Rosweyd is not the one Ado placed at the head of his work, but rather an abridged summary drawn from Ado, no older than the eleventh century. He would certainly not deny it the name Roman if he believed it truly to be the Martyrology that was sent from the Roman pontiff to a certain holy bishop at Aquileia and found and copied by Ado at Ravenna.

The learned man incorrectly assumes that Ado found and copied at Ravenna no other Martyrology than the Hieronymian itself, such as he testifies to having discovered joined to Ado in one or another manuscript.

The next article is directed against Florentinius. For the present, therefore, the controversy remains only with Valesius, who, after unsuccessfully trying to deprive the greater and older Martyrology mentioned by Saint Gregory of the designation “Roman Martyrology,” finally turns to Rosweyd’s Martyrology:

“And this is enough concerning the passage of Gregory the Great. As for Ado of Vienne’s testimony, the answer is not difficult. For, besides the fact that Ado is more recent and not sufficiently qualified to confirm a monument of such great antiquity, nothing can be drawn from his words to prove that there was any Roman Martyrology. Ado says that a very ancient Martyrology was handed over to him by someone, and that it had once been sent by the Roman pontiff to Aquileia. Ado does not say that the Martyrology was Roman, but only that it was sent by the Roman pontiff to Aquileia. But the monk who made this claim to Ado undoubtedly deceived him, in order to obtain greater authority for his manuscript and to advertise the favor he had done Ado by lending it to him for copying. For that Martyrology was composed not at Rome but at Aquileia—the one Ado placed at the head of his Martyrology and which Rosweyd later published for us as the old Roman Martyrology.”

84. Valesius defines many things here, in a few words, rather roundly and confidently in the interest of his authority. Beginning at the end, I openly deny his final two assertions: that the monk deceived Ado, which is stated with great rashness, and that the Martyrology was composed at Aquileia, which is asserted with no less levity. For nowhere does there appear any trace indicating that Rosweyd’s Martyrology was composed at Aquileia rather than at Jerusalem; nor do we believe that Valesius has been granted the right to accuse a religious man so boldly of lying without cause.

The most learned Mabillon, unless I am mistaken, saw this before me in the preface to the fourth century of the Benedictines, part 2, p. LXXXVIII and following, where he quotes Valesius’s very words. Yet, bound by some religious obligation, he added:

“I would not wish entirely to refute this opinion of a most learned man, whom I hold in the highest esteem; but nevertheless I cannot conceal the authority of the Council of Clovesho,” and so forth—namely, the authority of the council whose words, together with those of the Council of Aachen, we have just quoted.

For my part, I humbly respect and venerate Valesius and all learned men, but only up to the altar; not, I insist, to the point of accepting from them, in exchange for the truth already established, anything they devise without guarantor or witness. Valesius’s authority is not so great for me that I cannot regard the testimony both of the religious brother—whether he was a monk or someone else—and of Ado as sincere and true. Nor will I allow this conviction to be taken from me unless it is more clearly disproved by contrary arguments.

85. From the testimony of both men I have a Martyrology, and a venerable and very ancient one at that; I have one sent from the city of Rome to Aquileia to a certain holy bishop by the Roman pontiff. What, I ask, follows spontaneously from this? Surely that the Martyrology was written and used at Rome, and could consequently be called Roman, just as the older Martyrology commonly called Hieronymian was commended by Saint Gregory. Learned men everywhere, together with Bollandus and Florentinius, agree that this latter Martyrology may truly and properly be called Roman, whatever Valesius may argue against it—a position in which Florentinius has refuted him most fully.

Nor should you object that it would then follow that there were two Roman Martyrologies. There is nothing more objectionable in that than in the succession of several Sacramentaries, one after another: the Gregorian succeeding the Gelasian, the former more ornate and exact than the latter. In the same way, the lesser Roman Martyrology, more polished and clearer, could easily have replaced the greater and more confused one, even if seven or eight days now appear empty, perhaps having been left so through the carelessness of copyists.

But no example of this kind has been found at Rome. What then? Who found the Hieronymian Martyrology at Rome? Who does not know that those ancient Roman Martyrologies—whether called the greater or the lesser—entirely disappeared after the Usuardine Martyrology, more convenient and elegant, was introduced into almost all the churches of the West? More light will be shed on this by what follows.

[Col. 0503D] 86. Valesius continues: “Almost the whole of that Martyrology which was published by Rosweyd was copied from the Ecclesiastical History of Rufinus, a presbyter of Aquileia, including even the errors found in Rufinus.” He proves this for the entire course of the year from five days: the day before the Nones of February; the Ides of April; likewise the nineteenth of October; the second of November; and the fourth of that same month. There he correctly observes that Theodotus of Laodicea was improperly listed among the saints by the compiler of the Roman parvum, as we discussed at greater length under 2 November.

Nevertheless, I will not conceal that Valesius is again using considerable exaggeration here, since neither the whole, nor half, nor even a fifth part of the Roman parvum was composed from Rufinus [Col. 0504A]. I admit, nonetheless, that these are the only things said in that dissertation which could be worthy of so great a man, and which we have repeatedly impressed throughout our work in our Observations on numerous Usuardine texts.

But Valesius’s entire conclusion collapses: namely, that the Martyrology which Ado of Vienne prefixed to his own Martyrology could in no way be called Roman. As for the further charge which he adds—that it is riddled with serious errors—it comes down to a single case, that of Theodotus of Laodicea.

87. Yet this error in that Martyrology will easily be pardoned its author if we remember that he accepted it in good faith from Rufinus, being a man neither sufficiently learned nor sufficiently critical to discover from other sources that Theodotus had persisted in the Arian heresy—a fact which escaped many other learned men [Col. 0504B] after him. We know, for example, that Eusebius of Caesarea held a place among the saints in Usuard’s Martyrology for so many centuries, until the reformers of the Roman Martyrology finally removed him from it.

If Theodotus had been as dear to Valesius as Eusebius was, perhaps he would have fought just as vigorously to assert Theodotus’s orthodoxy. Thus Castellanus once frankly admitted to me in a letter that he recognized the unfairness of Valesius’s procedure: “For he seems,” he said, “to have been induced, in defending Eusebius, chiefly by the fact that he was distressed to see Theodotus erased from the Roman Martyrology, and therefore to attack more sharply the fact that he survives in it. Equity demanded that he either condemn both or defend both.”

Whatever the case may be, Valesius does indeed assert—I nearly said, he guesses—but in no way proves “either that Ado deceived us by publishing this Martyrology as having been sent by a Roman pontiff, or that the monk who made this claim to Ado imposed upon him.” We believe that both men reported the truth, and that the Martyrology published by Rosweyd must in no way be deprived of the title Roman.

88. Certainly, no great number of arguments is needed to refute what is asserted without proof. Throughout that entire dissertation, Valesius did not undermine either Ado’s sanctity or the faithfulness of the religious brother—at least not in the eyes of sensible people. To confirm our position admirably, the aforementioned Claudius Castellanus—who, as I said above, was my chief encourager and instigator in publishing Usuard—offers, in the preliminary notice to his edition of the first two-month portion of the Roman Martyrology, illustrated with his lengthy notes [Col. 0504D], a prudent, learned, truthful, sensible, and exact judgment on page 17. I translate it here from French into Latin:

“The Little Martyrology, sent from Rome to Aquileia, was published by Rosweyd under the name OLD ROMAN—whether he found this title in the manuscript preserved at Cologne among the Carthusians in the church of Saint Pantaleon, or whether he himself added it: in either case he would certainly have done so most deservedly, since in that manuscript the Martyrology prefixed to Ado’s longer Martyrology is found, and since it is evident that that holy archbishop of Vienne asserts in the preface to his Martyrology that, at the beginning of his work, he placed a venerable and most ancient Martyrology, sent from Rome to Aquileia by a Roman pontiff [Col. 0505A] to a certain holy bishop. ‘A religious brother,’ he says, ‘lent it to me for several days, and while I was staying at Ravenna I copied it.’ Who could believe that the Roman pontiff sent to Aquileia any other Roman Martyrology than the one then in use at Rome?”

89. “But what proves more clearly that the Martyrology found at the beginning of Ado’s work at Saint Pantaleon’s in Cologne is certainly an ancient Roman Martyrology, intended for the use of the Roman Church and a true copy of the one which the Roman pontiff had sent to Aquileia, is not only the fact that it contains saints proper to the city of Rome and completely unknown to the Hieronymian Martyrologies—such as Martina, Dafrosa, Papias, and Maurus [Col. 0505B], all in the month of January alone; nor merely the fact that the Chair of Saint Peter is marked on its proper day and correctly distinguished from the Antiochene Chair; but also the fact that among the various dedications of the Roman churches there appears that of the upper chapel of the Castle of Saint Angelo, expressed by the words ‘BETWEEN THE CLOUDS,’ and that on the feast of Saint Sebastian his burial is said to have taken place ‘AT THE FOOTPRINTS OF THE APOSTLES,’ by which words the Catacombs are designated, where the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul rested for some time.

“And how, he asks, after this, have certain modern writers, following one another’s footsteps, dared to assert that the Martyrology published by Rosweyd is not an old Roman Martyrology, but rather a copy of the Hieronymian Martyrology? What else does this show than that those men, if indeed they examined that Martyrology, read it only superficially [Col. 0505C]? For apart from what we have already said about the Roman saints and the distinctive dedications of the Roman churches, even the slightest attention or application plainly shows that the entire text of Rosweyd’s Martyrology is entirely different from all the known copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology.”

90. All this was observed with complete accuracy by Castellanus. He would undoubtedly have said more if he had probed somewhat more deeply into the secrets of the Roman parvum, which are set more clearly before our eyes throughout this work. Nevertheless, let us hear the comparison which he made between our Little Martyrology and the Hieronymian Martyrologies:

“In Rosweyd’s Martyrology there are vacant days; in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, however much abbreviated, every day is full. Again, in the former everything is composed [Col. 0505D] and orderly; in the latter there is great confusion, since the text has often been copied from various exemplars. In Rosweyd’s Martyrology several prophets of the Old Testament are recorded; in the older copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology there is not one. In the former there are martyrs and other saints taken from Rufinus, but not the martyrs of Lyons; in the latter there are the martyrs of Lyons and a few others. Thus one must admit that Rosweyd’s Martyrology is an old original work, prepared with great care, and in no way derived from another.

“Hence it may reasonably be conjectured that the Romans, weary of the Hieronymian Martyrology, in which only the names of martyrs and the places of their contests were noted, preferred another in which selected and newly introduced saints—both martyrs and others—would be announced in smaller numbers, with the emperors or judges under whom they suffered [Col. 0506A] and other circumstances added. All these things are very aptly expressed in the old Rosweyd Martyrology.

“Moreover, is it not credible that this is the very Martyrology of the Roman Church known throughout the West from the year 747, when the Council of Clovesho was held in England, whose canon 13 supplies these definitive words . . . ?” You have this above, no. 81.

91. Castellanus goes on to show that Ado, when writing his Martyrology around the year 858, could rightly have called the guide he found at Aquileia equally most ancient and venerable. Nor does he allow himself to be challenged by the few additions to the Roman parvum, such as Erminon, or Erminus of Lobbes, on 25 April; the discovery of relics at Stabæte on the twentieth of the same month; or the dedication of Malmedy on 17 November [Col. 0506B]. It is sufficiently clear that similar items could very easily have been added by monasteries that had once possessed that manuscript or something like it. The same applies to Quirinus on 30 April—together with the vigil of the Apostles on that same day—and to other such minutiae, which we admit do not belong to the Romans.

For from many other details it is entirely clear that Ado described each of the solemnities proper to Rome in such a way that he always seems to point out his precursor before him, as it were with his finger. Otherwise, Castellanus—and anyone ought to find this remarkable—thinks it astonishing that so ancient and so complete a codex should have survived to our own times.

Whether the feast of All Saints should be counted among the additions, we shall discuss in its proper place. He admits, however, that Theodotus of Laodicea was added by mistake by the author of that Martyrology, who followed Rufinus too blindly; we shall say more about him elsewhere [Col. 0506C].

Other arguments of Castellanus in favor of the authenticity, antiquity, and authority of the Roman parvum are scattered throughout the first two-month portion published by him with his excellent notes. May we one day be permitted to see the completion of that work! But what has already been said is, if I am not mistaken, more than sufficient to overthrow completely the objections of Valesius and the others.

92. At this point the reader must be warned that, while I am writing this, my venerable teacher Daniel Papebrochius should in no way be counted among my adversaries. He has been called by the Lord—as we confidently believe—to the crown of his labors, weighed down by age and merits. I repeat: he should not here be set against me, although in various places in our great work on the Acts [Col. 0506D] of the Saints, especially in volume V of June, page 550, letter C, he incidentally supports the opposing view.

He long ago and often admitted that he belonged to the group of whom Castellanus had just said that, although otherwise most learned men, they copied one another without sufficiently examining the matter and therefore failed to judge the Roman parvum according to its merits. There Papebrochius certainly summarized Florentinius’s opinion in a few words; but after hearing the more solid force of our arguments, he wished that this unfair judgment, adopted both in that place and elsewhere in the Acts, should be entirely withdrawn and erased.

It has now also been demonstrated that the arguments of Florentinius, cited above, and of the other opponents of the Roman parvum, miss the mark no less than those of Valesius and in no way weaken the authority of the venerable and most ancient Martyrology of Rosweyd [Col. 0507A].

## ARTICLE II

The adversaries vainly attempt to show that the Roman parvum is not the very Martyrology which Ado admits to have assisted him and which he asserts that he prefixed to his own Martyrology.

### § I.—Andrew Saussayus and John Fronto Refuted

93. We have already heard from Castellanus that certain modern writers, without giving the matter the slightest consideration, and merely copying one another, nevertheless dared to assert that our Roman parvum, published by Rosweyd, was an abridgment contracted from the larger and older Roman Martyrology, commonly called the Hieronymian.

I remember finding only a few such men; but [Col. 0507B] whoever they may be, they must be utterly inexperienced in matters of this kind, since a collation of the codices covering even one month, or indeed only a few days, can prove beyond all doubt that the author of that Martyrology was so far removed from the Hieronymian Martyrologies that on most days he does not record even one name found in the Hieronymian texts. I therefore judge that such adversaries do not deserve a refutation.

More trouble is caused by those who, deceived by a superficial and deceptive appearance of similarity, have persuaded themselves that our Little Martyrology is nothing other than a pure epitome of Ado’s Martyrology, produced at least two centuries after Ado himself. The principal men among these are the aforementioned Andrew Saussayus, cited by Florentinius in his work on mystical writers [Col. 0507C]; John Fronto, in section 8 of his preliminary notes to the Calendar published in 1652; and Franciscus Maria Florentinius, in preliminary admonitions 4 and 5 to the Hieronymian Martyrology.

I shall begin with Fronto. His paragraph is all the easier to overturn because his rounded assertion, unsupported by any reason, can be just as roundly, plainly, and completely demolished by an opposing denial. The title of his paragraph is: “What should be thought about the old Roman Martyrology published by Rosweyd?” The answer is categorical; attend to it.

94. “That Martyrology is nothing other than an epitome of Ado’s Martyrology, as anyone who compares them will easily recognize: it has the same errors, it often has the same words; some things have been added. In short [Col. 0507D], it is in no way Roman, nor is it old.

“That it is not old is demonstrated by the fact that it records the solemnity of All Saints, which certainly does not precede the time of Gregory III, who sat in the year 731, or of Charlemagne, who died in the year 813, as I demonstrated under 1 November.

“It is not Roman, for when it speaks of Saint Felix on 14 January, or the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, it writes as follows: ‘At Nola, Felix the presbyter, buried at Pincis.’ And who does not know that PINCIS is a place in Rome, not at Nola, as I demonstrated under that day? This error does not belong to a Roman writer but comes from Ado. Let no one say that I am indulging in conjecture here; the matter is certain.

“Otherwise, it makes no difference to me whether that Martyrology is Roman or not Roman; but we are bound to state what is true.”

By this sort of reasoning one could easily argue that the Greek Menologion translated into Latin by Cardinal Sirleto was not transferred by Baronius into the Roman Martyrology, but that the Menologion itself had been extracted from the modern Roman Martyrology.

95. Certainly, this most learned man disposes of much in a few words, and would have settled the matter if he had supported his judgment with solid considerations. If I declare with a single breath that the entire passage is not only uncertain but superficial and false, no one can rightly say that I am indulging in conjecture, since I shall prove each statement individually.

It matters no more to me than it does to Fronto whether that Martyrology is Roman [Col. 0508A]; but if we are bound to state what is true, then by the same religious duty we are bound to identify what is false—or at least what plainly appears to be false [Col. 0508B].

Come now: what follows from the claims “it has the same errors” and “it often has the same words”? Does this imply that the Roman parvum derives from Ado? Or does it not more clearly imply that Ado received it from the Roman parvum, especially since Ado himself so clearly testifies that, while he was staying at Ravenna, a religious brother lent it to him for several days, that he copied it with diligent care, and that he placed it at the beginning of his own work?

Let the errors be the same; let all the words be the same; let the punctuation marks be the same. What else, I ask, can one infer from this except that the man who expressly professes to have copied it did in fact copy it?

“But it is neither old nor Roman.” The latter has already been amply demonstrated and will be demonstrated further; and the unfortunate title “AT PINCIS” will not deprive us of it. On this, see the Observation under the cited day, 14 January [Col. 0508C].

As for its antiquity, we shall settle the matter briefly, so that the feast of All Saints will provide Fronto with no support. For the present, it is enough for our purpose that it is sufficiently old to have been a genuine guide for Ado in arranging his Martyrology.

96. Two adversaries remain, Saussayus and Florentinius, whose definitions must be answered not with definitions but with arguments. Not long ago we reported Saussayus’s magnificent praises of Rosweyd, poured forth on account of the publication of that old Roman Martyrology. Elsewhere, however, he turns these accumulated praises into reproaches. Since I find them in Florentinius, I shall not take the trouble to seek them in their original source.

Let us therefore listen to Florentinius and follow him step by step. Saussayus was first at fault in comparing Rosweyd’s codex with Bede’s Martyrology [Col. 0508D] and ridiculously asserting that it was merely an index of Bede’s Martyrology. Perhaps, since he knew no other Bede than the Plantinian one, badly stitched together from Ado, he could easily be led to make one the epitome of the other—just as Florentinius judged it an epitome of Ado when he compared it with Ado.

But Rosweyd had injured Saussayus in the pupil of his eye by attacking Hilduin’s views about Dionysius from his own codex. Hence those sharper attacks on Rosweyd; hence the long series of arguments with which Saussayus attacked him and asserted that most serious and learned men denied that Rosweyd’s Martyrology was the old Roman Martyrology praised by Ado [Col. 0509B] and depicted by Saint Gregory, and so forth.

In a word, he declares it spurious, different from the true Martyrology and to be rejected—indeed, corrupted, falsified, and drawn from a thoroughly corrupt codex [Col. 0509A]. Thus those who pronounce rashly on matters that they have not sufficiently discussed or weighed fall disgracefully into the opposite extreme, driven now by love, now by hatred.

I readily admit that Rosweyd’s Martyrology is not Gregorian. But that it is not the very Martyrology praised by Ado—that I emphatically deny. Nor will the arguments of Saussayus or Florentinius ever force me to concede it. To summarize their substance, I shall proceed in order.

97. Saussayus, as I see it, argued from the word *natalis* (“feast-day”), but with a weapon as weak as it is unworthy of refutation.

“But stronger objections are urged,” says Florentinius, “by what the critic then brings forward: namely, that this Martyrology cannot possibly be the one praised by Ado and from which he admits having received so much assistance.

“First, because of the three ancient codices which Rosweyd used, he found it prefixed to Ado in only one. In that codex it could more properly have been prefixed as a Calendar, and it actually presents something not inconsistent with such a function. Hence Rosweyd is attacked for having supposed that Ado everywhere followed the footsteps of the old Roman Martyrology, whereas the passages he notes clearly show that this supposed Roman Martyrology differs from Ado in many places and is fuller in some.”

If Saussayus has nothing stronger to urge than this, he truly shows that he attacks Rosweyd only in order to defend Hilduin. What if Rosweyd had found ten, or twenty, codices of Ado without the Roman parvum, and had found it happily prefixed only to one, in the twenty-fifth position [Col. 0509C]? Would that, I ask, make the long-sought and long-desired treasure less valuable?

Is Bede, published by our predecessors and received everywhere with the applause of all learned men, of less value because that text was absent from hundreds of codices and was found in only one or two—or even in two fragments, one Roman and the other Divionese?

98. Let someone now bring to light so many hidden works of antiquity. Even if they are absent from thousands of other codices, I will ensure that they are received gratefully and favorably by all learned men, provided they suffer from no defect other than rarity.

We know that Aloysius, after a long and burdensome search, found a copy of Ado in comparison with which he considered all gold worthless. Who, I ask, ever thought of criticizing its publication [Col. 0509D] on the ground that it was the only copy and the first?

Mabillon saw other copies, more or less complete, as did others; in some of them the Roman parvum was absent, and in some even Ado’s preface was missing. Yet no learned man on that account regarded with suspicion what Rosweyd had so successfully delivered to the scholarly world.

Moreover, the aforementioned Mabillon testifies in the fourth Benedictine century, part II, page 272, that in several handwritten copies of this Martyrology of Ado which he had seen, Ado’s name did not appear. Will Saussayus perhaps infer from this also that the Martyrology transmitted under Ado’s name was wrongly attributed to him because Ado’s name does not appear in many copies?

[Col. 0510A] 99. Here is another equally tasteless argument: Rosweyd’s Martyrology could more properly have been prefixed to Ado as a Calendar.

Has Saussayus already forgotten what he said shortly before—that it was merely an index of Bede’s Martyrology? Bede, even the spurious Bede, and Ado are certainly very different from one another—at least sufficiently so that the same index or Calendar cannot suit both.

Nor do I understand with what plausibility the Roman parvum can be presented as Ado’s Calendar if it is clearly shown to differ from Ado in many places and to be fuller in some. If an index or Calendar does not correspond to the work, it cannot properly be called the index or Calendar of that work—any more than a Calendar prefixed to the Roman Missal could be fitted to a Greek or Coptic liturgy.

Here [Col. 0510B] I see an excessive itch to scrutinize trifles and then quibble over them, where a more moderate judgment suited to the facts is required. Let us make some allowance for ancient codices, and let us admit, with Florentinius, that these sacred records—Sacramentaries, Diptychs, and Martyrologies—could not have reached us so intact that, through the extreme negligence of scribes or ecclesiastical copyists, they were not mutilated or interpolated.

To subject such codices to an excessively rigid criticism is therefore almost to tear them apart, as Florentinius has learned sufficiently from his own Hieronymian codices, and as those who frequently handle ancient codices—especially books intended for regular use, such as Martyrologies—experience only too often.

100. In his edition of Ado, Mosander marked many passages with an asterisk [Col. 0510C] as though they should be denied to the author; Rosweyd relegated more of them to an appendix. But behold: Mabillon, in the place already cited, thinks that most of them should be restored, while other passages that others had judged genuine were inserted by an interpolator.

We bring this forward only to show that it is scarcely humanly possible for such codices to reach us intact—a circumstance that occurs in almost every day of this edition of Usuard.

It will therefore be no great wonder if some things were added to the Roman parvum and others removed here and there, although we have found that this happened rarely.

How, then, do they continue to attack Rosweyd’s Calendar because many days are vacant of martyrs? Saussayus is truly obtuse. Let us first count how many days are vacant in the Roman parvum. When the calculation is made, we find that the total is seven: 27 February, 24 April, 23 May, 8 June, 15 October, 20 October, and 16 November [Col. 0510D].

And these are the “many days” vacant of martyrs? Must we abuse language by calling days “many” when, out of 365, only seven are lacking? Indeed, if this argument is properly weighed, the more numerous the vacant days in the Roman parvum, the less it will resemble what Saussayus calls Ado’s Calendar or what Florentinius imagines as Ado’s epitome.

101. Saussayus presses the point: “If Ado had used this Martyrology in arranging the feast days—which in any case were badly distributed day by day and according to the Kalends—then, since some days were also lacking in it, he could certainly not have used it to supplement Bede [Col. 0511A] as augmented by Florus.”

This is a new scruple. Ado nowhere wrote that he had used the Roman parvum to supplement every day that was missing from Bede through Florus’s abbreviation. Rather, he admits that it assisted him so that the days of the martyrs might be marked with complete accuracy—that is, distinctly. They were accustomed to appear confused in the Kalends, though not necessarily confused in Bede and Florus, but in the older Hieronymian Martyrology, from which Florentinius has not yet removed all the confusion.

Let there therefore have been seven vacant days. Can Ado not otherwise rightly profess that he was assisted, when he found 358 days full? Were there no other saints with whom he could fill those few days?

Let us resolve everything. On 28 February he brought in, from the neighboring region, Romanus, abbot of Jura. On 24 April [Col. 0511B] Bede was not vacant, yet on that very day Ado added Saint Alexander of Lyons, whom Bede had marked under 23 May. It was not necessary to go far in order to mention Desiderius of Langres—or indeed his namesake of Vienne; see our Usuardine Observation there.

On 8 June he had Medardus in Bede, but was not satisfied with him. On 15 October he supplied Antiochus of Lyons and Maurus of Cologne. On 20 October the local Saint Caprasius was not far to seek. Finally, on 16 November there was Eucherius of Lyons.

You see that Ado received no great assistance from elsewhere, so that it remains entirely true that he was assisted chiefly and above all by that venerable and most ancient Martyrology.

102. There follows an argument which I do not know how Saussayus could have extracted or manufactured, nor with what shadow of truth Florentinius could have reported it. Prick up your ears [Col. 0511C]:

“Moreover, it cannot be denied,”—I continue to quote Florentinius—“that the statements which Saussayus adds assign that Martyrology to a later period, namely to the year 1049. For since, under 20 October, it records at Rheims the solemnity of Saint Remigius, which had previously been celebrated on the day of his departure, 13 January, and since this was transferred to the same day at the Council of Rheims while Pope Leo IX was present, no one can allow that this is the Martyrology which Ado, bishop of Vienne, prefixed to his own autograph around the year 875—better, he should write, around the year 858—but rather one composed or written in the later part of the eleventh century.”

Not even Oedipus himself could explain to us what Saussayus and Florentinius ultimately intend by this imposing heap of material, unless they openly admit that they never examined Rosweyd’s old Martyrology—at least not on the very day they cite, 20 October [Col. 0511D].

103. I repeat that I simply cannot understand how such a thought could have entered the minds of men otherwise learned. For if 20 October is genuinely brought forward as an example, they are inventing monsters which they can safely destroy, since that day is precisely one of the seven which we said were vacant in the codex.

Nor is any other solemnity of Remigius recorded in the entire month except the one entered on the Kalends, in these words: “And at the city of Rheims, Saint Remigius, bishop.” Indeed, this is the one and only solemnity concerning Remigius [Col. 0512A] found in our Roman parvum.

But if this solemnity was first instituted in the year 1049, while Pope Leo IX was present, consider, I ask, how many absurd consequences would follow. All our Martyrologies—those of Bede, Wandalbert, Rabanus, Ado, Usuard, and Notker, and even the Hieronymian Martyrologies themselves—would then have been composed or written in the later part of the eleventh century, since the very same solemnity is explicitly announced in all of them.

If that is not enough, Gregory of Tours, who is five centuries older than all of them, would become younger than they, since in the History of the Franks, chapter 21, he states: “It happened that after a few days the feast of Saint Remigius arrived, which is celebrated at the beginning of October.”

Leo IX selected a day which he well knew had formerly been assigned to the feast of Remigius.

[Col. 0512B] 104. I am struck more by amazement than admiration when I see such quibbles, trifles, indeed sheer fabrications, being brought forward and even passed from hand to hand by learned men—things eagerly seized upon by non-Catholics and marketed to our discredit, while supplying them with an opportunity and a path for inventing similar claims.

The aforementioned Beckius certainly adorned his supposed Martyrology of Germany splendidly with such flowers gathered from Saussayus, Valesius, and Florentinius, and, lest he yield the palm to them, enriched it with an utterly foolish commentary.

After portraying Rosweyd from Valesius as something like a braggart soldier—one who, using words a foot and a half long, had addressed the Roman pontiff while mixing in childish details—he finally picks up a little stone from his own pouch and thinks that, with the blow he has chosen, he is destined to overthrow Goliath [Col. 0512C].

Hear how cleverly he argues, on page 22:

“The more recent age of Rosweyd’s Martyrology is also proved by what is read under the fourth day before the Nones of July: ‘On the same day, at Augsburg, Saint Ulrich, bishop and confessor.’ Yet he lived in the tenth century and was certainly not canonized immediately.

“Ado could not have drawn these waters from this source, since he lived in the ninth century, unless we say that these words were added by a later writer. This is the view taken by Mosander and Rosweyd in the appendix, where these passages seem suspect to them and to have been added by a later hand—perhaps that of a Benedictine monk, in whose codex alone they were found and were absent from the other three manuscripts.”

105. Forgive me, reader, if such an inept, foolish, and mendacious piece of nonsense [Col. 0512D] provokes my indignation. It is as similar to Saussayus’s argument as one egg is to another, and rests on precisely the same foundation.

For it is blatantly false that the words about Saint Ulrich of Augsburg cited here by Beckius are found anywhere in Rosweyd’s entire old Roman Martyrology, much less under the fourth day before the Nones of July, as this man boldly invents. Perhaps he found the quoted words in Rosweyd’s appendix to Ado and built upon them a mass of imaginary claims, clearly showing that he rushes about like a blind swordsman, knowing neither the argument at issue nor the books he had in his hands.

He links Mosander with Rosweyd, as though Mosander too had published the Roman parvum. That is a second falsehood.

Third, he calls something Mosander’s “appendix,” although Mosander never even dreamed of preparing an appendix. In Ado’s own text [Col. 0513A] he merely used an asterisk to mark passages that seemed suspect to him.

Fourth, he invents some codex belonging to a Benedictine monk, which supposedly served the edition of the Roman parvum together with three others, although Rosweyd expressly states that in editing Ado he used only three codices, and that the Roman old Martyrology prefixed to Ado was absent from two of them.

To conclude in a word: the entire Beckian construction is fabricated, futile, and empty. If only men otherwise most learned and worthy of my respect, carried away by false prejudices, had not shown the way to its invention!

106. I return to Florentinius, who continues the Saussayan web:

“Finally,” he says, “Saussayus proves that Rosweyd’s work—whether it is a Martyrology or a Calendar—is not the one desired by Baronius.”

Whether [Col. 0513B] this is sufficiently correct I do not examine, since it makes no difference to our case whether the great author of the Ecclesiastical Annals sought the larger or the smaller Roman Martyrology, provided that it remains true that Rosweyd published the one from which the Viennese Martyrologist admits having received assistance.

“But lest Saussayus omit anything that might remove all authority from Rosweyd’s Calendar, and conclude that the little book is entirely without certainty or weight and covered with thick errors, he adds, by way of a ridiculous climax, that it also contains certain absurdities. He attempts to prove this from the notes under the sixth day before the Ides of November: ‘On that same day, the Four Crowned Martyrs,’”—it should read, “And on that day”—“and so forth.” [Col. 0513C]

But those absurdities have, unless I am mistaken, been clearly disposed of in our discussion under the sixth day before the Ides of November. Here Florentinius also resolves them, correctly observing at least on one occasion that “Saussayus is far too exacting when he stubbornly insists that Dionysius of Paris is the same person as the Areopagite, because he conjectured that this identity was somewhat weakened by both Rosweyd’s Martyrology and his notes.”

107. This, then, is the whole source of the mischief. Inflamed by it, Saussayus, as he scrutinized everything with bulging eyes, imagined that he had discovered absurdities, nonsense, anachronisms, and I know not what else in the Roman parvum, into which he had previously inserted everything select and golden:

“Heribertus, certainly, himself an extraordinary ray of the sun of wisdom, a stream from the living fountain of faith, a branch from the trunk of flourishing justice, and already a beautiful and eternal star of heaven.”

I ask you: how quickly has that excellent color changed?

The distinguished Castellanus, from whom I had requested information about Saussayus’s book on mystical writers cited by Florentinius [Col. 0513D], would explain the matter sincerely and frankly. He replied that he did not know the work himself, but knew very well that all Saussayus’s works were held in profound contempt at Paris (*profonde mésestime*).

He further said that the great work of the Gallican Martyrology, divided into two volumes, was contemptuously called “a wagonload of lies.” Finally, he said that Saussayus was an exceptionally stubborn Hilduinist, and that for this reason he considered it a religious duty to rise up as fiercely as possible against the little work which so carefully distinguished the two Dionysiuses from each other.

Naturally, it made no difference to him what truth suffered, so long as he encountered something contrary to his prejudices (*à ses entêtements*).

With this, we order Saussayus to leave the arena.

### § II.—Florentinius’s More Plausible Objections Dispersed

[Col. 0514A] 108. Our controversy with Florentinius remains. In examining it, we must deal with matters which John Fronto had recently determined more by a categorical verdict than by solid arguments, while Florentinius, adducing reasons, attempts to demonstrate them more plausibly—but, as befits a most learned man, with the greatest modesty—by comparing the Roman parvum and Ado with one another.

It is worthwhile to examine his individual arguments in order. He proceeds as follows:

“Yet just as I would readily concede to Saussayus that the Martyrology attributed to Rosweyd is not the old Roman Martyrology indicated by Saint Gregory and sought by Baronius, so I would by no means agree that it was abridged from Bede’s Hagiology, since anyone who compares it with Ado could much more plausibly [Col. 0514B] regard it as an excerpt from Ado, a more concise Calendar.

“I have indeed compared many days of each month, and from those same passages excerpted from Ado and reduced for particular use in a style either more obscure, mutilated, or recent, I easily recognized that it was not Ado who transferred material from this Calendar into his Martyrology as from an ancient Aquileian codex. Rather, it was a later writer who assembled his little index from Ado.”

I ask you to observe carefully that Florentinius derived this from Saussayus and repeatedly assumes that the Roman parvum was written in the later part of the eleventh century. Armed with this prejudice, he easily gathers other features which seem to him to bear the marks of a more recent style.

“Let us,” he says, “if you wish, run briefly through one or two months.” Indeed, I am willing—and gladly so—to go through all twelve [Col. 0514C], and through the selected days. I want us to compare each and every one of them simultaneously with Ado and with our own Martyrology, so that not only the truth of the assertion but also the age of our older Martyrology may become evident.

109. To avoid confusion, I wish these matters to be joined to our subject; and, granting without hesitation whatever antiquity may belong to the Hieronymian copies for which he alone contends, I shall insist only on a comparison of Ado and the Little Roman Martyrology, so that it may clearly emerge which took from the other. Florentinius begins right from the outset as follows: “Rosweyde’s Martyrology begins the year, according to a more recent custom than ours, from the Kalends of January.” Indeed, it begins the year from the Kalends of January; but from this nothing follows less necessarily than that its custom is more recent. Florentinius labors greatly, but almost in vain, in his second dissertation to extract from somewhere the antiquity—or, to speak more clearly, the priority—of these customs for beginning the year [Col. 0514D], and so far has been unable to produce fixed pivots on which we might hinge the matter; nor is the judgment required for fixing them either easy or straightforward. However that may be, Florentinius is plainly disarmed by an argument ad hominem when he attacks Rosweyde here. For the oldest among his Hieronymian copies, written, as is established, at the beginning of the eighth century, likewise begins the sequence of its sacred year from the Kalends of January; and Bede, an exact contemporary of Willibrord, does the same. I do not dispute the prerogative of age with the Hieronymian manuscripts; it is enough for me if Florentinius grants the Little Roman Martyrology equal standing with the Epternacensis and Bede.

110. No more would be needed to weaken Florentinius’s entire first [Col. 0515A] argument completely. Yet, for the benefit of the curious, I am pleased to inquire further whether it is a more recent ecclesiastical practice to begin the year from the Kalends of January rather than from the Nativity, or from the vigil of the Nativity, or from some other point—for learned men still regard this matter as sufficiently uncertain and ambiguous. Let us run through the ancient Ritual books and Martyrologies.

It is certain that the Calendars of Allatius and Fronto are regarded as ancient, that they resemble one another, and that they do not differ greatly in age. The Allatian Calendar was inserted at the end of the work *On the Agreement of the Western and Eastern Churches*, four years before Fronto’s, namely in 1648. Compare the two: you will immediately notice that the Allatian begins with the First Sunday of Advent, and marks the days, in the manner of the ancient Romans and of our Martyrologies [Col. 0515B], by Kalends, Nones, and Ides. Fronto’s edition, by contrast, begins with the day of the Lord’s Nativity, and proceeds through the days of the whole year according to the modern custom, by ordinal numbers.

In the Sacramentaries edited by Menard and Thomasius, the beginning is taken from the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. Of the three Gallican Sacramentaries published by Thomasius and later by Mabillon, there is not one whose beginning you can determine to have been similar to that of another. Mabillon himself does not conceal that conjectures on these matters are doubtful and uncertain, in *On the Gallican Liturgy*, p. 98, no. 3; p. 176, no. 5; and elsewhere.

111. I think that the practice of beginning the Martyrologies was equally— that is, not fixed but arbitrary—and that nothing sufficiently certain can be established about it. I have already spoken of the Hieronymian Epternacensis and of Bede [Col. 0515C]; Blumianus must be added to them. The Lucensis and Corbeiensis, however, do not begin from the vigil of the Nativity, as does Ado’s copy of Rosweyde, but, like Fronto’s Calendar, begin the year from the eighth day before the Kalends of January, that is, from the very day of the Lord’s Nativity.

Moreover, Aloysius and Mosander edited Ado in such a way as to make the beginning fall at the Kalends of January. Rosweyde, however, speaks as follows in the last paragraph of his preface:

> “You should know that the beginning in Ado’s Martyrology is taken not from the Kalends of January, as it has hitherto been edited, but from the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity because this was done according to the custom of the Roman Church, which formerly had Christ’s Nativity as the epoch of the year and began the year from the Vespers of that Nativity’s vigil. Three manuscript copies which I used consistently presented it in this way.”

Was the most exacting of men perhaps then forgetful that his own ancient Roman Martyrology, much older than Ado, begins from the Kalends of January [Col. 0515D]? If all the manuscript copies of Ado were compared with one another, I believe that more would be found which in this respect conformed to the Little Roman Martyrology.

112. Wandalbert was Ado’s contemporary, indeed older than Ado and a Martyrologist before him, since he wrote in the year 842; nevertheless, he begins his work as follows:

> “From the Kalends of January to the end of the year, I have set forth in verse the festivals occurring on each day”—

that is, the Martyrology. The same was done by the man whose assistance and support Wandalbert chiefly used: the holy and celebrated Florus, subdeacon of the Church of Lyons, compiler of the expanded Martyrology of Bede.

Add to these [Col. 0516A] Rabanus, himself older than Ado; add Notker, nearly Ado’s equal in age; and it will be evident that what I said above is true: at that time this manner of beginning the year was highly arbitrary in ecclesiastical books, especially in Martyrologies. Indeed, the greater and more ancient number of our Martyrologists so establishes the authority of the Little Roman Martyrology that it rather follows that, in the very eighth century, the practice of beginning the year began from the Kalends of January, than that it can in any way plausibly be regarded, on Florentinius’s conjectures, as a more recent custom.

I conclude with Bolland’s preface, by which he begins his work on the first day of January:

> “The Kalends of January have always been celebrated by Christians with especial religious observance, because of the octave of the Lord’s Nativity, the memory of Christ’s most sacred circumcision [Col. 0516B], and the most august name of Jesus, in which all human beings must surely be saved. The Church therefore rightly preferred, in beginning the year from this day, to follow the ancient Romans rather than the other peoples who appointed some different beginning, so that this day itself might bear before us the sacred emblem of our salvation.”

But enough of this.

113. Let us continue our brief excursion with Florentinius:

> “On the very day of the Kalends,” he says, “besides the octave of the Nativity and the circumcision, it presents no others than three martyrs and a single confessor, leaving with Ado the crown of thirty Roman martyrs, Euphrosyna the virgin, and Eugendus the abbot.”

Let us pause here for a moment and ask Florentinius whether the compiler of a Martyrology can properly have composed his alleged epitome, index, or Calendar while leaving three entire notices in Ado untouched [Col. 0516C]. I would reject such an index, or Calendar, even from this one point alone as unfaithful and spurious.

Let us ask again whether he begins his comparison at an especially suitable point, where there is such great disagreement between Ado and the Little Roman Martyrology. Why did he not proceed to the second day of January? There he would certainly have found a much greater conformity.

But, lest it become too tedious to weigh everything individually here—for these are Florentinius’s words—I shall settle the matter in a single statement: whether the Little Roman Martyrology agrees with Ado’s notices, or differs in number, or is deficient, or is more abundant, nothing contrary to the Little Roman Martyrology follows from this. For the Calendar text cited by Florentinius must convince every reasonable person that Ado, being later, took from the earlier work whatever it contained, and added what he had found elsewhere or what was closer to hand at Lyons, where he was writing his Martyrology [Col. 0516D].

114. The most learned man could and should have remembered what he himself had said shortly before: that Ado did not accommodate himself so closely to the traces of the Little Roman Martyrology that he did not depart from them even by a hair’s breadth. Indeed, he had to depart from it whenever assistance came from elsewhere, as the Kalends of January clearly demonstrate. Elsewhere, when he found no other saints—as on the second day of January and often elsewhere—he adorned no saints except those whom the Little Roman Martyrology had suggested to him.

But if the reverse had happened—if, for example, the Little Roman Martyrology had taken from Ado—what conceivable reason, I ask, could there be for the author of the little index to have selected only five of Ado’s eight notices, leaving aside saints who were the most famous [Col. 0517A]? Again, what reason could there be for his altering even Ado’s first and more celebrated notice by adding “and the circumcision,” words absent from the Viennese copy?

Will Florentinius say that even the designation of the circumcision belonged to a more recent usage? But we are cutting useless arguments far too finely. Ado himself has explained the matter with excessive clarity; he has indicated his guide and standard-bearer so distinctly and openly that this will be plainly demonstrated in the following article.

115. In any event, Florentinius’s arguments must be examined one by one, and each must receive its proper answer. Let us weigh them all. He proceeds as follows:

> “Let the curious reader compare, in this same first month, the thirteenth day, which he mutilates by the name of Corona and by the names of forty soldiers; and the nineteenth, where from many sources he gathers Pontianus, condemned to the beasts.”

Nothing new is brought forward here that was not already brought forward and answered in the preceding reasoning.

There follows Florentinius’s false but perpetual assumption, drawn from Saussay, that the Little Roman Martyrology is not older than the eleventh century. Observe here how he attempts to confirm it. He begins thus:

> “But let him especially observe the twentieth day [of January], and he will recognize that Fabian is called bishop of Rome by Ado, while the Breviary, in more recent fashion, calls him pope. Since it assigns this title everywhere and consistently to the Roman pontiff, whereas it is found only very rarely in Ado, this seems clearly to indicate that the author of the Calendar lived after Gregory VII, who in the year of Christ 1073 established that the name ‘pope,’ hitherto common to other bishops and more distinguished priests, should henceforth be the proper and distinctive designation of the Roman pontiff.”

116. This is the hypothesis which I have pointed out more than once: Florentinius’s proposal, by which our Little Roman Martyrology is dragged down to the late eleventh century. To speak truthfully, it rests on a more plausible argument than the preceding one; nevertheless, it is wholly invalid. For an argument drawn from the principles of the school proves nothing when it proves too much, and with his own sword he cuts down the adversary himself.

If Florentinius’s reasoning truly stands, then by the same argument the Lucensis Hieronymian, and even the Corbeiensis, must be brought down to the eleventh century, since those very codices very distinctly announce, on July 1, “Gagi, pope” [the reading is uncertain]; on July 2, “Melciadae, PP.” or “Miltiadis, pope”; and on September 10, “Hilary, pope”; and perhaps the same designation recurs elsewhere, though there is no need to investigate further.

What more? Bede himself frequently uses the name “pope,” as do all the Martyrologists of the ninth century—men whom someone would absurdly and ridiculously presume, on such a basis, to send forward into the eleventh century.

As for Florentinius’s statement that the name “pope” is found only rarely in Ado, it is astonishing and completely false. It occurs twice on p. 47 alone, again on the following page, p. 52, and likewise on p. 54 and in many other places, which it would be superfluous to enumerate individually [Col. 0518A]. Other weapons are needed if the antiquity of the Little Roman Martyrology is to be shaken.

117. But the fact that the author of this Martyrology consistently applies the title “pope” to the Roman pontiff should itself, among other things, serve us as an argument that the Martyrology in question was written and used at Rome, and probably continued in use until the Usuardine Martyrology was admitted at Rome, as in all the other Western Churches.

Additional force and authority are given to our assertion by the ancient Roman Calendar, both as edited by Allatius and as edited by Fronto. There the name “pope” frequently recurs; yet no one could reasonably argue from this that the Calendar is later than the eighth century, and it would be still more disgraceful to try to banish it to the eleventh.

As for Florentinius’s sending the reasonable reader to January 20, 21, 29, and 30; then to March 11, April 1, September 7, November 1, November 10, 26, and 28; and finally to December 18 and 19, so that from these dates he may argue that everything breathes pure Ado—I gladly choose that same reader as judge of whether, from these cited days, indeed from almost all the days of the entire year, the exact opposite is not altogether apparent: namely, that wherever Ado does not impose saints sought from elsewhere, Ado breathes pure Little Roman Martyrology.

Accordingly, nothing could be less probable than that Florentinius’s statements establish that the ancient Roman Martyrology—or, with Bolland, the Lesser Roman Martyrology—was abridged from Ado rather than that it preceded Ado as a work of extreme antiquity. For, once the arguments of our opponents have been refuted, we are about to demonstrate the precise opposite [Col. 0518C].

118. One point remains with Florentinius, by which I shall briefly show that the distinguished man, carried away by excessive zeal for praising and embellishing his Hieronymian Martyrology, wished to force that very work into the place of the Little Roman Martyrology and fit it with the characteristics which Ado assigns to the latter: namely, that it was venerable and extremely ancient, sent from the city of Rome to Aquileia by a Roman pontiff to a certain holy bishop.

> “This is suggested,” he says, “by our two codices, in which the Martyrology ascribed to St. Jerome and presented by us is joined directly to Ado’s work. The ancient characteristics, which clearly prove it to be Gregorian, scarcely leave room for doubt that this is the very work which Ado calls ‘venerable and extremely ancient,’” and so forth.

Do we believe it because those who love such things ask us to? Certainly, if the juxtaposition of codices proves anything, our predecessors found so many works juxtaposed, and so many have been collected and juxtaposed in our museum, that anything whatever could be proved from them—for example, that Usuard was compiled from Rabanus and Bede from the Hieronymian Martyrologies alone, than which nothing could be more absurd.

If Florentinius had taken even a little trouble to compare the Hieronymian copies with Ado, he would have discovered, clearer than midday, that Ado’s affinity with the Hieronymian Martyrologies is scarcely greater than his affinity with the Calendars of Bucherius, Carthage, Allatius, and Fronto. Consequently, it is wholly gratuitous and wrong to say that the Hieronymian copies could have preceded Ado as his source and guide [Col. 0518D].

119. Let this suffice concerning Florentinius’s more specious objections. Yet, lest we seem entirely unwilling to concede anything to him, we shall not refuse him the point with which he concludes his fourth admonition—namely, that the Hieronymian Martyrology

> “must be considered older than everything published up to now, on the sole inspection of its nomenclature, the age of its additions, and its style of expression; and that it precedes the edition published by Rosweyde by as much as it surpasses all others in the marks of antiquity, and by as much as it exceeds it in the abundant yield of its simplest harvest of martyrs.”

This, I say, we freely grant to Florentinius, whether generously or merely as a due acknowledgment: that the Hieronymian Martyrology surpasses our Little Roman Martyrology in age, antiquity, and the number of martyrs.

But we ask that the favor be returned to us in ample measure: that the Little Roman Martyrology, in polish, arrangement, exact distinction of the Kalends, and finally in the whole symmetry of its composition, should be regarded as so greatly superior to all the Hieronymian codices that they cannot in any way be compared with it on these points [Col. 0519B].

But it is now time to examine thoroughly the very heart of the controversy: Rosweyde’s ancient Martyrology, our Little Roman Martyrology.

**ARTICLE III. Ado delineated the Little Roman Martyrology in such a way that his preface proves it to be precisely the work which he placed before his own Martyrology.**

120. Now that the arguments of the various opponents who attack the Little Roman Martyrology in various ways have been refuted in order and individually, it remains for us to draw from the Martyrology itself those conclusions concerning its true kind, authority, style, age, and other distinctive features which have finally persuaded us—after long study and repeated comparison over several years of all the Martyrologies, especially the Little Roman Martyrology itself and Ado’s—that no other Martyrology could have been designated in Ado’s preface than that very ancient, or Little, Roman Martyrology published by Rosweyde.

I believe that I have discovered, unless I am gravely mistaken, that this work served Ado as a kind of chain serves a weaver: as a model, as material, and as the foundation of his work; that it first shone before Ado, and thereafter before Usuard and Notker.

I do not conceal, however, that great labor, continuous attention, and unceasing study were required to drive from my mind a preconceived opinion, previously drawn from Fronto, Valesius, Florentinius, and others. That opinion, adorned with so many attractive illusions, had easily been absorbed by numerous learned men—whom I shall refrain from naming here. I had to expel it, I say, from a mind in which it had long been rooted.

Every day, in my observations on Usuard, I had to struggle against the same enchantment, so to speak, appearing before my eyes: namely, that the boundaries of the Little Roman Martyrology seemed so similar to those of Ado that I could not help recognizing something Adonian in the Little Roman Martyrology [Col. 0519D].

121. Let us state what is true. This struggle lasted long and intensely, and at first I could not yield to the most pressing arguments of Castellanus, who had more than once challenged me. But at length, after prolonged meditation, constant examination, and repeated reflection—bringing the notices of both Martyrologies together and comparing them with severe scrutiny; then weighing Ado’s own remarkable testimony, and continually encountering, in the very heart of the matter, many things that truly showed the Little Roman Martyrology to be older than Ado—I carefully balanced everything with myself, surrendered, and recognized the truth of Castellanus’s statement, reported above at no. 87: namely, that all those men, however learned, had not examined the matter with sufficient care, but had been captivated and deceived by that one deceptive resemblance, and had copied one another.

I share the arguments by which I established this with the reader, prepared to return to my former opinion if anyone should contend against me with a greater weight of reasons. For, to repeat Fronto’s words, it makes no difference to me in the least whether that Martyrology is Roman or not, ancient or recent, whether it preceded Ado or did not precede him—for the purity or integrity of Usuard does not depend on this. But we are obliged to set forth what is true and to take whatever precautions we can, lest the deceptive image that long deluded us should lead others into error [Col. 0520B].

122. If a sound judgment is to be made concerning this entire dispute, with partisan feeling excluded, the statements which the holy bishop of Vienne sets forth most expressly in his preface must never be absent either from the mind or from our sight. I think they must be reduced to six points.

First, Ado carried out his work at the command and instruction of holy men, so that the days which had been marked in the Martyrology that had grown through the labor of the venerable Florus and the work of Dom Bede, but stood without the names of martyrs, might be supplied.

Second, Ado sought days on which the martyrs had been recorded with complete accuracy, since they were customarily found confused in his Calendars. Here you can easily observe that “true” is set against “confused,” so that, in place of “most accurately,” one may without hesitation understand “most distinctly.”

Third, in accomplishing this he was assisted by some venerable and extremely ancient Martyrology.

Fourth, that very Martyrology had been sent from the city of Rome to Aquileia, by a Roman pontiff to a certain holy bishop.

Fifth, that the same Martyrology was later lent to Ado for several days by a certain religious brother, and that Ado, staying at Ravenna, copied it out with diligent care.

Finally, Ado thought that this very work should be placed at the head of his own work.

From these points it is perfectly clear that this was truly and uniquely the Martyrology from which Ado supplemented and enriched his own work after Bede and Florus, and that all the predicates contained in the six points just enumerated agree with it without controversy [Col. 0520D].

123. A second principle for deciding the dispute is one which none of our opponents can reasonably deny: no Martyrologies older than Ado can so far be identified—at least none by which he was assisted—other than the one circulated under the names of Eusebius and Jerome; the Little Roman Martyrology; and the work which grew through Florus’s labors upon Bede’s work and which Ado supplemented from that other, more ancient Martyrology.

If, therefore, I demonstrate that the six points established from Ado’s preface cannot possibly fit the Hieronymian Martyrology, and if, conversely, I prove that they fit Rosweyde’s Martyrology most aptly and unmistakably, I think that no one will thereafter dare to detract from the antiquity rightly due to the Little Roman Martyrology or from the praise deserved by Rosweyde.

Come, then, let us examine Ado’s individual statements.

As for the first point, I do not deny that Ado could have received some assistance from the Hieronymian Martyrology in supplying vacant days. I shall even grant our opponents something they perhaps did not know: Ado’s use of the Hieronymian Martyrology is demonstrated by Ado himself, since on February 24 he expressly cites it in these words: “And in the Martyrology marked with the names of Eusebius and Jerome.”

This proves that it could have been used to supply vacant days. But that he actually used it—that is the point which the opponents neither attempted to establish nor will ever establish. Merely reading our observations on Usuard will convince anyone who is not obstinate in nearly every single day that the contrary is true [Col. 0521B].

124. Let us approach the matter itself and demonstrate clearly, with respect to the first point of Ado’s preface, that Ado did not use the Hieronymian Martyrology in supplying Bede’s deficiencies.

Florentinius’s method will serve our purpose: as a specimen, we shall make a brief excursion through one or two months, comparing both Martyrologies, Jerome’s and Ado’s. No more will be needed for us to perceive most clearly that Ado had nothing less in mind than to restore from the Hieronymian Martyrology the days left vacant in Bede.

If you wish to touch the truth briefly and tangibly, run through only the first two months, January and February. In those two months alone you will find nearly forty days on which not a single notice of Ado agrees with any of the Hieronymian notices.

If some notices elsewhere seem to agree in some respect, at least in name, they always differ in some other way, and in a sufficiently significant way. I solemnly declare that in my observations on Usuard—where I chiefly labored to trace the memories of the saints back to their most ancient root—I often had to work hard to force out, now from one Hieronymian copy and now from another, some sort of affinity between them and Ado, as though by twisting their necks [Col. 0521C].

125. What I say here about the two months the reader will discover no less clearly and distinctly in all the months that follow. He will often be astonished that so many things concerning these Martyrologies and the Little Roman Martyrology have been determined and defined so boldly and rashly from a superficial comparison of perhaps one or two passages.

Earlier they loudly complained that Rosweyde’s Calendar was more open to attack because it had many days vacant of martyrs, although those many days scarcely amounted to a complete week. Yet here, if heaven approves, they will argue that from the Hieronymian Martyrology the days left vacant in Bede could have been supplied, when in the whole month of February scarcely four or five notices can be identified that can in any way be reduced to the Hieronymian notices.

There is neither time nor need to run through the days individually. The matter speaks for itself, and throughout the whole work of Usuard the same point had to be impressed and repeated almost to nausea [Col. 0522A]. Conversely, there, on nearly every single day, the origin of the notices from the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, Usuard, and Notker is brought before our eyes with as much exactness as possible and with such continual clarity that anyone who denies all this, though it is plainly demonstrated, must knowingly and willingly blind himself.

126. It is no less clear that Ado’s second statement is very far removed from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

Ado did not lack a copy of the Hieronymian Martyrology.
