But when he noticed in it an enormous confusion of materials—both in the bare names of the martyrs, which were very often truncated and distorted, and in the Kalends, or individual entries themselves, which had been completely disordered—he saw that he needed assistance from which he could record with complete accuracy the days of the martyrs whom he found confused in the Hieronymian copies.

He found this both opportunely and successfully in the Martyrology discovered at Ravenna. That Martyrology’s every trace is displayed most clearly and distinctly by the ancient work of Rosweyde, our Little Roman Martyrology, of which we are speaking here.

We call it “venerable and extremely ancient”: venerable in form, arrangement, and the whole elegant economy of its composition; extremely ancient in age, since we consider it unquestionably more than a hundred years older than Ado.

These two epithets could indeed also be applied to the Hieronymian Martyrologies on account of their antiquity. But since they are wholly lacking in the other respects, it is sufficiently clear that Ado found at Ravenna another treasure, by which he was assisted in composing his Martyrology. This fits the Little Roman Martyrology most plainly and fully, since Ado shows himself assisted by it on each day, rarely omitting the saints and rarely neglecting the very words in which the saints are announced in the Little Roman Martyrology. We have just said that this is the whole continuous demonstration of our work [Col. 0522C].

127. Fourth, Ado testifies that the Martyrology at Ravenna had been sent from the city of Rome to Aquileia, by a Roman pontiff to a certain holy bishop.

Allow me to remind you of what was said above at no. 122: Ado knew the Martyrology marked with the names of Eusebius and Jerome. Who, then, could regard it as even plausible that Ado would use those words and that phrase if the little book communicated to him at Ravenna by a religious brother had borne those same names of Eusebius and Jerome?

No one, as the proverb has it, should see three things in two or throw dust in his eyes. The two Martyrologies are designated here by such different characteristics that the one Ado acknowledges as having assisted him cannot possibly be the Hieronymian Martyrology.

But the description fits our Little Roman Martyrology perfectly: written and composed at Rome, truly Roman, and then used at Rome, it could have been sent by the Roman pontiff to a certain holy bishop at Aquileia, so that the bishop might conform himself to the Roman rite.

We believe that this was practiced at Aquileia and in other churches until the Usuardine method became more pleasing and gradually gained such strength that, once it had also been adopted at Rome, it deserved to be called, long before the time of Belinus of Padua, the Martyrology according to the custom of the Roman Curia.

128. If someone perhaps prefers the opinion of Henschenius and Papebrochius, expressed in the prologue to Bede before the second volume of March, no. 11, I shall not strongly resist, since they assert nothing there that does not fit our view extremely well. They write:

> “First of all, we find that we possess three manuscripts of Bede’s Martyrology, each of which presents the complete Bede, only moderately expanded and supplemented as regards the vacant days, with such fidelity that we were entirely persuaded that, in most Roman basilicas, after the use of the Hieronymian Martyrology had been abolished, and after that work which, as we noted above, had been sent by the pontiff to the bishop of Aquileia had perhaps been received only in the Lateran and a few other churches, Bede was so approved by others that many considered it appropriate to use him after he had been suitably expanded, until Usuard was seen to be more suitable for ecclesiastical use.”

Papebrochius explains this somewhat differently elsewhere, in the appendix to article 18 of his *Responses*. But before his death he requested that all his statements and writings concerning the material of the Martyrologies be brought back and adapted to this view of ours. Yet we would almost be straying from our purpose.

129. As for the fifth point, namely, that the Martyrology mentioned above was lent for several days by a religious brother and copied by Ado with diligent care, what could this more plainly signify than that it was not the Hieronymian Martyrology?

The holy Ado had been a monk of the monastery of Ferrières in the Gatinais; afterward he had moved to Prüm. Since he was a diligent investigator of matters, there is no doubt that he had visited other monasteries of his order and had certainly seen other Martyrologies, as well as—most certainly—a Hieronymian copy, or perhaps copies, which did not need to be sought at Ravenna or copied there [Col. 0523C].

Let us speak plainly: Ado would not have written in this way about a codex lent to him if he had received for copying the Martyrology marked with the names of Eusebius and Jerome.

Indeed, Ado discovered something there that had previously been unknown to him and to his own people. Because of the exact sequence of the Kalends and because of the names of the martyrs, so clearly distinguished, he valued it so highly that, thinking he had unearthed almost the riches of Croesus—just as Jerome spoke of Paul’s cloak—he proposed that single work to himself as a rule.

With the Kalends accurately marked, he would describe, from the records of the passions collected from every source, the praises of the saints at somewhat greater length and with greater clarity. Thus the weaker brethren might have, in the commemorations of the martyrs, a concise reading, in a small booklet, for which they would otherwise have to search through many other codices with great labor [Col. 0523D].

130. The sixth and final point of Ado’s preface remains, and it is by no means to be dismissed. In it the Martyrologist of Vienne declares that he thought this very Martyrology copied at Ravenna should be placed at the head of his work.

He did not say that it should be joined to his work or combined with it as one work. He expressly said that he thought it should be placed at the head of his work, so that, together with his own work, it would constitute, in a certain sense, one and the same work; so that his own preface would stand before both works; so that it would plainly affect both works; in a word, so that it would encompass both works as one and the same whole [Col. 0524A].

If Florentinius, or any other of our opponents, should somewhere produce a Hieronymian copy placed at the head of Ado’s Martyrology in this fashion, then, if you please, we can investigate in debate whether this last of Ado’s six points can in any degree be applied to the Hieronymian Martyrology.

For the present it seems certain to us that all those points agree with the Little Roman Martyrology as aptly, clearly, and manifestly as it is evident that all those descriptions are utterly foreign to the Hieronymian Martyrology—unless perhaps one excepts the fact that we do not deny that it can be called venerable and extremely ancient, if all its venerability derives solely from antiquity.

[Col. 0524B] 131. From these considerations I think it can most rightly be concluded that the ancient, or Little, Roman Martyrology has been depicted for us by Ado himself in such colors that scarcely anyone could have drawn it more vividly from life.

The most keen-sighted Rosweyde had seen and carefully observed all these features before he dared assert to the reader that Ado always follows the traces of this ancient Martyrology; before, confident of the truth, he addressed the reader so boldly:

> “Indeed, anyone who has even lightly inspected this ancient Roman Martyrology will not hesitate to assert that it is the source of all the other Martyrologies”—

for he did not yet know the Hieronymian Martyrology or the genuine Bede.

> “Certainly Ado drew his waters from this source. And just as a spring’s water, moving away from its origin, gradually grows, becomes a stream, and passes onward as waters flow into it from every side, so this Martyrology gradually grew: now through Bede”—

by “Bede” he means the Plantinian Martyrology, which he thought had been taken from Ado—

> “now through Usuard”—

whom he considered older than Ado—

> “now through Ado, now through others. It will now be possible always to point toward the source. For this purpose I have brought into the open the head of the spring, which until now lay concealed.”

These were Rosweyde’s words, the product of a discerning, mature, and sound judgment, within the limits of the knowledge of the Martyrologies then available.

The connection of the rivulets and streams with that first source of our series emerges throughout the entire course of Usuard’s Martyrology, day by day, from our observations in so sensible and palpable a manner that it seems unnecessary to roll this stone further here.

But since other arguments also exist which wonderfully illuminate the authenticity of the Little Roman Martyrology, I am pleased to set them forth in an orderly way in the following article [Col. 0524D].

**ARTICLE IV. The authority of the Little Roman Martyrology is demonstrated from its distinctive characteristics, style, kind, and age.**

132. We have now presented from Ado’s preface an image of the Little Roman Martyrology which can and should be recognized with the greatest ease; once recognized, it will be most ready to shatter all the quibbles of our opponents.

Let us grant Fronto, Florentinius, Cointius in the year 518, p. 315, and all the others who remain in the same boat, let us grant, I say, that everything in the Little Roman Martyrology and Ado’s Martyrology agrees so completely that in both there is the same style, the same order, the same words [Col. 0525A], the same solecisms, and the same errors—so that they differ in nothing and are altogether alike. Even so, it would not follow in any way that the Little Roman Martyrology had been abridged from the other, unless Ado’s entire preface were proved to be manifestly false and an utterly fabricated statement. We do not know that this has ever entered anyone’s mind, even in a dream.

Yet the most holy bishop of Vienne candidly and sincerely declares that, in order to supply Bede’s vacant days, he was assisted by a venerable and extremely ancient Martyrology, lent to him at Ravenna, copied by him, and placed by him at the head of his own work.

That very Martyrology is found placed at the head of Ado’s work. Its traces appear everywhere, marked out so clearly by Ado; and each and all of them belong so properly to the Little Roman Martyrology that they cannot possibly fit any other Martyrology.

And after this there will still be people who, virtually accusing the holy Ado himself of falsehood, pronounce to us, as though from a tripod, that our Little Martyrology, the ancient work published by Rosweyde, is nothing but an epitome of Ado’s Martyrology, in which everything breathes pure Ado.

I confess that I cannot understand how Florentinius, accustomed to scrutinizing everything more deeply, could have been persuaded of this. But let us vindicate the truth and depict the Little Roman Martyrology in its own living, distinctive, and native colors.

### 133.

The first distinctive mark of antiquity, and one different from Adonian method, is derived from the *Romanum parvum* in this respect: whereas Ado and the other Martyrologists of the ninth century always piously prefix the designation “saint” or “blessed” to martyrs and confessors, the author of this Martyrology, although he sometimes adds it, more often tends to omit it. For out of the sixty-two announcements of January in which the title “saint,” “blessed,” or “saints and blessed” could have been prefixed, it is found in only thirty-one. In February, out of forty-five announcements, twenty-seven lack the addition. Again, in March, out of forty-four, only sixteen are so marked. If you run through the other months, still fewer commemorations appear in which the author of that Martyrology was concerned to attach the designation “saint” or “blessed,” so that throughout the whole of November it is scarcely found four times, and in December only twice. You may conclude that this is a definite mark of antiquity from the fact that the Hieronymian codices—both the larger ones published by Florentinius and the smaller ones which we reviewed in the preceding chapter—rarely prefix titles of this kind, and indeed do so the more rarely the older they are. This is extraordinarily clear in the Echternach copy, in which the designation “saint” or “blessed” is scarcely ever found; and wherever it is added, it perhaps deserves to be deleted as an interpolation. [Col. 0525D]

### 134.

A second—and indisputable—mark of antiquity must be recognized in the *Romanum parvum*: throughout the entire cycle of the year, as Martyrologists speak, it very rarely marks the vigils of saints; indeed, most certainly no more than one, perhaps proper to Rome, that of Saint Lawrence, together with a second, the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. Yet Bede is found to have included, besides those two, the vigils of Saint John the Baptist and of Saints Peter and Paul. From this one might draw the not implausible conclusion that our Martyrology was composed before Bede’s time, although we think its date should begin somewhat after Bede’s death.

But that the omission of vigils must plainly be counted among the sure signs of antiquity is proved again by the Hieronymian copies. Concerning 24 December, Florentinius notes as follows: “Since neither in our codices nor in the most ancient Martyrology—for example, the Antwerp or Echternach one—is the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord indicated in today’s calendars, this supplied an occasion for doubt: whether this was not a practice of the most ancient Church, or at least that it is certain that, in the older Martyrologies, vigils are not indicated.” If the distinguished scholar had examined the *Romanum parvum* somewhat more carefully, and had noticed that it marks only one vigil of Lawrence and another of the Nativity of the Lord, although several others are found in Ado, he would not so readily have declared that “he had recognized that Ado had not transferred this from that Calendar into his Martyrology as from an ancient Aquileian codex, but, on the contrary, that a more recent writer had compiled his little index from it.” [Col. 0526B]

Nor should you say that the vigil of the Apostles is marked on 30 April, for it is sufficiently clear that it has been inserted there ineptly, just as Quirinus is placed on the same day, added there for the sake of the people of Neuss and incorrectly repeated from 30 March.

### 135.

To disarm all epitomizers once and for all with a brief argument, I ask them to submit solid answers to the following questions.

1. If the compiler of the old or little Roman Martyrology had Ado’s Martyrology before his eyes, tell me why he left seven days empty, when he could have filled those seven days just as conveniently as all the others from Ado?

2. What sufficient reason can be devised for his omitting the vigils so clearly marked in Ado, especially since we have discussed separately the Vigil of the Assumption of the Mother of God under 14 August?

3. Why did he suppress the title “saint,” so distinctly set out in Ado?

4. Why are there so many announcements in Ado, but fewer in the *Romanum parvum*? Thus, on 14 April Ado has four in full, whereas this one has only a single one; why, on 4 May, out of five commemorations; on 26 May, out of six; on 12 June and frequently elsewhere, are four again reduced to only one?

Examples of this kind are numerous and occur almost daily; they are sometimes examined in the *Observations*. I freely confess that the weight of this argument was so great with me that, beginning to investigate it, I perceived the entire structure erected by Rosweyd’s opponents to be thoroughly ruinous. [Col. 0526D]

### 136.

For I was saying to myself: what—what alleged epitomizer could have deterred himself from extracting at least the names of the saints from Ado, when it is not unusual for him to present four or five saints, indeed as many announcements, on a single day? As I proceeded from there to investigate other matters, ever new and ever brighter light arose, by which the value and esteem of this Martyrology increased in a remarkable way for me. Yet this, as I said, was almost the beginning of my investigation.

So that we do not wander farther afield, let the reader compare only the month of January. Why is the Circumcision placed on the first day, although Ado passed it over? Why are the thirty soldiers omitted? Why Euphrosyna, why Eugendus? Why, on 3 January, did the *Romanum parvum* select only Antherus, omitting Genovefa and Florentius? Why, on 17 January, is there nothing concerning the Three of Langres? See our observation there.

Proceed to the other days, no less unequal, and, I ask you, devise—even an absurd—reason why these or those saints could have been selected from Ado in preference to others. A sufficiently long catalogue is at hand, running through all the months and days of the year; I do not produce it, to avoid tedium, since from the examples already given I think we are dealing with a matter perfectly clear. [Col. 0527A]

### 137.

But let us also close the mouths of the detractors with another argument. They maintain that the same errors are found in the *Romanum parvum* and in Ado; here too they are egregiously mistaken, as many examples in our *Observations* demonstrate.

Let us give more than one specimen. On 2 January, the *Romanum parvum* had correctly written concerning Argeus and his brothers, whereas Ado’s elogium goes astray. On 7 May, the *Romanum parvum* has: “At Nicomedia, [the feast] of Augustus and Augustine”; Ado, adding something of his own, again falls into error, for he has: “of Flavius, Augustus, and Augustine, brothers.” See what we noted on this matter for that day.

On 19 June, the *Romanum parvum* reads: “The commemoration of Nazarius and Celsus”—correctly, I think, as Rosweyd judged in his notes; meanwhile Ado passed over that commemoration on that day. On 29 June, the announcement of the *Romanum parvum* is extremely simple; what ought to be corrected in Ado, you will understand from our observation for that day.

On 7 August, the *Romanum parvum* writes “Faustus,” while Ado has “Justinus”; one or the other is in error, but not both. On 31 August, the *Romanum parvum* correctly reports Aristides from Book IV, chapter 3, of Rufinus, while the Viennese writer adds much to his source there and departs from the straight path.

I should become tiresome if I pursued these matters individually here, since differences of this kind recur more frequently in our Usuard. There you can also easily demolish another ridiculous statement of Fronto, when he asserts that both Martyrologists use the same words. I have a catalogue of the differences ready, but it is enough to have indicated a few here, from which the inquisitive reader may judge of the others. Besides the days cited, one may consult 11, 12, and 28 January; 20 March, 11 July, and 27 August. . . . We proceed to other marks proper to the *Romanum parvum*. [Col. 0527D]

### 138.

What has already been said shows that it is ancient—at least older than Ado, and perhaps older than Bede—so that the first prerogative assigned to it by Rosweyd is fully vindicated. I shall also ensure that those who vainly gnaw away at its other title acknowledge that it is Roman.

As far as I know, no one except Valesius alone has yet dared to disparage Ado’s testimony, received from the mouth of a religious man; nor do the other opponents attack it directly. For once the truth proved above is admitted—namely, that that old or little Roman Martyrology was found by Ado at Ravenna and certainly preceded him—Florentinius, nor those who agree with him, will not deny that the Martyrology in question is truly and properly Roman, since the Viennese Martyrologist most explicitly testifies that it was sent from the city of Rome to Aquileia, to a certain holy bishop, by the Roman pontiff.

One must be ignorant of the conduct of the Roman pontiffs and completely unfamiliar with Roman affairs not to see that it follows from those words that the indicated Martyrology was compiled at Rome, written at Rome, and used at Rome at that time, and that it was sent to Aquileia for no other reason than that that church might conform itself more purely to the Roman Church, mother of the other churches.

I am thoroughly convinced that these facts, resting on the faith of that religious man and of Ado, are evident to all sensible and courageous judges. Now, lest anyone continue to doubt, let us display in the Martyrology itself sufficiently clear traces of its Roman origin. [Col. 0528B]

### 139.

Here we must repeat what we cited above from the distinguished Castellanus. Since he did not think it credible that any Martyrology other than a truly and properly Roman one had been sent by the Roman pontiff, he continues his argument as follows:

“But what proves more manifestly that the Martyrology found at the head of the Adonian work at Saint Pantaleon in Cologne is certainly the ancient Roman Martyrology, intended for the use of the Roman Church, and a true copy of the one which the Roman pontiff had sent to Aquileia, is not only the fact that it contains saints proper to the city of Rome and wholly unknown to the Hieronymian Martyrologies—such as Martina, Dafrosa, Papias, and Maurus, in January alone—nor merely the fact that the Chair of Saint Peter is marked on its proper day and most correctly distinguished from the Antiochene Chair; but also the fact that, among various dedications of Roman churches, there occurs the dedication of the high chapel of the Castle of Saint Angelo, expressed by the words ‘AMONG THE CLOUDS,’ and that on the feast of Saint Sebastian his tomb is said to be ‘AT THE FOOTPRINTS OF THE APOSTLES,’ by which words the Catacombs are designated, where the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul rested for some time.”

These observations were made as skillfully as they were truthfully by that great investigator of Martyrologies. He judged that nothing more was necessary to convince anyone who was not stubbornly obstinate of a truth whose rays, like those of the sun, strike the eyes of anyone who is not blind on every page of the little book. Nevertheless, I shall append here further evidence for the clarification and confirmation of the same matter. [Col. 0528D]

### 140.

From January alone, so as not to range farther afield—from that month alone, I say—Castellanus could have added saints proper to Rome and entirely absent from the Hieronymian Martyrologies: on 3 January, Pope Antherus; on 4 January, Priscus and his companions; on 5 January, Pope Telesphorus; on 22 January, Anastasius at the Aquae Salviae; on 23 January, Emerentiana; and finally, on 28 January, Agnes for the second time, expressed in a properly and precisely Roman manner.

Among the Roman dedications, besides the one already mentioned, which is recorded on 29 September and concerns the church of the Archangel built by Pope Boniface in the Circus—a place called “AMONG THE CLOUDS”—the following are especially noteworthy and, if one may speak so, especially Roman. The same Martyrology records them on the day before the Nones of May:

“And of Saint John the Apostle, when he was cast before the Latin Gate into a cauldron of boiling oil.”

And again, on the Ides, that is, 13 May:

“The dedication day of Saint Mary of the Martyrs is celebrated, established by Pope Boniface,” namely Boniface IV, who sat from the year 606 to 614.

What could be called more Roman than what is entered on 6 July?

“The first entry of the Apostle Paul into the city of Rome.”

Likewise, the same Martyrology records on 14 September in these words:

“The Exaltation of the Holy Cross, brought back from the Persians to Jerusalem by the emperor Heraclius; at that time also, in Rome, the life-giving wood of the Cross, found by Pope Sergius, is venerated by all the people.”

The dates of Sergius are well known: from the year 687 to 701. [Col. 0529A]

### 141.

Nor shall I hesitate to add the feast established at Rome by Gregory III between the years 731 and 741, in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary and of all the saints, as an expansion, so to speak, of the earlier dedication celebrated by Boniface IV.

The *Romanum parvum* records this feast in such terms that the author almost indicates that it had first begun during his own lifetime and, in a manner of speaking, before his own eyes. Observe the wording:

“The feast of the saints, which is celebrated at Rome as a solemn and general feast,”

as though he wished to say that it was a recent feast, celebrated only at Rome and not yet spread to other kingdoms or churches.

No clearer witness to this matter can exist than Ado himself. From his words, the distinction of the periods seems plainly indicated, when he adds:

“But in Gaul, at the prompting of Gregory IV, the pontiff of holy memory, the most pious emperor Louis, with all the bishops of his kingdom and empire agreeing, established that the feast of all the saints should be solemnly celebrated annually and perpetually on the aforementioned day”—1 November.

I do not understand what more the opponents of the *Romanum parvum* could desire in the face of such obvious evidence. [Col. 0529C]

### 142.

Fronto discusses this feast of all the saints not ineptly in his notes on the Roman Calendar cited above, from page 142 to page 145. There he rightly judges that its institution at Rome on 1 November must be assigned entirely to the time of Gregory III. For the extension of the same feast, see Ado and Usuard.

If Menard’s conjecture concerning the age of his Sacramentary is correct, that same feast must have been received in Gaul before the time of Charlemagne, since it is clearly expressed in that book. But this has nothing to do with us, since we are concerned only with the Roman feast, whose institution we, with Fronto, attribute to Gregory III.

And here, after having now traversed the whole of Usuard, we think the date of our little Roman Martyrology should be fixed: namely, it should be regarded as having been composed around the year 740.

From this and the other arguments already established, we consider its antiquity proved; from the saints and feasts proper and peculiar to Rome, its origin, homeland, and date of birth; in short, we regard it as established that it is OLD and ROMAN. We also showed above, against Florentinius, that this can be inferred from the name of the pope, repeatedly and almost deliberately inserted there. [Col. 0529D]

### 143.

It remains for us briefly to gather the other characteristics of the *Romanum parvum*, which are singularly conspicuous in it.

Whether its author had seen the Hieronymian Martyrology, or at least consulted it while preparing his own, we have not dared to declare more openly anywhere in our work, nor do we dare to do so now. Although the same saints are sometimes recorded in both, as may be seen on 26 February, we judge it more probable that those saints were received by the author of the *Romanum parvum* from the calendars of Rome and other churches, since they were generally better known.

I note three features proper to the *Romanum parvum*.

First, a large part of it was formed from the *History of Eusebius* in Rufinus’s translation, as we have pointed out repeatedly in this work with an almost literal indication. This is the one point that Henricus Valesius, the latest translator and commentator on Eusebius, could conveniently have noticed, and did carefully establish. He would have served his own reputation better if he had passed over the other matters, little worthy of his learning and scarcely relevant to his field. February alone, not to mention more fertile months, abundantly confirms Valesius’s assertion on 4, 8, 9, 18, and 27 February. December will provide still more saints, as our observation for 19 December will show you. [Col. 0530B]

### 144.

An observation on 10 January, concerning Nicanor, will provide a second genuine indication of the *Romanum parvum*, and the same point will be emphasized more frequently elsewhere: namely, that the author of the *Romanum parvum* took particular care to assign fixed days to the disciples of Christ the Lord and of the Apostles whom he found named in the sacred writings—assigning them, indeed, according to his own judgment, but so that such illustrious propagators of our faith would not be deprived of the worship due to them.

The examples are obvious; here are a few. On 21 January, Publius is commemorated; on 23 January, Parmenas; on 25 January, Ananias; on 2 February, Cornelius; on 3 February, Agabus; on 16 February, Onesimus; and so forth.

Since these and so many others are not known in the older Martyrologies, who would dare deny that they were first collected by the author of this Martyrology?

Castellanus already noted the third feature above, showing that the prophets of the Old Testament, passed over by the Hieronymian Martyrology, were again marked by the compiler of our Martyrology according to his own choice. To say nothing of Habakkuk and Micah on 15 January, Jeremiah on 1 May, and Elisha on 14 June, the single month of July supplies commemorations of five prophets. Of these, only the first, concerning Aaron, is known in the Hieronymian Martyrologies; in Bede, only Isaiah is found, although he mentions a few others, following the method and arrangement explained by Papebrochius in volume I of the April *Acta*, page 857. [Col. 0530D]

### 145.

A fourth feature may be added to these, and in this matter it is the last, but it is entirely proper to the *Romanum parvum* alone in comparison with the Hieronymian Martyrologies and Bede.

In those works you will scarcely find any commemoration of African martyrs who suffered in the Vandal persecution; in this Martyrology such commemorations are sufficiently frequent, as the *Usuardine Observations* will make clear. To avoid a lengthy search, inspect 29 March; 13 July; 6 September; 13 and 28 November; and 6 and 15 December—these are the ones that happen to remain in my memory.

Let the impartial reader, I ask, gather together all the characteristics enumerated throughout this section, characteristics so peculiarly owed to the *Romanum parvum* that they suit no other work. Let him recall in his mind the portrait so naturally represented by Ado; let him compare what has been argued throughout this chapter; and let him decide with me that the praise deserved by Rosweyd must at last be restored.

Let honor be returned to Rosweyd, I say; let the reputation of his name be restored; let the glory of that most learned man endure, for he was the first to bring to light, the first to publish, and the first to point out the source from which the Adonian Martyrology, and from that our Usuardine Martyrology, flowed.

It remains to trace the genealogy of these two in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER III. On the Descent of Ado and Usuard.

[Col. 0531B]

### 146.

Having exhibited, enumerated, and proved the progenitors of Ado, we have brought the genealogy of the Martyrologies to this point, so that it remains to discuss Ado himself and his legitimate offspring, Usuard, whom we have undertaken especially to elucidate.

Indeed, the whole preceding chapter has sufficiently demonstrated the first proposition which I had stated in §78: namely, that in preparing his Martyrology Ado used Rosweyd’s *Romanum parvum* as a kind of thread, if one may speak so, and copied almost the entire work virtually word for word. This has moreover been shown so clearly throughout our work, in the continuous observations attached to each Usuardine text, that anyone who dared to doubt so evident a truth would have to be blind as a mole.

The second proposition now follows, equally clearly proved in the observations mentioned above and formulated in §78 in these words:

“Usuard followed Ado, whom Florus called the second book, in everything so closely that he may truly be called an abridgment of Ado.”

Let the reader remember that our predecessors, after Molanus and other most learned men, were repeatedly mistaken in believing Usuard to be older than Ado, or at least so nearly contemporary with him that neither had seen the other’s Martyrology. This error was proclaimed in countless places throughout the first half-year of the *Acts of the Saints*, until Papebrochius, in volume V of the June *Acta*, page 250, column 1, at the end, began to observe the contrary.

What may still be desired for a living portrait of Ado and Usuard, beyond what we and our predecessors have already said, must now be treated here. [Col. 0531D]

## ARTICLE I. On the Martyrology of Saint Ado, Bishop of Vienne.

### 147.

Bollandus does not seem to have spoken of Ado with sufficient regard to his merits, when in chapter 4, §8, page LII, of the general preface, he discussed him briefly as follows:

“Saint Ado, bishop of Vienne in Gaul in the same century—the ninth—of whom we shall speak on 16 December, wrote a more extensive Martyrology. James Mosander published it; afterward Rosweyd, collated with three manuscripts: the manuscript of Everbode, that of Saint Pantaleon, and that of Peter Scriverius, following the latter especially. We possess a copy collated with three other manuscripts, namely those of the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liège—although the letter of Usuard to King Charles is prefixed to it—of the church of Thérouanne, and of the monastery of Dobiensis.”

Thus Bollandus, mentioning nothing of the first and oldest edition, prepared by Aloysius Lipomanus, which appears in volume IV of Ado’s works, beginning on page 150.

Aloysius offers several remarks there, based on the common opinion then accepted, which we now recognize as false. But the words in which he expresses his incredible joy at having discovered a copy of Ado deserve the greatest attention:

“How greatly I rejoiced then, God knows. I considered all gold to be nothing in comparison with it . . . and I gave immense thanks to our God and to his Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, as well as to the faithful friend who had honored me with so great a gift.” [Col. 0532B]

### 148.

One point should be noted in this edition of Aloysius: the distinguished Veronese prelate distinguished between the “lives,” as he himself calls them—that is, Ado’s longer elogies, embellished from passionaries—and distinguished, I say, between those described more briefly and those described in a fuller style.

“For,” he says, “most of the shorter ones are those commonly found in the Martyrology of Saint Jerome. In publishing Ado, therefore, I followed this method: whatever is found in Saint Jerome I omitted entirely, since it is readily available to everyone, unless something additional was found attached to it. Whatever is not found there, I inserted in full.”

He means that he omitted all the shorter commemorations and printed only the longer elogies.

But who, skilled in these matters, could understand “shorter lives” to be found in Saint Jerome’s Martyrology? In fact, such an idea is infinitely distant from the style of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in which only the names of the martyrs, the place, and the day of their passion are given. Anyone who finds more than this in some Martyrology should conclude with certainty that the work before him is not a pure Hieronymian Martyrology. [Col. 0532C]

### 149.

The difficulty is aptly resolved by the perceptive observation of Molanus on this subject, in chapter 2 of his preface:

“Many people cite the Martyrology of Saint Jerome, which is commonly available. But,” he says, “they do not cite the Martyrology of Eusebius and Jerome itself; rather, they cite Usuard’s, which he compiled from Eusebius, Jerome, Bede, Florus, and elsewhere, through the care and command of Charlemagne.”

Molanus is mistaken on several points here, but he truly asserts that many people—including Peter of Equilino and, at that time, virtually everyone—cited the Usuardine Martyrology as the Hieronymian, although they had never seen the latter, at least not one properly deserving that name, such as the examples published by Florentinius.

There was then such confusion among the Martyrologies that any work bearing on its front the famous letter of Chromatius and Heliodorus—which was found in almost all Usuardine copies—was called the Hieronymian Martyrology. Thus, for several centuries, Jerome’s name clung to the Usuardine Martyrology.

To make the matter clear, compare Usuard with Aloysius’s edition, and you will immediately see that all the shorter announcements have been omitted, whereas wherever Usuard condensed longer elogies from Ado, those elogies are restored in full and in Adonian form by Aloysius.

Here again you see the seeds from which the proposition established above grows: namely, that Usuard either copied or condensed almost his entire Martyrology from Ado. [Col. 0533A]

### 150.

Furthermore, Rosweyd sufficiently established that Saint Ado the Martyrologist was not, as Aloysius, Mosander, and many others wrongly thought, from Trier, but was an archbishop of Vienne; and at the present time this is acknowledged by all learned men.

Mabillon has illustrated his life—or rather, an abridgment of his life taken from the Breviaries of Vienne and Rome—with other learned documents, in Part II of volume IV of the Benedictine history, beginning on page 262. From there I shall briefly relate what concerns the age of that most holy and learned man and his Martyrology.

He is said to have arisen “from a noble family” in the district of Wastine or Sens, and to have been born “around the year eight hundred,” “for, having reached the age of seventy-six, he died in the year of Christ 875.”

He seems to have been entrusted to the discipline of the monks of Ferrières, having been received there while still an infant or boy by Abbot Sigulf. “There,” according to Lupus, “having conducted himself well, he surpassed all his contemporaries in literary studies.”

From there he was sent, at the request of Abbot Macward, to the monastery of Prüm, where he remained for some time, until, assailed by “the plots of certain envious men,” he went to Rome “to visit the house of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, for the sake of prayer.” After five years he returned to his homeland, and at Ravenna found and copied that Martyrology, about which we have argued at length in the immediately preceding chapter. [Col. 0533C]

### 151.

After departing from Ravenna with his excavated treasure, he “reached Lyons, where the distinguished prelate Remigius, worthy of blessed memory, was then in charge. He piously received God’s servant Ado and most graciously supplied him with whatever he needed.”

Detained there, therefore, because of his reputation for learning and probity, he remained at Lyons for some time. And if the Romans Breviary tells the truth, Remigius “assigned to Ado the church of Saint Romanus, with its adjoining properties, for his service, so that he might devote himself more privately to prayer”—and indeed, without doubt, to literary studies and especially to preparing his Martyrology, at the urging of Remigius and other bishops, whom in his preface he may have intended by the phrase “the command and order of holy men.”

Here we agree with Mabillon, Castellanus, and others that the date of his Martyrology should be placed before he was raised to the see of Vienne, which he certainly occupied in 860. It is therefore most probable that the aforesaid Martyrology was written around the year 858, or perhaps a little earlier.

“For he composed his other works,” says Mabillon, “when he was already a bishop; but he undertook this one before his episcopate.” That is, while he had returned from Ravenna and was wholly occupied in collecting the saints and describing their passions at greater length, “serving the weaker brethren to the praise of almighty God,” and so forth.

No time could be assigned more suitably for preparing this work than the leisure he enjoyed at Lyons for that purpose. In this dating of Ado’s Martyrology, all learned men today readily agree with Mabillon. [Col. 0534A]

### 152.

I am not equally satisfied with certain arguments brought forward by the esteemed Mabillon for this purpose, based on a certain Adonian codex—dear to him, I do not know why—which he says was copied by hand six hundred years earlier. From it he confidently argues, around the middle of page 273, that the commemoration of Saint Maurus the abbot, Saint Scholastica, and almost all the other saints whom Mosander and Rosweyd eliminated “must be restored” to Ado.

At the beginning of the page he had likewise said:

“The same judgment should be made concerning almost all the names which Mosander and Rosweyd relegated to a separate section.”

Much as I would like to grant this to so learned a man, and one who during his lifetime was so devoted to our work, I cannot grant it at all, since I have repeatedly observed that the aforesaid codex—which he alone, throughout the Benedictine *Acts*, frequently invokes—differs most widely from all our printed and manuscript copies.

More than one example occurs in the *Usuardine Observations*, on 6 July, 13 September, 12 November, and elsewhere.

To make it still clearer that Mabillon’s codex is not truly and purely Adonian, I ask learned readers merely to compare Ado for themselves with Usuard and Notker. Since these two generally either abridge or copy the earlier work, there is no more reliable means of determining what belongs properly to Ado and what must be attributed to his many interpolators. For this purpose scarcely anything more is needed than to consult our aforementioned observations, in which the streams are daily compared with their source. [Col. 0534C]

### 153.

It will be useful to place the matter before one’s eyes through an especially clear example.

Mabillon, on page 272, a little below the middle, writes as follows:

“In addition, in our manuscript codex the dedication of the church of the monastery of Celle, made in the year 850, is accurately described on 16 October, in the same manner in which it was related above under the year 873, where we discussed the translation of Saint Frodobertus the abbot. The reason that moves me not to regard this as an addition by an interpolator is that a man of a later age would not have known the individual circumstances, as they are called, so accurately.”

Mabillon wished to discover Ado’s date from this, although it is derived elsewhere more accurately and securely. All these arguments fail if tested by the proposed rule.

Usuard and Notker do not say a word about that detailed description of the dedication of the church of Celle. Moreover, neither in Aloysius’s Ado, who nowhere neglects the longer histories, nor in the editions of Mosander or Rosweyd, nor finally in the manuscripts of Liège, Queen Christina of Sweden, Tournai, or Lobbes, nor in the Adonian codices listed by Papebrochius in his prologue to Bede, nor in our other manuscripts, is any memory of the aforesaid dedication found.

It follows most clearly, therefore, that Mabillon’s highly praised codex is very far from Adonian purity.

No one need have devoted as much labor to examining the Martyrologies as I have spent in these last few years in order to be completely convinced that no manuscript of Ado, however ancient, can in any way be compared with Rosweyd’s edition. [Col. 0535A]

### 154.

Let no one be angry with me if I claim the well-deserved palm for Rosweyd, although I do not regard his edition as so complete and perfect in every respect that I never freely depart from his judgments.

I do so especially when I have the agreement of Usuard and Notker according to the rule proposed above: namely, when an announcement rejected by Rosweyd into an appendix is found in his two descendants. In that case I do not think there should be much doubt that the same announcement must also be attributed to Ado.

To make the matter clear with one example, let the reader consult our observation on Usuard for 20 March. There we think that Archippus, the fellow soldier of the Apostle Paul, should be restored to Ado, whatever may have been marked with an asterisk by Mosander and rejected by Rosweyd into an appendix. We are led to this conclusion because it is explicitly recorded in both of Ado’s descendants, Usuard and Notker, besides being reported by Ado’s ancestor, the *Romanum parvum*.

If the Adonian codices, both manuscript and printed, are examined more scrupulously according to this standard, I think the way can very easily be prepared for producing a simple, complete, genuine, and authentic edition of Ado. [Col. 0535B]

### 155.

I have also sometimes followed another path of investigation, although I do not consider it equally secure. It is this: whenever I find in Usuard and Notker a commemoration expressed in the same sense and in the same phrase, and one not taken from Bede, I am then not reluctant to believe that it should be attributed to Ado.

If anyone can bring forward more reliable criteria, we shall gladly and willingly accept them.

Meanwhile, neither Mabillon’s authority nor that of anyone else will move us to allow things that are not Adonian to be marketed under Ado’s name.

Let Florentinius and Hilasius again serve as an example. On 27 September, the esteemed Mabillon attempts to impose them on the Viennese Martyrology from Peter of Natalibus, Book VIII, chapter 124.

By Hercules, the bishop of Equilino is not a sufficiently reliable authority to testify on behalf of the genuine simplicity of Ado, which we undertake to establish from such diverse copies. All of those copies lack the two martyrs just mentioned; Usuard received them from elsewhere into his own Martyrology, as appears in our observation already cited for 27 September.

Long experience has now taught me that it is not only Peter and many others, but even the most eminent Cardinal Baronius, who sometimes cite Ado’s Martyrology incorrectly. [Col. 0535D]

### 156.

I shall not dispute with Mabillon concerning the remaining matters relating to Ado; they will have their place in the *Acts* for 16 December.

His conjecture concerning additions to Ado’s Martyrology should not be rejected entirely. He expresses it in these words:

“The fact that different things are lacking in different parchment manuscripts arises from two causes. First, because when this Martyrology was used in divine services throughout various churches, some people abridged it, while others removed certain saints unknown to their province or church. Second, because the author himself enlarged his Martyrology on many occasions by adding various saints who were not present in the first version. Consequently, those who copied the primary exemplar do not have as many entries as those who used secondary copies.”

I do not reject this prudent conjecture, since I have sometimes had to admit it, especially concerning the bishops of Vienne. Since Usuard frequently lacks them, I consider it probable that Ado added them to his Martyrology after completing it at Lyons, when he was later at Vienne.

But when the original simplicity is being sought, we decide the matter not conjecturally but certainly: it must be derived not from one or another codex, but from the collation of several equally trustworthy ones, just as we have done throughout this work in purging Usuard of additions. By this single argument alone—even if the other arguments were lacking—all Mabillon’s examples, brought forward in many places, must be entirely denied to Ado. [Col. 0536B]

[Cols. 0536C–0536D]

157. Here I pass over many matters; the rest will be explained by our *Usuardine Observations*, in which it has been sufficiently proved that not only Bede augmented by Florus and the *Romanum parvum*, but also the *Hieronymianum*, at times preceded Ado; I do not see why Castellanus denied this in the preliminary notice to the first Bimester, p. 22, although I fully admit that traces of the Hieronymian texts conforming to Ado’s style occur very rarely in Ado. If you join what has been said thus far with what had to be discussed in the preceding chapters concerning the holy Martyrologist, you will see that nothing further is needed regarding the date and genealogy of Ado’s Martyrology. Let us hear only how he himself explains the character of his entire work, addressing the reader in his preface as follows:

> “Ado the sinner sends greetings to the reader. Do not suppose that I have labored in vain in this work, or undertaken something unnecessary; I shall briefly disclose to you the reason for what I have done. First, there was the command and injunction of holy men that the days which had merely been marked in the Martyrology without the names of martyrs—[the Martyrology] which had been enlarged through the venerable Florus’s labor upon the work of Lord Bede—should be supplied. Then codices of Passions collected from every source so greatly stirred my mind that I described more fully and somewhat more explicitly not only the festivals of days already passed, but also those of others which had been set down there, day by day, throughout the year, serving weaker brothers and those less able to read, to the praise of almighty God, so that in the memorials of the martyrs they might have a concise reading, and in a small book what others seek out with great labor through many codices.”

[Cols. 0536D–0537B]

158. Hence those long histories drawn from the martyrs’ Passions in Ado’s Martyrology; hence also the great inequality among the days, since, where the Acts were lacking, almost bare names of saints were reported. Beyond doubt, those who had perhaps begun to use Ado’s Martyrology in the divine offices were thereby moved—as Mabilio recently said—to remove the names of unknown saints; or rather, as I consider more probable, to abridge the histories so that the individual days might be reduced to some uniformity.

Usuard was most successful in this task, abridging and polishing Ado’s Martyrology; but, strangely, he did so without knowing the author’s true name. Since Usuard knew no other Martyrologists besides Jerome, Bede, and Florus, and since Ado’s style differed very greatly from the Hieronymian work but closely resembled Bede augmented by Florus, he believed it to be Florus’s second book, by which all the empty days of the Calendar were supplied.

You will perhaps argue that the immense difference between the two Martyrologies ought surely to have struck Usuard’s eyes; I know this and admit it. Yet to me it is so certain and evident that Ado’s work was the book Usuard calls the second book of Florus that one must either admit the paradox—namely, that the Martyrology bearing Ado’s name is not Ado’s but Florus’s—or invent a miracle by which we may acknowledge that Florus and Ado wrote so alike that, like the Menæchmi, they produced twins from different births. But it is pointless to imagine such things. Let us now look closely at Usuard himself, the hero, so to speak, of our drama.

### ARTICLE II. On the Martyrology of Usuard the Monk

[Cols. 0537C–0537D]

159. Our entire discussion of Martyrologists and Martyrologies had to be brought to this point, so that, after Usuard’s ancestors, parentage, kinship, and affinity had been set forth, he himself—or rather his offspring—might at last be displayed more clearly to all.

There is neither time nor need here to set out what many highly learned men, besides our predecessors, long ago reported about him: Adrian Valesius, Jean Mabilio, Gerard du Bois, and most recently Claude Castellanus. They all agree against the opinions of Sigebert, Trithemius, and other earlier writers on the following points:

1. Our Usuard was a monk and priest of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, or Saint Vincent, at Paris.
2. He flourished not under Charlemagne but under Charlemagne’s namesake grandson, Charles the Bald, and dedicated his work to the latter, not to the former.
3. He composed his Martyrology around the year 875.

You will find all this solidly proved in Mabilio’s *Prolegomena to the Fourth Benedictine Century*, part II, p. 88, and in the *History of the Church of Paris* by the distinguished du Bois, part I, p. 467. We entirely agree with them in establishing Usuard’s date and profession. We disagree on this precise point: Bollandus, Henschenius, Papebrochius, and all the others—with Castellanus alone excepted—place Usuard before Ado, or, even if they regard them as nearly contemporary, nevertheless suppose that they wrote their Martyrologies so that neither knew the other and that each applied himself to his work at roughly the same time. These are the words of the ecclesiastical historians just cited. Add to them Mabilio’s somewhat timid assertion, no. 174, that Ado’s Martyrology almost approaches Usuard’s in authority. What should have been said is that Usuard possesses no more authority than he transcribed from Ado; no more than a stream possesses in comparison with its source; no more than a child in comparison with its parent.

[Cols. 0538A–0538C]

160. I have often noted that Papebrochius finally recognized this reversed order in volume V of the June volume, p. 250, col. 1, at the end, and did so at Castellanus’s suggestion, from whom the reversal was first derived. He restored the Viennese Martyrologist to his proper place of priority, and showed by the following brief calculation that Ado preceded Usuard in writing his Martyrology by approximately eighteen years.

Usuard’s Martyrology is dedicated to Charles the Bald, already emperor. But Charles the Bald was not emperor before the year 875; therefore the work was composed, or at least completed, either in that year or in the following year. Ado, however, as stated in no. 151, wrote his own work around the year 858. Thus the exactness of our calculation stands.

Here we must expressly pursue only this argument: that Usuard took almost all his material from Ado. Continuous proof of this is provided by our daily *Observations on Usuard’s Martyrology*, from the first day of January to the last of December. In them I examine the text of each Martyrologist, comparing, as we say here, announcement with announcement, phrase with phrase, and the very words with the words. After making the comparison, I show with a clarity which, if I am not mistaken, no one could reasonably demand to be surpassed in these matters, that Usuard’s little sections were copied from Ado’s, abbreviated and condensed, and occasionally modified slightly from Bede.

But by doing this, you will say, I accuse Usuard of plagiarism. Away with the charge of plagiarism! Listen to Usuard himself explaining the character of his entire work, and you will understand what he claims to have contributed from himself and what he openly admits to have received from the Martyrologies of other holy Fathers. His principal aim was to reduce the commemorations of the saints, by a suitable method, to a convenient uniformity for each day of the Calendar.

[Cols. 0538C–0539A]

161. Let us examine Usuard’s own preface from our distinguished Herinian codex. Bollandus published it in chapter 4, § 7; it is also found in other ancient codices, and even in Ado’s Leodiensis of Saint Lawrence, and elsewhere:

> “To the venerable lord Charles, most pious of kings (elsewhere: Augustus), Usuard, although an unworthy priest and monk, wishes prosperity in the present age and the glory of eternal blessedness.
>
> “Your Highness, reverend prince, is certainly not unaware how we are urged, by imitating the studies of the ancients, either to supply, as far as possible, whatever in books—especially those appropriate to ecclesiastical teaching—is found to be less complete than it ought to be, or to desire that it be supplied.
>
> “This consideration, arising from pious concern and reinforced by the command of your dignity, compelled me to gather the recurring festivals of the saints from various Martyrologies of the holy Fathers into a certain unity. For I recalled, during the sacred solemnities of the saints, the many kinds of excess arising from my own negligence; and this greatly compelled me to discharge this service for them in the love of God—although I was not sufficiently qualified for it, being unlearned, yet trusting that it might be aided by divine assistance and by the help of those saints, despite my unworthiness.
>
> “I was also stimulated by the writings of the venerable priests Jerome and Bede on this subject. One of them, devoting himself greatly to brevity, while the other left very many days of the Calendar untouched, is shown to have passed over many things necessary to this little work. Accordingly I employed the collected materials from many sources in the same undertaking of the second book of the memorable man Florus, which I judged especially worthy of imitation in those things that seemed suitable and worthy of remembrance, because he both corrected and added many things with the greatest care—things which I touched upon briefly.”

[Cols. 0539A–0539C]

162. These final words sketch Ado in the most vivid colors. Although in the common version of Usuard’s preface, edited by Greven, Molanus, and others, they are expressed somewhat differently, careful consideration shows that they amount to exactly the same thing. There we read:

> “The former, devoting himself to brevity, while the latter left very many days of the Calendar untouched, are found to have passed over many things necessary to this work. Nevertheless, following them, I judged that I should also follow the broader traces of the memorable man Florus in this same undertaking, especially in his second book; for there he both corrected and added many things which he had omitted in the first.”

Observe that Bede is here described as having been completed by Ado—not merely in part, as Florus had done, but in full. From these words it plainly follows that Usuard had three Martyrologies before his eyes, from which he assembled his little work. He says as much in the aforementioned common preface:

> “But if anything has been enlarged or altered by me in the present work beyond what I received from them, it will be possible to recognize that I investigated it by diligent inquiry.”

And here the charge of plagiarism, which I mentioned just now, completely disappears, once everything that can properly be called Usuardian is reduced to that single phrase “if anything”: material received from the registers of the Cordoban Martyrs, from which Usuard had sought out the relics of Saints George and Aurelius; from the neighboring churches of Gaul; from books of Passions; and from a few other documents, which we have not neglected to indicate and enumerate in their proper places.

[Cols. 0539C–0540A]

163. Nevertheless, Usuard sincerely acknowledges that he took almost everything principally from three Martyrologies: from the Hieronymian texts; from Bede as he had been augmented by Florus—these being the “broader traces of the memorable man Florus in the same undertaking”; and from Florus’s second book, where he “both corrected and added many things which he had omitted in the first.”

The Herinian preface expresses this still more clearly:

> “Accordingly I employed the collected materials from many sources in the same undertaking of the second book of the memorable man Florus, whom I judged especially worthy of imitation in those things that seemed suitable and worthy of remembrance, because he corrected and added many things with the greatest care, which I touched upon briefly.”

Whom, I ask, could Usuard have imitated more plainly than Ado, briefly touching upon what Ado had added with the greatest care in his long praises, and selecting what seemed suitable and worthy of remembrance?

Moreover, our *Observations* very frequently show that Usuard consulted the *Hieronymianum* and Bede; they also prove no less clearly that he never saw that Florus edited by Henschenius and Papebrochius. That other book of Florus torments the ingenuity of scholars and troubled our predecessors to an extraordinary degree. We know that it was sought in vain for so many centuries, especially in the immediately preceding period, and that it will continue to be sought in vain unless, as I said above, we invent either a paradox or a miracle for ourselves, remaining sober and vigilant.

[Cols. 0540A–0540C]

164. Only the name of Florus causes difficulty. Had Usuard not mentioned it, the work cited would refer to Ado so clearly, openly, and unmistakably that the eyes of readers and comparers would be flooded with the light of truth by its distinctive features alone.

It describes materials collected from many sources for the undertaking of the Martyrology, materials omitted from Bede’s earlier work as augmented by Florus; but here added so that the many days of the Calendar left untouched might be filled in on every side and all the necessities of such a little work might thus be present.

Yet Ado’s supplementation is not always suitable, nor is it always worthy of being included in Martyrologies as a memorial, since the histories are longer, and Usuard was therefore compelled to touch upon them briefly. But this is precisely the genuine labor of Ado, as it appears in the preface quoted above in no. 157:

> “Do not suppose that I have labored in vain in this work . . . First, there was the command and injunction of holy men that the days which had merely been marked without the names of martyrs in the Martyrology—which had been enlarged through the venerable Florus’s labor upon the work of Lord Bede—should be supplied. Then codices of Passions collected from every source so greatly stirred my mind that I described not only the festivals of days already passed . . . more fully and somewhat more explicitly,” and so forth.

These features reveal themselves everywhere throughout Ado’s work. When compared by us day by day with Usuard’s abridgement, they display the parent and indicate the lineage so clearly that no son could better reproduce his father; that is, no epitome previously discovered is more suitable, more worthy of remembrance, or more necessary for a little Martyrology.

Who, then, could still doubt that Usuard copied Ado’s Martyrology under the name of Florus, or in place of Florus’s second book?

[Cols. 0540C–0541A]

165. You may say that these are novel claims and protest that they are astonishing; nevertheless, what we write will remain certain and indubitable. You will uncover it most clearly if you compare the offspring with the father, Usuard with Ado, or, to spare yourself the labor, if you examine our daily *Observations*.

“But, I ask,” you will say, “how could Usuard have thought of naming Florus if Ado himself, the true author of the Martyrology, was perhaps still alive, and expressed his name so clearly at the head of the work: ‘Ado the sinner sends greetings to the reader’?”

I myself wonder and do not know how this happened. But I believe that I have discovered, through continuous comparison over several years, that the matter was as follows.

Castellanus employs an escape in the preface to the first Bimester, p. 23, avoiding the difficulty by saying that Usuard does not assert that he copied Florus. Yet in his own work, p. 764, he admits more accurately that Usuard copied and abridged Ado’s manuscript, sent to him from Lyon, as though it were Florus.

For what else do those words mean:

> “I employed the collected materials from many sources in the same undertaking of the second book of the memorable man Florus”?

Or these:

> “I judged that I should follow the broader traces of the memorable Florus in this same undertaking, especially in his second book”?

Throughout that entire second book I see no one but Ado; I sense no one but Ado; I hear no one speaking but Ado.

[Cols. 0541A–0541C]

166. If, while persisting in the question before us, you continue to press and torment me by asking how Usuard could have thought of naming Florus when Ado himself was probably still alive and had so clearly expressed his own name at the head of the work—“Ado the sinner sends greetings to the reader”—I have no answer to that question except one highly probable conjecture, in my opinion.

Namely, the work of the Viennese bishop sent from Lyon to Usuard may have been acephalous—that is, lacking its head. Perhaps it had lost its preface and the *Romanum parvum*, to which the preface itself is prefixed.

Do not think that I am inventing this without grounds. I ask whether it seems sufficiently credible that Usuard would nowhere have said a word about that *Romanum parvum*, which Ado had discovered at Ravenna, if he had seen it at the front of the work sent to him.

The *Romanum parvum* was therefore absent; consequently Ado’s entire preface was absent as well. Yet Ado had expressed his name there, whereas he had undoubtedly omitted it in the course of the entire work. There is therefore nothing very astonishing if Usuard did not know the true name of the author of the Martyrology sent to him.

Once this is granted, the remaining points seem to follow naturally, including the very reason why Usuard thought that the work should be attributed to Florus.

[Cols. 0541C–0542A]

167. I conceive the matter as follows. Ado had long since left Lyon, having been raised to the see of Vienne by at least the year 860, and the work left behind at Lyon was without its author’s name. Some fellow Benedictine monk sent it to Usuard in Paris. Usuard, comparing it with Bede’s Martyrology as revised by Florus and recognizing everywhere the astonishing similarity between the two, immediately decided that the two offspring were either twins or at least descended from the same parent.

From another source, Usuard, no less than Wandalbert, could have known that the famous Florus, subdeacon of the Church of Lyon, possessed several ancient and corrected codices. What could be easier than for him to conclude that a second and fuller Martyrology book had been composed by Florus, since so many days of the Calendar had remained untouched in the first?

I do not say this because I believe that those various corrected codices of Florus were Martyrologies, still less that Florus had composed a complete and finished Martyrology. I say rather that the fame of his name could easily have suggested to Usuard, who was seeking an author for an acephalous Martyrology, that Florus had prepared the work, since the reputation of his distinguished learning still endured at that time.

If these conjectures do not satisfy, I shall gladly learn from more expert authorities what more plausible opinion may rightly be held in this matter. Meanwhile, it remains utterly certain that the work was purely and simply Ado’s—the very work that Usuard, misled either by his own error or by someone else’s, called the second book of Florus.

[Cols. 0542A–0542B]

168. Believe me with confidence: under the wrongly assigned name of Florus there was Ado himself, the holy bishop of Vienne—or rather, his Martyrology. It was Usuard’s perpetual and inexhaustible source, from which the greater part of our entire Usuardian work was formed.

Add to this the *Hieronymianum* and Bede enlarged through Florus’s labor. If I may again use a textile metaphor, from these you will make the warp or chain, into which Usuard inserted the weft, especially from the better-known Gallic saints and from the recently acquired knowledge of the Cordoban Martyrs.

In the course of the work you will often find us uncertain whether Usuard added other saints, sought from elsewhere, to those leaders whom he has listed here. We know only a few such saints, but we do know some. Asclas, on 23 January, is not recorded by the earlier authorities, nor are Philemon and Apollonius on 8 March. We have indicated several others elsewhere.

Gregory of Eliberris in Baetica, on 24 April, now comes to mind; perhaps he would better have been omitted. On 21 September there is Pamphilus, a Roman martyr, whom I sought elsewhere in vain. Again, on 28 September, 12 November, and 4 December, the entire text is properly and exclusively—so to speak—Usuardian.

In October certain saints are commemorated whom Usuard drew from elsewhere, as may be seen there on the 1st, 3rd, 11th, 14th, 20th, and 25th. These examples are sufficient.

[Cols. 0542B–0542D]

169. It remains to ask where Usuard began his Martyrology. This controversy has been treated sufficiently fully in chapter 2 of this preface, beginning at no. 109.

Bede, Florus, Wandalbert, Rabanus, and Notker began the ecclesiastical year on the Kalends of January, as did the *Romanum parvum* and the Epternacense *Hieronymianum*. Nevertheless, we believe that Rosweyd judged correctly that Ado began on the ninth day before the Kalends of January—that is, on the vigil of the Nativity—and we think that Usuard followed him. This is shown by two of our finest and most ancient codices, the Pratensis and the Heriniensis, although most other codices disagree with them.

Meanwhile, following the first and most accurate editors of Usuard—Muneratus, Belinus, Greven, and Molanus—and indeed the custom now most widely received, we preferred to begin with the eighth day of the Nativity and the Circumcision of the Lord, that is, with the Kalends of January.

Here we set the limit of our entire martyrological genealogy, bringing the tree down to Usuard, who is the material, end, and object of our work. Since no Martyrologist left behind offspring so numerous, and since his descendants gradually diverged from the natural image of their parent, our chief task must be to gather traits from here and there and attempt to sketch the parent’s true and complete likeness.

Let us now examine the whole offspring of Usuard.

### ARTICLE III. The Earlier Editions of Usuard’s Martyrology Reviewed

[Cols. 0543A–0543B]

170. At the very beginning of this preface I have already anticipated the most obvious objection that could be raised here: why, after so many editions of Usuard’s Martyrology—editions that are in everyone’s hands—should this new and laboriously prepared edition appear?

I can settle the matter with a brief answer by saying that no edition has yet been found that did not leave behind a desire for another. There is none in which experts in martyrological matters have not detected serious defects and numerous excesses. Indeed, many learned men, most recently among them, have urged the highly learned Benedictine Fathers of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, almost by constant insistence, to make their autograph—or supposed autograph—publicly available. This they have so far been unable to obtain from them, as we sufficiently indicated above.

I shall not repeat the reasons mentioned there. Let our Bollandus’s plan, contemplated for so many years, stand for all of them: someday to publish Usuard in his native simplicity. In recovering that simplicity we have received more aids than either Rosweyd or Bollandus was able to gather at the beginning of the work on the *Acts of the Saints*.

For a proper judgment to be formed concerning this edition of ours, the criticism of all the others must first be presented; thereafter the characteristics of the individual manuscript codices must be set forth, so that from all these materials it may be determined that we have not devoted excessive or useless diligence to this work.

Here, then, is the promised review.

[Cols. 0543B–0543D]

171. The first of all editions, and the oldest at least of those known to us, is the edition of Usuard most frequently cited under the name of the *Maxima Lubecana*.

Our predecessors state in the *Acts* that it is Lubecana and was first published in print in 1475, and I find the same in many of their notes. The year does not appear in the work itself, since it is a portion torn from a larger volume which, as the epilogue says, contained “the whole scope of the sacred history of the entire world, arranged in fascicles.”

This is evident from the page number written by hand at the top center of the first side. It begins with 409 and continues to 435, always numbering only one side of each leaf.

The work is spread out in a broad, thick folio format; hence we rightly call it *Maxima*, distinguishing it from another Lubecana of 1490, which we shall discuss below.

This edition contains little to recommend it. The German or Gothic type itself is very imperfect, and the entire work teems with innumerable errors. The Martyrology itself departs very far from Usuardian purity: it is often enlarged and interpolated and resembles a manuscript codex which, since I could not designate it by its proper name, I simply call Antuerpiense, to distinguish it from two others, the larger and the largest.

Let the reader note that the Ughellian codex is usually joined with the Lubecana and Antuerpiense, as I shall explain elsewhere. The edition under discussion is therefore not of the first or best rank. Together with two others it forms a nearly distinct class between the primary and the intermediate witnesses, although it often occupies a place among the primary ones.

[Cols. 0543D–0544B]

172. The massive volume from which, as we said, this Martyrology was torn away later came to our Museum under the title *Rudiment of Novices*. The year of the edition has been correctly noted, for at the end of the very extensive index and of the whole work we read:

> “In the year, according to the flesh, of the Nativity of the Son of God 1475, on the very day of the most holy king and martyr Oswald, which is 5 August, under the most holy Father in Christ and our lord Sixtus IV, pope; under the most illustrious Frederick III, of the most illustrious house of Austria, invincible emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus, who is at present residing in Cologne; in the imperial and noble city of Lübeck, by the art of printing, invented by special divine grace for the salvation of faithful souls: this epitome, divided into six parts according to the six ages of the world, previously found nowhere else, which it pleased [the makers] to title *Rudiment of Novices*, has, with the help of God, who powerfully, gently, and peacefully orders heavenly and earthly things, been happily printed and completed by Master Lucas Brandis of Schass.”

It is not my concern here to pass judgment on that entire accumulation of material. It seems to possess value from no other source than the age of its printing, which we may readily allow to pass into the Martyrology as well, although otherwise we cannot accept it as a pure Usuardian text.

[Cols. 0544B–0544D]

173. In chronological order this is followed by the Belgian edition, or translation, of Usuard. Only its first six months survive in our possession, intermingled with a Belgian edition of Jacobus de Voragine’s *Golden Legend*, printed in small folio at Utrecht in 1480.

But antiquity has not added value even to this edition, since it is rarely pure. It was extracted from some codex similar to the Leydense and to others which we customarily call intermediate witnesses and shall describe more fully below.

To this may be joined the edition prepared at Florence by Francesco de Bonaccursiis in 1486. Henschenius found it in the Strozzi Library and compared it with Greven’s edition and with two other manuscript Usuardian codices, one from the same Strozzi Library and the other from the Medici Library.

I cannot here state my judgment of it in full, since Henschenius left only extracts copied in his own hand. We cite these frequently among the *Auctaria* under the name of the Florentine codices.

Their very frequent excesses show how little purity the aforesaid edition possesses. Papebrochius noted somewhere that its exemplar was preserved at Naples, at the Church of the Holy Apostles, corrected by Giorgio Antonio Vespucci, provost of the cathedral church of Florence.

This information is reported from others.

[Cols. 0544D–0545B]

174. Besides the *Maxima Lubecana*, the other Lubecana of 1490 is often cited in the *Acts*, together with another Cologne edition, entirely similar to the former and published in the same year.

The latter has the form of a small folio and bears at the end the following inscription:

> “Here ends the Martyrology of Usuard the monk, as it is found augmented, as is evident; diligently printed by me, Johann Roelhoff of Lübeck, citizen of holy and fortunate Cologne of Agrippina, and happily completed in the year of salvation and grace 1490, on the vigil of the most holy Three Kings, perpetual patrons and protectors of the aforesaid city.”

Rosweyd noted that it was once appended to the *Golden Legend* and differed greatly from Usuard. The latter point is proved most convincingly by the daily supplements drawn from this and the other Lubecana edition, intermingled with or added to Usuard’s text. Most of these properly belong to Cologne.

That other Lubecana, certainly derived from the earlier Cologne edition or at least from a very similar manuscript, is intermingled with the *Doctrinale of Clerics* in quarto-minor format. It differs from the earlier edition in beginning with the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.

At the end appears:

> “This little book alone directs each person directly to heaven. Here ends the *Doctrinale of Clerics*, together with the Martyrology of the Saints, diligently printed at Lübeck in the year from the Nativity of the Lord 1490.”

Several observations could be made with interest from this *Doctrinale*, but they have no relevance whatever to the present undertaking.

[Cols. 0545B–0545D]

175. There is no time to discuss at length the author or augmenter of this Martyrology, printed twice in the same year.

When Bollandus once asked Father Jacobus Kritsradt, of our Society, to investigate with certainty something about the life and writings of Hermann Greven, the Carthusian of Cologne, he replied on 5 March 1650 that he had approached the vicar of that Carthusian house. From him he learned that the aforesaid Martyrology of 1490 had been taken in every respect from a certain manuscript marked V. 38—the number of the Carthusian library.

Moreover, in the margin of the printed Martyrology cited, in the final empty column on the right, Father Garnevelt, now deceased, of the Carthusian house, had written by hand:

> “The author is the venerable Father Hermann Greven, or Grefgen, a professed priest of the Carthusian house of Cologne, who died in the year 1480, on 5 November.”

But it is clear from another note reported by the same Kritsradt that this is not sufficiently established: on the first page of the same codex it had been written in an ancient hand a hundred years earlier:

> “Elsewhere it is written thus: Johannes Grefgen, of our house at Cologne, enlarged Usuard’s Martyrology.”

And below:

> “Johannes Grefgen died on the Kalends of April.”

Below that again:

> “GRIFGIN, Carthusian.”

Now listen to the note written by the hand of the Carthusian vicar of Cologne himself, Brother Johannes Lotley. It reads:

> “I know nothing concerning the homeland and family of Father Hermann Greffgen. The other man whom I mentioned was Johannes Scherfgen, a patrician of Cologne, whom I reported because of the similarity of the names; I do not know whether he wrote anything.”

The author’s name appears in no edition; it had to be conjectured from other evidence.
