[Cols. 0545D–0546A]

176. I pass over the other matters investigated in connection with this question, since they are equally uncertain. It is sufficiently clear that efforts to discover the name of the author who augmented or arranged for the printing of that Cologne edition of Usuard from 1490 were fruitless.

For that reason our predecessors always called it simply the Cologne edition of that year. In my *Usuardian Auctaria*, I join it with the Lubecana and always designate both by a single name, under the title *Lubeco-Cologne Edition*, whether it was prepared by one or more Carthusians or by someone else.

I did not wish to separate one from the other, since they report exactly the same material and the Lubecana appears to have been taken from the Cologne edition in the same year. No one will find this very surprising if he observes that the former was completed on the vigil of the most holy Three Kings.

A different judgment must be made concerning the authors of the two other Cologne editions, from 1515 and 1521, which we shall briefly review. Bollandus, Henschenius, and Papebrochius consistently cite them under the name of Usuard of the Cologne Charterhouse, or as the *Additions of the Cologne Charterhouse to Usuard*, or under an equivalent description conveying the same meaning.

Most frequently, however, they cite them under the name of Greven—not Johannes but Hermann—although, if the latter died in 1480, he could not have been the author of those editions.

Whatever may finally be decided about the truth of the matter, we call both of those later editions Grevenian, and throughout the work we consistently use that designation.

[Cols. 0546A–0546D]

177. In that same year, 1490, another edition of Usuard appeared in Paris in folio, under the sole title *Martyrology*, as Rosweyd reports. He compared it with a second edition from 1536, printed by Ambroise Gérard in large quarto and preserved in our possession; the earlier edition was preserved at Louvain in the Standonck House.

Its author or editor was Jean le Munerat, cantor and scholar, a Parisian theologian, as Colvenerius noted somewhere.

Castellanus accepts the proper name but assigns him no other title than “Boursier of the College of Navarre,” in the first Bimester, p. 668. There, unless I am mistaken, he errs in two matters:

1. He gives 1535 instead of 1536.
2. He speaks as though the edition had first been made in that year, although it is certain that the earlier one was forty-five years older, and highly probable that Munerat did not survive until the second edition.

The title assigned in the later edition deserves notice. It reads:

> “Martyrology, that is, a review or catalogue of the martyrs, in which it is briefly and truthfully recounted what the holy martyrs of God suffered and accomplished for the Church and faith of Christ; and the festivals of those same martyrs are indicated according to the day of each month on which they occur. It was arranged after the example of Eusebius, Jerome, and other sacred authors, through the care and command of the emperor Charlemagne, with moral readings inserted that contain the rule of ecclesiastical discipline, written by mandate of Louis, most Christian and most glorious, ever Augustus, in the year 816 from the birth of Christ.”

These statements could easily be corrected. If only the entire edition were not likewise filled with other errors, especially typographical ones!

Otherwise, it is counted among the purer Usuard editions, though it is excluded whenever it departs in another direction.

[Cols. 0546D–0547A]

178. The Usuard editions described thus far are surpassed in renown by the one prefaced with the title:

> “Martyrology according to the custom of the Roman Curia.”

At the end it reads:

> “Here ends the Martyrology, most carefully corrected by Master Belnus of Padua, of the Order of the Hermit Brothers of Saint Augustine, and made abundant—elsewhere: abundant—through the additions of the Fathers of other religious orders. Printed at Venice by order and at the expense of the noble Florentine Luca Antonio de Giunta, and by the printing art of Johann Emerich of Speyer, in the year 1498, on the Ides of October.”

You can easily observe that the author’s name was badly printed as *Belnum* instead of *Belinum*, which is corrected in another edition, or as *Bellinum*.

This last form is the one our predecessors generally used in the *Acts*, and not incorrectly, since it is written that way in the short preface before the Kalends of January.

I have followed another formation because I considered it more accurate: in the Paris edition the name is clearly printed at the end, and it is sufficiently apparent that the letter *I* was absorbed in the first Venetian edition. Whichever inflection you choose makes no difference to us.

The reader should be warned that in the *Acts* the Venetian edition is sometimes cited through a lapse of memory under the year 1488 instead of its true year, 1498; this occurs in volume II of the May volume, p. 657, and elsewhere.

179. May I pause here to ask whether that printer, Joannes Emericus de Spira, was the son or grandson of Joannes Spira, or de Spira, or whether he was the very same man who in 1469, at Venice, printed Caius Pliny’s *Natural History* in an exceedingly elegant, round, or Roman type [Col. 0547B], in a very large format and indeed on parchment—a work which the most illustrious and devoted student of ours, Guillelmus Albertus, Baron of Grisperre, Goyck, and Libersaert and Chancellor of Brabant, wished to present to our hagiographical museum as a gift worthy of eternal remembrance. I mentioned it briefly in the dedication of my *Treatise on the Alexandrian Patriarchs*, inscribed to that same patron and benefactor of ours before volume V of June. The following metrical epigraph, appended to the volume mentioned above, raises a doubt:

> Though once so rare that a reader could scarcely obtain me,  
> and though, broken, I was almost impossible to read,  
> Joannes Spira has recently restored me at Venice  
> and has printed my books with metal type, etc.

[Col. 0547C] What makes me think that Belinus’s edition should be attributed to a son, rather than to the grandson or some other relative, is the immense diversity of the type and the method of printing, which was so little careful that Belinus’s Usuard cannot be compared even in its shadow with the Pliny. But let us return to Belinus.

180. He himself places before his customary prefaces another one, perhaps his own distinctive preface, also published by Molanus, in which he admits that he recognizes only two Martyrologists as earlier than Usuard—namely, Jerome and Bede.

> “The third,” he says, “was Usuard, a monk, whose work is more widely used among many churches, which are also believed to have added something to his work in various places, especially concerning the saints and feasts belonging to those churches. His is the Martyrology which we have judged should be selected for the most part and retained above the others.”

He speaks frankly and truly when he says “for the most part,” for he too added saints and feasts at his own discretion, as will often be evident from the Usuardine supplements. Nevertheless, Scardeonius, *On the Antiquity of the City of Padua*, book II, class 7, p. 154, praises Belinus not merely as editor but as corrector of “the Martyrology which, once publicly read only in choirs and convents because of its rarity, has now, through his work, been made available for everyone to read,” etc. Add to this the words of Castellanus, *First Bimonthly*, p. 134, who attributes to Belinus the distinction that, just as Notker is the last among the ancient classical Martyrologists, so Belinus is the first among the more recent. The most learned man certainly knew that other editions had preceded the Belinian one; but he wished to give this one first place because it was more common and more widely circulated.

181. Besides that first Venetian edition of 1498, we possess a later Parisian edition of 1521; these alone are the editions I have cited throughout the work, since I have found no later impressions, whether Venetian or otherwise, in our museum. Molanus speaks of some others in his 1573 edition, in the preface to the reader, p. VII:

> “The Martyrology of Belinus was printed at Venice, at the sign of Hope, in the year 49, and at Paris in the year 21”—

and Molanus chiefly uses the latter edition.

> “It appears also to have been enlarged somewhat with saints of Padua, of the Venetian church, and of various religious orders. There are also other Martyrologies of the Roman Church, which I have not seen. For the Church of Saint Peter uses a Martyrology printed at Venice in the year 60, which Alexander Peregrinus of Brescia, chaplain of Julius III, published after correcting it. The Lateran Church, however, uses a Martyrology printed by Hieronymus Cavalcalupus in 1564.”

I seem to remember editions dated 1548 and 1566 being mentioned somewhere, unless the numbers were perhaps mistaken, with 66 given for 64 and 48 incorrectly rendered for 49. Whatever the case may be, we refer only to the two editions mentioned above; the later of them departs more greatly from Usuardine purity. Its additions and omissions are described in their respective places in the supplements.

182. A pair of Cologne editions, from the years 1515 and 1521, is much more corrected and accurate than the Belinian editions. I recently said, and continued thereafter to say, that both had been attributed by our predecessors to Hermann Grefgen or Grefgin—more softly inflected as Greven—and I have called both editions by no other name than Greven’s. I know that they are sometimes cited under the more general designation of the Cologne Charterhouse or the Cologne Carthusians; but it is futile to attribute to several men what was undertaken by one alone, as will become clear from his words a little later. There is not much difference between the two in substance, somewhat more in style; but the last is more accurate, and it has been compared with the earlier edition in such a way that the wording of each can be discerned from the other. We possess both and consulted both whenever the variation of the commemorations seemed to warrant it.

Greven—or whoever prepared and corrected those editions—certainly rendered an excellent service to Usuard by carefully distinguishing, with an appended sign, the Usuardine text itself from the additions of various churches, though even his text has not always been completely purified. I do not wish to go through here all the days on which it departs from complete purity; the reader may do so if he wishes merely to count the codices appended to the Usuardine texts. The following points, which we have observed as peculiar to the Greven edition, should be noted here.

183. It is sufficiently certain that Greven—as we may call the author from now on—had the earlier Cologne edition before his eyes. But in order to separate the genuine text from the additions, he was assisted by some Usuardine codex received from Gaul. That it was from Chartres is proved by additions peculiar to that church, which I detected here and there, for example on 14 March:

> “On the same day at Chartres, Saint Leoninus, bishop and confessor.”

Likewise on 16 May:

> “In the district of Chartres, the passion of Saint Emanus, and of Mauricius and Almarius.”

The month of October alone supplies four examples. Thus, on 7 October:

> “At the city of Chartres, the discovery of the body of Saint Caletricus, bishop of that city.”

Then on the 16th:

> “At Chartres, the birthday of Saint Priscus, martyr, beside the River Andure.”

Again on the 17th:

> “At Chartres, Saint Solina, virgin. Near the same city, the dedication of a basilica in memory of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Finally, on the 25th:

> “At Chartres, the dedication of the church of Saint John the Baptist and of Saint Vincent, deacon and martyr.”

These and other observations made occasionally throughout the work clearly show, unless I am mistaken, that such entries could not have been attributed to Usuard except because they were found in a proper Chartres codex, the only one Greven possessed and set before himself as the pure Usuard to be followed.

184. Greven uses another sign, formed approximately like this: L. He speaks of it as follows in his preface, fol. 5:

> “Sometimes a small L is placed to indicate that the saint before whom it is set has been added to Usuard, although another sign may have been placed before it. This, however, has not at all been observed in the feasts of the Conception, Presentation, and Visitation of Blessed Mary, of Saint Thomas, bishop and martyr, and of Saint Catherine, virgin and martyr.”

But whether those things added to the Usuardine text bear a sign or not, we have sufficient reason—as we have said more than once elsewhere—to exclude Greven from the number of the pure codices. This is apparent on the days already cited, and likewise on 1 April, 5 and 20 August, 13 September, and elsewhere.

At the end of the entire work he explains why he did not think certain saints should be inserted into the Martyrology. Among other things, he speaks in a way from which it may truly be inferred that the whole collection had not several authors but one. Here are his words:

> “The end of the Martyrology of Usuard, monk, with additions collected with much labor from various Martyrologies, and added separately for the second time in the year of the Lord 1521, at Cologne.
>
> “In these additions, the person who collected them, following the judgment of Saint Jerome or Bede, simply accommodated his faith either to the history he was reading or to the writings of various men most devoted to this matter, entreating the charity of the Holy Spirit that his labor might attain its fruit in the advancement of the devout, to the glory of God and his saints.”

What may be added here will easily be understood from what follows immediately.

185. Among the editions of Usuard enumerated thus far, the last in order utterly surpasses the others in polish, elegance, and purity. It was prepared with particular care by Joannes Molanus, theologian of Louvain, whose true Belgian surname was Vermeuten. Castellanus renders this in French in the preface to the *Universal Martyrology* as *de la Meule*. I would rather translate it as *de Moulin*.

Valerius Andreas, in the *Belgian Library*, testifies that Molanus was born at Lille in Flanders in 1533:

> “To which place,” he says, “his father had gone with his pregnant wife for the sake of learning the French language.”

It is strange that he adds that Molanus “knew only his maternal and native language, that is, Brabantian, and preferred to be called a Louvain man,” on account of his mother’s homeland, although his father was from Schoonhoven. From Molanus’s manner of writing, I had become entirely convinced that he was skilled in French—indeed, somewhat scrupulous in preserving French orthography—since he everywhere carefully avoids forming the letter W, a practice we have generally retained in his supplements. Perhaps this was overly meticulous, but it follows the same orthographic practice that is commonly preserved in other Usuardine codices, so that curious readers may on this basis also form a conjecture about the value of each.

[Col. 0550B] 186. But what if Valerius made a slight mistake concerning Molanus’s native language, since he did not consult the editions of his Martyrology with sufficient accuracy? For when listing Molanus’s writings, Valerius gives first place to the following:

> “The Martyrology of Usuard, enlarged with annotations, Louvain, 1573 and 1577. Printed by Hieronymus Wellaeus.”

Here Valerius nodded off; for the first Wellaean edition bears the year 1568, the second 1573, and the third is the Antwerp edition printed by Nutius in 1582. It was also inserted at Paris, in the same year 1583, into the large volume of the *History of the Ancient Fathers* by la Barre. I know of no others that have appeared to date.

A second error of this kind concerns, unless I am mistaken, the distinguished man V. C. du Pin. In his *Library of Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the Amsterdam edition, section IX, p. 200, col. 2, he cites some impression—whatever it may have been—of Antwerp, assigning it to the year 1588, when he evidently means the earlier Louvain edition of 1568. I infer, however, that the most learned man either read it incorrectly or perhaps found the figures transposed, just as, for the year of the last edition, 1583, he may have seen 1538. That would certainly be an easy slip; but it was more disgraceful for the same bibliographer, in that very column cited, to substitute Bollandus for Mosander and to make Surianus the author of the supplement.

187. Whatever may be the truth about Molanus’s birth or native language, it is certain that he was famous for his learning and writings, which Valerius explains there, but most famous for his first edition of the Usuardine Martyrology. This is the one which, as I said above, surpassed all the older editions, chiefly because he restored Usuard’s text, with the greatest diligence possible, to its native purity and simplicity.

All the Hagiophiles praise, celebrate, and rightly revere this edition. It was held in such high esteem by Cardinal Baronius that he wished to leave this enduring monument of his appreciation in the preface to the *Roman Martyrology*, chapter 9:

> “I cannot calmly allow even a brief sheet of such a great man, who has rendered the best service to the Church of God and to Catholic truth, to perish. To him—for I shall speak frankly—I owe all these things insofar as, being the first to enter that thick forest, he opened a way for me and for others. For this reason both I and all learned men willingly acknowledge and confess that we owe him a very great debt.”

There Baronius also praises the later edition—or, if you prefer, the later editions, since whoever knows one knows them all. But to me, and to all worshippers of Usuardine simplicity in its purity and native form, the first edition alone is uniquely dear and supremely precious. In that edition alone Usuard is recognizable; the later edition or editions, deformed by alterations, transpositions, and interpolations under the direction and counsel of I know not whom, make it seem almost as though Usuard had vanished from sight.

Accordingly, we used the earlier edition to recover Usuard’s text; the others generally served to enlarge the supplements. Let us now hear Molanus himself discussing that first edition of his in chapter 4 of his preface.

188. I pass over the points on which he departed from the truth with Sigebert or others. He continues there as follows:

> “In the first prologue, among those ordinarily placed before Usuard, it is noted that Usuard’s work is more widely used than Jerome’s or Bede’s among many churches, which are also believed to have added something to his work in various places, especially concerning saints and feasts specifically belonging to those churches.
>
> “Because of these additions to Usuard, it is not easy to put Usuard alone into print, without additions indistinguishably mixed with him. Nevertheless, I hope that I have done so, although I am somewhat doubtful whether a few things may have escaped our efforts.
>
> “I did insert certain things into Usuard himself from Bede, Ado, various church Martyrologies, and elsewhere, but in a different type and with a letter placed before them, by which the reader can very easily notice that they are not Usuard’s. I compared the Usuard Martyrology printed at Cologne in octavo in 1521 with the Martyrology of the Roman Church, for that Martyrology uses Usuard with additions; likewise with various Martyrologies printed in France, all of which are Usuard’s but enlarged; and finally with several manuscripts.
>
> “From this comparison I observed that the Usuard printed at Cologne in the year mentioned had only a few additions indistinguishably mixed with Usuard; it has many additions, but they are distinguished from Usuard’s words by some mark. Once those indistinguishable additions have been removed from Usuard, this Martyrology contains Usuard himself alone, in larger type, corrected with the assistance of various exemplars.
>
> “In all these I find the name USUARD written, once and again HUSUARD; nevertheless, Trithemius and several Germans call him ISUARD.”

189. A few points from this passage must be considered and explained. I think Molanus is entirely correct in saying that, because of the additions to Usuard, it is not easy to print Usuard alone, without additions indistinguishably mixed with him. For despite employing all his diligence, he departed from Usuardine purity in more than thirty places, as the reader will find in our Observations.

No one should suppose that I am flattering myself to the point of thinking I have attained complete simplicity; I do not see how that could be accomplished conveniently, since among so many editions already reviewed and so many manuscript codices—which we shall review further—I have found none that does not suffer from numerous excesses or deficiencies.

In comparison with Molanus, we had this advantage: numerous codices of every kind were available to us. Assisted by his skill and that of others, and having brought to light, consulted, and compared the sources of Usuard, we were in a much better position to separate the false from the true, the genuine from the spurious, and dross from silver.

If anything escaped our efforts, we are fully confident that we shall be granted both an opportunity to recognize the error and permission to be forgiven for it. I judge it superfluous to repeat here the arguments advanced on both sides for recovering and proving the purity of Usuard, since this is the subject matter of our entire work, drawn out day by day.

190. Molanus continues:

> “I also compared the Usuard Martyrology printed at Cologne in octavo [in a smaller format] in MDXXI [1521].”

He means Greven, whom we discussed immediately before, with the Martyrology of the Roman Church, since that Martyrology uses Usuard with additions.

This is the Belinus edition, which Molanus accepted as the Roman Martyrology. For this he was criticized by Baronius, though the most eminent man calls it an error that was tolerable and worthy of pardon, since Molanus, being so far away, did not know what those who lived in Rome had obtained only with great labor, vigilant diligence, and the utmost industry.

That is, if they actually obtained or could have obtained it, since those matters still lie in obscurity. For although Baronius clearly teaches that there was some ancient Roman Martyrology copied by Saint Gregory, he is nevertheless compelled to admit that he himself had never seen such a Martyrology. We, however, demonstrated at the beginning of the preceding chapter that Gregory’s characteristics do not at all correspond to the Martyrology found by Ado at Ravenna. No harm has thereby been done to the Romans, since in place of one we have vindicated for them two true, genuine, ancient Martyrologies, long since made public.

Since Molanus did not know these things, while Belinus had prefixed to his edition the splendid title *Martyrology according to the custom of the Roman Curia*, that small error by which Molanus called Belinus’s Usuard the Martyrology of the Roman Church was certainly most worthy of pardon.

191. It is entirely certain from comparison alone that Molanus used both the Greven and Belinus Martyrologies, to such an extent that he often adopted their errors, or at least relegated them to the supplements, especially from that other Parisian edition of Belinus. The first and purer Venetian edition of 1498 does not seem to have been known to him.

Molanus also compared Usuard with various Martyrologies printed in France, all of which are Usuard’s but enlarged. He himself explains which those various Martyrologies were in chapter 12 of his preface; they are chiefly reduced to the two editions of Muneratus and the Belinian edition of 1521, of which we spoke above.

I wish Molanus had enumerated his manuscript codices more distinctly, especially the one he cites under the letter Q, which I consider precisely identical with our distinguished Herinien codex. It could easily have come into Molanus’s hands, since it had been possessed by Augustinus Hunnaeus, theologian and canon of Louvain and a contemporary of Molanus.

He identifies the codex he praises somewhat more clearly in the letter to the reader accompanying the second edition, on the verso of p. 6, calling it a Usuard manuscript that had scarcely any additions except those concerning the saints of Reims. This is precisely the most native form of our Herinien codex.

Meanwhile, from the continual comparison of Molanus’s edition with our codex, I do not see that everything which could have been useful as assistance was employed, as our Usuardine observations will make clearer.

192. There is one matter which I have not yet been able to investigate sufficiently: namely, how Castellanus, *First Bimonthly*, p. 196, learned that Molanus had used, in the additions, a manuscript Martyrology of the Church of Paris, copied from an older one in 1316 and transcribed again in 1529.

Certainly, among all the matters Molanus discusses at length in the prefaces to both the first and the later edition, he nowhere mentions such a Parisian manuscript, as far as I know. Let the reader consult chapters 12 and 13 of the first preface and section 10 of the letter accompanying the second edition.

If Castellanus had said that the editions of Muneratus and Belinus had taken precedence, he would have stated this correctly, since Molanus himself asserts that he compared Usuard with various Martyrologies printed in France.

I also seem able to infer that Molanus did not see the true or alleged autograph kept at Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, nor was a copy of it sent to him; otherwise he would certainly not have failed to mention it to his readers.

In any event, since Molanus’s edition was prepared from so many codices, both manuscript and printed, I wish all of them to be counted among my sources, so that considerable authority may accrue to this latest edition of ours, since it has been extracted, reviewed, corrected, and purged from so many exemplars.

193. In addition, the reader will find cited several times in January a certain Usuard that is fairly pure, published with the *Acts of the Martyrs*, or with the book bearing this title. Would that we possessed it complete! But since only that one month survives, I shall say no more about it.

We also possess a Martyrology, or *Violet of the Saints*, in the Strasbourg edition of 1508, which our predecessors mention more than once in the *Acts*. But we did not use it, because through its very frequent and extensive interpolations it departs too greatly from Usuard’s style.

Almost the opposite is true of the Martyrology of the Order of Saint Benedict, which we possess both in manuscript and in print. It belongs no more to the Benedictines than to any other religious order, and no indication of place or year has been appended.

We were not lacking an excellent and abundant harvest of other codices. The *Hagiologion of Frankish Gaul*, edited by our Labbe, did not deserve the name “authentic Martyrology”—“most authentic,” as Castellanus calls it on p. 654. It is plainly incomplete, and whatever good it contains, apart from its proper entries for Bourges, is almost entirely excerpted from Usuard.

For the same reason I did not think that Maurolycus, or other more recent men who were not editors of Usuard but interpolators, should be consulted in the search for his genuine text. Likewise, I disregarded the German edition of Walasser, sometimes cited under the name of our venerable Petrus Canisius, although it generally reproduces Usuard, but with very extensive additions.

Again, no account was taken of Papebrochius’s manuscript additions to the Cologne edition of 1490, taken from the codex of the Abbey of Saint Michael at Antwerp, since they generally departed very far from our Usuard.

To conclude the matter briefly: so many codices were available from other sources that seeking more would have been superfluous. On the other hand, I sometimes observed that the supplements had grown so excessively that I more than once considered removing certain items rather than procuring new ones.

So much for the published books of Usuard. We now proceed to the manuscripts.

## ARTICLE IV. On the Manuscript Usuardine Codices

### § I. On the Purer Codices, and First, on the Pratensis Usuard

[Col. 0554B]

194. Among the seventeen complete manuscript Usuardine codices that we possess, and the more than thirty collated with Greven or others, apart from eighteen Chiffletian codices and several others—in short, among all of them—one codex has always held first place with us, if not under the title of complete purity, at least under that of antiquity. It is the codex which is held in the highest esteem at the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés as having been written by the author’s own hand, or as an autograph. I have been unable, despite every effort, to obtain it even for a short time, so that I might proceed more securely with this edition.

Bollandus mentions it in his preface, p. 51, writing as follows:

> “Our Sirmondus considers that codex to have been written in Usuard’s time, or not long afterward. With his customary courtesy, he carefully compared my copy of it with another of easily four hundred years’ antiquity, or even older, which is kept in the same monastery of Saint-Germain in Paris.”

A notice prefixed to our codex states that the former is designated by the letter A and the latter by B. Sirmondus continues in the same place:

> “This copy of ours was transcribed from the former. The things marked below with little lines were either placed in the margin of autograph A or inserted into the text itself at the end of each day, by another hand, although almost certainly an ancient one. From this it appears that they do not belong to Usuard’s Martyrology, but were added later by the monks, especially those of Saint-Germain, to whom for the most part they pertain.”

[Col. 0554D] 195. How carefully we have followed the guidance contained in this notice is abundantly clear from our Observations. At the bottom of the page another hand reads:

> “I compared this Martyrology of Usuard with the codices cited here, together with the Reverend Father Jacobus Sirmondus, at Paris in the year 1631. Joannes Baptista de Cortas, priest of the Society of Jesus.”

The celebrated Sirmondus’s expertise in comparing and distinguishing ancient codices is widely known. Nevertheless, when I had observed here and there, from Castellanus’s citations, some discrepancy from our copy, I turned to Sirmondus himself, asking him to instruct me distinctly, minutely, and exactly concerning the aforesaid codex. He did so, returning to the source once, twice, and a third time, with such diligence and almost scrupulous conscientiousness that he might seem not to have omitted a single letter.

Nevertheless, our learned Stephanus Chamillart, who supplied Castellanus’s place with no less goodwill, noticed some blemishes in the final comparison.

For the rest, Castellanus, beginning a new complete comparison with Molanus’s first edition, noted with great skill the variations, however slight, day by day in a letter dated 31 May 1709. Strongly encouraged by this assistance, I was moved to undertake more boldly a work filled with the most wearisome investigations.

I shall frankly acknowledge here, to the praise of this hagiophile, that he continued to extend his helping hand throughout his life with no less constancy than he had promised at the beginning, after he had reported with some sorrow in a subsequent letter dated 31 July of the same year that the superiors of the monastery of Saint-Germain had absolutely not been persuaded, through the efforts of the learned Theodoricus Ruinartius, to send the codex here.

196. During this period we carried on a friendly discussion, not only about the antiquity but especially about the authenticity, purity, and simplicity of the codex so often mentioned. It could not be denied that the codex was covered with so many erasures, deletions, overwritings, additions, omissions, and alterations.

When I opposed to it our own codices, especially the Herinien, everywhere complete, clean, full, and venerable for its antiquity and splendor, he finally resorted to the argument by which Mabillon defends it: namely, that the Necrology appended to the codex proves that it was written in Usuard’s time and consequently by the author himself.

As for the interpolations, erasures, deletions, overwritings, superscriptions, and other features of this kind, they seemed to him signs by which it ought truly to be considered an autograph—one that Usuard himself, at different times and as new information became available, had truncated, enlarged, reduced, and altered, just as learned men know commonly happens in autographs written by the first hand.

To prove its antiquity, he therefore sent me a Notice prefixed by Mabillon’s own hand to that codex. Since I find it published in the frequently cited preface to the fourth Benedictine century, part II, p. LXXXVII, I prefer to transcribe it from there. The learned and always highly esteemed Mabillon writes as follows:

197.

> “And indeed we possess a very ancient exemplar of his Martyrology, written at that time—that is, in the ninth century, when Usuard was living—with the appended Necrology. In it, the death of Queen Irmintrudis, wife of Charles the Bald, is marked by the primary hand on the Nones of October; but the death of Charles II, emperor, is written by a more recent hand on the day before the Nones of October.
>
> “Accordingly, this codex was written during the interval that elapsed between the year 869, the death of Irmintrudis, and the year 877, when Charles the Bald died. This is also confirmed by the death of Ebroin, bishop and abbot of Saint-Germain, which occurred in 838 and is entered by the first hand on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, whereas the deaths of his successors Hilduin and Gozlin, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, and of Ebolus, on the sixth day before the Nones of October, are written by a second hand.”

Mabillon’s sincere reliability is too well established to me, and his skill in distinguishing ancient scripts too evident, for me to wish to call into question the death notices he adduces or their demonstrable difference, although, if I had been permitted to inspect the codex itself and examine that Necrology with stricter criticism, arranging and comparing all its elements with one another, perhaps some things might have emerged that would weaken the force of the argument or at least provide grounds for exceptions.

198. Nor does the conviction which Castellanus impressed upon me arise from the years marked in the Necrology. For what if that entire codex was written a hundred—or, if you wish, two hundred—years after Usuard’s death? Could not the same first hand have continued the Necrology for some distance, while some later hand added the remaining entries?

Mabillon’s argument may be admitted as highly probable, but by no means as conclusive. It would be more conclusive if there were not features that do not greatly support the commendation of the codex.

Certainly, from other matters to be brought forward shortly, one of two alternatives may perhaps appear more probable: either Usuard wrote different Martyrologies, or variant copies of the same Martyrology, from one of which our Herinien codex and others proceeded, just as the major Antwerp codex, the Rosweyd codex, and the Aquicinctine codex appear to have been taken from another similar Pratensis exemplar; or the Pratensis manuscript in question cannot reach back to Usuard’s lifetime and must therefore be called more recent, having been written later and interpolated and reworked—or rather deformed—in the manner in which it now exists by monks of the same institution in later generations.

Mabillon can easily see that this objection continually presents itself from the entire structure of the codex, from the varying script, from the addition of the same script at different times and in different ink, and from the numerous other blemishes that occur.

199. Let us hear how he protects himself against these points in the passage recently cited. He continues:

> “In that autograph of Usuard—for so it may be called—various additions are found here and there, and also certain erasures and writings apparently overwritten at the same time, perhaps by the author’s own hand, who repeatedly revised his work.”

I certainly do not deny that this could have happened, as Castellanus told and repeated to me more than once. I only wish it could be made as plausible as it pleases the defenders of that codex to claim as an escape.

For below we shall argue that, if Mabillon’s chief argument is sound, Usuard did not live long enough to introduce so many variations into his autograph.

I therefore think that I have examined the entire matter at greater length, with greater maturity and accuracy, and more expressly than they have, by comparing each day’s text—and indeed the individual commemorations within each text—with other Usuardine codices that are purer and more complete.

From this comparison I encountered difficulties that render the aforesaid autograph—whether genuine or alleged—suspect in many respects, at the very least, although in other matters I have always assigned it first place among the others.

Permit me to set forth my hesitations and the doubts that have repeatedly arisen, which I would like the most learned men, the possessors of this oft-praised codex, to resolve.

200. I shall not repeat the points that throughout the work I was compelled to oppose individually in my Observations to that Pratensis autograph. It will suffice here to indicate several days where they may be found.

The reader should consult January: 1, 9, 12, 13, 14, 16, 22, 26, 28, 29, 30, and 31.

February: 3, 8, and 17.

March: 10, 17, 18, 26, 27, 29, and 30.

April: 2, 12, 17, 19, 22, 23, and 26.

May: 10, 11, and 27.

June: 1, 4, 5, 9, 10, 15, 17, 21, 25, 26, and 30.

July: 1, 7, 11, 18, 20, 22, and 28.

August: 12, 23, 26, 29, and 30.

September: 1, 3, 5, 23, and 25.

October: 13, 16, 17, 19, 24, and 30.

November: 1, 2, 13, 19, 21, and 23.

December: 4, 22, 25, 29, and 31.

At nearly eighty places, as well as at others not recorded here with equal exactness, the Pratensis Usuard differs from other simpler codices, both printed and manuscript—although this difference has not always been a reason for excluding it from the number of the pure codices. In short, it has been altered, enlarged, abridged, or interpolated in so many places. What other conclusion can reasonably follow than either that this codex is not an autograph, or at least that there existed one or more other autographs from which our Herinien and other codices, purer than the Pratensis and to be discussed below, were copied?

201. I know that, with Mabillon and Castellanus, I must be answered that many of the variations just cited are of such a kind that, although written over erasures, added at the end, or transferred, transposed, and twisted around, they could nevertheless have been entered or added by Usuard himself as he repeatedly revised his work.

I know the poet’s saying: “The strictest justice is often the greatest malice”—or, as others read it, “injustice.”

I do not wish to be an excessively rigid exactor; I do not wish to argue; I do not wish to shake, much less overthrow, the most ancient and primary exemplar of Usuard. Indeed, I would very much like the venerable codex to be freed from every suspicion, however slight, of being spurious.

But when naked truth is being sought, it is wrong to conceal anything. I state everything openly.

This scruple nevertheless remains, and I have so far been entirely unable to remove it. Let us grant that many additions, alterations, interpolations, overwritings, and transpositions were made by the author himself. I have still not seen how the variations can be adequately explained which are expressed by the very first hand within the text of the Pratensis codex itself, yet are found in no codices, or only in very few, whether written or printed.

From this it becomes plausible—an argument I hinted at above—that either the Pratensis codex is not a genuine autograph at all and therefore not Usuard’s own manuscript, or that Usuard himself wrote several autographs, from one or more of which our Herinien and the other codices were copied.

This remains to be explained somewhat more clearly and distinctly.

202. The Pratensis codex, so often called—and henceforth to be called by us—expresses its second announcement for 12 January as follows: “At Caesarea in Mauretania, of Saint Arcadius, etc.,” with no erasure anywhere and no visible over-writing. Yet that location, or place of martyrdom, at Caesarea in Mauretania occurs in none of our other codices, whether printed or manuscript, except the Aquicinctine extract. Therefore the other codices were not copied from the Pratensis autograph; consequently, either it is not an autograph, or we must admit that more than one autograph existed, with some codices copied from one and others from another. What Castellanus replied to this argument [Col. 0558B] will be found explained on that day and, unless I am mistaken, thoroughly refuted. For my part, this reasoning has always seemed extremely compelling, and of such a kind that it cannot easily be weakened by any exception or evasion, whatever methods I have tried in order either to blunt its force or at least to soften it somewhat, as I shall explain more fully below.

Lest you think that I reach this conclusion from that single commemoration, observe what has been said on the same subject in other places: 16 and 31 January, 12 and 17 April, 15 and 17 June, 12 and 23 August. Let us add one or two further examples. On 17 April, in the penultimate place, before the announcement of the Cordubans, we read: “In the East, of blessed Nicephorus, etc.” Nicephorus is absent from all the best-established codices and is found only in the Rosweydine, Aquicinctine, and Brussels codices; [Col. 0558C] therefore he was not in the autograph from which the other codices of the highest quality were taken.

203. Castellanus noted that, in the Usuardine text, the Pratensis entry for 5 June had been rewritten (*redécrit*) on an added leaf, beginning with Boniface and omitting the Egyptian martyrs. I ask whether this was done by the original hand or by a later one. If by the original hand, the argument is valid; if by a later hand, it is no less pressing. For here too the Pratensis agrees with its almost constant companions, the larger Antwerp, Rosweydine, and Aquicinctine codices, while differing entirely from all the others.

Again, all the codices except the Pratensis and those same three read, in the middle of the text on 17 June: “On the same day, Saint Vulmarus the confessor, of admirable [virtue], etc.” Those three, together with the Pratensis, on that very day and in that very place treat of Gundulf of Bourges. A still greater confusion recurs on 20 July, to which some interpolator transferred Vulmarus, deleting there Paul, the martyr of Córdoba, whom nearly all the other codices consistently mark. I cannot readily believe that these and similar alterations were made by Usuard himself, as I show at greater length for those days. The conclusion follows once more that our chief and purer codices, from which the text of Usuard ought to have been taken, were copied from somewhere other than the Pratensis codex. Anyone who consults the other days assigned here, and many more besides, will easily draw the same conclusion.

204. To reconcile or in some fashion preserve these points, I see chiefly two possible approaches. First, one may grant that the author of the Martyrology, Usuard, copied his work himself, or had it copied, once, twice, and perhaps a third time, so that those exemplars copied successively—perhaps as they were to be presented to the emperor or to others—were afterward corrected, polished, or altered here and there by the author himself, with new information, whether true or false, being added, as commonly happens. From these different transcripts, moreover, the apographs were taken that do not entirely agree with the autograph left at Saint-Germain.

But this latter copy was subsequently so often deleted, erased, over-written, interpolated, and disfigured that Mabillon himself doubted its genuine authenticity. Certainly, in my opinion, we must admit that something was lacking, since those learned men, editors of so many ancient manuscripts, abstained for so long from publishing it, despite being repeatedly urged to do so—undoubtedly deterred by the multitude of erasures and intervening alterations. Whatever may have held them back from publishing their Usuard, the procedure just proposed has always seemed to me the most probable and, for everyone else, the easiest way of blunting and to some extent explaining the difficulties raised.

205. Nevertheless, I suggest another possibility, or another way of disentangling ourselves from the objections mentioned above, although it rests on no equal degree of probability: namely, that the earliest copyists of the Usuardine autographs may through carelessness have omitted certain things, or on their own authority have selected what pleased them, [Col. 0559C] and with the same authority passed over what did not please them. I do not deny that this can be devised with sufficient plausibility; but will those experienced in such matters allow themselves to be persuaded of it? Will they believe that this could so easily have happened—or at least been permitted—in that particular Martyrology which, by what may be called imperial authority, was intended for the common use of the Gallican churches? We can indeed allow that they were permitted to add the proper feasts of their own churches; but to remove saints or alter commemorations—this, we do not think, was tolerated under the principles then prevailing.

These, then, are more or less the considerations that we have candidly judged relevant to suspecting, defending, or preserving the antiquity of the Pratensis codex. Our sole concern is that even the age of Usuard himself should remain intact for it, and that all the corrections, interpolations, and so forth in which the same hand appears should be admitted as having been made by Usuard himself—although this is extraordinarily difficult to believe, because of another argument that I now present.

206. Those who long ago assigned Usuard to the time of Charlemagne did so on the ground that his Martyrology had been dedicated to Augustus Charles. Others, however, have rightly replied with us that this proves nothing, since Charles the Bald was also Augustus, that is, emperor, and the work may have been offered to him as emperor. Above, following Mabillon’s conjecture, we accepted that the Martyrology was written between the years 869 and 877; indeed, it must be admitted that it was written, or at least completed, after the year 875, when the Bald first became emperor, and therefore, in all probability, in the immediately following year, 876.

If we follow Mabillon’s conjecture, it will also follow that Usuard died before Charles the Bald, since the latter is entered in the Necrology in another hand; Usuard therefore survived, at most, until the beginning of the year 877—approximately one year after completing and presenting his Martyrology to the emperor. Who, then, will believe that within an interval of one year or slightly more so many things occurred to Usuard that, in a Martyrology only just communicated to the emperor and consequently to the Gallican churches, they had to be erased, altered, obliterated, transposed, and interpolated? Indeed, who would dare suppose that this was either permitted to Usuard or left open to him after the Martyrology had been accepted by the emperor and the churches? Again, who would persuade us that the same hand returned so many times, adding, removing, and so forth, while at the same time another ink, or other indications, so often appear as to prove convincingly that many years certainly intervened during which corrections were made?

207. There is another consideration that makes the authenticity, or autograph character, of the Pratensis codex uncertain: it is impossible to establish with certainty which was the writer’s original hand. For if only the hand that presents the actual text is the autograph and Usuardine hand, then whatever is added in another and later hand, whether in the margin or at the foot of the page, must be attributed to Usuard. Yet it often happens that similar additions, found in their proper place in all the other codices, clearly demonstrate that they are genuinely Usuardine; hence it follows that everything contained in this codex was not written by Usuard’s original hand, or that he used a different script. Either alternative will not easily satisfy the defenders of that autograph, whether genuine or alleged.

Among various examples, I take as evidence the entry for 7 November in the eulogy of Herculanus, bishop of Perugia: “Whose body, after the severing of his head, etc.,” taken from Book III, chapter 13, of Gregory the Great’s *Dialogues*. This is found in all the copies, whether of the first, second, or any other class, manuscript or printed, with the exception of the Tournai and Pulsan codices, which are especially accustomed either to shorten such eulogies or to cut them away entirely.

But this very eulogy is added in the margin of the Pratensis codex and, according to Castellanus, “in the margin and in letters less ancient than the text,” that is, in a later hand. Therefore, in the aforesaid codex, some things that are genuinely Usuardine are nevertheless written in a later hand; therefore it is not established that the original hand is Usuardine. Which hand, then, is it? I wish to be corrected and instructed, but so many defects, additions, over-writings, mutilations, and so forth plainly give rise to the suspicion that this codex, whatever its character, is no more endowed with the prerogative of autograph status than the others.

208. I wish the most learned and highly esteemed Reverend Fathers, the Benedictines of Saint-Germain, to receive these and whatever other matters have been said back and forth in the *Usuardine Observations* concerning that illustrious codex in the spirit that they were discussed and debated solely for the sake of discovering the truth. For so many years, and from such varied exemplars, we have sought only that simplicity—Usuard’s own simplicity; and if it could have been drawn from the Pratensis manuscript alone, I do not think that the possessors of that codex would, through so many centuries, have deprived all learned men, most eager for so great a treasure, of it.

Everywhere, Molanus’s edition is generally valued far more highly than that repeatedly praised codex, whether it is genuinely or supposedly an autograph; nor would I dare deny that I belong among those who think so. If I am mistaken, let some learned person from that celebrated Congregation, experienced in these matters, remove the error from me and from the others; let him explain and dispel my doubts, indeed my mistakes, into which I have fallen because I was deprived of the codex itself. I shall be the first to retract most readily whatever may perhaps be said to have been unjustly thought by me about that autograph.

I shall nevertheless seem to have rendered sufficient service to the republic of letters if I have extracted from those men, even somewhat importunately, what no one has so far been able to obtain by prayers and exhortations: namely, if my doubts induce them at some point to make their own Usuard public, restored in his native simplicity and equipped with whatever annotations they wish; indeed, if by the same effort they attempt to shake our Usuard, and he falls, it will be a triumph. We all have the same goal before us: that, once the darkness has been dispersed, errors may be driven away, truth brought to light, and ecclesiastical antiquity illuminated even by rival efforts, to the greater glory of God and the saints.

§ II.—On our principal Herinien codex

209. In the passage of the general preface cited above, p. 51, after praising the Pratensis codex and another codex of Miraeus, Bollandus continues as follows:

“Yet the copy of ours that I cited above I greatly prefer to both of those, and I judge it purer and more genuine. For that most ancient Parisian codex has, on the Ides of January, the following: ‘On Mount Verziacus, of Saint Viventius the confessor,’ although it is established that the relics of Saint Vincentius were transferred to Vergiacum after Usuard’s time—unless perhaps he wrote in the final years of Charles the Bald and lived on long afterward, adding this entry then. But these words are absent from our copy, and for that reason I consider it more genuine. It once belonged to the Carthusian monastery called the Chapel of the Blessed Virgin Mary, or of Herines” (from this we derived the designation HERINIENSIS), “near Edingen, or, as it is now called, Enghien, a town of Belgium; afterward it belonged to Augustine Hunnaeus, a celebrated man, and was later donated to our college at Louvain.”

I am not at all surprised that Bollandus prefers our distinguished Herinien codex to the Pratensis; he might perhaps have preferred it even more had he known the blemishes and stains with which, as Castellanus has taught us, it is sprinkled. Anyone who has examined and compared both will prefer it, unless I am greatly mistaken. Yet Castellanus removes the force of Bollandus’s argument by honestly testifying that the announcement “On Mount Verziacus, etc.” was added to the Pratensis codex by a secondary hand, as we recognize under 13 January—something that Sirmond and Cortasius had not observed.

210. If the question concerns the antiquity of the two manuscripts, I readily and willingly admit that our Herinien parchment codex yields the palm entirely to the Pratensis, even if attention is paid only to the form of the script. According to Castellanus, the Pratensis preserves the most ancient manner of writing, which he calls Carolingian; the Herinien is somewhat more elegant and polished, but at least two centuries later.

If, however, we consider purity, genuineness, integrity, and simplicity, there is no doubt that our codex far surpasses the other. Its script sufficiently establishes its antiquity, although it was executed by a most skilled scribe; and, unlike almost all other codices, it consistently forms the diphthong *ae* clearly with *e*, in accordance with the usage received in the eleventh century. Our predecessors rightly assigned the codex to that century, since no saints later than that period are added.

Thus, on 19 April, the following is appended to the Usuardine text: “Burial of Lord Leo the pope, who dedicated the church of Saint Remigius”—but, as you see, without the title “saint”; he died, namely, in the year 1054. Likewise, on 1 June it reads: “At Trier, burial of blessed Simeon the monk, etc.,” who is known to have died in 1035. He is called “blessed,” a customary title that Martyrologists continued to bestow even after his canonization, which took place in 1042.

Since the translation of Saint Nicholas is recorded on 9 May, if this truly occurred in the year 1087, it follows that our codex must have been written near the end of the century.

211. I know that our predecessors occasionally changed their opinion slightly concerning the age of this codex according to the varying circumstances that arose, as may be found concerning Henschenius in volume I of June, p. LXXXVIII, letter D; but its genuineness and purity could never be doubted. I shall not deny that some additions differing from Usuard occur here and there; but if the Rheims saints, or those of the province of Rheims—which extended almost as far as Trier—are removed, it will become clearer than daylight that among all the Usuardine codices, printed and manuscript alike, this one most deservedly holds the foremost place, and that it was once copied from some Usuardine autograph, or at least from an exceptionally pure apograph.

The difficulty perceived by Henschenius was that, on 15 October, the following was inserted second in the text: “On the same day, Saint Oswald, bishop and confessor,” as may be seen in volume III of February, p. DCCL. At that time Henschenius held the opinion that our codex was older than the tenth century, since he had not yet considered the other passages that show it to be later.

If you ask why the codex’s copyist recorded Oswald on that day rather than on 28 or 29 February, I shall confess that I do not know the true reason. If anyone wishes to hear conjectures, they must be sought in Henschenius at the place cited. We admit that Oswald’s announcement is an addition arising from the cult which he enjoyed in Gaul, especially in the province of Rheims, under some particular title.

212. Such Rheims additions occur more frequently in this codex of ours. If they were absent, scarcely any others would be found, so that Molanus rightly called it above, at no. 191, a Usuardine manuscript having hardly any additions except those concerning the saints of Rheims.

I have no doubt whatsoever that this was the codex’s homeland. It must have been transferred from there to the Herinien Charterhouse, formerly Saint Mary of the Desert, or Mont-Dieu, which was among the earliest Carthusian houses in all Belgium.

My conjecture, and at the same time the codex’s age, is confirmed by this commemoration, added by a later hand in the margin under the Second Nones, that is, 6 October: “In Calabria, the burial of blessed Bruno the confessor, first founder of the Carthusian order.” I believe this was added solely because of the exceptional reverence that this charterhouse showed toward its founder, since it is otherwise known how late the Church decreed public cult for Bruno.

These facts sufficiently establish the age, homeland, origins, and migrations of this Herinien Usuard. To leave nothing out, I will also add its format, which according to customary usage is now called quarto. It is bound together with a manuscript treatise of Saint Jerome on the Pauline and other Catholic Epistles; at the end of this is appended a calendar containing the anniversaries of the Herinien monastery. I stated above, at no. 169, that in this codex, as in the Pratensis, the year begins with the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.

213. Now, to form an opinion of its simplicity and purity, run through the individual months and separate the Rheims additions: you will immediately see that few additions have been inserted, interpolations are rare, and erasures scarcely one or two.

Under 4 January, Rigobertus, archbishop of Rheims, is recorded; under the 15th, Mauro is added, “disciple of blessed Benedict the abbot.” Finally, I do not know from where the most blessed Hildephonsus was brought in on the 23rd, unless he enjoyed a particular cult either in this province of Rheims or in the monastery to which the codex once belonged.

In February, Blasius has been moved back to the 3rd; on the 8th, Paul of Verdun is added, perhaps likewise a local saint. In March, some defect is found only on the first day. In April, apart from the Rheims additions, there are, on the 18th, Maternius; on the 19th, Leo IX; on the 24th, Bova and Doda; and on the 30th, Madernianus. The only other occurrence is Mary of Egypt, entered under the 9th.

There are five days on which it differs from Usuard: the 1st, concerning Marculfus; the 8th, concerning Gibrien; the 9th, concerning the translation of Nicholas; the 20th, concerning Romanus the monk; and the 29th, concerning the translation of Remigius. Yet I am greatly mistaken if all these do not belong specifically to the province of Rheims.

In June, something is missing under Medardus on the 8th; Leutfredus is omitted on the 21st; and Felix of Sutrium is missing on the 23rd, just as his companions Irenaeus and Mustiola are missing on 3 July. See our *Observations* concerning them.

214. Moreover, in July there is one erasure at the beginning, which I think concerns the translation of Saint Benedict; on the 18th, Arnulfus is added; and then, on the 20th and 23rd, occur the translations of Theodosia and Nicasius, celebrated by the people of Rheims.

In August, Bertulfus the abbot is added to the text on the 19th, apparently from the monastery’s own institution. Then, on the 25th: “In the district of Vermandois, Saint Hunegundis.”

In September, the 1st treats of Aegidius, Sinicius, and Nivandus as though they were from Rheims; Remaclus is added on the 3rd; and the 7th, 25th, and 27th likewise concern people of Rheims. The 10th, however, is somewhat mutilated, and the 20th interpolated, as our *Observations* explain more fully.

In October, the 1st is not pure; on the 27th, the Vigil of Saints Simon and Jude is entered, though it may be questioned whether this is not Usuardine. On the 11th, 15th, 16th, 20th, 21st, and 25th, it exceeds Usuard only in matters concerning the people of Rheims.

In November: the 1st, 2nd, 6th, 9th, 15th, 18th, 23rd, and 26th. Finally, in December, most of the additions on the 4th, 16th, and 29th are purely Rheims additions.

Let some curious person calculate the matter, compare the Herinien with the famous Pratensis autograph, and weigh the excesses and deficiencies of each in an even balance and on a just scale. If he is led by no partisan zeal, I dare promise that, once the reckoning has been properly made, he will go over to our opinion, body and soul.

§ III.—On the Tournai codex and the other especially approved ancient codices

215. We consider the codex called Tournai among us to be second after the Herinien. That it was once in use in that extremely ancient cathedral would be sufficiently demonstrated, even if we had no other evidence, by the additions proper to that church. We believe, however, that it was brought to Tournai from the monastery of Hautvillers near Rheims, or perhaps copied long ago from some codex of that monastery, as I said in my *Observations*, especially under 4 July.

Whatever the codex’s ultimate origin, it has an ancient and elegant appearance. It is written on parchment in a large format and divided by elegant, though somewhat worn, ruled columns; at times the text seems to have been fitted to the columns rather than the columns adapted to the text.

You may probably determine its age from the accompanying Necrology, written, apparently, by the same but more compressed hand, if you note that Anselm and Geraud, or Gerald, bishops of Tournai in the twelfth century, as well as Stephen and Goswin, otherwise Goscelin, who died in 1203 and 1218, are entered by the original hand. Walter, however, a native of Tournai and bishop of this church, to whom the Sammarthani attach the surname Marvis and who held the see from 1219 [Col. 0564D] to 1252, is recorded in the aforesaid Necrology under 16 February by a secondary hand, as are his successors Walter of Mandra, who died in 1262, and John of Buchel or Buchiaul, who died in 1266. It is therefore very probable that the Martyrology was written between 1219 and 1252. So much for the age of the codex.

216. Fair-minded readers will form their judgment of its genuineness and simplicity from our *Observations*. It certainly departs considerably from the first two, not usually in the number of saints, but through some abbreviation of the announcements, as though the Usuardine little book really had to be fitted into prepared columns, as I said above; or because the scribe thought himself permitted, with less scruple, sometimes to proceed more freely and contract longer passages.

Had that writer—whoever first tampered with the codex—taken care to avoid this, the codex would nearly have rivaled the Herinien in native simplicity. It would be too tedious to enumerate each contraction. Generally speaking, it is either pure throughout or close to pure. It deviates somewhat on 16, 17, and 18 July, and likewise on 19 October, where one may excuse the scribe for having improperly attributed certain local, Hautvillers, or other additions to Usuard, or at least to the Martyrology under Usuard’s name.

It is truly regrettable that the negligence or boldness of copyists deprived so distinguished a codex of its proper beauty and splendor. Its title and prefaces have been torn away, and it has a conspicuous gap from 9 August [Col. 0565B] to 26 September, because precious leaves were torn out through the fault of ignorant persons. We have begun to speak of the accompanying and fairly extensive Necrology; from it the benefactors of the church of Tournai could easily be recognized and enumerated in large numbers.

217. Comparable in age to the Tournai codex, which our predecessors considered much older, is the codex of the professed house of the Society of Jesus at Antwerp. Henschenius judged it to have been written six hundred years ago: in several places, including volume II of April, p. CCCCXLV, below E; volume II of May, p. CXXXI, below B; in the *Praetermissa* concerning Saint Letardus; again on 18 May, in the *Praetermissa* concerning Saint Mildreda the virgin; volume IV, p. CXXXVI, below A; and elsewhere.

Bollandus produced specimens from it among Bede’s copies in the general preface, p. XLIX, where he correctly observed that it had been entitled with Bede’s name, but by a later hand. He also notes, truly, that it is English, since on several days, as we have often shown elsewhere in their proper places, it displays added English material.

This is peculiar to the codex: it is not uniform. In some places, for example in January, it is fuller; elsewhere it is generally pure Usuard; in October and November it has been supplemented by a somewhat later hand. What we said about the Herinien—that, once the Rheims material is excluded, it is exceptionally pure—could nearly be said of this codex too, if the English additions and certain freer additions at the beginning were absent.

For the English appendices, consult the individual months, where several days are usually involved. I have noted the following: from July, 2, 6, 7, 8, 15, 17, and 31; from August, 24; from September, 4, 16, and 30; from October, 6, [Col. 0565D] 8, 11, 12, 13, and 15, and so forth.

218. These facts abundantly establish the codex’s homeland. As for its age, I think that worn rubrics, abraded letters, and torn leaves here and there misled Henschenius. In my judgment, two centuries may be subtracted from his six hundred years, so that it belongs to the thirteenth century.

The form of its letters agrees sufficiently clearly with the Tournai codex. A decisive argument, however, is supplied by the translation of Saint Thomas the martyr appended under 7 July, where I believe the archbishop of Canterbury is certainly indicated; his translation is known to have taken place on that day, or at least in that month, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Honorius III, namely 1223.

It is therefore clear that I was right to say at the outset that this codex is comparable in age to the Tournai codex. This is also shown by the commemoration of Saint Catherine, added to both on 25 November, unknown in the older Pratensis, Herinien, and subsequent Rosweydine codices, among others.

Furthermore, so that this codex might be designated among the Usuardines by a particular name, we call it, in abbreviated form, the larger Antwerp codex, to distinguish it from the smaller one in octavo, which we simply call the Antwerp codex, and from another large volume called the largest Antwerp codex. For our present codex is a parchment quarto, bound together with Bede of the church of Arras, from which that Florus published by our men was chiefly drawn.

I noted above that various passages are found here and there in which it agrees with the Pratensis, especially when the latter departs from the rest of the group.

219. Slightly older than the last two Usuardines described here is an altogether distinguished codex, written in a most elegant hand on parchment in a large format, or folio. It belonged to the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Utrecht and was once so highly esteemed by Rosweyd that he considered producing a genuine Usuard from it in that great manuscript collection of Martyrologies in two volumes, which is preserved among us and has been cited at the beginning of this preface and elsewhere more than once.

Hence the codex itself received its name. To avoid repeatedly using the long phrase “of the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Utrecht,” we have always called it, in Rosweyd’s shorter nomenclature, the Rosweydine.

Our manuscript certainly possesses a brilliance, ornamentation, and elegance that captivate the eyes of readers. Yet although in these respects, and even in its antiquity, it surpasses the first two, the Tournai and larger Antwerp codices, it occupies only fourth place among the Usuardines of our museum, since it is inferior to them in purity and genuineness by as much as it surpasses them in antiquity.

This scribe does not make many contractions, but freely expands the text according to his own license. His frequent additions from Hieronymian codices have sometimes led me to suspect that Greven, in enlarging Usuard, used either this codex itself or at least its exemplar.

220. As for the age of this codex, Henschenius noted in volume II of April, p. VII, below letter A, while citing this Martyrology, that it appeared to have been copied from some English Martyrology five hundred years ago. Here Henschenius correctly identifies both its age and its homeland.

He discusses the five hundred years again in volume IV of June, p. CCCCLVI, column 1, near the end. But on 5 June, p. 456, letter D, in the entry for Boniface, bishop of Mainz, he determines the proposed age more precisely, stating that it was written around the year 1138.

In my opinion, this is correct and exact. Henschenius could infer it from the very brief chronicle prefixed to the Martyrology, which extends to the year 1138 and in which the same hand as that which wrote the entire Martyrology is clearly visible.

I do not think that the age of an ancient codex can be established by a more convincing argument. This is what I meant when I said that it is older than the Tournai and larger Antwerp codices. Another highly probable indication is that it lacks the announcement of Saint Catherine the virgin on 25 November.

Indeed, if I am not mistaken, it can be established most clearly from the fact that it is completely silent about Saint Thomas, bishop of Canterbury, the most celebrated martyr of the twelfth century, although he is explicitly named in both earlier codices, as may be seen in the Appendices under 29 December.

221. The reason it is placed after those others in the order of simplicity and consequently of authority is the freedom of the copyist already mentioned. He interpolated the Usuardine Martyrology too frequently from the Hieronymian codices and from Ado, or enlarged it from other sources, or moderately abbreviated it, as our daily *Observations* and Appendices plainly show.

Add to this the English additions—which is why Henschenius earlier identified its homeland. It is enough to touch on a few; the reader will easily notice the rest in their proper places. Under 12 March, Elfragus, bishop of Winchester, is added. Under 6 July, the burial of Sexburga. Not to pursue every individual case, see 13, 15, and 31 August; 4 September; and many other places.

I nearly failed to note that something rare in the other codices is found here, from which a conjecture about its antiquity may be made: like the Herinien, it writes the diphthong *ae* with an *e* marked by a small stroke, as we carefully noted above concerning our principal Herinien codex.

Finally, we must repeat what was observed about the larger Antwerp codex: the Rosweydine manuscript of which we are speaking, together with the aforesaid codex and the Aquicinctine, generally follows the traces of the Pratensis, while the Pratensis departs from all the rest.

222. Henschenius called another codex illustrious in volume I of April, p. XIV, below letter E. It is called the Pulsan codex from its principal announcement, placed under 20 June, because there it treats of John, abbot of Pulsano, in such a way as to make it entirely clear that it was once copied in that monastery from an older Usuardine exemplar, though very frequently contracted and shortened.

From the year of John’s death—1139 in the year of the Incarnate Word—Papebrochius inferred, in volume IV of June, p. 39, no. 8, that this Martyrology was so ancient that it appeared to have been written under the immediate successor of the saint, since it contains no names of other saints of Pulsano.

I readily agree, since it bears signs that strongly commend its antiquity. It gives a clear indication of this when it mentions Thomas of Canterbury in the margin and in a more recent script, as in the Appendices under the 29th of December cited above.

The manner in which it came to us is explained by the Papebrochius cited in that place, from a note prefixed to the codex by Bollandus. It is written on parchment, in octavo, and is mutilated at the beginning by four days.

I have already said, and our entire work makes clear, that Usuard is abbreviated many times and that certain things are sometimes omitted with excessive freedom. I add that in June Usuard is occasionally abandoned and supplemented from the Hieronymian codices, perhaps because in the Usuardine exemplar from which this codex was copied some things were missing that had to be taken from elsewhere.

223. Also old, written on parchment in a smaller format, is the codex that, since we cannot refer it to another, we simply call the Antwerp codex. It bears no certain signs of age apart from its script, which seems unquestionably to suggest the thirteenth century. I am all the more easily persuaded of this because it marks no saints later than that century.

In the calendar prefixed to it are Saint Thomas the confessor on 7 March and Robert the abbot on 29 April, clearly the man who first began the Cistercian order. Then, on 20 August, in illuminated letters, Bernard the abbot appears; from this it may reasonably be conjectured that the codex once belonged to some Cistercian monastery.

Francis is placed under 15 October, and Elizabeth under 19 November. It must be noted, however, that the calendar is by a much later hand than the Martyrology to which it is prefixed; certainly, no saints later than Francis or Elizabeth occur in the latter.

The Appendices will show that it is not a completely pure Usuard. I noted above, at no. 172, that the first and oldest edition of Lübeck, from the year 1475, was made from a manuscript of this kind. Hence in our work these two Martyrologies are always cited together as “Antwerp” and “Greater-Lübeck.” They are usually joined by another codex, of which we possess only an extract or collation, from the library of the celebrated Abbot Ughelli. From him it received the name Ughellianus; we shall discuss it together with the other extracts below.

224. The Marchiennes codex must also be counted among the better-quality Usuardine manuscripts. We think that it no longer survives complete in the abbey itself, since we received from it only the month of February, together with a fragment of March. From this specimen [Col. 0568C] you can easily recognize the rest. Would that, if they still survive, they might at some point be sent to us! We have often already tried, but always in vain, to obtain this through some of our Fathers.

Because of its proximity, I append to the Marchiennes copy the Aquicinctine exemplar. Although we likewise do not possess it entire and complete, that deficiency is abundantly supplied by a most accurate collation of it with Molanus’s second edition of 1573, in which all variant readings are set down with as much diligence as possible, allowing a judgment to be formed concerning the purity and simplicity of the entire codex.

From the extracts mentioned above, I think one may conjecture that this codex is not later than the thirteenth century; the same judgment applies to the Marchiennes codex. The following is common to our Aquicinctine codex, the larger Antwerp, and the Rosweydine: whenever the Pratensis departs from the others, the Aquicinctine, together with its two usual companions, forms that distinctive group of which we have already spoken so often above and in our *Usuardine Observations*.

225. To all these must be added, if not on grounds of purity or simplicity, at least by right of antiquity, the old codex of Saint Richarius, which we designate Centulensis after the former name of that monastery—and rightly so, since from 4 June, 26 August, 2 December, and other days it is clear that it was once written and used there. Rosweyde wrote in his own hand that he had obtained his Martyrology from the Abbey of Saint Vedast, from which he had previously arranged for a copy to be made; I found it stored among the collected manuscripts relating to Bede. Its title was misleading, expressed as follows: “Here begins the Martyrology according to Bede, through the cycle of the year.” Consequently Bolland placed it first among Bede’s copies in the general preface, p. XLVIII, extracting the first six days of the year, although the writer begins the Martyrology with the vigil of the Nativity. Those six days alone prove that the entire Martyrology contains nothing in any way attributable to Bede. It is evident to me that the writer, whoever he was, had Usuard before his eyes and altered, shortened, and interpolated him according to his own inclination or convenience, with the principal aim of abbreviating most entries for each day. I have already said that the Martyrology begins with the vigil of the Nativity; I add here that its opening is such that, had the copyist continued the remainder in the same manner, the codex would rightly be counted among the first- and finest-quality Usuardian manuscripts.

226. It is not easy to determine to which century it should be assigned from the style of its writing; for here, unless I am greatly mistaken, the appearance of antiquity is more pronounced than is warranted. The compressed script, sufficiently elegant and somewhat large, on quarto parchment, much worn at the beginning, would seem to indicate approximately the twelfth century, were it not that I read there, under 4 Kalends of May, that is, 28 April: “On the same day at Milan, Saint Peter the martyr, killed by heretics.” Likewise, under 25 August: “In France, Saint Louis, king of the Franks and most glorious confessor—[text uncertain: ‘XII, lc. in cap.’].” These entries clearly indicate that it was written only at the beginning of the fourteenth century. Yet this age, whatever it may be, is the codex’s principal claim to some esteem; otherwise it very rarely attains purity except at the beginning and must always be relegated to the Supplementa.
