For the most part it forms a distinct class, as does another codex formerly belonging to the monastery of the Carthusians of Utrecht, which has been placed among the extracts under the name Matricula. It is therefore cited daily among the additions under the title “Matricula of the Utrecht Carthusians”; it too is a thoroughly Usuardian abridgment, often deficient even in the mere number of saints. Both have been granted a kind of privilege: their texts were to be transcribed in full for each day.

§ IV.—On the codices that we call of middling quality

[Col. 0569D]

227. We have given the following codices, mostly Belgian, the designation “of middling,” or at least “of inferior,” quality, because in respect both of age and of Usuardian simplicity they cannot at all be compared with the superior ones. They appear to flow from the same, or at least a not very different, source, being here and there sprinkled with longer elogies; but, surprisingly, they are not enlarged by many Belgian saints or other local figures. Among them, the principal and most splendid—having received its name from the size of its volume—is the enormous codex, written in an elegant hand on parchment and bound in pigskin. Since I have so far not discovered its true home, I thought it should be called the Great Antwerp Codex, after its long residence there. Its Belgian origin is certain from the proper feasts marked in its calendar. Under 10 July, notably, with the special distinction of a separate rubric, appears Saint Amelberga; since she is celebrated with particular solemnity at Blandinium, this suggests that the codex was once used either in that abbey or at least at Ghent. By investigating its age, I found that among the short works appended to the Martyrology there appears, before the *Provinciale of all the regions of the world*, in the explanation of the Paschal verses, the year 1425, written in the same hand as everything else. You may understand the codex’s splendor and magnificence from the fact that each page corresponds to the Usuardian texts for individual days; its faithfulness will be clear from the entire course of our work.

228. Comparable or nearly equal to this Great Antwerp Codex is the Utrecht Usuard, likewise quarto, on parchment, and neatly written. At its end, before a collection of various blessings, it identifies both its locality and its house in these words: “It belongs to the house of the Clerics of Saint Jerome at Utrecht.” This supplied the basis for its surname. To distinguish it from two other Utrecht Usuardians, we have above called the more important and notable one—the one that belonged to the church of Blessed Mary and which Rosweyde valued so highly—the Rosweydian; the other, printed in type, of which only the first half-year has reached us and which we mentioned in no. 173, we have decided to call the Belgian Utrecht edition; this one we shall now call simply the Utrecht Codex. No certain indications of its age occur anywhere; but, if I judge correctly, it cannot be much older than the Great Antwerp Codex. I would not rashly determine what precise period is indicated by the feast of the Sacred Stigmata, placed first under 16 September. Whatever the case may be, we do not wish to detract anything from that codex, even though in the series of Usuardian manuscripts of middling quality it is placed after the Great Antwerp Codex.

229. Next come two codices bound together in quarto, one written in Belgian vernacular on parchment, the other in Latin on heavier paper. The former, written in the vernacular, was intended for the use of the regular sisters of Lake Saint Mary near Leiden, as Bolland noted in volume I of the January Acts, p. 165; the other is called in the Acts the Usuard of Saint Cecilia of Leiden. We have retained this nomenclature for both, so that otherwise they would have to be called the Leideners of the Netherlands by a longer circumlocution; or, more simply, “Leideners,” by which an inexperienced person might easily confuse Leiden in the Netherlands with Lyon in France. There can be no doubt that both codices are Usuardian, but they are enlarged and closely resemble the preceding two, the Great Antwerp Codex and the Utrecht Codex. I admit that the Belgian one, although poorly rendered, sometimes reports somewhat purer readings, in which it occasionally agrees with the Great Antwerp Codex, as has been indicated in the proper places. Yet these matters are everywhere of so little importance that for this reason the Belgian should not greatly be preferred to the Latin. Whenever I find them in agreement—as they usually agree—I include both under the one name Leiden. Neither appears to exceed the fifteenth century in antiquity.

230. More elegant than the two just outlined, but, unless I am greatly mistaken, of the same period, is another codex of the same format, written on parchment, which we call the Leuven Codex after our Leuven college, formerly its owner. You would think that it had been copied from the Great Antwerp Codex, or the Great Antwerp Codex from it, were it not that it more often presents the elogies of the saints shortened or mutilated. Bolland remarked somewhere that this Leuven Martyrology had formerly belonged to some Belgian church, since it records saints of the diocese of Cambrai, such as Gudula, Rumold, Gaugericus, Nicasius, and others. But the last two are Usuardian, so that the conjecture must be supported only by Gudula and Rumold. From elsewhere it can be gathered with sufficient certainty that it belonged to some monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, since it consistently gives the most holy Doctor the title “our Father,” not only in the body of the Martyrology itself but also in the appended works, which I believe were once bound with the Martyrology and used by those Augustinian religious. I infer that it served Canons Regular rather than Hermits from the fact that it does not mention Saint Nicholas of Tolentino.

231. The sixth codex of middling quality takes its name from the monastery whose ownership mark it bears in these words: “Book of the monastery of Blessed Anthony at Albergen, of the Canons Regular, given by the venerable lord Henry Mathie, vicar at Werselo.” From Miraeus, in the *Origins of the Canons Regular*, I learned that the aforementioned monastery was situated in Twente, formerly in the diocese of Utrecht, from which this codex records most of its saints. Its format and script agree sufficiently with the Latin Leiden Codex, but it is sometimes fuller. It appears to have been written for the use of the Fathers of the Order of Saint Francis, as is evident from 4 and 11 October, 13 and 20 June, and other places. Nor should this seem surprising, since the Albergen monastery was first begun in 1406, as an old manuscript codex of ours, marked + ms. 34, records in describing its foundation. It relates that brothers were summoned there from the congregation of Zwolle, which at that time was especially renowned, together with the congregation of Deventer, for its observance of regular discipline and reputation for holiness, as our aforementioned manuscript codex and other Transisaline histories of the fifteenth century testify. This is enough to say concerning the codex’s provenance.

232. In arrangement and fidelity it is inferior, though perhaps somewhat earlier in date: our Danish Codex. It was purchased at Lübeck in 1584 by a certain knight, Henry surnamed Rancou, and came to the professed house of our Society at Prague, where it was given as a gift to Bartius and Janning in 1688, while they were residing there. On the first page these words are written: “Book of the convent of Nystad in the province of Denmark.” That the convent belonged to the Franciscan family is proved by a later inscription in the lower margin of the folio for 17 September: “At Mount Alvernia, the impression of the sacred stigmata of blessed Francis, a major double feast.” Likewise, under 19 August, in a newer hand: “At Marseille, blessed Louis, bishop and confessor, of the Order of Friars Minor, a major double feast.” Again, under 11 October: “Translation of Saint Clare, virgin, a minor double feast.” And under 8 November: “Likewise, the translation of Saint Louis the confessor.” Bernardine is similarly added in the margin under 20 May, Bonaventure under 14 June, and so forth. Francis occupies the first place in the text, under 4 October and 25 May: “At Assisi, the translation of our most blessed Father Francis.” Since the translation of Anthony of Padua took place in 1349 or 1350, and the entries we first cited are by another hand, it seems possible to infer that the codex is not earlier than the fourteenth century. Its homeland is revealed by 10 and 11 July, Kanute and Ketillus, and by other places. How far it departs from Usuardian simplicity will be shown by the daily additions.

233. Two complete codices remain, respectable ones, quarto, on parchment and fairly old: the Brussels and Hagenoy Codices. They had to be given the last place among the manuscripts of middling quality because, more freely and abundantly than the others, they have been enlarged and interpolated; besides which, they must yield to the others in style, order, and the less competent manner of writing. The Brussels Codex consists of two volumes, with a calendar prefixed and a treatise on the ten persecutions inflicted on the Church by the pagan Roman emperors, etc. These are followed by a preface of a Brussels canon, who, after praising the efforts of the ancient Martyrologists, especially Usuard, argues as follows among other things:

“Yet until now it has not been free from the fault of negligence, since no commemoration was made in the reading of the Martyrology of those saints whom the Church of Brussels commemorated, on the days on which we celebrate their feasts. This matter, through a certain pious concern, compelled the venerable lords, my teachers, the dean and chapter of this collegiate and parish church of the holy archangel Michael and the virgin Gudula, the mother church of all the churches of this distinguished town of Brussels in the diocese of Cambrai, to give the order, and compelled me, their unworthy canon, to obey, so that from the Martyrologies of the aforesaid Fathers the solemnities of the saints …”

He then wandered more freely, collecting much material, but arranged it poorly according to his own judgment, as immediately becomes apparent to anyone reading the additions. From them he will also understand how far it is from the brevity of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, a matter discussed in no. 38. No one will easily determine its age; unless I am mistaken, it belongs to the end of the fourteenth or the beginning of the fifteenth century.

234. We call the Hagenoy Codex by the name of its place of residence, or of its owner, Master Nicholas Schick, of Hagenau; for the rest, I do not see why it should be assigned to Hagenau rather than to any other city of Alsace or the Palatinate. The scribe indicates his name in four verses of rather coarse workmanship added at the end. From these we learn that the Martyrology was written in the year 1412, on 16 June: “The pen makes the letters; Wido Krentzelin has glued these together.” The date of the writing could reasonably be inferred from 27 September, where Elzear, count of Ariano, is said to have been recently canonized by Urban V. Since that canonization took place in 1469, the codex could not have been far removed from the end of the fourteenth or beginning of the fifteenth century. Moreover, if this Krentzelin, cited somewhere by Castellanus, was the compiler of this Martyrology, he did not win great praise, mixing in everywhere certain stories very remote from the style of Usuard and of the other Usuardian codices, which I have often been reluctant to reproduce. The codex nevertheless could not be excluded from the Usuardian class, since it generally records the same saints, often indeed in Usuard’s own phraseology, though corrupted and dislocated. So much concerning the full and complete codices that we have used in this edition and recension.

## ARTICLE V. On the codices from which we possess only extracts or variant readings

235. We rightly distinguish these codices from those which we have so far listed as full and complete, whether printed or manuscript. By extracts or variant readings I mean here those passages in which they either exceed or fall short of Usuard’s text. To make the matter clearer, I shall briefly explain what my teacher of blessed memory, Papebroch, often told me, when giving this account of the extracts, especially the later ones. While he travelled with Henschenius through Germany, Italy, and France in the years 1660, 1661, and 1662, collecting monuments concerning the saints, both Greek and Latin, by which our Museum was splendidly enriched, they adopted the following method so as not to be detained too long in copying the Usuardian Martyrologies, of which we possessed so great an abundance. Taking Greven’s edition as their model because it was easily portable and more convenient, wherever they came upon a manuscript Usuard they compared the whole of it with Greven’s edition of 1521, recording the variants or additions in their notebooks. Thus, with a considerable saving of time, they conveniently compared everything that would otherwise have required a longer stay and greater expense—for example, if each of these codices had had to be copied word for word by them or by scribes. All the material that was thus noted and extracted we call Usuardian variant readings or additions, and we thought that it should be placed among our additions.

236. The aforesaid extracts, or lists of variants, number nearly thirty; they therefore represent nearly as many codices. If these are added to the fourteen editions listed above that we used, the seventeen manuscript codices, and the eighteen others collected by Chifflet, it will be clear that this latest edition of ours has been prepared, illustrated, and purified from nearly eighty codices. I do not, however, wish to conceal that there is something in the collations and recensions made by Henschenius and Papebroch that displeases me, since from the form of our indexes I have seen that not all interpolations were included. I discovered this clearly in the Ughellian Codex, and frequently in the similar great Lübeck edition and the Antwerp manuscript: all the additions of the former were recorded with the utmost exactness, but not those that had undoubtedly been inserted into the middle of the text. When I formerly pointed this out to Papebroch, he candidly admitted that they had arranged their collations of the manuscripts with Greven in such a way that they concerned themselves only with the first and last announcement. It was necessary to give this warning, so that the reader may recognize how sincerely and rigorously all the documents from which this Usuardian edition of ours has been fashioned were weighed and examined. I shall now briefly present the extracts, together with the codices from which they were taken, omitting nothing that could be desired for adequate knowledge of all of them.

237. The first place in our collection is occupied by the Aquicinctine Codex, collated not by Henschenius and Papebroch but by someone else, perhaps a monk of that monastery, with the greatest accuracy and clarity, without neglecting even the minor details occurring in the text. We began to discuss it above, in no. 224, where it was assigned a place among the older and purer manuscript codices together with the Marchiennes fragment, and where it was noted that it agrees in many respects with the Pratensis, the Great Antwerp, and the Rosweydian, especially when these are separated from the rest of the group. Here I shall briefly note what may define the age of the Aquicinctine Codex with some clarity. The person who compared the manuscript with the second edition of Molanus, 1568, carefully noted under 25 August, after transcribing the final commemoration, “On this day, at Paris, the elevation of blessed Louis the confessor,” that these words had been added in a much later hand. Likewise, under 21 October, at this final announcement, “At Cologne, of the eleven thousand holy virgins,” he added: “These are in a later hand.” Such indications seem sufficiently to prove that the autograph codex itself was written in the thirteenth century or perhaps earlier. We shall discuss this one somewhat more fully and enumerate all the others much more briefly, describing only what the collators observed.

238. In order of antiquity and simplicity, the manuscript Usuard of Marchiennes, also praised in no. 224, ought to follow here; but since only two fragments are in our possession, namely the month of February and part of March, I shall say no more about it.

239. The Victorinus could have been cited under two names, since it was collated with another; but it is enough to indicate that here in a word. The variants or extracts were written in Henschenius’s hand, with this title prefixed: “The Parisian Usuard, manuscript of Saint Victor, and the printed edition of Molanus, collated with the manuscript of the Most Serene Queen of Sweden, which in 1521 belonged to Bernard Hannetreau, priest and curate of Blessed Mary in the church at Senlis.” It appears to have belonged to some monastery in the diocese of Nevers. It very frequently agrees with, and is therefore often cited in the Additions alongside, another codex of the Queen of Sweden marked no. 130, which will be discussed below.

240. Next come certain fragments of a codex of the church of Pulsa and of Messina, and then of the Pleschion Martyrology. The first is of little importance; the second, somewhat larger, was taken from a Lombard manuscript which was probably either incomplete or at least impossible to read in full.

241. The next extract, also transcribed by Henschenius, has the following prefatory note: “The manuscript Usuard of the Queen of Sweden, which belonged to the most illustrious prince, Lord Don Peter Vok Ursinus, lord of the House of Rosemberg, the last and eldest, and one of the most distinguished, most exalted, and most ancient men of Bohemia; collated in 1609 with the Utrecht manuscript in quarto and with the printed edition of Molanus.” Its antiquity is disproved by the commemoration of Saint Bernardine placed under 20 May, since that saint died in 1444.

242. From the papers of the Feuillants at Paris there is inserted here a list of saints, which I do not dare to determine to be wholly Usuardian. It begins: “From the most ancient manuscript Martyrology of the priory of Daveron, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Chartres.” It is cited in the Additions under the name of the Daveron Codex. An ancient series of the kings of France is mixed into it. Then follows: “Index and catalogue of the saints whose passions and Lives are contained in the manuscript Legendarium of the Reverend Fathers of the Discalced Carmelites of the suburb of Saint-Germain at Paris.”

243. The final part of the whole work is the manuscript Martyrology of the church of Amiens. Since I found it among the series of Usuardians, I cited it as such in the Additions.

244. Above, in no. 116, we spoke of a certain complete codex placed among the extracts under this title: “A Compendious Martyrology, excerpted from the register of the Utrecht Carthusian house, written on parchment and, at least in its first arrangement, already two hundred years old or more.” The describer of this codex, who compared it with the Roman Martyrology, could have determined its age somewhat more precisely had he noticed that under 30 July it reads: “Bridget, a religious woman, from whom the observant women of that Order originated, who in modern times began to arise in the diocese of Utrecht.” Bruno is not included under 6 October. It is a mere abridgment of Usuard, always transcribed in full in the Additions, as we said at the cited number.

245. The three Bigotian Usuards ought to be fairly pure, since Henschenius and Papebroch found few additions; Papebroch added notes to each. Concerning the first he writes: “Usuard collated with the Martyrology of the Bigot Library, under the name of Eusebius, Jerome, and Bede, formerly belonging to some convent of the Fathers of the Celestines, shelfmark P. 5.” Of the second he writes: “From an old codex of the same library, marked E 4 or E 40, which belonged, as is thought, to the church of Saint Stephen at Caen, containing almost the simple text of Usuard and very few of Bellinus.” Scarcely any additions were found in this one, nor many in the third: “Usuard collated with a third, older codex, marked D 9.” All begin with the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, which is how we said in no. 169 that Usuard himself began his Martyrology.

246. Next comes a folio in the manuscript of P. Chifflet, under this title: “Extracts from the Martyrology of Saint Benignus of Dijon,” which itself is Usuard’s Martyrology, with a few items inserted into the text or written in the margin, most of which we have collected here. I find that only a few things were added to Usuard. Those said to have been placed in the margin concern dedications of altars or chapels, of which there are many in the famous Pratensis Codex; but we omitted nearly all of them unless they are expressed in other sources. Another collation, in Papebroch’s hand, is described as follows: “Usuard’s Martyrology, collated with the manuscript of Saint Benignus of Dijon, which is at Cîteaux.” We first called this the Dijon-Cîteaux Codex. There are other extracts among the Chiffletian materials, to be discussed in their proper place.

Next comes Usuard’s Martyrology, collated with a Cluniac manuscript. The small number of additions sufficiently shows that this codex should be counted among the purer ones.

247. “Usuard’s Martyrology, collated with the manuscript of the monastery of Saint Lawrence of the Canons Regular in the city of Augensis [place uncertain].” Papebroch found few additions in this one as well; and therefore, if the collation was properly carried out, it too joins our pure Usuards.

248. Somewhat fuller is the one that Papebroch designates as follows: “Usuard’s Martyrology, collated with the manuscript of the Conventual Friars of the monastery of Saint Mary at Chambéry, with a calendar appended, containing the obligations and notable deaths of that convent.”

249. The following collation was made with two manuscript Usuards of the Queen of Sweden, one of which bears the number 130; it is the same one that we said above often agrees with the Victorinus Codex. The second is distinguished by the number 428. The Additions will show that both are fuller and consequently depart considerably from Usuardian simplicity.

250. To distinguish the next three adequately, Papebroch’s entire title must be given: “Usuard’s Martyrology, collated first with manuscript A of Lord Le Mare, which belonged to the college of the Canons of Saint Lazarus at Autun and has written in its margin the deaths and obligations of that college by virtue of bequests, etc., which are expressed with the greatest accuracy. Also with manuscript B, in which is written ‘Saint Augustine, our Holy Father.’ And manuscript C, which belonged to some Franciscan convent, as is evident from the feasts proper to the Order.” Both were written after the fourteenth century and belonged to D. Du Cheval at Dijon, although it is certain that the first had been written six hundred years earlier. All the extracts are so intermingled that I am scarcely confident of the correct citation of each. Here the poet’s saying truly applies: “While I strive to be brief, I become obscure.” The same confusion will recur shortly in the Florentine codices collated by Henschenius.

251. The Vatican Usuardian Codex, marked no. 5949, is abundantly enlarged and, conversely, abundantly contracted. It is written in Lombard script and is called by Papebroch “a new collection made from Usuard, Ado, and others for the Beneventan church.” That it was collected or composed for that church is sufficiently suggested by the title of Saint Sophia, repeatedly mentioned in the text. It has scarcely anything from Ado; rather, it appears to have been interpolated from some Hieronymian Martyrology. Papebroch attempted to conjecture its age to some extent when he said that it mentions Saint Romuald and Thomas of Canterbury. But it is not worth discussing this matter at greater length.

252. Here follows that codex of which I have mentioned more than once above: the Usuard of Abbot Ughelli, or the Ughellian, which I think agrees in every respect with our Antwerp Codex and the oldest great Lübeck edition. Had it been collated more accurately, it would undoubtedly never have been separated from those two. I would not, however, affirm this so confidently, since it may easily disagree with them in some details.

253. Papebroch correctly observed that the Altempsian Codex had been enlarged in England, since additions of this kind frequently recur. How it reached Rome has not been explained, nor have I been especially concerned to investigate its age more closely. I did observe, however, that the codex once belonged to the church of Winchester, since under 30 October it reads: “On this day, the ordination of our most holy bishop and patron Swithun”; others write Swithuni. Our collation begins with the month of March, January and February having been placed at the end. I suspect that the autograph itself was once written in this way, or perhaps that the codex was badly bound.

254. Here is the confusion among the Florentine codices of which I spoke in no. 250. Henschenius wrote the following at the beginning: “Usuard’s Martyrology, collated, first, with manuscript D of Carlo Strozzi, Florentine senator, in quarto. Secondly, collated with the Florentine Martyrology, published at Florence in 1486—elsewhere 1484 is noted, but we have retained the first number—by Francesco de’ Bonaccursi, priest, and belonging to the same Strozzi; where something is absent, it is marked (+ absent). Thirdly, collated with the manuscript of the Medicean Library, on parchment, in quarto. Where it agrees, the result is written below; where other readings occur alone, a line is drawn above.” Everyone can see how liable this arrangement is to error. I have tried, with all possible diligence, to assign each item to its proper codex; if I have gone astray anywhere, the prudent reader will readily forgive me. These codices do not appear to exceed the fifteenth century, and certainly they are almost continuously overflowing with additions.

255. Next come extracts, or other collations made at Florence and elsewhere, with other Martyrologies derived from Ado and from other heavily interpolated sources. Henschenius did not recognize them as Usuardians, and we did not wish to enlarge our Additions with their material, which is already sufficiently extensive and numerous from other sources. But since most of the Chiffletian materials appear to have been taken from Usuardian codices, greater attention has been given to them. We shall therefore go through their names one by one, so that nothing may recur in the whole work without being fully explained. Papebroch prefixed the following title to all of them:

“Extracts from various Martyrologies by the Reverend Father Peter Francis Chifflet.”

256. From the old manuscript Usuard of Saint Rigaud—that is, Saint Rigaldi—in the territory of Mâcon. If the purity of the codex may be judged from its additions, it must be a sound one, since they are few in number.

257. From the Martyrology of the Jura monastery of Saint Ragnobertus, composed, Papebroch says, from Ado and Usuard. But if you weigh the individual items carefully, it shares very little in Ado’s style. I would rather believe that it is Usuard adapted to the practice of others, but not greatly interpolated.

258. From the Martyrology of the church of Saint Stephen at Lyon, “under the name of Bede,” Papebroch again says, “but more similar to Ado.” I do not sufficiently understand where this similarity again comes from, for most of the Additions, if they do not reflect Usuard himself, at least almost preserve his manner of phrasing announcements.

[Col. 0578B]

259. From the Usuardian Martyrology of the church of Bordeaux. Nothing has been added from which its age can be determined. How far it is from its original simplicity, you may understand from the Additions.

260. From the old Martyrology of Château-Chalon—or, if you prefer, from the monastery of Saint Mary of Château-Chalon. I admit that the place has so far been unknown to me. If the codex is Usuardian, it does not appear contemptible.

261. From the Martyrology of Saint Paul at Besançon. It contains little by which it can be said to belong more to that city than to any other. To this may be added other extracts of little importance, taken from the Luxeuil Martyrology. I find no particular information recorded about that one either, nor was I myself able to observe anything.

[Col. 0578C]

262. From the Martyrology of Saint Anatolius of Salins. These extracts are followed by a few others from the Martyrology of the Franciscans of Salins. I give only the names, since I do not wish to indulge in uncertain conjectures.

263. Equally obscure are the materials that Chifflet took from the Martyrology of the Abbey of Gigny.

264. Likewise from the Martyrology of the Holy Mountain, except that in it Romaric—after whom the place is named, so that it is “the mountain of Saint Romaric”—and the other saints associated with him or belonging to the same monastery are more elaborately celebrated.

265. From the Usuardian Martyrology of the priory of Caudiac. I remember finding this codex somewhere in the Acts under the name Candracensis, but the nomenclature by which I chiefly used it in the Additions must be preserved. This single codex has as many additions as are found in the following four together.

266. From the Martyrology of Balerne. Only two announcements were extracted; since they are sufficiently well known elsewhere in the Additions, they did not deserve to be cited from this codex.

267. From the Martyrology of Saint Vincent of Chalon. It indicates its homeland with complete clarity, since everything it contains is proper to that place.

268. From the Usuardian Martyrology of the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon. We cited the same name from Chifflet’s own manuscript above, in no. 245; but the extracts do not entirely agree. In the earlier source only six announcements are found, whereas here there are eleven. The discrepancy is not important enough to detain us in explaining it at greater length.

269. From the Dijon Martyrology of the church of Saint Stephen. This codex too supplies little. Among its eleven additions, only two are proper to Dijon.

270. From the very old Martyrology of the church of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris at Reims. This codex is very full, abounding in more additions than any of the preceding ones. Chifflet did not explain whether it is truly Usuardian.

271. From the Martyrology of Saint Mary of Beaune. This too truly bears its name, since it contains nothing but material proper to Beaune. See the excellent specimen under 26 April.

[Col. 0579B]

272. From the Martyrology of Accinctum. It has a single commemoration: “In the territory of Besançon, at the monastery of Bellevaux, the translation of Saint Peter, bishop and confessor.” See 8 May.

273. Finally, at this place among the Chiffletian materials there is added an extract of no great importance from the Usuardian Martyrology of Abdinghof in Westphalia, which scarcely fills a page. Other materials from the same codex are appended, but do not belong here.

## Other codices not used in this work

274. Besides the long series of Usuardian codices described at sufficient length above, we possess other manuscripts that could have increased the number, had there not been such an abundance of others. We have another Utrecht codex of the church of Saint Mary of the Canons, written in Belgian hand and in folio, to which Rosweyde once added the note that it was not Usuardian. This is correct if he meant that it was not pure; but anyone familiar with Usuard will immediately see that it was compiled from Usuard and other sources. Molanus cites, in chapter 13 of his preface, the Usuard of the Bruges Williamites, which he used in his edition. I find two months copied from it, from which I infer that it agrees greatly with our Leiden Usuards, especially the Belgian one; hence those two months were bound together with the same codices. There is also another small codex, written in a more recent hand, which we simply call the Bruges Codex. I think we cited it once or twice, but subsequently rejected it because it deviated too often from Usuard. I add to these another very small codex, covered in black leather, which could almost be called Usuardian, were it not excessively and, as it were, deliberately abridged. The Acts frequently cite the “manuscript Additions of the Brussels Charterhouse,” but these have nothing to do with Usuard, since they are mere augmentations added to Greven’s edition. Papebroch collated the Lübeck-Cologne edition with a certain codex of the Premonstratensian Abbey of Saint Michael at Antwerp; but in that one too, additions have been placed on top of additions. Finally, the *Florarium Sanctorum* frequently recurs in the Acts, in which Usuardian material is mixed with much else. The codices already listed, which had to be examined day by day, were sufficient for me, so that I could easily leave all the others untouched.

[Col. 0580A] **275.** Perhaps someone, from Bollandus’s words cited at the beginning of this preface, will ask why, among so many Usuards already listed in order, that Prague manuscript which he names there together with the Brussels manuscript has no place. I shall say candidly that I know no distinct Prague manuscript. Nevertheless, I shall not deny that in our collection of Martyrologies there is a certain Prague Martyrology, which Henschenius called the specifically Prague Martyrology; and rightly so, since it marks only those days on which some feast is celebrated at Prague, on account of the relics of the saints procured and brought there in great number by the Emperor Charles IV. In our manuscript, in Papebrochius’s hand, it is noted that Father Gamans formerly sent the manuscript itself, the Prague one, to Bollandus, but that it was returned to the said Father in [Col. 0580B] 1681. In any case, I am sufficiently certain that Bollandus was not speaking of such a Martyrology in the general preface. I prefer to believe that our Prague Fathers, formerly owners of the Danish Usuard, sent Bollandus certain extracts and specimens, from which he could very easily judge that the praises of the saints had been expanded and many names added. If, besides this one, he either saw or had lent to him another Prague Martyrology, it is certain that it does not exist today in our Museum. If, moreover, the reader should find other manuscripts cited in the Acts under the name of Usuard, let him remember that they are incomplete, or that certain extracts were sent to our superiors, as we said concerning the Tamlactan Hieronymian, in no. 25 of this preface.

## ARTICLE VI. The reliability, method, and order of this edition

[Col. 0580C]

**276.** What I testified at the beginning of this preface, I now dare confidently to assert again near its end: throughout this entire new recension I have kept chiefly before my eyes the aim of presenting, besides the genealogy of the Martyrologies, the purest and most genuine Usuard. In this undertaking, I shall say boldly, I omitted no work, no labor, and no diligence on my part. I assigned sources so thoroughly cleansed and purified that I consider the clear truth to have been drawn from them; and therefore I can safely and without incurring anyone’s displeasure apply to this Usuard what Rosweydus asserted to Pope Paul V concerning his own Ado: “It has been revised with such faithfulness and care that I do not hesitate to affirm that it differs little from the author’s pen and mind. [Col. 0580D] It was certainly in the interest of the Christian commonwealth that nothing should be read under the title of a great man which was not his own; that nothing corrupted should be circulated under his name, sewn on by another hand; that posterity, following the authority of the man, should not weave the cords of error; and that nothing should be taken away from Usuard, for whom the unanimous testimony of the manuscripts supplied the most certain witness.” But lest, by piling up further arguments on this matter, I prolong still more a preface already sufficiently, perhaps excessively, diffuse, anyone who will take the trouble to consult our Observations will perceive the sincerity of my assertion in the case of each day.

**277.** Only a very few things remain to be said about the method and order of the work. At the head of each day is placed [Col. 0581A] the Usuardian text itself, derived from the collation of the principal—indeed, of all—the manuscripts. The names of those which were found pure for that day are placed beneath it in smaller italic type, as confirmation of the Usuardian text set above. Whenever no manuscript was found wholly pure and simple, a short dissertation is appended, by which the reader is fully informed about the simplicity of the text. Once the text has been purged on the basis of the more authoritative manuscripts, everything else that we judge should be denied to Usuard is relegated to the catalogue which we have called the *Appendices*. Furthermore, in the order of the work there follows a collection of variant readings occurring in the Usuardian manuscripts cited for that text. If minute details of exceedingly slight importance should happen to be observed there, let the reader remember that here I had to accommodate myself to everyone’s taste, and therefore to make some concession also to fastidious antiquarians. Anyone who knows these men knows that one is dealing with minds for whom it is a matter of religion to neglect not even the smallest point in such matters. Those who take no pleasure in details of this kind, I advise to pass over the Variants without concern and proceed to the Observations, where they will find everything that we judged could contribute to the elucidation of our Appendices.

**278.** My first concern was to uncover and explain the genesis of the Usuardian text, so that readers might daily possess the connection of Usuard with his father, grandfather, or grandfathers and great-grandfathers, with his relatives and kindred, which I mentioned above, precisely in the manner that I attempted to represent at the beginning of the preface. Besides the Martyrologists, in order to demonstrate the antiquity and continuity of the cult of the saints, I have more than once brought forward ancient calendars, especially those enjoying at this time the greatest authority among scholars. Among these is that famous and most ancient calendar first published by Bucherius in his commentary on Victor of Aquitaine’s Paschal Canon, p. 267 onward, and again edited by Ruinart among the *Sincere and Select Acts of the Martyrs*, in the Paris edition—which alone I used—from p. 692 onward, and in the more recent Amsterdam edition from p. 617 onward. In both editions another Carthaginian Calendar is appended, also extremely ancient; it was first discovered, published, and furnished with notes by the often-mentioned Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. III, p. 398 onward.

**279.** There are two others—or perhaps the same calendar in two editors’ versions—which Leo Allatius first inserted into his work *On the Perpetual Agreement of the Western and Eastern Church*, published in 1648, beginning at col. 1487. Fronto, whom we discussed above, published it in 1652 under a nearly different title; see above, no. 110, and frequently throughout our work. Add to these the Sacramentaries edited and revised by Menardus, Thomasius, and Mabillon, all of which have been introduced in their proper places to establish the antiquity of the cult of the saints.

Another question, raised almost every day, concerned the encomia of our Martyrologies, or the Acts themselves, from which those encomia were taken and composed by Bede and Ado. Here the difficulty is generally greater, but, in accordance with the purpose of this work, it has been dispatched briefly, so that during the first half of the year the matter has usually been decided on the basis of the reliability of our commentaries on the Acts; during the second half, however, we have briefly discussed the more intricate heads of controversy by means of monuments—whether printed or manuscript—within our possession, and have referred them to a larger work. Here I occasionally cited authors whom I had not yet examined with sufficient care, especially Sebastian Lenain de Tillemont, in his laborious French work entitled *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical History*, divided into sixteen volumes. I wish him, and anyone else cited in the same connection, to be understood as receiving no weight whatsoever from their authority if their statements do not wholly agree with the consent and approval of the Roman Church.

**280.** This warning to the learned reader is more than sufficient, which is all that we seek; for the inexperienced in these matters no explanation of our monuments can ever be given that would suffice for everyone’s understanding. Let nearly the same be said of the entire system of orthography, which in the Usuardian text itself has generally been preserved from the manuscripts and has likewise been employed throughout the Appendices, so that no one ought or can take offense if he finds many things incorrectly written, both in the matters themselves and in proper names. Thus in the text one commonly finds *presbiteri*, and so forth, *Dionisii*, *Hieronimi*, *Hierosolimis*, and so forth; the rationale of all these forms is given in the article which we distinguish under the title “Various Reading.” In the Appendices many much more absurd forms recur; nevertheless, it seemed appropriate to restore the diphthong *ae*, which is found in no manuscripts except the Pratensis, Heriniensis, Rosweydian, and Molanus’s edition. Augustine will provide a defense of the barbarisms we have preserved, as cited by Molanus in his note on 9 January. Here I set the limits of the preface; for if I wished to go through every item of this kind, there would never be an end. Perhaps such details will provide enough tedium elsewhere; it is not worthwhile to waste time on them again here. I shall satisfy both myself and everyone if I present Usuard’s Martyrology pure, genuine, authentic, and simple—which, as we have already said more than once, is the chief purpose of our work, directed toward the one and greater glory of God and the saints.

## NOTES FOR THE INDICES

**281.** To avoid the confusion found in Molanus’s index between the Usuardian saints and others mentioned only in the additions, we have appended two indices to the entire work. The first contains saints who are purely Usuardian, or other feasts that truly belong to Usuard; the second contains all the saints of the Appendices, but arranged in such a way that most of the errors of the manuscripts themselves from which they were taken, as well as the confusion arising from transforming, multiplying, and altering the names of the saints, and from often repeating the same names, have not been removed. In this too we wished our fidelity to be demonstrated to the reader. Nor was this the place to restore those saints to their proper natal days or to resolve other disputed matters, since this is the proper purpose of our commentaries on the Acts themselves; we have judged that all such matters should be referred and deferred to that work.

[Col. 0583]

# PROLEGOMENA OF THE EDITION

[Note: [Col. 0583C] Title: *The Genuine Martyrology of Usuard, a monk of Saint-Germain, edited according to the authority of the autograph preserved in the Abbey of Saint-Germain, and vindicated from the Observations of the Reverend Father Soller of the Society of Jesus. The work and study of D***, priest and Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur. Paris, at the shop of Pierre-François Giffart, bookseller, Jacob’s Street, under the sign of Saint Teresa. 1718, with the approval [Col. 0584C] and privilege of the king.] J. BOUILLART.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0583A] At last the autograph of Usuard’s Martyrology, preserved for nine centuries with such care, so eagerly desired by scholars, and so often demanded, now emerges from the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. The Reverend Father John Bollandus—whose pious and learned labors no oblivion will ever erase—had arranged for that distinguished monument to be copied for him and compared with another, more recent manuscript of the same abbey, and had promised that he would publish Usuard (*Preface to the Acts of the Saints*, vol. I). The Benedictines, who, provided only that the republic of letters might be enriched from their resources, regarded any return of thanks to themselves as nothing, were not even thinking of having it printed. They not only calmly permitted a man who had deserved so well of the Church to enjoy that glory, but even rejoiced that something of their own had contributed to the Collection which was destined to bring abundant fruits to the Christian world. They persuaded themselves that their manuscript would be held in the highest esteem by that learned man and his assistants, and that they would regard it as a matter of conscience neither to add nor to remove anything.

[Col. 0583B] Nor did they fear that, in his preface, that celebrated Jesuit seemed to favor the Heriniensis manuscript more than the Pratensis. Since the Heriniensis had not appeared to him superior to the Pratensis except because the latter announced, on the Ides of January, the translation of the relics of Saint Vincent to Verzy, nothing would have been easier than to remove that very slight scruple from his mind. It would have been enough to inform a man who loved truth that this translation had been added by a more recent hand; that the difference in the scripts was obvious even to a blind man; that in a work of this kind it was not surprising that certain things had been added; unless he wanted to suppose that a new manuscript had been written from time to time for new feasts; and that the autograph lost none of its authority on this account, since it sufficiently protected and defended itself by the antiquity, clarity, and elegance of its script.

But our expectation deceived us. After having kept everyone waiting for seventy years, the Jesuits of Antwerp at last bring a Martyrology into the light, calling it Usuard’s, but making it so impure that, if Usuard were to come back to life, he would look for himself in it in vain. For what reasons did they allow themselves so much license? Because in the Pratensis autograph there are erasures, and certain things written over the erasures that are absent from the other copies of Usuard’s Martyrology. It is surely strange to see erasures in an autograph, as though the work that had restrained many things by erasure were not thereby especially worthy of praise; and what do certain overwritten passages take away from the autograph’s reliability, when the hand that wrote over them is the same as the one that wrote the rest of the manuscript?

It was neither proper nor permissible to conceal the great injury inflicted upon our manuscript. For if the chronological notes presented by that manuscript; if the form of the letters in which it is written; if its silence concerning those who were afterward enrolled among the saints; if its omission of feasts instituted in subsequent periods; if our care, vigilance, and fidelity in preserving manuscripts cannot make Usuard’s autograph secure from suspicion—what certainty will ever remain in written documents? Of all the authors whose works have come from our libraries, whose manuscript do we have or have we had whose antiquity and excellence rest upon more numerous and stronger arguments? It is a kind of rule of textual criticism that, the older a manuscript is and the closer it stands to the author, the less it should be suspected of interpolation. What, I ask, will become of that rule if it is permissible to declare adulterated a manuscript known to have been written by the author himself, or under his direction?

“But,” you will say, “the Jesuits Sirmondus, John Baptist de Cortas, and Stephen Chamillart inspected that manuscript [Note: [Col. 0584D] See Soller’s edition, preface to Usuard’s Martyrology, ch. 3, art. 4, § 1, no. 195]; Castellanus as well, a canon of the Church of Paris, collated it once and again. How could men trained in recognizing and collating manuscripts have been deceived so often?”

This too seemed incredible to me until I had seen the manuscript with my own eyes. Indeed, I long doubted whether Castellanus had really reported what the last editor of Usuard, the Reverend Father Sollerius of the Society of Jesus, claims to have received from him; nor would I have believed it, unless I had trusted Castellanus’s reliability as much as he showed little fear of having it suspected by the Benedictines. In any event, our library is open to all; the manuscript will be available, and everyone may act as judge. The work must be judged by sight. And so that everyone may know what gave rise to the controversy, we wished not only to have an entire page engraved on copper, but also to display the autograph whole, exactly as it is. Whatever was added by another hand is certainly written in a different character; whatever was placed in the margin remains in the margin; whatever is defective and mutilated will likewise be seen to be so. Thus the reader himself will judge what should be denied to Usuard and what should be attributed to him.

Who this Usuard was, at what time he wrote the Martyrology, and from what sources he drew it, the critics dispute among themselves, and the prefatory matter placed before Sollerius’s Usuard is entirely devoted to these questions and is extremely lengthy. Since I have no desire for a large volume, I shall give a brief account of what I have been able to learn from reliable monuments.

Usuard was a man of great probity [Note: [Col. 0584D] Aimoinus, *Translation of the Body of Saints George, Aurelius, etc.*, p. 4], a priest and monk of Saint-Germain of Paris [Note: [Col. 0584D] Prologue to Usuard’s Martyrology]. As early as 838 he had entered his name into the monastic profession [Note: [Col. 0584D] *Spicilegium*, vol. IV, p. 229; Aimoinus, ibid., p. 40]. At that time he subscribed an instrument by which the monks of Saint-Germain-des-Prés established a fellowship of prayers with the monks of Saint-Remi at Reims. About nineteen years later, when the city of Valencia, destroyed by the Saracens or Moors, had given the monks of Saint-Germain-des-Prés hope that they might easily find in its ruins the body of their patron, the blessed Vincent the Levite, Abbot Hilduin II judged no one more suitable than Usuard to undertake this pious and arduous journey. Having set out with Count Odilard, and being unable to go to Valencia because the Moors infested the roads, he went to Córdoba, from where at last, in 858, he brought back to the village of Egmond—belonging to the monks of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and situated in the diocese of Sens—the bodies of Saints George and Aurelius and the head of Saint Natalia.

In 863, after the Northmen who had burned the monastery of Saint-Germain had returned to their homeland, Usuard returned to Paris with the other monks and, by order of Charles the Bald, devoted himself to the Martyrology. He himself gives the reason why this task was assigned to him in the Prologue. At that time many writings of this kind had been published. For, besides those bearing the names of Jerome and Bede, Florus—whoever he may have been—had either composed a work of his own or merely enlarged Bede’s. Rabanus, Archbishop of Mainz, and Wandalbert, a deacon and monk of Prüm in the diocese of Trier, had composed works of the same kind; Ado had followed them, first a monk of Ferrières and afterward bishop of Vienne. From all these Martyrologies our Usuard composed one.

I say “from all of them,” although he does not name them individually. He clearly indicates that, besides the Martyrologies of Jerome, Bede, and Florus, there were others that he used. The words of the Prologue are: “This matter, by pious concern—with your command, if you remember, graciously applied—compelled me, unworthy though I am, to collect into a certain unity the sacred feasts of the saints that are to be commemorated annually, from certain Martyrologies of the Fathers who preceded us.” Thus, before Usuard, there existed certain Martyrologies of preceding Fathers. Now the works of Rabanus, Wandalbert, and Ado had been composed before Usuard set his hand to his own. The matter is beyond dispute with regard to the first two. As for Ado’s Martyrology, scholars agree that Ado composed it before he occupied the see of Vienne, which he assumed in 860.

It is now clearer than daylight that Usuard composed his work after returning from Spain. This is proved both by the many saints from Spain whom he inserted into the sacred calendar and by the receipt of the bodies of Saints George and Aurelius, recorded in the first hand, on 20 October [Note: [Col. 0585D] Aimoinus, *Translation of the Bodies of Saints George and Aurelius, etc.*, p. 51]. He came to Egmond in 858. To suppose that he wrote at Egmond, without any books at his disposal, is utterly absurd. It is no less absurd to suppose that Charles the Bald thought about a Martyrology while the Northmen were besieging the royal city and devastating its surroundings with fire and sword. Aimoinus, an eyewitness and companion of the return, relates that Usuard did not return to Paris with the other monks before 863 [Note: [Col. 0586D] Aimoinus, book I, book II, *Miracles of Saint Germain*, ch. 15]. Usuard therefore did not turn his mind to the Martyrology before 863.

Ado’s Martyrology, then, had been written before Usuard’s; this explains why in both Martyrologies encomia are often expressed in nearly the same words. Yet Usuard does not name Ado or the others, because he did not claim to be composing an original Martyrology, and those Martyrologists were known to everyone at that time.

“But,” you will say, “the Martyrologies of the Fathers who preceded him are the Martyrologies of Jerome, Bede, and Florus.” Usuard’s words contradict this. A little farther on he continues: “Moreover, I was urged on by the pious, although concise, writings on this subject of the venerable priests Jerome and Bede.” No one will compare these words attentively with what precedes them without understanding that the Martyrologies of the preceding Fathers are not the same as those pious writings of Jerome and Bede that he mentions.

Moreover, he says that he undertook the Martyrology because, in the very solemnities of those same Martyrologies of the preceding Fathers, he recalled how many shortcomings due to their negligence there were. Yet he does not accuse Jerome, Bede, or Florus of this fault. Thus, first, of Jerome he says: “One of them, devoted to brevity.” If he devoted himself to brevity, brevity was not negligence. Then, of Bede: “The other, leaving many days untouched, noted—as he himself testifies at the end of his epitome—all whom he was able to find.” If, therefore, both had omitted many things necessary to this work, the one erred through devotion to brevity, the other through ignorance; neither through negligence. Finally, so far from accusing Florus of negligence, he judged that Florus should be followed: “I resolved to follow the broader tracks of Florus, who was renowned in this very undertaking,” and so forth.

Thus, besides the Martyrologies of Jerome, Bede, and Florus, Usuard had before his eyes those of Rabanus, Wandalbert, and Ado, and perhaps the particular Martyrologies of certain churches, which we know had been composed before Usuard.

Nor did Usuard follow the footsteps of his predecessors so closely that he did not sometimes dare to depart from them. He retained none of the faults that had displeased him in the others. He expanded the Hieronymian Martyrology, which was excessively brief; he supplied what was necessary but lacking in Bede; and he compressed the longer narratives of Florus—or, if you prefer, of Ado, for the question whether the second book he resolved to follow is really Florus’s or Ado’s very own Martyrology is still undecided—into shorter accounts. He also added much of his own: more saints whom, while traveling to Spain, he had learned were venerated in that kingdom; all the feast days proper to his own monastery; and other matters that he had investigated with diligent inquiry. Therefore anyone who denied that Usuard had mentioned a particular saint merely because other Martyrologies were silent about that saint would be acting foolishly, since Usuard himself expressly declares that he did not imitate the other Martyrologies in everything. “But if anything,” he says, “has been treated or altered in this work beyond what I received from them, it may be recognized as having been investigated by me through diligent inquiry.”

A work polished with such labor and completed with such industry could not fail to please everyone. Yet, lest there be those who suspected that he had been led to correct other Martyrologies more by fickleness of mind than by the usefulness of the undertaking, he judged that it should be dedicated to Charles, who was not yet emperor, as is clear from the most ancient Usuard manuscripts of this abbey, of the Royal Library, and elsewhere. He was also moved by the not obscure hope that a book fortified by such authority would carry greater weight among contemporaries and posterity. The matter succeeded according to his wishes. For this Martyrology pleased people by its polished and elegant brevity so much that, scarcely completed, it was adopted by almost all churches.

How long Usuard lived afterward is unknown. One thing is certain: his life cannot have extended beyond 877. For in the Necrology, which is of the same period and by the same author as the Martyrology, the death of Queen Ermentrude, wife of Charles, is recorded in the first hand; the death of Charles is recorded in another and more recent hand. Ermentrude died in 869, Charles in 877. Usuard therefore died sometime within that period, and on the Ides of January, for on that day Usuard the priest is commemorated in red letters in the same Necrology.

# To the Reverend Father John Baptist Sollerius, priest and theologian of the Society of Jesus

D***, priest and Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, sends greetings.

[Col. 0587B] At last you have discharged the task which, seventy years ago, your leader Bollandus had promised. It is certainly a great work and one requiring great labor. Your learned preface is as useful as it is lengthy. For there is no doubt that learned men will be greatly pleased by what you have argued concerning Bede’s Martyrology, enlarged through Florus’s diligence, and that, overcome by your arguments, they will judge Henschenius and Papebrochius to have been deceived when they attributed to Bede what belonged to Bede and Florus, and assigned to Florus what ought to be ascribed to an unknown interpolator.

The republic of letters also owes you much for the edition of Rosweydus’s Roman Martyrology, which you vindicated. Your triumph is all the more glorious because you had more numerous and more formidable adversaries: Henry Valesius, Saussayus, Fronto, and Florentinius. Nor can I fail to praise your conjecture concerning Florus’s second book, namely, that it is nothing other than Ado’s pure and unadulterated Martyrology—if one may call a judgment supported by so many and such solid arguments a conjecture. What you affirm, against the opinion of all learned men, namely that Ado wrote before Usuard and was almost copied by Usuard, appears to me so evident that I cannot sufficiently wonder how the critics could have denied it.

Your Observations will not be useless either. It is true that, since Usuard himself candidly confessed in his Prologue through whom he had advanced, it was not especially necessary to identify the sources from which the greater part of his Martyrology flowed. But because four or five books would have had to be collated simultaneously—books which those readers either will not possess or will not have leisure to collate—they will not begrudge being relieved of this labor. Finally, the Appendices either supply the names of unknown saints or teach where the memory of known saints belonged; and this is certainly no slight benefit.

All this is beautiful, good, and correct. If only the rest corresponded to such splendid principles—what an excellent book! What a Martyrology worthy of being exalted with every possible praise! But, with your permission, I must say that in the judgment you passed on the manuscripts I recognize neither the corrector of Henschenius and Papebrochius nor the champion of the Roman Martyrology: I see nothing that reflects your critical power; nothing that could bring you honor. Upon this judgment, however, the value and usefulness of the edition depended. For no one who merely needs Usuard even reads the Preface. The principal matter is the author himself, and your chief task as editor was to ensure that you presented Usuard himself, if possible, or, if not, in as little interpolated a form as possible.

The whole issue therefore lay in the selection of manuscripts. You neglected, without any reason, the oldest and most intact manuscript of all, the one best suited to reproducing Usuard’s sentences and words and, to put the matter in a word that most strongly commends the manuscript, Usuard’s own autograph. You preferred manuscripts of which none was entirely pure, some more contaminated than others, and none of which could be useful to you for editing Usuard.

This is the gravest fault an editor can commit, and I shall undertake to demonstrate that you have fallen into it. In doing so I shall take the greatest care that nothing escape me which might offend your mind even for a moment. But if, anywhere, an incisive temperament, a warmer zeal for truth, the unfairness of your criticism, or somewhat less cautious reflection led me to repay injury with injury, I ask you, in your humanity, to forgive me. I begin.

First, I maintain that our manuscript is the autograph. Hear my reasons.

1. It is clear that the script belongs to the ninth century. This is a judgment of the eyes, from which no one can appeal unless he is blind or obstinately unreasonable.

2. It is certain that the manuscript was written before 877, since in the Necrology, which was written by the same hand, the death of the emperor Charles, who died in that year, is recorded by another hand. I know what suspicion you have cast upon this argument. “What if,” you say, “the whole manuscript was written one hundred—or, if you wish, two hundred—years after Usuard’s death, and the same first hand nevertheless continued the Necrology for some distance, while some unknown secondary hand added the rest?” Reverend Father, in what kind of game did you learn to evade certain facts with suspicions? What if the Jews fabricated or adulterated the sacred Scriptures? What if the Benedictines were not guardians but fabricators or corrupters of the ancient Fathers? What if historians, orators, and poets came from the same workshop? You know where such license of suspicion would lead.

[Col. 0589A] I return to the point from which I digressed.

3. That the work was dedicated to King Charles while he was not yet emperor is confirmed by the Pratensis manuscripts, those of the Royal Library, and many others, whose Prologue simply calls Charles not emperor but a most pious king.

4. That the manuscript was written in the Abbey of Saint-Germain is evident. The Martyrology records all the solemnities proper to the monastery; the Rule of Saint Benedict, customarily read in the chapter, is appended to the Martyrology; the abbots and monks of that same abbey are commemorated in the Necrology; and all three were written by the same hand.

5. It is beyond controversy that Usuard was a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. This is indicated by the subscription to the Prologue itself: “Here ends the Prologue of Usuard, monk of Saint-Germain of Paris.” Nor can it be suspected that this subscription was added later, for it is inserted between the Prologue and Augustine’s testimony in such a way that, if it had not been there earlier, it could not have been introduced by any artifice.

6. No one will doubt that this very manuscript remained in use at the abbey for at least three centuries. This is proved by the solemnities added in the margin, which began to be celebrated after Usuard, and which, in other copies of the same Martyrology that were written in the same monastery after the Necrology had been completed and are still preserved there, were transferred into the text itself.

7. It is certain that the library of this monastery was never burned or plundered from the ninth century onward.

8. No one has accused the Benedictines of forging or corrupting the books of the ancients except someone who wished to evade the authority of the ancients.

What is your position, Reverend Father? Are these not certain marks of an autograph? Can these arguments be weakened by mere conjectures? Would it be permissible to disregard such numerous and so firm supports in your case? I would in fact disregard them if I were speaking with any reader; but since they have led you away from the truth, it will be useful, if not to everyone, at least to you, that they be dismantled.

First [*Preface*, ch. 3, art. 4, § 1], you think that so many erasures, deletions, overwritings, additions, omissions, and alterations are wholly inconsistent with an autograph. [Col. 0589C] The accepted vocabulary was lacking, by which you could adequately express your aversion to the Pratensis manuscript; it was therefore necessary to devise new expressions, unheard of by Latin ears. How different human judgments are! Nothing leads me more strongly to believe that our manuscript belongs to the author himself than the fact that I see so many things deleted, erased, overwritten, added, removed, and altered. Was there ever an autograph of even a moderately good work that was free of erasures? Has it ever been considered a fault to condemn what had pleased one, or to discover what had escaped one? Was Usuard alone not permitted to know that a style does its work no less by deleting than by writing?

I am certain that you would erase from your own papers whatever you said about the Pratensis manuscript without sufficient consideration. The fact that I can bring myself to believe this is due both to your acknowledged probity and to the love of truth that you display. But suppose that ten years after your death someone visiting the house of the Antwerp Jesuits were shown your writings, amended and corrected in this manner, by one of the members. Would that member endure someone arguing as follows?

[Col. 0589D] “Look for a foreign copy; those writings are not autographs. I accept nothing except what the author himself published. There was some associate who, wishing to protect the reputation of the learned writer, judged that his own style should be adapted to that writer’s. If that work had to be printed again, I would use the copies disseminated among the public and place no reliance on what you call the autograph. Those copies are polished and splendid, with no addition or interpolation; this one, however, is rough, dirty, and disfigured throughout by erasures and interpolations.”

Consider, Reverend Father, by what arguments your associate would repel that ungenerous quibble, and understand that by those same arguments we repel your own.

You may say [*Preface*, ch. 3, art. 4, § 1, no. 199]: “Usuard did not live long enough to introduce so many alterations into his autograph.” To make this seem probable, you calculate the periods of time. “The Pratensis manuscript,” you say, “was written, according to Mabillon, during the interval between the deaths of Ermentrude and Charles, the emperor, her husband. In the Necrology, the death of Queen Ermentrude is marked by the first hand on 7 October, while Charles’s death is marked by a more recent hand on 6 October. Ermentrude died in 869; Charles died in 877. The Martyrology was therefore written between 869 and 877.”

You continue [*Preface*, ch. 3, art. 4, § 1, no. 206]: “Indeed, it must be admitted that it was written, or at least completed, after 875, when the Bald was first made emperor, and therefore, most probably, in the following year, 876.” If one insists upon Mabillon’s conjecture, it will also follow that Usuard died before the Bald, since the latter is entered in the Necrology by another hand, and Usuard therefore survived, at most, until the beginning of 877. Thus, after performing these calculations, you think that Usuard lived for approximately one year after completing and offering the Martyrology to the Emperor Charles; and you judge that, in so short a period, it is not credible that so many things could have occurred to Usuard which he might alter, erase, or add in the Martyrology.

Do you say, Reverend Father, that a whole year is not enough to correct a work so small [Col. 0590B] in approximately fifty places? For there are no more than that in which Usuard changed the wording. And what sort of corrections are they? Here there is merely an erasure; there a saint’s name has been added; elsewhere only the designation of a place has been altered—so that all the corrections together would scarcely fill ten pages.

And from where do you derive the claim that the Martyrology was dedicated to the Emperor Charles? The preface placed before your Herinian codex had taught that it was dedicated not to Augustus, but to the most pious king. Does that highly commended codex have no authority except where it conflicts with the Pratensian? Neither it nor the Dervensis codex preserved in the royal library—the antiquity and value of which I shall discuss later—bears the name of Augustus. What, then, weighs against these three codices—the multitude of more recent ones?

Even if, therefore, the Martyrology had been written between 869 and 877, as our learned and revered Mabillon wished, Usuard could easily have survived the completed and presented Martyrology by four or five years [Col. 0590C]—a sufficiently long interval, and longer than necessary, for erasing what displeased him and adding what he judged more suitable.

Moreover, whether Mabillon was distracted by more important affairs when he wrote his conjecture, or whether I am slow to understand, I simply cannot see why, merely because the death of Charles’s wife Ermentrude was recorded in one hand and Charles’s death in another, this Martyrology must have been written during the interval that elapsed between their two deaths. What prevents it from having been written two, four, or six years before the Necrology? Is it because the hand is the same? A hand does not change with the years, especially not over so short a period.

It could also have happened that, when Usuard was writing the Necrology, no one had died whose death needed to be entered on the Nones of October. For it was customary that those who wrote Necrologies should first arrange all the days of the year and afterward assign each deceased person to the day on which his death had occurred. This is why in Usuard’s Necrology many days remain entirely [Col. 0590D] empty even today, while many others have been filled by a later Usuardine hand.

You add (Preface, ch. 3, art. 4, § 1, no. 206): “Who would dare suspect that Usuard had either the right or the freedom to make corrections after the Martyrology had been accepted by the Emperor and the churches?”

You are jesting, Reverend Father. Was it ever enacted by law that no one might add or remove anything from Usuard’s Martyrology? Was it not granted to all the churches that each might add its own solemnities? And is not the variety of the codices itself evidence that the text could be changed, enlarged, or abridged with impunity?

You continue (ibid.): “Who would suggest that the same hand repeatedly returned to add, remove, and so forth, while nevertheless a different ink or other indications so often appear—indications that sufficiently prove that many years certainly intervened during which corrections were made?”

Here you loudly proclaim that different ink often appears, while throughout your entire volume, if I remember correctly, you complain about the ink only twice. But perhaps one kind of ink and then another was often used. Does an ink bottle last for many years? Have you not often experienced yourself that ink fades after a week has passed? Surely those ancients did not plan for the long term. They ought to have foreseen that their writings would possess greater or lesser authority among their descendants on account of the ink, and therefore should have taken care that what they sold would not soon turn yellow.

What those other indications are that supposedly required Usuard to spend many years correcting the codex, I do not know. I shall refute them when you are able to specify them.

Now, if you ask how it happened that the Pratensian codex was corrected while the others were not, the explanation is obvious. The author offers a copy of his Martyrology to King Charles. It is immediately approved by everyone and copied. Meanwhile his own copy remains at home. As time passes, new information is added. The author comes across Acts that he had not previously seen. Whenever he takes up the work again, he regrets—as happens—that he wrote certain things, omitted certain others, and failed to record still others suitably. He adds, erases, moves passages, restrains what is excessive, [Col. 0591B] brings what is disordered into line, composes what is loose, and corrects everything with the utmost precision. There is your reason why the Pratensian was corrected.

The other codices, however, were not corrected because they had doubtless been copied in different months, and it would have been inconvenient to notify all the churches whenever something seemed in need of correction. Perhaps he did notify them; but either they were unwilling to incur new expenses or, for some other reason I do not know, they refused to follow his instructions.

Why do we rack our brains to explain something that happens every day? There is no author who, a year after publishing a work, does not notice that he omitted much that he wishes he had said and said much that he wishes he had omitted. Yet it would neither be agreeable nor convenient for learned men to purchase new volumes by the same author on the same subject every year. To use an example more closely relevant to the matter: would you regard Baronius’s martyrology as pure and intact despite any error whatsoever? Yet it is in use, and no new edition is contemplated whenever critics find some blemish in it. [Col. 0591C] Usuard corrected his work in precisely the same way; but the other churches either did not know of it or neglected it. So much for erasures.

I now come to the argument to which you award the palm and on account of which you exalt yourself so magnificently. You enumerate, with great display, sixty-six days of the year (Preface, ch. 3, art. 4, § 1, no. 200) on which the Pratensian Usuard differs from other simpler codices, both printed and manuscript. From this you conclude either that that codex is not the autograph, or at least that there was another autograph—perhaps more than one—from which the Herinian and the other purer Pratensian copies were transcribed. How groundlessly you have excluded the Pratensian codex from the number of the pure copies will be made clear by the Notes. Here I shall examine only the argument itself.

If we believe you, then, the Pratensian codex is not the autograph because it departs from the others, and does so frequently. Do you honestly think, Reverend Father, that this is a valid reason? To me it seems entirely beside the point. For if the codex is the autograph, your argument proves only that the codex was copied without fidelity. You should first have proved that it was not the autograph; only afterward could you have added that there was nothing surprising in its differing so often from the other codices.

For however great the discrepancy between an autograph and other copies may be, it can never serve as an argument that the former is not an autograph. I think you perceive the first defect in your argument.

As for your further conclusion that there was another autograph, I would not deny it. But that the purer Pratensian copies were transcribed from that other autograph, I cannot in any way concede. There is an old proverb, worn smooth by age: “Later thoughts are wiser” (δεύτεραι φροντίδες σοφώτεραι). The file smooths; it does not disfigure—unless Usuard happened to resemble those physicians who cut even healthy limbs. So far was he from doing that, however, that I could wish he had corrected still more.

Next I carefully read and reread everything you observed concerning those days on which you struck the Pratensian from the register of pure codices. When I sought the basis of so inequitable a judgment, this seemed to me to have been your reasoning: that the codex is corrupt wherever it is sullied by erasures. For you restore as genuine all the saints whom the Pratensian codex presents without erasure.

Thus, whenever your older codices mention certain saints who are absent from the Pratensian, or announce them differently there, if there was an erasure in those places in the Pratensian you never fail to put your own codices first, as though they had attained Usuard’s original simplicity, which you maintain has been removed or corrupted in ours by another hand. Do I understand your meaning correctly? Yet this reasoning is so little suited to diminishing the authority of the Pratensian codex that it is astonishing that it could have occurred to you, a man of such great acumen and judgment.

Come, Reverend Father, lend truth ears as receptive as you promised they would be. An erasure is made only so that either nothing remains where something had previously been written, or something different is read in place of what had been written. Your erasures, therefore, will be of no use to you unless either the same saints are always read in the other codices at the places where an erasure occurs in the autograph, or the saints written over the erasures are never the same as those who appear in the corresponding places in the other codices.

For if it sometimes happens that, where an erasure was made in the autograph, your codices report no saints, or that your codices have the same saints as those found in the autograph’s erasures—and even if it were occasionally true that saints were absent from the autograph where some of your codices mention them, or that the autograph mentioned saints different from those reported by your codices—you still could draw no judgment about the autograph from the erasures.
