Why? Because a rule that disagrees with itself and contradicts itself is no rule.

However much I strive for clarity, I fear that this argument may seem complicated to you. I shall compare examples. On 17 April you refused to follow the Pratensian codex because it contains Nicephorus, who is absent from your codices. But precisely where Nicephorus is now read in the Pratensian, there was formerly an erasure. Thus, if you are to be certain that the original simplicity of Usuard should be recovered for that day from your codices, one of them ought to contain a saint who stood in the Pratensian before the erasure. Yet you admit that no trace of this erasure appears in your codices. How, then, could the mention of Nicephorus have been a reason for thinking that your codices, rather than the Pratensian, preserve the fragrance of Usuard’s original simplicity?

Likewise on 14, 28, and 30 January; 10, 17, 29, and 30 March; 2, 17, 22, 23, and 26 April; 15 June; 23, 26, and 30 August; 25 September; 17 October; and 21 and 23 November, you judged the Pratensian codex defective because a commemoration of certain saints had been made in the erasures, while your codices are completely silent about them.

But on 16 and 19 March; 8, 13, and 29 August; 20 and 21 September; 17 October; 2 November; and other places, the Pratensian codex is likewise disfigured by erasures, yet your codices do not depart from it by even a hair’s breadth. Thus, just as your codices sometimes differ from the Pratensian where the latter has erasures, so they also sometimes agree with it in such places. [Col. 0592D]

The erasures, therefore, cannot serve you as a rule by which to judge the Pratensian codex, since there is no rule that remains consistently the same. To sum everything up briefly: the erasures in the Pratensian codex cannot be used to depress its authority unless you show either which saints were entered by Usuard before the erasures, or that those entered over the erasures were different from those Usuard himself had designated.

Your codices can establish neither point, since they often reproduce the saints who are read in the erasures without any trace of those erasures, and often reproduce the very same saints who appear in the erasures. You therefore wasted your effort when you attempted to overwhelm and crush the Pratensian codex by the number and bulk of your codices rather than by their value and dignity.

What do you say to this, Reverend Father? Does this argument fail in any respect? Is any escape left? I see one, and I shall gladly point it out to you. Say that you did not use erasures alone as your rule, but erasures together with discrepancies among the codices; that in some places you rejected the Pratensian because, in addition to the erasures, it differed from the others, while in other places you followed it because, although it had erasures, it nevertheless agreed with the other codices.

Would that satisfy you? Yet nothing is easier than to close off this refuge as well. The left hand is not more like the right than the hand that wrote the saints you rejected is like the hand that recorded those you admitted. I appeal to everyone’s eyes. If there is even the slightest difference in the scripts, I say nothing more: let the codex be considered not only not an autograph but the worst of all codices. Since, then, the same script appears in both sets of erasures, the discrepancies among the codices can in no way help us investigate Usuard’s original simplicity.

What now troubles you is how it could have happened that the Herinian and Tournai codices, in comparison with which you despise the Pratensian, accepted some corrections but not others. I believe I can untie this knot without difficulty. Before Usuard ordered the Martyrology to be copied for presentation to King Charles, there were undoubtedly already erasures in the autograph. It is a learned work requiring extensive reading, and in works of this kind something new comes to mind every day that calls for correction.

Everything that had been corrected in the autograph was transferred into its first copy, which may be called a second autograph. Your codices were derived from this. That is why they reproduce some corrections of the first autograph but not others: Usuard repeatedly introduced new material into his own copy which escaped the notice of the other churches or was neglected by them.

I hasten to your final argument. You say that certain things are read in the margin of the Pratensian codex which, although added by a later hand, are nevertheless found in all the oldest codices of Usuard and therefore belong to Usuard. From this it seems to follow for you either that not everything was written by Usuard’s own hand, or that he used a different script.

Among the many examples that you misleadingly suggest could be produced in large number, one seemed especially apt to you. Thus, on 7 November, the first hand in the Pratensian codex reads concerning Saint Herculanus: “At Perugia, a city of Italy, the birthday of Saint Herculanus, bishop.” In the margin, a later hand adds: “whose body, after his head had been cut off, was found on the fortieth day so united and sound, as Saint Gregory the pope writes, as though no incision of iron had touched it.”

Yet every codex of Usuard’s Martyrology, even the most ancient, contains this latter and longer part of the eulogy. Which hand, you ask, is the autograph? I admit that this miracle is related in the oldest codices, as I copied it from the Dervensis. Nor can it be denied that it was added in the margin by a later—and indeed unskilled—hand. For instead of “as though no incision of iron [had touched it],” it wrote “as though any incision of iron,” words which are devoid of sense. I will also readily grant that the entire eulogy belongs to Usuard. Does it follow, then, that the first hand was not Usuard’s? This is your conclusion, Reverend Father.

To me, who have the codex before my eyes, the matter appears quite otherwise. Between the commemoration of Saint Herculanus and that of Blessed Amarantus there is a space about a thumb’s breadth wide, scraped with a knife, but in such a way that even today one can easily read what was written there by the first hand. From this you, who have been writing for so long and have so often experienced how readily the mind approves, rejects, prompts, or restrains the hand, can easily resolve the difficulty.

I understand the matter as follows. When Usuard committed that day’s entry to writing, he first intended to adorn Saint Herculanus’s eulogy with a miracle. After writing the opening words, he rejected the plan he had initially formed. Later, while dictating the codex to be offered to King Charles, it occurred to him that this would add considerable ornament to the entry. He dictated it, [Col. 0594A] but did not add it to his own codex because no space had been left. Two hundred years later, some fellow, whether in another codex or in the Dialogues of Blessed Gregory, read the miracle, was delighted by it, took it hard that Usuard had omitted it, and added it.

But even if elsewhere in the remaining codex there were one or two commemorations written by another hand, provided that the passage occurs in all the copies, it seems to me to matter little to the credibility of the autograph whether it was written by the same hand or by another hand of the same period. For that alone is not an autograph which the author’s own hand wrote. It is enough that it was written under his dictation or direction.

Once this is granted—which you cannot deny—is the same scribe always at hand? For a work that everyone needed to read, Usuard undoubtedly chose someone who would write more neatly and elegantly. But that scribe could have been absent or ill when something occurred to the author that he wished to add to the codex.

The conclusion is this: whatever is older than all the copies, whether it was written by the same hand or by another hand of the same period, must belong to the autograph. Whatever corrections, therefore, are found in all the copies of Usuard, even if they are written over erasures in the Pratensian codex, even if they are marked by another hand, must be claimed for Usuard himself. Have I sufficiently explained and dispelled your doubts—or rather, your errors?

What if I demonstrate to you that your codices could have been useful neither for judging the Pratensian codex nor for publishing Usuard?

You know that an autograph is a codex written by the author himself, or one written under his dictation or direction, and therefore one from which it can be determined with certainty what he did or did not write. Since, then, you have declared from the Herinian, Tournai, and other codices that the Pratensian is not the autograph, you must have learned from them what Usuard did and did not write.

Yet I strongly suspect that you could have learned neither. For you could have known either point only if the autograph had come into your hands, or at least the purest copy; and I am fully convinced that you had neither. On what grounds? You shall hear.

In Paris, in the royal library, there is preserved a codex of Usuard’s Martyrology of extraordinary antiquity, written in Carolingian script, with scarcely any erasures and very few additions, in which it is quite easy to recognize a later hand. I have no doubt that it belongs to the end of the ninth century or at least the beginning of the tenth.

At its end, a certain catalogue of books was added by a later hand, with a title stating that these were the books found in the chest of Adso, abbot of Dervy, after he had departed for Jerusalem. He departed in the year 992. That later hand, therefore, belongs to the tenth century. How close the codex itself must approach Usuard’s time, since the later hand is separated from it by so small an interval!

Certainly either there is no purest copy, or this is it. Add that this distinguished codex once belonged to the monastery of Dervy, which had been heaped with so many benefits by Charles the Bald that there can be no doubt that, when it was heard that the Martyrology had been prepared at the king’s command, its abbot and monks transferred it for their own use.

Add also that the commemoration of Saint Odo is written by a later hand, although he died in 944 and was honored with public worship immediately after his death. Yet in that copy, although it generally agrees with your codices, there are many places where it differs from them. Do you want me to list some?

On 15 February, the entry begins with Saint Blasius, as in the Pratensian. On 28 May it says nothing about Saint Charaunus, not even mentioning him. On 5 June it has nothing about Saint Boniface, bishop. On the 30th it reports these words: “yet not on the same day, but after the passage of a year, as the eloquent poet Arator writes”—words which you deny were written by Usuard.

On 8 July, after Ciliani martyr, it adds “and his companions.” On the 12th it is silent about Saint Dyo. On the 20th it reads: “on the very day of Saint Margaret, virgin.” On 28 August it likewise reads: “On the Portuensis Way, of the holy martyrs Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrix, in the time of Diocletian,” and so forth—martyrs whom your codices pass over on this day.

On 7 September, Saint Clodoaldus is simply called a priest and confessor. On the 19th, it calls Saint Sequanus not a priest but an abbot and confessor. On 8 October, Libaria the virgin is joined to Pelagia the sinner. On the 9th, Eleutherius, one of the companions of Dionysius, is called not a deacon but a priest. On the 20th it announces Syndulfus and Adraudus. On the 23rd it is completely silent about Benedict the confessor. On the 30th it says nothing about Germanus of Capua, but instead reads: “At Medio-vicus, of the holy martyrs Pientius and Agentius and Saint Columba, virgin.” I omit the rest.

You plainly understand, even without my saying so, what follows from this variety of readings. Your codices stand far apart from two others, one of which is certainly an autograph and the other of which is, in all probability, derived from another autograph rather than from yours. How, then, could they have been copied from the autograph, or at least from the purest copy? How could you infer from them what Usuard did or did not write? By what right did you declare from them that the Pratensian is not the autograph?

The condition of your edition is truly pitiable. I see it between two reefs, upon one or the other of which it must be wrecked. For the more accurately an edition reproduces what the author wrote and his words, the purer and more carefully corrected it is considered. Nothing presents either with greater accuracy than the autograph; and from Usuard’s autograph, whichever of the two it may finally prove to be, you are very far removed.

But I wish to deal kindly with you. Let it be granted that your codices reproduce Usuard pure and simple, except for a few additions which you have most sagaciously detected. Let it be granted that the Pratensian codex does not deserve the title of autograph and ought to be counted among the copies. Even with this granted, see whether it was not the act of an unperceptive and imprudent man to prefer any other codex to the Pratensian.

First, you admit that all the others yield to the Pratensian in antiquity. Did this confession escape you, Reverend Father, without reflection? [Col. 0595C] Did you consider it sufficiently? Did you notice how dangerous it was to grant the Pratensian codex that degree of honor?

Certainly, the nearer water is to its spring, the less it is mixed with foreign water. And if the Pratensian is not the spring itself, it is at least so near the spring that scarcely any interval can be discerned between them. For the Herinian, by your own testimony, although it belongs to the eleventh century, is nevertheless two hundred years more recent than the Pratensian.

The Pratensian codex, therefore, was written in the ninth century. Again, by your own calculation of the dates, Usuard died in the year 876. The copy is therefore at most twenty-three years later than Usuard.

You will also admit, I know, that it was derived from the autograph. For it is scarcely credible that the codex was obtained elsewhere when there was a need to copy another codex because the autograph had become too worn. Was the autograph really too worn, Reverend Father? Was there a need, after twenty-three years, to copy a parchment codex that was taken into the hands only once each day, and on each day only during four periods of time? Can this seem credible to you, when in our churches paper books can be seen which, although they have been handled day and night every day for sixty years or more, nevertheless remain intact?

But let us suppose that the autograph lasted only that brief time. At least you will concede that the monks of Pratensian, in order to restore a book composed by one of their own fellows and used by them for twenty-three years, would not have borrowed a codex from elsewhere.

You must also admit that no church or monastery could appear less open to suspicion of interpolation. For what reason, and under what pretext, would the monks of Pratensian have altered the Martyrology? During the period between Usuard’s death and the tenth century, did the church of Paris add or remove any saints from its calendars? Was the abbey of Saint-Germain enriched with new relics? Did it enter into an association with another monastery by which it became bound to venerate that monastery’s saint?

I can foresee what you will answer. “The first hand,” you will say, “faithfully reproduced the autograph; but afterward another treacherous hand attacked the entire codex and substituted other material for what Usuard had written.”

You throw yourself into that hiding place in vain, Reverend Father; I have you in my grasp. The hand that made the erasures and introduced new material into them is plainly the same hand that wrote the rest of the codex. If you refuse to concede this voluntarily, I shall extort it from you even against your will: the erasures are earlier than the tenth century.

For the Dervensis codex—which the form of its letters, the appended chronological notes, and learned men all testify was written at the end of the ninth century or the beginning of the tenth—reproduces intact many of the entries that are written over erasures, while it contains not a word of what had been written before the erasures. Those erasures, therefore, were already in the Pratensian before the Dervensis codex was written.

Nor can you say that the Pratensian was corrected from the Dervensis. [Col. 0596B] Otherwise, why do traces of the earlier corrections survive in one place rather than another? Why do none of the earlier corrections remain, while some traces of later ones do? The hand of all the corrections is the same. Therefore all belong to the ninth century. The codex was therefore copied and corrected in the same period.

There was no reason in the ninth century for the Pratensian monks to alter the Martyrology. You must therefore admit that no church or monastery could be less liable to suspicion of interpolation.

Now let your codices come forward and contend with the Pratensian for honor and superiority. As to age, I have a confessing defendant. “I freely and willingly admit,” you say (Preface, ch. 3, art. 4, § 2, no. 210), “that our Herinian parchment codex yields the palm entirely to the Pratensian . . . being at least two centuries later.”

A great interval of time, Reverend Father—one in which, even if it were true that nothing new had been inserted into Usuard, you could nevertheless judge that less confidently of the Herinian than of the Pratensian. That alone was sufficient reason for preferring the Pratensian.

By what argument could you persuade yourself that the Herinian or the other codices were copied from the autograph or from the purest copy? By what sign could you distinguish what bore Usuard’s character from what was contrary to Usuard?

The Hieronymian indexes, Bede, Florus, Ado, and all the other martyrologists who preceded Usuard could provide no assistance, since Usuard himself clearly indicates that he sometimes departed from them when he says in his Prologue: “But if anything has been done or changed in this work beyond what I received from them, it will be possible to recognize it as having been sought out by me through careful investigation.”

Nor were all the martyrologies written after Usuard any more helpful. You will scarcely find two that agree with one another on every day of the year. The Herinian is packed with saints of the province of Reims; the Tournai codex mixes in many from England; others include others.

You may say that these can easily be distinguished from Usuardine material because certain saints belong properly to particular churches. But how many saints are found in Usuard whom certain churches venerate in their own particular and distinctive manner?

On 18 April you exclude Saint Maternus from Usuard, as though he were proper to Trier. Why would Usuard not have recorded Maternus just as he recorded Maximus, whom the people of Trier likewise honor with a distinctive cult?

On the 24th of the same month, your much-vaunted Herinian codex is disgracefully relegated among the impure because it mentions Saints Bova and Doda, who belong properly to the people of Reims. Why is it considered pure when it announces Saints Basolus and Theodoricus, who belong properly to certain villages of the same province?

It has also sometimes happened that, without any reason, you did not brand those codices and others of greater value with the mark of interpolation, while you blamed them for what should have been attributed to purity.

On 10 February you preferred them to the Pratensian. Wrongly: in the Pratensian, Saint Austreberta is written over an erasure, and the first hand, as you call it—the hand which I identify with the autograph presented to King Charles—did not mention her. [Col. 0597A] That saint is absent from the Dervensis codex.

Your codices were also pure on 16 March. Usuard added Hilary and Tatian to his codex after deleting the entire entry he had previously written. Eustachius was likewise deleted, and Eulogius of Córdoba added, on 20 September. Your codices, like the Dervensis, reproduced the first hand, or first autograph. Why did you wrong them?

You were no fairer to them on 1 November. The eulogy of Marcellus had not been altered in them; it was genuinely Usuardine and belonged to the first autograph. Thus nothing certain can be established once one has departed from the rule.

Your codices, therefore, supplied no mark by which you could distinguish Usuardine from non-Usuardine material. Let me ask you again, then: on what grounds did you persuade yourself that they had been copied from the autograph, or at least from the purest copy?

Finally, there is no need for me to prove that other churches and monasteries are more reasonably open to suspicion. The matter speaks for itself. When Usuard’s Martyrology reached them, they already possessed their own solemnities. In neighboring regions there were also others which they had long since adopted for themselves. Beyond doubt they added all of these to the new Martyrology. Since Usuard himself could have marked them, you cannot distinguish them from Usuardine material by any indication unless you approach the source itself or come as close to the source as possible.

No streamlet, as you yourself acknowledge, is nearer its source than the Pratensian, which I have been permitted to call a copy. Was it not therefore the act of a perceptive and prudent man to prefer the Pratensian codex to the others, even if it were as certain that it was a copy as it is certain that it is an autograph?

Even if it is true—as it certainly is—that the Pratensian ought to have been preferred to your codices, what confidence can your edition deserve, since you preferred yours to it? They therefore could have been of no use for publishing Usuard.

This is enough, Reverend Father. To interrupt your literary business with a longer discourse would be to injure the public interest. I believe I have omitted nothing that could henceforth lead you to think more favorably of the Pratensian codex.

I have established by the form of the letters, the chronological notes, continuous use, and faithful preservation that it is the autograph. I have demonstrated that the erasures—undeniable signs of an autograph—were made by Usuard, and that he was prevented from making them neither by any law nor by death.

I have made clear that the autograph’s divergences from the copies favor the autograph, not the copies. I have overturned the foundation on which your entire criticism rests: the claim that the Pratensian is corrupted wherever it contains erasures or corrections that do not appear in the other codices—since the others themselves often admit the corrections, and often contain nothing of what had been written before the erasures or corrections.

Since the script in the corrections is everywhere alike, either the rule must be applied to all the places, or there is no rule. I have shed light on the example that had made you suspect that Usuard’s hand was inconsistent with itself.

It was not enough to destroy the argument drawn from the variety of readings; I went further and showed that your codices differ from both autographs and therefore could not be used to judge the Pratensian.

And lest a harsher criticism exasperate your mind, I did not hesitate to descend to your view and grant that the Pratensian codex is a copy, or at least an autograph defiled by a later hand. [Col. 0598A] But I proved that, even if this were granted, it was a copy of such a kind that you ought to have preferred it to all the others: first, because it is the oldest of them all; second, because it is more probable that it was copied from the autograph than that any other was; and finally, because no other could be less open to suspicion of interpolation.

I hope, Reverend Father, that these arguments will remove every scruple from your mind, restore the Pratensis manuscript to your good graces, and persuade you to regard as withdrawn whatever you have said somewhat harshly and less than accurately about the authenticity and integrity of the autograph. I readily forgive you this. For how could you have judged that manuscript correctly when you were relying on other men’s eyes—and eyes not especially perceptive at that—and were hearing testimonies often directly opposed to one another? Bollandus and Henschenius, great men and well trained in this field, considered the manuscript far from pure; Sirmondus and Mabillon, no less distinguished, asserted that it was an autograph; Castellanus reported one thing, Stephanus Chamillart another. Blurred erasures here and there, and certain additions, made the matter difficult; it was easy to go wrong when entangled in so many complications.

I am convinced that you would have dealt much more kindly with the Pratensis manuscript had you been able to examine it with your own eyes. Yet you have no reason to complain of our superiors. You are not unaware how important and valuable a unique monument of this kind is. It was not safe to transport it so far into foreign and hostile regions. Was it not enough to allow the whole manuscript to be transcribed? To allow your Sirmondus to compare it with another copy? To allow Castellanus afterward to examine it once, twice, and a third time, and to record with the greatest diligence, day by day, every variation, however slight? (Soller., Preface, ch. 3, a. 4, § 1, no. 195.) If all these testimonies did not satisfy you, why did you not inquire by letter on what grounds we defended the autograph of Usuard’s Martyrology; why it contained erasures; why certain things had been written over those erasures that were absent from other manuscripts; why solemnities had been added in the margin; whether the same hand appeared everywhere or different hands? There is no one here to whom you would not have given great pleasure; no one who would not have considered it a duty to inform you most carefully about everything.

I wish you had adopted that prudent course. Since, however, you preferred to attack our Codex publicly, and since we are now publicly avenging it, I ask and earnestly entreat you to take this in good part. I have no fear that I shall fail to persuade you. You yourself not only requested but even demanded (Preface, a. 4, § 1, no. 208) that one of our number explain and dispel your doubts—or rather, your errors—into which you fell because you lacked access to the Codex itself. You promised that you would most readily retract anything that you might be shown to have thought unjustly about our autograph. Indeed, you seemed to have deserved well of the republic of letters if, through your doubts, you brought it about that we eventually made our own Usuard public, vindicated in its native simplicity and furnished with whatever annotations we wished. I was certainly entitled to expect such fairness from a learned man who belongs to the number of those who (ibid.) have all set themselves the same goal: that, once the darkness has been dispelled, errors may be driven away, truth brought to light, and ecclesiastical antiquity illuminated even by emulous scholarship, to the greater glory of God and the saints. Farewell.

[Col. 0599]

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF USUARD BEGINS, THROUGHOUT THE CYCLE OF THE YEAR

## PROLOGUE

[Note: This prologue was missing from the manuscript Codex which we are publishing, because its first leaf had fallen out through extreme age. The distinguished Pithaeus supplied it to us from a copy almost identical both in script and in age, as D. Jacques du Breul, a monk of this monastery, testifies; he prefixed this observation to the beginning of the Prologue. It should also be noted that it is not found in Soller’s edition of Usuard. BOUILLART.]

### TO CHARLES THE BALD

To the most pious lord of kings, CHARLES, Usuard, an unworthy priest and monk, sends an everlasting crown in Christ.

It is by no means unknown to Your Highness, most wise prince, how we are admonished to imitate the labors of the ancients, so that whatever is found in their works—especially in matters consonant with ecclesiastical doctrine—to be less than perfect, we should either complete as far as possible or at least desire to see completed. This pious concern, applied graciously at your command, if you remember, compelled me, unworthy though I am, to gather into a single whole the sacred and annually commemorated feasts of the saints from certain Martyrologies of our predecessors.

As I recalled their solemnities themselves, I also recalled how many excesses of my own negligence had occurred, and I wished that these too might be cleansed by such a task. Moreover, I was encouraged by the pious though concise writings on this subject of the venerable priests Jerome and Bede. The former, pursuing brevity, and the latter leaving many days untouched, are nevertheless found to have passed over much that was necessary for this work. I nevertheless decided to follow them, as well as to follow the broader path already traced in the same undertaking by Florus, that memorable man, especially in his second book. There he both corrected and added many things which he had omitted in the first.

But if anything has been done or altered in this work beyond what I received from those authors, it will be recognized as having been sought out by me through careful investigation. In any case, most gracious lord, I preferred to insert this little preface of my insignificance into this small work so that it might be understood that I did not undertake this effort out of frivolity, but rather obeyed your commands—as was fitting—commands ordinarily concerned with the benefit of Catholic believers.

Therefore, I beg you to do what belongs to you: if this work is judged just, let it be strengthened by the anchor of your personal protection; that is, let it be confirmed both for the present by the authority of royal examination and for the future by the judgment of so great an authority. May the Lord, King of kings, deign to guard the excellence of your greatness through many cycles of years. Amen.

[Note: This second prologue is lacking in the edition of Usuard prepared by Sollerius; but it is found in nearly all the handwritten copies of the same Usuard preserved in the Pratensis library, as well as in many others. BOUILLART.]

## ANOTHER PROLOGUE FROM THE BOOKS OF BLESSED AUGUSTINE: HOW THE SAINTS ARE TO BE HONORED

[Col. 0599]

The ancient Fathers decreed that the feasts of the holy apostles and martyrs should be celebrated as a mystery of veneration, either to arouse imitation, or so that we might be joined to their merits and aided by their prayers (Augustine, Book XX Against Faustus, ch. 21). Yet this is done in such a way that we sacrifice not to any of the martyrs but to God himself, although we establish altars in the memorials of the martyrs.

For no one standing at an altar in the places where the saints’ bodies lie has ever said: “We offer to you, Peter, or Paul, or Cyprian.” Rather, what is offered is offered to God, who crowned the martyrs, so that the affection aroused by love of those places may rise toward an increase of charity—both toward those whom we can imitate and toward him with whose help we are able to do so.

We therefore honor the martyrs with that form of love and fellowship with which holy men of God are honored in this life, whose hearts we perceive to have been prepared for such suffering on behalf of evangelical truth. But we honor the martyrs with greater devotion because they are more secure. We proclaim them with more confident praise as victors already in the happier life than as those still fighting in this one.

But with that worship which in Greek is called *latria*—which cannot be expressed in Latin by a single word, since it is a particular service owed to the Divinity—we neither honor nor teach that anyone should honor any being except the one God. Since the offering of sacrifice belongs to this worship, and since those who offer it even to idols are called idolaters, we in no way offer or command anything of the kind to be offered either to any martyr, any holy soul, or any angel.

Anyone who falls into this error is corrected by sound doctrine, whether so as to be reformed or so as to be condemned. For the saints themselves, whether human beings or angels, do not wish to have offered to them what they know is owed to God alone.

This was shown in the case of Paul and Barnabas, when the Lycaonians, moved by the miracles performed through them, wished to sacrifice to them as gods. Tearing their garments, confessing and persuading the people that they were not gods, they forbade this to be done to them (Acts 14:14). It was also shown in the case of the angels, as we read in the Apocalypse, where an angel forbids himself to be worshiped and says to the one worshiping him: “I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers; worship God” (Apoc. 19:10).

The martyrs, therefore, are to be honored for imitation, not worshiped as a religious act. They are to be honored with charity, not with servitude.

# THE MONTH OF JANUARY HAS THIRTY-ONE DAYS

[Col. 0601]

## On the Kalends. Day 1

[Note: That Usuard is represented here in his original simplicity is proved by most of the manuscripts on which I chiefly relied, as I indicated in the preface: namely, the Pratensis Codex—whether merely Pratensian or truly autograph—with which exemplar B always agrees, as do perhaps other similar manuscripts in the same collection. Likewise the Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Antwerpiensis, the great Lübeck edition, Muneratus, Grevenus, and Molanus; in these no discrepancy of any greater importance is found, as will soon become clear.]

[Note: The matter of *presbiteri* and many other such minor orthographical details was treated above in the preface, and there will often be occasion to discuss it elsewhere. I read *Circumcisio* with the Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Antwerpiensis, and several manuscripts and printed editions, as it is found in the forefront of Bede and the Romanum parvum. Usuard undoubtedly formed his entry from the earlier announcement. The Pratensis writes *Circuncisio*. Grevenus and Molanus add *secundum carnem* (“according to the flesh”), words used by the Hieronymian copies and by Bede; but that Usuard deleted them, as he often abridges much material, is proved by all the purer examples, both printed and manuscript.

I also omitted *Alippio*, although it is found in Ado—and, I think, more correctly as *Alypio* in Bede—for the same reason: this name is not found in our manuscripts and may have been deliberately omitted by Usuard, although it is quite plausible that Faltonius Probus Alippius administered the prefecture of the City in the time of Honorius, when Almachius or Telemachus was killed.

Here too, if I am not mistaken, *Eugendi*, not *Augendi*, is correctly read, contrary to the Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, and Muneratus, where *Augendus* is written for *Eugendus*. I prefer *Eugendus*, as our predecessors read it in the Acts on this day, and as Usuard ought to have read it when describing Ado. Other manuscripts cited for the text likewise show that it was read this way in ancient copies. Let others judge on which side the derivation of the French name *Oyend* lies.

In *Eufrosinae* I have preserved the spelling of the manuscript and printed copies, whatever more correctly Ado may have written as *Euphrosynae*, an orthography perhaps corrected by the editor. The distinguished Castellanus noted that in the supposed Pratensis autograph an erasure appears after *Augendi abb.*, after which, on the same parchment, *atis. Alexandriae* was written, followed by: “of Saint Euphrosina the virgin, whose life shone forth full of virtues and miracles.” This manifest transposition, to put it as mildly as possible, certainly diminishes the authority of that manuscript; nevertheless, on this first day it holds a place among the purer witnesses, though elsewhere it must often be excluded because of more serious defects.

Finally, I observe that in the Tornacensis copy a few words have been altered; nevertheless, they leave the substance of the whole matter unharmed and untouched.]

[Note: I cannot easily say why Ado omitted the Circumcision, which he took from the Romanum parvum, or why Usuard omitted the Lord’s octave, expressly included by both of those authorities and by Bede. The remaining matters concerning this first announcement are discussed in the Variants.

Almachius was first identified by Bede, without mention of his nationality or institution; hence it may be doubted whether he had Theodoretus, cited by Bollandus and others, before his eyes. Nevertheless, whether for that reason or another like it, the desire to distinguish Theodoretus’ Telemachus from our Almachius has more the appearance of a scruple than of a solid argument.

The Romanum parvum treats him more briefly but declares that he was beheaded; Ado did not venture to assert this, simply following Bede’s account. Whether Usuard and Notker copied from one or the other is left to the reader’s free judgment.

Someone may object that the very ancient Epternacensis Hieronymian copy contains a different reading—the manuscript which Florentius calls Antwerpiensis. In the specimen printed in the Bollandist preface, p. XLVI, and again in the antiquarian Propylaeum reprinted from copper plates before volume II of April, we read: “The feast of Corona, who, at the command of Asclepius, etc.” It would therefore seem that the original source of the Almachian notice must be sought in the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

But the objection is easily answered. It is perfectly clear that the confusion in that manuscript’s little column for this day must be corrected from all the other Hieronymian copies, both those edited by Florentius and those preserved among our manuscripts. To put the matter briefly, it is entirely foreign to these Martyrologies to record encomia of this kind anywhere. Moreover, the words belong not to Saint Corona—for there is no Corona here—nor to Stephen, whom one might perhaps suppose to be intended, but exclusively to Almachius.

It must therefore be concluded that Laurentius, the writer of the manuscript probably brought from England by Saint Willibrord, received the encomium either from the saint himself or from writings contemporary with Bede, and inserted it there rather inappropriately. This will be perfectly understood by those experienced in such matters and could be demonstrated at greater length if our other Hieronymian copies, closer to the genuine text, were ever printed; in none of them have we found a similar phrase anywhere.

The foolish little argument of some ignorant Englishman, deriving Almachius from *almanac*, must also be rejected. Merely to have mentioned it here is more than enough, since it deserves neither to be called an argument nor to be refuted—although the distinguished Castellanus, whom we have praised and shall often praise in the future, nevertheless did refute it.]

In our text there follows: “the corona of thirty soldiers,” which in Ado is placed after the announcement of Concordius and is taken directly from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. In those texts, Corona appears to be wrongly distinguished from the soldiers; this arrangement did not satisfy the Viennensis, nor our author, though Notker restored it.

I am not repeating what has already been said; if you want more, consult Bollandus and Florentius. At Rome, the Romanum parvum mentions Martina the virgin. Ado composed a lengthy encomium from the Acts; Notker produced a shorter version from Ado; Usuard presents only the condensed substance, as will become perfectly clear to anyone who compares them. Although Rabanus draws from the same source, he generally follows a different path.

Again, “And at Spoleto, Saint Concordius the martyr” are the words of the Romanum parvum. The encomium is Ado’s, drawn from the Acts; here Usuard gives a condensed version, while Notker’s is somewhat fuller. Rabanus again has a different account, assigning Concordius to Rome.

Basil is not known to the older Martyrologists. Notker records rather more about him, while Wandalbert sings:

> And sacred Basil shines in the honor of his merits,

and he also celebrates the Nativity of the Lord, Euphrosina, and Almachius, omitting all the others.

I myself think that the very holy bishop is purely Usuardine. As for the statement that his principal feast is celebrated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, I have so far been unable to discover, despite careful inquiry, how otherwise learned men understand this as referring to his ordination as bishop.

Finally, the Romanum parvum has: “And in the church of Ruspe, Saint Fulgentius the bishop.” Ado accepted this and praised him at greater length; Notker transcribed the encomium, while our author moderately abridged and polished it.

In Ado, Euphrosina appears in the next-to-last place, with an epitome of her life; Notker expanded it slightly, and it was copied into more recent Usuardine manuscripts, as will soon be seen. Usuard transferred little more than the name from Ado and placed it last. Bollandus, however, moved it, for the sake of the Carmelite Fathers, to 11 February. See Papebrochius’ reply, article 10, no. 44.

Eugendus belongs to Ado on this day, not the following day as Notker placed him. The words used by Usuard are composed from Ado’s wording. From these examples the reader may begin to see how true was our recent statement that Ado’s Martyrology is the source from which almost the whole of our Usuard has flowed.]

[Note: The Antwerpiensis-major inserts *secundum carnem* (“according to the flesh”). After *gladiatoribus*, it adds, with Bede, *hac de causa* (“for this reason”). In the entry for Martina, the words *sub Alexandro* and what follows are absent. It reads: “At the city of Spoleto in Tuscia.” After *triginta* it adds: “these, for confessing the true faith, under …” Of Basil it reads: “a bishop, a man of admirable faith and learning.”

Euphrosina’s life is described from Ado as follows: “She was born through the prayers of her father Paphnutius from a barren mother. When she had reached childhood, she secretly had her hair cut and sought the monastic life, taking for herself the name Smaragdus. Later, remaining for twenty-eight years in seclusion in all holiness, when she was struck by illness and recognized that death was approaching, she revealed herself to her religious father, who had repeatedly sought her with tears.” Thus far the text is from Ado. It adds: “When she had died, the faithful buried her in the church.” At the end it adds: “At Ravenna, Saint Severus the bishop and martyr.”

ROSWEYDUS. In second place he has Basil the bishop, omitting the encomium. In third place: “At Rome, Saint Martina, the wife of Hadrian. And Corona the virgin.” Then: “And the feast of Saint Almachius, under Olympius,” etc. He also reads: “At the city of Spoleto in Tuscia.” In the entry for Fulgentius, the entire encomium is absent. Finally, Euphrosina precedes Eugendus.

[Col. 0604C] PULSANEN. It is headless and lacks approximately the first four days.

ANTWERP.-MAXIM., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC. alter the order somewhat but remain sufficiently close to Usuardine purity. They uniformly begin the day as follows: “The octave of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and his Circumcision.” They then continue in second place: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the burial of Saint Basil the bishop, who in the time of Valens, distinguished for doctrine and wisdom and founded upon every virtue, shone forth wondrously.” I have no basis for determining why the manuscripts just mentioned omitted Usuard’s words about the celebration of his feast on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July.

The aforesaid manuscripts append the following to the text concerning Saint Martina: “There was a great earthquake during her passion, and on that day thirteen hundred souls believed.” The earthquake is taken from Ado; where and from whom this extraordinary conversion was transferred here, I do not know.

LOVANIEN. It begins in the same way and preserves the same order, but entirely removes the encomia of Basil, Martina, Almachius, Concordius, and Fulgentius.

CENTULEN.: “The octave of the Nativity of Jesus Christ our Lord, and his Circumcision. At Rome, Saint Almachius the martyr. Likewise at Rome, Saint Maxima the virgin.” I am still investigating who this Maxima may be; perhaps she should be joined with Magnus and Maximus, concerning whom see below under Belinus.

The manuscript continues: “Likewise on the Appian Way, twenty holy soldiers [why not thirty Corona soldiers?] who suffered under Diocletian. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Basil the archbishop and confessor. In Africa, at the city of Ruspe, Saint Fulgentius the bishop, illustrious in life and doctrine. At Spoleto, Saint Concordius the martyr. In the territory of the Jura, Saint Eugendus the abbot. At Alexandria, Euphrosina the virgin.”

BRUXELLEN. It begins: “The Circumcision of the Lord according to the flesh, and the eighth day of the Lord’s Nativity.” In the entries for Almachius and Concordius it is sufficiently pure. For Martina it has the same text as Antwerp.-Max., etc., but corrupts the name, writing *Marmena*. In the entry for the soldiers it is sufficiently pure; in that for Fulgentius it has been moderately interpolated from Ado.

Regarding Basil it inserts: “a man of admirable faith, life, and doctrine, whose principal feast of elevation …” The encomium of Euphrosina from Ado is somewhat mutilated. Then: “At Ravenna, Saint Severus the confessor.” The Hieronymian Martyrologies also mention him, but in the Acts his feast is deferred to 1 February.

“On the same day, Saint Pagoda”—by which it means Paracoda, or, as Mosander has it, Paragoda—the seventh bishop of Vienne. It continues: “In the territory of Lyon, in the monastery of the Virenses, Saint Eugendus the abbot,” etc. Finally: “At Silviniacum, Saint Odilo, fourth abbot of Cluny, who for fifty-six years ruled and advanced the monastery with wondrous religious zeal.” See below, Grevenus’ supplement.

HAGENOYEN.: “The Circumcision of our Lord Jesus Christ, when he himself was presented to the priest for circumcision on the eighth day, on which occasion he first shed blood for us sinners, showing that he had assumed a true human body.”

In the entries for Almachius, Martina, and Concordius it is then sufficiently pure. It continues: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the burial of Saint Blasius”—for *Basilius*—“the bishop. He was the first to write rules for monks, and was sent into exile by the emperor, but at last returned to his own church. The blessed Ephrem the hermit saw him on a pillar of fire, whose head was in heaven and feet on earth. He shone forth through the spirit of prophecy and, in the time of the emperor Valens, distinguished for wisdom and doctrine and adorned with every virtue, shone forth wondrously. His feast …” etc.

In the entries for Fulgentius and Eugendus it is sufficiently pure; in that for Euphrosina it does not entirely agree with the passages above. At the end, the thirty soldiers of the Corona are given in pure form.

AQUICINCT. At the end: “On the same day, Saint Maxinus the martyr.” See below concerning Magnus.

VICTORIN. At the end: “On the same day, Saint Odilo the abbot.” Then, in a later hand: “At Ravenna, Severus the bishop and martyr.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJ.: “The Circumcision of our Lord Jesus Christ. Almachius the martyr, at Rome. Thirty soldiers of the Corona. Fulgentius the bishop and confessor. Martina the virgin and martyr. Euphrosina the virgin.”

[Col. 0605D] QUEEN OF SWEDEN, under no. 130: “On the same day, Saint Odilo.”

STROZZIAN.: “On the same day, Saint Magnus the martyr.” See, as I said, under Belinus.

MEDICAEUS: “At Ravenna, Saint Severus the bishop and martyr.” The Florentine edition of 1486 partly agrees with this.

SELINENSIS OF THE FRANCISCAN FATHERS, written in a later hand: “Saint Venerius the martyr.” Could it be Severius?

THE LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION. Concerning the Circumcision, it is almost like the Bruxellensis. Then: “In the East, Saint Jaspar the king, whom the blessed apostle Thomas fully instructed in the faith and afterward ordained bishop of his own country, as he did the other two. He fell asleep in the Lord on this day, after the divine sacrifice had first been celebrated and received in the church.”

Concerning Basil, it is almost like the Antwerp.-Max., etc. Then: “At Rome, Saint Marcina the virgin and martyr, who, being of noble birth, born to a consul and exceedingly rich in possessions, which she generously distributed to the needy, was arrested by the emperor Alexander and ordered to sacrifice to Apollo. When she refused, she was subjected to various tortures,” etc., as above.

In the entries for Almachius and the thirty soldiers it is sufficiently pure. Concerning Concordius it inserts: “Who was Roman by nationality, born to Gordianus his father, and arrested,” etc. In the entry for Fulgentius it is pure. Concerning Eugendus it adds, “in the monastery of the Virenses.” What it adds concerning Euphrosina is not worth transcribing. At the end: “At Ravenna, Saint Severus the bishop.” See what has been said.

BELINUS inserts “in the monastery of the Jurenses.” He also wrote *Olympius* for *Alypius*. But the principal supplement at the end is: “On the same day, Saint Magnus the martyr,” perhaps copied from a manuscript like the Strozzianus. Molanus took this from Belinus, and no other manuscript mentions him. See the conjecture of the distinguished Castellanus in the notes, p. 15, and in the Universal Martyrology, p. 665. In any case, neither Baronius, nor Bollandus, nor anyone else has discovered anything about Magnus, Maxinus, or Maximus—at least nothing that can be applied to this martyr.

GREVENS begins with Euphrosina, almost as above. Then: “On the same day, Blessed Odilo the abbot, whose life, illustrious for virtues and miracles, Peter Damianus described in elegant style. He was the first to institute in his monasteries a general commemoration of the departed after the feast of All Saints, an institution which we see has been beneficially established in the Church. He also walked upon the waters with companions full of faith. In the East, the falling-asleep of Saint Jaspar, who was one of the three Magi. Having been taught the faith by the blessed Apostle Thomas and ordained bishop, he rested in peace. In Apulia, Potitus the martyr.” He is also celebrated on other days. See the Acts under 13 January.

“Stephen and Martin, martyrs. Secundus the martyr. Trophimus the martyr. Severus the bishop and confessor. On this day the memory is also celebrated of blessed Fulgentius, bishop of Utricoli, concerning whom Gregory, in Book III of the Dialogues, relates that, having been enclosed by the Goths within the outline of a circle, he did not feel the rain during a very heavy downpour. Corona the virgin.”

Grevenus most probably received this from some Hieronymian copy; but, as I said, there is no such virgin Corona, wrongly torn away through the copyists’ error from the thirty soldiers mentioned in the text. Besides Florentius, one may also consult the distinguished Castellanus, notes, pp. 8 and 12.

MOLANUS inserted in the text itself, in smaller Italic letters, concerning Fulgentius: “His life, full of virtues, is extant.” After “in the territory of Lyon,” he adds “in the monastery of the Jurenses.” At the end he has the same material concerning Magnus, in the same type, which he copied from Belinus; but we have already discussed him there.

This is followed, in smaller Roman type, by an encomium of Fulgentius of Utricoli taken from Grevenus. But in the preface, chapter 13, Molanus correctly observed that this Fulgentius had been placed on this day at the discretion of the Cologne Carthusians. In the Acts he is commemorated on 22 May. Castellanus commemorates him in the Universal Martyrology on 3 December.

The same type continues: “Clarus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Marcellus at Vienne and confessor, a man of great holiness. At Melun, the burial of Saint Aspasius the confessor, whose principal church is dedicated there to his name, although his life is entirely unknown. At Corbie, the burial of blessed Adelard, abbot and confessor. Ratbertus the abbot wrote his life.”

Later editions add, concerning Clarus of Vienne, “whose life is preserved.” It is also found in the Acts. Concerning Aspasius, the wording is as in the earlier edition.

There is no need, on this or any of the following days, to add the formula—whose antiquity I do not discuss here—“and many other saints, martyrs, confessors, and virgins.” The answer is: “Thanks be to God.”

[Col. 0601]

The Circumcision of our Lord Jesus Christ. At Rome, the feast of Saint Almachius the martyr, who, when he said, at the command of the prefect of the City, “Today is the octave of the Lord’s day; cease from the superstitions of idols,” was killed by gladiators. On the Appian Way, thirty soldiers of the Corona, under the emperor Diocletian. Likewise at Rome, Saint Martina the virgin, who, tortured under the emperor Alexander with various kinds of torment, finally gained the palm of martyrdom by the sword.

At Spoleto, Saint Concordius, priest and martyr, in the time of the emperor Antoninus. He was first beaten with clubs, then hung on the rack, and afterward tormented with iron in prison. There he was comforted by an angelic visitation, and finally ended his life by the sword.

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the burial of Saint Basil the bishop, whose feast is especially commemorated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July. In Africa, blessed Fulgentius, bishop of the church of Ruspe, who, having been exiled for the Catholic faith and his outstanding learning, was at last permitted to return to his own church; illustrious in life and word, he rested in a holy death.

In the territory of Lyon, Saint Eugendus [Bouillart: Augendus] the abbot, whose life shone forth full of virtues and miracles. At Alexandria, Saint Euphrosina the virgin.

## On the Fourth Day before the Nones. Day 2

[Note: Thus the Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, the first edition of Muneratus, Grevenus, and Molanus. Consequently there can be no doubt about the simplicity of the reading.]

[Note: Some write, with the Heriniensis, *Isidori*. I think that Usuard wrote it as it stands in the text. All read *Thomis*, *Argei*, *tyrones*, and *Macharii*; it must unquestionably be judged that our author read the same.]

[Note: Our first announcement was received by Usuard not from his customary source but from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Had he preserved it intact, perhaps the many different names—*Isidori, Isiridoni, Siridoni, Spiridonis, Stridonis*, and I know not what others—would not have been produced from a single original.

Most of those copies printed by Florentius read: “At Antioch, Siridon, bishop of that place.” The true form of the name will soon be demonstrated from this. In any case, this astonishing variation of names, however it may ultimately be pronounced, has exercised the minds of learned men considerably and gave Baronius the occasion to enter into the Martyrology, besides Isidore of Nitria—or rather of Hermopolis, who has been identified in some inexplicable way—another Isidore of ours, of Antioch, and another Siridon, likewise a bishop.

He honestly admits that he cannot determine to which city that bishop Siridon belonged. Bollandus, however, labors considerably to reconcile or distinguish Usuard’s Isidore and the Hieronymian Syrodon; certainly the matter is not straightforward.

Here I shall present the judgments of two learned men, leaving the reader to decide as he thinks best. Heribert Rosweydus, in a letter dated 12 May 1628, the penultimate year of his life, apparently destined for Rome and addressed to one of our number—found among his papers by our predecessors, or at least examined more carefully, in the year 1668—expresses the following judgment, or uncertainty, concerning these bishops Isidore or Siridon:

“Baronius,” he says, “cannot restore either of these bishops to his own see. If I may disclose my opinion, I greatly fear that two bishops have been produced from a single name read in different ways. For, if I reason correctly, no ancient Martyrology will be found to have these two bishops on 2 January, ISIDORE and SIRIDON; rather, the letters of the old manuscript will represent either Siridon or Isidore, according to how each reader interprets them.

I seem to infer what I am saying from the Martyrology of Jerome alone. In it—namely, in the Epternacensis—we have on 2 January: ISIRIDONI, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH. Since there were three bishops named Donus, or Domnus, of Antioch”—he might have added, “but no Isidore or Siridon”—“I scarcely doubt that one of these is intended.”

Thus Rosweydus. Bollandus produced another conjecture substantially along the same lines. But, unless I am greatly mistaken, Holstenius looked more deeply into the matter, clarified and excluded Rosweydus’ insufficiently expressed opinion, in a letter to the distinguished Florentius, dated 29 January 1658, where he says:

“Those who on the second day of January are presented by Baronius as different persons—Blessed Isidore the bishop, and shortly afterward Saint Siridon the bishop—are two false persons substituted for one, both created through ignorance of the true reading, as I discovered from the oldest manuscripts. In these the reading appears once, simply: ‘At Antioch, Syrodon, bishop of that same place.’ From this I easily perceived both the true reading and the origin of the error.

For who does not see that the reading should be: ANTIOCH OF SYRIA, DOMNUS, BISHOP OF THAT SAME PLACE? Once the true possessor of that see has thus been restored, the two substitute figures must be removed.”

If these things are true—and they can clearly be confirmed by the Martyrology of the Queen of Sweden, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Columba at Sens, which Cassiodorus, according to Castellanus, attributes to Jerome, and which Holstenius published almost in its entirety in his *Animadversions*, while we possess it among the Hieronymian manuscripts as number XIII—where it reads *Doni*; if, I say, these things are true, then Usuard’s reading is also false, although we have preserved it as the author’s pure and genuine text. See more on this in the works of the repeatedly mentioned Florentius and Castellanus.]

The second announcement, concerning the three brothers of Tomis, flows in the customary order from the Romanum parvum through Ado, and is placed second in both. In the Romanum parvum it reads: “And at Tomis, the martyrs Argeus, Narcissus, and Marcellinus.” It would have been better for Ado to leave this unchanged, for the encomium which he attributes only to Marcellinus, and which our author copied from him, was long ago observed by Notker to belong to another, although Notker himself erred in the name, writing “the bishop Phili,” while Rabanus on the following day writes “the bishop Titus.” What should probably be read is “the bishop’s son,” namely the son of Theogenes, whose Acts report the events which are rightly attributed neither to Marcellinus alone in Ado nor to him and his brothers in the more recent Usuardine manuscripts. This may be seen in the Acts under 3 January, on which day the three brothers are reported in the Hieronymian copies together with many others. Florentius’ note on that passage may be consulted.

In first place the Romanum parvum records: “Blessed Macarius”; Ado has: “The feast of blessed Macarius the abbot.” Thus far correctly, and the Hieronymian Martyrologies indicate nothing more on this day. But when Usuard, showing more initiative than his sources, prefixed “In Thebaid,” he complicated the matter; neither Rabanus nor Notker, following him, clarifies it, since they read: “At Antioch, Macarius the abbot.”

Nor do our current Supplements help, since they now identify this Macarius as the Alexandrian, and another, celebrated on 15 January, as the Egyptian. You will find this complicated and confused matter elucidated by Bollandus on this day and on the aforementioned 15 January, and summarized no less learnedly by Castellanus in his notes beginning on p. 40.

From these works you will understand how little those surnames “Alexandrian” and “Egyptian” amount to, since both men were inhabitants of Libya: the one celebrated today lived in the Cells, the other in Scetis. See January, p. 1005, no. 5, and those who after Bollandus have attempted to distinguish the Acts of the various Macarii more carefully.

Finally, let Wandalbert be heard, as he commemorates this one alone:

> Macnarius marks the fourth day before the Nones with a star  
>  
> Who, a pious inhabitant of the desert, held and taught its way of life.

[Note: [Col. 0607D]]

[Col. 0608]

ANTWERP–MAIJUS. The text is more deformed:

“In the Thebaid, the deposition of the blessed Macarius, abbot, a man of great virtues. And in Pontus, in the city of Tomis, the three brothers Narcissus, Argeus, and Marcellinus the boy. When they had been arrested among the recruits under Licinius and refused to serve, they were beaten to death and completed their martyrdom; after being tormented for a long time in prison, they were thrown into the sea. Their bodies were carried to the shore and [by] devout men [Col. 0608D] buried, and they shine with great miracles.”

He says nothing about Isidore.

ROSWEYD. “At Antioch, Isidore, bishop, and the blessed Macarius, abbot.” Of the three Tomitan martyrs he gives the text in the plural. At the end he adds: “At Jerusalem, Saints Stephen and Vitalis.” The names, separated in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, have been joined together.

PULSANEN. It is still blank.

[Col. 0609A] ANTWERP and MAXIMILIAN–LÜBECK, otherwise pure, add at the end from Usuard: “On the same day, the octave of Saint Stephen.”

MUNERATI. The more common second edition stitches onto the text: “On the same day, at the monastery of Silviniacum, the deposition of Lord Odilo, abbot.” He will recur here, although Castellanus thinks he should be placed on 31 December.

ANTWERP–MAXIMILIAN, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, DANIC, and the Belgian Utrecht edition have first: “The octave of Saint Stephen the protomartyr.” Concerning Isidore they all write: “Bishop and martyr.” Regarding the Tomitan martyrs, as though wishing to make Usuard’s construction clearer, after the words “and Marcellinus the boy,” they repeat: “who [were] Marcellinus, etc.,” so that one almost doubts whether Ado, and Usuard himself, did not write it that way. They then compose Macarius’s elogium in this form:

“This Macarius was Alexandrian; but Macarius, of whom there is an account below, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, was Egyptian by birth. Both flourished in Egypt, and both were disciples of Antony.”

See what has been said in our Observations.

[Col. 0609B] CENTULEN. “In the Thebaid, the deposition of the blessed Macarius, abbot, a man of great virtues. In Pontus, in the city of Tomis, the three brothers Narcissus, Argeus, and Marcellinus the boy. At Antioch, the passion of Saint Isidore, bishop. On the same day, the octave of Saint Stephen.”

BRUSSELS also begins with “the octave of Saint Stephen the protomartyr.” In the Tomitan entry it is sufficiently pure. Then:

“Of Isidore, bishop and martyr. In the Thebaid, the feast of Saint Macarius the Alexandrian, abbot, disciple of the blessed Antony, a man of great virtues. And of Saint Sindanus, bishop.”

This is, unless I am mistaken, another inflection of the name Syrodon, unless the reference is to Silanus.

HAGENOY. In the octave of Saint Stephen, and in the entries for Isidore and the Tomitan martyrs, it resembles the preceding witnesses; but it adds on its own:

“Likewise, in the same city, Marcellinus the boy, drowned in the sea.”

You will note that in the earlier announcement Marcellinus is not called a boy, and that the whole elogium is put in the plural. It continues:

“In the Thebaid, Saint Macarius the abbot. He was Alexandrian, [Col. 0609C] but Macarius, of whom there is an account below, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, was Egyptian by birth. Both flourished in Egypt, both were disciples of the great Saint Antony, both were men of great virtues and performers of great miracles.”

AQUICINCT. At the end:

“On the same day, Saint Spiridion, bishop. Likewise, Saint Barbatianus, confessor. At Silviniacum, Saint Odilo, abbot, holy and most blessed. The octave of Saint Stephen the protomartyr.”

[Col. 0610A] MATRIC–CARTUS–UTRECHT:

“The octave of Saint Stephen the protomartyr; Isidore, bishop and martyr; Argeus, Narcissus, and Marcellinus, brothers.”

A second hand adds: “Frontasius the martyr with his companions.” See the Acts.

CLUNIAC. “Likewise, Saint Barbatianus, confessor.” Bollandus refers this to 31 December.

CAMBRAI, Saint Mary’s: “Saint Baldulfus, confessor.”

ALTEMPS. “Saint Barbatianus, confessor. In the city of Périgueux, Saint Silanus the martyr,” in my opinion a companion of Saint Frontasius.

FLORENTIN. “On the same day, Saint Spiridion, bishop, and Saint Barbianus, confessor. He diligently searched out the deeds of the martyrs from the notaries and deposited them in the church.” But this is the carelessness of copyists, transferred here from the Adonian elogium of Antherus the pope, on the following day.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. It agrees entirely with ANTWERP–MAXIMILIAN, etc., except that at the end it adds: [Col. 0610B] “On the same day, Saint Baldulfus, confessor. On the same day, Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny.”

BELIN. “The octave of Saint Stephen.” In the remainder the text is fairly pure, and the following is appended:

“At Silviniacum, the passing [*transitus*] of Saint Odilo, abbot, whose feast, although it is observed on the Kalends, is commemorated here more fully. On the same day, Saint Spiridion, bishop.”

The later edition has *Syridon*. But enough has been said about these matters.

GREVEN. “The octave of Saint Stephen. At Jerusalem, Stephen and Vitalis. Likewise at Tubiae, Rutilia and Vitalis.” These names are to be taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. It continues:

“Stridon, bishop and confessor. Frontasius the martyr and his companions. Baldulfus, confessor.”

MOLAN. “The octave of Saint Stephen. At Silviniacum, Saint Odilo, etc.,” exactly as in BELIN. Then:

“On the same day, Saint Siridon, bishop.”

See above. Later editions place before the text, in italics: “The octave of Saint Stephen.” At the end:

“At Silviniacum, Saint Odilo, etc. At Corbie, the deposition of Saint Adalard, abbot. On the same day, Saint Siridon, bishop.”

It is remarkable that no Usuardine codex contains a commemoration of Saint Telesphorus the pope, who is celebrated today by Florus, Rabanus, and, from him, Notker, with an elogium. We shall discuss him on the fifth of this month.]

[Col. 0605]

At Antioch, the passion of the blessed Isidore, bishop. And in Pontus, in the city of Tomis, the three brothers Argeus, Marcellus [Col. 0607] [Bouillart: Narcissus] and Marcellinus the boy, who, having been arrested among the recruits under the emperor Licinius and refusing to serve, was beaten to death and, after being long tormented in prison, completed his martyrdom. In the Thebaid, Saint Macarius the abbot.

The third day before the Nones. Day 3. [Note: [Col. 0609D]

Taken from Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, Greven, and Molan. In the later editions he altered it, although in this first edition he had correctly placed it according to Usuard; accordingly, as often happens in those editions, he corrupted its text.]

[Note: [Col. 0609D]

I wrote *Antheros* with the best-attested codices. The same ending occurs in Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, and Ado, who more correctly have *Anteros*. Pratensis omits the word “pope,” which the other codices, together with the Martyrologists already cited, consistently retain. It is remarkable, however, that the title “martyr” is absent from all of them, although it is clearly expressed in the older witnesses—perhaps Usuard deliberately removed it. I printed *cimiterio*, although the codices spell it in different ways, generally in this form. Likewise *Calixti* with the last four witnesses; the Pratensis reading is *cymiterio Calisti*, as Castellanus, who consulted the source, informed me. In Herinien there is wrongly *Ellesponto*, and more wrongly in Greven *Hellesponta*; the text is better restored from the others. In *Cyricus* and *Theogenes* I preserve the reading which I judge purer from our witnesses. I write *Parisius*, according to the most anciently established usage, not *Parisiis*, as Molan repeatedly corrected it. It should be written *Autissiodorensi*, not *Altissiodorensi*, as Molan has it; but the ordinary reading of the codices, which recurs frequently, is *Autisiodorensi*. Some wrongly have *Antisiodorensi*.]

[Note: [Col. 0611A]

The Little Roman Martyrology mentions only Anterus. Ado enlarged Bede’s elogium concerning him; our author interpolated it in error, designating the tyrant as Maximian, where with Ado he ought to have written Maximin. Certainly Anterus cannot in any way belong to Maximian’s time, as is clear from his age. Nor should you understand here the Maximin who, at the beginning of the fourth century, cruelly drenched the Eastern Church in blood; the reference is to the man who succeeded Alexander after Alexander had been murdered near Mainz in the year 135, and who soon cut short the hope of the faithful for a happy and lengthy pontificate under Anterus. Here too is another error of Usuard, accepted from Bede and Ado, concerning thirteen years of pontificate; this is rightly corrected by Labbe, Papebrochius, and other chronologists. What should be thought of his martyrdom Tillemont correctly explains in volume III of his *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, p. 278. If anything from that source or elsewhere proves useful, we shall employ it in the Supplement. Florentinius, under 24 November, p. 997, mentions several matters concerning Anterus, although I do not know whether they have been devised with sufficient appropriateness. I find less objectionable what others infer concerning his ordination, perhaps performed on that day. In any case, Usuard removed some material from Ado’s elogium of Anterus, which we shall show restored among the additions from other codices. Rabanus mentions Peter Balsamus, killed by the sword, on the following day, and Notker copied his material from him. In Florus, Peter was crucified today in the city of Auclara. Bollandus teaches, in the *Praetermissa* under 11 January and today, while illuminating his Acts, that this is the same man as Abselamus, commemorated in the modern Roman Martyrology on 11 January. Castellanus follows him in his notes, pp. 50 and 170. So too Theodoric Ruinart in the *Sincere and Select Acts*, beginning on p. 554, where he reproduces the Acts published by Surius and Bollandus; wherever it is worthwhile, they should be compared with ours. Tillemont disagrees with them in volume V, p. 417. He attempts to extract two Peters from Eusebius, *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, chapter 10, and from the Acts; his arguments will have to be assessed in the Supplement. It is not known where Usuard obtained his Peter, nor am I yet persuaded that he ever saw the genuine Florus. It remains most plausible to conjecture either that he possessed Acts translated from Greek by Anastasius the Librarian, his contemporary, or at least that some information reached him from that source. Cyricus, otherwise Cyrinus, Primus, and Theogenes were taken by our author from the Epternacian Hieronymian Martyrology or one like it; on this day they are no more familiar to the usual guides than Peter, whom we have just discussed. In those Martyrologies they are assigned to Paretia; see Florentinius and Castellanus, p. 51. Concerning Theogenes, called Diogenes by others, we spoke separately on the preceding day. Florentinius considers Genovefa an addition to the Hieronymian Martyrologies; but Bede certainly mentions her, and Rabanus from him. The Adonian elogium was copied by Notker, shortened by our author, and fully recited in the additions. We now proceed to these, the Usuardine purity having been amply demonstrated. Why Florentius of Vienne, included by Ado, was omitted here I do not understand; the reader may observe with me in the course of the work that this was often done in the case of Viennese saints. I add Wandalbert’s verse in honor of Genovefa, the only one for today:

“The third day before the Nones celebrates Genovela.”]

[Note: [Col. 0611B]

ANTWERP–MAIJUS. In the first announcement, after “pope,” he adds with Ado:

“and martyr, twentieth after the blessed Peter, who, after ruling the Church for twelve years, one month, and twelve days, suffered under Maximian and was buried in the cemetery of Calixtus on the Appian Way. In the city of Aulana, the passion of Saint Peter,” etc.

The third announcement is absent. Then:

“At Paris, the feast of Saint Genovefa,” etc.; but after “she flourished,” he restored from Ado: “and grew old in Christ’s service until she was eighty years old.”

ROSWEYD. In the entry for Anterus he resembles the preceding witness. The entry for Genovefa likewise agrees with it. The second and third announcements are absent. At the end he adds from Ado:

“On the same day, Saint Florentius, bishop and martyr of Vienne, the eighth bishop of that city.”

PULSANEN. Blank on this day also.

ANTWERP and MAXIMILIAN–LÜBECK shorten Genovefa’s elogium with these words:

“She was consecrated to Christ by Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre.”

At the end they add: “And the octave of Saint John the Evangelist.”

MUNERATI. The larger and first edition also adds from Ado [Col. 0611D]: “And until her eightieth year,” etc.; the second, smaller edition adds further:

“Her body rests in the assembly of the apostles Peter and Paul, on the hill of Paris.”

ANTWERP–MAXIMILIAN, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and the Belgian Utrecht edition have first:

“The octave of Saint John the Evangelist.”

Concerning Anterus they insert:

“Who was the eighteenth after the blessed Peter, and, after twelve,” etc., purely to the end, except that some write *Dyogenes*. At the end, concerning Genovefa, they add: “and until eighty years in Christ,” etc.

LOUVAIN. It agrees entirely with the preceding witnesses, except that at the end it has deleted Genovefa’s entire elogium.

ALBERGEN and DANIC differ in this respect: after “pope,” concerning Anterus they read:

“He established, I think the text should be *ne*, that bishops cannot be transferred from one see to another; and he also diligently searched out the deeds of the martyrs from the notaries and deposited them in the church, for which reason he was crowned with martyrdom. He, the eighteenth … suffered under Maximin,” etc.

CENTULEN. “At Rome, Saint Anterus, pope and [Col. 0612C] martyr. In the city of Aulana, Saint Peter the martyr.” Cyricus, etc., is absent. “At Paris, Saint Genovefa, virgin. On the same day, the octave of the most blessed John the Evangelist.”

BRUSSELS begins with “the octave of Saint John the apostle and evangelist. At Paris,” etc., concerning Genovefa as above. “At Rome, the feast of Saint Anterus, pope and martyr. He diligently searched out the deeds of the martyrs from the notaries and deposited them in the church. For this reason he was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Maximin.” Nothing further. The entry for Peter of Aulana and the Hellespontine martyrs is fairly pure; at the end it adds: “And Saint Florentius, bishop.”

HAGENOY, with the octave placed first, invents the following after “pope” concerning Anterus:

“Who was appointed supreme pontiff against the will of the clergy by Pope Cyriacus, who suffered at Cologne with eleven thousand virgins. This Anterus governed the Church for three years, two months, and fifteen days; he was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Maximin and buried in the cemetery of Calixtus. He established that bishops could not be transferred from one see to another without the consent of the Roman pontiff. He himself diligently searched out the deeds of the martyrs from the notaries and ordered the sentence of excommunication to be hurled against rebels. He was Greek by nation and the eighteenth after the blessed Apostle Peter.”

In the next two announcements it is reasonably pure. Then, after “dedicated to Christ,” concerning Genovefa it adds:

“and consecrated with the sacred veil.”

Again, after “she grew old”:

“Of this virgin it is read that she wept from devotion whenever she looked upon the heavens. And, like Stephen the protomartyr, she often saw Jesus at the right hand of the Father. Symeon, who stood upon the column, also used to entrust himself to her prayers. Likewise, Saint Marinus the martyr.”

VICTORIN and the SWEDISH REGISTER, under number 130: “Likewise at Rome, Saint Marinus the martyr.” Is this the man celebrated on 26 December?

[Col. 0613A] MATRIC–CARTUS–UTRECHT:

“The octave of Saint John the apostle. Genovefa, virgin. Anterus, pope and martyr. Peter the martyr, who suffered crucifixion. Theogenes the martyr.”

ALTEMPS. “In the city of Périgueux, Saint Eumasius, confessor.” Castellanus has *Eumachus*, concerning whom there is nothing today in the Acts.

FLORENTIN. “In the city of Padua, Saint Daniel the martyr.” See the Acts.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. “The octave of Saint John the Evangelist and apostle.” It collected nearly everything about Anterus stated above. It is pure in the entry for Peter. Then:

“In Hellespont, Saints Cyricus and Primus, martyrs. Likewise at Cyzicus in the Hellespont, the passion of Diogenes the martyr under King Licinius, who, after many sufferings, was finally thrown into the sea and honorably buried by the faithful.”

See what we said on the preceding day about Theogenes. The entry for Genovefa and Florentius of Vienne follows as above.

BELIN. “The octave,” etc., is placed before the text, and the following is appended: [Col. 0613B] “In the city of Padua, Saint Daniel the martyr.”

GREVEN. “The octave of Saint John.” Concerning Florentius, from Ado, as above.

“In Africa, Marcialis, Ciricus, and Claudion.”

These names were transcribed, rightly or wrongly, from some Hieronymian witness, as often happens here.

“At Padua, the blessed Daniel, levite and martyr. In the year 767, he revealed to a blind man whom he had restored to sight the place where his body lay, pierced by pagans with nails through his head and all his limbs. Angela, virgin, of Foligno.”

It is better to place this on the following day with Bollandus, who notes that she was not a virgin but a widow.

MOLAN. At the end he adds the material found in both editions of Munerati. Concerning the octave, Daniel of Padua, and Florentius, see above. Then:

“Likewise, the translation of the head of Saint James the apostle,”

and in smaller type:

“Brother of Saint John. At Arras, at the monastery of Saint Vaast. Angela of Foligno. The finding of the blessed Quintinus the martyr by Saint Eligius.”

See the addition to Bede and the Acts.
