Other editions place first, in italics: [Col. 0613C] “The octave of Saint John the Evan [Col. 0614A] gelist.” They alter Anterus’s text, removing the years and substituting Maximin for Maximian—correctly, indeed, but contrary to the author’s intention. At the end, concerning Genovefa, as in the first edition. Then:

“On the third day, Saint Malachi the prophet and Saint Gordius the martyr.”

Concerning Florentius, as above.

“In the territory of Vermandois, the discovery of the body of the blessed Quintinus the martyr by Eligius, bishop, and its translation.”

Concerning the translation of Saint James’s head, almost as above. And in different type:

“On the same day, the death of Angela of Foligno.”]

[Note: [Col. 0614A]

From Rosweyd’s letter cited on the preceding day.

I call this an appendix because it does not belong to Usuard or to his additions; nevertheless, I think the observation of a very learned man concerning the Roman Martyrology will be agreeable to the reader. On this very day it celebrates “Zosimus, Athanasius, Theopemptus, and Theonas.” Accordingly, after citing the text and Baronius’s note, he begins:

“It must be considered whether four errors have been committed here. [Col. 0614B] 1. These four saints are placed as having suffered on 3 January, although Zosimus and Athanasius suffered on 4 January, while Theopemptus and Theonas suffered on 5 January, as is clear from the Menaea. The Menologion is corrupted where it reads, ‘On the third or fourth day.’ 2. These four martyrs are all said to have suffered in Cilicia, whereas the Menologion and the Menaea place only Zosimus and Athanasius in Cilicia. 3. These four are said to have suffered under Diocletian, although only Theopemptus and Theonas suffered under him; Zosimus and Athanasius certainly suffered under Domitian, as the Menologion and Menaea state. 4. The notes say that Zosimus and Athanasius suffered under the emperor Domitian; but they suffered under Domitian the governor. Cardinal Sirleto did not translate *praeside* correctly, since the Greek has *ἄρχοντι* [under the ruler/governor].”

See also Bollandus in the Acts, and Castellanus in his notes, pp. 51 and 73, where some material is brought forward for discussion in the Supplement. Add also what is said in the appendix to volume I of January, p. 1087.]

[Col. 0609]

At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of the blessed Anterus, pope [Note: [Col. 0609D] The Pratensis codex omits the word “pope,” says Sollerius, and reads *in the cemetery of Calixtus*. In both places, the text restored here by us shows that the reading of his informant was false. BOUILL.], who, after ruling the Church for twelve years, suffered under Maximian and was buried in the cemetery of Calixtus. On the same day, Saint Peter, who was put to death by crucifixion at the city of Aulana. In the Hellespont, Saints Cyricus, Primus, and Theogenes, martyrs. In the city of Paris, Saint Genovefa, virgin, who, dedicated to Christ by the blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, became widely renowned for admirable virtues and miracles.

The second day before the Nones. Day 4. [Note: [Col. 0613]

So nearly all the codices read, but complete simplicity is obtained only from Pratensis, Tournai, Munerati, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0613D]

Greven and Molan have *Eugene* instead of *Eugendus*, and *Marcianus* instead of *Martianus*; likewise, after Theodotus, they add, with several other manuscripts, the conjunction “and.” Other variations in the names occur in the codices, such as Theodorus for Theodotus, etc.; from our oldest witnesses we prefer the text’s reading and do not think that every minor detail needs to be enumerated scrupulously. All write *Tryphon*. For *religious*, some have *glorious*; many codices, however, add *woman*, a word that necessarily seems to have to be supplied, as Ado supplied it, so that the sense does not remain incomplete, since neither *glorious* nor *religious* means anything there without a substantive. In any case, what is sought is not correct syntax from us but Usuardine purity; and, unless I am greatly mistaken, that has been exhibited from the best-attested codices. Greven and Molan disagree: against the manuscripts once again, they read *they completed* instead of *they fulfilled*. Then, “afterwards” instead of “then” needs hardly any comment. Molan correctly writes *Aggaeus*, but, more correctly according to Usuard’s intention, *Aggeus*, as do others. Likewise *Gaius*, although printed witnesses more commonly have *Gaii*, *Gagii*, or *Gagi*. Munerati’s edition is insufficiently corrected and accurate here and elsewhere. Here are examples: *Affrosa* for *Dafrosa*, *to the prefect* for *to the aforesaid*, and a few other scarcely noteworthy matters.]

[Note: [Col. 0613D]

The Little Roman Martyrology again preceded Ado; Ado preceded Usuard and Notker, who today compiled almost his entire entry from Ado’s and Rabanus’s texts. What I said about our first source is most evident in the three commemorations on this day. To begin with Titus, his first remembrance in the sacred calendars is reported as belonging solely to the Little Roman Martyrology:

“At Crete, Titus, disciple of the apostles.”

In nearly these words he is celebrated by Ado in the Martyrology and from him by Notker. But the elogium was taken by Usuard from the feasts of the apostles and moderately shortened. Bollandus collected some material about Titus’s life and deeds from various sources; more recently Tillemont composed a more accurate synthesis from Scripture and the Fathers, volume II, beginning on p. 139, which may perhaps prove useful in the Supplement. The company of seven African martyrs is not known from the Little Roman Martyrology; Ado transferred it from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, adding the epithet “most illustrious martyrs.” Likewise, the deeds of these martyrs are said to exist, although our author certainly did not see them himself, since otherwise he would presumably have supplied at least some extract; nor has anyone else yet been able to bring them to light. The third announcement, concerning the Roman martyrs Priscus the presbyter, Priscillianus, and Benedicta, again first flows from the Little Roman Martyrology. The material added by Ado and shortened by our author Bollandus considers to have been extracted from the Acts of Saint Pigmenius, whom we shall discuss with Usuard on 24 March. Castellanus does not altogether reject it, so the accompanying chronological indications must be examined afresh and more accurately. Meanwhile consult the said Castellanus, pp. 66 and 808. The Little Roman Martyrology, cited for the third time, likewise simply gives Dafrosa. The brief elogium which our author borrowed from Ado is a small stream from the preceding source, not entirely pure. The marked dates of Julian’s reign are again objectionable; Castellanus argues with Tillemont that the Diocletian dates should be substituted. Dafrosa’s husband was called not Fabianus but Flavianus; concerning him and the daughters, see Bollandus today. The final group is Hieronymian, transferred here by Usuard alone from those sources, and not completely or faithfully, since the beginning is omitted, namely: “In the East.” That necessary phrase would have closed the way to countless conjectures. Against all the older texts Baronius inserted the tyrant Maximian, as Rosweyd observed in the manuscript letter cited above. There too he carefully notes that we learn from Jerome’s Martyrology—specifically the Epternacian one, which alone he saw—that Bononia here is not Bononia in Italy but Bononia in the East, or Illyricum. For there are two Bononias, he says, one in the East and one in the West; this is clear from the authorities. Thus Rosweyd, who nevertheless should have read in the Martyrology the very clearly expressed form *Bononia*. Castellanus thinks he found that Bonania or Bononia in Moesia, writing in French, “from Bodon”; see his notes for this day, pp. 66–67, and Baudrand in the *Geographical Dictionary*. Bollandus, however, noted that in our vernacular Usuardine codex of Leyden one reads *Balonia* (*Baloen*) in Thrace, which is entirely correct; the same reading is found in the published vernacular Utrecht edition. [Col. 0616B] But I think it unnecessary henceforth to cite the Belgian Leyden codex, since it agrees entirely with the other, Latin Leyden codex. Wandalbert’s verse is the only one for today; it reads:

“Then, on the day before the Nones, the festival of Eugendus returns.”

Recent writers generally think that Eugendus the abbot is commemorated here, the subject of 1 January. Bollandus largely assigns the reference to Eugene, in the African group; I think the matter requires further deliberation.]

[Note: [Col. 0615B]

HERINIEN. The entire text is very purely Usuardine; at the end it has an addition proper to the province of Rheims:

“On the same day, the feast of Saint Rigobert, archbishop of Rheims.”

ANTWERP–MAIJUS. It is mutilated. It begins:

“The feast of Saint Titus, disciple of the apostles.”

In the second and third entries it follows Ado, though it is more similar to Usuard. Then:

“Likewise at Rome, the blessed Dafrosa, wife of Fabianus the martyr.”

The remainder is absent.

ROSWEYD. “In Crete, the feast of Saint Titus, disciple of the apostles.” In the second, third, and fourth entries he copied Ado rather than Usuard. The last is absent; in its place are substituted:

“On the same day, Celsus the confessor. At Ghent, Pharaildis, virgin.”

That is, and widow.

PULSANEN. Perhaps two lines are missing; the remainder sufficiently shows that the text is close to pure. It lacks the final announcement.

ANTWERP and MAXIMILIAN–LÜBECK append to their fairly pure text:

“The octave of the Holy Innocents.”

ANTWERP–MAXIMILIAN, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC begin:

“The octave of the Holy Innocents.”

In the remainder their text is fairly pure. At the end they transpose the names Hermes, Gaius, and Aggeus.

LOUVAIN. Exactly like the preceding witnesses, but it cuts the elogium of Dafrosa.

CENTULEN. “At Crete, Saint Titus, disciple of the apostles. In the city of Bononia, Saints Hermes and Aggeus. In Africa, Saints Aquilinus … most illustrious martyrs, whose deeds, etc. At Rome, the passion of Saints Priscus … a most religious woman, who suffered martyrdom under the impious Julian. Likewise at Rome, Saint Dafrosa, wife of Fabianus the martyr, under Julian. And the octave of the Holy Innocents.”

BRUSSELS, after the octave of the Innocents, has second:

“And Saint Pharaildis, virgin, sister of the blessed Gudula, who rests at Ghent.”

Castellanus makes several observations about her which he could not distinguish because of his ignorance of the Belgian language. The entry for Titus follows, but not completely. Likewise in Priscus and his companions; in Dafrosa and the Bononian martyrs the text is reasonably pure. Concerning the African martyrs it adds:

“Who endured many contests, great punishments, and dreadful sufferings for the faith of Christ, as their deeds, which are extant, relate.”

See above.

HAGENOY also has the octave. The entry for Titus is pure. Then:

“On the same day, at Langres, Saint Gregory, bishop and confessor.”

The Africans follow, then Dafrosa, then Priscus and his companions, concerning whom the text is fairly pure. [Col. 0616C] At the end:

“In the city of Bononia, the holy martyrs Hermes, etc.”

The preceding witness also has this.

MATRIC–CARTUS–UTRECHT. “The octave of the Holy Innocents. Titus, bishop of Crete, disciple of the blessed Apostle Paul. Dafrosa the martyr. Rigobert, archbishop of Rheims.”

ALTEMPS. “In the territory of the city of Uzès, Saint Freteolus, bishop.” Molan mentions Ferrutius the martyr here, and Bollandus, in the *Praetermissa*, cites Ferrutius, Ferrutio, etc. This is Ferreolus of Uzès; see the *Praetermissa* under 1 April.

FLORENTIN. “At Nicomedia, the holy martyrs Theopemptus, bishop, and Synesius.” More will be said about them on the following day.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. After the octave comes the text, purer than usual. At the end, after Aggeus—for he is placed last here—it adds “martyrs,” and corruptly writes *Banomia* for Bononia. Then:

“At Trier, Saint Celsus, bishop and confessor of Christ, who rests in the cemetery of Saint Eucharius. At Bourges, Saint Fausta, virgin.”

See the *Praetermissa* concerning her.

“On the same day, Saint Pharaildis, virgin.”

BELIN also places the octave first. In Titus, instead of “appointed a worthy minister,” it has “a minister appointed by God,” etc. It continues:

“At Langres, Saint Gregory, bishop and confessor.”

In the remainder the text is fairly pure; at the end, “Aggeus and Gaius, martyrs.”

GREVEN. “The octave of the Holy Innocents. At Trier, Celsus, bishop and confessor. At Bourges, Saint Fausta, virgin. In Flanders, at Ghent, Pharaildis, virgin. At Langres, Gregory, bishop and confessor, whose life Vincent of Beauvais briefly abridges in the *Historical Mirror*, book XXII, chapter 52. At Nicomedia, under Diocletian, Theopemptus, bishop, and Synesius, martyrs. Likewise Neophista, virgin and martyr.”

MOLAN. At the end, after Gaius, he also appends “martyrs.” Then:

“The octave of the Holy Innocents. At Langres, Saint Gregory, bishop and confessor, whose deeds are extant. On the same day, the feast of Saint Rigobert, archbishop and confessor of Rheims. At Ghent, the feast of Saint Pharaildis, virgin. And Saint Ferrutius the martyr.”

See what we said concerning the Altemps codex. In other editions the last announcement there is deleted. They begin in italics:

“The octave of the Holy [Col. 0618A] Innocents.”

At the end, concerning Gregory, Rigobert, and Pharaildis, as above. It is followed by:

“On the fourth day, Saint Theoctistus, commander in Cucumus. And the gathering of the seventy apostles.”

Finally, in smaller type:

“At Todi in Tuscany, Saint Rogerius, confessor, of the Order of Friars Minor, whose memory is celebrated there with the consent of Gregory IX.”]

[Col. 0613]

The feast of the blessed Titus, who, ordained by the Apostle Paul as bishop of the Cretans and most faithfully fulfilling the office of preaching, attained a blessed end and was buried there, near the church where he had been appointed a worthy minister. In Africa, the most illustrious martyrs Aquilinus, Geminius, Eugendus, Martianus, Quintus, Theodotus, and Tryphon, whose deeds are extant. At Rome, Saints Priscus, presbyter, Priscillianus, cleric, and Benedicta, a religious woman; they completed their martyrdom by the sword under the emperor Julian. Likewise at Rome, Saint Dafrosa, wife of Fabianus the martyr, who, after his death, was first banished into exile and then, by order of the aforesaid ruler, sentenced to death by beheading. In the city of Bononia, Hermes, Aggeus, and Gaius.

The Nones. Day 5. [Note: [Col. 0617]

Thus many codices, but the only completely pure witnesses are Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, Antwerp, Maximilian–Lübeck, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0617B]

*Natale* for *natalis*, or the reverse, is used almost indiscriminately by Ado, Usuard, and others, and therefore is received in the same way by our codices; it is not worthwhile to keep observing the matter henceforth. I write *Thelesphorus* with most printed and manuscript witnesses, although it has been corrected in Molan. Likewise *Simeonis*, in which the codices vary greatly; today many prefer *Symeonis*. *Extitit* is also an ancient form of writing, still used by some.]

[Note: [Col. 0617B]

At the end of the entry for 2 January above, we indicated that Saint Telesphorus the pope is celebrated on that day by Florus, Rabanus, and Notker. The author of the Little Roman Martyrology first transferred him to this day in these words:

“At Rome, Saint Telesphorus, pope and martyr.”

From there he passed into Ado, who adorned him with a brief elogium, a small part of which Usuard adopted; the remainder will be supplied in the additions. Here I would have the reader observe what we said in the preface: although Florus, Rabanus, and Ado appear to have had the same Acts of the saints before their eyes, they nevertheless differ so widely and repeatedly in wording or phrasing that it is evident that one did not see the other. There is another opinion concerning Ado’s relation to Bede and Notker’s relation to Rabanus and Ado. As for the forms *Coelifloria*, *Coelesphorus*, and *Coelisphorus* in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, I do not know whether Bollandus and Florentinius have guessed correctly. Nor do I approve Castellanus, who asserts too roundly that Pope Telesphorus is found in most Hieronymian Martyrologies. Even if we granted that Telesphorus was extracted by Notker from the names cited, it would not yet follow that Pope Telesphorus is being commemorated there. See more in Castellanus’s notes, p. 79. Papebrochius will explain what should be thought of the Life of Telesphorus imposed by Zeger Paul Bollandus and inserted by him into the Acts, in his *Replies* to Article XI, beginning at number 38. Tillemont gave a shorter but more truthful account of Telesphorus’s life in volume II, p. 251. The Hieronymian copies mention the monk Symeon Stylites, once famous throughout the world and even during his lifetime; I do not see why Florentinius regards him as an interpolation, especially since the principal codices agree in reporting him. In the same witnesses the earlier Symeon is also marked, the one who received an answer from the Holy Spirit, etc. On this occasion Florentinius inserted an excursus, which the reader should consult. Both Symeons are commemorated on this very day by Florus, both by Rabanus, and from him by Notker. The Little Roman Martyrology treats only of the Stylite:

“At Antioch, Saint Symeon the monk.”

Ado provides an abridgement of his life, which Notker largely copied, while Usuard compressed it into very few words. Bollandus published more than one Life and excavated the material with the greatest care, preserving, as usual, the authors’ original phrasing. From these sources Tillemont chiefly composed his French account, embellishing it with material from Allatius’s *Symeons* and other works, in nineteen articles, volume XIV, pp. 347–392. Wandalbert joined both our saints in two verses:

“Thus the gracious confessor Symeon possesses the Nones.

Pope Telesphorus likewise shines forth with them.”]

### ANTUERP.-MAJ.

Here, contrary to custom, he appended the whole Adonian elogium to Usuard. To Telesphorus [he himself writes *Thelesforis*] he added only: “He sat [in office] for 11 years, 3 months, and 21 days.” But concerning Symeon, everything is given as follows:

> “Near Antioch, the deposition of Saint Symeon the monk. In the thirteenth year of his age, renouncing this world, he sought the enclosure of a monastery; there, with extraordinary abstinence—allowing himself food scarcely on the seventh day—he learned the Psalter in less than four months. Then, because of his excessive determination to subdue his body, he tightly bound his loins with a rope of palm branches and was severely lacerated. After that, shutting himself up in a certain well, and being forcibly brought back from it to the monastery by the brothers, he secretly fled and sought the desert. Having remained there for a long time, he enclosed himself in a lofty column, burning with holiness; from there he permitted himself to be seen neither by a strange woman nor even by his own mother. To this day no woman enters the basilica of that column, for a certain woman, dressed in male clothing, attempted to enter, but as soon as she touched the threshold, she fell backward dead.”

This last material Ado took from Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 26.

### ROSWEYD.

Here he supplies almost the entire elogium of Telesphorus [Col. 0618C] from the same Ado, adding the following to what has already been stated:

> “He established that a fast should be observed for seven [Ado: six] weeks before Easter, that Masses should be celebrated during the night of the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, and that the angelic hymn—that is, *Glory to God in the highest*—should be sung at the hour of the Mass sacrifice.”  
>   
> Then: “Also, the deposition of Simeon, who offered the Lord. At Antioch, Saint Simeon the monk and confessor, a man of admirable virtue, who stood upon a column.”  
>   
> Finally: “And Saints Felix and Amandus.”

### PULSANEN.

He begins: “The return of the child Jesus from Egypt.” Concerning this, see below, on the seventh day before the Ides, or 7 January. Then: “And the Vigil of the Epiphany.” Otherwise the entire text is sound.

### MUNERAT.

He alone inserts, after “illustrious martyrdom,” these words: “He led it under the prince Hadrian.”

### ANTUERP.-MAX., LEYDEN-BELG., LOVANIEN., and EDITIO ULTRAJ.-BELG.

They begin: “The Vigil of the Lord’s Epiphany.” Otherwise they are sound, except that concerning Telesphorus they insert, as above, “under Hadrian,” and so forth.

### ULTRAJECTIN., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC.

They also have the Vigil first. Concerning Telesphorus:

> “He established that a fast should be observed by all clerics for seven weeks before Easter; that three Masses should be celebrated on the Nativity of the Lord; and that the angelic hymn, namely *Glory in the highest*, should be sung at Mass. Finally, he underwent an illustrious martyrdom under Hadrian, and so forth.”

### CENTULEN.

> “At Rome, Saint Thelesphorus, pope and martyr, who underwent an illustrious martyrdom. At Antioch, Saint Simeon the monk, who stood upon a column, whose life was gloriously radiant with virtues and miracles.”

### BRUXELLEN.

The Vigil comes first. Then:

> “At Rome, Saint Thelesphorus, pope. He established that the angelic hymn, *Glory to God in the highest*, should be sung at the hour of the Mass sacrifice, and that three Masses should be sung on the feast of the Lord’s Nativity. Finally, under the emperor Hadrian, he underwent an illustrious martyrdom for Christ and was buried in the Vatican at Saint Peter’s.”

In the case of Simeon, he describes and abridges a large part of Ado’s elogium.

### HAGENOYEN.

Concerning the Vigil, as above. Likewise concerning Telesphorus, with an elogium almost entirely Adonian. Then:

> “Near Antioch, the feast of Saint Simeon, who was initially a shepherd of his father’s sheep and was wonderfully converted through his desire to know what the substance of the soul was. He was ordered to enter a monastery and there to be instructed concerning this matter. He did so, and progressed so far that in three months he learned the entire Psalter—only [or, I believe, ‘the whole reading’]—and the rules of the monks.”

The remainder differs little from what we have reported from Ado. At the end he adds: “At Batania, Severinus the confessor.” I find twelve Severinuses; whether this is one of them, I have not yet been able to determine with sufficient certainty.

### AQUICINCT.

Concerning Telesphorus, after “he underwent,” the following is added:

> “He established that all clerics chosen for God’s service should fast from meat for seven full weeks before Holy Easter, and that Masses should be celebrated during the night of the Lord’s Nativity, with *Glory to God in the highest* sung at the Masses.”

### VICTORIN.

He has all the same material, but with the wording somewhat altered.

[Col. 0619C]

### MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.

> “The Vigil of Simeon the monk, who stood upon a column. Of Pope and martyr Telesphorus. He established the Lenten fast. Of Edward, king of the English.”

### VATICAN.

The codex marked with number 5949 has nothing concerning Simeon Stylites; but concerning the earlier, Gospel Simeon it adds:

> “At Jerusalem, Saint Simeon the prophet.”

### EDITIO LUBECO-COL.

> “The Vigil of the Lord’s Epiphany.”

The material concerning Telesphorus is assembled from what was stated above.

> “Near Antioch, Saint Simeon the monk, who in the thirteenth year of his age renounced this world and sought a monastery, where, with extraordinary abstinence—allowing himself food scarcely on the seventh day—he learned the Psalter in less than four months. On the same day, Saint Edward, king and confessor. On the same day, Saint Verlac, hermit and confessor.”

He means Gerlacus; but how often G is changed into V, and conversely, I shall perhaps explain more carefully elsewhere.

### BELIN.

The first edition prefixes only the Vigil to the text. The second, however, after “he underwent martyrdom,” concerning Telesphorus inserts:

> “He established that Masses should be celebrated throughout the night on the Nativity of the Lord.”

At the end:

> “At Ghent, Saint Pharaildis, virgin.”

See concerning Pharaildis, on the preceding day, in the Appendices.

### GREVEN.

> “The Vigil of the Lord’s Epiphany. On the same day, Edward, king of England and confessor. Tillo the confessor. In Africa, Felix, Secundus, Honoratus, Lucianus, Candidus, Januarius. Gerlacus, hermit and confessor. At Sens, Honobertus and Henulphus, bishops and confessors. At Rome, blessed Emiliana, virgin, aunt of blessed Pope Gregory.”

Concerning her and her sister Tarsilla he says in Homily 38:

> “United by one ardor, living under the strictness of a rule in their own house, they led a common life and began, through daily progress, to grow in love for their Creator. Though they were here in body alone, each day they were passing over into eternal things.”

> “In the Thebaid, blessed Amata, virgin and abbess,” concerning whom Vincent speaks in the *Speculum historiale*, book XVIII, chapter 92.

In the Acts she is also called Talida. Tillo is treated on 7 January.

### MOLAN.

In the first edition he adds only in italic type: “The Vigil of the Lord’s Epiphany.” Then, in smaller type, he copies from Greven everything recently reported concerning Emiliana. Likewise concerning Edward and Gerlacus, but nothing concerning the others. Then, in smaller type:

> “At Barcelona, blessed Raymond the confessor, third master of the Order of Preachers. Although he has not been canonized, his feast is nevertheless celebrated by the people of Barcelona, with the consent of Paul III, on the day after the Epiphany of the Lord.”

In later editions he placed “The Vigil of the Lord’s Epiphany” first, in italic type. At the end, concerning Edward, king of the English. Then:

> “On the fifth day, Saints Theopemptus and Theonas, martyrs.”

To this may be referred what is noted here in the Appendix for 3 January from Rosweyd’s letter, where Zosimus and Athanasius are also discussed—saints whom Baronius joined to these on that day.

Molan admits that he took his Greek saints, whom he reports in the later editions, from the Greek *Horologion*, in which Theopemptus and Theonas are also celebrated on this day. It is absolutely certain that they were previously unknown to the Western martyrologists; they were transferred from the martyrology of Galesinius, or more probably from Sirlet’s *Menologion* by Baronius, although they are not commemorated by everyone on the same day.

Castellanus thinks that this Theopemptus and Theonas should be identified with Theopompus and Senesius, whom we discussed yesterday from the Florentine codices. See his note on 4 January, page 73.

The following is then found in our Appendices in smaller type:

> “At Utrecht, Gerlacus, formerly a soldier, now hermit and confessor. Also, as Metaphrastes notes, blessed Apollinaris, virgin.”

[Col. 0619]

At Rome, the feast of blessed Pope Thelesphorus, who, ordained as the seventh pontiff after the apostle Peter, underwent an illustrious martyrdom. Near Antioch, Saint Simeon the monk, whose life and conduct were sufficiently remarkable.

## Eight days before the Ides. Day 6.

[Note: [Col. 0619D]]

Thus agree the Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Belin., Greven., and Molan. Likewise the codices of middling authority: Antuerp.-Max., the Editio Ultraj.-Belg., Ultrajectin., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., and Danic.

[Note: [Col. 0619D]]

The Rhemensis and Remensis codices write this, generally following the final form. Max.-Lubec., although plainly an incorrect edition, often differs—as I have said—not so much in substance as in manner of writing; nor is there always time to examine every small detail. Thus here it reads *Rictionario*; Belin., *Riciovaro*; Antu.-Max., *Rictionaro*. The correct reading ought to be *abscissis*, but the codices commonly have *abscisis*, which must be followed. Some have the worse form *abcisis*; Greven., *excisis*.

The Usuardine reading is *migravit ad Dominum* (“he departed to the Lord”); Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. have *migravit ad Christum* (“he departed to Christ”). Some write *Melani*, as Antuerp.-Max. does, and this is better in the text.

In the final announcement various blemishes recur. In Praten. and Tornacen. it is *emigravit a saeculo* (“he departed from the world”). Antuerp. has *jugiter intentus in coelo* (“continually intent upon heaven”); Max.-Lubec., *jugiter intentus migravit* (“continually intent, he departed”); Antuerp.-Max. and others, *jugiter coelo intentus* (“continually intent upon heaven”). Finally, Belin. expands the phrase: *jugiter coelo intentus, gloriosus migravit* (“continually intent upon heaven, he departed gloriously”), and so forth; this is the reading preserved by Baronius.

[Note: [Col. 0621A]]

“Epiphany”; “the Epiphany of the Lord”; “the Epiphany of Our Lord Jesus Christ”: these are the various forms by which the Hieronymian copies express the most ancient and most celebrated feast of the whole Catholic Church.

Bede preferred the second form, which Florus expanded; Rabanus used the third. Notker, in a longer discourse, brought together various elements. The *Little Roman Martyrology*, in second place, put it this way: “The Epiphany of the Lord, that is, the manifestation or appearance of the Lord.”

Could Valesius really have perceived from this that the *Little Roman Martyrology* was abridged from Ado, when Ado wrote only “The Epiphany of the Lord”? In any event, Our author copied the words of Ado—or of Bede, or, if one prefers, of some Hieronymian copy.

Baronius and Florentinius briefly discuss in their notes several mysteries customarily commemorated on the feast of the Epiphany, and Bollandus in the Acts. But no one seems to have examined the entire matter more carefully from the beginning than Castellanus, whose learned investigations the curious reader may consult.

Nor should Wandalbert’s verse be omitted:

[Col. 0621B]

> “On the eighth before the Ides, holy Theophany is celebrated.”

Macra is not found in the Hieronymians, Bede, Florus, or Rabanus. The first to record her, and that in first place, was the author of the *Little Roman Martyrology*:

> “Saint Macra, virgin, under the governor Rictiovarus.”

I do not know which Acts served as Ado’s source. Certainly his brief elogium seems to contain more than is represented by the Acts published and illustrated by Bollandus. Tillemont discusses their critical evaluation in volume IV, pages 497 and 734.

Our author took all his material from Ado, with the wording somewhat polished; some codices preserved it intact. Castellanus refers Macra to 2 March, on which day the aforementioned Acts expressly state that she was crowned; he thinks that on this day her body was revealed or elevated.

Wandalbert did not write *Magra* or *Marcia* on 3 March; but unless I am greatly mistaken, he wrote:

> “Macra defends the Quines with pious love on the Nones.”

For some reason others transfer her to 11 June.

Concerning Melanius of Rennes, the oldest Epternacensis reads today:

> “In the city of Rennes, the feast of Saint Melanius, bishop.”

Other copies join on this very day his birth, ordination, and passing, just as Notker subsequently described them.

I do not doubt that Our author received the saint from the Hieronymians mentioned above, adding a little praise that could be applied to most saints. You have a life illustrated by Bollandus, from whom and from Castellanus you will learn what should be decided concerning the varying celebration of the feast.

[Note: [Col. 0621B]]

### ANTUERP.-MAJ.

> “The Epiphany of Our Lord Jesus Christ. In the city of Antioch, the feast of Saint Julian the martyr, Basilissa, Celsus the boy, Martianilla his mother, Antonius the priest, and Anastasius, under the governor Martianus, in the time of Diocletian and Maximian.”

Our codices place these under 9 January, but here they have been moved back to their proper day, on which they are mentioned in the Hieronymians and adorned by Florus with an elogium taken from the Acts. Concerning them, Castellanus must certainly be consulted on this day, page 105, where he gathers much material carefully and learnedly for identifying or distinguishing the Julians, with which the martyrologies are excessively crowded.

[Col. 0621C]

The codex next has Macra, who for it is Maria, and concerning whom it says only:

> “At the command of Rictiovarus, she was rolled in burning coals and, praying, departed to the Lord.”

On the same day: “The translation of the body of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, bishop, a man of admirable faith, learning, and virtues.” He is also included by others, but this should be referred to his feast on 31 July.

### ROSWEYD.

In the first edition he is sound; in the second he gives not the Usuardine but the Adonian announcement, concerning which variation we spoke above. He omits the third entirely.

### PULSANEN.

He begins:

> “The appearance of the incarnate Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ. Since its veneration is adorned by the mystery of his first miracle and baptism, it thereby becomes stronger in devotion and richer in salvation.”

The elogium of Macra has been removed. In the case of Melanius he is sound, except that instead of *Rhedonis* he writes *Seddonis*. At the end:

> “In Antioch, the feast of Saint Julian the martyr, Celsus the boy, Martianilla, Antonius the priest, and Anastasius, whose wondrous passions are read.”

Concerning these, as I noted above, see 9 January.

### MUNERAT.

> “The Epiphany of the Lord, that is, his appearance, displayed today in many ways.”

Otherwise the text is sufficiently sound.

### CENTULEN.

> “The Epiphany of Our Lord Jesus Christ. At Antioch, the passion of Saints Julian, Basilissa, Celsus the boy, Marcianilla his mother, Antonius the priest, and Anastasius, in the time of Diocletian. In the territory of Reims, the passion of Saint Macra, virgin.”

This same codex reports Macra with her companions on 2 May, but neither here nor there can it be determined who those companions were.

> “At Auxerre, the translation of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor.”

Nothing concerning Melanius.

### BRUXELLEN.

> “The Epiphany of Our Lord Jesus Christ, whom the Magi adored as an infant, whom John baptized in the Jordan when he was beginning his thirtieth year, and who in the following year changed water into wine; and who, in the next year thereafter, fed a great crowd of people with a few loaves. Thus four events coincide on this day, the first of which is celebrated as the principal one.”

See the ecclesiastical office and what Castellanus observes on page 95.

He calls Macra “Machea”; throughout the announcement he follows Ado. The complete Usuardine announcement concerning Julian, Basilissa, and their companions follows, as it appears under 9 January. In the case of Melanius he is sufficiently sound.

### HAGENOYEN.

> “The Epiphany of the Lord. Note that there is a threefold appearance of the Lord, by which he appeared today. First he appeared to the Magi, who offered him the first gifts that were offered to him in the flesh. Second, he appeared to John the Baptist at the baptism, when he heard the Father in the voice, baptized the Son in the river, and saw the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove. Third, he appeared to the guests at the wedding, when he made wine from water.”

Thus far it is sufficiently good, as above. Whether what follows can be accepted, let others judge; he continues:

> “Through this miracle that he witnessed, John the Evangelist, whose wedding this was, abandoned his wife at his voice and clung faithfully to Christ.”

In the case of Macra and Melanius he is sufficiently sound. At the end is added:

> “Also at Trier, Saint Agricola, bishop and confessor.”

He means “at Trier.” See Greven on 13 January and our Acts on the same day.

### MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTKAJ.

> “The Epiphany of the Lord. Macra, virgin and martyr. Melanius, bishop and confessor. Julian, Celsus, and companions, martyrs.”

It is correctly noted in the margin of our copy that Julian is not found on this day in the Roman Martyrology; he should have been sought under 9 January.

### CAMBERIEN, MONASTERY OF SAINT MARY

> “On this very day, Saint Saltanus and his companions, martyrs.”

In the *Praetermissi* I find Sulcanus; there Maurolycus is noted, in whom the commemoration of Sultan the martyr is observed. Bollandus suggests that perhaps Solochanus is meant, concerning whom see 17 May in the Acts.

If I may sometimes be permitted to conjecture, I would suspect that Saltanus—or Sulcanus—with his companions the martyrs is none other than Julian, under a corrupted name, and so forth.

### FLORENTIN.

> “In Antioch, the feast of Saint Julian the martyr, Celsus the boy, Martianilla, Antonius the priest, and Anastasius, whose wondrous passions are read.”

Julian recurs so often that this confirms the preceding conjecture.

### JURENSIS

For Macra, he incorrectly wrote Martha.

### REMENS. SS. TIM. ET APOLL.

> “The translation of the body of Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre.”

Concerning this, see above.

[Col. 0623A]

### EDITIO LUBECO-COL.

In both the first and second editions, otherwise sound, he inserts:

> “In the East, Saint Melchior, king and bishop, who fell asleep in the Lord on this day, after divine sacrifice had first been celebrated and received in the church.”

That is, by the same kind of death by which he earlier related that Gaspar died on 1 January. Instead of *Melanii* he writes *Melani*; otherwise he is sound.

Then:

> “At Langres, Saint Gregory the martyr, whose deeds are recorded.”

Is this not the same man who is called bishop and confessor on 4 January? See the *Praetermissi*.

> “On the same day, Saints Sulcanus and his companions, martyrs.”

See above under CAMBERIEN.

### GREVEN.

> “In the East, Saint Melchior, bishop, who was one of the three Magi and rested in peace on this day, and so forth. At Langres, Saint Gregory the martyr … Also Peter and Mark.”

From the Hieronymians, these have been separated from the others.

> “Sulcanus and his companions.”

See what was said above.

> “At the city of Famagusta in Cyprus, blessed Peter Thomas, patriarch of Constantinople, of the Carmelite order. Renowned for his life, teaching, and miracles, he rested in peace at the appointed time during the reign of Charles IV. In the city of Florence, blessed Andrew the Carmelite, bishop of Fiesole.”

Peter is referred to 29 January, Andrew to the 30th.

> “Also, the blessed memory of Gertrude of Oosten, Beguette [why not ‘Beguine’?] of Delft, who bore the stigmata of Christ impressed upon her body. Also, according to Vincent, book XIII, chapter 188, on this day blessed Julian and his companions suffered; they are placed below, on the fifth day before the Ides. Also, the holy memory of John Birellus, Prior General of the Carthusian order, conspicuous for his life and miracles.”

See the *Praetermissi*.

[Col. 0624A]

### MOLAN.

> “On the same day, the translation of the body of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, bishop, a man of admirable faith, learning, and virtues. At Famagusta, a city of Cyprus, blessed Peter Thomas, patriarch of Constantinople, a very celebrated teacher and professed member of the Carmelite order, who, after many victories over the enemies of the holy cross, after writing many books and performing miracles, happily fell asleep on the day and at the hour he had foretold. In the city of Florence, blessed Andrew the Carmelite, bishop of Fiesole, shining far and wide with the fragrance of his virtues.”

Later editions begin in italic type:

> “The Epiphany of the Lord, by which he began to be manifested to the nations when the Magi—Melchior, Balthazar, and Gaspar—adored him. On this day the Church likewise celebrates the grateful memory of his sacred baptism and of the first of all Christ’s miracles, as well as of the other miracles by which his divinity was gloriously manifested.”

At the end, concerning Peter Thomas and Andrew of Fiesole, as in the earlier edition. Then, in smaller type, concerning Raymond also, as above. Finally, in the same type:

> “At Delft, in the court of the Beguines, the death of the venerable Gertrude of Oosten. In ancient times the announcement of Easter Day was made by a deacon.”

Concerning this rite, see Castellanus, page 94.

[Col. 0619]

The Epiphany of the Lord. In the territory of Reims, the passion of Saint Macra, virgin, who, when at the command of the governor Rictiovarus she had been thrown into the fire and remained unharmed, was then afflicted by having her breasts cut off and by the filth of prison; afterward, having been rolled over extremely sharp potsherds [Bouillart adds: “and burning coals”], she departed to the Lord in prayer. At Rennes, Saint Melanius, bishop and confessor, who, after signs of virtue, continually intent upon heaven, departed from the world.

## Seven days before the Ides. Day 7.

[Note: [Col. 0623C]]

Again there is broad agreement among the codices: so the Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. Likewise Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., and the Editio Ultrajectin.-Belg.

[Note: [Col. 0623C]]

Concerning *Aegyptus*, as I have said once and will say again, I preserve the correct spelling from those codices that use diphthongs, such as Praten., Herinien., Rosweyd., and others, although many write *Egypto* or *Egipto*.

The form *presbiteri* is different, since it is the writing-form of all the codices. All our copies correctly write *Maximini* after Ado, except Max.-Lubec., where I think *Maximiani* has entered through error, as also in the more recent editions of the modern Roman Martyrology, contrary to what Baronius read.

If one appeals to the Acts published by Bollandus, I readily admit that they require considerable correction. It ought to be written *Bithyniae*, as it is in our Pratense copy and in Molan; but I follow the other codices, in which the form is simply *Bithiniae*, or, worse, *Bitiniae*.

Whether the reading in Munerat—*qui professionis gloria*—is a printer’s error or an error of Munerat’s editor, I have no means of determining.

I read *Felicis, Januarii* without the conjunction, which the purer copies—Praten., Herinien., Tornacen.—reject, although it is expressed in several others. The codices of middling authority add *martyrum*; I think this was the choice of a copyist.

[Note: [Col. 0623C]]

The Hieronymian codices nowhere mention the Return of the Child Jesus from Egypt, unless the old Gellonense is brought into the discussion. It was published by Acherius in volume XIII of the *Spicilegium*, and at the very end reads:

> “The bringing of Jesus out of Egypt.”

Bede and Florus are also silent. Rabanus, however, has on 11 January:

> “The bringing of the Lord out of Egypt.”

When Notker transcribed these words from that day, he added:

> “According to some, it is celebrated on the seventh day before the Ides of January; according to others, on the Nones of January, because of the journey lasting many days.”

Let that explanation stand, if it can; Castellanus will provide a more probable one.

The root and source of our text is the *Little Roman Martyrology*, whose very words passed clearly from there into Ado, and from Ado into Our author. Wandalbert likewise included no more than this in his verse:

> “The seventh celebrates Christ brought back from Egypt.”

Concerning the illustrious martyr Lucian, the Hieronymians have:

> “At Nicomedia, Lucian the priest, who was made into four parts,”

or:

> “who was plunged into four parts.”

Concerning this dismemberment and drowning, and also his restoration to wholeness, see Florus’s elogium.

The *Little Roman Martyrology* records him thus:

> “And Saint Lucian, martyr of Antioch.”

The encomium entered in the list is Ado’s, but Our author altered it somewhat and reduced it by nearly half; Notker mixed it almost entirely with Florus’s words.

Much could be observed concerning this most renowned martyr, but I prefer that the reader seek it in Baronius, Bollandus, Florentinius, and Castellanus. Ruinart had John Chrysostom’s homily, appended by Bollandus to the Acts of whatever quality, reprinted among the *Sincera et Selecta*, beginning on page 559.

The prefatory notice there, and the Gallic life composed by Tillemont from various sources in volume VI of his *Life*, page 474, may be considered in the Supplement, when the Greek passion from the parchment manuscript of Father Sirmond—or of our Parisian college—on 15 October, together with other material of this kind, if it proves worthwhile, will be brought here and illustrated.

Wandalbert composed this verse concerning Lucian:

> “The Antiochene people also commemorate their own Lucian.”

Thus Florus commemorates Cleri the deacon, in a way that seems to produce at least two men from one, though not many, as Castellanus wrongly rendered his words. For he reads:

> “Also, Clerici and the deacon, who were tortured seven times, and so forth.”

Who could render this in French as “*les clercs et les diacres*” unless the Latin were *clericorum et diaconorum*? The most learned man certainly knew that the names of martyrs are announced not in the nominative but in the oblique case.

The Epternacensis Hieronymian codex mentions today Lucerius the deacon, who recurs in the same codex on the 14th, where others have Cleri or Cleti; then again on the 15th under the name Luceris the deacon, with others reading Licerius or Lecerius. In all likelihood this is the same man, simply recorded by the *Little Roman Martyrology* as:

> “And Cleri the martyr.”

It is uncertain from where Florus or Ado derived their brief elogia, since no Acts are known to exist, at least not any that are extant. This is certain: Our author and Notker rendered Ado word for word.

Felix and Januarius were accepted by Usuard from the Hieronymians; in those codices they are again placed on 14 February, as Bollandus thinks, and Florentinius does not strongly object. Here he congratulates Our Master for not having listened to the fables of Bivarius and similar writers.

This is sufficient concerning the origin of the Usuardine text.

[Note: [Col. 0625A]]

### ANTUERP.-MAJ.

With the opening transposed, it reads:

> “The return of the child Jesus from Egypt. On the same day, the feast of Saint Lucian, priest and martyr of the Church of Antioch, a most learned and eloquent man.”

In this it again approaches Ado.

> “Also, near Antioch, Bilicerius [instead of Cleri], the deacon, who on account of his confession of Christ, and so forth.”

This is sound. But the final announcement is entirely absent.

### ROSWEYD.

Rather Rabanian than Usuardine, he begins:

> “The bringing of the Lord out of Egypt. At Nicomedia, Lucian the priest, who during the persecution of Maximian was broken into four parts and plunged into the sea, but on the following day was found whole. Also, near Antioch, blessed Clerius, deacon and martyr.”

Everything else is absent.

### PULSANEN.

He is otherwise quite sound, except that here he omits “The return of the child,” and so forth. From this source we reported it under the Nones in the Appendices there, perhaps following the custom of those who were accustomed to recite the Gospel concerning the return of the child Jesus on 5 January.

### ALBERGEN.

To a sufficiently sound text he appends:

> “At Dortmund, Saint Reynold, martyr, a man of exceptional virtue, whose deeds are recorded.”

From this the codex seems clearly to indicate its homeland.

### DANIC.

> “Also in Dacia, the province of Zealand, the passion of Saint Canute, duke and martyr.”

In the preceding material it is sufficiently sound.

### CENTULEN.

A continuous abridger of Usuard, he is sound in the first part. Then:

> “On the same day, Saint Lucian, priest and martyr of the Church of Antioch, a most learned and eloquent man. Also at Antioch, blessed Licerius, deacon and martyr.”

In the final item concerning Felix and Januarius he is likewise sound.

### BRUXELLEN.

> “The return of the seven-year-old child Jesus from Egypt into Nazareth, where a stone is shown on which he is said to have lain at night and sat by day for twenty-three years. The fragments of this stone are rightly venerated by Crusaders and pilgrims as though they were relics of the saints.”

Concerning Lucian, after “Maximian,” it has:

> “He was torn into four parts and bound to four stones, then sunk into the sea; but on the following day his body was found whole at Helenopolis in Bithynia and was buried there.”

See Notker. In the case of Clerius it is sound; in that of Felix and Januarius it resembles the codices of middling authority. Then:

> “Elsewhere, Tillo the monk. Also Saint Valentinus, bishop. Also Saint Luciana, virgin.”

Bollandus discusses Tillo and Valentinus; but which Luciana is meant, I confess that I do not know.

### HAGENOYEN.

> “The return of the child of Our Lord Jesus Christ from Egypt, when Joseph his foster-father obeyed the angel’s admonition and returned with Jesus, his mother the Virgin Mary, and the rest of his household from Egypt to the land of Israel. This return took place after the death of Herod and his other friends.”

This conforms more closely to Sacred Scripture than what we presented above from the Brussels codex. Everything else is sufficiently sound.

### MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.

> “The return of the child Jesus from Egypt. Lucian, priest and martyr of Antioch.”

[Col. 0626A]

### CODEX BICOTIAN.

Marked D. 9:

> “Also at Fécamp, the translation of the holy bodies that rest in the same church.”

This undoubtedly indicates Saint William, and perhaps others resting in that famous monastery.

### CAMBERIEN, MONASTERY OF SAINT MARY

> “On this very day, Saint Isidore, bishop, a man of great holiness.”

This Isidore is nowhere better known, as you will understand from the list of the *Praetermissi*. Hence the material concerning the Isidores belongs to 2 January.

In the VATICAN codex, number 5949, the final announcement concerning Felix and Januarius is absent.

### EDITIO LUBECO-COL.

It begins:

> “The return of the child Jesus from Egypt, in the sixth year of his age, in the forty-eighth year of the reign of Augustus Caesar, and in the thirty-eighth year of the reign of Herod, who had then died.”

What follows concerning Lucian is sufficiently sound. Then:

> “At Dortmund, Saint Reynold, martyr, a man of exceptional virtue, whose deeds are recorded: he suffered at Cologne, but was given to the people of Dortmund.”

In the two other commemorations the text is also sufficiently sound. Finally:

> “At the monastery of Solignac, blessed Stillo [others read Tillo and Hellonius, as in Bollandus], monk and confessor. On the same day, Saint Canute, duke and martyr.”

He must be distinguished from the one whose Acts we shall give on 10 July, although his office is celebrated in the Church on 19 January. See Bollandus on this day, beginning at page 390.

### BELIN.

He reads the first item as follows:

> “The return of the child Jesus Christ from Egypt.”

Instead of *Maximini* he has *Maximiani*; otherwise the text is sound. He adds:

> “On this very day, Saint Julian. Also at Pavia, Crispinus, bishop and confessor.”

Concerning Julian, I should note that he is reported here simply and without any addition. Baronius, however, who had Belin before his eyes, for some reason applied to him the title “martyr.”

Bollandus, without having sufficiently examined the matter, multiplied the Julians, inserting one in the Acts for today who will probably later have to be excluded.

Castellanus thinks that this is the same Julian whom we discussed yesterday and shall discuss again on 9 January. But, unless I am mistaken, this is another Julian, neither a martyr nor a keeper of a hospice. Belin added him to Usuard from particular knowledge, as Rosweyd also judged before me in the manuscript observations cited above more than once. He observes as follows:

> “I scarcely doubt that it should read: ‘On the same day, Saint Julian,’ with ‘martyr’ omitted. First, because this is how the old Roman Martyrology of Belin represents him, printed one hundred years ago at Venice and Paris. Second, because I think that the Julian intended here is Julian the confessor of Novara, who was the deacon of Saint Julius the priest, whose feast occurs on 7 January in Ferrarius’s *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*.”

Thus Rosweyd.

Further material concerning such new additions to the modern Roman Martyrology may be supplied by Papebrochius’s *Responses*, part II, article 18, in the appendix, where Nicetas is specifically discussed from Holstenius’s letter to Florentinius.

Nor should another observation by the same Rosweyd concerning this very day be omitted, regarding “Theodore the monk, who lived in the time of Constantine,” and so forth.

[Col. 0627A]

After first giving the text together with Baronius’s note, Rosweyd says:

> “Here I ask: first, on what authority from an ancient book is this Theodore placed here on this day, since he is not found in the ancient Roman Martyrology? Second, how can Baronius say in his notes that this Theodore was a disciple of Saint Antony—something he repeats in his note on 28 December because of another Theodore—and derive and prove this from the *Life of Antony* written by Athanasius, when Athanasius in chapter 32 of the *Life of Antony* does not say that he was a disciple of Saint Antony, but of Ammonas of Nitria, as is also found in chapter 1 of the *Life of Saint Pachomius*, on the authority drawn from that same life of Antony written by Athanasius? Palladius says the same in chapter 8.”

### GREVEN.

> “The return of the child Jesus took place in the sixth year of his age, in the forty-eighth year of the reign of Augustus Caesar, and in the thirty-eighth year of the reign of the deceased Herod.

> At Dortmund, in the diocese of Cologne, the translation of Saint Reynold, monk and martyr. Born of illustrious lineage and vigorous in arms, he became a monk at Saint Pantaleon’s in Cologne, renowned for his life and miracles. He was killed by the masons over whom his abbot had placed him in charge and was thrown into a lake. From there, when the Lord revealed the matter, he was recovered and given to the people of Dortmund.

> Also, Canute, duke of Slavia, martyr, son of the king of Dacia. At the monastery of Solignac, blessed Stillo, monk and confessor. Fausta, virgin and martyr.”

See Rabanus, Notker, and the index of the *Praetermissi*. She is celebrated on 20 September.

> “Melania the elder, Roman senator.”

See the *Praetermissi*.

> “Also, the holy memory of Duke Wedekind of Westphalia, resting at Enger.”

Read from the Acts: Wittekind, duke of the Saxons, and Enger.

MOLAN: “On that same day, of Saint Julian. Also at Pavia, of Crispin, bishop and confessor. At the monastery of Solignac, of blessed Stilo, monk.” Then, in smaller type: “At Dortmund, in the diocese of Cologne, the translation of Saint Reinold, etc.,” as above, except that here, after “was given to them,” the following is added: “They had most devoutly asked the archbishop of Cologne to give them the body of some saint, so that their land might be held in greater reverence and be safer from enemies. Also, of Canute, duke of Slavia, martyr, son of a king of Denmark.” In other editions, concerning Julian and Crispin, as in the first. Then: [Col. 0628B] “On that same day, of Saint Canute, duke of Denmark and martyr, son of King Eric. At the monastery of Solignac, of blessed Stilo, monk.” Then, in smaller type: “At Padua, of the most blessed Valentine, bishop of Rhaetia.” Finally, concerning Reinold, with a few changes that contribute nothing to the substance of the matter.]

[Col. 0623]

**The return of the boy Jesus from Egypt.** On the same day, of blessed Lucian, presbyter of the church of Antioch and martyr, who, distinguished enough for learning and eloquence, suffered at Nicomedia for confessing Christ under the persecution of Maximinus, and was buried at Helenopolis in Bithynia. Near Antioch, of Saint Clerius, deacon, who, tortured seven times for the glory of his confession and long weakened in prison, was finally beheaded and completed his martyrdom. At Heraclea, of Felix and Januarius.

**VI Ides. Day 8.**

[Note: [Col. 0627B]

Thus, in its original purity, the Pratense, Heriniense, Tornacense, Pulsanense, Grevenian, and Molanian copies read it. Molan, however, incorrectly altered the text in his later editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0627C]

The Pulsanense writes *Neapolis* incorrectly instead of *Neapoli*, just as it has *Beluati* instead of *Beluaci*. I have retained *Beluacus*, in the ancient manner, with the older Pratense and Heriniense manuscripts; Florus also used this form. The Tornacense writes *Beluago*, while others have *Beluaci* or *Beluaco*. In the Pulsanense there is “Lucian, bishop; Maximian, presbyter; and Julian, deacon.” But these titles do not properly belong to the persons named later: Lucian is no one other than the man placed in the text. Moreover, of his companions, the first should not be read as Maximian, as Florus incorrectly has it, nor as Messianus, as Ado has it, but, according to nearly all our manuscripts, as Maxianus; the French analogy also demonstrates this, as Castellanus shows on page 135. Molan wrote *Maximiniani*, Greven *Maximiani*, as did Belin, whom Baronius undoubtedly followed. The Pulsanense translates *viva voce confiteri* (“to confess with a living voice”) simply as “in one voice,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0627C]

The entire first announcement, or encomium of Severinus, has plainly been abbreviated from Ado, while retaining the confusion among the Severini that was taken from the *Small Roman Martyrology*, its first author—or, as someone else might say, its seducer—and accepted by Ado. Bollandus and Castellanus corrected this on the present day; for Severinus, bishop and brother of Victorinus of Amiternum, is sought in vain at Naples, since he is to be found among the people of Septempeda. See what we say on 5 September; the matter will be examined more fully in the Acts at its proper time. Molan noticed the confusion, but wrongly removed it from the text of Usuard in his later editions, whereas he ought to have preserved the text intact and corrected what required correction in the notes, as he does elsewhere. For it is certain that Usuard read “Severinus, bishop and confessor, brother of the most blessed martyr Victorinus,” just as he had found it written in Ado.

Among the Hieronymian copies, only the Corbie manuscript today mentions the apostle of Beauvais and his companions in the following manner: “In Gaul, in the city of Beauvais, the passion of the holy martyrs Lucian, Marian, and Julian,” where *Marian* is read through a slight error instead of *Maxian*, elsewhere called *Massian* or *Messian*. Bede says nothing about these martyrs. Rabanus placed only Lucian the presbyter, with an encomium, on 4 January; Notker copied his words there, while on this day reading again: “At Melloacia” (for *Bellovaci*), “of Saint Lucian, companion of blessed Dionysius.” [Col. 0628C] He also has “of Messianus,” which might seem to have been taken from Ado, were it not for the mention of Dionysius; for Ado himself simply says: “At Beauvais, of Saints Lucian and Messianus.”

From this, however, conclude that no Acts were known to Ado that Usuard certainly consulted, especially those written by an anonymous author, from which he very plainly extracted his encomium. Or did he also use Florus? Castellanus thinks so, on page 131, persisting in a preconceived opinion: namely, that Usuard inspected the additions of Florus of Lyon to Bede. I, however, believe that Usuard never saw them, since he knew no other Florus than those more favorable or more extensive traces that are the very Martyrology of Ado, as we demonstrated in the preface, without Castellanus disagreeing with us on this point. To make the present text of both an example, I appeal to your own eyes, reader: compare the encomium of Florus with our Usuardine text, and I shall surrender if it appears, even in the faintest outline, to have been abridged from it.

Learned critics debate the reliability and sincerity of the Acts; among them the aforementioned Castellanus made many careful observations, as did Tillemont in volume IV, beginning on page 537. These may perhaps be examined more accurately in the Supplement. Usuard gave Eugenianus as an otherwise unknown martyr, although no one under this inflection is found anywhere. For if he consulted the Hieronymian Martyrologies, however much expanded, he found there no one but Egemonium, Egonomium, or Aegemonum, and that with the title of bishop, as Rabanus also expressly indicates. Eugenianus, whoever he may have been, is unknown to the older sources, unless one accepts Wandalbert, who fitted him into verse as follows:

> On the sixth after the Ides, vows are offered to Eugenianus.

Bollandus, with keener judgment, considered it highly probable that Eugenianus was the same person as Egemon or Hegemon (however the name may be inflected), bishop of Autun. Indeed, he would have considered this certain with Castellanus, had he not attributed too much weight to Saussay. Several of the following additions fall into the same error, of which we shall often hear concerning the same matter.]

[Note: [Col. 0629A]

**ANTWERP–MAURISTS:** “At Naples in Campania, of Saint Seve—[read: Severinus] the confessor, brother of the most blessed Victor, a man most illustrious for miracles. At Beauvais, of the holy martyrs Lucian the presbyter, Maximian, and Julian. Maximian and Julian were first punished by the persecutors with the sword. Then blessed Lucian, after enduring excessive slaughter,” etc. The final announcement is entirely absent.

**ROSWEYD:** “Near Naples in Campania, of Saint Severinus the confessor, brother of the most blessed Victorinus, a man most illustrious for miracles. He too, imitating his brother, after the marks of many virtues, full of holiness, rested in peace. At Autun, of Eugenius, bishop and martyr.” In this respect the manuscript approaches the truth as much as it departs from Usuard. “At Beluago, of the holy martyrs Massian, Lucian, and Julian. At Regensburg, of Herhard, bishop. Also, of Eucherius, bishop.”

**MUNERAT:** To the otherwise sufficiently pure text he adds: “At Reims, of blessed Rigobert, bishop and confessor.” See 4 January. “In Greece, of Saint Timothy. Near Brussels, the birthday of Saint Gudula, virgin. At Metz, of Patient, bishop and confessor.” This does not seem to concern the Timothy whom Usuard places on 22 January, but another. See the Acts.

**ANTWERP, MAXIMILIAN–LÜBECK, and UGHELLIAN**, whose manuscripts generally agree, add at the end after the text: “In Greece, of Timothy; at Autun, of Eugenianus.” Max.-Lübeck incorrectly has *Eugemani*.

**ANTWERP–MAXIMILIAN, LEYDEN, ALBERG, DANIC, and the ULTRAJECTINE–BELGIAN EDITION**, concerning Lucian, insert “blessed Peter’s disciple.” To the text they add: “In Greece, of Saint Timothy. At Autun, of Saint Egemon or Eugenion, bishop. Near Brussels, the birthday of Saint Gudula or Gudila, virgin. At Metz, of Patient, bishop and confessor.”

**LOUVAIN** is similar to the preceding copies, except that it has omitted the encomium of the people of Beauvais.

**UTRECHT** is shortened by the announcement of Saint Gudila; otherwise it agrees with the copies just mentioned.

**CENTULAN:** “At Naples in Campania, of Saint Severinus, bishop and confessor, brother of blessed Victorinus the martyr. In the city of Beauvais, of Saints Lucian, Maxian, and Julian.” In its final part it is pure.

**BRUSSELS** begins: “Burial of Saint Gudila, virgin, our patroness. The relics of her sacred body are venerated here. In Greece, of Saint Timothy. At Beauvais, of the holy martyrs Lucian the presbyter, blessed Peter’s disciple, and Maximus the presbyter and Julian the deacon. They were punished with the sword for confessing Christ, after many tortures. Near Naples in Campania, of Saint Severus, bishop and confessor, brother of blessed Victorinus the martyr, renowned for miracles. He too, imitating his brother, full of holiness, rested in peace.” In this respect it surpasses various manuscripts: whereas those manuscripts forged two false names from the genuine name Eugenianus, this one writes only: “At Autun, of Saint Eugenion, bishop; at Metz, of Patient, bishop and confessor.”

**HAGENOYEN** also slightly varies the wording: in the first section it is relatively pure; in the second it likewise inserts “disciple of Saint Peter.” Then: “On the same day, of Saint Eugiminianus, martyr. In Greece, of Saint Timothy. At Autun, of Saint Eugenion, bishop. In the city of Metz, burial of Saint Pacient, bishop and confessor. Near Brussels, of Saint Gudila, virgin. At Regensburg, of Erhard, bishop. At Verona, of Saint Rusticus, confessor.” He is honored there, as a martyr, on 9 August.

**AQUICINCT** correctly writes *Maxiani* in the text. After [Col. 0630A] the pure text it adds: “In Greece, of Saint Timothy. At Autun, of Egemon, bishop.”

**VICTORIN** and the **SWEDISH REGISTRY**, marked number 130, likewise write: “In Greece, of Saint Timothy. At Autun, of Egemon, bishop.” The later manuscript has “Egemon.”

**MATRICIAN, CARTUSIAN, and UTRECHT:** “Of Lucian the presbyter, Maximian and Julian the martyrs, Severinus the bishop and confessor. Of Patient, bishop, disciple of Saint John the Evangelist. At Brussels, of Gudula, virgin. [Col. 0630B] She was lifted from the sacred font by Saint Gertrude.”

**The CODEX OF DOM DU CHEVAL**, marked B, and the **FLORENTINE** copy: “In Greece, of Saint Timothy.”

In the **VATICAN MANUSCRIPT**, number 5949, Eugenianus is absent. It adds again: “In Greece, of Saint Timothy.”

**ALTEMPS:** “Burial of Saint Ulfrin, bishop. Translation of Saint Judoc.” See 13 December. “Also, burial of Saint Pega, virgin.”

The **LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION**, slightly interpolated in its first and second forms, is pure in the third. The additions follow: “In Greece, of Saint Timothy the confessor. At Autun, of Saint Egenion, bishop and confessor. Near Brussels, the birthday of Saint Gudula, virgin. In the city of Metz, of Patient, bishop and confessor. On the same day, of Saint Erhard, bishop and confessor of Regensburg. On that same day, of Saint Afflin, bishop and confessor. At Troyes, of Saint Frodobert, abbot.”

**BELIN** writes: “Of Victor: at Belvati, of Lucian, bishop; Maximian, presbyter,” etc. Before Eugenianus he inserts: “On the same day, of Saint Maximus, bishop and confessor of Pavia.” At the end: “In the city of Metz, of Patient, bishop and confessor.” The second edition adds: “In Greece, of Timothy. At Autun, of Egemon, bishop.”

**GREVЕN:** “Of Agmon, [elsewhere Egenion], bishop and confessor of Autun [elsewhere martyr]. In Greece, of Saint Timothy the confessor, who was transferred to Constantinople on 9 May. Near Brussels, of Saint Gudula, virgin. At Metz, of blessed Patient, bishop and confessor, disciple of blessed John the apostle. On the same day, of Saints Erhard and Heribald, bishops and confessors of Regensburg.” The first edition speaks only of Erhard; see the Acts. “Of Saint Afflin, bishop and confessor. At Troyes, of Saint Frodobert, abbot. At Reims, of blessed Rigobert, bishop and confessor. Of Severinus, abbot, who, after Attila, king of the Huns, had died, became renowned through prophetic spirit, life, and miracles. On the same day, of Saint Maximus, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0630D] MOLAN, concerning Patient of Metz, Maximus of Pavia, and Rigobert of Reims, has as above; his account of Gudila is much more extended, as follows: “Burial of Saint Gudila, virgin, our patroness, whose sacred bodily relics are venerated here.” Thus far from the Brussels copy; he continues: “At her tomb near Ham in Brabant, during the winter season, a poplar tree suddenly grew up without the hands of pruners, and became green and leafy like a grove. Both things were marvelous: it was marvelous that the tree suddenly sprouted, and even more marvelous that during winter it flowered, although nature does not grant this. But God did both, by the operation as he knew and willed, and by the power he possessed, as a testimony to that same virgin in the house of the Lord, like a flourishing palm. On that same day, of Saint Afflin, bishop.” Concerning Frodobert, as above. Then, in smaller type: “On the same day, of blessed Laurence Justiniani. And of Erhard, bishop and confessor of Regensburg. At Laon in Gaul, of blessed Baldwin, archdeacon and martyr. [Col. 0631A] His deeds are contained in the life of his mother Salaberga. In Noricum, burial of Saint Severinus, abbot, who became widely renowned through the spirit of prophecy and miracles, and was transferred near Naples to the castle of Lucullanum.” We have discussed above at length the alteration made in the later editions. The additions too have been abridged. Thus, at the end: “At Autun, burial of Saint Egemon, bishop and confessor.” [Col. 0632A] After “became leafy” in the account of Gudila, he joins together the words “both things were done by God,” etc. The account of Frodobert follows, as above. Then: “At Regensburg, of blessed Erhard, bishop and confessor.” Next, the accounts of Patient and Maximus, again as above. Finally: “On the eighth day, of Saint Dominica, mother; and of the holy fathers George Chozebites and Aemilianus the confessor.”]

[Col. 0627]

At Naples in Campania, the birthday of Saint Severinus, bishop and confessor, brother of the most blessed martyr Victorinus. Severinus, after accomplishing many virtues, rested full of holiness. At Beauvais, of the holy martyrs Lucian the presbyter, Maxian, and Julian; Maxian and Julian were first punished by the persecutors with the sword. Then blessed Lucian, after excessive slaughter, because he had not feared to confess the name of Christ aloud, also received the sentence imposed on the former two. On the same day, of Saint Eugenianus, martyr.

**V Ides. Day 9.**

[Note: [Col. 0631B]

Thus read nearly all the Usuardine manuscripts that I have been able to consult, or that our predecessors, together with Greven and Molan, formerly compared. So too do Max.-Lübeck, Munerat, Belin, and all the others who have so far published Usuard, however much expanded. The Pratense manuscript alone differs from the others, as I shall explain shortly in the Variant Readings. Those who cite two Pratense manuscripts increase the number, not the authority, since one was copied from the other, with only additions or marginal material transferred into the text, as explained in the preface.]

[Note: [Col. 0631C]

I pass over here such minor details as *Anthiochiam*, *Dioclitiano*, *Dyocleciano*, *Basiliscae*, and similar forms. With the Pratense, Heriniense, Pulsanense, Munerat, Greven, and nearly all the varying manuscript and printed copies, I wrote “Basilissa the virgin” without an addition. Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, and Lübeck–Cologne read “Basilissa, his wife,” as do most of the middle-quality manuscripts. Others have “his spouse.” Belin and Molan, however, have “Basilissa the virgin, his wife.” I judged the older manuscripts preferable, although the *Small Roman Martyrology*, and Ado after it, expressly give “wife” or “spouse.”

I likewise preferred these same manuscripts, which agree here with Ado in the name *Antoninus*, against other printed and manuscript copies that transformed *Antoninus* into *Antonius*, and which Baronius, Bollandus, and others commonly imitate today. [Col. 0631D] There remains a somewhat more difficult problem, in which I said above that the Pratense differs from all the others. Omitting Martiana and the martyrs of Smyrna, it concludes the day as follows: “In Africa, of the holy martyrs Revolutus and Firminus, with three others.” Castellanus, who inspected the manuscript himself, observes in the First Bimester, page 809, that a leaf was once torn from that alleged autograph and later restored in an ancient script; on it, perhaps, as he conjectures, the change was made while Usuard was still alive. But I cannot understand how anyone could be persuaded of this, in the face of the clearest contradiction from the common and especially reliable Usuardine manuscripts. Whoever the interpolator was, he incorrectly wrote *Revolutus* instead of *Revocatus*. For the time being, therefore, we have judged that the genuine reading of Usuard should be defended. Some write *Marciana*; with the earlier copies, the *Small Roman Martyrology*, and Ado, we write *Martiana*. Manuscripts of middling quality add “deacon” after Fortunatus, while Belin added “martyrs.” I write *Smyrna* with the manuscripts generally.]

[Note: [Col. 0631D]

The very famous martyr Julian and his companions should already have been treated above, on 6 January, as some maintain, the day on which the Hieronymian Martyrologies place them in this form: “At Antioch, the passion of Saint Julian and Basilissa. In India, of Celsus and Julian.” On the same day, together with the longer narrative drawn from the confused Acts, all are mentioned by Florus. Rabanus assigns them to 13 January; Wandalbert to 13 February. The transposition of this feast is remarkable; Castellanus believes it arose because of Epiphany, as did the multiplication of the name Julian, to such an extent that the number given by him on page 106 almost exceeds belief.

Usuard followed his usual predecessors, with the *Small Roman Martyrology* leading the way: “And of Saint Julian, and Basilissa his wife, and Celsus and Marcionilla, and twenty soldiers.” To this Ado attached a long series from the Acts, already accepted in his own time, to be evaluated according to their reliability. Our author, without hesitation, abbreviated his encomium from that material, while Notker transcribed more of it.

Bollandus had performed excellent work in illustrating the aforementioned Acts of these saints, but Papebrochius later examined them more carefully in volume III of the May series, page 295, and more fully in the *Responses*, volume II, article 15, section 28, beginning at number 316. The reader should consult him, and also the curious observations of Castellanus on the various symbols of Julian and other matters relating to his extremely widespread cult, already cited once and again above; these too will not be useless in the Supplement. Tillemont offers a few remarks in volume V, pages 799 and 809, in connection with Julian of Cilicia, concerning whether he should be identified with the present Julian, or whether this Julian should rather be called the Antiochene or Antinopolitan, Syrian or Egyptian; the question remains undecided.

But those who demand that the Julians be confused because both are said to have suffered under the governor Martianus should consider whether another Julian should not also be included: the one produced by Florus on 11 January, who likewise suffered under the governor Martianus, but in Achaea and in prison. We have already begun to discuss Martiana in the Variant Readings. It is clear that she is not known today in the Hieronymian Martyrologies; nor, in our view, can *Martialem* there be understood as *Martiana*. It is not sufficiently probable that she is found there under the name *Mariana* on 11 July. The fact that some place her on the fifth day before the Ides of July could easily have arisen from abbreviations in the manuscripts.

Martiana is no better known in Bede, Florus, or Rabanus. It remains, therefore, that she was first marked in the *Small Roman Martyrology*, with her name somewhat deformed: “In Caesarean Mauretania, of Macra, virgin and martyr.” Ado restored the name to its proper form, but it may be inferred that he lacked the Acts because the entry has no encomium, however brief. Our author offers no more than what he found in the Viennese copy, with which Notker also agrees.

Baronius rightly judged that this is the same Martiana who is honored here and in July. The Spaniards should not be allowed to make two persons from one unless they produce more certain documents than those derived from Bivarius or similar sources. For the remaining matters relating to this subject, see Bollandus, Castellanus, and Tillemont, volume V, beginning at page 263.

There is scarcely anything to add concerning the last martyrs. They were taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but badly arranged by Usuard and no better restored by the Pratense interpolator. I have no doubt that the true reading of Usuard, which we have presented, is the one also shown by Wandalbert’s verse:

> On the fifth, Vitalis, Fortunatus, and Revocatus.

[Col. 0634B] Bollandus and Florentinius discuss on this day the distinction between the people of Smyrna and the Africans found in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, as does Castellanus most recently in his notes, beginning at page 146.]

[Note: [Col. 0633B]

**ANTWERP–MAURISTS** transferred the first announcement to the sixth of this month; here it is pure in the other two, but places one before the other. Usuard, inserted into the *Acts of the Martyrs*—of which only the January volume is extant—agrees with this manuscript; there too Julian, etc., is given today on the sixth, while Martiana and the people of Smyrna are expressly placed here.

**ROSWEYD:** “Near Antioch, of Julian the martyr and Basilissa his wife. These chaste spouses therefore lived together for several years in a most holy vow, preserving their flesh in virginity. They established monasteries from their possessions, since they were very distinguished in parentage and lineage, so that the father Julian became the father of ten thousand monks, while Basilissa became the mother of many virgins. After she had already sent their multitude, victorious, to the Lord, she too rested after many exercises. Julian, tortured by the governor Martianus, was at his command struck down with the sword by soldiers, together with the boy Celsus, the son of the aforementioned governor. On the same day, of Antony and Anastasius, martyrs, together with Marcionilla the martyr, the governor’s wife. On the same day, of Saint Marciana, virgin and martyr.”

**CENTULAN** also marked Julian and his companions on 6 January. Today it has: “In Asia, at Smyrna, of Saints Vitalis, Revocatus, and Fortunatus. In Caesarean Mauretania, of Saint Marciana, virgin and martyr.”

**BRUSSELS**, after “under the emperors,” continues as follows: “And under the governor Martianus, after the passion of the holy martyrs Julian and Basilissa his wife, whose day of passion is commemorated on the eighth day before the Ides of January. Antony the presbyter, Anastasius, and the boy Celsus, together with his mother Marcionilla, the wife of the governor Martianus, and many others, suffered.” This division of the martyrdoms is sufficiently appropriate, but on what is it based? The account of the people of Smyrna and of Martiana follows, in pure form.

**HAGENOYEN**, after “his wife,” continues: “This Julian became the father of ten thousand monks, all of whom were burned by fire; at their funeral the angels were heard in heaven at the same place.
