Basilissa, however, was the mother of a thousand virgins, who were also burned for Christ; Basilissa herself had already died in peace. Julian was beaten with clubs by the governor Martianus and then imprisoned; the fingers of his hands and feet were bound with oil-soaked wicks [Rosweyd restored *liciniis* in Ado] and set alight; afterward he was beheaded. After them Antony the presbyter, Anastasius, and the boy Celsus, who rests in the cathedral church at Spires, together with his mother, and many others, were killed by various punishments.” The rest is pure, except that at the end it has “with Fortunatus the deacon.”

[Col. 0634B] **AQUICINCT** has neither “deacon” nor “martyrs” at the end, but adds “with three others.” I suspect that the names were not correctly assigned, and that this manuscript therefore agrees here, as often happens, with the Pratense.

**VICTORIN** reads *Marinae* instead of *Martianae*.

**MATRICIAN, CARTUSIAN, and UTRECHT** begin: “Of Martiana, virgin and martyr. Of William, bishop of Bourges, noble by birth, who served God from childhood. Of Julian the martyr and Basilissa the virgin, with many other martyrs.” You should note that William of Bourges is commonly commemorated by others on the following day. See the Acts there.

**DIJON:** “At the monastery of Saint Benignus, near the castle of Dijon, the birthday of Saint Paschasia, virgin and martyr.” This is cited as extracted from the codex of that monastery, from which we have several other entries.

**FLORENCE:** “At Ancona, of Saint Marcellus. In the city of Bourges, of Saint William, bishop and confessor.” A manuscript fragment on parchment adds: “Consecration of the church of Saint Laurence of Florence, consecrated in the year of the Lord 1060 by Pope Nicholas II. Formerly he was bishop of Florence.”

The **LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION**, after “the passions,” inserts: “And although they were joined in a true marriage, nevertheless they secretly ended their lives in virginity. From their community also,” etc., in fairly pure form. Concerning Martiana it adds: “In Caesarea she shattered the image of Diana and, handed over to wild beasts, was finally killed for Christ by a leopard.” To the people of Smyrna it adds “martyr deacons.” “On the same day, of blessed Agetius the confessor.” See the entry in the *Praetermissi*. “At Trier, discovery of Saint Symeon the confessor.”

**GREVEN:** “In Africa, of Jocundus, Quintus, and Saturus, martyrs.” From the Hieronymian Martyrologies or Rabanus he selects here and there certain saints, whom he generally tears from their context or transfers carelessly. Thus he continues: “On the same day, of blessed Marcellinus [this should be read, not Marcellus, as above], bishop of Ancona, concerning whom blessed Gregory relates in Book I of the *Dialogues* that when he was placed by attendants before a fiercely burning fire, because he was unable to walk, the fire was completely cooled. Also, of Saint Agecius the confessor. Is this not Agritius, concerning whom see 6 January and again 13 January? At Trier, discovery of Saint Simeon the confessor. Of Bartwald, archbishop and confessor of Canterbury. In Kent, of Adrian, abbot and confessor. On the same day, of Felan, abbot and confessor.”

**MOLAN.** In a different typeface he inserts into the text Ado’s words concerning chaste marriage, the monasteries established, the monks, and the virgins subject to their discipline, which we quoted above from Rosweyd’s manuscript. Then, at the end, in smaller type: “At Dijon, of Saint Paschasia, virgin, whom Gregory of Tours mentions.” Marcellinus follows, with the encomium taken above from Greven. “In Kent, of Adrian, abbot and confessor. Of Bertwald, archbishop and confessor of Canterbury, whom Bede mentions in his history of his people.” He certainly mentions him, but Castellanus warns that he should be called neither Bertunaldus nor Bertwaldus, as Greven has it, but Berechtwaldus with the Bede mentioned above, or Brithwaldus with Goscelin. Consult him in the notes for this day, page 153. The later editions contain the same account of Adrian the abbot as the first; the text is the same, but everything else has been excluded. In its place is put: “In Normandy, burial of blessed Waning, confessor. He founded the noble monastery of Fécamp and sheltered Leodegarius in exile.”]

[Col. 0631]

At Antioch, under Diocletian and Maximian, the birthday of Saints Julian and Basilissa the virgin, whose marvelous sufferings are read. From their community also, a venerable multitude of priests and ministers of the church of Christ was burned by fire; they had fled to them because of the savagery of the persecution. After them, Antoninus the presbyter, Anastasius, and the boy Celsus, together with his mother, and many others, suffered. In Caesarean Mauretania, of Saint Martiana, virgin. At Smyrna, of Saints Vitalis, Revocatus, and Fortunatus. [According to Bouillart: “... suffered.” [Note: [Col. 0631B] Castellanus, who inspected the manuscript itself—the words are Soller’s—observes that a leaf was once torn from that alleged autograph and afterward restored in an ancient script, on which the change was made. Since the other Usuardine manuscripts have “At Smyrna, of Saints Vitalis, Revocatus, and Fortunatus,” I admit that it is another leaf; whether it is another hand, I doubt. Certainly the same character of the letters and the same age of writing are evident in both.

Perhaps Usuard replaced a leaf dirtied by erasures or corrections with another; the same scribe may not have been available. I do not make this conjecture rashly. For wherever the Dervensis manuscript differs from the Pratense, there are erasures in the latter; or, if the page is clean, I notice a hand that is indeed similar but nevertheless different. To anyone investigating the cause, the following explanation seemed probable and is confirmed by the constant practice of authors.

Before Usuard dictated the Martyrology, he had corrected many things; after dictating it, he corrected many more. When a leaf had become too dirty for the writing to be read conveniently, he tore it out and substituted another. Thus grant that Vitalis, Revocatus, and Fortunatus belonged to the first autograph. In the second, their place was given to Revolutus and Firminus. From where were these taken? I do not know. New Acts of the saints emerge every day from the corners of libraries. Perhaps those which Usuard saw will also emerge.

It cannot be asserted that Revolutus and Firminus came from the Africans or Smyrnaeans whom the other Martyrologies record on this day, unless Usuard was, perhaps, ἀναλφάβητος—that is, illiterate. For neither does the number agree, nor is there any relationship among the names. BOUILLART.]

In Africa, of the holy martyrs Revolutus and Firminus, with three others.]

**IV Ides. Day 10.**

[Note: [Col. 0635]

Taken from the Pratense, Heriniense, Tornacense, Pulsanense, the first edition of Belin, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0635B]

I am compelled to write *Nicanor* with the better-quality manuscripts, Greven, and others; I believe that Usuard followed this spelling, although the etymology of the name favors following the *Small Roman Martyrology* and Ado, who may perhaps have been corrected by Rosweyd, just as Usuard was corrected by Molan.

After “of the first seven,” I thought it appropriate to add from Belin what he may perhaps have found in Ado, namely “deacons”; the simplicity of Usuard is evident from the other manuscripts. Molan reads “crowned gloriously,” but the others, together with the manuscripts, generally have “crowned most gloriously.” In Ado these words are joined with “at Cyprus” in the following form: “At Cyprus he was crowned most gloriously,” from which it may be understood that he obtained the martyr’s crown through a bloody death. Usuard’s transposition left Castellanus uncertain whether the crown referred to martyrdom or heavenly glory.

Instead of *Thebaide, natalis, heremitae*, some copies write *Thebaida, natale, eremitae*, and instead of *ad coelum*, *ad coelos*. But I have already sufficiently indicated above that such trifles should be disregarded in the course of the work, especially since no fixed spelling can be maintained by us when we often follow variant manuscripts or even their errors.]

[Note: [Col. 0635B]

Those whom Ado records among the feasts of the apostles, although on different days, are collected together among the Greeks on 28 July: Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, and Parmenas. I wished to place them here together at a glance, so as to indicate that these four deacons, unknown to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, and the other ancient writers, were first distributed among particular days by the author of the *Small Roman Martyrology*, in my opinion on his own authority.

Thus, taken over by Ado, Usuard, and Notker, they are honored today: Prochorus on 9 April, Timon on 19 April, and Parmenas on 23 January, as will be repeated in their proper places. Therefore Nicanor’s original placement is owed solely to the *Small Roman Martyrology*: “And in Cyprus, of Nicanor, one of the seven deacons.” These words remain scarcely altered in Ado’s Martyrology and are marked only in third place, since both authors treat Paul first.

I have not yet discovered from where Ado extracted his brief encomium. No Acts have been published, and Tillemont, most recently, found nothing in volume II, page 70, except that he rejected the material together with Bollandus. Yet if Ado’s words are weighed—“At Cyprus, crowned most gloriously”—there can be no doubt that they must be understood of the martyr’s crown, however uncertain the matter may otherwise be; this is expressed more roundly by some of our fuller manuscripts.

Usuard perhaps seems to speak cautiously, or at least obscurely, when he combines both of Ado’s texts and transposes his phrase without sufficient clarity, while Notker follows the thought of his source more closely.

Concerning Paul, the *Small Roman Martyrology* mentions him first: “In Thebaid, of Saint Paul the hermit.” But Paul’s commemoration is older, having first been entered by Bede in the sacred registers, where it is adorned with a brief encomium, slightly expanded by Rabanus and copied by Ado and, from him, by Notker. Notker nevertheless incorrectly read XCIII for CXIII, an easy mistake resulting from the transposition of numeral letters. Our author abbreviated Ado’s encomium in such a way that he omitted both the age and the period spent in the desert.

So much for our text, which is demonstrably genuinely Usuardine and taken almost word for word from Ado. I say nothing about the Acts: concerning the two lives edited, illustrated, and vindicated by Bollandus, there is not much that later writers can either oppose or add.

But what shall we say was the reason that Ado omitted Pope Melchiades, whom Bede, whom Ado was copying, and the Hieronymian and other ancient sources expressly record? Again, why is Hyginus substituted, unknown to all the older sources? I prefer to confess ignorance rather than speculate by conjecture.

In the same Ado there is also, in fourth place, the translation of Saint Hermes the martyr. But Usuard entirely omits both announcements. Concerning the translation of Hermes, one may read Rosweyd’s annotations on Ado’s Martyrology, page 225, and our index of the *Praetermissi* for this day.

Why Paul was transferred in the modern Roman Martyrology to 15 January, since all the earlier days were occupied by other ecclesiastical offices, is clearer than to require explanation. Wandalbert joins Melchiades and Paul today in the following way:

> On the fourth, Melchiades and Paul the hermit,  
> > raised up by a blessed end, rejoice in the heavenly citadel.

] [Note: [Col. 0635D]

**ANTWERP–MAJOR.** Preserving Usuard’s order, it places Ado’s text beneath it almost verbatim:

“Birth of blessed Nicanor, who was one of the first seven deacons. He, through the grace of faith and admirable virtue, was gloriously crowned in Cyprus and was reverently buried there. In Thebaid, the birth of blessed Paul, the first hermit, who from the sixth year of his age—‘tenth’ has been omitted—until his one hundred and thirteenth year remained alone in the desert. His soul, etc.”

**ROSWEYD:** “In Thebaid, the birth … He who from his fifteenth year [Col. 0636D] until his one hundred and third remained alone, etc. Of Pope and confessor Hyginus.” Concerning him, see the Additions for the following day. “Likewise at Rome, of Pope and confessor Melchiades.” Consult the Omitted Notices. “In Cyprus, of blessed Nicanor, who was one of the seven deacons.”

**ANTWERP, MAX-LÜBECK, and UGHELLI,** generally conforming, add to the pure Usuard: “At Rome, of Pope Melchiades. At Bourges, of Saint William, bishop and confessor.” I find this last notice added by a more recent hand to the **PULSANO** manuscript in the following form: “On the same [Col. 0637A] day at Bourges, the feast of Saint William, archbishop and confessor.”

**MUNERATUS,** otherwise also pure, ends as follows: “At Bourges, the feast of Saint William, archbishop of that same city, glorious in life and miracles.” Usuard’s manuscript, which we said had been mixed with the Acts of the Martyrs, is exactly similar to this.

**ANTWERP–MAXIMUM, LOUVAIN, LEYDEN, BELGIAN, and the Utrecht–Belgian edition** likewise have the Ado material concerning Paul, as above, but read “sixteenth.” Then, in second place, they insert: “At Rome, of Saint Pope Agatho.” In third place, they give Nicanor, in the pure form. At the end: “At Bourges, the feast of blessed William, bishop and confessor, glorious in life and miracles.”

**UTRECHT and LEYDEN–LATIN** exceed the immediately preceding manuscripts in adding the following about Paul:

“His cloak, however, woven from palm leaves, Antony claimed for his own use at every solemn celebration. When Jerome had written the life of this holy man, he said: ‘I beg that whoever reads this may remember Jerome the sinner, who, if the Lord granted him a choice, would much rather choose Paul’s tunic together with his merits than the purple robes of kings together with their kingdoms.’”

**ALBERGEN and DANIC** have all the same material, but add concerning Agatho:

“He was the eighty-first after blessed Peter, sat for five years, six months, and fifteen days.”

See the Acts.

**CENTULE:** “In Cyprus, of blessed Nicanor, who was one of the first seven deacons and completed his life by martyrdom.” The passage about Paul follows Ado, but reads “from the fifteenth year of his age, etc.”

**BRUSSELS.** It is sufficiently pure in the passage on Nicanor and continues as follows:

“At Rome, the feast of Saint Pope Hyginus and confessor. He organized the clergy, distributed the offices by degrees, and established that a sponsor should lift up the person being baptized or confirmed. And at Rome, of Saint Pope Melchiades, who prohibited fasting on Sunday.”

It offers nothing new concerning [Col. 0637C] Paul. Then:

“Likewise at Rome, of blessed Pope Agatho, who, when he kissed a leper, the latter was immediately cleansed.”

Concerning William, as above.

**HAGENOY.** The passage on Nicanor is also sufficiently pure. Then:

“At Rome, of Pope Agatho, who sat in the Apostolic See [for] five years and six months. He established that men and women should have distinct dress and hairstyles. This pope condemned those who denied that Christ had two wills and two operations, at the Council of Constantinople. In Thebaid, of Paul, the first hermit and confessor. Accused by his brother-in-law, who wanted to possess his inheritance because he was a Christian, he fled into the desert: at first out of necessity, to escape bodily death, but eventually he turned necessity into an act of will and hid for ninety-seven years in a certain cave, where he devoted himself solely to God and where he was sustained by God with heavenly bread. His soul … Antony rejoiced in his glory [Col. 0637D] and was greatly comforted by his death. Antony found the dead body of this holy man with his knees bent and his hands raised toward heaven, and buried him with the help of a lion.”

[Col. 0638A] **AQUICINCT:** “At Rome, of Pope Hyginus. He organized the clergy and distributed the degrees.” This is Ado’s material.

**VICTORIN and the SWEDISH REGISTER,** marked number 130: “At Rome, of Saint Pope Melchiades.”

**MATRICULARY–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT:** “Of Paul, the first hermit. Of Nicanor, deacon and martyr, one of the first seven. Of Polyeuctus, martyr.” He is referred to 13 February. “And of Nearcus.” I do not know this man. Then follows the material about Vitalis, etc., from the preceding day.

**SWEDISH REGISTER,** under number 428: “Likewise at Bourges, the feast of blessed William the confessor and archbishop, who shone forth through many miracles.”

**IN THE VATICAN MANUSCRIPT,** under number 5949, Nicanor is absent. The following is added: “At Rome, of Saint Pope Melchiades. And the feast of Saint Gregory Nazianzenus, at Saint Sophia.” This is the monastery at Benevento.

**FLORENCE:** “Near the city of Bourges, of Saint William, bishop and confessor.”

**THE CHURCH OF RHEIMS OF SAINTS TIMOTHY AND APOLLINARIS:** [Col. 0638B] “At Amiens, the translation of the body of Saint Firminus, bishop and confessor.” Since he is the younger, he bears the title “confessor”;” but it is surprising that our Amiens manuscript contains nothing about him.

**THE LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION** has in first place concerning Paul the same material as Utrecht and Leyden. Concerning Agatho it likewise agrees with them, etc. It is sufficiently pure in the passage about Nicanor. Concerning William, again, it agrees with the manuscripts cited.

The second edition of **BELIN** fails in that its passage on Paul is not Usuard’s but Ado’s.

**GREVEN:** “On the same day, of Saint William, whom we Germans call Wilhelm, archbishop of Bourges, of the Cistercian order, renowned for his life and miracles. This saint was almost always cheerful and pleasant, which displeased certain austere men. Likewise, of blessed Pope and confessor Agatho, who was the eighteenth after Peter—everyone can see the palpable anachronism—and sat for five years and six months. Likewise, of blessed Pope Gregory X and confessor.”

His canonization was formerly treated at Rome, and is being treated again. Finally: “Of Polyeuctus, martyr.”

**MOLAN:** “At Bourges, the feast of Saint William, of that same city, etc.; at Amiens, the translation of Saint Firminus, bishop and confessor.” See what has been said. Concerning Melchiades, simply. “On the same day, the elevation of the body of Saint Wasnulf, confessor.” Then, in smaller type: “At the castle of Dijon, of Saint Florida, virgin, whom Gregory of Tours mentions.”

In the second and third editions I do not understand why he disgracefully mutilates Usuard by deleting Paul’s eulogy. After “hermit” he adds in italics, on his own authority: “but he is transferred after the octave of Epiphany to the fifteenth day of the same month.” In these editions he does not mention Melchiades or Florida; instead, from his Greek Horologion, he substitutes:

“On the tenth day, of Saint Domitian, bishop of Melitina. And of Saint Marcian, priest and steward of the Great Church.”

I do not know what sort of extract from that Horologion Molan possessed, or who supplied him with the translation [Col. 0638D]. Certainly it is clear from many indications, as we have said elsewhere, that he did not consult the source. Let the omission here of the person placed first—Gregory, bishop of Nyssa—serve as an example.

[Col. 0635]

In Cyprus, of blessed Nicanor, deacon, one of the first seven, who was gloriously crowned through the grace of faith and admirable virtue. In Thebaid, the feast of blessed Paul, the first hermit, whose soul Saint Antony saw being carried by angels into heaven among the choirs of apostles and prophets.

### The Third Day before the Ides. 11 January

[Note: [Col. 0637]]

Thus read Pratensis, Herinianus, Tournai, Antwerp–Major, Pulsano, Centule, Antwerp, Max-Lübeck and Ughelli, Muneratus, Greven, and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0637D]]

In Antwerp–Major, after Salvius, “martyr” is added. I read “In hujus” (“on this one’s [feast]”); I think our author took this from Ado, although the sense would seem clearer if, with Bede, I wrote “in cujus” (“on whose [feast]”), as do Rabanus, Notker, and several Usuard manuscripts, both manuscript and printed, such as Centule, Brussels, Hagenoy, Muneratus, Belin, etc.

Belin, Greven, Molan, and others write “of Carthage”; many manuscripts, more correctly with Bede, have “at Carthage.” But our purer manuscripts require “at Cartage,” as it appears in the text, although the more exact spelling is “Carthage,” as Ado wrote.

After Alexandria, Antwerp–Major inserted “feast,” etc. There is no doubt that “of Severus” should be written, although Tournai, Antwerp, Max-Lübeck, and others give “of Severinus”; Muneratus read “of Salinus,” and Belin “of Silvius” instead of “of Salvius.”

There is no greater variation, however, than in the name of Leucius. Usuard correctly placed it here, perhaps correcting Ado from the Hieronymian manuscripts; Ado had followed the earlier but mistaken author of the Little Roman Martyrology. In our manuscripts some write Leucius, Lencius, Leuticius, others Genucius, Leontius, Loucius, Euthitius, and so forth—plainly, unless I am mistaken, scribal errors.

The Pulsano manuscript is remarkable in distinguishing the last three saints. It reads:

“At Alexandria, of Saint Leucius, bishop and confessor. Likewise at Alexandria, of the holy confessors Peter and Severinus, whose acts are preserved.”

This, however, does not remove the difficulty that will shortly be discussed.

[Note: [Col. 0639A]]

The antiquity of the commemoration of Salvius in the sacred calendars is demonstrated especially by the Carthaginian Calendar published by Mabillon and reprinted by Ruinart, in which this day clearly reads: “Of Saint Salvius, martyr.”

The Hieronymian copies mix him with other martyrs—not Spanish but African, if they are indeed contained in those manuscripts. Whatever the case may be, the other Martyrologists mention him separately and alone: Bede, from whom Ado, and from Ado Usuard, transcribed him with altered phrasing. I wish it to be observed that their notice is placed in such a way that nothing concerning the manner of his death can be inferred.

Here our Viennese Ado clearly preferred Bede to the Little Roman Martyrology, since the latter plainly reads: “In Africa, of Salvius, martyr.” Indeed, not only the Calendar and the Hieronymian copies just cited prove that Salvius ought to be called a martyr; Bollandus demonstrates it from Possidius, carefully distinguishing our saint from another person of the same name, who was a Donatist heretic.

It is altogether astonishing that Rabanus, describing Bede, gives Salvius the title “confessor,” whereas Notker, who had both Bede and Ado before his eyes, calls him a martyr. Wandalbertus decides nothing on either side when he sings:

“From here Salvius consecrates the third Ides at Carthage.”

[Col. 0639C] A more intricate knot arises concerning three other saints unknown to Bede, Florus, and Rabanus, whom the Little Roman Martyrology mentions first in this form:

“At Alexandria, of the confessors Peter, Severus, and Lucius,” in a wholly unusual manner of expression.

Ado follows, using precisely the wording copied by our author, omitting the word “feast” and changing “Lucius” into “Leucius,” as stated above. Notker has the same reading, following the Hieronymian manuscripts in writing “Leucius,” and deleting the final words, “whose acts are preserved.”

To make the whole difficulty clearer, compare these words with the Hieronymian manuscripts’ first notice:

“At Alexandria, of Peter, Severus, Saint Leucius the confessor, and Absolamus, or Alolamus, or Assolamus.”

Only the Lucerne manuscript adds after Absolamus: “whose acts are preserved.”

What are we now to conclude? Did the Little Roman Martyrology badly copy its text from the Hieronymian manuscripts? I do not find that likely. Did both authors err? Florentinius tries to untangle the matter with his customary modesty, and so far I find nothing in his conjectures that can rightly be criticized.

Castellanus accuses the Little Roman Martyrology of more than one error and does not spare Ado, because he may have added the closing phrase, “whose acts are preserved,” taken from the Hieronymian manuscripts. This is indeed correct, for if he had seen those manuscripts he would not have spoken of them so meagerly.

Everything is confused by the title “confessors,” applied by the Little Roman Martyrology to all three, but by the Hieronymian manuscripts only to Leucius. This title seems all the more strange to me because in these manuscripts and in the Little Roman Martyrology the designation of either saints or confessors occurs less frequently and perhaps never with the meaning that we commonly assign to it.

In this perplexity, I prefer to accept the conjectures of others rather than pile new doubts upon doubts. Let Leucius alone be the confessor, perhaps a bishop of Brundisium, whom the Echternach copy mentions on 7 January. Let Peter and Severus of Alexandria be granted the crown of martyrdom. Let Peter, wrongly placed at Alexandria, be the same as Basalmus, Absolamus, and the saint of Aulanum, concerning whom see 3 January.

Thus it will be true to say of Leucius and Absolamus, “whose acts are preserved,” although the Leucian material at least requires extensive correction. If this matter interests you greatly, see Bollandus and the two authors cited immediately above. If new light should shine upon us from elsewhere, it will be communicated in the Supplement.

[Note: [Col. 0639C]]

**ROSWEYD** begins quite purely with the Alexandrians. Then:

“In Africa, of Salvius, bishop. On his feast, etc. Likewise, of blessed Gregory Nazianzenus, bishop.”

In the Omitted Notices he is rightly referred to 9 May. Then:

“In Aquileia, of Paulinus, patriarch.”

See the Acts.

**ANTWERP–MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and LOUVAIN,** otherwise pure, announce near the end:

“At Rome, the feast of Saint Hyginus—also written Iginius and Higinius—pope and martyr.”

From Ado, **BELIN** adds:

“He organized the clergy and distributed the degrees.”

**ALBERGEN and DANIC** add somewhat more:

“He was the eighth after blessed Peter, governed the Church beneficially for four years and three months, organized the clergy, and distributed the degrees; after completing his martyrdom, he was finally buried near the body of blessed Peter.”

**THE ACTS OF THE MARTYRS** end with:

“At Rome, the passion of Saint Pope Hyginus, who succeeded the martyr Telesphorus in the pontificate.”

**LEYDEN–BELGIAN** and the **Utrecht–Belgian edition** place Hyginus at the beginning. The first manuscript calls him the eighth after blessed Peter; the second, the tenth. Both, however, repeat Hyginus at the end, precisely as the middle-quality manuscripts do.

**BRUSSELS** reports the Alexandrian notice quite purely in first place. Then:

“In Africa, of Saint Salvius, confessor [Col. 0640C] and martyr. On whose feast, etc.”

This is an entirely new formula for the notice.

**HAGENOY** has the text throughout as the preceding manuscripts do, inserting the notice of Peter, Aventinus, etc. Then:

“Likewise, on the same day, of Polyeuctus, Candidus, and Florinus, martyrs, burned with fire. Likewise at Rome, on the Lavican Way, of the crown of forty soldiers, whom [which] under the emperor Gallienus, for their confession of the true faith, were worthy to receive.”

These martyrs, however, have been wrongly transferred here from the following day. Perhaps a copyist found them in some older manuscript, or transposed them through his own carelessness.

It is more surprising in Baronius, who placed the same crown on both days. I think he was misled by a manuscript of Saint Cyriacus, which he admits he used extensively; there the forty soldiers are wrongly joined to the four Africans—Zoticus, Modestus, Rogatus, and Castulus, if they are Africans at all—whereas from the purer Hieronymian copies it is clear that they belong to the following day, as we shall report them there with Usuard.

**CENTULE,** in his customary abbreviated form, has:

“At Achaia, of Saint Satyrus, martyr. On the same day, of Saint Arcadius, martyr.”

**AQUICINCT.** We have already discussed at length the location of Saint Arcadius “in Caesarea of Mauretania.” It continues:

“In the city of Nicomedia, the passion of Saints Pastor and Victor.”

**MATRICULARY–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT:** “Of Martiana, virgin and martyr.” In the margin “Tatiana” is noted, together with the Roman Martyrology.

**AUGUSTA:** “In the city of Nicomedia, the passion of Saints Pastor and Victor.”

**ALTEMPS:** “In the city of Nicomedia, of Saints Pastor and Victor.” Then it adds:

“Near the monastery of blessed Peter the apostle, which is called Piremuthe, the burial of blessed Benedict, abbot, whose Life Bede the priest wrote.”

The place is called Wirimunda by others. See Bollandus and also Castellanus in the notes, p. 183.

**THE LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION** is, as usual, more pure, for it adds no saint. At the end of Saint Satyrus’ eulogy, after “he was beheaded,” it adds: “by the idol’s worshipers.”

**GREVEN:** “Of John, bishop, otherwise pope and martyr. In Egypt, of Aventinus and Castulus; of Eugenius, the first pope, confessor, who, beloved and kind to all, governed around the year of the Lord 651.”

He should better have written 654 or 655. See 2 June in the Acts.

“Likewise, of blessed Claudia, a Roman matron.”

Concerning her and Pope John, see Bollandus in the Omitted Notices.

**MOLAN,** in smaller type:

“Of the holy martyrs Eutropius, lector; Tygrius, priest; and Olympia, a holy matron, concerning whom the Tenth Book of the Tripartite History speaks.”

Bollandus treats the first two today. He refers Olympia to 17 December. See Castellanus’ notes beginning on p. 179.

Then:

“Of Benedict, confessor, the first abbot of Vutrimund in England, whose history Bede admits that he wrote.”

See the homily published by Bollandus.

The later editions read:

“At Wirimunda in England, of Saint Benedict, the first abbot. Likewise, of Saint John, bishop of the Church of Jerusalem, a professor of the Carmelite order.”

In the Omitted Notices Bollandus asks who this John, bishop of Jerusalem, was, inclining to believe from Palaeonydorus that John II is meant, commonly numbered forty-fourth. Under his name appears the famous book *On the Institution of Monks*. I pass over further discussion of it here, since our master Papebrochius has treated the matter fully in his *Chronological Treatise on the Patriarchs of Jerusalem* and in his *Replies to the Presentation of Various Errors*, at several places; consult the index of that work.

Finally, in these editions Molan places:

“On the twelfth day, of Saint Tatiana, martyr.”

As usual, this was taken here from the Greek Horologion. Concerning the confusion of her Acts with those of others, see Bollandus on this day and Castellanus, p. 176.

Finally, contrary to custom, Wandalbertus’ verse is found at the end:

“The people of Achaia recall their Cyriacus on the preceding day.”

But we have already presented this verse above in Bollandus’ improved form.

[Col. 0637]

In Africa, the feast of blessed Salvius. On his feast Saint Augustine preached a sermon to the people at Cartage. At Alexandria, of the holy confessors Peter and Leucius, whose acts are preserved.

### The Day before the Ides. 12 January

[Note: [Col. 0641C]]

Thus read Herinianus, Tournai, Antwerp–Major, Rosweyd, Pulsano, Antwerp, Max-Lübeck and Ughelli, Albergen, Bruges, Muneratus, Belin, Greven, Molan, and the Acts of the Martyrs. To these add all the manuscripts cited in the preface, insofar as they reproduce the text, except Pratensis and Aquicinctinus, as I shall immediately explain.

[Note: [Col. 0641D]]

Rosweyd departs somewhat from the purity of the text by beginning:

“Of Saint Satyrus, martyr, a citizen of Arabia, who, etc.”

Usuard certainly read “at Achaia,” as Ado found it in Bede, whom he followed, although in the Little Roman Martyrology he found “at Antioch.”

What “citizen of Arabia” means in Bede and Ado has so far remained under investigation. I omitted these words, following our purest manuscripts, both manuscript and printed, and I have no doubt that Usuard did likewise, and rightly so. For, as Castellanus correctly observed, a person is properly called a citizen not of a region but of a city.

Some, with Rosweyd and Belin, write “had blown upon it”; but no purer manuscript has the article “in,” which could have been added, nor do the older Martyrologists mentioned above.

Antwerp–Major inserted “feast” before Saint Arcadius. As for my having written “of Arcadius” in the text, no one should be surprised, since I profess to follow the reading of the manuscripts.

There is controversy concerning the place of Saint Arcadius’ martyrdom [Col. 0642D], which nowhere appears in the older Martyrologists from whom our author took his material. The Acts explicitly name Achaia, and I consider it most likely that the martyr suffered in that region, as will be said in the Observations.

Here the issue concerns only the location added in Pratensis and, following it, Aquicinctinus: “in Caesarea of Mauretania.” But this appears in none of the other manuscripts, none whatsoever of the Usuard manuscripts whose long series we presented in the preface.

Nevertheless, someone argues for that location on the authority of the manuscript’s alleged autograph character, as those know who have read Castellanus’ note on p. 178. Before I seriously undertook this work, there was a friendly exchange of letters between us on this subject; here the learned man’s zeal in defending his beloved manuscript revealed itself.

When, among other points raised against his observations, I presented this passage to him, and no escape remained open, his argument finally came down to the following. I translate it from the French letter he sent me on 29 November 1709:

“It may have happened,” he says, “that the person who first copied the Pratensis manuscript, knowing no Caesareas other than the Cappadocian and the Palestinian, thought that Usuard had suffered a lapse of memory. Perplexed by doubt as to which Caesarea he should prefer, he excluded both and substituted only: ‘On the same day.’”

No one, I think, can fail to see how inadequate this response is. Whoever that scribe was had seen and read Caesarea of Mauretania elsewhere, and most recently in Usuard, on 9 January; and then, three days later, if heaven permits, he supposedly deleted that same Caesarea as though it were unknown.

I would rather state the truth: namely, that the Pratensis manuscript, both here and in several other places listed above in the preface, is not purely and genuinely Usuardine, and therefore has rightly been excluded by us today from the number of authentic manuscripts. This matter has been treated more fully elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0643A]]

On this day Ado must again be said to have preferred Bede to the Little Roman Martyrology, if his reading is genuine: “In Achaia,” rather than “at Antioch,” as in the two copies cited by Bollandus.

I am convinced that the Little Roman Martyrology simply wrote: “At Antioch, of Satyrus, martyr,” a phrase that does not have the flavor of the Hieronymian wording.

The oldest manuscript here, and, unless I am mistaken, also the purest, is the Echternach manuscript, in which alone we read:

“In Achaia, of Cyriacus, Moscentius, Satyrus,”

without the eulogy that was subsequently taken from Bede, but thoroughly deformed and intrusively inserted into other Hieronymian manuscripts contrary to their style. Acherius nevertheless did not faithfully delete it from the Corbie manuscript that he published; Florentinius rightly asked why this copy was not reproduced in full in the *Spicilegium*.

The true descent of our text seems to flow from a pure Hieronymian manuscript into Bede, and from Bede into the others. Henschenius and Papebrochius judged with considerable probability that Bede originally read in full:

“In Achaia, of Cyriacus, Mosantius, Satyrus, a citizen of Arabia, etc.”

as Rabanus copied it from him.

But the Viennese author, perhaps having obtained a copy in which he read only “at Achaia, of blessed Satyrus, etc.,” and finding the same in the Little Roman Martyrology, excluded the first two names and left us one alone. Usuard took this from him and transmitted it to all later copies, but entirely deleted what seemed redundant to him: “a citizen of Arabia.”

Castellanus’ observation that Florus’ inadvertence led Ado and Usuard into error derives from the preconceived opinion refuted above. It was not Florus, as is clear to anyone, but Bede himself who served as the light before Ado and perhaps Usuard.

As for the true place of the martyrdom, it will be debated as long as the Acts are lacking, since only from them can it be firmly determined. Nor is it yet clear where Bede obtained the material for his eulogy.

For the present, it is enough for us to have shown both Usuard’s genuine view and its derivation. Wandalbertus—whether rightly or wrongly I do not dispute—assigns Cyriacus alone to Achaia today. Bollandus restores his verse against Molan as follows:

“The people of Achaia recall their Cyriacus on the preceding day.”

Whether Notker derived his division from this is of no concern to us.

The author of the Little Roman Martyrology was the first to mention Arcadius the martyr. Ado had nothing to add except the commonplace praise, “renowned by birth and miracles.” These words passed into Usuard and Notker, but without any explicit indication of the place or location of the martyrdom. Castellanus therefore torments himself in vain trying to vindicate Caesarea of Mauretania for Usuard; we have discussed that matter in the Variants.

From the aforesaid Pratensis manuscript, and from a few manuscript copies of the Acts, contrary to all the others, Ruinart, in *Selected and Genuine Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 590, thinks it not obscurely follows that Caesarea of Mauretania, rather than the Achaia expressed in the Acts, should be preferred.

But I frankly confess that I still do not see why the Acts themselves, otherwise candid and genuine, should be trusted less than certain scraps sewn on later—unless one wishes, with almost the same right, to chatter with Bivarius because he happily found in the famous Chronicle of Dexter that Ursaona in Baetica had been consecrated by the blood of so great a martyr.

[Note: [Col. 0643C]]

**ANTWERP–MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, DANIC,** and the **Utrecht–Belgian edition** add after “Satyrus, martyr,” the words “a citizen of Arabia.” Between the two notices that they have purely from Usuard, they insert:

“In Egypt, of Saints Peter, Aventinus, and Castulus.”

They were certainly taken from some Hieronymian copy, with Philoromus and Zoticus omitted along with their companions.

**BRUSSELS** has the same material at the beginning as those just cited. In second place it also gives Peter, Aventinus, etc. Then:

“In the city of Nicomedia, the passion of Saints Pastor and Victor.”

They are referred to 29 March. Then follows the pure notice of Arcadius. At the end:

“Likewise, of Saint Firiacus, bishop.”

Concerning him, see the Omitted Notices.

**HAGENOY** has the same text throughout as the preceding manuscripts, with the notice of Peter, Adventinus, etc., inserted. Then:

“Likewise [on the same] day, of Polyeuctus, Candidus, and Florinus, martyrs, burned by fire. Likewise at Rome, on the Lavican Way, of the crown of forty soldiers, whom [which] under the emperor Gallienus earned the right to receive for confessing the true faith.”

These martyrs, however, were wrongly transferred here from the following day. Perhaps the copyist found them in some older manuscript or transposed them through his own carelessness.

It is more surprising in Baronius, who placed these crowns on both days. I think he was deceived by the manuscript of Saint Cyriacus, which he admits he used extensively, where the forty soldiers are wrongly joined to the four Africans—Zoticus, Modestus, Rogatus, and Castulus, if they are Africans—whereas the purer Hieronymian copies plainly show that they belong to the following day, as we shall report them there with Usuard.

**CENTULE**, the usual abbreviator, has:

“At Achaia, of Saint Satyrus, martyr. On the same day, of Saint Arcadius, martyr.”

**AQUICINCT.** We have already discussed at length above the location of Saint Arcadius “in Caesarea of Mauretania.” It continues:

“In the city of Nicomedia, the passion of Saints Pastor and Victor.”

**MATRICULARY–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT:** “Of Martiana, virgin and martyr.” In the margin “Tatiana” is noted, together with the Roman Martyrology.

[Col. 0644D] **AUGENSIS:** “In the city of Nicomedia, the passion of Saint Pastor and Victor.”

**ALTEMPS:** “In the city of Nicomedia, of Saints Pastor and Victor.” Then it adds:

“Near the monastery of blessed Peter the apostle, which is called Piremuthe, the burial of blessed Benedict, abbot, whose Life Bede the priest wrote.”

The place is called Wirimunda by others. See Bollandus and Castellanus’ notes, p. 183.

**THE LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION** is purer than usual. It adds no saint and, near the end of Saint Satyrus’ eulogy, after “he was beheaded,” adds: “by the idol’s worshipers.”

**GREVEN:** “Of John, bishop, otherwise pope and martyr. In Egypt, of Aventinus and Castulus; of Eugenius, the first pope and confessor, who, beloved and kind to all, governed around the year of the Lord 651.”

He should better have written 654 or 655. See 2 June in the Acts.

“Likewise, of blessed Claudia, a Roman matron.”

Concerning her and Pope John, see Bollandus in the Omitted Notices.

**MOLAN**, in smaller type:

“Of the holy martyrs Eutropius, lector; Tygrius, priest; and Olympia, a holy matron, concerning whom the Tenth Book of the Tripartite History speaks.”

Bollandus treats the first two today. He refers Olympia to 17 December. See Castellanus’ notes beginning on p. 179.

Then:

“Of Benedict, confessor, the first abbot of Vutrimund in England, whose history Bede admits that he wrote.”

See the homily published by Bollandus.

The later editions read:

“At Wirimunda in England, of Saint Benedict, the first abbot. Likewise, of Saint John, bishop of the Church of Jerusalem, a professor of the Carmelite order.”

Bollandus asks in the Omitted Notices who this John, bishop of Jerusalem, was, inclining to believe from Palaeonydorus that John II is meant, commonly numbered forty-fourth. Under his name appears the famous book *On the Institution of Monks*. I pass over further discussion here, since our master Papebrochius has treated the matter fully in his *Chronological Treatise on the Patriarchs of Jerusalem* and in his *Replies to the Presentation of Various Errors*, at several places; consult the index of that work.

Finally, in these editions Molan places:

“On the twelfth day, of Saint Tatiana, martyr.”

As usual, this was taken here from the Greek Horologion. Concerning the confusion of her Acts with those of others, see Bollandus on this day and Castellanus, p. 176.

Finally, contrary to custom, Wandalbertus’ verse appears at the end:

“The people of Achaia recall their Cyriacus on the preceding day.”

But we have already presented this verse above in Bollandus’ improved form.

[Col. 0641]

At Achaia, the feast of blessed Satyrus, martyr, who, passing before a certain idol, blew upon it and, making a sign upon his forehead, it immediately fell. For this reason he was beheaded.

On the same day, of Saint Arcadius, martyr, renowned by birth and miracles.

[At Bouillart: [Note: [Col. 0641C]]

Usuard states here that this Arcadius suffered at Caesarea in Mauretania, whereas both the Acts of that same Arcadius and other Martyrologies of Usuard attest that he suffered in Achaia. What are we to conclude from this conflict? That our manuscript, as Sollerius thinks, was not written by Usuard’s hand? Certainly not.

Rather, the Acts of Saint Arcadius may have been wholly unknown to Usuard, or he may not have seen them; hence he fell into the error that later writers of his Martyrology corrected. Some copies may then have come into Usuard’s hands in which the same error had more easily entered, since it seems to have been common in that age.

Our Ruinart cites several examples in *Selected Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 590, naming in particular two Colbertine manuscripts: one belonging to the Reverend Fathers of the Fulian order, the other given to the monastery of Remiremont by Hincmar, bishop of Rheims. In both it is read that Saint Arcadius suffered at Caesarea in Mauretania.

The same bishop also gave that monastery a copy of the treatises of Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona, whose thirty-ninth tractate of the first book is entitled: “On the feast of Saint Arcadius,” which says that his feast is on the day before the Ides of January, in the city of Caesarea in Mauretania.

**BOUILLART.]**

At Caesarea in Mauretania, of Saint Arcadius, martyr, renowned by birth and miracles.

### The Ides. 13 January

[Note: [Col. 0645]]

Thus read Pratensis; in its original purity, Herinianus; Tournai; Muneratus; Greven; Molan; and the Acts of the Martyrs.

[Note: [Col. 0645B]]

The disagreement between the Herinian manuscript and the others on this day is as follows. Although it otherwise reproduces Usuard’s text with complete integrity, since it belonged to the province of Rheims, as we have shown elsewhere, it has this distinctive feature: it places the notice of its own Remigius first among the others and, instead of “bishop,” gives “apostle of the Franks.”

I write “Gallienus,” as the manuscripts generally have it, although in some I find it corrected by a second hand. The Tournai manuscript has “of the Christian faith” instead of “of the true faith.”

The same manuscript reads “in the city of Poitiers” for “at Poitiers,” omitting “feast”; but the more common reading, and the purer reading of our text, is to be preferred.

It may perhaps be attributed to the typesetters’ error that “metropolitan” is not read in Muneratus.

Greven and Molan add “and confessor” after “bishop” in the passage about Remigius. In Molan, after “confessor,” “man” is absent; and in Greven, after “by reason of his faith,” “his own” is missing.

Bollandus once wrote that the Pratensis manuscript on this day read:

“On Mount Verziacus, of Saint Viventius, confessor.”

On this basis he attacked its antiquity. Castellanus refuted him, both in his notes on p. 200 and in a letter sent to me, explicitly asserting that these words had been added to the Pratensis manuscript by a later hand. This had not been explained in our copy, and therefore Bollandus, who had never seen another one, must be excused.

For this reason I noted above that I count the Pratensis manuscript among the genuine ones, but with the qualification that its text is in its original purity.

All the Hieronymian Martyrologies published by Florentinius mention Corona of the forty soldiers; they also specify the Via Labicana, except for the Lucan manuscript, which gives the Via Latina. Nothing about them appears in Bede or in his followers, Florus and Rabanus. Moreover, the Little Roman Martyrology more clearly shows that Corona is no more a martyr here than on 1 January, when it says: “At Rome, on the Via Labicana, forty soldiers, under the emperor Gallienus.” From this Ado copied the entry, prefixing the name *crown* to *soldiers*; Our author preserved this, but changed the case and number, as is clear: what appears in Ado to be a singular genitive is nominative plural in Usuard, contrary to the more usual manner of announcing saints. The rest has also been moderately expanded with paraphrastic elegance.

Notker, if I am not mistaken, wished to display excessive acumen by separating Corona from the soldiers both here and on 1 January; and today he changes *Secundus* of the Hieronymian Martyrologies into *Secundina*, in precisely this form: “At Rome, and so forth; of Secundina, Corona, and forty soldiers, under the emperor Gallienus” [Col. 0645D].

What is said about the renowned bishop Hilary of Poitiers was first written by Bede, somewhat enlarged by Ado, and taken from him by Our author. Here again, by comparison, you can see how greatly the phrasing of Florus differs from that of Ado and Usuard [Col. 0646C]. Notker here too followed Ado, not Rabanus. The Little Roman Martyrology had put it very briefly: “At Poitiers, Saint Hilary.” The Hieronymian Martyrologies have: “At Poitiers, the deposition of Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor.” Observe here the title *confessor*, which Jerome and other Fathers attributed to Hilary in a particular sense; Florentinius also noted this.

The Acts of the most glorious defender of the Catholic faith against the Arians have been most diligently elucidated by Bollandus. Castellanus added a few careful observations, while the most learned Benedictine Fathers treated the entire matter at length in the new Life composed by them and prefixed to the latest edition of Hilary’s works, likewise prepared by them. Tillemont was no less exact, in volume VII, beginning at page 432. The metrical encomium of Wandalbert must not be passed over:

> On the Ides, Hilary, for the city of Poitiers,  
> The devoted people serves, whom he illumined with the honor of its shepherd.

Concerning Remigius, the other most celebrated bishop of Gaul [Col. 0646D], the more ancient authorities record nothing today, except Florus in his supplement to Bede, who treats the saint in a brief eulogy, but one very different from that of Usuard. The Hieronymian copies, I do not know for what reason, transfer the deposition of Remigius, or Remedius, to 15 January [Col. 0647A], and again, together with all the other Martyrologists, announce him on 1 October, joined to Germanus, Vedastus, and Plato, without any mention of a translation, as will be said there.

It is certain that the feast of Remigius is celebrated on the Kalends of October, as the Roman Martyrology has it; nevertheless, as our Motherius notes in his most recent French translation, this is to be understood of places where the Roman rite has been received. At Reims and throughout the diocese of Reims, Remigius has customarily been celebrated on this day with religious and solemn observance—or, as we say, as a feast of obligation—even though both there and throughout [Col. 0648A] Gaul he is honored with a double office on those very Kalends of October. See much additional material concerning Remigius and his deeds in the learned Castellanus’s first Bimester, beginning at page 223.

Ado’s final commemoration concerns Verus, bishop of Vienne; but Usuard omitted this, as you will find repeatedly in the course of the work, especially when the bishops of Vienne are being discussed. Let whoever wishes divine the reason. Yet what Usuard left out we generally find restored by later writers in the Appendices, as we shall shortly see in the case of Verus, whose name has been altered here and there.]

[Note: [Col. 0647A]

PRATENSIS. We have already said that the following was added later in that manuscript: “On Mount Verziac, Saint Viventianus, confessor.”]

ANTWERP–MAJOR. In the first recension it is Adonian, simply reading: “under the emperor Gallienus.” In the second it is pure. The third abbreviates it as follows: “At Reims, the birthday of Saint Remigius, bishop and confessor.” See Mosander’s Ado.

ROSWEYD. In the entry concerning the eleven soldiers it is also purely Adonian. Then, in large red capital letters, he inserts: “The Octave of the Epiphany.” Concerning Hilary, correctly. Then: “At Vienne, Saint Severus, bishop, who presided over the Church after Saint Eventius.” These words were taken from Ado, but with the name corrupted. Then: “At Reims, the translation of Saint Remigius, archbishop and confessor.”

PULSANO. In the text, which is not entirely corrected, he inserts in second place: “On the same day, the eighth day of the most sacred manifestation of the Lord and our Savior.” At the end he adds: “Nevertheless, the feast of this holy man is celebrated on the Kalends of October.” See the Observations.

ANTWERP, MAXIMUS–LÜBECK, and UGHELLI. Their entire text is sufficiently pure; at the end they add: “At Verziac, the birthday of Saint Viventianus, confessor of Christ. On the same day, Saint Longisius, or Longisius, confessor.” Bollandus calls him Leogisolus and complains that he found nothing else about him beyond his bare name in the Martyrologies. See Castellanus, pages 200–201, where the forms Launogisilus and others are discussed.

ANTWERP–MAXIMUS, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, DANIC, and the Belgian edition of Utrecht begin: “The Octave of the Epiphany.” They are pure in the entry concerning the forty soldiers and in that concerning Hilary. Then follows: “At Reims, the metropolitan city, the deposition of Saint Remigius, bishop, a man of exceptional virtue. His translation is celebrated on the Kalends, or Kalends of October.” Then: “At Trier, Saint Agritius, bishop and confessor, a man of admirable holiness and learning. When he was bishop of the city of Antioch, at the request of Saint Helena he was sent by Pope Sylvester to convert the people of Trier, who, after the time of Saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus, had largely returned to their former vomiting forth of paganism. There the holy man, a second Eucharius, rescued the people from their ancient error of idolatry [idololatry], and there he ended his life in peace.”

Agritius is known among the ancients only to Rabanus, though Bollandus prefers that he be called Agraecius [Col. 0647D]. Baronius did not find him in the genuine Ado, and considers him to have been added even by Mosander. The Bede cited there is not genuine. On the patriarchate of Antioch, see Bollandus. Castellanus noted a few further points on page 198.

“At Versiac, the birthday of Saint Vincent, confessor of Christ. On the same day, Saint Longisius, confessor.” Not Longinus, as in the Albergen manuscript.

LOUVAIN. It differs from the preceding witnesses in omitting the longer account of Agritius.

CENTULE. In the first recension it follows Ado. Then: “At Poitiers, Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor, magnificent in faith and virtue. At Reims, the metropolitan city of the Franks, the deposition of Saint Remigius, archbishop and confessor. At Amiens, the discovery of Saint Firmin, bishop.”

BRUSSELS. It begins: “The Octave of the Lord’s Epiphany.” In second place it treats Agritius at length, as above. Then: “At Reims, the deposition of Saint Remigius, archbishop, a man of exceptional virtue, who on this day happily migrated to the Lord” [Col. 0648A]. What follows concerns Hilary and is nearly pure. The forty martyrs are treated last. Finally it adds: “At Vienne, Saint Severus, bishop, who worthily presided over that Church after blessed Eventius.” See the material above, and the purer text in Ado himself. “At Vertiac, Saint Vincent, confessor of Christ. On the same day, Saint Longisius [Col. 0648B], confessor. Also Saint Firmin, bishop.”

HAGENOY. “The Octave of the Epiphany. On this day, as Chrysostom says, there is a special commemoration of the three kings. The first of them died while praying at the Circumcision, another at the Epiphany, but the third today. And because their commemoration cannot then be held, the Church of Constantinople now celebrates their memory and feast.” How this agrees with what was said above about the three Magi, I for my part do not see. Yet it is quite customary for the author of this manuscript to introduce marvels found nowhere else, without troubling to investigate them, since they are often not even plausible. He has somewhat interpolated what was said above about Agritius. The account of Hilary follows, and that of Remigius, also slightly expanded. Concerning Viventianus and Longisius, as above.

AQUICINCT. “At Amiens, the discovery of the body of blessed Firmin, bishop and martyr.”

VICTORINUS and the SWEDISH REGISTRY, marked number 130: “On the same day, Saint Potitus.”

[Col. 0648C] MATRICHT, CARTHUSIAN, and UTRECHT: “The Octave of the Epiphany. Hilary, bishop and confessor. Remigius, bishop and apostle of the Franks, of exceptional holiness. Viventianus, confessor.”

BIGOTIAN, formerly belonging to the Celestine Fathers, marked P. 5: “On the same day, Longisius, confessor.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, marked B: “At Verziac, the birthday of Saint Viventianus,” and so forth; and concerning Longisius, as above.

In the VATICAN MANUSCRIPT no. 5949, Remigius is absent; the following is added: “The birthday of Saint Potitus, martyr.”

ALTEMPS: “In Scotland, in the city of Glasgow, Saint Kentigern, or Munguntus, bishop and confessor.” See Greven.

FLORENTINIUS, besides the commemoration of Viventianus and Longisius—for whom Longius is written—reports a saint unknown to the others: “At Rome, Saint Demetria, martyr, who suffered under Julian the Apostate and was buried by Saint John the presbyter beside the palace of Julian.” The printed edition [Col. 0648D] has Luceanus.

CODEX OF THE CASTRUM OF CHARLES: “The dedication of the basilica of Saint Peter of the monastery of Balmey.”

THE LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins: “The Octave of the Lord’s Epiphany.” It is sufficiently pure in the entries concerning the eleven soldiers and Hilary. Then: “At Reims, the metropolitan city, the deposition of Saint Remigius, bishop, a man of exceptional virtue and holiness. He converted the nation of the Franks, devoted to the worship of idols, together with their king, to Christ, and completed seventy years and more in the episcopate. Among other miracles, he is said to have raised a girl from the dead.” Concerning Agritius it has what was described above. Then, concerning Viventianus, it says: “At Verziac, the birthday of Saint Viventianus, priest and confessor of Christ, who believed at the preaching of blessed Gregory. When he died at the age of one hundred and twenty, blessed Maxentius, abbot, buried him at the fortress of Gravion.” Concerning Longisius, as above.

BELIN. At the beginning he has the entry concerning the octave, and at the end adds [Col. 0649A]: “On the same day, at the monastery of Versiac, Saint Vincent, confessor,” instead of Viventianus.

GREVEN. After the Octave he treats Agritius almost as above. Then: “At Vernac, the birthday of Saint Juventius, priest and confessor. By birth a Samaritan, converted in childhood, renowned for his life and miracles, he was buried in the 120th year of his life at the fortress of Gravion, where Saint Hilary of Poitiers had given him a place to stay, by blessed Maxentius, abbot.” See Bollandus for this day, and Castellanus in his notes beginning at page 198. Concerning Verus, as in Ado. “In Scotland, Saint Kentigern, bishop of Glasgow and confessor. Longisius, confessor. In the monastery of Eistad, the blessed-memory Count Godefrid of Capenberg.”

MOLANUS. In his first and more accurate edition he adds: “The Octave of the Epiphany. On the same day at Versiac, Saint Viventianus” [Col. 0650A], “confessor. At Trier, blessed Agritius, bishop and confessor. When he was patriarch of Antioch, he was sent to that same city through blessed Helena, for the strengthening of the Catholic faith.” Then, in smaller type: “In the territory of Liège, Jutta [Ivetta], a very holy recluse and widow, died.” The later editions are corrupted again. “The Octave of the Epiphany” is prefixed in different type. In the text, Hilary’s eulogy is deleted here, and the addition is made: “It is deferred to the following day.” At the end, concerning Viventianus and Agritius, as in the first edition. Concerning Verus, from Ado. Then from the Horologium: “On the thirteenth day, Saints Hermylus and Stratonicus, martyrs.” Finally, in smaller type, concerning Kentigern, from Greven. The woman whom the first edition called Jutta is here written Juetta.]

[Col. 0645]

At Rome, on the Via Labicana, a crown of forty soldiers, who under the emperor Gallienus were deemed worthy to receive it for their confession of the true faith. At the city of Poitiers, the birthday of Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor, who, because of the Catholic faith, was banished for four years to Phrygia; among his other virtues, he is said to have raised a dead man. At Reims, the metropolitan city, the deposition of Saint Remigius, bishop, a man of exceptional virtue. The Frankish people famously recalls the praise of his holiness, on account of its worthy faith, with the worship of due veneration. [Bouillart adds, in italic type: [Note: [Col. 0645B] Castellanus correctly observed that these words, “On Mount Verziac,” and so forth, were added by a more recent hand. This addition alone, however, gave Bollandus reason [Col. 0646B] to consider the Herinien manuscript purer than the Pratensian. BOUILLART.]] On Mount Verziac, Saint Viventianus, confessor.

The nineteenth day before the Kalends. Day 14. [Note: [Col. 0649B]

That Usuard wrote this way is proved by the Herinien, Tournai, Greven, and Molan manuscripts, which transmit the pure text, as do many others that differ only in a few details, as will be evident below.]

[Note: [Col. 0649B]

I read “of the presbyter,” not “of the bishop,” as in the Pratensian manuscript, which inserted this title contrary to almost all the codices, both manuscripts and printed editions. Nor does the fact that in a more recent hand in the Aquicinct manuscript it is written that he may be called a bishop carry any authority, since it is certain that, although the dignity was offered to him, Saint [Col. 0649C] never accepted it. Some call him a martyr, among them Belin, who differs somewhat from the others when he writes: “Saint Felix in Pincis, priest and martyr.” On this title, see Bollandus and the other writers cited below. But the addition *in Pincis* greatly perplexes scholars. It should be read purely as *in Pineis*, as the careful investigator of such matters, Castellanus, judges. Yet whichever way it is read, that designation has nothing whatever to do with Nolanus, as Bollandus carefully discusses in his Preliminary Commentary, § 6. Ruinart likewise treats it in *Sincere and Select Acts*, beginning at page 255, in the preliminary admonition.

There is a difference in the wording of the testimony of Paulinus. Greven and Molan have: “Of whom blessed Paulinus, bishop, writes.” Pulsano: “Of whom Paulinus writes,” and so forth. Pratensis reads: “Pauline bishop.” I follow the Herinien and Tournai manuscripts, as well as the Pratensian itself with respect to the position of the verb; and I think Usuard wrote this way, since he was not accustomed to bind himself to the wording of those whom he was copying.

All write *cocleis*; I shall refrain from saying what stricter orthography requires. Bede reads *eductus sit* [Col. 0649D]; all the purer codices read *eductus est*, whatever Pulsano and others may have. In the same manuscript it is *Efrasii*; I write *Eufrasii*, with all the others except Greven and Molan, who incorrectly have *Eufrosii*. Others would prefer *Euphrasii*. If one invokes the Greek root, as though the etymology derived from φράζω (*phrázō*, “to declare” or “make known”), I shall not strongly object, although I know well that many names today are pronounced with φ and written *ph* in Latin, though that letter is plainly superfluous in French, Spanish, German, and other names. Why should not Alfonsus, Arnulfus, Adolfus, Rodolfus, and others of that kind be written more correctly in this way rather than with the Greek φ, when they have contracted no relationship whatever with it? Whether Eufrasius has contracted such a relationship you will be able to determine from the Observations.

There remains the principal variation, by which the Pratensian manuscript again diverges from the others. It forms the second announcement as follows: “Also on the same day, Saint Felix, priest and confessor.” You see an ambiguous and undetermined saint, whom, in my judgment, Usuard did not place here. I therefore think the other codices must be preferred entirely; our text agrees with them, and this is how I have always been convinced that Usuard wrote it.

Nevertheless, so that I might not appear to trust my own opinion too much, I wished to consult Castellanus about the alleged autograph. On 21 July 1709 he replied that he had discovered that the earlier announcement in the said manuscript—whether it concerned Eufrasius or someone else—had been struck out or erased, and that another, “Felix, priest and confessor,” had been written over it, rightly rejected by us. He also thinks that the word *priest* was erased in the first entry [Col. 0650D] and *bishop* written in its place. Thus it is again clear that our text is the genuine text of Usuard and that, where it mentions Eufrasius, it was taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, as you will see below.]

[Note: [Col. 0649D]

Felix of Nola found so distinguished an encomiast that, even for this reason alone, he has always been most renowned throughout the Catholic Church. The Carthaginian Calendar, in Mabilion’s edition, correctly places him on the nineteenth day before the Kalends; the Ruinartian edition incorrectly has the eighteenth, with these explicit words: “Saint Felix of Nola.” He is probably the same person in Fronto and Allatius. You will find the Sacramentaries in Florentinius; to these may be added the work published a little more than thirty years ago by Joseph Maria Thomasius, recently added by Pope Clement XI, our most holy lord, to the college of cardinals.

All the Martyrologies, especially the Hieronymian, sing his praises: “At Nola in Campania, Saint Felix,” or “the passion of Saint Felix.” Here you see the difficulty previously examined: whether he should be honored with the title of martyr or only with the distinguished title of confessor. On this matter see Bollandus and, after him, Florentinius and the others already cited or about to be cited. In brief, both titles apply, each contributing to the saint’s glory; it is unnecessary to explain this at greater length here.

We have discussed the episcopate in the Variants. The Little Roman Martyrology has: “At Nola, Felix the priest, buried in Pincis.” This perhaps gave Ado the opportunity, in his longer account, to confuse the Felixes; Bollandus shows that he did so, and some of our codices did likewise, being excessively Adonian in this respect. Notker followed nearly the same path, here again imitating Ado rather than Rabanus.

Bede composed for Felix a brief, elegant, and truthful eulogy. He rendered in prose the Life of the saint, which Paulinus had bound together in verse. This is the very eulogy that Our author copied from Bede, abandoning Ado. Rabanus likewise customarily follows Bede, but, besides our Nolan Felix, he introduces another Felix, his brother [Col. 0651B]; having avoided Ado’s Charybdis, he falls into Scylla, as you will easily understand from Bollandus.

Whether Florentinius reached the goal more successfully by distinguishing the Felixes in his own manner will have to be examined in the Supplement. Ruinart’s admonition cited above may be useful there, as may the French Life excavated by Tillemont, volume IV, beginning at page 226. Let this suffice concerning Felix of Nola, or, if you prefer, the Pauline Felix, at least for the purposes of our present undertaking. Receive the verses of Wandalbert:

> The day that is established as the nineteenth before the Kalends of February  
> Is adorned by holy Felix, priest and confessor.

In the Hieronymian Martyrologies, the deposition of Bishop Eufrasius—or Euphrasius—is consistently placed last. It is strange that Florentinius calls him Euphrates in his notes; otherwise he supplies little that helps us identify the saint, apart from what Bollandus [Col. 0652A] suggested to him. Relying too heavily on Galesinius, Baronius places Eufrasius in Africa and confuses him with Euchratius, perhaps more correctly Encratius, to whom Cyprian’s Letter 62 is extant and who is found to have participated in the Council of Carthage under that same Cyprian.

Meanwhile, concerning the entry in the Roman Martyrology mentioned above, Rosweyd indicates three points in the frequently cited manuscript letter, and these must not be passed over. He notes:

1. All the books have “Euphrasius, bishop,” not “Euchratius,” so that there can be no suspicion that this concerns Eucrathius, who participated in the Council of Carthage.

2. Baronius inserted *in Africa* into the text on his own authority—one might say that he received it from Galesinius—for it is absent from all the ancient books and even from Belin’s Roman Martyrology, which Baronius undertook to edit. But because he himself thought that the Euchratius who is known from other sources to have lived in Africa should be inserted here, he inserted *in Africa* into the text as well.

3. “I think,” says Rosweyd, “that this concerns Saint Euphrasius, the thirteenth bishop of Clermont, who died in the year 548, and concerning whom Gregory of Tours writes in Book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 30, and Book III, chapter 2.”

You will conclude from Castellanus, page 245, that these observations of Rosweyd are correct. He may have found Rosweyd’s opinion in Bollandus, where it is not entirely accepted. Yet I scarcely doubt that it is true, and uniquely true. Castellanus admits there that Eufrasius is mentioned by Usuard, but perhaps he did not then notice that Eufrasius is absent from the alleged autograph, unless he assumed with certainty that Usuard himself had written the name in the first hand and that it had been erased by a later hand; this is not known to me.

Ado continues: “At Vienne, Saint Caaeldus, bishop”; Mosander has *Caldeoldus*, others *Eoldus*. Usuard is silent about him, as we have already said more than once: the saints of Vienne are often passed over by him.]

[Note: [Col. 0651C]

PRATENSIS. We have already said enough about its supplement. It is worth noting here the various ways in which that other Felix, whoever he may be, is announced.

ANTWERP–MAJOR. It copies much concerning Felix of Nola from Ado, as do other codices; but, so as not to fill the present page needlessly, we refer the reader to the source itself. It says nothing about Eufrasius, but in second place has: “On the same day, the birthday of Saint Clerus, deacon, one of the ancients, who, after many tortures, was thrown into the sea.” See 7 January. Then: “At Spoleto, the passion of Saint Pontianus, martyr, in the time of the emperor Antoninus, under the judge Fabianus.” Clerus was transferred here from many codices, perhaps because they followed Rabanus. See Usuard, 19 January.

ROSWEYD. He has the same concerning Pontianus. Then he gives more concerning Felix of Nola, from Ado.

ACTS OF THE MARTYRS. The Usuard inserted here transmits the first announcement in pure form, but, omitting Eufrasius as well, fabricates the second as follows: “Also at Rome, the passion of another Felix, priest, who is called Felix [Col. 0651D] in Pincis.”

MUNERATUS. He treats purely only of Felix of Nola, nothing further, perhaps because he was uncertain whether to prefer Eufrasius or another Felix.

ANTWERP and MAXIMUS–LÜBECK. Pure in the text, they add after “Eufrasius, bishop”: “Clerus, deacon,” without a conjunction.

ANTWERP–MAXIMUS, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and LOUVAIN. They begin with Pontianus, with the same eulogy that Usuard gives under 19 January, so that it need not be copied here. In second place: “At Rome, on the Via Portuensis, in the place called Pincis, the birthday of Saint Felix, priest and martyr. He was crowned with a glorious death by decapitation during the reign of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian.” An Oedipus is needed to distinguish the Felixes; Bollandus has two on this day and seven others among those passed over. As for that Felix of the Via Portuensis, as the companion of Adauctus, he is referred to 30 August. I think this is incorrect, and I do not see on what basis Bollandus said it.

ALBERGEN. It has nothing concerning Pontianus; it begins with Felix of the Via Portuensis, concerning whom it agrees with the preceding witnesses. It is pure in the entry concerning the Nolan Felix. Then: “Eufrasius, bishop, and Clerus, deacon.”

DANIC. It begins in the same way and agrees in the remainder except at the end, where, together with four other witnesses, it has: “Eufrasius, bishop, and Clerus, deacon and martyr, one of the ancients, who, after many tortures, was thrown into the sea and completed his martyrdom.”

LEYDEN–BELGIAN and the Belgian edition of UTRECHT have Pontianus first, but the eulogy has been entirely deleted. In the rest they agree with the preceding witness and the other four.

CENTULE: “At Nola in Campania, Saint Felix, confessor. At Spoleto, Saint Pontianus, martyr, in the time of the emperor Antoninus. On the same day, Saint Clerus, deacon and martyr, one of the ancients. On the same day, Saint Eufrasius, bishop.” To speak once for all about Clerus: Florus also places him on this day, with an eulogy again different from that of Usuard, which we reported on 7 January [Col. 0652D]; see our observation there.

BRUSSELS. It begins correctly and purely, but after *he was released* adds: “And after he had patiently endured the grievous tortures he suffered for Christ, the truly happy man ascended to blessed realms and was buried near the city in a place called Pincis, where he shines through miracles. At the same place, Felix the priest, brother of the preceding man. He fought bravely for the confession of Christ, but the Church holds him to be a confessor rather than a martyr.” Enough has been said about these matters. It continues: “At Rome, on the Via Portuensis, in the place called Pincis, Saint Felix,” and so forth, as above. It also treats Clerus, whom it calls Cletus; enough has likewise been said about him. Finally, it is pure in the entry concerning Eufrasius.

HAGENOY. It surpasses all the others, for after *he was released* it adds this concerning the Nolan Felix: “Then he was tied to untamed mules and dragged through all the streets of the city for so long that his body was stripped from the shoulders to the waist, and so forth.” This specimen is sufficient. Concerning Felix of the Via Portuensis, Eufrasius, and Clerus, it agrees with the foregoing. Finally, concerning Pontianus, after “he completed his martyrdom,” it adds: “His bones were transferred from Spoleto to Milan, and from Milan to Lower Utrecht.”

AQUICINCT. It agrees with the Pratensian manuscript in deleting Eufrasius. There is, however, this difference concerning Felix: in the first hand it has only “Saint Felix, priest, and so forth,” to which a more recent pen added “martyr, at Rome under Diocletian.” Presumably this is to be understood of Felix of the Via Portuensis. It is almost the only witness, together with the Pratensian, to give Felix of Nola the title “bishop.”

VICTORINUS and the SWEDISH REGISTRY, under number 130: “At Spoleto, Saint Pontianus, martyr.” They incorrectly write *Potianus* and *Pocianus*.

MATRICHT, CARTHUSIAN, and UTRECHT: “Felix in Pincis, confessor. The feast of Pontianus, martyr, is celebrated in the city”—namely, Utrecht—“because his body is present there in the church of Saint Martin.” These words are added in the margin.

In the VATICAN manuscript no. 5949, Eufrasius is absent. The following is added: “The birthday of Saint Felix in Pincis. At Benevento, Saint Memorius, bishop.” He is unknown to the others and is counted by Bollandus among those passed over.

FLORENTINIUS: “At Rome, Saint Felix in Pincis, martyr.” Then the STROZZIAN manuscript: “In Sardinia, blessed Ephysius [or Ephylius], martyr.” Others call him Ephysius and treat him on the following day.

THE LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins with Felix of the Via Portuensis and adds, besides what has already been given: “With the judge Draccho presiding, by decapitation,” and so forth. Concerning the Nolan Felix, after *he was released*, it adds: “At last, when peace had been restored, he returned to his church and rested there in peace. Now, on the Lord’s day,” and so forth. In this Ado confused the Felixes. Then: “On the same day, Saint Eufrasius, bishop, and Clerus, deacon. Also, the discovery of Saint Firmin, bishop and martyr.” It could have added, with Greven, “At Amiens.” Bollandus, on the preceding day—for Firmin also recurs there—refers Firmin of Amiens among those passed over, together with Usuard, to 25 September. On this day he treats another Saint Firmin, bishop of the Gabali, concerning whom see Castellanus, page 247.

BELIN. The second edition has at the end: “On the same day, Saint Eufrasius, bishop, and Clarus, deacon.”

GREVEN: “Clerus, deacon. At Rome, on the Via Portuensis, in the place called Pincis, the birthday of Saint Felix, priest and martyr, brother of the blessed Felix mentioned above. He, under Diocletian and Maximian, with Draccho presiding as judge, after the torment of the rack, by decapitation,” and so forth. He indicates Ado, where the following is read under 19 January: “He completed his martyrdom on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, and his body, taken up by Christians, was buried on the fifteenth day before the Kalends. His solemn day is celebrated on the fourteenth day before the Kalends”—Rosweyd reads this, not the sixteenth, as Castellanus cites it—“of February, when his sacred body was transferred a second time.” Perhaps it was then transferred.

Greven continues: “At Vienne, Saint Eoldus, bishop and confessor. Or Cadeoldus,” as we said above. “At Amiens, the discovery of Saint Firmin,” and so forth.

MOLANUS, in italic type: “The passion of Saint Pontianus, precious martyr, in the time of the emperor Antoninus, under the judge Fabianus [Col. 0654A], whose relics are kept in Lower Utrecht.” Then he names Caldeoldus; subsequently, in smaller type: “At Milan, Saint Datius, bishop, of great holiness, concerning whom there is an account in the *Dialogues* of blessed Gregory.” The second and third editions add: “He is listed with several other bishops of that place in the Litanies of the Church of Milan. In the territory of Tours, Saints Maura and Britta, virgins, whom Gregory of Tours mentions.” Bollandus treats these virgins, together with the Gallican Martyrology, on the following day.

The later editions add: “On the fourteenth day, the holy Fathers murdered on Sinai and at Raithu.” The indefinite number is correct; for when Baronius determined it, he gave occasion for this observation of Rosweyd, found in the manuscript cited above. I judged the entire passage, as it stands, worthy of the reader’s curiosity and have therefore reproduced it.

Baronius’s text reads: “On Mount Sinai, thirty-eight holy monks, killed by the Saracens for the faith of Christ.” In the notes: “Thirty-eight monks [Col. 0654B]; the Greeks also treat of them in the Menologion. Abbot Saint Nilus, who wrote the deeds of the aforesaid martyrs, crowned in his own time, says concerning them: ‘They died,’ he says, ‘after the seventh day of the Lord’s Epiphany, which is the fourteenth of January.’ But a little further on: ‘Others also were killed many years earlier; their commemoration too, because of the length of the journey and the multitude of those who assemble, they celebrate on the same day.’”

To this Rosweyd responds:

> “Two points must be noted concerning this day.
