First, the text here places thirty-eight monks, who in the notes are said to have been killed in the time of Nilus, since Baronius thought that Nilus was speaking about these thirty-eight monks when he says: ‘They died after the seventh day of the Lord’s Epiphany.’ This cannot refer to the thirty-eight monks who were killed long ago on Sinai, but to an uncertain number of monks killed in the time of Nilus. For the Menologion of Sirlet places those thirty-eight monks long before the time of Nilus, or of the emperor Anastasius, and Nilus merely mentions them in passing in these words: ‘Others also were killed many years earlier’—namely, in the time of the emperor Diocletian and Peter of Alexandria, as the Menologion has it—‘and their commemoration too, because of the length of the journey and the multitude of those who assemble, they celebrate on the same day.’
>
> “Second, from the words just cited it follows that those thirty-eight monks did not suffer on 14 January but on another day. Yet because on 14 January the Fathers gathered on Sinai to celebrate the feast of the monks killed in the time of Nilus, whose number is not specified, so that they would not be forced to assemble a second time on another day when those thirty-eight ancient monks had been killed—and because the journey was long and would impose hardship on many—they celebrated both commemorations together, on the day when the feast of the monks killed in the time of Nilus recurred annually; that day was 14 January.”

Thus far Rosweyd has observed the matter accurately enough [Col. 0654D]. See further concerning both classes of martyrs joined together by Baronius in Bollandus’s *Acts* and in Castellanus’s notes for this day, page 244. What has since Bollandus been published concerning both of these classes of martyrs, whether by Combefis, Possinus, or others, in Greek or Latin, will enlarge the Supplement. Meanwhile, see the appendix to volume I of January, beginning at page 1113.]

[Col. 0649]

At Nola in Campania, the birthday of Saint Felix, priest [Bouillart: bishop] [Note: [Col. 0649B] Castellanus also examined this point closely. The small space where *bishop* is written in the first hand had been erased. Likewise, the announcement of the second Saint Felix lies in an erasure, at least these words: “Also on the same day.” Whether it was enough for Usuard that Saint Felix had been designated and elected bishop by the people, so that he called him a bishop, I do not intend to investigate. I must preserve not the author’s intention but his words. As for the addition of the other Felix, if it is a fault, it was not Usuard’s alone. Ado himself mixed together the deeds of two Felixes, one of whom other Martyrologists before Usuard called the brother of the other. Wretched is the fate of the man who follows guides that are not at all safe; and in this matter Sollerius ought to be all the more equitable toward Usuard, since he himself is more clearly liable to the fault that he would blame in Usuard. BOUILLART.] and confessor, concerning whom blessed Paulinus writes: when he was being sent by persecutors into prison and was lying covered with shells and potsherds, he was released by an angel during the night and led out. On the same day, Saint Eufrasius, bishop.

The eighteenth day before the Kalends. Day 15. [Note: [Col. 0655]

The Pratensian, Tournai, Antwerp, Maximus–Lübeck, Greven, and Molan manuscripts have this in pure form.]

I wrote *Abbacuc*, *Micheae*, *Archadio*, and *Macharii*, as the manuscripts commonly do. Concerning Egypt, I said on 7 January that I would preserve the correct spelling, although few manuscripts use the diphthong *AE*, and I shall follow that practice hereafter. In the variant reading for Isidore, I preferred what is found in the text and is better: “In holiness of life, faith, and miracles.” I think Usuard read it this way, although the printed Ado has lost the preposition *in*. Why Greven and Molan wrote *fideque* is not worth investigating. I wrote *Boniti*, not *Bonitti*, as it is read in Praten., perhaps through a copyist’s error; certainly all the others call him Bonitus. From the manuscripts cited it is clear that Maurus was placed simply, as he is in our text, by Usuard himself, who presumably never thought of him as a disciple of Saint Benedict. Add to these many others collated with Greven and Molan, in which no trace of that matter appears anywhere. Indeed, if the authenticity of the Pratensis manuscript has any force, whether genuine or false, it here clearly demonstrates, as we say *ad hominem*, that in the mature ninth century the Angevin Maurus was not accustomed to be counted among Benedict’s disciples even by the Benedictines themselves. For who could soberly believe that Usuard would have kept silent about this, when shortly before, in the same text, he had proclaimed Macarius a disciple of Antony? I was therefore greatly surprised to read these additions in the Herinien manuscript: “A disciple of the blessed abbot Benedict.” And in Muneratus, otherwise pure: “A disciple of the blessed Benedict, whose body is magnificently placed, honored, and venerated near the city of Paris.” Other manuscripts will recur below. In any event, I think it beyond doubt that these and other additions were made later and were never known to Usuard.

[Note: [Col. 0655B]]

Only the memory of the prophet Habakkuk—or *Abbacuc*—is found in all the commonly circulated Hieronymian manuscripts except the Epternacensis. Neither this prophet nor Micah is known to Bede or Florus. Rabanus records the deposition of the first and then the discovery of the relics of both under Arcadius and Honorius; Notker preserved this arrangement from him. The first author to join the feast of the two prophets was the compiler of the Small Roman Martyrology: “Habakkuk and Micah, the prophets.” The remainder was added by Ado, taken over verbatim from him by Our Author, and passed into all the more recent versions. Baronius nevertheless correctly observed—and expressed the same point in the Roman Martyrology—that those bodies were discovered under the elder Theodosius, as Bollandus deduces from his *Ecclesiastical History*. Bollandus discusses learnedly both prophets—whether they are one or two homonymous persons—and other matters relating to them, as Florentinius acknowledges; Florentinius’s note is also worth reading. Wandalbertus, following the opinion of the Small Roman Martyrology, which I think he took from Ado, composed his little verse:

> The twice-nine [day] honors Habakkuk and Micah together.

The Small Roman Martyrology continues: “And Macarius the abbot, a disciple of Antony.” Ado added, “Most renowned for life and miracles”; Our Author prefixed, “In Egypt”; Notker lacks both additions. Nothing further remains to be observed about the Macarii; see what we said on 2 January and consult the authors cited there. The companion or colleague of Macarius in the Small Roman Martyrology seems to be the following priest and monk, in these words: “And Isidore,” to whom Ado appended a sufficiently commonplace eulogy, from which Usuard and Notker took theirs. I do not know whether later writers can say more about his life and deeds than has been collected with the greatest care in our Acts. Up to this point it is entirely clear that our text is Adonian. Bonitus, thirtieth bishop of Clermont, was first recorded by Usuard and also furnished with a commonplace eulogy. Add to Bollandus’s commentary what Castellanus noted on pages 282 and 283. Maurus, like Bonitus, also belongs solely to Usuard, concerning whose placement we have said enough in the Variants. It is not the place here to investigate further whether this Maurus was a disciple of Saint Benedict. The curious may consult the distinguished Castellanus, who discusses the entire controversy at length in his notes, from page 252 to page 281. Papebrochius tried more than once to untie the same knot in the Acts, and more recently in his *Responses to the presentation of errors*. Ruinartius composed an apology for the mission of Maurus against both these writers and others. Finally, so many others have woven and rewoven this fabric that it seems superfluous even to name them. Note also that on this day Ado records the translation of Sulpitius of Bourges. But Usuard and the other Martyrologists who follow him, together with the modern Roman Martyrology, treat this saint on 17 January, where Bollandus carefully distinguishes the various Sulpitii.

[Note: [Col. 0655D]]

**PRATEN.** See above in the Variants what was additionally inserted in this manuscript of Usuard.

**ANTUERP.-MAJ.** writes simply of Macarius: “Macarius, a disciple of Antony.” In other respects it is not entirely sound. After *confessor* concerning Bonitus it has: “Whose life, the merits of whose virtues, and the glory of whose miracles were distinguished.” Then: “In the territory of Angers, the deposition of the blessed Maurus, monk, abbot, and confessor, a disciple of Saint Benedict.”

**ROSWEYD.** varies the wording concerning the discovery of the prophets thus: “Discovered when divine grace revealed them.” In the entry for Isidore it is not entirely pure. Bonitus is absent, and this is substituted: “At Bourges, the translation of Saint Sulpitius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the passing of Saint Maurus the abbot.”

**PULSANEN.** inserts Maurus in second place in this form: “On the same day, of the most blessed Maurus, confessor and abbot, disciple of Christ’s confessor Benedict.”

**MUNERAT.** and **THE ACTS OF THE MARTYRS** agree in the matters reported above in the Variants.

**ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVAN.,** and the **ULTRAJ.-BELG.** edition add only at the end: “A disciple of the blessed Benedict.”

**ALBERGEN.** and **DANIC.** begin as follows: “In Gaul, in the territory of Angers, of Saint Maurus the abbot, a disciple of Saint Benedict. Educated regularly under his discipline from childhood, he showed how much progress he had made in it by several deeds performed while he was with him, including walking on foot over the waters.” Then they give the entries for Habakkuk and Micah without alteration. Next: “In Egypt, of the blessed abbot Macarius, a disciple of the blessed Antony, renowned for life and miracles, and so forth. Having received divine grace against aerial spirits, in the healing of human beings, and also in announcing future events, he completed sixty years in the deserts, into which he entered at the age of thirty. When someone asked him why his body was so dry, he replied: ‘The fear of God consumes even the bones.’” In the remaining portions the text is fairly pure.

**CENTULEN.** is nearly pure. It omits Bonitus’s eulogy and adds concerning Maurus, “a disciple of Saint Benedict.”

**BRUXELL.** begins: “The octave of our blessed virgin Gudila, our patroness.” It is pure in the prophets. Concerning Macarius it adds only his age, repeating what it said about the other Macarius on 2 January. It then proceeds to Isidore, purely. Then: “At the city of Bourges, the translation of Saint Sulpitius, bishop and confessor.” It is fairly correct concerning Bonitus. It postpones Maurus to the following day, perhaps because this day is occupied by the octave of Saint Gudila.

**HAGENOYEN:** “Of the prophet Habakkuk (*Abacuch*), who was carried by the hair by an angel to Babylon to provide food for Daniel. Also of the prophet Micah (*Nycheae*). Their bodies, and so forth.” It has the longer eulogy for Macarius given above. It is pure concerning Isidore and Bonitus. Then it also has the account of Maurus the abbot as above.

**AQUICINCT.** continues concerning Maurus after *abbot* as follows: “and confessor and Levite, a disciple of the most holy Benedict; educated under his discipline from childhood, he revealed how much he had advanced in it by several deeds performed while he was with him, an unprecedented event after Peter, namely by walking on foot over the waters. Then sent by Benedict himself into Gaul, renowned for the glory of his miracles, he rested in peace.”

**VICTORIN.** agrees with the preceding not entirely in words but in sense.

**MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.:** “Of Macarius the abbot, a disciple of the blessed abbot Antony. Of Maurus the abbot, a disciple of the blessed abbot Benedict. Of Isidore the confessor. Of Sabinus, Marcellinus, and Exuperantius, martyrs.” Concerning these, see Usuard’s first announcement, 30 December. It continues: “Of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah.” Finally: “In Auvergne, of Saint Bonitus.”

**CLUNIACEN.:** “In the territory of Angers, of Saint Maurilius the abbot.” Was he not a bishop? See below.

**REG. SUEC.** no. 130, and **VICTORIN.** above: “In Africa, of Saint Restituta the virgin.” If this is Restituta of Sora, see the Acts for 27 May.

**CODEX D. LE MARE**, designated A, formerly belonging to the Canons of Saint Lazarus of Autun: “At the city of the Aedui, the translation of Saint Symphorianus the martyr.” See 22 August.

In the **VATICAN** manuscript no. 5949 Bonitus is absent. It adds: “At Bourges, the translation of Saint Sulpitius, bishop and confessor.” Maurus is placed first, in red letters.

**FLORENTIN.:** “In the territory of Angers, of Saint Maurilius the abbot.” It continues: “At Bourges, of Saint Sulpitius,” and so forth.

[Col. 0658A]

**LUGDUNEN.:** “The feast of Saint Bonitus, bishop and confessor of Auvergne.”

**BURDEGALEN.:** “In the territory of Angers, the translation of Saint Maurilius, bishop and confessor. And the dedication of the church of Saint Maurilius.” Usuard treats him on 13 September under the name Maurilio and calls him a bishop. This explains the reason for the doubt mentioned above.

**LUBECK-COLOGNE EDITION:** “In the city of Angers, near Paris in Gaul, of Saint Maurus the abbot, a disciple of Saint Benedict. Under whose discipline … walking on foot over the waters, by order of Saint Benedict he rescued a boy from drowning.” It is pure in the prophets and has the account of Macarius given above. It is also pure in Isidore and Bonitus. At the end it adds: “Likewise, a commemoration of Saint Joseph, the Lord’s foster father.” This is also read in Greven, probably because of a special feast customarily celebrated among the people of Cologne.

**BELIN.** in the first edition omitted Saint Bonitus’s eulogy. The rest is fairly pure, except that concerning Maurus it has everything reported above from **AQUICINCT.**

**GREVEN.:** “Of Felix, bishop of Tubizacum and martyr. At Alexandria, of Tonita, otherwise called Cointa, virgin and martyr. Of Remedius, bishop and confessor.” These are from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, as we said on the preceding day. “A commemoration of Saint Joseph, the Lord’s foster father.” See the Index of Saints Omitted for all these matters.

**MOLAN.** adds to the account of Maurus, taken from Muneratus, beyond what has already been said: “Whose body is magnificently placed, honored, and venerated near the city of Paris. Likewise, the celebration of the most sweet name of Jesus.” I find the beginning of this feast indicated in the manuscript Martyrology of Saint Michael at Antwerp, under the name of Usuard, although it is enormously interpolated; it reads as follows: “This feast began in Antwerp in the year of the Lord 1458, through the foresight, devotion, and arrangements of an honorable citizen, Hippolytus. In our monastery, however, we began to celebrate this same feast solemnly in the year of the Lord 1492.”

Molan continues in smaller type: “In Burgundy, of Saint John Calinitus (*Joannis Caliniti*) the confessor, whose holy body rests happily in the city of Constantinople, shining with many miracles; but the city of Chrysopolis—Besançon—is incomparably enriched by the precious treasure of his head.” Other editions have: “On the fifteenth day, of the holy father John Calybites. ‘Whose precious …,’ etc.” Rosweyd’s observation on this passage, which was inserted differently into the Roman Martyrology, is as follows:

> “Two questions may be raised here. First, from which old manuscript did Baronius insert the Martyrology’s text concerning John Calybites? Second, how can he place him at Rome when the *Menaea* expressly locates him at Constantinople? The answer is that Metaphrastes means New Rome, not Old Rome. Indeed, the text of the Life seems sufficiently to indicate that all these events took place at Constantinople.”

See Bollandus’s preliminary commentary, section 2, where several further considerations are carefully weighed; and Castellanus’s briefer treatment of the same matters in his notes, page 283. Later editions of Molan have the entry for Maurus and that for the name of Jesus almost as in the first edition. Then: “On the same day at Malbodium, the deposition of the blessed Ablebert, or Emebert, bishop of Cambrai, who preceded Saint Autbert in the bishopric of Cambrai.”

[Col. 0653]

Of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah, whose bodies were discovered under the emperor Arcadius through divine revelation. In Egypt, of the blessed abbot Macarius, a disciple of the blessed Antony, most renowned for life and miracles. Likewise, of Saint Isidore, distinguished in holiness of life, faith, and miracles. At the city of Clermont, of Saint Bonitus, bishop and confessor, whose life shone with virtues. In the territory of Angers, of Saint Maurus the abbot.

[Note: [Col. 0656A]]

From the fact that Usuard does not call Saint Maurus a disciple of the blessed Benedict, Sollerius—insufficiently mindful of his own dialectic—concludes that Usuard never thought of him as a disciple of Saint Benedict, and that in the mature ninth century the Angevin Maurus was not accustomed to be counted among Benedict’s disciples even by the Benedictines themselves. The only conclusion that follows from this is that at that time no other Angevin Maurus was known apart from the disciple of Saint Benedict, and therefore that Usuard thought it superfluous to add any designation by which the Angevin Maurus might be distinguished from another.

“But,” he says, “who could soberly believe that Usuard would have kept silent about this, when shortly before, in the same text, he had proclaimed Macarius a disciple of Antony?”

No sober person fails to see why he said this about Macarius: namely, because there were several abbots named Macarius, but only one disciple of the blessed Antony. I in turn ask: Who could prudently believe that a holy abbot who was an ornament and propagator of the Benedictine family never came to the mind of a Benedictine and was omitted from a catalogue of the saints being compiled? **BOUILLART.**

**XVII Kal. The 16th.**

[Note: [Col. 0657D]]

Only the Herinien and Tornacense manuscripts read this way, and, as I believe, correctly.

[Note: [Col. 0659A]]

I wrote *Maximinus*, as the two cited manuscripts expressly have, together with Praten., Munerat., and others; nor had Usuard found any other form in Bede and Ado. Greven, Molan, and other manuscripts give *Maximianus*. Which is better? Perhaps neither: for from *Maximinus* and *Maximianus* one might easily suppose Maxentius, to whose tyranny both the death of Marcellus and whatever sufferings he endured seem by some to be referred. Whatever one decides, it is most probable that Marcellus died not strictly as a martyr but properly as a confessor in the seventh year of the Diocletian persecution, in the year of Christ 310, as Tillemont correctly believes in volume V, pages 95 and 626; Papebrochius had already taught this before him. The quibbles of Pearson and others can easily be refuted from these writers.

The Pratensis manuscript reads between Honoratus and Furseus: “Likewise, at the city of Odobergia, of Saint Titianus, bishop and confessor.” For a long time I remained uncertain what judgment to make about this announcement. It was not easy to determine where Usuard had obtained this saint, unknown to the Martyrologists whom he followed, since he was not accustomed to travel beyond the Alps or to other regions—except Spain—to add saints to Ado or the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

Meanwhile Muneratus, Greven, Molan, and several manuscripts followed the Pratensis, while others, together with the Herinien and Tornacense, said nothing about Titianus. Although I place great confidence in the authority of the latter two, I had thought that I should almost yield to the current of the majority. I therefore asked the distinguished Castellanus to consult the Pratensis manuscript again, and, after detecting the corruption, he admirably confirmed the original simplicity of those two manuscripts.

> “Whatever was written in the Pratensis manuscript by the original hand between *Arelate* and *Saint Furseus*—excluding both—was later erased, and I found written in another, much-abbreviated hand what is read in Molan’s first edition, with this sole difference: *TITIANI* and *PARRONA* occur instead of Molan’s *TICIANI* and *PERONA*.”

This observation by my friend completely moved me to remove Titianus. If others judge otherwise, I shall willingly yield to better arguments. *Arelaten* for *Arelatem* in the Herinien manuscript is a copyist’s error. *Parrona* was formerly written for *Perona*, as nearly all the manuscripts prove; some wrote *Parona*.

[Note: [Col. 0659B]]

At Rome, on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla, the deposition of Marcellus, bishop and confessor. These are the words of most of the Hieronymian manuscripts; Florentinius’s careful note may be consulted concerning them. The Small Roman Martyrology differs little: “At Rome, on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla, of Saint Marcellus the pope.”

This is brief; but Bede, who had seen the not-very-genuine Acts of Marcellus, or the deeds of the pontiffs, adorns the saint with a longer eulogy. Rabanus and Ado copied it, Notker somewhat interpolated it, and Our Author, whether he took it from Bede or from Ado, shortened it by more than half; even so, it is not sufficiently exact in every respect.

Everywhere here I read *Marcellus*, never *Marcellinus*, except in Bucherius’s Calendar, which could very easily have been corrupted through the similarity of the names, as in fact happened on the indicated day, XVIII Kal., instead of XVII Kal. Fronto’s Calendar proves this, for on this exact day it expressly reads not *Marcellinus* but *Marcellus*, as does the Sacramentary of Thomasius, praised above.

Nor am I moved by the authority of the Greeks, which, unless I am mistaken, has been sufficiently shaken by Henschenius in his treatment of Marcellinus on 26 April. Castellanus argues vigorously in today’s notes for the identity of the two and again insists on the same opinion in his universal Martyrology. But when I had pressed my friend more than once on this matter in private conversation, he finally admitted in his last letter to me—written by another hand after he had been struck by a fatal apoplexy, on 31 January 1711—that he had retracted what he had written concerning the identity of Marcellus and Marcellinus.

We established the date of his death in the Variants. For the other matters transferred here and there, whether genuinely or under pretense, see Bollandus, who also preserves the celebrated epitaph. Even if one denies that it was truly composed by Damasus, one will not deny that its antiquity makes it worthy of veneration. Wandalbertus sang of Marcellus:

> The seventeenth day shines with the martyr Marcellus,  
> The supreme pontiff, in merit and in name.

Honoratus of Arles is considered an addition to the Hieronymian copies. He was first placed by Ado, and Our Author transferred him from Ado in almost the same words. Rabanus reported him in different wording, adding the miracle of the dragon driven from the island of Lérins; Notker copied this text. The Life, illustrated by Bollandus, is presumed to have been written by Hilary, likewise bishop of Arles, but Henschenius casts this into doubt on 1 June, in his treatment of Saint Caprasius. See other material in Castellanus, page 292.

I explained above whether Titianus of Opitergium should be attributed to Usuard. There can be no doubt that Furseus truly belongs to Usuard. Florus had recorded him earlier, but this passage will again make clear how unknown he was to Our Author. Castellanus corrects the errors made by some concerning this saint on page 295. Whether the Life published and illustrated by Bollandus was composed by an excessively credulous writer will be examined elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0659D]]

**PRATEN., MUNERAT., GREVEN.** and **MOLAN.** have Titianus of Opitergium inserted in the text, concerning whom see above.

**ANTUERP.-MAJ.** reports nearly the whole of Bede concerning Marcellus. It is almost pure in Honoratus. Then: “At the monastery of Parrona, of Saint Furseus the confessor. He was very distinguished both in word and example, showing salvation to many; worn out by a good old age, he happily departed to Christ. He was first buried in the monastery of Lagny, then transferred to Parrona, where he rests, [renowned] for many miracles.” It says nothing about Titianus.

**ROSWEYD.:** “At Rome, on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla, the feast of Saint Marcellus the pope and martyr. By order of Maximianus he was beaten with clubs and assigned to the service of animals; there he died. At Arles, of Saint Honoratus the bishop, whose life, teaching, and miracles shone forth,” as Ado has it. “On the same day, the feast of Saint Furseus the confessor.” It also says nothing about Titianus.

**THE ACTS OF THE MARTYRS**, at the end: “At the monastery of Perona, of Saint Furseus, bishop and confessor.” The rest is as in **PRATEN.**

**PULSANEN.** abbreviates Bede somewhat in its first section. In the second it writes *Honorius* for *Honoratus*. It includes Titianus and Furseus. At the end it adds on its own: “At Rouen, of Saint Melantius, bishop and confessor.” See the Omitted Saints.

**ANTUERP.-MAX., LUBECK,** and **UGHELLIAN.** have Titianus of Opitergium as do many manuscripts. At the end they add: “At Rome, of Saint Priscilla.” But unlike others, they do not call her a virgin.

**ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVAN., ALBERGEN.** and the **ULTRAJ.-BELG.** edition insert in the penultimate place: “On the same day, at Rome, of Saint Priscilla.” Concerning Furseus they read: “Abbot and confessor, brother of Saint Foillanus the martyr.” In other respects they resemble those that record Titianus, and so forth. Concerning Priscilla, see Castellanus, page 285.

**DANIC.** resembles the earlier witnesses; a later hand has added the names of five martyrs of Morocco, concerning whom much will be recorded below from Greven.

[Col. 0661B]

**CENTULEN.:** “At Rome, the feast of Saint Marcellus the pope and martyr. At the city of Odobergia, of Saint Titianus, bishop and confessor. At the monastery of Parrona, of Saint Furseus the confessor, who was very distinguished both in word and example. At Relato, of Saint Honoratus, bishop and confessor.” I think this is a copyist’s error, since he did not sufficiently distinguish *Arelate* or *Arelato*; a later hand subsequently tried to shape the word.

**BRUXELL.** postponed Maurus here, concerning whom we spoke on the preceding day. Then: “At Rome, on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla, the feast of Saint Marcellus the pope and martyr. When he refused to sacrifice to the gods, by order of the emperor Maximianus he was beaten with clubs and assigned under public guard to the service of animals. On the same day, at Rome, of Saint Priscilla.” It is not entirely pure in Honoratus. “At the monastery of Parona, of Saint Furseus, abbot and confessor, and brother of Saint Foillanus the martyr. Distinguished in word and example, he finally, worn out by a good old age, happily departed to the Lord. At Rouen, of Saint Melantius, bishop and confessor. Likewise, at the city of Odobergia,” and so forth.

**HAGENOYEN.** scraped together some material concerning Marcellus that does not deserve to be reported. Concerning Honoratus and Titianus it agrees with the account above. Then: “On the same day at Rome, the deposition of Saint Priscilla.” Concerning Furseus it adds: “abbot and brother of Saint Foillanus the martyr.”

**AQUICINCT.** offers a new addition concerning Furseus, namely: “Whose head is kept at Canterbury.”

**VICTORIN.** adds after “he died” concerning Saint Marcellus: “He built the cemetery on the Salarian Way and established twenty-five titular churches in the City for the baptism and penance of many who are converted from paganism, and for the burial of martyrs.” These additions were taken from the Acts. At the end, with the same error as others, it writes: “At Rome, of Saint Priscilla the virgin.” The **CODEX REG. SUEC.** no. 130 writes the same.

The **CODEX REG. SUEC.**, formerly belonging to Prince Ursinus Rosenberg, has: “At the city of Brescia, of Saint Libera, wife [or perhaps rather virgin?] and sister of Saint Faustina, who, leading a strict life in a certain monastery, ended her life. Double minor, second class.” Let Bollandus be consulted on this day among the Omitted Saints, and on the 18th of this month, where he treats her.

**VATICAN** no. 5949, omitting Titianus of Opitergium, adds: “At Benevento, of Saint Peter the martyr, in Saint Sophia.”

**STROZZ.:** “On the same day at Morocco, the passion of the blessed martyrs Berard, Peter, Accursius, Adjutus, and Otto, of the Order of Friars Minor”; concerning these, more extensively below.

**JURENSIS OF SAINT RAGNOBERT:** “At Grenoble, of Saint Ferreolus, bishop and martyr.”

The first edition of **BELLINI** is tolerable, adding only Priscilla and the Moroccan martyrs in the way already reported from the Strozzi manuscript. But the second, Paris edition is disgracefully corrupted and distorted. There “Odobergia” is cited twice, and first “Cyrianus,” then “Titianus,” is attached to it as bishop. The eulogy of the Moroccan martyrs, torn away from the martyrs themselves, yields no meaning; I therefore thought it preferable to quote it below from Greven.

The **LUBECK-COLOGNE EDITION** has awkwardly combined various material about Marcellus found in other witnesses; it has likewise collected material found concerning Furseus. It makes Priscilla a virgin and adds at the end: “On the same day, of Saint Remundus the confessor.” Greven also mentions him, but it is not easy to determine which Remundus is meant; Bollandus thinks Pennafort may be indicated.

**GREVEN’S** appendix is longer than usual and begins as follows: “Of Poleuctus [printed *Poleucti*], Candidianus, and Philoromus, martyrs.” I believe he intended *Polyeuctus*, as we corrected it again above on the 10th of this month. Bollandus treats them on the 11th. It continues: “Of Foillanus, bishop and martyr, and his companions. Likewise, of Felix, bishop of Tubabocum, who, when questioned by the judge Anolinus under Diocletian and Maximianus, replied only this: ‘I am a Christian.’ Then bound and lying in a small boat beneath the feet of horses, weakened by starvation, he finally completed his martyrdom by being beheaded at Nola in Campania.” Concerning Foillanus and Felix, Bollandus should be consulted among the Omitted Saints.

Greven continues:

> “At Morocco, around the year of the Lord 1350 (1220)—the passion of the blessed martyrs Berard of Carpio, Peter of Geminiano, Accursius, Adjutus or Adutor, and Otto, of the Order of Friars Minor. Inflamed with divine zeal and burning with love of martyrdom, they crossed over to the lands of the unbelievers to preach the Gospel of Christ. Martyred by the king of Morocco, they became renowned through many signs of miracles. Their bodies were brought from Morocco by Don Pedro, the Infante, brother of the king of Portugal, and honorably placed in the monastery of Santa Cruz at Coimbra. Of Honoratus, bishop of Amiens, renowned for miracles. Once, while celebrating Mass, he saw the hand of Christ holding the host and extending it to him as he was about to receive Communion. The memory of Honoratus the abbot is also observed here. As Gregory relates in the first book of the *Dialogues*, while still in the years of childhood, in the region of Samnium he burned with love of the heavenly homeland through abstinence. Restraining himself also from idle speech, after founding a monastery he became the father of nearly two hundred monks and, giving examples of outstanding conduct all around him, rested in peace. Likewise, of Melantius the bishop and confessor—Molan writes *Mela*—to whose church, as is said in the *Tripartite History*, those who had come by order of King Huneric to deport into exile the bishops resisting the Arians found him preparing candles and tending lamps, as though he were the church’s lowest minister. For this reason they did not recognize that he was a bishop until he himself voluntarily disclosed it, so that he might be carried into exile for Christ.”

You will find the false material mixed with the true distinguished by Bollandus, and perhaps at some point further illuminated. “At Reggio in Gaul, of Faustus the bishop, who, chosen from the abbacy of Lérins, is praised by Gennadius as full of holiness and constantly devoted to the divine Scriptures.” Enough has been said about Remundus and Priscilla.

**MOLAN.** copied Greven almost entirely in the matter of the Mauritanian martyrs and what follows, except for Faustus and Remundus, whom he omitted. He correctly removed the title “virgin” from Priscilla. To Furseus he added: “Whose deeds are recorded.” Then: “On the same day, the discovery of the body of Saint Foillanus, bishop and martyr, at Ampollin.” Ampollin, or Ampolines, is the place where Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, says that Saint Foillanus suffered martyrdom, as will be related in the Acts for 31 October. Another edition of Molan considers this Priscilla to be the same woman celebrated in the Acts of the Apostles; finally it adds: “On the sixteenth day, the adoration of the precious chain of the most holy and most blessed apostle Peter.”

[Col. 0657]

At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the feast of Saint Marcellus the pope, who, because he defended the Catholic faith, was first beaten with clubs by order of the tyrant Maximinus, then assigned under public guard to the service of animals, and after serving there for many years died wearing a garment of haircloth. At Arles, of the blessed Honoratus, bishop, whose life, teaching, and miracles were illustrious.

[Inserted by Bouillart.: [Note: [Col. 0657D]]

Sollerius removed Saint Titianus, although there is a consensus among the manuscripts, which he thought should almost be followed like a torrent. The reason for his resistance was the following observation by his informant: that in the Pratensis manuscript everything between *Arelatem* and Saint Furseus written by the first hand had been erased. There is indeed an erasure here. But the person who erased the passage also wrote what precedes it. He merely compressed the letters somewhat more tightly to make room for Saint Titianus, whom he had omitted in the original autograph.

This Titianus is the bishop of the city of Opitergium, whom the published Martyrologies of Usuard and the German Martyrology commemorate on this day; Ferrarius composed his Acts from the ancient records of the church of Opitergium. Bollandus reports these Acts on this same day. **BOUILLART.]

Likewise, at the city of Odobergia, of Saint Titianus, bishop and confessor. At the monastery of Parrona, of Saint Furseus the confessor.

**XVI Kal. The 17th.**

[Note: [Col. 0663A]]

This is how Praten., Herinien., Pulsanen., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven., Molan., and the Acts of the Martyrs read it. Belin nearly agrees, but neither edition is correct.

[Note: [Col. 0663A]]

In the Pulsanensis, concerning Saint Antony, instead of “whose body,” which I find placed through the copyist’s freedom, there is “his venerable body.” Nearly all write *Alexandriae*; Ado had more correctly placed *Alexandriam*, as Usuard wrote in the Acts of the Martyrs, but we determine his reading from other manuscripts.

Pulsanen., Munerat., and the Acts of the Martyrs omit *Baptistae*, while some other appendices substitute *Evangelistae*; the reading in the text, taken from Ado, is correct. How varied the spelling is in forming the names of the Gemini, you will find in Bollandus. I think that Usuard wrote as the text reads, especially on the basis of Praten., Herinien., Pulsanen., and Munerat.; in this form the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, Rabanus, and Notker also announce them, although today the Martyrologists and some of our Usuardine manuscripts eagerly and almost universally follow Ado.

Bollandus differs in *Eleusippus*, but retains *Melasippus*; the Acts of the Martyrs have *Melanippus*. Let each person choose freely. The Acts of the Martyrs incorrectly have “fifteen years.” Likewise, *Conilla* occurs for *Jonilla*, as also in Munerat., although Bollandus presents a varied nomenclature for this name as well.

Usuard expressly noted “in the time of Aurelian” from Bede and Ado, but with an obvious anachronism taken from the Acts of Warnaharius. Whether and how that can suitably be corrected, I prefer that you gather from Bollandus and others rather than that I introduce anything new on my own. See Villemontius, volume III, page 603 onward, and Castellanus, page 313 onward. For now, it is enough to present Usuard’s reading.

In the Acts of the Martyrs *Bituris* is incorrectly placed. Pulsanen. seems to have intended to write more elegantly than *Bituricas civitate*: “At the city of Bourges.” Just as that first and largest Lubec edition is extremely corrupt, so here it reads *Sulpicii* for *Sulpitii*; the Antwerp manuscript almost always agrees with it, at least here.

[Note: [Col. 0663B]]

The most celebrated memory among all Martyrologists is that of the patriarch of cenobites. Bede copied the Hieronymian Codices here: “In Egypt, the deposition of Antony the monk.” Rabanus copied it, adding an eulogy different from that of Ado. The short Roman Martyrology differs little: “In the Thebaid, of Antony the monk.” Ado appended a brief encomium, copied by Notker and contracted by Our Author in such a way that the beginning has been joined to the end, with the intervening material omitted; we shall provide most of that material below from several fuller codices. As for the remainder concerning his life, Bollandus has illustrated it so learnedly that nothing seems capable of being desired, [Col. 0663C] unless one wishes to consult Raynaud’s chronology. The Life itself, whether received in Greek from Athanasius or in Latin from Evagrius, is so authoritative that even the hypercritics find nothing which they can reasonably gnaw away. What our Acts relate about the Three Twins of Langres is less straightforward: there has been much dispute about them among the aforementioned Bollandus and Castellanus, as well as Florentinius, Tillemont, and others. The question is: of what country are they—Cappadocians or Gauls? Where, how, and at what time did they suffer? To put it as mildly as possible, some things have been transferred, mingled, and confused. To avoid dwelling on them here, the learned reader should consult the writers cited. The point especially worth observing for our present purpose is that the short Roman Martyrology makes no mention whatsoever of them. Hence one may incidentally note the frivolous quibble of those who, with Valesius, imagine that the short Roman Martyrology was abridged from Ado. The conjecture of the distinguished Castellanus is instead strengthened: namely, that all knowledge of those Three Twins flowed from the inauthentic Acts of Warnaharius addressed to Ceraunus, bishop of Paris, among the Transalpine peoples, and that their names may consequently have been inserted into the Hieronymian Martyrology; certainly their eulogies were added by Bede, Ado, and others, and these require considerable threshing. Usuard abridged them, but even so it will be evident to anyone moderately skilled in these matters that they were not sufficiently worked over. It is especially astonishing that in the Usuardine copy from Tournai, which I count among the purest, the entire series of those Langres saints has been omitted. Whether the scribe of the codex regarded the whole narrative as suspect, I would not dare assert by conjecture; I am sufficiently certain that Usuard wrote it as it is found in our little register. [Col. 0664C] Wandalbertus sings of Antony and the Langres saints in verse as follows:

> The sixteenth is distinguished by Antony’s virtue;  
> this day too has the shared honor of the twins,  
> Whom the people of Langres celebrate, covered beneath one marble.

We said that Sulpicius was marked by Ado on 15 January, where we also noted that Bollandus carefully distinguishes the various Sulpicii occurring on this day. The one added to the Hieronymian Martyrologies is considered by Florentinius to be the elder. I do not know which one Florus intends; but whoever is indicated by him is indicated in such a way that his wording differs greatly from Usuard’s, as is also most evident in the shorter eulogy of that saint. I therefore have no doubt that our Sulpicius, surnamed Pius, must plainly be regarded on this day as the Usuardine Sulpicius. Besides the two Lives edited and illustrated by Bollandus, I find a third cited somewhere. If it should come into our hands, it may be published in its proper place.

[Note: [Col. 0663D]]

**TOURNAY.** We have already said that in this codex the second announcement concerning the Twins of Langres is missing.

**ANTWERP MAJOR:** “In Egypt, in the Thebaid, the birthday of blessed Antony the monk, who, father of many monks, lived most illustriously in life and miracles. His body . . . was buried in the church of blessed John the Evangelist.” In the second entry it is sufficiently pure. Then: “At Bourges, the deposition of Saint Sulpicius, bishop and confessor, who, instructed in sacred letters from childhood and conspicuous for the radiance of holy conduct, also shone in virtues while still a layman. Later, after laying aside his hair, he became the father of monks, and then, raised to the episcopal chair, illustrious in life, rested in peace.”

**ROSWYD:** “In Egypt, in the Thebaid, the deposition of blessed Antony the monk, who, father of many monks, lived most illustriously, venerable in life, and, having completed [Col. 0665A] his course, happily rested in peace. His body, etc. At Langres, of Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Melasippus, etc.” Finally: “In Africa, of Sulpicius the bishop.” Bollandus still has two Sulpicii among the *Praetermissi*, but so far I have found nothing concerning the African one. The translation of Sulpicius of Bourges was treated in the codex for 15 January.

**ANTWERP MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and the UTRECHT-BELGIAN EDITION** begin as follows: “In Egypt, in the Thebaid, of blessed Antony the monk, whose Life Athanasius, bishop of the Alexandrian church, treated in a distinguished volume.” The rest is as in the text, except that they add “and confessor” concerning Sulpicius.

**ALBERGEN and DANICUS** additionally insert: “Who flourished under Constantine the Great and, father of many monks, lived most illustriously, venerable in life; having completed his course, he happily rested in peace in the one hundred and fifth year of his age. His body,” etc.

[Col. 0665B] **LOUVAIN** agrees with **ANTWERP MAXIMUM**, etc., but completely cut out the eulogy of the Twins.

**CENTULE:** “In Egypt, in the Thebaid, the deposition of blessed Antony the abbot, who dedicated many thousands of monks to the service of Christ and lived most illustriously in life and miracles. At Langres, of the holy twins Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Meleusippus. When they were . . . , they suffered under Aurelian. At Bourges, of Saint Sulpicius, bishop and confessor.”

**BRUSSELS.** Concerning Antony it gathers almost everything stated above, adding about his body: “Which, as is said, has now been transferred to Vienne in Gaul. At Langres, the passion of the holy twins Speusippus, Elasippus, and Melasippus. Benignus the priest, sent into Gaul by blessed Polycarp, the disciple of Saint John the Apostle, together with Andochius and Thyrsus, taught them the faith of Christ. When they were twenty-five years old, they were bound to a tree with their hands and suspended and stretched by their feet, so that the joints of their limbs seemed destined to be dislocated. Afterwards they were thrown into the fire, yet were not harmed; amid words of prayer, in the time of the emperor Aurelian, they were crowned with martyrdom and together departed to Christ. Their grandmother Leonilla and Lonilla, together with Neon, the recorder of the acts, seeing this, openly confessed themselves Christians. Because of this, after being afflicted with many tortures and refusing to deny Christ, they were killed together by the sword and received the crown of martyrdom. Turbon, who was writing the victories of those confessing Christ, also suffered martyrdom not long afterward.” See Bede and Ado. The entry for Sulpicius is pure.

**HAGENAU.** It begins with the Langres saints, and is sufficiently pure. Besides what has already been said about Antony, it adds the following on its own authority: “In him discernment of spirits shone forth wonderfully, and against them he received from God a marvelous power; they too were testing him beyond human measure.” Likewise: “Renowned also in the spirit of prophecy, he offered himself to the judges out of desire for martyrdom; but since they could neither would nor were able to harm him because of the divine grace which they saw shining in him, he retired into the desert (the text has *successit*; read *secessit*), where, having completed the course of his life, he died in peace in the one hundred and fifth year of his age, etc.” The entry for Sulpicius is also pure.

**VICTORINUS and the CODEX REGIUS OF SWEDEN**, no. 130, have: “At the Ancients, the dedication of the Lord and Savior, which is situated in the Lateran.”

**Another CODEX REGIUS**, numbered 428: “Likewise, Saint Genulfus the confessor.”

[Col. 0666B] **VATICAN CODEX**, no. 5949: “At Piacenza, Saint Sabinus the bishop.”

**THE LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION** agrees with **ALBERGEN** and **DANICUS** in the entry for Antony and is pure in the rest. It further adds: “On the same day, Saint Genulfus, bishop and confessor. At Valendar, a village in the territory of Trier below Confluentia, the translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, martyrs.”

Greven has the same material, in nearly the same words, and additionally: “At Vienne, blessed Marcellus the bishop.” See the Acts for this day among the *Praetermissi*, and 9 April, where he is treated.

**MOLANUS**, in italic type, inserted concerning Saint Antony what Ado had received from Augustine, namely: “Although he had no knowledge of letters, he is said to have understood the divine Scriptures by hearing them repeatedly and to have retained them by prudent reflection.” Likewise, also in italic type, after “the emperor Aurelian”: “But Turbon, writing the victories of those confessing the Lord, suffered martyrdom not long afterward.” [Col. 0666C] Then, in smaller type, he added: “On this day, the emperor Theodosius died at Milan. At his death the most holy bishop Aurelius Ambrose delivered a sermon on the commemoration of the fortieth day after his death, with Honorius, his son, attending as ruler.” In later editions he treats Genulfus in italic type as follows: “On the same day, Saint Genulfus, first bishop of Chartres and confessor.”

[Col. 0663]

At the Thebaid, of blessed Antony the monk, whose body, discovered by divine revelation under the emperor Justinian, was brought to Alexandria and buried in the church of Saint John the Baptist. At Langres, the birthday of the holy twins Speusippus, Elasippus, and Melasippus. When they were twenty-five years old, they were crowned with martyrdom together with their grandmother Leonilla and Lonilla, together with Neon, in the time of the emperor Aurelian. At the city of Bourges, the deposition of Saint Sulpicius the bishop, whose life and precious death are commended by glorious miracles.

**XV Kal. The 18th.**

[Note: [Col. 0665]]

Thus read Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, Antwerp, Maximum-Lübeck, Greven, Molan, and the *Acts of the Martyrs*.

[Note: [Col. 0665D]]

Among the purer codices I number Herinien here, as elsewhere, although it departs somewhat from Usuard’s native simplicity by reading “dedication” instead of “chair”; we shall discuss this matter more fully in the Observations. It also agrees with Molan, who has “first at Rome,” etc.; others, following the short Roman Martyrology and Ado, have “which.” Antwerp and Maximum-Lübeck, instead of “and the passion,” have “on that very day, the passion.” The version inserted in the *Acts of the Martyrs* reads: “At Rome, of Prisca the virgin and martyr.” Our reading is purer. What title and what laurel Prisca deserves we shall investigate immediately.

[Note: [Col. 0665D]]

That the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter the Apostle celebrated today was ancient in the Church is clearly proved by the copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology, in which it is generally prefaced by: “The deposition of the most holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary.” On this Florentinius’s fifth dissertation may be consulted. As far as our subject is concerned, the very ancient Echternach codex has briefly: “The deposition of Saint [Col. 0666D] Mary and of Peter’s chair at Rome”; the Lucca codex has: “And the dedication of Saint Peter the Apostle, on which Peter the Apostle first sat at Rome”; while the Corbie codex has: “The dedication of the chair of Saint Peter the Apostle, on which he first sat at Rome.” Florentinius discussed these matters sufficiently accurately, demonstrating the antiquity of the feast after Baronius and Bollandus. It is therefore strange that the distinguished Castellanus should argue as though he wished to indicate that the feast of the Roman chair was peculiar to the Gauls before the time of Charlemagne, while at Rome and throughout Italy it was entirely unknown. It seems more probable to me that it was known no less at Rome than in France, although perhaps it was not celebrated with a distinctive cult or a special Mass, since another feast on 22 February was accustomed to be understood equally of the Roman and Antiochene chairs, as Belethus notes, cited there by Castellanus, and as several others also observe, both on that day and on the 12th of February already mentioned. I readily admit that several matters arise here which could provide material for a longer dissertation: both the original origin and institution of the feast, and the circumstances of its spread from Rome to other Churches. But to settle the point of this controversy, the authority of the short Roman Martyrology is sufficient. Since it was copied from an older Roman codex and, as Castellanus admits, sent from Rome to Aquileia, he cannot possibly deny that it is much older than Charlemagne. In it one reads most explicitly: “The Chair of Saint [Col. 0667B] Peter, on which he first sat at Rome.” Ado added nothing to this, nor did Usuard, except the single word “apostle.” Consequently, he ought to have admitted that even before the time of Charlemagne the present feast of the Chair of Saint Peter was accustomed to be commemorated—not only in churches of the Gallican rite, but also at Rome and in churches of the Roman rite, at least in the Martyrologies, which alone are under discussion here. Nor does the silence of Bede, Florus, and Wandalbertus constitute an obstacle, unless one wishes by the same reasoning to argue for erasing nearly innumerable commemorations of saints. Rabanus explained the matter at greater length; Notker copied his entire text with only a few changes, differing chiefly in that where he found in Rabanus “the dedication of Saint Peter the Apostle,” he himself wrote, undoubtedly from another Hieronymian source, “the Chair of Saint Peter,” etc. Florentinius further examines whether both feasts—namely, the dedication of the church of Saint Peter and the commemoration of the establishment of his chair—are correctly proclaimed on this very day. Perhaps we shall discuss the same matter at greater length in the Supplements [Col. 0667C] to January and February. The Appendices will supply other ways of expressing it.

Fronton’s Calendar gives only Prisca, omitting the Chair of Peter. The Gregorian Sacramentary calls her both virgin and martyr. The copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology do not speak uniformly: one has “At Rome, Saint Prisca the virgin,” while another mentions her only as a martyr. Bede reads: “The birthday of Saint Prisca the virgin and martyr.” The short Roman Martyrology has: “And Saint Prisca the martyr”; Rabanus says no more, generally following Bede. In Ado there is a change, for there again she is called “virgin and martyr,” and Notker preserves this. Whether deliberately, or perhaps through carelessness or forgetfulness, Our Author assigned her only the title “virgin” is uncertain. Bollandus considers Prisca very probably deserving of both laurels, and in my judgment the authority of the Gregorian Sacramentary seems to vindicate her. If Castellanus’s conjecture expressed in his notes at page 328 were true—namely, that this Prisca was the wife of Aquila—perhaps she would deserve neither title. [Col. 0668B] What Wandalbertus thought may be gathered from his verse:

> The fifteenth rejoices together for Prisca as a martyr.

I would not dare defend the reliability of the Acts. Whether they are primitive, and whether other writers formed from them the Acts of Martina and Tatiana cited above, may be examined elsewhere. The Hieronymian Martyrologies mention Mosei and Ammonii, and Ado supplied an eulogy of them, I do not know from where, substituting “Mosaei” for “Mosei.” With this one exception, Usuard took the whole from Ado, as did Notker, who wrote “Moysei.” The copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology in Florentinius seem to express the place of martyrdom more distinctly, but it is not easy to find it. Nor do they leave it sufficiently clear whether the series of other martyrs, generally associated with these, belongs to Pontus, Nicaea, or somewhere else—a matter doubtless attributable to the ignorance of copyists. Regarding Usuard’s reading there is sufficient certainty; regarding the truth of the matter [Col. 0668C] there is no basis for a secure judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0667C]]

**ANTWERP MAJOR**, sufficiently pure in the text, adds: “At Alexandria, Saint Maximus the bishop, who became sufficiently renowned and distinguished by the title of confession.” Other codices also discuss him, but the matter is referred to 27 December. “On the same day, the passion of the holy martyrs Thyrsus, Leucius, and Gallenicus.” These were taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. See below.

**ROSWYD** would be entirely pure if it did not omit the eulogy of Moseus and Ammonius.

**PULSANO** begins as follows: “At Rome, the establishment of the chair of blessed Peter the Apostle, after, that is, his first chair in the holy Church of Antioch.” In the remainder it is sufficiently pure.

**MUNERAT.** I do not know why the first announcement concerning the Chair, etc., has been omitted here.

**ANTWERP MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, [Col. 0667D] DANICUS, and the UTRECHT-BELGIAN EDITION** are pure, except that they begin the day with Saint Prisca, in these words: “The passion of Saint Prisca the virgin, who, when she was thirteen years old, bravely endured wondrous tortures for Christ and finally, struck by the sword, happily completed the contest of martyrdom.” The Louvain codex has “in her thirteenth year.” Others omit the age, and more safely so, since nothing certain is known about it. See Bollandus.

**CENTULE:** “The Chair of Saint Peter the Apostle [‘on which’ is missing], on which he first sat at Rome. And the passion of Saint Prisca the virgin. And in Pontus, of the holy martyrs Moseus and Ammonius. At Alexandria, Saint Maximus the bishop and martyr. At Apollonia, of the holy martyrs Thyrsus, Leucius, and Gallenicus.” These are referred to 28 January.

**BRUSSELS:** “At Rome, the passion of Saint Prisca the virgin and martyr. She bravely endured wondrous tortures for Christ and finally, struck by the sword, happily completed the contest of her [Col. 0668C] martyrdom.” In the other two announcements it is sufficiently pure. Then: “At Alexandria, Saint Maximus the bishop and confessor. At Tours, Saint Leopardus the confessor.”

**HAGENAU:** “The Chair of Saint Peter the Apostle, on which he first sat at Rome, which he gloriously governed for twenty-five years, six years [he means months], and nine days, under the emperors Claudius and Nero. On that same day at Rome, the passion of Saint Prisca the virgin and martyr, under the emperor Claudius. When she was ten years old and was suffering wondrous things for Christ, she was finally led, after being afflicted by having her hair shorn, to an idol so that she might worship it; but she did not consent. Finally, she completed her martyrdom by the sword. At the island of Pontus, the birthday of the holy martyrs Moseus, etc.,” sufficiently pure. At the end: “Likewise, of Christicola the confessor.” He means Deicola.

[Col. 0668D] **AQUICINCT:** “At Tours, Saint Leobardus the confessor.”

**VICTORINUS** has “Amoseus” instead of “Moseus,” as some write “Ammonis” for “Ammonius.” At the end, together with the Swedish Royal Codex numbered 130, it adds as above: “At Tours, Saint Leobardus the confessor.”

**DAVERON:** Concerning Leobardus, more fully as follows: “At the Major Monastery, blessed Leobardus the confessor, who wisely rejected the world and, carrying Christ’s cross upon his head, shut himself away in a very narrow cave at that same monastery.”

**MATRICULARY OF THE CARTHUSIANS OF UTRECHT:** “Of Prisca the virgin and martyr. The crowning of Saint Peter, and of Moseus and Ammonius, soldiers and martyrs. Deicola the abbot and confessor.”

In the **VATICAN CODEX**, no. 5949, it is said that the following is added: “At Rome, the birthday of Saint Prisca the martyr.”

**DIJON, CHURCH OF SAINT STEPHEN:** It reads as above: [Col. 0669A] “At Alexandria, Saint Maximus the bishop. He became sufficiently renowned and distinguished by the title of confession.”

**THE LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION**, pure in the entry for the Chair, adds:

> “Because of Simon Magus, although by the hidden will of God, he came to Rome and, preaching the Gospel there, held the pontificate of that city for twenty-five years. At Rome, on the Ostian Way, the passion of Saint Prisca: . . . under the emperor Claudius she happily completed the contest of martyrdom, etc. At Pontus, the birthday of the holy Moseus, etc.”

At the end: “At the Major Monastery, Saint Leobaldus the confessor.” Greven had written the same in his first edition; in the second, as will soon be clear, he placed with the others “At Tours, of Leopardus,” correctly in neither place, for “Leobardus” must be read.

**BELIN**, in both editions, has: “On this same day, the passion of Saint Prisca the virgin and martyr.” Likewise in both: “Mosey and Amonis.” Finally, at the end: “On this same day, Saint Liberata the virgin.” Molan copied this from Belin and added nothing by which she could be identified. It seems certain that the reference is not to Faustina’s companion from Como. There remains, therefore, that very famous woman whom Greven seems to indicate, whether Spanish or Lusitanian, who in Belgium and elsewhere is called Wilgefortis. More will have to be said about her on 20 July, the day on which Bollandus rejects her among the *Praetermissi*.

[Col. 0670A] **GREVEN:** “Saint Prisca, when she was thirteen years old, endured wondrous tortures for Christ and finally, under Claudius, completed the contest of martyrdom by the sword. At Alexandria, Maximus the bishop, Fortunatus, Leo, and Lucius. Likewise, Thyrsus the martyr. At the city of Abitina, Saturninus and his companions, martyrs. In England, Wirminus the soldier and martyr. On the same day, blessed Deicola the abbot, disciple of Saint Columbanus; among other marks of his faith and works, it is read of him that once, tired from his journey, he hung his cloak upon the rays of the sun, as though on a pole. At Tours, Leopardus the confessor. At the monastery of Conches, Marcia and Liberata, virgins. At Venice, the translation of Saint Lucy the virgin and martyr. In England, Osia the martyr.”

**MOLAN**, in smaller type, followed Greven concerning Deicola; but instead of “Leopardus” he more correctly wrote “Leobardus,” adding: “Gregory, bishop of Tours, wrote a book about his life. In the same place, the birthday of [Col. 0670B] Saint Volusianus, archbishop of Tours and martyr.” In later editions he arranged the Appendix differently: “At Tours, the birthday of Saint Volusianus, seventh archbishop. In the same place, the deposition of Saint Leobardus the confessor. At Clermont, Saint Venerandus the bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Deicola, abbot of Santenay, disciple of blessed Columbanus.”

[Col. 0665]

The Chair of Saint Peter the Apostle, on which he first sat at Rome. And the passion of Saint Prisca the virgin. At Pontus, the birthday of the holy martyrs Moseus and Ammonius, who, being soldiers, were first assigned to the mines and finally handed over to the fire.

[Bouillart in the margin: “At Paris, in the monastery of Saint Germanus, the dedication of an altar in honor of the most victorious cross, and of the blessed, glorious, ever-virgin Mary, and of the holy martyrs Mauritius and his companions.”]

**XIV Kal. The 19th.**

[Note: [Col. 0669B]]

Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, Antwerp, Pulsano, Maximum-Lübeck, Munerat, and Greven. We shall briefly note below what is missing in Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0669C]]

Greven writes “Saint Germanicus” instead of “blessed Germanicus,” as in Ado. Munerat, together with certain codices, incorrectly reads “Marcus Antonius”; our text is purer. Antwerp and Maximum-Lübeck, everywhere consistent, insert “for himself” before “the beast,” as it is also read in the aforementioned Ado; Pulsano prefixes that word to the adjective, reading “the beast prepared for him.” I think the genuine Usuardine reading is represented here. Antwerp again has “in the time of Antoninus” instead of “during the times.” Where the other codices read “by whom he was not harmed at all,” Pulsano has “emerging unharmed from them.” Likewise, in “After all these things, by lead, etc.,” the word “all” is superfluous. But I note that in most codices, even the purest, *Postque* is written, almost by abbreviation, as though it meant “and afterward,” although the sense seems to require *quae* as the case governed by the preceding particle. This is not surprising in ancient writers, at least those of the Middle Ages, who scarcely observed the diphthongs. I therefore believe that the ignorance of copyists caused the conjunction or enclitic *-que* to intrude in place of the relative *quae*. It is certain that Launomarus was both priest and abbot, yet our codices—except Antwerp and Maximum-Lübeck—do not call him abbot. They variously write “the district of Dorcas” or “Dorcassinus”; Greven calls it “the district of Chartres.” Either is acceptable, as one finds in Bollandus. We have preferred the first reading as properly Usuardine.

[Note: [Col. 0669D]]

I find no one who first entered Germanicus into the sacred calendars other than the author of the short Roman Martyrology, who writes on this day: “At Smyrna, Saint Germanicus the martyr, condemned to the beasts.” To ask why he chose this day rather than another is mere conjecture. We have already shown elsewhere that the compiler of this Martyrology, on his own authority alone, assigned fixed days to many saints taken from Rufinus and elsewhere and unknown to the older Martyrologists. Nor do I think that that author ever saw the celebrated letter of the Smyrnaeans, in which he might have found some more precise, though not entirely certain, indications regarding the day of the martyrdom. Ado followed the short Roman Martyrology, adding an eulogy from the same Rufinus or Eusebius, the complete passage of which Bollandus reproduced. Our Author took everything from Ado, but not word for word; Notker, in a rarer example, transcribed only the words of the short Roman Martyrology. [Col. 0670D] The same eulogy of Ado also recurs among the feasts of the apostles, where Polycarp is treated on 26 January. Thus far, concerning the derivation of our text and the splendid laurel of Germanicus, everything is clear and straightforward. The question of the actual day of his martyrdom is uncertain, for it seems possible to argue about it by the same reasoning through which Bollandus, in the first section of his learned commentary, attempted to assign Polycarp’s contest to a fixed day, namely 7 Kalends of April, or 26 March. No one will deny that Bollandus established this with considerable probability; yet he did not regard it as so certain that he thought the day fixed by the Martyrologists for so many centuries should therefore be changed. Castellanus did so, transferring both saints to March: Polycarp to the 26th, and our Germanicus to the 29th. Ruinart correctly observed this uncertainty among the *Selecta*, page 26, where he brings Valois and several others to the same opinion. Tillemont, in volume II under Polycarp, seems to prefer the Greek calendars; others go in a different direction. I admit that from the aforementioned letter of the Smyrnaeans it is perfectly clear that our Germanicus completed his contest several days before Polycarp, but nowhere does it become apparent that the interval was precisely a full week. Nevertheless, since Castellanus, having transferred Polycarp to 26 March as we have said, thought—apparently as a consequence—that because Germanicus is celebrated here on 19 January, he too should be transferred to the 19th of March. Whether others have judged rightly or wrongly, we were obliged to adhere to our Martyrologies and to the Usuardine witnesses that precede them.

We have spoken more than once about Pontianus, the martyr of Spoleto, on 14 January, on which day he is commemorated with great zeal by Rabanus, Notker, and many Martyrologies, especially Belgian ones, because his body was transferred to Utrecht. Here, however, he also appears in the short Roman Martyrology, specifically on this day, with these distinctive details: “And at Spoleto, Saint Pontianus the martyr, who suffered on 19 Kalends, was buried on the 15th, and was transformed in the tomb on the 14th, when his more celebrated day is observed.” Ado has the same, together with a longer account drawn from the Acts, whose elegant abridgment Our Author adapted to his brevity, as represented in the text. See Bollandus on 14 January, or Castellanus’s note, pages 248 and 249. The fact that Launomarus was added by Usuard himself to the first two is clearly shown by the codices cited above and by nearly all the other Usuardine codices. I do not know why Molan deleted him. Certainly this first taught me that the opinion of those who think Molan published his Usuard from the Pratensis codex is false, since in many other places he openly disagrees with it. Wandalbertus’s verse may perhaps be read as follows:

> Twice seven shines for Nicetus and Launomarus.

[Note: [Col. 0671B]]

**PRATENSIS.** In our copy it is said to be added in the margin: “At Paris, in the monastery of Saint Germanus, the dedication of an altar in honor of the most victorious cross, and of the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy martyrs Mauritius and his companions.” Castellanus, however, reported in a letter to me dated 31 May 1709 that this belongs to the preceding day. In any event, these entries are particular to that monastery, as are others which will be indicated from time to time.

**ANTWERP MAXIMUM, CENTULE, VICTORINUS, THE SWEDISH ROYAL CODEX**, no. 130, **and BURDIGALA:** “At Jerusalem, Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus.” These were taken from the Hieronymian Martyrology, as Rabanus, Notker, and others also have them. Indeed, in the Victorinus codex every possibility of escape is closed to those who imagine that Mary and Martha have been substituted for Maria and Martha; for there all are explicitly named: the men at Rome, and the women at Jerusalem. The most ancient Cluniac Calendar calls both women virgins on this same day. All these matters will be discussed more extensively in the Acts for the following month of July. See the Sacramentary of Thomasius, p. 144, where Maria, Martha, Audifax, and Abacuc are joined to Sebastian on 20 January, perhaps through the error of a copyist. The first codex continues: “And at Smyrna, the birthday of Saint Germanicus the martyr. In the district of Dorcas, at the monastery of Corbion, the birthday of Saint Launomarus the abbot, whose deeds are renowned.” The codex of Amiens and Molan also have this.

**ROSWYD.** Adonian: “At Smyrna, the birthday of Saint Germanicus the martyr. When he flourished in the beauty of early youth, excluding the fear of bodily weakness through the grace of God’s virtue, he voluntarily challenged the beast prepared for him, having been condemned by the judge; and by its teeth,” etc., purely. “Marius and Martha and their sons Audifax and Abacuc, noblemen from Persia.” These belong to the following day.

**ACTS OF THE MARTYRS.** The entire announcement is appended to the sufficiently pure text: “On the Cornelian Way,” etc., as on the following day.

[Col. 0671D] **ALBERGEN and DANICUS** have the aforementioned announcement at the beginning, and at the end write: “In the district of Dorcas, at the monastery of Corbion, the deposition of Saint Launomarus the abbot and confessor.”

**ANTWERP, MAXIMUM-UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and the UTRECHT-BELGIAN EDITION** also prefix “On the Cornelian Way,” etc., but since they treated Pontianus on 14 January, they omit that announcement here. They also have at the end “the abbot,” etc. **CENTULE** agrees with them and writes concerning Germanicus as **ROSWYD** above.

**LOUVAIN** agrees with the preceding, except that it mutilated roughly half of the eulogy of Marius, etc.

**BRUSSELS** begins: “At Rome, on the Cornelian Way,” etc. Then: “At Jerusalem, Martha and Mary, sisters of Lazarus.” Its entries for Germanicus and Pontianus are sufficiently pure. It then has: “And the passion of Saint Thyrsus, the glorious martyr, with his companions,” taken from the preceding day. At the end: “the abbot and confessor.”

[Col. 0672B] **HAGENAU.** In the first entry concerning Germanicus it is sufficiently pure. In the second place: “In the district of Dorcas, Saint Lauromarus the abbot.” The third is: “At Rome, on the Cornelian Way,” etc. It treated Pontianus with the others on 14 January.

**MATRICULARY OF THE CARTHUSIANS OF UTRECHT:** “Germanicus, the renowned martyr, who was delivered to the beasts. Launomarus the priest and confessor.”

In the **VATICAN CODEX**, no. 5949, Launomarus is missing.

**ALTEMPSIAN**, augmented by the following entry: “In England, the translation of Saint Burghwaladus, bishop and confessor.”

**BELINUS**, in both editions, after Germanicus and Pontianus, reports the same things concerning Marius and Martha, etc., which we have already said Usuard more correctly places on the following day. In both editions it also has: “At the city of Laude, Saint Bassianus [others write Bassiani], bishop and confessor.” Launomarus is missing from the first edition. It is not useful to catalogue typographical errors.

**THE LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION** begins as follows: “At Cologne Agrippina, the translation of Saint Antonina and six other virgins and martyrs from that noble company of eleven thousand virgins, to the parish church of Saint John the Baptist.”

**GREVEN**, after the complete text of Usuard, continues as follows:

> “This Launomarus, while still a little boy and tending his parents’ flock, distributed his food to the needy and to travelers; he himself frequently prolonged his fast until sunset. Later, having been given over to the study of the liberal arts and having become a priest, he went into the desert. There, among other wonders of virtue, he healed a lame man, extinguished the force of fire by opposing to it the sign of the cross, and by the power of that same cross moved an ancient oak to whatever place he wished. In England, John Brangualator, the hermit. On the same day, according to some, Marius and Martha with the others whom Usuard places on the following day. In Africa, according to Bede” (what copy of Bede he saw is uncertain: no printed or manuscript copy has so far become known to us in which the sequence of martyrs appended here occurs in this order, namely):

> “The holy martyrs Paul, [Col. 0672D] Quintus, Gerontius, Januarius, Saturninus, Successus, Pia, Germanus, Julius, and Gagus.”

> “In Sweden, blessed Henry, archbishop of Uppsala and martyr. An Englishman by birth, governing the aforesaid Church in the time of Saint Eric, king of Sweden, he went with him to convert the people of Finland and was murdered by a certain criminal on account of his zeal for justice. When that same murderer tried to remove from his head the cap of the holy martyr, which had been placed there, he tore away his own skin together with the flesh. In England, Saint Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester and confessor. When his rivals, presiding at a synod, ordered him, as an unlearned man, to resign his pastoral staff, he said, ‘Gladly I resign it, but not to you.’ Saying this, he drove the staff itself into the hardest stone with which the tomb of Saint Edward the king was covered, so that no one could move it. Ashamed by the miracle, they ordered him to take the staff back. At Cologne Agrippina, the translation of Saint Antonina, virgin and martyr, and of six others from the company, as above from the Lübeck-Cologne edition. Of Bassianus, bishop of Laude, renowned for life and miracles. When he visited blessed Ambrose of Milan, he foretold his death to Ambrose’s clergy and buried him after his death. On the same day, of Hugh the archbishop. Likewise, of Contextus the bishop and confessor.”

MOLANUS. After Usuard’s words “he was struck with a sword,” he adds, largely from Ado: “He completed his martyrdom on 15 January, and his body, taken up by Christians, was buried on the 18th. His solemn day, however, is celebrated on 19 January, when his sacred body was transferred a second time.” He then continues: “On the Cornelian Way, etc.,” as on the following day. “In the city of Lodi, of Saint Bassianus, etc. At Lyon, of Nicetius, bishop. In the monastery of Corbie, in the district of Dourdan, [Col. 0674A] etc. On the same day, of the blessed Contextus, bishop and confessor.” What he prints in smaller type concerning the African saints according to Bede, the blessed Henry of Uppsala, and Saint Wulfstan is taken word for word from Greven. Later editions depart farther from Usuard. The beginning is “On the Cornelian Way, etc.” After this comes a noteworthy remark: “Their celebration,” he says, “is anticipated by one day, because the day of their passion is assigned solely to the martyrdom of Saints Fabian and Sebastian.” It is very well known that feasts are transferred; their anticipation is much rarer, although I do not deny that examples exist by which this can be demonstrated against Castellanus. One new feature in these editions is that a place is assigned to the blessed Contextus, namely: “On the same day, at Bayeux, etc.” For Henry of Uppsala, the year of his martyrdom is given, namely 1151.]

[Col. 0669]

At Smyrna, the birth into eternal life of the blessed martyr Germanicus, who, under Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius, by the grace of God’s power, casting out fear of bodily weakness, voluntarily challenged the beast prepared for him. Crushed by its teeth, he deserved to be incorporated into the true bread—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ—by dying for him.

At Spoleto, Saint Pontianus, martyr, in the time of the emperor Antoninus. Because of Christ, the judge had him beaten most severely with rods, then ordered him to walk barefoot over burning coals. Since these did him no harm, he was ordered to be hung on the rack with iron hooks and thus thrown into prison, where he deserved to be strengthened by an angelic visitation. After this he was drenched with boiling lead and finally struck with a sword.

In the district of Dourdan, Saint Launomarus, priest.

13th day before the Kalends. Day 20.

[Note: [Col. 0673]]

Taken from Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck. Munerat., Greven., and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0673B]]

Pulsanen., against all the other manuscripts, limits Fabian’s pontificate to twelve years; the other martyrologists extend it excessively, as will be said in the Observations. “He presided” is less exact syntactically, but nevertheless this is Bede’s wording, from whom all the others and our manuscripts derive it, except Molanus, who reads “had presided,” here and elsewhere correcting the ancient simplicity rather freely.

The manuscripts we follow generally have *cimiterio*. In *Callisti*, *Calisti*, and *Calixti* they vary frequently, so it should not seem strange if we too do not maintain a fixed spelling. Molanus wished to write more elegantly *apud Catacumbas*. Pulsanen. and Munerat. have *ad Catacumbas*; the others, neglecting the preposition, put *Eodem die Catacumbas*, and although this is more barbarous, we have thought it should be read so.

*Ligari in medio campo* is undoubtedly Usuard’s reading, according to Bede and Ado; Tornacen. and Munerat. write *religari*. In Pulsanen., *fusticari* for *fustigari* is a scribal error. More noteworthy is the fact that where all the others correctly write *nobilium de Persida*, that manuscript alone has *hi nobiles fuerunt viri de Siria*. “They came to Rome”: Greven. has *Romae*, but *Romam*, found in the others, is better. Again, Greven. and Molan. have *temporibus Claudii* instead of *tempore*, etc. Pulsanen. has *manuum praecisiones*; Bede’s and Ado’s singular reading should be retained. Likewise, in the same Greven. and Molan., *in nympha* should be read for *in lympha*, as Bollandus rightly proves; Castellanus explains this more fully on p. 340, where he also makes several careful observations about these saints.

[Note: [Col. 0673C]]

Among the ancient martyrologists I observe an extraordinary agreement in recording these same saints. All the Hieronymian copies have these saints, unusually consistent here; so do Bede, Rabanus, and Notker; and in our series, the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Usuard.

Florentinius asks what is meant by the indefinite formula of most of the Hieronymian manuscripts: “At Rome, in the cemetery, of Fabian the bishop and Sebastian.” He thinks, quite appropriately, if I am not mistaken, that it should be understood antonomastically from Cyprian as referring to the cemetery of Callistus, and confirms this from Bucherius’s Calendar, though he does not quote the passage in full. It should be read as follows: “13 days before the Kalends of February: Fabian at Callistus, and Sebastian at the Catacombs.”

I consider it superfluous to cite other calendars or sacramentaries, since the memory of these illustrious saints has been sufficiently consecrated throughout every age.
