Bede’s text is noteworthy: “At Rome, Fabian, bishop, who, after presiding over the Church for twenty-five years, suffered martyrdom in the time of Decius and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus.” Rabanus copied this from him, adding some material from the Pontificals, and all of it passed into Notker, who expanded it slightly further from the same source. In the Little Roman Martyrology it is simply stated: “At Rome, Fabian, pope and martyr.”

Ado follows Bede, but with this precaution: while taking the rest from him, he substitutes for twenty-five years: “He who ruled for fourteen years, eleven months, and twelve days.” Our author borrowed his text from one or the other, but rejected both calculations and wrote “who comes closest to the true chronology.” See the rest in Bollandus and, more recently, Tillemont, vol. III, beginning on p. 362.

In the Hieronymian text for the preceding day, the Lucensian manuscript places last: “At Rome, the passion of Saint Sebastian, martyr.” There you will find the reason for, or at least a conjecture about, the duplication of the feast. The Little Roman Martyrology reads third: “And Sebastian, buried at the memorials of the Apostles.” Ado copied Bede’s entire longer eulogy, omitting only Sebastian’s homeland, Milan. Rabanus left Bede unchanged, while Notker followed Ado. Our author shortened his encomium from those fuller accounts, whether Bede’s or Ado’s, correctly expressing “at the Catacombs.” On these, see the Acts for 24 June, p. 439 onward, and Castellanus, who gathers much learned material about Sebastian and his translation, beginning on p. 353.

It is reasonably doubted whether the Acts were truly composed by Ambrose from autograph and authentic sources. Nevertheless, everyone, with Hesselius in Molanus, Bollandus, Ruinartus on p. 295, and others, admits that they are excellent, weighty, and worthy of belief. Nor would Tillemont deny this; his summary, worth reading, is in vol. IV, beginning on p. 515.

Wandalbertus sings today:

“After the thirteenth, the third day flourishes for Bishop Fabian;

With equal virtue Sebastian is joined to him,

Whom joyful Suesse now honors, brought from Rome.”

The third announcement in the Hieronymian Martyrologies suffers from the same defect: “In the cemetery, of Marius, Martha, Audifax, and Abbacuc.” Here Florentinius does not use the benefit of antonomasia, but considers the unnamed cemetery to be the Arenarium on the Cornelian Way, which is marked in the Epternacian manuscript and in Usuard.

The Little Roman Martyrology gives only the names, whose first and last are variously distorted by some: *Maris* or *Marini* for *Marii*; *Ambacum*, *Ambacuc*, *Abacum*, [Col. 0676A] and so on. Everything else that Rabanus, Ado, Usuard, and Notker transferred into their texts is again derived from Bede. Of these, Usuard seems to depart least from the source, except in the placement—namely, “On the Cornelian Way,” which he alone prefixed, perhaps finding it in the Acts or in some Hieronymian copy.

Bollandus seems to have had fewer doubts about the authenticity of the Acts than Baronius; Ruinartus excluded them from his collection of selected Acts. I consider the subject, so to speak, of the whole history sufficiently genuine, but I regard it as extremely difficult to smooth over all the objections Tillemont raises in vol. IV, beginning on p. 673. If anything can nevertheless be added to or clarified by the Bollandist investigations, we shall provide it in its place, and with that zeal for truth which we ordinarily bring to such matters.

[Note: [Col. 0675A]]

ANTUERP.-MAJ. The section on Fabian is Adonian. It also mixes in some material about Sebastian as follows: “He was so dear to the emperors Diocletian and Maximian that they entrusted him with command of the first cohort. When Diocletian learned that he was a Christian and could not be recalled from the faith, he ordered him to be tied in the middle of the field, like a target for shooting, and shot by the soldiers. When he was covered with arrows like a hedgehog, they thought him dead and departed.” The remainder is absent; it is better read together with the preceding material in Bede or Ado. The third announcement is likewise incomplete: “On the same day at Rome, the birthday of the holy martyrs Marius . . . and Abacuc, noblemen, who had come to Rome for prayer in the time of the emperor Claudius.”

ROSWEYD. The section on Fabian is also Adonian. From the same source he extracts somewhat different material about Sebastian: “Who, by order of . . ., was placed like a target for arrows and was so filled with arrows that he appeared like a hedgehog. Then, recovering his health within a few days, he openly reproached the emperors themselves for their unjust persecution of Christians. He was captured again and received martyrdom in a blessed consummation, and was buried at the Catacombs beside the memorials of the Apostles.” Concerning Marius, etc., see the preceding day.

THE ACTS OF THE MARTYRS assign fourteen years to Fabian. The section on Sebastian is pure. For the others, see the preceding day.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJ., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., and the Utrecht-Belgian edition, just as they reported the Persian martyrs on the preceding day, omit them today. Their section on Sebastian is pure. Concerning Fabian, after “pope,” they insert only: “Who was the nineteenth after the blessed Peter.”

ALBERG. and DANIC. agree with the preceding witnesses, but after “buried” they add: “He established that chrism should be celebrated every year on the Lord’s Supper.”

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, the passion of the blessed Fabian, pope and martyr. On the same day, Saint Sebastian, martyr, through whose faith and teaching many were crowned with martyrdom. Likewise on the same day at Rome, the holy Marius and Martha, with their sons Audifax and Abacuc, noblemen of Persia, who had come for prayer in the time of the emperor Claudius.”

BRUXELLEN. begins as follows: “At Rome, the birthday of Saint Sebastian of Milan and his companions, who, when . . .,” not entirely purely. Then, after “he failed”: “They threw him, thought dead, into a sewer. His body was found by a certain Licineus and buried in a crypt beside the memorials of the Apostles.” Then, concerning Fabian, after “pope and martyr,” it continues: “While the see was vacant and the election of the future pontiff was being discussed, he was present with the others. Suddenly a white dove descended from heaven upon his head and said: ‘You shall be ordained bishop of Rome.’ Thus divinely elected, after a praiseworthy life he was beheaded by Decius for the faith of Christ. He established that chrism should be consecrated every year on the Lord’s Supper, and took exact care that the Acts of the martyrs should be collected in full.” Concerning the Persians, see the preceding day.

HAGENOYEN. It announces Fabian somewhat differently at the beginning: “He was the nineteenth after the blessed Peter, and through the sign of a dove descending divinely upon him he was elected pope under the emperor Gordian. [Col. 0676B] He presided over the Church for thirteen years. This Fabian restored—or, rather, resisted—Emperor Philip, who wished to take part in the solemn celebration of Easter, until he confessed his sins and performed penance.” See Bollandus. “He appointed seven subdeacons to collect the Acts of the martyrs. Finally, under the persecution of Decius, he completed his martyrdom by decapitation.”

Concerning Sebastian, it reads: “At the Catacombs, the blessed Sebastian, soldier and martyr, who strengthened many in faith and in suffering and converted many to the faith. When he had . . .” not very purely. “But afterward presenting himself to the emperors, he reproached them for the unjust persecution of the saints, and therefore was ordered to be beaten to death and his body thrown into a sewer.” Concerning the Persians, see the preceding day.

VICTORIN. From Rabanus, after “buried,” it has the following concerning Fabian: “He divided the regions among the deacons and appointed seven deacons to supervise the seven notaries and collect the Acts of the martyrs in full.” [Col. 0676C] It then adds: “During his time Novatianus came from Africa—he means Novatus—and separated Novatianus from the Church after Moses the confessor died in prison; he had been there for eleven months.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJ.: “Fabian and Sebastian, martyrs; Marius and Martha with their noble sons; Marcellianus and Marcus, and their father Tranquillinus, martyrs.” These belong to 18 June, but here they may have been joined to Sebastian because their Acts are included in his.

REMENS. CHURCH, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “At Lyon in Gaul, Saint Clement, priest.” The Hieronymian copies also remember him, as do our Acts very briefly.

LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION. It inserts only the following concerning Fabian, as above: “Who was the nineteenth after the blessed Peter.” On the same day at Rome, at the Catacombs, the birthday of Saint Sebastian, martyr, who, when he had,” etc., as above. Concerning the Persians also, see the preceding day.

[Col. 0676D] BELIN. Neither edition is entirely pure in its text. It omits the Persians, of whom it dealt with on the preceding day, and in both editions the following is added: “In the city of Turin, of the holy martyrs Solutor, Adventor, and Octavius.” These belonged to the famous Theban Legion and are referred in the Omissions to 20 November, on which day the Roman Martyrology mentions them.

GREVEN., contrary to custom, has this one addition: “On the same day, the blessed Polychronius, martyr.” Two Polychronii are mentioned in the Omissions; which of them is intended we do not yet know.

MOLAN. In the first edition: “In the city of Turin, of the holy martyrs Solutor, Adventor, and Octavius,” from Belinus; “At Lyon in Gaul, Saint Clement, priest.” Concerning him, see above. In later editions it adds: “On the twentieth day, the holy and God-bearing father Euthymius the Great.” His Acts treat of him at length, and perhaps other material may be added in the Supplement. Then, in smaller type: “On the same day, Saint Maurus, bishop of the city of Cesena and confessor, a man of outstanding holiness. King Dagobert of the Franks died. It was established by Lord John the abbot and the entire chapter of Marcianus that his anniversary should be solemnly celebrated, because that glorious king and his queen Mathilda, when they had received the blessed virgin Eusebia from the saving font, bestowed Villa Verniacum and the wine brought from France for our use with royal generosity.” See the Omissions.]

[Col. 0673]

At Rome, the birthday of the blessed Fabian, pope, who, after presiding over the Church for thirteen years, suffered martyrdom in the time of Decius and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus.

On the same day, at the Catacombs, Saint Sebastian, martyr, who, having held command of the first cohort, was ordered by the emperor Diocletian, on the charge of Christianity, to be tied in the middle of the field and shot by soldiers, and finally to be beaten until he died.

On the Cornelian Way, the holy martyrs Marius and Martha, with their sons Audifax and Abacuc, noblemen of Persia, who had come to Rome for prayer in the time of the emperor Claudius. After enduring beatings, the rack, fires, claws, and the cutting off of their hands, Martha was killed in a pool; the others were beheaded, and their bodies were burned.

12th day before the Kalends. Day 21.

[Note: [Col. 0677]]

From Prat., Herin., Torn., Pulsan., Munerat., Greven., Molan., and the Acts of the Martyrs.

[Note: [Col. 0677B]]

Pulsan. writes “Saint Publius,” and so do the later manuscripts generally, together with Antu.-Max., the Lübeck edition, and others. He also reads *Areopagite*, as do Herin. and Tornac.; we noted in the preface that this is scarcely worth observing. Greven. and Molan. have transposed the words, reading “he nobly ruled” instead of “he ruled nobly.” Pulsan. went further, thinking it more elegant to read: “He nobly ruled the Church of the Athenians.” Munerat. in the second edition, I do not know how, translated “and illustrious in virtues” as “and preaching virtues.” The Acts of the Martyrs do the same.

Again, instead of “is gloriously crowned,” Pulsan. has “gloriously fell.” Greven. and Molan. add “virgin” and “martyr.” Munerat., by omitting “under the governor,” produces a broken sense. All reliable manuscripts read *Symphronio* after Ado; Pulsan. and others, perhaps imitating Bede, read *Simpronio* or *Sempronio*. Likewise, he has *Tarracona*, while the others, with Munerat. and the Acts of the Martyrs, have *Terracona*. I do not dispute which is more correct.

I regard *Tugurii* for *Augurii* in Pulsan. as a scribal error, as also *Galeni* for *Galieni* in the Acts of the Martyrs. *Gallieni* would be better written, but we follow the manuscripts. I read “thrown into prison,” since I think Usuard wrote it that way; Ado had said more correctly “into prison.” Pulsan., Greven., and Molan. depart from this, thinking it should be corrected. The Acts of the Martyrs have *expassis* for *expansis*. Greven. omitted the word “praying” before “so that they might be burned,” perhaps because he noticed that the sense was obscure. But the liberty taken by the Pulsan. manuscript is especially objectionable, for it corrects the passage as follows: “They were thrown into prison; then they were cast into flames to be burned. But when their bonds had been burned away and their hands had been stretched out in the form of a cross, by praying they obtained the palm of martyrdom.”

All write *Trecas*, following the style of the Middle Ages; the freer Greven. has *Trecis*, together with the Acts of the Martyrs. Usuard’s reading, whatever its quality, is preferable.

[Note: [Col. 0677C]]

Our Usuardine manuscripts of the best quality unanimously announce Publius first. Several others, with Belinus, put Agnes first. So too do the Hieronymian copies, the Little Roman Martyrology, Rabanus, and Ado. It is not easy to guess why Usuard and Notker thought this should be changed. Nor can chronological order be pleaded, for on that basis the most famous Agnes would have had to be relegated to the last place, even if, with Bollandus, one holds that she obtained the crown of martyrdom under Valerian and Gallienus rather than under Diocletian, as the more probable opinion maintains.

Thus Publius is placed before all the others. We consider him one of those whose first memory in the sacred calendars is owed to the author of the Little Roman Martyrology. For the person who appears in the Hieronymian copies as Puplius, Publius, or Publius among other martyrs has no connection with this Publius, and I think Castellanus plainly mistaken in believing that the name was taken from those notices.

Here are the words of the Little Roman Martyrology: “At Athens, Saint Publius, bishop, who was ordained bishop of Militus by Paul.” Ado has it differently: “Likewise at Athens, the blessed Publius, bishop, crowned with martyrdom for Christ.” In this way the chronological difficulties are excluded—difficulties into which he becomes entangled in the festivals of the Apostles when he makes Publius of Militus the immediate successor of Dionysius the Areopagite. Baronius and Halloixius, cited by Bollandus, noticed this, and Tillemont more recently attacks it in several places in vol. II.

Whether our author, shortening Ado, wished to avoid the difficulty he had noticed is not easy to say. Certainly he formed the announcement in such a way that he reached the truth, or at least something close to it.

Jerome very truly states in Letter 8 to Demetrias—974 in the new edition—near the end, that Agnes’s life is praised in the writings and languages of all nations, as the excellent encomia of Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, and so many others prove. “Especially in the Churches,” the same Jerome says; indeed, “in all the most ancient calendars, martyrologies, and sacramentaries.” The Bucherian Calendar expressly reads: “Agnes at the Nomentan.” The Carthaginian Calendar: “Saint Agnes, martyr.” Fronto’s, apparently to distinguish a duplicated feast: “The birthday of Saint Agnes from her passion,” where *Agnes* in the nominative would be better than *Agne*.

The Hieronymian Martyrologies place first: “At Rome, the passion of Agnes, virgin.” More briefly, the Little Roman Martyrology has: “Saint Agnes, virgin.” Bede’s eulogy is copied almost word for word by Rabanus and Ado in the Martyrology; our author probably borrowed the rest, and this as well, from the latter.

In that same Ado, however, a fuller history is woven among the festivals of the Apostles. One could call it a summary of those Acts commonly circulated under Ambrose’s name, from which Notker also extracted several details. Whether Bollandus truly believed the Acts to be Ambrosian is doubtful; in any case, modern scholars generally deny them to that holy teacher. Nor should this be considered a great loss, since it is abundantly compensated by Ambrose himself, Book I *On Virgins*, chapter 2, by Prudentius, Maximus of Turin, and many other Fathers.

See Ruinartus among the selected Acts, beginning on p. 503, where he illustrates Prudentius’s hymn 14 and the cited passage of Ambrose. Tillemont, vol. V, beginning on p. 344, and Castellanus in his notes for today, make several observations that may be examined in the Supplement.

Wandalbertus sang of Agnes alone:

“The twice-sixth day honors Agnes, virgin and martyr.”

The Hieronymian Martyrologies commemorate the martyrs of Tarragona; Florentinius made a few observations about them, perhaps to be discussed elsewhere. Castellanus is again mistaken when he says that their names appear in all prose martyrologies, since neither Bede nor the Little Roman Martyrology mentions them.

Florus marks them with an encomium of his own. Ado composed a more elegant account from the Acts, which our author reduced to fewer words. Rabanus selected only Fructuosus and wrongly attributed to him rules for monks, which were composed many centuries later by Fructuosus, bishop of Braga; Notker preferred to follow Ado.

Ruinartus admits that the Acts illustrated by Bollandus are authentic; see him beginning on p. 219, and Tillemont, vol. IV, p. 198. Patroclus of Troyes was also taken from the praised Hieronymian Martyrologies: “At Troyes, the passion of Saint Patroclus by martyrdom,” whom Acherius wrongly counted among the additions. Rabanus and Ado received him from this source, with the difference that the former neglected to indicate the place, while the latter gives it more distinctly: “At Troyes.” Why our author wrote less elegantly, or why Notker omitted him, is not worth investigating. It is clear enough that Usuard took all his material from Ado. When you notice here and elsewhere that Baronius or Bollandus cite Bede, understand this as referring to the long-published Bede mentioned above, which Bollandus commonly indicates as a precaution. Bollandus deals carefully with the Acts and translation of Patroclus; add to this Tillemont’s more recent observations in vol. IV, p. 203.

[Note: [Col. 0679A]]

ANTUERP.-MAJ. begins with Agnes, and is sufficiently pure in that section. Then: “At Athens, the birthday of Saint Publius, bishop and martyr.” The Tarragonese saints lack an encomium. Finally: “At Troyes, the passion of Saint Patroclus, martyr, in the time of the emperor Aurelian. After various struggles which he endured for Christ, he completed his martyrdom by decapitation and was buried not far away.”

ROSWEYD. The section on Agnes is good. On Publius, as Ado has it in the Martyrology: “Likewise at Athens, the blessed Publius, bishop, crowned with martyrdom for Christ.” He compresses the encomium of the Tarragonese saints: “In Spain, in the city of Tarragona, the birthday of the holy Fructuosus, bishop, and Augurius and Eulogius, deacons, who were crowned with martyrdom in the time of Gallienus under the governor Aemilianus.” The final section is pure.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LÜBECK. are sufficiently pure throughout the text, but in the encomium of the Tarragonese saints they supplement from Ado what Usuard omitted: “And immediately certain people—the brothers and the governor’s daughter who was standing there—saw the souls of the saints ascend to heaven crowned.” Manuscripts of middling quality have the same.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJ., LEYDEN., ALBERG., DANIC., and the Utrecht-Belgian edition are no less faithful, except that they place Agnes before Publius.

[Col. 0679C] LOVANIEN. also places Agnes first, but is additionally mutilated, lacking the entire encomium of Publius.

CENTULEN.: “At Athens, Saint Publius, bishop and martyr, whom Saint Paul the Apostle taught and ordained. At Rome, the passion of Saint Agnes, virgin, under the judge Symphronius.” In the Tarragonese notice, after “deacons,” it adds “and martyrs,” but lacks the encomium. In the final section it is pure, but adds “in the time of Aurelian.”

BRUXELLEN. adds concerning Agnes: “Whom we commemorate daily in the canon of the Mass.” Concerning Publius, it combines Ado’s encomium among the festivals of the Apostles with Usuard’s, approximately as follows: “At Athens, the blessed Publius, bishop and martyr. Formerly he was ruler of the island called Melitene. When he had received the blessed Paul, sailing to Rome, as a guest for three days and treated him hospitably, and Paul had healed his father, who was suffering from fever and dysentery, by the laying on of hands, he began to cling to Saint Paul. Paul later ordained him bishop and sent him out to preach. He was the second after Dionysius,” etc.

The Tarragonese section is not entirely pure, and from Ado it adds the same material mentioned above. At the end: “On the same day at Troyes, in the time of the emperor Aurelian, the passion of the glorious Saint Patroclus, martyr, who rests at Sens.” See Bollandus.

HAGENOYEN. is sufficiently pure in Publius, whom it places second. [Col. 0680A] It has the Tarragonese saints as in Antwerp and the others above. Concerning Agnes it reads: “At Rome, the passion of Saint Agnes, virgin and martyr. In her youth she chose God as her bridegroom and therefore refused the son of the governor Symphronius. For this reason she was shamefully stripped naked, but was covered by God with her hair and guarded by an angel in a brothel. After she had restored to life the governor’s son, who had wished to violate her, she was thrown into the fire and killed, but was not harmed by the flames. Finally she was struck with a sword and underwent death. On the same day at Troyes,” etc.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJ. reads: “The solemnity of Agnes, virgin and martyr.” In the margin: “By special permission of the chapter, because her body is present in the church of Saint Martin at Utrecht, where it is solemnly placed in a gilded silver reliquary.” In later editions Molanus inserts into Usuard’s text, in italics, concerning the same saint: “Her relics are kept in Lower Utrecht.” See Bollandus and Castellanus.

BELIN. The first edition is mutilated, the second nearly complete, but both differ from Usuard in assigning first place to Agnes.

LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION. Also beginning with Agnes, it inserts into Usuard’s encomium after “virgin” the words: “Who, in the thirteenth year of her age, in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, under the governor of the city,” etc. Its section on Publius is pure. In the Tarragonese martyrs it copies Ado rather than Usuard. Concerning Patroclus it reads: “On the same day at Troyes, Saint Patroclus, martyr, who was beheaded in the time of the emperor Aurelian.”

GREVEN.: “This Patroclus was a citizen of the city of Troyes, but, for love of Christ, despising riches, after enduring fetters, burning chains, and beatings, he reached the palm of martyrdom by the cutting off of his head. Vitalis, martyr of Agaunum. Meinrad, hermit and martyr. The translation of Saint Vincent, deacon, at Clermont; Avitus, bishop. Hermis, bishop. Also Saint Celestine.”

MOLAN. First edition, in small type: “At Ancyra in Galatia, Saint Busyris, an outstanding martyr.” From the *Tripartite History*, Book VI, chapter 13. “Meinrad, hermit and martyr of Reichenau.” The later editions read: “On the island of the monastery of Reichenau, Meinrad, hermit and martyr, in the year 960. On the twenty-first day, Saint Maximus, holy confessor, and Saint Neophytus. On the same day, the holy martyrs Eugenius, Canidius, Valerian, and Acyla.” Concerning Maximus, see the Omissions. Whether that Neophytus is Anastasius, I do not know. See the Acts for the preceding day and the Omissions for today.]

[Col. 0677]

The birthday of the blessed Publius, bishop, who, second after Dionysius the Areopagite, nobly ruled the Church of the Athenians, and, illustrious in virtues and resplendent in teaching, was gloriously crowned by martyrdom for Christ.

At Rome, the passion of Saint Agnes, virgin, who, after being thrown into the flames under the city prefect Symphronius, had the flames extinguished by her prayer and was struck with a sword.

In Spain, in the city of Tarragona, the holy martyrs Fructuosus, bishop, and Augurius and Eulogius, deacons, who, having first been thrown into prison in the time of Gallienus and then cast into the flames, obtained by prayer—after their bonds had been burned away and their hands stretched out in the form of a cross—that they might be burned.

At Troyes, Saint Patroclus, martyr.

11th day before the Kalends. Day 22.

[Note: [Col. 0681]]

The text is taken from Herimen., Tornacen., Munerat., Greven., Molan., and the Acts of the Martyrs.

[Note: [Col. 0681A]]

The slight discrepancies are scarcely worth noting. Greven. and Molan. write “Saint Paul” instead of “blessed Paul.” The same Molan. and others have “ordained bishop,” and likewise “at Ephesus”; the others, better in agreement with the text, have “ordained bishop at Ephesus.”

In Tornacen., where Vincent is announced, “on the same day in the city, etc.,” the word “day” is omitted through a copyist’s error; Munerat. likewise writes *Gispaniarum*. Herinien. places “after many struggles for Christ”; the transposition in Usuard, “after many struggles which he endured for Christ,” is certain and somewhat more elegant.

The same manuscript again reads: “whose passion was that of a noble triumph.” The text’s reading is better and is truly and genuinely Usuardine throughout Vincent’s announcement—not the reading attributed to Usuard by Bollandus, who was misled by the Pratensian manuscript and cites the following: “At Valencia, a city of Spain, Saint Vincent, deacon and martyr, whose triumph of combat, in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, after excessive slaughter and grievous torments, the text of his passion declares to have been completed under the governor Dacian.” [Col. 0682A]

I could never bring myself to believe that this was genuinely Usuard’s, since all the other manuscripts, except Aquicinctinus, oppose it. How correctly I had long perceived this was subsequently taught me by Castellanus, whom I can never praise enough as an assistant in consulting the aforementioned Pratensian manuscript. He wrote that the entire encomium of our text, as it had first been written there, had perhaps been erased by some incompetent person and that the words we have just cited were written above it. From this it is clear that this manuscript too was once in agreement with our others, and consequently that the very Usuardine reading is the one we have presented in the text.

The Acts of the Martyrs have “at the waters of the Salinae”; Molan. has “at the waters of Salvias.” Finally, Molan. and Greven. write: “In Gaul, in the city of Embrun.” Everyone can see that the reading of our text is to be preferred to the others. Greven. has something redundant.

[Note: [Col. 0681B]]

As authentic as the deeds of Timothy are—for their chief witness is the Doctor of the Nations himself—so uncertain is the day on which he earned the laurel of martyrdom.

Baronius begins his note on 24 January as follows: “The other Latins celebrate the same man on this day, 24 January, but the Greeks on the 22nd of this month.” He speaks truly of the Greeks, but not of the Latins. For the Hieronymian Martyrologies—and, if it may be counted among them, the manuscript of Saint Cyriacus used by Baronius—as well as Florus, mark him on 27 September; Wandalbertus on 16 May. Usuard, however, his principal manuscripts, Belinus, and other recent witnesses announce him expressly on this day, 22 January.

Thus the others derive from Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, Rabanus, and Notker. Bede’s, the Little Roman Martyrology’s, and Rabanus’s wording is very brief; Notker’s is somewhat longer and comes from Ado among the festivals of the Apostles. Our material also derives from there, with only the translation of the relics omitted—the translation that Usuard treats on 9 May, transferring some Adonian material from today to that place.

What moved him to abandon the customary tracks I nowhere find, unless, contrary to his custom, he wished here to imitate the Greeks. Bollandus has admirably illustrated the Acts written by Polycrates and the fuller account by Metaphrastes. See also Castellanus’s note beginning on p. 493 and Tillemont’s carefully prepared summary of the life in vol. II, beginning on p. 142.

“As far as either the Roman Empire or the Christian name extends,” Augustine says, “every region and every province rejoices to celebrate Vincent’s birthday.” Hence his memory is famous in the ancient monuments of the Church. He is not honored only in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but is joined to Bishop Valerius and eighteen, indeed even more, companions. Bollandus deals carefully with this group, and after him Florentinius in his notes. Take the names of most of the companions from the distinguished hymn of Prudentius, and learn from the cited writers on which day each should be placed.

[Col. 0682C] The Little Roman Martyrology leaves the place of his martyrdom indefinite: “Saint Vincent, deacon and martyr, in Spain.” Bede did not write more clearly. Ado composed an encomium from the most reputable Acts, although they are not official proceedings. Our author, because of his particular devotion to Saint Vincent, fashioned an encomium that some rejected and others did not render faithfully. Florus wove a different history, and Rabanus another, but Notker copied Ado.

In our Acts you have the material laboriously collected concerning the translations and miracles. See also Ruinartus beginning on p. 387, Castellanus’s note on p. 375, and Tillemont’s life in French, vol. V, beginning on p. 215.

The Little Roman Martyrology mentions “Anastasius the monk at the waters of Silvias,” instead of Salvias. Bede is somewhat fuller, and the Viennese manuscript has a still more expansive encomium. Rabanus followed the former; Notker the latter, and Usuard refined it, omitting the translation, as we have reported it in the text. His Acts have been so excellently illustrated by Bollandus [Col. 0682D] that nothing seems capable of being desired.

Wandalbertus joined Vincent and Anastasius in this way:

“The sacred Levite Vincent adorns the eleventh day;

To him valor joins the excellent Anastasius.”

The final announcement is purely Usuardine, not Adonian, as Rosweyd rightly decreed, in my opinion. I cannot conjecture where Usuard obtained that Caucoliberitan Vincent and his companions, [Col. 0683A] but, unless I am greatly mistaken, this is the same Caucoliberitan Vincent who is commemorated by the Hieronymians, Ado, and others, indeed by Usuard himself, on 19 April, as Papebrochius correctly observed there, p. 622; Castellanus followed him [Col. 0684A] in his notes, p. 37, as did Tillemont, vol. V, p. 62. That today’s Vincent has companions, whereas the other is alone, can easily be reconciled elsewhere. For the present, we wished to preserve Usuard’s pure and simple reading intact.]

[Note: [Col. 0683A]

PRATENSIS. The alteration made in that manuscript has been discussed sufficiently in the Variants.

ANTWERP–MAJOR. It moves Timothy to 24 January. It therefore begins: “In Spain, in the city of Valencia, the passion of Saint Vincent, Levite and martyr.” In Anastasius, Vincent, Orontius, and so forth, it is entirely pure.

ROSW EYDIAN. It also postponed Timothy: “In Spain, Saint Vincent, deacon and martyr, who, under the most impious governor Dacian, after suffering many tortures, deserved to be crowned with martyrdom. On the same day, in Gaul, in the city of Ebredunum, Saints Vincent,” and so forth. In Anastasius, whom it records last, it is plainly Adonian.

PULSANENSE. Pure in Timothy and Vincent, it closes the day as follows: “At Rome, at the Salvian Waters, Saint Anastasius, monk and martyr.” All the others are omitted, I do not know through whose fault.

[Col. 0683B] ANTWERP and MAXIMUS–LÜBECK, also having transferred Timothy to the 24th, begin as follows: “In Spain, in the city of Valencia, under Dacian, the most impious governor, Saint Vincent, Levite,” and so forth; the entire remainder of the text is pure.

ANTWERP–MAXIMUS, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, DANICUS, and the UTRECHT–BELGIAN edition resemble the preceding witnesses in transferring Timothy to the 24th and are almost identical in the other respects as well.

LOUVAIN is additionally defective in having mutilated the encomium of Anastasius.

CENTULES: “In Spain, in the city of Valencia, the passion of blessed Vincent, archdeacon and martyr, under the governor Dacian. At Rome, at the Salvian Waters, Saint Anastasius, monk and martyr. On the same day, in Gaul, in the city of Ebredunum, Saints Vincent, Orontius, and Victor, martyrs.” Timothy is placed on the 24th.

BRUSSELS: “In Spain, in the city of Caesaraugusta, or Valencia, under Dacian,” and so forth, quite purely. Then concerning the three Ebredunian martyrs, as above. In Anastasius [Col. 0683C] it is Adonian. At the end, however, a later hand adds: “Also, Saint John the Almsgiver, who was patriarch of Alexandria.” See the Additions for the following day.

HAGUENAU: “Near the city of Valencia, the passion of Saint Vincent, Levite and martyr, under the emperor Diocletian, with Dacian acting as governor of Spain: they beat him with clubs, hung him on the rack, pressed a burning plate against his chest, sprinkled his wounds with salt, put him in a dark prison, and rolled him over sharp potsherds; and when he had overcome all these things, he died on a soft bed. The noble [account] of whose passion,” and so forth. In Anastasius and the Ebredunians it is quite pure. At the end: “Also, the translation of the body of Saint Urban, bishop and confessor.” This was undoubtedly intended to refer to Urban of Langres; see the Acts for the following day.

[Col. 0683D] AQUICINCTUS has the same encomium for Vincent [Col. 0684A] that we quoted above from the Pratense. In the remaining items it is pure.

VICTORINUS and the ROYAL SWEDISH MANUSCRIPT, under no. 130: “And the feast of Saint Dominic, abbot.”

CAMBRAI, of the Conventuals of Saint Mary: “Also, Saint Ulf, martyr.” Bollandus records him among the Praetermissa, because sufficient documentation concerning his cult, and so forth, was lacking.

BIGOTIANUS, marked D 9, has the translation of Saint Urban as above. But the BESANÇON manuscript is somewhat clearer: “At Dijon, the translation of the body of Saint Urban, bishop and confessor.”

VATICAN, marked no. 5949, says nothing about Timothy. It adds: “The passing of Lord Dominic, priest and monk.”

ALTEMPS: “At Sardica, Saint Potitus, martyr, under the emperor Antoninus.” In my opinion, this is the saint whom we discussed from other sources among the Additions on 13 January.

[Col. 0684B] FLORENTINE: “Also, the burial of Saint Gaudentius, bishop of the city of Novara, confessor, a man of great holiness.”

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. Timothy is transferred. Some of Vincent’s tortures are enumerated from Ado. In Anastasius also it is Adonian. Then: “At Blandinum, Saint Berdulphus, confessor.” See below. At the end, the entry concerning the Ebredunians is quite pure.

BELIN. In the text it is not entirely pure: it rearranges the announcements so that Vincent occupies the first place and Timothy the third. At the end it adds: “On the same day, at Novara, the burial of Saint Gaudentius, bishop and confessor.”

GREV EN: “On the same day, Epiphanius, bishop of Ticinum, that is, of Pavia, and confessor. Anastasius, abbot, who, as Gregory I reports in the Dialogues, was initially a notary of the Roman Church, but, desiring to devote himself to God alone, entered a monastery situated near the city of Nepi; there he led a life of holy conduct for many years and subsequently governed that monastery with diligent care. At Blandinum, Saint Berdulphus, confessor.” Bollandus more correctly calls him Bertulphus, at Blandinium, but refers the Acts to 5 February.

MOLANUS inserts Ado’s entire encomium of Vincent in different type; I judge it superfluous to copy it here, since it can be read more purely in its original source. At the end, in smaller type, he transferred from Greven the passage concerning Anastasius that we have just given. Then: “On the same day, Epiphanius, bishop of Ticinum, that is, of Pavia, and confessor, who was translated to Hildesheim.” Finally: “At Rome, Saint Blesilla, matron, concerning whom Saint Jerome wrote to Marcella.” Other editions again depart from Usuard’s purity by transferring Timothy from this place to the ninth day before the Kalends. At the end they add what was given above: “On the same day, at Novara, the burial of Saint Gaudentius, bishop and confessor. At Pavia, Saint Epiphanius, bishop and confessor.”]

[Col. 0679]

The feast of Saint Timothy, blessed Paul’s disciple. He was ordained bishop of Ephesus by that same Apostle and, after many struggles for Christ, was crowned with martyrdom. On the same day, in the city of Valencia, under Dacian, governor of Spain, Saint Vincent, Levite and martyr. The conspicuous poet Prudentius lucidly celebrates in verse the noble triumph of his passion; Saint Augustine also commends, in a certain sermon, how worthy of praise and honor the proclamation of this same martyr is. [Bouillart. He reads: [Note: [Col. 0681A] Bollandus, who preferred our reading, says that Sollerius was misled by the Pratensian manuscript. But if he himself had not been misled by his badly sighted informant, he would have shown much greater honor to his colleague. For it is false that, as Castellanus observed, someone perhaps incompetent erased the encomium reproduced by Sollerius. The hand that first wrote Sollerius’s text and later erased it substituted Bollandus’s—or ours—in its place. I appeal to competent judges of this kind of writing. But how do these things fit together? Nothing is easier to explain. Usuard allowed his copy to be transcribed as he had first written it. Hence the copies from which Sollerius drew his encomium of Vincent. After he had received his own manuscript back, however, he obliterated what seemed less correct to him and added what pleased him more. Thus Sollerius here presents Usuard pouring out whatever came into his mind; we, with Bollandus, have published Usuard as revised and restored by himself. BOUILLART.] In the city of Valencia in Spain, Saint Vincent, Levite and martyr, whose triumph in the contest, after excessive slaughter and grievous tortures in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, the text of the passion declares to have been completed under the governor Dacian.] At Rome, at the Salvian Waters, Saint Anastasius, monk and martyr. After enduring many tortures of imprisonment, blows, and bonds, which he had suffered from the Persians in Caesarea of Palestine, he was finally afflicted with much punishment and at last beheaded with seventy others. On the same day, in the city of Ebredunum, Saints Vincent, Orontius, and Victor, martyrs.

The tenth day before the Kalends. Day 23. [Note: [Col. 0683]

Thus read the Pratensian, Pulsanensian, Antwerp, Maximus–Lübeck, Greven, Molan, and Acts of the Martyrs. The Antwerp–Maximus, Utrecht, Leyden, Albergen, Danic, and Utrecht–Belgian edition may also be added, although they differ slightly from the others.]

[Note: [Col. 0685A]

In the Acts of the Martyrs, this concerns seven deacons. The Pulsanensian added a superfluous word to the text, reading “of the first seven deacons”; for it is sufficiently understood from the number that they were among the first, even with that word omitted. Add that it transposes what follows: “handed over by the brothers to the grace of God, and having completed the duty entrusted,” and so forth. Moreover, where the text reads “and, while also defending those praying from the assault of the pagans,” and so forth, the same manuscript cuts out “and while also [defending] those praying” and reads “that [she might defend them] from the pagans,” and so forth. In Greven, Mauricania is a scribal error for Mauritania. I wrote Cneocaesarea, as our principal manuscripts require. Molan, following his usual practice, corrected it to Neocaesarea, as Bollandus also has it, although he admits that Gneocaesarea is commonly read, as in various of our manuscripts, or Geneocaesarea, as in Belin, and so forth. I do not wish to argue over the word, provided it be conceded, against Galesinius, that this city must be located not in Macedonia but in Mauritania. Nor is it necessary to waste effort enumerating the variant readings of the Maximus–Lübeck manuscript: it is enough to have indicated once, and now again, that the first edition of Usuard teems with typographical errors [Col. 0685B], from which other editions are not immune, especially those of Munerat and Belin.

Until now we have recognized the Herinien manuscript as pure; scarcely any addition was found in it except the proper Reims addition for the fourth of this month and a little word concerning Saint Maurus on the fifteenth. [Col. 0686A] Today, however, after Usuard’s completely sound text, it adds the following: “At Toledo, the most blessed Hildefonsus, archbishop and confessor.” I suspect that the church or monastery from which this manuscript originated had a particular cult for him, and that from there the entry passed into other manuscripts. It is also surprising that the entire announcement of Ascla has been omitted in the Tournai manuscript. Was it because he was not found among the ancients? Certainly the following has been substituted in its place: “At the monastery of Resbais, the translation of Saint Agilus, abbot. On the same day, Saint Macarius, martyr.” I do not understand at all what Agilus’s translation has to do with the people of Tournai, since no mention is made of his feast on a proper day. Nevertheless, other manuscripts too speak of this translation. The feast of Macarius, either alone or joined with Eugenius or Emerentiana, was once highly celebrated in various churches of Gaul and Belgium, as their calendars, Rabanus, manuscript codices, and Munerat’s edition prove. Nor does an earlier memorial seem necessary than the one expressly recorded in the Hieronymians. His Acts will be given on 20 December. The manuscripts of middling quality [Col. 0686B] depart from complete purity only in this respect: together with the Small Roman and Ado, they place Emerentiana before Parmena and insert the account of Ascla, who, under the governor Arius, first … See the Observations at the end.]

[Note: [Col. 0685B]

Above, on 10 January, we indicated in passing that four of the first seven deacons—namely Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, and Parmena, who is commemorated today—were first entered into the sacred calendars by the author of the Small Roman. Here I set down the words of that Martyrology: “At Philippi, Parmena, deacon, one of the seven.” Nearly the same words are reported by Ado in his Martyrology, but in the feasts of the Apostles he composed a brief encomium, which Notker transcribed in full, while Our Author altered and abridged it very slightly. There is little about Parmena in our Acts, and little in Tillemont, vol. II, pp. 69–70. Emerentiana is not absent from all the Hieronymian copies, but I believe that she is legitimately placed in none of them. Castellanus, p. 385, indicates clearly enough that she too was first recorded by the Small Roman; this cannot be denied if we consider Beda older than its author. For Emerentiana is celebrated by the Beda mentioned above with an encomium that Rabanus, Ado, and Notker took almost word for word from him. Whether Our Author drew from the source or from the stream makes little difference; certainly he cut away a few words from theirs. The Small Roman had written: “At Rome, Saint Emerentiana, virgin,” with the inflection in which we recently showed Agnes to be read. There she is adorned with no title other than “virgin”; Beda, however, most distinctly proclaims her a virgin of Christ and a martyr and briefly includes nearly everything that the Acts of blessed Agnes preserve concerning this saint of ours. Wandalbert alone praises her in this verse:

“After Emerentiana, on the tenth day, a great praise shines forth.”

[Col. 0685D] The Hieronymian copies announce first: [Col. 0686B] “In Mauritania, in the city of Neocaesarea, the passion of Saint Severinus and Aquila his wife.” Whether those who are usually added to these are their companions is made doubtful by the Echternach manuscript; concerning this, Florentius may be consulted. The Small Roman differs little from the preceding, except that it writes Severianus and does not add the designation “wife” to Aquila. Ado of Rosweyd restored everything to the sense of the Hieronymians, adding the manner of death. Nevertheless, if conjecture is permitted, I think that Ado wrote not Severinus but Severianus. Usuard and Notker demonstrate this; it is not credible that they would have altered anything in the martyr’s name while transcribing everything else from Ado. The conjecture is confirmed by Mosander’s edition, in which Severianus is also expressly read. Apart from what is said here in the text, Bollandus and, as far as I know, no one else have so far discovered anything about these martyrs. I add here another conjecture that seems, unless I am mistaken, sufficiently probable: namely, that Usuard saw the Acts of certain Egyptian martyrs, which had been unknown to the earlier Martyrologists and even to his contemporaries. From them he extracts today Asclas, the celebrated martyr of Antinoe; Philemon and Apollonius he extracts on 8 March. Some wish Asclas to have suffered on the 21st and to have been buried on this day. I discuss neither his cult among the Greeks here nor elsewhere. Bollandus published Acts sufficiently genuine; if these are compared with our encomium, it will clearly appear that the latter was once extracted from them. Tillemont, in vol. V, beginning at p. 353, connects several Egyptians who suffered under Arius, first the cruel persecutor and later himself a martyr, including Asclas on p. 358. From what has been said concerning the origin and genuineness of Usuard’s reading, I believe the matter has been sufficiently established.]

[Note: [Col. 0685D]

HERINIEN and TOURNAI. We have given the additions of both above among the variants.

ANTWERP–MAJOR. It follows Beda, or perhaps Ado, rather than Usuard. It has this first: “At Rome, Saint Emerentiana, virgin of Christ and martyr, who was the foster-sister of Saint Agnes. And while she was praying at her tomb, and praying together,” and so forth. In Severianus and Aquila it is quite pure. In Parmena it is more Adonian. The encomium of Ascla is missing. At the end: “In the city of Toledo, the feast of Saint Hildefonsus, bishop and confessor, most illustrious in faith and doctrine.”

ROSW EYDIAN. In Emerentiana it agrees almost entirely with the preceding. Then: “And in Mauritania, in the city of Neocaesarea, the feast of Saint Severianus and Aquila his wife, who received martyrdom by the punishment of fire. At Philippi, Parmena, deacon, who was one of the seven deacons.” Nothing about Ascla. In its place: “Also, Macarius, martyr.”

MUNERAT adds to the text: “On the same day, Saint Macarius, martyr.”

LOUVAIN is defective only in the encomium of Ascla, which it omitted.

CENTULES: “The feast of Saint Parmena, who was one of the first seven deacons and, having attained the glory of martyrdom, rested at Philippi. At Rome, Saint Emerentiana, virgin. At Antinoe, Saint Asclas, martyr. In the city of Toledo, Saint Hildefonsus, bishop and confessor, most illustrious in faith and doctrine, who with wondrous devotion cultivated the praise and honor of the blessed [Col. 0687A] Mother of God and ever-virgin.” The Mauritanian martyrs are absent.

BRUSSELS is almost pure in Emerentiana and purer in Parmena and the Mauritanians. Concerning Ascla it has: “At the city of Antinoe, Saint Asclepius, martyr. He was most cruelly tortured under the judge Arius, then burned in flames, and finally …” Then: “On the same day, Saint Sabina, virgin.” Is this the Sabina whom Beda mentions on the following day? “And Macarius, martyr. In Gaul, at Vienne, the burial of Saint Bernard, confessor and archbishop of Vienne. And on the same day, the translation of Saint Agilus, abbot and confessor.”

HAGUENAU is quite pure at the beginning. Of Emerentiana it says, “virgin, who was the foster-sister of blessed Agnes the virgin and a catechumen; and while she was praying,” and so forth. In the remaining entries it is purer than usual.

AQUICINCTUS, after “she was stoned by them,” inserts into the text: “On the same day, Saint Macarius.”

VICTORINUS is defective in Saints Severianus and Aquila. [Col. 0687B] At the end, however, together with the Royal Swedish manuscript under no. 130, it adds: “In the city of Toledo, the feast of Saint Hildefonsus, bishop and confessor, most illustrious in faith and doctrine.”

DAVERON: “At the monastery of Resbais, the translation of blessed Agilus, confessor and abbot of that same monastery.”

MATRICIAN, CARTHUSIAN, and UTRECHT: “Emerentiana, virgin and martyr. Hildefonsus, bishop and confessor. Ascla, martyr, and his companions.” By these he undoubtedly means the others who suffered under Arius. “Parmena, deacon, who was one of the first seven. Severianus and Aquila his wife, burned with fire.”

DIJON, Saint Benignus: “At the monastery of Dijon, the translation of Saint Urban, confessor, bishop of the city of Langres,” which belongs to this day, as we said yesterday from Bollandus. It is therefore wrong that in another manuscript of Saint Benignus preserved at Cîteaux all these entries are assigned to the eighth day before the Kalends of February, that is, 25 January.

[Col. 0687C] AUGEN: “At the monastery of Resbais, the translation of Saint Agilus, abbot. On the same day, Saint Macarius, martyr.”

ROYAL SWEDISH MANUSCRIPT, under no. 428: “On the same day, Saint Macarius, martyr.”

[Col. 0688A] In the VATICAN manuscript marked no. 5949, the commemoration of Ascla is absent.

ALTEMPS: “On the same day, in the monastery of Resbais, the translation of the body of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Agilus, first abbot of that same monastery. Also, Saint Felicianus, bishop and confessor.” In the Acts, 24 January.

FLORENTINE: “Also, the translation of Saint Agilus, abbot and confessor. At Toledo, Saint Hildefonsus, bishop and confessor.”

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins: “At Cologne Agrippina, in the church of Saint Cunibert, archbishop, the commemoration of eleven thousand virgins and martyrs.” In Emerentiana it follows Ado and, after “she was stoned by them,” adds: “And by such a martyrdom she gave up her blessed spirit. Her body the parents of blessed Agnes buried honorably at night with the priests beside the tomb of that same Agnes.” It then proceeds to Parmena and the others, quite purely.

Both editions of BELIN are somewhat truncated in [Col. 0688B] the encomium of Ascla; both begin with Emerentiana. The second, however, adds at the end: “On the same day, Saint Macarius, martyr.”

GREV EN: “Macarius, martyr. Also Eugenius. On the same day, John, patriarch of Alexandria, who on account of his outstanding mercy toward the poor was called the Almsgiver. At Toledo, blessed Hildefonsus, archbishop and confessor.”

MOLAN: “At Toledo, Hildefonsus, bishop and confessor. At Alexandria, the feast of Saint John, patriarch, a man of God, most devout in suffering and generosity in almsgiving. On the same day, Saint Macarius, abbot and martyr.” Later editions have the same concerning Hildefonsus; concerning the Almsgiver, more clearly: “At Alexandria, the feast of Saint John, patriarch, a man of God, most devout in compassion and generosity of alms. At Vienne in Gaul, Saint Bernard, bishop of that city and confessor, in the time of Louis the Pious. In Burgundy, Saint Maibodus, martyr.” [Col. 0688C] In the Acts he is called Maimbod. “And elsewhere, the passion of Saints Eugenius and Macarius. On the twenty-third day, Saint Clement, hieromartyr of Ancyra, and Saint Agathangelus, martyr.” See them in the Acts, together with their companions, who are enumerated there.]

[Col. 0683]

At Philippi, blessed Parmena, who was one of the seven deacons. He, handed over by the brothers to the grace of God and completing with full faith the duty of preaching entrusted to him, attained the glory of martyrdom. At Rome, the feast of Saint Emerentiana, virgin and martyr, who, while praying at the tomb of Saint Agnes and defending those praying with her from the assault of the Gentiles, was stoned by them. In Mauritania, in the city of Cneocaesarea, Saints Severianus and Aquila his wife, burned with fire. At the city of Antinoe, Saint Asclas, martyr, who was first tortured most cruelly by hanging, then burned with flames applied to his sides, and finally, having been thrown into a river, surrendered his precious soul to God.

The ninth day before the Kalends. Day 24. [Note: [Col. 0687C]

The Pratensian, Herinien, Tournai, Pulsanensian, Munerat, the first edition of Belin, Greven, Molan, [Col. 0687D] and the Acts of the Martyrs agree. The Antwerp–Major and Maximus–Lübeck manuscripts, the second edition of Belin, and all the manuscripts of middling quality should also be added, except that today they record Timothy first, as we shall say below in the Additions.]

[Note: [Col. 0687D]

Belin incorrectly formed Babille instead of Babylas, perhaps because he wished in some measure to imitate Beda. The Hieronymian copies generally have Basillae; others Babellae, and so forth. Following the Small Roman and Ado, Babylae ought to be written, as Molan and the Acts of the Martyrs read; but we followed our manuscript codices. Herinien has “martyr and bishop.” Munerat, Belin, Greven, and Molan read “had glorified God”; with the manuscripts we have “the Lord,” and we believe that Our Author read it in this way, as he had found it in Ado. There is much variation in the names of the children; greater variation can be observed in the Acts. The more accurate manuscripts conform to the text, although Tournai has Epholonus, Greven Pepolenus, and Molan Eupolenus. Bollandus gives a different form, perhaps from Beda, and others pronounce the name differently; but, unless I am mistaken, the proper spelling must be elicited from the agreement of several manuscripts, as will also apply in the following class. Munerat has In Caesarea; Molan again has Neocaesarea. The Pratensian has Cneocaesarea, which, if not more correct, is at least more consistent with the earlier form; Herinien and others have Gneocaesarea. But, as recently, we have reduced these to a single nomenclature. The first edition of Munerat writes Mulonis; the second, in agreement with the text but incorrectly, Merilli instead of Metelli. Belin has Musionis; others Misonii, others Musonii, as can be observed in Bollandus; we read it with Usuard. The particle “and” is superfluous in the Pulsanensian and in Molan before Metelli. The Pulsanensian called the river Ausus, but Munerat, Belin, and Molan have the river Axus; the best manuscripts, following Ado, have “the river Axus,” while Belin incorrectly added at the end, “they are reported to have been.” There was no need here to be excessively ingenious.]

[Note: [Col. 0689A]

The first part of our text would seem to derive from more than one source, if all the ancient witnesses proceeded uniformly. In this they certainly agree: that they celebrate on this day the renowned Babylas, bishop of Antioch, not on 4 September, as the Greeks do; Tillemont, and after him Castellanus, rightly argue against them from the order of Saint John Chrysostom’s homilies. Meanwhile, the Hieronymians read at the beginning: “At Antioch, the passion of Saint Basil, bishop, with three children.” Beda’s text has Babyla, and the children’s names Urbanius, Prilidianus, and Epolonius are added; Rabanus appended a few details to these. The author of the Small Roman had another source, Rufinus, I think, from which he recorded only this: “At Antioch, Saint Babylas, bishop.” Ado followed him, drawing other material from Eusebius, though material that also concerns Babylas alone. Our Author transcribed the first part of this word for word, adding a closing clause about the three children, omitted by Notker, whom he could have obtained from no other source than Beda. I admit that Florus too expresses the children’s [Col. 0689B] names mentioned above; but that Usuard drew nothing from this source is proved by the great difference between his encomium and Ado’s: they differ most extensively in the tyrant’s name, the manner of death, and everything else, since Ado drew his account from Eusebius, while the other drew his from the Acts. This is the variety of differing records that has rendered Babylas’s life so encumbered with insuperable difficulties that no one has yet been able entirely to explain them. Bollandus performed excellent work in distinguishing the various Babylases and in embellishing this Babylas of Antioch, nor do I see more precise accounts produced by later writers. Tillemont extracted some material from Chrysostom, vol. III, beginning at p. 400; whether it can be sufficiently reconciled with the Acts will have to be examined elsewhere. The remaining material has been so well illuminated by Bollandus from ecclesiastical history that there is no need to linger over a familiar subject. Wandalbert has a single verse:

“On the ninth day the courage and martyrdom of Babylas shine forth.”

The next announcement of the Hieronymians reads as follows: “And in the city of Neocaesarea, Mardonius, Mosonius, Eugenius, Metellus.” Nothing appears concerning them in the Small Roman, Beda, Florus, or Rabanus. In Ado the names have been smoothed, and a brief encomium added, which Our Author and Notker transcribed in every detail. If you ask where Ado could have drawn this from, I shall answer that I cannot conjecture it even by divination, unless he saw some Acts that have now perished. From that encomium, however, arises the controversy concerning the place of their passion, which you certainly cannot easily determine unless the river Axus is first found, beside which Cneocaesarea or Neocaesarea lay. The time of their martyrdom and the other circumstances are equally uncertain; but Usuard’s text is entirely certain, and we have set out its origin and simplicity.]

[Note: [Col. 0689B]

We noted above that Beda, the Small Roman, Ado, Rabanus, and Notker place Timothy on this day, as is preserved in the modern Roman Martyrology. Since the scribes of certain Usuardine manuscripts imitated those Martyrologists, the following were excluded for that sole reason from the number of pure Usuards: ANTWERP–MAJOR, ANTWERP and MAXIMUS–LÜBECK, ANTWERP–MAXIMUS, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, DANICUS, the UTRECHT–BELGIAN edition, and likewise the second [Col. 0689C] edition of BELIN. It should be noted, however, that the manuscripts just cited record Timothy’s announcement purely and in full from the 22nd, and in first place, whereas that second edition of Belin adds it only at the end: “On the same day, blessed Timothy, apostle.”

ROSW EYDIAN begins: “At Ephesus, Timothy, blessed Paul the Apostle’s disciple.” It is pure in Babylas but lacks the final clause concerning the three boys. In the last announcement also it is correct.

CENTULES: “At Ephesus, Saint Timothy, bishop and martyr, disciple of Saint Paul the Apostle. At Antioch, Saint Babylas, bishop and martyr, martyred with three boys. In the city of Gneocaesarea, Saints Mardonius, Mosonius, Eugenius, and Metellus, martyrs, all of whom were delivered to the fire.”

BRUSSELS also begins with Timothy, quite purely. Then: “At Antioch, the feast of Saint Babylas, bishop and martyr. During the persecution of Decius, he gloriously met the end of his life in bonds. With him,” and so forth. [Col. 0689D] In the other announcement it is quite pure. At the end it adds: “Also, Basil, bishop.” Nothing is said elsewhere about this Basil. Perhaps he had read Basil somewhere in place of Babylas and derived Basil from it?

HAGUENAU records Timothy not entirely purely; in the text it is more even.

AQUICINCTUS: “At Cambrai, the elevation of Saint Autbert, bishop and confessor.” He is commemorated on 13 December.

VICTORINUS draws from the preceding day concerning Saints Severianus and Aquila, and adds: “On the same day, Saint Felicianus, bishop, who suffered under Decius.” At the end: “At Troyes, Saint Sabinianus, martyr.” Florus treats him today under the same name, joining to him “Sabina” as sister, whereas Beda had spoken only of her. See our other manuscripts below.

MATRICIAN, CARTHUSIAN, and UTRECHT: “Babylas, bishop and martyr, with the three boys who suffered with him. [Col. 0690B] Also, Saints Mardonius, Mosonius, Eugenius, and Metellus, martyrs, who were delivered to the fire.”

CAMBRAI: “Near the city of Gévaudan, blessed Severianus, bishop.”

ROYAL SWEDISH MANUSCRIPT, under no. 130: “On that same day, Saint Felicianus, bishop. At Troyes, Saint Sabinianus, martyr.”

In the VATICAN manuscript marked no. 5949, Timothy and Ascla are commemorated on this day.

[Col. 0690C] UGHELLIAN is similar to the manuscripts of middling quality cited above at the beginning.

ALTEMPS: “On the same day, Saint Cadoc, confessor.” Castellanus places him among the Emeri, or saints without a day, p. 910; perhaps this concerns Sophia, or Sophius of Benevento. See the Acts, vol. II, pp. 602–603.

FLORENTINE: “In the province of the Franks, at the city of Troyes, Saint Sabinus, martyr, who suffered under the emperor Aurelian …” I think Sabinianus is meant; see 29 January. The STROZZIAN adds: “Also, Saint Felicianus, bishop and martyr.”

The LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins with Timothy quite purely. The text too is close to pure. At the end: “At Troyes, blessed Sabinianus, martyr, who, after an iron bed, fire, and other tortures of various kinds, was beheaded. Through him also more than nine thousand Gentiles who confessed Christ suffered similar martyrdoms.” Concerning the number of his companions, see vol. II of January, [Col. 0690D] p. 938. It continues: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Eric, king and martyr.”

GREV EN: “Timothy, blessed Paul’s disciple, here according to Ado and certain others,” and so forth. We have discussed these above. “In the territory of Troyes, Sabinianus, otherwise Sabinus, martyr; the emperor Aurelian ordered him, bound to iron bars, to be beaten and a burning helmet to be placed on his head; then, after he had been put into fire but was unharmed, he ordered him to be beheaded. Usuard, however, places him first on the fourth day before the Kalends under the name Sabianus”; whom “Vincent follows in book XII, chapter 105.” Usuard commemorates Sabinianus on the cited day, and therefore, if Vincent wrote Sabianus, he followed Usuard incorrectly. Bollandus discusses Sabinianus and his sister Sabina on 29 January. It continues: “The translation of Saint Eric, king of Sweden and martyr.” See the Acts for 18 May. “At Herford, the translation [Col. 0691A] of blessed Pusinna, virgin.” Her life is given on 23 April. “The commemoration of blessed Augustine, bishop.” Bollandus did not know the reason for this feast, nor can I guess it. Finally: “Leonilla, widow and martyr.” She does not seem to be different from the mother or grandmother of the triplets discussed above under 17 January.

MOLAN. In the first edition, after “in bonds,” he inserts the entire Adonian text in different type. Let it be consulted in the source. At the end he adds: “On the same day, blessed Timothy [Col. 0692A] the Apostle. At Cambrai, the elevation of the body of Saint Autbert, bishop and confessor.” The other editions are not pure, since they place Timothy first. Concerning Babylas they give the same material from Ado. At the end: “At Clermont, Saint Artemius, bishop and confessor, of remarkable holiness. On the twenty-fourth day, Saint Mother Xena.” In the Acts she is also called “Eusebia.” Concerning the elevation of “Autbert” of Cambrai, as in the first edition.]

[Col. 0687]

At Antioch, the feast of Saint Babylas, bishop, who, during the persecution of Decius, after glorifying the Lord frequently through his sufferings and tortures, met the glorious end of his life in bonds. Three boys are also reported to have suffered with him, namely Urbanus, Prilidanus, and Epolonus. In the city of Cneocaesarea, Saints Mardonius, Mosonius, Eugenius, and Metellus, all of whom were delivered to the fire, and their remains were scattered into the river Axus.

The eighth day before the Kalends. Day 25. [Note: [Col. 0691B]

Thus the Pratensian, Herinien, Tournai, Pulsanensian, Antwerp, Maximus–Lübeck, Munerat, Belin, Greven, Molan, and the Acts of the Martyrs. The Antwerp–Maximus, [Col. 0692B] Louvain, Leyden–Belgian, and Utrecht–Belgian edition may also be added.]

[Note: [Col. 0691B]

The Pratensian and a few others write “blessed Paul”; I followed the majority, both manuscripts and printed editions, which unanimously have “Saint Paul.” In Belin, “which was” is incorrectly read instead of “which came,” as in the Herinien, in the second year after the Ascension. The Pulsanensian and the manuscripts of middling quality somewhat transpose the second announcement as follows: “At Damascus, Saint Ananias,” and so forth. Aniana in Munerat is a careless scribal error. Castellanus noted in a letter addressed to me that the Pratensian manuscript reads Prijecti instead of Praejecti. There is great variation in Arvernis: Tournai has Alvernis; the second edition of Belin, Greven, Molan, and others have Avernis; Munerat has Arvennis; the first edition of Belin has Arvenis, and so forth. The more accurate [Col. 0692B] manuscripts and the Acts themselves prove that Amarini should be written; nevertheless, Antwerp, Greven, Molan, and the manuscripts of middling quality generally have Marini. The Pulsanensian has Amilini; Belin, however, “and the man of God Martin.” The Pulsanensian put Gabalis for Gavalis; it may be disputed which is preferable. We follow the nomenclature of the better manuscripts, by which Ganalis is certainly excluded. All correctly read Severianus; I do not know what moved Belin, or rather his editor, to print Severinus in the second edition. Nothing need be noted concerning ammirandae; it is a formula of the Middle Ages. The final line of Munerat is wholly incorrect; it reads: “And a man in holiness of doctrine.” The sense requires “a man of holiness and doctrine,” as correctly given in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0691C] (no further text supplied)]

The Hieronymian copies of the Vulgate, in remarkable agreement on this day, announce in second place: “At Rome, the translation of the Apostle Paul.” No other festival of Paul is mentioned in those manuscripts, whatever Florentius may cite in favor of the Conversion from the Dungal Martyrology and two other Lucca codices. More could be observed here, but, lest I repeat what has already been examined elsewhere by our predecessors, let the reader consult Papebrochius’s discussion in the Acts, volume V for June, p. 467 onward, concerning Paul’s translation and, together with it, his conversion and its liturgy.

It will be enough to have reviewed the Martyrologies. Neither Peda nor Florus discusses either festival. Rabanus joined both together: “At Rome, the translation of the Apostle Paul, and the conversion at Damascus”; and Notker copied all this from there. Since in Rabanus those words are connected with the rest of Bede’s text, I would not find it surprising if someone judged them also attributable to Bede.

But, to draw nearer to our Usuard, he followed his customary guides, of whom the first author of the Little Roman Martyrology reads as follows: “The Conversion of Saint Paul the Apostle” [Col. 0691D]. Ado has it more briefly: “The Conversion of Saint Paul.” The details relating to the time of that conversion were added by Usuard, and several more are added among the Appendices. On this controversy, see Baronius’s note and Tillemont, volume I, p. 544. We shall give Wandalbert’s verse below.

The Little Roman Martyrology attached the commemoration of Ananias to Paul’s conversion: “At Damascus, Saint Ananias, who baptized Paul,” presumably because it did not know the certain day of his death or martyrdom. Castellanus was misled by memory when he stated on p. 402 that Ado had first done this, and he candidly admitted as much in his last letter to me, dated 31 January 1711. Meanwhile, the words of the Little Roman Martyrology, slightly altered, are found in the Ado mentioned above, almost as they are presented in the text, and were also taken from it by Notker.

The present text of Bede is as follows: “Saint Gregory the Theologian, and the feast of Saint Projectus.” The same reading occurs in Rabanus [Col. 0692C] and Notker; but it is well known that Gregory belongs to 9 May. Concerning Projectus, whom others more correctly call Praejectus, Florus added: “Who, chosen from the womb in prophetic fashion, preserved his purple robe in triumph.” You can see how entirely different this is from our eulogy.

Ado placed only this, at the end: “Likewise, the feast of Saint Praejectus, bishop of Arvernus.” Usuard consulted a fuller source, namely the Acts themselves, from which he took the perpetrators of the death and Amarinus, the companion in martyrdom—something Mabillon wrongly attributes also to Ado when he quotes the Acts mentioned above from Bollandus and illustrates them with new observations in the second Benedictine century, from p. 460 onward.

Wandalbert joins our Praejectus to Paul’s conversion in this way:

> On the eighth day, celebrating Paul, converted from the world,  
> The Arvernian honors and adorns his own Praejectus.

In third place Ado records Severianus, bishop of Gabala, from whom our Usuard and Notker received him in nearly identical words. One may well wonder why that saint was removed from the modern Roman Martyrology—something Rosweyd had already wondered at before me. In the often-cited letter he observes:

> It may be asked why Baronius omitted expressing these things—namely, what is placed in Usuard’s text concerning Severianus—in his Martyrology. Did he omit them because he thought the reference was to Severianus, bishop of Gavalum, whom Jerome mentions in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 21, and whom, from book I, chapter 10, of the *Tripartite History*, we know to have been an enemy of Saint Chrysostom? Yet there is also a place called Gavalis in Gaul, where on 25 January Saint Severianus is celebrated, the first bishop of Gavalum, or Mimatensis. It may therefore perhaps have to be considered whether this paragraph should be restored to the new Roman Martyrology, since it is found in the old printed Roman Martyrology—namely, Belinus—in Bede’s common text, in Usuard, and in Ado.

Thus far Rosweyd. It is not sufficiently clear whether Bollandus saw this observation of Rosweyd, unless one wishes to infer it from the agreement of their judgments [Col. 0692D], by which both conclude that the similarity of the names gave occasion for the error.

“Peter of Natalibus,” says Bollandus, “first supplied the opening for this error, in book III, chapter 23. Molanus followed him, writing in the margin beside the name of Severianus in Usuard’s Martyrology: ‘Concerning him, Gennadius, chapter 21.’ Yet Gennadius in that passage is speaking of the Syrian Severianus.” In his later edition Molanus also cites Socrates and Sozomen. See there the other supporters of the same confusion. I shall not discuss it at greater length here.

## [Col. 0693A] Variants

**ANTWERP–MAJOR.** “The Conversion of Saint Paul the Apostle at Damascus, when a light from heaven surrounded him and he heard a voice from heaven saying to him: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ The translation of his sacred body is also celebrated at Rome on the same day. On the same day, the feast of blessed Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, who is called the Theologian.” Its text is sufficiently pure in the notices of Praejectus and Severianus. At the end: “At Poitiers, Saint Savinianus the martyr.” See the *Praetermissi*. It contains nothing concerning Ananias.

**ROSWEYD.** “The Conversion of Saint Paul the Apostle.” In the notice of Ananias, correctly. It then reads: “At the city of Gabala, Saint Severinus the bishop, of admirable …” [Col. 0693B] Read “Severianus. Likewise, the feast of Saint Praejectus, bishop and martyr of Arvernis” [*Arvennensis* instead of *Arvernensis*].

**UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERG, AND DANISH.** These sufficiently show that the date of Saint Paul’s conversion was disputed, since they defend it in the following terms:

> Nor should it trouble us if it is sometimes found to have occurred in the first year; for the statement concerning the first emerging year is to be understood according to the Hebrews, whose year begins in March, whereas the statement concerning the customary year is to be understood according to the Latins, whose year begins on the Kalends of January.

See what we briefly touched upon above in the Observation. In other respects, the manuscripts are extremely pure.

**CENTULE.** “The Conversion of Saint Paul the Apostle at Damascus, which occurred in the second year after the Ascension of the Lord, and the translation of whose sacred body is celebrated at Rome on the same day. On that day, Saint Ananias, who baptized that same apostle. Likewise, Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, bishop, who is called the Theologian. At Arvernis, Saint Praejectus the bishop and Marinus the martyr. At the city of Gabala, Saint Severianus the bishop and confessor, a man of great holiness and learning.”

[Col. 0693C] **BRUSSELS.** “The Conversion of Saint Paul the Apostle”—in red letters—“which is read to have taken place at Damascus, sometimes in the first year after Christ’s Ascension and sometimes in the second. The first, emerging year ends where it begins—see above; the second is the customary year, which according to the Latins is renewed at the Kalends of January.” Its notice of Ananias is sufficiently pure. Then:

> In the city of Arvernis, Saint Praejectus, bishop and martyr. He was crowned with martyrdom by the nobles and chief men of his city in revenge for Hector, the patrician of Massilia, whom Hilderic, king of the Franks, had killed because of the injustices he had inflicted upon the church of Arvernis. And Marinus, a man of God, who was slaughtered together with the aforementioned bishop Praejectus by the nobles of that city of Arvernis on account of justice. And Saint Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, who is called the Theologian; for he was as distinguished in learning as he was remarkable in conduct. Finally, as blessed Jerome writes, after appointing another bishop in his place, he himself practiced the monastic life in the countryside. At the city of Gabala, [Col. 0693D] Saint Severinus the bishop, a man of admirable learning, life, and holiness.

See above.

**HAGENAU.** “The Conversion of Saint Paul the Apostle, when by the voice of God from heaven he was changed from a persecutor into a preacher. This conversion took place in the second year after the Ascension of the Lord. Nor should this trouble us, etc.” It adds concerning Ananias: “a man of great holiness.” In the two final notices its text is sufficiently pure.

**VICTORINUS AND THE SWEDISH REGISTRY**, marked number 130: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, who is called the Theologian. On that day, Saint Arthemas the martyr.” This has until now been unknown to me, unless Saint Artemas the boy is concealed under the feminine name; Bollandus discusses him on this day [Col. 0694A], or perhaps another Arthemas, mentioned by the Hieronymian copies and, from them, by Greven on the following day. We know that men’s names are sometimes transformed into women’s names, and vice versa. See Castellanus, p. 430.

**DAVERON.** “In the district of Tours, Saint Liventius the confessor.” I do not know what place this is, nor have I time to investigate. Many, with Bollandus, read *Linentii*; Castellanus praises Maurolycus for correctly writing *Liventii*. The form, whether derived or perhaps a primitive Gallic name, *Louent*, seems to support that reading. Others below wrongly write *Lineti*.

**MATRICHT–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT.** “The Conversion of Saint [Col. 0694B] Paul the Apostle.” The margin adds: “A celebrated feast in the city of Utrecht.” It was celebrated elsewhere too, especially at Antwerp, with solemn observance—“a suspension of business,” as Bollandus notes, from legal affairs and other servile labor. But this festival was subsequently abolished, along with several others, and therefore, according to Castellanus, p. 402, it ought to be deleted. The manuscript continues:

> Of Ananias, the disciple who baptized Paul; of Projectus, bishop and martyr; of Marinus, abbot; and of Severianus, bishop and confessor, of admirable …

**ALTEMPS.** “At the fortress of Lucas, Saint Liventius the confessor.” I do not know what place this is, and have no time to investigate.

The **Lübeck–Cologne edition**, concerning Paul’s conversion, agrees with the Utrecht manuscript and the others, except that it adds, with several others:

> The translation of the body of this most holy Apostle is also celebrated at Rome on the same day. At Damascus, Saint Ananias the presbyter and confessor, who …

Its texts concerning Praejectus and Severianus are sufficiently pure.

> On the same day, at the town of Nazianzus, Saint [Col. 0694C] Gregory the bishop, who, after many teachings, ordained another bishop in his place, as Jerome reports—having himself been instructed by him in the divine books—and practiced the monastic life in the countryside. In the district of Tours, Saint Linetus the confessor.

**GREVÉN.** “Note: when it is said that the conversion of blessed Paul took place in the first year after the Ascension, this must be understood of the first emerging year, which according to the Hebrews begins in March. What is said here, however, is to be understood of the second customary year, which according to the Latins begins at the Kalends of January. On the same day at Rome, the translation of blessed Paul the Apostle. Likewise, the deposition of blessed Gregory of Nazianzus, who is placed on 9 May, namely the day on which he was ordained. Likewise, Saints Vitus, Castula, and Agileus.”

For the first and last, see the *Praetermissi*.

> Poppo the abbot. Linetus the confessor. Likewise, blessed Semina the virgin,

passed over by Bollandus as unknown.

> On that day, the matron Lucina.

See concerning her in the Acts for 30 June.
