[Col. 0694D] **MOLANUS**, in the first edition, adds in smaller type:

> On the same day, the blessed martyrs Juventinus and Maximus, on whose feast-day John Chrysostom delivered a sermon.

Later editions, in similar type, have:

> On the following day after Babylas, the feast of the blessed martyrs Juventinus and Maximus. In Metaphrastes, Saint Eusebia, who is called “the hospitable” or “the foreign woman”—

namely Xene, concerning whom see the preceding day.

> At Stavelot, the Lord Poppo the abbot died.

See Bollandus and Castellanus.

> On the same day, Henry Suso died, who was of outstanding holiness.

The occasion for the error concerning Severianus of Gabala, which we discussed above at the end of the Observations, may have arisen from the marginal note in the first edition, where Gennadius is cited.

## [Col. 0691] Usuard’s Text

The Conversion of Saint Paul, which occurred in the second year after the Ascension of the Lord. On the same day, Saint Ananias at Damascus, who baptized that same apostle. At the city of Arvernis, Saint Praejectus the bishop, and Amarinus, a man of God, who suffered at the hands of the nobles of the aforesaid city. Likewise, at the city of Gavalis, Saint Severianus the bishop, a man of admirable holiness and learning.

**Seven days before the Kalends. Day 26.**

[Note: [Col. 0695]]

This pure reading of Usuard is preserved by the Herinien manuscript. It is also found in the first Venetian edition of Belinus, Greven, and Molanus.

[Note: [Col. 0695A]]

Greven and other manuscripts read *Smirnam*, which we again follow; others more correctly have *Smyrnam*. Molanus correctly reads *Polycarpi*, although nearly all the printed and manuscript copies have *Policarpi*. Again, Greven and Molanus use *adversus* instead of *adversum*, in agreement with Saint Jerome. The difference is slight, but the ancient simplicity of Usuard should nevertheless be preserved, even if it were less correct. Belinus wrote worse by omitting *adversus eum* and substituting only *coronati sunt* for *martyrio consummati sunt*.

In that same edition, *Kathildis* is a printer’s error; in the second edition it is corrected to *Bathildis*. Molanus followed this form, while Greven has *Batildis*. I preferred the reading of the Herinien manuscript because the Pratensis codex, number 30 of this month, and Muneratus also have it, although I plainly believe the orthography of Belinus and Molanus to be better and more widely accepted, whatever Castellanus may write—*Baldechildis*. *Parisiensi* and *Parisiacensi* amount to the same thing. Belinus wrote the former, the others the latter, which we have judged should be retained.

The Pratensis codex supplies two variations, from which two controversies arise. The first concerns the time at which it asserts that Theogenes suffered martyrdom, namely under the emperor Licinius; the second concerns Bathildis, whom it transferred to 30 January [Col. 0695C].

As for the first, the aforesaid Pratensis codex has very few followers, apart from the Aquicinctine manuscript and the corrupt Parisian edition of Belinus. I was therefore strongly inclined to suspect that it was a recent addition, probably taken from the similarity of names in the entry for 3 January. Castellanus, an exceptionally sharp-eyed inspector of the codex itself, as I have said elsewhere, confirmed this splendidly by accurately noting that the memory of Queen Bathildis had there been erased or half-erased [Col. 0696B], and that the words “under the emperor Licinius” had been written in their place—words which we had rightly judged should be excluded from Usuard.

There could be greater controversy concerning the commemoration of Batildis, since it is absent from other manuscripts—namely, the Tornacensis, Muneratus, the *Acts of the Martyrs*, and others—and many Martyrologies cited by Bollandus in the Acts place her on one or the other day; indeed, Wandalbertus places her on the following day.

But, to settle the matter briefly, I wish you to know in advance that I am not here undertaking a discussion of the true day of her death or cult. On the basis of Castellanus’s notes and many other proofs supplied in his letters, we may for the moment admit both that Queen Bathildis died on 30 January and that on that very day she is celebrated by the Parisians, Cellenses, and Corbeienses.

The sole question is: what did Usuard truly write in his Martyrology? Here we entirely agree with what the manuscripts cited above sufficiently demonstrate concerning the text: namely, that Bathildis was entered by him on 26 January. This is proved even by the Pratensis codex itself, from which we clearly discover through Castellanus that she was introduced there [Col. 0696C]. It is therefore evident that we are presenting Usuard’s genuine and simple text, although erroneous in this respect.

[Note: [Col. 0695C]]

We discussed Polycarp at considerable length on 19 January, in connection with Germanicus, who preceded that most glorious bishop by several days in undergoing martyrdom. There you may seek information concerning the day of his martyrdom and other related matters in the celebrated letter of the Smyrnaeans, which for the sake of brevity we must omit here.

In most of the Hieronymian manuscripts we now find: “At Nicaea of Smyrna, the passion of Saint Polycarp the bishop.” The most ancient Epternacensis, omitting the rest, appended only the name Polycarp to the end of its list [Col. 0695D]. Concerning that Nicaea—whether of Bithynia, Macedonia, or some other region—I have nothing to propose beyond Bollandus or Florentius. Let the reader see there what can most probably be determined.

Bede simply wrote: “The feast of Saint Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, who under Marcus Antoninus …” Florus develops this at greater length, but the Viennese text does so in an entirely different style, and our Usuard followed it. These are the words of the Little Roman Martyrology: “Saint Polycarp, disciple of Saint John the Apostle, suffered at Smyrna.”

The aforesaid Ado composed two eulogies, one longer in his Martyrology, in which the Smyrnaeans’ letter is abridged, and another shorter one among the feasts of the apostles. The latter was copied almost word for word by Usuard [Col. 0696C]. Rabanus follows Bede; Notker abridges Ado’s eulogy from the Martyrology.

This is sufficient concerning the origin of our text. See the rest in Bollandus and in those cited in the Observations for 19 January, but above all consult Florentius’s *Exercise VI*, appended to 23 February, p. 340 onward. There he undertakes a long dissertation intended to consecrate that day to the martyrdom of Saint Polycarp, which must be examined in its proper place.

Wandalbertus explains Polycarp’s martyrdom clearly enough:

> Soon the seventh day shines with Polycarp’s blood,  
> Whom Smyrna truly celebrates, burned for the King.

The same Hieronymian copies that mention Polycarp at Nicaea of Smyrna also commemorate Theogenes—or Theogen—and thirty-five anonymous companions who were martyrs.

Florentius strongly inclines to take the name *Leudicius*, or *Laodicius*, which immediately precedes Theogenes, as referring to the city of Laodicea, and therefore, with Peter of Natalibus and other Martyrologists, regards it as the arena of this whole company. Bollandus was not far from this opinion, nor do I see why it should be rejected altogether.

I admit that our Martyrologists do not specify the place, as is clear from the Little Roman Martyrology, which simply writes: “And Theogenes with thirty-six others.” This was transmitted by Notker in nearly the same form. Our Usuard copied Ado’s text word for word.

I admit, I say, that the arena is missing here because the author of the Little Roman Martyrology undoubtedly did not know it, and Ado could not find it in any Acts. I therefore believe without hesitation that this is Usuard’s judgment, as shown in the Variants.

Usuard alone entered Bathildis in the calendars on this day. See what was said in the Variants, Bollandus in the Acts, and Mabillon in the second Benedictine century, from p. 775, and in the fourth century, concerning her translation, from p. 448. The observations of that most learned author may also be consulted there.

It remains to compare the modern Roman Martyrology’s notice of Theogenes with the Usuardine—or rather Adoian—notice. From this comparison it will become clear that Baronius attributed to that martyr several details which neither Bollandus, nor Florentius, nor other men highly experienced in this field accept.

Rosweyd’s judgment, preserved for us in the letter cited above, will suffice. He begins with the Roman text:

> At Hippo Regius in Africa, Saints Theogenes the bishop and thirty-six others, who, in the persecution of Valerian, despising temporal death, attained the crown of eternal life.

Baronius’s note follows.

**THEOGENES THE BISHOP:** “Concerning him and his companions, Bede—though spurious—Usuard, and the others on this day. This is recognized as that Theogenes, bishop of Hippo, who took part with Saint Cyprian in the Council of Carthage, as appears from his Acts, which are preserved in Cyprian and Augustine, book VI, *On Baptism against the Donatists*. There was at Hippo a basilica named for Saint Theogenes, which Saint Augustine mentions in Sermon 101, *On Various Matters*, where he says: ‘When you heard at the memorial of Saint Theogenes, “I offer you, Peter; I offer you, Paul,” did you ever hear …’”

Rosweyd then continues:

> After Baronius had discussed the martyrdom of Lucius, Montanus, Flavianus, Julianus, and Victoricus, ministers who suffered at Carthage on 24 February after Cyprian, who had suffered the preceding year, he adds—in volume II of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 262:
>
> “Theogenes, bishop of Hippo, also suffered at the same time. He is found numbered among the bishops who took part in the Council of Carthage held concerning the question of baptism. Since the Catholic Church therefore lists him, together with the other bishops of that council who died by martyrdom, among the martyrs, and celebrates their feasts, it is sufficiently clear that they, like Cyprian, departed in peace and in communion with that same Catholic Church.”

And the rest, which I omit in order to come to the point. He continues:

> Who, reading these things in Baronius, both in the Annals and in the Roman Martyrology, would not regard them as certain and fully attested? He constructs his Annals from the authority of the Catholic Church—that is, from the Roman Martyrology. Yet the Roman Martyrology did not possess these statements until recently, but only from Baronius’s time; so that it seems that the authority to be cited belongs not to the Church, but rather to Baronius. Three new elements, therefore, appear to have been inserted here by Baronius into the text of the Roman Martyrology, if it is compared with the ancient manuscripts or even printed editions.
>
> “1. That he says Theogenes suffered at Hippo Regius in Africa—or, if he does not mean that he suffered there but that he was venerated there. Who will assert that this Theogenes, whom the Roman Martyrology mentions, is the African who is venerated at Hippo Regius, especially since all the ancient Martyrologies simply place Theogenes without adding any indication of place?
>
> “Moreover, Peter, in the *Catalogue*, book III, chapter 25, after treating in the preceding chapter of Polycarp and his twelve disciples, who came from Laodicea and suffered after him, adds in the following chapter:
>
> “‘Theogenes the martyr and thirty-six other Christians suffered martyrdom in that same city of Laodicea, when the persecution already mentioned—of Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, under which Polycarp had suffered martyrdom—was pressing upon them. Despising temporal death, they attained the crown of eternal life on 26 January, as Jerome says.’
>
> “Maurolycus and Galesinius took their account from this passage of Peter, and they too place Theogenes at Laodicea. Other ancient Martyrologies, however—such as the Old Roman Martyrology, which I formerly prefixed to Ado, and also the spurious Bede, Usuard, and Ado—give no place of martyrdom.
>
> “2. That he calls this Theogenes a bishop, without the authority of any ancient book. Indeed, Augustine, who mentions Saint Theogenes, does not say that he was a bishop. The fact that a certain Theogenes, bishop of Hippo Regius, is found to have taken part in the Third Council of Carthage can have no bearing on the matter, since that council was convened contrary to the judgment of the Roman Church, nor is there any other evidence that this Theogenes, bishop of Hippo Regius, suffered martyrdom.
>
> “3. That he says he suffered ‘in the persecution of Valerian.’ This too occurs in no Martyrology, manuscript or printed—as far as I have seen, although I have seen very many. Indeed, Belinus’s Roman Martyrology for 26 January considers him to have suffered under Licinius, writing:
>
> “‘On the same day, Saints Theogenes and thirty-six others, who, despising temporal death under the emperor Licinius, attained the crown of eternal life.’
>
> “It seems, however, that Belinus confused Theogenes, mentioned in the Roman Martyrology on 3 January, with this one. The earlier Theogenes did indeed suffer under Licinius.”

Thus far Rosweyd’s judicious note.

Whether those words, “under the emperor Licinius,” were inserted into the second edition by Belinus himself or only by the Parisian editor-printer, I would not dare rashly to pronounce. This much certainly remains true: the clause was unknown to all the ancient Martyrologists, including Usuard, as we proved above.

As for Theogenes of the Hellespont, you will find in the Appendices for 3 January that he suffered under King Licinius.

[Note: [Col. 0697D]]

Concerning the Pratensis, Tornacensis, Aquicinctine, Antwerp–Major, and Lübeck–Major manuscripts, Muneratus, and the second edition of Belinus, enough has been said above in the Variants.

**ACTS OF THE MARTYRS.** This codex is nearly identical with the Pratensis, also omitting the third notice.

**ANTWERP–MAJOR.** It gives a more extended eulogy of Polycarp, composed almost entirely from fragments of Ado; the source contains a purer text. For Theogenes it writes *Theologenes*; otherwise that notice is sufficiently pure. It then adds:

> At Bethlehem, the falling-asleep of Saint Paula. Saint Jerome, writing of her life, admirable for its virtues, testifies that she was crowned by a long martyrdom.

See the following day.

> In the Parisian territory, at the monastery of Chelles, the deposition of Lady Queen Bathildis.

**PULSANEN.** Its text concerning Polycarp is pure; it says nothing about Theogenes, but instead treats Paula in the words already reported.

[Col. 0698D] **ROSWEYD.** After the words “he was the chief man,” it varies the wording as follows:

> Later, for the love of Christ, he endured many things from the enemies of the Catholic faith and, under Aurelius the proconsul, was handed over to the fire with twelve others. On the same day, the feast of the holy martyrs Theogenes and thirty-six others. Likewise, at Bourges, blessed Sulpitius the bishop and confessor.

**ANTWERP–MAX., UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERG, DANISH, AND THE UTRECHT–BELGIAN EDITION.** They expand Polycarp’s eulogy somewhat, in fewer words, as follows:

> When he had been condemned to the fire and stood in the midst of the flames, the fire bent itself like a vaulted chamber and stood above the martyr’s body. The body, placed in the midst, was not like burning flesh, but as though gold or silver were glowing in a furnace. When the agents of wickedness saw that the fire could not consume him, they pierced with a sword the body from which the fire had recoiled.

[Col. 0699A] **LOUVAIN.** Similar to the foregoing in its treatment of Polycarp, but it lacks the shorter eulogy of Theogenes.

**CENTULE.**

> At Smyrna, Saint Polycarp the bishop and martyr, who was a disciple of blessed John the Apostle and was ordained bishop by him. He was the chief man of all Asia; twelve others suffered with him. On the same day, Saint Theogenes the martyr with thirty-six others. At Bethlehem, the falling-asleep of Saint Paula, a most noble matron, whose life Saint Jerome described for imitation, etc. In the territory of Paris, at the monastery of Chelles, Saint Baldetildis the queen.

**BRUSSELS**, in addition to the fuller material concerning Polycarp given above, adds from Jerome’s *On Illustrious Men*:

> When the heretic Marcion met him, he said, “Recognize us.” He replied, “I recognize you as the firstborn of Satan.” But when Polycarp had courageously resisted him and the other heretics, under Marcus Antoninus, etc.

It mutilated the eulogy of Theogenes, but added on its own authority:

> Saint Augustine mentions him in his homilies on Pentecost.

[Col. 0699B] Molanus inserted these words into the text in italics. Concerning Paula it adds only:

> The mother of Eustochium, the virgin of Christ,

which are Ado’s words for the following day.

**HAGENAU.** It has this distinctive statement concerning Polycarp:

> He sent disciples for many years to the regions of Gaul, Spain, and Italy to preach the word of God.

It then adds:

> At the city of Bourges, the deposition of Saint Supplicius—Sulpitius, concerning whom see above under 17 January—the bishop and confessor. From childhood he had been instructed in the sacred writings and was conspicuous for the light of his holy conduct, so that, while still a layman, he shone with virtues. After cutting his hair, he became the father of many monks; then, advanced to the episcopal chair, he was glorious throughout all the days of his life for miracles and teachings, and finally rested in peace.

**VATICAN, no. 5949, AND JURENSIS OF SAINT RAGNOBERTUS.** On this day they report Sulpitius of Bourges with the eulogy which we previously quoted from Usuard under 17 January and among the Appendices under 15 January:

> At the city of Bourges, Saint Sulpitius the bishop and confessor, whose life and precious death are commended by glorious miracles.

The Jurensis continues:

> Blessed Maurus, abbot of the monastery of Bodacum, whose life, full of virtues, the illustrious patrician Dynamius wrote.

It means Marius of Bobacum, more correctly Bodonensis, concerning whom see the following day.

The aforesaid codex had also added to the eulogy of Saint Polycarp:

> His relics are kept at Lyon in a crypt.

**STROZZI AND MEDICI**, in first place:

> At Florence, a city of Tuscia [the other has “in the city of Florence,”] the translation of Saint Zenobius, bishop and confessor of that same city. This translation took place in the year of the Lord 428 [or 429], through blessed Andrew, his successor as bishop. After many miracles, a dry elm, when it was touched by his bier beside the church of the Baptist, suddenly put forth leaves and flowers; a marble column still stands there.

The **Lübeck–Cologne edition**, after the material concerning Polycarp which we have reported from the manuscripts of middling quality and others, adds:

> From his blood, which flowed abundantly, the entire fire was extinguished. His soul was also seen by those standing around to be carried into heaven in the form of a dove. Twelve others suffered with him, etc.

It then adds:

> At Trier, Saint Marius the bishop and confessor, who rests in the church of Saint Paul.

After Theogenes it continues:

> In the Parisian territory, at the monastery of Chelles, the deposition of Saint Paula the virgin.

Greven has the same, but Bollandus found nothing concerning her.

> On the same day at Le Mans, blessed Silvinus the bishop and confessor. At the city of Bourges, Saint Julianus the bishop and confessor.

Greven has these same notices; Bollandus placed both among the *Praetermissi*.

**GREVÉN** adds:

> At Rome, Fabianus, otherwise Sabianus the martyr, according to Bede.

I do not know which Bede he means; he would have indicated Jerome more correctly. See Bollandus’s conjecture.

> At Pozzuoli, Artemas. Tryphon the martyr. At Trier, Marius the bishop and confessor. The translation of blessed Zenobius, bishop of Florence and confessor. Likewise, the blessed memory of Haseka the virgin, a recluse, who, serving the Lord in great simplicity and wisdom beside the church of Schermbeke, once restored butter spoiled by age to perfect freshness through prayer.

**MOLANUS’S** first edition lacks this addition, but in its notice of Polycarp it inserted the following words in italics:

> In the midst of the pyre, after being pierced with a sword, he poured out so much blood that he extinguished the fire.

Later editions add Marus of Trier. Then:

> On the twenty-sixth day, Saint Xenophon the father and his companions.

## [Col. 0693] Usuard’s Text

At Smyrna, the feast of Saint Polycarp, who was a disciple of blessed John the Apostle and was ordained bishop by him; he was the chief man of all Asia. Later, under Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius, while the entire people of that same city were shouting against him in the amphitheater, he was handed over to the fire. Twelve others, coming from Philadelphia, also suffered martyrdom with him in the aforesaid city.

On the same day, Saints Theogenes and thirty-six other martyrs, who, despising temporal death, attained the crown of eternal life.

[**Bouillart:** …]

[Note: [Col. 0695A]]

These words, “under the emperor Licinius,” had been regarded as suspect by Sollerius. But after Castellanus informed him that in the Pratensis codex the memory of Queen Bathildis had been erased or half-erased and that the words “under the emperor Licinius” had been written in their place, he set aside all hesitation, deleted that addition—as he calls it—and restored the memory of Queen Bathildis. Yet certainly no one will approve this.

For, besides the fact that exactly the same hand repaired the erasure, it cannot be held against Usuard that he said Theogenes died a martyr under the emperor Licinius. I wish it were true that his death occurred under Valerian, as is commonly believed. But that emperor did not bear only one name [Col. 0696A]. I have seen in Mezabarba, Vaillant, and other collectors of coins that he too was called Licinius. It is also certain that that emperor, who bore two names, persecuted Christians.

To establish this I shall not cite the many Martyrologies, nor shall I use Augustine’s authority, since I am pursuing brevity. What, then, did Usuard get wrong when he assigned the death of Theogenes to the time of Licinius?

The memory of Saint Bathildis was indeed erased, but it was transferred by the same author to another day for just reasons, as will be noted below.

**BOUILLART.** [Bouillart reads: “Under the emperor Licinius, they attained the crown of eternal life,” omitting what follows.]

In the Parisian territory, Bathildis the queen.

**Six days before the Kalends. Day 27.**

[Note: [Col. 0699]]

Thus read the Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp, Lübeck–Major, Molanus, and *Acts of the Martyrs* manuscripts. Add the Antwerp–Major, Louvain, Leyden–Belgian, and Utrecht–Belgian editions.

[Note: [Col. 0699D]]

There is little here worthy of observation. The forms *Johannis*, *Crisostomi*, *Chrisostimi*, *Chrisostomi*, *Bethlehem*, *martiris*, *Jeronimus*, *Jhieronimus*, *Affrica*, and *Aphrica* are simply spelling variations, some of which are not wholly rejected even today; in the text we have followed the manuscripts as usual.

The Antwerp–Major manuscript adds *and confessor* after *bishop of Constantinople*. The Antwerp manuscript slightly transposes the words, reading *plurimum profuit Christiana*, etc., instead of *plurimum Christianae profuit*.

It errs more seriously when, together with the Antwerp–Major, Louvain, and others, it makes *Mauri* out of *Marii*. *Dynamius* is likewise corrupted by many; but these matters will be discussed again in the Observations.

In Molanus one particle is superfluous: “in Bethlehem of Judea, in the falling-asleep.” This is a printer’s error.

Julianus, the apostle of the people of Le Mans, ought to belong here, since the Tornacensis, Antwerp–Major, Rosweyd, Muneratus, Greven, and others place him on this day, while our Pratensis copy places him on the following day. We have excluded him from Usuard’s text on both days because he is not found in our other manuscripts.

Castellanus, the inspector of the Pratensis codex, also informed us that Julianus was added there in more recent ink. Hence, in his notes on this day, he wonders why the ancient Martyrologists preserve no memory of so great a man.

Whatever Usuard drew from older sources comes from the *Little Roman Martyrology* and Ado—unless perhaps African Avitus [Col. 0700D] (whom Wandalbertus likewise renders in this form) has some relationship with the Vitus of the *Hieronymian Martyrologies*, concerning whom below, in his proper place. Thus neither the *Hieronymian Martyrologies*, nor Bede or his followers, nor Wandalbertus mention Chrysostom at all. The author of the *Little Roman Martyrology* says briefly: “At Constantinople, John Chrysostom.” Ado says nothing more, except that he paraphrastically explains the preceding words: “The feast of Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, who is called Chrysostom.” Our text is Usuard’s; Notker composed another, only slightly fuller. Bollandus discusses the various festivals of this most illustrious doctor, especially among the Greeks, in his list of those passed over, explaining why the saint’s Life had to be assigned to another day. We shall give it, from Palladius and other ancient sources, on its proper day of death, 14 September; then it may be illustrated by a fuller commentary based on the learned works published after Bollandus’s death, among which Hermantius’s celebrated work and Tillemont, volume XI, from the beginning through page 405 in 154 entire articles, seem especially important. This is truly remarkable in the case of so illustrious a saint: among our ancient martyrologists, indeed among so many Usuardine codices, scarcely any is found that mentions him even in a word on 14 September, although that was his actual feast day.

Marius’s entire announcement is taken from Ado, with some abridgment by Notker. Bollandus most carefully distinguished the many matters concerning this saint that had previously been confused and obscure; Castellanus added no less interesting observations in his notes from page 424 onward, correcting various errors made by those who went astray in writing both the saint’s name, and the place and author of his Life. Our text correctly reads *Marii* with Ado, where others have *Mauri*, *Macerii*, and so forth; hence ignorant writers fabricated new saints. Yet Usuard errs in changing the name of the place, thereby giving rise to considerable confusion. He had probably read in Ado *Bodanensis*, or, as in the common text, *Badonensis*. Following neither, he wrote on his own authority *Bobacensis* [Notker: *Bodacensis*], which others variously altered and thereby transferred our saint to various and wholly distant places. One must read *Bodonensis* or *Bodanensis*, “of the valley of Bodon,” as the cited authors rightly prove; in their works one will find the final traces of that monastery.

Again, he correctly wrote *Dynamius*, as the author of the Life is truly called. Belinus has incorrectly *Damianus*; others have *Dinandus*, *Didamius*, *Dinavius*, and so forth. The curious reader will not regret consulting the writers who have investigated these matters. Ado speaks more fully of Paula than of Chrysostom, and Notker follows him. Our text, omitting the intervening material, took the first and last words, namely those that we introduced among the Additions on the preceding day. Bollandus, Florentius, and Castellanus discuss Avitus at greater length; I have nothing to add to their conjectures. The main question here is whether Avitus arose from the Vitus of the *Hieronymian Martyrologies*. Castellanus suspects that Wandalbertus lengthened the name for metrical reasons, and that Usuard took it from him. I have not yet been able to ascertain with certainty whether Usuard ever knew that metrical Martyrology. Whatever conclusion one reaches, it is certain that this Avitus, unknown to the other martyrologists, was first recorded by Usuard, from whom he passed into the others and into the Roman Martyrology. The aforementioned Wandalbertus added Sulpitius, Bathildis, and Aldegund to the Avitus just mentioned; we shall treat them in their proper places. Here are his two verses:

> In the sixth place Punic soil venerates its own Avitus.  
> Sulpitius, Bathildis, and Aldegund also flourish.

### Notes

**[Col. 0701B]**

The Tournai manuscript, beneath the pure text, adds: “At Le Mans, the feast of Saint Julian, bishop and confessor.”

**ANTWERP MAJOR**, not quite correctly: “At Constantinople, the feast of Saint John, bishop, who is called Chrysostom.” From Ado. Then: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Marius, abbot of the monastery of Bobacum, whose life, full of virtues, the patrician Dinavius records.” Paula was treated on the preceding day. At the end: “At Le Mans, the deposition of Saint Julian, bishop and confessor.” Nothing about Avitus.

**ROSWEYD:** Also takes Chrysostom from Ado. In Marius it is fairly pure. Then: “Likewise in Gaul, at Le Mans, Julian, bishop and confessor. Likewise at Bethlehem, the repose of Saint Paula, widow.” Avitus is also absent.

**PULSANO:** Is very mutilated. It treated Paula on the preceding day; today it lacks Chrysostom and begins: “In the monastery of Bobacum, Saint Marius, abbot, whose life, etc.” Its notice of Avitus is pure.

**MUNERATUS:** Instead of *Marii*, writes *Mauri*; instead of *Dynamius*, *Dinavius*. After *martyrio* in the section on Paula, it adds: “Whose feast is celebrated at Paris on the fourth day before the Kalends of February.” At the end: “At the city of Le Mans, the feast of Saint Julian, bishop and confessor.”

**GREVEN:** Adds to the text: “At the city of Le Mans, Saint Julian, bishop and confessor.”

**UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC:** Would be pure Usuardine texts if they did not place before the text: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Vitalian, pope, who, after blessed Peter, was the seventy-eighth and sat for nine years and six months. He composed the chant of the Romans and harmonized it with a sweet-sounding organ.” I do not know who first added this; see what Bollandus carefully collected about him.

**CENTULE:** “At Constantinople, Saint John, bishop, who is called Chrysostom. On the same day, Saint Marius, abbot, whose life shone forth full of virtues.” It also treated Paula on the preceding day and entirely omitted Avitus.

**BRUSSELS:** Is not entirely pure in its notice of Chrysostom; at the end it adds: “He died after being sent into exile for the third time. On the same day, Saint Vitalian, pope, who composed the chant of the Romans and [Col. 0702C] made it harmonious with the sweetest [organ], etc.” It writes *Mauri* and *Badonensis*.

**HAGUENAU:** Is usually distinctive in various ways. Here, concerning Chrysostom, it adds to the pure text: “When he once wished to write about God, the devil poured ink upon him; he immediately dipped the pen into his own mouth and wrote golden letters with it, and therefore he was called ‘Golden Mouth.’ This Chrysostom was sent into exile three times for the truth of his teaching and the strictness of his discipline, and finally died there.” It also adds to the text concerning Paula: “And especially praises her for contemplation, abstinence, devotion of mind, and the governance of her sisters.” Nothing about Marius; concerning Vitalian, almost as above, except that some names are distorted.

**VICTORINUS:** “At Le Mans, blessed Julian, bishop and confessor, who was sent by blessed Pope Clement to Le Mans and ordained, etc.,” followed by a long encomium from the Life.

**MATRICULA OF THE CARTHUSIANS, UTRECHT:** “Of John Chrysostom, [Col. 0702D] bishop and confessor. Of Paula, widow, whose life blessed Jerome describes. Of Marius, abbot.” The final announcement is absent.

In the **Vatican manuscript no. 5949**, the commemoration of Avitus is also absent.

**ALTEMPS:** “Likewise Saint Saturninus and three others. In Lesser Britain, Saint Gildas, abbot.” Gildas is commemorated on the 29th; I cannot sufficiently distinguish the others, unless they are to be commemorated on 31 January.

**STROZZI and MEDICI:** “On the same day at Rome, Saint Vitalian, pope and confessor.”

The **Lübeck–Cologne edition** begins with Vitalian, to whom, in addition to nine years and six months, it assigns twenty-one days. Concerning Chrysostom, after “in religion,” it adds “as his Acts clearly testify.” Instead of *Marii*, it writes *Mari*; instead of *Dynamius*, *Dinandus*. After “Saint Paula,” it adds “widow, mother of Saint Eustochium, virgin of Christ.” It continues: “In Africa, Saint Amicus, martyr,” intending Avilius, whom Belinus in the first edition called [Col. 0703A] *Adjuti*. “On the same day, Saint Julian, martyr.” This is undoubtedly the Julian whom Baronius claims for Sora, while others assign him to Atina, situated not far from Sora. Castellanus explains the basis of this in his notes, and we shall examine it in the Supplement. Finally: “At Le Mans, Saint Julian, bishop and confessor.”

**BELINUS**, in both editions, reads: “The deposition of Saint Julian, the first bishop of that city, glorious for the holiness of his life and his miracles.” In the first he writes *Cinomannis*, in the second *Cenomannis*.

**GREVEN:** “On the same day, Emiliani, Publius, Artemius, Armata, Julian, Celian, Saturus. Vitalian, pope, seventy-eighth after Peter. Paul, pope and confessor. He visited the cells of the sick by night with a few companions, supplying what was necessary and rescuing prisoners; endowed also with other holy works, he rested in peace.” He is commemorated on 28 June. “At Orléans, blessed Adjutor, abbot of Chartres and confessor. When the people gathered for his annual feast, a certain man, contemptuously cultivating his vineyard, was struck by a terrible affliction and thereby gave testimony to the saint’s holiness.” This is referred to 19 December. “Likewise John, priest of Antioch, who, according to Jerome’s book *On Illustrious Men*, shone remarkably under the elder Theodosius in holiness and wisdom. The prophet Jonah.” See the section on those passed over.

**MOLANUS**, in the first edition, writes about Julian of Le Mans as Belinus does. Then: “The deposition of our holy father Sulpitius, bishop and confessor.” The second edition says “of the monastery of Celle,” omitting “our.” Inserted there is: “At Chalon, Saint Lupus, bishop of that city.” Then: “On the twenty-seventh day, the translation of the relics of our holy father John Chrysostom.” Concerning Vitalian, almost as above.

### 28 January

**[Col. 0699]**

The feast of blessed John, bishop of Constantinople, surnamed Chrysostom, who by word and example greatly benefited the Christian religion. Likewise Saint Marius, abbot of the monastery of Bobacum, whose life, full of virtues, the illustrious man and patrician Dynamius records. At Bethlehem in Judea, the repose of Saint Paula. In writing her Life, admirable for its virtues, Saint Jerome testifies that she was crowned by a prolonged martyrdom. In Africa, Saint Avitus, martyr.

**Five days before the Kalends. Day 28.**

### Notes

**[Col. 0703A]**

From the Pratensis, Herinian, Tournai, Pulsano, the second edition of Belinus, Greven, and Molan.

**[Col. 0703B]**

Belinus and Greven incorrectly have *Apolonia*. The text correctly has *Thyrsi* after Ado, whereas Tournai, Greven, Molan, and others have *Tirsi*; Herinian has *Thirsi*, others *Tyrsi*. I retained Usuard’s reading *Calinici*, although *Callinici* would be the better spelling. Herinian and Greven have *Calenici*. Molan has *Galenici*, perhaps from Ado. *Leuticii* and *Calenitii* in Pulsano, and *Galanici* in Belinus, are obvious errors. For the various other forms of these names, see Bollandus here and Castellanus in his notes from page 435 onward. Herinian reads *cruciati* instead of *excruciati*. I printed *abscisione*, as it is written by the Pratensis, Herinian, Tournai, Belinus, and Ado himself; Pulsano, Greven, and Molan instead have *abcisione*. Tournai, Belinus, and Greven have *celesti* for *coelesti*; we have discussed this and other diphthongs elsewhere. *Cirilli* instead of *Cyrilli*, and *praedicator* instead of *propugnator* in Belinus, are not especially surprising. But *praeclarus* for *praeclarissimus* should be called another error in Pulsano. Ado wrote *Reomanensis*, and Molan likewise. Our text has *Reomensis*; all are wrong. Tournai, Pulsano, and Belinus have, worse still, *Remensis*. It should be written and pronounced *Reomaensis*, from the French *Reomay*, today Montier-Saint-Jean in Burgundy. This must also be corrected in Baronius’s Martyrology, or the present Roman Martyrology, where it has *Rhemensis*.

**[Col. 0703C]**

This second commemoration of Agnes is found in all the ancient martyrologies. Most of the *Hieronymian* copies read: “At Rome, the birth of Saint Agnes, virgin.” Florentius discusses this birth quite carefully; whether his view is acceptable you will understand if you compare it with what Bollandus in the Acts and Castellanus in his notes on page 363 examine under the 21st of this month. Bede’s wording agrees with the Calendar of Fronto: “The birthday of Saint Agnes, virgin, from her birth.” Rabanus, acting as an interpreter of the final phrase, inserts after “virgin” *genuinum*, that is, “true,” and so forth; Notker has almost the same. Whether these words make an already obscure matter even more obscure, let others judge. I would believe that Rabanus took *genuinum* from some *Hieronymian* copy; in the Echternach manuscript Florentius found *ingenuinum*, whose meaning he admits he does not know.

To make the sense clear in a word: I would prefer *genuinum* to be understood of the true birthday, that is, the day of martyrdom, rather than that Agnes’s birth according to the flesh is said to be celebrated with solemn worship. Nevertheless, the entire doubling of the feast probably arose from the fact that on 31 January the faithful gathered at the virgin’s tomb on the Nomentan Way, while on the eighth day the very place of her martyrdom in the Forum Agonalis was honored with a new celebration.

We possess an exceedingly ancient Calendar of the church of Paderborn, copied from parchment by Father John Grothusius and annotated by him. Its text reads: “The octave of Saint Agnes.” Grothusius notes there that the ancient title “octave” is correctly retained. “For,” he says, “the meaning of the old Roman Calendar, from which this title was taken, is not that it is the eighth day of the celebration, but the eighth day of the passion.” This is the opinion of that most learned man. The present manner of announcing the feast, however, was taken from the *Little Roman Martyrology*. It simply reads: “Of Saint Agnes, the second,” and Ado, our text, and the others have nearly the same. Wandalbertus sings:

> On the fifth day let Rome’s noble offspring proclaim Agnes.

**[Col. 0705A]**

Bollandus and Castellanus, whom we must often commend, show at length and learnedly that the Apollonian martyrs, whose names we presented shortly before in various forms, were honored in various places and on various days. In the *Hieronymian Martyrologies* under 18 January one finds: “And the passion of Saint Thyrsus with his companions Leucius and Gallinicus,” with no mention of the stadium. Hence Florentius doubts whether these are the same martyrs who are listed on the 20th: “At Nivedunum, Thyrsus, Quiriacus [in Echternach, Leucius], and Gallinicus.” There is likewise doubt whether the same names, placed separately on other days, refer to these same martyrs—something one would more readily admit if one observes in their Acts that they suffered on different days and in different places. Florus assigns only Thyrsus to Miletus, with an encomium, on 25 January.

It is certain, however, that our martyrologists consistently record them on this day. The *Little Roman Martyrology* mentions only Leucius and Thyrsus. Ado, adhering to the order of the Acts, joined the three on this day, with an encomium that Notker copied in full; our text softened it, rejecting what seemed less credible. Baronius, however, by reversing the order of the names, assigns to Leucius what, according to the ancient sources, must most certainly be attributed to Thyrsus, as is immediately clear.

As far as I know, Ado was the first among the Latin martyrologists to place Cyril on this day; Usuard, Notker, and the later writers generally copied his words. The Greeks celebrate him on 9 June, on which day Baronius thinks he died. In my chronological treatise on the patriarchs of Alexandria, it seemed more probable to me that he ceased to live on the 27th of that month, unless the Coptic calculation is to be entirely rejected—which, so far as I am concerned, may certainly be done. Bollandus collected a good deal concerning Cyril’s deeds, but Tillemont carefully traversed the whole sequence of his life, which no one had previously followed in full, in volume XIV, pages 267–676.

The commemoration of John—“not Nicanus,” as Notker incorrectly read—is also copied entirely from Ado. Bollandus illustrated his Life; this may be compared with what Mabillon supplied in the appendix to the first century of the Benedictines, beginning on page 632. We have already said enough about Reomaus; a clearer expression of the place may be seen among the Additions in the Antwerp Major codex.

### Notes

**[Col. 0705B]**

The Pratensis and the *Acts of the Martyrs* add to the text: “At Le Mans, Saint Julian, the first bishop of that city.” But since, as we showed on the preceding day, this was added to the Pratensis codex, there is no objection to its having a place today among the purer Usuardine witnesses. The same addition occurs in Antwerp Major and Lübeck, and almost in the same form in the first, or Venetian, edition of Belinus.

**ANTWERP MAJOR**, fairly pure in its first notice, says nothing of the Apollonians. It is also pure in Cyril. Finally, concerning John of Reomay, it speaks more distinctly as follows: “In the territory of the city of Langres, at the castle of Tornodorus, in the monastery of Robonium, the feast of Saint John, priest and abbot, who was the first inhabitant of that place and the father of various monks, and who, worn out by long old age and illustrious in virtues, rested. He was buried not far from the monastery.”

**ROSWEYD** begins: “The octave of Saint Agnes. And in the city of Apollonia, Leucius, Thyrsus, and Callinicus, martyrs, who in the time of the emperor Decius, tortured by various kinds of torments under the governors Cambritius, [Col. 0705C] Silvanus, and Baudo, completed their martyrdom. On the same day at Alexandria, blessed Cyril, bishop and confessor.” The final announcement is absent.

**ANTWERP MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC** give Julian’s announcement second, as above. Moreover, for some reason I do not know, they transfer Alexandria to Greece. What they say about Charlemagne will be given immediately, when you find collected what is read about him in the various codices.

**LEYDEN BELGIC and the BELGIC UTRECHT EDITION** begin: “The octave of Saint Agnes, virgin.” Otherwise they resemble the others, as usual.

**MUNERATUS**, at the end: “Likewise Saint Charles, emperor.” **ANTWERP MAXIMUM and LOUVAIN:** “At Aachen, the deposition of Saint Charles, king of the Franks and emperor of the Romans.” **MATRICULA OF THE CARTHUSIANS, UTRECHT:** “Of Charlemagne, king and emperor of the Romans, [Col. 0705D] the most steadfast champion of the Christian faith.”

**UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC**, somewhat more fully, add to the words previously cited: “When he had pacified and enlarged his kingdom and empire, had devoutly ordered the condition of the holy Church, and had zealously extended the faith, in the year of the Lord 814, in the seventy-first year of his age, the forty-seventh of his reign, and the fourteenth of his empire, he passed to the Lord. Because of the greatness of his deeds he was surnamed ‘the Great.’”

The **Lübeck–Cologne edition** differs from these by scarcely three words, agreeing with Greven in shortening his age by one year and omitting the years of his reign. Molan sets out the matter most fully in these words:

“On the same day, at the basilica of Aachen, the feast of Saint Charles the confessor, the first of the Frankish race, by divine ordination Augustus of the Romans: from the beginning of his life, despising the pomp of the world, he converted Gascony, Germany, and Gaul by the sword of imperial power, by the word of holy preaching, and by the example of a saving life. He also converted Frisia, Alemannia, and Saxony to the Lord by a threefold trophy. At his own expense he also built, for the praise and honor of the holy and undivided Trinity, twenty-seven churches, among which the church of Aachen holds the distinction of excellence, glorious through its present intercessions. Having most zealously extended the faith, devoutly ordered the condition of the Church, and enlarged and pacified his kingdom, he rested in peace in the year of the Lord 814, in the seventieth year of his age and the fourteenth of his empire. Because of the greatness of his faith and works he was surnamed ‘the Great.’”

In smaller type it adds: “And he was numbered among the saints by Pope Paschal in the year 1196.”

**BRUSSELS** begins as follows: “At Rome, Saint Agnes’s second feast from her birth. In the city of Apulia, Saints Leontius, Thyrsus, and Gallienus, etc.” It continues with Julian of Le Mans. Then: “At Alexandria in Greece, the deposition of blessed Cyril, etc.” Then John of Reomay. “Hence at Maubeuge, blessed Aldetrudis, virgin, daughter of Saints Vincent and Waldetrudis, and niece of blessed Gudula, who succeeded Saint Aldegund, her maternal aunt, in the abbey of Maubeuge.” See 25 February. What was said about Saint Charles is sufficient. “Likewise the translation of blessed Thomas Aquinas, holy doctor of the Order of Preachers.”

**HAGUENAU** has this distinctive statement about Charlemagne: “He died in peace, his sins having been forgiven through the intercession of Saint Giles, abbot.”

**CENTULE** makes Cyril a martyr. It is silent about the Apollonian martyrs. Concerning John it writes: “In the territory of Langres, in the monastery of Reomay, Saint John, abbot, a magnificent man, who extinguished a basilisk by prayer.”

The **Lübeck–Cologne edition** begins the day in this way: “At Cologne Agrippina, the translation of Saint Ursula, queen, and her eleven thousand companions, virgins and martyrs, which was carried out by Saint Cunibert, archbishop of the city of Cologne. At Rome, the octave of Saint Agnes, virgin and martyr.” In its treatment of the Apollonian martyrs, Cyril, John, and Charles, it is broadly like the codices cited. At the end: “At Toulouse, the translation of Saint Thomas Aquinas.”

**GREVEN:** “In Africa, according to Bede (not genuine), Saints Censorianus, Victor, Festus, and Marina.” Concerning Charles’s encomium, in which it differs from the others, we have made observations above. It continues: “Likewise Saints Paul, Victor, Hippolytus, Honoratus, and Petrosia. Severus, bishop of Bourges and confessor, disciple of Saint Martin. In Britain, Gildas, abbot. Vitalis, abbot. [Constantius, if I am not mistaken,] bishop and martyr of Perugia.” Concerning Charles’s encomium, in which it differs from the others, we have made observations above. It continues: “The translation of blessed Thomas Aquinas from the monastery of Fossanova to Toulouse. At Cologne Agrippina, the translation of Saint Ursula, virgin, and her companions, carried out by [Saint Cunibert], etc. Margaret, virgin of blessed memory, of Hungary.”

**MOLAN**, speaking of Censorianus and his companions, agrees with Greven. Then: “Julian the hermit, surnamed Sabbas, whose deeds, dedicated to God—that is, the history of the *Philotheus*—Theodoret says he recorded in Book II, chapter 24, of his *Ecclesiastical History*.” In the later editions, after the commemoration of Charles, he writes in smaller type: “At Porphyrion, according to Symeon, Saint James the hermit. And at Nicomedia, the holy martyrs, including Domnes and twenty thousand who suffered under Maximian. On the same day, the death of the most illustrious Margaret, virgin, daughter of the king of Hungary, of the Order of Preachers.”

### 29 January

**[Col. 0703]**

At Rome, the feast of Saint Agnes, the second. And in the city of Apollonia, Saints Leucius, Thyrsus, and Callinicus, martyrs, who in the time of Decius, tortured by various kinds of torments, completed their martyrdom: the first and the last by beheading, while the one in the middle, summoned by a heavenly voice, gave up his spirit. At Alexandria, blessed Cyril, bishop, who proved a most distinguished champion of the Catholic faith. In the monastery of Reomay, the deposition of John, priest, a man of God.

**[Added by Bouillart]**

**[Col. 0703B]**

Sollerius excluded Julian from the number of saints of this day, on the ground that, as Castellanus notes, that blessed bishop was added in the Pratensis codex in fresher ink. Learned gentlemen, I appeal to your good faith! When it is certain that the hand is the same, has the character of the ink ever been, or ought it to be, taken into account? For I should like to know by what mark the age of ink can be discerned. Is it because it is blacker than in the remaining lines? If that is the case, all ancient monuments of writing are lost to us; for I think there are few in which the ink is everywhere of precisely the same blackness. Or does it not very often happen to us that, when the ink is changed, the colour of the writing changes? Is it therefore inserted by another hand because it has a different colour?

Moreover, by the same argument John’s encomium ought to have been cut away. For the words *presbyteri viri Dei* [“priest, man of God”] are written over the same erasure and in the same ink as *Cinomannis*, etc. Castellanus, I suppose, did not point this out; or Sollerius, having been warned of it, prudently suppresses it in silence. In any case, Usuard appropriately commemorates Saint Julian on this day, on which the Parisian Church, where he lived and wrote, venerated him. —BOUILLART.

“At Le Mans, Saint Julian, the first bishop of that city.”

**Four days before the Kalends. Day 29.**

### Notes

**[Col. 0707A]**

There is complete agreement here among a great many codices: the Pratensis, Herinian, Tournai, Pulsano, Antwerp, Maximum–Lübeck, Muneratus, Belinus, Greven, Molan, and the *Acts of the Martyrs*. Also the codices of middling authority: Antwerp Maximum, Utrecht, Leyden, Louvain, Albergen, Danic, and the Belgian Utrecht edition.

**[Col. 0707B]**

*Mauro* for *Mauri* in Muneratus is an error. In Albergen, the first word, “martyrs,” is redundant. There is considerable disagreement among the codices in writing the name *Laudicius*. Antwerp has the incorrect *Laucius*; Herinian, Tournai, Molan, and others, following Ado, have *Laodicius*. In the text I follow the reading of Bede, Pulsano, Muneratus, Belinus, and Greven. I would not object if one preferred another reading, or thought that, with the Pratensis, *Lauditius* should be read—indeed perhaps *Laodicius*, as Castellanus seems to have read it in that codex.

Muneratus again incorrectly has *profectus* for *praefectus*. I do not understand which manuscripts Greven and Molan followed; both omit the words “And thus have them thrust back into prison,” which all our copies, without exception, express very clearly. The only difference is that Antwerp, Maximum–Lübeck, Utrecht, and others have *trudi* instead of *retrudi*. That clause should indeed be expressed according to Bede and Ado, who copied him.

Whether the final phrase should read *ad ultimum* or *in ultimo* is uncertain; the best codices vary. Herinian and Tournai write the first form; we think Usuard wrote the second. Muneratus alone has *ultimo*. Molan, wishing to make the wording clearer, corrupted the text by adding from Ado the word *percuti*, thus reading: “and at last to be struck with leaden weights.” Pulsano omits *atque* and has “and in the end with leaden weights.”

In Muneratus, *Treveris*; in the first edition of Belinus, *Valeris*: these are to be attributed to the printer. Some write *Trecassino*, *Sabiani*, or *Saviani*, especially the less genuine codices; one has *Fabiani*, and Muneratus *Saviniani*. The text is taken from the purer witnesses. Pulsano, Antwerp, and Belinus have *Aurelio* for *Aureliano*. Moreover, Utrecht, Leyden, Louvain, Albergen, and Danic announce Valerius last, placing Sabinian before him.

Among the purer codices is again our Pratensis copy, although today it contains an addition concerning the octave of Saint Vincent. Castellanus writes to me that this was added to the supposed autograph, noting that the last five letters of the text, *us est*, have been erased, from which the addition begins.

**[Col. 0707C]**

The *Hieronymian* copies say nothing about Papias and Maurus. Bede was the first to mention them, with a notable encomium that Rabanus slightly altered. The *Little Roman Martyrology* had written: “At Rome, Papias and Maurus, soldiers, under the emperor Diocletian.” Ado seems to have polished Bede’s prepared encomium somewhat. Whether Notker followed him is of little importance; our text certainly rendered what it found in one or the other more elegantly and briefly.

I said that Bede has *Laudicius*, which Ado translates as *Laodicius*, as do Rabanus and Notker. Whether *Laudicius*, preserved by Usuard, can indicate that he chose Bede rather than Ado as his model is not worth investigating. The remaining matters concerning these saints should be sought again in the Acts of Saint Marcellus, pope, under 16 January.

Valerius of Trier is placed in all the *Hieronymian* copies in such a way that he certainly does not appear to be an addition. That he was venerated as a confessor is shown by the prefixed formula *depositio*; thus one reads: “At Trier, the deposition of Valerius,” or “of blessed Valerius,” or “of most blessed Valerius, bishop.” Indeed, the Corbie copy expressly adds “confessor,” a title that, as we have said elsewhere, occurs more rarely in these codices. Rabanus took his notice from this. What is proper to Ado, however, is the addition in our text that he was a disciple of Saint Peter; Notker consulted the same source.

The sense in which this is to be understood is explained not ineptly by Castellanus on page 451. It cannot be taken in its literal or ordinary sense, as one may gather from the *Hieronymian* copies, in which those first bishops of the first two centuries of the Church commonly receive the epithet “ancient.” In this very little section it is applied to Hippolytus. But these matters will be discussed more fully either in the January Supplement or on 14 September in the Life of Saint Maternus. If one remembers that Maternus flourished in the time of Constantine the Great, one will easily determine the period of this Valerius.

Wandalbertus comprises our two announcements in these metrical lines:

> On the fourth day the martyrdom of Papias and Maurus shines forth;  
> And then Trier rejoices in Valerius as its bishop.

Of Sabinian, martyr of Troyes, whom we have hitherto thought must be distinguished from the Sabinian of Sens, only Usuard among the ancients speaks on this day—and incorrectly, as our predecessors observed before Castellanus. His feast is celebrated throughout the diocese of Troyes on 24 January, and Castellanus shows that this was already customary before Usuard’s time. Nor is this surprising, since his Acts report that Sabinian was crowned with martyrdom on that very day. Florus seems to have known this, when he joined Sabina, his sister, to him on the aforementioned day. From this one may again infer how unknown to Usuard were Florus’s supplements to Bede.

Below we shall note another error of Usuard: namely, that he postponed this Sabina of Troyes to 29 August, in order to connect her with the Roman Sabina. In our Acts she is better commemorated on this day, and on the authority of the Martyrologies is joined to her brother and to many other martyrs, whose deeds are collected and examined there. See the other days in the Acts on which their names are repeated, either together or separately.

I think this is sufficient for our purpose. Whatever judgment one may reach concerning the historical truth, it remains certain that the very reading, genuine and proper to Usuard, is faithfully and simply represented by us in the text.

### Notes

**[Col. 0709A]**

**ANTWERP MAJOR:** “At Rome, the passion of Saints Papias and Maurus, soldiers, in the time of Diocletian.” It is fairly pure in Valerius. It translates the last notice as follows: “On that same day, the feast of Saint Savina, virgin.” The clearer codex VICTORINUS and the REGIUM SUECICUM, marked no. 130, read: “At Troyes, Saint Savina, virgin.” The codices cited among the Additions joined her to Sabinian on the 24th of this month. I would not dare determine with certainty whether she belongs more appropriately to that day or to this one; nevertheless, I would prefer either of those days, and especially this one, to 29 August, to which Usuard assigns her while joining her with the Roman Sabina.

Again, whether she should be called *Savina* or *Sabina* is the same question that could be raised concerning the names *Saviniani* and *Sabiniani*. The Altempsian codex and some others called him *Sabinus*.

**ROSWEYD** is not entirely pure in its first and second notices and omits the third altogether.

**CENTULE:** “At Rome, Saints Papias and Maurus, soldiers, under Diocletian. In the territory of Troyes, Saint Sabinian, martyr. At Trier, the deposition of blessed Valerius, bishop, disciple of the apostle Peter. And the octave of Saint Vincent, martyr.” See the Variants at the end.

**BRUSSELS**, in an inverted order, announces Papias and Maurus last, with an encomium somewhat interpolated from Ado. It begins as follows: “At Trier, the deposition of blessed Valerius, bishop, disciple of the apostle Peter. When he came to Trier with the blessed Eucharius and Maternus, after Eucharius’s death he held the honor of the episcopate there for fifteen years. His preaching was so forceful that, while he was still alive, throughout Gaul and Germany Christians surpassed the pagans both in number and in religion.” It is pure in Sabinian.

**HAGUENAU** begins differently, namely: “In the territory of Troyes, the passion of Saint Sabinian, martyr. He was the only son of Sabinus, the prefect, who was miraculously converted by an angel of the Lord and received holy baptism. Leaving his father and homeland, he went forth to teach others; he endured endless punishments from the emperor Aurelian and finally completed his martyrdom by being beheaded.”

It changes nothing in Papias and Maurus. Concerning Valerius, it adds only this to the text: “Together with blessed Eucharius and Maternus he converted a large part of Gaul to faith in God; after Eucharius he became bishop there and rested in peace.”

**VATICAN, no. 5949:** “At Penvia [or perhaps Perugia?], Saint Constantius. At Benevento, the feast of Saints Felicissimus and Cassianus at Saint Sophia.”

**STROZZI and MEDICI:** “Near the city of Cebena [perhaps Cellensis], beside the castle of Corneto, Saint Flavian, martyr, who suffered under the emperor Claudius with his entire household, men and women indiscriminately, seventy-five in number. They were baptized by blessed Theodore, priest, and completed their course through martyrdom, as is read in the Acts of Saint Maximus, martyr.” These obscurely confused matters require much clarification and must be examined again together with the Acts of Saint Severa and others. See volume II of the January Acts, page 946.

The **Lübeck–Cologne edition**, after “Papias and Maurus, soldiers,” inserts from Ado: “in the time of the emperor Diocletian, who, seeing the steadfastness of Saints Saturninus and Sisinnius, deacons, were converted to the faith. Their faces, etc.” Concerning Valerius it adds: “Whom the same apostle sent to Trier, together with his disciples Eucharius and Maternus, to preach to those peoples.” At the end: “At Bourges, Saint Severus, bishop and confessor, disciple of Saint Martin, bishop.” See below in Molan’s addition.

**[Col. 0710C]**

**GREVEN:** “Likewise Saints Paul, Victor, Hippolytus, Honoratus, and Petrosia. Severus, bishop of Bourges and confessor, disciple of Saint Martin. In Britain, Gildas, abbot. Vitalis, abbot. Constantius, if I am not mistaken, bishop and martyr of Perugia.”

MOLANUS, in smaller type: “On the same day, the holy Sulpitius Severus, bishop of Bourges and confessor, disciple of Saint Martin, concerning whom Gennadius [writes], etc.” Everywhere there is confusion among the Sulpitii; for this man, the bishop of Bourges, cannot in any way belong to the time of Saint Martin, as Bollandus demonstrates on this day. Later editions: “In Britain, Gildas, abbot and confessor.” Then concerning Sulpitius. Finally: “At Perugia, Saint Constantius, bishop and confessor.” In all editions, after the elogium of Papias and Maurus, there is inserted in italics, from Bede and Ado: “It is written in the Acts of Blessed Marcellus.”]

[Col. 0707]

At Rome, on the Nomentan Way, the heavenly birthday of the holy soldiers Papias and Maurus, whose mouths Laodicius, prefect of the City, ordered to be crushed with stones at their first confession of Christ; then he had them thrown back into prison, afterward beaten with clubs, and finally flogged with lead-weighted scourges until they died. On the same day at Trier, the deposition of Blessed Valerius, bishop and disciple of the apostle Saint Peter. In the territory of Troyes, Saint Sabinianus, who, by order of the emperor Aurelian, was beheaded for the faith of Christ. [Bouillart adds:

[Note: [Col. 0707B] Castellanus wrote to Sollerius that the octave of Saint Vincent had been added to the Pratense manuscript, and likewise that the final five letters of the text had been erased so that there might be room for the addition. Everything is false. Nothing was erased. Only five letters were contracted into two in this form: t9 e. Nor was anything added. And indeed it is not surprising that Usuard should mention the octave of Saint Vincent. It was customary among the Benedictines for the brethren, assembled in chapter, to be forewarned by the reading of the Martyrology [Col. 0708B] which feasts they were to celebrate and whose saints’ memory the Church would honor on the following day. That the Martyrology was composed for this purpose is demonstrated by the Rule of Saint Benedict and the Necrology inserted in the manuscript, which were usually read after the Martyrology. Could the Pratense monk have forgotten an octave that he knew to be dedicated to the patron of his abbey? BOUILLART.]

And the octave of Saint Vincent the martyr.]

III Kalends. Day 30. [Note: [Col. 0709]

Thus purely [read it] Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Belin., Greven., Molan., and the Utrecht-Belgian edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0711A]

Only Munerat. wrote *sancti* instead of *beati*. I wrote *Ypoliti*, in a sufficiently barbarous form, but one supported by the considerable, though whatever its quality, authority of the manuscripts: Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Antuerp., Munerat., and many others, as you will also see on 13 and 23 August. Molan. correctly wrote *Hippolyti*; immediately after him Praten. has *Hippoliti*; Belin. and Greven. have *Hypoliti*. You may prefer what is best; let us be permitted to follow even the distorted spelling of our manuscripts. In the Hieronymian Martyrologies it is *Epoliti*, etc. The first edition of Belin., instead of *Novati*, wrote *Novatiani*: both contributed to the schism [Col. 0711B]. It also has, together with other manuscripts, *scismate*. Tornacen. and Munerat., instead of *correctus*, read *correptus*. With the same freedom with which the others write *Ypoliti*, I write *Hierosolimis*, etc., concerning which elsewhere. Instead of *sanctissimi*, the Tornacensis has *sancti*, and Belin. has *gloriosissimi*. Some manuscripts write *Mathaei* and *Mathei*; Molan. has *Matthaei*; the first edition of Belin. has *Nathei*; Praten. more correctly has *Mathiae*, which is the preferable reading. In most of our manuscripts [Col. 0712A], and in the best ones, *narrant* is found, which I believe is how Usuard read it. Pulsanen., Belin., Greven., and Molan. perhaps more correctly have, with Ado, *narrantur*. Again, Greven. and Molan. have *finierit*. Tornacen., instead of *ipso die*, has *eodem die*. Pulsanen., Greven., and Molan. omit *passio*. *Flavii* in Pulsanen., instead of *Flaviani*, is an error, as is also *Malboydo* in the same manuscript, *Moalbodio* in Greven., and *Aldegunde* in Belin.

Above, on 26 January, I noted the erasure in the Pratense manuscript of the commemoration of Bathildis, as Castellanus had observed. The same scholar notes on this day that Aldegundis was likewise inserted in the aforesaid manuscript, transferred to 13 November, and that Bathildis was substituted here in its place. This is the reason why the manuscript has also been excluded from the number of the pure witnesses for this day. How some have combined both women, while others have written differently, you will understand from the Supplementary Witnesses. The genuine reading of Usuard is abundantly confirmed by the manuscripts cited for the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0711B]

On the preceding day we carefully observed that the Hieronymian Martyrologies mention Hippolytus as a bishop, one of the ancient figures, although his name is distorted there; likewise on this day, when the aforesaid copies read first: “At Antioch, the passion of Saint Epolitus.” From the different forms of expression, most people wish these to be different men, although in these manuscripts it is by no means unusual for the same saint to be repeated once and again [Col. 0711C]. I openly confess that I remain uncertain about the Hippolyti when I examine more deeply the conflicting opinions of learned men. The earlier one, the bishop “of the ancients,” should apparently be understood as that most celebrated writer among the ancient teachers of the Church, as Florentinius rightly judges, in my opinion, on this day. But is he the one whom some call bishop of Porto? Or the one honored on 22 or 23 August? Or the one celebrated by Prudentius? Opinions differ.

Who, then, is this Hippolytus of ours who suffered at Antioch? I am sufficiently inclined to say that he is that same great writer “of the ancients,” a bishop of uncertain locality, in no way to be confused with the martyr of Porto. But this is obstructed by the fact that the Hieronymian Martyrologies distinguish one from the other. The stumbling-block is Antioch. You will solve or cut the knot, if it is permissible to assign the great Hippolytus to Antioch, as the bishop of some Eastern church, who is commemorated by our martyrologists on 22 or 18 August; and to call this man a Roman presbyter, who perhaps, together with Pope Pontianus, as it is recorded in the Henschenian catalogues before volume I of April, suffered exile, became involved in the Novatian schism after Cornelius was elected, but, gloriously repenting, underwent an illustrious martyrdom when already worn out by age—not at Antioch, but most probably at the mouths of the Tiber—and was splendidly praised by Prudentius. He was not confused with the other, as Baronius wishes, and is honored by beautiful Rome on the Ides of August, as we shall say there.

These matters had to be prefaced in order to expose the confusion introduced into all the Martyrologies through Ado. The Little Roman Martyrology briefly read: “At Antioch, the passion of Saint Hippolytus.” But, unless I am mistaken, Ado alone complicated the matter by adding that elogium, which Usuard, Notker, and later writers generally received from him, and which I consider to belong exclusively to Prudentius’s Hippolytus—not, certainly, to the Antiochene—unless someone, in order to favor Ado, should invent some other Hippolytus deceived by the Novatian schism and martyred at Antioch. This certainly does not seem plausible to me.

We esteem our martyrologists very highly, but not so highly that we should everywhere prefer them to Prudentius, who lived so many centuries earlier [Col. 0712B]. Wandalbert appears to follow the sense of the Hieronymian Martyrologies in his single verse:

“And the third resounds with Hippolytus for the city of Antioch.”

Castellanus, on page 461, suggests repeatedly that Usuard was the first to place Matthias of Jerusalem, although it is perfectly evident that all his words here too have been copied, with only very slight alterations, from Ado [Col. 0712C]. Ado had received him from the Little Roman Martyrology, where he is mentioned as follows: “At Jerusalem, Matthias the bishop, who was the eighth after James.” Notker transposed Ado’s phrase somewhat; he is not known among the other martyrologists. Whether Ado handled the matter more successfully here than in the earlier announcement—and what and of what character those remarkable and wholly trustworthy Acts are—you may see in the Acts and in the Chronology of the Patriarchs of Jerusalem before volume III of May, page 6.

In Ado there follows Alexander the martyr, likewise reported by Notker. Why he was omitted by Usuard I understood only after repeatedly examining and turning over Ado’s elogium and learning that it had once again been badly translated and applied. All the words, in fact, are taken from Rufinus, book VI of the *History*, chapter 29, where the struggles of Alexander of Jerusalem are plainly described. This is the same Alexander who is expressly placed by the Little Roman Martyrology and Ado on 18 March. Thus this Alexander of Ado’s entry is redundant, unless the author of the Little Roman Martyrology indicated some other Alexander who also suffered in the Decian persecution and who has hitherto escaped our notice. We refer the rest to 18 March.

Castellanus undoubtedly observed this as well, but seems to suffer from another defect when, in his notes on page 461, he postpones the aforementioned Alexander to 12 December, as though he were the same person who is announced on three different days by the Little Roman Martyrology and Ado. I do not understand his intention clearly, unless he wishes to follow the Greeks, who commemorate Alexander of Jerusalem on that day. For the Alexander who is celebrated there by our writers with his companion Epimachus is as far removed from Alexander of Jerusalem as Alexandria is distant from Jerusalem, as Rufinus explains sufficiently distinctly in the cited book, chapters 31 and 35; likewise Eusebius of Valesius, book VI, chapters 41 and 46.

The Flavianus substituted here by Usuard is known by no identifying features, being placed without any indication of location or time, and I cannot guess where he obtained him [Col. 0713A]. I admit that Castellanus places this Flavianus at Centumcellae, while Baronius assigns him to Rome on 28 January. But I find such a variety of materials piled together that I cannot distinguish them. Nor do I find any more light than the Acts provide, on pages 833 and 946. Nothing further need be said about Aldegundis. The particular elogium concerning her belonging to Rabanus and, through him, to Notker, reported by Molan., we shall list among the Supplementary Witnesses.]

[Note: [Col. 0713A]

PRATEN. and the *Acts of the Martyrs*, with Aldegundis deleted, as I said in the Variants, substitute: “In the territory of Paris, Queen Bathildis.”

ANTUERP.-MAX. is sufficiently pure throughout the text up to *vitam finivit*, but then adds from Ado: “He was the eighth after the apostle James and ruled the Church of Jerusalem. On the same day, the passion of Blessed Alexander the martyr.” Concerning Aldegundis, it is correct.

ROSWEYD. The elogium is absent under Hippolytus. Under Matthias it is sufficiently pure. Then: “Likewise, Blessed Alexander the martyr, who suffered in the time of Decius. In Africa, 124 martyrs.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies. “Likewise, the martyr Lucius and his companions.” I do not know whom else this could indicate except Leucius, concerning whom see the 28th of this month. “Likewise on the same day, the death of Saint Bathildis.” Under Aldegundis it is pure.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., MUNERAT., ANTUERP.-MAX. LOVANIEN., and LEYDEN. BELGIC. are all pure in the text, but exceed it by adding Queen Bathildis.

ULTRAJ., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC. write somewhat more about Alexander than Ado did. They read as follows: “Likewise at Jerusalem, the heavenly birthday of Blessed Alexander the bishop. During the Decian persecution he was brought before the tribunal for his confession; and, after being handed over to imprisonment, while his venerable white hair shone with the dignity of great age, after he had often glorified the Lord through his sufferings, he was led now from tribulations [ULTRAJ. and LEYDEN. read this; the others more correctly have ‘from tribunals’] to chains, now from chains to tribunals; amid the tortures that succeeded one another in turn, he rested in a blessed end.” Nearly the same is found elsewhere.

[Col. 0713C] VATICAN., no. 5949, and STROZZ., etc. GREVEN. and MOLAN. more correctly and simply read: “Likewise, Blessed Alexander. During the Decian persecution he was brought before tribunals for confessing the faith and handed over to prison bonds. When he, with the venerable white hair of great age,” etc. GREVEN. adds: “He seems to be the same man whom Usuard places on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.” This is also what we think, though it is not altogether certain. See Bollandus on this day.

CENTULEN. The abridger of Usuard begins with Matthias, reading almost as the Little Roman Martyrology does: “At Jerusalem, Blessed Matthias, bishop and martyr, who, the eighth after James, ruled the Church of Jerusalem.” Hippolytus follows. Then: “On the same day, Saint Alexander the martyr.” At the end he wrongly adds: “At Alexandria, Saint Metranus the martyr,” who belongs to the following day.

BRUXELLEN. begins as follows: “At the monastery of Malbodium, the deposition of Saint Aldegundis, virgin and abbess, sister of Blessed Waldetrudis and niece of Saint Gudila.” Under Hippolytus and Matthias it is nearly pure. It contributes nothing new concerning Alexander. Flavianus follows. Finally: “In the territory of Paris, the death of Saint Bathildis, queen of the Franks, who built the monastery of Corbie.”

HAGENOYEN. is distorted and defective; it calls Hippolytus *Novaypolitus*, Flavianus *Flaviarius*, assigns Aldegundis to the territory of Paris, Bathildis to Malbodium, etc.

[Col. 0714B] MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJ.: “Aldegundis, virgin, sister of Saint Waldetrudis the widow. Flavianus the martyr. Likewise, Saint Hippolytus the martyr, whose passion Prudentius describes.”

ALTEMPS., enlarged in England: “Likewise, Saint Bellianus the martyr.” I think the name is corrupt, perhaps derived from *Pellicanus*, or some similar name, which may have been taken from the Hieronymian copies.

The LUBECK-COLOGNE edition agrees with the manuscripts cited above, adding this distinctive passage: “At the monastery of Malbodium, *sancti* [*sanctae*] Aldegundis, a most noble virgin, who, born of royal stock, chose Christ as her perpetual bridegroom; he also loved her so greatly that he often sent her a visible angel for consolation.” But Molanus expresses this more elegantly from Rabanus and Notker: “Born of noble stock in the time of Dagobert, king of the Franks, she chose the purpose of virginity and remained in it; an angelic vision was often revealed to her, exhorting her to persevere in her purpose. Finally, amid great brightness of heavenly light, she departed to eternal life.”

GREVEN.: “In Africa, Pellicanus, Clericianus, Philippianus, and 124 others.” From the Hieronymian Martyrologies. See Bollandus. “Lucius the martyr and his companions. Bathildis, queen of France, who, after the death of her husband Clovis, entered a monastery and, abasing herself in great humility, strove to be conformed to Christ. She is also placed on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, but more appropriately here.”

MOLAN., in addition to what has been said, writes in smaller type: “On the same day, the blessed memory of Antonius Peregrinus of Padua, born of the Manzi family, who visited all the holy places and died in 1267.” In the later editions he omitted Alexander, undoubtedly because, together with Greven., he began to doubt whether this was not the same man as the one placed on 18 March.]

[Col. 0709]

At Antioch, the passion of Blessed Hippolytus the martyr, who, having been somewhat deceived by the Novatian schism, was corrected through the operation of Christ’s grace and returned to the love of the Church, for which [Bouillart adds: “and in which”] he completed an illustrious martyrdom. At Jerusalem, the most holy Matthias, bishop, concerning whom they relate wonderful things, with full confidence, because after suffering many things for Christ he finally ended his life in peace. On the same day, the passion of Saint Flavianus the martyr. At the monastery of Malbodium, Saint Aldegundis, virgin. [Bouillart has: … Flavianus the martyr. In the territory of Paris,

[Note: [Col. 0709D] The queen Bathildis mentioned here is the reason why the severe censor of the Pratense manuscript did not deign to count it among the pure witnesses for this day. Yet the anonymous author of Bathildis’s Life, her contemporary, records the queen’s death on the third day before the Kalends, in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, volume II, and in Bollandus, volume II of January. [Col. 0710D] The very ancient calendar of the abbey of Corbie, written more than seven hundred years ago, assigns her death to the same day; the Martyrologies likewise mention Bathildis on that day. These include the Martyrology of Saint Jerome, the Pontisarense of the twelfth century, the Fossatense, Colbert manuscripts A and D, Victorin. A and B, Sandionys., Fuliens. B, Montisburg., the Parisian [Col. 0711A] Church, and the monasteries of Corbie and Chelles, which, founded and ennobled by Bathildis’s benefactions, celebrate this day as a festival and solemn observance. Yet Sollerius could not be persuaded by all these arguments to believe that Usuard had assigned this day to Bathildis’s death. What, then, holds him back? The authority of Castellanus, naturally, who stated that Bathildis had been substituted in place of the erased Aldegundis [Col. 0712A]. I do not deny the erasure; but the observer ought not to have omitted the fact that the same hand which copied the rest of the manuscript announced Bathildis’s memory here. Let judges trained in this branch of learning decide. We are prepared to provide a copy of the manuscript. BOUILLART.]

Queen Bathildis.]

The day before the Kalends. Day 31. [Note: [Col. 0713] Only Herinien., Tornacen., and Antuerp.-Major are considered the purer manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0715A]

There is scarcely anything worthy of notice except the difference between Antuerp.-Major and the two other manuscripts cited for the text.
