That manuscript appears to have preferred Ado’s pure reading, only slightly altered into Usuard’s form. Thus, instead of *beati*, it reads *sancti*. Then, after *martyris*, it continues as follows: “Whom the pagans, after seizing him, ordered to utter impious words; but when he refused, they crushed his whole body … [lacuna] … and there, whatever spirit remained in him,” etc.

The same manuscript forms the second announcement as follows: “Of Thyrsus, Saturninus, and Victor, whose Acts are extant.” Others write *Tyrsus*; we prefer Ado’s spelling, which we likewise used above on the 28th. Again, Antuerp.-Maj. begins: “On the same day,” etc. Herinien., however, incorrectly writes *Vigili* for *Vigilii*.

There remains a new controversy arising from the Pratense manuscript and others: namely, whether Vigilius of Trent was entered by Usuard himself on this day or on 26 June. Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., [Col. 0716A] Greven., and Molan. agree with the Pratense; that is, the greater number of manuscripts, on whose authority Usuard’s simplicity is for the most part to be determined. Although many other manuscripts, especially Herinien. and Tornacen., give the opposite reading, I had thought that they should yield until Castellanus made me more certain of the true reading of the Pratense.

In his most recent letter, delivered to me in another hand on 31 January 1711, he replied in these words: “While [the manuscript] is at Saint-Germain-des-Prés, an erasure appears—[concerning] 31 January, about which I had inquired—probably [the name] of Saint Vigilius, who recurs again on 26 June, but written by the same first hand by which the rest was written.” What should be deduced from this, when compared with the announcement of 26 June, we have explained in the preface. Here it is enough for me to have established one point: that in the oldest copies of Usuard, such as the Pratense certainly ought to be considered, Vigilius was formerly placed on this day, and consequently in Usuard’s very first autograph; therefore our reading is genuine and pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0715B]

The singular zeal of the author of the Little Roman Martyrology in collecting saints from Rufinus, which appears frequently throughout the work, is clearly evident here in the glorious Alexandrian elder named Metra. We spoke of him briefly in the chronological treatise on the patriarchs, no. 164; but here, following the customary manner of writing, we call him Metranus, as do our Martyrologies.

This man was first recorded by the Little Roman Martyrology as follows: “At Alexandria, Saint Metranus the martyr.” The source was the famous letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Fabius of Antioch, which, taken from Eusebius and Rufinus, you have reprinted in Ruinart’s *Sincere and Selected Acts*, beginning on page 103. From there Ado took his entire elogium; Notker left it intact, while Our Author, abbreviating it slightly, made it more obscure, as is made clear by the Antuerp.-Major manuscript in the Variants.

The second announcement belongs to Ado alone and is expressed by him without specifying the place: “Likewise, Saints Saturninus, Thyrsus, and Victor.” Notker preferred the Hieronymian Martyrology, in which at least some distinction is found between these and other martyrs [Col. 0715C]. Usuard confused the matter by assigning the arena to Alexandria, whereas in the aforesaid Hieronymian Martyrologies a different group of martyrs is assigned there.

Bollandus rightly and solidly observed on page 1080: “When the Acts exist, it is difficult to establish with certain confidence the birthdays of holy martyrs; the place where they won the palm is often either omitted by copyists, expressed erroneously, or rashly attributed to several persons as though they were one; companions are sometimes omitted, sometimes brought in from elsewhere because punctuation was neglected, or wrongly repeated because of similarity of names. When all these matters are kept before our minds here, even what we might conjecture is not sufficiently clear.” Nor is it easy for us to separate these confused materials.

In any case, Usuard’s error passed into later writers, and was corrected in part, quite successfully, from the manuscript of Saint Cyriacus by Baronius. It may be asked whether Wandalbert’s verses did not give others the occasion to select those three from a larger number. He sang as follows:

“Saturninus, your glorious trophy, and that of Thyrsus,

and likewise of Victor, delimit the world of January.”

We are entirely convinced that Vigilius of Trent was recorded by Usuard on this very day, after the Little Roman Martyrology and Ado, as was said above in the Variants. Thus the author of the Little Roman Martyrology first announces him: “At Trent, Saint Vigilius, bishop and martyr.” Hence Ado placed him in the same words, which Usuard and Notker copied from him. See his illustrated Acts on 26 June, on which day he is reported by the modern Roman Martyrology.]

[Note: [Col. 0715C]

I begin with the omission I noted above in the manuscripts PRATEN., PULSANEN., ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., MUNERAT., GREVEN., MOLAN., and the *Acts of the Martyrs*, all of which omitted Vigilius on this day.

ROSWEYD., in the first announcement, is neither wholly Adonian nor Usuardian, although it agrees with them in substance. In the second it is likewise not entirely pure. It too lacks Vigilius, in whose place it adds: “And the heavenly birthday of fifteen priests.” These items were taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. But what is meant by the added phrase, “And Blessed Julius the confessor”? Does it concern the presbyter who, together with his brother Julian the deacon, is placed at Novara in Italy in the Acts?

ALBERGEN. begins as follows: “The heavenly birthday of the blessed martyrs Cyrus and John.” LOVANIEN. adds: “The first of whom was born at Alexandria, the metropolis of Egypt, and the second at the city of Edessa.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., DANIC., and the ULTRAJ.-BELGIAN edition add the following to complete the elogium: “Who, in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, were first seized and thrown into prison, then beaten with rods and scorched with flaming torches, drenched with vinegar and salt, rubbed with sackcloth, and covered with boiling pitch; finally, they were beheaded and completed their martyrdom.” Concerning Saturninus and his companions they all add, “whose Acts are extant”—if only that were true! [Col. 0716C] LOVANIEN. alone is pure in having Vigilius at the end, as in the text above.

CENTULEN. dealt with Metranus on the preceding day, as may be seen there among the Supplementary Witnesses. Here, however, it reads: “At Alexandria, the holy martyrs Thyrsus, Saturninus, and Victor, whose Acts are extant.” Under Vigilius it is pure.

BRUXELLEN. reads Cyrus and John, together with the middle-grade manuscripts cited above. Under Metranus it has Ado’s pure elogium. Under Saturninus, etc., it reads as above. Then it joins together unrelated material of its own as follows: “And at the city of Trent, Vigilius, pope and martyr; because he refused to restore to his see Anthemius [Anthimus], bishop of Constantinople, condemned for heresy, he was disgracefully treated by order of the emperor and sent into exile. There, by worthily repenting of what he had unjustly done to Pope Silverius, his predecessor, he found a place for pardon and happily ended his life. He established that Masses should be celebrated in churches facing east. Likewise, Bishop Gelasius.”

HAGENOYEN. After Usuard’s pure and complete text, adds: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Eustacius [Eustadius], bishop and confessor.” It then follows with Cyrus and John, as above. Then: “Likewise at Modena, Saint Geminianus, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0717A] AQUICINCT. reads *Tyrsimi* instead of *Thyrsi*.

VICTORIN., at the end: “And Saints Abba, Cyrus, and John. On the same day, at the city of Trent, Blessed Vigilius, bishop and martyr.” CODEX REG. SUEC., no. 130, and VATICAN., no. 5949, have *Trientinam*, as above. ABDINGHEFF. has “At Trent.” STROZZ. and MEDIC. have: “At the city of Trent, the heavenly birthday of Saint Vigilius, bishop and confessor.” MATRIC. CARTHUS.-ULTRAJ. without a place: “Vigilius, bishop and martyr.”

AMBIAN. has: “In Gaul, at Amiens, the passing of Saint Vulphia.”

DIVION. of Saint Benignus: “At Dijon” [another copy has “at Dijon”] “the translation of the body of Saint Eustadius, presbyter and confessor.”

REG. SUEC., no. 130: “And Saints Abbacyrus and John.” Another manuscript, no. 438: “At the city of Grenoble, the heavenly birthday of Saint Patroclus the martyr, bishop of that same city.”

AUGUSTODUN. D. LE MARE: “At Dijon, the removal [translation] [Col. 0717B] of Saint Benignus the martyr.”

VATICAN., no. 3949: “The heavenly birthday of Saints Cyrus and John. And Saint Cyriacus, bishop and martyr. On the same day, the heavenly birthday of Saint Paschasius, abbot.” It places Vigilius in the penultimate position.

STROZZ. and MEDIC.: “Likewise, the translation of Saint Geminianus, bishop and confessor, at the Italian city of Modena, a man of great holiness.” They also discuss Vigilius.

BELIN. After the text, where it writes *Trisi* for *Thyrsi*, adds: “On the same day, Saints Cyrus and John the martyrs. Likewise at Modena, Saint Geminianus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Julius the confessor. On the same day, the translation of Saint Mark the Evangelist from Alexandria in Egypt to the city of Venice.” In another edition it adds: “At the city of Trent, Saint Vigilius, bishop and martyr.”

The LUBECK-COLOGNE edition begins with the elogium of Cyrus and John, as reported above from the middle-grade manuscripts [Col. 0717C]. Usuard’s first announcement follows, fairly purely. Then the second concerning Saturninus and his companions, with the addition “whose Acts are extant.” Then: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Mark the Evangelist. In the territory of Troyes, Saint Pontanius the confessor. On the same day, Saint Aedan, bishop and confessor.” Vigilius is omitted.

GREVEN.: “Cyrus and John, martyrs, who by order of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian were first seized, then thrown into prison, afterward beaten with rods and scorched with flaming torches, and finally beheaded,” etc. “At the city of Trent, according to Ado, Saint Vigilius, bishop and martyr, who is placed on the sixth day before the Kalends of July. The passion of Saints Ponticus and Blandina, concerning whom see 2 June. Tarsicius, Zoticus, and Aminonius. Likewise Pullius, Gelasius, Hippolytus, and Julius the confessors. Aurelianus the martyr. Torquatus [I believe this should be Torquatus], bishop and confessor. Geminianus, bishop and [Col. 0718A] confessor of Modena, at whose funeral Saint Severus of Ravenna said that he had been present, carried away in spirit during the solemn celebration of the Mass. Julius and Julian, brothers. Saint Gaudus of York [Gaudus of Évreux], bishop and confessor. In the territory of Troyes, Saint Potanius the confessor. In England, Keneswitha, abbess. At Amiens, Vulpha, virgin. The translation of Saint Mark from Alexandria to Venice, in the year of the Lord 465 [certainly several centuries too early]. Aedan, bishop and confessor.”

MOLAN.: “On the same day, Saint Veronus [Veronius] the confessor. On the same day, the holy martyrs Cyrus and John. Likewise at Modena, Saint Genimianus [a faulty transcription of Belin., where *Geminiani* appears above], bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Julius the confessor. On the same day, the translation of Saint Mark the Evangelist from Alexandria in Egypt to Venice. At the city of Trent, Saint Vigilius, bishop and martyr. In Gaul, at Amiens, the passing of Saint Vulphia. At the city of York, Blessed Gaudus, bishop of that same city.” [Col. 0718B] Then, in smaller type: “Marcella the widow, to whom Blessed Jerome writes.”

The later editions present a different order, in which “Vigilius of Trent” is reported first. Then: “In Gaul, at Amiens, the passing of Saint Vulphia.” Concerning Bishop Gaudus, it is more correctly written here: “At the city of Évreux. On the same day, the holy martyrs Cyrus and John, wonder-working and silver-free.” These titles are taken from the Greek elogium, οἱ ἅγιοι καὶ θαυματουργοὶ ἀναργὺροι, which is better translated in the Acts as “holy wonder-workers who heal the sick without payment.” It follows: “Likewise at Modena, Saint Geminianus,” etc. Concerning Julius, as above.

Here again it is more correctly written: “At Castrilocus, the translation of Saint Veronus the confessor. On the same day, the translation of Saint Mark the Evangelist,” etc., as in the earlier edition. The year of the translation of the body of the most holy evangelist, which was incorrectly recorded above as 465, is prudently omitted. It is certain that the aforementioned [Col. 0718C] feast is solemnly celebrated on this day at Venice in that magnificent ducal basilica, dedicated to the patron and protector of the Most Serene Republic. Yet, after many investigations by learned men, nothing sufficiently certain has so far been established concerning the actual day, month, or year of the translation. I openly confess that, when I was writing about the patriarchs of Alexandria and was investigating this matter with the greatest diligence, I nowhere managed to find sufficiently clear traces of the said translation.

However the matter may have occurred, the more probable opinion holds that the venerable body was not brought from Alexandria to Venice before the beginning of the ninth century; and, if we believe the history of the translation, the time of Leo the Armenian, between the years 813 and 820, should be noted. Thus it happened, as I correctly indicated above, several centuries after the year 465 assigned by Greven. See the Acts on 25 April, beginning on page 353, and Tillemont, volume II, beginning on page 98.]

[Col. 0713]

At Alexandria, the heavenly birthday of Blessed Metranus the martyr. When he refused, at the pagans’ command, to utter impious words, they beat his entire body with clubs; piercing his face and eyes with sharp reeds, they drove him outside the city amid tortures, and there expelled the spirit that remained in him by stoning him. Likewise at Alexandria, the holy martyrs Saturninus, Thyrsus, and Victor. At the city of Trent, Saint Vigilius, bishop and martyr. [Bouillart omits: “At the city of Trent … martyr.”]

[Note: [Col. 0713D] Sollerius adds to this article: “At the city of Trent, Saint Vigilius, bishop and martyr.” Thus the Herinien. and Tornacen. manuscripts close the article for this day. So too the much older Dervensis. Therefore there is no doubt that Usuard’s first autograph mentioned Vigilius of Trent on this day [Col. 0714D]. Usuard had imitated the Martyrologies composed before him by Bede, Florus, and others. Later, after reading Vigilius’s Acts, he corrected the error. How appropriately he did so will be said on 26 June. BOUILLART.]

THE MONTH OF FEBRUARY HAS TWENTY-EIGHT DAYS.

[Col. 0717]

On the Kalends. Day 1. [Note: [Col. 0719]

From Praten., Herinien., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0719A]

Greven. and Molan. have *natale* instead of *natalis*, which he corrected in the other editions. Likewise, after *Blessed Peter*, the others omit the word *blessed*, as Ado did. Herinien. transposed the words, reading *ecclesiam rexit* (“he ruled the Church”) instead of *rexit ecclesiam* (“he ruled the Church”). Greven. and Molan. have *traditur* instead of *mittitur*, but Molan. corrected this in the other editions. Herinien. reads *Praesente Trajano*; Munerat. more correctly has *Eo praesente* in the text. Munerat. inserts the phrase *ac circumsedente*. In our Pratense copy, *affecto* is read instead of *affectus*, perhaps through the scribe’s error. Instead of *dehinc*, Greven. and Molan. have *deinde*. Herinien. and Munerat. incorrectly form the name Pionius: here the former has *Pronii*, the latter *Pinonii*. In Munerat., *scalorem* for *squalorem* is an error. Greven. and Molan. change *vitae finem* into *finem vitae*. Herinien., with Greven., has *Effrem*. Munerat. has *Effren*; the other editions of Molan. have *Ephraem*. The reading of the text, supported by the other manuscripts, should be retained. Munerat. and Greven. write *Edissenae*. Greven. displays excessive cleverness when he says: “In the town of Tricaster, otherwise Tricassinus.” Molan. is no better with *Trecassino*, taken from Ado. Here *Schothia* or *scotia* means Ireland, where I read *Brigidam*, not *Brigitam*, as in the Pratense.]

[Note: [Col. 0719A]

No earlier commemoration of the Most Holy God-bearer (*Theophorus*) exists in our Latin Fasti than that first entered on this day by the Little Roman Martyrology: “At Antioch, Ignatius, bishop and martyr.” I believe its author saw those Acts which, published by our predecessors after other writers and formerly abridged by Ado, most explicitly state that he completed his martyrdom on this very day, the Kalends of February, in the eleventh year of Trajan, during the consulship of Atticus and Marcellus. From Ado’s abridgment Usuard extracted those few words of his, included among the Feasts of the Apostles, though even thus they do not correspond sufficiently closely to the truth.

Usserius was the first to publish the genuine and authentic Acts of Ignatius, in 1647. It is remarkable that Henschenius did not know them, although otherwise he pursued the deeds of that illustrious martyr with the greatest diligence. Ruinart had the same Usserian Acts reprinted among his Selected Acts, beginning on page 9; he also appended the original Greek source, fortunately found in the Colbertine Library, together with a new translation, beginning on page 695. In these the martyrdom is clearly assigned to the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, that is, 20 December, to which day Castellanus referred him—more scrupulously than was justified, if I am not mistaken.

Other recent writers have exercised their style in praising Ignatius; it is enough to mention Tillemont, volume II, pages 190–212, besides the notes. We shall say more about these matters in the Supplement to February.]

The Hieronymian Martyrologies deal with Pionius in such a way that an interpreter and commentator is needed, such as Florentinius proved himself to be. The Romanum parvum clearly reads: “At Smyrna, Pionius the martyr and fifteen others.” Ado appears to have had the more reliable Acts before him; from them he first composed his text, which Our Author transcribed for the most part, excising the disputed sentence beginning, “During the persecution of Antoninus Verus, etc.” See the Acts themselves, carefully examined by Bollandus, whose prolegomena explain the difficulties that even in our own time provide learned men with material for dissertations, as in Ruinart, p. 120 onward, and Tillemont, vol. III, p. 367 onward. I admit that the Acts assign another day, namely the fourth day before the Ides, or 12 March (although the martyrdom certainly seems to have occurred around the middle of that month); but I do not yet sufficiently understand why Castellanus transfers Pionius to 5 April.

Nor is it any clearer on what grounds that same Castellanus could assert that the most illustrious Ephraem died on 9 July. On this day Ado first reported him—I do not know for what reason—and from Ado Our Author, and from him the others, received the notice almost everywhere. Bollandus omitted nothing that might gather together everything written about him; I have no leisure to examine what more recent writers added. Tillemont constructed a continuous account of his life in vol. VIII, pp. 259–319.

Paulus Tricastrinus is also from Ado, but is wrongly assigned there, perhaps through a copyist’s error, to the city of Trecassina; Notker preserved this, while Our Author prudently corrected it, as we believe, although it remained in many of his copies. See the Acts, p. 93, and Castellanus, p. 487.

Only Bede mentions Brigida on this day. Florus added a brief eulogy in his own manner; Ado added a singular miracle, which belongs among the supplements; Our Author borrowed from Ado only what the text presents. The very ancient cult of this virgin is proved by most copies of the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Rabanus changed “Scotland” into “Ireland,” not without reason, as did Notker, who nevertheless wrote “Brigitta.” I believe that Castellanus skilfully distinguished among the saints who otherwise bear similar names: one Brigida, celebrated on this day; another, the Gallic Britta; and finally the Swedish woman, now best known, who ought to be called Birgitta.

In matters concerning the patroness of Ireland, Bollandus allowed nothing to be lacking, illuminating five different lives, which modern scholars, at least in part, rightly regard as suspect. From what has been said it is clear that our text flows entirely from Ado, with only some alteration of order; Notker added what he had found in Rabanus besides Brigida. Wandalbertus celebrates only her today:

> Brigida, mighty virgin, makes the first of February her own;  
> Celebrated among the Scots with wondrous devotion.

[Note: [Col. 0719D]]

**TORNACEN.** Usually pure and complete, but today it lacks the eulogies of Pionius of Smyrna and Paulus Tricastrinus; nevertheless, after “Pionius the martyr,” it does not omit the statement: “and fifteen others suffered with him.”

**MARCHIANEN.** Has a pure text, except that Paulus is entirely omitted.

**ANTUERP.-MAJ.** Here too the eulogy of Pionius has been erased. In Ephraem it is fairly pure. Concerning Brigida, it adds from Ado to the text:

> “When she touched the wood of the altar as a testimony to her virginity, it immediately became green.”

In Paulus it is pure; afterward it inserts:

> “On the same day, the translation of Saint Audoenus, archbishop.”

At the end, concerning Ignatius, it has only this from Ado’s Martyrology:

> “On this day, Saint Ignatius, bishop and martyr.”

**ROSWEYD.** It also omits the eulogy of Ignatius. In Pionius it is interpolated and mutilated. It then reads:

> “At Ravenna, Severus, bishop and confessor.”

In Ephraem it is pure.

> “In Scotland, Brigida the virgin,”

as in Bede.

> “On the same day, Saint Paulus, bishop and confessor of the city of Castrina.”

**PULSANEN.** Is silent about Pionius and Ephraem; at the end, however, it adds:

> “On Mount Gargano, the deposition of Paschasius, blessed abbot. So far nothing whatever has been found about this Paschasius.”

**ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC. and UGHELLIAN.** Are sufficiently pure throughout the rest of the text; they add concerning Brigida from Ado what we gave above. At the end they add:

> “On the same day, the holy bishops Polycarp and Severianus.”

See the historical note in the Acts, p. 933. The same saints will often be mentioned below.

**ANTUERP.-MAX., LEYDEN.-BELG. and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition** Differ from the preceding copies only in order, placing Polycarp and Severianus before Brigida; they also assign Pionius only ten or twelve companions.

**LOVANIEN.** Would be entirely similar, if it did not lack the whole eulogy of Pionius and also the fifteen companions.

**ULTRAJ., LEYDEN., ALBERG. and DANIC.** After the words of the text, add concerning Ignatius:

> “At one time, carried up into heaven through a vision, he saw and heard how the angels sang hymns to the Holy Trinity by the alternation of antiphons. Instructed by this vision, he established that antiphons should be sung in the church of Antioch according to the pattern of the vision. Then, through blessed Ambrose, the rite of singing passed from the Greeks to the Latins.”

They add only twelve companions to Pionius. They place Polycarp and Severianus second from last, and finally add Brigida as above.

**CENTULEN.**

> “At Rome, the passion of Saint Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, a disciple of blessed John the apostle, who was the third after blessed Peter to govern the church of Antioch. At Smyrna, Pionius the martyr and fifteen others. On the same day, Saint Ephraem, deacon of the church of Edessa. In Scotland, Saint Brigida the virgin. At Trecas, Saint Paulus, bishop and confessor.”

Whether this Paulus is different from the Tricastrinus, see *The Saints Passed Over* and the Acts, p. 93.

**BRUXELLEN.** Begins as follows:

> “In Scotland, Saint Bregida the virgin. When she touched the wood …”

It adds:

> “Her life was distinguished by many miracles.”

It composed a special eulogy for Ignatius, which I did not think necessary to transcribe. It follows with:

> “Likewise, Gallenitus the martyr, who suffered with the blessed Ignatius mentioned above.”

It gives a damaged form of Pionius’s encomium. Ephraem is given almost as in the text.

> “Likewise, Saint Paulus, bishop of the city of Trecassina, or of the town of Castrum Yppidotum, whose life …”

Then:

> “On the same day, the blessed bishops Polycarp and Severianus and Praecordius the priest. And the translation of Saint Andoenus [Audoenus], archbishop of Rouen.”

His life will be given on 24 August.

**HAGENOYEN.** Also devised a eulogy for Ignatius on its own initiative. In Pionius, Ephraem and Paulus it is fairly pure, except that it assigns Pionius only twelve companions. It then reads:

> “In Scotland, Saint Brigida the virgin, who had been foretold by many, both pagans and Christians. When at a certain time, etc. On the same day, the holy bishops Polycarp and Severianus.”

See what was said above.

**AQUICINCT.** Instead of Trecassinus, or rather Tricastinus or Tricastrinus, it reads *Tegastri*.

**VATICAN., no. 5949.**

> “At Ravenna, Saint Severus, bishop.”

**VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC.** Add: “the glorious man.”

**DAVERON.** Incorrectly has on this day:

> “Likewise, Severus, bishop, surnamed Sulpitius, blessed Martin of Tours’ disciple, pontiff of the city of Bourges, most illustrious in birth and wisdom.”

Several Severuses recur on this day; concerning them, see the index of *The Saints Passed Over* and Castellanus, pp. 486–487.

**BIGOTIAN., formerly of the Congregation of the Celestines:**

> “On this day, the holy bishops Polycarp and Severianus.”

**ALTEMPS., expanded in England:**

> “At Périgueux, Saint Suri the confessor.”

In the Acts he is called Sorus.

[Col. 0722A]

**Codex S. RICALDI:**

> “Agrippianus, bishop and confessor of Le Puy.”

In the Acts: Agrippanus.

**STROZZ. and MEDIC.**

> “In Scotland, Saint Brigida the virgin … Her life, admirable for virtues and miracles, is commended in writing by Saint Donatus the Scot, bishop of Fiesole. Likewise, the translation of the body of Saint Aldoenus, archbishop, when it was transferred from Gaul to Rouen through a vision of Robert, the illustrious king of the Normans, in the year 918 from the Incarnation of the Lord. Likewise, the holy bishops Polycarp and Severianus. At the city of Ravenna, the feast of Saint Severus, archbishop. Likewise, Saint Praecordius the martyr.”

Could this not be Praecordius of Corbie?

**LUBECO-COL. edition:**

> “At Antioch, the feast of blessed Ignatius, etc.,”

as above from the ULTRAJ. and other copies. It follows:

> “In Scotland, Saint Brigida the virgin. When she had received from the hand of a bishop the veil customary among nuns, after prayers had been read over her head, she bowed her head and touched the wood of the altar as a testimony to her virginity; it immediately became green, and remained forever green and incorruptible.”

In Pionius it reproduces Ado. After Ephraem and Paulus it places Polycarp and Severianus. Last of all:

> “At Poitiers, Saint Leo the confessor.”

**BELIN.** Is fairly pure in Ignatius. In second place it has:

> “In the town of Trecassinus, etc.”

It follows:

> “In Scotland, etc.,”

as in the codices above.

> “At Ravenna, Saint Severus, bishop and confessor.”

Then it gives Pionius, whose eulogy it mutilates. Finally it gives blessed Ephraem.

**GREVEN.**

> “At Ravenna, the deposition of Saint Severus, bishop and confessor. Seeking his livelihood through wool-working, he was designated by a dove sent from heaven as the one to be taken up into the episcopate. Others maintain that this is his commemoration, together with Vincentia his wife and Innocentia his daughter, while his deposition is on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November. On the same day, the holy bishops, etc. Likewise, blessed Severius, bishop and confessor, whose body is reverently displayed to the people on this day in the metropolitan basilica of Saint Mary of Rouen. At Poitiers, Saint Leo the confessor. Eubertus, bishop and confessor. At Metz, Sigebert the confessor, and Severus the priest and confessor, of whom Gregory relates in the First Book of the *Dialogues* that, when summoned to a sick man, he delayed for a little while because of the work of pruning his vineyard; when the man had died, he recalled him to life while weeping bitterly. Others, however, place this saint on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March. Likewise, Saints Dionysius and Publius.”

From the Hieronymian codices.

**MOLAN.** Concerning Brigida:

> “She, when she touched the wood, etc.”

Concerning Severus and Severius, as in Greven.

> “At Vastiacum, the feast of Saint Praecordius the confessor.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “At Metz, Sigebert the confessor and king, who among his other virtues built twenty monasteries. The passion of Saints Vindemialis, Eugenius and Longinus, concerning whom Gregory of Tours writes in the *Chronicles*, Book II. At Lille, Saint Eubertus the confessor, whose life, although known to God and unknown to men, is nevertheless believed to have been of distinguished merit. His body rests in Saint Peter’s.”

In other editions there is also the following concerning Severus of Ravenna:

> “Whom God raised from the wool-working trade to the episcopate. On the first day, the prefect Ypapantes of the Lord and God, our Saviour Jesus Christ. And Saint Tryphon the martyr. At the city of Augusta, Saint Ursus, bishop of that same city. At Poitiers, Saint Leonius, fellow priest of Saint Hilary, most holy from his earliest age.”

Finally, in smaller type:

> “In Iceland, Saint Goedermund, bishop and martyr.”

He is not yet known among the saints, unless he is taken for “Jón Ogmund.” See *The Saints Passed Over*.

[Col. 0717]

## The Feast of Blessed Ignatius, Bishop and Martyr

He was the third after the apostle Peter to govern the church of Antioch. During the persecution of Trajan he was sent bound to Rome, where, in the presence of Trajan himself and with the Senate seated around him, he was first subjected to the most savage punishments; afterward he was thrown to the lions and strangled by their teeth, becoming Christ’s sacrificial victim.

At Smyrna, Saint Pionius the martyr, who, after the squalor of prison—where by his exhortations he strengthened many of the brethren to endure martyrdom—was afflicted with many tortures, nailed fast, and placed upon a burning pyre, thus obtaining a blessed end of life for Christ. Fifteen others suffered with him.

On the same day, blessed Ephraem, deacon of the church of Edessa.

In the town of Tricastrinum, Saint Paulus, bishop, whose life shone with virtues and whose precious death is commended by miracles.

In Scotland, Saint Brigida the virgin, whose life shone with miracles.

## Fourth Day before the Nones. Day 2.

[Note: [Col. 0723]]

Almost all our codices are fairly pure, but only the Pratensian, Herinian, Tornacensian and Marchian codices exhibit the original and simple purity of Usuard.

[Note: [Col. 0723A]]

I wrote *Ypapanti*, the ending found in all the cited codices, which lack aspiration; the Pratensian actually reads *Yppapanti*. The other printed and manuscript witnesses vary considerably. The greatest discrepancy concerns the name of Fusculus of Orléans, whose different inflections I could almost number twelve; they may be seen in Bollandus and Castellanus on this day. I retained the reading of the Pratensian, Herinian and Marchian codices, although some judge the Tornacensian preferable, where *Flosculi* is written instead of *Fuscoli*—in French, Saint Flou—and our Motherius interprets it in this way in his note for the day.

[Note: [Col. 0723A]]

Bede reads *Hypapante Domini*, whom Rabanus here abandons while following the Hieronymian Martyrologies, though he somewhat expanded their wording. The Romanum parvum agrees with Bede, and the phrase is exactly the same in Ado, so that Our Author was not without models to imitate. Why our codices generally use another ending is not worth discussing. The Greek upsilon, incorrectly rendered in Latin, undoubtedly introduced the whole variation. Notker did not wish to depart either from Rabanus or from Ado, joining both forms of announcement, although he does not adhere entirely to the wording of the former.

The Hieronymian copies in Florentinius speak as follows:

> “The Purification of Saint Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Henschenius treats this feast at length and with learning, followed by Castellanus from p. 498 onward. In any event, Bede, the Romanum parvum, Ado and Our Author clearly demonstrate that the Greek name of this feast had been received by ancient usage in the Latin Church, although other names were also adapted to it. I leave it to others to consider what Wandalbert’s verses precisely mean; they run as follows:

> On the fourth day before the Nones, the Lamb brought into the temple speaks:  
> When God purifies it, the believing people in one temple,  
> With pious mind, place and lay down the tribunal they have received.

The centurion Cornelius, found by Ado in the Romanum parvum, was given an expanded eulogy, which Our Author took from him, preserving the circumstance that baptism was conferred by the apostle Peter—a detail that, strictly speaking, does not seem to conform to the sacred text. Some also doubt whether he was truly ordained bishop of Caesarea by Peter. On these matters see Bollandus in the Acts, where he discusses Caesarea’s prerogatives and the door to faith opened to the Gentiles through Cornelius; Tillemont treats the matter more briefly in vol. I, p. 154 onward.

Notker’s eulogy neatly condenses the whole history of Cornelius from the Acts of the Apostles. Bede mentions Apronianus only by name; the Romanum parvum calls him a martyr at Rome; Ado adds more, which one could scarcely believe Our Author reduced to a summary. Certainly Ado did not express Christ’s words, “Come, you blessed …,” and other witnesses do not give them uniformly. We may perhaps say that this was the reason why they were interpolated in many codices, so that only four were found which, as we judged above, transmitted the genuine and simple sense of Usuard.

Rabanus had before him the same source, namely the Acts of Saint Marcellus, which we discussed on 16 January, and drew from it his brief eulogy. Notker copied it; although it does not agree with Ado’s longer version word for word, it agrees in sense. Fortunatus, together with three other martyrs, was selected by Our Author from among the many names in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, as was probably also Fusculus of Orléans, while Sicaria was omitted. Florentinius wrongly attributes her to Bede and Usuard. Rabanus has only the latter; Notker has both.

[Note: [Col. 0723C]]

**ANTUERP.-MAJ.** Begins:

> “The Purification of Saint Mary the Virgin.”

It is fairly pure in Cornelius:

> “On the same day at Rome, Saint Apronianus the martyr, under the emperor Maximian.”

**ROSWEYD., in red letters:**

> “The Purification of Saint Mary.”

In the second entry it is not entirely pure:

> “On the same day at Rome, Saint Apronianus the martyr, who after suffering much during the persecution of the emperor Maximian was finally beheaded on the Salarian Way at the second milestone. In Africa, Victor and eighty others. Likewise at Rome, Fortunatus and thirty-two others.”

See the Acts and Florentinus, where these groups of martyrs are distinguished more accurately.

**PULSANEN., ANTUERP.-MAX., LUBEC., GREVEN. and MOLAN**, along with many other codices, give a longer form of the voice heard by Apronianus:

> “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you.”

**BELIN.** Adds “from the foundation of the world,” omitting “believing.”

**MOLAN.** Also inserts Ado’s words into Usuard’s text in different lettering. Thus, after “still a pagan,” it reads:

> “During the persecution of the emperor Maximian, when he had brought blessed Sisinnius the deacon before the eyes of Laodicius the prefect, having led him out of prison—for Apronianus was the prison clerk.”

And after “was baptized”:

> “by the deacon Sisinnius,”

and:

> “to be confirmed with the sacred Chrism, he was brought before Pope Marcellus.”

**PULSANEN.**, in large illuminated capitals, begins:

> “The Purification of the holy and perpetual Mother of God and Virgin Mary.”

The text follows with the addition already mentioned. At the end it constructs the sense so that, after “Candidus,” it reads:

> “Aurelianus and Fusculus the bishops,”

as though these were two martyrs, companions of the others. Muneratus has the same reading and likewise departs from Usuard’s simplicity at the beginning, writing:

> “The Hypapante of the Lord, which in Latin is ‘meeting,’ namely when holy Simeon met the Lord in the temple.”

**BELINI.** Since we have already discussed the first edition, it should also be noted in what respect the second departs from purity. It concludes the day:

> “At Orléans, Saint Flostulus, bishop and confessor, and Sicharia, consecrated to God.”

**ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJ., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC. and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition** All begin the day in this form:

> “The Purification of the Blessed Virgin and the Hypapante of the Lord,”

presumably because they wished to exclude neither feast, or at least neither form of announcing it. In the voice heard—“Come, you blessed,” etc.—they agree with the witnesses cited above. At the end, after “bishop,” most add “and confessor”; they form the name Fusculus in various ways.

[Col. 0724D]

**CENTULEN.**

> “The Hypapante of the Lord, which is the embrace or reception of the Lord the Saviour. At Caesarea, the most blessed Cornelius the Centurion, whom blessed Peter the apostle baptized and who, elevated to the episcopate in that same city, rested. At Rome, Apronianus the martyr. Likewise at Rome, the holy Fortunatus, Felicianus, Firmus and Candidus. At Orléans, Saint Fusculus.”

In a space erased by a later hand, these words were written:

> “At Sebaste, the beheading,”

prefixed to what had been written by the older and first hand:

> “Saint Blasius, bishop and martyr.”

Thus one may rightly doubt whether these words belong to this day or the next.

**BRUXELLEN.**

> “The Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary and the Hypapante of the Lord. This feast began at Byzantium, or Constantinople, in the time of the emperor Justinian. And Saint Symeon, who, holding Christ presented in the temple in his arms, sang the song: ‘Now dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace.’”

Otherwise it is pure, including the heavenly voice perceived by Apronianus. It nevertheless has “confessor” at the end.

**HAGENOYEN.**

> “The Purification of blessed Mary, Mother of God, when she offered her son in the temple to the priest and redeemed him with offerings according to the law of Moses. There he was recognized by Saint Symeon and Saint Anna the widow. This feast was solemnly instituted by the emperor Justinian because of the pestilence then raging in Constantinople; Pope Pelagius also confirmed it.”

After “was baptized,” concerning Apronianus, it adds:

> “And out of devotion he presented himself, complaining that he had wasted his days. The judge said to him: ‘Today you will truly lose your days,’ and immediately ordered him to be beheaded.”

Instead of Firmus it reads *Sirinus*.

**MATRICULA-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJ.** Omitting Apronianus and Fusculus, it places at the end:

> “Telerin, the confessor, and other martyrs.”

It means Celerinus and his companions, but they belong to the following day.

**VATICAN., no. 5949.** Does not have Fortunatus and his companions, nor Fusculus.

**ALTEMPS.**

> “On this day in Kent, at Canterbury, Saint Langacius, archbishop.”

[Col. 0726A]

**STROZZIAN.**

> “At the castle of Florentine, Saint Verdiana the virgin, whose life is admirable for its virtues.”

It nevertheless leaves doubtful whether this saint belongs to this day or the preceding one.

> “Likewise, the passion of Saint Sotheris the martyr. Likewise, Saints Zotici, Herennius and Hyacinthus, martyrs.”

The MEDIC. codex and the FLORENTINE edition of 1486 also treat these saints.

**LUBECO-COL. edition** Begins like the middle-grade codices above. It is pure in Cornelius, but in Apronianus it is interpolated from Ado. After “Fusculus, bishop and confessor,” it adds:

> “On the same day, blessed Sorus the confessor.”

Greven also mentions him. In the Acts he is placed on the preceding day.

**GREVEN.**

> “In Africa, Saints Victor and eighty other martyrs. Likewise, Saints Marinus, Perpetua, Julia and Privatula.”

See the Acts. Sorus follows; then:

> “Laurentius, archbishop of Canterbury, who succeeded blessed Augustine, the first bishop of that city. Likewise, according to some, the seven women who collected drops of Saint Blasius’s blood and gloriously died for Christ. At Orléans, Sigaria, a virgin consecrated to God. Hadeloga, the virgin, kinswoman of Saint Boniface the bishop.”

Molan’s additions mention only Sicharia and Laurentius of Canterbury. The material inserted into the text was given above.

[Col. 0721]

## The Hypapante of the Lord

At Caesarea, the most blessed Cornelius the Centurion, whom blessed Peter baptized. Elevated to episcopal rank in the city mentioned above, he rested there.

At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the passion of Saint Apronianus, who, while still a pagan, heard together with the deacon Sisinnius a voice from heaven saying, “Come, you blessed of my Father,” and the rest. Believing, he was baptized, and afterward, in confessing the Lord, received the sentence of capital punishment as the end of his life.

Likewise at Rome, Saints Fortunatus, Felicianus, Firmus and Candidus.

At Orléans, Saint Fusculus the bishop.

## Third Day before the Nones. Day 3.

[Note: [Col. 0725]]

There is now a scarcity of pure codices. Only Greven and Molan appear free of every addition or alteration. The reason will soon be given.

[Note: [Col. 0725C]]

I wrote “Africa” in accordance with custom, although both witnesses write *Aphrica*. Greven has Laurentius, together with many other codices; Molan, following the Romanum parvum and Ado’s *Laurentini*, more correctly has the form found in the text. I write *extat*, as elsewhere *extitit*, etc. Greven has *Vapincum*, Molan *Vapingum*; both are correct. See the other names and places, and the names of the saints themselves, in the Acts. Here are the other variations of greater importance, on account of which so many codices have been excluded from the number of the genuine witnesses.

That the Pratensian codex is not pure is clear from the fact that Castellanus warned me long ago that everything in it had been erased, beginning with the word “saints” and continuing to the end, and that the following was written over it in smaller characters:

> “the martyrs Laurentius, Ignatius, etc.,”

as above.

Then:

> “At the city of Sebaste, blessed Blasius, bishop, confessor and martyr. At the city of Nicaea, the passion of Saint Tryphon, in the time of the emperor Decius. At the town of Vapingum, etc.”

Finally it adds:

> “At Latiniacum, the feast of Saint Deodatus, bishop and confessor.”

Who would not see that Blasius of Sebaste has been wrongly read here, since Usuard, following the Romanum parvum and Ado, treats him at length on 15 February under the name Blavius? Unless someone wishes to distinguish this Blasius from Blavius—a distinction no one today would accept.

For a long time I thought that the name Blasius first became famous in the West when the returning Crusaders enriched our churches with the relics of the illustrious martyr, and that only then did his commemoration begin to be celebrated more prominently on this day. But when I found him placed so explicitly on this very day in Rabanus, I rejected that conjecture as vain. Nevertheless, this circumstance may have caused many codices to place Blasius on this day, either with or without the designation of his arena, because they perhaps considered him different from Blavius in those times. Others may have moved the entire announcement, which Usuard placed on the fifteenth, to this day; this was done by the Herinian and others. However one decides the matter, I consider it certain that, according to Usuard’s intention, Blasius does not belong to this day at all.

The martyr Tryphon of Nicaea has been inserted with no stronger foundation. He is plainly different from the one discussed on 4 January, whom Bollandus moved to 10 November, because the patron of that name is celebrated on that day at Ascrivium, commonly Cattaro, a town in Venetian Dalmatia. We placed the name of another Tryphon, or perhaps the same one, among the additions on the first of this month; Bollandus placed him among the saints passed over. Castellanus distinguished four saints of this name in his universal Martyrology. These matters must be examined elsewhere in detail. See below the addition of Greven from Vincentius.

For our present purpose it is enough that this Tryphon, of whatever sort he may have been, was unknown to Usuard, who, as we have said elsewhere, rarely adds Eastern saints to Ado unless he has found them in the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Finally, Deodatus, placed last in the Pratensian, found a place among the additions only in Greven; he is undoubtedly the same saint whose Acts are illuminated on 19 June.

The Marchian and Aquicinct codices agree with the Pratensian. They too name Tryphon, but simply call Blasius a martyr, without specifying the place, so that he might equally be understood as Blasius of Oreto, Caesarea or Sebaste. That they distinguish Blasius from Blavius is manifest from the fact that they report the latter with Usuard on the fifteenth, as does the Pratensian.

The Herinian and Tornacensian are closest to Usuard’s purity. The latter is simpler, calling Blasius merely a martyr, like Marchian and Aquicinct, and placing Blavius also on the fifteenth; the former is clearer, removing the ambiguity and assigning the entire eulogy of Blavius to Blasius—who must not be duplicated—on this day. There is no mention of Tryphon.

The Pulsanian, excluding Tigris and Remedius, likewise transfers the whole eulogy of Blasius to this day; Muneratus gives it in mutilated form. More will be said about these matters in the additions.

[Note: [Col. 0727B]]

Among the Hieronymian copies, the Corbeian more clearly gives the name Celerina, joined with Felix and Felicitas. Florentinius observes that several Africans bearing similar names are often, though not always correctly, designated by these names.

Bede, Florus and Rabanus know none of the saints celebrated today. Our announcement is found originally in the Romanum parvum as follows:

> “Blessed Celerinus the deacon, and Celerina his [relative], and Laurentius and Ignatius.”

Ado explains this somewhat more fully, reporting Cyprian’s words from Letter 34. Bollandus illustrated that letter, together with other matters concerning their glorious origin, in an excellent dissertation, from which the entire memory of these distinguished saints may be recovered. Add Tillemont, vol. III, p. 395 onward, and the other writers who composed commentaries on Cyprian’s works and life, as well as Castellanus’s note on p. 508.

Our text is taken from Ado, except that it omits the circumstance that Celerinus was the uncle and Laurentius the maternal uncle; Notker preserved this circumstance, together with the title “deacon,” which the cited authors rightly maintain should not be applied to Celerinus.

Whether Wandalbertus saw the Romanum parvum is uncertain. That he received his material from the same source from which the author of the Romanum parvum drew his is indicated by these two verses:

> Celerinus with Celerina shines through pious blood,  
> And blessed Ignatius and Laurentius likewise.

We have already shown at sufficient length in the Variants that Blasius, Tryphon and Deodatus do not belong at all to today’s text. Why Usuard did not discuss Lupicinus I do not know; certainly he was known to Wandalbertus and Rabanus. From the latter Notker copied him together with Blasius.

In any event, Our Author extracted Tigris and Remedius from the Hieronymian codices. The first name appears as *Tigris*, *Tingides*, *Teridus* and *Terridus*; the second is inflected in more than one way. Whether these saints were martyr bishops or confessors, as the term “deposition” suggests; whether both died on this day; and when and for how long they governed that church do not appear sufficiently established. Consult Bollandus, Florentinius and Castellanus, who attempt to offer the more probable explanations.

From what has been said thus far, we think it can be established completely that the simple and original text of Usuard has been represented by us in the upper column.

[Note: [Col. 0727C]]

**PRATEN.** The matters exceeding the pure text of this codex are recorded in the Variants.

**HERINIEN.** Gives the entire text concerning Blasius; see the fifteenth of this month.

**TORNACEN., MARCHIANEN. and AQUICINCT.** Add beneath the text:

> “On the same day, Saint Blasius the martyr.”

The last also adds:

> “At Lyons, Lupicinus the bishop, Felix and Celerinus.”

See in the Acts how improperly all these notices are joined together.

**PULSANEN.** Omits Tigris and Remedius, but it too brings back to this day the entire text assigned to Blavius on 15 February.

**ANTUERP.-MAJ.**

> “In Africa, blessed Celerrimus [so written instead of Celerinus], deacon and confessor, and the holy martyrs Celerrima, his grandmother, and Laurentinus and Ignatius; the former was his paternal uncle, the latter his maternal uncle. The feast of Saint Blasius, bishop and martyr.”

As in the codices mentioned above.

**ROSWEYD.**

> “In Africa, blessed Celerinus, deacon and confessor, and the holy martyrs Celerina, his grandmother, and Laurentinus and Ignatius. At Vienne, the feast of Eventius, the glorious bishop. On the same day, the passion of Saint Blasius, bishop and martyr. At Lyons, Lupicinus, bishop and confessor. And Saint Waltrudis the virgin.”

See below for the more accurately expressed name.

**MUNERAT.** After the pure text, appends a mutilated eulogy of Blavius from the fifteenth, as follows:

> “At the city of Sebaste, the passion of blessed Blavius the bishop. He, the performer of many miracles, after prolonged scourging and suspension on a wooden stake, during which his flesh was torn apart with iron combs, and after a most terrible imprisonment and immersion in a lake, from which he emerged unharmed, completed his martyrdom by beheading, at the command of the judge mentioned above, together with two boys.”

See this passage more purely and completely on the fifteenth.

**ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC. and UGHELLIAN.** Give the pure text of Usuard, adding at the end:

> “At Lyons, Lupicinus the bishop, Felix and Celerinus.”

We have discussed this incongruous conjunction above. It will recur more than once below.

**ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERG., DANIC. and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition** All begin by reporting Blasius of Sebaste, together with Usuard’s eulogy from the fifteenth. At the end they add, as above:

> “At Lyons, Lupicinus the bishop, Felix and Celerinus.”

Finally:

> “At Bremen, Anscharius, the first bishop of that place.”

DANIC. adds:

> “and apostle of Denmark.”

See more in Greven’s *Supplement*.

**CENTULEN.** Seems almost, but not entirely, pure. It reads:

> “In Africa, blessed Celerinus the deacon, Celerina his grandmother, and Laurentinus and Ignatius the martyrs. At the town of Vapingum, the holy bishops Tigris and Remedius.”

**BRUXELL.** Begins:

> “Saint Waldetrudis the chosen, niece of blessed Gudula. Drawn from conjugal love to the love of God, and having abandoned earthly possessions, she followed Christ devoutly, founded a monastery at Mons in Hainaut, and her body rests there.”

Bollandus refers her to 9 April. Only her translation is celebrated at Mons on this day; in some calendars it was transferred to the fourth because of the concurrence of Blasius.

The notice of Blasius and Celerinus follows as above in the middle-grade codices. Then:

> “At the city of Nicaea, the feast of Saint Tryphon, who suffered in the time of the emperor Decius. At Vienne, Saint Eventius, the glorious bishop. At Lyons, Saints Lupicinus, etc.”

At Vapingum the text is pure. At Bremen:

> “Saint Anscharius, the first bishop of that place.”

**HAGENOYEN.** Blasius, with his complete eulogy, is also placed first. A fairly pure text follows. Then comes Lupicinus with his companions, as above. Afterward:

> “At Rome, Tryphon the martyr. At Bremen, Saint Anscharius, etc. Likewise, Waldetrudis the widow and Wetpurga the virgin.”

He meant Wereburga, whom Greven mentions below and the Acts assign to this day. We call her Gecburg in the vernacular.

**VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC.**, under no. 130, add at the end:

> “Likewise, Saint Tryphonius the martyr.”

**DAVERON.**

> “At Lyons, Lupicinus, etc.”

The D. DU CHEVAL codex reads more clearly:

> “At Lyons, Saints Lupicinus, etc.”

**MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJ.**

> “Blasius, bishop and martyr, at Sebaste in Cappadocia, and the seven women who collected the drops of blessed Blasius’s blood. Waldetrudis the widow. Berlendis the virgin.”

[Col. 0729B]

**LUBECO-COL. edition** Begins with Blasius, as do the codices above. In second place, concerning blessed Celerinus and his companions:

> “On the same day, Saint Tryphon the martyr, who shone with many miracles from childhood and was finally crowned with the sword in the city of Nicaea under Decius.”

The notice of Tigris and Remedius follows. Then:

> “At Lyons, Saints Lupicinus the bishop, Felix and Celerinus the martyrs. At Bremen, Saint Anscharius, etc. On the same day, Saint Hadelinus, confessor of Aquitaine. At Auxerre, blessed Julian the martyr. At Vienne, Saint Evencius, bishop and glorious confessor. Likewise, Saint Waldetrudis the widow.”

**BELIN.** After Blasius and the text, adds:

> “At Lyons, Lupicinus and likewise Felix.”

Greven: “On the same day, Saint Blaise, bishop and martyr, whom Usuard places after Ado on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March under the name Blavius. At Lyons, Lupicinus, bishop, and the martyrs Felix and Celerinus. At Auxerre, blessed Julian, martyr. In Africa, Felix and Felicitas. Tryphon, martyr. From the seventh year of his age, he shone with miracles; under Decius, in the city of Nicaea, he was lacerated with claws for Christ, dragged naked by the feet of horses through the snow, and, nails having also been driven into his feet, was led around; finally struck by the sword, he triumphed. Vincent, book XII, chapter 47, says that he suffered on the third day before the Nones of May; others say on the Nones of December. Anschar, the first bishop of Bremen and confessor, whom Louis, son of Charlemagne, appointed a worthy shepherd and bishop together with the newly converted Christian people of the Saxons. Hadelin, confessor of Aquitaine. At Vienne, the glorious bishop and confessor Eventius. Likewise, according to the Catalogue of the Saints, the burial of blessed John the Almsgiver. Gaudentius, bishop of Novara, a disciple of Saint Martin, who endured exile for Christ with Saint Eusebius of Vercelli. Radegund, virgin. Likewise, Wereburga, virgin. On the same day, Waldetrudis, widow and countess of Hainaut, who had four children distinguished for holiness.”

Molanus, in the first edition, adds: “At Lyons, Lupicinus and likewise Felix,” from Belinus. Blaise follows with his eulogy; in other editions he is wrongly placed in the text. Then: “And Saint Hadelin, confessor, at the town of Visé. On Mount Castrilocus, Saint Waldetrudis, widow. At Bremen,” and so forth. Finally, in smaller type: “In the Brabant village of Meerbeke near Ninove, Saint Berlindis, virgin.” Later editions read: “On Mount Castrilocus, etc. At the town of Visé, Saint Hadelin, confessor. At Lyons, Lupicinus, etc. At Meerbeke, the burial of Saint Berlindis, virgin. At Bremen, Saint Anschar, first bishop of the united sees of that place and Hamburg. At Besançon, Saint Anatolius, most holy bishop and confessor of that metropolis. On Mount Calvus, Saints Oliveria and Libertata, sisters and virgins. At Vienne, the glorious bishop Eventius.”

[Col. 0725]

In Africa, the feast of blessed Celerinus, deacon and confessor, and of the holy martyrs Laurentinus, Ignatius, and Celerina; concerning the glorious praises of all of them, there exists a letter of blessed Cyprian. Bouillart inserts:

[Note: In Sollerius’s judgment, this entire article is thoroughly corrupt. Three and a half lines have been obliterated; the mention of blessed Blaise and Saint Tryphon has been inserted; and a commemoration of Saint Deodatus has been added. It is astonishing how fiercely he attacks these faults. Castellanus is responsible. If the monks of Pratis had been consulted, Sollerius would have received this answer: in the Pratis manuscript whatever space lay between “of the saints” and “of Remedius” had been erased. But the inserted material reproduces the same form of writing, although perhaps in slightly smaller letters and with the letters brought somewhat closer together than usual. The mention of Blaise is worthless, since it was smeared into the margin of the manuscript by a much later hand. Nor should you linger over Deodatus. An older hand than the one that wrote Blaise, but still not contemporary with the first hand, added him in the margin. Usuard added Tryphon. Correctly, for the Greeks venerate his memory in this month, and he suffered among them. His Acts, edited by Thierry Ruinart, attest that Tryphon and Respicius were tortured in the harshness of winter and in the violence of a storm. This agrees better with February than with November, in which the Roman Church celebrates Saint Tryphon. Bouillart.]

“At Nicaea, the passion of Saint Tryphon in the time of the emperor Decius.” And in the margin: “Blessed Blaise, bishop and martyr.” “At Latiniacum, the feast of Saint Deodatus, bishop and confessor.” At the town of Vapingum, the burial of the bishops Tigris and Remedius.

The Ides. Day 4.

[Note: The Pratis, Herinien, Tournai, Marchiennes, Poussan, Antwerp, Mainz-Lübeck, Munerat, Greven, and Molan manuscripts agree.]

[Note: Pratis correctly writes “Egypt,” as Molan also has it; in the other manuscripts it is generally Egypti or Egipti, as stated above. They also frequently stumble over the word Thmuis: Herinien has Chinuis; Tournai, Thinius; Marchiennes, Thapnis; Antwerp, Tinnius; Munerat, Thymus; and others have other forms. Although Greven wished to proceed confidently, he did not reach the truth. He writes Taphnis, adding that elsewhere it is Thynius, Thymus, or Thymnis; all these forms are mistaken. In the text the others have Filea and Filoromus, although I have no doubt that Molan and the more recent manuscripts’ reading, Philea and Phileromus, is altogether preferable. Nevertheless, I followed the oldest manuscripts—Pratis, Herinien, Tournai, and others—from which Usuard’s genuine reading must be extracted. Munerat writes Filoronius; Greven, Phileromus. Poussan seems to have fused two persons into one, whom he called Florianus, and consequently has “with whom” instead of “with them.” The fourth stumbling-block, against which nearly all repeatedly collide, is Forum Sempronii. The text has Foro Simpronii, preserving Usuard’s reading according to Pratis, Herinien, Tournai, and Molan. Marchiennes, Antwerp, Mainz-Lübeck, and Munerat have Foro-Symphronii or Simphronii. Greven has Sympronii; most disgracefully, Poussan has inphoro Simpronii. In Molan, the conjunction et before Donatus is superfluous. Trecas is the very common medieval spelling, correctly amended by Greven and Molan. Trecio in Munerat is certainly attributable to the printer. Likewise, through the copyist’s error, Aventinionis and Gallasii entered the Poussan manuscript in place of Gelasii.]

[Note: The little Roman Martyrology today speaks of the famous martyrs Philea and Philoromus in these words: “In the Egyptian city of Thmuis, blessed Philea, bishop of that city, and Philoromus, tribune, and an innumerable multitude of martyrs.” There seems no doubt that the author of this Martyrology received them from the customary source, namely Rufinus’s translation of Eusebius. Ado copied a large part not only from that ecclesiastical History but also from the Acts, which Henschenius first published and illustrated more fully under the name of the Gregory whose excellent account of the passion Rufinus says he revised, book VIII, chapter 10. Many today, however, deny that they can agree with Henschenius. Ruinart thinks that he has put forward somewhat purer Acts, though they appear acephalous, in the Sincere and Select Acts, from page 547 onward. See the same author from page 343, where he incorporates Eusebius’s eighth book into his Acts; and Tillemont, volume V, page 484 onward. Our author contracted Ado’s more expansive eulogy into very little, though whether he preserved the name of the tribune and the place of martyrdom correctly will be discussed elsewhere. Notker took rather more from the same Ado. The Hieronymian copies express the names of these martyrs so corruptly that they greatly exercised Henschenius and Florentinius—and will exercise anyone who tries to restore the words “Themoi, Philea the bishop, with his daughter” to a sensible meaning, unless, from Florentinius’s longer notice, he finally inclines to judge that “Philea the bishop with his daughter” are different from Philea and Philoromus. Our concern is only with Usuard’s text, which we have given in its purest form. Furthermore, whether the Acts published by Combefis, after our February volume had appeared, among the Selected Triumphs—perhaps translated into Latin from the Greek of Metaphrastes—are important enough for these saints to be moved, on their authority, to 18 May, as Castellanus does against the authority of our Martyrologies, will be examined elsewhere.

There is more than one error in the following class of martyrs. The location is falsely placed, since Rome is joined with Forum Sempronii; the spelling is not sufficiently correct, as the variants show; nor is the treatment of the names more exact in the Hieronymian copies. From these facts Castellanus rightly conjectures that the exemplar used by Usuard was extraordinarily damaged and corrupted. Rabanus and Notker contain more confused material, which you will find explained more clearly in the Acts; and the names of saints fabricated through scribal negligence—derived from Thmuis, Themojus, or Themius, and from Forum Sempronii, Symphorianus, and so forth—are rightly rejected. For the present, let this remain beyond dispute: our author wrote as the text reads. Wandalbert celebrates only Aquilinus, joining the first two to him:

“Then, on the day before the Nones, the kindly Aquilinus claims his place,

and Philea shines as bishop together with Philoromus.”

Aventinus, unknown to the earlier martyrologists, first obtained a place in Usuard, specifically at Troyes, although he was not buried there; I believe that he preferred that better-known city. Virtually all the manuscripts call him a bishop, so that there can be no doubt that this represents Usuard’s true reading. The author was mistaken, as Bollandus shows, but his text was improperly mutilated in the later editions of Molan. Bollandus also discusses on this very day Aventinus of Châteaudun, whose episcopal dignity may have been transferred to the earlier Aventinus; nevertheless, Castellanus places him among the *aemeri*, that is, saints of uncertain day and perhaps uncertain cult, in his Universal Martyrology.]

[Note: Antwerp-Major: “In the Egyptian city called Tinuis, the passion of blessed Philea, bishop of that city, and Phyloromus, tribune of the Roman soldiers; with them an innumerable multitude of the faithful from the same city, following the footsteps of their shepherd, was crowned with martyrdom in the persecution of Diocletian. At Troyes, the feast of Saint Aventinus, bishop and confessor, whose deeds are recorded.” In these matters it approaches textual purity, but the second announcement is missing.

Rosweyd begins: “At Rome, the holy martyrs Aquilinus, etc.,” correctly. Then follows: “In Egypt, the passion of Saint Philea, bishop, and Phyloromus, etc.,” as above. Everything else is absent.

Antwerp-Maxi­milian, Leiden-Belgium, Louvain, and the Utrecht-Belgium edition prefix to the text: “The feast of blessed Gilbert, confessor.” Their text is not entirely correct, and after “tribune” they wrongly insert “under the persecution of Decius,” which Rosweyd also indicated that he had found in Ado’s copies.

Utrecht, Leiden, Albergen, and the Danish manuscript have the same as the preceding witnesses and add at the end: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Liefard, bishop and martyr of the English.”

Centule: “In the city of Thymius, the passion of blessed Philate, bishop of that city, and Philoromus, tribune of the Roman soldiers.” In the other two copies the text is fairly pure.

Brussels, in the first announcement, is not entirely pure and inserts “under the persecution of Diocletian.” It forms the second as follows: “At Rome, the holy martyrs Aquilinus,” etc. Then: “Likewise, Symphorianus, martyr. On the same day, Saint Liphard, bishop and martyr of the English.” To the last it adds: “whose deeds are recorded.”

Hagenoyen, after reproducing the complete text, adds: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Gilbert, confessor. Likewise, Saint Luthard and Eliphard, bishops and martyrs of the English.” It is quite clear that two false names have been fabricated from one genuine name. At the end follows: “Likewise, Veronica, widow,” concerning whom see the Acts.

The Matricular, Carthusian, and Utrecht manuscripts wrongly write Silea and Florianus instead of Philea and Philoromus.

A manuscript belonging to Lord Le Mare, formerly belonging to the Canons of Saint Lazarus at Autun, reads: “At Celtic Rome, the dedication of the basilica of Saint Symphorianus, established in the suburb of that city.” What this means, I do not know.

Altemps, expanded in England: “On the same day, Saint Alelarus, bishop and confessor of Claudio-Cestria.”

Strozzi and Medici: “Likewise, the feast of Saint Gilbert, confessor.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition differs very little from the manuscripts cited above—Utrecht and the others—and only adds concerning Aventinus, “whose deeds are recorded”; instead of Liefard it writes Liophard.

Belinus, reversing Usuard’s order, first announces the martyrs of Forum Sempronii, to whom he immediately adds: “At Troyes, Aventinus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Gilbert, bishop and confessor.” The title “bishop” is wrongly assigned here; it suits none of the Gilbert under discussion today, who was the man of Sempringham. Baronius fell into another error in his Notes, as Rosweyd observed. The present Roman text reads: “On the same day, Saint Gilbert, confessor.” Its note is as follows:

“Gilbert, also called Gilibert or Guibert, was the noble founder of the monastery of Gembloux. Sigebert calls him Wibert and says that he died in the year of the Lord 962. Peter discusses him in the Catalogue, book III, chapter 83, as does Molan in the Index and in the Birthdays of the Saints of Belgium. His Life, written by Sigebert, a monk of that monastery, was included by Surius in volume III, on 23 May.”

Rosweyd responds:

“Baronius’s entire note at this place in the Roman Martyrology is irrelevant. For that Gilbert, who is celebrated on 4 February, has nothing in common with Guibert of Gembloux. That Gilbert was an Englishman, a Canon Regular, and abbot of Sempringham; his life is given in the *Legenda Angliae*, formerly compiled by the Carmelite Capgrave. He flourished around the year 1140 and died in 1175, in the 106th year of his life. He was enrolled among the saints in 1202 by Pope Innocent III. Guibert, on the other hand, was the founder of the monastery of Gembloux. He was a Belgian, in the diocese then of Liège and now of Namur; he flourished around 940 and died in 962. His feast falls on 23 May, on which day Surius gives his life; his translation is celebrated on 23 September. There was another Guibert, the thirteenth abbot of Gembloux, who wrote an apology for Sulpicius Severus; Baronius, in his Notes for 29 January, confuses him with Guibert, the founder of Gembloux.”

Thus far Rosweyd’s observation.

Greven: “Donatus, Themius.” The first name should be Donatus; the second is a badly distorted form derived from Thmuis. “Leopardus, bishop and martyr of the English. Likewise Richard, king and martyr of the English. Rembert, archbishop of Bremen and confessor, who, raised by Saint Anschar, bishop of that city, succeeded him in its government; he ruled his own people commendably and also frequently announced Christ to unbelievers. In England, Gilbert, abbot and confessor, who taught many to live according to a rule. Sanascla,” or, if you prefer, “Sanasola, priest,” hitherto unknown; “Hugh, priest,” likewise unknown. In Scotland, Modan, abbot.”

Molan, after Aventinus, adds: “whose deeds are recorded. At Binche, Ulgis, bishop and abbot of Lobbes, a man of astonishing holiness. At Soissons, Saint Vodalus, confessor. On the same day, Saint Gilbert, confessor. On the same day, Saint Lietphard, archbishop and martyr of the English.” Concerning Richard and Rembert, he follows Greven. Later editions read: “On the same day, Saint Gilbert, confessor, who rests at Sempringham, in the monastery that he founded. At Hunecourt on the same day, Saint Lietphard, etc. At the monastery of Lobbes, the burial of Saint Vulgisius, bishop and confessor. On the fourth day, Saint Isidore of Pelusium, father.” In smaller type: “Likewise, Rembert, archbishop, whose more solemn feast is on 11 June. On the same day, Metaphrastes places the penance of Theophilus, through the intercession of the most glorious Mother of God, with Eutychianus, the servant of this Theophilus, as author.”]

[Col. 0729]

In the Egyptian city called Thmuis, the passion of blessed Philea, bishop, and Philoromus, tribune, with whom an innumerable multitude of the faithful from the same city was also crowned with martyrdom, following the example of its shepherd, as the eighth book of the Ecclesiastical History relates. At Rome, at Forum Simpronii, the holy martyrs Aquilinus, Geminius, Gelasius, Magnus, and Donatus. At Troyes, Saint Aventinus, bishop and confessor.

[Note: After the commemoration of Saint Avienus, almost the entire verse was erased, and this occurred before the copy of the Martyrology was offered to Charles, since in the Dervensis manuscript Saint Aventinus is announced last. Bouillart.]

The Nones. Day 5.

[Note: The text of the Pratis, Herinien, Tournai, Marchiennes, Antwerp, Poussan, Mainz-Lübeck, Munerat, Greven, and Molan manuscripts agrees—indeed, almost that of all the others.]

[Note: Only Herinien writes “Sicily,” but it has the Pratis manuscript as its companion in “of the Catenians.” Marchiennes has Catinensium; Poussan, Chateniensium; Munerat, Catenensium. In the text I followed Tournai, Antwerp, Mainz-Lübeck, Munerat, Greven, and Molan, although the aspiration seems wholly superfluous. Again, Pratis and Herinien nearly agree: the former writes Agathes, the latter Agates; the inflection of the text is better, unless I am mistaken. I read *equuleum* with the more reliable manuscripts and printed editions: Tournai, Marchiennes, Antwerp, Poussan, and Mainz-Lübeck have *eculeum*, which recurs elsewhere more than once. *Martires*, *torciones*, *Quinciano*, *abscisionem*, *ammirabili*, *eresis*, *hereseos*, and similar forms belong to corrupt medieval spelling, which has been discussed sufficiently in the preface. Mainz-Lübeck, as it is usually the most incorrect, has here twisted several things through printer’s error; we easily corrected them from the Antwerp manuscript, to which it everywhere closely corresponds. Both manuscripts read *mirabili* instead of *admirabili* and omit the word *Arianae*, as does Pratis. All the others express it clearly, and we think it should be expressed, following Ado. Herinien, Tournai, Poussan, Munerat, Greven, Molan, and others write *Arianae*. Whichever reading one prefers is immaterial to me.]

[Note: Whoever has called Agatha the glory of the Sicilians and especially of the people of Catania—or, if you prefer, of the people of Palermo—has said enough. The calendars, such as the most ancient Carthaginian and the Frontonian, and all the Martyrologies speak of the rest. Castellanus enumerates the further honors owed to the most illustrious virgin, page 537. The Hieronymian copies agree; in almost the same words they place first: “In Sicily, at Catania, or in the city of Catana, the passion of Saint Agatha, virgin.” The little Roman Martyrology has no more: “Saint Agatha, virgin, at the city of the Catanians.” Bede’s eulogy was copied by Rabanus and also by Ado in his Martyrology, with this true and noteworthy variation: in place of the emperor Diocletian he substituted Decius, and Notker correctly followed him, as you will find demonstrated by Bollandus. Ado gives a longer account of her life among the feasts of the apostles; and our author, intent on brevity, extracted his material from the shorter encomium of the Martyrology. Since, however, he was uncertain from the disagreement between Bede and Ado which tyrant’s reign should chiefly be named, he named neither and was content with the name of the proconsul Quintianus as judge. Bollandus laboriously gathered whatever might contribute to Agatha’s deserved praise and commendation, illustrating and confirming the Acts with such evidence that, although they cannot approach the most reliable sources, they easily escape the criticism of the strictest critics. Tillemont gives a summary of them in volume III, beginning on page 409; nor should one neglect what Castellanus collects with sufficient care at the place indicated above. Thus Wandalbertus writes of Agatha:

“On the Nones, Agatha makes the peoples of Sicily subject to herself;

the virtue of the virgin is celebrated for her outstanding beauty.”

We find Avitus of Vienne, under the praenomen Alcimus, very well known among ecclesiastical poets and celebrated for other writings, mentioned in most of the Hieronymian copies. Whether he truly belongs among the additions, as Florentinius thinks, is not worth discussing at length. Rabanus also mentions him, although he is not known from Bede or Florus. It is certain that Usuard again borrowed everything here from Ado, omitting only the words “in the time of King Gundobald,” which have been restored in Notker and many fuller manuscripts, as will immediately become clear. See what is accurately discussed about Avitus in the Acts, and more briefly in Castellanus’s note, pages 541–542. In Rabanus and Notker, the ordination of Andrew the Apostle to the episcopate is marked from the Hieronymian copies, but it has nothing to do with Ado and consequently nothing with our author.]

[Note: Antwerp-Major. In the first part it describes Bede, in the second Ado; here is its text: “Near the Sicilian city of the Catanians, the passion of Saint Agatha, virgin, under the emperor Diocletian and the proconsul Quintianus. After slaps and imprisonment, after the rack and torture, after the cutting off of her breasts—but their healing by the Lord—and after being rolled over potsherds and coals, she finally died in prison. At Vienne, blessed Avitus, bishop, whose faith, diligence, and admirable teaching, in the time of King Gundobald, [defended Gaul] from the attack of the Arian heresy,” etc.

Rosweyd: In the first part it follows Ado; of the second it has only: “At Vienne, the bishop and confessor.” The saint’s name is missing.

Antwerp-Maximilian, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, Albergen, Denmark, and the Utrecht-Belgium edition are all fairly pure, except that they omit the three words cited above concerning Avitus, “in the time of King Gundobald.” They themselves write Gundebald.

Centule: “Near the Sicilian city of Catania, the passion of Saint Agatha, virgin, under the emperor Decius and the proconsul Quintianus. At Vienne, Saint Anitus [for Avitus], bishop and confessor. In the territory of the Morini, the passing of Saint Bertulf, confessor and monk, whose bones rest at Ghent.”

Brussels adds concerning Agatha: “whose name we recall in the canon of the Mass.” In the final place: “At Blandinium, Saint Bertulf, confessor.” The rest is fairly pure.

Hagenoyen, interpolated in the account of Agatha, says after “the cutting off of her breasts”: “She was imprisoned again, and visited and healed by the blessed apostle Peter. Then she was rolled over coals and glass potsherds; finally, under Quintianus,” etc.

The Victorine and Swedish Royal manuscripts, marked number 130, and the Lombard Vatican manuscript, number 5949, add at the end: “On the same day, Saint Theodore, martyr,” unknown to the others, unless someone recognizes Isidore under the name Theodore; concerning him see “Those Passed Over,” etc.

The Matricular, Carthusian, and Utrecht manuscripts place after Agatha: “Aleydis, virgin and abbess.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition, in the account of Avitus, agrees with the manuscripts of the middle class. After “coals” in the account of Agatha it inserts only: “Finally, in the time of the emperor Decius, under the judge Quintianus,” etc.

Belinus appends to Usuard’s text at the end: “In the city of Brixen, the holy confessors Geminius and Albinus, bishops, whose life is glorious for its miracles.” See below for the true names of these saints.

Greven: “On the same day, Saturus, Avitus [or was it not Revocatus?], Felix,” from the Hieronymian Martyrology. “At Landun” [I think he meant Blandinium], “Bertulf, confessor. At Poitiers, Babilonius, deacon and confessor.” Bollandus found nothing about him. “Ingela, virgin,” likewise unknown. “Alheydis (Adelheydis) and Bertrada, virgins, and Gerberta (Gerberga), their mother.” So far I have found no evidence that the last two were venerated.]

Molan, concerning Geminius and Albinus, copies Belinus. “At Vilika, the burial of Aleidis, virgin and abbess, of remarkable holiness. In the monastery of Blandinium, Saint Bertulf, confessor.” The later editions of Molan begin with Bertulf. Then: “At Soissons, Saint Vodalus, confessor.” Geminius and Albinus follow. Their true names are Ingenuinus and Albuinus; Castellanus postpones the former to 5 September. “At Vilika, the burial,” etc. Then, in smaller type: “At Alexandria, the martyrdom of Saint Isidore, glorious martyr.”]

Near the Sicilian city of the Catanians, the feast of Saint Agatha, virgin and martyr, who, after slaps and imprisonment, after the rack and tortures, after the cutting off of her breasts, and after being rolled over potsherds and coals, finally died in prison under the judge Quintianus. At Vienne, blessed Avitus, bishop and confessor, through whose faith, diligence, and admirable teaching Gaul was defended from the attack of the Arian heresy.
