The Eighth Day before the Ides. Day 6.

[Note: This is found in Pratis, Herinien, Tournai, Marchiennes, Munerat, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: Tournai and Greven have “of Cappadocia”; the spelling of the others is preferable. Enough has been said elsewhere about *eculeus*, “the rack.” The others retain *scolasticus* in the text, as all the manuscript codices have that reading. Only Molan wrote “and then on the same rack”; the others more correctly have “the same.” Herinien has Antolanus; Greven, Antolianus; Molan, Anatholianus. I believe the text is entirely pure, whatever others may say in calling it into doubt. Our Pratis copy has *existit* instead of *exstitit*, perhaps because the letters were distorted in the supposed autograph; certainly everyone reads it as in the text. “Of the Adartans and of the Trectans” is Usuard’s formula according to the manuscript codices, but it was corrected by Munerat and Molan; Henschenius should be consulted here. Greven preserved “of the Trectans,” but wrongly wrote “of the Atrebatians.” Rabanus and Notker depart from everyone else, giving Aderatus, from which Arras probably derives. Florus had written differently: Atrebata.]

[Note: The Hieronymian manuscripts of Lucca and Corbie distinctly record the passion of Saint Dorothea at Caesarea in Cappadocia; but because the former reads “Ethiopolis and the Scholasticus” in such a way that they appear to be different martyrs, the others express it more clearly: “The passion of Saints Dorothea and Theophilus the Scholasticus.” As for the fact that martyrs bearing the same names are found among several Alexandrians on 12 February, I do not see why this should create such great difficulty, since examples of martyrs with identical names are daily occurrences, especially in this Martyrology. Whether this Alexandrian virgin, whom Rufinus called Dorothea, is indicated on one day or the other, and whether Baronius believed her to be the famous Catherine, we leave to the examination of others. Our announcement unquestionably refers to the ordinary source, namely the little Roman Martyrology, which reads: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Dorothea, virgin, and Theophilus the Scholasticus.” Ado composed his encomium from the ancient Acts, and our author inserted its essence into his brief list. Rabanus has a different eulogy, in which Christa and Callista are added, both mentioned in the Acts cited above; Notker combined his account from Rabanus and Ado. Tillemont gives a sufficiently exact summary of the Acts in volume V, beginning on page 497. Wandalbertus offers only this verse today:

“On the eighth day before the Ides, the martyr Dorothea shines.”

Florentinius doubts whether Antolianus, who is placed in the Hieronymian Martyrology, is the same as our present martyr of Auvergne. The doubt seems unfounded: for Antholianus was undoubtedly taken from Ado, and from him by Usuard. Antholianus, I say, not Anatolianus—our oldest manuscripts agree with Ado himself. See Bollandus’s historical commentary on him.

Castellanus argues that Usuard lacked precision in joining Amandus with Vedastus, since they had little in common and were separated in age by almost a century and a half. Yet, if there is any fault, it should be attributed not to Usuard but to his predecessors, among whom Florus, Wandalbertus, Rabanus, and Ado show that this conjunction had long been customary. They report the two as joined either on the same day or at least in the same connection: Florus and Rabanus on this day, the other two on 26 October, as will be said there. That both saints are correctly assigned to this day could not be demonstrated more clearly than by the fact that the deaths of both fall on this very day, as you will find in the Acts at the places cited below. You will now plainly understand that Usuard once again took almost everything here from Ado if you compare their words for the days mentioned above. Rosweyd relegates them today to an appendix, in which Vedastus appears again on 1 October. Florus’s eulogy is entirely different, with the order reversed, since the younger Amandus is placed before the older Vedastus. The accounts in Rabanus and Notker are not sufficiently exact. For us, however, it is enough to have presented Usuard’s genuine text. For matters relating to the other celebrations of Vedastus, see the preliminary commentary on the Acts, sections 4 and 5, beginning on page 785; concerning Amandus, page 840. There you will find the deeds of both teachers of the Belgians wonderfully set forth and most diligently illustrated by Henschenius.]

[Note: Poussan, slightly interpolated in the account of Dorothea, mutilated the eulogies of Vedastus and Amandus.

Antwerp, Mainz-Lübeck, and Ughelli’s edition add to the pure text: “On the same day, Saints Saturninus, Theophilus, and Revocata.” Theophilus could have been omitted, since he was probably the same as the Scholasticus. See the Acts.

Antwerp-Major is defective; it reads: “Near Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Dorothea, virgin, who, under Apricius, governor of that province, was first tormented by being stretched on the rack, then beaten for a very long time with palms, and finally punished by capital sentence. At Auvergne, the feast of Antholianus, who was crowned with martyrdom at the city of Auvergne.” In the final section nothing is missing; it writes Atrebatensium instead of Adartensium.

Rosweyd gives Dorothea as the earlier witness does, but adds: “The Scholasticus Theophilus also suffered with her.” Antholianus is likewise as in the preceding witness. Then: “In Gaul, Vedastus and Amandus, bishops and confessors. Likewise, Helena, queen.” Her feast is celebrated on 18 August.

Antwerp-Maximilian, Utrecht, Leiden, Albergen, Denmark, and the Utrecht-Belgium edition place the account of Vedastus and Amandus second and add concerning the latter: “He governed the church for three years.” Then: “But, seeing his labor there to be fruitless, choosing an eremitical life, he remained in a certain cell near the city of Tours for fifteen years, clothed in a hair shirt and sustained by barley bread and water.” These matters are not correctly divided chronologically. The Danish manuscript adds, quite suitably, that Amandus was bishop of Upper Trajectum. Henschenius’s most careful commentary on these two apostles of ours should be consulted. The account of Antholianus follows, where they add, as above: “who was crowned with martyrdom near that same city.” At the end: “On the same day, Saints Saturninus, Theophilus, and Revocata.” Louvain also has the last item, together with the preceding clause about the three years, but omits the rest.

Centule: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Dorothea, virgin, under the judge Sapricius; and Theophilus the Scholasticus. At Auvergne, Saint Antholianus, bishop and martyr. At Arras, Saint Vedastus, bishop and confessor. At the monastery of Helno, Saint Amandus, bishop and confessor.”

Brussels likewise gives an expanded account of Dorothea. Concerning Vedastus and Amandus, after “glorious,” it reads: “Of these, the former governed the churches of Cambrai and Arras, while the latter governed that of Utrecht above the Meuse.” Antholianus, Saturninus, and the others are as in the manuscripts of the middle class.

Hagenoyen is more generous than all the others in expanding Dorothea’s eulogy, but the material is not important enough to deserve a place here. He omits Antholianus. His eulogy of Vedastus and Amandus is almost the same as that already given above, but adds: “Afterward he made a pilgrimage to Rome, where blessed Peter appeared to him in a vision and commanded him to preach in Gaul; he did so and died in peace.”

The Bigotian manuscript, formerly belonging to the Celestine Fathers, and the Strozzi and Medici manuscripts: “On the same day, Saints Saturninus, Theophilus, and Revocata,” as above.

The Swedish Royal manuscript, marked number 130: “On the same day, Soteris, virgin.” The Vatican manuscript, marked number 5949, gives the location: “At Rome, the passion of Saint Soteris, virgin.” But in this latter manuscript the commemoration of Saints Vedastus and Amandus is absent. Concerning Soteris, see the tenth day of this month.

The Castle of Charles manuscript: “In the territory of Lyons, the feast of Saint Amandus, bishop and confessor.” Could this be Amantius of Tricastinum? Certainly it cannot in any way refer to Amandus of Utrecht, or of Strasbourg, or of Worms, nor finally to Amandus or Marcus Amandus, concerning whom Bollandus treats among the saints passed over.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins with a feast proper to Cologne: “At Cologne Agrippina, the translation of the ashes of Saint Pantaleon, martyr, which took place together with certain relics of Saint Quirinus, martyr.” The material inserted into Dorothea’s eulogy is more authentic in Ado. In the accounts of Vedastus and Amandus, Antholianus, Saturninus, and the others, it differs nothing from those cited above.

The first edition of Belinus is defective in that after “of the Atrebatians” it does not say “the latter of the two governed the church of Utrecht.” It adds at the end: “On the same day, Saints Saturninus, Theophilus, and Revocata”; the second edition further adds: “And on the same day, Saint Soteris, virgin.”

Greven: “On the same day, Saints Saturninus, Theophilus, Revocatus, and Soteris, virgin. Lubentius, priest and confessor, who, entrusted by blessed Martin of Tours for upbringing to Saint Maximinus of Trier, after giving examples of an eminent way of life, rested in peace. His body was placed on a boat, which, against the force of the Rhine, ascended onto the land, driven even upward by invisible power. He is celebrated on 13 October. Christa and Callista, sisters. After they had apostatized from the faith, they were converted through Saint Dorothea and deserved to attain the palm of martyrdom. At the monastery of Eike, Harlindis and Relindis, virgins.” See the Acts. “At Silvolde, Gerwis, virgin,” of whom nothing has yet been discovered. “At Cologne Agrippina, the translation of the ashes of blessed Pantaleon, martyr.” This belongs to his feast day, 27 July.]

[Col. 0738D] Molanus’s entry on Saint Dorothea is fuller than Ado’s, just as the entries on Amandus and Vedastus are; they will be read more satisfactorily in Molanus himself. It continues:

“On this day, Saturninus, Theophilus, and Revocatus. At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery bearing the same name, the passion of Saint Soter, virgin. At Praeneste, Saint Garinus, bishop and confessor. At the monastery of Eike, Harlindis and Relindis, virgins.”

Then, in smaller type:

“At Maastricht, the feast of all the bishops of Maastricht: Servatius, Monulphus, Gondulphus, Martin, Valentinus, Candidus, and the rest.”

The later editions abridge the entries, after which they add:

“In the territory of Loon, near the village of Maes-Eike, at the monastery of Eike, Herlindis and Relindis, virgins.”

Concerning Guarinus, see above.

“On the sixth day, Saint Buculus, father and bishop of Smyrna.”

Instead of Revocatus, he more correctly gives Revocata here.

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Dorothea, virgin, who was first tortured on the rack, then beaten for a long time with palms, and finally punished by beheading. During her confession of faith, a certain Theophilus, a scholar, was converted; soon afterward he too was tortured most cruelly on the rack and finally struck down with the sword. At Clermont, Blessed Antholianus, martyr. On the same day, Saints Vedastus and Amandus, bishops, whose life and death alike were glorious through many miracles. [Note: [Col. 0735C] Sollerius observes that the autograph has *existit* instead of *exstitit*. What a diligent author! He overlooks nothing, and [Col. 0736C] therefore conjectures that the letters of the autograph are distorted. Nothing could be emptier than this conjecture.] Of these, the former governed the church of Arras, the latter that of Maastricht.

### The Seventh Day before the Ides. Day 7

[Note: [Col. 0739]

Pratensis, Herinien­sis, Tornacensis, Antwerp, Maximilian-Lübeck, Muneratus, the first edition of Belinus, Grevenus, and Molanus agree. Antwerp-Maximilian likewise agrees with them.]

[Note: [Col. 0739A]

Pratensis writes *Britaniis*; Muneratus, *Britannia*; the others have the reading in the text. Belinus alone has “in the city of Augsburg.” Utrecht gives *Augalii*; the others have *Augulii*; the first edition of Belinus has *Aulei*. Some prefer *Augurii* or *Atigulii*; the correct name is given in the marginal list. Enough has already been said elsewhere about the spelling of *martyrium*. Antwerp and Maximilian-Lübeck, together with most manuscripts of the Middle Ages, have *complens* instead of *explens*. Only Tornacensis reads *Moisetis* for *Moysetis*. *Primus* for *primum* is an error in the Danish manuscript. All read *heremo*; Molanus more correctly has *eremo*, but we preferred to follow the manuscript reading. Pratensis alone omitted the word *magnifice*. Manuscripts that have been less thoroughly corrected, such as Antwerp-Maximilian and others, incorrectly have *innotuit* for *innotuerat*. I wrote *Sarracenorum*, following all the manuscripts except Pratensis and Molanus. Antwerp and Maximilian-Lübeck suppress three words, namely *grandi ex parte*; in Muneratus there is a solecism, *grandi cum ex parte*.]

[Note: [Col. 0739A]

Nowhere do the Hieronymian copies define a saint more clearly and precisely than when, on this day, they identify Augulus: “In Britain, in the city of Augusta, the feast of Augulus, bishop.” The reading *Auguria* in the Echternach manuscript could easily have arisen through a simple corruption of *Augusta*. Bede agrees with this: “In Britain, at Augusta, the feast of Augustus, bishop and martyr”; here one sees another scribal error, *Augusti* for *Auguli*. There can be no serious doubt about this, since Rabanus, who reports Bede’s material with the greatest care, distinctly reads *Auguli*. Ado followed Bede almost word for word. Our author, contrary to his usual practice, added something of his own, but it applies no more to Augulus than to anyone else, since he merely paraphrastically explained the title “martyr.” Henschenius investigates learnedly which Augusta of Britain this was and in what period the martyr lived. I entirely fail to see why Castellanus attacks him on page 558: whether one assigns the name Augusta to London or to York, the Acts will scarcely contradict it. Thus Wandalbertus addresses the saint himself in a single verse:

> Augulus, by conquering the world, triumphs through seven days.

[Col. 0740A] Moses was taken from the Small Roman Martyrology, where he is commemorated in these words:

“Saint Moysetis, who, at the request of Mauvia, queen of the Saracens, was made bishop of that people.”

Ado composed his entry from ecclesiastical records, and our author elegantly adapted it to his customary brevity. How famous the name of this great man, the peacemaker, was under the emperor Valens can easily be gathered from Socrates, Sozomen, and the other Greek writers cited by Henschenius. From the same sources one can expose the error of those who, following more recent martyrologists, confused this Moysetis with another man of the same name, an Ethiopian, as is accurately explained in the Acts. See also Tillemont, volume VII, beginning at page 593. From him I would have you consider more carefully how appropriately he is counted among the inhabitants of Carmel by Alegrus and his associates. In any case, the memory of Moysetis was also exceedingly famous throughout the West, as is proved most clearly by our martyrologies. Notkerus, however, is gravely mistaken when, copying Ado’s entry, he transfers Moysetis to Britain—unless we should say that this happened through a scribe’s negligence, so that, with Augulus’s name omitted or erased, the homeland of one passed over to the other.

[Note: [Col. 0739C]

Marchianus begins with the local feast: “The translation of the body of Saint Rictrudis.” In the rest he is a very pure follower of Usuardus. See 12 May.

Pulsanensis, after Augulus, continues as follows:

“Likewise, Saint Moysetis, bishop. On the same day, the burial of Blessed Laurentius, bishop of Siponto.”

This is correct, as may be seen in the Acts; the following material is not:

“In the district of Malens, Saint Austreberta, virgin, at the place called Pauliacus.”

The first part of the sentence is corrupt: instead of *Malensi*, read *Rothomagensi*. Similar errors occur elsewhere, when the initial letters of a word have been erased and the final letters are sometimes corrupted as well. Thus here I believe that, instead of *Malensis*, *Magensis* was originally read. See 10 February.

Antwerp-Major:

“In Britain, in the city of Augusta, the feast of Saint Augulus, bishop and martyr. On the same day, Saint Moysetis, venerable bishop and confessor. In the province of Asia, Saint Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis, a most learned man.”

See the Acts.

Rosweyd:

“In Britain,” and so forth, as in the preceding text.

“Likewise, Saint Moysetis, who at first led a solitary life in the desert and had become greatly renowned through his merits, virtues, and the signs that God performed through him. Later, at the request of Auvia, queen of the Saracens, he was made bishop of that people; he kept inviolate the fellowship of the Catholic faith and converted a large part of the people over whom he had been appointed bishop to the faith of Christ. Thus he rested in peace.”

From Ado.

Centulensis first announces Augulus in Ado’s words, almost as do the two manuscripts cited immediately above. Then:

“In Asia Minor, Saint Apollinaris, bishop, a most learned man.”

It mutilates Moysetis’s entry in this way:

“On the same day, Saint Moysetis, venerable bishop, who converted a large part of the Saracen people.”

Brussels writes *Anguli* for *Auguli*; otherwise its announcement is not Usuardine but also Adonian. From the same Ado it has interpolated Moysetis’s entry. Then, with others, it adds:

“In Asia, Saint Apollinaris, a most learned man, bishop of the city of Hierapolis and confessor.”

Finally, at the end:

“Likewise, Queen Helena.”

We said yesterday, in the Additions, that her feast is 18 August.

[Col. 0740D] Hagenoyen is indeed Usuardine, but reports the wording somewhat more confusedly. At the end he incorrectly appends:

“Likewise, Saints Theophilus, Saturninus, and Revocata, martyrs.”

See what was said on the preceding day in the Additions.

Victorin, at the end:

“In Asia, Saint Apollinaris, bishop [Col. 0741A] of Hierapolis, a most learned man. On the same day, Saint Austreberta, virgin, and Saint Theodore, martyr,”

without doubt the Heracleian Theodore, one of the four Great Martyrs, concerning whom see the Acts.

The matricularies of the Carthusians of Utrecht insert between Moysetis and Augulus another Moses, abbot. I believe this is the man who completed his martyrdom in Egypt with six companions. More recent martyrologists incorrectly assigned him to Scythopolis in Egypt, although, from the Lives of the Fathers quoted here by Henschenius at page 46 and elsewhere, it is clear that he was killed not at Scythopolis—which is the metropolis of Second Palestine—but in the desert of Scete, by marauding barbarians, together with six brothers. See the additional material collected by Henschenius from Cassian, Sozomen, and others.

Camberiensis of the monastery of the Conventual Saint Mary:

“At the monastery of Altimlarense [he means Altovillarense], the arrival of Saint Helena, empress.”

This will be discussed on 18 August.

[Col. 0741B] Regin-Suec., under number 130:

“On the same day, Saint Austreberta, virgin, and Saint Theodore, martyr.”

See above.

Vatican manuscript 5949:

“In Gaul, Saint Austreberta, virgin.”

I have already said that this belongs to 10 February.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition, nearly pure in its first announcement, adds the following to the second after “had become greatly renowned”:

“After he had converted to the faith of Christ the people of the Saracens, over whom he had been made bishop, he returned to the desert, where he was killed by barbarians together with six hermits.”

The matters confused here are explained in the Acts. It continues:

“In the province of Asia, Saint Apollinaris, bishop and confessor of the city of Hierapolis, a most learned man. On the same day, Saint Richard, king, father of Saint Walburga, who abandoned everything he possessed for Christ and undertook a very long pilgrimage, and finally died happily.”

The second edition of Belinus, at the end:

“On the same day, the arrival of the body of Saint Helena at the monastery of Altovillare; while she was the mother of the emperor Constantine, by living religiously she deserved to attain the honor of becoming the discoverer of the most sacred cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

See what was said above.

Grevenus:

“Likewise, Anatholius, Ammon, Statianus, and Lucius,”

from the Hieronymian Martyrology.

“In England, Odo, bishop and confessor. In the same place, William, bishop and confessor.”

See the index of the Omitted Saints concerning both.

Concerning Apollinaris and Richard, it is almost the same as in the Lübeck-Cologne edition. The following are added:

“Amantius, bishop and confessor. Frindrudis, virgin. Apollonius, senator and martyr, father of Saint Apollonia.”

See also the cited index concerning these three, and specifically concerning the last, in that same index under 9 February.

Molanus:

“At Binche, Amolwinus, bishop and abbot of Lobbes.”

He copied Belinus concerning Helena. At the end, in smaller type:

“On the same day, Richard, king, father of Saint Walburga, who undertook a very long pilgrimage for Christ.”

In the other editions it begins as follows:

“At Comines, the feast of Saint Chrysolius, [Col. 0742B] who came here, sent by Pope Marcellus to preach.”

It should be noted that this is correctly placed on this day, whereas in the first edition it is placed on the following day, with the clause:

“who, known to Dionysius, came here.”

It continues:

“At Binche, from Lobbes, Blessed Amolwinus, bishop and confessor. In England, Saint Odo, bishop and confessor. On the seventh day, Saint Parthenius, bishop of Lampsacus, and Saint Luke, in Storo of Greece. At Marchiennes, the translation of the body of Saint Rictrudis.”

Helena has already been discussed. Later, in smaller type:

“In Phrygia, the feast of the blessed and numerous martyrdom suffered together by an entire city of Christian citizens. Its author and leader was a man distinguished for piety and religion, named Adauctus. When the whole people followed his steadfastness in confessing Christ, men with women, the children with the old, the city with its citizens, they were burned by the fire that had been set, so that no one at all departed from that city, even when the opportunity was offered. On the same day, at the city of Lucca, Richard, king, etc.,”

as above.

[Col. 0739]

In Britain, in the city of Augusta, the feast of Blessed Augulus, bishop, who, completing the course of time through martyrdom, deserved to receive eternal rewards. Likewise, Saint Moysetis, bishop. At first he led a solitary life in the desert and had become greatly renowned through signs and virtues [Note: [Col. 0739] Only Pratensis, as Sollerius observes, omitted the word *magnifice*. I attribute the false observation either to Castellanus or to the person who first transcribed the manuscript at Bollandus’s command. Bouillart.] but afterward converted a large part of the people of the Saracens, over whom he had been made bishop, to the faith of Christ, and thus, glorious in merits, rested in peace.

### The Sixth Day before the Ides. Day 8

[Note: [Col. 0741]

From Tornacensis, Pulsanensis, Albergen­sis, the Danish manuscript, Muneratus, Grevenus, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0741D]

The others in the text have Dionysius and Aemilianus, following Tornacensis, Pulsanensis, Muneratus, and others. Albergen­sis, the Danish manuscript, and Grevenus write the inferior form *Dyonisii*; Molanus correctly has *Dionysii et Aemiliani*. Pulsanensis contains the error *Juliani*. The name of the Alexandrian martyr has been corrupted in nearly eighteen different ways in the Acts. Grevenus reads *Coyntae*; Molanus, *Cointhae*; Tornacensis, *Conitae*; Pulsanensis, *Chontae*; Muneratus, *Corinthae*. I preferred the reading *Cointae*, with Albergen­sis and the Danish manuscript, because it is the reading of the Small Roman Martyrology and is closer to the Latin *Quintae*, whatever Ado may have written differently; choose whichever you prefer. Enough has been said elsewhere about the word *idola*. Muneratus incorrectly has *correctam* for *correptam*. Pulsanensis mutilates the sense by writing *execrasset* instead of *execrans recusaret*, and omits the words “fastening fetters to her feet.” The Danish manuscript’s error, *disc­erserunt*, has been corrected by assuming that the *p* was misread.]

There is difficulty concerning the placement of Salomon, in which a few manuscripts differ from all the others. Among the purer witnesses, Marchianensis reads:

“In the province of Lusitania, in the city of Corduba”;

Rosweyd more briefly:

“In the province of Lusitania, Saint, etc.”

The Pratensis manuscript largely agrees, reading:

“In the province of Lusitania, in the city of Corduba.”

Castellanus therefore believed that Usuardus had written it in this way. When I objected that it was absurd to assign Corduba, the seat of the Saracen kings, to a region so far removed from it, he replied that the connection of disparate matters proved nothing more than that Usuardus had been an ignorant geographer. I, however, am not persuaded that the author could have made such a blunder concerning provinces that he had almost seen with his own eyes. I therefore judge that the preceding words do not belong to Usuardus and that those manuscripts, which differ from the others in this respect, cannot be counted among the pure witnesses. There is also another addition in the Pratensis manuscript, which we shall discuss in the Additions.

[Note: [Col. 0743A]

The principal and more distinct information about these three Armenian martyrs is obtained solely from the Hieronymian copies, which at least state their homeland, whereas the Small Roman Martyrology omits it. The former read:

“In Lesser Armenia, the feast of Dionysius, Emilianus, and Sebastian.”

The latter gives only the names:

“Saints Dionysius, Aemilianus, and Sebastian.”

Ado consulted the former source and shaped the announcement that was copied almost word for word by Usuardus and Notkerus. Whether anything beyond their names and province is known about them, and whether they were ennobled by their contest—for they are considered martyrs—you will learn from Bollandus in the Acts. See also Florentinius’s note, which further confirms Bollandus’s opinion. Among other things, he carefully observes that the manuscript Acts of Saint Aemilianus in his possession were so corrupt in places that their meaning could scarcely be understood. Indeed, something that escaped the very sharp-eyed Bollandus: with only the names changed, they contain the same material that appears in Peter de Natalibus’s Life of Saint Pantaleon, and, what is more, are constructed in almost the same words. This is what he says. Whether this is sufficient to remove Jacobilli’s Acts from our work will be seen in the Supplement. In Wandalbertus’s verse there was no place for Sebastian; he sings as follows:

[Col. 0744A]

> Dionysius and Aemilianus adorn the sixth day.

I have no doubt that Cointa, or Quinta, the faithful woman, was taken from Rufinus. Thus the first author of the Small Roman Martyrology speaks of her:

“At Alexandria, Saint Cointa, martyr.”

Notkerus copied Ado’s encomium in full, which was composed almost entirely from the words of the celebrated Rufinus; our author reproduced it with scarcely any alteration. Above, under 31 January, when we were discussing the old man Metra, we cited the famous letter of Dionysius of Alexandria, from which Cointa on this day and Apollonia on the following day were taken. See the passage of Ruinart indicated there, or rather the original source in Rufinus, Book VI, chapter 31. There is another translation of Eusebius by other hands, from which Cointa’s martyrdom is also variously explained in Bollandus. Whether the title “virgin” can be assigned to her remains uncertain. Salomon, martyr of Corduba, is reported only by Usuardus, presumably because he possessed a more recent memory of that Arab persecution; for we know of no other Salomon who suffered for the faith at Corduba. By others, and by the modern Roman Martyrology, he is placed on 13 March with Rudericus, a priest, as may be seen in the Acts. The remaining matters that may belong here are discussed under the Variants.]

[Note: [Col. 0743B]

Pratensis, in addition to the inserted words discussed under the Variants, adds at the end:

“At Verdun, Saint Paul, bishop and confessor.”

Several other Usuardine manuscripts also speak of this Paul, but in such a different form that it is plainly an addition.

Herinien­sis, after the pure and complete text, treats of the same Paul in this wording:

“At Verdun, Blessed Paul, bishop and monk, restorer and ruler of that church.”

Antwerp-Maximilian, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition differ from the preceding only in adding, after “ruler,” the epithet “distinguished.”]

[Col. 0743C] Marchianensis and Rosweyd have the form described under the Variants, with no other addition, and are therefore closest to the pure text.

Antwerp-Major is almost genuine in the Armenian martyrs and in Cointa, whom it calls Conida; it says nothing about Salomon.

Centulensis, Usuardine in its first announcement, continues:

“Saint Chointa, virgin and martyr. At Verdun, Saint Paul, bishop and confessor. At the city of Concordia [for Corduba], Saint Salomon, martyr.”

Antwerp, Maximilian-Lübeck, and Ughellian, after reporting the pure text, append:

“At Rome, Paul, bishop, Lucius, and Cyriacus.”

Concerning this association of the three saints, see Bollandus and Castellanus here; it is repeated far too often below.

Brussels, usually purer, inserts after “they tore her apart”:

“In Spain, in the city,” etc.

At the end:

“At Rome, [Col. 0743D] Saint Paul, bishop and confessor. And Saints Lucius and Cyriacus.”

Hagenoyen turns Cointa into Torrita; otherwise he is close to the pure text. At the end, however:

“At Brescia [or perhaps Pavia?], Iventius, bishop and confessor. At Rome, Saints Paul, bishop, Lucius, and Cyriacus, martyrs.”

See the writers mentioned above.

The first edition of Belinus writes *Coytae*; the second, *Corinthae*. In the rest it adds the same material as Antwerp and Maximilian-Lübeck.

Aquicinctensis:

“At Rome, Paul, bishop, Lucius, and Cyriacus.”

The same wording has everywhere been transmitted from one witness to another.

The matricularies of the Carthusians of Utrecht begin:

“Paul, bishop and martyr. Mengoldus, soldier and martyr. Saint Helena, queen, mother of the emperor Constantine.”

Then:

“Dionysius, etc.”

They say nothing about Cointa or Salomon.

Codex 3 of the Bigotian manuscripts, marked D. 9:

“On the same day, Saint Cuthmann. The name”

is written differently by others.

The D. Le Mare manuscript, note C, formerly Franciscan:

“At Rome, Paul, bishop, Lucius, and Cyriacus.”

The Vatican manuscript 5949 adds only:

“At Rome, Saint Paul, bishop,”

as do the Hieronymian copies.

Altemps:

“In the territory of Dol, Saint Jacutus, confessor.”

Concerning him, see the Omitted Saints for this day.

“At the monastery of Fécamp, Saint Geuthmann, bishop and confessor of Limoges.”

In the very ancient Missal of Jumièges he is called Cuthmann, confessor. The Bigotian manuscript reads almost the same above.

[Col. 0744C] Strozzi and Medici:

“Likewise, at Rome, Saints Paulinus, bishop, Lucius, and Cyriacus, martyrs. Likewise, Saint Eventius, or Inventius, bishop and confessor. And Saint Helena, virgin.”

It is sufficiently clear that this Paulinus is the Paul of the other witnesses. I do not know which Helena the virgin is.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition, nowhere more similar to Usuardus, adds at the end only the martyrs mentioned above:

“At Rome, Saints Paul, bishop, Lucius, and Cyriacus, martyrs.”

Grevenus announces the same persons in the same manner. Then:

“Likewise, Pope Julius,”

whom Ado and Usuardus place on the day before the Ides of April.

“Eudoaldus, bishop of Lyon and confessor.”

He is probably Chagnoaldus of Laon, concerning whom see 6 September.

“Paul, bishop of Verdun and distinguished restorer. Thyadgermus, second bishop of Halberstadt and confessor, resting at Werden.”

See Bollandus in the index of the Omitted Saints.

“Iventius, bishop of Pavia and confessor. Chunibaldus, confessor. Mengoldus, soldier. Gislarius, priest.”

Concerning this man and Chunibaldus, see the cited index.

“The translation of Helena, the most Christian queen.”

Her translation and life will be given on 18 August.

Molanus:

“At Rome, Paul, bishop, Lucius, and Cyriacus. On the same day, the burial of Saint Paul, bishop of Verdun,” etc.

“Likewise, at Huy, the feast of Blessed Mengoldus, glorious martyr. The feast of Saint Chrysolius, who, known to Dionysius, came here, sent by Pope Marcellus to preach.”

The last items are corrected in the other editions and more properly transferred to the preceding day. In those editions it reads:

“On the same day, the feast of Saint Nicetius, bishop of Besançon and confessor, a man of outstanding holiness. On the same day, the burial of Saint Paul, etc. On the eighth day, Saint Theodore, the Great Martyr, commander of the army,”

concerning whom we spoke yesterday.

“At Rome, Paul,” etc.

Finally, in smaller type:

“In Bithynia, Blessed Eugenius and Maria, his daughter, concerning whom Metaphrastes writes.”

Bollandus assigns them to 17 July, because on that day they were translated to Venice.

In Lesser Armenia, the feast of Saints Dionysius, Emilianus, and Sebastian. On the same day at Alexandria, Saint Cointa, martyr: the pagans seized her and led her to the idols, compelling her to worship; when she, execrating them, refused, they fastened fetters to her feet and dragged her through the streets of the whole city, tearing her apart by a horrible punishment. [Bouillart: [Note: [Col. 0741] Sollerius has such an opinion of Usuard that he would not allow him to offend against the rules of geography; hence he denies that Usuard wrote Lusitania, because he placed Corduba in it. Whether Usuard’s memory failed, I do not know. Certainly his hand slipped. BOUILLART.] In the province of Lusitania, in the city of Corduba, Saint Salomon, martyr. And in italic type: *At Verdun, Saint Paul, bishop and confessor.*] At the city of Corduba, Saint Salomon, martyr.

### The Fifth Day before the Ides. Day 9

[Note: [Col. 0745A]

Only the manuscripts Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Muneratus, Grevenus, and Molanus report the pure text. Most of the other manuscripts chiefly exceed it by adding, whether from Pratensis or elsewhere, Saint Ansbert, bishop of Rouen, as you will soon learn from the Additions.]

[Note: [Col. 0745B]

The virgin’s true name is Apollonia, not *Appolonia*, as Muneratus has it, nor *Apolonia*, as Grevenus does. For *vivam se eam*, Heriniensis has *vivam eam se*; Grevenus and Molanus, *eam se vivam*. All are correct, and both later witnesses also follow Ado more closely here in inserting the word *ageret*, reading “what she might do, within herself,” and so forth. I readily admit that this contributes to clarity, but all the manuscripts, both handwritten and printed, plainly resist that reading. Muneratus has the worse form *paululum quidem*, and *exilivit* for *prosilivit*. The manuscripts consistently express *Suevo*, not *Sueno*, as Castellanus wants. Tornacensis has *Sievo*; Muneratus, *Sieno*; Grevenus, *Suevi*. These should be rejected, as should *Avinionis* for *Ammonis* in the Muneratus mentioned above. See in the Acts the other inflections of *Suevo* or *Sueno*, where you will discover that the place is unknown.]

[Col. 0746B] In our Pratensis copy, *Fontenella, Saint Ansbert, bishop and confessor* is appended at the end. But since those words have been underlined by Sirmondus and are noted as occurring in the text of manuscript B, in the same hand, this is evidence that they were added to the purported original manuscript. I therefore judged that manuscript should be retained among the pure witnesses. The announcement in question could have been taken from some Hieronymian manuscript, especially the Lucca manuscript, formerly belonging to Saint Wandregisilus, where its location is correctly marked:

“At Altum-Mons above the Sambre.”

But whoever enlarged that manuscript shaped the announcement differently, and from it it passed into other manuscripts, where it is not expressed uniformly, as will be clear from the Additions.]

[Note: [Col. 0745B]

This is that remarkable Apollonia, a virgin of advanced age and an illustrious martyr, whom, on the preceding day, we said had been taken from the cited passage of Rufinus together with Metra, or Metranus, and Cointa, or Quinta. She was first extracted from that source by the author of the Small Roman Martyrology:

“At Alexandria, Apollonia, virgin,”

with the day selected, I believe, at his discretion. Ado again composed an entry for this day from a translation of the celebrated Rufinus; Notkerus copied it in full, while our author shortened it only very slightly. In this series of martyrologists Apollonia is celebrated, but she is unknown to the Hieronymian manuscripts, Bede, Florus, Rabanus, and Wandalbertus. I cannot sufficiently conjecture why Baronius places the martyrdom of this saint under Decius, just as he does those of Metra and Cointa, since it is perfectly clear from the often-cited letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Fabius of Antioch that these events occurred during the fury of the pagan populace against the Christians, while Philip was still alive. We assigned the cause and date of her passion in our Treatise on the Alexandrian Patriarchs, no. 164; these matters are explained more fully by Tillemont, volume III, beginning at page 293. Whether, besides these, other Acts fabricated later may be admitted, and whether a second Apollonia may properly be assigned to the time of Julian, see Bollandus and below in the Additions of Grevenus.]

[Col. 0746B] In the Lucca Hieronymian copy, the names of Ammon and Alexander have been wrongly divided by the insertion of the announcement cited above:

“Saint Asbert, for Ansbert, bishop.”

The remaining witnesses keep the two together, with *Sueno* or *Suevo* near Cyprus. The Echternach manuscript omits the place of the contest and adds twenty unnamed companions. You will find these men and others confused by later writers restored to their proper classes in the Acts, with several points also accurately noted in Florentinius’s commentary. We are certain that Usuardus took his announcement from some Hieronymian manuscript in which he probably found it just as we read it in the text, unless perhaps he himself placed one before the other. Rabanus copied his material from the same source; Notkerus copied from him. Both explicitly agree with Usuardus in reading *Suevo*, while the editor marks *Soli* in the margin with an asterisk, perhaps because he found it elsewhere; from there the reading probably passed into the modern Roman Martyrology. Wandalbertus speaks only of Ammon, but since three persons of the same name are commemorated on this very day in the Hieronymian manuscripts, I leave it to others to determine which one he intended. His verse is:

> The devout prayers of the faithful commemorate blessed Ammon in groups of five.

[Note: [Col. 0745D]

Marchianus, pure in the text, adds:

“On the same day, Saint Ansbert, bishop of Magensis.”

I believe that, after the first letters had been erased, an ignorant scribe formed *magnensis* from *magensis*, which is the final part of *Rothomagensis*. I do not see how this can otherwise be understood.

Antwerp and Maximilian-Lübeck add:

“At the monastery of Fontenella, Saint Ansbert, archbishop of Rouen and confessor.”

Pulsanensis begins:

“At Canusium, a city of Apulia, the burial of Blessed Sabinus, bishop and confessor.”

It mentions Apollonia without an encomium. Then:

“At Cyprus, Saints Ammon and Alexander. On the same day, Blessed Ansbert, archbishop of the church of Rouen.”

Antwerp-Major:

“At Alexandria, Saint Apollonia, virgin and martyr.”

The remainder of the text is absent, replaced by:

“In the province of Pontus, Saint Athenodorus, bishop, brother of Blessed Gregory, who was called the Theologian. At the monastery of Fontanella, the departure of Blessed Ansbert, bishop.”

It omits the words that others explain more clearly:

“of the church of Rouen, etc.”

Rosweyd, pure enough in the first part, adds:

“At Blandinium, Saint Ansbert, bishop and confessor. At Cyprus, Alexander, martyr, and Ammon, confessor.”

The title “martyr” suits both equally.

Antwerp-Maximilian, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition add to the pure text:

“On the same day, at the monastery of Fontenella, the feast of Saint Ansbert, bishop and confessor of Rouen.”

Albergen­sis and the Danish manuscript treat of “Paul of Verdun,” etc.

Centulensis lacks Apollonia’s encomium. Then:

“In the city of Gneocaesarea in Pontus, Saint Athenodorus, bishop, brother of Blessed Gregory. At the city of Rouen, Saint Ansbert, archbishop and confessor.”

Brussels begins:

“The commemoration of Blessed Mary, ever-virgin.”

I believe this indicates the octave of the Purification. It is moderately interpolated in Apollonia’s entry.

“At Cyprus,” etc., as in Pulsanensis.

It continues:

“On the same day, the translation of Saint Ansbert, archbishop and confessor of Rouen, who had been sent into exile at the monastery of Altimont, buried at Fontenella, and afterward translated from there on this day to Blandinium. At Verdun,” etc.

See above.

Hagenoyen adds to Apollonia’s encomium:

“And they customarily invoke her when suffering from toothache.”

At the end:

“Likewise, at the monastery of Fontenella, the burial of Saint Ansbert, archbishop of Rouen. At Verdun, etc. In Bavaria, Alton, confessor.”

He was abbot at Altenmünster.

Aquicinctensis:

“On the same day, Saint Ansbert, archbishop of Rouen.”

Victorin and the Swedish Register, under number 130:

“In the province of Pontus, Saint Athenodorus, bishop. At the city of Canusium, Saint Sabinus, bishop.”

The matricularies of the Carthusians of Utrecht:

“Apollonia, virgin and martyr, with many others: Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, exhorter of the aforementioned martyrs.”

See the observations.

The Vatican manuscript 5949, in Lombard script, formerly Beneventan and already often cited above, places first:

“The feast of Saint Sabinus, [Col. 0747C] bishop and confessor of Canusium.”

Ughellian:

“At the monastery of Fontenella, Saint Ansbert, bishop of Rouen and confessor.”

Strozzi and Medici:

“In the East [why not in the South?], Saint Sabinus, bishop. At the monastery of Fontenella, [Col. 0748A] Saint Ansbert, bishop and confessor of Rouen.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition writes concerning Ansbert, Paul of Verdun, and Athenodorus as above. At the end:

“On the same day, Blessed Alton, confessor.”

Belinus, in both editions, writes *Amsubertus* for *Ansbertus*. The earlier edition has:

“Suevo in Egypt,”

concerning whom see the Acts.

Grevenus:

“The octave of the Purification of Blessed Mary. Ammon, Thomas, and thirty-seven others. Likewise, Emilianus.”

Here the names from the Hieronymian Martyrology have been confused.

“At the monastery of Fontenella, Saint Ansbert, bishop of Rouen, who, when he had been betrothed to a noble girl named Angadrisina and both preferred celibacy, obtained through prayer that she should become extremely ugly and leprous. But afterward, when she had been consecrated to Christ by Saint Audoenus, archbishop of Rouen, she was restored to her former beauty. Ansbert, meanwhile, first became a monk under Saint Wandregisilus, abbot of Fontenella; then he became abbot; finally, succeeding Saint Audoenus worthily in the episcopate, he rested in peace. In Britain, Teyllianus, confessor. In Ireland, Trovanius, bishop and confessor. In the province of Pontus, Blessed Athenodorus, bishop and confessor, brother of Blessed Gregory of Nyssa. Alton, confessor. In Ireland, Tarabata, virgin.”

Thus far both editions, 1515 and 1521. The latter adds the following, plainly apocryphal:

“On the same day, another Saint Apollonia, virgin and martyr, whom Julius Caesar first had beaten with rods for the faith of Christ, then ordered to be suspended on the rack and flayed alive, with pieces cut from her flesh; finally, after her teeth had been cruelly pulled out, he had her pierced through with a sword and made her a martyr of Christ.”

See Bollandus and Castellanus here.

Molanus, first edition:

“At the monastery of Fontenella, Saint Ansbert, archbishop of the holy Gallican see of Rouen.”

In the other editions:

“At Ghent, at Blandinium, from the monastery of Fontenella, Saint Ansbert, archbishop of the holy Gallican see. At Huy, Saint Maingoldus, duke and martyr, son of Hugh, king of the English,”

whom the first edition more correctly places on the preceding day.

“On the ninth day, Saint Nicephorus, martyr.”

This is the man who won the palm before Sapricius.

[Col. 0745]

At Alexandria, the passion of Saint Apollonia, virgin, whose persecutors first knocked out all her teeth. Then, when they threatened to burn her alive unless she uttered impious words with them, she deliberated briefly within herself, suddenly broke free from the hands of the impious, and leaped into the fire they had prepared. At Suevo in Cyprus, Saints Ammon and Alexander.

[Bouillart adds in cursive type: At Fontenella, Saint Ansbert, bishop and confessor.]

### The Fourth Day before the Ides. Day 10

[Note: [Col. 0747] The text is found in Pratensis, Marchianensis, Rosweyd, Antwerp, Maximilian-Lübeck, Muneratus, Grevenus, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0747D]

It should have read “Irenaeus and Hyacinth,” as Molanus corrected it. But since no manuscripts read it so, I thought the medieval reading should be preserved more scrupulously. Munerat, instead of *Zotici*, incorrectly has *Zonei*. Likewise *Hyrenei*, which is also found in Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck. In Pratensis, *Jacinti* appears for *Jacincti*. *Amancii* for *Amantii* is a common error in many manuscripts. Marchianensis writes *Soteris*; this reading would be preferable if all the manuscripts did not oppose it. Pratensis alone has *Casinum*, correctly, I think, but all the others have the reading in the text; they also agree on *Scolasticae*, although Molanus corrected it to *Scholasticae*. *Rothomagensi* is found in nearly all copies except Pratensis, who also reads *Austrobertae*, together with Marchianensis and Greven; the others have the reading in the text. Molanus alone writes *Austreberthae*.

[Note: [Col. 0747D]]

Of the first four martyrs, some are joined with Soter or Soteris in the copies of Jerome, but are distinguished by Bede, where the four names are expressed more clearly and precisely. The Small Roman Martyrology, perhaps corrected in orthography by Rosweyd—as Henschenius and Papebrochius probably did in Bede—also writes the names accurately, as does Ado, who plainly lacked material for the eulogy. The same Small Roman Martyrology mentions Soteris, without making her grammatical position clear, unless one thinks that the conjunction *et* should be connected with the preceding Roman martyrs. Ado, however, understood the text of the Small Roman Martyrology differently: perhaps misled by the Greek origin of the name, he was the first to transfer Soteris to the East, and in doing so he had Our Author as his follower. Not so Notker, says Castellanus, who preferred to imitate Rabanus and the earlier authorities, perhaps observing that she more probably died in Italy, since she was a relative of Saint Ambrose.

He could not have meant any “earlier authorities” except the copies of Jerome; nevertheless, here this otherwise careful man allowed his diligence to fail him, since Notker—whether he made one Soteris or two—reproduces Ado’s very words for this day exactly. What may have misled Castellanus is that he read Notker’s announcement under the eighth day before the Ides, that is, on the sixth of this month, formulated in these words: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of the same place, the passion of Saint Soteris, virgin and martyr.” We readily admit that all this, except the final word, was taken from Rabanus, as we stated on the saint’s own day from Greven. Again, Soteris, the most holy virgin, is recorded by Ado and Notker on 12 May, as we shall indicate there.

Here Florentinius doubts whether the name Soteris should be applied to a man or a woman, and also whether the same virgin is announced twice, as we have seen happen with Agnes. But these matters belong to another investigation and another place. Our Author copied the little eulogy that Ado composed for her. To avoid dwelling on this longer, one may consult Bollandus’s commentary, in which passages from Ambrose are brought forward that may pertain to the virgin’s true praise, together with other matters relating to her cult. Ruinartius, in the *Selecta*, p. 405, also cites passages from Saint Ambrose. Castellanus briefly collected the more curious points in his notes, pp. 600–601. Tillemontius, however, joined her with Pancratius in vol. V, beginning at p. 259.

There follows the group of ten soldiers, who are recorded in the Small Roman Martyrology, Ado, Our Author, and Notker only by their names. Scholastica was added by Our Author; Rabanus, and Notker after him, embellish her with a more extensive encomium. But what are we to say about Austreberta, who is named only by Our Author? I shall speak frankly: I do not doubt without good reason whether she was inserted by Usuard himself. This is especially because the two manuscripts that I value most highly, Heriniensis and Tornacensis, do not mention her; yet until now they have not usually omitted what is genuinely Usuardian, particularly among the Frankish saints. I therefore cannot in any way imagine what could have moved the scribes to suppress a saint otherwise so well known, if she had been expressly included in Usuard’s autograph.

Nevertheless, she had to be retained in the text, lest I appear to define Usuard’s simplicity according to my own judgment rather than on the authority of other manuscripts. Let another interpreter explain what Wandalbert indicates in his verses:

> Soteris, Irenaeus, and the virgin Scholastica shine alike  
> With the fourfold distinction of their outstanding merits.

[Note: [Col. 0749B]]

I have already said that Heriniensis and Tornacensis do not mention Austreberta. Pulsanensis agrees with them; it is distinctive in disturbing the order of the Roman martyrs and writing *Amarini* instead of *Amantii*. It then reads: “Likewise at Rome, Saint Soteris, virgin.”

Antwerp-Max., Lovanium, Leyden-Belg., and the Utrecht-Belgian edition depart from the pure text only in announcing Scholastica first and, at the end, writing *Austrebergae* instead of *Austrebertae*, a form also found in certain other manuscripts. In the Belgian edition, the name of one of the first four martyrs is absent.

Utrecht, Leyden, Alberg, and Danish likewise give Scholastica first, but add the following to the Usuardian text:

> “He saw her soul leave the body and penetrate the secrets of heaven in the form of a dove. Rejoicing with her in such great glory, Saint Benedict gave thanks to God and announced her death to the brothers. He immediately sent them to bring her body to the monastery and place it in the tomb that she had prepared for herself, so that, since their minds had always been one in God, their bodies also might not be separated by burial.”

Whether this connection is sound is disputed elsewhere.

Centula, after a somewhat abbreviated text, adds at the end: “At Saintes, Saint Trojan, bishop and confessor,” words that Antwerp-Major also included, but between Scholastica and Austreberta. This Trojan belongs, however, to 30 November.

Brussels, whose text concerning Scholastica is drawn from Utrecht and is partly mutilated, reads after “penetrate the secrets”:

> “When he saw this, he himself had the body of his deceased sister brought to his own monastery and buried in the tomb that he himself had prepared. It was later transferred to Le Mans.”

It then proceeds concerning Soteris, omitting the Roman martyrs. Then follows the group of ten soldiers. After *Rothomagensi* it inserts:

> “In the place called Pauliacus. On the same day at Nivelles, the elevation of Saint Gertrude, virgin.”

Finally, in a more recent Belgian hand:

> “Likewise in the valley called ad Stabulas Rodis, blessed William, confessor. He had been the most ferocious count of Poitiers and duke of Aquitaine, but became a most strenuous and steadfast hermit of exemplary life and a most powerful worker of miracles.”

These matters are discussed with the greatest care and precision in the *Acta*.

[Col. 0750B] Hagenoyen mixes in further material concerning Scholastica that is not equally well attested. After the entry for Saint Benedict the abbot, it speaks as follows:

> “She was the ruler of many holy virgins who were religious women. One day, when Saint Benedict had come to visit her and wished shortly afterward to depart, she obtained from God rain with thunder, and thus he unwillingly spent the night with her. Shortly afterward Benedict, her brother, saw her soul leave the body in the form of a dove,” and so forth.

Victorin writes *Amarii* instead of *Amantii*. At the end, as in Centula, it has the entry for Saint Trojan.

Altemps, enlarged in England: “On this day, Saint Vivinna, abbess.”

Strozzi and Medici place first:

> “In the region of Tuscany, in the place called Pauliacus, the passing of Saint William, hermit and confessor, a man of great holiness and glorious for his miracles.”

The codex of Mont-Saint-Michel reads: “At Saintes, the deposition of Saint Trojan, bishop, and of Baldegundis, abbess.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition records Scholastica first, as Utrecht and the others do. It continues:

> “On the same day, Saint William, confessor. He had first been duke of the Aquitanians and excessively dissolute, but afterward, moved by divine prompting, he repented, renounced the world, and assumed the monastic habit, becoming the servant of the servants of God. He bent his knees a hundred times by night and day, passing from the active to the contemplative life. He also attained such perfection that he shone with the spirit of prophecy. Later, strengthened in body and having partaken of the blood of Christ, he departed to the Lord.”

The text also inserts that Soteris suffered under the emperor Diocletian. Then: “At Saintes, Saint Trojan, bishop and confessor.”

Belin is somewhat more correct in his second edition; in both editions he announces first:

> “The birthday of Saint William, confessor, of the order of the hermits of Saint Augustine.”

See the *Acta*.

Greven has:

> “At Saintes, Trojan, bishop and confessor. The elevation of Saint Gertrude, virgin. William, count of Poitiers and confessor, who, after first giving himself wholly to wickedness and supporting the schism of Peter Leon, was terrifyingly rebuked by Saint Bernard, finally came to his senses, put on an iron shirt next to his flesh, led an austere life, and, founding an order bearing his name, rested in peace.”

The confusion everywhere has been skillfully removed by Henschenius.

Molanus copied Belin in the entry for William. Then:

> “In Campania, the birthday of Saint Silvianus, bishop and confessor.”

Rabanus writes this. Jerome and Notker name him Silvanus. It continues:

> “And of Baldegundis, abbess,”

whom some have transformed into a man. Other editions begin: “At the Stabulae Rodis, the birthday of Saint William,” and so forth, as above. Then:

> “At Clermont, the deposition of Saint Sigo, bishop of that distinguished city, of great holiness and a confessor, in the time of King Chlothar. On the tenth day, Saint Charalampus, martyr.”

Concerning Silvianus and Baldegundis, see above. Finally, in smaller letters:

> “At Dordrecht, the commemoration of Saint Sura, virgin and martyr, under the name Soteris, which in Latin means ‘saviouress.’”

See Bollandus for this day. Castellanus certainly does not sufficiently establish that this Sura, or “Zuwarda,” of Dordrecht should be identified with the Roman or Eastern Soteris.

[Col. 0747]

At Rome, the birthday of the holy martyrs Zoticus, Irenaeus, Hyacinth, and Amantius. In the East, Saint Soteris, virgin, who, after being severely and for a very long time beaten with slaps and overcoming every other kind of punishment as well, completed her martyrdom by the sword. Likewise at Rome, on the Lavican Way, the ten soldiers.

[Note: [Col. 0747C]]

In order to make room for Austreberta in the final line, this entire passage was deleted from Usuard, and the following was written in somewhat smaller letters: “sister of Saint Benedict the abbot.” Saint Austreberta was absent from the first exemplar. Sollerius ought to have followed his manuscripts; or, if Pratensis seemed preferable to him here, it ought to have seemed preferable everywhere, since the writing of this addition is the same as that of the others. I do not mention here that Saint Austreberta is appropriately remembered. Everyone agrees that that holy virgin died on this day. Bouillart.

At Casinum, Saint Scholastica, virgin, sister of Saint Benedict the abbot.

[Note: [Col. 0748D]]

These words are written in Bouillart’s copy in the margin: “These are not Usuard’s. See the *Acta Sanctorum* of Mabillon, third century, part I, p. 28 A.”

In the district of Rouen, Saint Austreberta, virgin.

The third day before the Ides. Day 11.

[Note: [Col. 0751]]

Thus read Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Marchianensis, Antwerp-Major, Pulsanensis, Munerat, Greven, and Molanus.

[Note: [Col. 0751B]]

In Tornacensis, *Laudonensi* is incorrectly written for *Nantonensi*; Munerat is worse, having *Nannetensi*; Greven has *Nautoniensi*, also incorrectly; Molanus has *Nantoniensi*. Pratensis, Marchianensis, and Munerat read *Acaunensis*; Antwerp-Major, *Aganensis*; Pulsanensis, *Athaunensis*; Greven, *Augaunensis*: the reading in the text is better.

The alleged autograph writes *Flodovehus* or *Flodovechus*; another manuscript, Pratensis, and Antwerp-Major have *Flodoveus*, as do Heriniensis, Pulsanensis, and Greven. Munerat, probably through a typesetter’s error, has *Clodoneus*; the true reading is that of the others and of the text.

Pulsanensis and Antwerp-Major omit “king.” Marchianensis has *diuturna* for *diutina*; Antwerp-Major simply writes, “he was freed from his illness.” The others have the reading in the text. *Eufrasiae* is supported by the agreement of all the manuscripts, although Tornacensis more correctly reads *Eufrosinae*, as will be explained more fully in the Observations.

[Note: [Col. 0751B]]

On this day Usuard passes over saints who are explicitly named by Bede and Ado. Bede mentions Callocerus and Parthenius, and Rabanus follows him; Ado mentions Simplidus of Vienne, none of whom Our Author commemorates.

I am especially astonished with Castellanus that Ado, who is otherwise so generous in listing the holy bishops of his own church, including on this very day, does not announce that distinguished predecessor of his in the same church, Desiderius, whom Bede explicitly places here: “On the same day at Lyons, Desiderius, bishop.” Nor does Rabanus’s silence present an obstacle, since Bede’s text is confirmed by Wandalbert.

The placement is certainly unsatisfactory; nor should the title “martyr,” deservedly assigned to him by others, have been omitted. At the command of the famous Brunhild he was first punished with exile and then, at Prisciniacum—not at Lyons—was stoned, beaten with a club, and killed, as Notker recounts more fully from Ado’s own account on 23 May, when he commemorates the translation.

Here we must ask whether Ado recorded him on neither day, since Rosweyd relegates him to the appendix on both occasions. Castellanus turns the matter in various directions, but finally, in the Corollary at the end of the volume, thinks he can infer from Notker’s words on 23 May that Ado did not mention him at all in the Martyrology. Notker’s words are:

> “Since the venerable Father Ado, bishop of our same church in his time, had him present before him and therefore known to all his own people in every respect, he considered it superfluous to say anything particular about him.”

Let others judge how weighty this argument is. For my part, I should nevertheless believe that Notker’s text for today is genuinely Adonian, were I not prevented by Usuard’s silence. Usuard would not have neglected the opinion of his guide if he had found it in Ado’s Martyrology; nor would he have added the title “confessor” to Bede’s words, where Desiderius is so plainly declared crowned by martyrdom. Florus likewise says so on 23 May, as will be explained in its proper place.

To avoid going on longer, consult the *Acta*, especially those for 23 May, where the whole matter is developed and illuminated at greater length. Wandalbert’s verses clearly flow from Bede’s text for this day:

> From here Desiderius thrice crowns the walls of Lyons;  
> Rome shines with Parthenius and Calocerus.

The memory of Severinus, abbot of Agaunum, most renowned for miracles, is found in no ancient Martyrology. Our Author was the first to insert him in his own. Why the name *Clodoveus* was commonly transformed into *Flodoveus* or *Flodovehus* is not worth investigating. Learned men admit that his life, written by an anonymous author and published in the *Acta*, has been interpolated. Whether the original version published by Mabillon in the appendix to the first century of the Benedictine order, p. 568, is free from every blemish will be examined in the Supplement.

We recorded Euphrosyne with Usuard above, on the Kalends of January, drawn from Ado, whose eulogy you will find among the Appendices. As we said there, Bollandus placed her among the *Praetermissi* on this day, while Castellanus assigned her to 25 September. Here, however, the Small Roman Martyrology, Ado himself, and Our Author in both places mention not Euphrosyne but Euphrasia. It appears from the eulogy, and is proved by other evidence, that the same saint is concealed under both names. Hence the modern Roman Martyrology correctly assigned Euphrosyne to 1 January, while Ado and Usuard placed Euphrasia here. See what was said there in the Observations.

Nor is the saint celebrated by the Greeks on 25 September a different person; she should more probably be thought to have died on that day and is adorned with the great praises fully recounted in the *Acta*. Whether these praises are sufficiently sincere and true is doubted by many learned men, including Tillemontius, vol. X, p. 50. Their arguments will be examined more carefully in the February Supplement.

[Note: [Col. 0751D]]

Antwerp-Max. and Lübeck record on this day the saints whom Our Author places on the following day. They read:

> “In Africa, the holy martyrs Saturninus the presbyter, Dativus, Felix, Apuleius, and their companions, who suffered for Christ under Anolinus the proconsul. At Lyons, Desiderius, bishop. At Alexandria, the burial of Euphrasia, virgin, who, as her life relates, is known to have shone in the monastery through the remarkable virtue of abstinence and through miracles.”

They say nothing of Severinus.

Rosweyd inserts near the end of his text: “At Rome, Calocerus and Parthenius, martyrs.” Instead of *Eufrasiae* he writes *Eufraxiae*; otherwise his text is fairly pure.

Antwerp-Max., Utrecht, Leyden, Lovanium, Alberg, Danish, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition are almost like the first two. They read:

> “In Africa, the holy martyrs Saturninus, Danitus, Felix the presbyter, Apuleius, and their companions, who suffered for Christ under the emperor Julian and Anolinus the proconsul.”

The entry concerning Desiderius follows in pure form. Then:

> “At Alexandria, the burial of Saint Euphrosyne, virgin, who, as her life relates, is known to have shone in the monastery through the remarkable virtue of abstinence and through miracles.”

Severinus is omitted in all of them.

Centula reads:

> “At Lyons, Saint Desiderius, bishop and confessor. In the district of Vexin, at the fortress of Mantes, Saint Severinus, abbot of the monastery of Agaunum, through whose prayers Clodoveus, the God-fearing king of the Franks, was freed from his illness. At Alexandria, Saint Euphrasia, virgin.”

It seems that *Flodoveus* had previously been written, but the upper part was erased, including the *f*, so that what remains forms a *c*.

Brussels begins: “At Vienne, Saint Simplidus, bishop and confessor.” It then gives the passage concerning Severinus in pure form. Concerning Euphrasia it agrees with Antwerp above.

Hagenoyen, concerning Saturninus, Dativus, and the others, agrees with Antwerp, but adds “and under the emperor Julian” at the end. The rest generally corresponds to the text. At the end: “Likewise Yminia, virgin.” Is this perhaps Solinia?

Victorin and the Royal Swedish codex, no. 130, end with: “Likewise Saint Amasius, bishop and confessor.” He is found neither in the *Acta* nor among the *Praetermissi*.

The Vatican codex, no. 5949, reads: “In Campania, Saint Castrensis, bishop and confessor. At Rome, Calocerus and Parthenius.” The latter two are celebrated on 19 May.

Ughellian begins: “In Africa, the holy martyrs Saturninus,” and so forth, as in Antwerp.

Altemps: “At the monastery of Glasgow, Saint Blesius, martyr.” I have not yet been able to discover who this may be.

Strozzi and Medici: “Likewise Saint Calocerus, archbishop of Ravenna.” See Henschenius’s commentary.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins with Severinus. It then gives Saturninus and his companions, and Euphrasia, as above. It closes the day with: “At Vienne, Saint Sinniplidus, bishop and confessor.” Read *Simplidis*.

Belin begins with Saturninus, as in Antwerp. Its entry for Desiderius is pure. For *Eufrasiae* it writes *Euphrosinae*. At the end: “At the fortress of Nanthoniense,” and so forth.

Greven mixes together these mutilated and confused items from a corrupt text of Jerome:

> “In Campania, Basilianus, Amantius. In Africa, Victor, Felix, Januarius, Zoticus, Irenaeus. In Apamea, Basilianus, Penis.”

See Bollandus and Florentinius. “In Ireland, Ecianus, bishop and confessor. There also, Solinia, virgin.”

Molanus: “In Africa, the holy martyrs Saturninus the presbyter, Dativus, Felix, Apuleius, and their companions, who suffered for Christ under Anolinus the proconsul.” These items are omitted in the other editions, in which there is added only: “At Clermont, Saint Desideratus, bishop and confessor.” See the *Acta*.

[Col. 0751]

At Lyons, the birthday of Saint Desiderius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, at the fortress of Nantonense, Saint Severinus, abbot of the monastery of Agaunum, through whose prayers Clodoveus, the God-fearing king, was freed from his long illness. At Alexandria, the burial of Saint Euphrasia, virgin, who also shone in the monastery through the virtue of abstinence and through miracles.

The day before the Ides. Day 12.

[Note: [Col. 0753]]

Thus read Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Marchianensis, Munerat, Greven, and Molanus.

[Note: [Col. 0753C]]

In Marchianensis and the others, *Hyspaniis* is incorrectly written; likewise *Daviti* in Heriniensis. I placed *Apelii* in the text on the authority of Pratensis, Marchianensis, and Greven. Heriniensis and Tornacensis have *Apeli*; Munerat has *Pellii*; Molanus has *Apulcii*. I shall add the true name below, which Molanus correctly gave in his other editions. In Munerat, *sociorumque* appears instead of *et sociorum*; this is a slight alteration. Heriniensis reads “under Julian the proconsul.” In the Appendices for the preceding day we saw Julian the emperor, incorrectly joined with Anolinus, perhaps because certain ancient manuscripts wrote *Juliano* for *Anolino*, as Heriniensis does here. Marchianensis, Munerat, and Molanus have *infantium*, which the last corrected in his other editions.

[Note: [Col. 0753C]]

Bede alone among the ancient martyrologists either did not know of Eulalia of Barcelona or at least did not include her in the sacred calendars. The others announce her, although none expresses the manner of her martyrdom as explicitly as the modern Roman Martyrology does. For how this Eulalia is to be distinguished from the Eulalia of Mérida, celebrated on 10 December, and which details belong separately to the Acts of each, see Bollandus in the *Acta*.

Ado borrowed her from the Small Roman Martyrology, while also speaking of others whom Usuard judged should be named only on their proper days, since, although they suffered under the same Dacian executioner, they did not complete their martyrdom on the same day. More ought to be said about those synonymous virgins, unless a proper place remained on 10 December, where discussion will return to the more celebrated Eulalia of Mérida, splendidly praised by Prudentius in Ruinartius, p. 496 and following. To that place I refer the rest, adding here only Wandalbert’s verses in honor of Eulalia of Barcelona:

> The feast and blood of Eulalia shine on the preceding day;  
> Barcelona rejoices in its illustrious martyr.

Here it must again be noted that Ado records Damian, whom Our Author omits—an unusual occurrence, as I recently said. Saturninus and his companions are mentioned neither by Jerome, nor by Bede, nor by any ancient authority before Usuard. He was the first to record these four names, without expressing the other forty-five, concerning whom Augustine recounted the Conference of Carthage; we therefore suppose that Our Author obtained them from him.

Why the more recent manuscript codices and the modern Roman Martyrology have preferred the preceding day to this one, I do not know. Augustine certainly explicitly states that the hearing was held on the day before the Ides of February, and the same day is clearly expressed in the title of the proconsular Acts. It is therefore certain that none of these martyrs suffered before that day; but on what day they actually gained the crown is nowhere recorded.

Whether Ruinartius correctly assigns some of them to particular days in his preliminary notice, p. 408, may be examined elsewhere. There the same author reproduces the Acts, omitting the preface and conclusion appended by the Donatists; both are found in Baluzius, vol. II of the *Miscellanea*, beginning at p. 56, and the first in Henschenius’s *Acta*, where his commentary and notes should be consulted. See also Tillemontius, vol. V, beginning at p. 231. If any small blemishes inserted by the Donatists still remain, they do not compromise the purity of the Acts.

Furthermore, the person called *Apelus*, *Apelius*, and *Apuleius* in the manuscripts seems rather to have been named *Ampelus* or *Ampelius*. For the rest, see above, in Castellanus’s notes, and in the Appendices for the preceding day.

There are several points concerning Modestus that should be noted in the modern Roman Martyrology, but they belong elsewhere. Modestus and Ammonius were taken from Ado, who called them both infants, although they are not called such in the Small Roman Martyrology. The copies of Jerome do not distinguish them sufficiently. Rabanus, adding Zoticus to the infants, joins them with Damian in Africa. Usuard follows Ado without further examination. For the group of martyrs from which Modestus and Ammonius were separated, see Bollandus and Castellanus.

[Note: [Col. 0755A]]

Pulsanensis is defective in the first announcement concerning Saint Eulalia; otherwise it is pure.

Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck begin: “The birthday of Saint Macarius, Saint Rufinus, and Saint Justus.” See the Appendices for 28 February. “And at Alexandria, Ammonius,” and so forth. Nothing is said of Eulalia. They dealt with Saturninus and the others on the preceding day.

Antwerp-Major, Adonian in its first section, reads:

> “In Spain, Saint Eulalia, virgin and martyr, who suffered under the emperor Diocletian, under Dacian, prefect of Spain; at the same time, under the same ruler, Saint Cucuphas at Barcelona and Saint Felix at Girona are known to have received the glorious crowns of martyrdom, as is written in the passion of Saint Leocadia.”

It calls Modestus and Ammonius infant martyrs. At the end: “In Africa, the passion of Saint Damian, soldier.”

Rosweyd is today more obscure and confused. Its text is as follows:

> “In the lands of Spain, Saint Eulalia, virgin, who is known to have received the glorious crown of martyrdom in the city”—he means Barcelona—“under the emperor Diocletian.”

Then:

> “In Africa, Damian, soldier, and the holy martyrs Saturninus, and so forth. In Alexandria, Julian, martyr, and eighteen other companions, or saints. In the same place, the holy infants Modestus and Ammonius, and the holy martyrs Quiriacus and Simplicius.”

See these matters explained more distinctly in the *Acta*.

Centula, as usual an abbreviator, summarizes everything briefly and adds something:

> “In Spain, Saint Eulalia, virgin, under the governor Dacian. In Africa, the holy martyrs Saturninus the presbyter, Dativus, Felix, Apelius, and their companions. At Alexandria, Modestus and Ammonius, infant martyrs. In Africa, Saint Damian, soldier.”

Antwerp-Max., Lovanium, Leyden, Belgian, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition begin as follows:

> “At Rome, Saint Gregory II, who, the ninety-second after blessed Peter and a Syrian by nationality”—here Gregory II is incorrectly confused with his namesake successor—“occupied the see for ten years, eight months, and fourteen days, in the time of the emperors Leo and Constantine.”

Utrecht, Leyden, Alberg, and Danish have nearly the same beginning and perhaps add from some Adonian manuscript:

> “This man, chaste and learned in the divine Scriptures, preached the word of salvation in Germany through Saint Boniface, bishop. He also established that a fast should be observed on Thursday during Lent, and arranged the office for the solemn celebration of Mass on that day—which previously had not been done—taking most of it from the Sunday offices.”

The latter passages are taken from Anastasius the Librarian. They do not show, as Bollandus thought, an improper custom of earlier times in which Thursday of Lent was not a fast day; rather, they indicate the ecclesiastical rule then established, as may be seen in Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 20, and elsewhere. For just reasons, when those circumstances ceased, Gregory II restored that Thursday to the order of the other days, as we shall say in the Supplement to Note 2, no. 10, p. 703.

Meanwhile, see the fuller discussion by our Papebrochius concerning this pontiff, who is assigned by others to the following day. According to Papebrochius’s calculation, however, he died on 17 January. Father Simon Motherius takes the opposite view in the note appended to 13 February in his recent French translation of the Roman Martyrology, where he wishes him to have died on 11 January. As for Motherius’s citation there of Bede and Ado, he did not obtain it from their genuine editions. Bede’s date makes clear that he could not have known Gregory II. In Mosander’s Ado he is included; more correctly, I think, Rosweyd relegated him to the appendix.

The manuscripts then proceed with Modestus and the others. At the end: “On the same day, the birthday of Saints Macarius, Rufinus, and Justus.” Eulalia of Barcelona is absent from all of them. They dealt with Saturninus and his companions on the preceding day.

Brussels, interpolated in the passage concerning Eulalia, has Damian in second place, as Antwerp-Major does. It says that Saturninus and his companions suffered under “the emperor Julian.” The infant martyrs follow. At the end it has the entry concerning “Macarius, Rufinus, and Justus,” as above.

Hagenoyen announces Eulalia first; Gregory second, nearly as in the middling-class manuscripts; Macarius and his companions third. The rest is as in the small entry.

Victorin, the Royal Swedish codex no. 130, and the Vatican codex no. 5949 end with: “In Africa, the passion of Saint Damian, martyr.”

Ughellian begins: “The birthday of Saint Macarius, and of Saint Rufinus, and of Saint Justus.”

Altemps: “Likewise at Oxford, the translation of Saint Frideswide, virgin.” This should be referred to 19 October.

Strozzi and Medici: “Likewise Saint Gregory IV, pope. He established the feast of All Saints in the year 808.” I have so far read nothing concerning the cult of this pontiff. The error in the dates is obvious. But this and other matters properly connected with it will be discussed in their proper place.

[Col. 0756C] The Lübeck-Cologne edition has the same beginning of the day as Utrecht and the others. It then continues:

> “At Alexandria, the birthday of the holy infant martyrs Modestus and Ammonius. Likewise at Alexandria, the birthday of the holy martyrs Macarius, Rufinus, and Justus. In Africa, the passion of Saint Damian, soldier and martyr. On the same day, the birthday of Saint Livinus, bishop and confessor. Likewise the commemoration of Saint Eulalia, virgin and martyr.”

Belin dealt with Saturninus and his companions on the preceding day. In the passage concerning Eulalia he is pure. “At Alexandria, Modestus,” and so forth. “Likewise Macarius, Rufinus, and Justus.”

Greven:

> “The third translation of blessed Barbara, virgin and martyr, namely from Rome to Piacenza. In Africa, Damian, soldier and martyr. Likewise there, Julian, Donatus, Heraclius, and Zoticus. Ludanus, confessor. At Alexandria, Quiriacus and Simplicius, martyrs. Macarius, Rufinus, and Justus, martyrs. On the same day, Saint Livinus, bishop and confessor”—or is it Licinius? See Bollandus among the *Praetermissi*.

He is recorded on the following day. Livinus will be treated on 12 November, and Lebuinus on the same day.

Molanus:

> “Likewise Macarius, Rufinus, and Justus. In Africa, the passion of Saint Damian, soldier.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “Susanna, the most holy matron, who is read of in Daniel.”

In the later editions, Macarius and the others being omitted, he begins with Damian. Then:

> “On the twelfth day, Saint Meletius, father and archbishop of Great Antioch.”

Finally, in smaller letters:

> “Likewise at Constantinople, Saint Antony, great among God’s bishops and admirable among the patriarchs.”

This is the Antony surnamed Cauleas in the *Acta*.

[Col. 0753]

In Spain, the birthday of Saint Eulalia, virgin, who is known to have received the glorious crown of martyrdom under the emperor Diocletian, in the city of Barcelona. In Africa, the holy martyrs Saturninus the presbyter, Dativus, Felix, Apelius, and their companions, who suffered for Christ under Anolinus the proconsul. At Alexandria, Modestus and Ammonius, infant martyrs.

The Ides. Day 13.

[Note: [Col. 0757]]

From Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Marchianensis, Pulsanensis, Munerat, Greven, and Molanus.

[Note: [Col. 0757A]]
