Pulsanensis begins: “At Antioch.” Munerat has “in the Acts of the Apostles.” The true reading of Usuard is in the text. All write *Militana* and *Poliocti* except Tornacensis, which has *Polieucti*; Munerat has *Policeti*, and Molanus *Polyocti*. The true name is known to be *Polyeuctus*. In Munerat there is a typographical error: *militum orans* for *multum orans*. Heriniensis, Munerat, and Molanus have *Lucinii*; Pulsanensis has *Licinii*. The *Acta* admit both under alternative forms, while also reporting other versions. The reading of the others seems preferable to me.

[Note: [Col. 0757A]]

The Hieronymian copies say nothing about Agabus, nor do Bede or his followers. The author of the Small Roman Martyrology was the first to mention him, in these words: “Agabus the prophet in the New Testament, at Antioch.” The Viennese author expands this slightly, adducing two passages from the Acts of the Apostles in which Agabus is shown to have prophesied; Henschenius explained them correctly.

Our Author, passing over the sacred texts, copied the rest from Ado. Notker briefly added that Agabus had predicted the famine and Paul’s imprisonment. This entry also derives from that same source, the Small Roman Martyrology.

Polyeuctus is there recorded as follows: “At Melitene in Armenia, Saint Polyeuctus, martyr.” Ado added only the interpretation of the name, from which Usuard and Notker took their material, though with some alteration in spelling, discussed in the Variants. How many ways the name *Polyeuctus* has been corrupted has already been abundantly shown, since it recurs so often and on several days, while the true day on which he should be celebrated remains uncertain.

Castellanus indeed argues from the Hieronymian copies that he received the crown of martyrdom on 7 January. But what if the same manuscripts instead support 14 February, on which day he is explicitly recorded just as on 7 January? Consult Florentinius in both places and Henschenius’s commentary for this day. See also the *Acta* themselves, edited and illustrated by the aforementioned Henschenius, from which Tillemontius drew his material in vol. III, beginning at p. 424.

Whether the accounts promised long ago by Combefisius in the *Lecti triumphi*, p. 185, are purer—he claimed that they were composed by Near-chus, the martyr’s friend—cannot yet be determined. It will be possible if they are ever brought to light.

Usuard alone among the ancient martyrologists entered Licinius of Angers into the sacred calendars. Bollandus published two highly regarded lives of him, later translated into French by others. He himself wrote *Licinius* or *Lucinius*; I would prefer *Lizinius* or *Lezinius*, as I have displayed them from the manuscripts in the small entry. From this inflection the French name *Lezin* seems more correctly to be derived, or perhaps the reverse. Castellanus assigns his birthday to 1 November.

Wandalbert’s verses do not pertain to today’s text, since they concern Julian and Basilissa. See 9 January.

[Note: [Col. 0757B]]

Antwerp-Major:

> “The birthday of blessed Agabus, prophet in the New Testament, at Antioch. In the city of Melitene in Armenia, the birthday of Saint Polyeuctus,”

and so forth, in pure form.

> “At Angers, Saint Licinius, bishop and confessor, whose sacred body is honored by frequent miracles.”

[Col. 0757C] Rosweyd begins: “At Lyons, Saint Stephen, bishop and confessor.” The pure text follows, with this added at the end: “In Britain, Saint Ermenhild, virgin.” Is this not Queen Ermenhild of Mercia?

Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck append to the pure text: “At Lyons, the feast of Saint Stephen, bishop, and Saint Julian,” without any punctuation. Hence certain more recent martyrologists and the reformers of the modern Roman Martyrology took occasion to place Julian also at Lyons. See more in the Acts.

Antwerp, Max.-Utrecht, Leyden, Louvain, Alberg, Danic, and Utrecht-Belgian read *in Antiochia quiescentis* (“who rests in Antioch”) instead of *apud Antiochiam* (“at Antioch”). Alberg and Danic incorrectly write *Lupicini*; others have *Licinii*. They all then add: “In the territory of Trier, Saint Castor, confessor, whose deeds are recorded.” He is venerated at Koblenz, as is said below. “At Lyons, the feast of Saint Stephen, bishop. At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Julian, martyr.”

[Col. 0757D] In the Centulensian manuscript the text is abbreviated.

Brussels is almost pure in Agabus; in second place it has Gregory, concerning whom see yesterday in the Appendices. It continues with Polyeuctus. Then: “At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Julian, martyr. At Lyons, Saint Stephen, bishop and confessor.” Concerning Lizinius it adds: “Whose body is honored by frequent miracles. At Trier, Saint Castor,” and so forth, as above. “Also, the translation of Saint Edward, king and martyr.”

Hagenoyen, after an almost pure text, announces Stephen, and at the end has: “In the territory of Trier, in the place called Koblenz, Saint Castor, priest and confessor, who first sought the desert, remained there for many years, and, having grown old there, rested in peace.” Indeed, he also became renowned for many miracles.

[Col. 0758B] Aquicinct, after the text, adds: “At Lyons, Saints Stephen, bishop, and Julian. At Rome, Pope Gregory IV, who ruled the Church for sixteen years,” and so forth, as was said the previous day concerning Gregory II.

Victorin and the Swedish Register, marked no. 130, differ from the preceding in that they correctly name Gregory [Col. 0758C] II, and at the end have: “At Lyons, Saint Stephen,” and so forth.

The Matrician-Carthusian-Utrecht manuscript, after the announcement of Agabus, inserts: “Stephen, confessor, who was the father of many monks.”

Codex I Bigotianus, formerly belonging to the Celestines, marked P. 5: “At Lyons, Saints Stephen, bishop, and Julian.” See the Acts, pp. 656 and 672.

Swedish Register, no. 428: “At the city of Meaux, the feast of Saint Gislebert, bishop of that same city.”

Codex D. du Cheval, marked B: “At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Julian, martyr.”

The Vatican manuscript, no. 5949, omits Lizinius but adds: “At Rome, Blessed Gregory II, pope, who ruled the Church for fifteen years, in the time of the emperors Leo and Constantine. At Lyons, Saints Stephen, bishop, and Julian, martyr.”

Altemps: “On this day, in Britain, Saint Ethormethisda, virgin, and Saint Huna, priest [Col. 0758D] and hermit.” Nor are they known among the persons omitted.

Strozzi and Medici: “At Lyons, Saint Stephen, bishop and martyr. Also, Saint Julian, martyr. In the district of Trier, at Cardona, Saint Castor, confessor. Also, Saint Antoninus, confessor.” I think this means the abbot of Monte Cassino, who is celebrated on the following day.

Codex S. Ricaldi: “Saint Fulcran, bishop of Lodève”; concerning him, see the Acts for this day.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins: “In the territory of Trier, Saint Castor, priest and confessor, whose deeds are recorded. In the time of his youth, he was joined by his noble parents to Saint Maximin, bishop of Trier. After receiving the priestly order from him, he entered the desert, where he faithfully served God, and at last rested with a good end.” Concerning Agabus, as above. In the entry for Polyeuctus the text is pure. Concerning Lizinius, Stephen, and Julian it writes as the Brussels manuscript does. At the end: “On the same day, Blessed Ermenhild, virgin.” He meant to say widow, and so forth. See the Acts.

The Belin edition writes *Mauritana* for *Militana*, and *Policrati* for *Poliocti*; these readings were corrected in the later edition. Afterward, following *multum orans* (“praying much”), it continues: “At Rome, Saint Tranquillinus, priest, who, converted to Christ through the preaching of Saint Sebastian, martyr, was baptized by Saint Polycarp, priest, and ordained priest by Saint Caius, pope. When he had gone to the confession of Saint Paul for the sake of prayer, he was seized by the pagans and stoned.” See 6 July. Here it inserts Lizinius, whom it calls Lucinius. Then: “At Rome, Saint Gregory II, pope, who ruled the Church for sixteen years, in the time of the emperors Leo and Constantine. [Col. 0759B] At Torcello, Saint Fusca, virgin and martyr.” The second edition adds: “At Lyons, Saint Stephen, bishop.”

Greven: “At Nicomedia, Julian, martyr. Cyriacus. In Alexandria, Tullianus, Anchirianus, Ammon, Fusca, martyr. Gregory II, and so forth,” as on the previous day, except for the final sentence concerning the Thursday of Lent. “In the territory of Trier, Saint Castor,” and so forth, almost as in the Lübeck-Cologne edition. “In Britain, at the monastery of Ely, Ermenhild, queen. Stephen, bishop of Lyons and confessor. Stephen, deacon and confessor, who first began the Order of Grandmont around the year 1076; strict toward himself but kind toward his subjects, he governed the same order and, full of good works, rested in peace. Also, Amulric, of revered memory, bishop and confessor of the church of Münster. Blessed Jordan, of revered memory, master general of the Order of Preachers. Also, Blessed Beatrice, virgin, [Col. 0760A] of the Carthusian Order. She was borne with such ardent love toward Christ’s wounds that she could think of nothing but wounds and desire nothing but wounds.” Concerning this Beatrice and Amulric of Münster, see Bollandus among the persons omitted.

Molan transcribed Belin, adding material of his own from other sources. “In the territory of Trier, at the castle of Koblenz, Saint Castor, confessor, whose deeds are recorded. At the city of Meaux, Saint Gislebert, bishop and confessor.” Then, in a different typeface: “Jordan, of blessed memory,” and so forth, from Greven. “Amulric, bishop of Münster in Westphalia, not yet canonized. Stephen, deacon,” and so forth, also from Greven: “Also, Eustochia, nun, of Saint Prosdocimus, near the walls of the city of Padua, of blessed memory: born in sacrilegious childbirth from a nun, she blossomed like a most beautiful rose from rough and piercing thorns. For when scarcely four years old, she was seized by a most evil demon and cruelly tormented until the final day of her life; yet with unconquerable patience of spirit she endured all his tortures, including the dreadful prison into which she was confined by order of the bishop, at the devil’s instigation, because he suggested that she was a sorceress and wished by her magic and means to remove the new abbess. At last she flew up to heaven in the twenty-fifth year of her age, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1469.” Bollandus omitted her, but we later obtained excellent evidence concerning her sanctity, to be published in due course. “At the city of Rieti, Saint Stephen, abbot and confessor, concerning whom Blessed Gregory writes in the *Dialogues*.” Later editions vary considerably. Concerning Gregory they add “that he preached the word of salvation in Germany through Bishop Boniface.” Concerning Fusca, as in Belin: “In Britain, Ermenhild, virgin.” Concerning Stephen, Castor, and Gislebert, as above: “On the thirteenth day, Saint Martinian, father.” In smaller type, they abbreviate what was said concerning Stephen and Eustochia. Concerning Jordan and Amulric, they repeat almost the same material.]

[Col. 0755]

The feast of Saint Agabus the prophet at Antioch, of whom Blessed Luke writes in the Acts of the Apostles. In the city of Militana in Armenia, Saint Polyeuctus, martyr, whose name is interpreted in Latin as “praying much.” At the city of Angers, Saint Lizinius, bishop, a man of venerable holiness.

The sixteenth day before the Kalends of March. Day 14.

[Note: Col. 0759]

From Pratensis, Heriniensis, Rosweyd, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, Munerat, Belin, Greven, and Molan.

[Note: Col. 0759C]

*Sanctitatum* for *sanitatum* (“healings”) is an error of Munerat, who also omitted *et* (“and”); thus Belin reads *Feliculi* for *Feliculae*, and Greven *Felicolae*. In Munerat, *Iteramnis* is written for *Iterannis*. Likewise Belin has *diutinam* for *diuturnam*, *Protholici* for *Protolici*, *Tyroni* for *Cyrionis*, *Moysetis* for *Moyseos*, and so forth. Rosweyd, instead of *mediae noctis silentio* (“in the silence of midnight”), substitutes *medio*, and so forth. Heriniensis, Antwerp, and [Col. 0760C] others write *Cirionis*; Rosweyd has *Chirionis*. I followed the reading of the other manuscripts, which is also that of Ado. Pratensis alone has *Bassiniani*. Greven and Molan seem to have wished to correct the text by writing *igne* instead of *igni*; the word is absent, however, from Munerat and Belin. Concerning Dionysius the priest and similar matters, enough has been said elsewhere.

[Note: Col. 0759C]

Several Valentini occur on this day; Henschenius has performed excellent work in distinguishing them, and Florentinius, in his present notes on the Hieronymian Martyrology, departs in no respect from his opinion. Others hold a different view. The principal issue is whether the two persons distinguished in the list, the Roman and the Interamnian, ought to be merged into one, as Castellanus considers obvious from the Hieronymian copies [Col. 0759D] for this day, which are neither sufficiently uniform nor sufficiently correct; or whether the distinction should rather be maintained, in agreement with Bede, Rabanus, the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Notker. Our author agrees with these: he transcribes the first notice from Bede and Ado, and also contracts the second from both or one of them. This controversy properly belongs to the Supplement for this month; but since Castellanus’s opinion undermines the foundations of our text, the first elements of the question must at least be set out here, from the very manuscripts from which that author derives his arguments.

Among the Hieronymian copies, only the Epternacensis has this in first place: “At Interamna, on the Flaminian Way, the feast of Valentinus.” The Corbeiensis, including the copy published by Acherius, speaks somewhat differently in second place: “At Interamna, on the Flaminian Way, sixty-four miles from the city of Rome, the feast of Saint VINCENTIUS.” Here are the words of the Lucensis: “In Tuscany, in the city of Spoleto, the feast of Saints Vitalis, Cyrianus, and Marcianus. VALENTINUS. At Interamna, on the Flaminian Way, sixty-three miles from the city of Rome, [Col. 0761A] the feast of Saint VINCENTIUS.” The Blumianus remains, but in it the name Valentinus is also missing. Here, reader, you have the very words, extracted with complete fidelity, of all the most ancient copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology published thus far. Consider carefully whether Castellanus’s assertion follows correctly from them—an assertion that he presents as certain on p. 644, namely, that the older copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology today mark Valentinus as follows: “AT INTERAMNA, ON THE FLAMINIAN WAY, SIXTY-FOUR MILES FROM THE CITY OF ROME, SAINT VALENTINUS,” when among the five copies at least that he was able to consult, not one expresses the text he constructed. Nevertheless, the learned author relies exclusively upon these witnesses, believing himself clearly to have established his case and declaring outright that the two Valentini recorded in our text must be completely fused into a single Interamnian Valentinus. To conceal nothing: from the Epternacensis alone Castellanus could infer that some Valentinus was commemorated at Interamna, which we readily admit, although the other manuscripts substitute Vincentius. But I entirely fail to understand what reason could dictate his wish to exclude the Roman Valentinus. If that man, always most friendly toward us, were still alive, I scarcely doubt that, given the teachability with which he was endowed, he would retract the identity here asserted of the Valentini as readily as he rejected the identification of Marcellus and Marcellinus, which was discussed on 16 January.

Meanwhile Tillemontius uses an argument from the Hieronymian Martyrology of equal force in volume IV, p. 678 onward, and with his customary modesty insinuates the same opinion, adducing other records for that purpose. I readily acknowledge that in the calendars of Fronto and Allatius, and likewise in certain sacramentaries, only some Valentinus is mentioned—either simply or with the addition “martyr”—without any designation of rank as priest or bishop. But what follows from this? At most, it follows that innumerable holy martyrs, both bishops and priests, exist who are either not found in those calendars and sacramentaries or are not portrayed there with sufficient individuality; this is certainly beyond doubt. Yet the clear distinction of at least two Valentini made by Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, Rabanus, [Col. 0762A] Ado, Usuardus, and Notker will nevertheless remain unshaken until it is overturned by stronger and more reliable evidence. If that happens, the Supplement will correct whatever Henschenius has argued about them that is less true or less probable. I would also point out that those calendars and sacramentaries, being Roman, can be understood as referring to no Valentinus other than the Roman one. The ancient Gellonensis Martyrology, published by Acherius, explicitly indicates this when it writes first: “At Rome, Valentinus.” Thus, if the writers mentioned above wish to argue from these records, they are destroyed by their own weapons, for from these very sources they must acknowledge one Roman Valentinus and another Interamnian Valentinus. In any case, Bede and his copyist Rabanus discuss only these two Valentini, while Wandalbertus remembers only one Valentinus; it is uncertain which one he means. I append his verses here:

[Col. 0762B]

Then, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends,

the martyr Vitalis shines, and the virgin Felicula;

and their deeds celebrate blessed Valentinus.

Of the remaining classes of martyrs listed in the calendar, I can say only that Ado divided and distinguished them in this way from the cited Hieronymian copies, rightly or wrongly understood—for on this day they are extraordinarily extensive and confused. Our author copied all of them from Ado, without much hesitation or examination. The first three, Vitalis, Felicula, and Zeno, do not seem to have been correctly joined, although they are likewise united in the Gellonensis. Certainly Felicula—whether the same woman or another I do not know—is placed by all the ancients on the Ides of June. There is no less dispute concerning the Alexandrians: about the formation of the names themselves, their location or arena of martyrdom, and finally the very kind of contest, as will readily be seen from our Acts and from Castellanus. It is enough to indicate these matters here; they may be discussed more fully elsewhere, if worthwhile. [Col. 0762C] There is absolutely no reason to doubt the genuineness of the Usuardine text.

[Note: Col. 0761C]

Marchianus is pure throughout and places first the feast proper to his monastery, in these words: “The octave of Saint Rictrudis.”

The Tournai manuscript is mutilated today: the eulogy of Valentinus of Interamna is missing, and the entire notice of Cyrianus, Moses, and the others is omitted.

Pulsanensis has nothing concerning the three classes of Alexandrian martyrs.

Antwerp-Major is supplemented for several days by a later hand; otherwise it is pure in the first section. The second is missing. It gives the third as follows: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Valentinus, bishop and confessor of Interamna.” The rest is sufficiently pure.

Antwerp-Maximum, Utrecht, Leyden, Louvain, Alberg, Danic, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition incorrectly add after the words “under Claudius Caesar”: “and by Saints Marius and Martha and their sons, he was reverently [Col. 0761D] committed to burial.” More correctly, after the words “could not be overcome,” they add from Bede or Ado: “by order of the furious Placidus, prefect of the city.”

Centulensian: “At Rome, Saint Valentinus, priest and martyr. At Interamna, Saint Valentinus, bishop and martyr.” It gives Bassianus the title of lector and Agatho that of exorcist; otherwise it is pure in the Alexandrian entries. At the end, without a location or place-name, it adds: “On the same day, Saints Vitalis, Felicula, and Zeno, martyrs.”

The Brussels manuscript expands the eulogy of Valentinus of Interamna from Bede or Ado, adding to the words “could not be overcome” as follows: “By order of the furious Placidus, prefect of the city, he was beheaded in the silence of midnight. Then his disciples Proculus, Ephebus, and Apollonius buried his body by his church during the night. When they were seized by the pagans and could not be recalled from the faith of Christ, they were beheaded and buried not far from Saint Valentinus.” Concerning Bassianus and Agatho it has the same as the Centulensian.

Hagenoyen writes concerning the Roman Valentinus as the manuscripts of middling quality do. Concerning the Interamnian, after “and martyr,” it adds: “He healed the son of Crato, an orator, who had his head between his knees; because of this many came to Christ. Therefore Blessed Valentinus was cruelly beaten and committed to close confinement; and when he could not be overcome, by order of the furious Placidus,” and so forth.

Vatican, no. 5949: “In the city of Nicomedia, Saint Pantaleon, martyr, and the feast of Saint Modestinus, bishop and martyr.” Concerning the former, see the Acts; concerning the latter, 27 July.

Strozzi and Medici: “On the same day at Padua, the translation of Saint Antony of the Order of Friars Minor.” Bollandus transfers this to the feast of 13 June. Moreover, the Medici manuscript alone also has: “Also, Saint Eleuchadius, archbishop of Ravenna. Also, the passion of Saints Proculus, Ephebus, and Apollonius, martyrs, in the city of Interamna.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins the day as follows: “At Cologne, Saint Valerius, king and martyr, of the company of Saint Ursula, virgin. Also at Cologne, the discovery of Saint Cordula, virgin and martyr, of the company of the eleven thousand holy virgins, which took place in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1268.” See Bollandus among the persons omitted. The entire sacred legion will be treated on 21 October. In the rest, this edition resembles the manuscripts of middling quality mentioned above.

Greven: “On the same day, Waltfrid, abbot and confessor.” His life is given in the Acts for the following day. “Eleuchadius, priest, or rather bishop, of Ravenna. Marcianus.” Two Marciani are given in the Acts today. “At Cologne, the translation of Saint Valerius, king, of the company of Saint Ursula. Also there, the translation of Saint Cordula, virgin and martyr, of the same company, carried out by the late Albert the Great, formerly bishop of Regensburg. Also, the life and miracles of Sisinnius, bishop of the city of Thaumas, which is near Ephesus, a man renowned for both.” Is this the same person who is called Bishop Teius among the persons omitted? Certainly no other Sisinnius occurs on this day.

[Col. 0764A] Molan, in small type: “Also, Saint Meletius, archbishop, whose encomium Saint John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople, wrote. There is also an oration delivered at his funeral by Gregory of Nyssa.” Concerning him, see the Acts for the twelfth of this month. In other editions of Molan only this is added: “On the fourteenth day, Saint Auxentius, father.”]

[Col. 0759]

At Rome, the feast of Blessed Valentinus, priest, who, after many distinguished healings and teachings, was beaten with clubs and thus beheaded under Claudius Caesar. Also at Rome, Saints Vitalis, Felicula, and Zeno, martyrs. At the city of Interamna, Blessed Valentinus, bishop, who, after a prolonged beating, was committed to custody; and when he could not be overcome, was taken from prison in the silence of midnight and beheaded. At Alexandria, Saints Bassianus, Antonius, and Protolichus, martyrs, who were drowned in the sea. Also, Cyrianus, priest; Moses; Bassianus; and Agatho, all of whom were burned in the fire. Also Dionysius and Ammonius, who were beheaded.

The fifteenth day before the Kalends. Day 15.

[Note: Col. 0763]

Only the Pratensis, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, and Marchianus manuscripts are pure today.

[Note: Col. 0763B]

I wrote *Blavius*, as all the ancient manuscripts, both handwritten and printed, have it, rather than *Blasius*, as Antwerp-Major has. Concerning him we dealt with on the third of this month. Nearly all read *Agricolano*, except Rosweyd; they likewise read *Brixa*, and we think this is what Usuardus read. Antwerp-Major, among other blemishes, has *Agricolano*; *diurnam* for *diutinam*; *laci* for *laici*; *documento* for *documentis*; and *Nacionensi* for *Vasionensi*. Here, as elsewhere, we write *Agape* with the text itself and with most of the manuscripts. Again, the manuscripts have *Quinidi* for *Quinidii*; but here there is no less diversity in the pronunciation of the city than in that of the name, as you will see in the Acts. Marchianus writes *Quiri* in the most corrupt manner of all. Several others have *Jobitae*; Antwerp-Major, *Sobitae*; Rosweyd, *Jovitiae*: we read the form used by Usuardus. Today Rosweyd’s manuscript alone, unusually exact and accurate, omitting the title *virginis* after *Jovitae*, adds by abbreviation *martyrum* (“of the martyrs”).

The scarcity of pure manuscripts arises chiefly from the fact that many of them, on the third of this month, in accordance with the Church’s more solemn custom then prevailing, announce Blavius—whom we today call Blasius. This was evident in the Heriniensis, otherwise extremely pure today. The Tournai manuscript was also discussed there. There is, however, this difference between the two: the eulogy of Blasius has been contracted from the final section; the account of Crato has been completely cut out; and the Pulsanensis, Antwerp, and Max.-Lübeck manuscripts are deficient in other respects. Munerat resembles the Heriniensis; it also has Blasius on the third, but is otherwise pure. In general, one should observe that neither these nor almost any other of our manuscripts ever mention Joseph, deacon of Antioch, whom Greven and Molan nevertheless append to Usuardus’s text, followed in their opinion by Baronius and others. I am unhesitatingly of the opinion that the authority of our manuscripts outweighs those two witnesses, and I suspect, not implausibly, that this notice entered a few Usuardine manuscripts from Rabanus or Notker. This Joseph is known in the Hieronymian copies under the names *Jusippus*, *Joseppus*, and *Josippus*, everywhere with the title “deacon” and as the leader of a larger cohort. Molan’s edition further differs from the others in that it transposed the text itself, announcing Faustinus and Jovita before Crato.]

[Note: Col. 0763C]

We have already discussed Blasius, or Blavius, in the Variants for the third of this month, and again above for this day. Castellanus, p. 507, asserts without hesitation that this saint is commemorated in the Hieronymian Martyrology on 16 February under the name *Plesus*, as in the Epternacensis, or *Blesus*, as in both the Corbeiensis of Acherius and that of Florentinius. Our predecessors did not recognize there Blasius, or Blavius, bishop of Sebaste; I readily confess that I do not see more clearly than they did. He is explicitly placed on this day by the Little Roman Martyrology: “At Sebaste, the passion of Saint Blavius, bishop.” Ado saw some Acts, from which he fashioned an eulogy, contracted by our author and transcribed in full by Notker. Bollandus’s commentary for 3 February should be read. Whether the Acts themselves ought wholly to be rejected, as Tillemontius suggests among more recent writers in volume V, [Col. 0763D] pp. 170 and 649, will be examined in the Supplement. The memory of Crato is likewise found in the Roman Martyrology: “At Rome, Saint Crato, martyr.” The additions in the calendar are taken from Ado, who supplied further material from the Acts of Saint Valentinus of Interamna, concerning whom we dealt yesterday. But it remains uncertain where the assertion comes from that he completed his martyrdom with his wife and entire household.

Faustinus and Jovita, with their names somewhat altered, are placed by the Hieronymian copies on the following day in Britain; from this it is certainly evident that their cult was very ancient in the Church. But what does “in Britain” mean here? If some conjecture is permitted, I would believe that the name of Brixia, once abbreviated or not adequately expressed, gave ignorant Gallic scribes the opportunity to construct the more familiar name Britain. In the same way, and together with Henschenius, we should charitably explain what is read elsewhere: “at the city of Cologne”—namely, that it should be “at the city of Brixia, a Roman colony.” These explanations are surely more tolerable than Castellanus’s recourse to Ovid’s *Fasti* in order to derive from them a resemblance between Jupiter and Faunus. Aloysius and Mosander consistently attribute both saints to Ado with an extensive eulogy; but Rosweyd rightly relegates this to an appendix. I suspect this most probably because not a word of the whole story is found in Notker, who nevertheless mentions Faustinus, nor has anything been extracted from it by Usuardus, so that it is not sufficiently clear from where he obtained it—especially since no one before him had given Jovita the title “virgin.” I scarcely doubt that he thought her a woman, since he was never accustomed to grant that distinction to men. See the rest in the work of the aforementioned Henschenius, and, much more briefly, in Tillemontius, volume II, [Col. 0765A] p. 228. The entire notice of Quinidius is taken word for word from Ado; see Bollandus’s commentary and the life edited by him. Agape is clearly marked in the Hieronymian Martyrology: “At Interamna, the feast of Saint Agape, virgin”; but some companions seem to have been added, whom our author omitted. Whether her martyrdom can truly be doubted, see the Acts and Castellanus, p. 653. Wandalbertus writes of her as follows, placing her before Faustinus and Jovita:

From this, on the fifteenth day, Agape’s merit shines;

and on this day Brixia venerates

Faustinus, struck by cruel punishments,

and the famous and holy Jovita.

[Note: Col. 0765A]

Pulsanensis mentions only Crato, apart from Faustinus and Jovita; it is astonishing that Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck omitted him.

Antwerp-Maximum, Utrecht, Leyden, Louvain, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition are sufficiently pure, except for the single notice of Blasius, which, as we said, they placed on the third of this month.

Alberg writes concerning Faustinus and Jovita: “In Italy, at the city of Brixia, the feast of Saints Faustinus and Jovita, deacons, who, under the emperor Hadrian, were exposed to most savage beasts and flames; their arms were ordered to be bound and suspended on high, and they were there violently tortured. Then, with lamps lit and placed at their sides, they completed their glorious martyrdom by decapitation. More than three thousand people, strengthened by their passion, believed.” At the end it adds: “Also, the translation of Saint Antony, confessor.” This final addition was inserted by a later hand in the Danic manuscript; in the other copies it agrees with Alberg, except that it writes *Brixia* for *Brictia*, *confringi* for *constringi*, and *compleverunt* for *consummaverunt*.

The Centulensian, abbreviating everything, adds: “In the territory of the Morini, the burial of Saint Silvinus, bishop and confessor of Toulouse,” concerning whom see more on the seventeenth of this month.

The Brussels manuscript, interpolated in Crato and mutilated in Blasius, has in third place: “At Antioch, Joseph, deacon.” It alone among all our manuscript codices mentions Joseph. It follows with: “At Brixia,” and so forth, contracting the preceding eulogy somewhat. [Col. 0765C] Then: “At Padua, the translation of Saint Antoninus, confessor.” It means Antony of Padua, concerning whom several manuscripts speak. Concerning Agape and Quinidius, it is almost as in the text. At the end: “On the same day, Saint Silvinus, bishop and confessor of Tournai.”

Hagenoyen, quite pure in Crato, has concerning Faustinus and Jovita almost the same as Alberg above. After Agape it adds: “Also, Blessed Austregisilus, bishop and confessor.” Bollandus assigns Austregisilus to 20 May, although Florus also records him today.

Victorin, at the end: “On the same day, Saint Silvinus, bishop of Tournai. In the province of Valeria, Saint Severus, priest, concerning whom Blessed Gregory writes.” Mosander inserted this same Severus into Ado’s text.

The Matrician-Carthusian-Utrecht manuscript: “Agape, virgin and martyr, and Chionia, her sister.” I do not know where this sister came from. If they are Agape and Chionia, they are celebrated on 3 April.

[Col. 0765D] Codex Bigotianus, marked P. 5, formerly belonging to the Celestines: “At the city of L’Aquila, the translation of Blessed Peter, confessor, of Marrone, formerly Pope Celestine.”

The Swedish Register, under nos. 130 and 428: “On the same day, Saint Silvinus, bishop of Tournai.” The earlier codex alone adds: “In the province of Valeria,” and so forth, as in Victorin.

The Vatican manuscript, no. 5949: “In the province of Alteria, Saint Severus, priest.” It meant “in Valeria,” and so forth.

The Altempsian: “In the territory of the castle of Bedriacum, the arrival of the most illustrious confessor of Christ, Botolph, over whose bier a column of light sent from heaven shone before everyone’s eyes.” See the Acts for 17 June.

The Medici codex: “Also, at the city of Aquileia, the translation of the body of Saint Peter, confessor, who is called of Marone, in the monastery of Collemaggio.”

The Codex of Monte Cassino: “The translation of the bishops, the blessed confessors Amatus, Romaric, and Adelphius, who were relocated together.”

The Priory of Caudiac: “At Clermont, the translation of Saint Georgia, virgin.” She is celebrated on this day.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins as follows: “At the monastery of Meyfeld near Koblenz, Saint Severus, priest and confessor, concerning whom Blessed Pope Gregory writes in the *Dialogues*: At Rome, Saint Crato, martyr, who had a son named Cerimon, a student. When the latter fell into a very serious illness, Crato brought him to Blessed Valentinus, bishop, for healing, on the condition that if the boy were healed, he himself with his entire household would become Christian. When the boy was healed through the prayer of the holy bishop, Crato fulfilled what he had promised and was baptized with his wife and entire household; not many days later he completed his martyrdom.” Concerning Faustinus and Jovita it writes almost as Alberg does. Concerning Quinidius and Agape, purely. “Also, the translation of Saint Antony of Padua, confessor, of the Order of Saint Francis. On the same day, Blessed Ebbo, bishop and confessor.” See Bollandus among the persons omitted. “Anania [Antioch], Saint Joseph, deacon and confessor. On the same day, Saint Sigfrid, bishop and confessor. Also at Ravenna, the translation of Saint Severus, bishop and confessor.” He was discussed on the first of this month, when his life was edited.

The beginning of Belin is this: “At Brixia, the feast [Col. 0766C] of Saints Faustinus and Jovita, martyrs, who, when examined under the emperor Hadrian, said to him: ‘Listen, Hadrian, twisted serpent, indeed most savage snake: you run through winding paths and bends so that you may make us stray from the straight road. Let this be known to you: we shall not obey your barking, nor shall we offer incense to the gods; rather, to the Lord our Creator we continually offer incense and libations together.’ When the people from the city of Milan heard this, they gathered together because of the saints’ steadfastness, came to the blessed martyrs of God, and had themselves baptized. Then Hadrian, hearing this, inflamed with fury, immediately had them punished with the sword and beheaded.” It continues with Agape. Then: “On the same day at Padua, the translation of Saint Antony, of the Order of Friars Minor.” At the end: “At Antioch, Saint Joseph, deacon.”

Greven: “Faustinus and Jovita, as Vincent records in book II, chapter 83: exposed by the emperor Hadrian to most savage beasts and flames, they were unharmed; bound by the arms, suspended on high and tortured, then burned with lamps lit and brought near their sides; finally they completed their martyrdom by decapitation. They believed, and so forth: John, Adventus, Saturninus, and Castula.” They are not correctly joined from the Hieronymian Martyrology; see the persons omitted. “At the monastery of Meyfeld, and so forth, who is also mentioned above on the Kalends of February.” Here he confuses the two Severuses. The translation of Severus of Ravenna and of Antony of Padua follows. “Ebbo, bishop and confessor of Tournai [perhaps he means Teroanensis; but even thus he is unknown]. Silvius, bishop and confessor [is this not Silvinus?], Marcellus, bishop. In Ireland, Berachius, bishop and confessor. Faustus, monk and confessor, disciple of Blessed Benedict, who wrote his life.” See Castellanus, p. 625, around the middle.

Molan inserts in italic type into the text what we reported from Belin concerning Faustinus and Jovita. Also concerning Quinidius, “whose deeds are recorded.” Then he adds: [Col. 0767A] “On the same day at Padua,” and so forth. “On the same day, Blessed Severus,” and so forth. Finally, in smaller type: “His [Severus’s] body was brought from Italy by Rupert, bishop of Trier.” See the Acts and Castellanus. In other editions the text of Usuardus is mutilated. The translation of Saint Antony of Padua is also omitted. But the following is added: [Col. 0768A] “At Vexio in Dacia, Saint Sigifrid, bishop, a man of outstanding holiness, who converted Sweden to the Lord.” Again in smaller type: “At Constantinople, the dedication of the church of Saint Sophia.” I find no other reference to this. See the dedication of that church in Cangius, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, book III.]

[Col. 0763]

At the city of Sebaste, the passion of Saint Blavius, bishop, a performer of many miracles. Under the governor Agricolanus, after a prolonged beating and suspension on a wooden frame, during which his flesh was torn by iron combs, and after a most dreadful imprisonment and immersion in a lake, from which he emerged unharmed, he was beheaded by order of the aforesaid judge, together with two boys. Finally, seven women who were collecting the drops of his flowing blood were discovered to be Christians; after terrible tortures, they too were struck with the sword. At Rome, Saint Crato, martyr, who, instructed in the proofs of the faith by Blessed Valentinus, completed his martyrdom with his wife and entire household not many days later. At the city of Brixa, Saints Faustinus and Jovia, virgin, martyrs. In Gaul, at the city of Vaison, Saint Quinidius, bishop, whose death is attested as precious in the sight of the Lord by frequent miracles. At the city of Interamna, Saint Agape, virgin.

The fourteenth day before the Kalends. Day 16.

[Note: Col. 0767]

Thus the Pratensis, Heriniensis, Marchianus, Antwerp-Major, Belin, Pulsanensis, Greven, and Molan manuscripts.

[Note: Col. 0767B]

Older codices read *Honesimi*; we therefore judged that their spelling, although incorrect, should be retained. Pulsan has *sancti* instead of *beati*. Antuerp.-Max. among other blemishes has *Phylomeni* for *Philemoni*; Belin has *ordinavit* for *ordinans*. In the Herinien. manuscript the particle *eum* is redundant before *reliquit*. Pulsan has the worse reading *requievit* for *reliquit*. Herinien. and Belin have *In civitate Cumis*. What Pulsan intends by *Ticitii* [Col. 0768B], I do not know. *Julianes* for *Julianae* in that same manuscript is extraordinary. Likewise, in Greven and Molan, *deinde* instead of *dein* is not noteworthy, as several manuscripts have *Egyptum*. Greven omits *martyris* after *Juliani*. Pulsan alone of all the codices substitutes *with five soldiers* for the universally asserted *with five thousand others*.

### [Note: Col. 0767B]

Onesimus is unknown to the Hieronymian Martyrology; he is recorded by Bede and, following him, by Rabanus, and in precisely the same formula by the *Romanum parvum*: “Saint Onesimus the apostle.” The designation “apostle” is commonly given by both Greeks and Latins not only to the Twelve, but also to their other disciples and fellow workers. In the text of his Martyrology Ado prefixed only *natale* (“feast”). Mosander, confusing Ado’s words, transferred here what had been said among the festivals of the apostles. There he is adorned with an eminent eulogy [Col. 0767C] drawn from Paul’s Letter to Philemon and from another letter of Ignatius to the Ephesians. Since the latter makes it clear that Onesimus was bishop of Ephesus, Ado thought that title should unquestionably be assigned to him, and he continued with the rest concerning his martyrdom, which Notker describes; Our author embraces it more briefly.

Henschenius has illustrated all this in an excellent commentary, without doubting that this was the same Onesimus, Philemon’s slave, the Apostle’s disciple, and subsequently, after Timothy, bishop of the Ephesians. Some more recent scholars disagree, among them Tillemont, in *Life of St. Paul*, vol. I, p. 289 onward, and in the notes on p. 576. He presses especially the point that the man baptized by Paul around the year 61 does not seem likely to have lived until 107, the year in which Ignatius’ letter is presumed to have been written.

For my part, whether in this matter or in the other arguments advanced by Tillemont, I have so far seen nothing that compels me to depart from Henschenius’ opinion. To put it briefly: let us suppose for the moment that Onesimus was first an apostolic bishop [Col. 0767D], or a bishop of uncertain location—a status commonly allowed both for apostles and for other disciples. Suppose next that he succeeded Timothy in 97, and assume that Paul baptized him when he was twenty years old, or, if one prefers, thirty. What difficulty, I ask, would there be if, surviving beyond the age of seventy into the year 107, he received Ignatius at Ephesus?

The arguments Castellanus brings on p. 666 from the silence of Rabanus and Wandalbertus are even less alarming, for they collapse of themselves if Ignatius’ letter can be understood as referring to our Onesimus. I therefore wish to warn the reader that Papebrochius’ sentence in the *Ephemerides Graeco-Moschae*, p. XVII, has been wrongly understood by some, as though he were there retracting what Henschenius had correctly established. This is precisely what Papebrochius meant to indicate, as I write these words while he is still alive and in good health.

For the rest, if more compelling arguments should later be brought forward against Henschenius’ view, we shall examine them carefully in the Supplement.

### [Col. 0768B]

Hesselius had earlier rejected the Acts of Juliana of Nicomedia in Molanus, on the strength of several arguments. Bollandus easily answered these in the present commentary, though without in any way asserting the complete authenticity of the aforesaid Acts. We may admit that he was somewhat more indulgent in accepting them, as Papebrochius shows in his *Responses*, art. II, no. III, and elsewhere. It will be our task at the proper time to investigate and assess what was there promised.

As for the memory of the illustrious saint [Col. 0768C], she is recorded in the most ancient sacred calendars. Whatever Florentinius may think was introduced through scribal license into the Corbie copy—the title “martyr,” for example, in the announcement: “At Nicomedia, the passion of Saint Juliana, virgin and martyr,” an unusual formula in these codices—and likewise in the Epternacensis, where we read: “In Campania, at Cumbas [for Cumas], the feast of Juliana,” the reader should consult the note of the cited editor.

For us, it is enough to cite our martyrologists Bede, Rabanus, the *Romanum parvum*, Ado, Usuard, Notker, and Wandalbertus himself, who sings of her together with Onesimus:

> The fourteenth day shines with Juliana the martyr,  
> And honors blessed Onesimus, taught by Paul.

The *Romanum parvum* simply records: “And at Cumae, Saint Juliana the virgin.” Bede composed the eulogy from the Acts; Rabanus and Ado took it from him [Col. 0768D], and Notker from Ado; Our author has greatly abridged it. This is sufficient concerning the antiquity of her cult among the Latins; add to it the Sacramentary of Thomasius. Among the Greeks, more will be found on different days. Whether this is truly a celebration of her martyrdom or of the translation of her relics, I leave undecided. See Castellanus, cited above, p. 666, and Tillemont, vol. V, p. 155.

The Hieronymian Martyrology explicitly reads *Julianus with five thousand Egyptians*, or *five thousand*, or *of five thousand*. Ado followed it, adding on his own authority the location *in Egypt*. Hence Usuard and Notker; but in them no textual indications can be found by which this Julian might be distinguished from the number of doubtful Julians. The discarded John the Deacon confuses the matter still further.

To avoid excessive length: after everything has been properly weighed, this Julian seems to me most probably to be the one who appears in the Acts with Theodulus on the following day, and who is joined in the Eusebian group in the Hieronymian Martyrology to the illustrious Pamphilus [Col. 0769A] and his other companions, himself being the last to receive the crown of martyrdom. Among that group were also the five anonymous Egyptians mentioned here, who had assumed the names of the prophets Elijah, Jeremiah, Isaiah, Samuel, and Daniel, as may be gathered from Eusebius in Valesius’ edition, *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, chap. II.

Eusebius’ words are cited in the Acts on this day, where Elijah and the others are discussed; on 17 February, where Julian and Theodulus are discussed; and on 1 June, where Pamphilus is treated separately from our martyrologies, as we shall explain there. For that date, see Papebrochius’ commentary, from which Castellanus took what he presents on pp. 667 [Col. 0770A] and 668. See also p. 673 and Florentinius’ careful note.

From all this it will be understood that those who, according to Eusebius and the Hieronymian Martyrology, ought to have been collected on this day under the number twelve have been separated and scattered over various days. At the same time one sees that the Pulsan codex, cited above, read quite aptly—though not according to Usuard’s intention—when it substituted *five soldiers* for *five thousand*: namely, those Egyptians whose proper names are not given in the Hieronymian Martyrology. The martyrdom of Pamphilus and his companions, translated from Eusebius into French, may be read in Tillemont, vol. V, p. 418 onward.

### [Note: Col. 0769A]

**ROSWEYD.** It could have been counted among the pure manuscripts, since it differs only in not writing, concerning Juliana after *ferventem* (“boiling”), what the others have: “she completed her martyrdom by beheading; but, with her bridegroom Evilasius taking away her head, [she completed] martyrdom,” and so forth.

**TORNACEN.** It is defective: it omitted the final part [Col. 0769B] of Saint Onesimus’ eulogy, which concerns his martyrdom, and the whole of Juliana’s eulogy—perhaps because it rightly regarded both as suspect.

**ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC.** They also cut short Juliana’s eulogy.

**ULTRAJECT.** It inserted three words concerning Juliana into the text: “in the time of the emperor Maximian”; otherwise it is sufficiently pure.

**ANTUERP.-MAX., LEYDEN., LOVAN., ALBERG., DANIC.**, and the **ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition**, besides those three words, add at the end: “At the city of Metz, the feast of Saint Symeon, bishop and confessor.” See the Acts.

**MUNERAT.** “On the same day, Saint Honestius the martyr.” See Bollandus’ commentary, and compare with it what Castellanus has on this day, p. 668.

**CENTULEN.** “At Rome, the passion of Saint Onesimus, bishop of the Ephesians, who was stoned by the Romans. At Cumae, Saint Juliana the virgin.” In the last part it is sufficiently pure.

**BRUXELLEN.** First: “At the city of Cumae, the passion of Saint Juliana the virgin. In the time of the emperor Maximian [Col. 0769C], she was stripped and beaten with rods, suspended by her hair, and drenched from the head with molten lead; then she was taken into prison, where she openly fought with the devil. Afterwards she overcame the torments of wheels, flames, and a boiling cauldron, and completed her martyrdom by beheading.” It presents Onesimus’ eulogy somewhat more fully; we shall report it better below. Julian is then added in the margin, by the same hand. Symeon follows as above.

**HAGENOYEN.** It is almost pure concerning Onesimus, but invents something else about Juliana: “At the city of Cumae, the passion of Saint Juliana, a most noble virgin and martyr, who, after being stripped, was scourged for a very long time by her betrothed because she would neither consent to marry him nor worship the gods. She was suspended by her hair for six hours [Col. 0770A], and boiling lead was poured over her, but the virgin was not harmed. She was bound with iron and imprisoned, where she fought with and conquered the devil. She was thrown among the blades of wheels and into the fire, and cast into a cauldron full of molten lead; finally, by beheading, she completed her martyrdom.” Julian appears as in the text. At the end [Col. 0770B]: “At the unnamed city [Metz], Saint Symeon, bishop and confessor.”

**AMBIANEN.** “On the same day, the feast of Saint Honestius, priest and martyr.”

**REG. SUEC., no. 428.** “On the same day, Saint Honestius the martyr.”

**VATICAN., no. 5949.** First: “The holy virgins Fusca and Maura.” See the Acts for the 13th of this month.

The **LUBECK-COL. edition** varies somewhat from the preceding manuscripts in Onesimus and Juliana; insofar as the substance is concerned, we shall give it below from Molanus. It has Symeon of Metz in third place and Julian with five thousand at the end, as above.

**GREVEN.** “Faustinianus, Plesius, Fabianus. Sebastian the martyr.” In the first edition of 1515: “Saint Honestius the martyr. In Africa, Paul the Hermit. At Metz, Symeon, bishop and confessor. In Sweden, Sigfrid, bishop and confessor.” For Sebastian, Paul, and Sigfrid, see those omitted today.

**MOLAN.** After *reliquit*, he inserted into the text, in different type, the following from Ado [Col. 0770C]: “Concerning him blessed Ignatius, writing a letter to the Ephesians, says: ‘Since I have received your multitude in the name of the Lord, in Onesimus our beloved teacher, but your bishop, I urge you, according to Christ Jesus, to love him, and all of you to be in him in concord. For blessed is God, who has granted you to have in Christ such a bishop.’”

Concerning Juliana, after *consummavit*, he adds from the same Ado: “She indeed suffered at Nicomedia, but after a short time, by God’s providence, she was transferred to Campania.” At the end, concerning Symeon, as above. In other editions there is an additional entry: “On the same day at Amiens, Saint Honestius the martyr.”

### [Col. 0767]

The feast of blessed Onesimus, concerning whom Saint Paul writes to Philemon; the same apostle ordained him bishop and, entrusting him with the word of preaching, left him at the city of Ephesus. Brought to Rome, he was there stoned for the faith of Christ; from there his body was carried back to the places where he had been ordained.

At the city of Cumae, Saint Juliana the virgin, who, after various torments and imprisonment, openly fought with the devil. Then, overcoming flames and a boiling cauldron, she completed her martyrdom by beheading.

In Egypt, Saint Julian the martyr, with five thousand others.

### XIII Kal. Day 17

[Note: Col. 0769D]

Taken from Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Marchian., Pulsanen., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. Codices of middling authority may also be added, as I shall say in the Appendices.

### [Note: Col. 0771B]

The reading should be *Polychronius*, as found in the author of the *Romanum parvum* and in Ado, unless I am mistaken that the editor corrected them. I, perhaps excessively scrupulously, follow the Usuardine codices: Praten., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Marchian., Munerat., and others, although Herinien. and Greven have *Polichronius*; Pulsan, *Polychronius*; Molan, *Polycronius*. Let the reader choose whichever reading seems preferable.

Pulsan has *Babiloniae* for *Babylonia*. Greven and Molan have *praesidente* for *praesente*. Pulsan is worse in reading *Diocletiano* instead of *Decio*; perhaps it would be better to omit the presence of both. Pulsan changes *raising his eyes to heaven* into *with his eyes raised to heaven* [Col. 0772B]; Munerat has *lifting them toward heaven*. Thus Marchian changes *Concordia* into *Corduba*, and *eighty-six* into *eight hundred six*; Pulsan likewise has *Formuli* for *Romuli*. Some place *Scotia*; the form in the text is better.

Marchian reads *Finanus*; Pulsan, *Funtanius*; Munerat, *Funtanus*. We have given the true name. All write *Silvinus*; I do not know why more recent writers prefer *Sylvinus*. Our Pratensis has *Tarvenensis*; Herinien, *Tarwanensis*; Greven, worst of all, *Targuanensis*; the others have *Taruanensis*, a word omitted by Pulsan. See below at the end of the Observations.

### [Note: Col. 0771B]

The name Polychronius occurs only in the Epternacensis copy of the Hieronymian Martyrology, in this form: “At Babylon, Polychronius”; and again, in that same codex, at the end of 30 April: “The burial of Polychronius, bishop”—whether the same man or another, who can explain? Bede, in the entry for today, adds “bishop of that place,” but no more correctly writes *Polocronius*, as does his transcriber Rabanus. We have said that this inflection, or one very close to it, is common in the Usuardine codices.

The *Romanum parvum* does not specify the episcopal see, reading: “In Persia, blessed Polychronius, bishop and martyr.” Ado joins Babylon and Ctesiphon as two sees, while also introducing Bede’s eulogy, which Rabanus and Notker adopted in full. Our author has shortened it only slightly, while retaining what requires correction, as may be seen in the Acts, in Castellanus, p. 676, and in Tillemont, vol. V, p. 561.

Here lies the chief difficulty: Bede and those who follow him testify that the eulogy was taken from the Acts of Saint Lawrence. Those Acts are now judged by all learned scholars, at least as Baron and Henschenius considered them, to be so highly suspect that they can neither be wholly defended nor easily purged. From the same source come Olympias and Maximus, 15 April; Parmenius and the others, 22 April; and others on other days. Their memory is certain enough in our calendars, but the sequence of their lives or martyrdoms, taken from those Acts, is rejected, as will be said on 10 August.

Wandalbertus’ verses are not entirely clear, when Donatus is joined to Polychronius from the following group:

> On the thirteenth day Polychronius’ feast returns,  
> And Donatus’: faith, blood, and altar unite them.

There is no need here to argue at length concerning the Concordian martyrs, whom Our author confused because of the disordered classes of the Hieronymian copies. It is certain that the genuine text of Usuard should be restored [Col. 0772B]. Notker placed other classes, concerning whose arrangement or restoration we shall speak in their proper place. Meanwhile, see the Acts, Florentinius, and Castellanus here.

Fintanus belongs to Usuard alone; *Scotia*, according to the usage of that period, means Ireland. Silvinus’ death seems to belong to 15 February, as Castellanus holds, and some of our Appendices place it on that day. Nevertheless, more recent martyrologists generally follow Usuard, together with the modern Roman Martyrology and the Acts.

Bollandus illustrated his life with an excellent commentary, and Mabillon reproduced it in *Benedictine Centuries*, century III, part I, p. 294 onward. In the preliminary observations, however, that most learned man must have been asleep when he wrote: “Ado, bishop of Vienne, had seen those Acts; in his genuine Martyrology these words occur: 15 Kalends of March, Saint Silvinus, bishop and confessor of Tervan, whose deeds are recorded.”

As I say, he must have been asleep, for so far I have been unable to find those words in any of the printed or manuscript Martyrologies that are genuinely Adonian. It seems rather certain to me that the entire announcement of Silvinus is wholly Usuardine. Castellanus conjectures what sort of Acts Usuard possessed on p. 659, where he also discusses his episcopate on the basis of Bollandus.

Certainly it is far from the truth that our Pratensis copy reads “bishop of the city of Toulouse,” and Castellanus admits that this was added to the supposed autograph above the earlier announcement, the one we present here, which had been erased with a knife [Col. 0772D]. I would not dare call our announcement true, but it is genuinely Usuardine; all our codices agree in it except Marchian, which, together with the aforementioned Pratensis, reads: “In the district of Tervan, Saint Silvinus, bishop of the city of Toulouse.” Antuerp.-Maj. differs only in wrongly writing “in the district of Caritatis” instead of “in the district of Tervan.”

### [Note: Col. 0771D]

**ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC.**, and the **ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition** scarcely depart from the pure text. The name Romulus is omitted from the group of Concordian martyrs, and Fintanus is placed after Silvinus [Col. 0772D]. The variation in the forms of Polychronius and Tervanensis is unsurprising.

**ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC.** Omit Fintanus, and also omit the name Romulus.

**ROSWEYD.** Third, it inserts: “At Aquileia, Chrysanthius the martyr and ninety others.” See the Acts. For Fintanus it writes *Finianus*. At the end, concerning Silvinus, it agrees with Pratensis.

**CENTULEN.** Omits Silvinus here, having treated him on the 15th, as will be found there among the Appendices. In his place it adds at the end: “At Verdun, Saint Pulchronius, bishop and confessor.”

**BRUXELLEN.** Also treated Silvinus on the 15th; otherwise it is pure, except that it inserts into the text “bishop of Babylon and Ctesiphon.”

**HAGENOYEN.** In the penultimate place it introduces saints unknown today in all the other manuscripts. It reads: “On the same day, the holy martyrs Montanus and Gemellus, who, when they were imprisoned with other saints, saw in a vision a young man enter the prison carrying two phials full of milk. He gave all the prisoners to drink and said, ‘A third phial is still reserved for you,’ and departed.” I would be mistaken if this did not concern the martyrs to be assigned among the Usuardine additions on the 24th of this month. Otherwise, scarcely anything is lacking from the purity of the Hagenoyen codex.

**AQUICINCT.** Reads *Cordula* for *Concordia*, and *Finani* for *Fintani*. At the end: “At Clermont, the translation of Lupianus the confessor.” This is also found in the Bordeaux, Cluniac, Altempsian, Daveron, Caudiac Priory, and D. Le Mare codices, designated C, formerly belonging to the Franciscans, with the sole difference that some add the saint’s name. See those omitted.

**VICTORIN.** At the end, instead of Silvinus: “On the same day, Saint Morsetus.”

**REG. SUEC., no. 130.** Reads: “On the same day, Saint Moiretius,” almost certainly for *Moisetus*.

**VATICAN., no. 5949.** Says nothing of Fintanus and Silvinus, and adds at the end: “Saint Valentinianus.”

### [Col. 0773C]

**STROZZ. and MEDIC.** “At the city of Fiesole, in the regions of Tuscany, the translation of the bodies of the saints: Romulus, the first bishop of that city; Alexander, bishop; Donatus and Romanus, bishops of the aforesaid city; and the holy martyrs Carissimus, Crescentius, and Dulcissimus, together with the relics of other saints and holy women.”

The **LUBECK-COL. edition** inserts between Fintanus and Silvinus: “On the same day at Trier, Saint Bonosius, bishop and confessor.” At the end: “On Mount Siberg, the translation of Saint Benignus, priest and martyr, performed in the year 1073 of the Lord’s Incarnation by Saint Anno, archbishop of Cologne.”

**BELIN.** Has an almost pure text; at the end it adds: “At Clermont, the translation of Saint Lupianus the confessor.”

**GREVEN.** “At Trier, Saint Bonosius, bishop and confessor. In Africa, Chrysanthus, Concordia, and Justa.” The order is incorrect. “On Mount Siberg, in the diocese of Cologne, the translation of Saint Benignus, etc. In Scotland, Fimianus, bishop”—or is this not Finanus of Lindisfarne? “Sabinus, bishop of the city of Canusium, of whom Gregory reports, in *Dialogues* III, among other things, that when poison had been administered to him by his archdeacon, who was aspiring to the episcopate, he learned of it by prophetic inspiration and drank it without harm, saying to the archdeacon: ‘I am drinking poison, but you will not be bishop.’ At that very hour the archdeacon died.” This is certainly Sabinus of Canusium, concerning whom see the 9th of this month.

**MOLAN.** In the text concerning Polychronius, in Italic type, he adds Ado’s words: “It is written in the passion of Saint Lawrence,” which many consider apocryphal. At the end, after *bishop*, he attaches the words earlier rejected: “Of the city of Toulouse, in the district of Tervan, whose deeds are recorded.” Concerning Lupianus and Bonosius, as above. Then, in smaller type: “Sabinus, bishop of the city of Canusium, concerning whom Gregory reports in Book III of the *Dialogues*.”

In other editions he added concerning Silvinus: “At the monastery of Sithiu”—why not at Alciacum, commonly called Auchy? Finally, at the end: “On the seventeenth day, Saint Theodore the recruit, martyr.”

### [Col. 0769]

In the Persian city of Babylon, the feast of blessed Polychronius, bishop and martyr, who, while the persecutor Decius was present, had his mouth beaten with stones; stretching out his hands and raising his eyes to heaven, he gave up his spirit.

At the city of Concordia, the passion of the holy martyrs Donatus and Secundianus; Romulus with eighty-six others.

In Scotland, Saint Fintanus, priest and confessor, a man of great virtue.

On the same day, Saint Silvinus, bishop of Tervan.

[At Bouillart: “…a man of great virtue.” [Note: Col. 0769D] Castellanus wrote to Soller that this “bishop of the city of Toulouse” had been added to the Sangermanensis autograph, the earlier announcement having been erased. That announcement had been: “On the same day, Saint Silvinus, bishop of Tervan.” I confess that, when I read Castellanus’ warning, I could not refrain from calling either his reliability or Soller’s into question. For I already knew from several examples that Castellanus had inspected the codex with his eyes covered; but who would have believed him so bleary-eyed as to think he saw an erasure here?

Yet so it is. I give my word that scarcely any page of the codex is cleaner. The whole page is untouched by the point of a knife. Nevertheless, I do not deny that the Sollerian reading belonged to the Carolingian autograph—so may I call it briefly, meaning the Martyrology presented to King Charles. It was corrected by Usuard in the Pratensis.

But since this and perhaps other erasures may have made the page less legible, a leaf was torn out and another pasted beside it. The handwriting is the same, or at least the distinction is so obscure that all the learned men who inspected it at our request considered it the same. The only difference I can see is that, instead of the red pigment used elsewhere in the codex to paint the Nones, Ides, and Kalends, a violet color was used here.

It is uncertain how Usuard learned that Saint Silvinus was bishop of the city of Toulouse. The Acts of that prelate, published by Guilielmus Catellus, Bollandus, and Mabillon, do indeed testify that he was raised to episcopal dignity, but they do not identify the see. Perhaps Usuard saw Acts that have since perished. Whatever the case, it cannot be determined whether he was mistaken.

Soller therefore pronounced too boldly that the reading of the Pratensis autograph was contrary to the truth. On the other hand, it is certain that the reading he derived from the Carolingian autograph is false. Saint Silvinus was never bishop of Tervan, since the bishops who held that Church’s see throughout the period when the saint lived among the Morini are known. According to Mabillon, they were Drausius, Bainus, Ravengarius, and Erkembodo, who survived until 737.

An old and elegantly written manuscript of Ado that I have before me does favor Soller’s reading. It reads, under 15 Kalends of March: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Silvinus, bishop and confessor of Tervan, whose deeds are recorded.” But I would not wish to declare that codex genuine. Its having been written after the tenth century is indicated by the commemoration, in the first hand, of Saint Maiolus the abbot on the fifth Ides of March; Maiolus died in 994.

Thus our Theoderic Ruinart, who had called that codex genuine in the first edition of the Acts, p. 203, changed his opinion in the second edition, where, abandoning the codex, he praised the common text of Ado on p. 205. BOUILLART.]

In the district of Tervan, Saint Silvinus, bishop of the city of Toulouse.]

### XII Kal. Day 18

[Note: Col. 0773]

From Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.

### [Note: Col. 0773D]

Herinien., Tornacen., and Molan read *Simeon*, which we follow here as elsewhere; Praten. and Antuerp.-Maj. have *Simon*; Munerat. and Greven, *Symeon*. I wrote *dinoscitur* (“is known”), as it appears in almost all the manuscripts, however scrupulous I may seem in such details. I likewise did not correct *Hierosolimorum*, since it is so commonly read corruptly, as we have said elsewhere.

Tornac. omitted the article here; we wrote *Jherosolimitanorum*. Munerat has *consummatur* for *consummatus est*. In Antuerp.-Maj., after *mirantibus* and before *CXX annorum*, *ut* is missing. Herinien., Tornacen., and Antuerp.-Maj. have *Hostia*; the others agree with the text.

Praten. and others have *Prepedigne*; I thought the final diphthong should at least be retained. Tornacen. omitted *cum essent praeclarissimi generis*; Munerat has *Deo*.

It should be noted in passing that two otherwise sufficiently genuine codices, Marchian and Aquicinct, are very badly disordered for six full days, up to the 23rd of this month: the saints found in Usuard are transposed and others unknown to him are added, so that they appear to have been deliberately and arbitrarily corrupted by someone.

### [Note: Col. 0774D]

Simeon, or Simon, who is said to have been one of the brothers of Christ the Savior, first becomes known in the martyrologies through the *Romanum parvum*: “At Jerusalem, Simeon, bishop and martyr.” In the edition of Ado’s Martyrology by Rosweyd, Ado added: “Who is reported to have been related to the Savior according to the flesh.” No further discussion of that kinship appears in the festivals of the apostles on 2 May, where Simeon is recorded and from which Usuard took everything except the inserted clause concerning the brotherhood of Joseph and Cleophas. Rosweyd, following Mosander, removed that clause from Ado’s Martyrology and relegated it to an appendix; in my opinion, incorrectly, since it is present in full in Notker, in the form I give the reader: “It is established, however, that he was the son of Cleophas, whose brother Joseph was.”

It is commonly known how many controversies and dissertations concern the physical kinship of Christ the Lord with those four brothers, James, Joseph, Simon, and Jude, so clearly named in Matthew 13 and Mark 6. Were they Joseph’s sons from another marriage, as Nicephorus Callistus reports from the divine Hippolytus, in Schelstrate, vol. I of *Illustrated Antiquity*, p. 507? Or cousins, through Mary of Cleophas, whom many regard as the sister of the Blessed Virgin Mary? Or paternal cousins, through Cleophas, the brother of Joseph, as our text says? Or must this kinship be explained in some other way? It is neither the place nor the time to decide these questions.

They may be examined at a later opportunity in the February Supplement, or perhaps elsewhere, when the Acts provide the occasion. Anyone unwilling to wait should consult the interpreters. Besides the present commentary in the Acts, see Florentinius’ Exercise IV, p. 161; Henschenius’ dissertation on James, 1 May; the *Chronology of the Bishops of Jerusalem* [Col. 0775B] before the third volume of the May Acts and elsewhere; Tillemont on this Simeon, vol. II, p. 186 onward, and on James the Less, vol. I, p. 365 onward; and finally Castellanus’ note, pp. 682–683.

What concerns Simeon’s martyrdom is taken from Rufinus’ translation of Eusebius, Book III, chap. 31 [Col. 0776A]. Castellanus seems to have been mistaken when he thought Usuard added something from Rufinus to Ado, for Usuard in fact took everything from Ado himself. The learned man could easily have discovered this had he consulted the aforesaid Martyrology in the festivals of the apostles on 2 May.

Maximus, Claudius, Praepedigna, and their sons Alexander and Cutia are announced by the *Romanum parvum* not at Ostia on the Tiber but at Rome, in this order: “And at Rome, the martyrs Claudius, Praepedigna, Alexander, Cutia, and Maximus.” Ado preserves the same order, but perhaps uncertain about the location, did not specify it.

Our author placed Maximus first and omitted the names of the sons. I do not see what led him to name Ostia, unless it was because the burned bodies of Claudius, his wife, and their sons are said to have been thrown there into the *rheuma*—a flowing stream—and buried by Christians beside that same city.

The rest of the eulogy is entirely abridged from Ado’s narrative, and Ado’s narrative from the Acts of Saint Susanna, concerning whom see 11 August. I do not decide here what credibility those Acts deserve; some think they should be wholly rejected. We have otherwise demonstrated the origin and authenticity of our Usuardine text.

### [Note: Col. 0775B]

**MARCHIANEN.** Mixes today’s text with the following day’s; certainly, it has the complete announcement of Gabinus. Then: “In Africa, the holy Pulius [Publius] and Julian.” See the index of those omitted.

**ROSWEYD.** Pure in the first part, it joins the second part to the following day; here it adds only at the end: “Pimenius the martyr.” See the Acts.

**PULSAN.** Defective in the section on Simeon and slightly interpolated elsewhere.

**ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC.** Pure in the section on Simeon; among the Ostian martyrs they omit Maximus; at the end they add: “In Africa, Rutulus, Silvanus, and Maximus.” See the other companions in the Acts.

**ANTUERP.-MAX., LEYDEN., ALBERG., DANIC.**, and the **ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition** agree in a modest interpolation of the text. They add after Joseph: “the Savior’s foster-father,” and call Maximus Claudius’ brother. At the end they consistently add: “On the same day in Africa, the holy Rutulus,” and so forth.

The **LOVAN.** manuscript has the same addition, but omits everything concerning the Ostian martyrs after “with two sons.”

**CENTULEN.** As an abridger, shortens Simeon; concerning the others, it adds from Ado: “At Rome, the holy martyrs Claudius, his wife Praedigna, and their sons Alexander and Cutia, and Claudius’ brother Maximus, who, being of most distinguished birth, were baptized by Pope Caius through the agency of their brother Gabinus, a priest, and afterward put to death by Diocletian in various ways. At Alexandria, blessed Dionysius, bishop and martyr. At the monastery of Centula, the burial of Saint Angilbert, abbot, who, seventh after blessed Richarius, successfully governed the monastery of Centula. His body, after being buried for twenty-eight years, was found incorrupt.”

**BRUXELLEN.** After a text considerably interpolated, it adds: “In Africa, the holy Rutulus, Silvanus, and Maximus. At Alexandria, blessed Dionysius, bishop, who became renowned through many confessions. At Metz, Saint Legontius, bishop and confessor of that city.” Dionysius is celebrated on 17 November; whether he should be honored with the title “martyr” will be said elsewhere.

**HAGENOYEN.** Almost pure, it adds: “In Africa, the holy martyr Rutulus,” and so forth.

**AQUICINCT.** Joins the text of this day to that of the following day, adding: “Likewise, Saints Rutulus,” and so forth. Its confusion has been discussed above.

**VICTORIN.** and **REG. SUEC., no. 130**, at the end: “At Alexandria, blessed Dionysius, bishop. In Africa, the holy martyrs Rutulus, Silvanus, and Maximus.”

### [Col. 0776B]

**CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, marked B.** “On the same day in Africa, the holy Rutulus, Silvanus, and Maximus.”

**UGHELLIAN. and CAUDIACENSIS.** “In Africa, Rutulus,” and so forth. The names have already been repeated often enough.

**ALTEMPSIAN.** “On the same day, Saint Constantina, virgin and martyr. At Alexandria, blessed Dionysius, bishop, who, having often become sufficiently renowned through many confessions, was made glorious by the diversity of his sufferings and torments; he rested in peace in the time of the emperor Gallienus.”

**STROZZ. and MEDIC.** “On the same day, Saint Constantia, virgin,” the daughter of Constantine. I would believe her to be the same as the Constantina of the Altempsian codex, unless the latter added the title “martyr.” See the Acts.

The **LUBECK-COL. edition** begins: “At Cologne, the commemoration of the bones of Saint Pantaleon, physician and martyr. When the head of that most holy martyr was translated from Constantinople to the city of Cologne by Henry, a knight and lord of Ulmen, in the year 1208 of the Lord’s Incarnation.” It is astonishing that Rabanus records the feast of Saint Pantaleon on this day with a long eulogy. In the remaining material, that edition is broadly similar to the middling-authority codices cited above.

**BELIN.** Has a pure text in the second edition; in the first, it wrote “one hundred and nine” instead of “one hundred and twenty.” Both editions add: “In Africa, Lucius, Silvanus, and Maximus.”

**GREVEN.** “At Rome, Pimenius, priest, and Faustus, martyrs. Likewise Rutulus, Classicus, Damasus, Tullus, Lampasius, Maiolus, Silvanus and Maximus, Elasicius, Secundinus [Col. 0776D], Fructulus, and Paulus.” These were taken from some copy of the Hieronymian Martyrology.

“In Ireland, Culanus, bishop and confessor. Likewise Berethus and Marcellus.” These could have been counted among the preceding group and assigned to the following day.

“Likewise Colomannus, bishop and confessor. At Cologne, the commemoration of the bones,” and so forth, as above.

**MOLAN.** Appends to the text: “And afterward, having been cast at Ostia into the *rheuma*, their relics were sought out by Christians and buried beside the city.” These are Ado’s words.

“In Africa, Lucius, Silvanus, and Maximus. At Cologne, the commemoration of the bones of the most holy martyr Pantaleon, when his head,” and so forth.

In other editions there is a further addition, in smaller type: “At Patara, the holy martyrs Leo and Paregorius.” See the Acts, published among the *Sincere and Select* by Ruinart, p. 610 onward.

### [Col. 0773]

Natal of blessed Simeon, bishop and martyr, who is recognized as having been related to the Savior according to the flesh, and as the son of Cleophas, who was the brother of Joseph. He was ordained bishop of Jerusalem after James, the Lord’s brother; during Trajan’s persecution he was afflicted with tortures for a long time and was brought to completion through martyrdom. Everyone present, and the judge himself, marveled that an old man of one hundred and twenty years had endured the punishment of the cross. At Ostia, the holy martyrs Maximus, Claudius, his wife Prepedigna, and their two sons. Although they were of very distinguished lineage, they were arrested at Diocletian’s command and deported into exile; afterward they were burned, and rendered to God the fragrant sacrifice of martyrdom.

Eleven days before the Kalends. Day 19. [Note: [Col. 0777]]

From the Pratense, Heriniense, Tornacense, and Antwerp-Major.

[Note: [Col. 0777A]]

Several codices, both manuscript and printed, read *Gabini*, but incorrectly, since Usuard most probably followed Ado, and Ado the Little Roman Martyrology; in both, however, the form is *Gabinii*, as also in Notker. Among the codices, the Heriniense, Antwerp-Major, and others preserve this reading. Similar transformations of the name occur in Bollandus. Concerning *presbyter*, *Diocletian*, *Africa*, and such minor details, enough has been said. *Pretiosi morte*, instead of *pretiosa morte*, in the Antwerp-Major is attributable to the copyist’s carelessness, as are several other blemishes in one or another leaf, worn away or torn out and subsequently recopied. Thus there too one reads *Plubii* for *Publii*. The scarcity of pure codices is caused by the addition at the end of the third name, namely *Marcelli*, which is added in the codices of the best quality—Munerat, Belin, Greven, and Molan—but we have judged the reading of the others preferable.]

[Note: [Col. 0777A]]

From the Acts of Saint Susanna cited on the preceding day, today’s notice concerning Gabinius was also extracted, and was again first marked by the Little Roman Martyrology: “At Rome, Gabinius, priest and martyr.” Ado composed a brief eulogy, in which, besides what Our Author transcribed verbatim, he inserts only this: “father of the most blessed Susanna.” He could have added what is occasionally appended in many copies of Usuard, namely that Gabinius was the brother of Pope Caius [Col. 0777B]. Tillemont, continuing his history in French, treats in volume IV, page 572, Susanna, Claudius, Prepedigna and the others of the preceding day, as well as our Gabinius; in his usual sufficiently modest manner, but not sufficiently in favor of the Acts, he gives his judgment. Bollandus gathers together the Gabinian material in a brief commentary, referring the reader to the frequently cited Acts of Susanna.

Henschenius, discussing at greater length on this day Publius, Julian, and their African companions in martyrdom, says: “There is a splendid crown of twelve champions of Christ who won the palm [Col. 0778A] of martyrdom in Africa.” For this he cites the manuscript Martyrology of the church of Blessed Mary at Utrecht, which we call Rosweyd’s Usuardine manuscript; its words will be given first among the Additions. All the names must be compared with the very dissimilar Hieronymian manuscripts, both in the number of martyrs and in their nomenclature, as Florentinius shows here; and this is also plainly evident from Rabanus and Notker, their copyists. [Col. 0778B] Castellanus, who is exceptionally careful in investigating and arranging these matters, does not complete the number twelve. But whatever may be decided concerning the other ten companions, certainly our purer codices mention only those two, Publius and Julian; some fuller copies add Marcellus, others one or more persons at will, as we stated in the Variants and as will become clearer below. Our notice is purely Usuardine, and Wandalbert agrees with it in this verse:

“Publius and Julian together adorn the eleventh.”

] [Note: [Col. 0777B]]
