Rosweyd. We said on the preceding day that he brings here from that day the notice: “At the city of Ostia, the holy martyrs Maximus, Claudius,” etc. In the case of Gabinius he is pure. Then he adds: “In Africa, the holy martyrs Publius and Julian and ten others.” Concerning this number, from this very Rosweyd manuscript, received by Henschenius [Col. 0777C], we spoke in the Observations.

Munerat: “In Africa, the holy martyrs Publius, Julian, and Marcellus. At Trier, Saint Leguntius, bishop and confessor.”

Marchian. On this day he placed what we shall report with Usuard on the twentieth: “At Tyre,” etc.

Pulsan. After Gabinius he inserts into the pure text: “On the same day, at the city of Benevento, the natal of blessed Barbatus, bishop and confessor.”

Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck: “In Africa, the holy Publius, Julian, and Marcellus.”

Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Albergen, the Danish codex, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition, after *martyr*, insert: “father of blessed Susanna and brother of blessed Pope Caius,” etc. “In Africa, the holy Publius, Julian, and Marcellus. At Trier, Saint Leguntius, bishop and confessor.”

Centulense inserts “father of the most blessed Susanna,” like many others from Ado.

[Col. 0777D] Brussels has everything found in the codices of middling quality and, in addition, adds at the end: “Elsewhere, Saint Pantaleon, martyr.” See the Omitted Notices. He will be treated on 27 July.

Hagenoyen, fuller than the others, after “Pope Caius,” adds: “and a kinsman of the emperor Diocletian. Because he refused to give his daughter Susanna [his own daughter] in marriage to a pagan man, the son of Diocletian, Maximius, Diocletian kept him in chains for a long time,” etc. “In Africa, the holy Publius,” etc., as above. “At the city of Trier, Saint Leguntius, bishop and confessor. He was transferred to Scasusan.” I do not know what place is meant here, unless perhaps, from the similarity of the name, one might conjecture Schaffhausen among the Helvetians. But I find nothing concerning this translation in the others. For whether there was one Leguntius or two, and for other matters pertaining here, see the Acts for this day and the preceding one.

[Col. 0778C] Aquicinct also has on this day, as does the Marchian codex, matters that ought to be placed on the following day.

Vatican, formerly Beneventan, no. 5949, has first: “At Benevento, Saint Barbatus, bishop and confessor.” So too the Italian codices.

Strozzi and Medici: “Also Saint Susanna, virgin. Also Saint Barbatus, archbishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Eustachius, patriarch of the Church of Constantinople.”

Codex Abdinghoffensis: “At Trier, Saint Licontius, bishop and confessor.” This is the same person as Leguntius above. This fragment of the codex is defective.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition agrees with the codices of middling quality.

Belin, pure in the notice concerning Gabinius, adds with most others: “In Africa, Publius, Julian, and Marcellus. On the same day, Saint Eustachius, patriarch of the Church of Constantinople.” See the Omitted Notices.

[Col. 0778D] Greven also adds Marcellus with Molan, as I said above. His Addition begins as follows: “The aforementioned Gabinius was the father of Saint Susanna, virgin and martyr, concerning whom below, on the third day before the Ides of August. He was also the brother of Saint Pope Caius.” See the Observations. “On the same day at Trier, Saint Leguntius, bishop and confessor. Also Julian, martyr. Also Marubius. Decentius, confessor.” Concerning him, see the Omitted Notices. The other two seem to have been taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; here and elsewhere they have been carelessly heaped together.

Molan. We spoke above of Marcellus, added to the pure text. [Col. 0779A] “On the same day, Saint Eustachius,” etc., as in Belin. “At Trier, Saint Leguntius,” etc. Then, in smaller type: “Boniface, bishop of Lausanne in Burgundy, died. Born at Brussels, he rested at the monastery of the Cistercian order at Cambron, near that town, in the year 1260; he was renowned for miracles during his life and after his death.” In later editions, instead of *Eustachius*, he writes *Eustathius*, and adds to him and to Leguntius: [Col. 0780A] “At the city of Benevento, Saint Barbatus, bishop and confessor.” After this, in smaller letters: “Also Saint and glorious worker of admirable deeds, Father Auxibius, archbishop of Soli, who was a disciple of Saint Mark, the blessed apostle and evangelist. On the same day Boniface died,” etc., as above, except for the final words, “in the year 1260, renowned for miracles during his life and after his death.”]

[Col. 0777]

At Rome, the natal of Saint Gabinius, priest and martyr, who, afflicted for a long time by imprisonment and chains under Diocletian, obtained the joys of heaven through a precious death. In Africa, the holy Publius and Julian.

Ten days before the Kalends. Day 20. [Note: [Col. 0779]

Thus the Pratense, Heriniense, Antwerp-Major, the second edition of Belin, Greven, and Molan have it purely.]

[Note: [Col. 0779B]]

Molan writes *incitabat* instead of *indicabant*, incorrectly. Belin contains more than one error of this kind: *Tyrannius* for *Tyrannio*; *Pelagius* for *Peleus*; *episcopus* for *episcopi*. One ought to read *Nilus*, as it is found in Ado and Eusebius, indeed even in Usuard on 19 September; but here we are compelled to follow the erroneous codices. The Pratense and Greven have *Cipro*; the others have the better reading found in the text. Again, Greven and Molan have *Pothamii*; I prefer the others. Belin omitted the title *priest* at the end. The Antwerp-Major is marred by more serious corruptions: the words *quorum numerum* are missing; *tormentis tormentorum suppliciis* is wrongly read; and after *addita* one finds *feritatem ignis ferro*. After *Alemannia* there appears “Secundinus of Saint Gall,” perhaps because the incompetence of someone filling blank pages inserted Secundinus from the following day here. I count the Pratense codex among the pure ones because in our copy the text is complete, and even the notice of Saint Gall is plainly expressed—whatever Castellanus may have meant when he said that it is found neither on 20 February nor on 16 October in the alleged autograph.]

[Note: [Col. 0779B]]

Concerning the first band, or company, of martyrs, the compiler of the Little Roman Martyrology, the first among the martyrologists, wrote as follows from the frequently cited and customary author Rufinus’ Eusebius: “At Tyre, martyrs whose number only God’s knowledge gathers together, whom Veturius, master of the army, killed by various tortures at Diocletian’s command.” That Veturius was added either from the Chronicle of Eusebius or from some Acts—whose loss Bollandus supposes—though I do not know which. Ado greatly expanded the brief period, transcribing much of his eulogy from Book VIII, chapter 7, of the praised author. So far as he follows Rufinus here, it is true and genuine; elsewhere, however, it is confused with chapter 14 of the same author, when the episcopal instigators are added. Most of these plainly belong to nearly different places, certainly to different times, and some even completed their contest by another kind of death, as will be clear from 19 September and 29 October, where we shall discuss certain of them separately. From Ado are derived the notices received by Usuard and Notker, and by more recent martyrologists from them, preserving the confusion which Bollandus believes was found in the anciently interpolated Acts. Moreover, Ado did not know the number of the Tyrian martyrs, since Rufinus himself did not state it, and in Eusebius of Valesius it is enclosed in parentheses and reduced to only five [Col. 0779D], who seem to have been extended, from the phrase of the Little Roman Martyrology, to the many “whom only God’s knowledge gathers together.” See Bollandus’ historical commentary, in which those bishops and others are assigned their proper days, as we have begun to indicate above. Tillemont, volume V, page 440, and Castellanus, pages 696–697, followed Bollandus. Nothing is read concerning these Tyrian martyrs in the Hieronymian copies, Bede, Florus, Rabanus, or Wandalbert. I know that Molan wished to attribute these verses to this metrical martyrologist:

“Soon the tenth recalls the praise and crowns the fame

Of those who shine at Tyre, their blood in multitudes poured forth.”

[Col. 0780B] But Bollandus rightly judged this supplement to be rejected, ending Wandalbert’s single verse in this way:

“Soon the tenth recalls the praise and crowns the fame of Corona.”

[Col. 0780C] Concerning this martyr, joined with Victor, see the Hieronymian Martyrologies for this day, and Rabanus, Notker, and Henschenius, who explain several uncertainties in his commentary.

Potamius and Nemesius were taken from a somewhat purer copy of the Hieronymian Martyrology, but separated from Didymus, whom Rabanus and Notker correctly joined with others. *Potamiae*, *Potaminae*, *Misis*, *Nemesis*, *Nemersi*, and similar forms seem attributable to the carelessness of copyists. We certainly think that *Potamia* or *Pantamia* was fabricated from this, a name that will recur frequently in the Additions, wrongly appended to Caius and Victor. Whether there were further companions of Potamius and Nemesius, as seems to emerge from the Corbie codex, is uncertain.

Ado called Saint Gall an abbot, a man of extraordinary holiness and a disciple of Saint Columbanus the abbot; Our Author calls him a priest and confessor. Both celebrate him on this very day, although Notker refers his natal to 16 October, to which Bollandus transferred him; on the following day, he places his translation. I do not see why Ado celebrates him on this day, unless perhaps another translation or elevation is involved. I see even less how Baronius could have cited the aforesaid martyrologists for 16 October, where Gall is marked with an asterisk by Mosander and relegated by Rosweyd to an appendix. Perhaps he was misled by some manuscript of Ado. Certainly Usuard, at least in its pure form, mentions no Saint Gall on that day, unless Baronius accepted Belin’s text as Usuard’s.]

[Note: [Col. 0779D]]

Marchian places today what belongs to the following day, omitting only the name Servulus.

[Col. 0780D] The Tornacense begins with its local notice: “At the city of Tournai, the restoration of Saint Eleutherius, bishop and confessor.” [Col. 0781A] See the Acts. It then presents an incomplete list, a whole leaf having been torn from the codex, so that only the twenty-sixth of February, the fourth day before the Kalends of March, remains complete. We shall discuss the larger lacuna on 9 August.

Rosweyd. The first notice is: “At Rome, the burial of Caius, bishop.” It is taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; Our Author places it on 22 April. It follows: “On the island of Cyprus,” etc. Then the Tyrians, fairly purely. Nothing concerning Gall.

Pulsan would be almost pure, were it not defective in the final notice concerning Saint Gall.

Aquicinct, with the order disturbed, has here matters that should be assigned to the following day; and after the twentieth, at the end, adds: “In Hasbania, at Saint Trudo, the burial of Saint Eucherius, confessor and bishop of Orléans, who was sent into exile by Charles Martel and there rested in Christ.”

Victorin shapes the last notice as follows: “In Alemannia, Saint Gall, bishop and confessor.”

Antwerp-Major-Lübeck and Ughellian omit [Col. 0781B] the commemoration of Saint Gall, substituting in its place: “At Rome, the holy Caius, Victor, and Pantamia.” The second codex writes *Pantania*; but however it is inflected, it can be no other than Saint Potamius, as we said above. The Bigotian codex, marked P. 5, and D. du Cheval, marked B, agree with the codices cited. Nowhere is the correct connection of these three found. We have already said that the first belongs to 22 April; the last name is almost certainly fictitious. From the Hieronymian copies, Victor must be joined with Corona, who are reported in the Acts on this day.

Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Albergen, the Danish codex, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition place second: “At Rome, the holy Caius, Victor, and Pantamia.” Then they treat Potamius and Nemesius purely. Finally: “On the same day, Saint Eucherius, bishop and confessor of Orléans, who, banished into exile for the faith of Christ, rested honorably with Saint Trudo.” The final notice is missing in all of them.

[Col. 0781C] Centulense has a different beginning from the others: “At Alexandria, the holy martyrs Julian, Eunius, Macarius, Epimachus, Alexander, Metranius, Apollonia, Ammonaria, Chorinta, and ten others.” The Lübeck-Cologne edition below is almost the same. For the proper natal days of these martyrs, see the catalogue of the Omitted Notices for this day. It mutilates the eulogy of the Tyrians, omitting Potamius and Nemesius. “In Alemannia, Saint Gall, abbot.”

Brussels is somewhat expansive in the case of the Tyrian martyrs, but what exceeds the text does not deserve to be transcribed. In second place it has: “On the same day at Rome, the natal of Saint Eleutherius, pope and martyr, to whom Lucius, king of Britain, requested by letter that he be made a Christian. The pope sent two religious men, who baptized the king and his people. Finally the pope himself was crowned with martyrdom.” In the Omitted Notices he is referred to 26 May. “On the same day at Rome, the holy Caius, Victor, and Pantamia. On the island of Cyprus, etc. Also [Col. 0782A] Saint Eucherius, bishop and confessor of Orléans, who, banished into exile for the faith of Christ, rests honorably in Hasbania with Saint Trudo.”

Hagenoyen, almost pure in the matter of the Tyrian martyrs, has in second place: “On the same day, Eucherius of Orléans,” etc., as in the codices of middling quality above. It follows with Potamius, etc. Then Caius, etc. At the end: “At Tournai, blessed Eleutherius, bishop and confessor.”

Munerat adds the following to the pure text: “At Orléans, Saint Elutherius [he means Eucherius], bishop and confessor, who, banished into exile for the faith of Christ, rests honorably with Saint Trudo.”

Matric.-Carthus.-Utrecht: “At Tyre, very many martyrs who suffered with their companions at the exhortation of Silvanus. Eleutherius, bishop and martyr. Eucherius, bishop of Orléans.”

Belin omitted the notice of Saint Gall in his first edition.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition, somewhat interpolated in the case of the Tyrian martyrs, has in second place: “At Rome, the holy martyrs Caius, Victor, and Pantamia.” [Col. 0782B] It follows with Potamius and Nemesius. “On the same day, Saint Eucherius, bishop of Orléans, etc. At Alexandria, the passion of the holy martyrs Julian, Eunius, Macarius and Epimachus, Alexander and Metranius, Apollonia and Ammonaria, and Chorinta with ten others, under the emperor Decius.” We discussed these above from the Centulense.

Greven: “At Rome, Caius, Victor, and Pantamia, martyrs. At Orléans, Saint Eleutherius [read Eucherius], bishop and confessor, who, banished into exile for the faith of Christ, rests honorably with Saint Trudo. Julian and Eunius, his ministers, martyrs, whom Ado and Usuard place on the third day before the Kalends of March with the martyr Corona and others.” These are joined to Victor and his companions on the twentieth in the Acts, more appropriately than Victor is joined to Caius and Pantamia. “Eustochium, virgin. Humberga, countess.” See the Omitted Notices. Didymus the martyr should be joined to Potamius and Nemesius.

Molan adds concerning Gall what we noted above from Ado: “an abbot, a man of extraordinary holiness, a disciple of Saint Columbanus the abbot. At Sarchinium, in the monastery of Saint Trudo, the burial of blessed Eucherius, who, as bishop of Orléans, was banished into exile by Charles. That he nevertheless endured this for justice is shown by the frequent miracles which divine clemency grants to be performed through his holy merits.” In other editions Gall is omitted. The Addition begins: “At the city of Tournai, the burial of Saint Eleutherius, bishop and confessor of that church. At Sarchinium, etc. On the twentieth day, Saint Leo, father and bishop of Catania in Sicily.” In smaller type is added: “In Persia, Saint Sadoth, bishop, and one hundred and twenty-eight who suffered martyrdom with him in the second year of Sapor’s persecution.” The Acts of this excellent bishop and his companions are both serious and genuine; Ruinart reproduced them from our work beginning on page 642.]

[Col. 0779]

At the city of Tyre, the blessed martyrs whose number only God’s knowledge gathers together. At Diocletian’s command they were killed by many tortures, one after another. First they were torn throughout their bodies by scourges; then they were handed over to various kinds of beasts, but were preserved from them by divine power. After the ferocity of fire and iron had been added, they completed their martyrdom. Tyrannio and Silvanus, and also the bishops Peleus and Linus, as well as the presbyter Zenobius, stirred this glorious multitude to victory; Zenobius, in a blessed contest, gained the palm of martyrdom together with them. On the island of Cyprus, the holy Potamius and Nemesius. In Alemannia, Saint Gall, priest and confessor.

Nine days before the Kalends. Day 21. [Note: [Col. 0781D]

Taken from the Pratense, Heriniense, Antwerp-Major, Pulsan, Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck, Munerat, Belin, [Col. 0782D] Greven, and Molan. Add Antwerp-Max., Leuven, Leiden-Belgium, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0781D]]

The Leuven codex differs from the others in reading “through various kinds of tortures.” Thus Belin, instead of “the crown of his confession,” placed “the crown in his confession.” The Heriniense, [Col. 0782D] Pulsan, Munerat, Belin, Antwerp-Major, and Leuven write “prepared for him by Christ”; the text agrees with Ado. Antwerp-Major omitted both *prepared* and *made ready*. In his first edition Belin read *Secundi* for *Secundini*, but this was corrected in the second. *Neroli* in Max.-Lübeck is one of the errors with which that edition is everywhere overburdened; similarly, in Antwerp-Major, *Vetoli*. Certainly all our codices write *Veroli*, not *Veruli*, as later writers do together with the present Roman Martyrology.]

[Note: [Col. 0783A]]

Here again we have a crown of anonymous martyrs, of whom the Hieronymian copies, Bede, and the other martyrologists cited on the preceding day are silent. They are mentioned, however, by those martyrologists who form part of our series, with the Little Roman Martyrology leading the way in these words: “In Sicily, seventy-nine martyrs who suffered various tortures under Diocletian.” Ado, next to this source, says the same thing in a somewhat paraphrastic manner, in the very form taken from him and expressed in our text. Notker copied him. I think that the fact that Canisius’ edition reads seventy-four instead of seventy-nine arose because the copyist did not distinguish the numeral letters correctly, an easy alteration of LXXIX into LXXIV. Here you have the very source from which the other martyrologists drew, in great number and with much labor enumerated by Henschenius; not so Galesinius and Ferrarius, who seem to have indulged their imagination somewhat: the former by assigning these martyrs to Zaragoza, the latter by gratuitously stating that they suffered the punishment of the cross. To avoid prolonging the matter, it is more probable that they should be assigned to Syracuse; concerning their contest, however, you will seek in vain elsewhere for more than what is expressed by the Little Roman Martyrology. Nor does Galesinius correctly cite Wandalbert, in whom you will find none of those celebrated in the present text.

Concerning the Adrumetines, the distinguished Henschenius considers three questions in his historical Sylloge: What arena of victory was established for these athletes? How many were there, and what were their names? At what time did they flourish, or in what persecution were they killed? These questions he also tries to excavate from many Martyrologies with his customary diligence. It is necessary to return to first principles by going back to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, from which that whole company, mostly anonymous, was first taken—then by Rabanus, Our Author, and Notker, each in a different manner, whence the variety that arose in the more recent writers. Speaking only of Usuard, they are correctly located at Adrumetum from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; but in number and names neither those copies, nor Rabanus and Notker among themselves, nor they with [Col. 0784B] Our Author agree. Castellanus thinks that Usuard determined the number sufficiently exactly from the earliest sources; I do not wish to add anything to the observations of Henschenius and Florentinius. Nothing concerning the time of the persecution or slaughter was handed down by the ancients. I suspect that Galesinius introduced the reformers of the Roman Martyrology to designate the Vandalic persecution, contrary to the silence of the Usuardine codices and of Belin himself. What old manuscript Baronius calls upon in his notes, I do not know; if he is indicating the Martyrology of Saint Cyriacus, one must admit that this eminent man suffered a lapse of memory. What Peter reports in the Catalogue, Book II near the end, no. 75, seems to have been taken from Usuard.]

[Note: [Col. 0783B]]

In our Pratense, the following is written in the margin: “At the monastery of Saint Germanus, the consecration of an altar in honor of the blessed martyrs John and Paul, and of Saint Blaise, as well as of the holy confessors Benedict, Lupus, and Giles. Also, the consecration of an altar in honor of the holy Innocents and of the holy virgins Columba, Margaret, and Catherine.”

Marchian remains in confusion, placing here what Usuard has on the twenty-third, with a few changes that will be restored there.

Utrecht, Leiden, Albergen, and the Danish codex add to the pure text: “At the city of Metz, the natal of Saint Felix, bishop and confessor, who sat for forty-two years and six months.”

Rosweyd, fairly pure in the text, adds on his own after “twenty”: “who were killed by various tortures at Diocletian’s command.”

Centulense writes seventy-eight instead of seventy-nine.

Brussels reports an almost pure text; it adds: “At Metz, Saint Felix, bishop and confessor, who sat, etc.” Then: “At Landen, a great city of Brabant, the burial of Pippin, duke and father of Saints Begga and Gertrude. As mayor of the palace and governor of the kingdom, he excelled in courage in war and in justice in peace. For he was most faithful toward the king and most steadfast in equity toward the people, and in judging the case of both he persisted with the firmest judgment. He paid no attention either to the gifts of the people for overturning royal justice or to the king’s favor for overwhelming the people’s justice. He rests at Nivelles with his daughter Gertrude.”

Hagenoyen inserts in second place: “At Grandvalle [the word is mutilated; it means ‘in Grandvalley’], Saint Germanus, abbot and martyr. At Rome, Siricius, pope. In Africa, at the city of Adrumetum, the holy martyrs Ferreolus, Secundia, Servulus, and twenty of their companions. At Quedlinburg, in the territory of the diocese of Hildesheim, Saint Corona, split apart among the trees. On that same day, at the city of Metz, the burial of Saint Felix, bishop [Col. 0784B] and confessor, who happily sat there for forty-two years and six months, governing the people entrusted to him by word [Col. 0784C] and example.” Siricius and Corona are not mentioned in the Acts on this day, not even among the Omitted Notices.

Aquicinct agrees with Marchian in the transposition of the days.

Victorin reads *Secundiani* for *Secundini*.

Matric.-Carthus.-Utrecht has at the end Bertulf, confessor. Concerning him, see the Acts for the fifth of this month.

Altemps: “In the district of Meaux, Saint Dercangota, or Descangota, virgin.” She was unknown to Bollandus. Whether, and who she was, will be examined in the Supplement, unless perhaps she is the same woman who is called Earcongota in the Acts on 22 February.

Strozzi and Medici: “At the city of Ravenna, Saint Maximian, archbishop and confessor.” In the Acts this is deferred to the following day.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition is entirely similar to the codices of middling quality.

Greven: “Hilary, pope and martyr.” Hilary was not a pope or martyr, and does not belong to this day but to 10 September. “Also Siricius, Saturninus, Fortunatus, [Col. 0784D] Jocundus, bishop, Victorinus, Peter.” All these belong among the Adrumetine martyrs, except the last two. But where Greven found that Jocundus was a bishop, I do not know. “At Metz, Saint Felix, bishop and confessor, who sat for forty-two years and six months. Bertulf, confessor. Serena, martyr. Eleutherius, bishop. At Rome, Symmachus, pope and confessor.” Concerning the last four, see the index of the Omitted Notices.

Molan: “At the city of Metz, etc. And the burial of Eleutherius, bishop.” Then, in smaller type: “Of Tournai, resting in the cathedral church. In Gaul, Vitalina, most holy virgin.” Then: “The book of anniversaries among the canonesses of Nivelles: the scattered vigils of Saint Pippin.” I find no explanation, either in this or in the other editions, of what “scattered vigils” are. Moreover, these further additions occur: “On the twenty-first day, Saint Timothy, father, who was in Symbola. At Milan, the feast of Saint Ambrose, on account of the victory obtained at Parabiago in the year of the Lord 1338 through his invocation.” See concerning this festival of whatever sort the Omitted Notices. It is followed again, in smaller type: “On the same day, the death of Saint Pippin, and the scattered vigils of Saint Pippin, whose body rests at Nivelles in a portable tomb and is carried around in the Litanies, as is that of Iduberga and of Saint Gertrude’s nurse.” See Bollandus for this day, page 259.]

[Col. 0781]

In Sicily, the holy martyrs numbering seventy-nine, who under Diocletian, through various tortures, deserved to receive from Christ the crown of their confession prepared for them. In Africa, at the city of Adrumetum, the holy Verolus, Secundinus, Servulus, and twenty others. [Bouillart, in the margin of the page: “At the monastery of Saint Germanus, the consecration of an altar in honor of the blessed martyrs John and Paul and Saint Blaise, as well as of the holy confessors Benedict, Lupus, and Giles. Also the consecration of an altar in honor of the holy Innocents and the holy virgins Columba, Margaret, and Catherine.”]

Eight days before the Kalends. Day 22. [Note: [Col. 0785]

From the Pratense, Heriniense, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Pulsan, Max.-Lübeck, Belin, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0785B]]

Pulsan and Belin write “Peter the apostle”; the text is pure from Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, and Ado. Not Belin alone, but all the codices write “blessed Papias,” so I am surprised that Castellanus noted this as a point of difficulty in Belin, page 709, at the end. Here too *Hierapolitanae* is correctly read; incorrectly, the Heriniense has *Jerapolinae*; Pulsan, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, Greven, and Rosweyd, *Jerapolitanae*; Belin, *Hierapolitanae*; Antwerp-Major, *Terapolitanae*. The same codex wrote *discipulus* for *condiscipulus*; Rosweyd, for *sodalis fuit*, repeated *auditor fuit*. The Pratense and most other codices have *Policarpi*, concerning which enough has been said elsewhere. Pulsan, having added the title “apostle” to Peter, removed it from John, and after Polycarp omitted *autem*. Thus Belin in his second edition; instead of *auditor*, he wrote *adjutor*. Rosweyd has seventy instead of seventy-two. Again, in his first edition Belin placed *Abiti*; Pulsan has the worse *Babbilii*. Rosweyd reads twelve instead of thirteen. Whether one says *annos* or *annis* makes no difference. In his first edition Molan omitted *sacerdotium*, restoring it in later editions. Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, and Belin read *vita conspicuus* instead of *virtute conspicuus*; Pulsan inserts a word and has: “he faithfully administered.” In Rosweyd *virtute* is missing.]

[Note: [Col. 0785B]]

The most ancient Calendar, which we commonly call Bucherian after its editor, announces this day as follows: “The natal of Peter of the Chair.” This means the celebration, festival, or solemnity of the chair, as Florentinius explains here, and Castellanus at greater length where he treats the word *Natalis* under 6 January, page 100. Gregory’s Sacramentary agrees, simply reading: “The Chair of Saint Peter.” Thus far the statement is indefinite, so that it is entirely impossible to determine whether the Antiochene chair or the Roman chair is intended, just as we began to say on 18 January; and John Fronto, drawing quite appropriately on Menard and Pamelius, holds this view concerning the Calendar, page 28. See Menard himself in the notes to Gregory’s Sacramentary, pages 46–47.

The Hieronymian copies speak differently. Among them, the Epternacense says most briefly: “The Chair of Peter in Antioch”; the Lucense: “The natal of the chair of Saint Peter the apostle, which he occupied at Antioch”; the Corbie copy somewhat differently: “The natal of the chair of Saint Peter the apostle, in which he sat at Antioch”; the version published by Acherius, more simply: “The Chair of Saint Peter, in which, etc.” Certainly all agree in establishing this feast as different from the Roman Chair. All the following martyrologists adopt this view: the Little Roman Martyrology, Bede, Rabanus, Ado, Usuard, and Notker. Their words are the same as those recited in our text, since the very brief additions of Rabanus and Notker [Col. 0785D] in no way diminish the integrity of the whole matter. The remaining matters, which we previously said had long been subject to several dissertations, the curious reader may investigate in Bollandus’ present commentary and in Florentinius’ annotation, where Beleth’s words concerning the feast of Blessed Peter of the Feasts, reported by Bollandus, and other related matters are examined more carefully. More was discussed in the preliminary commentary for 29 June, section 5, beginning on page 407, and among the Analecta, sections 12 and 13, beginning on page 456; add to these Castellanus’ note beginning on page 706. Wandalbert’s exposition, arranged in numbered verses, agrees completely with the martyrologists mentioned:

“On the eighth, Peter’s Chair and teaching shines forth,

and the joyous city of Antioch flourishes, where he first served as bishop.”

The name of Papias is recorded in none of the Martyrologies earlier than the Viennese one; but I scarcely think anyone will approve the conjecture of Castellanus, who supposes that it was inserted because of its resemblance to the name *papa* (“pope”). For the rest, Ado expressly calls Papias a hearer of the holy apostle John, and Notker follows him almost word for word. Our author, somewhat polishing Ado’s phrasing, further mentions his special association with Polycarp. Baronius seems to have been troubled by a scruple when he substituted the elder John, or *presbyter* (πρεσβύτερος), for the Evangelist, as Henschenius learnedly demonstrates; see also Castellanus, p. 708, and Tillemont, vol. II, p. 296. In these authors and in other learned modern writers one will find little that ought to be included in the Supplement.

The first commemoration of Aristion was consecrated by the *Romanum parvum*, not on this day but on 17 October: “And of Aristion, who was one of the seventy disciples of Christ.” Ado repeats these same words there, perhaps forgetting that on this day, I think on the occasion of the feast of Saint Papias, he had already treated Aristion. The only difference between the two texts is that here Ado wrote “who was one of the seventy-two,” a phrase that Usuardus and Notkerus preserve exactly, celebrating the saint only on this day. Bollandus has gathered in a brief commentary the few details that can be recalled about Aristion from Eusebius and others; Tillemontius found no more, associating him with Papias.

Abilius—also called Avilius, Melius, Milius, or Melianus—the patriarch of Alexandria, more probably died on 20 August, as we established in our *Chronological Treatise* against Tillemontius, no. 71. Nor do we think that one should depart from the calculation there established on the authority of the Martyrologies, since Abilius was first entered on this day in the *Romanum parvum*, purely according to its author’s discretion, as he often does. It reads: “At Alexandria, Abilius, bishop.” Ado added the order and duration of his administration; Usuardus added two words, “conspicuous in virtue”; Notkerus is purely Adonian. In Ado, Paschasius of Vienne, of admirable holiness, is placed last; but here he is omitted by Usuardus together with several others, Ado’s predecessors, although he is entered in certain fuller manuscripts, as will soon be seen.

[Note: [Col. 0787A]]

**PRATEN.** Someone here adds another consecration of the altar proper to that monastery of Saint Germanus, in these words: “On the same day, the consecration of the altar in honor of the blessed martyrs Eustachius and his companions, and of the holy confessor of Christ, Medardus.”

**MARCHIAN.** It is almost pure, but is excluded because it still wanders on the following day.

**TORNACEN.** It is blank, as stated above.

**ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERG., DANIC.** and the **ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition**, after “the apostle Peter,” continue as follows: “How, after Simon Magus, who had deceived them into believing in him and stoning Peter, had been expelled by the people of Antioch, Peter himself was received and exalted to the pontifical chair.” All these manuscripts, except **ALBERG.**, add at the end, from Ado: “At Vienne, Saint Paschasius, bishop and confessor, a man of admirable holiness.”

**CENTUL.**: “At Antioch, the chair of the holy apostle Peter. At Alexandria, Saint Abilius, bishop, who was second after blessed Mark and governed the Alexandrian Church.” Thus it reads on this day, but on 17 May it repeats the same Papias with precisely the eulogy found in our present text. Had Castellanus seen this manuscript, he would not have set it against Ado on p. 709. “On the same day, blessed Aristion, an ancient disciple of Christ.”

**BRUXELL.** In speaking of Peter’s chair, it says: “After Christ’s Ascension, he held the priestly chair in the eastern regions for four years; then he came to Antioch and, after Simon Magus had been expelled, assumed the pontifical chair, which he held there for seven years. When these years had been completed, Peter, in order to overcome Simon Magus, went to Rome; there he presided worthily over the Roman Church for twenty-five years, seven months, and eight days. He had no successor who thereafter completed so long a period in the administration of the supreme apostolate.” In the entries for Aristion, Papias, and Abilius it departs little from the pure text; then it adds: “At Vienne in Gaul, Saint Pacasius [Paschasius], bishop and confessor, a man of admirable holiness, and Thecla, virgin.”

**HAGENOYEN.** It speaks differently about the chair: “In which he sat, governing and teaching the people laudably and confirming his teaching by miracles. This chair was first erected for him in the Church of Antioch when he raised from the dead the son of Theophilus, the city’s governor, who had been dead for fourteen years. Saint Peter sat in this see for seven years.” In the entries for Papias and Aristion it is almost pure. “At Alexandria, Saint Abalius, bishop, who was the second bishop after blessed Mark and served for thirteen years. He was the second priest, conspicuous in every virtue. At Vienne, Saint Paschasius, bishop and confessor, a man of admirable holiness.”

**AQUICINCT.** Here too it agrees with the Marchian manuscript.

**CODEX D. DU CHEVAL.,** marked C, formerly belonging to the Franciscan Fathers, has at the end: “The nativity of Saint Thecla, virgin.” On her, see the index of the saints omitted from the main text; and at the source, Rabanus and Notkerus.

**ALTEMPS.**: “On the same day, the nativity of Saint Thecla, virgin. Also at the monastery of Wenlock, the most blessed Mildburga, virgin. At Saint Edmund’s, blessed Firminus, confessor, brother of Saint Ethedra, virgin.” Mildburga is treated on 23 February. Firminus requires another investigation.

**STROZZ.** and **MEDIC.**: “Also at Rome, Saint Romana, virgin.” See the Acts for the following day, where Romana of Todi is discussed.

**MUNERAT.** adds to the pure text: “At Vienne, Saint Paschasius, bishop and confessor, a man of admirable holiness.”

The **LUBECO-COL. edition** has the same account of the chair as the manuscripts of middling authority mentioned above, adding only at the end: “In which he completed seven years.” It also has at the end: “At Vienne, Saint Paschasius,” and so forth.

**GREVEN.**: “In Africa, Victorinus, Palatinus, Donatus, Fortuna, and twenty-nine others.” They were taken from some Hieronymian manuscript. “At Rome, Siricius, pope and martyr.” See the section on those omitted from the main text. “Dionysia, virgin and martyr.” See the omitted saints. “At Vienne, Paschasius, bishop, etc.; Thecla, also called Teda, virgin.” See above.

**MOLAN.** has Paschasius as above. “The translation of the body of Saint Guduval, archbishop.” Other editions state it more explicitly: “At Ghent, the translation of the body of Saint Gudwal, archbishop.” The annual commemoration of this translation is observed on 3 December; his feast is on 6 June.

[Col. 0785]

At Antioch, the Chair [Bouillart: “Chair”] of Saint Peter. On the same day, blessed Papias, bishop of the city of Hierapolis, who was a hearer of the apostle John but a fellow disciple and companion of Polycarp. Also, Saint Aristion, who was one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ. At Alexandria, Saint Abilius, bishop, who, second bishop after blessed Mark, served in the priesthood for thirteen years, conspicuous in virtue. [In Bouillart, in the margin of the page: “On the same day, the consecration of the altar in honor of the blessed martyrs Eustachius and his companions, and of the holy confessor of Christ, Medardus.”]

**VII Kal. — 23rd day**

[Note: [Col. 0787]]

Taken from **Praten., Herinien., Rosweyd., Pulsanen., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven,** and **Molan**.

[Note: [Col. 0787D]]

**Sirmium** is transformed into **Firmum** by **Antuerp.** and **Max.-Lubec.**, and into **Smyrna** by **Munerat.**, as Notkerus wrote it incorrectly, leading others into error. We have retained **Syrmium**, which is how the manuscripts generally write it; **Rosweyd** incorrectly has **Sirnium**. These same witnesses vary in the name of **Sinerus**: **Antuerp.** has **Sirenerus**; **Max.-Lubec.**, **Siverus**; **Munerat.**, **Sinetus**; **Rosweyd.**, **Serenus**; **Greven** and **Molan**, following Ado, have **Syrenus**. More will be said about him in the Observations.

Only our Praten manuscript writes *duum* instead of *duorum*; all the other manuscripts have the reading found in the text. **Pulsanen** added *militum* (“soldiers”), but is singular in this respect; **Antuerp.-Max.-Lubec.** and **Molanus** in the first edition print “seventy-two,” whereas in later editions the latter restored the pure Usuardian reading. Enough has been said elsewhere about the orthographic errors of the Middle Ages, such as *Policarpi presbiteri*. In **Max.-Lubec.**, *consumentes* appears for *consummantes*; in **Muneratus**, *mensura* for *mansura*—hardly noteworthy misprints. **Pulsanen** incorrectly reads “blessed Stephen” for “blessed Sebastian,” “the palm” for “glory,” and *exortando* for *exhortando*. In the 1521 edition **Greven** seems to append the Vigil of blessed Matthias to the text; but since he clearly distinguished it in the earlier edition, I have counted him among the pure manuscripts.

[Note: [Col. 0787D]]

We read **Sinerus** with the best Usuardian manuscripts, whatever may be said about the various forms of this name found elsewhere; Bollandus discusses them at length on this day, and Castellanus on the preceding day. In the *Romanum parvum* it is written: “At Sirmium, Sirenus, monk.” The *Acts* prefer this spelling, together with **Sirenus**. The Lucense Hieronymian manuscript on the preceding day—which is more probably the day on which he suffered, judging from the final clause of the *Acts* edited by Ruinartius on p. 546—gives the following entry: “At Sirmium, the feast of Saint Serenus and sixty-two others.” The Epternacense reduces the number of companions, reading “and sixteen others”; both Corbeienses increase it, reading “and seventy-two others.” Perhaps the Gellonense wrote better and more simply, though without a place designation: “Senerus,” adding “and elsewhere sixty-one.”

Certainly, in the genuine and sincere *Acts* of both men, first published by Bollandus and subsequently among the selected Acts, no mention whatever is made of companions. In the Hieronymian Martyrologies this entry occurs on 8 Kalends, that is, 22 February; on the present day, however, the Florentinian manuscripts place first **Senerotus**, or **Senerotus**, who is joined to three others expressly named by Rabanus, Notkerus, and Bollandus. Only Senerotus is named in the Gellonense. To this must ultimately be reduced the long heap—one might almost say confusion—of names found in Castellanus, p. 710.

I do not understand on what basis that distinguished man conflates various saints into one, especially Senerus or Serenus and Senerotus, who are correctly distinguished both in the Hieronymian Martyrologies and in the *Acts*. Even if we grant that they suffered in the same place, it certainly does not follow that they underwent martyrdom at the same time. Nor have I discovered in which Hieronymian manuscripts Castellanus found this same Senerus appearing under another form on 21 February, so that one and the same martyr would recur on three consecutive days.

Whatever may be said about the inflections of the Hieronymian names, it is certain that Ado wrote **Syrenus**, Notkerus **Synerius**, and others other forms, thereby multiplying the saints through varying nomenclature, as may be seen in the authors cited above and in Florentinius. Our only concern here is the Usuardian reading, which we have established from manuscripts of better quality. Those who investigate etymologies may judge whether this spelling has a closer relationship to the French forms **Serneu, Cerneux, Cerneuf**.

Ado took the saint’s eulogy from the *Acts*; Notkerus copied it from Ado; our author contracted it more elegantly. Likewise, in the notice of the sixty-two who suffered at Sirmium, as stated here and drawn from the same source of the *Romanum parvum*, he gave the wording a somewhat more polished and elegant form. The *Romanum parvum*, as edited by Rosweyd, reads **XLII** instead of “sixty-two,” presumably through a scribal error corrected by Ado. More recent martyrologists, together with the modern Roman Martyrology, write **LXXII**. I believe this arose from the difference among the Hieronymian manuscripts or originally from Notkerus, and was then copied from Usuardian manuscripts that were not sufficiently pure in this respect.

Bollandus shows in his commentary how incorrectly certain Italian martyrologists transfer Saint Sinerus to Firmum in Picenum, and how absurdly the Spaniards place him in Baetica, at Sexti Firmum. Tillemontius translated the often-cited *Acts* into French in vol. V, p. 254 onward.

The third announcement of the *Romanum parvum* is: “At Rome, Polycarp, priest.” Ado correctly believed him to have been a companion of Saint Sebastian; our predecessors held the same view and included him as such in the *Acts*, with a historical collection composed from the life of that illustrious martyr. Usuardus copied word for word what he had found in Ado; Notkerus omitted only a single word.

The Hieronymian manuscripts here record another Polycarp, namely the celebrated bishop of Smyrna, about whom we have already spoken at some length above, under 19 and 26 January. The present entry, however, brings up the sixth *Exercitatio* of Florentinius, in which he argues that the true day of his martyrdom coincides with 23 February according to the Greek reckoning. Castellanus, p. 724, condemns all this too decisively as an error. Wandalbertus agrees with our account, composing these verses about today’s Polycarp:

> The seventh shines with the glorious honor of Polycarp;  
> A priest in speech, who followed Christ’s commands in faith,  
> By martyrdom he was able to preserve a faithful throng.

[Note: [Col. 0789C]]

**ANTUERP.-MAJ.** frequently reveals itself to have belonged formerly to some church in England, as we showed in the preface. Here it adds to the pure text: “In Britain, blessed Milburga, virgin, who was renowned for her virtues and miracles.” See the *Acts*.

**CENTULEN.**: “At Sirmium, Saint Sirenus, monk, who was beheaded under Maximian. And sixty-two others who suffered there.” These are Ado’s words. Then: “At Rome, Saint Polycarp, priest and confessor, who flourished as an assistant and fellow worker.” I think “of Saint Sebastian” ought to be added. Yet this Polycarp is again placed in the same manuscript on the following day; whether by design or through the scribe’s carelessness, who can say?

**MARCHIAN.** Being empty today because of the transposition of the days, it obtained a supplement from a Hieronymian manuscript that is corrupt in many places. It is worthwhile to present the entire entry. Here are its words: “The feast of the holy martyrs Inpannonius, Senerotus, Antigonus, Rutulus, Libius, and Rogatianus.” See the *Acts*. “In Asia, Polycarp, bishop, with twelve other martyrs. At Smyrna, the feast of the holy Herotes, Carpus, and Gerontius. In Africa, Chrysogonus, Zeno, Menander, Carinianus, Arion, Hippolytus, Diodorus, Menelaus, Athora, Peter, Lambesis, Luciana, Felix, and thirty-six others. In Asia, Lascon, Synorius, Herutus, Zeno, Menalippus, Sinestes, and Syrices with their companions.”

**ANTUERP.-MAX., LEYDEN, LOVANIEN., ALBERG., DANIC.** and the **ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition** begin: “The Vigil of Saint Matthias the apostle.” They write **LXXII** instead of **LXII**; otherwise they are pure.

**BRUXELLEN.** inserts almost everything from Ado that Usuardus had omitted. It reads: “At Smyrna, Saint Syverus, monk. When, in the time of the emperor Maximian, he had more sharply rebuked and driven away the wife of one of the emperor’s household servants, whom he found walking at an unsuitable hour in a garden that he himself cultivated, he was arrested at Maximian’s command. After confessing that he was a Christian, he was beheaded. Also at Smyrna, the feast of sixty-two saints,” and so forth. The remainder is pure.

**HAGENOYEN.**: “The Vigil of Saint Matthias the apostle. At Smyrna, blessed Syrenus,” and so forth, with the text somewhat interpolated. At the end: “Also Wildeburgis, virgin, in England.” Read **Milburgis**.

**AQUICINCT.** Like the Marchian manuscript in its confusion, is also supplemented from a Hieronymian manuscript, but somewhat more accurately. It reads: “The feast of the holy martyrs in Pannonia, Senerotus,” and so forth. It omits “In Asia, Polycarp,” and so forth. After Gerontius it inserts: “The nativity of Saint John the Evangelist.” In the number of the remaining martyrs the manuscripts agree, although they pronounce the names differently. A later hand adds at the end: “Also the Vigil of blessed Matthias the apostle.”

**VATICAN.,** marked no. 5949: “At Smyrna, the feast of Saint Herotes.” See **MARCHIAN**.

**ALTEMPS.** reproduces almost everything that, as stated, is found in the Marchian and Aquicinct manuscripts, with names truncated and distorted from some Hieronymian copy.

The **LUBECO-COL. edition** begins: “The Vigil of Saint Matthias the apostle.” Concerning Sinerus it has the same material that we said was restored from Ado in **BRUXELLEN.** It also gives **LXXII** instead of **LXII**. Then: “At Trier, the discovery of Saint Celsus, bishop.” The entry concerning Polycarp follows. Finally: “On the same day, Saint Milburga.”

In the first edition **BELIN** makes Polycarp a bishop and confessor. Both editions have **LXXII**, and at the end: “On the same day, the Vigil of blessed Matthias the apostle.”

**GREVEN.**: “The nativity of Saint John the Evangelist.” This is treated on 27 December. “In Asia, Polycarp, Herotes, Felix, and twelve others. Also Senerotus, Antigonus, Rotulus, and Labius.” These have already been discussed sufficiently. “In Hungary, the passion—or, according to others, the translation—of Saint Gerard, bishop of Morisena and martyr. He was Venetian by nationality and a canon of Saint Mark. Desiring perfection, he assumed the religious habit and led an eremitical life. Later, through the agency of Saint Stephen, king of the Hungarians, he became a bishop; finally, he was captured by unbelievers and killed with many others.” See the index of the omitted saints. “Milburga, virgin, daughter of the king of Mercia. At Trier, the discovery of Saint Celsus, bishop and confessor. In Ireland, Timinus, bishop and confessor.” Whether this is Tianus or Tiamanus, who is discussed among the omitted saints, I do not know. “Also Saint Serenus, abbot, of whom it is read in the *Lives of the Fathers* that by divine gift he attained the highest purity of mind and body.” He too appears among the omitted saints.

[Col. 0792A]

**MOLAN.** inserted Ado’s words about Sinerus into the text in a different typeface. At the end: “On the same day, the discovery of Saint Celsus, confessor of Christ. On the same day, the Vigil of blessed Matthias the apostle.” Then, in smaller type: “This is celebrated in most places with observance of a fast. Milburga, virgin, daughter of the king of Mercia, whose Life was written by Cardinal Atto.” In other editions it is more correctly stated: “Celsus, bishop.” And at the end: “In the territory of Auvergne, Saint Syrenus, distinguished martyr.” This is the same man who is called Sinerus in the text, venerated by the people of Auvergne because his relics were brought there from the East, or from Pannonia. See more in Bollandus and Castellanus.

[Col. 0787]

At Sirmium, blessed Sinerus, monk and martyr, who, arrested at the command of the emperor Maximian, was beheaded after confessing that he was a Christian. Also the feast of sixty-two men who, completing the contest of martyrdom in the aforesaid city, received kingdoms that shall endure. On the same day, Saint Polycarp, priest and confessor, who together with blessed Sebastian converted many to the faith of Christ and, by exhorting them, led them to the glory of martyrdom.

**VI Kal. — 24th day**

[Note: [Col. 0791A]]

The entries are pure in **Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Marchian., Pulsanen., Munerat., Greven,** and **Molan**. Add **Albergense**. **Belinus** differs only in placing Sergius before the discovery of the Forerunner’s head.

[Note: [Col. 0791B]]

There are a few points worthy of notice. **Mathias** and **Matthias** are written indiscriminately; here we prefer the reading of the martyrologists. In **Herinien.** I find the words written above the line: between *sorte* and *electus* it places *est*, and after *electus* the particle *et*; **Martiani** is commonly read. If one prefers **Marciani** with **Antuerp.-Maj.**, I have no objection. **Praten.** and **Muneratus** write *quando isdem*, apparently out of an excessive concern to avoid cacophony. *Capud* in **Pulsanen.** for *caput* is a scribal error; *Capadociae* for *Cappadociae* recurs frequently elsewhere. In **Antuerp.-Maj.** the noun *gesta* has been omitted.

[Note: [Col. 0791B]]

It is not so certain as Castellanus claims on p. 732 that the Hieronymian Martyrologies commemorate the apostle Matthias on 21 May. For although the Lucense manuscript there reads near the end, “And elsewhere, the feast of Saint Matthias the apostle,” other copies—such as the very ancient Epternacense, both Corbeienses, and even the Gellonense, if it may be counted among the Hieronymian manuscripts—clearly express Saint Matthew in the same place.

Nevertheless, Florentinius accepts Matthias on that day, p. 543, and thinks the commemoration on 24 February to be of more recent institution because his feast is recorded on that date in both Corbeienses. I do not see here a feast of so recent an institution, since it is celebrated today in the Gregorian Sacramentary edited by Menardus under this title: “The feast of Saint Matthias the apostle.” Nor are the Corbeienses so recent, in which precisely these words, except for *sancti*, are placed first. Add to these the other Martyrologies cited by Henschenius, as well as our own, which we shall examine in the customary order.

Bede first has the following on this day: “The discovery of the head of John the Forerunner.” Then: “And the feast of Saint Matthias the apostle.” The *Romanum parvum* has simply, and first: “Saint Matthias the apostle.” Ado’s Martyrology reads: “The feast of Saint Matthew the apostle.” These entries are more fully explained among the feasts of the apostles; from there Usuardus took everything added in the text.

It is surprising that Rabanus departed from Bede and Notkerus from Ado, since both write: “In Palestine, the nativity of Saint Matthias the apostle, who, one of the seventy disciples, was chosen by lot for Judas the traitor and appointed to the apostleship, and preached the Gospel in Judaea.” I admit that the difference is more in wording than in substance, as is also found in Florus; but nowhere is the time, place, or manner of martyrdom specified.

For the rest, Henschenius has abundantly illustrated everything concerning Matthias’s deeds, cult, the translation of his body or of parts of it, and his miracles. Those who prefer abridgements may read Tillemontius, vol. I, p. 406 onward, together with the notes relating to this matter.

We have already spoken, from Bede, of the discovery of the Forerunner’s head. There will be another occasion to discuss the Hieronymian Martyrologies. The *Romanum parvum* reports the same event in the same manner, and Ado took it from there; our author took it from Ado, but everywhere omitted the proper name, using a sufficiently distinct appellative instead.

Our text suggests that this was the first discovery, as is also asserted in the modern Roman Martyrology—apparently solely on Usuardus’s authority, since he added the word *primam* (“first”) to Ado. But that investigation does not belong here. Consult the Acts of Saint Prodromus for 24 June, admirably illustrated by Papebrochius, where the various discoveries of the venerable head are treated at length in chapter 3; see also Tillemontius, vol. I, p. 103 onward, and the notes beginning on p. 494.

The material about this particular discovery, made under the emperor Martianus and set out by Ado with citations from the Hieronymian Martyrology, and greatly expanded by Notkerus, was summarized by our author in his usual manner, but with the insertion of a particle noted above. Wandalbertus likewise joined the two feasts:

> The sixth, Matthias, shines with apostolic virtue;  
> And the Baptist reveals the head long hidden.

Sergius, martyr of Caesarea in Cappadocia, is most probably the same man who is commemorated on this day with Herulus and Lucius in the Hieronymian manuscripts, from which Notkerus took them. Ado does not seem to have consulted those sources, following the *Romanum parvum*, where Sergius alone is placed: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Sergius, martyr.” Our author took everything from Ado, preserving even the final words, “whose deeds are held to be most illustrious.” If those deeds ever existed, would that they might be recovered from somewhere! For the material produced in our Collection from Tamayo Salazar requires, at the very least, a wholly new and careful examination. With God’s favor, we shall undertake it in its proper place.

Molanus, in the first edition of his Usuardus, had cited Gregory of Tours; but in later editions he seems to doubt whether that holy writer, when he recounts miracles of some Saint Sergius in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 97, had our Sergius in mind. Before his time, however, scarcely anyone doubted that Gregory was speaking there of Sergius, the companion of Bacchus, concerning whom Usuardus and others write under 7 October. See Henschenius’s commentary, no. 7, where he also shows that the Gregory of Tours cited in book VII of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 31, names no other Sergius than the one who, as Baronius too attests, is venerated on the aforementioned 7 October.

[Note: [Col. 0793A]]

**ROSWEYD.** forms the first announcement as follows: “In Judaea, Matthias the apostle, who, one of the seventy-two, was chosen by the lot of the apostles and appointed in the place of Judas after the Lord’s Ascension.” The remainder is pure.

**ANTUERP.-MAX. LUBEC.** and **UGHELLIAN.** have nothing about the discovery of the Forerunner’s head. The **ALBERG.** manuscript agrees with them, as would **DANIC.** in every respect if it did not add at the end: “At Trier, Saint Modestus, bishop and confessor.”

**ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LOVANIEN.** and the **ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition** insert the following words into the first announcement: “And appointed in the place of the traitor Judas.” Otherwise they are pure, adding at the end: “At Trier,” and so forth—a supplement that also recurs several times in other manuscripts below.

**CENTULEN.**: “The feast of Saint Matthias the apostle. On the same day, the discovery of the head of the Lord’s Forerunner, in the time of the emperor Martianus.” The third announcement is absent and is replaced by a repetition of Polycarp, about whom we spoke yesterday: “At Rome, Saint Polycarp, priest and confessor, of whom it is read in the deeds of blessed Sebastian.”

**BRUXELLEN.** reads: “The feast of Saint Matthias the apostle, who after the Lord’s Ascension was chosen by lot by the apostles and appointed in the place of Judas the traitor, and preached the Gospel of Christ in Judaea. The body of this blessed apostle was transferred by Queen Helena from Judaea to Rome; Pope Saint Sylvester, together with many other relics, sent it through the blessed bishop Agritius to Trier, as is said. On the same day, the discovery of the head of blessed John the Baptist, the Lord’s Forerunner, who, as is clear from the Gospel, was beheaded when the feast of Passover was approaching; and who, in the time of the emperor Martianus, revealed to two monks where his head lay hidden. They searched for it and were worthy to find it on this day.” It gives Sergius fairly well. Then: “At Trier, Saint Modestus, bishop and confessor, who after Miletus governed the Church of God there with much fruit.”

[Col. 0793C]

**HAGENOYEN.** invents many additional details about Matthias. Although I recognize that these are neither sufficiently clear nor sufficiently well attested, I nevertheless wish to reproduce them here, so that it may be evident how many varied and often quite absurd matters, introduced by unskilled men with ever-increasing freedom, entered even ecclesiastical books. Our manuscript reads:

“The feast of blessed Matthias the apostle, who immediately after the Lord’s Ascension was instituted as an apostle by the apostles in the place of Judas the traitor. He had previously been **Demicius**—I cannot read it otherwise—and was one of Christ’s seventy-two disciples. He added this article to the Apostles’ Creed, and received Judaea by lot so that he might preach there. But he was handed over to the Jews to be stoned under Nero Caesar, while Anianus the Younger, a Jewish priest, was acting as deputy prefect. Later, according to Roman custom, Anianus had him struck with axes as though he were an ox; and then the apostle Matthias, raising his hands and eyes toward heaven, gave up his spirit.”

In the second announcement, concerning the discovery of the Forerunner’s head, the manuscript is fairly pure. Then: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, blessed Sergius, martyr, whose illustrious deeds are said to have been recorded.” Finally it adds: “At Trier, the burial of Saint Modestus, bishop and confessor.”

**REGINAE SUEC.,** marked no. 428: “At the city of Paris, about five miles from the city, the dedication of the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius.”

**VATICAN.,** no. 5949: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Primitiva.” See the *Acts*, where the name is more correctly **Primitivus**, joined in the Hieronymian manuscripts with a companion named Paulus at the Roman harbor.

**STROZZ.** and **MEDIC.**: “Saint Matthias, whose body was transferred from Nicaea [Judaea] to Rome and afterward to Trier; nevertheless, his head is displayed by the canons of the church of Saint Mary Major of the holy City with the greatest reverence. The discovery of the head of the Lord’s Forerunner, which now rests in Rome in the church of Saint Sylvester and is displayed there with the greatest devotion to all the faithful of Christ.” See 24 June in the *Acts*.

The **LUBECO-COL. edition**: “The feast of blessed Matthias the apostle. After the Lord’s Ascension he was chosen by lot by the apostles and appointed in the place of Judas the traitor; he preached the Gospel of Christ in Judaea. He had previously been one of Christ’s seventy-two disciples. First he was seized by the Jews and covered with stones as a blasphemer. After this he was struck with an axe like an ox and beheaded. In such martyrdom, first fixing his eyes upon heaven, he gave up his spirit. The venerable Helena Augusta, a native of Trier, after many years transferred him from Judaea to the city of Rome and honorably buried him in the church of Saint Mary Rotunda. He now rests at Trier by translation.” The account of the discovery of the head follows, and so forth. Then: “At Trier, in the church of Saint Eucharius, the burial of Saint Modestus, bishop and confessor of that place.” The entry for Sergius is correct. At the end: “On the same day, blessed Meforius, confessor. Also Saint Athelbert, king.”

**GREVEN.** has almost the same eulogy of Matthias that we quoted from the **LUBECO-COL. edition**. Then: “At Rome, the holy martyrs Primitivus and Paulus, Rutulus, Serapion, Herodion, and Lucius. Also Lucius and Flavianus. Montanus and Gemellus, martyrs.” These are confused; in the *Acts* you will find them somewhat more clearly distinguished. Concerning Modestus, as above. “Athelbert, king of Kent, or of England. Converted through the preaching of blessed Augustine, whom the holy Pope Gregory had sent, he showed himself an energetic fellow worker in extending the faith and building churches, and, full of good works, rested in peace. On the same day, blessed Meforius, confessor, and Olympias, holy matron. Also Hisca and Hinna, holy women.” See the omitted saints.

**MOLAN.**: “At Trier, blessed Modestus, bishop.” Then, in smaller type: “Ethelbert, king. His history was written by Bede in books I and II of his *History of His People*. At Rouen, the passion of Saint Praetextatus, bishop of that city, concerning whom Gregory of Tours writes in the *Chronicle*, book V, chapter 18; book VII, chapter 16; and book VIII, chapter 31.” In other editions: “At Trier, blessed … In England, Ethelbert, king of Kent,” and so forth. Again in smaller type: “On the same day is recorded the life and martyrdom of Saint Montanus and his companions Lucius, Julianus, Victoricus, Flavianus, and the rest, written in an elegant style partly by the martyrs themselves and partly by their associate, who was present.” See the excellent *Acts*, of the highest quality, illustrated by Henschenius and reviewed anew by Ruinartius beginning on p. 232.

[Col. 0791]

The feast of blessed Matthias the apostle, who after the Lord’s Ascension was chosen by lot by the apostles and preached the Gospel of Christ in Judaea. Also, the discovery of the head of the Lord’s Forerunner in the time of the emperor Martianus, when that same Forerunner first revealed to two monks where his head lay hidden. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Sergius, martyr, whose deeds are held to be most illustrious.

**V Kal. — 25th day**

[Note: [Col. 0795]]

Taken from **Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Marchian., Pulsanen., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Belin., Greven,** and **Molan**. Add the **Albergense** manuscript.

[Note: [Col. 0795A]]

I read **Aegyptum** (“Egypt”), as it ought to be read with the better manuscripts. That **Egyptum** and **Egiptum** are often written according to the practices of different periods is too well known to require another note here. **Nicophorus** is written by the *Romanum parvum* and by Ado as edited by Rosweyd, not **Nicephorus**, as in the more recent witnesses. Only Molanus followed the earliest manuscripts. Codices of the best quality confirm the text. **Pulsanen** and **Munerat** have wandered: the former writes **Nicyphorus**, the latter **Nichoforus**. **Antuerp.-Maj.** reads worse, **Nicofirus**, a scribal error of the sort also found in **Diascorus** and **Serapion**. **Pulsanen** is likewise wrong in reading **Claudius** for **Claudianus**; Molanus’s editor stumbles still more disgracefully here, placing **Claudianus** first and then transforming the same person into **Claudius**. There is also a typographical error in **Muneratus**, where **constanti** is incorrectly printed for **constanter**.

**Pulsanen** altered the phrase, rendering *suppliciorum genera* (“kinds of punishments”) as *tormentorum supplicia* (“the punishments of tortures”). Thus **Marchian** substituted *reliqui* for *reliqui quatuor* (“the remaining four”), namely, “the remaining.” The first edition of **Belinus** incorrectly has **reliquae** for **reliqui**. **Pulsanen** has **injecti** where **incensi** is required. **Alberg., Ant.** and **Max.-Lubec.** read **continue, gladio caesi** (“immediately struck down by the sword”), while all have **celebre** … [the remainder is defective in the supplied text]. **Munerat.** has **omnesque** for **omnes itaque**.

Only the class of Egyptian martyrs recurs today in Usuard, taken from Ado, whose eulogy he abridged. Here, as usual, he followed the Roman Parvum, where those seven are expressed most distinctly on this day: “In Egypt, Victorinus, Victor, Nicophorus, Claudianus, Dioscorus, Serapion, and Papias.” Most of these [Col. 0795B] are recorded on the preceding day in the Hieronymian copies, in this enumeration: “In Egypt, the passion of the holy Victorinus, Victor, Nevecta [Nivitta, Nivitita, Nincentia], Nicophorus, Serapion, and Dioscorus.” Seven are repeated, whether the same persons or namesakes, on 28 February, but mixed with several others and without any indication of place. Their series can be arranged as follows: Serapion, Claudianus, Victorinus, Victor, Nicophorus, Diudorus, and Papias—who, if they are indeed the same persons, would constitute the seven named above.

“Henschenius says that the Acts of these martyrs seem formerly to have been composed from their eulogies, which are found in various and very ancient Martyrologies.” But what he here calls “many Martyrologies” ought, in my judgment, to be reduced to Ado alone. Perhaps he had seen some Acts from which he chiefly derived the account of the various kinds of torments suffered by these martyrs, which Our Author reported more briefly. Accordingly, those various announcements from other Martyrologies which the aforementioned Henschenius adduces in the Acts [Col. 0795C] contribute little to our present purpose.

It is worth observing that in Ado, both in Mosander and in Rosweyd, the emperor Numerian is named, with the duke Sabinus acting, whereas the name Numerian would surely better have been omitted here, perhaps having been inserted into the Acts by some interpolator and not by Ado himself, since Notker transcribes the same text of Ado in full. We possess, however, an Adonian copy belonging to the Queen of Sweden, formerly apparently from the abbey of Fulda, in which the reading is corrected and says only: “Under the duke Sabinus”—whom we know to have cruelly persecuted the Christians in Egypt—not under Numerian, who is nowhere reported to have been hostile to them, but under Decius, as the patriarch Dionysius relates more fully in his letter against Germanus [Col. 0796A], preserved by Eusebius in Book VI, chapter 40. When Usuard selected from Ado what could serve his purpose, he chiefly selected the detail concerning the time of the martyrdom, which he could more safely have omitted, striking out the duke Sabinus, as is clear from our entry.

The place of the martyrdom is even less certain, unless we wish to borrow it from the Greeks, who commemorate these martyrs on other days, as John, bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône, seems to have done, if the *Topography of the Holy Martyrs of Christ* published and revised by Maurolycus is his. In that work, under the name Diopolis, he places these seven martyrs of ours there under Numerian. While Henschenius was examining this question carefully and learnedly, he inexplicably went wrong concerning the true first name of the author of the *Topography of the Saints* and attributed it to Peter of Chalon-sur-Saône.

The learned Castellanus astutely noticed the error in his notes, p. 763, charitably interpreting it as a typographical oversight—correctly enough, and in keeping with his devotion to our work. Yet while correcting Henschenius himself, he fell into another very similar error, whether his own or typographical. I readily understand what misled him: without examining the matter further, he followed Maurolycus and substituted the name Primus, thereby allowing his otherwise tireless diligence to fail him [Col. 0796C], since he did not consult the catalogue of the bishops of Chalon, where there is no Primus. Instead, for the year in which Maurolycus is said to have written the aforementioned *Topography*, there appears John Germain—called John X by some and John XI by the Sammarthani—a very learned man known for other writings. Perhaps the initial letter J. attached to his first name gave Maurolycus the opportunity to form “Primus,” as Papebrochius observed before me from Raynaudus, in volume V of the June Acts, p. 491, no. 27.

See in the works of the aforementioned Sammarthani whether Maurolycus’s *Topography* should not be understood as a *Spiritual Map of the World*, together with the book composed upon it, which is there listed among the other works of John of Chalon-sur-Saône, and which Raynaudus, volume XI, p. 287, calls the *Sacred Map*. We return to our subject.

### [Col. 0795C]

**ROSWEYD.** In his first edition, which is pure, adds: “In Bavaria, Saint Walburga, virgin. In Africa, Donatus and Justus, martyrs, and twenty-one others.” These were taken from the Hieronymians; see their companions in the Acts.

**LOVANIEN.** Even in its otherwise pure text, appends: “In Phoenicia, Saints Ananias the presbyter and Peter his jailer.”

**ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., DANIC.,** and the **ULTRAJECT.-BELG. edition** have the same beginning and continue as follows: “The first of them was scourged under the governor Maximianus; his wounds were sprinkled with salt and vinegar and rubbed with the roughest sackcloth. Then, together with the aforementioned Peter, who had been converted by his steadfastness, after various punishments they were thrown together into a heated furnace; with seven other soldiers they were cast into the sea and attained the glory [Col. 0796C] of martyrdom.” See the Acts illustrated by Bollandus [Col. 0796D].

**CENTULEN.** Lacks the entire text, but reads: “In Africa, the birthday of Saints Donatus, Justus, Ingenia, and fifty others. Also the birthday of Saint Aldetrudis, virgin.”

**BRUXELLEN.** Presents almost the whole context of Ado, although not entirely pure, as follows:

> “In Egypt, the birthday of the holy seven brothers Victorinus, Victor, Nicaphorius, Claudianus, Dioscorus, Serapion, and Papias, under the emperor Numerian, with the duke Sabinus acting. The first of them was put into a hollow wooden ball, pierced all around, and for a very long time pierced through each of its openings; when a great quantity of blood flowed out, he was taken from the ball and beheaded. The second, after his hands and feet had been cut off, was put into the same ball, endured the tortures of the first, and was finally beheaded. The third, when he had entered the ball of his own accord, angered the judge, who ordered him to be taken out and roasted for a while on a grate with burning coals beneath it, and turned from side to side. When he persisted in his confession, he was taken away, cut to pieces with a sword, and gave up his spirit. The remaining four—Claudianus and Dioscorus were burned in flames, while Serapion and Papias were killed by the sword—completed a celebrated martyrdom.”

Concerning Ananias and Peter it has the same account as the manuscripts of the middle class. At the end it adds: “Also Aldetrudis, virgin, daughter of Saint Bavo.” It means Vincent, the count. See our Acts, where Henschenius explains several difficulties concerning the time of Aldetrudis’s life, the day of her death, and other matters not yet sufficiently understood.

**HAGENOYEN** composed another text:

> “In Egypt, the birthday of the holy martyrs Victorinus and Victor, Nicophorus, Dioscorus, Claudianus, Serapion [Col. 0797B], and Papias, under the Roman emperor Numerian. The first, second, and third, steadfastly enduring various kinds of punishments devised for their confession of the Godhead, while the others were burned in flames and the last two were beheaded, all dedicated a solemn martyrdom.”

The announcement of Ananias follows, in which it expresses the location or site of the martyrdom as follows: “In Venice, the holy martyrs Ananias the presbyter and Peter his jailer. The first of them,” etc., as in the manuscripts of the middle class above. At the end: “Walburga, virgin.”

**AQUICINCT.:** “The discovery of the head of Saint Paul the Apostle.”

**CODEX D. DU CHEVAL**, marked B: “In Phoenicia, [Col. 0798A] Saints Ananias the presbyter and Peter his jailer.”

**ALTEMPSIAN.:** “At Rome, the discovery of the head of Saint Paul.”

**STROZZ. and MEDIC.:** “Also Saints Justus and Herenaeus, martyrs, and Saint Victor, bishop and martyr.”

The **LUBECO-COL. edition**, whose text is almost pure, adds only: “In the district of Troyes, blessed Victor, confessor.” This pertains to the following day.

**GREVEN.:** “In Africa, Donatus and Justus, martyrs, and fifty-one others. Also Hereneus, Pysion, Nestor, and Casta.” As usual, these were taken from some Hieronymian copy. “Ananias, martyr. At Rome, Aglaes, martyr.” See the index of omissions. “In the district of Troyes, blessed Victor, confessor. Aldetrudis, virgin, daughter of Saint Bavo [read: Vincent, the count],” who himself is also venerated as a saint on 24 July. “The translation of Saint Walburga, virgin.” It is more probable [Col. 0798B] that she died on this day, as may be seen in the Acts.

**MOLAN.:** “Also Saint Aldetrudis, virgin, daughter of Saint Waldetrudis.” Then, in smaller type: “On the same day, our holy father Tarasius, archbishop of Constantinople.” Other editions place the supplement as follows: “Also Saint Aldetrudis, virgin, daughter of Saint Waldetrudis, who was the second abbess of the monastery of Maubeuge. In Sicily, Saint Gerlandus, from Burgundy, bishop of Agrigento, in the time of Count Roger. On the twenty-fifth day, our holy father Tarasius, archbishop of Constantinople.” See Henschenius’s outstanding commentary on him, and the Life translated from Greek into Latin by Gentianus Hervetus and excellently illustrated.

### [Col. 0793]

In Egypt, the birthday of Saints Victorinus, Victor, Nicophorus, Claudianus, Dioscorus, Serapion, and Papias, under the emperor Numerian: the first, second, and third steadfastly enduring various kinds of punishments devised for their confession of the Godhead; while the remaining four—Claudianus and Dioscorus were burned in flames, and Serapion and Papias were struck down by the sword. Thus they all completed a celebrated martyrdom.

**IV Kalends. Day 26.**

### [Col. 0797]

**Note:** Taken from Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Ant.-Maj., Marchian., Pulsan., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.

**Note:** Pulsanen. and Munerat. write *Pergem* for *Pergen*. I read *Pamphiliae* with nearly all the manuscripts, although I readily admit that Molanus’s reading, *Pamphyliae*, is better. The text correctly has *orationi insisteret* (“he devoted himself to prayer”); only Pulsanen. differs, writing *incumberet*. Thus Molanus, against everyone, wrote *mirabili* instead of *mira libertate*. Some have *eculeo*; I followed the more common and accurate spelling. In place of *exin*, Greven. and Molan. read *exinde*. Pulsanen. and Munerat., who print *et in*, do not seem wholly to depart from the true meaning [Col. 0798C]. The scribe of the Antuerp.-Maj. manuscript wrote *ex tamen*, which means absolutely nothing. Marchian. omits the title *bishop* after Alexander. They commonly write *Arrium*; Antuerp.-Maj. incorrectly has *Arritum*. There is variation in *Nicaeno*. “He condemned” preserves the orthography of its own age. Greven. at the end has *damnavit eumdem*; Molan. has *eumdem damnavit*—in both cases the construction is correct.

We have said elsewhere that, among the various opinions concerning the author of the Roman Parvum, one is deeply rooted in many minds: that he compiled his little work from the Hieronymian Martyrology. But from the continuous comparison in which I have been engaged for so long, I judge the opposite to be far more probable. Although I do not deny that the same saints sometimes occur on the same day in both works [Col. 0797D], I am nevertheless firmly convinced that that author rarely took anything from the Hieronymian copies.

To approach today’s text: when he announces it in this form, “At Perge in Pamphylia, blessed Nestor, bishop,” he must clearly have followed another guide. To make this evident, here is the Hieronymian entry for this day: “The birthday of Saints Alexander, Nestor, Theon, Epion, and many others.” What correspondence is there here, I ask? But perhaps he could have taken it from the preceding day. I do not think so; let us compare the words.

The Lucca manuscript has there: “In Pamphylia, the birthday of Saints Nestor and Casta.” The Corbie manuscripts: “In Pamphylia, the birthday of Saints Nestor and Casta, Claudianus.” Finally, the Echternach manuscript: “In Pamphylia, the birthday of Saint Nestor.” Nowhere is the place determined, nor is a title attached; almost everywhere companions are added, whom everyone must remove from our Nestor [Col. 0798D]. If these details are sufficient to say that the first author drew from the later entries, I am mistaken if anyone skilled in these matters would think so.

I believe that Nestor of Magydus became known to the author of the Roman Parvum through the Acts. Since he did not find a sufficiently definite day there, he chose this one at his own discretion, as he sometimes does, before the others. From similar Acts Ado composed an excellent eulogy, which Notker transcribed and Our Author elegantly adapted to his customary brevity.
