See the Acts themselves, approved by Baronius and Henschenius, though Tillemont considers them subject to many doubts in volume III, beginning at p. 351.

Which Nestor is celebrated by Wandalbert is clear from his verse:

> “With Nestor the fourth, Theon likewise is joined.”

What we think concerning Nestor applies, with even greater force, to Alexander, patriarch of Alexandria: he is certainly not indicated in that group of many martyrs which is recorded on this day in the Hieronymians, and indeed without any indication of place. Wherever the author obtained him—I do not doubt that he took him from Rufinus—and whatever his reason, when the author of the Roman Parvum assigned him to 26 February, it is certain that the entry reads: “At Alexandria, Alexander, the glorious aged bishop.” It is certain that Ado constructed Alexander’s eulogy from the account of Rufinus’s Eusebius; Usuard and Notker copied it almost word for word, and from them it spread into the other Martyrologies.

Some recent scholars attempt to evade the authority of that Martyrology by transferring Alexander’s death from 26 February to 17 April, contrary to what seemed to me correct in the *Chronological Treatise on the Alexandrian Patriarchs*, no. 193 onward. I shall not repeat what I said there; I merely wish to observe that all the conjectures which the most learned Montfaucon piles up and ingeniously twists in his preliminary notice to the Life of Saint Athanasius, p. 46, collapse. He argues that the author of the Roman Parvum incorrectly punctuated and confused the Hieronymian texts in order to place Alexander of Alexandria on this day and, if it please heaven, even make him a martyr. I shall refute him more clearly on the following day.

I shall suggest a better and shorter course to the learned man: let him say plainly that the author of the Roman Parvum sometimes assigned saints, almost at his own discretion, to particular days when he did not possess certain knowledge of the day of their death. We shall readily admit that this is true; but whether it applies here is established neither for him nor for me.

Among those recent opponents I also count Castellanus, who habitually exercises excessive freedom in changing the days which, for so many centuries, the unanimous agreement of our martyrologists had consecrated to the veneration of the saints. I pass over the rest, since the origin and genuine simplicity of our text have been sufficiently demonstrated.

**Note:** Rosweyd gives the pure text, but at the end adds: “Fortunatus, bishop.” Other manuscripts add companions, though they do not agree on their number; see Henschenius and Florentinius, who distinguish those classes with sufficient accuracy.

**Note:** Antuerp.-Max.-Lubec., Ughellian., Belin., Antuerp.-Max., Vatican manuscript no. 5949, Ultraj.-Leyden., Lovanien., Danic., and the Ultraj.-Belg. edition, all also sufficiently pure in their text, have at the end: “Also Fortunatus, Felix, and twenty-seven others.”

**Note:** Albergen., I do not know why it departs from the usual companions, inserting into the text from Ado the following concerning Nestor: “He joyfully sang, saying: ‘I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth.’ But the governor, astonished at such endurance and wishing to draw him away from the faith with flattering words, said to him: ‘Do you wish to be with us, or with your Christ?’ Saint Nestor replied to him with great joy: ‘With my Christ I was, am, and shall be.’ Then from the cross,” etc.

**Note:** Centulen., I think through the scribe’s carelessness, has confused two announcements in this manner: “In the city of Perge in Pamphylia, Saint Fortunatus, bishop and martyr, and thirty-two others.” See the Acts.

**Note:** Bruxellen., whose text is almost pure, nevertheless preserves its customary addition at the end: “Also Felix the martyr with twenty-seven companions.”

**Note:** Hagenoyen also reports an almost pure text. In the supplement it agrees with the manuscripts above: “Also Fortunatus and Felix with twenty-seven other martyrs.”

**Note:** Aquicinct., instead of *Nestoris*, reads *Nestorii*, and adds at the end with the others: “Also Fortunatus and Felix with twenty-seven others.”

**Note:** Victorin. and the Royal Codex of Sweden, marked no. 130, have at the end: “At Nevers, Saint Agricola, bishop and confessor.” Others call him Agricola; see the Acts.

**Note:** Strozzi and Medici put a local saint first: “At the city of Florence, in the parts of Tuscany, the birthday of Saint Andrew, bishop and confessor of that same city, successor of the glorious bishop and confessor Saint Zenobius, a man of distinguished holiness, praiseworthy life, and great renown, whose body rests in the cathedral church of the aforesaid city, beside the altar of the aforesaid Saint Zenobius.”

**Note:** The Lubeco.-Col. edition inserts something from Ado concerning Nestor after “he was guarded,” in these words: “Having been arrested by a certain Irenarchus, chief magistrate of the city, he was brought before the governor Pollio. While confessing the Lord’s name with remarkable freedom and eagerness, he was subjected to many kinds of torture and cruelly tortured on the rack. Then,” etc. It continues with Alexander. Then: “Also Saints Fortunatus and Felix, with twenty-seven other martyrs. At Arvernis, blessed Agricola, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Arciacum, Saint Victor, confessor.”

**Note:** Greven.: “Also the holy martyrs Theon, Epion, Justus, Donatus, Ampliatus, and Ingenius. Also Fortunatus, bishop, Felix, and twenty-seven other martyrs.” Concerning Agricola and Victor he has the same as the Lubeco-Col. edition: “In Ireland, Oghani, bishop.” He is among the omissions. “Also Jacelinus, of holy memory, the tenth prior of the Grande Chartreuse after Bruno, a man of great holiness and merit. When a deceased Carthusian monk began displaying miracles, he restrained him by a command of obedience from continuing to do so.” He is noted only among the omissions for this day and the preceding one.

**Note:** Molan., in the first edition: “Also Fortunatus and Felix with twenty-seven others. In the territory of Arciacum, Saint Victor, confessor.” Later editions add: “On the twenty-sixth day, our holy father Porphyry, archbishop of Gaza.” See his outstanding Life, written by Mark, his disciple, translated into Latin by Gentianus Hervetus, and illustrated in our Acts by Henschenius. It is astonishing that our martyrologists make no mention of so great a man.

### [Col. 0797]

In the city of Perge in Pamphylia, the birthday of blessed Nestor, bishop. During the persecution of Decius, while he devoted himself to prayer day and night, asking that Christ’s flock be guarded, he was arrested and confessed the Lord’s name with remarkable freedom and eagerness. He was cruelly tortured on the rack. Then, victorious, he departed through suspension on a cross. At Alexandria, Saint Alexander, bishop, a glorious old man. After blessed Peter, he expelled his own presbyter Arius, corrupted by heretical impiety and convicted by divine truth, from the Church; later, among the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, he condemned him again at the Council of Nicaea.

**III Kalends. Day 27.**

**Note:** This is found in Praten., Herinien., Marchian., Pulsan., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan.

**Note:** Munerat., after *is cum*, omits *ita*, which is required for correct syntax. In Pulsanen., *potuisset* is incorrectly read for *posset*; in Munerat., *Uno* appears for *Euno*, as also in Marchian. Belinus has *Enuo*. Here again, instead of *inspectante*, he reads *spectante*, and Munerat. agrees, writing *Hispalis* for *Hispali*. *Hyspaniis* and *Hyspali*, which occur in some copies, must be attributed to the defective spelling of the age. The first edition of Belin has *Recharendum*; the second, with all the manuscripts, has *Recharedum*. Guided by their authority, we have retained that form in the text. Munerat. omitted the three words *per Recharedum regem*. I wrote *Ariana*, as on the preceding day. Marchian., Pulsanen., the first edition of Belin, and Greven. read *Baldomeri*, correctly, I think, although I yielded to the stream of the other manuscripts, which, with Ado and Notker, consistently write *Baldomeris* or *Baldemeris*. Molan., in the second edition, likewise has *Baldomeri*, and also corrects what he had incorrectly printed in the first edition, *ipsius verberibus* for *ipsis*.

The commemoration of Julian and Euno belongs to the author of the Roman Parvum, who took those saints from nowhere other than Rufinus’s Eusebius. They belong to the number of those whose contests Dionysius of Alexandria praised in his frequently cited letter to Fabius of Antioch, preserved by Eusebius in Book VI, chapter 41, and from which all the others derived their account.

The aforementioned Martyrology reads: “At Alexandria, Julian the martyr and Euno, who persevered with the old man in confession.” Here one will notice that Euno’s proper name, Cronion, has been omitted. Ado fashioned a eulogy from the words of Eusebius, which Our Author presents more briefly.

Montfaucon’s observation in his notice to the Life of Athanasius, whom we also mentioned the preceding day, is quite extraordinary. There he accuses the author of the Roman Parvum of disorder and confusion, as though he had fused different persons into one, and specifically as though the words “who persevered with the old man in confession” indicated that Euno suffered martyrdom together with Alexander the patriarch, since Alexander, as we saw on the preceding day, is called a glorious old man.

But how slight the conjecture on which these and Montfaucon’s other arguments rest is shown plainly by the reading of that Martyrology, Ado, and Notker. He could have corrected himself by his own eyes had he even glanced at Eusebius in the cited passage. I shall quote his words here:

> “Among them was Julian, a man afflicted with the pains of gout, so that he could neither stand nor walk. He was brought in together with two others who carried him. One of these immediately denied the faith; the other, named Cronion and also called Euno, and the old Julian himself, after confessing Christ,” etc.

Here Montfaucon has the old man with whom Euno persevered in confession; he has the man—not by whom the Roman Parvum is accused of confusion, but by whom he himself is convicted of confusion, namely, because he has conflated the entirely different texts of two days into one.

Concerning Leander, that famous bishop of Seville, none of the martyrologists older than Ado makes mention. Ado himself announces him first, in these words:

> “In Spain, in the city of Seville, Saint Leander, bishop and confessor, to whom blessed Gregory wrote the books of the *Moralia*. Through Leander’s preaching and diligence, the entire Gothic people was converted from Arian impiety to the Catholic faith through King Reccared. He also converted his brother, King Hermenegild, while their heretical father was still alive, from the same Arian heresy to the Catholic faith, and by his exhortations led him even to the glorious suffering of martyrdom.”

Notker also transcribed all this, likewise placing it first. Usuard, changing the order, followed Ado’s meaning. Leander is transferred in the Acts to 13 March for the reasons given there, the chief being that throughout nearly all Spain he is celebrated on no other day.

Castellanus thinks that the martyrologists took the occasion for commemorating Leander of Seville on this day from the fact that a certain Leander is mentioned among the Smyrnaean martyrs in the Hieronymian copies. I do not agree. In Ado and those who followed him, at least so far as I have been able to observe, this lacks precedent.

The metrical martyrologist left us this verse concerning Leander:

> “The third shines for Hesperia with Leander as bishop.”

Baldomerus was likewise first entered into the calendars by Ado, whose words Usuard and Notker transcribed. The Gallic name *Galmier* or *Geaumier* is difficult to derive by proper analogy from the primitive form. See the little that Chiffletius discovered concerning him in the Acts illustrated by Henschenius. There is no remaining doubt concerning our text.

**Note:** Tornacen. adds to its pure and simple text: “On the same day, Saint Honorina, virgin and martyr.” She seems to have become known chiefly through her translation, as Henschenius explains in the Acts.

**Note:** Antuerp.-Maj. is mutilated here; it reads: “In Spain, in the city of Seville, the birthday of Saint Leander, bishop, to whom blessed Gregory wrote the books of the *Moralia*. Also on the same day in Alexandria, the birthday of Saint Julian [Col. 0801D], martyr.”

**Note:** Rosweyd, in his first edition, is pure; he transfers the next two announcements to the following day, but here substitutes: “Also in Africa, Dion, martyr, and twenty-three others.” He intended Dionysius. Others count twenty-four anonymous companions.

**Note:** Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. add at the end: “On the same day, Alexander, Abundantius, and Fortunio.”

**Note:** Antuerp.-Max., Ultrajec., Leyden., Lovanien., Alberg., Danic., Hagenoyen, and the Ultraj.-Belg. edition, pure enough at the beginning and end, insert in the second after “confessor” concerning Saint Leander: “To whom blessed Gregory wrote the books of the *Moralia*.” At the end they have, as above and as several manuscripts below: “On the same day, Alexander, Abundantius, and Fortunio.” These were detached from the Hieronymians’ class of Thessalonian martyrs; see the remaining companions properly ordered in the Acts, where one can easily detect what has gone wrong in the modern Roman Martyrology.

**Note:** Centulen. does not reproduce a single word from the whole Usuardine text, reporting only this from the Hieronymians: “In Africa, Saint Dionysius and twenty-four other martyrs.” I have already said that the manuscripts do not have a single reading here, since some count only twenty-three companions.

**Note:** Bruxellen. begins with Leander: “In Spain, in the city of Seville . . .,” as in the manuscripts of the middle class. It continues with Julian and Euno. Then: “On the same day at Alexandria, Abundantius and Formion.” The manuscripts above have the better reading. “At Lyons, Saint Baldunetus . . .” Finally: “Also Fortunatus, martyr.”

**Note:** Aquicinct., at the end: “Also at Alexandria, Abundantius and Fortunio.” We already know the error. “And Saint Honorina, virgin.”

**Note:** Victorin., the Royal Codex of Sweden marked no. 30, and Ughellian.: “Also Saint Alexander, Abundantius, and Fortunio.” This is an addition that frequently recurs.

**Note:** Martrician. and Carthus.-Ultraj. add after a thoroughly mutilated text: “The discovery of Saint John the Baptist”; but in the margin: “Perhaps John, son of Eutropius.” More probably neither. See the index of omissions.

**Note:** The Bigotian Codex marked P. 5, formerly belonging to the Celestines: “Also Alexander, Abundantius, and Fortunio.”

**Note:** The Royal Codex of Sweden marked 428: “On the same day, Saint Honorina, virgin and martyr.”

**Note:** Codex D. du Cheval, marked B: “On the same day, Alexander, Abundantius, and Fortunio.”

**Note:** Vatican manuscript no. 5949: “Alexander, Abundantius, Fortunio, and twenty-four others.”

**Note:** Strozzi and Medici: “Also Saint Januarius.” Is he one of the companions of Saints Alexander, Abundantius, and the others?

**Note:** The Lubeco-Col. edition appends after Leander: “The calling of Saints Peter and Andrew the apostles to the apostolate.” It continues with Baldomerus. Then: “On the same day, Saints Alexander, Abundantius, and Fortunio, martyrs. On that day, blessed Onesima, virgin.” Read *Onesima*, concerning whom see the Acts for today.

**Note:** Greven.: “At Thessalonica, Alexander, Abundantius, Antrogonus, and Fortunio, martyrs. In Africa, Dionysius, Tacianus, Dion, and thirty-three other martyrs.” We have already observed that Greven commonly begins his additions from Hieronymian copies. “Onesima, virgin. Also Macarius. At Castro Conflando, Honorina, virgin. Also blessed John, monk, son of Eutropius, master of the soldiers of the city of Rome. After living in the monastery for seven years in complete holiness, he returned to Rome; he remained unknown in his parents’ house and, revealing himself to his parents at the end of his life, died in their arms. Also blessed John, abbot in Scetis, who, when the brothers asked him to leave them some word of salvation, replied: ‘Since I became a monk, I have never done my own will, nor taught anything that I had not first done myself.’ Also another John in the desert of the Upper Thebaid, distinguished in life, conduct, and abstinence. Also another John, who shone in the desert of Sutria with such a gift of consolation that, whatever sadness oppressed anyone, they were filled by his few words with joy and cheerfulness.” Concerning these three other namesakes, see the index of omissions.

**Note:** Molan.: “On the same day, blessed Honorina, virgin and martyr.” Thus in the first edition. The later editions have: “On the same day in Normandy, blessed Honorina, virgin and martyr. On the twenty-seventh day, our holy father Procopius of Decapolis, confessor.” Finally, in smaller type: “Also according to Metaphrastes, Saints Andronicus and Athanasia.” In the index of omissions they are referred to 9 October.

### [Col. 0799]

At Alexandria, the passion of Saint Julian the martyr. He was so afflicted by gout that he could neither walk nor stand. Together with Euno, his servant, he was offered to the judge in a chair. They were ordered to be placed upon camels, led around the entire city, and torn with whips here and there before the watching people, until they met their end through the very scourging. In Spain, in the city of Seville, the birthday of Saint Leander, bishop and confessor, through whose preaching and diligence the whole Gothic people was converted from Arian impiety by King Reccared. At Lyons, Saint Baldomerus, a man of God, whose tomb is made illustrious by frequent miracles.

**Pridie Kalends. Day 28.**

**Note:** The text is taken from Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Marchian., and Pulsanen. Munerat. agrees, but adds the translation of Saint Augustine. Greven. and Molanus, by contrast, omit Macarius and Rufinus in the final announcement [Col. 0804B]. Ant.-Max., Lubec., and many of the other manuscripts contain an excess concerning Justus and Theophilus. See the Observations for more; the rest is in the Appendices.

**Note:** There are no variants here.

Whatever is included in our present text concerning Romanus, the abbot of the Jura, Usuard took from the Viennese manuscript, and Notker likewise reproduced it in the same words. Both omitted Ado’s final paragraph, which reads: “His venerable body lies in the territory of Besançon.” We shall present that paragraph below, restored in some fuller manuscripts.

What Ado briefly mentions here was investigated fully and carefully by Henschenius, who with equal diligence illustrated the Life of the same Romanus, written by a contemporary and recovered by Pierre-François Chifflet. Whether the interpolations which a recent critic thinks he has detected in the aforementioned Life are genuine will be examined in the Supplement.

I have already said that the name of Romanus is absent on this day from the other ancient martyrologists; I add here that the Roman Parvum is entirely silent, so that I may occasionally recall how implausibly some suppose the author of this shorter Martyrology to have been a compiler of Ado—since here he failed to record even one saint whom it is most evident [Col. 0803D] had appeared in Ado.

Concerning Macarius and Rufinus, and likewise Justus and Theophilus, the aforementioned Henschenius treats on this day. He prudently assigns them to two larger groups of the Hieronymians, to one or the other of which they seem to belong: the last perhaps to the earlier group of Alexandrians, the first to the other. The obscurity of the Hieronymian texts is evident to anyone who reads them; nor did Florentinius possess the means to distinguish the classes more accurately or restore them to their proper locations.

For us the question concerns only Usuard’s reading, that is, only Macarius and Rufinus. It is surprising that Castellanus, p. 803, should assert so categorically that in Usuard, as in Ado, no other saint is recorded on this day except Romanus alone. Unless I am greatly mistaken, he must have relied on Molanus’s edition. Certainly he had not then consulted the precious Pratense manuscript, nor did he wish to take account of the other manuscripts cited by Henschenius. He would not have doubted the truth of the matter if he had been able to consult the long series of manuscripts of this kind.

The Hieronymians vary concerning the gender of our martyrs; if one follows them more closely, both Macarius and Rufinus might seem to have to be transformed into women. But since Wandalbert also clearly says:

> “Rufinus, blessed, is joined to Macarius on the preceding day,”

we must acknowledge that they were found somewhere in that form, and we may not depart from the judgment of our author.

But for what reason these two were selected above so many others by these martyrologists—who can guess? I believe that the choice was arbitrary, just as Rabanus and Notker selected four others: “At Alexandria, Saints Celerus, Pupillus, Legici [Notker has Gaius], and Serapion,” preserving no memory of their companions. This occurs countless times in those two martyrologists, and recurs frequently in Our Author as well.

How correctly Galesinius arranged those martyrs, and others after him, see in the Acts, p. 723. There can be no doubt about the authenticity of our text, whatever Greven. and Molan. may do in departing from the agreement of the other manuscripts.

**Note:** Antuerp.-Maj. restores Ado’s concluding clause, forming the announcement as follows: “In the territory of Lyons, in the Jura region, blessed Romanus, abbot, who, first living there as a hermit and distinguished by many virtues and miracles, later became the father of many monks. His venerable body lies in the territory of Besançon.” Only two manuscript copies of Usuard are found without Macarius and Rufinus: this one and the Centulensis.

**Note:** Rosweyd, in first and second place, reports two announcements concerning Leander and Baldomerus, which we noted on the preceding day as having been wrongly transferred to this manuscript. The full and pure text of today follows.

ANTWERP and MAX.-LÜBECK report the second entry [Col. 0805A] as Henschenius printed it in the *Acta*: “On the same day, of Saints Macarius, Rufinus, Justus, and Theophilus.” These are found joined in this way in several manuscripts, undoubtedly first taken from copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology, although the first three—or at least their namesakes—appear among the Additions on 12 February. See the index of the Omitted Saints for this day.

ALBERICUS and DANICUS, together with the similarly marked manuscripts to be cited shortly, insert into the text, with only a very slight alteration, certain details about Romanus. These have been wrongly confused solely because of the similarity of his name to that of another Romanus, as you will find in our index of the Omitted Saints under the name of Saint Romanus, abbot of Fontisrogo, and more clearly under 22 May. The words of all those manuscripts are: “He is believed to have given the monastic habit to blessed Benedict and to have supplied him with the necessities of life at the sound of a little bell.” Then, at the end, they add the entry mentioned above: “On the same day, of Saints Macarius, Rufinus, Justus, and Theophilus.”

[Col. 0805B] ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, and the UTRECHT-BELGIAN edition add further: “Also, the translation of Saint Augustine, bishop and confessor, from Hippo to Sardinia.” You will note that both Leyden manuscripts and the Louvain manuscript insert the words “our Father”; from this you may easily infer that those manuscripts were written for the use of monasteries or convents of the Order of Saint Augustine.

CENTULA begins: “The feast of Saints Publius [or perhaps Pupillus?], Justus, Theophilus, and Felix, martyrs.” Here is another selection from the Hieronymian Martyrology plainly made arbitrarily. Of Romanus it has only this: “In the territory of Lyon, Saint Romanus, abbot.”

BRUSSELS adds about Romanus what the others have above and appends from Ado: “Whose venerable body is situated in the territory of Besançon. On the same day, of Saints Macarius, Rufinus, Justus, and Theophilus. And at Pavia, the entombment of the body of blessed Augustine, bishop of the church of Hippo.”

HAGENOY adds still something to what was said above about Romanus, namely: “He is believed to have been an assistant to blessed Benedict, father of the black and grey monks, etc.” Then, after “to have supplied,” it adds: “On the same day, of Julius and Julian, confessors.” I do not find who these men were, or where they were taken from. Whether they were local Alsatian saints will be investigated later. “Also on the same day, of Saints Macarius, Rufinus, Justus, and Theophilus. On the same day, of Saint Donatus, martyr, who suffered at Carthage under the commander Ursacius and the tribune Marcellinus.” The feast of Donatus is anticipated; see the following day.

AQUINCINCT, after “of monks,” adds: “He also proved an assistant and fellow worker to blessed Benedict at the beginning of his conversion. On the same day, of Saints Macarius, Rufinus, Justus, and Theophilus. In Alexandria, of Saints Dionysius, Claudianus, and Theophilus.” It would not be easy to say where this Dionysius was taken from.

VICTORINUS, at the end: “At the city of Pavia, the entombment of Saint Augustine, our Father, bishop. On the same day, of Saints Macarius and Rufinus, Justus and Theophilus, martyrs.”

MATRICULA-CARTHUSIANS-UTRECHT: “Of Romanus, abbot. Of Macarius and Rufinus, martyrs. Of Oswald, archbishop of York [in the margin: alternatively, of Worcester], a man of great holiness.”

THE VATICAN MANUSCRIPT numbered 5949 and UGHELLI: “Of Saints Macarius, Rufinus, Justus, and Theophilus.”

MUNERATUS: “On that day, the translation of blessed Augustine, bishop and confessor.”

BELIN begins as follows: “At Pavia: the translation of Saint Augustine, our Father, bishop and confessor.” At the end, however: “On the same day, of Saints Macarius and Rufinus, Justus and Theophilus.”

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE edition also confuses Romanus with Saint Benedict’s assistant, adding with the Brussels manuscript, from Ado: “His venerable body is situated in the territory of Besançon.” It continues: “The calling of Saint Philip to the apostolate. On the same day, of Macarius, etc. On that day, of Saint Rufina, virgin.” It could also have added Macaria. See above in the Observations, and in the *Acta*, p. 748. “The translation of blessed Augustine, bishop, from Hippo to Sardinia, made in the year of the Lord 498, in the time of Pope Symmachus and the Emperor Anastasius, in the sixty-second year after the death of that holy man. And this translation of his is called the first.” This belongs to 28 August.

GREVEN: “Of Macarius, Rufinus, Justus, and Theophilus, martyrs. Also of Saints Celer, Pupillus, Claudius, Macarius, Gaius, and Serapion. In Britain, of Saint Oswald, bishop of Worcester and confessor, and of Symphronia, matron and martyr.” See the Omitted Saints. “Of Pynnosa, virgin and martyr. Of Rufina, virgin. The first translation of Saint Augustine, bishop, from Hippo to Sardinia, made in the year of the Lord 498, in the sixty-second year after his death. Of Luitberga, enclosed, of blessed memory. The calling of Saint Philip the apostle in the thirtieth year, on Thursday, concerning which see John I.”

MOLANUS: “At Pavia, the translation of Saint Augustine, our Father, bishop and confessor. On the same day, of Saint Macarius and Rufinus, Justus and Theophilus.” In other editions there is added only: “On the twenty-eighth day, of the holy father and confessor Basil, fellow ascetic of Saint Procopius,” namely, Procopius of Decapolis; concerning both, see the *Acta* for 27 February. Here Molanus follows the Greek *Horologion*, about which we spoke above. The Greek calendars do not agree in every respect. Henschenius preferred to join both saints to the preceding day on the basis of the Menologia, both that edited by Canisius from Sirlet’s translation and the other called that of Basil the Emperor. See more in the cited Commentary of Henschenius.

[Col. 0803]

In the territory of Lyon, in the Jura region, the entombment of blessed Romanus, abbot, who was the first there to lead the eremitical life and, distinguished by many virtues and miracles, later became the father of many monks. On the same day, of Saints Macarius and Rufinus.

THE MONTH OF MARCH HAS THIRTY-ONE DAYS.

[Col. 0805]

On the Kalends. Day 1.  
[Note: [Col. 0805C]

From Pratensis, Tournai, Pülsen, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0807A]

“Clodius” instead of “Claudius” is an error of Muneratus. “The condemned,” “the arena,” and similar matters scarcely deserve to be noted. Nearly all write *amphitheatro*, except Greven and Molanus; we have followed the latter, as was done earlier. I do not know why Greven reads *Clonae* for *Donati*. The Marchian fragment has *Donae* instead; but I refrain from citing fragments in the order of the text. The manuscripts have *Ursacius* or *Ursatius* indiscriminately; I preferred the form in the margin. Pratensis, Tournai, Pülsen, and Muneratus read *Cartagini*; that spelling had to be retained. The remaining two are errors of the Pülsen manuscript, namely *Marsilia* for *Massilia* and *Abiani* for *Adriani*.]

[Note: [Col. 0807A]

Concerning the first anonymous company of martyrs in our text, Henschenius pronounced as follows in the *Acta* for this day:

“The illustrious memory of these holy martyrs has been preserved in various very ancient Martyrologies, and especially in the *Acts of Saints Marius and Martha*, husband and wife, etc. From these sources, surely, the author of the *Little Roman Martyrology* first introduced them into the sacred calendars, reading as follows: ‘Of 260 holy martyrs, in the time of Claudius, who, while digging the arena, were condemned.’ A somewhat fuller and clearer text from the same *Acts* was given by Ado, copied by Notker, and polished by our author; and Henschenius shows from the passage cited above that nothing more can be commemorated concerning those martyrs. Moreover, there is one and only one entry of the *Little Roman Martyrology* and Ado; the others were first placed by Usuard, most probably taken from some copy of the Hieronymian Martyrology.

“It is certain that the Hieronymian copies remember some Donatus on this day, beginning as follows: ‘The feast of Saints Leo, Donatus, etc.’ In the most ancient Epternacensis, the place is prefixed: ‘In Africa.’ The question is whether this Donatus is our Donatus, whom Usuard says suffered at Carthage; I mean, whether he is the same man who is mixed with others in the Hieronymian Martyrology. ‘After a long discussion,’ says Henschenius, ‘we judge that they must be distinguished; I think so because he is distinguished by different marks.’ I willingly defer to the authority of our predecessors, although, after a long and careful comparison of the Martyrologies with one another, I believe that Usuard had no source besides the Hieronymian Martyrology from which to bring forth Donatus; and it is probable that Wandalbert likewise drew from it, since he joined Albinus immediately to him in the following verse: ‘The Kalends hold Donatus and Albinus.’ But who can conjecture from where Usuard determined the place of the contest, or from where he obtained the names of the commander and tribune? Let us admit that he possessed information from another source which has not reached our own times.

“Albinus is recognized in the Hieronymian Martyrology by very distinctive characteristics. Acherius considered him an interpolation; if one considers only their age, very many such figures occur here and there in those manuscripts, for they are much later than Eusebius and Jerome. The very form of writing in both editions of the Corbie manuscript betrays novelty: ‘At the city of Angers, the entombment of Saint Albinus, bishop and confessor.’ The Epternacensis comes closer to the ancient style: ‘At Angers, the entombment of Albinus, bishop,’ without the title ‘confessor,’ which is sufficiently indicated by the entombment in those manuscripts and is not included in the Lucensis. Rabanus and Notker have almost the same form. Usuard’s little embellishment, if one may use a familiar expression, records nothing except the Common of Saints. Henschenius’s Commentary will provide more extensive and painstakingly investigated material.

“Concerning Hermes and Adrian, the difficulty is greater: namely, how and for what reason Usuard places these two together at Marseilles, when in the Hieronymian Martyrology they are separated by vast distances—one Marseillian, the other African. Thus the manuscripts unanimously read: ‘In Africa, of Adrian, Victurus, etc. In Marseilles, of Hermes, Gittheus, etc.’ Henschenius considered this matter long ago and, observing that the Adrians must be distinguished for serious reasons, assigned one to Africa, one to Rome, and one likewise to Marseilles. Here I find nothing that would turn me away from the careful discrimination of my learned master, and I embrace it all the more willingly because it better serves to protect and preserve Usuard’s authority.”]

[Note: [Col. 0807C]

HERINIEN is excluded here from the number of pure manuscripts because, after “they would be sent,” it omitted these words: “And in the amphitheatre of the same city they would be killed by the soldiers’ arrows.”]

ANTWERP-MAJOR follows Ado rather than Usuard in the first entry. It then gives the material concerning Albinus and Donatus quite accurately. The Marseillian martyrs are absent, but it adds: “At the city of Antinoüs, the passion of blessed Leonides, who was killed by various tortures by the same judge under whom Saint Asclas suffered.” Is this the Leonides about whom see the *Acta* for 28 January? See the Omitted Saints.

ROSWEYD is quite pure in the first entry; in the second, after “suffered,” it adds: “And of fourteen others,” from which it is clear that our Donatus was once taken from the Hieronymian Martyrology. In the third and fourth entries it is pure; at the end, however, it adds: “On the same day, of Saint Suitbert, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0807D] ANTWERP and MAX.-LÜBECK, at the end, after the pure text: “The passion of Saint Leo, martyr.” Several manuscripts to be cited below discuss him. I do not see that he can be anyone other than the one placed first in the first class of the Hieronymian Martyrology; for if Leo of Rouen were intended, the title “bishop” would have to be added.

The MARCHIAN manuscript reads *Donae* instead of *Donato*, as we said above.

ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, DANICUS, and the UTRECHT-BELGIAN EDITION, after the pure text, append: “At the imperial town called Werden, the feast of Saint Switbert, bishop and confessor of Werden, who in the time of Pepin, together with Saint Willibrord, preached the word of salvation to the nations. [Col. 0808C] Among other kinds of illness, he was accustomed to cure the disease which physicians call *squinantia* [quinsy].” The LOUVAIN manuscript agrees, but omits the time of the preaching and the companion.

CENTULA again departs from Usuard: “At Rome, of the forty holy martyrs who had been condemned to dig the arena for the name of Christ. At Angers, the entombment of Saint Albinus, bishop and confessor.”

BRUSSELS: In the 260 martyrs and in Donatus it is almost pure; in the third place it has: “At the city of Antinoüs, the passion of Leonides, martyr, father of Origen, who was beheaded for Christ. Origen his son would also have perished with him had he not been stripped of his clothes and forestalled by the stratagems of his mother.” On the confusion of the Leonides, see the index of the Omitted Saints. It then proceeds to Hermes and Adrian. Next: “At Angers, [Col. 0808D] Saint Albinus, bishop and confessor, whose life shone forth full of virtues and miracles. At the imperial castle called Werden …” as above in the middle-class manuscripts. “On that day, of Saint Sintherius, bishop and confessor.” Whether one writes *Sinthecius* or *Suithecius*, he is omitted as unknown in the *Acta*. “And of Saint Senardus, abbot.” He means Siviardus of Anisole, concerning whom see the *Acta* for today.

HAGENOY, in the first entry, is quite pure; in the second place it has: “In the city of Tua, in England, Saint David, bishop of that city, a man of admirable holiness.” Unless I am mistaken, it concerns David of Menevia, who is also mentioned below. It then proceeds purely with Albinus. Then: “The passion of Saint Leo, martyr. [Col. 0809A] At the city of Marseilles, of Saints Hermes and Julian. At the imperial town …” as above.

AQUINCINCT, in the penultimate place, inserts: “At Tours, of Saint Simplicius, confessor.” The Daveron manuscript has the same. Both could have added “bishop,” for the reference is to the archbishop of Bourges.

VICTORINUS and the SWEDISH REGISTRY 130: “At the city of Antinoüs, the passion of blessed Leonides.”

MATRICULA-CARTHUSIANS-UTRECHT begins: “Of David, bishop and confessor, whose remarkable deeds and those of his disciples are described.” Everything else is taken from the text, but all of it is mutilated.

The BIGOT manuscript, numbered P. 5, together with the CLUNIACENSIS and UGHELLIANUS: “The passion of Saint Leo, martyr.”

ALTEMPS: after Adrian, adds “Julian.” Then: “The passion of Saint Leo.”

STROZZI and MEDICI: “Also the passion of Saint Leo, martyr. In the city of Perugia, the translation of the body of Saint Herculanus, bishop and martyr of that city.”

BRUSSELS: “In the city of Marseilles, of Saints Hermes [Col. 0809B] and Adrian, and the passion of Leo, martyr.”

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE edition, in the first place: “In the territory of Mons, in the imperial town …” as above. It follows with the pure text; at the end: “At the city of Antinoüs, of blessed Leonides, martyr. On that day, of Saints Simplicius and Senardus, confessors. On the same day, of Saint Clona, martyr.” We have already said that this is Donatus. “Also of Saint David, bishop and confessor. On that day, of Saint Monanus, confessor.”

BELIN: “On the same day, at Perugia, of Saint Herculanus, bishop and confessor.” Its second edition incorrectly reads “Herculianus.”

GREVEN: “In Africa, of Donatus and fourteen other martyrs. At the city of Antinoüs, of Saint Leonides, martyr. Also of Saints Abundius, Leo, Arcastus, and Polochronius. On the same day, of blessed David of Menevia, archbishop [Col. 0810A] and confessor. Saint Patrick, patron of Ireland, foresaw by divine revelation for thirty years that this man would be born. When he was born and was about to be baptized, a spring of water suddenly burst forth. Once, while writing the Gospel of Saint John, he left hastily for the work of God when a bell was rung, with his work unfinished; on returning, he found it completed in letters of gold by angelic ministry. At length he died full of days, in the 146th year of his life.” These matters are discussed more carefully in the *Acta*. “In the territory of Mons, in the imperial town called Werden, the feast of Saint Switbert, bishop of Werden and confessor. As Bede relates in his *Deeds of the English*, when he was ordained bishop in the time of Saint Willibrord, he preached the word of salvation to the nations and obtained from King Pepin a place of residence on an island in the Rhine. There, after building a monastery—which his heirs still possess—he led for some time a life of complete continence and rested in peace. Among other things, he … On that day, of Senardus, abbot. Of Simplicius, confessor. In Scotland, of Monanus, Levite and confessor. [Col. 0810B] Also at Perugia, according to some, the passion of Saint Herculanus, bishop and martyr, who is placed on the seventh day before the Ides of November.”

MOLANUS inserts in italic type concerning Albinus: “Whose life was written by Fortunatus the priest.” Then at the end: “The feast of the guardian angels of individual human beings. On the same day, at Perugia … At the city of Antinoüs … At the imperial town …” And in smaller type: “On the same day, of blessed David …” through “foresaw.” In other editions there is also added: “On the same day at Marseilles, of Saint Adalongus, bishop.” He is omitted in the *Acta*. “On the first day, of the most holy martyr Eudocia. In the territory of Le Mans, the feast of Saint Siviardus, abbot. In Britain, of blessed David of Menevia, archbishop and confessor. At the city of Antinoüs, the passion of blessed Leonides.”

[Col. 0805]

At Rome, 260 holy martyrs, whom Claudius first ordered, because of the name of Christ, to dig the arena after they had been condemned. Then he ordered them to be sent outside the walls at the Salarian Gate and killed in the amphitheatre of the same city by the soldiers’ arrows. On the same day, of Saint Donatus, martyr, who suffered at Carthage under the commander Ursacius and the tribune Marcellinus. At Angers, of Saint Albanus [Bouillart: Albinus], bishop and confessor, a man of outstanding virtue and holiness. At the city of Marseilles, of Saints Hermes and Adrian.

The sixth day before the Nones. Day 2.  
[Note: [Col. 0809]

Thus Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, Pülsen, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0809]

The whole entry is taken from Pülsen, who writes *Joniani* instead of *Jovini* and places *in* before *extremo*, reading *in exilio*.]

[Note: [Col. 0809C]

We recall repeatedly what we have already noted more than once, and what will recur frequently for further notice: namely, that the author of the Martyrology which we always call the *Little Roman* was not accustomed to borrow his saints from the Hieronymian Martyrology; Ado, moreover, generally follows in his footsteps, while our author and Notker follow both of them, though they very often obtain other material from elsewhere. The sequence of Ado, Usuard, and Notker from the other source is demonstrated most clearly by today’s text, which was first recorded by the *Little Roman* in this form: “At Rome, of Jovinus and Basileus. And of many martyrs condemned to capital punishment under Alexander.” Ado expanded the first entry in the form copied word for word by our author and Notker. Henschenius shows that the knowledge of both saints was extracted from the *Acts of Saint Stephen the pope*, while explaining the other matters handed down in their memory. Concerning the martyrs who suffered under Alexander, scarcely anything is found beyond what we quoted from the aforementioned *Little Roman*, expressed by Ado in harsher language; our author took his text from Ado after somewhat smoothing it, and Notker copied it all from him. The emperor Alexander’s favorable disposition toward Christ and the Christians is well known, although Ado calls him impious; nevertheless, this disposition could not prevent the fury of the notorious Ulpian and his other ministers from raging against our people, even against the emperor’s will, as our *Acta* teach here and on 1 January, where Saint Martina is discussed. Let this suffice concerning the text; Wandalbertus sings quite differently, and his verses have no connection with it.]

[Note: [Col. 0809C]

ANTWERP-MAJOR again indicates his native country here, when he adds an English saint to Usuard’s text [Col. 0809D]: “On that day, of Saint Cedd, bishop.” Others write “Ceadda,” but he perhaps followed the English pronunciation.

ROSWEYD also has the pure text here, but adds other material: “On the same day, of Simplicius, pope. In Caesarea of Cappadocia, of Lucius, bishop.” See the manuscripts that follow immediately [Col. 0810C]. “At Ghent, of Winnualoc, confessor.” [Col. 0810D] See his Life in the *Acta* for the following day.

ANTWERP and MAX.-LÜBECK add at the end of the pure text: “Also of Lucius, bishop, Absalonius [MAX.-LÜBECK: Absolinus], and Lorgius. These names recur in the manuscripts with various inflections; I do not know whether they have been correctly joined together and separated from others. Certainly, among the Hieronymian copies from which they were undoubtedly taken, Absolonius [Col. 0811A] and Lorgius, or Georgius, together with his companion Herolius, lack a placement in the most ancient Epternacensis. Lucius is explicitly assigned to Caesarea of Cappadocia, while ‘Primitivus, Secundola, and Januaria’ belong to the Roman port. But these matters belong elsewhere, where the observations of Florentinius may be compared with our *Acta*.]

ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, LOUVAIN, LEYDEN-BELGIUM, and the UTRECHT-BELGIAN edition, at the end: “At Werden, the feast of Saint Willeicus, confessor, priest of Saint Switbert, bishop.”

UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, and DANICUS, in the first place: “At Rome, of Saint Simplicius, pope. He was the forty-ninth after blessed Peter and condemned Acacius of Constantinople and Peter of Alexandria, bishops, because of the Eutychian heresy. He also established that no pope should appoint his own successor.” The text follows; at the end they have the same material as the Louvain manuscript concerning “Willeicus.”

CENTULA again has nothing from Usuard, but appears to have understood Jerome’s meaning better, though not completely. It reads: “At Caesarea of Cappadocia, [Col. 0811B] of Saints Lucius, bishop, Primitivus and Secundola, martyrs.” It also has “Januaria”; why not “Secundola” as well?

BRUSSELS reports the pure text, but in the wrong order. At the end it adds: “Also at Rome, of Simplicius, pope, who sat for fifteen years. Also of Cedd, bishop. And of Lucius, bishop, Absolonius, and Largius. Also the translation of Benedicta and Felicitas, holy martyrs.” Could these be from the Confraternity of Saint Ursula, whose bodies rest in the abbeys of Vicoigne and Marchiennes? See the Omitted Saints. They will be treated fully on 21 October.

HAGENOY, after a fairly pure text, gives Simplicius almost as in the middle-class manuscripts above. Then: “In England, of Cedd, bishop and confessor. Also of Lucius, bishop, Absolonius, and Lorgius. At the town of Werden, of Willeyricus, priest and confessor, chaplain of Saint Switbert.”

AQUINCINCT: “Also of Saints Lucius, bishop, [Col. 0811C] Absolonius, and Georgius. In Britain, the entombment of Saint Cedd, bishop. At Rome, of Simplicius, pope. He condemned Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, and Peter, bishop of Alexandria, as Eutychians.”

The MARCHIENNES fragment: “In Britain, the entombment of Saint Cedd, bishop.”

MATRICULA-CARTHUSIANS-UTRECHT: “Of Simplicius, pope. Of Tartranus or Tauranus, martyr, and of many others.” If it intended to indicate Ceraunus, the martyr of Chartres, he is celebrated on 28 May, as can be seen in the *Acta*: “Of Charles, count of Flanders and martyr, who rests at Bruges.”

CLUNIAC: “Of Lucius, bishop, Absolonius, and Georgius.” But in the calendar of the same monastery it reads: “Of Lucius, bishop, Januarius, and Primitivus.”

The DU CHEVAL manuscript, marked C: “Of Lucius, bishop, Absolonius, and Georgius.”

The VATICAN manuscript, numbered 5949, reads first: “Of Simplicius, pope, who sat in the episcopate for fifteen years.”

UGHELLIAN: “Also of Lucius, bishop, Fbsalonius, and Lorgius.”

[Col. 0812A] STROZZI and MEDICI: “At Florence, the translation of the arm of Saint Philip the apostle into the basilica of Saint John the Baptist, in the year 1204, under Pope Innocent III.” See the history of this translation in the *Acta* for 1 May, p. 15.

The REMENSIS manuscript of the church of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “In the district of Reims, the passion of Saint Macra, virgin.” We discussed her with Usuard on 6 January.

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE edition has Simplicius almost as above. At the end: “On the same day, of Saint Cedd, bishop and confessor. At Werden, the feast of Saint Willericus, confessor, priest of Saint Switbert.”

BELIN: “Also of Lucius, bishop, Absolonius [the second edition: Absoloni], and Lorgius.”

GREVEN: “At Rome, of Saints Georgius, Heraclius, Absolonius, Paul, Januarius, Primitivus, and Secundola.” The confusion is obvious. “Of Charles, count of Flanders, martyr. Of Tauranus, martyr.” Concerning him, see above. “Also, of 400 captive martyrs, concerning whom Gregory reports in *Dialogues* 3.28 that, when the Lombards compelled them to worship the head of a goat consecrated to the devil, the greatest number of them refused and were killed by them.” So far I have found no evidence of a cult. “At Rome, of Simplicius, pope and confessor, who was the forty-ninth after blessed Peter and sat for fifteen years. He condemned Acacius [the text has Agatius], etc. In England, of blessed Cedd, bishop of the Mercian and Lindisfarne peoples, whose virtues Bede, recounting them in books III and IV of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, praises, among other merits of his virtues, as full of fear of the Lord and constantly mindful of his last things. Of Lucius, bishop of Caesarea and confessor.” Why not “and martyr”? “Of Leporius, bishop and confessor.” Perhaps this is “Herolius,” the companion of Lucius. “Also at Caesarea of Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Luke, bishop.” The names have been wrongly multiplied. “At Werden, of Willericus, priest and confessor, disciple of blessed Switbert, bishop. In Ireland, of Tidgna and Monendabbis, abbots,” unknown even to the Irish. “At Ghent, of Winnualoc, [Col. 0812C] priest, disciple of blessed Samson, archbishop of Dol, concerning whom see 14 November.” See the *Acta* for 3 March. “At Perugia, of Aegidius, disciple of Saint Francis, of blessed memory. Also of William, priest and confessor.” Consult the index of the Omitted Saints concerning both.

MOLANUS: “Also of Lucius, bishop, Absolonius and Lorgius. And of Simplicius, pope, who sat for fifteen years. He condemned Acacius … In the Roman port, of Secundola, Januaria, and Saints Paul and Heraclius. At Werden, the feast of Saint Willeicus …” Afterwards, in smaller type: “Also of 400 or more martyrs …” as in Greven. “In England, of blessed Cedd … Of Charles, count of Flanders, martyr of blessed memory, resting at Bruges in the cathedral church of Saint Donatian.” In other editions it varies as follows: “Also of Lucius, bishop, at Caesarea of Cappadocia. And of the holy martyrs Absolonius, Lorgius, and Heraclius. And of Simplicius, pope,” as above. “In the Roman port, of Paul, Secundola, and Januaria.” Again in smaller type: “At Bruges, the death of Charles, martyr and count of Flanders.”]

[Col. 0809]

At Rome, on the Latin Way, of the holy martyrs Jovinus and Basileus, who suffered under the emperors Gallienus and Valerian. Also at Rome, of many martyrs whom the emperor Alexander, after they had long been tortured, condemned to death at the end.

The fifth day before the Nones. Day 3.  
[Note: [Col. 0811A]

From Pratensis, Herinien, Rosweyd, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, Muneratus, Belin, Greven, and Molanus; the Antwerp-Maximum, Utrecht, Leyden, Albergen, Danicus, and Utrecht-Belgian-edition manuscripts are also added.]

[Note: [Col. 0813A]

Only Pratensis reads *Astyrii* correctly enough; with Herinien, Belin, and Molanus, we have followed the *Little Roman* and Ado in reading *Asterii*, not *Astirii*, as many other manuscripts have it. Muneratus omitted *fuisset* after *accusatus*. Concerning *abscisione*, as the manuscripts generally write it, and *abcisione*, it has been stated elsewhere. The other manuscripts have *subjectis humeris* (“supported on the shoulders”) in the text, as do the more reliable manuscripts with Ado, although with Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, and other manuscripts one should read *subvectum humeris* (“carried on the shoulders”). Herinien, Rosweyd, Muneratus, and Greven have *subtracta veste*; the sense clearly indicates that *substrata* should be written, as it is in the text. *Qui martyrii* instead of *quem martyri* is an error of Muneratus or his printer. The *Little Roman* reads *Hemitherii*; Ado, *Emiterii*; Pratensis, *Emitherii*; Herinien, *Emytherii*; Muneratus, *Enutherii*; Belin, *Emitterii*; Greven, *Emicherii*; Molanus, *Hiterii*; others have still other forms. In this disagreement among the manuscripts, I followed the inflection which our predecessors in the *Acta* judged preferable. Again, the *Little Roman* and Ado have *Cheledonii*, followed only by Molanus. The other manuscripts, and indeed the more reliable ones, read *Celedonii* with the *Acta*. The forms *Galliae* in Muneratus and *Gallatae* in Rosweyd, Belin, and Molanus are easily corrected from the circumstances. Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, and Belin omit *milites*. Greven and Molanus have “they were crowned with martyrdom,” which differs in no respect from the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0813A]

It seems certain that the martyrs commemorated in the text passed from the *Little Roman* into Ado, and from Ado into Usuard’s calendar here as well. Here are the words of the earlier source, reported in second place: “At Caesarea, of Marinus, soldier, and Asterius, senator.” I do not concern myself with those who claim that they were taken from copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology, led to this conclusion by the fact that certain namesakes are found there on this day. I do not concern myself with them, I say, for although a certain Marinus—or even two Marini—and Asterius are found there, they are so different and so separate that they have absolutely no connection with the Caesareans, who were evidently taken from Rufinus, as Florentinius himself admits and our *Acta* appear to have assumed. Therefore it is clear that these most glorious martyrs were taken from Rufinus, Book VII, chapters 13 and 14; it is equally certain that Ado took his eulogy from there, and that Notker copied it from Ado while our author abridged it. Wandalbertus has the same opinion in the verses cited below. In short, the judgment of the Martyrologists, derived from Rufinus and the *Little Roman*, is one: Asterius—or Astirius or Astyrius—like Marinus, attained the glory of martyrdom. Because this is not expressed in Eusebius, Tillemont regards it as suspect in volume IV, p. 21 onward, and Ruinart, following Eusebius, mentions only Marinus among the Selected Saints, p. 274. For the time being, let Asterius retain his crown, or let it be claimed for him solely on Rufinus’s testimony.

“What I said at the outset concerning the Caesarean martyrs—that they were not taken from the Hieronymian Martyrology but from elsewhere—I also understand of the martyrs of Calahorra. Although Emeterius, Emeritus, Meterius, and Celedonius, Cellendonius, Cellidonius, and Eceledonius are named in the Hieronymian Martyrology, anyone who takes the trouble to compare the texts will recognize that they are entirely different from our martyrs, unless I am greatly mistaken. I admit that Henschenius and Florentinius labor considerably to turn the name *Galogori*, which appears in the Hieronymian Martyrology, into the name of a city and to reconcile the corrupt names of those manuscripts with the Emeterius and Celedonius of our Martyrologies; but in the perplexity of the Hieronymian manuscripts, one will scarcely find a place where it is safe to set one’s foot. As for our martyrs, the author of the *Little Roman* first mentions them in this way: ‘Of Saints Hemitherius and Cheledonius, crowned with martyrdom at Calahorra.’ They are likewise placed in Ado with a longer eulogy, the first part of which our author copied word for word, omitting the remainder, which may be found in full in the Additions. ‘The acts of their martyrdom,’ says Henschenius, ‘were committed to writing by contemporary authors’; their loss through the violence and fury of tyrants is lamented by Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, to whose diligence we owe all our knowledge of these martyrs. See there his hymn and the other matters concerning them, carefully arranged. The final two verses of Wandalbertus comprise our text; I do not examine what the preceding one means:

‘Macra [Bollandists: Magra; why not Macra?] with pious love guards the fifth Nones.

With these, Emeterius, Chelidonius, and Marinus,

And Asterius shine, renowned for their shed blood.’]

[Note: [Col. 0813C]

TOURNAI is deficient in that part of the eulogy which concerns Asterius, omitting these words, and, from “with the following,” through “martyr.” Did the copyist of the manuscript perhaps not believe him to be a martyr?]

ANTWERP-MAJOR is more mutilated and reads: “The feast of the holy martyrs Enutherius and Theledonius in Spain, who, having first been soldiers at the Gallic city of León, when the storm of persecution arose, were subjected to many torments for confessing the name of Christ, brought to Calahorra, and crowned there with martyrdom. At Caesarea of Palestine, of the holy martyrs Maurinus, soldier, and Asterius, senator, under the persecution [Col. 0813D] of Valerian.”

PÜLSEN and LOUVAIN give only this concerning the Spanish martyrs: “On the same day, of Saints Emeterius and Celedonius.” They are pure in the other passages.

CENTULA: “In Africa, of Saints Gaiolus, Felix, Nicephorus, and Claudianus. In lesser Britain, the entombment of Saint Wigualoc, abbot.” This is Winwaloc or Winwaloe.

BRUSSELS is only moderately interpolated in the account of Marinus and Asterius. Concerning the martyrs of Calahorra it restores from Ado the material which we said above Usuard had omitted. Thus, after “they were crowned,” it adds: “When the executioner cut off their heads, a great miracle appeared to the people. For the ring of one and the handkerchief of the other were received by a cloud and carried up into heaven. All who were present saw these things, and for as long as the range of their eyes could reach, they followed the gleam of the gold and the whiteness of the linen with astonished gaze.” By “handkerchief,” understand a *sudarium*. It continues: “In the monastery of Monasteriolum, of Saint Winnoc, abbot.” He is the same as the Winwaloc mentioned above. Finally: “Also of Maurinus, bishop and martyr,” unknown elsewhere.

HAGENOY is almost pure; among the two entries it inserts only this middle one: “On the same day, of Cunegund, empress.”

VICTORINUS and the SWEDISH REGISTRY, numbered 130: “Also of Simplicius, pope, who sat at Rome for fifteen years. He condemned the bishop of the city of Constantinople and the bishop of Alexandria as Eutychians.” [Col. 0814D] See more on the preceding day.

The VATICAN manuscript, no. 5949: “At Benevento, of Saint Arthelais, virgin.” The Pleschonian manuscript writes *Athelais*.

The Lübeck–Cologne edition begins as follows:

“Ordination to the pontificate of Saint Anno, archbishop of Cologne, Agrippina, and confessor. At Caesarea in Palestine, of the holy martyrs Marinus, a soldier and citizen of Jerusalem, and Asterius, a senator of the city of Rome. Of whom … On the same day, in Spain, the feast of the holy martyrs Emeterius and Celedonius … On the same day, of Saint Cunegund, empress, who was the daughter of the Palatine Count of the Rhine and was joined in marriage to Saint Henry the emperor. Both of them were virgins, preserved their virginity until the end of their lives, and now lie buried together in the city of Bamberg.”

Greven: “Of Felix and Justus, Fortunatus, Florianus, Donatus, Paula, Gaiolus, Julius, Castus, Solus, Marcia, Hierotes, Antigonus, Januarius, Tutilla, Gabianus, and Quiriolus. Also of Winwalocus, abbot and confessor—according to others, on the preceding day. Of Cunegund, virgin and empress, daughter of the Palatine Count of the Rhine. She, serving Christ in virginity together with her husband, Saint Henry, the first emperor of that name, rested in peace, full of good works. Also of Queen Eufenissa.” She is listed among the Praetermitted as unknown. “At Cologne Agrippina, the ordination to the episcopate of Saint Anno, archbishop and confessor.”

Molanus, after the eulogy of Marinus and Asterius, adds in italics from Ado: “It is written in the Ecclesiastical History.” After the second eulogy he adds: “Aurelianus [Ado: Aurelius] Clemens writes this in the book of the crowned [Ado: crowns]. In the monastery of Blandinium, of Winwalocus, abbot.” Then, in smaller type: “Of Caluppanus, priest and hermit. Also at Bamberg, of Cunegund, virgin and empress …,” as in Greven above. In other editions, instead of Aurelianus, Aurelius is more correctly written. “At Blandinium, etc.; at Bamberg, of Saint Cunegund, virgin. On the third day, of the holy martyrs Eutropius and his companions, Cleonicus and Basiliscus.”

[Col. 0811]

At Caesarea in Palestine, of the holy martyrs Marinus, a soldier, and Asterius, a senator, under the persecution of Valerian. When the former had been accused by his fellow soldiers of being a Christian, and he openly declared in a very loud voice that he was a Christian, he received the crown of martyrdom by the cutting off of his head. When the latter then received the beheaded body of the martyr upon his shoulders and upon the garment that had been spread beneath it, he immediately himself received the honor that he had rendered to the martyr. On the same day, the feast of the holy Emeterius and Celedonius, who were first soldiers at the city of León in Galicia. When the storm of persecution arose, they were subjected to many tortures for their confession of Christ’s name, brought as far as Calahorra, and there crowned with martyrdom.

IV Non. Day 4. [Note: [Col. 0815B]]

Pratensis, Herinianus, Tournacensis, Rosweyd, Pulsa, Greven, and Molan agree in this. Four other Antwerp manuscripts, Max.-Lübeck, Munerat, and Belinus differ only in adding to Caius Palatinus twenty-seven companions, as we shall say in the Appendices.

[Note: [Col. 0815B]]

They offer scarcely anything worthy of notice, since *cemeterio*, *cimiterio*, and *caemiterio*; *Ceciliam*; *Gaii* and *Gagi*; *Apia*; and *saeculi* are either echoes of the manuscripts or scribal errors. Some of these we follow here and elsewhere on the authority of the purer manuscripts. Rosweyd incorrectly wrote *eighty* for nine hundred.

[Note: [Col. 0815B]]

The whole text, as it stands, is taken from Ado, with this sole difference: the eulogy of Lucius in our marginal column has been reduced by half. What Usuard omitted will be supplied below in the Appendices. Lucius and those nine hundred Roman martyrs had earlier been placed in the Little Roman Martyrology: “Of Lucius, pope and martyr, and of the nine hundred martyrs who are buried in the cemetery at Saint Cecilia.” Ado’s eulogy was formed from the lists of the Roman pontiffs, in which there are several matters that learned men cannot immediately accept. Henschenius was unable to smooth out all the controversies; more recent scholars investigate and attempt to resolve others from the letters of Saint Cyprian. Among them Pagi discusses Lucius at considerable length under the year of Christ 252, beginning at number 14, while Tillemont treats him more briefly in volume IV, page 18.

Let us return to our text. Caius, and specifically Caius Palatinus, derives from some Hieronymian copy, although the question remains whether *Palatinus* should not be understood as the martyr’s proper name. Who added twenty-seven others to some Usuardine manuscripts is not easily guessed.

The Acts present another aspect—or rather another sequence of names. According to the more credible reading of the Lucense and Blumian manuscripts, that Caius Palatinus, whether there was one Caius or two, is placed at the head of a long company of martyrs. Those twenty-seven companions, however, are joined not with him but with Bishop Julius, Roto, and others. Another, no lesser, difficulty troubles Florentinius: namely, whether Julius has not been substituted for Lucius in the Hieronymian manuscripts, or Lucius for Julius in the Little Roman Martyrology and our manuscripts.

The matter, however, is now sufficiently clarified in the Acts. That bishop Julius is separated from Lucius and Julius, the Roman pontiffs, while the proper day of Julius the pope—who was not a martyr but a confessor—is preserved as 12 April, as will become clear in its proper place. Rabanus perhaps perceived the difficulty but did not solve it correctly when he marked a bishop Julius on this day and, on the following day, Lucius, pope and martyr. Notker preferred Ado.

Indeed, the ancient Bucherian Calendar had once clearly distinguished the pontiffs Lucius and Julius: it placed Lucius not on the fourth but on the third day before the Nones of March, at the cemetery of Callistus, and Julius on the day before the Ides of April, on the Via Aurelia.

Wandalbert remains. He agrees with our manuscripts concerning the true martyrdom of Lucius but substitutes eight hundred for nine hundred. Henschenius, although the Hieronymian texts vary, thinks that nine hundred and ten should be counted. I have no basis for determining anything more probable. Meanwhile, even if the historical truth is uncertain, the simplicity of Usuard’s text is fully evident. Here is the metrical encomium of the aforementioned Wandalbert:

> Hence, on the fourth day, Pope Lucius shines by a precious death,  
> a most excellent throng of eight hundred martyrs  
> [Molanus in the margin: “by martyrdom, and of nine hundred.”]

[Note: [Col. 0815D]]

Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck, Munerat, and Belinus append only what we indicated above to the pure text, namely: “And twenty-seven others.” Other examples occur below.

Antwerp Major inserts the following from Ado concerning Lucius, after “he completed”: “He was buried on the Appian Way at Saint Sixtus. He sat in the episcopate for three years, three months, and three days.” The rest of the text is pure. It continues: “At Nicomedia, the passion of Saint Adrian with twenty-three others. His body was transferred to Rome and buried on 8 September, where his passion is also recorded.” See that day. He is also listed on this day in the Hieronymian manuscripts.

Antwerp-Maximum, Louvain, Leiden, Belgian, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition have the same statement about the twenty-seven at the end. In addition, concerning Lucius, they insert into the text: “Who was the twenty-third after blessed Peter.”

Utrecht, Leiden, the Latin manuscript, Albergen, and the Danish manuscript also contain the same statement about Lucius. After “he completed,” they restore from Ado what we said above Usuard omitted. They read:

“He established that in every place two priests and two deacons should not leave the bishop, for the sake of ecclesiastical testimony.”

Also, after “were thrown into the sea”: “And twenty-seven others at Nicomedia; the feast of Saint Adrian with twenty-three others. His body was transferred to Rome and buried on 8 September” [Albergen incorrectly reads December].

The Centulense manuscript has only this today: “At Rome, of Saint Julius, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0817A] Brussels, in third place: “At Nicomedia, the feast of blessed Adrian with twenty-three others, all of whom, under Diocletian, after many punishments, completed their martyrdom by the breaking of their legs [the intended reading is *crurifragio*, ‘by the breaking of the legs’]. On the same day, the passion of Saint Gagius Palatinus, who was thrown into the sea, and of twenty-seven others.”

Hagenoyen, with the order almost reversed, begins with the nine hundred martyrs. In second place he gives Caius with his companions. In third place comes Lucius, to whom he adds the same appendix that we reported above. Then:

“At Nicomedia, the passion of Saint Adrian, martyr and soldier, with twenty-three others. Adrian was urged to martyrdom by his own mother and wife. After many punishments, imprisonment, and hunger, all of them completed their martyrdom by the breaking of their legs under the emperor Diocletian. After some years had passed, on 8 September, the body of blessed Adrian was transferred to Rome. On the same day, the translation of Saint Wenceslaus, duke of Bohemia and martyr.”

Aquicinct adds concerning Lucius as above. As it agrees with the Victorine manuscript in writing “three deacons,” or “deacons,” instead of “two,” I think this was caused by a scribal error, as was the fact that Aquicinct alone gives two hundred instead of nine hundred and Agius instead of Caius.

Manuscript D of Le Mare, marked C, formerly belonging to the Franciscan Fathers, reads: “Also of Agape, virgin; Gorgonius; and Firmus.” I do not know why these three have been inserted here today. It will become clear later that they belong to 10 March.

Ughellian and Altemps add, as above, the statement concerning Caius and the twenty-seven others.

The Lübeck–Cologne edition inserts still more concerning Lucius, beyond what has already been mentioned: “Who was the twenty-third persecution after blessed Peter, etc.” Concerning Caius, as so often above:

“At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Adrian with thirty-three others. After many punishments, all of them completed their martyrdom under the emperor Diocletian. After several years had passed, the body of blessed Adrian was transferred to Rome and buried on 8 September, a day which is held in greater honor in the Church. At Trier, of Saint Basinus, bishop and confessor. At the city of Prague in Bohemia, the translation of Saint Wenceslaus, duke and martyr. Also the translation of the holy martyrs Felix and Adauctus, namely, their heads, which are now kept at Cologne in the church of the holy Apostles.”

Greven: “With this Caius, twenty-seven others are said to have suffered. At Nicomedia, the passion—or, as others prefer, the elevation—of Adrian the martyr, Gregory, Julius, and thirty-three others, whose more solemn feast is held on 8 September, when blessed Adrian was buried at Rome. Of Basinus, archbishop of Trier and confessor. At Prague … At Cologne Agrippina, the translation of the heads of the holy Felix and Adauctus. In Ireland, of Saint Moggrudon, bishop and confessor,” hitherto unknown. “Also of Boson, of holy memory, priest and confessor, sixteenth prior of the Great Charterhouse after Bruno, a man of great holiness. When a man had been crushed and killed by the collapse of a building, Boson restored him to life by prayer. Herbs also, growing above his tomb, have given and continue to give many the desired remedy of health, with the Lord glorifying his saint.” In the index of the Praetermitted, it is said that no cult or veneration is shown him in the Charterhouse itself.

Molanus: “And twenty-seven others at Nicomedia; of Saint Adrian with twenty-three others. His body was transferred to Rome and buried on 8 September, where his passion is also recorded. At Trier, of Saint Basinus, bishop.” In other editions there is added: “On the fourth day, of the holy father Gerasimus, who lived in the Jordan.” It would be better written *Gerasimus*, for he belongs not to this day but to the following one. At the end: “On the same day, the elevation of the body of blessed Adrian the martyr.” This refers to the statement that his relics were transferred to Belgium and most recently placed, in the year 1110, at Mount Gerard, a town of Flanders, as will be examined more fully in its proper place.

[Col. 0815]

At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of blessed Lucius, pope and martyr. During the persecution of Valerian and Gallienus, he was banished into exile for the faith of Christ, and afterward, by divine providence, was permitted to return to his church; he completed his martyrdom by being beheaded. Also at Rome, on the Appian Way, of the nine hundred holy martyrs who are buried in the cemetery at Saint Cecilia. On the same day, of Saint Caius Palatinus, who was thrown into the sea.

III Non. Day 5. [Note: [Col. 0817C]]

Pratensis, Herinianus, Tournacensis, Rosweyd, Pulsa, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, Munerat, Belinus, Greven, and Molan agree again, as do the intermediate manuscripts Antwerp-Maximum, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, Albergen, the Danish manuscript, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition.

[Note: [Col. 0817C]]

All the manuscripts read *Focas*, and I have left it untouched. “Passus est,” instead of “est passus,” changes nothing in the text. “Even today to the peoples” is Usuard’s true reading. Many manuscripts simply have “today to the peoples”; Greven and Molan have “today also.” Belinus preferred to vary the phrase. His first edition reads: “Today it is made known by the gathering of the people.” The second: “Today the peoples make it known by their gathering.” It has already been said more than once that the great Lübeck edition abounds in typographical errors. I think one of them is that it reads *Sacae* instead of *Focae*. It is generally enough for me to indicate such slips in a general way.

[Note: [Col. 0817C]]

On this day Usuard proceeds almost as on the preceding one. He presents half of Ado’s eulogy of Phocas; of Eusebius, because the sentence is shorter, he makes his own, neglecting the word “also” and adding “passion.” The Little Roman Martyrology mentions both, and the Viennese martyrologist always draws from that source; he took the eulogy of Phocas from Gregory of Tours, as is clear in the Acts.

A certain Phocas, and specifically a Phocas of Antioch, is also mentioned in Hieronymian copies, where the name appears both as “the Virgin” and with the forms *sanctae Focae* and *Focatis*. I would not dare affirm with certainty whether the author of the Little Roman Martyrology received the name from there or from elsewhere, although I incline more toward the negative view for reasons given elsewhere. Whoever desires more should consult Florentinius.

I should nevertheless not omit what will have to be repeated among the Appendices: the very ancient Centulense manuscript gives Phocas the title of bishop, in this form: “At Antioch, the feast of Saint Phocas, bishop and martyr, under the judge Afficanus [Afric**a**nus].” But it is probable that Phocas of Sinope the bishop has here been confused with the Phocas of Antioch commemorated today. See Henschenius here and what we shall say on 14 July.

The Little Roman Martyrology assigns only eight companions to Eusebius Palatinus, perhaps through a scribal error. Its copy must necessarily have had Ado more correctly. There are also Eusebiuses today in Jerome, and also Palatini, placed among the holy martyrs in another class of African martyrs. Whether the designation Palatinus suits Eusebius on this day better than Caius on the preceding day is for others to judge.

Certainly Notker seems to have understood the meaning of the Little Roman Martyrology correctly when he distinguishes Palatinus from Eusebius and reads: “Of Eusebius and Palatinus and eight others.” In the Acts, meanwhile, another Palatinus, Peter, Rusticus, Herebus, Mare, and nine other unnamed men are counted as soldiers of the same company.

I refrain from investigating or bringing forward more on this subject, since Henschenius and Florentinius have discussed it with all the diligence that can be applied to such obscure and tangled combinations of names. It is enough for us to have presented Usuard’s simple text. I take it as established that he wrote as he found it in Ado.

Here may be added Wandalbert’s verses about Saint Phocas, alluding to the cures of venomous bites mentioned by Gregory of Tours in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 99, and referred to by Ado in his eulogy:

> Threefold is the martyr Phocas in the name of his merits:  
> by blood he conquered death,  
> by virtue the dragon.

[Note: [Col. 0819A]]

Antwerp Major abbreviates the text in the first announcement as follows: “At Antioch, the passion of Saint Phocas the martyr. Also on the same day, of Saint Eusebius Palatinus, etc.”

Rosweyd, fairly pure in the first announcement, expanded the second in this way: “On the same day, the passion of Saint Eusebius and Palatinus and eleven other martyrs.” He should have read, more correctly with Notker: “and eight other martyrs.” I suspect that the numeral letters had been transposed.

The Centulense manuscript, as we have already said, writes today: “At Antioch, of Saint Phocas, bishop and martyr, under the judge Afficanus.”

[Col. 0819B] Brussels, with the text interpolated from Ado in the first announcement, expands it further in second place:

“At Antioch, the passion of Saint Phocas, companion of blessed Eusebius, a worker of great miracles. After suffering many insults for the name of Christ, he is today declared to the people as having triumphed over the ancient serpent. Finally, if a serpent should coil around someone and pour venom into its bite, the person who has been bitten is immediately saved when, believing, he touches the door of the basilica of Phocas the martyr, for the power of the venom has been emptied. On the same day, of Saint Eusebius Palatinus and nine other martyrs beheaded for Christ. At Soissons, of Saint Drausius, bishop and confessor.”

One may consult the French dissertation inserted in the *Trévoux Journal* in June 1711, which concerns the cult of Saint Drausius or Draucinus.

Hagenoyen composed an almost entirely new eulogy of Phocas on his own initiative, in these words:

“At Antioch, the feast of blessed Phocas the martyr, who was hung up and torn with claws. After this he was thrown into a fire for three hours, where he praised God and came out unharmed by the fire. Then he was placed for three days in a heated furnace, where, while praying, he died; after three days his body was found unburned, intact, and filled with a very pleasant fragrance. Today he is proclaimed to the people for the praise of God as one who triumphed over the ancient enemy.”

He gives Eusebius without alteration.

Aquicinct adds at the end: “At Soissons, the deposition of Saint Drausius, bishop and confessor.”

Marchian, in a fragment, reads eleven instead of nine others, as above.

Matric.-Carthus.-Utrecht: “Of the illustrious martyr Phocas under Trajan.”

Altemps: “Of Saint Kyrianus,” instead of *Kerani*; in the Acts he is called *Kieranus*.

The Lübeck–Cologne edition adds to the text: “In Ireland, of Saint Keranus, bishop and confessor.”

Greven: “In Africa, of Adrian and Euvolus. Also of Victor, Pamphilus, Siris, Saturninus, and Peter.” They have been separated from their companions and, as is often the case with Greven, largely fashioned at will. “In Ireland, of Keranus, bishop and confessor. Of Helda, abbot,” more probably “Hilda, abbess,” who is referred to 25 August. “The conversion of Terentiana and her five sons.” Nothing else is read about her.

“Of Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea, formerly called the Tower of Strato. As Saint Jerome testifies in his book *On Illustrious Men*, he shone forth under the emperor Severus, distinguished by wisdom and holiness. The translation of Saint Landrada, virgin.” Whether that translation occurred on this or another day will be stated under 8 July, to which the Acts refer it.

Molanus: “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Drausius, bishop and confessor.” In smaller type is added: “Of Soissons.” Then: “Of Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea, etc.,” from Greven. In other editions he reads: “At Soissons, of Saint Drausius, bishop and confessor.” Again in smaller type: “At Caesarea in Palestine, of Saint Adrian the martyr.
