On the festival day when the feast of the Caesareans’ Fortune is customarily celebrated—for so it was believed—he was first thrown to a lion to be torn apart and was then slaughtered with a sword.”

[Col. 0817]

At Antioch, the feast of blessed Phocas the martyr, who, after suffering many insults for the name of the Redeemer, is proclaimed even today to the people as having triumphed over that ancient serpent. On the same day, the passion of Saint Eusebius Palatinus and nine other martyrs.

The day before the Nones. Day 6. [Note: [Col. 0819C]]

Pratensis, Herinianus, Tournacensis, Rosweyd, Pulsa, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, Munerat, Belinus, Greven, Molan, and the intermediate manuscripts Antwerp-Maximum, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, Albergen, the Danish manuscript, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition agree again.

[Note: [Col. 0819D]]

Munerat’s reading is an error: “Victor, Vitalis, Victorinus.” Likewise, in the Pulsa manuscript: *triennio* instead of *per triennium*; *Claudio* instead of *Claudiano*; and *Balsa* instead of *Bassa*. More shamefully, the Danish manuscript has “Clarus the deacon.” Belinus alone writes “with his wife.” Some read “they completed the course of his life”; others, “they completed his course of life.” The Danish manuscript omits *suae*. In Greven, *citate* is a printer’s error. The same may perhaps be said of *Tolleto* in Belinus: and likewise of *habebatur* for *habetur* in the same Greven, who may have found it written that way in Rosweyd’s manuscript, or rather in one similar to it.

[Note: [Col. 0819D]]

Florentinius says that all the published martyrologies assign Victor and Victorinus of Nicomedia to this day. He might at least have excepted Rabanus. As I have often noted, Usuard and Notker copy Ado in many places here as elsewhere, but they frequently add certain saints to him. Ado follows the Little Roman Martyrology closely, where he found: “At Nicomedia, of Victor and Victorinus, who completed the course of their life in prison.” Hence it is not surprising that Victor and Victorinus appear in all these sources, as they do in many more recent ones.

But how were Claudianus and Bassa added to them? When Henschenius prefaced the genuine Bede to volume II of March, he suspected that the eulogy found in Ado might have been present in some manuscript written by Bede himself. I am compelled to disagree. Since Rabanus, who habitually plundered Bede carefully, did not place any of these names today, it follows that whatever is recorded in our text about the four Nicomedian martyrs must be attributed to Ado alone. Certainly the author of the Little Roman Martyrology did not find them there; nor would he have omitted them if he had had the other source before his eyes.

Wandalbert praises only the first two when he writes:

> Victorinus rejoices on the day before, and Victor,  
> shut away in prison,  
> who with lofty flight  
> penetrated the stars.

Whether the Viennese received the bare names of the two later martyrs from some Hieronymian source, I do not clearly see, unless he had a copy similar to the Antwerp manuscript, which alone mentions Claudianus and Bassa after Victor and Victorinus.

Usuard alone added Julianus, unknown to the earlier sources. His proper day seems to be not this day but 8 March, as Papebrochius explains more fully there in the preliminary commentary, suggesting that the day of his death, originally recorded as the day after the Nones, may have been changed into the day before the Nones. It is sufficiently plausible that Usuard brought knowledge of this saint from Spain into Gaul together with many others. Certainly the agreement of the manuscripts does not permit doubt that he marked him on this day.

[Note: [Col. 0821A]]

Antwerp Major seems to have altered the text arbitrarily. It reads:

“At Nicomedia, the feast of the holy martyrs Victor and Victorinus, in the time of the emperor Claudius. At the city of Toledo, the deposition of Saint Julian, bishop, who among the inhabitants of that place is held in the highest renown because of the excellence of his holiness.”

Centulense: “At Nicomedia, of the holy martyrs Victor and Victorinus.” Nothing further.

Brussels, somewhat interpolated in the first announcement, has in second place:

“At the city of Toledo, the deposition of Saint Julian, bishop, who among the inhabitants of that place is venerated because of the excellence of his holiness.”

Hagenoyen is less pure than Brussels in the case of the Nicomedian martyrs. Concerning Julian he follows the text but adds:

“This Julian some people are accustomed to invoke in order to obtain good lodging for the night.”

It is strange if the author of this Martyrology did not confuse the Julians. Certainly that invocation, “in order to obtain good lodging for the night,” would fit better and more correctly the Julian called *Zenodochus*, who is commemorated on 9 January.

It continues: “In Seconia, of Saint Fridolin, or Frydolin, confessor.” Unless I am very much mistaken, he intended Fridolin, the abbot of Seckingen in Germany, concerning whom see the Acts for this day.

Aquicinct writes Claudio instead of Claudiano, and Vigiliano instead of Juliano.

Altemps: “In Britain, the deposition of Saint Balter [the Acts read *Balther*], priest and confessor. At the monastery of Burgo, of the holy women Kyneburga, Kyneswitha, and Tibla.” The Acts have *Tibba* or *Tilba*.

The church of Rheims, of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “At the city of Toledo, the deposition of the most blessed Julian, bishop and confessor.”

Abdinghof: “At Trier, of Saint Quiriacus, priest.”

The Lübeck–Cologne edition, after the text, adds: “At Trier, of Saint Quiriacus, priest and confessor. On the same day, of Saint Cyril, priest and confessor, of the Carmelite Order. On the same day, of blessed Fridolin, abbot and confessor. Also of Saint Baldred, confessor.” He is the same as Balther, mentioned above.

Greven: “At Nicopolis, of Papias, Alexander, and Jocundus. At Nicomedia, of Saturninus, Cassius, Victor, and two others, Papias and Nicephorus.” This is the usual confusion in Greven, who takes martyrs from Hieronymian copies.

“At Terdona, the passion of Saint Marcian, bishop and martyr, under the emperor Hadrian. When he had been brought out of prison and had remained unharmed after glowing iron plates had been placed upon his head, he completed his martyrdom by beheading. Also of Diodorus, Claudianus, Carisius, and Margolus.” This is another Hieronymian fragment, not arranged very accurately.

“Of Victor, martyr, *Mosovensis*.” He intended *Mosomensis*, in Belgic Gaul; see the Praetermitted and the Acts for 9 February.

“In Scotland, of Baldred, bishop and confessor.” Whether he should correctly be called a bishop is discussed in the Acts.

“At Metz, of Saint Chrodegang, bishop and confessor. On Mount Carmel, of blessed Cyril, priest and confessor, to whom God, as to a faithful friend, revealed many things secretly concerning the future condition of the world. At Trier, of Saint Quiriacus, priest and confessor. On the same day, of Fridolin, abbot and confessor. Of Keneburga, virgin. Of Victoria, a married woman.” I find nothing about her.

“At Ghent, of Colette, of holy memory, a nun and the first reformer of the Poor Clares.”

[Col. 0822B] Molanus took his material from Greven. He treats of Cyril, Quiriacus, Chrodegang, Fridolin, and Colette. There is one difference concerning Cyril: he writes:

“On Mount Carmel, of blessed Cyril, priest, a most devoted hermit of Carmel. To whom God, etc.”

In other editions he repeats the same material concerning Cyril and Quiriacus. Then:

“At Seckingen, the deposition of Fridolin, abbot and confessor. On the sixth day, of forty-two martyrs, recently discovered at Ammorium.””

Then, in smaller type:

“At Ghent, the death of blessed Colette of Corbie, in the year 1447, who founded the Colettine Poor Clares. At Metz, of Saint Chrodegang, archbishop and confessor.”

It will not be out of place to append here what Rosweyd left written among the manuscript observations cited above, under this day, 6 March. The present Roman text is prefixed:

“In Cyprus, of Saint Conon the martyr, who under the emperor Decius was ordered to run before a chariot with nails driven through his feet. Falling upon his knees, he gave up his spirit in prayer.”

Baronius’s note follows:

“Conon: the Greeks also treat of him in the Menologion on this day. They say that he was from Nazareth and was ennobled by the distinguished contests he undertook for Christ, while they describe his martyrdom in brief summary.”

Rosweyd says that three things must be noted here.

1. How can Baronius place this Conon on 6 March and say that the Menologion also treats of him on this day, when the Menologion has him on 8 March?

2. The days in the Menologion seem to be confused, since the Menaea place Conon on 5 March; the Acts likewise placed him there.

3. How can Baronius place him in Cyprus when the Menaea say that he suffered at Mandae, a city of Pamphylia?

But Baronius was misled by a corrupt reading of the Menologion on 7 March, which reads:

“Saint Conon, τοῦ κυπρίου [of Cyprus], from Nazareth of Galilee. Under the emperor Decius, because of his confession of the Christian faith, he was ordered to run before a chariot with iron nails driven through his feet. Falling upon his knees and praying, he gave up his spirit to Christ the Lord.”

It should instead read *τοῦ κυπροῦ*, that is, “the gardener.” Therefore the text of the Roman Martyrology seems to require this correction:

“At Mandae, a city of Pamphylia, of Saint Conon the gardener, martyr.”

[Col. 0819]

At Nicomedia, the feast of the holy Victor and Victorinus, who for three years, together with Claudianus and his wife Bassa, were afflicted by many tortures and confined in prison, where they completed the course of their life. At the city of Toledo, the deposition of Julian, bishop, who among the inhabitants of that place is held in the highest renown.

The Nones. Day 7. [Note: [Col. 0821]]

The simplicity of the text is found in Pratensis, Herinianus, Tournacensis, Antwerp Major, Rosweyd, Pulsa, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, Greven, and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0823A]]

There are no notes in the first three manuscripts. Antwerp Major writes “passion” instead of “feast.” Pulsa incorrectly reads *Turbitanorum*, as do the Hieronymian copies. In the first edition Greven and Molan read *Tiburbitanorum*, which Greven did not correct more successfully in later editions to *Thuburbitanorum*. Both editions of Greven incorrectly give *Mauricania* instead of *Mauritania*. Likewise, they have “of the holy martyrs” instead of “of the holy women,” as do Pulsa, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, and Molan. Pulsa transposed the companions and reads: “and with them Saturninus, Revocatus, and Secundolus.” It also has “thus they were handed over” instead of “they were handed over.” Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck read “the remaining ones,” instead of “all the remaining ones.”

[Note: [Col. 0823A]]

The unanimous judgment of all the ancient martyrologists is that the most glorious and celebrated contest of Perpetua and Felicity throughout the whole Church was completed on this day, whatever may also be listed on the preceding day in Hieronymian copies. Florentinius does not sufficiently explain the reason for this repeated entry.

How widely the fame of these truly Christian heroines has spread from every age is shown by the ancient Bucherian Calendar, the oldest of all. Among the African martyrs it mentions only them and Cyprian: Cyprian on his own feast, 14 September, and these women on this day, the Nones of March—Perpetua and Felicity of Africa.

I pass over the Sacramentaries and similar works. The Acts themselves are an incomparable and most precious monument of ecclesiastical antiquity; even Catholics are compelled to acknowledge this. Let anyone read them who delights in spectacles of ancestral courage and catholic piety.

The long-desired and long-sought hidden treasure was first successfully brought out of the library of Monte Cassino by the distinguished Lucas Holstenius. Possinus published it from there, and our predecessors made it known on this day. Other most learned men then edited it in renewed editions, including at Oxford, and supplied it with observations. Ruinart collected the more curious notes and added his own among the *Sincere and Genuine Acts*, beginning at page 81. Tillemont constructed the sequence of her life in volume III, beginning at page 136.

The reader should consult what has been discussed with the greatest care by these authors, while we explain the judgments of our martyrologists, whether true or false.

The martyrologists do not follow one uniform method in assigning the companions. These companions are placed variously and confusedly in Hieronymian copies and were omitted by Bede and consequently by Rabanus. The Little Roman Martyrology says no more, expressing only the names of Perpetua and Felicity—not “at Carthage,” as Bede more correctly reads, but “in Mauritania, at the city of the Tuburbitans.”

Ado follows the traces of the Little Roman Martyrology, but adds three companions from the Acts, which Bede had also seen; Usuard and Notker do not omit them. Satyrus, however, is everywhere lost, although according to the Acts cited above he would seem to deserve the first place among the men. Hence it is evident that Ado alone stood before Usuard, who transcribed the first part of Ado’s eulogy almost word for word; Notker, as usual, rendered the whole.

You will find the question of whether the place of martyrdom was Carthage or Thuburbo discussed in our preliminary commentary, in Florentinius, and more recently in Ruinart’s preliminary admonition and Tillemont’s notes.

Whether the error belongs to the printer or to Florentinius himself, when he says that *Turbitanorum* in Jerome should be restored from Augustine as *Tuburbinatorum*, is made doubtful by the fact that he immediately adds that the illustrious martyrs Perpetua and Felicity are called *TUBURBITANAE*. It is therefore clear that *Tuburbitanorum* is better—or at least less badly—written in the text, although it is more plausible that Augustine and others did not understand “the Tuburbitan martyrs” to mean these women, but rather Maxima and her companions, who are treated on 30 July.

Together with the Little Roman Martyrology and Bede, Wandalbert sings a victory song only for the two women:

> On the Nones, Felicity and Perpetua shine,  
> who dedicated their chaste life to Christ  
> by a happy death.

[Note: [Col. 0823C]]

The Danish manuscript appends to the text:

“At the province of Valeria, the feast of Saint Equitius, abbot, whom blessed Gregory mentions in the first book of the *Dialogues*.”

Antwerp-Maximum, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition have the same entry. They further add: “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Thomas, confessor and doctor.” Albergen gives it in this form: “On the same day, of Saint Thomas of Aquino, of the Order of Preachers, an outstanding doctor, who greatly benefited the Christian religion by his writings and teachings.”

The Centulense manuscript reads: “In Africa, at the city of Tiburba, the passion of the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicity, and with them Revocatus, Satyrus, and Secundolus.”

Brussels, after “under the emperor,” adds “on the day of his birthday,” words taken from Ado. Then: “In the province of Valencia [for Valeria], of Equitius. Also the deposition of blessed Thomas of Aquino, a holy doctor of the Order of Preachers.”

Hagenoyen invents many things today concerning the Tuburbitan martyrs and blessed Equitius, which do not deserve to be reported. As a specimen of its accuracy, consider the final announcement: “On the same day, of Saint Thomas, an outstanding doctor and archbishop of Canterbury, of the Order of Preachers.” It also calls Perpetua and Felicity virgins, and so forth.

Matric.-Carthus.-Utrecht places Thomas of Aquino first. It then composed an eulogy of Perpetua and Felicity, which need not be copied here.

STROZZ. and MEDIC., and already in the first place: “The feast of Saint Thomas of Aquino, confessor of the Order of Preachers; his burial at the monastery of Fossanova, [Col. 0824C] of the Cistercian Order, in Campania. He died in the year of the Lord 1274, at the beginning of the fiftieth year of his life.” I have no means of determining how that redundancy concerning his burial arose, unless perhaps one text was composed from various texts; certainly it is clear that his translation is not being discussed here. More will follow shortly.

MUNERAT. To the pure text he adds: “On the same day, the burial of blessed Thomas, confessor of the Order of Preachers, an eminent doctor.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition adds, as does the Brussels manuscript, “on the day of his death”: “In the province of Valeria, the commemoration of Saint Equitius the abbot, whom blessed Gregory mentions in the first book of the *Dialogues*. On the same day, in Campania, at the monastery of Fossanova, the commemoration of Saint Thomas of Aquino, of the Order of Preachers, an outstanding doctor [Col. 0824D] of the Church, who greatly benefited the Christian religion by his teachings and writings. It is also related of this same doctor that he never violated baptismal innocence, that he preserved virginity of mind and body until the end of his life, and that he never knowingly committed a mortal sin. In the territory of Mons, in the imperial town called Werda above the bank of the Rhine, the commemoration of Saint Willeycus, confessor and priest of Saint Swicbert the bishop.” He was treated above, on 2 March.

The first edition of BELIN: “On the same day, Saint Thomas of Aquino, confessor”; the second edition: “doctor and confessor, of the Order of Preachers.”

GREV. “Likewise, Saints Silvanus, Rogatus, and Ero. At Antioch, Eocus [or Leocus], Saturus, Saturninus, and others.” The eulogy of Saint Thomas is almost the same as the one we reported, with the addition of the year of his death, as was also stated above [Col. 0825A]. Enough has been said about Willeycus or Willericus. “In the province of Valeria, Saint Equitius the abbot, who, as blessed Gregory relates in the first book of the *Dialogues*, was regarded by everyone there as admirable on account of the merit of his life. He was very plain in his clothing, but such was the fervor that inflamed him to gather souls for God that he governed monasteries in such a way that he went about everywhere through churches, fortresses, villages, and even the homes of individual believers, stirring the hearts of his hearers to love their heavenly homeland.”

MOLAN. From Ado he adds the following to the text: “on the day of his death. While they were still being held in prison and Felicitas was giving birth, through the prayers of all their holy fellow soldiers it was obtained that she should give birth in the eighth month. In the province of Valeria,” as above in the Danish manuscript, etc. “On the same day, Saint Thomas Aquinas, doctor and confessor, in the city of Terracina in Campania, at the monastery of Fossanova. He descended from the noble family of the counts of Aquino and, against his father’s wishes, entered the Order of Preachers; applying himself diligently to literary studies, he was raised to the chair of sacred theology, illuminated the whole world with the splendor of his knowledge, and in the year 1274, at the beginning of his fiftieth year, ended his life.” The words “in the city of Terracina in Campania” may be deleted. In smaller type: “At Segenberg, Saint Volker the martyr. Likewise, Saint Redempta the virgin, concerning whom blessed Gregory speaks in a homily.” This is rightly omitted in the other editions. See the index of passages omitted. In these, however, the following is added: “On the seventh day, the most holy martyr bishops in Cherson: Basileus, Ephraem, Chariton, Eugenius, and the rest.” Then, in smaller type: “At Caesarea in Palestine, the commemoration of Saint Eubulus, who, preferring a glorious death for piety to a transitory life, was finally killed by the sword after being torn by wild beasts; and he sealed all the contests of the martyrs with his own blood. At Segenberg, Saint Volker the martyr.”

[Col. 0821]

In the city of the Tuburbitani in Mauretania, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicitas, and with them Revocatus, Saturninus, and Secundulus; the last of these died in prison, while all the others were thrown to the wild beasts under the emperor Severus.

## Eighth day before the Ides. Day 8

[Note: [Col. 0825B]

Pratensis, Herinien­sis, Tornacensis, Antwerp, Max.–Lübeck, Muneratus, Belinus, Grevenus, and Molanus agree. To these may be added Antwerp–Maximus, Utrecht, Leiden, Alberg, the Danish manuscript, the Utrecht–Belgian edition, and Hagenoyen for the most part.]

[Note: [Col. 0825B]

Only Tornacensis places the notice at the city of Antinoüs; Grevenus has Antynoum. The same Tornacensis has *Apollinii* instead of *Apollonii*. Belinus reads “deacons,” where probably neither was a deacon. The transposition by Grevenus and Molanus of “to sacrifice to idols” into “to idols to sacrifice” is not noteworthy. The fact that some write *Ydolis* has been discussed elsewhere. Antwerp–Maximus–Lübeck, Belinus, Grevenus, Molanus, and other manuscripts write *Adriani* instead of *Arriani*; why they prefer the *Acts of Arianus*, I do not know. Likewise, Herinien­sis has *Thetici*, and Grevenus *Teotici*, the latter better in the [Col. 0826B] text. Muneratus omitted *trium*. The middle-grade manuscripts add *piscis*—“fish”—after *delphini*. Antwerp writes *Kartagini*; Muneratus, *Cartagine*; Belinus, Grevenus, and Molanus, *Carthagini*; I prefer the ancient spelling preserved by the older witnesses. Muneratus and Belinus reverse the sense, reading “the deacon and blessed Cyprian.” The former is less mistaken in *in passionis illius*; the latter, in *in passionis ejus*. Herinien­sis, strangely enough, writes *clari et promeruerunt*, as though two persons were under discussion.]

[Note: [Col. 0825C]

The memory of Philemon, Apollonius, and the other martyr Antinoites recorded here in first and second place was unknown to, or passed over by, all the more ancient martyrologists; it is owed solely to Usuard, who incorrectly placed Philemon before Apollonius and, from their passion, did not determine the place, day, and other circumstances of their martyrdom with sufficient accuracy. Papebrochius explains this more precisely on this day, illustrating the Acts from various Latin manuscripts collated with the Greek text—Acts which learned modern writers now commonly attack and reject as fabricated and interpolated by Metaphrastes. Whether they are the work of Metaphrastes is another question. In any event, those more scrupulous scholars think so, even more strongly than Papebrochius himself; yet he would not now so readily prove what, at the beginning of his studies, before he was so well acquainted with these matters, he accepted. Whatever the truth may be, anyone who wishes to compare these accounts with Rufinus’s narrative in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter not 29 but 19, p. 476, excerpted by Ruinart and published among the *Selecta*, p. 539, will clearly see that they are by no means genuine. I do not know why our predecessors neglected to cite that account. Meanwhile, it cannot be denied that the passion illustrated by Papebrochius is older than Metaphrastes, since Usuard, who excerpted his eulogy from it, must certainly have seen it. He alone among all the ancient martyrologists—as we began to say in the observations on Saint Asclas, 23 January, on which day we also cited Tillemont on Arrianus—[Col. 0826C] did so. Tillemont’s two relevant articles, 4 and 5, may be read in volume V, beginning at p. 360, where the present martyrs are discussed also from Rufinus and Palladius, with the Usuardine Acts rejected. The praised Papebrochius had already observed, before Tillemont, that these Acts had not correctly assigned this 8 March to the saints’ contest, indeed had wrongly joined them all together; see the rest in Papebrochius. Nothing doubtful can arise concerning the simplicity of our genuinely Usuardine text amid such remarkable agreement among almost all the manuscripts.

Concerning Pontius, the small Roman Martyrology reads as follows: “At Carthage, Saint Pontianus, deacon of blessed Cyprian, who, always glorifying the Lord in his sufferings, earned the crown of life.” Ado enlarged this only slightly; the additions were copied by Notker. Our text, whether by accident or deliberately I do not know, omitted the words “always glorifying the Lord in his sufferings.” Nothing prevented their being left untouched, unless perhaps he thought they should be understood of a true martyrdom, which Pontius is by no means known to have endured. Here, by praising Cyprian, he left his own memory to posterity, for Henschenius derived his commentary from Pontius’s booklet on the life of the most glorious martyr Cyprian, splendidly vindicating Pontius against the excessively arrogant attacks of Rigaltius, as the reader will be able to see there; the matter will be proved more fully on 14 September. For us it is enough that Usuard’s text is genuine here also.]

[Note: [Col. 0827A]

ANTWERP–MAJOR. In the first edition the whole eulogy is missing; in the second the text is almost pure; in the third it is almost Adonian: “At Carthage, Saint Pontianus, deacon and disciple of blessed Cyprian the bishop, who, enduring exile with him until the day of his passion, left behind an excellent volume on his life and passion, and, always glorifying the Lord in his sufferings, earned the crown of life.”

ROSWEYD, pure throughout the text, adds at the end: “At Nicomedia, Quintillus, bishop and martyr. Likewise, in Africa, Cyril, bishop and martyr.” Both notices were taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, or from Rabanus or Notker. The verses of the contemporary Wandalbert have no particular bearing on the Usuardine text.

PULSANEN. The section on Arrianus and his companions is missing.

LOUVAIN. It could be regarded as purer than the middle-grade manuscripts were it not that it often abridges Usuardine eulogies. Here it omitted everything that Usuard reported in praise of Philemon and Apollonius.

CENTULEN. It has already often departed from Usuard; today it has only: “At Nicomedia, the holy martyrs Quintulus the bishop and Capitulinus.” This comes from some Hieronymian copy, in which *Quintili*, *Quintilli*, or *Quintilis* is commonly read instead of *Quintuli*.

BRUSSELS, after a text considerably interpolated, adds: “Likewise, Rogatus and Catillus, bishops.” See the Acts concerning Cyril the bishop, Rogatus, and others.

AQUICINCT. “And Saints Quintolus and Capitulinus.”

VICTORINUS reads “four” instead of “three.”

MARCHIAN. Its fragment has *Adriani* instead of *Arriani*, as do several manuscripts above.

MATRIC.–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT begins: “Cyprian the bishop and Pontius the deacon, martyrs; Asclas the martyr, Apollonius, Philemon, Arrianus, and his companions.” Asclas was discussed on 23 January.

ALTEMPS: “On the same day, Saint Felix of the East Angles, who was their preacher and bishop; after being transferred from there, he is now honored with great glory [Col. 0828A] in the monastery of Fameseye [Ramesey], where he also lies buried.” See this matter discussed more carefully in the preceding commentary on his Acts. “In Ireland, Saint Seinav, confessor and abbot [rather, bishop].” The Acts call him Senanus.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. To an almost pure text it adds: “On the same day, Saint Ducnatus [Duthacus], bishop and confessor. Likewise, Saint Hunfridus, bishop and confessor.”

GREV. “At Nicomedia, blessed Quintillus, bishop and martyr. Likewise, at Birona, Herenia, Felicitas, and Urbanus. In Africa, Cyril, bishop and martyr. Likewise, Silvanus, Quirillus, and Capitulinus the martyr.” Here you see various and confused Hieronymian martyrs. “Felix, bishop and confessor of the East Angles, who came from Burgundy and announced Christ to the nation of the East Angles. Receiving the episcopal see in the city of Dommoc, he presided for seventeen years in great holiness and then rested in peace. In Scotland, Saint Duchatus, bishop and confessor. In Ireland, Cenani, Conallus, and Crovani, bishops and confessors.” Concerning Conallus and Cronanus, not Crovani, see the index of passages omitted. “On the same day, Hunfridus, bishop and confessor. Cleopatronia, daughter of Dacianus.” On the form of the name *Cleopatronia*, see Castellanus, notes for January, p. 200.

MOLAN, in small type, copied from Grevenus the notice concerning Felix. Then: “Likewise, Hunfridus, bishop and confessor, whose body, after the destruction of the Morini by Charles V, was translated to Ypres.” In the other editions it reads: “In the district of Thérouanne, Saint Hunfridus, bishop of that city and abbot of Sithiu, whose body, after the Morini had been destroyed, was translated to Ypres. In England, Saint Felix, bishop and confessor, who came from Burgundy and announced Christ to the nation of the East Angles. On the eighth day, Saint Theophylactus, bishop of Nicomedia, father and confessor.”]

[Col. 0825]

In the city of Antinoüs, the commemoration of Saints Philemon and Apollonius the deacon, who, having been arrested and brought before the judge, steadfastly refused to sacrifice to idols. Their heels were pierced, and they were dragged horribly through the city; finally they were struck down with the sword and completed their martyrdom. On the same day, at the aforesaid city, the passion of Arrianus, Theoticus, and three others; the judge killed them by drowning them in the sea, but through the service of a dolphin their bodies were restored to the shore. At Carthage, Saint Pontius, deacon of blessed Cyprian the bishop, who, enduring exile with him until the day of his passion, left behind an excellent volume on his life and passion; and, renowned for his sufferings, earned the crown of life.

## Seventh day before the Ides. Day 9

[Note: [Col. 0827]

On this day I find only Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Rosweyd, Grevenus, and Molanus to be pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0827C]

There is almost nothing to note. I wrote *Nisenam* from Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Grevenus, and other manuscripts, simply to preserve the ancient Usuardine reading, which also seems to be present in our Pratensian copy. Molanus incorrectly printed *Nicenam* in the first edition, but corrected it in later editions by reading *Nyssenam*, which is certainly the correct form. Likewise, the others, together with Pratensis and Molanus, have *Caesariensis* in the text, as has now generally prevailed among scholars. Three others, disregarding diphthongs as they usually do, have *Cesariensis*. It should be written *Paciani*, but in the manuscripts cited for the text, and elsewhere commonly, it appears as in the text; Rosweyd, however, incorrectly reads *Potiani*.]

[Note: [Col. 0827C]

I have no doubt that the pure and genuine text of Usuard is represented here. This is demonstrated not only by the authority of the highly approved manuscripts listed above, but also almost daily by the fact that Ado evidently followed the small Roman Martyrology, adding a few things that our author copied almost word for word, as he often does. These are the words of the small Roman Martyrology concerning Gregory: “In the city of Nyssa, Saint Gregory the bishop, brother of Basil.” Papebrochius collected much about him accurately in his historical commentary, but Tillemont collected far more after others, in volume IX, from p. 561 to 616, in twenty articles. [Col. 0827D] The Hieronymian copies, Bede, his copyist Rabanus, and Wandalbert deal on this day with the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste; the Roman Martyrology did so before the time of Pope Innocent X, under whom they were transferred to the following day, yielding to the double office of Saint Frances of Rome. Nevertheless, their notice and eulogy are placed on this day, just as that of Saint Hilary is on 13 and 14 January, Saint Henry on 14 and 15 July, and Saint Didacus on 12 and 13 November—not, I think, for any other reason than the one just assigned, namely, the precedence of a greater feast. What moved Rabanus to place these same Forty Martyrs again on the 11th, and once more on 9 September, I certainly do not understand, unless he doubted the true day of their death, or through carelessness thought that different classes of martyrs were involved. [Col. 0828D] In later editions Molanus wrongly inserted them into today’s text, although, according to the small Roman Martyrology and Ado, whom Usuard follows, they should be reported on 11 March, as he did in the first edition—a first edition far preferable to the others, at least insofar as concerns recovering the simplicity of Usuard’s text, which is our sole object. For if the true day of martyrdom is being considered, Jerome’s and Bede’s placement may perhaps deserve preference, since it is confirmed by the Acts themselves. Hence it may reasonably be suspected that they were inserted from there into some of the more recent Usuardine manuscripts. It is enough for us to have presented the ancient and genuine reading of our martyrologist. [Col. 0830A] The small Roman Martyrology had only “At Barcelona, Pacianus the bishop”; the rest is Adonian, and was also almost wholly transcribed by Notker. Henschenius briefly reported what he had found in Jerome and other ecclesiastical writers; Tillemont made some passages clearer in volume VIII, beginning at p. 537.]

[Note: [Col. 0829A]

PULSANEN transferred the material, changing the ninth into the eleventh. For what we have reported today as genuinely Usuardine he himself placed on the eleventh, for reasons I do not know; but on this day he has the Sebastean martyrs, and only them, in pure Usuardine wording.

ANTWERP–MAJOR is not entirely pure in the text, to which it adds: “At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, the commemoration of the forty holy soldiers, in the time of King Licinius, under the governor Agricolaus. The names of these martyrs are: Domicianus, Eunoicus, Sisinnius, [Col. 0829B] Eradius, Alexander, John, Claudius, with their companions. They all completed their martyrdom by having their legs broken. The bodies of the saints were therefore burned and thrown into a river, but by divine providence their relics were found intact and buried with due honor.” This does not sound like Usuard; the following manuscripts reproduce the complete text.

ANTWERP and MAXIMUS–LÜBECK, MUNERATUS, BELINUS, ANTWERP–MAXIMUS, UTRECHT, LEIDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERG, the DANISH manuscript, and the UTRECHT–BELGIAN EDITION mention the Sebastean martyrs on this day, some at the beginning and others at the end. We shall give them, with Usuard, on the eleventh. In the last manuscript Gregory of Nyssa is missing.

CENTULEN: “The passion of the forty soldiers in the time of King Licinius, under the governor Agricolaus. In Africa, Saints Felix and Rogatus.” It has not a word of the whole text.

BRUSSELS, after somewhat interpolating the eulogy of the Sebastean martyrs, adds an almost pure version of today’s text.

[Col. 0829C] HAGENOYEN seems to have made eighty martyrs by doubling the groups of forty: he announces one group today in Cappadocia and another on the eleventh “at Sebaste in Armenia,” assigning different eulogies to them. Where he derived today’s account I do not know; certainly it does not deserve to be reported. In the rest of the text he departs little from purity.

AQUICINCT writes *Datiani* instead of *Patiani*. At the end it adds: “In Lesser Armenia, the forty holy soldiers. Likewise, Saints Felix, Philip, and Rogatus.”

REG. SUEC., numbered 130: “At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, the commemoration of the forty holy soldiers who suffered under the governor Agricolaus, in the time of King Licinius.”

[Col. 0830A] UGHELLIAN also deals with the forty soldiers.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION: “At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, the commemoration of the forty holy soldiers who, in the time of King Licinius, under the governor Agricolaus, after very frequent bonds and imprisonments, and after their faces had been struck with stones, were sent into a pool, where their bodies, stiffened by the ice, were broken apart during the night. When morning came, the satellites of the most impious tyrant found the jailer, counted among the martyrs, after one faint-hearted man had fallen away. They dragged them all to the shore, broke their legs with clubs, and thus [Col. 0830B] finally completed their martyrdom by having their legs broken. Their names are: Domicianus, Eunoycus, Sisinnius, Eraclius, Alexander, Joannes, Claudius, Athanasius, Valensis, Helianus, Melliton, Hecclicius, Achacius, Jubanus, Helyus, Theodolus, Cyrillus, Valerius, Flavius, Severianus, Quirion, Theudeon, Sacerdon, Priscus, Euticius, Smaragdus, Philoctimon, Actius, Michallius, Lysimachus, Dompnus, Theophilus, Euthychius, Xanctius, Aggius, Leoncius, Isicius, Gagius, Gorgonius, and Candidus. Quirion and Candidus were the most eminent among them.” See all this enumerated more carefully by Ado on 11 March, as we said above. The text follows, and at the end it adds: “At Paris, the commemoration of Saint Draconius the abbot.” In the passages omitted, he is said to be the same as Saint Droctoveus the abbot, whom Usuard mentions on the following day.

GREV. “On the same day, Saints Sicius, Philip, Marianus, Concessus, Sebastianus, Julianus, and Silvanus. [Col. 0830C] The names are carelessly confused from Hieronymian copies.” At Paris, Draconius the abbot. Likewise, according to some, the forty martyrs who are placed on the fifth day before the Ides.

MOLAN: “At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, the commemoration of the forty holy soldiers who, in the time of King Licinius, after very frequent bonds and imprisonments and after their faces had been struck with stones, were sent into a pool, where their bodies, stiffened by the ice, were broken apart during the night, and thus, when morning came, they finally completed their martyrdom by having their legs broken. Quirion and Candidus were the most eminent among them.” This is Usuard’s text, except for the details about the ice, which are inserted from Ado.]

[Col. 0827]

At the city of Nyssa, the commemoration of Saint Gregory the bishop, brother of blessed Basil of Caesarea, most illustrious both in life and in eloquence. At the city of Barcelona, Saint Pacianus the bishop, who, in the time of the emperor Theodosius, reached the end of his life in an excellent old age.

## Sixth day before the Ides. Day 10

[Note: [Col. 0829]

Today I find only Heriniensis and Tornacensis to be pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0831A]

*Apamia*, as Heriniensis has it, is closer to the true reading than *Appamia*, as the other has it. Both write *Gaii*. Tornacensis incorrectly has *Appollinaris*. The first reads *Hierapolitanus*, the second *Jherapolitanus*, the more correct form in the text. These manuscripts and many others commonly have *Catafrigas*; I thought the defective spelling could be retained. Heriniensis has *Droctovei*, Tornacensis *Drochtovei*. Why should anyone not prefer the more common form, as in the text? Let each prefer what he wishes; I have no objection.

But what are we to make of Attalus, or Attala, the abbot and disciple of Saint Columbanus? He is reported here in approximately these terms by the Pratensian manuscript, but it is not sufficiently certain whether this was written by the first hand or added later by another. For my part, I do not think that manuscript, however ancient, preserves the original purity of Usuard here. Certainly Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Antwerp–Major, Antwerp and Maximus–Lübeck, and Muneratus are silent about him. He is likewise absent on this day from the manuscripts which we commonly call middle-grade, from the Brussels manuscript, and from many others. It is not plausible that those manuscripts would have excluded Attalus [Col. 0831B] if there had been any memory of him in the copies from which they were first transcribed [Col. 0832A]. That he was added to the text seems also to be demonstrated by the fact that Grevenus and Molanus present the matter differently, namely: “At the monastery of Luxeuil, Saint Athalus [Attala], abbot.” For if the notice concerning Attala had been taken from the Pratensian manuscript, which many regard as an autograph, it would certainly have been expressed in the same terms. I therefore venture to suspect that the words of the Pratensian manuscript are more recent, added to Usuard’s text either by the first scribe himself or by someone else; understanding, as Notker correctly did, that Attalus should be assigned to the Italian monastery of Bobbio, he prudently omitted the location, or place of burial. I do not wish to quarrel over the matter. If you produce stronger arguments for restoring Attalus to the text, I shall readily agree, since I seek the truth alone. Among the Hieronymian manuscripts only the very old Antwerp, or Echternach, manuscript is found to mention Attala; if you wish to hold that he was drawn from there and entered into certain Usuardine manuscripts, I shall not strongly resist the proposal.]

[Note: [Col. 0831B]

Alexander and Caius—or rather Caius and Alexander, since the names have again been transposed—are first recorded by the small Roman Martyrology in these words: “At Apamia, Alexander and Caius of Eumenia.” From there they were taken by Ado, and from him by our author and Notker, almost with the same eulogy; they also appear in the additions to Bede, everywhere with the addition “of Eumenia,” except in Usuard. Understand this as meaning that they came from Eumenia, either *Eumenia prognati*, “sprung from Eumenia,” or *Eumenia oriundi*, “originating from Eumenia,” as Valesius translates it. Moreover, that Saints Alexander and Caius belong to the number of those whom the author of the small Roman Martyrology drew from Rufinus’s Eusebius will be obvious if you compare his text with what the cited writer relates in the *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 16, toward the end. Viennensis observed that the account was taken from Apollinarius of Hierapolis, from the same chapter and the one immediately preceding it. More and clearer information may be found in Henschenius’s brief commentary. Henschenius acknowledges the broad agreement of the Latin martyrologists in assigning to this day the commemoration of the forty-two martyrs, although no information is supplied concerning the time, the particular city or province, the persecution, or any of their names. The small Roman Martyrology records them: “In Persia, forty-two martyrs.” Thus they were transferred by Ado, and from him by Usuard and Notker. The Hieronymian copies vary in number: some write twenty-two, others forty-seven, although they seem clearly to indicate the same persons. Droctoveus the abbot was added solely by Usuard, since he was the first founder and superior of the monastery itself at Pratis. You have his life, published and annotated from manuscripts by Henschenius; Mabillon edited it anew in the first Benedictine century, p. 252. Wandalbert recalls the first two groups of today’s list in these verses:

“Caius and Alexander are honored at Siena. With them,

A band of forty-two is joined in blood,

Whom together we celebrate as slain in savage Persia.”]

[Note: [Col. 0831C]

PRATENSIAN. I have already almost fully indicated its supplement in the Variants. It reads: “On the same day, Saint Attalus the abbot, disciple of Saint Columbanus.”

PULSANEN. It has “fifty-two” instead of “forty-two.” At the end: “At the monastery of Luxeuil, Saint Attalus the abbot. Likewise, Saint Hugh, bishop and confessor.” I think it refers to the bishop of Rouen, who is commemorated on 9 April.

ANTWERP–MAJOR: “At Apamia, the commemoration of Saints Alexander and Caius of Umenia, who at Apamia were crowned with glorious martyrdom in the persecution of Antoninus.” In the second edition it is pure. Nothing concerning Droctoveus.

ROSWEYD, fairly pure in the first and second editions, writes *Clodovei* instead of *Droctovei* in the third. Then: “On the same day, Saint Attalus the abbot, disciple of Saint Columbanus.”

ANTWERP–MAXIMUS, LÜBECK, ANTWERP–MAXIMUS, UTRECHT, LEIDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERG, the DANISH manuscript, and the UTRECHT–BELGIAN EDITION omit Droctoveus, replacing him with: “On the same day, Saints Gorgonius and Firmus.” MUNERATUS has the same addition, but after the complete text, except that he writes *Campaniam* instead of *Apamiam*.

BRUSSELS inserts into the text concerning Alexander and Caius that they suffered at Vienna. In third place it has: “On the same day, Saints Gorgonius and Firmus.” The notice concerning Droctoveus follows. Attalus is absent. At the end: “At the monastery of Fontenelle, the translation of the body of Saint Ausbertus [Ansbertus], archbishop of the church of Rouen, who had been banished into exile at the monastery of Hautmont. [Col. 0832C] When he felt the end of his life approaching, he asked that his body be buried at Fontenelle, where he had professed the religious life.” See the material on Ausbertus in the supplements for 9 February and in the Acts for that day.

HAGENOYEN assigns the forty-two martyrs to the time of Sapor, king of the Persians. The notice concerning Droctoveus follows. Nothing about Attalus. At the end: “On the same day, Saints Gorgonius and Firmus, martyrs.”

CENTULEN has only: “In Italy, at the monastery of Bobbio, Saint Attalus the abbot.”

AQUICINCT writes about Attalus as the Pratensian does. At the end it adds: “At Antioch, Saint Agape the virgin, and Saints Gorgonius and Firmus.”

VICTORINUS and the QUEEN OF SWEDEN manuscript, numbered 130, have at the end: “Likewise, Saint Agape the virgin, and Saints Gorgonius and [Col. 0832D] Firmus.”

MESSANENSIS: “On the same day, Saint Heraclius.” Is this the one assigned by the Hieronymian Martyrology, through Rabanus and Notker, to Alexandria?

PLESCHIONENSIS: “At Antioch, Saint Agape. At Nicaea, Saints Gorgonius and Firminus.”

BIGOTIAN, numbered P 5: “On the same day, Saints Gorgonius and Firminus.”

CLUNIACENSIS: “Likewise, Agape the virgin, Gorgonius and Sirinus.” It joins them all together without distinguishing the places.

VATICAN, no. 5949, omits Droctoveus and Attalus. At the end it adds: “At Antioch, Saint Agape the virgin. At Nicaea, Saints Gorgonius and Forminus.”

UGHELLIAN likewise omits Droctoveus and Attalus. At the [Col. 0833A] end it has: “Saints Gorgonius and Firmus,” as do the other manuscripts above.

ALTEMPS: “At Alexandria, the commemoration of Saint Philonius the bishop, Candidus, Valerius, and twenty others; at Carthage, Saint Heraclius and others.” I suspect that the days have become confused.

STROZZ. and MEDIC.: “Likewise, Saint Hugh, bishop and confessor. Likewise, the holy martyrs Felix and Philip.”

The LÜBECK–COLOGNE edition, omitting Droctoveus and Attalus, has: “On the same day, Saints Gorgonius and Firmus, martyrs. On the same day in Scotland, Saint Kessog, bishop and confessor. Likewise, the translation of Saint Vitus the martyr.” This concerns the famous translation of Saint Vitus the martyr to Saxon Corvey; see the passages omitted for this day and those for 15 June.

BELINUS incorrectly writes *Dorothei* and *Dorothonei* instead of *Droctovei*. Concerning Attalus it has: “At the monastery of Bobbio, Saint Attalus the abbot.”

[Col. 0834A] GREVENUS. We have already spoken of Attalus. It follows: “Gorgonius, Firmus, and Candidus, martyrs, with their companions. Ereticia and Criduana, virgins and martyrs.” See the passages omitted. “Palastinus the martyr [perhaps Palatinus]. In Scotland, Kessog, bishop and confessor. Agapita the virgin.” The name is again corrupt instead of *Agapa*, Marina the virgin. “The translation of Saint Vitus the martyr.”

MOLAN, in smaller type: “In Ireland, Congallus the abbot. At Vissenaken near Mount Thienen, Saint Himelinus the confessor, who, a Scot by nationality and related by blood to blessed Rumoldus, died in the aforesaid place after being stricken by pestilential fever, while the Lord caused his death to be attended by many signs and miracles.” Concerning Congallus, see the passages omitted, where he is referred to 10 May; Molanus removed him in later editions. There, however, he adds: “On the tenth day, the holy martyrs Quadratus and his companions.” Concerning Himelinus he repeats what he had said in the earlier editions.]

[Col. 0829]

At Apamia, the commemoration of Saints Alexander and Caius, martyrs, who, as Apollinarius, bishop of Hierapolis, writes in his book against the Cataphrygians, were crowned with glorious martyrdom in the persecution of Antoninus Verus. In Persia, forty-two holy martyrs. At Paris, the commemoration of Saint Droctoveus the abbot, disciple of blessed Germanus the bishop. [Bouillart adds: “On the same day [Note: [Col. 0829D] Sollerius summons the Pratensian manuscript to court because Saint Attalus is added to the saints of this day. Yet not a few handwritten manuscripts, and manuscripts of very great value, do not mention that holy abbot, while others present him differently. It is not credible that he would be absent from those manuscripts if the source from which those streams flowed had contained him. He therefore suspects that the words of the Pratensian manuscript are more recent. To refute his own little arguments, I ask only that he come and inspect the manuscript. For what weight have conjectures against what actually exists? Nor should he object to an erasure. For the forty-two martyrs and the abbot Droctoveus, whom he admits to belong to Usuard, are also written in that same erasure, together with Attalus. I do not deny that Attalus may have been added, since the Dervensis manuscript is silent about him. But Usuard was permitted to enrich his Martyrology with his own additions whenever he wished and with whichever saints he wished. Nor was it necessary for him, as soon as he had corrected anything in his manuscript, to send it wherever he sent anything else, or to announce by letter what he had added or removed from the manuscript. Now, that this is the day on which Saint Attalus or Attala ought to be commemorated requires no proof. Everyone has his Acts in hand. BOUILLART.] Saint Attalus the abbot, disciple of Saint Columbanus.”]

## Fifth day before the Ides. Day 11

[Note: [Col. 0833A]

I consider Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Grevenus, and Molanus pure. Rosweyd may be added.]

[Note: [Col. 0833B]

The only issue is that Grevenus and Molanus read, after “their faces struck with stones,” whereas Pratensis omitted the word “more eminent.” I have added to the pure witnesses the manuscript [Col. 0834B] which I call Rosweyd’s; nevertheless, after “into the pool” it inserts “where their bodies were broken apart by the ice,” which is absent from the other manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0833B]

The most noble company of fellow soldiers at Sebaste has already appeared above, on 9 March, because on that day they are commonly celebrated by both Greek and Latin martyrologists, except by those who constitute our sequence, namely the author of the small Roman Martyrology, Ado, Usuard, and Notker. We have also spoken above of Rabanus’s three notices. Thus the first to mention them on this day is the foremost among the others: “At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, the forty soldiers, in the time of King Licinius.” Ado’s account is longer, drawn from the ancient Acts and giving the names of each individual; these may be read on the cited day, 9 March, in Grevenus’s supplement. Usuard excerpted passages from Ado’s text here and there to construct his own eulogy; unless you prefer to say that he copied Bede, which seems entirely plausible from the final words, “Quirion and Candidus were the most eminent among them,” although, apart from this, the material belonging to Bede is also found in Ado. Notker follows the day, but his wording differs from Bede and Ado, having been taken from the current text of Rabanus and somewhat interpolated. Henschenius disentangled and arranged the deeds of these illustrious martyrs, which had previously been quite confused, in excellent dissertations, and illustrated the Acts themselves with equal diligence; nevertheless, Ruinart did not believe them worthy of being counted among the sincere and genuine records, producing only Basil’s homily, beginning at p. 583, where the prefatory admonition may be consulted. If, therefore, stricter critics find anything to censure in the aforementioned Acts, the praises of Basil and the other holy Fathers, from which Tillemont seems chiefly to have drawn his material, will abundantly supply it; see volume V, beginning at p. 518. I refer here to Wandalbert’s verses, which he had reported above on 9 March:

“On the seventh day, the sacred temples of Lesser Armenia celebrate one feast under a company of forty soldiers.”]

[Note: [Col. 0833C]

PULSANEN. We have already said that the texts are transposed in this manuscript, so that on the ninth it placed what belongs to this day, while on this day it has what we reported with Usuard on the ninth.]

## Antwerp–Major

Here and in many of the codices below, which marked the Sebastenes on the cited day, 9 March, the names were borrowed from the Hieronymian Martyrologies to fill an empty space. In this codex it reads:

> “At Apana (see below), the commemoration of Saints Philo, bishop, Candidus, and Valerius, with twenty others. At Carthage, Saint Heraclius.”

See their companions in the other Appendices. The following verse of Wandalbert fits Candidus and Valerius:

> “Hence Candidus and Valerius each retain five for themselves.”

## Antwerp–Maximus; Lübeck

They alone give:

> “At Carthage, Heracli or Heraclii (Heraclius), Zosimus, Alexander, Candedus, Piperion, and twenty others.”

The Ughellian codex reads it exactly so. Henschenius also judged that it should be read approximately in this way. Others transformed Alexander’s name into *Alexandriae*, thereby duplicating the location; there is some controversy concerning this. Some of these martyrs, complete or corrupted, Rabanus announced on the preceding day; Notkerus refers the remaining Nicomedians to today. Others give other forms, as in the following Appendices; these, unless I am mistaken, arose from differences among copies of the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Let the Acts and Florentinius be consulted. The forty martyrs mentioned above under 9 March are also absent here.

## Antwerp–Maximus; Utrecht; Leiden; Leuven; Alberg; Danish; Utrecht–Belgian edition

> “At Carthage, Saints Heraclius, Zosimus, Alexander, Candulus, Piperion, and twenty others. Also at Carthage, Saint Constantine the confessor, a most distinguished man. At Alexandria, the commemoration of Saints Philomus—Philomius, Philo, or Philonius—bishop, and Valerius, with twenty-one others. At the monastery of Luxeuil, Saint Attalus, abbot, disciple of Saint Columbanus, abbot.”

Muneratus reads precisely the same, with nearly the same inflections; he also listed the nine Sebastene martyrs with these codices.

## Brussels

> “At Carthage, the commemoration of Saints Heraclius, Zozimius, Alexander, Candidus, Piperion, and twenty others. At Alexandria, the commemoration of Saint Philomus, bishop, and Valerius, with twenty-one others. At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, the commemoration of the forty holy soldiers, among whom Quirion and Candidus were the more distinguished. And at Antioch, of Agape the virgin and Marina. At Carthage, Saint Constantine the confessor, a most distinguished man. At the monastery of Luxeuil, Saint Athalus, abbot, disciple of the blessed Columbanus, abbot.”

## Hagenoyen

He first treats the Sebastene martyrs, then those of Carthage and Alexandria. He continues:

> “On Mount Panois, the blessed Emperor Henry.”

I do not know what Mount Panois is, or why Henry is mentioned on this day. If this concerns his canonization, it is mentioned by others on the following day; see “Those Omitted” there. At the end: “At the monastery of Luxeuil,” etc.

## Aquicinct

To the uncorrupted text it adds:

> “In the district of Arras, the burial of Saint Vindician, bishop. Also of Saints Agapita and Marina, virgins.”

## Victorinus

> “At Alexandria, the commemoration of Saints Philo, bishop, Candidus, and Valerius, with twenty others.”

## Pleschionen

> “At Alexandria, Saints Caius, Candidus, Alexander, and Neonas the deacon, and fifteen others. On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Firmianus, abbot.”

## Marchian

He adds:

> “In the district of Arras, the burial of Saint Vindician, bishop.”

## Matricularium; Carthusian; Utrecht

> “Saints Quirion and Candidus, with forty other soldier-martyrs.”

## Codex D of du Cheval, marked B, formerly belonging to the Augustinians

> “At Alexandria, the commemoration of Saint Philoromus, bishop, and Valerius, with twenty-one others.”

## Vatican, no. 5949

> “At Carthage, Saints Heraclius and Zosimus. At Alexandria, Saints Caius, Candidus, Alexander, and Neonas the deacon, and fifteen others. On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Firmianus, abbot.”

## Altemps

> “At Alexandria, the commemoration of Saints Philonius, bishop, Candidus, and Valerius, with fifteen others. At Carthage, Saint Heraclius and others.”

## Strozzi and Medici

> “Also, the passion of forty other martyrs”—that is, on account of the forty Sebastenes, who nevertheless have been transferred thence to the ninth day—“also of Saint Firminus, abbot, a man of great holiness.”

He is the same person as the Firmianus mentioned above, whom they also call Firmanus.

## Lübeck–Cologne edition

It begins:

> “In the territory of Würzburg, the commemoration of Saint Gumbert, confessor. He was first a most Christian and faithful soldier, to whom the administration of the entire bishopric of Würzburg was entrusted; he discharged this responsibility usefully. When the bishop died, he was unanimously elected bishop by all. But, considering himself unworthy of so great an honor, he asked the Lord for the opposite and obtained it. For, while the report was pending before the pope, he peacefully fell asleep in the Lord. And when he had already been buried, the letters announcing that his prayer had been heard were publicly brought forth. Then, when all the clergy wished to honor him more highly as a bishop and to place his bones in a more honorable location, he was found adorned in all the pontifical vestments, although he had been buried as a soldier and layman.”

This saint will have to be treated on the day, 15 July, on which he is honored by the church of Würzburg. The account of the Carthaginians follows, as above:

> “At Alexandria, the commemoration of Saints Philonius, bishop, Candidus, and Valerius, with twenty martyr companions. At Luxeuil, etc. In Scotland, Saint Constantine, king and martyr. On the same day, in Lesser Armenia, Saints Domitian and his fellow martyrs.”

They belong to the number of the forty Sebastenes. See the index of “Those Omitted.”

## Belin

He first treats the Carthaginian martyrs, where *Heraclii* and *Zosimi* are written *Heradii* and *Osimi*. Then:

> “On the same day, Gorgonius and Firminus.”

This belongs more properly to the preceding day.

## Greven

> “The names of the aforesaid martyrs are,” etc., as we enumerated them on the ninth of this month. Concerning the Carthaginian and Alexandrian martyrs, as above from Antwerp–Maximus, etc.:

> “In Scotland, Saint Constantine, king and martyr. Gumbert, bishop of Würzburg. When he was a soldier, etc. In the district of Arras, Saint Vindician, bishop of Cambrai and confessor. At Carthage, Saint Constantine the confessor, a most distinguished man. Also, according to some, Attalus, abbot, whom Usuardus places on the preceding day.”

See what we said there.

## Molanus

> “One of these, named Melito, when he was younger in age,”

and the rest, which follow in Ado up to the end. Concerning Constantine the Carthaginian confessor and the martyrs of that city, the same material is repeated here as so often before.

> “On the same day, Gorgonius and Firmus. In the district of Arras,” etc.

Then, in smaller type:

> “Gumbert, bishop of Würzburg. At Clermont, Saint Georgia, most holy virgin, concerning whom Gregory of Tours writes.”

In the other editions the text is absent, but everything just mentioned is printed in italics, and the following is added at the end:

> “On the eleventh day, Saint Sophronius, father and patriarch of Jerusalem.”

[Column 0833]

At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, the commemoration of the forty holy soldiers who, in the time of King Licinius, after very frequent bonds and imprisonments, after their faces had been struck with stones, were sent into a pond and finally completed their martyrdom by the breaking of their legs. Among them the more distinguished were Quirion and Candidus.

### IV Ides (12 March)

[Note: The Prato, Herinien, Tournai, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus codices.]

[Note: The Prato codex omitted the word “more distinguished.” This is Sollerius’s observation. Yet no word in the entire article strikes the eye more forcefully. Bouillart.]

Gregory and Innocent are combined in Muneratus; I think this is a typographical error, although “Innocent” is also found in the Prato and Tournai codices. Most read “Nicomedia,” which is more correct in the text. Molanus has *vere* where *veri* is expected. Here Greven has *Egduni*, while Muneratus has *Egdimi*. It is also written in other ways, as may be seen in the Acts. After “seven others,” Muneratus added “martyrs.” Other minor matters are sufficiently indicated elsewhere.

The combination of the holy pontiffs Gregory and Innocent under one announcement was unknown to Bede, who mentions only Gregory, almost in the words of the Hieronymian Martyrologies:

> “The burial of Saint Gregory, pope, of blessed memory.”

It was likewise unknown to the aforesaid Hieronymian Martyrologies. Among them, the Lucense adds “at Rome” and reads “bishop” instead of “pope”; the Corbeian has “pope”; the Epternacense, in an unusual phrase, has:

> “Saint Gregory, pope of Rome.”

In all of them he was added last. Innocent, however, is announced nearly in the middle of the text:

> “At Rome, Saint Innocent, bishop.”

Rasi has “bishop.” Concerning these matters, see Henschenius here.

Again, this combination was unknown to Rabanus and Wandalbertus; it should therefore first be attributed to the Little Roman Martyrology, and Ado evidently took the two from it in his customary manner. Our author likewise followed both, abbreviating Ado’s short eulogy, which Notkerus preserved, adding somewhat of his own—unless one insists that the material concerning Gregory and Innocent, which Rosweydus relegated to an appendix, belongs to Ado.

This is clearly the view of the received order of our text. More recent Usuardine codices plainly abandoned it; many must be cited in the Appendices under 28 July, when, together with the modern Roman Martyrology, they refer to Pope Innocent I, some indeed with the additional title “martyr.” But we reserve these matters for the month of July in the Acts. There, after Florentinius, we shall also investigate whether that bishop Innocent who is placed in the Hieronymian copies on 21 December is the same as this one or different from him. We shall attempt to bring to light the evidence demonstrated by Henschenius, who on page 106 distinguishes the present Innocent from the pope, and so forth. Tillemont’s study will be useful, volume X, pages 627–666. Henschenius discussed Gregory the Great with the utmost accuracy. Mabillon contends for his authorship of the Life in volume I of the *Analecta*, beginning on page 319. Other Lives of the most holy pontiff have been published more recently; they may be consulted when it seems worthwhile to complete the material for the month of March.

Now hear Wandalbertus singing today of Gregory alone:

> “The fourth day before the Ides soon consecrates your end, blessed Gregory,  
> by which you sought heaven in eternal praise.”

Peter of Nicomedia is also listed by the aforementioned Little Roman Martyrology:

> “At Nicomedia, Peter the martyr, companion of the martyrs Dorotheus and Gorgonius.”

Ado did not neglect to indicate that association with Dorotheus and Gorgonius. Our author drew only from the longer eulogy those elements that seemed more suitable to his purpose. They were taken from Rufinus and are read in Henschenius’s commentary, where he lists many fellow martyrs from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. We shall say more about them on 9 September, lest we exceed our customary limits here.

Egdunus—whose name is pronounced in various ways—was counted by Ado, whose words Usuardus copied exactly. Henschenius and Florentinius ask whether he was one person or two: Migdonus, Migdonius, or Egdonus. It seems to me beyond doubt that he belongs entirely to that enormous Nicomedian slaughter of Diocletian.

Ado clearly names a certain Maximilian, both in Mosander and in Rosweydus. Others call him Mamilianus, perhaps a corruption or diminutive of Maximus or Maximianus. Usuardus omitted him; Henschenius, following Baronius, assigned him to Rome—incorrectly, since he appears to belong to Africa, if the Acts published by Ruinartius among the *Selecta*, page 309, are his. Since these were not seen by our predecessors, they may enlarge the Supplement to March.

[Note: In the Pulsanensis, the final announcement concerning Egdunus and his companions is absent.]

### Antwerp–Major

The first version is more expansive:

> “At Rome, the commemoration of the holy confessors and pontiffs Gregory, apostle of the English, most renowned for life and doctrine, and Innocent, distinguished in faith and works. The former sat for thirteen years, six months, and ten days; the latter for fifteen years, two months, and one day. At Nicomedia, the passion of the blessed Peter, most glorious martyr, who was one of the companions of the martyrs Dorotheus and Gorgonius, who were the king’s chamberlains.”

The third version is uncorrupted.

### Rosweydus

The text is fairly pure, but at the end adds an English accession:

> “On the same day, the burial of Saint Elphragus, bishop and confessor of the church of Winchester, who, adorned with holy virtues, rested in a blessed end and was buried there with fitting honor.”

In the Acts he is called Elphegus.

### Antwerp; Maximus–Lübeck; Ughellian

They depart from the purity of the text only in failing to join Innocent to Gregory. At the end, after the text, they add:

> “At Rome, the burial of Saint Innocent, bishop.”

### Antwerp–Maximus; Utrecht; Leiden; Leuven; Alberg; Danish; Utrecht–Belgian edition

Omitting Innocent, they shape the first announcement as follows:

> “At Rome, the commemoration of blessed Gregory the Great, pre-eminent doctor of the Church. He was the first Gregory and, in the order of the popes, the sixty-sixth; in the year of the Lord 585 he governed the holy Church of God beneficially.”

Otherwise they are pure. Concerning the beginning and end of his pontificate, see the Acts.

### Centulensis

Here Usuardus is again abbreviated and slightly interpolated. It reads:

> “At Rome, the commemoration of the holy pontiffs Gregory, apostle of the English, most renowned for life and doctrine, and Innocent, distinguished in faith and works. At Nicomedia, Saint Peter, glorious martyr. Also at Nicomedia, Saint Ebdunus— for Egdunus—priest and seven others, who were strangled on successive days so that fear might be instilled in the others.”

### Brussels

It begins:

> “At Rome, Saint Gregory the Great, confessor and pontiff, pope and apostle of the English, a man most salutary both in life and in teachings, and the pre-eminent doctor of the holy Church. He added to the canon of the Mass: ‘And dispose our days in your peace.’ He instituted the Greater Litany and was the first of all the Roman pontiffs to write of himself, ‘servant of the servants of God.’ Also at Rome, Saint Innocent, pope, distinguished in faith and works, who established that the kiss of peace should be given at Mass and ruled the Church for fifteen years. The account of Peter and Egdunus follows as in the text.”

At the end:

> “And Saint Maximilian the martyr.”

### Hagenoyen

He first treats Peter, then Egdunus, fairly accurately. Finally he continues:

> “At Rome, on the same day, the burial of Saint Gregory, pope and first doctor. He is called the apostle of the Angels”—for “English.” “While still a layman, he built six monasteries in Sicily and a seventh within the city of Rome; he gave them extensive estates and made himself a monk in the seventh. At the time of a shipwreck he gave twelve gold pieces and a silver dish to an Englishman. This holy pope generously provided for all the poor. He left no treasures behind him. He established the litanies. He ordered the ecclesiastical offices. He published many books. He patiently endured the calumnies of many and died in peace.”

### Aquicinct

After the Greek article τὸ, “of the English,” it adds:

> “And Innocent. The former increased the canon with: ‘And dispose our days in your peace, and rescue us from eternal damnation, and command that we be numbered among your elect.’ The latter condemned the heretics Pelagius and Coelestius.”

### Matricularium; Carthusian; Utrecht

After Gregory and Innocent it places:

> “Saint Paul, bishop of León, confessor.”

It cuts out the eulogies of Peter and Egdunus.

### Cambrai, Convent of Saint Mary

> “At the city of Nevers, Saint Vincent, priest.”

The Royal Swedish Codex, no. 130, refers to him on the following day. The Acts require more certain information concerning his cult.

### Altemps

> “On the same day, the burial of Saint Elphegus of Wentan”—for Winchester—“bishop and confessor, who, adorned with holy virtues, rested in a good end and was buried there with fitting honor.”

### Strozzi and Medici

> “At Rome, Saint Innocent, bishop and confessor. At Rome, Saint Mamilianus, martyr.”

### Burdigalensis

> “At Plebs Lapidis, Saint Paul, confessor.”

He is the same person whom others call the bishop of León.

### Remensis of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris

> “At Rome, Innocent, pope.”

### Lübeck–Cologne edition

> “At Rome, the commemoration of blessed Gregory the Great, pope, confessor, and pre-eminent doctor of the Church of God, and apostle of the English. He was the first Gregory and, in the order of the popes, the sixty-sixth; in the year of the Lord 585—see the Acts—he beneficially governed the holy Church of God for thirteen years, six months, and ten days. He was endowed with such life and learning that he was called an earthly angel. He also added to the Mass: ‘And dispose our days in your peace,’ and composed many books. He was the first pontiff to write of himself, ‘servant of the servants of God.’ He also established that, for the remission of the sins of the human race, stations of the faithful should be held and devoutly celebrated each day of Lent in each church of the city of Rome.”

The account of Peter and Egdunus is nearly pure. It continues:

> “In Lesser Britain, blessed Paul, bishop and confessor. At Rome, the burial of Saint Innocent, pope and confessor, who ruled the Church for fifteen years, two months, and twenty-one days. On the same day, Saint Maximilian the martyr.”

### Belin

The first edition begins with Gregory alone. It omits Egdunus, but adds:

> “At Rome, the burial of Saint Innocent, bishop and confessor. At Rome, Saint Mamilianus, martyr.”

The second begins as in the text. The additions already noted are included, and at the end:

> “Also at Nicomedia, Saints Egdunus, etc.”

### Greven

> “The most blessed Gregory, the first pope of this name, was, after Peter, the sixty-second; according to Martin’s reckoning, the sixty-seventh. Because of his exceptional holiness and learning he was called an earthly angel. He added to the canon, etc. He was also the first to call himself ‘servant,’ etc. He established stations in the city of Rome on each day of Lent. He governed the Church for thirteen years, six months, and ten days. He fell asleep in the Lord in the year 606”—he meant 604.

> “Innocent, also placed here, was the first of this name. On the same day, blessed Maximilian the martyr. Pionius the martyr,” concerning whom see 1 February. Perhaps he was taken from Florus on this day.

> “Also Zemmeon,” hitherto unknown to me.

> “In Lesser Britain, Saint Paul, bishop of León and confessor, whose faith was so great that, placing pebbles on the seashore, he forbade the sea ever again to occupy the land beyond them. The sea is still seen to observe his prohibition. Also, according to some, Kessog, who is placed above under the sixth day before the Ides. Also near Metz, the translation of Saint Gorgonius the martyr.”

### Molanus

> “At Rome, Saint Maximilian the martyr.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “On the same day, Dionysius Richel died at Roermond; his life and catalogue of works were written by Theodoricus a Stratis, Carthusian of Cologne.”

In later editions:

> “At Rome, Mamilianus the martyr. On the twelfth day, Saint Theophanes, father and confessor.”

In smaller type:

> “He was also called Isaac and resisted Leo the Iconoclast with great steadfastness. In Lesser Britain, Paul, bishop of León, in the time of Justin the Younger.”

He has already been mentioned above. See Papebrochius’s commentary and the Life he illustrated.

[Column 0835]

At Rome, the blessed pontiffs Gregory, doctor and apostle of the English, and Innocent. At Nicomedia, the passion of Saint Peter the martyr. When he was a chamberlain of the emperor Diocletian and spoke with excessive freedom about the immense punishments of the martyrs, he was brought into the midst at the emperor’s command. First he was suspended and tortured for a very long time with whips; then, covered with vinegar and salt, he was finally roasted on a gridiron. Thus he proved to be the true Peter’s heir both in faith and in name. Also at Nicomedia, Saints Egdunus the priest and seven others, who were strangled on successive days so that the others might be frightened.

### III Ides (13 March)

[Note: The Prato, Herinien, Tournai, Pulsanensis, Antwerp, Maximus–Lübeck, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus codices agree. They are joined by Antwerp–Maximus, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Alberg, Danish, and the Utrecht–Belgian edition.]

[Note: “Nichomediam” and “Nycomediam” are medieval errors; it is not worthwhile to continue observing them. Greven incorrectly reads *Modestiae* for *Modestae*. I wrote *Nicea* with nearly all the codices, although Molanus’s reading *Nicaea* seems preferable. Tournai has *Nicena*. Pulsanensis alone has *Machedonii*. The manuscripts vary in *Theusetae*: Tournai has *Teusete*; Antwerp and Maximus–Lübeck, *Theosete*; Greven, *Theusece*; Molanus, *Theosetae*. *Theoaere* in Herinien and *Nempodere* in Pulsanensis are, unless I am mistaken, scribal errors, as is *Nimpedoi* in Muneratus. Likewise *Marcii* for *Marci* in Pulsanensis, and *Marci et Arabiae* in Muneratus. All write *Eufrasiae*. I did not think other minor matters worth noting in the five final codices.]

The agreement of almost all the ancient martyrologists in reporting the first class of martyrs is remarkable and nearly unparalleled. The Hieronymian copies explicitly record them, though they differ from the others in that the spelling is frequently more corrupt, as here in *Mitriciae* for *Patriciae*, etc. Bede, Rabanus, the Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Notkerus have nearly the same words:

> “At Nicomedia, or at Nicomedia, the birth of Macedonius the priest, Patriciae his wife, and Modesta their daughter.”

Our author preserved the names but suppressed the relationship. This is plainly established from the most trustworthy codices that I cited, whatever our Acts may indicate concerning some other codex—said to be Usuardus’s genuine one—in which the relationship is expressed. That genuine codex, whoever may have possessed it, was either merely lent out or has certainly perished. For it is not permissible to regard the great Utrecht codex of Saint Mary, which we have so often called Rosweydus’s, as an ancient and genuine Usuardine codex accepted by Henschenius, despite Rosweydus’s having arranged in his great collection of Martyrologies—Roman, Greek, the common Bede, Usuardus, Ado, Rabanus, and Notkerus—for that very Utrecht codex to be described as Usuardus’s authentic copy, along with the others, unless I am mistaken, for publication, as he seemed to promise in 1607 in his first plan for publishing the Acts.

How far that codex departs from Usuardus’s authenticity has often been clear and will become clear again. The same form of announcement is also found in the codex that I have always called the Antwerp Major; it is likewise found in the Centulensis. Yet from the purity of Usuardus both are so far removed that I have learned this fully from constant collation. Moreover, no other codex remains in our Museum; and if one did remain, it would not easily displace the authority of the others.

To the martyrologists already cited let Wandalbertus also be added, singing in harmony with the rest:

> “Macedonius the priest completes three, with his honorable  
> wife Patricia and their daughter Modesta accompanying him.”

The Nicene martyrs, with their names somewhat corrupted, are also found recorded in the Hieronymian copies. From there Ado very probably drew them, lacking his usual guide, since the Roman Martyrology makes no mention of them. Our author again followed Ado, and Notkerus likewise followed him; Rabanus adhered more closely to the Hieronymian wording.

Usuardus was the first to speak of Eufrasia, who may be called Egyptian on account of her residence. I say “Egyptian,” for it is not credible that Usuardus confused her with another Nicomedian woman mentioned in the Hieronymian text, whether he accepted the names as identical or nearly identical. The Acts judge that she should be called Euphrasia, or rather Eupraxia; there much material is assembled and learnedly discussed on the point, which the curious reader may consult in its place. We shall not repeat what has already been done. The Life, there illustrated by Papebrochius from ancient manuscripts collated with the Greek text, although it does not appear to be by a completely contemporary author, is nevertheless such that it may safely be tested against the touchstone of the strictest criticism.

### Antwerp–Major

Here again it is entirely Adonian. Its first announcement reads:

> “At Nicomedia, the commemoration of Saints Macedonius the priest, Patriciae his wife, and Modesta their daughter. At the city of Nicaea, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Theuseta and her son Horris, Theodora, Nimpodora, Marcus,” etc.

The third announcement is absent; we said above that Usuardus alone added it. See the observations above.

### Rosweydus

He forms the first announcement as follows:

> “At Nicomedia, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Macedonius the priest, Patriciae his wife, and Modesta his daughter, and thirty-two others.”

The rest is pure.

### Brussels

It is closest to the older text:

> “At Nicomedia, Saints Macedonius, Patriciae his wife, and their daughter Modesta. At the city of Nicaea, the holy martyrs Theuseta and her daughter Orris, Theodora, Mimphodora, Marcus, and Arabia. They were all handed over to the fire. In the Thebaid, the burial of Saint Euphrasia the virgin. Also Macedonius and Innocent, bishops”—perhaps “Innocent”—“also Pope Leo.”

See “Those Omitted.”

### Hagenoyen
