> “At Rome, at the Bear with the cap, the commemoration of Saint Innocent, pope and martyr”—this title could have been omitted. “He confined many Cataphrygians whom he himself had discovered in a monastery of exile. He established that whoever was born of a Christian woman must immediately be born again through baptism, which the heretic Pelagius denied. His feast is chiefly celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. At Nicomedia, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Macedonius the priest, Patriciae, and Modestia the virgins.”

In the rest it does not depart greatly from the pure text.

### Victorinus and Royal Swedish Codex no. 130

At the end:

> “In the territory of Nevers, Saint Vincent, priest and confessor.”

The Acts ask to be informed concerning his cult. See “Those Omitted.”

### Pleschionen

> “The commemoration of Saint Eldradus, abbot.”

### Marchian

For *Modestae* he writes *Modestiae*, as Greven did above.

### Matricularium; Carthusian; Utrecht

> “Euphrasia the virgin. Peter the martyr’s companions, Saints Dorotheus and Gorgonius, from 12 March. Theuseta with her companions, martyr.”

### Cluniac

> “On the same day, at the monastery of Cluny, the translation of Saint Consortia.”

Her commemoration is on 22 June.

### Vatican, no. 5949

At the end:

> “Saint Eldradus, abbot. On the same day, Saint Ansimius”—or Ansovinus—“bishop and confessor.”

### Altemps

> “On the same day, at the monastery of Cluny, Saint Consortia.”

### Strozzi and Medici

> “Also Saint Leo, pope. On the same day, at the monastery of Cluny, the translation of Saint Consortia.”

### Saint Ricaldus

> “The burial of Saint Eldratus, abbot and confessor.”

### Caudiac Priorate

> “At the monastery of Cluny, the translation of Saint Consortia the virgin.”

### Lübeck–Cologne edition

> “At Nicomedia, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Macedonius the priest, Modestia his daughter, and Patriciae his wife.”

The rest is nearly pure.

### Belin

> “At Nicomedia, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Macedonius the priest, Patritia his wife, and his daughter Modesta. In the city of Nicaea, the holy martyrs Theoseda and Horris her son,” etc.

At the end is added:

> “On the same day, at the monastery of Cluny, the translation of Saint Consortia.”

### Greven

> “Donatus, Advocatus, martyrs.”

See “Those Omitted.”

> “Desiderius, bishop and martyr.”

See the same place.

> “Constantine, king and protomartyr of Scotland.”

He is treated on the eleventh.

> “In Ireland, Mochomogus the confessor and Geraldus the abbot. Also Epipodia.”

Perhaps the name is corrupted from Epepodius, the Nicomedian martyr, concerning whom see the Acts.

> “Kevoca,”

rather, Kennocha the virgin.

### Molanus

> “On the same day, at the monastery of Cluny, the translation of Saint Consortia.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “And Saint Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople.”

Later editions add:

> “On the thirteenth day, the bringing back of the relics of Saint Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople.”

In smaller type:

> “He defended the useful veneration of sacred images against impiety.”

A brief eulogy has rightly been added here. It is also correct that what is celebrated is not his day of death, as the first edition seemed to suggest, but the bringing back of his relics. Indeed, the day is memorable for this additional reason: on 13 March he was punished with exile by the impious Leo the Armenian.

> “At Hermopolis, Saint Sabinus the martyr.”

He is one of those who suffered under Arianus, governor of the Thebaid—the famous man who later became a martyr, as we said elsewhere. Hence it probably happened that his Acts, published by Lipomanus and Surius, became confused with the Acts of Saint Ascla, who is celebrated on 23 January, and were therefore omitted by Papebrochius, with only the eulogies taken from the Greek Calendars being preserved.

[Column 0839]

At Nicomedia, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Macedonius the priest, Patriciae, and Modesta. In the city of Nicaea, the holy martyrs Theuseta, Horris, Theodora, Nimpodora, Marcus, and Arabia, all of whom were handed over to the fire. In the Thebaid, the burial of Saint Euphrasia the virgin.

### Eve of the Ides (14 March)

[Note: Only the Prato, Herinien, Tournai, Muneratus, and Molanus codices are pure.]

[Note: In the Tournai codex there is an ancient but faulty spelling, such as *Affrica* and *Aphrica*. Herinien, Tournai, and Muneratus, following Ado, read *Mamurtini*; the better reading is *Mamertini*, found in Prato, Molanus, and the most common spelling. *Fedei* for *fidei* in the Prato codex is a scribal error. All read *Eufrosii*; with Molanus, it should more correctly be written *Euphrosii*.]

Apart from the genuine codices cited above, there are several others, such as Antwerp, Maximus–Lübeck, and eight middle-grade manuscript codices, which may properly be counted among the pure ones, since they depart from Usuardus’s simplicity in only this respect: instead of forty-seven they read forty-nine.

Greven must plainly be excluded, since he alone inserted Leobinus of Chartres—whom he calls Leoninus—unknown to all our Usuardine codices, as we shall say in his Appendix. Otherwise, it is plainly evident from the source itself that the given reading must be preserved. By “source” I mean the Little Roman Martyrology, from which Ado customarily took them, enlarging the earlier wording somewhat. Our author in turn reports Ado’s eulogy complete and unchanged; Notkerus, strangely, truncated its final part, as you will also find noted in the Acts.

There is scarcely any doubt that the compiler of the Little Roman Martyrology took those martyrs from the Acts of Saints Processus and Martinianus, who are mentioned neither in the Hieronymian copies nor in the genuine Bede. Whether Florus or someone else subsequently appended them to Bede need not be investigated here; nor is there time to examine where the recently noted change from forty-seven to forty-nine first arose. It most probably entered the later codices through the carelessness of copyists.

Peter the African and likewise Euphrosius—or perhaps Euphrasius, for both are celebrated on this day—were torn from their respective classes, accurately distinguished in the Acts from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. No one earlier than Usuardus records them in that manner, unless Wandalbertus is excepted. If Usuardus did not take them from him, he could at least have done so, since Wandalbertus has:

> “Euphrosius shines on the preceding day, and Peter with the martyr.”

### Antwerp–Major

> “At Rome, the commemoration of the forty-seven holy martyrs who were baptized by the blessed apostle Peter. At Laodicea, Saint Sagaris, bishop, who in the time of Antoninus Verus, under Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Asia, was crowned with a glorious martyrdom.”

I leave the transposition as it stands, however inept it may be. That Sagaris, concerning whom others also write, is relegated in the Acts to 6 October.

### Rosweydus

> “At Nicomedia, Felicissimus and Dativus, martyrs.”

### Pulsanensis

The first announcement is pure; it omits the final two.

### Centulensis

He invents a new alteration of the number, writing:

> “At Rome, the forty-two blessed martyrs who, baptized by the blessed apostle Peter in prison, suffered under Nero.”

He says nothing about the other two.

### Brussels

Instead of forty-seven, it gives forty-eight. Then, in second place:

> “At Laodicea, Saint Sagaris, bishop, who in the time of Antoninus Verus, under Sergius Paulus the proconsul, was crowned with martyrdom.”

In the accounts of Peter and Euphrosius it is pure.

### Hagenoyen

He counts forty-nine. Then he adds to the otherwise nearly pure text:

> “At the city of Thessalonica, Saint Matrona, maidservant of a certain wealthy widow, and martyr. Her mistress bound her upon a bench and beat her; an angel released her; while she was praying, she was again bound and beaten and again released by an angel. Finally she was beaten to death with stout clubs, and in confessing Christ she surrendered her spirit undefiled.”

See the following day.

### Aquicinct

It begins:

> “The commemoration of Saints Felicissimus and Dativus.”

After “forty-seven,” it inserts “soldiers.”

### Victorinus and the Swedish Codex, no. 130

At the end:

> “Also at Laodicea, Saint Sagaris, bishop and martyr.”

### Daveronensis

> “The burial of blessed Leobinus, bishop of Chartres, a man of magnificent holiness and most distinguished in miracles.”

His name is formed in various ways, as will be clear from what has been said and what will be said.

### Altemps

> “At Laodicea, Saint Sagaris, bishop, who in the time of Antoninus Verus, under Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Asia, was crowned with a glorious martyrdom.”

The difference from the preceding versions is slight.

### Strozzi and Medici

> “At Rome, Saint Zacharias, pope.”

See the following day.

> “Also Saint Alexander the martyr. Also at Lyon in Gaul, the translation of Saint Bonaventure, cardinal, bishop of Albano, of the Order of Friars Minor.”

> “At Chartres, Saint Leobius, bishop and confessor.”

> “At the city of Metz, in the lower monastery, the translation of the body of Saint Glodesindis the virgin.”

She is celebrated on 25 July.

### Lübeck–Cologne edition

With the codices cited above, it reads forty-nine; and in second place has:

> “On the same day at Chartres, Saint Leoninus, bishop and confessor.”

Finally:

> “On the same day, Saints Innocent, bishop, and Euphrosius, confessor.”

Concerning Innocent, see “Those Omitted.”

BELINUS: Both editions also note XLIX and, after an almost pure text, append:

> “On the same day, of Zacharias the pontiff, who sat in Rome for ten years. Also at Lyon in Gaul, the translation of Saint Bonaventure, cardinal and bishop of Albano, of the Order of Friars Minor.”

GREVEN, together with the Lübeck–Cologne edition, inserts into the text:

> “On the same day at Chartres,” etc.

To the text he adds:

> “At Nicomedia, of the holy martyrs Felicissimus, Dativus, and Frontina. Also in Africa, of Alexander the martyr. Also of Pionus. Of Pope Innocent. At Lyon, the translation of Saint Bonaventure, bishop of Albano, of the Order of Friars Minor, cardinal priest of the Roman Church. [Col. 0844C] Also of Peter, abbot of Clairvaux, of blessed memory, distinguished by birth and manner of life. Mathilda, of blessed memory, mother of the first Emperor Otto, a matron of the greatest humility and patience. She was also so devoted to the virtue of continual prayer that she was accustomed to recite the entire Psalter before Matins. Finally, foretelling her death in a prophetic spirit, she departed to Christ. At Metz, the translation of Saint Glodesindis the virgin.”

MOLANUS:

> “On the same day, of Zacharias the pontiff, who sat in Rome for ten years. Also at Lyon in Gaul, the translation of Saint Bonaventure, cardinal and bishop of Albano. On the same day at Chartres, of Saint Leoninus the bishop.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “Mathilda, of blessed memory, a matron of the greatest humility and patience.”

In other editions, after the ten years of Zacharias, there is added:

> “He translated the four books of the Dialogues of blessed Gregory into Greek, and through Boniface, [Col. 0844D] bishop of Mainz, he raised Pippin, father of Charles, to the royal throne in the city of Soissons. On the same day at Chartres, of Saint Leoninus the bishop. And of Saint Alexander the martyr at Pydna.”

In smaller type:

> “At the monastery of Quedlinburg, in the diocese of Halberstadt, the repose of Queen Mathilda, mother of Otto I, the emperor, whose life was a mirror of virtue.”

[Col. 0841]

At Rome, the passion of the forty-seven saints. They were baptized by blessed Peter the apostle while he was being held in the Mamertine prison with his fellow apostle Paul, where they were detained for nine months; all of them, in the most devout confession of the faith, were slain by Nero’s sword. In Africa, Saint Peter the martyr. Also Saint Euphrosius.

On the Ides. The fifteenth day.

[Note: [Col. 0843]

From the Pratensis, Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, Muneratus, Belinus, Greven, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0845A]

There is an error at the beginning. Greven begins “Caesarea Cappadociae”; the Tornacensis is worse, omitting “In Caesarea” and beginning “Cappadociae”; *Cappadotie* occurs in Max.-Lübeck; *Capadocie* in Muneratus, Belinus, and Greven; and other such minutiae do not deserve to be recorded. The Pulsanensis added “city.” Thus Belinus wrote *ejus* for *ejusdem*, “his” for “the same,” and in the other edition added *militis*, “of the soldier,” just as he added *virginis*, “of the virgin,” concerning Matrona; Muneratus also reads this, omitting the particle *usque*, “even unto.” Belinus transposed the final words in this form: “He gave back his spirit to God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0845A]

Florentius says that almost all the Martyrologies, both printed and manuscript, treat on this day of Longinus the martyr of Cappadocia. Among these he wrongly counts the Martyrology of Ado, who explicitly remembers this Longinus not today but on the first of September, after the Little Roman Martyrology. Nor is he known to the genuine Bede, Florus, or Wandalbert. Rabanus and Notker genuinely treat of him: the former adorns him with a longer eulogy, which he says he composed from the Acts; the latter gives something not very different but more concise, though he does not write the same words verbatim, as through inadvertence it entered our Acts. The same Notker again mentions Longinus on the first of September, where he follows Ado’s eulogy.

It is sufficiently certain that some Longinus, and indeed one in Cappadocia, is mentioned in the copies of Jerome. Whether he can or should be identified with the man supposed to have pierced the side of Christ with a lance—a not entirely alien etymology; whether he is called a centurion or a soldier; whether the Latin Acts confused the persons of soldier and centurion; who their authors were; and many other matters concerning the homeland, deeds, cult, companions, relics, translations, invented histories, and so forth of the two men—Papebrochius has explained at considerable length in his entire preliminary Commentary, beginning on page 376.

He nowhere clearly states what credibility he thinks the Acts deserve; more recent writers accept neither account. See Tillemont’s criticism, volume I, page 453. Whatever authority one may judge the Acts themselves to possess, it is clear that our text, probably taken from Ado on the first of September, exhibits that Usuardine simplicity which alone concerns us.

The first author to introduce the martyr Matrona, silently omitting the title “virgin,” was the author of the Little Roman Martyrology. Ado composed his customary eulogy, which Notker reproduces in full; our author, as usual, condensed only the principal points. Concerning the two other Matronas, the one of Barcelona and the Lusitanian one, see the Acts for this day.

A singular case, noted once and again above, occurs here anew: namely, that in Ado of Rosweyde there is found today Pope Zacharias, whom Usuard completely omitted. I cannot discover the reason. In Mosander’s edition, moreover, he is placed with his eulogy on the day before the Ides; hence it is not surprising that Baronius observed it in this way in his notes, since he did not see Rosweyde’s more accurate edition, nor could he have seen it, having died six years before it appeared.

I had almost failed to record the verse which Wandalbert left about this Matrona:

> “The Thessalian people keep the Ides through the martyr Matrona.”

] [Note: [Col. 0845B]

ANTWERP–MAJ. passes over Longinus and treats only of Matrona, abbreviating Ado’s eulogy in this manner:

> “At the city of Thessalonica, the birthday of Saint Matrona. Since she was the servant of a certain *utilae* [someone wrote *vetulae*, “of an old woman,” above *utilae*; but *Plautillae*, “of Plautilla,” ought to be supplied], and secretly worshipped Christ and daily attended church for furtive prayers, she was discovered by her mistress, stretched out and bound on a bench, flogged almost to death, and then left bound to the bench throughout the night, with the doors carefully sealed. On the following day she was found miraculously freed and praying with great grace upon her lips.”

ROSWEYDE adds to the pure text:

> “At Nicomedia, of Lucius the bishop and martyr.”

These words seem to have been transferred here from Notker, unless they were instead taken directly from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

ANTWERP–MAX., LOUVAIN, LEYDEN, BELGIAN, and the UTRECHT–BELGIAN edition add the following concerning Longinus, after “he opened”:

> “He was baptized by the apostles, and while living in Cappadocia, distinguished for holiness, he was arrested under the governor Octavius. After confessing the faith, his tongue was cut out, his teeth were knocked out, and he was beheaded.”

I do not yet know who first transferred this eulogy into the more recent Usuardine codices. I do know that it was taken from Ado—not for this day, as I noted above, but for the first of September, a point that will have to be repeated.

UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERG, and DANISH begin as follows:

> “At Rome, the birthday of Saint Zacharias the pope. He translated the four books of the Dialogues of blessed Gregory into Greek, and through blessed Boniface, bishop of Mainz, raised Pippin, father of Charles, to the royal throne in the city of Soissons.”

They have concerning Longinus the same material that we have just quoted.

CENTULES:

> “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, of Saint Longinus the soldier, who opened the Lord’s side with a lance and was afterward baptized and beheaded by the governor Octavius.”

BRUSSELS has concerning Longinus the same material as above. Then:

> “At the city of Thessalonica, the birthday of Saint Matrona the martyr. Since she was the servant of a certain widow Plautilla [Col. 0846B], secretly worshipping Christ . . .”

As above. It adds from the same source:

> “Finally, beaten with clubs until death, she gave her spirit back to God in a good confession. At Rome, the burial of blessed Zacharias the pope, who translated the books of the Dialogues of blessed Gregory into Greek.”

HAGENAU invents many things concerning Longinus, which I do not wish to report. As we have seen, he treated of Matrona on the preceding day. In his account of Zacharias he does not differ much from the Utrecht edition and the others.

AQUICINCT agrees with ANTWERP–MAX. concerning Longinus. It follows:

> “At Rome, of Pope Zacharias, who found in the patriarchal church the head of Saint George the martyr.”

Matrona is called a virgin, a title with which Belinus likewise adorned her above.

VICTORINUS writes at the end concerning Zacharias as Aquicinct does immediately above, adding after “he found”:

> “It had been placed in a chest, in which he also found an epitaph, likewise written in Greek letters; and he was buried in the church of blessed Peter.”

These words are taken from Ado of Mosander on the preceding day; they are found in Rosweyde’s appendix.

MATRICULUM–CARTHUSIANS–UTRECHT treat of Longinus. They also treat of Zacharias and Matrona, but with almost all the eulogies cut away.

REG. SUECIAE, number 130:

> “Also of Pope Zacharias,” etc.

The remainder is not added, but I think it is the same as Victorinus suggested above, since this codex frequently agrees with him.

Codex D. DU CHEVAL, marked C:

> “Also of James the apostle and Lucius the bishop.”

From the Hieronymian Martyrology.

VATICAN, marked number 5949, omitted Longinus and wrote first:

> “At Rome, of Zacharias the pontiff, who sat in the episcopate for ten years.”

STROZZI and MEDICI, after reporting concerning Longinus what we described above from ANTWERP–MAX. and the others, add further, also from Ado on the first of September:

> “And with him the blessed Aphrodisius, the recorder, was crowned; the governor had ordered his tongue to be cut out. After his tongue had been cut out at the governor’s command, he nevertheless proclaimed Christ and his faith in a clear and fluent voice.”

Ado reads “he spoke.”

[Col. 0847A]

BORDEAUX:

> “Of the most blessed James the apostle and Lucius the martyr.”

From the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION:

> “At Rome, the birthday of Saint Zacharias the pope and confessor, who sat for ten years. He translated the four books of the Dialogues of blessed Gregory into Greek, and through blessed Boniface, bishop of Mainz, raised Pippin, father of Charles, to the royal throne in the city of Soissons. He also had King Carloman of the Franks, Pippin’s brother, made a cleric and sent him to the monastery of Cassino to become a monk; Carloman also bestowed many gifts and apostolic privileges upon the monastery.”

What it says more fully about Longinus and Matrona is taken from Ado or Notker.

GREVEN:

> “At Rome, of Zacharias the pope and confessor. He translated the four books of the Dialogues of Pope Gregory into Greek; and through Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, raised Pippin, father of Charlemagne, to the royal throne. Of Aphrodisius, the recorder, who suffered with Saint Longinus. Of Lucius the bishop. Also of blessed Fausta.”

From the Nicomedian martyrs he included this one alone [Col. 0848A]. See the remaining companions in the Acts.

MOLANUS inserts in italics into the text:

> “Since she was the servant of a certain widow Plautilla, secretly worshipping Christ, and daily attending church for furtive prayers.”

Concerning Zacharias, he collected the material set out above from the manuscript codices, except only that he wrote *pitacium* instead of *epitaphium*, on which see his Notes. Then, in smaller type:

> “At Rieti, Saint Probus the bishop, whom blessed Gregory mentions in the Dialogues. At Dijon, Saint Tranquillus the confessor, of whom blessed Gregory of Tours writes. Saint Speciosus the monk, of whom Gregory writes in the Dialogues, book IV, chapter 8. At Rome, the holy monks Merulus and Antony, of whom Gregory writes in the same book.”

Molanus omits all these in his later editions, in which only this is read:

> “On the fifteenth day, Saint Agapius the martyr and his companions.”

The Acts relegate him to 24 March; but they do not even mention Merulus and Antony among Those Omitted.]

[Col. 0843]

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the passion of Saint Longinus, who pierced the Lord’s side with a lance, as is found in the deeds of the same saint. At the city of Thessalonica, the birthday of Saint Matrona the martyr, who, after being discovered and afflicted in many ways, was finally beaten with stout clubs until death and gave her undefiled spirit back to God in the confession of Christ.

XVII Kalends. The sixteenth day.

[Note: [Col. 0847]

The Pratensis, Rosweyde, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, Muneratus, the second edition of Belinus, and Molanus appear to be pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0847C]

Some read *Hilari* with the Pratensis, others *Hylarii*, *Ylarii*, and so forth; in the text, I think, the purer form is found. Likewise *Tatiani* is better than *Taciani*. Muneratus has the incorrect *Heronius* for *Beronius*. *Dionysius*, *birthday*, *rack*, and *Cyriacus* do not deserve notice. Muneratus added *martyr* after *deacon*. I read *terminarunt*, “they completed”; others have *terminaverunt*, “they finished”; Belinus has *consummaverunt*, “they brought to completion.” The codices commonly write *reliquata*. The Pratensis incorrectly reads “stretched out, pulled apart, and already with the sinews . . .” More correctly, I think, with Molanus: “stretched out and pulled apart, even with the sinews, and . . . . .” whatever others may read, “pulled apart even with the sinews.” In Muneratus *caesus*, “struck,” is lacking; it is present in Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck. The Pratensis alone placed “the August Ides.” Belinus and Molanus have *Avernis* for *Arvernis*. Both words could have been omitted, as could Patricius himself. In Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck *sancti*, “of the saint,” is lacking.]

[Note: [Col. 0847D]

A considerable difference between the ancient Usuardine codices and the more reliable ones recurs today. Neither the Herinien. nor the Tornacen., nor Belinus’s purer edition mentions anything concerning Hilary of Aquileia and his companions. Hence one may reasonably doubt whether they were written by Usuard’s original hand, or whether they were subsequently added by someone else—or perhaps by the author himself—from some Hieronymian codex.

Certainly Bede, who treats today of Cyriacus and his companions, says not a word about Hilary. Rabanus copied Bede. Ado is also silent. Notker indicates only the name of Hilary and Aquileia, so that one clearly understands that these words were taken from a Hieronymian copy. Whatever the truth may be, the reading of the Pratensis and the other codices has been retained.

It may already have been noted, and will be observed throughout the work, that eulogies which are genuinely Usuardine—that is, which have not been copied or abridged from Bede or Ado—are exceedingly rare. Usuard composed this one himself from the passion of the martyrs, just as we have shown him to have done in the case of Ascla, on 23 January, and in the first two announcements on 8 March. See what was said about this matter in the preface.

Everyone agrees about Cyriacus. This could have been taken from the Little Roman Martyrology, together with Largus, Smaragdus, and Crescentianus, all of whom Ado also recites and adorns with a eulogy. I nevertheless believe that Ado borrowed all his material from Bede, whom he appears to copy almost word for word, while Notker is unusually mutilated in this section. Crescentianus is not expressed by Usuard, nor is Sisinnius, who is named at the beginning by Bede and Ado.

The codices vary concerning the name of the tyrant under whom they suffered: some call him *Maximianus*, others *Maximinus*. Under 16 January, where Marcellus was discussed—and where the deeds of Cyriacus and his companions, of whatever quality, are inserted—it is inferred that they and Marcellus suffered at almost the same time. There, I say, with the most reliable codices—whose genuine reading, although faulty, we are bound to report—we judged that *Maximinus* should be written; most writers today, together with the Pratensis, also give that name. Yet they are not sufficiently consistent, for on 8 August, where Cyriacus and his companions occur again, the time of Diocletian is indicated—perhaps his persecution continued.

Here it is enough to vindicate Usuard’s genuine reading. What should truly be read, how many the band of martyrs was, where the martyrdom took place, and so forth will be examined expressly under 8 August in our Acts.

Likewise, the final announcement concerning Patricius of Arvernis, or Avernensis, is retained in the text. Although unknown to the more ancient authorities, he is expressly mentioned by Usuard, from whom he entered the modern Roman Martyrology, even though it is sufficiently clear that there was never any Patricius of Avernus, if he is distinguished from Patricius of Ireland. Consult the index of Those Omitted, where you will find the source of the corrupt reading identified.

I cannot determine why Isicius, Isichius, or Esichius of Vienne, included by the received Ado, was omitted by Usuard, unless perhaps he was completely absent from the Adonian codex used by Usuard and was later added by some local copyist.

Let me append here Wandalbert’s verses in which he celebrates Cyriacus and his companions:

> “The seventeenth day, preceding the Kalends of April in the customary reckoning, shines with the honor of Cyriacus and Largus;  
> and at the same time blossoms with the precious blood of Smaragdus.”

] [Note: [Col. 0849B]

We have already indicated the lacuna in the HERINIEN. and TORNACEN.

ANTWERP–MAJ. here departs completely from Usuard, for it has only one announcement, concerning Cyriacus and his companions, copied verbatim from Ado. Seek it in that source itself.

The PULSANEN. ought to be called the purest, since it is entirely silent concerning Patricius of Avernus. Yet it should have been omitted because here it departs from the erring Usuard.

GREVEN is also excluded from the class of pure codices because of his final announcement, which was added to Usuard:

> “Also, the burial [why not the birthday?] of Saint Heribert, bishop of Cologne and confessor.”

It is truly surprising that Greven did not notice that Saint Heribert lived two centuries after Usuard, especially if he believed that Usuard offered his Martyrology to Charlemagne, which Greven certainly believed.

ANTWERP–MAX., UTRECHT–LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERG, DANISH, and the UTRECHT–BELGIAN edition have at the end:

> “At Cologne Agrippina, the birthday of Saint Heribert, bishop and confessor of the same place.”

Among these codices the only difference is that the Louvain codex departs somewhat from purity in the text. I do not think it worthwhile to record this more scrupulously.

CENTULES has only this:

> “At Rome, the passion of Saint Cyriacus the deacon and martyr, who, abounding in the great grace of healings, freed from a demon Artemia, daughter of the Emperor Diocletian, and Jobia, daughter of the king of the Persians.”

BRUSSELS begins with Cyriacus, whose eulogy it interpolated from Ado. Then it proceeds on its own:

> “On the same day, of Artemia the martyr, daughter of Diocletian, whom her brother Maximinus killed because she was a worshipper of Christ.”

See the index of Those Omitted.

> “At Nicomedia, of the holy martyrs Eugenius, Pamphilianus, Serenus, Castor, and Dionysius.”

The confusion of names is distinguished in the Acts. It is sufficiently pure concerning Hilary and Tatian, and likewise concerning Patricius. It follows:

> “At Vienne, of Saint Esichius the bishop and confessor. At Cologne Agrippina, the burial of Saint Heribert, archbishop and confessor of the same city, who, dying near the day he had foretold, began to become renowned through great miracles. Also Saint Eugenia the virgin.”

This belongs to the Nicomedian group, unless he intended to refer to Eusebia of Hamaticum.

HAGENAU, moderately interpolated in its account of Cyriacus, treats of Patricius second and Hilary third. Then:

> “At Cologne Agrippina, the birthday of Saint Heribert, bishop and confessor of the same place. His body, however, rests at Deutz beyond the Rhine, in the monastery which he founded himself, in the cloister of black monks. Also at Babylon, of Saint Agricola the bishop and confessor.”

What “at Babylon” is meant to signify will become clear on the following day, where Agricola of Chalon is discussed.

[Col. 0850B]

AQUICINCT begins:

> “At Hamaticum”—by which he means Hamage, the priory adjoining the abbey of Marchiennes—“the burial of Saint Eusebia.”

That correction, I do not know by whom it was added, could be called superfluous; Hamaticum appears to have been used interchangeably with Hamagia.

MARCHIENNES begins:

> “The burial of Saint Eusebia the virgin.”

MATRICULUM–CARTHUSIANS–UTRECHT briefly treat of Hilary, Tatian, and Heribert. Then:

> “Of Niretinus the confessor with his companions, whose marvelous deeds are read.”

Unless I am mistaken, this is Boniface, who is discussed in the Acts.

CAMBRAI, of the Conventuals:

> “At Cologne, of Heribert the prelate, Lucius the bishop, and Eugenia the virgin.”

I do not understand the basis for such a company among these saints.

STROZZI and MEDICI:

> “At Ravenna, the birthday of Saint Agapitus, archbishop and confessor, who was the ninth to rule and flourished after Apollinaris. Also Saint Gertrude.”

This too is recorded on the following day, and much more correctly.

ABDINGHOFEN:

> “At the city of Aquileia, the passion of Saint Felix the martyr.”

He has remained unknown until now.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins:

> “At Cologne Agrippina, the birthday of Saint Heribert, archbishop and confessor of the same place, who sat for twenty-three years, two months, and twenty-two days, and whose buried body rests across the Rhine in the monastery of Deutz, which that prelate had built from its foundations during his lifetime and consecrated in honor of the blessed Virgin Mary.”

Its account of Hilary is pure; that of Cyriacus is greatly interpolated from Ado. It follows with Patricius. Finally:

> “In Scotland, of Saint Boniface the bishop and confessor.”

GREVEN:

> “Of Isicius, bishop of Vienne and confessor. At Rome, of Alexander the bishop.”

See Those Omitted.

> “In Scotland, of Boniface the bishop. Of Albanus the bishop and confessor.”

Whether this is Abbanus or Abbenus, I do not know.

> “Also of King Colloquillus. Of Saint Kinitimus.”

That is, I think, of Boniface.

> “Of Abraham the priest and anchorite, and of Mary, his brother’s daughter, a penitent. In Ireland, of Finnian the abbot and confessor. On the same day, of Eugenia the virgin.”

Could this be Eusebia?

MOLANUS:

> “On the same day, the birthday of Saint Heribert, archbishop of Cologne. His venerable body rests honorably in the monastery of Deutz, across the Rhine; that holy man himself raised it from its foundations in honor of the holy Mother of God.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “Of Abraham the priest,” etc., as in Greven.

In later editions, concerning Heribert:

> “On the same day,” etc.

At Rees, in the territory of Cleves, the feast of Saint Dentinus, a boy of seven years. At Marchiennes, the burial of Saint Eusebia the virgin. On the sixteenth day, of the holy martyrs Sabinus and Papa.

Concerning Sabinus, see Those Omitted. Patricius is relegated to the end.]

[Col. 0847]

[Note: [Col. 0847B]

In the Carolingian autograph there was never any mention of Saints Hilary and Tatian. The Dervensis codex is silent concerning them and begins the article with Cyriacus. Moreover, in the Pratensis the whole article, from beginning to end, is affected by erasure, and wherever those saints were to have their place, the entire passage was written in smaller letters.

Nor do the Herinien. and Tornacen. codices mention those saints; these were generally the standard by which Soller judged the Pratensis. Here I ask Soller why, while preferring the Pratensis, he departed from his own principles. In the Pratensis there was an erasure, while the other codices varied. With these two arguments alone he judged everywhere that the Pratensis codex had been interpolated.

Therefore, at this point—or nowhere—his rule ought to have been applied. Yet Sollerus gives the entire article: it is wholly Usuard’s, pure Usuard. The censor says not even a word about the erasure. I suppose this is because he was informed that there was no difference in the handwriting there, and that Usuard deserved praise for having followed the example of distinguished writers, neither considering an erasure disgraceful in a written work nor fearing it.

Why, in the same matter, Sollerus did not always maintain the same attitude toward the Pratensis, I would rather not know than maliciously suspect anything about the love of truth with which he professes to burn.

BOUILLART.]

At Aquileia, the birthday of blessed Hilary the bishop and Tatian the deacon, who, under the governor Beronius, after the rack and other tortures, completed their martyrdom together with Felix, Largus, and Dionysius. At Rome, the passion of Saint Cyriacus the deacon, who, after a long imprisonment and torment, was drenched with molten pitch, stretched out on a frame, and pulled apart; then, beaten even with sinews and clubs, he was finally beheaded, together with Largus, Smaragdus, and twenty others, by order of Maximinus. Their feast, however, is celebrated on the sixth day before the Ides of August, when their bodies were taken up by blessed Pope Marcellus and buried with honor. At Arvernis, the burial of Saint Patricius the bishop and confessor.

XVI Kalends. The seventeenth day.

[Note: [Col. 0851]

Taken from the Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0851A]

The Pulsanensis, through a scribal error, reads *Caesarea* for *Scotia*; one copy writes *Scythia*. Refer here the *Scotia* of Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck, *Scochia* in Muneratus, and *Schocia* in the others. In Greven the title “bishop” is lacking; in Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck, “confessor” is lacking. The Pulsanensis reads *vigella erasoni*. Muneratus has *Migella*, Greven *Novigella*. Again, the Pulsanensis has *Geretrudis*, a form imitated by the other more recent codices.]

[Note: [Col. 0851B]

Bede and the Little Roman Martyrology treat of Patricius in wording not very different. Ado added a little of his own; our author copied Ado word for word. Rabanus departs somewhat from Bede in his manner of expression, and Notker from Ado; we thought it worthwhile to note this in passing.

Papebrochius skillfully extracted and arranged chronologically the sequence of deeds of the most famous apostle of Ireland from the disorderly accumulation of material, in the first work he undertook on the Acts of the Saints, where he allowed scarcely anything to remain wanting.

Some nevertheless complain that, from among the many Lives of Patricius, he preferred the one composed by Jocelin, which is farthest removed from the saint’s own time. Let them examine the reason for this choice in the preliminary commentary itself, sections 3 and 4; from these they will finally conclude what the aged emeritus still declares: namely, that he selected the Life which appeared to be less filled with fabulous marvels.

No account has today been taken of the Hieronymian copies, either by the ancient authorities or by the Usuardine codices, except the Pratensis, which—whether I should call it corrupted or altered—has this instead of Gertrude:

> “At the city of Nicomedia, of the holy martyrs Eugenius, Pamphilianus, Castor, and Serenus.”

They have been both wrongly connected and wrongly transferred to this day by some ignorant person, and indeed written over Gertrude’s erased announcement, as the distinguished Castellanus, an eyewitness who inspected the alleged autograph, informed me in a letter dated 31 May 1709.

As he himself believes, this happened because the Acts of the virgin were badly copied or misunderstood. Her birthday seemed to be postponed to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April; hence she was foolishly inserted in the list for that day, with two texts corrupted by one error, as will again appear on the following day.

Concerning Gertrude, see Henschenius’s dissertations prefixed and appended to the Life.

Our text agrees with Wandalbert’s metrical eulogy:

> “The eighteenth day shines with your name, Patricius,  
> compassionate teacher of the Scottish people through their towns.  
> On this day vows are also rendered to blessed Gertrude.”

] [Note: [Col. 0851C]

ANTWERP–MAJ.:

> “In Scotland, the birthday of Saint Patricius the bishop and confessor, who was one of the disciples of blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, and first preached the Gospel of Christ to that people. At Alexandria, the birthday of Saint Ambrosius, deacon of that church, who was renowned for the glory of his confession of the Lord. At the monastery of Nivelles, the burial of Saint Gertrude the virgin, whose illustrious deeds are recorded.”

ROSWEYDE, in second place:

> “At the city of Nicomedia, of the holy martyrs Eugenius, Pamphilianus, Castor, and Serenus. On the same day, the burial of Saint Witburga the virgin. At Nivelles, of Gertrude the virgin.”

ANTWERP–MAX., UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERG, DANISH, and the UTRECHT–BELGIAN edition insert after “virgin” concerning Saint Gertrude:

> “daughter of Duke Pippin, whose deeds are recorded.”

At the end:

> “At Chalon, the birthday of Saint Agricola the bishop and confessor.”

CENTULES:

> “At Alexandria, of Saint Ambrosius the deacon and martyr. In Scotland, of Saint Patricius the bishop and confessor, ordained and sent by blessed Germanus of Auxerre. At the monastery of Nivelles, of Saint Gertrude the virgin.”

BRUSSELS:

> “At Nivelles, the burial of Saint Gertrude, a virgin dear to God, daughter of Duke Pippin, who lifted blessed Gudula, her niece and our patroness, from the sacred font. At the very hour of her death she appeared at Trier to Saint Modesta the nun, and at that same hour of death, blessed Ultan, brother of Saint Foillan, saw Saint Patricius, leader of the soul of the blessed virgin Gertrude, present.

> “In Scotland, or Ireland, of Saint Patricius the bishop and confessor. He was the son of Conches, sister of Saint Martin of Tours, and one of the disciples of blessed Germanus of Auxerre. Pope Celestine sent him there, and he was the first to preach the Gospel of Christ to that people. But when he produced little fruit, he asked God for a sign by which they might at least be frightened into repentance. With his staff he marked out a large circle; within it the earth opened and immediately a very large and very deep well appeared. It was revealed to him that there was there a place of Purgatory, and that if anyone descended into it, no further penance for his sins would remain for him.

> “Thus he converted the whole people of that region to the faith of Christ and ruled over them for sixty years. When these years were completed, he died in the one hundred and twenty-second year of his age.

> “At Alexandria, of Saint Ambrosius of that church,” etc., as in ANTWERP–MAJ., above.

Concerning Agricola also, as stated above.]

HAGENAU is more generous than Brussels in embellishing Patricius and Gertrude. It makes her the sister of Charlemagne and records such things about him that they deserve to be omitted.

AQUICINCT and VICTORINUS have at the end:

> “At Chalon, of Saint Agricola the bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0853A]

PLESCHION:

> “On the same day, of Saint Gertrude the virgin and Saint Victorina.”

No Victorina is known to us today except the one counted among the Nicomedian martyrs in the Acts.

MARCHIENNES reads exactly as the Pratensis does. Hence our conjecture above was not wrong: that codex was taken from the alleged autograph. This would have become more evident if our predecessors had been able to procure the complete copy.

ALTEMPS:

> “At Alexandria, of Saint Ambrosius, deacon of that church, who was renowned for the glory of his confession of the Lord.”

FLORENTIUS treats of Gertrude in her proper place. He has:

> “In the city of Córdoba [one of the two codices seems to read *Cordula*], the passion of the holy martyrs Olympias and Maximianus under the Emperor Decius, as is found in the deeds of Saints Abdon and Senen. Vitellius, the deputy of Decius, ordered that their heads be struck with axes, and thus they gave up their spirit.”

They are relegated in the list of Those Omitted to 15 April.

[Col. 0853B]

RHEIMS, Church of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris:

> “At Alexandria, the birthday of Saint Ambrosius, deacon of that church.”

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION:

> “In Scotland, the birthday of Saint Patricius the bishop and confessor. He was one of the disciples of blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, and is said to have been the son of the sister of Saint Martin; he was the first to preach Christ in Scotland and to convert almost all Ireland to Christ through teachings, examples, and miracles.

> “At the monastery of Nivelles, of Saint Gertrude the virgin, daughter of Duke Pippin. Saint Amandus the bishop, together with her mother, placed the sacred veil upon her and appointed her over a community of many virgin nuns after her father Pippin had died. After she had governed them commendably, she departed to the Lord in the thirty-third year of her age.

> “At Alexandria,” etc., as in ANTWERP–MAJ.

> “At Chalon . . .” [Col. 0854A] also as above.

> “In Alexandria, of the martyrs Collegius the deacon, Rogatus, and Satyrus.”

Concerning these and those that follow, see Those Omitted.

> “In Campania, the birthday of the holy martyrs Quintus and Lucianus, Victor and Maurus. At Nicomedia, of the holy martyrs Apurilis and Servilus. On the same day, the translation of Saint Antony the abbot.”

BELINUS, after “preached Christ” concerning Patricius, adds:

> “and shone forth through the greatest miracles and virtues.”

GREVEN, concerning Ambrosius, as in ANTWERP–MAJ.:

> “Also of Theodulus, Cyriacus, and Dionysius.”

They are distinguished more accurately in the Acts.

> “Of Mary the martyr.”

See Those Omitted.

> “At Nicomedia, of Eugenius, etc. In Alexandria, of Collegius . . . In Campania, of Quintus . . . At Nicomedia, of Apurilis . . . At Chalon,” etc., as above.

> “In England, of Witburga the virgin. The translation of Saint Antony the abbot.”

MOLANUS: After “virgin,” he adds “daughter of Duke Pippin, whose illustrious deeds are recorded,” and then proceeds concerning Ambrosius:

> “And the birthday of Mary the virgin. Since she was the servant of a certain distinguished man named Tertullus, and refused on the birthday of his son to attend her master’s banquets, preferring instead to devote herself to fasting in the Christian manner, she was cruelly torn by lashes by that same master. But when this could not turn her away from the persistent service of Christ to the worship of idols, she was handed over to the public judge for punishment.”

This is almost a summary of what Rabanus and Notker relate more fully. Meanwhile the saint is transferred to 1 November.

> “At Lierre, the translation of Saint Gummarus, the distinguished confessor.”

He is especially honored on 11 October.

Concerning Agricola, in smaller type.

In other editions, after Nivelles, the word *transitus*, “passing,” is inserted in italics; the rest is as above. The same is done concerning Ambrosius, Agricola, and the translation of Saint Gummarus.

Finally:

> “At Donjon, the elevation of the body of Saint Regina.”

This belongs to 1 July, on which her feast is said in Those Omitted to be celebrated; there the elevation of another Regina at Flavigny is also noted from Saussay.]

[Col. 0849]

In Scotland, the feast of Saint Patrick, bishop and confessor, who first preached Christ there. [Col. 0851] On the same day, at the monastery of Nivigella, Saint Gertrude, virgin. [At Bouillart …: “he evangelized.” At Nicomedia, the holy martyrs Eugenius, Pamphilianus, Castor, and Serenus [Note: [Col. 0851A] Sollerius hesitates over whether he should call the manuscript corrupt or altered. Four holy martyrs are badly connected and wrongly transferred here. Gertrude has been expelled from her proper place and foolishly inserted among the saints of the following day; two texts have been corrupted by one error. And the man who shortly before calmly and patiently tolerated nine entire erased lines pours all these injuries into the erasure of a single line. What should I say to this? It is true that those holy martyrs were not mentioned in the Carolingian autograph, but whether they were badly connected or wrongly transferred here, by what argument will Sollerius establish it? Does he possess Acts that he can produce? I know that he will thrust the Hieronymian lists upon us; but in their oldest manuscripts not one of those whom Usuard mentions here is read. Nor was anything recorded on the preceding day. For in those lists, according to Henschenius: “At Nicomedia, Castor, Dionysius, Nonnus, Cyriaca, Milisa, Eugenia, Julianus, and Asclepiodotus.” Some manuscripts indeed announce Castor, others Serenus, and others, combining one from each of the two classes, Pamphilianus. What certainty can be extracted from that conflict of manuscripts? Perhaps Usuard had other lists; perhaps he combined both classes of Nicomedian martyrs on one day; perhaps he saw the Acts. Finally, I would rather conjecture anything than, like Sollerius, reject a manuscript that is in no way suspect without any argument. Concerning Saint Gertrude, shortly in the following article. BOUILLART.]]

XV Kalends. Day 18. [Note: [Col. 0853C]

Many manuscripts agree: Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp. and Max-Lubecana, Munerat., Belin., Greven., [Col. 0854C] Molan. Add Antuerp.-Max., Ultraj. and the remaining manuscripts of middling authority.]

[Note: [Col. 0853D]

It consists almost entirely of scribal errors. Some manuscripts read “and by her own” instead of “from her own.” Concerning Hierosolima, Jherosolyma, Jerusolima, Cappadocia, Caesarea, martyrdom, and so forth, see what was said elsewhere. Similar matters occur in Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., which read “relation” instead of “revelation.” In Munerat., “by divine revelation,” and “I completed” instead of “he completed.” In the Pratensis manuscript the announcement of Saint Gertrude from the preceding day has been added: “At the monastery of Nivigella, Saint Gertrude, virgin”; thus it is easy to see that this is an addition, both from a certain difference in the ink and from the more compressed characters used to express the whole announcement in the space left vacant after “he completed.” Nevertheless, the formation of the letters is very similar to the earlier writing, as the distinguished Castellanus, who reported the rest, testifies; and I readily believe this. Meanwhile, that manuscript had to be excluded even today from the number of the pure Usuardian manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0853D]

On 30 January we showed in passing that Alexander, recorded on that day by the author of the Roman Parvum, was adorned by the Viennese bishop with such a eulogy that he most clearly portrayed the bishop of Jerusalem commemorated today, from Rufinus, Book VI, chapter 29. This, then, is the most celebrated saint, placed on this day by the author of the Roman Parvum and accepted from him, as commonly happens; neither the Hieronymian lists, nor Bede, nor his followers remember him. Eusebius discusses Alexander in Book VI, in various chapters cited by Rosweydus, Henschenius, and Papebrochius; and Jerome follows Eusebius in On Illustrious Men, chapter 62. These, however, are the words of the Roman Parvum for this day: “Saint Alexander, bishop, who together with Narcissus assumed the governance of the Jerusalem church.” Alexander of Jerusalem could not, I think, be indicated more distinctly [Col. 0856A] even by a finger; and Adonis’s eulogy is no less clear, drawn from the celebrated Rufinus, Book VI, chapter 9, or from Eusebius, chapter 11. Notker copied it, and Our Author contracted it in the customary manner, as it appears in the text. Since the matter is so plain, we shall not linger over it; see Henschenius’s historical commentary, Catalogue of the Bishops of Jerusalem, p. 13, and also Ruinart in Sincere and Select Accounts, beginning at p. 114; Tillemont gives related material in volume III, beginning at p. 415. Wandalbert joins Alexander with Pigmenius, concerning whom more will be supplied in the Appendices.

“Bishop Alexander thrice five possesses the height,

And the presbyter Pigmenius purifies Rome with blood.”

] [Note: [Col. 0855A]

PULSANEN. appends to the pure text: “On the same day, Saint Pigmenius, bishop.” Unless I am mistaken, he means Pigmenius the presbyter and martyr. See the twenty-fourth of this month.

[Col. 0855B] ANTUERP.-MAJ.: “The feast of blessed Alexander, bishop and martyr, who, when he was already shining with the venerable grayness of extreme old age, was led to Caesarea during the persecution of Decius and shut up in prison; for his confession of Christ he was crowned with martyrdom.” The same hand adds in the margin: “On the same day, Saint Edward, king and martyr.”

ROSWEYD. after the text: “At Rome, Pigmenius the presbyter. At Nicomedia, twenty-three thousand martyrs.” See the Acts, where the number is ten thousand. I do not know from where the number in this manuscript has increased.

CENTULEN.: “The feast of blessed Alexander, bishop and martyr, who, while he was governing the church of Cappadocia and, in religious zeal, visiting the holy places of Jerusalem, was ordered by a voice falling from heaven to govern the Jerusalem church.”

BRUXELLEN. begins: “At Bethany, the raising of Lazarus after four days.” He is commemorated on 17 December. An eulogy of Alexander follows, slightly interpolated. [Col. 0855C] Then: “And at Rome, Saint Pigmenius, presbyter and martyr, buried beside the martyrs Saints Abdon and Sennen. On the same day, Saints Rogatus, Victor, and Lucian. Also Edward, king of England, who for Christ visited Rome as a pilgrim to the thresholds of the blessed Peter and Paul in the time of Pope Sergius; and in that same city, full of good works and almsgiving, grew old until the day of his death.” How awkwardly these items are connected, you will understand from the Acts. Finally: “At Metz, Saint Landricus, bishop of Metz and confessor, who was the son of Saints Vincentius and Waldetrudis and a relative of our patroness, blessed Gudula.” He is relegated among the Omitted Saints to 17 April.

HAGENOYEN. in the more extensively interpolated version of Alexander has, in second place: “At Bethlehem of Judea, the burial of Saint Joseph, spouse of blessed Mary, virgin [mother] of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh, and the Lord’s foster-father, who is highly commended by the Evangelists in the Gospel. This holy man showed great concern for Christ and his mother. By what death this holy man died, at what time, and in what place he was buried is completely unknown to most people.” [Col. 0855D] See the additions for the following day.

AQUICINCT.: “Also Saints Currentius and Timothy.” They belong to the class of Moorish martyrs.

PLESCHIONEN. and VATICAN no. 5949: “At Alexandria, Saints Collegius the deacon, Rogatus, and Satyrus,” or Saturus.

[Col. 0856A] REG. SUEC., which belonged to Prince Ursinus of Rosemberg: “At the city of Mantua, the burial of Saint Anselm, [Col. 0856B] bishop of Lucca and confessor.”

MARTRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJ.: “Alexander, bishop and martyr. Ancelinus [he means Anselm], bishop of Lucca.”

ALTEMPS.: “The feast of Saint Edward, king and martyr, whose death is attested as precious in the sight of the Lord by frequent miracles. On the same day, Saint Frigidianus, bishop and confessor.” His principal feast is his translation on 18 November.

FLORENTIN.: “The feast of Saint Anselm, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the feast of the most glorious archangel Gabriel.” In the Acts it is deferred to the twenty-sixth of this month.

LUBECO-COL. EDITION begins: “In Spain, the commemoration of Saint Gabriel the archangel.” The text follows. Then: “On the same day in Britain, Saint Edward, king and martyr.”

GREVEN.: “The venerable commemoration of the archangel Gabriel, the sponsor of our redemption. Pigmenius, Quartinus, Samphorus”—confused and dislocated names. “In England, Saint Edward, king and martyr. At Augsburg, [Col. 0856C] blessed Narcissus, bishop and martyr. Also the passion of Saints Luxorius, Cisellus, and Camerinus, martyrs.” They suffered in Sardinia on 21 August. “In Mauritania, blessed Surentius and Timothy. On the same day, the burial of Saint Apianus, bishop and confessor.” Concerning this Apianus, see the Omitted Saints. “Also Saint Speciosa, virgin.” She is commemorated on 18 July.

MOLAN. concerning the archangel Gabriel, Apianus, Speciosa, and Edward, is almost as Grevenus. Then, in smaller type: “At Augsburg, blessed Narcissus, bishop and martyr, who, after winning a new family for God in Rhaetia, departed after nine months for Spain, to the city of Gerunda, with Felix his deacon; there he won a great people for God for three years and completed the palm of martyrdom with Felix his deacon.” In other editions he omits Narcissus of Augsburg. In the Usuardian text, after “coming,” he inserts: “while Narcissus, bishop of that same city, already an old man, was governing the church”; and [Col. 0856D] after “governance,” he places “assumed with him.” Finally, in addition to the four named above, he adds: “On the eighteenth day, Saint Cyril, father and archbishop of Jerusalem.” In smaller letters: “He, a most ready defender of the apostolic doctrines, suffered the greatest persecutions from the Arians.” More could have been added about Cyril, that outstanding champion of the faith; see all this explained more fully and accurately in the Acts.]

[Col. 0853]

The feast of blessed Alexander, bishop, who, coming from Cappadocia, from his own city, to Jerusalem through a holy desire, afterward, by divine revelation, assumed the governance of that place; and after venerable old age was led to Caesarea and, during the persecution of Decius, completed his martyrdom because of his confession of Christ. [Bouillart adds: [Note: [Col. 0853C] This is the true place of Saint Gertrude. I am surprised that Henschenius and others could have been deceived, since they assigned the death of that holy virgin to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of this month. Usuard himself had been mistaken in the Carolingian autograph; but he conveniently corrected the error in his own copy: the same Acts that had deceived him, when examined more carefully, brought him back to the right path. The author of Gertrude’s life relates that, when the day of her death was approaching, she sent one of the brothers to the monastery of Fosses to ask Saint Ultan, an inhabitant of that place, on what day she would die. Ultan replied: “Today is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April. Tomorrow, during the solemn celebration of Mass, that servant of God and virgin of Christ will depart from the body.” Having received this message, Gertrude spent the whole night with the sisters [Col. 0854C] in psalms and prayers; on the following day, Sunday, she gave up her spirit. That Sunday, therefore, was the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April. Gertrude did not die in the year 664, as Henschenius thinks, or in 659, as the distinguished Baillet prefers, but in 658, when Easter fell on 25 March, the lunar cycle was 13, the solar cycle 23, and the Dominical Letter G. “Why,” you will ask, “do those same Acts report that she died on Sunday, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April?” The Acts, indeed, report this through a faulty transcription; but it is plainly evident that the reading which our Mabilio derived from the Fuldensis manuscript must be retained, since otherwise the author of the life is inconsistent with himself. For if Gertrude was to die on the day after the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, how could she have died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April? BOUILLART.] At the monastery of Nivigella, Saint Gertrude, virgin.]

XIV Kalends. Day 19. [Note: [Col. 0855D]

From Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0857A]

Pulsanen varies the wording somewhat, writing: “Who, originating from Syria, came to Italy and there, near the city of Penara, built a monastery, and became the father of many servants of God,” and so forth. Greven and Molan also write “Penarense”; our Acts have “Paranense.” Munerat was mistaken, for he has: “and there, near the city of Ariminum”; had he called it Spoletina, it could perhaps have been excused. [Col. 0858A] Praten. reads Quintili instead of Quintilli, perhaps from some copy of a Hieronymian manuscript; certainly he does not find it written that way in Ado. Munerat follows another inflection, making Quintilla, a woman’s name, stand for a man; several others do the same. The manuscript codices write “Brixa,” except Pulsan., which has “in the city of Brixia.” Greven and Molan have “Brixia.”]

[Note: [Col. 0857B]

John of Penara, or Panara, or, as our Acts write, Paranara, and elsewhere Pinnensis, is known neither to the Hieronymian lists nor to Bede, unless one wishes to conjecture that Rabanus’s words can be attributed to Bede. Rabanus certainly speaks here of John, but differently from our sources and not very accurately. In our series, therefore, he first recurs in the Roman Parvum: “In the city of Penara, blessed John, a man of great holiness.” Ado saw the life—or rather the surviving summary of the life—and derived his account from it; Notker abbreviated it somewhat, while Our Author contracted it into the customary wording. It seems certain to me that the matter proceeded in this order, not in the manner Henschenius reports, as though each writer had received a different eulogy from the same source. Wandalbert celebrates the same John thus:

“Twice seven [days] shine with John, the dweller of the desert.”

The Hieronymian copies mention the martyrs of Surrentum, or names closely resembling theirs; but as they are expressed in our text, they seem to have been taken from the Roman Parvum, with this difference: there “Martia” is written instead of “Marci,” and VIII instead of IX in the matter of Quintillus, as we said above. [Col. 0857C] Florentinius makes some observations about these martyrs, but Henschenius investigated the matter much more carefully and scrupulously. Nevertheless, after examining many manuscripts and weighing everything, he is forced to yield to the authority of our martyrologists—understand, the Roman Parvum, Ado, and the others—leaving aside the confusion that would disturb the sequence, change the names, enlarge them, or transpose them on the basis of the Hieronymian lists. Calocerus remains, brought forth by Usuard, I do not know from where; perhaps from the very long eulogy of Faustinus and Jovita on 15 February, which Rosweydus removed from the Adonian edition. Certainly Calocerus does not properly belong here, but seems to belong to 18 April, on which day he is recorded in the present Roman Martyrology and in the Acts. Castellanus carefully observed that the name Calocerus had been written in the purported Pratensis autograph over an earlier insertion or erasure. In any case, since all our manuscripts of the best authority, as well as the more recent ones, unanimously place him on this day, there is no reason to doubt the authenticity of the Usuardian text, either here or in the other announcements. Papebrochius had to say something about Calocerus in his Replies to Article XI, beginning at no. 56.]

[Note: [Col. 0857C]

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. are pure in the text, but append: “Also Saint Theodore, bishop. On the same day, Apollonius and Leontius, bishop.”

The PRATENSIS CODEX, distinct from the purported autograph, has in the margin: “At Vézelay, the translation of Saint Mary Magdalene.” This translation is also recorded in the very ancient calendar of Saint Mary Magdalene at Besançon and in the Appendices described below.

LOVANIEN. is mutilated in the passage concerning John. It is pure in the passage concerning the Surrentine martyrs. Then: “At the city of Brixia, Saint Calocerus the martyr, who entered before Hadrian and, seeing the instruments of torture empty and the ministers being tortured, said, ‘Great is the God of the Christians,’ and was brought to completion by him. On the same day, at Bethlehem of Judea, Saint Joseph, the Lord’s foster-father. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Theodore, bishop. On the same day, Apollonius and Leontius [Col. 0857D], bishops.” It means Apollonius, as ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC., and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. EDITION read; in these Appendices they entirely agree with the Lovaniensis and are purer in that they place the complete text first.

CENTULEN. has: “In Italy, near the city of Penara, Saint John, abbot, a man of great holiness. On the same day, at Surrentum, Saints Quintus, Quintillus, Quartilla, and Marcus with nine others.”

ANTUERP.-MAJ. differs little from the preceding.

ROSWEYD. appends to the text: “At Caesarea, Theodore the presbyter and martyr. Also in Africa, Apollonius the martyr and fourteen others. Landoaldus the confessor. At Bethlehem, Joseph, the Lord’s foster-father.”

BRUXELLEN., first: “At Bethlehem, Saint Joseph, foster-father of our Lord Jesus Christ. His own pupil on earth adorned him with twelve principal honors, which Lord Peter of Alliaco, bishop of Cambrai and later cardinal, described. [Col. 0858C] Near the city of Penara, blessed John the hermit, a man of admirable holiness, who, full of the prophetic spirit, foretold victories over tyrants to the most Christian emperor Theodosius.” It is sufficient to note this; the rest agrees. Concerning the Surrentines and Calocerus, it follows LOVANIEN. Then: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Theodore, bishop and martyr. On the same day, Apollonius, Leontius, and John, bishops. And at Ghent, Saint Landoaldus, archpresbyter and confessor, who, after blessed Amandus, administered the bishopric of Tongeren above the Meuse for nine years. During that time, instructing Saint Lambert, he led him into the way of God; and his body was translated to Ghent in the time of Pope Stephen VII.”

HAGENOYEN., pure in the text, has the addition concerning Calocerus already described. Then: “Also at Caesarea [Col. 0858D] in Cappadocia, Saint Theodore, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Apollonius and Leontius, bishops. Also at Chalon, Saint Agricola, bishop and confessor.” He is placed out of order.

AQUICINCT., after the pure text: “Also Saints Theodore, bishop, Apollonius, and Leontius, bishop. And Saint Landoaldus, confessor.”

PLESCHIONEN.: “In Africa, Saints Lucillus and Bassus, and Saint Leontius, bishop.”

MATRICULA-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJ. has: “The translation of blessed Mary Magdalene. John the confessor. Quintus and his fellow martyrs. Saint Joseph, the Lord’s foster-father.”

BIGOTIAN., marked P. 5: “Also Saint Theodore, bishop.”

CLUNIACEN.: “Also Theodore, bishop; Apollonius; Leontius, bishop.” I preserve the punctuation.

VATICAN., no. 5949: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, [Col. 0859A] Saint Theodore, presbyter. In Africa, Saints Lucillus and Bassus, and Saint Leontius, bishop.”

UGHELLIAN.: “Also Saint Theodore, bishop. On the same day, Apollonius, Leontius, bishop.” As above.

ALTEMPS.: “On the same day, Apollonius and Leontius, bishops. Also Saint Theodore, bishop. At Vézelay, the translation of Saint Mary Magdalene from the territory of Aix, from the place called Inpelliacus, where she is visited to this day by faithful peoples with fitting honor.”

STROZZ. and MEDIC.: “The feast of Saint Joseph [lacuna]. At Surrentum, Saints Quintus, Quintillus, Quartilla, and Marcus with eight others. At Brixia, Saint Calocerus the martyr. Also Saint Theodore. At Vézelay, the translation of Saint Mary Magdalene. On the same day, Saints Apollonius and Leontius, bishops.”

LUBECO-COL. EDITION begins: “The betrothal of the glorious ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of God, to Saint Joseph. At Bethlehem of Judea, the feast of Saint Joseph, foster-father of our Lord [Col. 0859B] Jesus Christ.” Concerning John, the Surrentines, and Calocerus, as above. It continues: “At the monastery of Vercelliacum, the translation of the body of blessed Mary Magdalene from Aquitania. At Caesarea, the feast of Saint Theodore, bishop and martyr. On the same day, Saints Apollonius and Leontius, bishops and confessor. Also Saint Lactinus, confessor.”

BELIN., first: “The feast of blessed Joseph, spouse of the most blessed Virgin Mary.” In second place, concerning Calocerus, whom he makes a bishop. Then concerning John and the Surrentines. Finally: “On the same day, Saints Apollonius and Leontius, bishops.” In another edition, “Apollonius [Col. 0860A] and,” where the following is added: “Also the translation of Saint Mary Magdalene.”

GREVEN.: “The betrothal of the glorious ever-Virgin Mary to Saint Joseph. The passing of that same blessed Joseph, spouse of the Mother of God, who also deserved rightly to be called the foster-father of our Savior. On the same day, Saints Apollonius, Bassus, Surentius, and Leontius, bishop. Also Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia and confessor. In Ireland, Saint Lactinus, bishop and confessor. Landoaldus, presbyter and confessor. The translation of blessed Mary Magdalene from Aquitania to the monastery of Vercelliacum.”

MOLAN.: “The feast of blessed Joseph, spouse of the most blessed Virgin Mary. On the same day, Saints Apollonius and Leontius, bishops. Also the translation of Saint Mary Magdalene. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Theodore the presbyter and seven others. The burial of Saint Landoaldus, bishop and confessor. He nourished the blessed bishop Lambert in childhood and instructed him in sacred letters. Also the feast of his companions, who rest honorably with him at Ghent, in the monastery of Saint Bavo.” In other editions he prefixed “Saint Joseph” to the text, but in italic letters. At the end, concerning Theodore, as above. Then: “At the port of Ghent, the burial of Saint Landoaldus, confessor and archpresbyter. He [Saint Landoaldus] nourished the blessed Lambert … Also the feast of his companions, Amantius the deacon, Adrian the messenger, and the others, who rest honorably with him at Ghent, in the church of Saint Bavo. On the same day, Saints Apollonius and Leontius, bishops. At the monastery of Vercelliacum, the translation of Saint Mary Magdalene.”]

[Col. 0855D]

The feast of blessed John, a man of great holiness, who, originating from Syria, came to Italy; and there, after building [sic] a monastery near the city of Penara, became the father of many servants of God for forty years and, famous for many virtues, rested in peace. On the same day, at Surrentum, Saints Quintus, Quintillus, Quartilla, and Marcus with nine others. At the city of Brixia, Saint Calocerus [Note: [Col. 0855D] Not only the name Calocerus, as Castellanus noted, [Col. 0856D] but the entire space from “the saints” [Col. 0857A] to the end has been erased. Nevertheless, this does not prevent Sollerius from thinking that the text of the Usuardian manuscript is pure. Nor is this without justification, since the same hand wrote it. But it is worth knowing why he accords so much honor to the Pratensis manuscript: namely, because all the manuscripts of the best authority unanimously place Calocerus on this day. The order of the argument may perhaps seem reversed, especially since in Sollerius the Pratensis manuscript holds first place by virtue of its antiquity. BOUILLART.] martyr.

XIII Kalends. Day 20. [Note: [Col. 0859]

From Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0859C]

It consists almost entirely of scribal or typographical errors. He wrote “to the Colossians,” although the manuscripts commonly read “to the Colosians”; Munerat’s “to the Collocensians” is worse. Likewise, with the Pratensis I wrote “anachoreta,” although the manuscripts have “anachorita”; Tornacen. has “anacorita.” Again, most manuscripts have “Chutbertus,” though I think “Cuthbertus” should be read; Bede has “Gutbertus,” Rabanus “Chudbertus,” and Tornacen. [Col. 0860C] “Cutbertus.” The remaining forms—Syria, Cerilli, and “all” instead of “the whole” in Munerat—need not be noted, nor does his “Nulfranni” instead of “Vulfranni,” as all the manuscripts have, whatever the Pratensis may have written, namely “Vulframni,” which may perhaps be the correct spelling, although we prefer “Wulfranni,” but not “Wlfranni,” as others read.]

[Note: [Col. 0859C]

Archippus’s commemoration is found in the Roman Parvum, the customary guide of Ado; hence it seems to me to follow that it should likewise exist in Ado himself, since he very rarely omits those whom he found in the manuscript copied at Ravenna. Mosander nevertheless thought it appropriate to add an asterisk, a sign, namely, of exclusion from the genuine text of Ado; Rosweydus, following him, relegated it to the appendix. Whether they did this rightly or wrongly is not for this place to examine. My conjecture is strengthened meanwhile by the fact that Notker, who customarily adheres closely to Ado’s footsteps, also mentions Archippus, and does so in almost the very words that Mosander and Rosweydus denied to the Viennese martyrologist. These are the words of the Roman Parvum: “Archippus, fellow soldier of the apostle Paul.” Notker added the title “bishop.” Concerning this, and also concerning the crown of martyrdom, Henschenius seeks the testimony of the ancients but does not find it; Tillemontius does not find it either, volume I, p. 289. Paul himself calls him his fellow soldier when writing to Philemon, and speaks of his ministry when writing to the Colossians; hence the formula in our text was added. Chutbertus, or Cuthbertus, of Lindisfarne, is mentioned by name only by Bede, who calls him Cutbertus, as we said above. A distinguished eulogy was added by Ado, taken, as he declares, from the very Life written by Bede; you will find it in our Acts. Usuard copied almost the whole of Ado’s eulogy, and Notker copied it entirely. Rabanus composed another on his own initiative. Wandalbert sings only of Cuthbert:

“On the thirteenth, shining with Cuthbert’s praise,

the English peoples are led through mystical joys.”

The Syrian martyrs were most probably drawn by Usuard from some Hieronymian manuscript; Notker also mentions them, but in different wording, adding after Eugenius “Serapion, Victoricus, and others,” without specifying the number. In the Acts, Henschenius added, besides Serapion and Victoricus, five other companions, naming them individually, but found nothing concerning their deeds. Wulfrannus is unknown to Bede, the Roman Parvum, Rabanus, and Notker; Florentinius assigns him to the Hieronymian manuscript of Lucca. It is highly probable that Usuard changed only the day, transferring Wulfrannus from 23 April in Ado to this day, his actual day of death. I would not presume to determine by conjecture what moved him to select this particular day; but the cited Lucchese manuscript reveals itself, formerly belonging to Fontenelle or Saint Wandrille, since it alone discusses Wulfrannus; and the older manuscript of Echternach shows itself to be English when it adds at the end: “Saint Cuthbert.” If you wish to accept the day of commemoration from the former manuscript, I shall not object, although it is certain that Wulfrannus does not belong to the genuine Hieronymian lists, as Florentinius admits. Meanwhile, I think it so certain that the list, as we have presented it, is entirely Usuardian that this cannot be disputed. See Henschenius’s commentary and the Acts illustrated by him; compare them with Mabilio’s Observations in the third Benedictine century, part I, beginning at p. 355, and, if possible, reconcile the opinions of both with that of Cointius concerning the year 704.]

[Note: [Col. 0861A]

PULSANEN., somewhat mutilated in the text, adds at the end: “On the same day, the vigil of Saint Benedict, abbot.” Below it will become clear that this was proper to certain Italian monasteries, from the Pleschionensis.

ANTUERP.-MAJ. begins with Cuthbert from Ado: “In Britain, the feast of Saint Cuthbert, who, from being a hermit, became bishop of the church of Lindisfarne and led an entire life, from childhood to old age, distinguished by signs of miracles. When his body had remained buried for eleven years, it was found incorrupt, as though the man had died at that very hour, together with the garment in which it had been covered. Saint Bede the presbyter writes this in the little book on his Life. On the same day, Saint Archippus, fellow soldier of the apostle Paul. At the monastery of Fontenelle, Saint Wulfrannus, bishop, a man distinguished in miracles and learning.” Ado has this account of Wulfrannus on 23 April. I do not know the reason; certainly his profound silence concerning this saint on that day is unjustly criticized by Mabilio in the Benedictine Acts, at the place cited in the Observations.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. are pure, except for the final formula of the announcement, which they read: “At the monastery of Fontenelle, Saint Wulfrannus, bishop and confessor.”

ROSWEYD. alone falls short of purity here. It has: “In the district of Rouen, Saint Vulfrannus, bishop of the city of Sens.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJ., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC., and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition insert after the eulogy of Cuthbert this passage from Ado: “His body, as Bede the presbyter writes, after having lain buried for eleven years, was found incorrupt with the garment in which it had been covered.” Then at the end: “At the monastery of Fontenelle, Saint Vulfrannus” (the manuscripts vary in their spelling), “bishop and confessor.”

BRUXELLEN. introduces new material and begins: “The first day of the world and the beginning of time, in which God created heaven and earth. On that day Joshua crossed the Jordan with the Hebrews on dry ground. On this day was Palm Sunday, when Christ drove the sellers from the temple.” It then follows the text concerning Archippus and the Syrian martyrs. Concerning Cuthbert, it is almost like the manuscripts of middling authority, except that it adheres somewhat more closely to Ado’s wording. At the end: “At the monastery of Fontenelle, Saint Wulfrannus, archbishop and confessor, whose body was later translated to Blandinium.”

HAGENOYEN. differs very little from the manuscripts of middling authority. It omits Bede’s title “presbyter” and inflects Wulfrannus as “Wolfframus.”

[Col. 0861D] CENTULEN. has, in its own style: “In Britain, the burial of blessed Cuthbert, bishop and confessor, a man of admirable holiness. At the monastery of Fontenelle, the burial of Saint Vulfrannus, formerly archbishop of Sens and confessor.”

AQUICINCT. adds “martyr” after Archippus.

PLESCHIONEN. ends with: “The vigil of Saint Benedict.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJ. is deficient in the martyrs [the text is corrupt] and gives the remainder very briefly.

FLORENTIN., first: “The feast of blessed Joachim, father of the glorious Virgin Mary and grandfather of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The CODEX OF MONTE SANCTO: “The feast or passion of Gertrude [Col. 0862B], virgin.” I do not sufficiently understand what this manuscript intends.

The LUBECO-COL. edition agrees almost with the text of the manuscripts of middling authority, but adds at the end: “On the same day, Saints Sabeanus and Pollio and their fellow martyrs.” Concerning them, see the index of the Omitted Saints.

BELIN. reads Arcippus instead of Archippus. In second place it discusses the Syrian martyrs. Then: “At the monastery of Fontenelle, Saint Vulfrannus, confessor. In Britain, Saint Gutbertus, bishop.”

GREVEN. appends to Wulfrannus: “This Vulfrannus, when he was bishop of Sens, crossed into Frisia and preached the Gospel of Christ. Returning from there, he took the monastic habit at the monastery of Fontenelle; completing his course in great holiness, he rested in peace in the year of the Lord 720. On the same day, Saints Joseph and Claudius.” See in the Acts how appropriately these two are joined. “At Metz, Saint Urbicius, bishop [Col. 0862C] and confessor. At Sens, Guericus and Ebbo, bishops and confessors.” See the Omitted Saints. “Heribertus, presbyter and confessor. When Saint Cuthbert, bishop, told him that he was going to depart from the world, he fell at his feet and begged him to obtain from the Lord that he might pass with him into eternal joys; and it happened as he had requested. Also, according to some, on this day there is the translation of blessed Mary Magdalene.” Concerning this, see the Appendices for the nineteenth.

MOLAN. concerning Wulfrannus: “The archbishop of Sens, at the monastery of Blandinium. Saint Joachim, confessor, father of the blessed Virgin Mary.” In later editions Wulfrannus’s announcement is changed. Concerning Joachim, as already stated. “On the twentieth day, the saints who are called the fathers slain at the monastery of Saint Sabbas.” Finally, in smaller type: “At Cologne, at the Steps, the death of Rixa, queen of Hungary, niece of Saint Anno, bishop.
