Although she was not canonized, her body is displayed on the great feasts.” She is discussed among the Omitted Saints on this day and on the nineteenth of this month.]

[Col. 0859]

In Asia, the feast of Saint Archippus, fellow soldier of blessed Paul, whom the same Apostle mentions in his epistle written to the Colossians. In Britain, the burial of Saint Cuthbert, who, from being a hermit, became bishop of the church of Lindisfarne and led an entire life, from childhood to old age, renowned for signs of miracles. In Syria, Saints Paul, Cyrillus, Eugenius, with four others. On the same day, Saint Wulfrannus, confessor.

XII Kalends. Day 21. [Note: [Col. 0861D]

Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Rosweyd., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. agree. The manuscripts of middling authority differ scarcely at all.]

[Note: [Col. 0861D]

The differences consist almost entirely in one or another transposition. The text has: “Blessed Pope Gregory writes”; Munerat has: “Gregory writes.” Likewise, instead of “he was illustrious,” Tornacen. has “he was illustrious” in the reverse order. In Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. “saint” is missing before Lupicinus. Enough has already been said concerning “anachoritae” and “anachoretae.”]

[Note: [Col. 0863A]

The most celebrated name of the great father of the black monks, Benedict, is commemorated on this day by all the ancient martyrologists. The Hieronymian copies remember him; thus the Echternach manuscript adds at the end of the list: “And Saint Benedict, abbot,” while the Corbie manuscript also has at the end: “And the burial of Blessed Benedict, abbot”; these words are placed first in the Lucchese manuscript. Bede is no less simple: “Saint Benedict, abbot”; one may compare with this the brief eulogy of Florus, which differs from ours. The Roman Parvum: “At the fortress of Cassino, Benedict, abbot.” Ado adorned the saint with a not lengthy discourse, the greater part of which Our Author borrowed; Notker took it all and added something, not very aptly connecting Cassino fortress with the city of Benevento. Rabanus was content to say that Benedict wrote the rule of the monks with great discernment. Henschenius treated at great length the deeds, translations, and miracles of the most holy patriarch; if these are insufficient, see the Acts of the Benedictines in the various places designated by Mabilio. Wandalbert’s encomiastic verse remains:

“Then, by faith and by the name of Benedict, the twelfth shines forth;

the monastic glory, under whose leadership the world rejoices.”

Serapion, noted here in second place, is not so familiar to me as he seems to have been to many others; nor is it entirely clear whether he first originated from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. I shall let you infer this from the various ways in which the Martyrologies record him. In the Hieronymian copies mentioned above, he is placed before approximately ten companions, in this manner: “In Alexandria, of Serapion the monk, Josephus, etc.” There can be no doubt whatever that a martyr is commemorated here.

Now take the text of the Little Roman Martyrology: “And of Serapion the anchorite.” Ado speaks in the same sense: “On the same day, of blessed Serapion the anchorite.” Here I understand a confessor, known to Ado by name alone, without any distinction of homeland, age, or dwelling-place; thus you are wholly unable to know which of several Serapions those authors mean. Rabanus and Notker do not dispel the darkness. Notker marks Alexandria and speaks in such a way that he seems to have followed the Hieronymian Martyrologies, although he had read in Rabanus, “the burial of Serapion.” What of our author? I admit that he too reads Alexandria, but the entire sense makes it clear that some confessor named Serapion is intended. Whom, I ask? The Arsinoite? The Sidonian? The bishop of Thmueos, concerning whom Henschenius writes on this day? Or the man who, in Baronius’s view, suffered exile at the hands of the Arians? Or Sindoneus, or the Sindonite, mentioned by Bollandus on 23 January, p. 508, col. 2, and hitherto, I do not know by what accident, omitted from our Acts? Here I raise many questions that may provide material for a more laborious investigation on 21 October. See Henschenius here, and Tillemont briefly in volume VIII, p. 618, and elsewhere.

Ado was the first to record Lupicinus, content with a brief eulogy, which Usuard truncated in its second part. Notker added much of his own from the Life itself, unless I am mistaken; this Life, written by a contemporary, is reproduced in the Acts. For the genuine simplicity of Usuard’s text, the cited manuscripts and printed editions, both, are entirely sufficient.

### Note: [Col. 0863B]

Pulsan., out of singular reverence, as I think, for the patriarch, expresses himself about Benedict as follows: “At the castle of Cassinum, of the most holy confessor and abbot Benedict.”

Belinus likewise departs from purity only in writing “of the most blessed.”

[Col. 0863C] Antuerp.-Max., Ultraj., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., Danic., and the Ultraj.-Belg. edition are also pure, with very few exceptions—namely, those words which they add: “In the second book of the Dialogues the blessed man writes, etc.”

Centulen. also inserts the words about Benedict already mentioned. In Serapion it is pure. It excises the brief eulogy of Lupicinus. Then, at the end, it has its own local notice: “At the monastery of Centula, the translation of Saint Vigor, bishop [of Bayeux] and confessor.” See the Omitted Saints, where this is referred to 1 November.

Antuerp.-Maj. adds about Benedict, “as Ado wrote in the books of the Dialogues.” It agrees with the text concerning Serapion. “And in the territory of Lyons, of Saint Lupicinus, abbot of the Virenses [Jurenses], whose life was illustrious for holiness and glory in miracles. His body is honored in the territory of Besançon, at the monastery of Latona.” This is the second part of Ado’s eulogy, cut away by Usuard, in which, however, one reads *Laocense*; [Col. 0863D] others write *Lauconense*; Mosander, *Lacionense*. Let the Acts be consulted.

Bruxellen. agrees with the manuscripts of the middle class. It is pure in Serapion; concerning Lupicinus it reads: “In the territory of Lyons, of Saint Lupicinus, magnificent abbot of the Virenses. His Life. And his body is honored in the territory of Besançon, in the monastery of Laocense.”

Hagenoyen. has this distinctive feature: it includes almost the whole life of Saint Benedict in a not lengthy encomium, in these words:

“This man, while still a young man, abandoned the secular schools and devoted himself to the divine schools. And when he felt temptations, he threw himself among nettles and brambles, and was cured. Only the Roman [Romanus] knew that he was hiding alone in a cave for three years, and he supplied him with food. This man shone with the spirit of prophecy and wrote rules for monks. He received from the Lord an exceedingly great discernment of the unclean. Having become abbot, he was stern toward dissolute brothers according to the rule; therefore, when they offered him a glass vessel containing poison, he shattered it by the sign of the cross. He went to the place of his solitude, where afterward he became renowned for many virtues, on account of which many came to him daily, and for that reason he built twelve monasteries there. He was also singular in the grace of contemplation, and saw spiritual visions: that is, he saw the soul of his sister Scholastica and of Germanus, bishop of Capua, carried into heaven by angels. The Lord also revealed to him a year beforehand the day of his departure, and he did not conceal it from the brothers. Six days before his death he began to languish from fevers; on the sixth day he had himself carried into the oratory and his grave opened, and then received Communion. Among the hands of his disciples, with his hands raised toward heaven, he breathed forth his last spirit amid words of prayer.”

[Col. 0864B–C]

Ambian.: “On this same day, the translation of Saint Firminus, bishop and confessor.” He is celebrated on 25 September.

Matric.-Carthus.-Ultraj.: “Of Benedict the abbot. Of Serapion the anchorite. Of Lupicinus the abbot, brother of Saint Romanus the abbot.”

The Lubec.-Col. edition differs scarcely at all from the manuscripts of the middle class.

[Col. 0864D] Greven.: “Of Joseph. Of Ammon.” From the Hieronymian Martyrology: “In Ireland, of Enda the abbot. Of Amos, hermit and confessor.” This is referred to the Omitted Saints under 4 October. “At Rome, of Felicitas the widow.” Under 23 November. “Here God made the lights of the world. Also of blessed Benedict the monk, concerning whom Gregory reports in Dialogue 3 that, although young in age but advanced in conduct, he was thrown by the Goths into a heated furnace and shut in, and was found completely unharmed the following day.” This must be referred to 23 March.

Molanus treats only this Benedict, identifying Gregory’s passage more precisely, namely Dialogue 3, chapter 18. In other editions: “On the twenty-first day, of Saint James, father and confessor, bishop.” Concerning him, see our Acts.

[Col. 0863]

At the castle of Cassinum, the birthday of Saint Benedict the abbot, whose life was glorious in virtues and miracles, as blessed Pope Gregory writes. In Alexandria, of blessed Serapion the anchorite, a man of great virtues. In the territory of Lyons, of Saint Lupicinus the abbot, whose life was illustrious for holiness and glory in miracles.

### XI Kal. — Day 22

#### Note: [Col. 0865]

Taken from Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.

#### Note: [Col. 0865A]

It returns to very little. In place of the city, Herinien. and Muneratus read “the city.” Praten. has *Byterris*; Tornacen., worse, *Biternis*. What remains is the various form of *Afrodisius*: Praten. has *Afrosidii*; Herinien., *Afradisii*; Munerat., *Affrodisii*, which Greven. also reads. Molanus, I think, has it best: *Aphrodisii*, while nevertheless preserving the spelling of almost all the manuscript codices, which I see has also been preferred in the Acts.

#### Note: [Col. 0865A]

Aphrodisius, or Afrodisius—however one finally writes it—I cannot explain the name. Whether he was Egyptian, Greek, or Roman is nowhere transmitted. This is certain: he was first discovered by Usuard and entered into the sacred calendars. I think this was done from the Acts of Saint Paul of Narbonne, where it is briefly said that he was ordained in his place at Béziers, as Henschenius shows here. He observes that these are nearly all the things that can safely be said about Saint Afrodisius, since other narratives are not free from errors; he rightly judges that several such accounts, from Maurolycus, Galesinius, and others, must be rejected.

Moreover, all the more ancient martyrologists—Hieronymus, [Col. 0865B] the Little Roman Martyrology, Florus, and Ado—as well as Rabanus, Wandalbert, Notker, and later writers, commemorate Paul himself, not Afrodisius, on this day. In our Acts there is a long enumeration of the Martyrologies in which Paul is recorded on this day, and of others in which Paul is recorded on 12 December. But unless I am greatly mistaken, the entire cause of the difference must be attributed solely and exclusively to Usuard, from whom nearly all the others who place Paul on 12 December received it.

Ado included Paul’s eulogy among the Feasts of the Apostles; Notker transcribed it in full, adding a few things of his own. [Col. 0866A] Usuard’s authority, however, was either rejected or disregarded by Baronius and the other revisers of the modern Roman Martyrology. The name of Afrodisius of Béziers was entirely removed from the Martyrology, and Paul of Narbonne was restored on the basis of the agreement of the Hieronymian copies, the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and the others.

I would not, with the Utrecht Carthusian Calendar, suspect that Baronius doubted whether Usuard had substituted Afrodisius for Epaphroditus; for, when the characteristics of both are distinguished, the difference is perfectly clear. Meanwhile, after Afrodisius of Béziers was excluded, Epaphroditus of Terracina took his place. As for us, there seems to be no possible controversy about Usuard’s true reading, since all the codices agree with the calendar. And although the Paul of Narbonne mentioned does not properly belong to Usuard’s present text, it has nevertheless seemed appropriate to append here Wandalbert’s couplet about him:

“On the eleventh Paul the bishop bestows pious light,

And Narbonne rightly exults in its own master.”

### Note: [Col. 0865B]

Pulsanen. appends to the pure text: “Also of Saint Paul the confessor,” omitting the title of bishop, as do other codices, especially the Hieronymian ones.

Antuerp.-Maj.: “In Gaul, in the city of Narbonne, the birthday of Saint Paul, bishop and confessor, whom the blessed Apostles, ordained bishop of the city of Narbonne, sent there. At Corinth, of blessed Dionysius the bishop, whose learning and grace, which he possessed in the word of God, many enjoy to this day.” This Dionysius is the Corinthian one, whom other codices also mention; he belongs to 8 April. The codex continues: “In the city of Béziers, the burial of Saint Afrodisius, bishop and confessor.”

Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., and Ughellian. differ from the other Usuardine codices, for they read:

“In Gaul, in the city of Narbonne, the birthday of Saint Paul, bishop, disciple of the Apostles, who was baptized by blessed Paul, sent into Gaul, and honored with episcopal dignity at Narbonne. In Africa, of Saturninus and nine others.”

The whole of Usuard’s text is absent.

Rosweyd., after the text: “In Africa, of Saturninus the martyr and nine others. Of Alexianus the deacon.”

Antuerp.-Max., Ultraj., Leyden., Lovanien., Alberg., Danic., and the Ultraj.-Belg. edition place first, with the three cited above: “In Gaul, in the city of Narbonne, the birthday of Saint Paul, bishop, disciple of the Apostles, [Col. 0865D] who was baptized by blessed Paul,” etc. Second, they have the blessed martyr Saturninus and his nine companions. Third and last, they append the pure Usuardine text.

Centulen. has the following: “In Gaul, in the city of Narbonne, of Saint Paul, bishop and confessor, whom blessed Paul the Apostle ordained and sent there. At Corinth, of blessed Dionysius the bishop, whose learning and grace, which he possessed in the word of God, many enjoy to this day. In the city of Béziers, of Saint Afrodisius, bishop and confessor.”

Bruxellen. also begins with Paul, whose eulogy it somewhat interpolates from Ado. It places Afrodisius second and is pure in that entry. Third it records Dionysius, as above. Finally: “In Africa, of blessed Saturninus and nine others.”

Hagenoyen., concerning Paul, as Antuerp. above. Afrodisius follows, as in the text. In third place, Saturninus and his companions. Finally: “Also of the martyr Fidelis.” He is celebrated on the following day.

[Col. 0866C] Pleschionen.: “In Africa, of Saints Fidelis, Saturninus, and nine others.”

Matric.-Carthus.-Ultraj.: “Of Afrodisius, bishop and confessor.” It then notes in the margin that in the Roman Martyrology Epaphroditus is placed in place of Afrodisius.

Vatican., numbered 5949, omitting the text, reads: “The birthday of Saint Paul the bishop, who, when he was going to Spain to preach, was left by the blessed Apostle Paul in the city of Narbonne. Having diligently fulfilled the office of preaching, he rested, crowned and renowned for miracles.” See what will be said under 12 December. It continues: “In Africa, of Saints Fidelis, Saturninus, and nine others.”

Florentin., at the end: “At the aforesaid Narbonne, of Saint Paul, bishop and confessor. In Africa, of the holy martyrs Saturninus and nine others.”

The Lubec.-Col. edition begins: “In Gaul, etc.,” as Antuerp. above. It continues: “In Africa, of blessed Saturninus and nine other martyrs, who were killed for the name of Christ.” In third place it adds the pure text.

The first edition of Belinus has exactly what we described above from Antuerp.; but in the second, an additional text is supplied: “At Septiviavia [Septimania], in the city of Bituris, etc.”

Greven.: “In Africa, of Saturninus, Dieronius, and eight other martyrs. Also of Arion.” Consult Florentinius and the Acts on this day concerning these. “Of Thomas, count of Lancaster and martyr.” See what is said about him in the index of the Omitted Saints. “Of Alexianus the deacon. At Rome, of Theodula the martyr.” Since she is unknown, she is passed over. [Col. 0867A] “Also, according to some, on this day, the birthday of Saint Paul of Narbonne, who is placed on the day before the Ides of December. Of Catherine, widow and virgin.” I am surprised that she was not noted among the Omitted Saints, since she is expressly placed on this day in the Roman Martyrology. See the Acts under 24 March.

Molanus has the same addition concerning Paul of Narbonne that we gave from Antuerp.; he further appends: “On the same day, at the monastery called Eike, of the holy virgins Herlindis and Relindis, sisters, and religious women, glorious in miracles. At Troyes, the burial of Saint Camelianus, bishop.” Then, in smaller type: “Of Lea the widow, concerning whom blessed Jerome writes that, after her husband’s death, she was converted and became head of a monastery and mother of virgins. Of Catherine the widow, daughter of blessed Bridget, whom Urban [Col. 0868A] VI canonized. At Dijon, of Saint Hilary the confessor. Also at Carthage, of Octavianus the archdeacon and martyr, with many thousands of men and women, concerning whom Gregory of Tours writes in Book II of the History of the Franks, chapter 3, at the end.” Concerning Camelianus and Hilary, see the Omitted Saints. In the Later Additions Paul is omitted. Saturninus is as in the others. Camelianus is as in the first edition. It continues: “On the twenty-second day, of the holy martyr Basil, priest of the Church of Ancyra. At the monastery called Eike, the translation of the holy virgins Herlindis and Relindis, sisters.” Then, in different type: “At Parthenopolis, a city [Magdeburg of the Saxons], of blessed Margaret, said to have been crippled, a virgin of great endurance, whose life exists in a book.” She is omitted from the Acts.

[Col. 0863]

At Septimiana, in the city of Béziers, the burial of Saint Afrodisius, bishop and confessor. He was ordained bishop of that city by Saint Paul, bishop of Narbonne; distinguished by proofs of faith and adorned with merits of virtue, he rested in peace.

### X Kal. — Day 23

#### Note: [Col. 0867]

Thus Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Rosweyd., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan.

#### Note: [Col. 0867B]

In Rosweyd’s codex one reads *Frumentii et Frumentii*, with one of the words deleted. I read *Wandalica*, as it must altogether be written and read—a form belonging to us Germans and other related peoples in spelling and pronunciation; there is no need to say more about it. Praten., Pulsanen., Muneratus, and others write *Vuandalica*; Tornacen., *Uuandalica*; Belinus, *Vandalica*. Muneratus has *apostle* instead of *bishop*. Rosweyd’s codex incorrectly has *Honerifico*; Pulsanen. is not much better with *Honorio*; Belinus, *Honorico*; Munerat. and Greven., [Col. 0868B] *Honerico*. It is evident that Huneric, or Hunneric, is meant, as the name is written indiscriminately in both forms. Muneratus’s transposition, “they were crowned with martyrdom,” changes nothing in the sense. Belinus alone has *Theodoli* instead of *Theodori*, and it is likely that Baronius’s *Theodulus* arose from this. Grevenus and Molanus: “In the city”—the preposition is redundant. *Affrica*, *Aphrica*, *martirum*, *supplitiis*, and *Cesarea* are common errors. Rosweyd’s codex lacks the penultimate word, *sancti*.

#### Note: [Col. 0867B]

This illustrious company of African martyrs is entirely absent from the Hieronymian copies, genuine Bede, Wandalbert, and Rabanus. The first author found to have recorded it distinctly and clearly is the author of the Little Roman Martyrology: “In Africa, of the martyrs Victorianus, Frumentius, another Frumentius, and two brothers, who suffered under King Huneric in the Vandal persecution.” From this source Ado extracted the same company and adorned it with a brief eulogy. It has often been said and demonstrated that Usuard and Notker are followers and copyists of Ado. Here Notker transcribed the aforesaid eulogy with almost no alteration; our author inserted a few words of his own, namely, “as Victor, the African bishop, writes.” I consider it more than evident that the rest was received from Ado. You will find more about these martyrs in the Acts, with notes and illustrations. Among other things, the errors of various writers concerning the true homeland, arena, and age of these holy martyrs are corrected there; all of this is splendidly confirmed from the Acts of their glorious martyrdoms, as produced there from Victor of Vita.

From the Hieronymian copies Usuard derived Theodore, priest of Antioch, and Julian of Caesarea. The former is placed quite distinctly and is expressed by Notker in exactly the same words; the latter, however, was drawn from a certain group that greatly exercised Florentinius and Henschenius, both in determining the true names and in identifying the place of martyrdom—if indeed all the martyrs were real, as these codices assume. Since discussion of these matters does not belong here, let the reader consult the cited authors, for it would be worthwhile to know more. Meanwhile our author wisely omitted the crown of martyrdom. How Baronius could have learned with certainty that Julian was only a confessor, I cannot discover. It is enough for us, and more than enough, to have established the source and genuineness of Usuard’s text.

Wandalbert’s combination is quite remarkable: in his couplet he seems to join Felix the African with Theodore of Antioch and Julian of Caesarea as though they had been crowned at the same time, in the same place, and by the same martyrdom, although this occurs elsewhere as well. Thus he sings:

“Here Felix the tenth, and Theodore with Julian,

Adorn the day, worthy to be borne with outstanding praise of virtues.”

#### Note: [Col. 0867D]

Antwerp., Max.-Lubec., Ughellian., and eight other codices, which we customarily call of the middle class, are all completely pure in the first announcement; in the last two they fail to include Theodore and Julian.

Antuerp.-Maj. agrees almost entirely with the preceding codices, but reads, with Centulen., *Victorini*, and adds at the end: “In Africa, of blessed Imdelis”—he intended to say *Fidelis*, the companion of Felix.

Centulen. has the following: “In Africa, of the holy martyrs Victorianus, Frumentius, another Frumentius, and two brothers, who, tortured with the most savage punishments, were gloriously crowned. In Africa, of blessed Fidelis the martyr.”

Bruxellen. is nearly pure in Victorianus and his companions. It continues: “Also in Africa, the birthday of Saint Felix the martyr. Also at Antioch, of Saint Theodore, priest and martyr. In the city of Caesarea, of Saint Julian. And of Saint Faith the martyr.” This Faith seems to be the one celebrated on 6 October, as you have in the catalogue of the Omitted Saints.

Hagenoyen. is likewise pure in Victorianus and his companions; in second place he writes: “At Antioch, of Saint Theodoric [Theodore], priest and martyr, who was struck with many blows. Bound upon a bench, he was stretched so far that he appeared eight feet long. After this two burning lamps were placed against his side, and finally he was killed with the sword.” It should be considered whether Theodoric, or Theodoritus, of Antioch is not indicated here—the man who suffered under Julian the Apostate, concerning whom we deal with Usuard on 23 October. The codex then has the final announcement in pure form: “In the city of Caesarea, of Saint Julian.”

Pleschionen. and Vatican., numbered 5949: “At Antioch, of Saint Theodore the priest, Paul, Julian, and Sabinus.” See the Acts, where you will observe that these men have been wrongly joined together.

Altemps.: “At the monastery of Barking, of Saint Hilda the abbess. And on the following day.” In fact, she is celebrated on the following day and is called by others “Hildelitha.”

[Col. 0869B] Burdegalen.: “The discovery of Saint Lupus, bishop of Angers.” This is referred from the Omitted Saints to his natal day, 17 October.

The Lubec.-Col. edition inserts, in the third-to-last place: “In Africa, the birthday of Saint Fidelis the martyr.” The rest is sufficiently pure.

Greven.: “In Africa, of blessed Fidelis the martyr. Also of Piomolus [others, from the Hieronymian Martyrology, have Thiomolus], of Felix, and of Theodoric the martyr.” This is referred among the Omitted Saints to 23 October, where the Lubec.-Col. edition is wrongly cited, since it does not mention him. “Of Hilaria the widow.” Whether she was the mother of Saint Afra or another woman cannot yet be determined. See also the Omitted Saints.

Molan.: “In Africa, the birthday of Felix and twenty others.” Thus the first edition. In the others: “On the twenty-third day, of the most holy martyr Nicon and his ministers, his disciples, martyred together with him. At Bergues, the elevation of Saint Winoc the abbot.”

[Col. 0867]

In Africa, of the holy martyrs Victorianus, Frumentius, another Frumentius, and two brothers who, in the Vandal persecution, as Victor, the African bishop, writes, suffered under King Huneric. For the constancy of their Catholic confession, they were tortured with the most savage punishments and crowned with distinguished martyrdom. At Antioch, of Saint Theodore the priest. In the city of Caesarea, of Saint Julian.

### IX Kal. — Day 24

#### Note: [Col. 0869A]

From Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Rosweyd., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. All the codices of the middle class could also be added, as will be clear below.

#### Note: [Col. 0869B]

Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. incorrectly read “bishops” instead of “the priest Pigmenius”; Pulsanen. adds no rank. Again, Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. have *enutrivit* instead of *nutrivit*. In Greven. and Molan. the sacred letters are treated indifferently. All the codices read “brothers,” except Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. These also write *Syria* together with Tornacen. I restored *Phrygia* with Molanus, [Col. 0870B] although most codices—Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., and Greven.—read *Frigia*; Praten., *Phrigia*; Rosweyd., *Frygia*. I had almost forgotten to mention that Muneratus alone reads *Secundi* instead of *Secundoli*, as in the modern Roman Martyrology. Grevenus and Molanus differ from the others in placing Agapitus before Seleucus.

#### Note: [Col. 0869C]

The martyrologists cited on the preceding day, the Hieronymian copies, Bede, Florus, Rabanus, and Wandalbert, all omit Pigmenius. Others mention him; their constant leader is the author of the Little Roman Martyrology, by whom he was first named and recorded in these words: “At Rome, Pigmenius the priest and martyr, buried in the cemetery of Pontianus.” Not content with this, Ado composed a long eulogy, probably from the Acts of Saint Bibiana, which in this part are at least very corrupt. Bollandus had once seen them and noted, under 4 January in the entry for Dafrosa, that the Acts of Flavianus, Pigmenius, Bibiana, and others had been mixed together, and were of such a kind that they required no small correction.

Henschenius, however, on this day, after examining with Baronius the fictions of the aforesaid Acts, especially those contained in Ado’s eulogy, judged them wholly unworthy of inclusion in our work. What if, then, Tillemont’s conjecture in volume V, pp. 119 and 633, should be accepted—that Epigmenius and Pigmenius, both recorded on this day in the modern Roman Martyrology, should be combined into one? Certainly the true substance of the matter would then remain, with the false circumstances removed. We refer further examination to the Acts under 14 September, where Crescentius the boy, baptized by the aforesaid Epigmenius, will be discussed.

Notker transcribed Ado’s entire history; our author abridged it in a manner consistent with his own brevity, but not equally with the truth. Thus far, the text is sufficiently clear and straightforward.

It is not equally easy, however, to connect Romulus with Secundolus, and indeed by a bond of brotherhood, as Usuard does. In all probability he is departing from the truth, and was himself the first craftsman of this confusion, as is plainly gathered from our Acts. For none of the Hieronymian codices—from which alone our author could have extracted these names—join Romulus and Secundolus in such a way that they even seem to be countrymen, although they express both names.

Romulus was torn away from a notable company of martyrs who were crowned with Timolaus in Caesarea of Palestine, as is reported from Eusebius in the Acts. Secundolus, however, belongs to an entirely different group that triumphed in Mauretania. Usuard may perhaps have seen Wandalbert, where he read this verse:

“Romulus fills the ninth, and likewise Secundolus.”

Meanwhile, whatever Usuard’s reading may be, it is genuine and entirely consistent in all the codices, both manuscript and printed, including the Centulen. codex, which, as will be evident in the Appendices, differs from the text only in phrasing and nevertheless omits the title “brothers.” What moved Baronius to substitute *Secundus* for *Secundolus*, I cannot divine either.

Seleucus and Agapitus likewise derive from the Hieronymian copies, from which they were placed by our author and in the Acts without any title, although Baronius makes Seleucus a confessor and Agapitus a bishop. For if this is the Agapitus who also appears in the Hieronymian Martyrologies under the name *Agapius*, he was truly a companion of Timolaus and therefore a martyr of Caesarea. Whether he was perhaps taken from elsewhere and was bishop of Synada, I do not see clearly enough. Florentinius is silent; Castellanus, in the Universal Martyrology, disagrees with Henschenius.

For the rest, Usuard’s reading as proposed in the calendar seems certain and beyond doubt, although perhaps only the penultimate announcement can be called true, since it is expressly placed first in all the Hieronymian Martyrologies. If any title is to be added there, it should certainly not be “confessor,” but “martyr.”

#### Note: [Col. 0869D]

All the codices cited for the purity of the text read “was killed in the Tiber,” [Col. 0870D] whereas Ado has the better reading, “was thrown down from the bridge”; this was imitated by Antuerp.-Max., Ultraj., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., Danic., and the Ultraj.-Belg. edition, in which alone they depart from Usuardine simplicity.

Antuerp.-Max. is mutilated here and reads: “At Rome, the birthday of Saint Pigmenius the priest. He nourished Julian the Apostate and impious man from childhood and instructed him also in the sacred letters. In Syria, the birthday of Saint Eleucus. On the same day, of Saints Romulus and Secundulus, who suffered for Christ in Mauretania.”

Centulen., in its own manner: “At Rome, of Saint Pigmenius the priest and martyr. In Syria, of Saint Seleucus. In Phrygia, of Saint Agapitus. On the same day, of Saints Romulus and Secundolus, who suffered for Christ in Mauretania.”

Bruxellen. presents Pigmenius’s eulogy with considerable interpolation from Ado. Then, in agreement with the text: “In Mauretania, of Saints Romulus and Secundolus, brothers and martyrs, who suffered for Christ. In Syria, of Saint Seleucius [it intends Seleucus]. In [Col. 0871B] Phrygia, of Saint Agapitus. Also of Saint Linus the martyr.” Concerning him, see the Omitted Saints.

Hagenoyen. has invented other material about Pigmenius, as fables are easily embellished with fables. We shall not linger over repeating it. In Romulus and Secundolus he is pure, except that he writes *Remuli* instead of *Romuli*. He continues: “In Syria, of Saint Seleucius the martyr. Also in Phrygia, of Saint Agapitus the martyr.”

In the comparison of the Aquicinctine codex with the second edition of Molanus’s Usuard, the following is found: “After Saint Agapitus he added: Also of Saints Agapitus, Romulus (or perhaps Romicius, for it cannot be read satisfactorily), and Rogatus.”

Victorin. and Reg. Suec., numbered 130, add: “On the same day, of Saints Victor and Corona.” You will find their proper day among the Omitted Saints, namely 14 May.

Pleschionen. agrees with Aquicinctine, expressing the matter more clearly: “In Africa, of Saints Agapitus, Romulus, and Rogatus.” How suitable this association is, see in the Acts, where they are assigned more properly to their respective places.

Matric.-Carthus.-Ultraj., with its customary brevity: “Of Pigmenius the priest and martyr, and of Romulus and Secundolus, brothers and martyrs.”

Vatican., no. 5949: “In Syria, of Saint Seleucius. In Africa, of Saints Agapitus, Romulus, and Rogatus.”

Codex Strozz.: “In Persia, of Saint Simeon the archbishop.” Concerning him, more is given among the Omitted Saints.

The Lubec.-Col. edition is pure concerning Pygmenius up to “instructed.” It then adds: “By him he himself was afterward thrown from a bridge into the Tiber for the faith of Christ. His body, found and gathered up, was buried in the cemetery of Pontianus, not far from Saints Abdon and Sennen. In Mauretania, of Saints Romulus and Secundolus, brothers, who suffered for Christ and the Catholic faith. In Syria, of Saint Seleucus the confessor. In Phrygia, of Saint Agapitus the martyr. In the city of Trent, the passion of Saint Simeon the boy and martyr.”

Belin., not entirely pure in the text, adds at the end: “In Persia, of Saint Simeon the archbishop.” This is the one celebrated on 21 April.

[Col. 0872B] Greven.: “Of Saturninus and Cyri(n)us, martyrs. At Trent, of blessed Simeon the boy, the new martyr, cruelly killed by the Jews in Holy Week in the year of the Lord 1475. God bore witness to his holiness through frequent miracles. Of Caninus the confessor. Of Jobia the virgin, daughter of the king of the Persians.” See the catalogue of the Omitted Saints.

Molan.: “In Persia, of Saint Simeon the archbishop.” In smaller type it continues: “At Trent, the passion of blessed Simeon the boy, the new martyr, cruelly killed by the Jews in Holy Week in the year of the Lord 1475. At Deventer, Florentius the priest died; he established the Brothers of the Common Life, and Thomas à Kempis wrote his Life.” This is in the first edition. The others have: “At Trent, the passion of blessed Simon the boy. At the monastery of Wasten, of Saint Catherine the abbess, daughter of blessed Bridget. On the twenty-fourth day, the pre-festival of the Annunciation.” Then, in different type: “At Caesarea, of the eight martyrs Timolaus, Dionysius, Romulus, Pausis, Alexander, Alexander, Agapius, and Dionysius. At Deventer,” etc. See the Acts concerning the Caesarean martyrs.

[Col. 0869]

At Rome, the passion of blessed Pigmenius the priest. He nourished Julian the Apostate from childhood and instructed him in the sacred letters; afterward Pigmenius himself was killed by him in the Tiber for the faith of Christ. In Mauretania, the birthday of Saints Romulus and Secundolus, brothers, who suffered for Christ. In Syria, of Saint Seleucus. Also in Phrygia, of Saint Agapitus.

### VIII Kal. — Day 25

#### Note: [Col. 0871C]

Today I find no Usuardine codex genuine and pure in every respect. In every respect, I say, for many fail in only a very few places, and in this way open a sufficiently convenient path toward recovering the text. Thus Belinus errs only by transposition, placing Cyrinus before Irenaeus; since he alone does this, he is certainly excluded from complete purity.

The Pratensis is marred by the error of writing *Theolae* for *Dulae*. Although three other codices—the Aquicinctine, Marchian, and Rosweyd codices—agree with it, it nevertheless represents Usuardine simplicity no better. Indeed, Rosweyd’s codex would be pure if it did not ineptly insert, in third place, “also the birthday of nine hundred saints.”

The Herinien. likewise departs from purity, expressing the first announcement as follows: “At Nazareth, a city of Galilee, as the Catholic faith believes, the angel Gabriel venerably salutes and adores and proclaims the Virgin Mary, who was to give birth to the Lord.” These words may also be found in some manuscript of Bede, included among Bede’s Appendices. [Col. 0872C]

In the Tornacen. Usuard, only the eulogy of Irenaeus is absent. In the Pulsanen. the name Hermelandus has been deleted. The same is true in Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., where the eulogy of Cyrinus has also been omitted.

Muneratus is disfigured by several errors, probably typographical; but its chief error is that, after the announcement of the Lord, it adds what is otherwise called the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ. Thus Grevenus and Molanus must be excluded, because they alone begin in this way: “Jesus Christ our Lord suffered.”

We shall present the additions of the other codices in their proper place. Meanwhile, from those already cited and those still to be cited, Usuard’s genuine simplicity is elicited by the fact that almost all agree in the sense of the calendar, as can readily be understood by comparing their omissions and additions. With these matters established—

#### Note: [Col. 0871D]

It remains to indicate the sources from which we believe Usuard drew his material. First, the following is the unanimous commemoration for this day in all the Hieronymian Martyrologies: “At Jerusalem, the Lord Jesus Christ was crucified.” They do not, however, agree so closely concerning his Annunciation or Conception; in the Epternacense this is entirely absent.

In Bede it is placed very briefly: “The Annunciation of the Lord.” Rabanus wrote: “The Annunciation of the Lord’s incarnation.” The Little Roman Martyrology has: “The Annunciation of the Lord and the Crucifixion.” Ado, however, removing the crucifixion and not following either the Hieronymian Martyrologies or the Little Roman Martyrology completely, expanded Bede somewhat by prefacing the city of Nazareth, where the mystery took place; in precisely that wording our author transferred it from Ado into his calendar.

By Ado I mean here Rosweyd’s Ado, not the one edited by Mosander, in which the crucifixion, the martyrdom of the Apostle James, the sacrifice of Isaac, and other types of Christ are joined together on this day. Notker combined Bede’s, Rabanus’s, and Ado’s words into one. Nothing concerning this solemnity can or should be added at length to Henschenius’s Commentary. Let us hear only Wandalbert:

“The angel announces the Lamb who will come on the eighth day.

And the Lamb himself is lifted upon the cross for the world’s death.”

The one who is listed here in second place is commemorated in the fourth and final place in the Little Roman Martyrology as follows: “At Sirmium, Irenaeus, bishop and martyr.” Ado also records him in that order, with an elogium which passed in its entirety into Notker, though Our Author somewhat adjusted it, while nevertheless taking everything from the same source. Ado undoubtedly once saw the Acts of Irenaeus of Sirmium. Neglected for many centuries, these were first brought to light by our John Gamans, then published and illustrated by Papebrochius; a Greek version, in more ornate language, was also added at the end of the volume. The Latin text itself was rightly counted by Ruinart among the *Sincera et Selecta*, at p. 432 onward; Tillemont may also be consulted, vol. V, p. 250 onward. Since the published Acts say that Irenaeus suffered on the eighth day before the Ides, that is, 6 April, it may once have been read as the eighth day before the Kalends of April. [Col. 0874A] The Martyrologies vary. I find no Irenaeus of Sirmium in the Hieronymian Martyrologies on 6 April; I admit that he is marked in Florus and Rabanus, indeed by both Notkers on both days. Nevertheless, I firmly judge that the ancient reading of our Martyrologists should be retained and not altered in any respect.

Cyrinus, called Quirinus by others, occupies the third place in the Little Roman Martyrology and in Ado. Here he is taken from Bede, in the same words used by Rabanus and Notker, who briefly recount what concerns him from the Acts of Saint Valentinus—or Marius—Martha, and Abachum. Usuard, however, departs from Ado, substituting another wording from the same source. Enough has been said elsewhere about the aforesaid Acts; see the commentary of Henschenius and the other material more recently given there concerning Cyrinus, of which Tillemont has a summary in vol. IV, p. 677.

Dula is found in the Hieronymian Martyrologies: “At Nicomedia, the feast of Dula.” The Little Roman Martyrology: “At Nicomedia, Dula, martyr.” Bede, and Rabanus from him: “The feast of Dula, a soldier’s maidservant, who was killed for her chastity.” Ado combined both texts, and Usuard and Notker claimed the combined text from him. Yet none of them thought that Theodola of the Hieronymian Martyrologies and Dula—the latter perhaps having received her name from her condition—were the same person. Castellanus nevertheless thought so in a brief note to the *Martyrologium Universale*; in my judgment that note should be removed, restoring to the text not the name Theola but Dula, which is what appears in the Roman Martyrology itself.

Hermeland, unknown to all the older authorities, was first introduced by Usuard. The correct reading is “on the island of Antrum in the Loire,” now swallowed by the river’s waters, not “on Andros,” separated by so many expanses of land, as the great Utrecht manuscript incorrectly reads. To distinguish it from the others, we commonly call this manuscript Rosweydi, or Rosweydinum.]

[Note: [Col. 0873C]

ANTWERP-MAJORITY: “At Nazareth, a city of Galilee, the Annunciation of the Lord, when the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee, to the blessed Virgin Mary, and said to her: ‘Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.’ When she saw him, she was troubled at his entrance and wondered what sort of greeting this might be. And the angel said to her: ‘Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.’ Glorified by so great a message, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, exalted above all by him who deigned to take flesh from her, she is blessed forever in reverence. At Sirmium, the feast of Saint Irenaeus, bishop and martyr, under the emperor Maximian. At Rome, Saint Quirinus, martyr.” In the last two entries it is pure. For “the island of Antrum,” it seems to read “Antico,” but this is corrected worse in the margin to “on the island of Andros.”

ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, DANIC, and the UTRECHT-BELGIAN EDITION, after “the Annunciation of the Lord,” add: “On the same day, our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified at Jerusalem and Isaac was sacrificed.” Likewise, after “At Rome,” they read “in the cemetery of Pontianus.” All are defective in the final account of the Annunciation.

CENTULEN: “At Nazareth, a city of Galilee, the Annunciation of the Lord, when, with the angel announcing and the power of the Most High coming upon her, the undefiled Virgin conceived the Son of the living God, whom she was to bear. On the same day at Jerusalem, the same God, the Son of God, was crucified by the Jews. At Sirmium, Saint Irenaeus, bishop and martyr. At Rome, Saint Quirinus, martyr. At Nicomedia, Saint Dula, martyr. On the island of Antrum, Saint Herkuland, abbot.” The true name is given above.

BRUSSELS, characteristically more expansive, heaps together much material here: “At Nazareth, a city of Galilee, the Annunciation of blessed Mary, ever Virgin. On the same day, the creation of Adam and his expulsion from paradise. Near the field of Damascus, Abel, the first martyr, was killed for righteousness. Christ praises him in the Gospel, and we name him every day in the canon of the Mass. On the same day, Melchizedek, the first priest, offered bread and wine to Abraham as a figure of the sacrament of the Eucharist. Melchizedek too has been inscribed in the canon of the Mass. On that day, Abraham offered his son Isaac to God upon the altar as a figure of the Lord’s Passion. Again on that day, the children of Israel passed through the Red Sea. On the same day, blessed John the Baptist was beheaded. At Jerusalem, our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified for the redemption of the world. And Saint James the Apostle, the Lord’s brother, was killed on that day. And Saint Peter was freed from Herod’s prison by an angel. At Rome, Saint Quirinus, martyr, who, after suffering many beatings, was killed by Claudius and thrown into the Tiber; he was found on the island of Lycaonia and buried in the cemetery of Pontianus, as is written in the passion of Saint Valentinus. At Smyrna [Sirmium], Saint Irenaeus, bishop and martyr, who, in the time of the emperor Maximian, under the governor Probus, completed his martyrdom after the harshest tortures by the cutting off of his head. At Nicomedia, Saint Dula, a maidservant . . . And the deposition of Saint Hermeland, abbot and confessor, whose glorious way of life is praised by the proclamation of miracles.”

HAGENAU: “At Nazareth in Galilee, the Annunciation of the Lord. Note that on this day many marvelous events occurred, which are recorded in these verses:”

Hail, festive day, which restrains our wounds.

An angel is sent. Christ suffers upon the cross.

Adam is made and on that same body [alternatively, time] falls.

Because of the merit of the tithe, Abel falls beneath his brother’s sword.

Melchizedek offers. Isaac is placed beneath the altar.

John the Baptist of Christ is beheaded [alternatively, Blessed John, Christ’s Baptist].

Peter is rescued; James is killed under Herod.

Many bodies of the saints rise again with Christ.

Yet the thief receives a sweet “Amen” with Christ [alternatively, through Christ]. [Col. 0875A] “That thief is crucified with Christ; there he confesses Christ to be the true God, asks for and obtains forgiveness, and, with his legs broken on the cross, gives back his spirit to the Creator. At Sirmium, the passion of blessed Irenaeus, bishop and martyr, etc.,” as in the text. For “the island of Antrum,” it reads “Nutrum.”

VICTORIN adds: “On the same day, Saints Taracus, Probus, and Andronicus.” They belong to 5 October.

MATRICHT-CARTHUSIAN-UTRECHT: “The Annunciation of the Lord’s Incarnation. At Rome, Quirinus, martyr. Hermeland, abbot.”

SWEDISH REGISTER, marked no. 130: “On the same day, Saints Taracus, Probus, and Andronicus. At Smyrna, blessed Thrasea, bishop and martyr.” It refers the reader to 15 October.

FLORENTINE: “On that day, the consecration of the cathedral church of Florence, Saint Mary of the Flower, by Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1436.” What follows is obscure: “But in the year 1481 Pope Sixtus IV granted this jubilee [I think he means, ‘that is, a plenary indulgence’], and his successor Innocent VIII confirmed it in the first year of his pontificate.”

DIJON, Saint Benignus: “At Bayeux, Saint Ragnobert, bishop and confessor.” It belongs to 16 May.

LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION: “At Nazareth, a city of Galilee, the incarnation of the Son of God. And the Annunciation of the blessed Virgin Mary, when the angel Gabriel was sent to her and said: ‘Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.’ Glorified by so great a message, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, he who deigned to take flesh from her exalted her above all and blessed her forever in reverence.” It then follows with the crucifixion, Isaac, Irenaeus, Quirinus, and Dula, almost as in the BRUSSELS manuscript above. “On the island of Antrum, Saint Hermeland . . .,” as in the text.

GREVEN: “The passion of Saint James the Greater, apostle. Also Josias, scribe and martyr, beheaded with blessed James.” See the *Praetermissi*. “At Nicaea, Victorinus, Alexander, Euphrates, Castula, Nicostratus, Lucilla, and four hundred other martyrs. The sacrifice of Isaac, son of Abraham the patriarch. Also Abel the Just, the protomartyr of the Old Testament. The passage of the children of Israel through the Red Sea. The victory of blessed Michael over the dragon. Also Simeon, abbot.” See the *Praetermissi*. “At Altona, a castle in the county of Mark, Saint Eynard, hermit and confessor. Saint Veronica, a matron, to whom the Lord left the image of his face impressed upon a cloth.” On this true image, consult the *Praetermissi*, Papebrochius’s *Responsiones* in various places, and the other authors whom he cites.

MOLAN, in italics, after “he was killed by the sword,” inserts from Bede: “It is written in the passion of Saint Valentinus.” Other editions add: “Also on that day, the deposition of Saint Humbert, most holy bishop and confessor of Christ, glorious for his virtues and miracles. On the same day, the creation of the world.” Then they speak of Isaac, the passage through the Red Sea, and Michael’s victory.]

[Col. 0871]

At Nazareth, a city of Galilee, the Annunciation of the Lord. At Sirmium, the passion of blessed Irenaeus, bishop, in the time of the emperor Maximian; he was first afflicted by extremely severe tortures, then tormented for many days in prison, and finally brought his martyrdom to completion by the cutting off of his head. At Rome, Saint Quirinus, martyr, who, after the loss of his possessions, after the filth of prison, and after suffering many beatings, was killed by the sword by King Claudius. At Nicomedia, the feast of a certain Dula, a soldier’s maidservant, who was killed for her chastity. On the island of Antrum, Saint Hermeland, abbot, whose glorious way of life is praised by the proclamation of miracles.

7 days before the Kalends. Day 26. [Note: [Col. 0875B]

Today Pratensis, Herinienensis, Tornacensis, Pulasnensis, Antwerp, Maximus-Lübeck, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus agree.]

[Note: [Col. 0875C]

Muneratus and Greven have “Pentapolis.” I know that “Libya” should be read, but since absolutely all the codices agree on their reading, with Molanus alone excepted, I thought their reading should be retained in the text. Thus all the same authorities have “Irenaeus” or “Hyrenaeus.” I preferred the former form because it is the reading of Pratensis, Herinienensis, Tornacensis, and Greven, whatever I may find elsewhere as “Irenaeus.” Greven and Molanus incorrectly write “Ammonis” instead of “Ammonius.” The chief difficulty concerns the name Castolus or Castulus. It is certain that all the ancient witnesses read “Castuli.” Yet it seems equally certain that Usuard read “Castoli,” if we may rely on the authority of our older codices. Pratensis, Herinienensis, Tornacensis, Pulasnensis, Muneratus, and Greven accordingly print it that way, and we follow them here, even when they are mistaken. Pulasnensis perhaps adds, for greater emphasis, “and likewise, crowned with martyrdom, he departed in confession.” At the end it makes a shameful error, writing: “At Sirmium, Saints Vincent, priest, and Maximus.” The remaining variant readings are mere scribal blunders. Thus Muneratus has “Maximae” for “Maxime in mare,” with the name Maxima needlessly repeated. Likewise “tertio,” “harenaria,” “Syrmio,” “Smyrnia,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0875C]

The first group of the Pentapolitan martyrs is indicated quite clearly in the Hieronymian copies, though the names are distorted here and there and the place of the contest is omitted; this is expressed most clearly only in the Epternacensis: “In Pentapolis of Libya, Theodore, bishop, Irenaeus, etc.” The Little Roman Martyrology knows nothing of the companions, or at least deliberately excluded them, reading: “At Pentapolis of Libya, Theodore, bishop.” In Ado our entire announcement is given word for word, and Notker also derived it from him. Nothing further worthy of mention is found concerning these saints, unless one enjoys sampling attractive little tales from the fabrications of Dexterinus and works of that kind.

Castulus is placed first in the Hieronymian codices cited, with the variations—whether of name or of burial place—which Henschenius and Florentinius explain fully. He is likewise first in the Little Roman Martyrology: “At Rome, Saint Castulus, chamberlain of the palace.” [Col. 0876C] The elogium added to this by Ado is taken verbatim from the Acts of Saint Sebastian, chapter 22, no. 83. I wished to warn the reader of this, lest, when reading Florus’s elogium, he should suppose that one author had ever known the other, on the grounds that in most respects they agree here. The truth is that both drew the same material from the same source, and thus agree quite well to that extent; but it can be established from the remaining details alone that each arranged his material independently. As usual, Notker followed Ado; Our Author uses his customary method of abridgment; Rabanus copied a few items from some Hieronymian codex.

In recording Montanus and Maxima, the Hieronymian Martyrologies again lead the way, and all the other martyrologists agree, except the Little Roman Martyrology. Henschenius and Florentinius discuss them and their forty companions. Bede records: “At Sirmium, Montanus, priest, Maxima his wife, and eleven others.” Rabanus removed the final clause, which Our Author also omitted, while the others retained it. Indeed, apart from Bede, the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Ado, Rabanus, Notker, Wandalbert, and many more recent authorities state that they were married. I confess that I cannot sufficiently conjecture why Usuard kept silent about this. I understand even less what could have moved him, while disregarding Ado’s words, which explicitly assert that they were thrown into a river, to prefer to write that they were drowned in the sea. Shall we say that he was entirely unaware that Sirmium is a city deep inland? I think this must be admitted, since we have shown sufficiently elsewhere that Usuard was not very well versed in geography. Nor do any Acts of these saints survive; for we do not think that, without violating the truth, they can be transferred either to Firmium or Firmum in Italy, or to Sexti Firmium in Spain. Let this passage from Wandalbert’s sacred poetry also be included:

The seventh recalls Montanus with his holy wife,

And with him, forty martyrs who suffered.

] [Note: [Col. 0877A]

ANTWERP, MAXIMUM-UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, DANIC, and the UTRECHT-BELGIAN EDITION, after the pure text, add: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Ludger [Luidger, Lutger, Luideger], bishop and confessor of Münster.” ALBERGEN further adds: “Disseminating the word of life far and wide, he became renowned for many virtues and miracles. For at his blessed passing, around midnight, a light coming from heaven illuminated the entire province. He flourished in the time of Charlemagne, who appointed him the first head of the church of Münster. He lies buried at Werden.”

ROSWEYD, in third place: “On the same day, Saint Liudger, bishop and confessor. At Sirmium, Saints Montanus, priest, and Maxima, his wife, who were seized and thrown into the river. And forty other martyrs.”

ANTWERP-MAJORITY and CENTULEN begin: “At Rome, the passion of Saint Castulus, martyr. On the same day, at Pentapolis . . .,” in pure form. “At Sirmium, Saints Montanus, priest, and Maxima, his wife, drowned in the sea.”

BRUSSELS: “The seventh day of the world, on which heaven and earth and all their adornment were completed, and on which God ceased from all the work he had made. Hence on that day Christ also rested in the tomb. At Rome, on the Via Labicana, in its cemetery, Saint Castulus, [Col. 0877C] martyr. As he was chamberlain of the palace and the host of the saints, as is read in the deeds of Saint Sebastian, he was seized and tortured by the persecutors; while he persisted in confessing the Lord Jesus, he was thrown into a pit, and a mass of sand was cast down upon him. Thus, with the palm of martyrdom, he departed to the Lord. At Sirmium, the feast of Saints Montanus, priest, and Maxima, his wife, drowned in the sea. And the deposition of Saint Ludger, bishop and confessor.”

HAGENAU, in its first and second announcements quite accurately, after “he departed to the Lord,” concerning Castulus adds something which I can scarcely read and nowhere else find: “But here he was transferred by hand to Messbg.” Concerning Montanus and Maxima, it agrees with the text. It follows: “On the same day, in a monastery of Westphalia, in the city, the deposition of Saint Ludger, bishop of that city, who is said to have been chaplain of Charlemagne and companion of Saint Willibrord. He drove wild geese into his house because of the damage they had inflicted upon him. He restored one of them after it had died, and forbade them all ever again to cause damage on his estate; this still continues.” The truth and duration of this miracle must be investigated elsewhere.

AQUICINCT, after “Castulus, martyr,” has: “chamberlain of the palace.”

PLESCHIONEN and VATICAN, no. 5949, add: “Saint Longinus, martyr.” See above, 15 March.

MATRICHT-CARTHUSIAN-UTRECHT, omitting the others, reads: “Ludger, bishop and confessor, patron of the church at Loenen, who was one of the companions of blessed Gregory, bishop of Utrecht.”

ALTEMPS: “In Africa, Victor, Saturninus, Solutor, and twelve others. At Sebaste, Saint Peter, bishop. At Heraclea, Martial, bishop. At Antioch, Timothy, Theogenes, and Macharius.” Belinus has similar material below. Consult the Acts and the *Praetermissi*.

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION begins: “At Cologne Agrippina, in the church of Saint Augustine, the commemoration of Saint Constantius, martyr, who was one of the company of the holy [Col. 0878A] Moors.” Was he one of the Thebaean martyrs? See the *Praetermissi*. It gives the account of Theodore and his companions in pure form. In its account of Castulus, whom it makes an official of the palace, it differs little from the BRUSSELS manuscript. The same is true of the Sirmian martyrs, except that it adds: “Their bodies were found not far from the city. At Trier, blessed Felix, the twenty-first bishop of that place and confessor. In the monastery of Werden, the deposition of Saint Ludger, the first bishop of Münster and confessor. On the same day, Saint Mohallok, bishop and confessor.”

BELIN. The first edition comes close to purity; in the second the following are inserted: “In the city of Sebaste, Peter, bishop. At Heraclea, Saint Martial, bishop. At Celer, Saint Cassian, bishop. At Antioch, Timothy, Diogenes, Macharius, and Maximus and Theodore, bishops. In Africa, Victor, Saturninus, Solutor, and twelve others.” I have already said above that the Acts and the *Praetermissi* should be consulted concerning these.

GREVEN: “Serotinus, martyr. Also Peter, Martianus, Capinus, and Kilianus.” See the index of the *Praetermissi*. “At Rome, Saint Quirinus, martyr, killed by the sword for Christ in the time of Claudius. Is this Cyrinus, concerning whom see 25 March? Felix II, archbishop of Trier and confessor. In the monastery of Werden, the deposition of Saint Ludger, first bishop of the church of Münster and confessor. Having been instructed by the abbot Alcuin, a most learned man, he was a deacon at York. Ordained a priest at Cologne, he announced the Gospel of Christ to the Saxon and Frisian peoples, and, renowned for his life and miracles, rested in peace. Also Saint Mohallok, bishop and confessor. In Ireland, Mottelog, abbot and confessor.” The Acts admit one Mochelloc or Kellenus, whether he was a bishop or an abbot. “At Cologne Agrippina, in the church of the hermits of Saint Augustine, the commemoration of Constantine, martyr, one of the company of the holy Moors.” He is called Constantius above, in the Acts under the *Praetermissi*.

MOLAN, concerning Castulus, gives in the text, in italics from Ado: “When he was chamberlain of the palace and host of the saints.” Then at the end: “Also at Werden, the deposition of Saint Ludger, bishop and confessor, who was the first bishop of Münster, in the time of the emperor Charlemagne. At that time the aforesaid Charles was staying at the palace of Aachen, when Saint Ludger departed from this world. At that very hour, going outside with a certain man named Aquo, an astrologer, so that he might gain knowledge by observing the stars, he saw a great brightness of fire coming from heaven, and it illuminated the entire province; a light also appeared before the eyes of all the people of France, in a wondrous sight. After some time had passed, it happened that Grifrid, Saint Ludger’s nephew, who had attended the holy man’s funeral, came to the king’s palace. When the king asked him about the holy man’s death and inquired about the day and hour, and he related everything in order, the king realized that at that same moment his beloved servant had departed to the Lord, and that the light had been shown to him by the Lord from heaven. Thus it is made clear how radiant his soul came before the Lord. On the same day, blessed Felix, bishop of Trier. At the monastery of Laubach, the elevation of the body of Saint Ursmar, bishop and confessor.” In other editions there is little concerning Ludger. To Felix of Trier is added “the second.” [Col. 0879A] Finally: “At Lobbes, the elevation of Saint Ursmar, bishop, which is celebrated on the Sunday before the feast of Saint John the Baptist.” This is more properly assigned to his feast day, which is celebrated on 18 April.]

[Col. 0875]

At Pentapolis of Libya, the feast of Saints Theodore, bishop; Irenaeus, deacon; Serapion and Ammonius, lectors. At Rome, on the Via Labicana, Saint Castulus, martyr, who, as is read in the deeds of blessed Sebastian, after being hung up three times and questioned three times by the persecutors, persevering in confessing the Lord, was thrown into a pit; when a mass of sand had been cast down upon him, he departed to Christ through martyrdom. At Sirmium, Saints Montanus, priest, and Maxima, drowned in the sea.

Six days before the Kalends. Day 27. [Note: [Col. 0879A]

There is broad agreement among Herinienensis, Tornacensis, Pulasnensis, Antwerp, Maximus-Lübeck, Muneratus, Belinus, Greven, and Molanus. To these may be added Antwerp-Maximum, Utrecht, Leyden, Louvain, Alberg, Danic, and the Utrecht-Belgian Edition.]]

[Note: [Col. 0879B]

It offers little worthy of note. Maximus-Lübeck reads “John the First,” through what I suppose is a printer’s error. All the codices consistently write “hermit,” and we follow even their errors, perhaps with excessive scrupulousness. Belinus, with a slight transposition of the wording, writes “full of the prophetic spirit.” In the Antwerp manuscript, “saint” is missing before Alexander. I had almost failed to mention that some codices write “victory” instead of “victories.” Concerning “Egypt,” “Egyptian,” “tyrant,” “martyr,” and such trifles, enough has been said elsewhere and more than enough. In the Pratensis there is an addition which is both badly expressed and incorrectly placed on this day, in these words: “On that day, Saint Eucherius, bishop of Tours.” Castellanus himself admits that this addition is not only present in the letters he sent me, but expressly stated in the first part of his *Bimestrium* under 20 February. He likewise admits that the announcement was not properly formed, since Eucherius was not bishop of Tours but of Orléans, as our *Auctaria* correctly state under the cited day, 20 February. If you wish to restore the aforesaid words to their true sense, write “Trudonensis” instead of “Turonensis.” It would then be understood that Eucherius, bishop of Orléans, was at some time called “of Trudo” from the place of his exile; a comma should be placed after “Trudonensis,” as follows: “On that day, Saint Eucherius of Trudo, bishop, etc.”]

[Note: [Col. 0879B]

John, a native of Lycopolis and an anchorite there, surnamed “the prophet,” elsewhere called an abbot and here called a hermit, was a most perfect exemplar of obedience, as he is portrayed vividly by Saint Ignatius, our holy father, and consequently of the other virtues as well; just as he was known throughout the Christian world, so he had nearly all the holy Fathers as his praisers. Nevertheless, the author of the Little Roman Martyrology was the first to bring him into the sacred Calendars on this day, from his Rufinus, the final book, chapters 19 and 32—whether quite appropriately I do not know: “In Egypt, John, hermit, a man of prophetic spirit.” Ado spoke somewhat more clearly from the celebrated History; Usuard and Notker rendered not his words but their sense. His life is extremely well known and, I think, not suspected of Origenism; Papebrochius has illustrated it, and Tillemont included it in French in vol. X, p. 9 onward. In any case, as I have already indicated, the Hieronymian copies, Bede, Florus, Rabanus, and Wandalbert have nothing concerning this illustrious saint.

Nor is there anything concerning this Alexander of Pannonia, equally unknown to Ado, Notker, and their source; nor can I, even by conjecture, sufficiently determine where Usuard could have obtained him. Here Henschenius’s appended observation is relevant, and it can be applied to many other saints bearing the same name. “Many,” he says, “who were called Alexander obtained the crown of martyrdom and caused some confusion in the sacred tables. From time to time the same individual is found entered in the Calendars on different days, as though he were distinguished from himself. Sometimes one and the same person is identified when in reality there were several, to be assigned to different days; and we plainly think that this last circumstance occurred in the case of this Alexander.” He goes on to demonstrate this by comparing this Alexander with the other one who is celebrated on 13 May. We ask by what records Usuard produced this Alexander of Pannonia, but in vain. Nevertheless, it remains absolutely certain that nothing except Usuard has been placed by us in the little calendar, as our printed and manuscript codices clearly show, whatever Alexander his words may ultimately be understood to concern.]

[Note: [Col. 0879D]

ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, following Ado, reads: “In Egypt, the feast of blessed John the hermit, a man of admirable holiness, who, being also full of the prophetic spirit, foretold to the most Christian emperor Theodosius victories over tyrants.” Alexander is absent. It follows: “At Smyrna, the feast of blessed Thrasea, bishop and martyr, whom the fifth ecclesiastical book mentions.” In the table of the *Praetermissi* he is referred to 5 October, because on that day he is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology, which we follow.

ROSWEYD begins: “The Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Wandalbert mentions this alone in his single verse:

The sixth day shines with the triumph of the rising Lamb.

Concerning John, as in the text. It follows: “In the district of Hasbania, Saint Eucherius, bishop of Tours and confessor.” In various codices this recurs under the same formula, “bishop of Tours,” concerning which we have spoken fully above in the *Variants*. Concerning Alexander, correctly. Then: “Martianus, bishop,” which belongs to 6 March. “Rudbert, bishop and confessor.” This means Rudbert or Rupert of Salzburg. See Papebrochius’s commentary and the Life illustrated by him.

CENTULEN: “At Jerusalem, the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh. In Egypt, Saint John, monk, a man of great holiness and prophetic spirit. At Smyrna, blessed Thrasea, bishop and martyr, whom the fifth ecclesiastical book mentions.” He is referred above to his feast day, 5 October.

BRUSSELS: “At Jerusalem, the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Concerning John, as in the text. It follows with Thrasea, as above. Then Theodore and the Pentapolitan companions, whom it omitted yesterday. Concerning Alexander, correctly. “Also elsewhere, Saints Pastor and Romulus.” He is the leader of the African martyrs. See the *Praetermissi* concerning Pastor.

HAGENAU gives a brief but, contrary to its custom, quite exact summary of John’s life as follows: [Col. 0881A] “In Egypt, blessed John the hermit, who, as is read in the *Lives of the Fathers*, foretold to the emperor Theodosius victory over the tyrant, and that Theodosius himself would shortly afterward die a natural death. No one entered his monastery from the fortieth year of his age until his ninetieth. To men who came, he rarely and at fixed times presented himself at a window to be seen, for their edification or consolation. No woman ever came into his presence. He had a guest cell for those arriving from far away, but he himself devoted his inner life to God alone: for the more he separated himself from human cares and conversations, the nearer God was to him. Because of his constant practice, he could no longer take food except in the evening, and then only a small amount. His hair and beard were sparse and thin, since no sufficient food nourished him. Even when he was living through his ninetieth year, he observed the same rule, taking no prepared food. His death was as follows: for three days he permitted no one to enter to him, and, placed in prayer, he gave up his spirit. In the cemetery of Pontianus at Rome, Saint Quirinus,” concerning whom see 25 March. “In Pannonia, Saint Alexander, martyr. In the bishopric of Salzburg, Saint Rupert, bishop and confessor.” See what we have already said more than once among the present *Auctaria* about this illustrious bishop, whom some assign to the church of Salzburg and others to that of Worms.

VICTORIN, at the end: “At Smyrna, blessed Thrasea,” etc., as above in ANTWERP-MAJORITY, where we noted that this saint belongs to 5 October.

PLESCHIONEN: “In Africa, Saints Romulus, Donatus, and Saturninus.” I have already said that Romulus was the leader of the African company; Donatus is seventh in order, Saturninus last. See the other nine in our Acts, where they are given by name.

MARCHIEN: adds: “In the district of Hasbania, Saint Eucherius, bishop of Tours.”

MATRICHT-CARTHUSIAN-UTRECHT: “John the hermit, who, as Augustine reports, was distinguished by the spirit of prophecy.” In the margin: “The Resurrection of the Lord.”

VATICAN, no. 5949, adds: “In Africa, Saints Romulus, Donatus, and Saturninus.”

ALTEMPS: “Saint Eustasius, abbot.” This seems to be Eustasius of Luxeuil, concerning whom see the Acts for 29 March. Let the reader see what we shall say there in our Observations concerning the aforesaid Eustasius. “In the district of Hasbania, Saint Eucherius, bishop of Tours. In Africa, Romulus, Acutus, Moralus, Successa, Matutina, Donatus, Saturninus.” These are given somewhat more distinctly in the Acts. “At Rome, Saint Calixtus, pope.” He is celebrated on 14 October. “At Smyrna, blessed Thrasea, bishop and martyr.”

FLORENTINE: “Also Saint Martin, bishop and martyr.” Does this indicate Martianus, concerning whom see the Acts for 6 March?

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION, after the text, adds: “At Smyrna, blessed Thrasea, bishop and martyr, whom the fifth ecclesiastical book mentions. At the castle of Conflans, Saint Honorina, virgin.” She is treated in the Acts on 28 February. “On the same day, Saint Rupert, bishop of Worms and confessor.” He is the same person who is called Salzburgian above; see Papebrochius’s learned commentary in the Acts for this day.

GREVEN: “The Resurrection of the Lord. At Smyrna, Thrasea, bishop and martyr, whom the fifth book of Ecclesiastical History mentions. Also Agutus, Missia, [Col. 0882B] Romulus.” The names are transposed and formed incorrectly by Greven, as he often does: “Ananias, priest, and Peter and seven other soldiers drowned under Diocletian.” Their passion is given in the Acts for 25 February. “In Africa, Saints Romulus, Marolus, and Successus.” Much confused material; see the Acts. “At Tortona, Saint Marcianus, bishop and martyr. Eucherius, bishop and confessor.” In the earlier edition of 1515, “of Tours” was added. “Rupert, bishop of the city of the Vangiones, now called Worms, and confessor. Eustasius, abbot and confessor. At the castle of Conflans, Saint Honorina, virgin.” See what was said above concerning these. “Also Neminia, virgin, and Cyriacus, deacon,” among the *Praetermissi*. “Also John, a monk, a man of remarkable obedience. At the command of his abbot he watered a dry piece of wood for an entire year without interruption, not judging the command of his superior.” Concerning him, see the text.

MOLAN: “At Jerusalem, the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Concerning Marcianus, as in Greven. Concerning Thrasea, as in the Lübeck-Cologne edition. Concerning Rupert, as in Greven, but in smaller type. In other editions, nothing is changed concerning the Resurrection or Marcianus. “At Worms, Saint Rupert, bishop and confessor. In the time of Childebert, he propagated the teaching of Christ in Bavaria, Austria, Styria, and all Noricum.” Then, in small type: “At Constantinople, Saint Isaac, man of God.” See the *Praetermissi*. “In Persia, nine martyrs.” Their names are given in the Acts.]

[Col. 0879]

In Egypt, the deposition of blessed John the hermit, who, among his other marks of virtue, being also full of the prophetic spirit, foretold to the most Christian emperor Theodosius victories over the tyrant. In Pannonia, Saint Alexander, martyr. [Bouillart adds: [Note: [Col. 0879A] Castellanus and Sollerius rightly deny that Saint Eucherius ought to have been placed by Usuard on this day. But that he was in fact placed here no one but a stubborn person, or someone entirely inexperienced in judging manuscripts, will deny. If Usuard erred, he did so at his own peril. BOUILLART.] On that day, Saint Eucherius, bishop of Tours.]

Five days before the Kalends. Day 28. [Note: [Col. 0881D]

The text is taken from Pratensis, Herinienensis, Tornacensis, Antwerp, Maximus-Lübeck, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus. [Col. 0882D] Add Antwerp-Maximum, Leyden-Belgian, Louvain, and the Utrecht-Belgian Edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0881D]

Greven and Molan omit the conjunction between Malchus and Alexander. The principal difficulty here is whether Usuard followed Adon’s reading in these words: “why he raged so violently against the blood of the righteous,” as found in Antwerp, Leuven, Max.-Lübeck, Greven, and Molan. I preferred the authority of the older codices—Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, and Munerat—from which I composed the text, although Herinien differs slightly, reading “those who shed the blood of the righteous,” and Tournai, through a scribal error, “in the blood of the impious.” Thus, I am entirely convinced, Usuard wrote it. Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck, together with many more recent witnesses, have “of Chalon”; others, conforming here to Ado, have “among the Chalonenses.” Leuven has “of Cabulon”; Herinien, “of Calon.” The remaining witnesses have *Guntramni* in the text, although the older spelling requires *Gunthramni*. Meanwhile, Herinien, Tournai, Antwerp, Greven, and Molan read *Guntranni*, while Max.-Lübeck has the worse form *Guntramii*. Again, the text has *spiritalibus* (“spiritual”) with Pratensis, Max.-Lübeck, Munerat, and Greven, although I have considerable doubt whether the reading of the others, agreeing with Ado, ought not to be preferred. Whichever you prefer, I shall regard with indifference. Tournai has *actibus* (“deeds”) instead of *actionibus* (“works”). Herinien repeats the particle *et*, thus: “both to churches and to the poor.” All write *Tharso*, except Herinien, Antwerp-Max., and others, and Munerat, where *Tarso*, the better reading, is found; we are compelled to follow the majority. Max.-Lübeck has the very poor form *Therso*. Among the more recent witnesses there are some who write *Siciliae*. The rest—such forms as *Cesarea*, *saevicia*, *martirum*, *Dorotei*, and similar variants—may be disregarded. I should nevertheless mention that *Palestinae* has been retained in the text, because all the codices form it in this way, with Molan alone excepted.]

[Note: [Col. 0883A]]

This day also owes to the *Little Roman Martyrology* those martyrs of Palestine who occupy the first place in the list and were delivered to the beasts during the persecution of Valerian. Ado set out the matter somewhat more fully, nearly in Rufinus’s own words, as did Notker, who followed him. Our author used a shorter style, but reported the same sense and nearly the same words, omitting only a few details. We have already discussed them above in the examination of the variant readings. Henschenius found nothing further in the Acts. In *Sincera et Selecta*, p. 252, Ruinart transcribed only the words of Eusebius, which Tillemont translated into French in volume IV, p. 17. Wandalbert expresses our first two announcements metrically in his couplet:

[Col. 0883B] “On the fifth, Priscus, Alexander, and Malchus are honored.”

The excellent king Guntram, departing this life, also adorns this day. Moreover, the holy king Gunthramn was first recorded by Ado in words which Our Author transcribed less scrupulously than Notker, though with very little difference. I know that in a certain Hieronymian copy the following was found: “At Canillon, the deposition of King Guntherannus”; but Florentinius rightly judged this to be wholly an addition. Henschenius’s preliminary commentary and the Life written by Gregory of Tours, which he elucidated together with Fredegar’s appendix, leave nothing further to be said about the excellent king. It is not altogether easy to determine whether Castor and Dorotheus of Tarsus should be joined together, nor from which Hieronymian copy they were taken, separately. If you are interested in investigating this, consult the commentary on the Acts. But why was Sixtus—or Xistus or Xystus—the third pope of that name omitted by Usuard, when he found him expressed so clearly in Ado? An Oedipus is needed. In any case, I believe that the genuine simplicity of Usuard’s text is established.]

[Note: [Col. 0883B]]

**BELIN.** He is pure in this matter, but excluded because of the transposition and because, instead of *Dorothei*, he reads *Theodori*.

**PULSANEN.** Almost entirely pure; he is plainly deficient in the final announcement.

**UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC.** They begin: “At Rome, the feast of Blessed Sixtus III, pope, who sat for eight years. He, accused by a certain man named Bassus, cleared himself together with fifty-six bishops; but he buried his accuser, who later died, with his own hands, using linen cloths and spices. He decreed that no bishop should presume to ordain in another’s parish.” The rest is pure.

[Col. 0883C] **CENTULEN.** “At Caesarea of Palestine, of the holy martyrs Priscus, Malchus, and Alexander. At Tarsus in Cilicia, of Castor and Dorotheus. At Chalon, of the holy king Gunthramn, who, having wholly abandoned the pomp of the world, devoted himself entirely to the service of the Lord.”

**ANTWERP-MAJOR.** In the first class, as in Centulen: “At the city of Chalon, of the lord Gutrand …” correctly; Castor and Dorotheus are omitted at the end.

**BRUSSELS.** “At Caesarea of Palestine, the feast of the holy martyrs Priscus, Malchus, and Alexander.
