When they saw the saints of God being martyred under the persecution of Valerian, inflamed by the divine fervor of faith, they voluntarily approached the judge and rebuked him for raging so violently against the blood of the righteous. He immediately handed them over, for the name of Christ, to be devoured by beasts; and thus they themselves completed their martyrdom. At Rome, of Blessed Sixtus III, pope and martyr. He decreed that no bishop should presume to ordain in another’s parish. At Tarsus,” etc., as in the text. “At the city [Col. 0883D] of the Chalonenses, the deposition of the holy and devout king Guntram of the Franks. He devoted himself so completely to spiritual works that, abandoning the pomps of the world, he distributed his treasures to churches and the poor. Once, when he had fallen asleep beside a stream after becoming tired from hunting, his armor-bearer saw a little animal emerge from his mouth and hurry toward the stream. He placed his sword over it as it went and returned. When the king awoke, he said that in his sleep he had crossed an iron bridge and found treasures on a mountain. The king himself found them, guided by his armor-bearer, and gave them to the churches.”

**HAGENOYEN.** In the first announcement, fairly pure; in second place, concerning Sixtus, nearly as in Utrecht and the others. Concerning Gunthramn, correct; instead of Dorotheus, he writes *Thorotheus*. At the end: “At Cologne of the Agrippinenses, of the holy Eugislus, bishop and confessor.” See below.

[Col. 0884B] **MARCHIAN.** At the end: “At Nicomedia, the passion of the holy Pastor and Victorinus.” See the twenty-ninth.

**MATRICULA-CARTHUSIAN-UTRECHT.** The text reports only the names, placing Gunthramn first and the Caesarean martyrs last.

**VATICAN, no. 5949.** Adds: “At Rome, of the holy Xistus, pope, who held the episcopate for eight years.” Nothing concerning Castor and Dorotheus.

In **ALTEMPS**, after Castor and Dorotheus, Adaucta is appended. See the commentary on the Acts.

**FLORENTIN.** “At Rome, of the holy Sixtus, pope.”

The **LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION** begins: “At Cologne [Col. 0884C] of the Agrippinenses, the translation of the holy Evergislus, archbishop and martyr, from the city of Tongeren, by Bruno, archbishop of the city of Cologne, to the church of Saint Cecilia, virgin. At Rome, the feast of the holy Sixtus …” as in Utrecht, except that at the end, after “should presume,” it adds: “and that no cleric should receive ordinations in the parish of another bishop.” Concerning the Caesarean martyrs, it again adds at the end, after “to be devoured”: “Their souls were received by angels, as is written in ecclesiastical history. At the city of Chalon, the deposition of the holy Guntraninimus [Gunthramn], king of the Franks, a devout man who …” The rest is pure.

**GREVEN.** “Also, of the holy Audactus and Castor.” This connection is explained in the Acts. “At Rome, of Blessed Sixtus …” as in Utrecht, but after “should presume” it reads: “Nor should a cleric in another’s parish receive ordinations.” The first edition is better: “receive the ordinations of another.” “Of Felix, bishop [Col. 0884D] of Trier and confessor.” He was treated on March 26. “Of Rogata, virgin.” Or *Rogatus*? See the omitted notices. Concerning Blessed Evergislus, almost as just stated.

**MOLAN.** “At Rome, of Sixtus, pope, who sat at Rome for eight years. And at the castle of Monte, the deposition of Saint Waldetrudis.” This should be referred to April 9. In the other editions this is omitted, where the following is found: “At Naxos, or Nesos, a town of Sicily, of Saint Conon, a Basilian monk, renowned for abstinence and holiness, in the time of Roger II, in the year 1236. On the twenty-eighth day, of Saint Stephen the Wonderworker and Saint Hilarion the Younger.” The former is treated in the Acts on this day, the latter on the twenty-fifth of this month. “At Rome, of Sixtus, pope, who sat for eight years. At Cologne, the translation from Tongeren of the body of Saint Evergislus, bishop.”]

[Col. 0881]

At Caesarea of Palestine, of the holy martyrs Priscus, Malchus, and Alexander, who, inflamed by the divine fervor of faith during the persecution of Valerian, voluntarily approached the judge and rebuked him for his cruelty toward the blood of the righteous; but he immediately handed them over, for the name of Christ, to be devoured by beasts. At the city of the Chalonenses, the deposition of the holy king Guntram, who devoted himself so completely to spiritual works that, abandoning the pomps of the world, he distributed his treasures to churches and the poor. At Tarsus in Cilicia, of Castor and Dorotheus.

**IV Kal. Day 29.** [Note: [Col. 0885A]]

From Herinien, Tournai, Pulsanen, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, Munerat, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0885B]]

All the Usuardine codices read *Armogasti* instead of *Armogastis*. They do not agree equally concerning *Archinimi*: Pulsanen, Munerat, and Molan have *Archimini*; Greven, *Archimimi*. Greven and Molan have *Saturi*, perhaps correctly; Tournai and Munerat, *Satiri*. I follow the others, in conformity with the *Little Roman Martyrology* and Ado. Concerning *Wandalicae* and *Guandalicae*, see what we shall explain more fully on May 23. The codices are almost universally in agreement on *Geiserico*. Some prefer *Genserico* or *Gensericho*, as Molan; not *Gerserico*, as Munerat has it, and much less *Honerico*, as Pulsanen erroneously reads. *Obpropria* has the flavor of medieval orthography, as shown by Herinien, Tournai, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, and Greven, although they vary elsewhere. I thought it could appropriately be retained in the text. Only Pulsanen has *compleverunt* instead of *impleverunt*, and he also has *Heustasii* instead of *Eustasii*. The question is whether Usuard placed the saint’s name first. Ado does not do so; neither do Herinien and Munerat. Nor did I think it should be added. Munerat wrongly omitted the particle *ferme*; worse, Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck read *ducentorum* (“two hundred”) instead of *sexcentorum* (“six hundred”); indeed, the latter codex, through what I suppose to be a printer’s error, lacks the words *exstitit monachorum* (“he was the father of monks”). Through a similar error, at the beginning it has *conversorum* (“converts”) instead of *confessorum* (“confessors”). Pulsanen fashioned a different sentence, reading: “Who, being the father of nearly six hundred monks, distinguished for life and holiness, etc.” We deliberately disregard other minor variations in spelling.

The Pratensis codex plainly reveals that its supposed autograph status is compromised in more than one way on this day: the Nicomedian martyrs Pastor and Victorinus have been added, improperly torn away from the larger group, and are found in no other codices except Belin, Rosweyd, Aquincinct, and Florentin, which certainly do not rise above mediocre quality. In addition, the entire announcement of Eustasius of Luxeuil [Col. 0886C] has been crossed out and completely erased, as Sirmond observed in our copy and the distinguished Castellanus more recently informed me by the letters cited above more than once. We recognize today as genuinely Usuardine only the text itself; apart from it, nothing is authentic. Concerning Eustasius, transferred to April 2 in the aforementioned Pratensis codex, we shall speak there.]

[Note: [Col. 0885C]]

This most noble class of three African confessors—thus are they adorned with a singular title—again proceeds from the *Little Roman Martyrology*, while the Hieronymian martyrologies, Bede, and Bede’s followers are silent. Ado attributed to them a brief but magnificent eulogy, followed by Notker. Our author cut away its core but preserved the rest word for word. We have already stated above which form of their names we prefer, based on the Usuardine codices; which form should actually be preferred is explained at greater length in Henschenius’s commentary, where certain difficulties concerning the second name [Col. 0885D] are clarified. There you have the entire history of their martyrdom [Col. 0886C] taken from Victor of Vita and from the more accurate edition of Pierre-François Chifflet. No one before Ado spoke of Eustasius, abbot of Luxeuil. Usuard uses his very words, though not precisely all of them, and so does Notker for the most part. Our author transposed only the opening words; the other altered both the beginning and the ending. See here also Henschenius’s commentary, together with the two Lives which he carefully elucidated. Wandalbert elegantly celebrates the praises of Eustasius:

“Eustathius shines with the fourth glory of virtue,

[Col. 0886D] the abbot who rightly flourished under Columbanus as master.”

] [Note: [Col. 0885D]]

Concerning **PRATENSIS** and **ROSWeyd**, enough has already been said; concerning Belin and the others, below.

**ANTWERP-MAX., UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LEUVEN, ALBERGEN, DANIC**, and the **UTRECHT–BELGIAN EDITION** depart very little from purity, adding to Eustasius the title expressed by Ado, “disciple of Saint Columbanus,” and writing *ducentorum* instead of *sexcentorum*.

[Col. 0886D] **CENTULEN.** “In Africa, of the holy Armogastus, Archiminus, and Satyrus. On the same day, the deposition of Blessed Eustasius, abbot, disciple of Saint Columbanus.”

**ANTWERP-MAJOR.** Reports the text concerning Eustasius almost exactly. It names the African martyrs without further description.

**BRUSSELS.** “At Nicomedia, of the holy martyrs Victor, Victorinus, Pastor, Saturninus, Julian, and four others. In Africa, of the holy martyrs Armogastus, Archiminus, and Satyrus. During the Vandal persecution under King Geiseric, they endured many severe tortures for their confession of the truth and completed the course of their glorious contest. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Eufragius, abbot of the monastery of Luxeuil, disciple of Saint Columbanus, a man of God. He was the father of nearly six hundred monks, distinguished for holiness of life, and also renowned for miracles. At Rome, the ordination of Blessed Gregory, pope.” Whatever memory of Saint Gregory is involved here, return to March 12.

**HAGENOYEN.** Does not differ greatly from the purity of the text; we omit its blemishes.

**AQUINCINCT.** After *impleverunt*, inserts into the text: “At the city of Nicomedia, the passion of the holy Pastor and Victorinus.”

**MARTYR.-CARTHUS.-UTRECHT.** “Of Pastor and Victor. Of Eustachius, abbot. Of Achacius, bishop and confessor.” In the margin, *Victorini* and *Eustasii* are corrected; the following words are added: “Usuard writes Achacius the martyr. Not on this day, at least; perhaps on the next? It will be seen there. He is properly commemorated on March 31, as can be seen in the omitted notices.”

**PLESCHIONEN** and **VATICAN, no. 5949.** “At Nicomedia, of Pastor, Victorinus, and Julian.” The number appears to have been changed arbitrarily.

**UGHELLIAN.** Has *ducentorum* instead of *sexcentorum*. In this it agrees with its two customary companions, Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck.

**ALTEMPS.** “At Antioch, of Theodore, priest, Juliana, and Acacia.”

**FLORENTIN.** “At Nicomedia, the passion of Pastor and Victorinus.”

The **LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION**: “In Africa, of the holy confessors Armogastus, Archiminus, and Satyrus. Since they were the most illustrious members of the Church of Christ …” These final words are Ado’s; the rest is pure. Concerning Eustasius, it writes *ducentorum*. Then: “At Nicomedia, [Col. 0887C] of the holy Victorinus, Pastor, Saturninus, Julian, and four others. On the same day, of Blessed Or, [Col. 0888A] a ninety-year-old hermit who was so devoted to abstinence that, as is read about him, he took no earthly food for three full years. To prevent himself from growing sluggish through idleness, he planted tree nurseries and cultivated a forest for the brothers.” See the index of omitted notices, where his acts are referred for examination on other days. “Also, of Saint Sophia, virgin and martyr. Also of Saint Macovalla, abbot.” Both are treated among the omitted notices.

**BELIN.** Instead of *Luxoviensis*, he writes *Lugdunensis*; instead of *sexcentorum*, *ducentorum*. At the end he adds: “At the city of Nicomedia, the passion of the holy Pastor and Victorinus.” Thus the first edition. In the second are added: “Saturninus, Juliana, and four others.” See the Acts, where the uncertain number is determined.

**GREVEN.** “At Nicomedia, of the holy Victorinus, Pastor, Saturninus, Julian, and four others. The feast of Blessed Achacius the martyr, whose passion is recorded.” Concerning him, above, under “Stephen, pope IX.” See the omitted notices. “Also of Gregory, bishop.” Perhaps Gregory of Nazianzus? “Of Macovalla, [Col. 0888B] abbot. On the same day, of Blessed Or, hermit, who possessed such great abstinence that he is said to have taken no earthly food during an entire period of three years. To prevent himself from growing sluggish through idleness, he planted tree nurseries and cultivated a forest for the brothers. At Rome, of Saint Sophia, virgin and martyr.” These matters have been discussed. “Also at Dola, of Juliana, virgin.” Perhaps the Nicomedian? But the locations are quite different.

**MOLAN.** “At Nicomedia …” as in the second edition of Belin. “And the passion of Saint Achard.” Then, in smaller type: “whose passion is recorded. On the same day, of the holy martyrs Jonah and Barachisius, under Sapor, king of the Persians. Their history was written by Isaiah, son of Adam, a knight of King Sapor and one who heard and witnessed the events that took place. On the same day, of Saint Berthold, confessor, of the Carmelite order.” In the other editions, concerning the Nicomedians and Berthold, as above. It continues: “On the twenty-ninth day, of the holy father Mark, bishop of Arethusa. And of Cyril, deacon, and others who contended under Julian [Col. 0888C] the tyrant.” Concerning Jonah and Barachisius, somewhat more briefly, and in different type.]

[Col. 0883]

In Africa, the feast of the holy confessors Armogastus, Archiminus, and Satyrus, who during the Vandal persecution under King Geiseric endured many severe tortures and insults for their confession of the truth, [Col. 0885] and completed the course of their glorious contest. On the same day, the deposition of Eustasius, abbot of the monastery of Luxeuil, who was the father of nearly six hundred monks and distinguished for holiness of life, and also renowned for miracles. [Bouillart, after the African martyrs: [Note: [Col. 0885A] This final commemoration of Saints Pastor and Victorinus is written in erasure by the same hand as the rest of the entry; afterward, a space of two and a half lines is left entirely blank, indeed scraped with a knife so thoroughly that not even the slightest trace of any letter can be detected by the eyes of a lynx. Other codices lack Pastor and Victorinus and append a lengthy commemoration of Saint Eustasius to the African confessors. Hence Soller’s complaint: that Pastor and Victorinus were added and Saint Eustasius expelled, and therefore that the codex was corrupted. If he had said that it was altered, I would have objected to nothing; for I readily admit that the Nicomedian martyrs were absent from the Carolingian autograph and Saint Eustasius was present. But who would prove from this that the codex was corrupted, as Sollerius claims? Is it because, as he says, Pastor and Victorinus were torn away from the larger group? Yet among the codices he cites in great number, scarcely two agree with one another concerning that group, so that even to Sollerius the number appears to have been changed arbitrarily. In other words, other codices could with impunity increase or diminish the group at will; [Col. 0885B] [Col. 0886A] only the Pratensis is at fault. I pass over the fact that he adds that those two martyrs are omitted by other codices. For this is false in the first place: they are indeed recorded among others by the Rosweydian and Aquincinctine codices, which Sollerius considers to be of the highest quality. The Gellonense martyrology, made publicly available by our Dacher, also records them. I do not include the Pratensis examples: that would be a matter of number, not authority. They are also found in the Carthusian-Utrecht Matricula and in the Galesinian edition. Moreover, even if they were absent from all the codices, nothing would follow from this against the Pratensis. It is a correction of which the other churches either were not informed, or, though informed, neglected it. I do not doubt that Usuard reserved Saint Eustasius for April 2 for valid reasons, although Ado of Vienne placed him on this day. He undoubtedly saw Acts which have now perished. Perhaps he was also led to this by the Hieronymian calendars, whose oldest codex, which I have before my eyes, is silent about Eustasius today and remembers him on April 2. BOUILLART.] At the city of Nicomedia, the passion of the holy Pastor and Victorinus.]

[Col. 0887]

At Rome, on the Appian Way, the passion of Blessed Quirinus, tribune and martyr, who, under the emperor Aurelian, after the cutting out of his tongue, suspension on the rack, and the severing of his hands and feet, completed the struggle of martyrdom by the sword. At Thessalonica, the feast of Saints Domninus and Victor. [Bouillart. [Note: [Col. 0887C] Most codices give Victor as Domninus’s companion, though he was never Domninus’s companion. Ours was the first to name the true companions, namely Philopolus and Achaicus; it was followed by Rosweyd, Marchian, Pratensis B, D, and E, and Conches. But I do not know by what fate it came about that Usuard, at first not knowing them, placed I know not whom there; afterwards, furnished with new information, he excluded that person and gave place to the other two. And this is enough for Sollerius to strike the Pratensis codex from the list of pure ones, to assert that the Usuardine sense has vanished, and to attribute the correction to some pedant. You will show the same hand in vain: his codices record Victor. Therefore Philopolus [Col. 0888C] and Achaicus are not Usuard’s. Thus the Pratensis codex must lose the title of autograph because Usuard, when he had first corrected something, did not take care to have it posted at every crossroads in every city, so that others too might correct what he had corrected. [Col. 0888D] Nor does Sollerius reproach only this fault in the article. He is also vexed that Saint Regulus, bishop of Senlis, was erased. He was certainly erased and transferred to 23 April, the day on which the church of Senlis celebrates his deposition. The reason why Usuard changed the place of the commemoration will be stated there. BOUILLART.] At Thessalonica, the feast of Saints Domninus, Philopolus, and Achaicus, omitting what follows.] At the fortress of the people of Senlis, the deposition of Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor.

**III Kal. Day 30.** [Note: [Col. 0887C]]

Herinien, Tournai, Pulsanen, Munerat, Greven, and Molan are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0887D]]

Greven and Molan read “of the martyr and tribune”; Munerat, worse, has *martyrum* (“of martyrs”) instead of *et martyris* (“and of the martyr”). Almost all have *abscisionem* (“cutting off”). What is preserved elsewhere had to be preserved here in the same form. We have also spoken elsewhere about the rack. In Pulsanen, *gladio* (“by the sword”) is missing, and *Domnii* is read instead of *Domnini*; Munerat renders this as *Doni: mini*.]

[Note: [Col. 0887D]]

The author of the *Little Roman Martyrology* commemorates Blessed Quirinus the martyr today in these words: “At Rome, of Quirinus, tribune [Col. 0888D] and martyr, father of Saint Balbina.” Ado composed a longer eulogy from the Acts of Saint Alexander, pope, [Col. 0889A] which appears under this day in Notker and is reported in the common Bede on April 30. In the Acts, p. 811, no. 4, I read the following: “But in the Bede printed for April 30, with the eulogy taken from Ado, which was made in the eleventh or twelfth century, after the body of Saint Quirinus had been translated to Neuss, as will be said below.” Understand this as meaning that we should not suppose that Ado’s eulogy was composed at that time, which would be absurd; rather, that around that period the feast happened to be transferred to the day noted by the common Bede. More closely relevant to our subject is that Usuard summarized from Ado whatever he thought sufficient for the martyr’s praise, retaining the chronological designation, which Henschenius corrects here. The matter will be taken up again on May 3, where it may be stated in its proper place what we should think about the Acts of Saint Alexander. In any case, in this first section of our list there is complete agreement among all the codices. The same is not true in the following class of Thessalonian martyrs, where the Pratensis is again corrupt—or, if you prefer, corrected by someone who wished to be too clever—in such a way that the Usuardine sense has completely disappeared. I confess that I cannot at all understand how Usuard could have joined Domninus, one of the Thessalonian group, with Victor, who is expressly placed elsewhere in the Hieronymian copies; nevertheless, our codices clearly prove that he did so. This is what I said had been noticed by some ignorant corrector and subsequently wrongly restored in the Pratensis: Victor’s name was erased and Philopolus and Achaicus were entered, who in fact were companions of Domninus, or Dominicus. [Col. 0890A] Yet that Usuardine conjunction of Domninus and Victor is ancient is also proved by Wandalbert’s verse for this day:

“On the third, Domninus shines with his companion Victor.”

Castellanus recognized the change just mentioned in the letters cited so often elsewhere. Another erasure now reveals a new defect in the Pratensis. The entire announcement of Regulus has been erased, although it is clearly expressed in all codices of any quality, with the sole exceptions of Rosweyd and Marchian. Thus there can be no dispute about the genuine Usuardine reading. Sirmond noted in our Pratensis copy that the line had again been crossed out; but Castellanus asserts more distinctly that everything concerning Regulus of Senlis had been erased. Regulus was therefore first added by Usuard, since he is not found in the older or contemporary witnesses. This is sufficient to establish the genuine simplicity of our list. Regulus will be discussed again on April 23, to which day he is read as having been transferred in the Pratensis; but, according to Castellanus, he was added by a hand that was not very old. This also proves that the addition of Philopolus and Achaicus was made long after Usuard’s time. Henschenius attempts to disentangle many very doubtful and complicated matters concerning Regulus, producing genuine Lives which Tillemont and other more recent writers altogether reject. In volume IV, at various places under the words *Regulus* and *Ricule*, he distinguishes Regulus of Arles from Regulus of Senlis and subjects other matters to sufficiently critical examination; these will be treated elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0889B]]

**PRATENSIS.** We have already sufficiently indicated its excesses and deficiencies. The Rosweyd codex agrees with it in every respect, as we shall often show in the course of the work.

**ANTWERP and MAX.-LÜBECK** add to the text: “At Orléans, of Pastor, palatine bishop.”

**ANTWERP-MAX., UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LEUVEN, ALBERGEN, DANIC**, and the **UTRECHT–BELGIAN EDITION** write concerning Regulus [Col. 0889C]: “bishop of the same place.” How plausible this is, see in the Acts. They then add: “At Orléans, of Saint Pastor, palatine or palentine bishop.” Whichever you choose makes no difference; you may even choose *Valentinus*, if you wish. This is an error common to the more recent Usuardine codices and also found in Hieronymian copies and elsewhere. An error, I say, for at Orléans there was neither a bishop Pastor nor a Palatine nor a Palentine. See the accurate commentary on this matter in the Acts, p. 829.

**ANTWERP-MAJOR**, mutilated at the beginning, writes: “At Rome, of Saint Quirinus, tribune, of the martyrs [for *martyris*] under Trajan.” The second edition is missing. Concerning Regulus, it adds at the end: “the first of that city itself.”

**CENTULEN.** “At Rome, of Saint Quirinus the martyr, under the emperor Trajan. At Thessalonica, of the holy Domninus and Victor. In France, at the city of Senlis, of Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor.”

**BRUSSELS.** It took Quirinus’s eulogy, longer than Usuard’s, almost from Ado. It is fairly pure concerning the Thessalonians. It continues: “At the city of Orléans, of Saint Pastor, palatine archbishop. At the fortress of the people of Senlis, the deposition of Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor. Also of Saint Quintinus. Also of Saint Eulalia, virgin.” I would believe that these names were polished from the Hieronymian martyrs. Quintinus is commemorated on October 31. We discussed Eulalia on February 12; another, of Mérida, is commemorated on December 10.

**HAGENOYEN.** In Quirinus’s eulogy it contains nothing of particular importance that is not read better in Ado. It is pure concerning the Thessalonians. It continues: “In the city of Asti, the passion of Saint Secundus, who was a vigorous soldier, an outstanding athlete of God, and a glorious martyr. He was taught the faith of Christ by Blessed Calocerus, commended in many ways by angelic testimony, and baptized through angelic ministry by Faustinus and Jovita, with water provided from a cloud. After he had buried [Col. 0890B] Blessed Marcian, he was seized by the governor Sapricius, stripped of his clothing, tortured on the rack, healed by the Lord, and finally imprisoned and released by an angel. The Lord appeared to him and strengthened him, and an angel led him to Calocerus. Finally, the governor ordered pitch and resin to be poured boiling over their heads and bodies and made them drink from it. And then [Col. 0890C] Secundus was beheaded and reverently buried by angels. Calocerus, however, was sent to Abyganus and punished there.” See the Acts.

**AQUINCINCT.** It resembles the Pratensis in Domninus, Philopolus, and Achaicus, but at the end adds: “At Orléans, of Saint Pastor, palatine bishop.”

**PLESCHIONEN** and **VATICAN, no. 5949.** “At Thessalonica, of the holy Domninus and Victor, Marcellus, and Saint Regulus.” The conjunction of all these is inept, as can be seen in the Acts.

**MARCHIAN.** At the end: “Of the holy Domninus, Philopolus, and Achaicus.”

**DAVERON, UGHELLIAN, and BORDEAUX.** “At Orléans, of Pastor, palatine bishop.”

**MATRICULA-CARTHUSIAN-UTRECHT.** “At Rome, of Quirinus, tribune and martyr. Of Secundus, soldier and martyr. Of Veronus, confessor; of Regulus, bishop and confessor.”

**ALTEMPS.** After Domninus, adds: “Of Philopius and Achaicus and Victor. At Orléans, of Pastor, palatine bishop. [Col. 0890D] On the same day, the passion of the holy Acescama and Eulalia.” The names have, unless I am mistaken, been formed incorrectly. “In eastern England, the translation of Saint Edmund, king and martyr, in the basilica of Saint Mary the Virgin.” This is referred to his feast day, November 20.

**STROZZI.** “At Orléans, of Saint Pastor the palatine.” Medicaeus inserts *bishop*.

The **LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION**: Concerning Quirinus, it has most of the material from Ado; but the matters concerning the tongue presented to a hawk, the six pairs of oxen, etc., which it adds, can be found discussed in the Acts. “At Thessalonica, the feast of the holy martyrs Domninus and Victor. At the fortress of the people of Senlis, the deposition of Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor of the same place. At Orléans, of Saint Pastor, palatine bishop and confessor. On the same day, of Blessed Acharius, bishop and confessor.”

**BELIN.** In the penultimate place: “At the city of Asti, [Col. 0891A] of Saint Secundolus the martyr,” in both editions, instead of Secundus. At the end, the first edition has: “At Orléans, of Pastor, bishop.” The second edition: “At the city of Orléans, the deposition of Blessed Pastor, bishop.”

**GREVEN.** “At the city of Asti, of Blessed Secundus, soldier and martyr, in the time of the emperor Hadrian. After molten pitch mixed with resin had been poured over his head and mouth, he completed his martyrdom by decapitation and was buried by angels. The deposition of Pastor, Victorinus, and four others. In Alexandria, of Pastor, bishop, and twenty-four others burned by fire.” Concerning these two groups, see the omitted notices. “Also of Philopoli, Eulalia, virgin, and six hundred and one others.” See the Acts concerning the cohort of martyrs whose leader is Victor. “At Orléans, of Pastor, palatine bishop and confessor. Of Acharius, bishop and confessor. Of Mamertinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, [Col. 0892A] confessor.” To April 20. “Of Veronus, confessor.” More properly, *Veroni*.

**MOLAN.** “At Orléans, of Pastor, bishop. On the same day, the passion of Blessed Simon, a boy from Trent”; concerning whom, above, on the twenty-fourth. “At the city of Asti, of Saint Secundus the martyr. And the deposition of Saint Veronus, confessor.” Then, in smaller type: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Maxentia, widow, mother of Saint Vigilius, bishop of Trent.” This belongs to April 30. Thus the first edition. In the others, after *Aureliano*, in italic letters is inserted: “Count of both military commands, and Trajan.” At the end: “In the Brabantine district, in the village of Lembeke, the passing of Saint Veronus. At the city of Asti,” as above. “On the same day, the feast of Saint Maxentia, widow, mother of Saint Vigilius. At Orléans, of Pastor, bishop. On the thirtieth day, of the holy father John, who wrote the *Ladder*; that is, *Climacus*.”

[Col. 0887]

At Rome, on the Appian Way, the passion of Blessed Quirinus, tribune and martyr, who, under the emperor Aurelian, after the cutting out of his tongue, suspension on the rack, and the severing of his hands and feet, completed the struggle of martyrdom by the sword. [Col. 0888D] Nor does Sollerius reproach only this fault in the article. He is also vexed that Saint Regulus, bishop of Senlis, was erased. He was certainly erased and transferred to 23 April, the day on which the church of Senlis celebrates his deposition. BOUILLART.] At Thessalonica, the feast of Saints Domninus, Philopolus, and Achaicus, omitting what follows.] At the fortress of the people of Senlis, the deposition of Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor.

**Pridie Kal. Day 31.** [Note: [Col. 0891A]]

Thus Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, Rosweyd, Munerat, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0891B]]

It contains scarcely anything worthy of note. I think *Timpora* in Herinien and Greven is a copyist’s error. All read *patriam devectus* (“carried to his native land”), omitting the preposition *ad*, except Greven and Molan, who also read *confixum* instead of *transfixum*. The Rosweyd codex writes *Anesii* instead of *Anesi*. Munerat has truncated the name, for it reads *Ansi*.]

[Note: [Col. 0891B]]

A brief commentary in our Acts deals with what could be said about Amos the prophet, whom Usuard here names first; there you will find the author of his death more clearly identified. It is certain that none of the ancient martyrologists—namely Jerome, Bede, Florus, the author of the *Little Roman Martyrology*, Ado, Rabanus, Notker, or Wandalbert—mentions him. It is likely that Usuard took from Isidore, cited in the Acts, what he records on this day about the prophet. Later writers, together with the modern Roman Martyrology, subsequently followed him. Ado took Balbina from the *Little Roman Martyrology*, expanding the history; Notker somewhat abridged it, while our author summarized it very briefly [Col. 0891C]. The same judgment must be passed on the deeds of Saint Balbina as on the Acts of Saint Alexander. Henschenius’s commentary will provide the remaining material concerning her. Florentinius disputes Diodolus (whom Baronius preferred to call Theodulus) and Anesus [Col. 0892B]; Henschenius, cited in the Acts, also discusses them. They do not agree in every respect. Nor is this the place to investigate the number or sequence of those African martyrs. I have no doubt that Usuard first received them from some copy of the Hieronymian Martyrology, either alone or joined with others, since he was not accustomed to examine whether he was selecting them correctly or incorrectly. Certainly, whatever his reading may be, I consider it, on the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts, incapable of being made clearer. Wandalbert again supports this, writing:

> “On the preceding day Diodolus and blessed Anesus shine forth.”

Moreover, among the more recent manuscripts of Usuard, we shall immediately give the companions of Diodolus and Anesus, though they are not everywhere listed in the same order.]

[Note: [Col. 0891C]]

PULSANEN., otherwise pure, again omits the final announcement of Diodolus and Anesus.

ANTUERPIEN. and MAX.-LUBEC. begin: “Of the prophet Amos,” cutting away the entire eulogy. They end: “In Africa, of the holy Diodolus, Anesus, Felix, Cornelia and Valeria, Portus and Abdas.” These are the companions whom I most recently said were found in the Hieronymian copies, with the order of the names altered here and there. It may be suspected that those companions were restored by some learned person, but in such a way that they were wrongly attributed to Usuard. In ANTUERP. *Babillae* appears instead of *Balbinae*. And likewise:

ANTUERP.-MAJ.: “At Rome, the birthday of Saint Babilla, virgin, daughter of Quirinus the martyr. On the same day, the birthday of the prophet Amos, whom King Uzziah of Israel killed by piercing his temples with a bar, and afterward, while still half alive, had carried back to his homeland, where he was buried.” Apart from the name Babilla, these two announcements are sufficiently sound; the third, concerning Diodolus and the others, is entirely absent.

ANTUERP.-MAX., UTRAJ., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN. and DANIC., pure in the entries for Amos and Balbina, continue: “In Africa, of the holy Diodolus, Anesus, Felix, [Col. 0892C] Cornelia, Valeria, Portus and Abdas. At Cologne Agrippina, the birthday of Saint Agilolphus, bishop and martyr of that same city.” This entry recurs below, but, to mention it only once, it must be referred to 9 July.

CENTULEN.: “The birthday of the prophet Amos, whom Uzziah, king of Judah, killed by piercing his temples with a bar. At Rome, of Saint Balbina, virgin, daughter of Quirinus the martyr. In Africa, of the holy Diodolus and Anesus.”

BRUXELLEN., pure in the entry for Amos, continues: “At Rome, of Saint Balbina, virgin, daughter of Saint Quirinus the martyr. After she had been healed, baptized, and instructed by Blessed Alexander the pope, she remained in virginity, rich in good works; and, when the course of this world had been completed, she was buried beside her father on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Praetextatus. In Africa, of the holy Diodolus, Anesus, Felix, Cornelia, Valeria, Portus and Abdas. At Cologne Agrippina, the birthday of Saint Agilolphus, archbishop of that same city. Charlemagne’s grandfather, Charles Martel, sent him there to negotiate peace; he was cruelly killed, crowned with martyrdom, and became renowned for many [Col. 0893A] miracles. And of the Roman monks.” On this, see *Those Omitted*.

HAGENOYEN. offers something new: “At Samaria, of the prophet Amos, whom Jeroboam, king of Israel, because he prophesied evil against him on account of the idolatry he practiced, pierced through the temples with an iron bar; afterward, while still half alive, he was carried back to his homeland, where he was honorably buried by his own people. At Rome, of Saint Balbina, virgin, daughter of Quirinus the soldier and martyr, whom Pope Alexander had cured of a scrofulous disease. She vowed her virginity to God. After she had overcome [the world], etc. In Africa, of the holy martyrs Diodolus and Anesius, Felix and Cornelia, Uleria, Portus and Abdas. At Cologne Agrippina, the birthday of Blessed Agilolphus, bishop and martyr of that same city.”

AQUICINCT. adds, in its proper place: “In Britain, of Saint Aldhelm, bishop and confessor.” (Refer to 25 May.)

PLESCHIONEN.: “In Africa, of the holy Felix, Anesius and Diodolus.”

MARCHIANEN., at the end: “In Britain, the falling-asleep of Saint Adelmus, bishop and confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJEC.: “Of the prophet Amos. Of the virgin Balbina, who was the daughter of Quirinus the martyr, the aforementioned tribune, and was buried with him.”

Codex D. DU CHEVAL., marked B: “At Cologne Agrippina, the birthday of Saint Agilolphus, bishop and martyr of that same city.”

VATICAN.: “In Africa, of the holy Anesius, Felix and Diodolus.” See what we said above about the companions of Diodolus and Anesus, under the second appendix.

UGHELLIAN. After Anesus it adds: “Felix, Cornelia and Valeria, Portus and Abdas.” As above.

ALTEMPS.: “At the monastery of Fontenelle, the translation of Saints Wandregisilus, Wulfram and Ansbert, by Blessed Babinus the bishop, in the church of Saint Peter the Apostle.” Each is referred to his proper feast day in the index of *Those Omitted*.

FLORENTIN.: “The birthday of Saint Julius, pope and confessor. Nevertheless, his feast is observed on the day before the Ides [Col. 0893C] of April.” See Usuard’s text there, and so forth.

The LUBECO-COL. edition begins with Balbina, composing a eulogy not very different from that of Hagenoyen. It follows with Amos, correctly. “In Africa, of the holy Diodolus, [Col. 0894A] Anesus, Felix, Cornelia, Valeria, Portus and Abdas the martyrs. At Nicaea in Bithynia, of Saint Arsacius the confessor, formerly a soldier and later a hermit, who cured a demoniac and killed a dragon.” This, I think, is the same man who has already been called Acharius, Achatius, and so forth; perhaps Acacius of Melitene, concerning whom Henschenius’s commentary should be consulted.

BELIN., not entirely correct in the text, inserts in third place: “On the same day, of Felix, pope and martyr.” Instead of Diodolus it reads Theodulus. Felix the pope is treated on 30 May.

GREVEN.: “In Africa, of Felix, Cornelia and Valeria, Portus and Abdas. The birthday of Blessed Agilolphus, archbishop and martyr of Cologne Agrippina. At Speyer, of Guido the abbot. At Paris, of Catulla the matron.” See *Those Omitted*. “At Nicaea in Bithynia, of Arsacius the soldier, hermit and confessor. Also, of Amos the abbot in the desert of Scetis, father of nearly five hundred monks. Of Ammonius the abbot, who, for those coming to him for conversion, was accustomed not only to build cells with the utmost care but also frequently to leave his own cell, together with everything in it. Of blessed memory, Lauduin, prior of the Grande Chartreuse. He was one of Saint Bruno’s companions and, after him, governed that house; having been handed over to prison by schismatics, he rested in peace.” These last three are also treated in the index of *Those Omitted*.

MOLANUS has Agilolphus as HAGENOYEN does. Felix as BELIN does. Then: “The elevation and translation of Saints Wandregisilus the abbot, and Ansbert and Wulfram, archbishops.” See above. Later, in smaller type: “At Speyer, of Guido, the first abbot of the monastery of Pomposa. His body, before a full year had passed after his death, glorified by very many miracles, was transferred with great honor from the city of Parma to Speyer by Emperor Henry.” Other editions read: “On the thirty-first day, of Saint Hypatius, illustrious for his miracles, bishop of Ancyra.” In the index of *Those Omitted* he is called bishop of Gangra and is deferred to 14 [Col. 0894C] November. There is another Hypatius as well; see there. “On the same day, of Felix, pope and martyr. At Blandinium, the elevation and translation, etc.”]

[Col. 0891]

Of the prophet Amos, whom Uzziah, king of Israel, killed by piercing his temples with a bar and afterward, while he was still half alive, had carried back to his homeland, where he was buried. At Rome, of Saint Balbina, virgin, daughter of Quirinus the martyr, who, after completing the course of this world, was buried on the Appian Way beside her father. In Africa, of the holy Diodolus and Anesus.

THE MONTH OF APRIL HAS THIRTY DAYS.

[Col. 0893]

On the Kalends — Day 1. [Note: [Col. 0893C]]

The following support the text: Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Munerat., the first edition of Belin, and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0893D]]

Munerat. and Belin. read simply “holy” instead of “most holy.” The same Belin has “and buried,” and after “brother” adds “her,” as does Molan; Tornacen. put “from the city of Rome” instead of “at Rome.” Otherwise, *Egipto*, *Egypto*, *Rhoma*, *Venancii*, *Martiris* are minor details. Something remains to be said about Greven, whom we excluded from the number of the pure witnesses on this day because he attaches to the text: “At Grenoble, of Blessed Hugh, bishop and confessor,” prefacing it with the sign LL, which also recurs elsewhere, for example on 5 and 25 August. This announcement ought to have been relegated among the Appendices, where you will find more about the same saint.]

[Note: [Col. 0893D]]

The *Little Roman Martyrology* begins this month as follows: “At Rome, of Theodora, sister of the martyr Hermes, who suffered martyrdom under Aurelian and was buried on the Salarian Way.” Ado adorned the saint with a brief but distinguished eulogy, from which Usuard took what is said in the text; Notker transcribed it without alteration. Here you see, on three successive days, the Acts of Saint Alexander serving as the source for the author of the *Little Roman Martyrology* and for those who follow him, [Col. 0894D] for this Theodora too was taken from there, as was the whole substance of Ado’s eulogy. In this matter, however, it is especially astonishing that, whereas elsewhere, when relating the same Acts of Pope Alexander, he always marks the time of Trajan, here he expressly asserts that she suffered martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian. See what we say on 3 May. The Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, and those in his succession are silent about Theodora; Wandalbert also, like all the others, deals on this day [Col. 0895A] with Agape and Chionia, separately from the other sister who is joined with those two in the Acts on 3 April, when our martyrologists also mention them, as we shall say there—unless perhaps today’s Chionia, Agape, and the others are different from those who are to be numbered among the Heracleans, a matter we leave unresolved. Venantius is purely Adonian, honored with the titles of bishop and martyr, although, as Henschenius says, it is nowhere explained which see he held, whether he died from the martyrdom he endured or survived it and was therefore also called a confessor, as will become clear in the Appendices. Usuard and Notker, investigating no further, were content to transcribe Ado’s words. Henschenius examines whether the body of this Venantius was transferred to Rome from Istria or Dalmatia, but rightly counts the alleged bishopric of Toledo among the fables of fabricated chronicles. Victor and Stephen were taken by Usuard alone from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; they are distinct, as Baronius correctly judged, from Victor and Corona, who are treated on 14 May, though of the latter almost nothing remains beyond their names. Ado placed this Walericus on this day, followed by Mosander and Rosweyd; Notker took it from him, while our author deferred it to 12 December, with which the more reliable manuscripts cited for the text and others agree. Others disagree, including Pulsanen., which Henschenius here praises as the illustrious parchment Martyrology brought from Italy, carefully examining which of the two was truly the day of death. Some manuscripts, such as Centulen. and Ambianen., assert a translation on this day. If you want more, consult Henschenius; for us it is enough to have established that this was Usuard’s original reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0895A]]

IN THE HERINIENSI manuscript, written in the margin by a more recent hand [Col. 0895B]: “In the city of Grenoble, the burial of Blessed Hugh, bishop and confessor.” It is sufficiently certain that this was added by some Carthusian monk.

PULSANEN., in second place: “In the district of Vinimau, above the sea-crossing, of Blessed Gualericus [Walericus], abbot and confessor. In childhood he left his earthly father and attached himself to serve the heavenly King. When he was old and full of days, loving the eremitical life, he ended his life in the Lord.” In the rest it is entirely pure.

ANTUERPIEN. and MAX.-LUBEC. append to the text: “On the same day, of Saint Walericus the abbot.” Max.-Lubec. wrongly writes *Valeriti*.

ALBERGEN., after an otherwise pure text: “In the district of Vinacum, above the sea, of Blessed Walericus, abbot and confessor.” LOVANIEN. adds: “In childhood he left his earthly father and attached himself to serve the heavenly King.” ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJ., LEYDEN., [Col. 0895C] DANIC. and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition add to the above, with PULSANEN.: “When he was old and full of days, loving the eremitical life, he ended his life in the Lord.” Later manuscripts write *Vimmacensi*, and so forth.

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, of the most holy Theodora, virgin and martyr, sister of Saint Hermes, prefect of the City. In the district of Vimacum, the translation of Saint Walericus the abbot, a man of extraordinary holiness. At Thessalonica, of the holy virgins and martyrs [Agape, added below by another hand] and Chionia, sisters. In Egypt, of the holy Victor and Stephen. In Sardinia, of Blessed Meriton, bishop, whose deeds were most renowned among men. On the same day, of Saint Venantius, bishop and confessor.” Two men named Venantius occur in the Acts today, but both are martyrs. See the Observations.

ANTUERP.-MAJ. resembles CENTULEN. in some respects, but differs in being silent about Walericus, Venantius, Victor and Stephen.

[Col. 0895D] BRUXELLEN., concerning Theodora, inserts into the text: “Whom Pope Alexander instructed, baptized, and taught the faith of Christ. In Sardinia, of Blessed Meriton, bishop, whose deeds were most renowned among men.” Whose name was Meriton—or rather Meliton—see in the Acts. It continues: “In Egypt …” Then follows Venantius, and so forth. “In the district of Vimacum above the sea, etc.,” as above; but instead of “he ended his life,” or “he is ended,” it has “he fell asleep.” “Also, of Blessed Hugh, of the Carthusian order, bishop and confessor.” See the Acts.

HAGENOYEN., somewhat interpolated in the text, adds at the end: “Also, the conversion of Blessed Mary Magdalene. In the district of Vimmacum, etc.,” as in ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others; but instead of *militaturus* it absurdly writes *militericiis*. “At the castle of the people of Senlis, the burial of Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor. At Orléans, the burial of Pastor, bishop and confessor of that city.” These have been placed incorrectly. See what was said above.

[Col. 0896A] ROSWEYD., pure in the entry for Theodora, departs from Usuard in the rest. In second place he has, from Bede: “At Thessalonica, of Agape and Chionia, who under Diocletian, after imprisonment, were cast into the fire but were unharmed; after prayer, they gave up their spirit.” The entry for Venantius follows. Then: “The birthday of Saint Quintianus and Anastasius. Also, of Walericus the abbot. In Egypt, etc. At Thessalonica, of Saints Agapitus and Quirinus, martyrs.” From the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

AQUICINCT. adds at the end: “Of Saint Walericus the confessor.” See what is said here repeatedly.

VICTORIN.: “The beginning of Christ’s preaching.”

AMBIANEN.: “In the district of Vimacum, the translation of Saint Walericus.” Many give the date of his death.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT. begins: “Of Hugh, bishop and confessor. Of Theodora, virgin and martyr, sister of Saint Hermes the martyr. Of Venantius, bishop and martyr. Of Walericus the abbot.”

CAMBERIEN. S. Mariae: “In Sardinia, of Blessed Militon, prelate, and Walericus the abbot.” The day is correct, but not the association of the place.

In VATICAN., manuscript no. 5949, Victor and Stephen are absent. It adds: “At Thessalonica, the birthday of Saint Ethionia, under the emperor Diocletian; she was first tormented in prison, then cast into the fire, and there, after pouring out a prayer, went to the Lord.” I think Chionia is indicated here.

UGHELLIAN., at the end: “On the same day, of Saint Walericus the abbot.” You see that this belongs to nearly all the manuscripts.

ALTEMPS.: “In Armenia: Partinus, Quintianus, Victor, Secundus. At Thessalonica: Ingenianus, Saturninus, Pattinius, Dionysius, Parthenius, Alexander.” See the names more accurately and distinctly formed in the Acts. “In the city of Grenoble, of Saint Hugh, bishop and confessor.”

FLORENTIN.: “The passing of Saint Walericus, abbot and confessor.” This is another formula for announcing the feast.

The LUBECO-COL. edition, slightly interpolated in the entry for Theodora, is pure in that for Venantius and is silent about Stephen and Victor. It continues: “In the district of Vimmacum above the sea, [Col. 0896D] of Blessed Walericus, abbot and confessor, whose tomb is made illustrious by frequent miracles. On the same day, of Saint Hugh, bishop and confessor, of the Carthusian order. In Sardinia, of Blessed Militon, bishop and confessor, whose deeds were most renowned among men. In the territory of Troyes, of Saint Leuconius, bishop and confessor.” In the Acts he is called Leuconius.

BELLINI’s second edition appends to the pure text: “In Armenia, the birthday of Blessed Partinus, Quintianus, Victor and Secundus. In the city of Heraclea, of Victor, Chionia, Agape and Hyrene. In Thessalonica, of Ingemana, Saturninus, Paternus, Dionysius, Panterius and Alexander.” They were taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; in the Acts all are expressed more correctly and distinctly.

GREVEN., after the sign LL and the words cited above, “At Grenoble, of Blessed Hugh, bishop and confessor,” adds: “This Hugh, a most holy man, saw in the wilderness of Chartreuse God building dwellings for his honor, and seven stars providing him with guidance on his journey. After this vision Bruno immediately arrived with six companions, seeking a place suitable for the eremitical life. Hugh received them and led them to the place divinely shown to him; he supported them with counsel and assistance and lived among them as one of them. At last, full of days and holiness, he rested in peace. Of Quintianus the martyr. In Armenia, of Partinus and Victor. In Sardinia, of Blessed Militon, bishop and confessor. In the district of Vimmacum above the sea, of Saint Walericus the abbot, disciple of Blessed Columbanus. Vincent, briefly summarizing his most holy life in Book 24, chapter 21, says among other things that his kindness and humility exceeded all measure. He was so full of divine compunction and grace that whenever he preached to his disciples or looked toward heaven while singing psalms to God, he poured forth tears. His face too, pale and wasted by emaciation, would glow with a rosy color and extraordinary radiance whenever, through him, the Lord brought healing to the sick, foretold future events, or revealed hidden things. Of Gilbert, bishop of Catania and confessor. Also, of Hugh, archbishop of Vienne, of blessed memory, who, having been a Carthusian monk, succeeded Saint Hugh during his lifetime in the episcopate of Grenoble, and afterward, having been made archbishop of Vienne because of the merit of his life, rested in peace.” He is among *Those Omitted*. “On the same day, of Hugh, abbot of Bonneval, of the Cistercian order, of good memory.” Also, “of Blessed Gertrude.” Or Genetrude: see *Those Omitted*.

MOLANUS: “At Grenoble, of Blessed Hugh, bishop and confessor, who lived the anchoritic life for many years and, renowned for the glory of his miracles, departed to Christ. On the same day, of Saint Valericus the confessor.” In other editions, the entry for Hugh is the same, while that for Walericus reads: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Vualericus the confessor, whose tomb is made illustrious by frequent miracles.” I have already noted that others write “birthday,” as is reported today in the Acts. See Henschenius.]

[Col. 0893]

At Rome, the passion of the most blessed Theodora, sister of the most illustrious martyr Hermes. She suffered martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian and was buried beside her brother on the Salarian Way, not far from the city of Rome. On the same day, Saint Venantius, bishop and martyr. In Egypt, Saints Victor and Stephen.

IV Nones. Day 2. [Note: [Col. 0897B]

Thus Tornacen., Pulsanen., Antuerpien., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. The following also concur: Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Alberger., Danic., and the Ultraj.-Belg. edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0897B]

Nevertheless, in this text the letter *c*, which Tornacen., Pulsanen., Antuerpien., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., and others reproduce, is inserted twice. Although this spelling is faulty, we thought it should be preserved for those curious about such ancient minutiae. Greven. and Molan. read “bonds and beasts,” omitting the word “waters” [Col. 0897C]. We likewise retained *abscisione* (“cutting off”), as nearly all the manuscripts have it, rather than *abcisione*, as Greven. and Molan. do. Munerat. has *Nececii*, “archbishop,” for *Nicetii*, “bishop.” Munerat. and Molan. likewise repeat the particle *et*, as though for greater emphasis: “whose life also,” as is read in Ado. Tornacen. omits “by miracles” before “is commended,” though that seems to carry some force. Some write “In Palestine,” but most, “At Palestine.” Munerat. omitted “Saint”; Greven. and Molan. read “Blessed.” Scribal errors have been discussed elsewhere. I wrote *Palestinam* as all the manuscripts have it. With these points stated, the principal variation remains.

For it might be doubted whether the celebrated Egyptian penitent was first entered in the sacred calendar on this day by Usuard himself, unless at least most of the manuscripts, both ancient and recent, agreed strongly on this point. Yet our Pratensis copy has an extraordinary reading today: namely, Egyptian Mary in third place, and Eustasius of Luxeuil in fourth. Something must have escaped Sirmond’s attention when he collated the aforesaid copy; for the distinguished Castellanus, who more than once carefully examined the alleged autograph for my sake, most recently testifies that Mary had been entered, in these words translated from French into Latin: “On 2 April, Saint Mary the Egyptian is erased, and Saint Eustasius put in her place.” In Herinien., Rosweyd., and Antuerp.-Max. there is today no commemoration of the Egyptian, having been transferred to 9 April, as we shall say there. From these and other manuscripts doubt may arise, but it is not so well founded as to overthrow the genuineness of the entry, which we judge to be genuine and straightforward.]

[Note: [Col. 0897D]

Theodosia had an eminent herald in Eusebius of Caesarea himself, Book 7 of the work on the Martyrs of Palestine. Henschenius placed his brief eulogy before all the Latin Acts; in his work there is much more material drawn from the Menologia and other Greek records, though not taken from the same day. These leave no doubt that Theodosia was tortured with harsh and dreadful torments at Caesarea, not in Cappadocia but in Palestine, as all the Hieronymian Martyrologies edited by Florentinius most clearly commemorate on the following day [Col. 0898D]: “At Caesarea in Palestine, the birthday of Saint Theodosia, virgin”; there one may see Florentinius’s note, which may perhaps resolve the difficulty proposed by Henschenius concerning the Sunday of the Resurrection on which, according to Eusebius, our Theodosia is said to have undergone martyrdom. That Sunday could not coincide with either 2 or 3 April in the expressly stated fifth year of Diocletian’s persecution, as Tillemont also considers in volume V, p. 85. Yet our text seems to have come from another source, for the author of the Little Roman Martyrology was the first to say: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Theodosia, virgin and martyr, beheaded.” Ado enumerates various kinds of tortures, and Notker does so from him. Our author did not include them all, and he especially took proper care not to make Caesarea in Cappadocia a maritime city. Whether deliberately or accidentally, it is certainly not by divine intervention that throughout our whole series of martyrologists this location is given—a location found not even in the Latin Acts themselves, in which the water, as in Eusebius, is rightly said to be the arena at Caesarea in Palestine. Rabanus, recalling Theodosia on the following day with a longer narrative, simply reads “Caesarea,” as if uncertain to which Caesarea the virgin should be assigned. Wandalbert too, on the following day, attached Theodosia to Evagrius and Benignus:

> “And the virgin Theodosia shines with equal splendor.”

[Col. 0899B] Nicetius of Lyons, omitted by Bede and Rabanus, is also absent from the Little Roman Martyrology. Yet it is certain that he is entered in all Florentinius’s Hieronymian copies, in the last or next-to-last place. In Ado he is placed first, under the usual formula of praise, copied word for word by Usuard and Notker. Florus embellished him with another phrasing: “A man who passed his life in every holiness, most chaste conduct, and outstanding charity”; thus you may again see how far that Florus is from our Usuard in both substance and style. For the rest, see Henschenius, together with the Life from Gregory of Tours which he edited. Wandalbert, doubtless for metrical reasons, makes *Nicetum* from Nicetius, celebrating him alone on this day:

> “On the fourth Nones, sacred Nicetus in the city of Lyons.”

Mary the Egyptian, otherwise very well known, seems to have been unknown to Latin martyrologists; no one earlier than or contemporary with Usuard entered her in the sacred calendar. For the occurrence of her name in Mosander’s Ado on 9 April was, in my judgment, rightly rejected by Rosweyd; this is confirmed, I think, by the fact that Notker, usually Ado’s faithful follower, did not enter her at all. Thus the aforesaid Mary must be attributed to Usuard alone, under the title “penitent,” drawn from I know not where and inserted for I know not what reason into this day’s entry, although the Greeks honor her differently, in association with the priest-monk Zosimas. Indeed, even the Usuard manuscripts are not consistent among themselves, as was said in the Variants and as will subsequently appear from the Appendices for 9 April and elsewhere. Papebrochius rendered outstanding service concerning this saint, happily uncovering in various dissertations her chronology, until then incorrectly determined, and other matters concerning her, arranging them carefully and elucidating them copiously. This is more than sufficient for our purpose.]

[Note: [Col. 0899B]

Nothing further need be said of PRATENSIS and HERINIENSIS.

ROSWEYD. inserts in second place: “In Africa, of the martyrs Amphianus and Victor, and ten other martyrs.” Why not fourteen, as the Hieronymian Martyrologies expressly read, from which the first two were taken? The entry for Nicetius follows correctly. And in the margin: “Also, of Saint Eustachius, abbot of the monastery of Luxeuil.” He means Eustasius, of whom there has already often been mention; but he omits the third announcement concerning Mary the Egyptian, which is also absent from the ANTUERP.-MAX. manuscript; in other respects it is pure.

CENTULEN.: “The birthday of Saint Nicetius, bishop of Lyons. In Achaia, at the city of Tomis, Saints Evagrius and Benignus.” It has put Achaia for Scythia and wrongly assigned to this day what belongs to the next, just as it defers Theodosia to tomorrow, though she ought to be entered today.

ANTUERP.-MAJ.: “The birthday of Saint Nicetius, bishop and confessor of Lyons. At Palestine, the burial of Blessed Mary the Egyptian, who is called a penitent; her deeds are found to be very wonderful and worthy of every praise.” Theodosia is likewise on the following day.

BRUXELLEN., fairly pure in Theodosia and Nicetius, adds at the end: “And Saint Eustachius the abbot. Also Urban the bishop.” I think this is the bishop of Langres, concerning whom see the Appendices for 23 January. Moreover, the following was added in a later hand at the first place, referred to by an asterisk: “At Palestine, the burial of Blessed Mary the Egyptian, whose conversion, when first a penitent, was wonderful, whose penance was vigorous and very acceptable to God.”

HAGENOYEN. is more or less pure in Theodosia; concerning Mary the Egyptian, as it is accustomed to do elsewhere out of singular piety, it attaches a longer history, or summary of her life, which does not seem to need copying here. Then: “On the same day, Saint Nixecius, bishop of Lyons, whose life was renowned for miracles and distinguished by virtues [was].”

AQUICINCT. is among those which defer Mary the Egyptian to 9 April.

VICTORIN. and REG. SUECIAE, marked no. 130, I do not know what saints they here group together; a proper day is assigned to each in the index of Those Omitted. Thus they have at the end: “On the same day, Saints Hereneus the bishop, Andochius the priest, Benignus the priest, Tyrsius the deacon, and Felix the merchant.”

DAVERONEN.: “At Tours, the translation of Blessed Anthony the confessor.” See Those Omitted. He is honored on 1 May.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-UTRAJECT.: “Nicetius, bishop of Lyons.” Nothing further.

ALTEMPS.: “At Tours, Blessed Anthony the confessor. Also [Col. 0900C] Saint Eustasius, abbot of Luxeuil.”

FLORENTIN.: “Also Saint Nicetus, bishop of Lyons, whose life was renowned for virtues and miracles. Also at Como, Saint Abundius, bishop and confessor.” This is absent from the printed edition.

The LUBECO-COL. edition gives Ado’s eulogy of Theodosia, but very interpolated. It is pure in Nicetius. “At the city of Palestine, the burial of Saint Mary,” etc.

BELIN. In both editions it treats Mary the Egyptian in second place. Then: “On the same day, the birthday of Nicetius [in the second edition, Nicenius], bishop of Lyons.” In the first: “Also Saint Abundius, bishop and confessor.” In the later: “Also at Como,” etc.

GREVEN.: “Amphianus, Victor, Urban, and Niertus, martyrs.” A conjunction of scattered persons. “Barlaam, hermit and confessor.” He is unknown, unless he is the one honored with Josaphat on 27 November.

MOLAN. immediately adds concerning Mary the Egyptian: “Her deeds are found very wonderful and most worthy of every praise [Col. 0900D]. Also at Como, Saint Abundius, bishop and confessor. Commemoration of the venerable confessors of Christ Ursmar and Erminus, when the people of Lobbes were freed from the Hungarians.” Then, in smaller type: “On the same day, Saint Francis of Paola, confessor, founder of the Order of Friars Minorites; who, among the other athletes of Christ, by his merits and examples, divine grace cooperating, adorned Holy Church in many ways, wonderfully illuminated the darkness of the present age by the splendor of his lamp, and was renowned for countless miracles both in life and after death. Leo X entered him in the catalogue of saints. Saint Musa, virgin, of whom Gregory writes in the Dialogues. On this day Nodger, bishop of Liège, died; his illustrious deeds are recorded.” See the index of Those Omitted. Later editions have Mary and Abundius as above. Then: “In Gaul, in the territory of Tours, Saint Francis of Paola, of the town of Calabria, founder of the Order of Minims. At Lobbes, commemoration of the merits of the venerable confessors of Christ Ursmar and Erminus, when the people of Lobbes were freed from the Hungarians through their merits [Col. 0901A].” Again in smaller type: “At Langres, Saint Urban, bishop and confessor, a man of great virtues, who often preserved vineyards by his prayers. At Caesarea in Palestine, the passion of another Theodosia, a virgin of Tyre, whom Eusebius of Caesarea writes of in Book Eight. On this day occurred the passing of the man of God Nodger, bishop of Liège, whose illustrious deeds are recorded.” This Theodosia is not different from the one reported in the text. Molan was deceived by the different location, or place of martyrdom. Concerning the various persons confused under the name Notger, see Those Omitted for 10 April.]

[Col. 0897]

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the passion of Saint Theodosia, virgin, who in the time of Diocletian voluntarily joined the confessors in custody, was stretched out and nevertheless tortured on the rack, and, by God’s power, after being delivered from bonds, waters, and beasts, finally completed martyrdom by the cutting off of her head. On the same day, the birthday of Blessed Nicetius, bishop of Lyons, whose life was renowned for miracles and whose precious death is likewise commended by miracles. At Palestine, [Note: [Col. 0897B] Sirmond had formerly read Mary the Egyptian in third place and Saint Eustasius in fourth. Later Castellanus wrote to Sollerius that Mary the Egyptian had been erased and Eustasius put in her place. I myself pity the lot of an author who uses others’ eyes. For how can these things be reconciled? If Sirmond reads Mary the Egyptian, how was she erased? If she was erased, how did Sirmond read her? If I had been in Sollerius’s place, this alone would have made me place no confidence in Castellanus’s eyes [Col. 0898B]. I now inform Sollerius how the manuscript stands at this point. The last two syllables of the word *commendatur*, the entire commemoration of Mary the Egyptian, and the words “also Saint Eustasius” are under erasure; of these, “abbot of the monastery of Luxeuil” runs first into the inner margin, and the other two words into the lower margin. All are in the same hand, but in different ink; in different ink because, in my opinion, it was at first beginning to fade. BOUILLART.] Saint Mary the Egyptian, who is called a penitent. [Bouillart adds: Also Saint Eustasius, abbot of the monastery of Luxeuil.]

II Nones. Day 3. [Note: [Col. 0901B]

From Praten., Herinien., Pulsanen., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., the first edition of Belin, Greven., and Molan. The following also concur: Antuerpien.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Danicus, and the Ultraj.-Belg. edition. Albergen. is lacking only in Pancratius.]

[Note: [Col. 0901B]

Scythia is written by the most reliable codices—Pratensis, Herinien­sis, Pulsanensis, Muneratianus, Grevenus, and others. Molanus has *Scythia*; Belinus, *Schitia*; Antwerp, *Scicia*: the forms in the other witnesses vary, and none reads *Schytia* correctly. We have followed the older codices in the text. Likewise, all write *in Thomis*. Muneratianus has *Evagii* instead of *Evagrii*; *Chiomae* instead of *Chioniae*; Pulsanensis, *Cyoniae*; Grevenus, *Scioniae*. There is a greater defect in Antwerp and Maximus-Lübeck, where one reads: “Under Diocletian, into the fire,” and so forth, with the intervening words entirely omitted. Pulsanensis, on the contrary, exceeds the others by inserting *permanentes* after *a flammis*. *Fusas* instead of *fusam* in Muneratianus is, unless I am mistaken, a typographical error, as also in Maximus-Lübeck. *Thauromentum* instead of *Tauromenium*, as the Hieronymian codices have it. Those same witnesses have *Pancracii* instead of *Pancratii*; Pulsanensis, *Panchratii*; the second edition of Belinus adds, “of the martyr Pancratius.”

[Note: [Col. 0901B]]

The fuller information concerning Evagrius and Benignus comes entirely from our Martyrologies. Thus today, in the second place, the Short Roman Martyrology reads: “At Tomis, Evagrius and Benignus.” The Usuardine text, only slightly longer and derived from Ado, is also described by Notker in nearly the same words. Bede, Florus, and Rabanus say nothing about them. In the Hieronymian Martyrologies, however, there is great confusion, from which Florentius does not easily extricate himself. Here are the various texts. The Echternach manuscript has: “In Sicily, the feast of Evagrius, Benignus …”; six others are then listed by name. The Corbie manuscript: “In Sicily, the feast of the holy Thomas, Evagrius, Benigna, and again six others.” The Lucca manuscript: “At Nicaea, the feast of the holy Thomas, Evagrius, and Benignus; add five fellow soldiers.” Reconcile these, if you can, satisfactorily. So much for the first position. But what can the same codices mean by what is read at the end: “Theumis,” or “Eumis,” or “Heumisiter”; “of Evagrius and Benignus”? Are these the same persons, or different from those named first? Florentius thinks the latter; Henschenius, the former. Follow whichever opinion you prefer; for us it is certain that our witnesses read as we have reported in the text, and Wandalbert agrees with them:

Evagrius shines forth, and martyr Benignus likewise.

The Hieronymian Martyrologies read on 1 April: “In the city of Heraclea, Victor, Chionia, Agape, and Herene”; and on the fifth day of the same month: “At Thessalonica, the feast of the holy virgins Chionia, Herene, and Agape.” Which day is preferable I leave to Florentius’s judgment. It was said in the Observations for 1 April that it might be questioned whether the same women are meant in both places. I do not wish to examine that here, while other matters remain to be considered. Today, in the first place, the Short Roman Martyrology is written as follows: “At Thessalonica, the virgins Agape and Chionia.” Bede perhaps more correctly omitted the title “virgin” on 1 April; Rabanus followed him closely in this. Ado copied Bede’s words, and from Ado Usuard and Notker did so as well. They retain, with their predecessor, the designation “virgin,” or rather “virgins”; indeed, the last adds Irene, whom he repeats on 5 April with a longer eulogy, as we shall again find the matter discussed there from our sources.

What must especially be noted is that Bede’s present eulogy, and that of Notker placed on 5 April, are taken from those Acts which were formerly passed off as the authentic proconsular Acts. They pleased Henschenius so much that he preferred them to the Greek Acts translated into Latin from the Crypta-Ferrata manuscript by Sirletus, Lipomanus, Surius, and Baronius, all of whom had judged the Greek text itself to be more genuine—indeed, uniquely authentic. Our teacher, a very experienced judge in such matters, had his reasons for reaching that conclusion. I read and weigh them, yet I do not find them such that I should not rather prefer the Sirletian text, and therefore I am compelled to admit, with the most learned recent scholars, that on this occasion at least a man otherwise remarkably perceptive nodded somewhat.

We are not driven by prejudices; we pursue truth alone, and when it is found we willingly yield to it. Here, therefore, with Baronius, under the year 304, no. 40, and the other authorities cited, we freely acknowledge the genuineness of the aforesaid proconsular Acts. On this subject see Ruinart, who treats it learnedly in *Sincera et Selecta*, p. 419 onward, and Tillemont, vol. V, p. 240 onward.

We think that the day of the glorious contest of these martyrs must be determined from the celebrated Acts as follows: Irene was crowned on 1 April, while the others were crowned several days earlier, and therefore at the end of March. The explicit mention of the Kalends of April, however, led the older martyrologists to record them all on the same day. Wandalbert followed them, speaking more explicitly of only the first two, and perhaps indicating the third by the word “companion”:

Distinguished Agape and Chionia by a virgin’s wreath,

They rightly consecrate the Kalends of April as companions to themselves.

Our third announcement from the Hieronymian Martyrologies is: “At Tauromenium in Sicily, the feast of the holy Pancratius.” In nearly this form, without a further eulogy—and indeed in a shorter form—the notice is also found in the Short Roman Martyrology, Ado, Usuard, and Notker; to the other martyrologists he is either unknown or omitted. It is the received opinion that he was the first apostle of the Sicilians. See what Henschenius carefully collected about him and distinguished from the apocryphal material. It is enough for us that he, like the others reported in the text, is truly Usuardine.

[Note: [Col. 0901D]]

This Tournai codex has a special addition unknown to all the others except Molanus. It reads: “In the monastery of Altovillari, the translation of the body of Saint Madelupus, priest.” See the observations in the index of the Omitted Saints. The rest will be said on 20 December.

[Col. 0903A] Rosweyd is pure in the notices of Evagrius and Benignus, and likewise in that of Pancratius. He discussed Agape and Chionia on the first day of this month, as we said there.

CENTULEN.: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Theodosia, virgin. At Tauromenium in Sicily, Blessed Pancratius, martyr. At Tours, Saint Antony, confessor.” See the additions for the preceding day.

ANTWERP-MAJOR discusses only Theodosia, with an eulogy drawn almost entirely from Ado.

BRUSSELS is nearly pure today. It begins with Agape and Chionia. Then, concerning Evagrius and Benignus: “At Tauromenium, a city of Sicily, Saint Pancratius, martyr.”

HAGENOYEN is pure in the first and second announcements; in the third place it has a notice of Nicetius, as we did yesterday. It then proceeds to Pancratius, purely. Then: “Likewise, in England, Richard, bishop. In Alsace, Saint Florentius, bishop and confessor.” The latter is referred in the Omitted Saints to 7 November.

[Col. 0903B] VICTORINUS and the SWEDISH REGISTRY, manuscript no. 130, add at the end: “At Caesarea in Palestine, Saint Theodosia.”

MARTYROLOGY OF THE CARTHUSIAN HOUSE OF UTRECHT: “The glorious Theodosia, virgin and martyr, whose various tortures and victories are read. Agape and Chionia, virgins and sister-martyrs.”

VATICAN, manuscript no. 5949, has at the end: “At Nicomedia, Saint Donatus.” See the Acts.

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE edition is pure in the first announcement, then continues: “At Thessalonica, the passion of the holy virgins Agape and Chionia, under the emperor Diocletian and the governor Sisinnius. They were sisters of Saint Irene, a virgin, and were first tormented in prison by various tortures, then thrown into the fire; but, remaining unharmed by the flames, after pouring out a prayer to the Lord, they gave back their souls to heaven. At Tauromenium, a city of Sicily, Saint Pancratius, bishop and confessor [he would have spoken more correctly had he said ‘martyr’]. On the same day, Saint Richard, bishop and confessor.”

GREVEN: “At Nicomedia, Saint Donatus. Likewise, Saints Sixtus, Benignus, Rufus, and Patricius. In England, Saint Richard, bishop of Chichester and confessor, and Burgundofara, abbess and virgin.” See the notices of her and of Sixtus with his companions in the Omitted Saints.

MOLANUS, in small type: “In England, Saint Richard, bishop and confessor of Chichester. Burgundofara, abbess and virgin. Saint Nicetas, father and confessor, for whom Theosterictus, the disciple of that most blessed man, wrote a funeral oration.” In other editions, immediately after Pancratius, in italic type, it adds: “bishop, killed by the pagan Archaganus, whose Life was written by Evagrius, his disciple.” But this account is everywhere rejected as fabulous. See Henschenius here and Tillemont, vol. I, p. 190. “In England, Richard,” and so forth, as above. “In the monastery of Altovillari, the translation of the body of Blessed Madelupus, priest. On the third day, Saint Nicetas, father and abbot of the monastery of Medion.” Again, in another type: “Likewise, the burial of Blessed Burgundofara, virgin and abbess of Evoriacum, concerning whom there is an account in the Life of Blessed Columbanus, abbot.” We have already said that the catalogue of the Omitted Saints should be consulted; it refers the reader to 7 December.

[Col. 0901]

At Tomis, a city of Scythia, the feast of the holy Evagrius and Benignus. At Thessalonica, the passion of the holy virgins Agape and Chionia under Diocletian. They were first tormented in prison, then thrown into the fire; but, remaining unharmed by the flames, after pouring out a prayer to the Lord, they gave back their souls. At Tauromenium in Sicily, Blessed Pancratius.

## 2 Non. Day 4

[Note: [Col. 0903B]]

From Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tournacensis, Pulsanensis, Antwerp, Maximus-Lübeck, Muneratianus, Belinus, the first edition of Grevenus, and Molanus. Add Antwerp-Major and all the codices of middling quality, discussed below.

[Note: [Col. 0903C]]

Antwerp and Maximus-Lübeck write *Mediolano*, as Bede and others occasionally do, as will become clear below. All read *Arrianae*; I would prefer *Arianae*, but I have followed the codices. Grevenus transposed the words to “the Catholic faith.” Molanus did worse by omitting “Catholic.” Pulsanensis has *Hyspalim* instead of *Hispali*, and *Hysidori* instead of *Isidori*. Tournacensis, Antwerp, Maximus-Lübeck, and Muneratianus have *Ysidori*. Grevenus and Molanus put *beati* instead of *sancti*, and *episcopi* instead of *antistitis*; the latter form is also found in Belinus.

[Note: [Col. 0903C]]

Scholars dispute the exact year and day on which the death of the great Father Ambrose should be recorded. Although on this day the Acts refer all Ambrosian material to 7 December, when the memory of the illustrious Doctor is celebrated more solemnly throughout the Church, Henschenius nevertheless wished, in a special dissertation before volume I of the April Acts, p. 38, to introduce the debate in a manner, setting out his opinion in advance “so that others,” as he says, “may rather express their own judgment.” From the Chronicle of Marcellinus Comes, with its explicit consular notation and several other records, especially Milanese ones, he attempts to prove that Ambrose’s death should be assigned not to 4 April 397, as Baronius had decided against the very ancient Milanese tradition, but to 17 April 398.

Against Henschenius stands the larger number of more recent scholars. Among them Pagius, in a decidedly emphatic tone, under the year 397, no. 19 onward, and the more restrained Tillemont, vol. X, note 56, p. 761 onward, argue more vigorously on behalf of Baronius’s opinion, relying also on the authority of our Martyrologies. I see weighty arguments on both sides, perhaps weightier ones favoring the Martyrologies. But those who undertake the Acts for December will decide the final point of uncertainty; here we shall remain within the bounds of the Martyrologies.

Among the Hieronymian Martyrologies, only the Corbie codex appended at the end of the list, in another hand and distinguished by Acherius as a pure addition: “At Milan, the burial of Saint Ambrose, bishop and confessor.” It is more certain that Ambrose is noted in all the Hieronymian codices on 30 November in approximately this form: “At Milan, Saint Ambrose, bishop, concerning the reception of baptism.” In the Lucca copy alone, on 3 December, we read: “The feast of Saint Ambrose.” Yet on 7 December none of those codices names Ambrose.

Let us turn to the day of his death. On this day, 4 April, the Venerable Bede is the first to celebrate Ambrose’s solemnity: “At Milan, the burial of Saint Ambrose, confessor.” Do not be surprised that the title “bishop” is omitted, for you will learn from more than one later passage that this was quite customary for Bede.
