Florus added on his own: “Who shone with immense learning and virtues.” Rabanus reads: “At Milan, the burial of Blessed Ambrose, bishop and confessor, whose distinguished life and teaching are proclaimed in the Church.” Here too he repeats Ambrose from the Hieronymian Martyrology on 30 November, without mentioning baptism.

Thus the Short Roman Martyrology has in our series: “At Milan, Blessed Ambrose, bishop and confessor.” Ado’s brief but elegant eulogy, taken from Jerome and explained by Baronius under 4 April and again under 7 December in his notes on the Martyrology, is reproduced verbatim in our text; Notker, contrary to his usual practice, greatly expands the Viennese wording. All these writers unanimously place Ambrose’s feast on this day, supported also by Wandalbert’s verse:

Ambrose entered heaven’s honor on the day before the Nones.

As for the Ordination, on 7 December there is no one who mentions it even in a word. I seek the beginning of the more solemn feast’s institution throughout the universal Church, but neither in Baronius nor elsewhere have I so far found sufficiently certain traces of its first origin, apart from what Henschenius briefly and somewhat obscurely indicates in the dissertation mentioned above. A fuller investigation does not belong here; it may conveniently be deferred to 7 December, where in the Acts, after the learned studies of Baronius, Hermantius, Tillemont, the Benedictine Fathers of Saint-Maur, and others concerning this incomparable champion of the faith, the whole sequence of his life will be arranged with greater labor and precision.

None of the ancient martyrologists mentions Isidore of Seville. It is therefore extremely probable that Usuard, who is known to have gone from Spain to obtain the relics of Saint Vincent, first brought him into Gaul, together with other confessors and martyrs, especially those of Córdoba, as we shall not fail to observe in their proper places. For the rest, consult the Acts, where Henschenius has most diligently collected everything that Nicolaus Antonius and other Spanish writers of better reputation could provide concerning the holiness, cult, and teaching of this noble bishop; to these should be added the appendix in the same volume, p. 900.

[Note: [Col. 0905B]]

ANTWERP-MAJOR, ANTWERP-MAXIMUS, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, the DANISH witness, and the UTRECHT-BELGIAN EDITION could all be counted among the pure codices. For concerning Isidore of Seville they add only this to the pure text: “Outstanding in faith and teaching.”

ROSWEYD reads: “At Milan, the burial of Blessed Ambrose, bishop and confessor, who, while both Arians and Christians were loudly calling out, was elected bishop from the laity, through whose zeal ….” The remainder is pure to the end of the list.

CENTULEN.: “At Milan, the burial of Blessed Ambrose, archbishop of that city, through whose zeal,” and so forth, purely. “In Spain, in the city of Seville, Saint Isidore, bishop and confessor, an illustrious man in life and teaching.”

BRUSSELS: “At Milan, the burial of Saint Ambrose, archbishop and confessor. While serving as governor and not yet baptized, he was elected archbishop by the consent of the whole people, with the approval and command of the emperor Valentinian; he received both the grace of baptism and the dignity of the episcopate. Through his zeal, in the time of the Arian perfidy, all Italy was converted to the Catholic faith. Blessed Paulinus of Nola, bishop, wrote his Life for Blessed Augustine [a recent hand adds: ‘bishop’]. At Seville, the burial of Saint Isidore of Seville, an eminent bishop, outstanding in faith and teaching. Among his other works, when arranging the book of natural history which he called the *Etymologies*, he carefully distinguished the ages of the world.” For the relationship between Isidore’s Chronicle and the book of the *Etymologies*, see Labbe’s *Historical Dissertations*, vol. I, p. 645.

HAGENOYEN composed a speech on Saint Ambrose much too long for our purpose. Among other insufficiently supported claims, it includes the assertion that Ambrose resisted the emperor Valentinian and forbade him to enter the church—an event commonly known to belong to Theodosius. We have judged these and similar matters worth omitting. Then: “In Spain, at the city of Seville, the burial of Saint Isidore, bishop and confessor, outstanding in faith and teaching.”

[Col. 0906B] MARTYROLOGY OF THE CARTHUSIAN HOUSE OF UTRECHT: “Isidore of Seville, eminent bishop and doctor, who produced many books, some of which are sufficiently well known.”

In the VATICAN manuscript, no. 5949, Isidore is absent. The following is added: “In Syria, Saints Taracus, Andronicus, and Probus.” They are also mentioned elsewhere and referred to 11 October.

ALTEMPS adds: “On the same day, the burial of Saint Senerthus, bishop.” He is omitted from the Acts and proposed to the curious investigator.

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE edition inserts after “confessor” in Ambrose’s eulogy: “and eminent doctor of the Catholic Church, through whose zeal ….” “At Seville, the burial of Saint Isidore, bishop, a man outstanding in faith and teaching, brother of Blessed Leander, to whom Blessed Gregory wrote a sacred exposition of the Book of Job.”

GREVEN: “At Thessalonica, Saints Agatho the deacon, Theodulus, Paul, Matutinus, and Urbanus. Likewise, Blessed Successus.” These are fragments, well or badly stitched together from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. “In Ireland, Beghanus, abbot. Likewise Ambrose the deacon, who, as Jerome reports in *On Illustrious Men*, was first a Marcionite, but was corrected by Origen and became renowned for the glory of confessing the Lord. In Scotland, Tigernach, bishop and confessor, according to others on the following day.” These persons are discussed in the index of the Omitted Saints.

MOLANUS: “On the same day, the translation of Saints Ulgisus, Amulguinus, Theodulf, Abel, and Hildulf, confessors.” See the Omitted Saints. It continues in smaller type: “In Persia, Saint Benjamin, glorious martyr: Tripartite History, book I, chapter 33. Likewise Ambrose the deacon,” and so forth, as in Grevenus. In other editions only this is added: “On the fourth day, Saints Joseph the hymnographer and George, who was at Maleum.” Henschenius collected little about this George in the present Acts. Joseph was reported on the preceding day, where a longer Life is given and everything concerning him is carefully explained by Papebrochius. It is enough to have indicated these matters; let the reader consult that section for the rest.

[Col. 0903]

At Milan, the burial of Blessed Ambrose, bishop and confessor, through whose zeal, among his other distinctions in teaching and miracles, all Italy was converted to the Catholic faith during the time of the Arian perfidy. At Seville, the burial of Saint Isidore, bishop.

## Nones. Day 5

[Note: [Col. 0905D]]

From Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tournacensis, Antwerp, Maximus-Lübeck, Muneratianus, the first edition of Belinus, Grevenus, and Molanus. To these are added Antwerp-Maximus, Leyden-Belgian, Louvain, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition.

[Note: [Col. 0905D]]

The first difficulty concerns the spelling of proper names. The Pratensis codex reads *Martiani, Nicandri*, whereas all the others, except Molanus and Louvain, explicitly have *Martianae, Nicanoris* or *Nichanoris*. I am firmly persuaded that Usuard wrote this way, unless he abandoned his guides, the Short Roman Martyrology and Ado, on his own authority.

Some codices incorrectly write *Appollonii*, *Appolonii*, or *Apolonii*; the form in the text, agreeing with Pratensis, Heriniensis, and others, is better. There is no less variation in the virgin’s name. The Hieronymian Martyrology has *Herene*; the Short Roman Martyrology and Ado have *Irene*, which I think should be written. The Usuardine reading is disputed. Pratensis has *Hireniae*; all the others have *Hirenis* or *Hyrenis*. Muneratianus alone writes *Herenis*. Heriniensis, Tournacensis, Antwerp, and Maximus-Lübeck support the first form, which we have preferred as closer to the truth. After “virgin,” Muneratianus adds “and martyr,” against the overwhelming majority.

Above, from the inflection of the codices, we placed *Agapis* in the text, from the nominative *Agapes*, just as here *Hirenis* is formed from *Hirenes*, although we customarily write it otherwise. Belinus alone has *Sissinio* and likewise *passae sunt*; nearly all the others have *martyrizatae sunt*; Heriniensis, *martyrizarunt*; Pratensis, *martyrizaverunt*, a form quite frequent in Ado. Since Usuard followed him so closely today, it would not be surprising if he copied this as well. Molanus correctly reads *Lyciae*; the others have *Liciae*, which we have retained in the text. *Liciniae* is an error in Heriniensis; *Ciliciae* occurs in Belinus.

[Note: [Col. 0907A]]

It is quite remarkable and unusual that none of the saints from the preceding list is recorded in the Acts on this day. The Egyptian martyrs are not included because they are recorded elsewhere, especially in the modern Roman Martyrology, on 5 June. Henschenius refers them to that date as the same persons who are commemorated on both Nones—those of April and those of June—under nearly the same names; this is his view there against Florentius. Indeed, in some Hieronymian manuscripts the same persons appear to be recorded on both days.

Thus, on this day, in the second place, the Lucca manuscript and Acherius’s Corbie manuscript have: “In Egypt, the feast of the holy Marciana, Nicanor, and Apollonius.” The Echternach manuscript has only: “In Egypt, Marcianus.” Bede’s series says nothing about them. But the Short Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Usuard announce the same three in the same manner, while Notker substitutes *Martiani* for *Martianae*, as do several of our codices in the remainder of the Usuardine text. The rest will be given under the aforesaid date, 5 June, where it will be discussed whether the double class of these three persons should be identified or distinguished.

Nor is Irene treated separately in our work, since she was mentioned with her sisters Agape and Chionia on 3 April, whose Acts are common, as we explained there at length. In the Hieronymian Martyrologies the three sisters are repeated on this day as well. The Short Roman Martyrology reads: “At Thessalonica, Saint Irene, virgin.” Ado’s eulogy, and consequently ours, was copied from Bede, moderately enlarged by Rabanus and extensively by Notker. The account of all of them must be tested rather strictly against the proconsular Acts, with the phrase “struck by an arrow” removed. I am surprised that Baronius, who corrected the rest properly, left it in his text. If I am not mistaken, Wandalbert followed Bede:

On the Nones the holy virgin Irene shines forth from death.

Finally, Amphianus also has no place in the present Acts, although he is explicitly noted in the Hieronymian Martyrologies: “At Caesarea, or Caesaria, in Lycia or Lycia, Amphianus.” Another Amphianus is read there in Africa on the second day, and another at Nicomedia on 3 April. Baronius, Henschenius, and Florentius do not doubt that this refers to that innocent lamb, divine martyr, portentously courageous, fearless, admirable, most holy and blessed young man Apphianus, whose glorious victory over the tyrant was accurately described by Eusebius, an eyewitness of the exceedingly harsh contest; from him the foregoing titles have been taken, in book 4 of *On the Martyrs of Palestine*. The whole account is reproduced in the Acts, and Ruinart reproduces it in full beginning on p. 334. The Gallic series is found in Tillemont, vol. V, p. 386; in a note on p. 737 he attempts to harmonize Eusebius’s chronology, which he had proposed to learned readers for further examination. See Henschenius, p. 59, letter F.

That our author wrongly places this Caesarea in Lycia should be blamed not so much on him as on Ado—or rather on the unskilled scribes who, while copying the Hieronymian text, removed, added, or changed something. Whether Florentius correctly restores the Hieronymian text by reading “At Caesarea in Lycia,” with reference to the martyr’s homeland and cult, I leave to others to consider. Since the martyrologists do not deal here with Aedesius, Apphianus’s brother, it is of no concern to our author either. It is enough to have presented the genuine text in every respect. See the modern Roman Martyrology for Aedesius on 8 April, and there consult our Acts, which report his martyrdom from Eusebius.

[Note: [Col. 0907C]]

PULSANENSIS lacks the final announcement; otherwise it is pure.

ROSWEYD, after Amphianus, adds “and others.” Then: “Claudius, martyr.” From the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

UTRECHT, LEYDEN-LATIN, ALBERGEN, and the DANISH witness append to the otherwise pure text: “In Scotland, Saint Tigernach, bishop and confessor.”

CENTULEN.: “At Thessalonica, Saint Herene, virgin and martyr. In Egypt, Saints Nicanor and Apollonius, martyrs. At Caesarea in Lycia, Saint Amphianus.”

[Col. 0907D] ANTWERP-MAJOR: “At Thessalonica, the feast of Saint Irene, virgin and martyr. In Egypt, the feast of Saints Marciana, Nicanor, and Apollonius, whose deeds are recorded.”

BRUSSELS says nothing about the Egyptian martyrs or Amphianus. In the notice of Irene it is sufficiently pure. It continues: “In Scotland, Saint Tigernach, bishop and confessor. Likewise Marina, virgin. And Saint Vincent of Valencia, doctor of the Order of Preachers, who was renowned for miracles both in life and after death.” Which Marina is meant here, I do not know.

HAGENOYEN, otherwise pure today, adds only: “On the same day, in Scotland, the burial of Saint Tigerilach [Tigernach], bishop and confessor.”

VICTORINUS and the SWEDISH REGISTRY, no. 130, have at the end: “Likewise at Carthage, Saint Pontianus, deacon.” No other Pontianus is known today, not even among the Omitted Saints. I am greatly mistaken if this does not refer to Pontius, the deacon of Saint Cyprian, discussed above on 8 March.

MARTYROLOGY OF THE CARTHUSIAN HOUSE OF UTRECHT: “Irene, virgin and martyr, sister of Agape and Chionia. Didymus of Alexandria, confessor, whom Jerome mentions.” Is this perhaps the martyr discussed in the Acts?

STROZZI: “The feast of Saint Vincent, of the Order of Preachers, a native of Valencia and a most renowned preacher, who rested in the British city of Vannes, whose holiness is attested by frequent miracles.”

REIMS has Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “At Châlons, the burial of Arulfus, bishop.” He is omitted from the index of the Omitted Saints as unknown.

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE edition treats Saint Vincent first, but its eulogy is mutilated in places; we shall give it more correctly below from Grevenus. Concerning the Egyptians it adds, “whose deeds are recorded.” The rest is as in the text. At the end: “In Scotland, Saint Tigernach, bishop and confessor.”

The second edition of BELINUS adds at the end: “Likewise, in the city of Vannes in Brittany, Blessed Vincent, confessor, of the Order of Preachers, most renowned for holiness, teaching, and miracles.”

GREVEN: “At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Claudianus, confessor.” Why not “martyr”? “Likewise, Didymus, confessor. Marcianus, Quintus.” He seems to indicate Alexandrian martyrs. “In Lesser Britain, in the city of Vannes, the feast of Blessed Vincent, priest and confessor, of the Order of Preachers. By origin a Valencian, shining with an angelic life and salutary teaching, he long nourished the various peoples of Spain and Gaul with the food of the divine word and converted more than twenty thousand Jews and Moors to Christ. Finally renowned for every kind of sign, he deserved to be numbered among the saints and adorned with the most distinguished honor of canonization.”

MOLANUS: “Likewise at Vannes in Brittany, Blessed Vincent of Valencia, surnamed Ferrarius [Ferrer], confessor of the Order of Preachers, most renowned for holiness, teaching, and miracles. He converted more than twenty thousand Jews and Moors to Christ. At Laon-Clavatus, the first translation of Saint Celinia, mother of Saint Remigius, bishop.” See the Omitted Saints. “In Scotland, Saint Tigernach, bishop and confessor.” Then, in smaller type: “At Liège, on Mount Cornillon, Juliana, virgin and prioress of that place, died and was translated to rest in the monastery of Villers, where her Life is also found.” In other editions, concerning Vincent, as above. “In Scotland, Saint Tigernach, and so forth. On the fifth day, Saints Theodulus and Agathopus, martyrs.” They are treated in the Acts for 4 April. “At Laon-Clavatus,” and so forth. Then, in smaller type: “On the same day, the holy martyrs Saint Thermes, with her sister and maidservant.” The notice is referred among the Omitted Saints to 22 April. “At Liège, on Mount Cornillon, Juliana, virgin and prioress of that place, died; on the third day after her death she was translated to the monastery of Villers and buried there among the sacred bodies. Her Life is also preserved there.” This account is given in the Acts and splendidly illustrated by Henschenius.

[Col. 0905]

In Egypt, the feast of the holy martyrs Marciana, Nicanor, and Apollonius. At Thessalonica, Saint Irene, virgin, who, after enduring imprisonment, was struck by an arrow by the governor Sisinnius; under him her sisters Agape and Chionia were likewise martyred. At Caesarea in Lycia, Saint Amphianus.

## 8 Idus. Day 6

[Note: [Col. 0909A]]

So read Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tournacensis, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp, Maximus-Lübeck, Muneratianus, Grevenus, and Molanus. Closest to these are Antwerp-Maximus, Leyden-Belgian, Louvain, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition.

[Note: [Col. 0909B]]

The issue concerns only the names Sixtus and Timothy. It is sufficiently certain that Heriniensis and the Great Lübeck Edition read the final name incorrectly as *Timothei*. The older spelling in Hieronymus and the Short Roman Martyrology seems to support *Xystus* or *Xistus*. Pratensis indeed has *Xysti*. But since all the other codices without exception read *Sixti*, together with Ado, we have judged that spelling preferable here; if the other form prevails elsewhere, it may be used there.

[Note: [Col. 0909B]]

Some copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology name two Sixtuses or Xistuses on this day. That they do not, however, concern the first pope of that name is proved by the groups of martyrs among whom they are mingled, separated from this Sixtus by place and probably by time. The person announced in the list is therefore taken from the Short Roman Martyrology, whose words are: “Sixtus, pope and martyr, who suffered under Hadrian.” Ado’s eulogy in Rosweyd is brief, while Notker gives it much more fully; unless Mosander’s edition is to be preferred, in which nearly word for word are found passages that one might easily persuade oneself belonged specifically to Notker. Our author shortened Ado’s wording as it appears in Rosweyd and softened it somewhat.

We believe that the first information about Sixtus was taken from the *Liber Pontificalis* by the Short Roman Martyrology. He is venerated as a martyr, whatever doubts some may have raised about that title. Florus gives a fuller account on 3 April; it is presented in our edition of Bede and in the Acts for this day. There Henschenius collected and distinguished everything that can be said about Sixtus I—his cult, age, Acts, burial, translation, and discovery—while other writers merely touch upon his deeds, as Tillemont does in volume II, pp. 238 and 240, in his treatment of Alexander. Wandalbert celebrated him in this couplet:

On the eighth day before the Ides, Sixtus, sacred martyr,

Shines forth, having suffered death under Caesar Hadrian.

On this day the Hieronymian Martyrologies agree in our final announcement concerning Timothy and Diogenes. Usuard must certainly have extracted it from some such codex, since they are entirely unknown to the other martyrologists, both earlier and contemporary, except Notker, who copied the same codices incorrectly, reading Nicomedia for Macedonia and Theogenes for Diogenes; Henschenius and Florentius rightly correct this.

There are two martyrs of the same names, Timothy and Diogenes; if they are not the same persons, they are read in the Hieronymian Martyrologies on the following day, with this difference: here they are said to have suffered in Macedonia and are joined to no companions; on the following day they are said to have suffered martyrdom with two or three companions at Antioch in Syria. Hence I do not know how Maurolycus came upon Philippi as the definite arena of our martyrs, nor is it sufficiently clear whether the two groups should be confused. The Acts are concealed, from which, as Henschenius says, we could present more certain information and distinguish these martyrs of today from the Antiochene martyrs on firmer grounds. Florentius’s notes on both days provide no greater clarity. We have given the Usuardine material in full.

[Note: [Col. 0909C]]

PULSANENSIS is pure in the notice of Sixtus, but omits Timothy and Diogenes, in whose place it has: “On the same day, Saint Celestine, pope.” It indicates Celestine I, who is discussed frequently below and in the Acts for this day.

ANTWERP-MAXIMUS, LEYDEN, BELGIAN, LOUVAIN, and the UTRECHT-BELGIAN EDITION expand the text as follows: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Sixtus I, pope and martyr, who was sixth after Blessed Peter, in the time of Hadrian,” and so forth.

UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, and the DANISH witness have the same, but moreover add after *temporalem*: “He established that the sacred mysteries should not be celebrated except by sacred ministers.”

CENTULEN shortens the text in this way: “At Rome, the passion of Blessed Sixtus, pope and martyr, in the time of the emperor Hadrian. In Macedonia,” and so forth, purely.

ROSWEYD, fuller than all the others, is pure in the notice of Sixtus. Then, in second place: “At Nicomedia, Firmus, bishop and martyr, and twenty-eight others.” Henschenius carefully examined in the Acts whether the episcopal dignity is rightly attributed to Firmus and how many companions he had. “In Africa, Epiphanius, bishop, and fourteen others.” We shall discuss this group with Usuard on the following day. “Likewise, Caelestina, virgin, with eight hundred others.” On the authority of almost this codex, this distinguished company is included in the Acts. “At Nicomedia, Saints Timothy and Diogenes.”

BRUSSELS transfers a large part of yesterday’s text to this day. It first treats Marciana, Nicanor, and Apollonius, then Amphianus. It proceeds to Sixtus, after whose pure text it adds: “He established that ‘Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth’ should be said in the Mass.” “In Macedonia,” and so forth, purely. “Likewise, Blessed Florentius, martyr.” Is this Florentinus one of the Sirmian martyrs? So far the matter is not sufficiently clear.

HAGENOYEN.: “At Rome, the commemoration of blessed Sixtus, first pope and martyr, who was sixth after blessed Peter and, in the time of the emperor Hadrian, after governing the apostolic see for nine years and five months, willingly endured temporal death in order to gain Christ for himself. He established that the sacred mysteries should not be celebrated except by sacred ministers.”

“Also on the same day, the commemoration of Saint Irenaeus, bishop and martyr of the people of Sirmium. After being worn down for many days in prison, he was finally killed by the sword, and his body was thrown into a river.” Among the martyrs of Sirmium there is no Irenaeus today, much less a bishop. Firmus is the leader of the Nicomedians; through an embarrassing mistake Rabanus transformed him into a man of Sirmium, and made Irenaeus, originally Firmus’s companion and otherwise a bishop, bishop of the same place. Florentinius had already observed this before me, attributing it to Notker, who, being younger than Rabanus, probably derived that episcopate from this source. The HAGENOYEN. writer could have drawn this from either error, unless perhaps he saw Florus, who mentions that Irenaeus today but assigns him a different eulogy. For Irenaeus of Sirmium, see 25 March. He continues: “In Macedonia, Saints Timothy and Diogenes.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked no. 130, add at the end: “At Troyes, Saint Winobaudus the priest.” Others express it differently, as will soon be evident.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Irenaeus, bishop and martyr, Timothy and Diogenes. Sixtus, pope and martyr.”

VATICAN., marked no. 5949, is silent about Timothy and Diogenes. At the end it adds: “Saint Celestine the pope, who sat at Rome for eight years.”

STROZZ.: “Also Saint Celestine the pope.”

REMENS. has Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “At Troyes, Saint Winobaudus the priest and confessor.”

[Col. 0911C] The LUBECK-COLOGNE edition: “At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Sixtus the first, pope and martyr, who, sixth after blessed Peter the apostle, in the time of the emperor Hadrian, [Col. 0912A] governed the Church for ten years, two months, and one day; and, in order to gain Christ for himself, willingly endured temporal death. He established that the sacred mysteries should not be celebrated except by sacred ministers, and that the altar cloth should not be made of silk, but of the purest woven linen, undyed. He also established that ‘Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth’ should be said three times at Mass. He was beheaded at the Appian Gate, where the Lord appeared to blessed Peter when he was saying, ‘Lord, where are you going?’ In Macedonia,” etc., accurately. “At Troyes, Saint Prudentius, bishop and confessor.” For more about him, see the Praetermissi. “On the same day, blessed Vermebandus the abbot.” Read Winebaudi; others have Winobaudi.

Both editions of BELINUS add at the end: “Also Saint Celestine the pope.” Concerning him, see above many times.

GREVEN.: “Firmus, bishop and martyr” (for him and those who follow, consult the Acta and the Praetermissi, so that you may distinguish the errors and confusions), “and his twenty-five companions. At Sirmium, Saints Rufina, Moderata, Maxima, and Macharia. Also Saints Herenneus, Romanus, Donatus, Clusius, Quiriacus, and Irenaeus, bishop of Smyrna. Celestine the virgin and eighty other martyrs. Lucia, widow and martyr. Anegra of Galatia, blessed Theodore the bishop, distinguished for wisdom and holiness. In Dacia, William the abbot and confessor. At Troyes, Prudentius, bishop and confessor. Vermebandus the abbot.”

MOLAN.: “Also Saint Celestine the abbot.” Is he not the pope? “And blessed Wermebandus the abbot.” Then, in smaller type: “In Ireland, Saint Celsus, archbishop of Ardinach and confessor, concerning whom Saint Bernard writes in the Life of Malachy. At Constantinople, the commemoration of our great and blessed father Eutychius, patriarch of Constantinople, whose Life and miracles were written by Eustachius, a humble priest.” Thus far the first edition. In the others, more briefly: “Also Saint Celestine the pope. And blessed Wermebandus the abbot. In Dacia, William, abbot of Roschild and confessor. On the sixth day, Saint Eutychius, archbishop of Constantinople.” The eulogy appended in the first edition is omitted. See the rest in the Acta.]

[Col. 0909]

At Rome, the commemoration of blessed Sixtus, pope and martyr, who, in the time of Hadrian, willingly endured temporal death in order to gain Christ for himself. In Macedonia, Saints Timothy and Diogenes.

VII Idus. Day 7.

[Note: [Col. 0911C]

The manuscripts of Pratensis, Herinien., Tornacen., Antwerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. are pure. Add Antwerp.-Max., both Utrecht manuscripts, both Leyden manuscripts, Lovanien., [Col. 0912C] and the Utrecht-Belgian edition. Belinus also belongs here, differing only in placing Pelusium before Hegesippus.]

[Note: [Col. 0911D]

For Epiphanius and Donatus’s thirteen companions, quite a few manuscripts give fourteen, as do Antwerp., Max.-Lubec., manuscripts of middling quality, and others. Whether the number in the text should be retained, see the Acta; we are certain that Usuard wrote this way, as is clear from the better manuscripts. I entirely agree that Hegesippus should be read, as the Tornacensis manuscript alone has it; Pratensis wrongly has Hejesippus, and Herinien. has the no better form Eiesippus. In the text, meanwhile, the others agree with all the other manuscripts and, after Ado in both editions, have Egesippus. Eusippus in Muneratus is attributable to a typographical error. Tornacen., Max.-Lubec., and the manuscripts of middling quality read Apostolorum temporibus, “in the times of the Apostles,” more elegantly instead of Apostolorum temporum. All the rest read as in the text; here Usuard did not correctly follow his source, who had accurately written, after Jerome, vicinus Apostolorum temporum, “near to the times of the Apostles.” In all the manuscripts the word omnes, “all,” follows; Greven and Molan omitted it, although both, together with other manuscripts of middling quality, add sermone simplici, “in simple language,” taken from Ado rather than Usuard. Muneratus wrote caractere, preserving the case used by the modern Roman text. But all the manuscripts I have seen use the accusative, and all likewise read as preserved in the text; if this is too scrupulous, it may be corrected at my discretion. I do not know where Greven found Peleusippi; Molan prefers Peleusii, along with Antwerp. and Max.-Lubec. We prefer the more common spelling represented in the text. It is enough to point out the scribal errors, such as Affricam, Aphricam, historias, and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0911D]

Henschenius composed a brief but accurate Commentary on Epiphanius and his companions, in which you will find the opinions of various Martyrologies concerning the day of their contest and the number of their companions. It would be superfluous to repeat them here. This, however, should be noted: Usuard appears to have been the first to place this group of martyrs on this day, whereas the Hieronymian Martyrologies generally announce them on the eighth day before the Ides, as Notker also did. Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Rabanus mention them on neither day. Hegesippus, first mentioned by the Little Roman Martyrology as near to the apostolic age, is adorned by Ado with a distinguished encomium, taken almost entirely from Saint Jerome’s book On Illustrious Men. Our author contracted it into a shorter form, wisely omitting those details that more properly belong to Saint Justin, as Henschenius correctly observed in the Acta. Notker is even briefer than usual in his eulogy of Hegesippus, cutting out the disputed period in which Ado wrongly attributes to Hegesippus the words fully given in Greven’s supplement: “For I myself, trained in the Platonic schools, hearing Christians slandered and seeing them fearless,” and so forth. Henschenius indicates here briefly that these words should be attributed to Justin; he proves the point more fully on 13 April. On this day he assembles several matters concerning Hegesippus from various passages of Eusebius, historically set out by Tillemont in volume III, page 47.

Pelusius, or Peleusius, unknown to the Little Roman Martyrology and to Ado, undoubtedly came from some Hieronymian manuscript in which he is called Pilusus; Usuard excerpted him from it. Rabanus calls him Pilosus; others express the name differently. Wandalbert’s verse seems to proceed from the sense of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in which Diogenes and Timothy are also placed today. It reads:

“Diogenes and Peleusius are said to be [here] on the seventh.”

For a time Henschenius judged that these were not the same pair of martyrs as those listed in yesterday’s entry for Macedonia and assigned today by the Hieronymian Martyrologies to Antioch in Syria. But enough about them on the preceding day. What has been said suffices for the truth of the text. The difficulty troubling Henschenius—whether Peleusius, Peleusus, Pelensius, Pelusus, and so forth is also called Clusius among the many names in the ancient copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology for the preceding day, and whether Eleusius and Peleusius are one and the same—belongs to the same great uncertainty that surrounds so many other martyrs drawn from those manuscripts. Since no further information about them can be obtained elsewhere, they scarcely leave us enough evidence even to distinguish one from another with any security by a merely probable conjecture. It seems safest to me to follow the traces of our Martyrologies until something more certain comes to light.”]

[Note: [Col. 0913B]

ULSAN. speaks as follows today: “In Africa, Saints Epiphanius the deacon, Donatus, and thirteen others. In Alexandria, Saint Pelusius the priest. On the same day, Saint Victor.” I do not know who this Victor is, unless he is to be counted among the Libyan martyrs.

ALBERGEN. and DANIC. begin in this way: “At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Celestine the pope, who established that David’s 150 psalms should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice, for previously only the Epistle and Gospel were recited.” Ado Mosander has something similar, so it is entirely plausible that this passed here from some copy of Ado. In the rest, the cited manuscripts are pure.

[Col. 0913C] CENTULEN.: “Hegesippus, a most holy man, near to the times of the Apostles. In Alexandria, Saint Pelusius the priest. In Africa, Saints Epiphanius the bishop, Donatus, and others.”

ROSWEYD.: “In Africa, Saints Epiphanius and Donatus, martyrs.” He then proceeds fairly accurately concerning Hegesippus. Then: “In Antioch of Syria, Timothy the martyr with six others. In Alexandria, Pelusius the bishop.” In the text, priest is better.

ANTUERP.-MAJ. places Hegesippus first with a longer eulogy, taken almost entirely from Ado. It gives Epiphanius accurately and says nothing about Pelusius.

BRUXELLEN. contains much that I considered worthy of the curious reader. It begins: “Hegesippus the confessor, a most holy man. Since he was near the times of the Apostles, he composed five books in simple language, weaving together histories of ecclesiastical events from the Passion of the Lord to his own age and gathering here and there many things useful to readers, so that in his manner of speaking also he might express the character of those whose life he followed.” Thus far is from Ado; what follows he added on his own: “At Rome, blessed Celestine the pope. He governed the Church for eight years. He established that the psalm Judica should be said before the entrance of the Mass. From his institution also come the Introit, Graduals, and Offertories, which are said in the Mass before the sacrifice and are drawn from the Psalms. Under him the Third Synod of Ephesus also condemned Nestorius the heretic. This Pope Celestine also sent Saint Patrick, son of Conches and nephew of blessed Martin of Tours, to Ireland; he converted everyone there to the faith of Christ.” In Epiphanius and Pelusius it is accurate. At the end it adds: “Also Saint Macarius the monk.” This is omitted.

HAGENOYEN. is, unusually, almost but not entirely pure in the text; concerning Celestine it has the same material that I quoted above from ALBERG. and DANIC.

REG. SUEC., which belonged to Prince Ursinus in Bohemia: “At Rome, Saint Celestine the pope. After blessed Peter he established that David’s 150 psalms should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice, for previously only the Epistle and the holy Gospel were recited.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Hegesippus the confessor, a most holy man, who wrote histories from the Passion of the Lord to his own age. Pelusius the priest and confessor.” Why not martyr?

VATICAN., marked no. 5949, passes over Pelusius but adds: “In Antioch of Syria, Saints Timothy and Diogenes.”

The LUBECK-COLOGNE edition: “At Rome, Saint Celestine the pope and confessor, who governed the Church for eight years.” [Col. 0914C] It follows with the material previously given from LOVANIEN. Then: “He also established that the psalm Judica me, Deus, et discerne causam meam, ‘Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause,’ should be said before the Entrance of the Mass.” In the African material it is quite pure. Concerning Hegesippus it has nearly the same as the Bruxellensis. At the end: “In Alexandria, Saint Pelusius the priest and confessor.”

GREVEN.: “The aforesaid Hegesippus reports the following in his books: ‘For I, too, trained in the schools of Plato, hearing Christians slandered and seeing them fearless in accepting death and enduring every punishment, considered that it was impossible for them to live in wickedness and lust.’” These words are taken from Ado, but, as we have said, should be denied to Hegesippus. “In England, Salvator the martyr.” He is unknown even to the English. “Also Eleusius, Macharia, and Philibert.” For what should be said about this conjunction, see the index of the Praetermissi. “Celestine the pope and confessor, who governed the Church for eight years. He,” etc., as in ALBERGEN. “Some place him,” he says, “on the following day.” Rather, on various days. “Brandanus, bishop and confessor. The translation of Saint Timothy the apostle and martyr.” See the Praetermissi concerning these. “Also in Eifel, at the monastery of Steinfeld, the blessed Hermann, who because of his simplicity was also called Joseph.”

MOLAN. gives the material already mentioned about Hermann in smaller type: “On the same day, Saint Aibertus, monk and priest of the monastery of Crespin, whose life was written by a certain archdeacon of Ostrevant.” Other editions add: “On the seventh day, Saint George, bishop of Melitene.” Mitylene is better. In still smaller type: “At Crespin, the Lord Aibertus died enclosed as a recluse; Crespin commemorates him in the monastery’s litanies. His feast is celebrated in the nearby chapel where he rests, on the day after the dedication of its oratory, which is 2 May. At Pompeii, Saint Calliopius the martyr. In Eifel, at the monastery of Steinfeld, the blessed [Hermann],” etc., as above.]

[Col. 0911]

In Africa, the commemoration of Saints Epiphanius the bishop, Donatus, and thirteen others. On the same day, Hegesippus, a most holy man, near to the times of the Apostles, who wove histories of ecclesiastical events from the Passion of the Lord to his own age, so that he might also express in his manner of speaking the character of those whose life he followed. In Alexandria, Saint Pelusius the priest.

VI Idus. Day 8.

[Note: [Col. 0915A]

From Pratensis, Herinien., Tornacen., Munerat., Greven, and Molan. Add Antwerp.-Max., Utrecht, Leyden, Lovanien., Albergen., Danic., and the Utrecht-Belgian edition. [Col. 0916A]]

[Note: [Col. 0915A]

The manuscripts differ very little, and in matters scarcely worth noticing. Herinien. alone writes Corintum. The others differ slightly; most have the reading in the text, and rightly. All read Dionisii, and we have thought that this should be retained, although Dionysii ought to be written. Greven and Molan wrongly have Thuronis. In Greven alone it is ammirandae.]

[Note: [Col. 0915A]

The Acta today discuss Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, the letters written by him, and the translation of his sacred body to the monastery of Saint-Denis under Pope Innocent III. Several Martyrologies are cited there in which the feast of Dionysius is commemorated on this day. Yet among them no Martyrology is older than Usuard, nor can any contemporary of his be found. Wandalbert’s [Col. 0915B] verse departs very widely from the text:

“Maximus and Solutor hold the sixth day before the Ides.”

These two saints can have come only from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Usuard’s announcement is therefore as distinctive as it is certain that he received it from no earlier martyrologist. Usuard gives no detail in his eulogy that could not be said of all the ancient writers of the Church, as is clear from what has been said and will become even clearer from what follows. He could certainly have drawn from Eusebius some details more specifically suited to this Dionysius, as the Acta present them in order, after removing those that were customarily attributed to him improperly. Tillemont kept Henschenius before his eyes in volume II, beginning at page 448. Furthermore, the controversy over whether the body resting in the monastery of Saint-Denis belongs to Dionysius the Areopagite of Athens or to this bishop of Corinth does not concern the present purpose.

The Little Roman Martyrology mentions Perpetuus, and after it Ado; Usuard took from Ado only what we have seen above to be common to several other saints, cutting out those details that applied specifically to Perpetuus. Notker gave a more faithful version of his own, and expanded Ado’s words with an angelic demonstration. The Ado text is given almost in full below by the supplements of the Brussels and HAGENOYEN manuscripts. So much for our Usuard, who here, as he often does, followed Ado. Some Hieronymian manuscripts cited by Florentinius write differently; under 30 December, at the very end, they read: “At Tours, Perpetuus, bishop and confessor.” Rabanus added on the same day: “He built the church of Saint Martin.” Florus had said somewhat more; see him either in the source or in the Acta. As for what is found concerning Perpetuus in the manuscripts of Ado, Mosander and Rosweyd rightly judged it, in my opinion, to be an addition. It is not easy to decide which day is preferable, since Gregory of Tours, from whom Perpetuus’s life is taken, neglected to indicate the day that was his last on earth and his birthday in heaven. See Henschenius for the rest.]

[Note: [Col. 0915C]

PULSANEN., ANTUERPIEN.-MAX., LUBECK, and BELINUS may be counted among the pure manuscripts. They differ only in omitting the very brief eulogy of Perpetuus of Tours, writing instead: “At Tours, Saint Perpetuus the bishop.”

ROSWEYD. would also be pure, except that between Dionysius and Perpetuus it inserts the following: “In Africa, Macharius the martyr and nine others.” I should like to be told how the writer of this manuscript was able to extract precisely a group of nine companions.

CENTULEN.: “At Toulouse, blessed Exuperius, bishop and confessor. This blessed man was very sparing [I think, ‘toward himself’ is understood], but toward the needy he was [generous] and compassionate.” ANTUERP.-MAJ., which will be cited immediately, gives this better from Usuard, but the material belongs to 28 September. CENTULEN. continues: “At Corinth, blessed Dionysius the bishop. At Tours, Saint Perpetuus, bishop and confessor.”

ANTUERP.-MAJ., omitting Dionysius and Perpetuus, supplements Exuperius’s eulogy in this way: “At Toulouse, [Col. 0915D] Saint Exuperius, bishop and confessor. Saint Jerome has commemorated this blessed man in a memorable account, showing how sparing he was toward himself and how generous toward others.”

BRUXELLEN. gives concerning Dionysius almost what we have in the text, though in a slightly different order. It then proceeds to Exuperius, as the immediately preceding manuscript does. Then: “Also at Rome, Calixtus the pope and martyr, whose principal feast falls on the fourteenth day before the Ides of October.” Whence, then, comes this lesser principal feast, unknown to others? Is it perhaps from some translation? See the Praetermissi, where it is assigned to that day, 14 October: “At Tours, Saint Perpetuus the bishop, a man of admirable holiness, by whose efforts [Col. 0916C] the church built over the bones of blessed Martin the bishop was completed, and his body was transferred there.” This is taken from Ado, though not word for word.

HAGENOYEN. is also almost pure concerning Dionysius. Concerning Perpetuus, after “a man,” it adds: “He built a church in honor of blessed Martin the bishop, caused the bones of blessed Martin to be transferred, and honorably placed them in that same church, as was fitting. Finally, after accomplishing many miracles, he himself died in tranquil peace.”

AQUICINCT. adds at the end, after “a man”: “At Rome, Saint Celestine the pope. He established that David’s psalms should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice, for previously only the Epistle was recited, and the holy Gospel.” You see that what we said is true: this saint is reported on various days.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Dionysius, bishop of Corinth. Perpetuus, bishop of Tours.”

[Col. 0916D] In VATICAN., marked no. 5949, the following has been added: “In Africa, Saints Macarius, Connexus, Concessus, and Maxima.” They have been taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

ALTEMPS.: “Also Concessus, Ammonius, and Successus.” These too are taken from the same source. See in the Acta where they are correctly joined.

FLORENTIN.: “At Rome, in the cemetery of Saint Priscilla on the Salarian Way, the commemoration of Saint Celestine the first, pope and martyr.”

The LUBECK-COLOGNE edition is pure concerning Dionysius. It has the following concerning Perpetuus: “At Tours, Saint Perpetuus the bishop, a man of admirable holiness, by whose efforts a church over the revered bones of blessed Martin the bishop was completed, and he was the founder of many other churches.”

GREVEN.: “In Africa, the commemoration of Saints Timor, Macarius, Connexus, and Maxima, and others. Also Concessus, Salutaris [why not Solutor?], Successus, Januarius, and Pinnarius, martyrs.” From different copies of Jerome. “Celestine the pope, according to others on the preceding day. Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse and confessor, who is listed below under 28 September. Gemmarius the abbot and confessor.” Could this be Genemarus? Henschenius thinks it is “Geremarus,” the abbot of Flay, who is celebrated, or at least reported by others, on 24 September. “Sexburga, queen and abbess, whom Bede mentions in Book IV of the History of the English People.” Her feast day is 6 July.

MOLAN. transcribed Greven concerning Sexburga or Sexburge in smaller type. It continues: “The burial of blessed Redemptus, bishop and confessor of the city of Ferentina, concerning whom Gregory speaks in the Dialogues.” Thus far the first edition. In the others: “Also blessed Albert, father of the Carmelite order, bishop and confessor of the Church of Jerusalem. At Marchiennes, the elevation of Saint Jonatus, confessor of Christ.” This is assigned to 1 August. “On the eighth day, Saints Herodian, Agabus, Rufus, and their companions, apostles.” Thus they are celebrated by the Greeks on this day and together in the Moscow Calendar; by the Latins separately, as can be seen in the index of the Praetermissi. It continues in different type: “Also Saint Bademus, archimandrite and martyr, whose martyrdom is recorded by Symeon Metaphrastes.” He is referred among the Praetermissi to the following day, where he is also called Badimus.]

[Col. 0915]

At Corinth, blessed Dionysius the bishop, through whose learning and the grace he possessed in the word of God many continue to benefit even to this day. This chosen servant of Christ also flourished in the time of Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius. At Tours, Saint Perpetuus the bishop, a man of admirable holiness.

V Idus. Day 9.

[Note: [Col. 0917B]

From Pratensis, Tornacen., Pulsanen., Antwerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven, and Molan. Add Antwerp.-Max., [Col. 0918B] Utrecht, Leyden, Albergen., Danic., and the Utrecht-Belgian edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0917B]

Most manuscripts read Procori, which I followed; the true reading is found in Pulsanen. and Molan. Muneratus omitted the word “seven” before “the first deacons.” Greven and Molan prefer to write “the first deacons.” Pulsanen. has only clarus, “famous,” instead of praeclarus, “very famous.” Pratensis has Syrmio; the form in the text, shared by the others, is better. In Pulsanen. “seven” is missing before “virgins.” This is certainly prudent, if it was done deliberately, as will be clear from what follows. Muneratus alone adds after “virgins” the words “and martyrs”; dyaconibus, martirio, mercata, eternam, and aetatem preserve the flavor of the age in which they were written.]

[Note: [Col. 0917B]

On 10 January we expressly listed the four deacons among the first, whom, omitted by all other martyrologists, we believe the author of the Little Roman Martyrology alone assigned to particular days. Among them, Prochorus, third in order, possesses this day as sacred to him, marked there as follows: “At Antioch, Prochorus the deacon, who is one of the seven.” Ado does not differ in his Martyrology, except that he placed him second. A brief encomium among the feasts of the Apostles reads: “Blessed Prochorus the deacon, a man most distinguished in faith and miracles, brought to completion by martyrdom at Antioch, and resting there.” Notker used this same wording; I do not know why Our Author altered it. Some of the manuscripts to be cited in the Supplements preserve it in full. It is not at all clear where Ado obtained his material, nor is anything sufficiently certain handed down about Prochorus apart from his election to the diaconate in Acts chapter 6. Nor can he be identified as the author of the apocryphal booklet, filled with fables and falsehoods, concerning the Life, miracles, and assumption of Saint John the Evangelist. Otherwise, our martyrologists and their followers are in fairly close agreement about Prochorus.

There is greater controversy concerning the seven virgins. In the copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology two classes of virgins are expressed very distinctly. The first, placed at Sirmium or in Sirmia, comprises not seven but only five, whose names “the Lord knows” or “God knows.” The other group of seven is recorded elsewhere, and in some manuscripts has a distinctive designation, namely the title Canonical—understand, sacred virgins—as Florentinius correctly conjectures, unless I am mistaken; the interested reader should consult his note. Nevertheless, Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, and Ado of Rosweyd, whom Usuard followed, explicitly assign seven virgins to Sirmium, as do Rabanus and Notker. In this all the martyrologists generally, including the modern Roman revisers, unanimously follow Usuard’s traces. In my opinion, they are wrong, unless someone argues that the oldest Hieronymian manuscripts, which entirely agree with one another, should be subordinated to other, more recent manuscripts—a position that, I believe, no expert in these matters will approve. Mosander’s edition of Ado differs greatly from the edition cited, since it expresses both numbers of virgins while preserving the positional error and confuses various items, differing in its proper places from Ado of Rosweyd. More may be found on these matters in the Acta and in the aforementioned Florentinius; for us it is enough to indicate the source or sources from which Our Author received his material, so that he may not be thought to have been the first to make the error. For the rest, I am entirely convinced that his genuine text is the one given in the entry. It remains to add from Wandalbert the distich by which he honors them in the same sense:

“On the Ides, a lofty lamp shines with sevenfold flame;

A radiant virgin blossom, beauty as well, shines together in heaven.”

]

[Note: [Col. 0917D]

We indicated above that the HERINIEN. manuscript, although otherwise highly reliable, differs from the others in transferring to this day: “In Palestine, Saint Mary of Egypt.” See our Observations on 2 April. Other manuscripts to be cited shortly agree with HERINIEN.]

LOVANIEN. is pure, except that after “was brought to completion” it adds, “and resting there.”

ROSWEYD. begins: “In Palestine, the passing of Saint Mary of Egypt, who is called the sinner.” It continues: “At Sirmium, seven canonical virgins,” [Col. 0918D] etc., correctly. “On the same day, the commemoration of blessed Prochorus, who was one of the seven deacons.” The rest is as in the text.

CENTULEN.: “The commemoration of blessed Prochorus the deacon, a man most distinguished in faith and miracles, brought to completion at Antioch, and resting there. At Sirmium, seven virgins, who were worthy to be crowned together.” Here Ado’s wording is placed before Usuard’s. “On the same day, the passing of the most blessed Mary of Egypt, who, with the help of our glorious Lady, ever Virgin and Mother of God, abandoned all the enticements of the flesh and became a vessel of election.”

[Col. 0919A] ANTUERP.-MAJ. treats Prochorus and the seven virgins of Sirmium together with the text and largely agrees with CENTULEN.; that is, it regularly copies Ado rather than Usuard. From this point onward it will approach greater purity.

BRUXELLEN.: “At Antioch, the commemoration of blessed Prochorus the deacon, a man most renowned in faith and miracles, who was one of the seven first deacons and was crowned by martyrdom. At Sirmium, the commemoration of the seven holy virgins, who were worthy to be crowned together and, by paying the price of blood, purchased eternal life. In Palestine, the passing of blessed Mary of Egypt, who is called the repentant sinner; her deeds are found to be exceedingly marvelous and worthy of all praise. In the mountains of Hainaut, the burial or passing of blessed Waldetrudis, niece of blessed Gudula.” For her, see the Acta.

HAGENOYEN.: “The commemoration of Saint Prochorus the martyr. He was one of the seven first deacons, appointed by the Apostles together with Saint Stephen to minister to widows. He was distinguished in faith and miracles and was crowned by martyrdom at Antioch.” It is pure concerning the virgins of Sirmium. “At Rome, the passion of very many martyrs whom Pope Alexander baptized in prison while he himself was being held in chains. The emperor Aurelian had all of them placed on an old ship, taken out into the open sea, and there, stones being tied around their necks, drowned in the depths of the sea.” This belongs to the following day.

AQUICINCT. also assigns Mary of Egypt to this day, in these words: “In Palestine, Saint Mary of Egypt, who is called the sinner.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUECIAE, marked no. 130, add at the end: “At Rome, Saint Celestine the pope, who governed the Church for seven years. He established,” etc., as yesterday and the day before yesterday among the Supplements.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “The seven virgin martyrs. Mary of Egypt. Prochorus the deacon.” See what has already been said about them more than once.

[Col. 0919C] ALTEMPS.: “Also Fortunatus and Donatus.” These names have been added from some copy of the Hieronymian Martyrology, as were others on the preceding day.

STROZZ. and MEDIC.: “The translation of Saint Monica from Ostia on the Tiber to Rome.”

The LUBECK-COLOGNE edition adds only the following to Prochorus: “And resting there. At Sirmium, etc.,” and is otherwise pure. It continues: “On the same day, blessed Dioscorus the abbot, who was the father of nearly one hundred monks. He often admonished the brothers who shared the Eucharist that they should approach Communion no otherwise than as people most diligently prepared for death.” This is omitted from the Acta for lack of sufficient proof of an ancient cult: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Monica, widow, mother of the outstanding doctor of the Church, Saint Augustine the bishop, from Ostia on the Tiber to the city of Rome.”

Both editions of BELINUS begin as follows: “The translation of the body of Saint Monica, mother of Saint Augustine, from Ostia on the Tiber to Rome, in the pontificate of Pope Martin V, in the thirteenth year of his pontificate; and it was deposited at Saint Augustine’s.” The rest is considerably longer.

GREVEN.: “Also, according to some, on this day: the martyrdom of James the Greater, the apostle; Demetrius; the deacon Hilary; Concessus; Marius; and Fortunatus.” From the Hieronymian Martyrology: “In Gaul, in the city of Rouen, blessed Hugh, archbishop of that city and confessor. Dioscorus the abbot, who was nearly,” etc., as above. “The burial of blessed Mary of Egypt, whom Usuard places on the fourth day before the Nones of April. On the same day, the translation of Saint Monica, mother of blessed Augustine, from the Ostia on the Tiber to the city of Rome, in the time of Pope Martin V. Waldetrudis, widow and abbess.”

MOLAN.: “The translation of the body of Saint Monica, etc.,” as in the LUBECK-COLOGNE edition. “In Palestine, Saint Mary of Egypt. In Gaul, in the city of Rouen, blessed Hugh, archbishop and confessor of that city.” It continues in another type: “His body is preserved with great reverence and shines in the provostship of Saint Vedast, called Haspre, in the diocese of Cambrai. Dioscorus the abbot, who was nearly,” etc., as in the LUBECK-COLOGNE edition and GREVEN. These passages, however, Molan prudently omitted in his other editions. It continues: “In the city of Die, Saint Marcellus, bishop and confessor of that city, concerning whom Gregory of Tours writes. Acacius, bishop and confessor of the city of Amida: in Book XI, chapter 16, of the Tripartite History.” Thus far the first edition. In the later editions it begins: “In Gaul, in the city of Rouen, etc.,” as above. “At Mont-Castrum, the passing of blessed Waldetrudis, who by Vincent, a noble man, bore the holy virgins Aldetrudis [Col. 0920C] and Madelberta; then, separated from him while preserving charity, she gathered together at Castrilocus a great army of holy virgins for spiritual discipline. On the ninth day, Saint Eupsychius the martyr.” He meant “Eupsychius.” “On the same day, the translation of the body of Saint Monica, mother of Saint Augustine, from Ostia on the Tiber to Rome, in the pontificate of Pope Martin V, in the thirteenth year of his pontificate.” Then, in smaller type: “In Palestine, according to the history, the burial of Saint Mary of Egypt, whose memory is celebrated by some on this day and by others on the fourth day before the Nones of April, where Usuard has noted her.” Enough has been said on both days.]

[Col. 0917]

The commemoration of blessed Prochorus, who was one of the seven first deacons; distinguished in faith and miracles, he was brought to completion by martyrdom at Antioch. At Sirmium, the passion of the seven holy virgins, who, having together paid the price of blood, purchased eternal life.

IV Idus. Day 10.

[Note: [Col. 0919D]

Thus Pratensis, Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Munerat., Belinus, Greven, and Molan. Likewise Antwerp.-Max., [Col. 0920D] Utrecht, Leyden, Lovanien., Albergen., Danic., and the Utrecht-Belgian edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0919D] ]

Only Pulsanen writes *Hezechielis*. Praten. and Belin. have “Babyloniam”; Greven. and Molan., “Babylonem”—either form is acceptable. Nevertheless, I have placed the former in the text along with the others. In place of *Sem*, Pulsanen has *Emath*. Tornacen. and Pulsanen read *Arfaxat*; Munerat., *Arfaxath*; Belin. and Greven., *Arphaxat*; Molan., *Arpaxat*. Choose whichever you wish; I preferred the reading of Praten. and Herinien., not because I consider it better—for it ought to be read *Arfaxad*. In Pulsanen the word *papae* is omitted. Belinus made a more shameful error when he wrote: “But Valerianus [did] all these things.” I do not sufficiently understand why Praten., Herinien., Munerat., Belin., Greven. and Molan. read *navi vetusta*; in my opinion Tornacen. and Pulsanen are more correct, after Ado, with *navi vetustae*, and so it appears in the marginal entry. At the end of this period Pulsanen omitted *maris*, reading: “He caused [him] to be drowned in the deep.” We have discussed the name of Apollonius elsewhere: Tornac. incorrectly has *Apolinii*; Munerat., *Appolonii*; and Belinus, *Apolonii*. I pass over the other minor points.

### [Col. 0921A]

Concerning the prophet Ezekiel and his commemoration by Bede, Papebrochius makes several observations today in the *Acta*, among which I consider this point entirely established: namely, that when that martyrologist names prophets, he indicates them almost solely by name. Yet this is no more peculiar to him than to the *Romanum parvum*, Ado, and Rabanus. It is clear from the course of the work that Usuard follows a different method. You will find in the aforementioned Papebrochius what degree of historical truth should be assigned to the account of Ezekiel given today. The additions supplied by the Hagenoyen manuscript are no less worthy of admiration, as you will immediately see for yourself.

To put it briefly: apart from the title of priest, which is inferred from Ezekiel’s own prophecy, the remaining details concerning his deeds, the period of his life, and the manner of his death lie concealed in obscurity—except that Athanasius records that he suffered on behalf of the people, because he foretold to the people what was to come. It is sufficiently probable that Usuard borrowed these details not from that source, but from certain apocryphal writings commonly circulated concerning Ezekiel. Hence Papebrochius judges that only the place of his burial derives from genuine tradition, since his venerable memory long remained among Jews and Christians. As for the claim that Sem and Arphaxad were once buried in the same place, he considers it freely transmitted—or rather invented—by the rabbis. Let us put it more mildly: it is highly uncertain and supported almost solely by Usuard’s authority.

Wandalbert imitates Bede’s brevity:

> The prophet Ezekiel, with holy mouth, declares fourfold.

### [Col. 0922A]

The Roman martyrs baptized by blessed Pope Alexander, and taken from his *Acts* together with Quirinus and Balbina, are commemorated in the *Romanum parvum* and, from it, in Ado. Our author followed his guide in the customary manner, adhering to the substance of the entire elogium, but not scrupulously to its actual wording—as we have often said is more characteristic of Notker.

The curious reader should note that the number of these captive martyrs can readily be determined as approximately twenty from the cited *Acts* of Saint Alexander, which Henschenius consistently declares to be entirely genuine. Likewise, Aurelianus, who is called their commander here, is named by Usuard above, on 30 March, where Saint Quirinus is discussed, as the emperor; yet he is one and the same prefect, or count of either military force, summoned by the emperor Trajan from Seleucia in Isauria to put all the Christians to death, as is expressly stated in the aforementioned *Acts*.

Meanwhile, neither these martyrs, however celebrated, nor the prophet Ezekiel are known in any of the Hieronymian copies. Nevertheless, Apollonius seems certainly to have come from these sources, first recorded by Our author with a company of five companions. Florentinius was unable to determine satisfactorily which five to select from the six named there. Perhaps our *Acts* have distinguished them more successfully; we leave the controversy open. Whether Usuard was in error or not, let that be judged by others: the agreement of almost all the manuscripts abundantly proves that we have reproduced his text pure and simple.

### [Col. 0921B]

Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. today followed Bede, the *Romanum parvum*, and Ado rather than Usuard, announcing the entry first simply as: “Of the prophet Ezekiel.”

Rosweyd adds to the unadulterated text, from the Hieronymian Martyrology: “In Africa, seventeen martyrs.”

Centulen.: “Of the prophet Ezekiel, stoned near Babylon and buried in the tomb of Sem and Arphaxad. At Rome, several martyrs whom blessed Pope Alexander baptized, and whom the commander Aurelianus cast into the sea. At Alexandria, Saint Apollonius the priest and five others.”

Antuerp.-Maj. is almost pure, but omits Apollonius.

Bruxellen. is also sufficiently pure in the text, but adds at the end: “Likewise, Saint Macarius, archbishop of Antioch. After undertaking a difficult pilgrimage for Christ, he came to Ghent and, dying there in the monastery of blessed Bavo, rested in a holy death.”

Hagenoyen. begins as follows:

> “Near Babylon, the prophet Ezekiel. He was given as a hostage from Jerusalem to King Nebuchadnezzar by Joakim, king of Judah, together with Daniel, the three boys, and Mordecai. He was a great prophet in contemplation directed toward God. He also saw wondrous visions, and he alone among all the prophets was called by God ‘son of man.’ He was a priest and, in the manner of a high priest, rebuked the people who were being led into exile, foretelling evils to them. And because he foretold to certain people that they would not return to the land of Judah, they killed him by dragging him through thorns and thistles. All the people buried him, in honor of the prophecy that was in him, in the tomb of Sem and Arphaxad, Sem’s son. At Alexandria, the passion of Saint Apollonius the martyr and five other martyrs.”

The Roman martyrs are omitted here; we said yesterday that they had been incorrectly placed.

Matric.-Carthus.-Ultraject.: “Of the prophet Ezekiel. At Rome, many martyrs.”

Codex Bigotianus, marked D 9, records on this day Saint Hugh of Rouen, whom other manuscripts more correctly assigned to the preceding day. It reads simply, without an elogium: “On this same day, the burial of Lord Hugh, archbishop of Rouen.”

Vatican manuscript no. 5949 adds at the end, from some Hieronymian copy: “At Antioch, Saint Theodore the priest. In Africa, seventeen holy martyrs.”

### [Col. 0922C]

Luxovien.: “At Lyon in Gaul, the burial of Saint Siagrius.” Greven. also has him below, but others place him on the following day.

The Lubec-Cologne edition, moderately interpolated in the text, adds at the end: “Here Apollonius converted Philemon, and the judge of Alexandria, who were all drowned for the glory of Christ.” It would have been better to omit these statements, since they do not fit the Apollonius of the present entry, as is shown by Florentinius and in the *Acts*.

Greven.: “In Africa, seventeen martyrs. In Thrace, the feast of Saint Gaianus. Of Antony the martyr. Likewise, of Saturninus and Granus.” These are customarily taken from the Hieronymian Martyrology, except for Antony, who is rightly omitted in the *Acts*.

“Of Macarius, patriarch of Antioch and confessor, resting near Ghent in the monastery of Saint Bavo. At Lyon, of Siagrius the confessor.” Concerning him, see above.

“Of Theodore the priest.” Is he also the Antiochene martyr? See the *Praetermissi*, where the following person is also discussed: “Of Mutius the hermit. The beheading of John the Baptist.” This is referred to 29 August.

“The translation of Saint Gertrude the virgin.” Her life and translations are discussed on 17 March.

Molan., in smaller type: “Of Malachi, bishop of Lesmore and confessor, concerning whom see the life of Saint Malachy.” Molan. mentions this in the first edition, but it is omitted in the later editions, as well as in our *Acta*. The later editions, moreover, have: “At Ghent, the burial of blessed Macarius, bishop and confessor. On the tenth day, of the holy martyrs Terentius, Pompeius, and their companions.” He means the African martyrs marked as belonging to the second class in the *Acta*. See there for their names expressed more distinctly.

### [Col. 0919]

Of the prophet Ezekiel, who was killed near Babylon by the judge of the people of Israel and buried in the tomb of Sem and Arphaxad. At Rome, many blessed martyrs whom Saint Alexander the pope baptized while he was being held in prison. The commander Aurelianus had all these men placed on an old ship, taken out into the open sea, and there, with stones tied around their necks, drowned in the depths of the sea. At Alexandria, Saint Apollonius the priest and five others.

## 10 April

### [Col. 0923]

The manuscripts of Praten., Herinien., Munerat., Greven. and Molan. are pure.

### [Col. 0923A]

Munerat., Molan., and most of the other manuscripts write *Calcedonensis*; I followed Praten., Herinien. and Greven., because I think this was the medieval manner of writing. Neither form is correct, nor is the form *Calchedon*, which was formerly widespread among other learned men and which I myself had followed elsewhere; after being corrected by Stephanus and others, one must read *Chalcedon*. Let this be said in passing on the present occasion.

Almost all the manuscripts have *Domionis*; the *Acta* give *Domnii* or *Domnionis*. Munerat. incorrectly has *Eustergi* for *Eustorgii*. It is enough to mention *Nichomediae*, *sinodus*, *preditus*, and so forth.

### [Col. 0923A]

“At Rome, of Leo the pope and confessor”: these are the words of the genuine Bede. Nothing concerning him appears on this day in the Hieronymian copies, nothing in the *Romanum parvum*, and therefore nothing in Ado, as Mosander also admits. Rabanus, removing something from Bede’s words, composed an elogium that is not entirely genuine; it was copied almost word for word by Notker. Our author drew a few points from his own resources, proclaiming above all the universally recognized glory of that truly great pontiff.

It must indeed be acknowledged that the present solemnity of the great Leo was formerly of exceptional importance among the Latins, although it is clear that this day cannot be called either the anniversary of his ordination or pontifical consecration, or more properly his heavenly birthday or burial. For this reason Henschenius and Papebrochius believe that the feast of some translation or elevation is being celebrated. Moreover, after the last editor of Saint Leo’s works, the aforementioned Papebrochius and Castellanus assign the actual day of his burial to 30 October; but this in no way pleases me.

Why should the antiquity of the observance on 10 November not prevail, since it is unanimously attested on that day in the Hieronymian Martyrology: “At Rome, the burial of Saint Leo the bishop”? Certainly, on that very day, 10 November, the notice is repeated not by Notker but by Rabanus, and it agrees perfectly with the ordination of his successor Hilary, as Henschenius and Florentinius show. Thus far I see no reason why the opinion of the most ancient martyrologists, confirmed by so many others, should be abandoned—much less why Pagius, at the year 461, should here congratulate himself so extravagantly as though he had unearthed a treasure, boldly declaring, contrary to the others and in his customary fashion: “His death, which until now has escaped everyone, occurred on the day before the Nones of November, that is, on the fourth day of that month.” His method of calculation is obvious there; with his permission, we think otherwise.

Anything else that might be examined here should be deferred to 28 June. Henschenius does not seem to have treated Leo’s deeds sufficiently fully, following the Life first composed and published by Canisius. Other learned men explained and expanded his effort more fully; among them Tillemont follows the entire course of the life at greater length, though not without partisan bias, in volume 15, pages 414–832, in 175 complete articles. I have neither the leisure to work through them nor the inclination to approve them all.

For now, accept this brief but sufficiently elegant metrical encomium by Wandalbert:

> With Leo, thrice shining as supreme pontiff,  
> He shines in face and hand, who fed Christ’s flock.

Philip of Gortyna is today the only entry in the *Romanum parvum*: “At Gortyna, of Philip the bishop, who flourished in the times of Antoninus Verus and Lucius.” Ado’s elogium, transcribed by Notker and translated by our author in a somewhat more polished paraphrase, says no more.

The compiler of the *Romanum parvum* wrote *Gortinae* correctly enough; others have *Gortynae*. Why Ado, and Notker after him, changed this to *Cortyna*, I neither wish to conjecture nor investigate. Nor do we inquire why the same Philip is repeated in the *Romanum parvum*, Ado, and Notker on 8 October, where Usuard more correctly omitted him, although it is clear that both entries concern the same person.

What Irenaeus, Eusebius, Jerome, and others transmit in praise of Philip’s virtues and learning is presented together by Henschenius. There is disagreement concerning the designation of the bishop of Salona; but it seems certain that Usuard wrote it as he had found it in some Hieronymian manuscript, from which he most probably took it, and we have considered it absolutely necessary to preserve it in the text.

If you prefer *Domnionis* with Notker—which we certainly admit is preferable—take care not to write *millium octo* instead of *militum octo*. Whether this number of eight is itself strictly historically accurate, Florentinius will show you; more are counted in our *Acta*. These matters, however, do not in any way impair the purity of Usuard’s text, any more than does his insufficiently scrupulous omission of Eustorgius of Nicomedia, the companion distinctly named in the Hieronymian Martyrology.

### [Col. 0923C]

The manuscripts suffer from defects on this day, but are otherwise generally pure. Tornacen. omitted Domnion. Pulsanen. omitted Eustorgius and part of Saint Philip’s elogium. Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. cut short the elogium of Pope Leo.

Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden, Lovanien., and the Ultraject.-Belg. edition could be counted among the pure manuscripts; nevertheless, they have been excluded because they write concerning Leo: “At Rome, the feast of blessed Leo I, pope and confessor, in whose time the fourth synod, namely Chalcedon, took place.”

Albergen. and Danic. add: “At which five hundred and thirty bishops assembled, expounding the Catholic faith and confessing, against the Eutychian heresy, the two natures in Christ, namely the divine and the human.” They are otherwise also pure.

Centulen. departs from purity only in this defect: in Philip’s elogium it omits the words beginning, “But he flourished…”

Antuerp.-Maj. is defective in the entry for Eustorgius, whose entire notice it has removed, and has substituted Ado’s elogium of Philip for Usuard’s.

Bruxellen., moderately interpolated in the entries for Leo and Philip, says concerning Domnion: “In the Dalmatian city of Salona, etc.” It is pure in the entry for Eustorgius. It then adds: “In Britain, Saint Guthlac the confessor and anchorite.”

Hagenoyen. begins with Philip. Domio follows. Then it gives an account of Leo almost like Albergen. and Danic. It is pure in the entry for Eustorgius.

Rosweyd. places second, after Leo: “In Britain, the burial of Saint Guthlac, confessor of Christ and anchorite, who endured many unheard-of torments for Christ from evil spirits and, finally overcoming their devices, departed to the Lord in an excellent manner of life.” Philip and Domio follow. Then: “In Africa, Donatus the martyr with two hundred and forty others. At Lyon, Siagrius the confessor.” Finally, it gives the entry for Eustorgius.

Aquicinct.: “In Britain, Saint Guthlac the confessor and anchorite, who, shining with many virtues, rested in peace.”

Matric.-Carthus.-Ultraject.: “Of Guthlac the confessor and hermit. Of Leo III, pope and confessor. Of Zeno, bishop and confessor of Verona.” Or was he a martyr? See the *Acta* for 12 April. Leo III, who is also incorrectly recorded today in the Lubec-Cologne edition, belongs to 12 June.

In Vatican manuscript no. 5949, Domio is omitted. The following is added: “In Mauritania, Saint Domninus the bishop and nine soldiers.” The confusion can easily be exposed and corrected.

Altemps.: “At Tours, Saint Agricius the abbot. At Lyon, Siagrius the bishop. Likewise, Fortunatus and two hundred and forty others.”

Codex Castri Caroli: “At Lyon, the burial of Siagrius, Patricius.” These are two names in the *Acta*, where no mention is made of Siagrius’s episcopate.

Montis Sancti: “Saint Agrestius the martyr, who was a companion of Saint Romaricus, whose body rests on this holy mountain of Rombech, formerly called Habendi-castrum.” I find nothing else about this saint; perhaps something will recur in the Life of Saint Romaricus on 8 December.

The Lubec-Cologne edition begins as follows:

> “At Rome, the feast of blessed Leo III, pope and confessor, who sat in the episcopate for twenty years, five months, and sixteen days, in the time of blessed Charlemagne, and conferred upon that Augustus the imperial diadem. He is said to have visited blessed Severinus in Cologne Agrippina, in his church, and to have delivered a longer prayer there; likewise, to have said these words to his companions: ‘Lord Severinus is at home, and therefore I did not dare to pass him by without greeting him.’ He was buried at Rome near Saint Peter.”

Nothing is said about Leo the Great. The entry for Philip is pure. For Domion it gives: “with eight soldiers, martyrs, who, unwilling to deny Christ, were killed for his name, in glory and honor.” To Eustorgius it adds: “the martyr.” “In Britain, Saint Guthlac the priest and confessor. On the same day, the holy martyrs Fortunatus and two hundred and forty others. On that same day, blessed Godeberta the virgin. Likewise, Saint Didymus the hermit, in whom there was much grace against poisonous things.”

Belin. In the first edition, after the emperors, inserts: “At Antioch, Saint Theodore the priest, whom Julian, the uncle of Julian the Apostate, after having seized and cruelly tortured him, finally ordered to be killed by the sword.” Concerning this Theodore, to say it once, see the index of the *Praetermissi*. The same appears in the second edition; in addition, after *Calcedonensis* it adds: “Of six hundred and thirty bishops.” At the end it also adds: “At Lyon, Siagrius the bishop; at Tours, Agiricus the abbot.”

Greven.: “In Africa, Saints Fortunatus, Donatus, and two hundred and forty others. The passion of Stanislaus, bishop and martyr of Kraków.” He is honored on 7 May. The notice concerning Theodore follows, as in Belin.; but instead of *mactasset*, “had slaughtered,” the better reading is *sauciasset*, “had wounded.”

“In Britain, Guthlac the priest, anchorite and confessor. Isaac the monk and confessor, who, as Saint Gregory reports in *Dialogues* 3.14, came from Syria and, near the city of Spoleto, lived in a humble dwelling. He was extraordinarily endowed with the virtue of abstinence, contempt for passing things, the spirit of prophecy, and devotion to prayer. There was only one feature in him that seemed blameworthy: he sometimes possessed such great joy that, unless he were known to be filled with all those virtues, it would have been impossible to believe it. Of Didymus the hermit and confessor, in whom there was much grace against poisonous things.” More certain evidence of veneration is sought, and therefore he is omitted from the *Acta*.

“Likewise, of blessed memory, Raynerus the solitary, who, enclosed near the church of Osnabrück, shone greatly through his life and miracles. On that same day, blessed Godeberta the virgin.”

Molan. gives Theodore, Siagrius, and Agiricus exactly as Belinus. Then, in smaller type: “On that same day, at Noyon, blessed Godeberta the virgin.” The entry for Stanislaus, Guthlac, Isaac, and Raynerus follows as in Greven. Finally: “On the same day, according to Metaphrastes, Saint Antipas, bishop and martyr of Pergamum in Asia, concerning whom the Lord says: ‘Antipas, my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.’”

This is in the first edition; in the others: “In Britain, Saint Guthlac the confessor and anchorite, who, shining with many virtues, rested in peace. At Noyon, Saint Godeberta the virgin. At Lyon, Sicarius the bishop. At Tours, Agricius the abbot. On the eleventh day, Saint Antipas the hieromartyr, bishop of Pergamum in Asia. In the monastery of Bronn, the arrival of Saint Leodegarius, bishop and martyr. Likewise, of blessed memory, Raynerus the solitary,” etc. See Greven. above.

### [Col. 0921]
