At Rome, the feast of blessed Leo the pope, in whose time the holy synod of Chalcedon took place. In the city of Gortyna in Crete, Saint Philip the bishop, who was endowed with great virtues and excellent studies. He flourished in the times of the emperors Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius. In Dalmatia, in the city of Salona, Saint Domnion the bishop with eight soldiers. At Nicomedia, Saint Eustorgius the priest.

## 12 April

### [Col. 0925]

I find only the Herinien. and Tornacen. manuscripts, together with the first edition of Belin., to be pure throughout.

### [Col. 0927A]

Among the manuscript copies there is no difference, apart from the usual omission of diphthongs in Tornacen., which we have discussed elsewhere. Belinus incorrectly reads *Constantino* for *Constantio*, and *jugo*—“on the ridge”—for *apud Vapingum*, “at Vapincum.” What he means by *jugo*, I do not know; for Vapincum was not situated on a mountain ridge but, if I remember correctly, at its foot.

### [Col. 0927A]

The memory of Pope Julius is announced in more than one way in the Hieronymian copies. The very old Epternacensis simply has: “At Rome, the burial of Julius the bishop.” Both Corbeienses have: “On the Via Aurelia, at the third milestone, the burial of Julius the bishop, where the cemetery of Calepodius is.” In the Lucensis this cemetery is attributed here to a certain Lupicinus, and thus the announcement agrees perfectly with the words of the Bucherian Calendar, which reads: “On the day before the Ides of April, Julius on the Via Aurelia, at the third milestone, in the cemetery of Callistus.”

These statements are clearly and plainly made about Julius; the same cannot be said of the matters Bede inserted into his elogium, more elegantly than truthfully. Rabanus copied it from Bede, Ado from Rabanus, and Our author from Ado, while nevertheless preserving Bede’s placement, that is, the place of burial. When reporting Ado’s account, Notker added several matters which we shall provide among the additions from the Aquicinctine manuscript—unless those too ought to be attributed to Ado, as Mosander did; we understand that the edition was prepared through his efforts.

The *Romanum parvum* had more correctly preceded Ado: “On the Via Aurelia, of Julius the pope and confessor, under Constantius the Arian.” For the statements about his exile and sufferings in the text have rightly been rejected by Baronius and all learned men. See Henschenius’s commentary and the other writers cited by Tillemont in volume 7, page 269 onward.

Wandalbert’s elogium is genuine:

> Bishop Julius returned to Rome’s walls the day before,  
> A pastor renowned for the Catholic doctrine.

Constantinus—called Constantius by others—was certainly taken by Usuard from the Hieronymian copies, since he is entirely unknown to the other sources already cited. In almost all those edited by Florentinius we read: “In the city of Vapincum, the burial of Constantinus the bishop.” Whether Acherius and Florentinius are right to count this among the additions is a question concerning the wording.

Henschenius correctly determines his period, as far as possible, against Baronius and Saussayus; but at the end his pen seems to have gone astray when he rebukes Peter de Natalibus, as though he had not correctly said that Constantius flourished on the day before the Ides of April. There is certainly no doubt that he belongs to the Usuardine text, since all the manuscripts agree on the matter, and Usuard was especially accustomed to append Gallic saints, or saints borrowed from the Hieronymian Martyrology, to other notices derived from Ado.

The earlier scholars, and notably Henschenius, did not judge Zeno of Verona in the same way. Henschenius expressly declares that Zeno was inserted into Usuard’s text on this day, although he appears in the supposed autograph of Praten. and in many others, in the wording that we shall report below.

The chief reason why I think we should not depart from Henschenius is the authority of the Herinien. and Tornacen. manuscripts, which has been sufficiently established elsewhere. Another reason is the principle already indicated: Usuard very rarely summons transalpine saints unless he has found them in earlier sources. I have observed this elsewhere with no little success, especially on 16 January in the case of Titianus of Oderzo, where I also appended the testimony of the distinguished Castellanus, which excellently confirms the genuine simplicity of two of our manuscripts.

Finally, to pass over the other considerations, there is the exceedingly doubtful narrative of the entire elogium, sufficiently discussed by Henschenius, which seems formerly to have moved Molan. to remove several passages from the first edition in the later ones. I would venture to suspect that there was someone among Usuard’s fellow-workers who, finding a mention of Zeno in Rabanus and in his copyist Notker, perhaps judged that he should adapt his style to Usuard’s.

If anyone teaches me better by solid arguments, I will certainly not refuse to accept them. But I am not greatly moved by the authority of the Praten. manuscript alone, which the others followed, since above we have so often shown that its authority has been shaken, and shall further demonstrate that it ought to be shaken. The force of the argument proposed in our preface will always remain: other things being equal, a manuscript approaches the original simplicity of any martyrologist more closely in proportion as its text is confined to fewer saints.

### [Col. 0927C]

Praten., Pulsanen., Rosweyd., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., the second edition of Belin., Greven., Molan., and almost all the other manuscripts announce second:

> “On the same day, Saint Zeno, bishop, who during the storms of persecution ruled the city of Verona wonderfully and was crowned with martyrdom in the time of Gallienus.”

Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden, Lovanien., and the Ultraject.-Belg. edition have the same, and additionally restore certain passages from Ado. They begin:

> “At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, in the cemetery of Calepodius, the feast of blessed Julius the pope, who under Constantius, the Arian emperor and son of Constantine the Great, for ten months,” etc.

Albergen. and Danic. add after “rested in peace,” from Notker:

> “He decreed that no cleric should conduct a public case except in a church.”

Centulen.: “At Rome, Saint Julius the pope and confessor. In Italy, Saint Zeno the bishop and martyr, who suffered under Gallienus. Likewise, the burial of Saint Constantinus the bishop.”

Antuerp.-Maj. treats today only of Pope Julius, differing little from the text.

Bruxellen. begins:

> “At Rome, the feast of blessed Julius the pope and confessor. He endured many tribulations and a long exile under Constantius Drrianus, the emperor and son of Constantine; after Constantius’s death he returned with glory to his own see, rested in peace, and was buried on the Via Aurelia, in the cemetery of Calepodius, three miles from the city. In his time the Council of Nicaea was celebrated, which condemned the heresy of Arius.”

In the rest it is almost pure. Where it found that the Council of Nicaea should be assigned to Julius’s pontificate, I neither know nor investigate.

Hagenoyen begins with Zeno, to whom it assigns certain details not sufficiently reliable to deserve repetition here. In addition to what has already been reported concerning Julius, it adds:

> “He also decreed that marriage should be blessed by a priest in the church.”

For the remainder, understand it from the additions given above.

Aquicinct., after the *τὸ* in *in pace*—“in peace”—adds several partly damaged passages; what remains is:

> “He decreed that … should conduct any case in public except in a church … should be collected by notaries, and whether securities or stri… donations, exchanges or transfers, wills, allegations, or manumissions, should be carried out by clerics in the church.”

Since these statements are taken from Notker, they should be supplied as follows. First: “that no cleric should conduct any case,” etc. Second: “that a written record of the faith should be collected by notaries.” Third: “or instruments or donations,” etc.

Matric.-Carthus.-Ultraject. treated Zeno yesterday as a confessor. Today: “Of Julius the pope. Of Zosima the abbot.” Concerning him, therefore, see the index of the *Praetermissi*. “Of Ermigild, king and martyr”: this belongs to the following day and is called Hermenegild.

In Vatican manuscript no. 5949, Constantinus is absent.

Florentin.: “Likewise, Saint Lazarus the martyr, who suffered under the emperor Antoninus in the city of Tergeste, under the *praesul* [*praeses*, “governor”] Pompeius. Since he was a deacon and faithful to Christ, and willingly received at his house those who continually gathered there, he was accused of being a Christian. Because he steadfastly preached the faith of Christ before the governor, he was ordered first to have his mouth beaten, then to be scourged with rods, and finally, after being beheaded, happily reached the eternal kingdom.”

Codex Remen. of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “At Reims, the translation of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris.”

The Lubec-Cologne edition has Julius almost as Albergen. and Danic.; at the end it reads:

> “He decreed that no cleric should conduct a public case, nor be publicly brought before it, except in a church.”

It also inserts something about Zeno after “emperor”:

> “He was crowned with martyrdom for the sheep of Christ entrusted to him.”

To Constantinus it adds: “the confessor.” Finally:

> “On the same day, Saint Zosima the abbot, concerning whom it is read in the deeds of Saint Mary of Egypt.”

See 2 April, on which day the *Acta* of both are elucidated.

Greven.: “At Capua, the feast of Saints Cyprian, Novella, and Silvanus. Likewise, Saints Carpus, Julius, Agapus, and Paulus.” These are fragments of the Hieronymian Martyrology.

“Of Erkenbodus, bishop and confessor. Of Zosima the abbot, concerning whom it is read in the deeds of blessed Mary of Egypt. Of John the hermit and confessor.” It is surprising that he is not named even among the *Praetermissi*.

“Of Zeno the monk, disciple of Abbot Silvanus, who in the Egyptian region, under the scorching heat of the fiercest sun, stood dried out for five days, wishing to test whether he could endure the torments of the future life.” This is referred to 19 July.

“Likewise, of blessed memory, Engeburga the virgin, daughter of the king of England.” See the index of the *Praetermissi*.

Molan., after “he was crowned,” inserts in italics:

> “Concerning him Gregory reports in Book 3 of the *Dialogues*: At the monastery of Sithiu, the burial of Saint Erkenbodus, bishop of the Morini.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “On this same day, the springs of the abyss were burst open and the flood occurred. On that day, Saint Sabas the Goth, martyr. When the magistrate of the Goths forced Christians to eat things sacrificed to idols, and certain pagans offered to their relatives things said to have been sacrificed although they had not been, blessed Sabas, when the matter became known, protested to everyone: ‘If anyone eats of those meats, he cannot be a Christian.’ The Church of God which is in Gothia writes to the Church in Cappadocia and to all the Christians of the Catholic Church (Book 7 of Aloysius). The report of Saint Renatus, bishop of Angers, from Italy to his own city.”

This is as far as the first edition goes. The others preserve what was said about Gregory. Then:

> “At the monastery of Sithiu, the burial of Saint Erkenbodus, bishop of the Morini and abbot of Sithiu. On the twelfth day, Saint Basil, bishop of Parion, holy father and confessor.”

Again in smaller type:

> “On that day, Saint Sabas the Goth, martyr,”

and so forth, up to “he cannot be a Christian,” omitting the remaining material reported above.

### [Col. 0925]

At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, the feast of blessed Julius the pope, who under the emperor Constantius endured tribulations and exiles for ten months; after Constantius’s death he returned with great glory to his own see and rested in peace.

Bouillart inserts:

> “On the same day, Saint Zeno the bishop, who during the storms of persecution ruled the city of Verona wonderfully and was crowned with martyrdom in the time of Gallienus.”

The mention of Zeno, although written on another folio, displays the same form of letters, the same ink, and the same parchment, so that no one could declare it to have been inserted after Usuard except a blind man or someone utterly inexperienced in assessing writing. There is no erasure, the script is clean, and there is nothing that could arouse suspicion even in excessively strict judges. Almost all the manuscripts known to Sollerius support it. Of those I examined, none disagrees: the four Praten. manuscripts of excellent quality, two of them more than five hundred years old; the two Victorini; Conchensis; Pontisarensis; Fulienses A and B; Colbertini A, B, C, and D; and Fossatensis. The more carefully and accurately printed books agree as well, as Sollerius admits. An ancient martyrology written at the beginning of the eleventh century and carefully preserved in Paris at the royal priory of Saint Martin reports the same reading. The Roman Martyrology also mentions the same Zeno on the same day. Should a reading supported by so many aids totter and be endangered?

Without doubt Sollerius saw manuscripts that he could set against the Praten. He did indeed see two, the Herinien. and Tornacen.; add the Dervensis as well—it makes no difference to me. Other churches did not take care to correct for themselves everything that had been corrected by Usuard. But, deprived of manuscripts, he perhaps fights with arguments, and with arguments that cannot be resolved. He must be heard.

“Usuard,” he says, “very rarely summons transalpine saints.” What then, I ask? If very rarely, then sometimes. Zeno, however, will be one of those cases. But Usuard’s account is more than doubtful. Why, then, did Henschenius hesitate uncertainly over whether to assert that Zeno was a pontiff and confessor only, or also a martyr? Has Sollerius discovered something new? Henschenius expressly declares—indeed, without any argument, but expressly declares—that Zeno was inserted by later hands.

I do not dare to reply. And what will the reader think of this urbanity of Sollerius? I would venture to suspect that there was someone among Usuard’s fellow-workers … who judged that he should adapt his style to Usuard’s.

Vapincum: the burial of Constantinus the bishop.

## 13 April

### [Col. 0929C]

Thus Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Rosweyd., Munerat., Greven. and Molan., together with Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden, Lovanien., Albergen., Danic., and the Ultraject.-Belg. edition.

Papirii is read, with the text, by Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., and Munerat. Perhaps Rosweyd., Greven., and Molan. are better: Papirii, as the Romanum parvum and Ado explicitly have it. Some write Papiri, as do the manuscripts of the middle class cited last; but among all the Usuardine manuscripts I find none that gives Papily, as do the modern Roman edition and our Acts. We are bound by the rule of following our older manuscripts, even when they are erroneous. The same applies to the spelling, as it stands in Pratensis, Tornacensis, Grevenianus, and others. Herinien. and Molan. give scripto; Rosweyd., scriptura; Muneratus, as he is everywhere disfigured by typographical errors, here makes a disgraceful slip into *scripture munerationem*. This seems to have arisen from some Pratensian manuscript, marked B by us and collated with another. Again, the others have *Erminigildi* in the text, along with Pratensis, Herinien., and Tornacensis, to which Munerat., Antuerp.-Max., and others prefix an aspiration. Creven. and Molan. are more correct with *Herminigildi*. But Munerat. wrongly inserts *regis*. The remaining forms—*dyaconi*, *Antonio*, *Justinius*—are almost certainly errors peculiar to him.

[Col. 0929D]

Nothing is read concerning today’s martyrs of Pergamum in the genuine Bede or Rabanus; nor do the Hieronymian copies clearly mention them, at least on this day, unless someone should contend that, by an analogy that in my judgment is insufficiently plausible, our Carpus was formed from Jerome’s Polycarp and Papirius from the same author’s Paul. For whatever modern writers may prefer from Eusebius—*Papylus* or *Papulus*, which would come closer to *Paulus*—the author of the Romanum parvum, who first received this announcement not from the Hieronymians but from Rufinus, choosing the day according to his own preference, most distinctly reads *Carpi et Papyrii*: “At Pergamum in Asia, of Carpus the bishop and Papirius, Agathonica, and many others.” Why not also the others, all of whom Ado reports as crowned with martyrdom for their proven confessions, from the same source? Here he does not expressly specify the time of their martyrdom, but Usuard derived it by a sound inference from Justin’s eulogy. This is not Ado’s only error; add also Notker’s, who writes “for blessed confessors” instead of “for proven confessors.” In any case, the names Antoninus Verus and Aurelius Commodus entered the Martyrologies for this reason: the martyrdoms both of these Pergamene saints and of the Justin who follows were taken from the Rufinus mentioned above, where they are placed almost immediately after the passion of Saint Polycarp. Ado, without making any distinction, judged all the martyrs mentioned in Book IV, chapters 15 and 16, to belong to the same period, and thus, as though in one continuous sentence, joined the remarkable man Justin with the Pergamenes, as we briefly indicated concerning Pionius on 1 February. This is the entire and sole explanation of the confusion. It should be attributed only to Ado—or, if one prefers, to Rufinus, who in a certain sense showed the way to the error—not to Usuard, as Papebrochius does on 1 June, nor to the other martyrologists. To proceed in order: perhaps Carpus, who is mentioned on the preceding day in the Hieronymians together with others at Pergamum in various forms, is the same man whom we said our authors received from Rufinus. From his Acts, embellished at least by Metaphrastes, it is clear that he and his companions fought gloriously under Decius, as Henschenius demonstrates at length here and elsewhere; Florentinius in his notes and Tillemont, volume III, pages 346 and 711, agree.

There is a separate controversy concerning the remarkable man Justin, commonly called simply “the martyr,” first raised by Papebrochius from Greek sources. On this day he became doubtful because this Justin is presented by Ado, Usuard, and Notker, while another Justin is celebrated by others on 1 June (or perhaps by someone on 12 June, as Castellanus noted in the *Martyrologium Universale*, I do not know). He inclines to establish two Justins on various grounds. Ruinart, however, opposed that duplication in *Sincera et Selecta*, page 38 onward, and Papebrochius himself, in his discussion of 1 June, had already moved not obscurely toward the common opinion before he had seen Ruinart’s work. Compare what has been most carefully investigated on both days. On the first, one will find the Life laboriously composed by Halloix and elucidated by Papebrochius; on the other, the Acts themselves, authentic Latin-Greek or Greek-Latin documents, in which the contest of Justin and his companions is set forth briefly, seriously, and sincerely. From both places and from other documents Tillemont derived a much longer, though in some measure encomiastic, Life in volume II, page 344 onward.

Before Ado, no martyrologist mentioned Hermenegild. Usuard transferred into his little calendar the eulogy composed by Ado from Saint Gregory—if not all of it, certainly its greater and more elegant part—while Notker transcribed nearly all of this and the preceding material almost word for word. Concerning the most renowned victim of Arian fury, it seems impossible to say anything that Henschenius has not diligently collected and learnedly illustrated. His cult in Gaul in the ninth century is also demonstrated by Wandalbert’s verses:

> On the Ides, gracious King Hermingild, you perceive your father raging;  
> yet you bear away a true triumph from death.

On this day Rabanus and Notker also commemorate from the Hieronymians Euphemia, that celebrated Chalcedonian martyr, whom Mosander added to Ado—distinguishing her with an asterisk, that is, adding her as doubtful—rightly conjecturing that she had been incorrectly called on this day by name alone, since she is praised by the same author on 16 September in a distinguished account. Whether there was one Euphemia or several, and whether she or they should be celebrated on this or other days, is briefly discussed in the Acts. I do not wish to draw out a contentious dispute, since nothing concerning Usuard on this day is involved, although the name repeatedly recurs in the supplements. With these points established, I do not see at all what grounds there could be for doubting the authenticity of our text. The items concerning altar consecrations and similar matters that we find written in the margins of the Pratensian manuscript, here and elsewhere, are so peculiar to that monastery that they have nothing in common with Usuard’s Martyrology; accordingly, we shall properly omit them hereafter, unless something worthy of notice occurs among them.

[Col. 0931B]

PULSANEN.: As far as can be conjectured, it is either pure or comes very close to purity. But since its worn text cannot be read, I preferred to exclude the manuscript from the pure witnesses rather than sell doubtful readings as certain ones.

ANTUERPIEN. and MAX.-LUBEC. are pure in the text, but at the end they add: “Also, Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr.” The FLORENTINE manuscripts likewise read this way.

CENTULEN.: “At Chalcedon, Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr. At Pergamum, a city of Asia, Saints Carpus the bishop, Papirius the deacon, and Agathonica, an excellent woman, and many others, who were crowned with martyrdom for their proven confessions. In Spain, the birthday of Saint Hermenegild, son of King Leovigild, whom his father, the Arian king of the Goths, had killed because of his unconquerable confession of the Catholic faith.”

ANTUERPIEN.-MAJ. resembles CENTULENSIS in the entry on Euphemia and the Pergamene saints, omitting Justin in both places. In the entry on Hermenegild, whom it calls Hermibald, it comes closer to Ado.

BRUXELLEN. begins as follows: “At Chalcedon, the birthday of Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr. She overcame for Christ tortures and prisons, scourges and instruments of wheels, fires and weights, wild beasts and blows from rods, axes and flaming frying-pans.” In the remainder of the text, apart from scribal errors, it follows Ado.

HAGENOYEN. is pure in the first entry. In the entry on Hermenegild it expands the wording, but not the substance. At the end: “On the same day, Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr.”

AQUICINCT. and CLUNIACENS.: “Also, Euphemia, virgin and martyr.” There is only a slight variation.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Carpus the bishop, Papirius the deacon, and many others. Justin the philosopher and martyr. Godeberta the virgin. Ida, countess of Boulogne, widow.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, marked C, which belonged to the Franciscan fathers: “Also, Euphemia, virgin and martyr.”

VATICAN., no. 5949: “Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr.” Thus do nearly all the manuscripts read.

[Col. 0932B]

UGHELLIAN.: “Also, Saint Euphemia, virgin.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., no. 130, omit even “martyr,” but prefix: “At Chalcedon.”

[Col. 0932C]

LUBECO-COL. EDITION. At the beginning it is sufficiently pure; concerning Hermenegild it reads: “In Spain, Saint Herminigild, king and martyr, whom his father Leovigild, the Arian king of Aragon and the Goths, ordered to be killed with an axe on the holy night of the Lord’s Resurrection because of his unconquerable confession of the faith; and by such a martyrdom the king and martyr entered the heavenly kingdom. Translation of Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr, at Chalcedon.” I have no certain knowledge whether any translation of Euphemia of Chalcedon truly took place. On the unity or plurality of Euphemias, see what is discussed in the Acts on this day.

BELIN.: “On the same day, Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr.”

GREVEN.: “The aforementioned Hermenegild, son of King Leovigild of the Visigoths, as Gregory reports in Book III of the *Dialogues*, was converted from the Arian heresy to the faith through the preaching of blessed Leander, bishop of Seville, and was crowned with martyrdom by his Arian father on the holy night of Easter. Also, Saints Eucapius, Secutor, and Paul.” These names are almost certainly corruptions from the Hieronymian text: “At Chalcedon, the birthday—or, according to others, the translation—of Saint Euphemia, virgin. Donanus the abbot. Godeberta the virgin. Also, the holy confessor Nicholas, resting at Nussia.” The last of these is treated among the omitted entries. Godeberta belongs to the 11th of this month. I find nothing anywhere concerning Donanus, not even in the index of omitted entries. Whether he is the one discussed in the Acts on 17 April, who was martyred with two disciples and fifty-two others, or rather another Donanus, who is simply called an abbot in Scotland in that same place, will be examined elsewhere.

MOLAN.: “On the same day, Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr.” Then, in smaller type: “In the territory of Auvergne, Saint Martius, abbot and confessor, concerning whom Gregory of Tours wrote.” See the Acts.

[Col. 0929]

At Pergamum, a city of Asia, the birthday of Saints Carpus the bishop, Papirius the deacon, and Agathonica, an excellent woman, and many others, who were crowned with martyrdom for their blessed confessions under Antoninus Verus and Aurelius Commodus. Together with them, the remarkable man Justin the philosopher, laboring greatly for the religion of Christ in his writings, received the reward of martyrdom for his faithful tongue. In Spain, Saint Hermenegild, who, because of his confession of the Catholic faith, was struck on the head with an axe and entered the heavenly kingdom, as king and martyr, in place of an earthly kingdom.

[Bouillart, in the margin: On the same day, at the monastery of Saint-Germain, the consecration of an altar in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity and the life-giving cross, together with the most blessed Mother of God Mary, Saint Wandregisilus, and all the saints.]

XVIII Kal. Day 14. [Note: [Col. 0933A]]

Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Rosweyd., Antuerpien., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan. are pure. Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., Danic., and the Ultraject.-Belg. edition would also belong here, if they had not inserted from Ado “in the cemetery of Praetextatus.”

[Note: [Col. 0933A]]

The forms *Tyburcii* in Heriniensis and *Tiburcii* in Tornacensis scarcely deserve notice. The greater difficulty is whether we should retain *ad plumbatas*, as we have placed it in the text from Pratensis, Heriniensis, and Tornacensis, or *plumbatis*, as nearly all the others read; not *a plumbatis*, as Munerat. has it. It is certain that this phrase, although harsher, appears in Rosweyd’s edition of Ado and in our manuscripts, with the sole exception of Lobiensis. Here the authority of three highly approved manuscripts is sufficient for us. The same witnesses, together with Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., and Munerat., write *exalaret*, which we retained in the text. The Antwerp manuscript, for excessive clarity, placed *duo primi* in the sentence itself. “It appeared glorious because of miracles” is wrongly read in Belin as “it shone by miracles.” Likewise *iteranis* is wrong; Munerat. has *iterannis*, Tornac. *interampnis*. But what should be made of the name of the virgin placed last? For *Domninae* stand Praten. (though I doubt it), Antuerp., Rosweyd., Greven., and Molan., among others. On the other hand, common usage prevails, which we were compelled to follow on the basis of all the more recent witnesses, the modern Roman edition, and our Acts. I nevertheless truly believe that this usage has wrongly gained currency and that we should read not *Domninae* but *Domnae*, as the Hieronymian copies, both editions of Ado, and all his manuscript codices most distinctly do. For *Domnae*, Herinien., Tornacen., and Munerat. not implausibly write *Dominae*. But *Domininae* in Max.-Lubecana, *Doninae* in one Belinus, and *Donninae* in the other are obvious corruptions. The same Belinus wished to be wiser than necessary when he preferred to write *sociabus* instead of *sociis virginibus*.

[Note: [Col. 0933B]]

As illustrious throughout the Christian world as the name of Cecilia is, consecrated by perpetual celebration in ancient Calendars and Sacramentaries, indeed in the very canon of the Mass, so venerable are her companions in martyrdom, Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus. In all the Hieronymian copies they are entered on this day in the first place, approximately in this form: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, the birthday of Saints Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus.” Yet they are often listed with many companions, concerning whom one may consult Florentinius’s customary fuller note, together with his note on 21 April, when the same saints are repeated in those copies, and Henschenius’s commentary with the *Analecta*, where translations and other matters of that kind are examined, though they do not belong here. The same names of the saints, and they alone, are reported on this day by the author of the Romanum parvum. Whatever else is added in the text belongs to Bede; from him it was transferred to Rabanus, Ado, Usuard, and Notker. Bede had taken it from the celebrated Acts of Cecilia. Henschenius praises those Acts in these words: “This very ancient solemn veneration of these saints grew greatly from the most certain knowledge of their virtues and martyrdom supplied by the ancient Acts of Saint Cecilia, which at that time—approximately the fifth century—were rubbed by everyone’s hands and have survived to this day in the principal and very ancient manuscripts.” This favorable judgment of Henschenius is one from which many, especially more recent writers, have eagerly withdrawn, including Tillemont in volume III, page 250 onward and in the note on page 689. They do not deny the antiquity of the Acts, but refuse to admit them as true or sincere, to such an extent that Ruinart seems deliberately to have abstained throughout his work even from mentioning Cecilia. There is neither room nor leisure here to weigh the controversy; it may be discussed in our Acts on 22 November. Meanwhile, it seems certain that Wandalbert agreed with the other martyrologists when he sang:

> As the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May passes,  
> Valerian triumphs, and his brother Tiburtius;  
> Maximus, a soldier, accompanies them with blood shed.

What is said in the calendar about Fronto, Frontonus, or Frontonius, the Egyptian abbot, is plainly taken from Ado. Rabanus constructed a much longer history from the *Lives of the Fathers*, and Notker made it somewhat shorter. It was undoubtedly taken from the Hieronymians, where, near the end of the calendar, it is read in approximately this form: “At Alexandria, Fronto the monk.” Henschenius published the Life from Rosweyd’s edition. On the occasion of the final clause, he became entangled in many difficulties from which Papebrochius happily extricated him, without resistance, on 14 May, in the Life of Saint Pachomius. The matter is treated at greater length in the *Responses* to article 15, section 13, beginning at no. 196; it is sufficient to indicate it here. Ado’s third announcement is likewise the notice of Saint Proculus, martyr of Interamna, whom he detached from the larger group of Hieronymian martyrs, just as he did the virgin Domnina or Domnia, who is placed last and crowned with her companions. I have nothing to add concerning them to Henschenius’s brief but exact commentary. Usuard added nothing to Ado either, merely revising his text almost word for word and changing only somewhat the order of the saints.

[Note: [Col. 0933D]]

PULSANEN. alone is deficient in the entries on Proculus and Domnina; in the other part it is entirely pure. I note that it too reads *ad plumbatas*, as we have in the text.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC., and the ULTRAJECT.-BELG. edition exceed the others only slightly, as we said: namely, by adding “in the cemetery of Praetextatus.”

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, Saints Tiburtius and Valerian, brothers, and Maximus, who were converted to the faith through blessed Cecilia and crowned under the prefect Almachius by the sword. At Interamna, Saint Proculus the martyr. Also, Saint Domna the virgin, crowned with her virgin companions. At Alexandria, blessed Fronto the abbot, glorious in virtues and miracles.”

ANTUERPIEN.-MAJ., in its first class, cuts out the eulogy. It continues: “At Interamna,” etc., purely. Then: “Domnina,” purely. “Fronto,” purely. “On the same day, the dedication of the basilica of Saint George the martyr, at Squantius.” I do not know what place is indicated here—a villa, fortress, village, or monastery.

BRUXELLEN.: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, the holy martyrs Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus, under the prefect Almachius. The first two, Tiburtius and Valerian, brothers, were baptized by Pope Urban; by order of the prefect Almachius they were beaten with clubs and pierced through with a sword. Maximus, however, was beaten with leaded scourges until he breathed out his spirit.” It then continues “At Interamna,” etc., purely. Then *Domninae*, and afterward *Frontonis*. Finally, at the end: “And the passing of Saint Lambert, bishop of Lyon, disciple of Saint Wandregisilus and the second rector after him of the monastery of Fontenelle.”

HAGENOYEN.: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, the birthday of the blessed martyrs Tiburtius and Valerian, brothers, who were converted through blessed Cecilia and instructed in the faith by blessed Pope Urban. After they had seen angels, begun to distribute all their possessions to the poor, and buried many martyrs of Christ, they were seized by the prefect Almachius and questioned about the faith. He first ordered them to be beaten with clubs and imprisoned, and finally beheaded. Also at Rome, blessed Maximus, a cornicularius, who was converted through Tiburtius and Valerian. When, with the permission granted in those times, he saw souls leaving their bodies like maidens adorned for the bridal chamber and ascending into heaven, he publicly confessed this miracle. Almachius therefore ordered him to be beaten with leaded scourges until he died. At Alexandria, the birthday of blessed Fronto the abbot, whose life was glorious in holiness and miracles. Through his prayers, eighty brothers [Rabanus and Notker, who describe this story more fully, read seventy], living in the desert and eating earthly bread and food, were preserved from the sin of murmuring by means of camels carrying loads of provisions divided and sent to them by God. At Interamna, blessed Proculus the martyr. Also Saint Domnina the virgin, with her other virgin companions crowned with martyrdom [more correctly, ‘crowned’].”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJ.: “The martyrs Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus. Fronto the abbot. Domnina the virgin with the others.”

LUBECO-COL. EDITION, besides the statements concerning Tiburtius and his companions, adds: “Their bodies were reverently buried by blessed Cecilia.” Concerning Fronto, it is pure. “At Interamna, blessed Proculus, Mephibius, and Apollonius, martyrs, disciples of Saint Valentine, bishop and martyr, beheaded under the consul Hennutius.” See our Acts concerning them. In the entry on Domnina, it is correct.

GREVEN.: “Together with the aforementioned Saint Proculus, disciple of Saint Valentine, bishop and martyr, Mephibius and Apollonius, his fellow disciples, suffered under the consul Hennucius. Lambert, bishop of Lyon and confessor. Also in Holland, in the town of Schiedam, the holy virgin Lydwid, who, gladly enduring unheard-of tribulations out of love for conformity to the Lord’s passion, using no bodily food for many years, frequently visited by the Lord through innumerable revelations, and full of good works, rested in peace in the year of the Lord 1433.”

MOLAN., in smaller type, gives the same material concerning Lambert and Lydwid, adding concerning the latter: “Her life was written by the venerable Thomas à Kempis. The death of Saint Abundius, concerning whom Gregory writes in the *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 25.” In the Acts, Book III of the *Dialogues* is cited, but chapter 22. In later editions, the notice concerning Lambert is repeated in the same type, as GREVEN. has it. It continues: “In Holland, in the town of Schiedam, the death of the virgin Lydwid, of extraordinary patience.”

[Col. 0933]

At Rome, on the Appian Way, the birthday of the most blessed martyrs Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus, under the prefect Almachius. The first two were beaten with clubs and struck with a sword; the last was beaten with leaded scourges until he breathed out his spirit. At Alexandria, Saint Fronto the abbot, whose life was glorious in holiness and miracles. At Interamna, blessed Proculus the martyr. Also Saint Domnina the virgin, crowned with her virgin companions.

XVII Kal. Day 15. [Note: [Col. 0935B]]

Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Rosweyd., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. are the witnesses. Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., Danic., and the Ultraject.-Belg. edition are also pure on this day. Hagenoyen as well is nearly pure, apart from a few scribal errors.

[Note: [Col. 0935C]]

For *Cordula*, Herinien., Rosweyd., and Molan. read *Corduba*, but incorrectly, as do most of the later manuscripts. There can be no doubt that Usuard followed Bede, the Romanum parvum, and Ado, in whom *Cordula* is explicitly given. Why Rabanus corrupted Bede’s reading is of no concern to us. Herinien. and Tornacen. perhaps write *tonsa* instead of *tunsa* through an error of the age. Pulsanen. is much more corrupt: “they were cut down with axes.” Again, the same manuscript gives *Vecticeris* for *Euticetis*; Rosweyd., however, has *Eutychetis*, which I entirely judge to be the correct reading, along with the Romanum parvum, both editions of Ado, and Notker. Nevertheless, the reading we consider proper to our author, on the basis of the other Usuardine manuscripts, had to be retained in the text. Rosweyd’s manuscript omits *Pontiam*, for which Munerat. corruptly gives *Pontitiam*. Pulsanensis seems excessively scrupulous when, after *fidem*, it adds *Christi*, although this is entirely clear from the sense. Munerat., on the contrary, removes what is necessary, omitting the word *variis*, which completes the sentence.

[Note: [Col. 0935D]]

Ado found a double announcement for this day in the Romanum parvum, which has briefly: “Cordula, Olympias, and Maximus”; then: “In Italy, Maro, Eutychetius, and Victorinus.” Bede also supplied him with the first, and Ado transferred Bede’s eulogy unchanged into his own Martyrology. Our author copied it word for word from one or the other—or, if preferred, from both—adding from himself the beginning, “In Persia.” These two martyrs, together with others to be reported on the 22nd of this month, were taken from the Acts of Saint Laurence, which we discussed on 17 February in the *Polychronion*. All are said to have been killed in Persia by order of Decius for the faith, as the very uncertain authority of those Acts indicates. Whatever judgment one forms about them, it is certainly clear from the Martyrologies that their cult is very ancient. Furthermore, whether they completed their contest in the city of Cordula, Corduba, or Corduena, as Baronius prefers, no one today could easily say, especially since places of this kind, or resembling them, seem unknown to geographers. From Henschenius’s Commentary you will learn how suitably these martyrs are drawn into Spain and numbered among the people of Corduba. Their widely accepted cult is also demonstrated by Wandalbert, who praises these alone:

> The seventh, joined to the tenth, displays blessed Olympias,  
> and another Maximus at the same time defends her.

Concerning the three other martyrs discussed by Florentinius and Henschenius, the question is whether they can be assigned to the first class of the Hieronymians, and whether the others who are Maro’s companions there should be connected with these three. Anyone who examines the matter will see immediately that this is very uncertain. What is beyond doubt, as I have already shown, is that our three are explicitly named in the Romanum parvum. Ado likewise received them from there and undertook to adorn them with a long discourse from the Acts of the martyrdom of Saints Nereus, Achilleus, and Domitilla, in which they are expressly named; our author reproduces the substance of that encomium in his calendar in his customary manner. Notker gives the whole history, though he does not leave it entirely untouched. The source from which everything first flowed will be disclosed on 7 and 12 May. Henschenius relates matters concerning the time at which they suffered separately, the various places where they were buried, and the different days on which they are celebrated; his account comes closest to probability. Victorinus will recur in our Martyrologies on 5 September.

[Col. 0938A]

On this day the aforementioned Notker describes what Ado records concerning the martyrs of Zaragoza in both editions and in the manuscript codices. Were they taken from Hieronymian copies? I would not dare assert this, since neither the number of martyrs nor their names agree at all. Henschenius thinks that eighteen are to be counted, who on 22 January are joined without names to Saint Vincent. I do not find it easy to guess why there is such variation in the names. It is clear that Ado drew his company from Prudentius’s hymn, furnished with four Saturnini; but why he chose this day, and why Usuard chose the following one, I do not find sufficiently explained. Perhaps our author excels in this respect: he took the sequence of names from the Acts, as will become clearer on the next day. Meanwhile, let the genuine simplicity of our entire text remain beyond dispute.

[Note: [Col. 0937B]]

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. are pure in the first announcement but mutilate the second as follows: “In Italy, the passion of the blessed martyrs Eutychetes and Victorinus.” Nothing more. The UGHELLIAN CODEX also reads this way and generally agrees with them.

CENTULEN.: “In the city of Cordula, Saints Olympias and Maximus, noblemen, who, under Decius, having been struck [perhaps ‘with axes’?], gave up their spirit. In Italy, Saints Eutychetes and Victorinus, who, after suffering a long exile with the most blessed Domitilla, were finally punished by various deaths through the agency of Aurelian. At the monastery of Reomaus, Saint Sylvester, disciple of Saint John.”

ANTUERPIEN.-MAJ. is pure in the entry on Olympias and Maximus; it completely truncates the second announcement and then adds a third concerning Saint Sylvester, which we shall presently report from BRUXELLENSIS.

BRUXELLEN. after a pure beginning adds the martyrs of Zaragoza in an order different from Usuard’s: “And in Spain, in the city of Zaragoza, the eighteen holy martyrs Optatus, Lupereus, Successus, Marcianus, Urbanus, Julius, Quintilianus, Publius, Fronto, Felix, Caecilianus, Evotius, Primitivus, Apodemus, Cassianus, Faustus, Januarius, and Saturninus. All of them were afflicted with various punishments and killed under Dacian, governor of Spain. In Italy, the birthday of the holy martyrs Maro, Eutichus [Eutychetes], and Victorinus. While they were leading a long exile with blessed Flavia and Domitilla on the island of Pontia and piously supporting her with consoling aid in the confession of Christ, they were handed over by the prince Nerva into slavery to Aurelian, her suitor and persecutor, whom she had despised for Christ’s sake. After they had converted many to the faith, they were ordered to be killed by various punishments, and thus their marvelous passion came about. At the monastery of Reomaus, the death of Saint Sylvester, disciple of blessed John the confessor.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked no. 130, have at the end: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Eptadius, priest and confessor.” He is celebrated on 24 August. Castellanus calls him a martyr on 22 August, unless perhaps he is a namesake, different from the former and unknown to the Martyrologists.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Olympias and Maximus, martyrs. Maro, Eutychetes, and Victorinus, martyrs.”

VATICAN., no. 5949: “In Spain, in the city of Zaragoza, the eighteen holy martyrs. In Mesopotamia, Saints Archelaus, Cyprian, and Diogenes.” See their companions in the Acts.

ALTEMPS.: “The translation of Saint Oswald, bishop of the Mercians.” See what is said about him in the index of omitted entries. His Life was given on 28 February, and we discussed him there.

CODEX REMEN. OF SAINTS TIMOTHY AND APOLLINARIS: “At the monastery of Reomaus, Saint Sylvester, disciple of Saint John the confessor.”

LUBECO-COL. EDITION, after a sufficiently pure text, adds: “At Helmarshausen, the translation of Saint Modowald, bishop of Trier and confessor, who was made [or ‘appointed’] by Lord Bruno, bishop of that church.” His birthday is assigned in the omitted entries to 12 May.

BELIN., at the end: “On the same day, blessed Quiricus the bishop, who found the Lord’s cross.” GREVEN. calls him Quirinus; others think he is the same as Saint Cyriacus. See the omitted entries.

GREVEN.: “Quirinus the bishop, who found the Lord’s cross. Also Saints Carcellus, Diogenes, George, Messor, and Franco, bishop and confessor.” Is this Fronto? More is said about him among the omitted entries. “Maximus, bishop of Constantinople, who, as Saint Jerome reports, was distinguished in doctrine and holiness in the time of Gratian.” See the index of omitted entries. “In Ireland, Candanus the bishop.” He is the same person who is called Rodanus or Ruadanus in the Acts. “At the monastery of Reomaus, blessed Sylvester the confessor. The translation of Saint Modowald, bishop of Trier and confessor. Eugaria, virgin and martyr. The passing of Saint Helena the empress.” See what is said about both among the omitted entries.

MOLAN.: “On the same day, blessed Cyricus the bishop, who found the Lord’s cross. At the monastery of Reomaus, the death of Saint Sylvester, disciple of Saint John the confessor.” Then, in smaller type: “Maximus, bishop of Constantinople, who, as Saint Jerome reports, was distinguished in doctrine and holiness in the time of Gratian. Franco, bishop of Worms.” In later editions he says nothing about the latter. He does, however, insert something into the text in italics after “the prince Nerva,” namely: “They were handed over into slavery to Aurelian, the bridegroom whom Flavia Domitilla had despised for Christ’s sake. He ordered them to dig the earth throughout the day, but in the evening to eat *cantabrum*; then, etc. At the monastery of Reomaus,” etc., as above. “On the same day, at the monastery of Helnone, the reception of a double cross, containing in two places pieces of the wood of the Lord’s cross. It was brought from Jerusalem by Walter of Warin, a noble soldier, and offered there to the church; it was received by the abbot and community with a solemn procession, with joy and exultation.” These matters have been added here, although they do not pertain to the Martyrology, especially not to Usuard’s; nor does what follows concerning the beginning of the First Council of Nicaea.

[Col. 0935]

In the Persian city of Cordula, the birthday of Saints Olympias and Maximus, noblemen, who, by order of Decius, were beaten with clubs and then with leaded scourges; finally their heads were struck with axes until they gave up their spirit. In Italy, the blessed martyrs Maro, Eutychetes, and Victorinus, who first endured a long exile on the island of Pontia in the confession of Christ and afterward, under the emperor Nerva, after converting many to the faith, were ordered to be killed by various punishments.

XVI Kal. Day 16. [Note: [Col. 0939A]]

Thus Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Rosweyd., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0939A]]

*Chorintum* in Pratensis and *Corintum* in Heriniensis are incorrectly written. Thus here *Coelesti* stands for *Calisti*, a form maintained by Praten. and Rosweyd., and apparently required by the Hieronymian manuscripts, whatever the Romanum parvum and Ado may read, namely *Callisti*. Our other manuscripts generally have *Calixti*, as is now more commonly received. Where we are free to choose, let us be permitted to imitate the purer sources. Pratensis has *Charisii*, and so do the Acts; I prefer *Carisii*, with the Romanum parvum, Ado, and the other manuscripts, not *Carisi*, as Muneratus has it. *Mari* and *Ceseree* in Pulsanen. are corruptions; nor is *Caesarea Augusti* in use, as Rosweyd. has it, where there is also *eighteen* instead of *eighteen* expressed as *ten and eight*. There is some variation in the names of the martyrs: Pulsanen. and Greven. write *Quintiliani* and *Marcialis*. The former again has *Evochi*, *Apodemii*, and *Juliani*; the latter *Luperti*; Munerat. *Fusti*; Molan. *Eventi*. All the ancient manuscripts read *Evoti*. “These, the Spaniards, having first been afflicted,” instead of “having been afflicted by punishments,” are characteristic errors of Pulsanensis, as is *Hyspaniarum* in Heriniensis.

[Note: [Col. 0939A]]

The Romanum parvum treats today only of the Corinthian martyrs: “At Corinth, Callistus and Carisius, drowned in the sea with others.” Ado uses the same phrase, except that he inserts the word *all* of his own. Florentinius thinks that the words “all drowned in the sea” clearly confirm that Ado composed his Martyrology from some Hieronymian copy, with seven names, which were expressed in the older version, cut away. When and to what extent Florentinius’s opinion applies, the inquisitive reader will understand from our continuous Observations for each day. It seems more plausible to me that Ado sometimes used both Martyrologies: the Hieronymian, which may be called the Great Roman Martyrology, and the one we call the Romanum parvum—on this day and on others as well. In any event, our author copied Ado’s text word for word. Rabanus gives the names of six Corinthian martyrs, which Notker in turn transcribed from him almost unchanged, adding that all were drowned in the sea, where Rabanus had written “and many other saints.” See the six additional companions in Henschenius. Wandalbert’s couplet agrees with our witnesses:

[Col. 0940A] The sixteenth day shines with Charisius and Callistus,

whom the sea blessed when it drowned them with seven others.

Concerning the second announcement of the martyrs of Zaragoza, almost enough has already been said on the preceding day, when it is recorded by Ado and by several fuller Usuardine codices; nor do I see how the accuracy of our text can be doubted. The remaining question is which order of those martyrs should be preferred: the Adonian or the Usuardine? I have already said that the former was taken from Prudentius’ hymn, who presumably attended more to metrical requirements than to preserving the ancient sequence of the names. The older sequence, if I am not mistaken, is presented by the Acts edited by Papebrochius; Usuard had long before taken it from them, and it is not very unlike the one found in the Hieronymian Martyrologies on 22 January, though the latter has many additional names. But since these matters have been sufficiently explained in our Acts, it is not worthwhile to discuss them at greater length. This alone is certain: Dacian’s executioners struck down the martyrs like flocks of lambs, who did not resist them, and, maddened and bloodstained by the blood of the innocent dead.

[Note: [Col. 0939C]]

TORNACENSIAN: Pure throughout the whole text, but omits the final clause about the governor Dacian, perhaps because the copyist was too tightly constrained by the limits of his columns.

ANTWERP, MAXIMILIAN–LÜBECK, BELIN, ANTWERP–MAXIMILIAN, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, DANISH, and the Utrecht–Belgian edition all agree in following, in their enumeration of the Zaragoza martyrs, not yesterday’s Usuardine text but Ado’s, as follows:

“Zaragoza [some copies: Caesaraugusta]: the feast of the eighteen holy martyrs, Optatus, Lupercus, Successus, Marcialis, Urbanus, Julius [some copies: Julia], Quintilianus, Publius, Fronto, Felix, Caecilianus, Evotus, Primitivus, Apodemus, and four others [others, more correctly: the remaining four], who are all reported to have been called Saturnini. All these,” etc.

CENTULENSIAN: “In Spain, in the city of Caesaraugusta, the eighteen holy martyrs who were consumed by various torments during Dacian’s persecution. [Col. 0939D] At Corinth,” etc., as in the text.

ANTWERP–MAJOR: Begins with the Zaragoza martyrs, whose names it reports neither all nor in full. Then: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Tiburtius, bishop and confessor of the city of Le Mans.” This is Thuribius, as is shown in the Acts. Finally, it gives the Corinthian martyrs quite accurately.

BRUSSELS: Pure in the first announcement, it adds:

“And at Rome, Saint Anicetus, pope and martyr, who sat for eleven years and was crowned with martyrdom in the time of Severus and buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He decreed that a cleric should not grow his hair or beard, but should have a crown in the form of a small sphere [or spherical crown]. Also, Bishop Paternus.” This is certainly the Paternus of Avranches.

HAGENOY: The text would be pure if it had not distorted the martyrs’ names and inserted the following after “the governor of Spain”:

“Under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, they were afflicted with various punishments and were cruelly put to death by the same man.”

AQUICINCT: At the end:

“At Rome, Anicetus, pope and martyr. He decreed that a cleric should not grow his hair, according to the Apostle’s command.”

He often recurs here today, but is celebrated on 17 April.

VICTORINIAN:

“At Rome, Saint Enicetus, pope, who occupied the episcopate for eleven years. He decreed that a cleric should not grow his hair, according to the apostolic command.”

AMBIANIAN:

“Also, the dedication of the church of Saint Maurice and his companions at Amiens.”

MATRICIAN–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT:

“Zaragoza, the seventeen holy martyrs, whose passion Prudentius recounts in verse. Caelestius and Charisius. The martyr Bassus.” Perhaps this is Vasus, the martyr of Saintes.

CAMBERIAN:

“On the same day, Saint Isidore the martyr.” He is referred among the omitted commemorations to 15 May.

VATICAN, no. 5949:

“At Rome, the feast of Saint Anicetus, who,” etc.

In the UGHELLIAN edition there is another order of the Zaragoza martyrs, and Julius is written Julia, as we also indicated above from other sources.

The Lübeck–Cologne edition, pure in its first announcement, continues as follows:

“Cologne, translation of Saint Albinus the martyr. The blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, brought him from Britain to the city of Rome; afterward the pious Roman empress Theophanu, wife of the emperor Otto I [or II], having received him as a gift from the pope, brought him to Cologne in the time of Lord Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, in the year of the Lord 885, and honorably placed him in the church of Saint Pantaleon the physician.”

The date is wrong by an entire century; see the Acts, where Albinus is celebrated on 22 June.

It continues:

“In Spain, at Zaragoza, the eighteen holy martyrs, whose names are these: Lupertus, Successus, Marcialis, Urbanus, Julius, Quintilianus, Publius, Fronto, Felix, Caecilianus, Evotus, Primitivus, Apodemus, and the remaining four, Cassianus, Matutinus, Faustus, and Januarius. All these are known to have been afflicted with various punishments and killed under Dacian, governor of Spain. At Le Mans, the blessed Tiburtius, bishop and confessor. Also Saint Amon, of whom it is read that he placed two dragons before the door of his cell, lest robbers carry away the bread on which alone he fed.”

He is referred among the omitted commemorations to 4 October.

GREVEN:

“Bassus the martyr.” We have already spoken of him above.

“In Dacia, Magnus, count and martyr.” Which Dacia is meant here, see in the Acts.

“Lupercus, bishop.” See the omitted commemorations.

“Paternus, bishop of Poitiers.” He is the Paternus of Avranches, born among the Pictones.

“At Le Mans, Tiburtius, bishop and confessor. Also Saint Ammon, hermit and confessor, of whom it is read, etc. At Cologne, translation of Saint Albinus, England’s protomartyr, whom Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, brought from Britain to Rome; afterward the empress Theophanu, wife of Otto I, having received him from the pope as a gift, transferred him to Cologne in the year of the Lord 985 and honorably placed him in the monastery of Saint Pantaleon the martyr. In Mauritania, Saint Basilla.” Concerning her, see the Acts.

MOLANUS begins from Notker:

“At Rome, Saint Anicetus, [Col. 0941C] pope, who occupied the episcopate for eleven years and, crowned with martyrdom in the time of Severus and Marcus, was buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He decreed that the clergy should not grow their hair, according to the Apostle’s command. At Cologne, the translation of Saint Albinus the martyr. The relics of this martyr, worthy of God, were first transferred from Britain to Rome by the blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre; afterward, through the empress Theophanu, wife of Otto II, they were transferred to Cologne and placed in the monastery of the most holy martyr Pantaleon, where they grant saving assistance to all who piously seek it.”

Then, in smaller type:

“In Cleves, at Xanthen, the feast of a martyr whom they call the nameless martyr, whose body was found on 16 April, clothed in purple and wearing shoes, with his head cut off; Archbishop Philip of Cologne transferred it. On the same day, at Palencia in Spain, the feast of Saint Turibius, bishop of Astorga, to whom Pope Leo wrote a letter against the Priscillianists. He was renowned for innumerable miracles and greatly strengthened the Christian religion and faith. At Sebourg, near Valenciennes, Saint Drogo the confessor, who, when invoked, wonderfully assists those suffering from stones and hernias. His deeds are recorded.”

This is as far as the first edition goes. Other editions have:

“In the same place, Engratia, or Encratis, virgin and martyr, and Caius and Crementius, who, having confessed a second time, tasted the flavor of martyrdom.” See our Acts.

It continues with Turibius, as above. Then it adds:

“Near Valenciennes, in the village of Sebourg, rests the renowned Saint Drogo the confessor, who, when invoked, wonderfully assists those suffering from stones and hernias. His deposition took place on 16 April in the year of the Lord 1186. In Sicily, near Castellum Bonum, beneath Mount Maro and the twin hills, in the monastery of Saint Mary of Childbirth, the deposition of the blessed William the confessor. In Dacia, Saint Magnus, count of Arcadia and martyr, in the year 1104.”

Concerning him, we have spoken above. Regarding the translation of Albinus, the same things are given above. See our Acts, volume IV of June, page 172 onward.

“The feast of the martyr of Xanthen, whom Archbishop Philip transferred, found clothed in purple and wearing shoes, with the top of his head cut off. We, who saw clots of blood clinging to the hairs in his tomb, have written this so that you may believe, and so that through the turning of the years you may venerate him on this day and continually. Nor should it disturb you that his name is not known, since the Legend of the Thebans scarcely contains the names of twelve martyrs.”

Finally, in smaller type:

“In the region of Coutances, Saint Paternus, bishop of Avranches and confessor, formerly abbot of Scissy.” See GREVEN above and the Acts for this day.

[Col. 0937]

At Corinth, the feast of the holy Callistus and Charisius, with seven others, all drowned in the sea. At Zaragoza, the eighteen holy martyrs Quintilianus, Cassianus, Matutinus, Publius, Urbanus, Marcialis, [Col. 0939] Faustus, Successus, Felix, Januarius, Primitivus, Evotus, Caecilianus, Optatus, Fronto, Lupercus, Apodemus, and Julius. All these were afflicted with punishments and killed together under Dacian, governor of Spain.

The fifteenth day before the Kalends. Day 17.

[Note: [Col. 0941]]

The text is taken from the Herinien, Tournai, Pulsa, Antwerp, Maximilian–Lübeck, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus editions.

[Note: [Col. 0941D]]

It scarcely presents anything worth noting. For Mappalicus, the Pulsa manuscript writes Ampilicus. More disgracefully, for Petrus it has Peto. Muneratus likewise has Hermogenes. At Córdoba, Greven and Molanus read Hermogenes; the others have it as in the text. The more reliable codices show that Helias should be written, not Heleas, as in Antwerp and Molanus, nor Helyas, as in Muneratus. Likewise, Herinien has Isydorus incorrectly; Tournai, Antwerp, Maximilian–Lübeck, and Muneratus have Ysidorus; Pulsa has Hysidorus. Concerning presbyter, Africa, Cyprianus, and similar matters, enough has been said. In the Maximilian–Lübeck edition, through the printer’s negligence, it reads:

“At Antioch, the holy martyrs Heleas the presbyter, Paul and Ysidore the monks, Peter the deacon, etc.”

At the end, however, the announcement of the Cordoban martyrs recurs in its proper order. Therefore all the words between “At Antioch” and “Peter” must be deleted. Here is a somewhat more difficult variation.

In our Pratense copy, in the penultimate place—that is, between the Antiochene and Cordoban martyrs—it reads:

“In the East, the blessed Nicephorus, crowned with martyrdom under Valerian and Gallienus for Christ.”

The same words are found in the Aquicinct, Brussels, and Rosweyd manuscripts—or rather in the very ancient manuscript of the church of Saint Mary at Utrecht. In it, as in the Pratense, the name is Nicoforus; in the Brussels manuscript, Nycoforus.

Long ago, on the authority of the other codices, I judged that this announcement must be wholly excluded from Usuard. Nor did Castellanus, otherwise the supreme patron of that alleged autograph, dare to resist; he openly admitted that what is said about Nicephorus is entirely interpolated, and, as he says, “by a hand not very ancient” (*ajouté de main peu ancienne*). This was said, of course, to excuse the codex.

But it must also be admitted that something else had previously been written in that place by an earlier hand, if indeed there was such writing, and that it was subsequently erased so that these words could be inserted anew. Yet no trace whatever of this matter appears in any of our other codices. Nor does the aforementioned Castellanus, as he usually does elsewhere, even mention an erasure.

Who could adequately understand how a more recent hand could have been joined to an older one in the middle of the text, unless either space had been left there—which seems absurd—or something had certainly been erased? Whatever may finally be brought forward in defense of the codex, we leave it to the judgment of experts in such matters whether additions of this kind, which Castellanus calls very mildly “additions,” greatly commend its authenticity. Meanwhile, the primitive simplicity of our little register is demonstrated to the eye by the other codices.

[Note: [Col. 0943B]]

On this day Ado again records certain saints who are also found in the Hieronymian copies, although one may altogether doubt whether they were taken from those copies. Mappalicus in particular is numbered among the African martyrs in the copies mentioned above, but in an entirely different manner: neither alone nor as the leader of his companions.

In the Roman Martyrology known as the Little Roman, however, he is alone:

“In Africa, Mappalicus.”

Ado most probably took him from there, adding the rest of the material in the eulogy from Cyprian’s laudatory letter. Our author transferred only Ado’s eulogy into his own text, excluding the letter; Notker truncated part of the letter. Neither Mappalicus nor any of his companions is known in Bede, Florus, or Rabanus.

Yet the memory of this illustrious martyr is found much earlier in the very ancient Carthaginian Calendar, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May (instead of the fifteenth): “the martyr Mappalicus.” Since he is also mentioned there alone, this makes the conjecture plausible that the Little Roman, and from it Ado, may have taken him from some calendar of this kind, or from Cyprian’s letter itself, rather than from the Hieronymian copies, which would at least have introduced the memory of his companions.

In the Acts you have the cited letter of Cyprian and more about his companions in the chapter appended by Henschenius. See also the notable Admonition of Ruinart prefixed to the Life and Passion of the most glorious bishop, p. 198. But no one appears to have traced the history of Mappalicus and the other Carthaginian martyrs and confessors who suffered under Decius more accurately than Tillemont, volume III, beginning at p. 378.

Wandalbertus speaks of Mappalicus in such a way that he almost assigns him to Antioch together with Peter and Hermogenes:

Mappalicus on the fifteenth, and Hermogenes and Peter,

shine forth, renowned in merit, virtue, and blood.

There is scarcely any doubt that Peter and Hermogenes derive from the same source as the Little Roman, since they are announced in exactly the same words there, in Ado, and in our author. Nevertheless, I do not deny that these very Antiochene martyrs, joined again to other companions, are listed in the aforementioned Hieronymian copies.

Notker adds: “Peter, Fortunatus, and Martianus,” whereas in Rabanus, after Hermogenes, he had read: “and in Africa, Fortunatus and Martianus.” The reading of Notker, supported by the Hieronymian copies, is to be preferred. Yet our text does not seem to have proceeded from there, whatever I must confess: I do not know from what source their memory—now preserved nowhere except in the Martyrologies—was formerly drawn.

Ado next has Pantagathus, a predecessor of his as bishop of Vienne. Why Usuard passed him over, we do not even conjecture here. In his place, however, were substituted the Cordoban martyrs, beheaded by the Saracens in Usuard’s own time. As we said elsewhere, Usuard may easily have acquired knowledge of them in Spain itself, where he had been sent to obtain the relics of the most renowned martyr Vincent. Henschenius reported a few things about them from Eulogius, p. 494.

[Note: [Col. 0943C]]

Concerning PRATENSE and ROSWEYD, we have already said enough above.

UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, and the Utrecht–Belgian edition begin as follows:

“At Rome, Saint Anicetus, pope. [Col. 0943D] He was the tenth after blessed Peter; after governing the Roman Church for eleven years, he was crowned with martyrdom in the time of Severus and Marcus and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus.”

This does not agree entirely with ANTWERP–MAXIMILIAN.

ALBERGEN and DANISH add to what has already been mentioned:

“He decreed that the clergy should not grow their hair according to the Apostle’s command, but that their tonsure should be spherical and round. Hence Pope Martin’s decree that clerics should walk with shorn heads and uncovered ears.”

Others report the same matter differently.

CENTULENSIAN:

“In Africa, Saint Mappalicus, who was crowned with martyrdom together with many others. At Antioch, Saints Peter and Hermogenes. At Córdoba, Saints Helias the presbyter, Paul and Isidore the monks.”

The usual abridgment of this codex.

ANTWERP–MAJOR is almost like the preceding source, but omits the final announcement.

BRUSSELS begins:

“Noah entered the ark.”

[Col. 0944C] It is pure in the sections on Mappalicus and the Antiochene martyrs, but inserts:

“In the East, the feast of the blessed Nicephorus, who was crowned with martyrdom under Valerian and Gallienus for the faith of Christ.”

[Col. 0944D] It continues:

“At Córdoba,” etc., accurately. Then:

“At Vienne, Saint Pantagathus [or Pantagotus], glorious bishop.”

HAGENOY is somewhat interpolated in the section on Mappalicus and, in second place, gathers together almost everything that we reported yesterday and today from various codices about Anicetus. It is pure in the sections on the Antiochene and Cordoban martyrs.

Concerning AQUICINCT, together with PRATENSE and the others, we have spoken above. See the Acts for 9 February.

MATRICIAN–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT:

“Mappalicus with several martyrs. Anicetus, pope and martyr.”

In the VATICAN manuscript, no. 5949, the commemoration of the Cordoban martyrs is absent.

FLORENTINIAN:

“Also, Saint Majolus, abbot, father of many monasteries, resting in the place called Cluny.” He is referred among the omitted commemorations to his feast day, 11 May.

The Lübeck–Cologne edition joins to the material on Anicetus what we presented above from Utrecht, Albergen, and the others. [Col. 0945A] The entire text that follows is pure. Then:

“In the East, the blessed Nicephorus, crowned with martyrdom under Valerian and Gallienus for Christ. At Vienne, Saint Pantagathus, bishop and confessor. In Egypt, another Saint Ammon, a man of incredible abstinence and father of innumerable monks.”

See the index of omitted commemorations.

Both editions of BELIN are faulty and confused. After “Mappalicus the martyr,” it inserts “who was scourged.” It reads “At Antioch” where it should have “At Córdoba,” and “At Córdoba” where it should have “At Antioch.” At the end, the first edition has:

“Also at Rome, Anacletus, pope and martyr.”

The second edition has Anacletus. It intended to say Anicetus.

GREVEN:

“At Rome, Anicetus, pope,” etc., as in Utrecht and the others.

“In Italy, Saint Domninus the martyr, who was one of Christ’s seventy-two disciples.” See the omitted commemorations.

“In the East, the blessed Nicephorus, crowned with martyrdom under Gallienus and Valerian for confessing Christ. Also Marcianus and Donatus.” From the Hieronymian Martyrology.

“Jobitas the martyr and three other beheaded men.” [Col. 0945B] See the omitted commemorations.

“Magnus the martyr.” In my opinion, a futile repetition of yesterday’s entry.

“At Vienne, Saint Pantagathus, bishop and confessor. At Tortona, Saint Innocentius, bishop and confessor. In Egypt, another Ammon, a man of incredible abstinence and father of innumerable monks.” Concerning him, see above.

“Helenus the abbot, whose faith was so great that irrational animals obeyed him at his command and, when disputing with a heretic, he entered fire and remained unharmed. In Libya, Paul the abbot, who was father of five hundred monks, whom he led into the way of salvation both by salutary admonitions and by an exemplary life. He did not work with his hands and did not take food until he had offered three hundred prayers to God on bended knees; he counted them by means of stones, returning one stone to his bosom at each prayer.”

Concerning these last two, see the index of omitted commemorations.

“Noah entered,” etc.

MOLAN:

“Also at Rome, Anacletus, pope and martyr.”

I would believe that he took this from Belin, who in a later revision restored it, writing Anicetus instead of Anacletus.

“At Tortona, Saint Innocentius,” as above.

“At Sonegias, the feast of Saint Landricus, bishop and confessor.”

In other editions it reads:

“Also at Rome, Anicetus, pope and martyr. He decreed that a cleric should not grow his hair, according to the Apostle’s command. In the East, the blessed Nicephorus, crowned with martyrdom under Valerian and Gallienus for Christ. [Col. 0946B] At Tortona, Saint Innocentius, bishop and confessor. At Sonegias, the feast of Saint Landricus, bishop and confessor. On the seventeenth day, Saint Acacius, bishop of Melitene.”

See what is said about him in the Catalogue of the Omitted. His Life, moreover, is given in our Acts under 31 March.

[Col. 0941]

In Africa, the feast of Saint Mappalicus the martyr, who, as blessed Cyprian writes in his letter to the martyrs and confessors, was crowned together with many others.

At Antioch, the holy martyrs Peter the deacon and Hermogenes.

[Bouillart inserts:

[Note: [Col. 0941C]]

In the Pratense codex, between the Antiochene and Cordoban [Col. 0941D] martyrs, Nicephorus is mentioned. The same man is mentioned there in the Aquicinct, Brussels, and Rosweyd manuscripts, in the three Pratense manuscripts B, D, and E, in the Conches manuscript, the Montisburg manuscript, and the Lübeck–Cologne edition.

Nevertheless, the Pratense was not worthy to be followed by Sollerius, both because of the other codices that lack Nicephorus and especially because Castellanus warned that what is said about Nicephorus is entirely interpolated, and by a hand that is not very ancient.

Must I hear the same thing so often? Must I so often weary the reader with the same matter? But here I wish Sollerius to learn more from me about our codex than he learned from Castellanus.

The last line of the page, where “Peter the deacon and Hermogenes” now appear, was formerly almost entirely erased, [Col. 0942D] and restored in another hand—although close to Usuard’s time—and in different ink. Let Sollerius consult his notes.

Perhaps his adviser spoke of those martyrs, whereas Sollerius understands him to have spoken of Nicephorus. Furthermore, the first two lines of the following page, where “Nicephorus” and “the Cordoban monks” now appear, were similarly erased.

But I ask Sollerius to believe me: the hand that wrote those saints is precisely the same as that of the rest of the codex, although the letters are smaller so as to make room for Nicephorus, whom Usuard undoubtedly inserted here after being deceived by certain Acts that claimed Nicephorus’ feast was celebrated on this day.

Certainly, in the manuscript collection of the Acts I read the following title prefixed to the Acts of Saint Nicephorus:

“The Passion of Saint Nicephorus the martyr, whose feast is celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.”

BOUILLART.]

In the East, the blessed Nicephorus, crowned with martyrdom under Valerian and Gallienus for Christ.

Also at Córdoba, the holy martyrs Helias the presbyter, Paul and Isidore the monks.

The fourteenth day before the Kalends. Day 18.

[Note: [Col. 0945C]]

Taken from the Pratense, Tournai, Rosweyd, Antwerp, Maximilian–Lübeck, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus editions. Also from Antwerp–Maximilian, Utrecht, Leyden, Louvain, Albergen, Danish, the Utrecht–Belgian edition, and almost from Hagenoy.

[Note: [Col. 0945C]]

Messana is written with nearly all the codices, although I have nowhere found a Messana in Apulia. For Anthia, Maximilian–Lübeck reads Anthya; Rosweyd and Antwerp, Ancia. In Muneratus, through a shameful printer’s error, *matrium* appears instead of *matris*. The same source, together with Antwerp, Maximilian–Lübeck, Greven, Molanus, and others, writes “oil, pitch, and resin,” but our register’s reading is to be preferred. `Hiis` is an error very common in the Maximilian–Lübeck edition. Muneratus has `Appoloni`. In Rosweyd, instead of “by sentence of the Senate,” it reads “according to the sentence of the Senate.” Again, Muneratus reads Praefectus instead of Perfectus; Antwerp and Maximilian–Lübeck have Cordoba instead of Córdoba’s genitive, Cordubae.

[Note: [Col. 0945C]]

The Hieronymian copies explicitly give the following today:

“At Rome, the feast of the holy Eleutherius, bishop, and Anthia—or Anchiae or Antiae—his mother, Parthenius, Calocerus, etc.,” with eight or nine persons named individually.

The Little Roman does not know the companions, writing only:

“At Messana in Apulia, Eleutherius, bishop, and Anthia, his mother.”

Ado differs somewhat:

“At Messana in Apulia,” etc., with a eulogy whose substance our author reproduced.

Concerning Mesana, Messana, Misena, and the other places, there is much in Baronius’ notes, much in Florentinius, and much investigation and many conjectures in our Acts. There are also further difficulties arising from Florus, Rabanus, and Notkerus. Florus assigns the passion to Rome, with a eulogy different from that of the others. Omitting the location, Rabanus says that Eleutherius was ordained bishop at Aquileia; he appears, unless I am mistaken, to have drawn the rest from the Acts at Rieti, while Notker preferred the Adonian material, though he still wrote Misena in Apulia.

All these matters are variously entangled in difficulties, and it is not easy either to examine them fully or to refute them. We consider the antiquity of the martyrs’ cult certain. Some Acts preceded the Hieronymian copies; others preceded the author of the Little Roman, whose Martyrology Ado perhaps enlarged from still other Acts. Finally, we see no light arising from Florus or Rabanus for saints already excessively obscured by darkness from other sources.

There is no need to labor over Usuard’s text. Whether he wrote correctly or not makes no difference; we are certain that he wrote as he found it in his perpetual predecessor.

Papebrochius delivered a judicious criticism of the root from which so many things—at the very least highly suspect—sprang. It was attacked by Joseph Perez, Benedictine monk of Saint-Facundus, as may be seen in the replies to article 11, no. 232, but was approved by Tillemont, volume II, pp. 227 and 587. In Perez’s dissertations I find nothing that shakes, much less overturns, the arguments of our master.

Nevertheless, let the true and certain memory of these illustrious martyrs remain, once celebrated by Wandalbertus as well:

Twice seven: Eleutherius, and his holy mother

Anthia, shine forth, following life through death.

It seems certain that Apollonius the Roman senator, mentioned in the register, is not the same person who is numbered among Eleutherius’ companions in the Hieronymian copies, but is entirely different from him. The author of the Little Roman first introduced him into the sacred calendars from Rufinus’ translation of Eusebius, book V, chapter 21; Ado then attached a brief eulogy to him, drawn either from the aforementioned Rufinus or from Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 42—or, why not, composed from both.

Certainly, wherever the dignity of a Roman senator is mentioned, it is clear that Jerome was before Ado’s eyes. It is no less evident that our author borrowed everything from Ado, while Notker transferred it almost intact.

Henschenius investigates the remaining matters concerning this illustrious defender of the faith and martyr of the senatorial order; Tillemont arranges them quite accurately in volume III, beginning at p. 55, without paying much attention to Joseph Scaliger’s quibble, which Ruinart mentions among the *Selecta*, p. 73.

The Viennese Martyrologist next has:

“The passing of Saint Ursmarus,”

although Usuard preferred to transfer him to the following day, undoubtedly because he considered that to be the true day of his death, as did many others.
