His place on this day was occupied by Perfectus, the Cordoban martyr, unknown to all the other earlier and contemporary sources, but worthy in Usuard’s time—when the memory of his recent glorious contest was still fresh—of a place in the ecclesiastical calendars. Our Acts present his Life, illuminated by Eulogius.

[Note: [Col. 0947A]]

HERINIEN: Extremely pure in the text, it adds at the end:

“At Trier, Saint Maternus, bishop and confessor.”

From this it may be inferred that the memory of this saint had long been celebrated with a particular cult in the church or monastery to which this codex once belonged. Other sources also mention him on this day, but most place him on 14 September.

[Col. 0947B]

PULSA: Deletes the eulogy of Eleutherius; otherwise it is pure.

CENTULENSIAN:

“At Messana, a city of Italy, the holy martyrs Eleutherius, bishop, and Anthia, his mother. At Rome, Apollonius the senator. At Córdoba, Saint Perfectus, presbyter and martyr. In the region of Sambria, at the monastery of Lobbes, Saint Ursmarus, bishop and confessor.”

See the following day.

ANTWERP–MAJOR: Mutilated in the sections on Eleutherius and Apollonius; it says nothing about Perfectus. At the end it adds:

“At Auxerre, the dedication of the altar of the older church of Saint Stephen the protomartyr.”

BRUSSELS:

“At Lobbes, Saint Ursmarus, bishop and confessor. After preparing the necessities required for the use of the monastery, he undertook to govern the monastery of Lobbes, founded by Landelinus, at the command of Pippin.”

The remainder of the text is sufficiently pure.

VICTORIN:

“At Córdoba, Saint Perfectus, bishop and confessor.” Read “presbyter,” as above.

“On the same day, Saint [Col. 0947C] Leo, pope.”

These final words are also found in the Swedish Royal Codex, marked no. 130, so that it is surprising that no mention of it is made among the omitted commemorations. It concerns Leo IX, as will become clear on the following day.

MATRICIAN–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT:

“Apollonius the senator. Maternus, bishop and confessor. Eleutherius, bishop and martyr, and Anthia, his mother.”

In the VATICAN manuscript, marked no. 5949, the entry for Perfectus, presbyter and martyr of Córdoba, is absent.

The MONTIS SANCTI codex:

“Translation of Saint Mary Magdalene.”

When and to what place, I do not know.

The Lübeck–Cologne edition, fairly pure in the text, adds at the end:

“On the same day, Saint Lacerianus, bishop and confessor.”

See in the Acts concerning Lafreanus or Molassius. He is said to have been an apostolic legate.

BELIN reports the text purely, but inserts between Apollonius and Perfectus:

“On the same day, Saint Calocerus the martyr.”

I think it concerns the Calocerus of Brescia, whose Acts are explained today—unless someone wishes to take him from the Hieronymian Martyrology and make him a companion of Eleutherius and Anthia, together with Parthenius and others.

GREVEN:

“Anastasius, pope and martyr.”

Is this referring to a translation or elevation? He is referred among the omitted commemorations to 27 April.

“Also Saints Septimus, Victoricus, and Donatus.”

A joining together of unrelated persons from the Hieronymian Martyrology.

“Calocerus the martyr. Ursmarus, bishop and confessor; according to Usuard, however, on the following day. Lacerianus, bishop and confessor. Peter the deacon and confessor.” [Col. 0948B] See the conjecture placed among the omitted commemorations.

“In Ireland, Lafrianus, abbot and confessor.”

I would be greatly mistaken if he were not the same as Lacerianus, or Lafreanus or Molassius, mentioned above, who was both abbot and bishop.

“In the territory of Hermopolis, Saint Apollonius, abbot and confessor, a man of great holiness.”

See what is noted about this Apollonius and the other Apollonius in the index of omitted commemorations.

MOLAN:

“In the monastery called Lobbes, the deposition of the blessed Ursmarus, bishop and confessor, whose deeds are recorded. On the same day, Saint Calocerus the martyr.”

Then, in smaller type:

“At Zaragoza, Saint Encratia, or Encratis, the martyr, of whom Aurelius Clemens writes in the book of the *Crowned Ones* that, after being torn to pieces in a horrible manner, she was kept in chains until her wounds and body rotted.”

Concerning her, see the Acts for 16 April.

Other editions add to the Usuardine text:

“At the monastery of Lobbes, the deposition of the most holy Ursmarus, bishop and confessor.”

This is treated as part of the text, except that one word and half of another are printed in italics.

The Supplement follows:

“His illustrious deeds are recorded. At Milan, the deposition of Saint Galdinus, which is always celebrated on the second Sunday after Easter. On the eighteenth day, Saint Father John, disciple of Saint Gregory the Decapolite. On the same day, Saint Jubinus, bishop and confessor, whose body rests at Lyon on the Rhône.”

He is omitted from the Acts as unknown.

“At Auxerre, the dedication of the altar of the older church of Saint Stephen, Christ’s protomartyr. For the ancient dedication, celebrated by blessed Amator, is found in the ancient Martyrologies on the fifth day before the Nones of October.”

Then, in smaller type:

“In the region of Mons, Aia, countess of Hainaut, illustrious in both blood and life, whose memory the church of Mons celebrates in the Litanies.”

This is the first mention found in the Martyrologies of this holy countess, likewise the wife of Saint Hidulph. Her cult, life, relics, and patronage in lawsuits have all been elucidated by Henschenius in a careful Commentary.

[Col. 0945]

At Messana, a city of Apulia, the feast of the holy martyrs Eleutherius, bishop, and Anthia, his mother. He was illustrious both for the holiness of his life and for the power of his miracles. Under the emperor Hadrian, he overcame an iron bed made fiery, a grating, and a frying-pan boiling with oil, pitch, and resin; he was also thrown to lions but remained unharmed by them. Finally, he was beheaded together with his mother.

At Rome, the blessed Apollonius the senator, who, after being betrayed by a servant under the emperor Commodus because he was a Christian, composed a notable volume, which he read in the Senate; then, by sentence of the Senate, he was beheaded for Christ.

At Córdoba, Saint Perfectus, presbyter and martyr.

The thirteenth day before the Kalends. Day 19.

[Note: [Col. 0947]]

Taken from the Tournai, Muneratus, first edition of Belin, Greven, and Molanus sources.

[Note: [Col. 0949A]]

Tournai, Belin, and certain other ancient codices read *Thimonis*, which we follow; Molanus more correctly has *Timonis*; Muneratus incorrectly, *Thinonis*; Greven, *Thymonis*. Belin begins incorrectly:

“The feast of Saint Thimonis”;

Muneratus:

“At Corinth.”

In Greven and Molanus the word “Lord” is missing. Muneratus somewhat reverses the sense: instead of “and there by the Jews,” etc., he writes “there, as it is reported, by the Jews.” After “injured,” *est* is omitted in Greven and Molanus.

I wrote *Militana* with all the codices; the Hieronymian copies, the Little Roman, Ado, and others likewise have this form. I have no doubt that Melitene is meant.

There is no single spelling for the martyrs’ names. For *Caii*, most read *Gaii*, as in Tournai, Muneratus, Belin, Molanus, and others. Greven, with some others, has *Gagii*. I preferred to follow the consensus of the older codices. Tournai, Greven, and Molanus read *Galathae*; I preferred the form of the others, *Galatae*. Only Belin has *Ruffi*.

Again, Belin has “In the city of Spain,” etc. *Calcoliberi* and *Vicentii* are errors of Muneratus. I wrote *Ursmari* so as not to depart from the more common designation, although Tournai, Muneratus, and Greven read *Orsmari*, while Belin has *Ursmari*. Matters such as *nihil*, *dyaconi*, and similar forms may be passed over.

[Note: [Col. 0949B]]

[The supplied source ends here, mid-note.]

Who, as we have shown under 10 and 20 January and 9 April, included most of the earliest deacons, was also the first to insert Timon into the ecclesiastical Martyrologies: the author of the *Little Roman Martyrology*, under 20 April, “At Corinth, Timon, one of the seven deacons.” From this source Ado transferred him and adorned him, among the festivals of the apostles, with the eulogy that Our Author reproduced almost word for word. In his own Martyrology, however, he announces him simply, as Notker does—Ado first, Notker last.

Henschenius might here, and occasionally elsewhere, be charged with a slight negligence: without consulting the festivals of the apostles, he attributed to Usuard what certainly belongs to Ado, as is truly the case with the entire present eulogy of Timon, printed in Rosweyde’s edition on page 36. Henschenius himself collected a few details about Timon—whether there was one Timon or two—which are even less well supported; nor does anything further appear to have been added by others.

The Armenian martyrs are found in the Hieronymian Martyrologies as well as in the *Little Roman Martyrology*, but with this difference: the aforesaid copies have additional martyrs, again in the same position, of whom the *Little Roman* makes no mention, and consequently neither does Ado, from whom Notker extracted them. They are everywhere marked by the same limits, since no fuller information about them exists anywhere. Wandalbertus concluded all of them in two verses:

> Gaius, Aristonice, Rufus, Hermogenes, and Galatas,  
>   
> With Expedite and the martyr, shine on the thirteenth day.

Vincent is likewise known in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but not in the *Little Roman*. Ado took him from the former, adding nothing, nor did Usuard—probably because they had seen no Acts, and none exist even now, unless they have been fabricated more recently. The multiplicity of the Vincents, and their identity in the Acts, is discussed elsewhere. See what we said on 22 January, and the Acts of Vincent, Orontius, and Victor, illustrated there by Bollandus.

It is surprising that Florentinius was unaware of Caucoliberis, which was known not only to the martyrologists but also to geographers. For the rest, see Papebrochius’s observations for this day, p. 622, and add Tillemont’s note, vol. V, p. 612.

We began speaking of Ursmarus on the preceding day because Ado reports him there—not under the name Orsmarus, as we read in some places, but under the name Ursmarus. Whether he was recorded by Usuard, however, is made doubtful by the numerous Usuardine codices, scarcely ever accustomed to omit anything from their author, in which he is nevertheless entirely absent. The doubt is increased by the varying manner of his announcement. The Pratensis and Rosweyd manuscripts read, “in the Hainaut district” (understand: Hainau, in Hainaut—a very vague expression); the other manuscripts cited in the text have the more precise and distinct reading, “at the monastery of Lobbes.” For this reason the Pratensis was excluded from the number of pure codices; it also adds the dedication of a church “in honor of Saint Symphorianus,” and so forth, although Castellanus testifies that this was added by a later hand, and Sirmondus indicates the same by striking out the lines.

Whatever the case may be, the announcement of Ursmarus preserved in the margin is more probably to be attributed to Usuard, after Ado—at least in the form in which we reproduce it—even though Ado read it somewhat differently, namely: “At the monastery of Lobbes, the passing of Saint Ursmarus, bishop and confessor.”

[Note: In the Pratensis, much has already been said.]

HERINIEN. differs today from the others by excluding Ursmarus and substituting in his place: “On the same day, at the church of Saint Peter in Rome, the burial of Lord Leo IX, pope, who dedicated the church of Saint Remigius.”

PULSANEN. is pure in the entry for Timon, immediately adding: “At the city of Caucoliberis, etc.” It is silent about the martyrs of Militina and also about Ursmarus.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. are likewise defective concerning Ursmarus.

ROSWEYD. writes *Timothei* instead of *Timonis*. In the other matters it follows the text, except that it reads “in the Hainaut district” and adds at the end: “In Kent, the passion of Saint Elphegus, archbishop and martyr, who was captured and killed by pagans and buried in London.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJ., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., DANIC. The ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition does not mention Ursmarus; otherwise it is nearly pure in the text. ALBERGEN. agrees in this omission but additionally excludes Vincent of Caucoliberis.

BRUXELLEN. also omits Ursmarus; otherwise it approaches the purity of the texts closely. At the end it adds:

> “On the same day, Saint Leo IX, pope and confessor. He was first bishop of Toul, was promoted to the papacy by Emperor Henry, and, because of this, considering his conscience, resigned. Having then been duly elected again, after a praiseworthy life he was buried in the church of Saint Peter, shining with miracles.”

HAGENOYEN. likewise deviates little from the text. It too is silent about Ursmarus. At the end it adds: “At Canterbury, Saint Elphegus, bishop and martyr.”

CENTULEN. begins with the martyrs of Militina, where it is pure. It continues:

> “In Septimania, at the city of Caucoliberis, Saint Vincent the confessor, whose deeds are preserved. On the same day, Saint Timon, one of the seven earliest deacons, who, crucified at Corinth, rests there.”

Papebrochius explains here which Acts of Vincent survive.

ANTUERP.-MAJ., in the Armenians and Vincent, follows the earlier witness without much difference and continues:

> “At the monastery called Lobbes, the burial of blessed Ursmarus, bishop and confessor, whose deeds are preserved.”

In the entry for Timon it abbreviates the text while preserving the substance.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “Elphegus, bishop and martyr of Canterbury, with many others. Timon, deacon and martyr.”

And in the margin:

> “The feast of the sacred lance is celebrated on the Friday after the octave of Easter.”

VATICAN., numbered 5949, omits Rufus among the Armenians. It says nothing about Ursmarus. At the end it adds: “At Rome, the burial of Saint Leo IX, pope, who sat in the pontificate for five years.”

UGHELLIAN. lacks Ursmarus.

FLORENTIN.:

> “At Florence, in the regions of Tuscany, Saint Crescentius, subdeacon of Saint Zenobius, bishop of that same city, who became renowned for his life, virtue, and miracles in the year of the Lord 424, was honorably buried in the cathedral church by Zenobius, then bishop there, and was praised in the letters of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, when his death had been announced.”

The ignorance of the encomiast is obvious.

BURDEGALEN.:

> “At the monastery of Lobbes, Saint Ursmarus, bishop.”

BIZUNTICEN.:

> “At Rome, the burial of Leo, pope and confessor, whose most holy life is attested by frequent miracles.”

The LUBECO-COL. edition is nearly pure in the text, but reads:

> “In the district of Hainaut, at the monastery of Lobbes, blessed Ursmarus,” etc.

Then:

> “At Solemniacum, Saint Tillo, bishop and confessor.”

Who this was, see under the *Omissions*. “On the same day, Saint Alphegus, bishop of Canterbury and martyr.”

BELINI. The second edition adds to the text: “At Rome, Saint Leo, pope and confessor.”

GREVEN.:

> “Donatus, Vitalis.”

The former was taken from the Hieronymian Martyrology; whose the latter is, I do not know.

> “In Kent, Saint Alphegus. He, as Vincent relates in book 26, was born of illustrious parents and educated in letters. When he had read what seemed sufficient for salvation, he turned all his philosophical study toward loving God. First bishop of Winchester, and then, in the year of the Lord 1006, made archbishop of Canterbury, he deserved, because of the holiness of his life, to attain the palm of martyrdom. The sweetest and dearest of the martyrs.”

For these, see the *Omissions*.

> “In Arabia, Saint Tymon, bishop and martyr.”

He is not known even among the *Omissions*. See concerning the other Timon.

> “At Solemniacum, Tyllion, bishop and confessor. At Rome, the burial of Saint Leo IX, pope and confessor. He was German by nationality and was first bishop of Toul, called Bruno. When the Romans had asked the emperor to give them a pontiff, and he could persuade no bishop of Germany to undertake this burden, this man at last consented. Governing the Church laudably and renowned for miracles, he died in the year of the Lord 1054.

> “In Upper Wesalia, in the diocese of Trier, the passion of blessed Wernher, a boy fourteen years old, who in the year of the Lord 1287 was hanged by Jews on the day of the Preparation, scourged, cut in all his limbs, and killed by a cruel death; he immediately became renowned for many miracles.

> “In Dacia, at the city of Odense, the translation of Saint Canute, king and protomartyr of Dacia.”

He is celebrated on 10 July.

MOLAN. gives, concerning Leo, the very words reported above from HERINIEN.:

> “At the monastery of Blandinium, the raising of the body of Saint Florbert, first abbot of that monastery.”

He is celebrated on 10 November.

> “On the same day, Saint Alphegus, bishop and martyr.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “He who was first at Winchester …”

as above.

> “In Upper Wesalia …”

also from GREVEN.

The later editions omit Ursmarus, who was mentioned on the preceding day. Concerning Elphegus, as above. Likewise concerning Leo. It continues:

> “On the nineteenth day, Saint Father John of the Old Laura.”

I find nothing altered concerning Florbert and Wernher.

[Col. 0947]

Saint Timon, one of the seven earliest deacons, who first sat as a teacher at Beroea and afterward, spreading the word of the Lord, came to Corinth. There, as is reported, he was first thrown into the flames by Jews and Greeks, but was unharmed; then he was fastened to a cross and completed his martyrdom. In the Armenian city of Militina, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Hermogenes, Gaius, Expedite, Aristonice, Rufus, and Galatas, crowned on one day. At the city of Caucoliberis, the passion of Saint Vincent the martyr. At the monastery of Lobbes, Saint Ursmarus, bishop and confessor.

[Bouillart.: … Vincent the martyr.]

[Note: Sollerius gives two reasons here why he considered the Pratensis codex less suitable for reproducing Usuard. He himself judges one of them useless; the other, however, would have been sufficient for everyone except Sollerius to choose the Pratensis. One reason is that the Pratensis adds to the present entry: “The dedication of a church in honor of Saint Symphorianus the martyr and the most blessed Nicholas the Confessor.” He immediately shows us how little weight he ought to have assigned to this reason, in these words: “although Castellanus testifies that this dedication was added by a later hand, and Sirmondus likewise indicates this by striking out the lines; nor would the custodians of the autograph deny it.”

The other reason is that, instead of “at the monastery of Lobbes,” it has “in the Hainaut district.” Yet nothing is more customary for Usuard than to designate a monastery by the district in which it is situated, as though he deliberately preferred this usage. Thus, apart from the present passage: on 29 December, “in the district of Oximus”; on 26 April, “in the district of Ponthieu,” instead of “at the monastery of Centula”; on 15 July, “in the district of Le Mans,” instead of “at the monastery of Anisola”; on 22 July, “in the district of Rouen,” instead of “at the monastery of Fontenelle”; on 30 August, “in the district of Meaux,” instead of “at the monastery of Rebais,” and so forth.

It is indeed true that Sollerius attempted everything to wrest all these places from us; but we have already given such examples of his ingenuity that the reader will undoubtedly foresee the outcome with which he attacked all of them.

BOUILLART.]

In the district of Hainaut, Saint Ursmarus, bishop and confessor. And in italic type: At the monastery of Saint Germanus, the dedication of a church in honor of Saint Symphorianus the martyr and the most blessed Nicholas the confessor.

XII Kal. Day 20. [Note: The Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Rosweyd, Munerat, Greven, and Molan manuscripts are pure.]

[Note: The Rosweyd codex alone reads *coronatus est* (“was crowned”) instead of *coronatur* (“is crowned”). Likewise, the Tornacensis and Munerat read *Supplicii* instead of *Sulpitii*, as some write *Sulpicii*. Rosweyd incorrectly prefixes *Publii*. Munerat, Greven, and Molan likewise have *Domicillae*. In Munerat, *Salviano* is an error for *Aniano*. Molan reads *Marcellinus*, and rightly, I think; the others have *Marcelli*. In the Herniensis, *ni* is written above the line. Greven has *Marcelli primi*. Munerat has *Dominio* for *Domino*. Otherwise, forms such as *Rhomae*, *natale*, *Ydolis*, *Ebredunense*, *Affrica*, *Aphrica*, and similar trifles are easily excused.]

[Note: It is clear that Victor the bishop is reported with three companions in the Hieronymian Martyrologies: “At Rome, the burial of Saint Victor the bishop, Felix, Alexander, and Papias.” Whether Victor is designated as a martyr is not sufficiently certain, unless this can be inferred from the circumstance of his companions. In the *Little Roman Martyrology* I find Victor the bishop and martyr, but without companions: “At Rome, Victor, bishop and martyr.”

Henschenius discusses whether he was a bishop of Rome or of another city, adducing other examples of foreign bishops who suffered at Rome. At the same time, he tries to prove that Victor, whoever he may be, mentioned in the Hieronymian copies on this day, was not the Roman pontiff of that name, since the latter is believed to have died on 28 July, when he is celebrated by Rabanus, Notker, other martyrologists, and especially the modern Roman Martyrology.

This observation had already been made by Molan, and caused him in later editions of Usuard to mutilate the text by transferring to July that Victor whom Ado most certainly understands on this day as Pope Victor—whether Ado himself was perhaps led into error by some ignorant person, as Henschenius suspects, or whether he was the first to make the mistake.

Our Author and others who followed him considered Ado’s eulogy safe to transcribe, with a few alterations. What is read in Mosander’s edition is somewhat longer, and Notker presents it in a still fuller form, where the author adds the very material that he had again transcribed from Rabanus under 28 July.

There is no doubt about Henschenius’s view. Papebrochius thought 20 April preferable and therefore agreed with Florentinius that the Victor commemorated in the Hieronymian Martyrology on this day was Pope Victor himself. Tillemont agrees, presenting Victor’s life in eight sections in volume III, beginning on page 100. Pagi, in his discussion of the year 201, no. 5, scarcely dares to determine the day of death, although he plainly assumes that the Hieronymian Martyrology announces Pope Victor on 20 April.

We touch on the various opinions here only briefly; they will be examined in the Acts under 28 July. Meanwhile, as we have often stated, we attempt to represent Usuard—whether he is mistaken or speaking the truth—in his native colors. Bede is entirely silent for seven days; the supplement of Florus for today commemorates not Victor but Pope Anicetus.

Sulpitius and Servilianus are mentioned by the *Little Roman* by name alone and are unknown to the Hieronymian Martyrologies. From the Acts of the saints Nereus, Achilleus, and Domitilla, with which we shall have to deal elsewhere more than once, Ado adorns them with a distinguished encomium, the chief portion of which Usuard was content to appropriate. Henschenius added much concerning the translations of these martyrs, the various Servilians, and related matters.

Marcellinus and his companions belong to Ado alone; Our Author formed his entry from Ado’s eulogy, while Notker gathers the entire harvest. The Acts published by us must have been seen by Ado; Mabilio discovered at least their scribe, if not their author, in his *Diplomatica*, p. 172, letter E, from a codex copied eight hundred years ago by Deodatus the presbyter. Tillemont runs through the life briefly in volume VII, beginning on page 561.

Why Ado’s *Marcellinus*, and most of our codices—including the best of them—have changed it into *Marcellus*, I have no basis for conjecture. I wrote *Marcelli*, since that is how I find it written. In the Heriniensis codex, as I have already indicated, the syllable *ni* may be seen added above the line, but by a more recent hand, in more recent ink. Let this suffice concerning the original simplicity of the entry. The first two verses of Wandalbertus, celebrating Marcellinus and his companions, follow; the remaining two will be added in the Appendices:

> Marcellinus, Domninus, and Vincentius,  
>   
> By name twice six they shine, in festival and faith.]

[Note: In PRATEN., added in the margin, I think, is: “The revelation of the body of Saint George of Bethlehem, monk and martyr, and of Saint Venantius, abbot”; but additions of this kind we generally disregard.

PULSANEN. and LOVANIEN. truncate the final lines of the text, stopping at “bishop and confessor,” and suppressing what follows.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. are pure, but add at the end: “At Auxerre, Saint Marianus.” This name has been twisted and deformed in various ways, not only in our codices but also in the Hieronymian Martyrologies; see Florentinius on this. Castellanus judges that it should be read as it stands here.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition likewise append to the pure text: “At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Marcianus”—many write this instead of *Marianus*—“priest and confessor.”

ALBERGEN. and DANIC. agree in the Appendix with the two preceding witnesses, but transfer the announcement of Saint Victor to 28 July.

CENTULEN., pure in Victor, continues: “Likewise at Rome, Saints Sulpitius and Servilianus, who, at the exhortation of blessed Flavia Domitilla, were converted to the faith and suffered under Aurelian [Anianus] for the love of Christ. At Auxerre, the holy confessors Mamertinus and Marianus, priests.”

ANTUERP.-MAJ. differs slightly from CENTULEN. in phrasing. Instead of *Mamertini*, it writes *Martini*.

BRUXELLEN. adds concerning Victor: “He established the Paschal limit and that Easter should always be celebrated on Sunday.” In the second announcement it is pure. In the third it appends from Ado: “So that the baptistery which he himself founded in the aforesaid city is, by divine power, each year suddenly flooded with water during the vigils of the most holy Paschal feast, and remains, with grace overflowing, throughout the seven days of that solemnity. At Auxerre, the holy confessors Mamertinus and Marcianus, priests.”

HAGENOYEN. begins: “In Mysia, Saint Hiltegundis, virgin.” The whole text follows fairly purely. Then: “At Auxerre, Saint Martianus, priest.” We have already said that he is better called Marianus. “At Nicomedia, Saints Sevelius and Theophantus; they were translated to the cell of Ratolf.” Whether these may perhaps be Synesius and Theopompus, see the index of the *Omissions* and 21 May. Wandalbertus sings today of a certain Synesius:

> And the feast of Synesius, kindly martyr, is celebrated,  
> Blessed with the title of bishop, with learning and with death.

Thus indeed the martyrologist-poet; but it has not yet been possible to explain sufficiently who this Synesius was, distinguished by the title of bishop and martyr. I do not wish to guess; let whoever has found such a Synesius anywhere inform us. Perhaps the name has been corrupted, but that too is equally uncertain; and therefore it is better to await light from some quarter.

AQUICINCT. begins thus: “At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Victor, pope, who, thirteenth after blessed Peter, ruled the Church for ten years and was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Severus. He established that holy Easter should always be celebrated on Sunday, and should be observed from the fifteenth moon of the first month until the twenty-first. He also established that, when necessity required, whoever of humankind came from the gentiles might be baptized under Christian profession, whether in a river, the sea, or springs.” These details were taken from some fuller copy of Ado, or from Notker.

DAVERONEN.: “At Auxerre, Saint Martin.” AQUICINCT. above has the same reading.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Victor, pope and martyr. Mamertinus, abbot. Macianus [Marianus], priest.”

VATICAN., no. 5949: “Likewise at Rome, on the Nomentan Way, Saints Aralacus and Donata.” See the entire company, and the correctly written first name, in the Acts.

UGHELLIAN.: “At Auxerre, Saint Martianus.”

FLORENTIN.: “At Auxerre, Saint Martianus.”

DIVIONEN., of the church of Saint Stephen: “At Auxerre, the holy confessors Mamertinus and Marianus, priest. And the translation of Saint Exuperia, virgin.” Read *Exuperantia*, as below. She is celebrated on 26 April.

REMENS., of the church of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “The translation of the body of Saint Exuperantia, virgin.”

The LUBECO-COL. edition refers Victor to 28 July. The other part of the text is fairly pure. At the end: “At Auxerre, the burial of the holy confessors Mamertinus and Marianus, priests.”

BELIN., in the last announcement, has struck out Marcellinus’s companions; otherwise it is pure. At the end the first edition adds: “At Auxerre, Saint Martianus.” The second adds “confessor.”

GREVEN.: “Likewise, Saints John, Victor, Donatus.” From the Hieronymian Martyrology. “Adelarius, bishop and martyr.” See the *Omissions*. “At Auxerre, Saints Marcianus and Mamertinus, priests. Likewise, Saint Hildegundis, a virgin of blessed memory, a nun of the Cistercian Order, who was also called Josepha.”

MOLAN.: “At Auxerre, Saint Martianus.” In smaller type, concerning Hildegundis, as GREVEN. In the other editions, as I have already said above, Pope Victor has been struck out. At the end, the same concerning Martianus: “On the twentieth day, Saint Father Theodore, who was at Trichina.” Again in smaller type: “At Schönau, the death of Hildegundis, virgin, of the Cistercian Order, who was also called Josepha.” Why does he not rather call her Joseph, since she was admitted among monks in male attire and lived there most holily, after many grave perils to which she had been exposed before entering religion? See her remarkable Life, written by a fellow novice, an eyewitness of all the things she did among men in monastic profession, and elucidated by Papebrochius.]

[Col. 0951]

At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Victor, pope, who, after blessed Peter, ruled the Church as the fifteenth for ten years and was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Severus. Likewise at Rome, the holy martyrs Sulpitius and Servilianus, who, converted to the faith of Christ through the preaching and miracles of the virgin Domitilla, refused to sacrifice to idols and were beheaded by Anianus, the prefect of the city. In Gaul, at the city of Embrun, Saint Marcellus, bishop and confessor of that city, who, coming from Africa by divine command with his holy companions Vincent and Domninus, converted the greater part of the Maritime Alps to the faith of Christ by the word and by wondrous signs, with which he shines even to this day.

[Bouillart adds in italic type: On the same day, at the monastery of Saint Germanus, the discovery of the body of Saint George of Bethlehem, monk and martyr, and of Saint Venantius, abbot.]

XI Kal. Day 21. [Note: Thus the Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Antwerp, and Max.-Lubeck, Rosweyd, Munerat, first edition of Belin, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: Pratensis and Molan write *Simeonis*; elsewhere we followed them together with several codices, but here the authority of other codices led us in another direction. If we fluctuate here and there, the fault is theirs, not ours, though it is easily excused.

Belin alone reads *apprehensus* instead of *comprehensus*, and in the same witness *Persidam* appears instead of *Persidem*. Molan placed *constantissime* adverbially. In some codices *erant* is inserted after “some were bishops, others presbyters, others …”; in the text, following the better codices, it is assumed to be sufficiently understood.

All the codices read *Ustazadis*, except Belin, which has *Ustozadis*. The Acts prefer *Usthazanes*, following Sozomen, yet the *Little Roman* and Ado read it as in the text. In Belin, *Epusitius* is written for *et Pusitius*. Only in the Heriniensis do I find *cum filia sua*. The Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Rosweyd, Greven, and others agree on *Fortuni*, which we therefore thought should be retained in the text, although, unless I am mistaken, others read *Fortunati* more correctly, while Munerat has *Fortunii*. Some include Vitalis as well, but the best witnesses omit him, as is customary with Usuard. *Honustus*, *Felicis*, and so forth need no annotation.]

[Note: The *Little Roman Martyrology* gives only one announcement on this day:

> “In Persia, Saints Simeon, bishop and martyr, with one hundred others, and Ustazades, Abdella, Ananias, and Pusicius.”

There this most noble company of martyrs first becomes known in the sacred Martyrologies, undoubtedly taken from Sozomen or the *Tripartite History*. From these same records Ado composed his eulogy, whose marrow Usuard extracted with considerable elegance; Notker, as usual, translated almost the whole of it.

For fuller details, both concerning the correct form of the names and concerning the different day of death of Usthazades and the others, see the explanations and illustrations in our Acts. There Henschenius seems chiefly to have aimed at more plausibly bringing the beginning of the fierce persecution that Sapor, the most implacable enemy of Persia’s flourishing Christianity, waged against it from Jerome’s chronology down to the time of Constantius. Sozomen had wrongly assigned it to the age of Constantine; among recent scholars, Ruinart, in *Sincera et Selecta*, beginning on p. 632, and Tillemont, vol. VII, beginning on p. 76, establish this correction. There the whole history is set out at length and in order.

Nevertheless, the aforementioned Ruinart, Tillemont, and others by no means agree with Henschenius in postponing the martyrdom of Simeon and his companions to the year 349. Our teacher was led to this by a plausible argument. Since Sozomen says that the martyrdom of these Persians occurred on the day on which the saving Passion of Christ is annually commemorated, he rightly judged that one should seek the year in which 21 April coincided with Good Friday. Since that coincidence did not recur before 349, he thought the contest of Simeon and the others must be placed there; Usthazades had been crowned on the preceding day.

He was right, I say, if he had rightly assumed that our Martyrologies always assign to a martyr’s feast the true and actual day of the passion, and that Simeon and his companions truly suffered on 21 April. Henschenius did assume this, but we cannot grant that he assumed it correctly. We know too well that the authors of the *Little Roman Martyrology* and Ado, as we have shown elsewhere, very often selected days either purely arbitrarily or on the basis of some conjecture. Such a conjecture could here have been suggested by Sozomen’s very phrase concerning the day on which the saving Passion of Christ is annually commemorated; both the twenty-one other martyrologists, Latin and Greek—poor chronologists though they are—and the Latin writers may have combined it with another day in April. This will become clear again on the following day and can be demonstrated more fully elsewhere.

To avoid departing further from my purpose, I frankly confess that I dare not place complete confidence in Henschenius’s calculation, especially since other considerations more plausibly show that Simeon and his companions suffered martyrdom near the beginning of Sapor’s persecution, around the year 344. In this Pagi’s criticism of Baronius under the year 343 is mistaken, since he describes and follows Henschenius’s opinion.

Yet I would not allow myself, with Castellanus, to be induced on this account to move from its place the solemnity that our martyrologists have established for so many centuries, and to which Wandalbertus likewise assigned it, bringing Gaius back from the following day:

> On the eleventh, Gaius and Simeon alike are celebrated.

The second class of Alexandrian martyrs derives from the Hieronymian copies, in which there is no complete uniformity, as Florentinius rightly observed. It is clear that Ado selected only five of them; Usuard took them from him, slightly changing the order and altering one name. Our best codices consistently call this martyr not *Fortunatus*, as Ado reads, but *Fortunus*.

You will say that the name is corrupt; so be it. We are nevertheless determined not to depart from our codices—just as, in the case of Ustazades, who should be called Usthazades or Chustazates, commonly Usthazanes, and Abdella, who is Abedechalas, we have perhaps adhered too scrupulously to the witnesses. From this the integrity of the Usuardine text is abundantly clear.]

[Note: PULSANEN. is mutilated, omitting what is said in the margin about Usthazanes and his companions between “to be beheaded” and “at Alexandria.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERG., DANIC., and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition, pure in the text, add at the end:

> “At Liège, in the church of blessed Lawrence, the burial of blessed Walbodus, bishop of that same city.”

The same Appendix is found in LOVANIEN., but it is defective in the same places in which PULSANEN. above is defective.

CENTULEN.:

> “In Persia, Saint Simeon, bishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon, royal cities, who, during the persecution of the king of Persia, was beheaded after other tortures. With him suffered Ustazades the eunuch, Abdella, Ananias the elders, and Pusicius with his virgin daughter. At Alexandria, the holy Fortunatus, Arator the presbyter, Felix, Silvius, and Vitalis, who found rest in prison. In Gaul, at Embrun, Saint Marcellinus, first bishop and confessor of that city, with Vincent”—add *Domninus*—“his companions.”

Concerning these we spoke yesterday.

ANTUERP.-MAJ. interpolates the text from Ado in the entry for Simeon. In the Alexandrian martyrs it agrees with CENTULEN. It follows at the end with Marcellinus, but purely, as we read yesterday in the text.

BRUXELLEN. begins:

> “At Rome, Saint Soter, pope. He sat for nine years and was then crowned with martyrdom. He decreed that no nun should touch the consecrated pallium, but should wear a veil.”

Many others record Soter on this day, although he belongs to the following day. It continues with Simeon, where these words from Ado are inserted:

> “Bishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon, royal cities,” etc.

In the Alexandrian martyrs it is pure. At the end:

> “At Liège, the burial of blessed Walbodus, bishop of that city.”

HAGENOYEN., fairly pure in Simeon, disgracefully confuses the following two announcements in this fashion:

> “At Alexandria, the holy martyrs Arator the presbyter and Fortunatus. Likewise at Liège, in the church of blessed Lawrence, Saint Walbodus, bishop of that city, Silvius, Felix, and Vitalis, who found rest in prison.”

A confusion of the announcements.

> “At Rome, Saint Agapitus, pope, who is greatly praised in pontifical deeds. He entered Constantinople and recalled the emperor Justinian from error, deposing Artemius”—Anthimus—“and appointing Mena, a Catholic man. This Artemius denied two natures in Christ. The pope died at Constantinople and was transferred to Rome, where he was buried with glory in the church of the apostle Saint Peter. He also enacted constitutions.”

Agapitus has been intruded here improperly; he is celebrated on 20 September, whatever many others, with Notker, report on the following day.

AQUICINCT. begins:

> “At Rome, Saint Soter, pope. He decreed that no nun should touch the consecrated pallium in the church or place incense upon it.”

The text follows.

VICTORIN. adds after “virgin”:

> “Likewise Saint Soter, pope. He decreed that no nun should touch the consecrated pallium or offer incense.”

REG. SUEC., belonging to Prince Ursinus of Rosenberg:

> “At Liège, in the church of blessed Lawrence, the burial of blessed Valbodus, bishop of that same church.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “Simeon, bishop and martyr, with many others under Sapor, king of the Persians, under whom sixteen thousand were crowned with martyrdom in various places and at various times.”

VATICAN., no. 5949, adds at the end:

> “At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Soter, pope, who sat in the episcopate for nine years.”

The LUBECO-COL. edition is nearly like BRUXELLEN. in its interpolation of Simeon and pure in the Alexandrian martyrs. It continues:

> “At Liège, in the church of blessed Lawrence, the burial of Saint Walbodus, bishop and confessor of that same city. In England, at the city of Canterbury, Saint Anselm, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0958B]

The second edition of BELIN.:

> “On the same day, the translation of Saint Oswald, bishop of York.”

He is celebrated on 28 February.

GREVEN.:

> “At Rome, blessed Soter, pope and martyr; according to Ado, however, on the following day.”

Indeed, Mosander places him on this day; he is not known in the ROSWEYD edition unless he has been wrongly relegated to the appendix.

> “In England, blessed Anselm, archbishop and outstanding doctor. Born near the borders of Lombardy and Burgundy, he came to Bec, drawn by the reputation of Lanfranc the master. There he first became a monk, then prior, and finally archbishop of Canterbury. He shone brilliantly in life and doctrine around the year of the Lord 1100.

> “Julian, bishop of Vienne.”

Rather Julian, concerning whom Ado could correctly have spoken; he places him on the following day, on which he is celebrated.

> “At Liège, Walbodus, bishop and confessor. Likewise the blessed memory of Victor III, pope and confessor. Among other things, it is read of him that he lived in great bodily continence, always wearing an exceedingly harsh hair shirt next to his flesh. At the tables of guests he often deceived the eyes of those present, touching food without tasting it. At night, after taking a little sleep, he would rise secretly from his bed and devote himself to prayers, prostrations, and tears. He also became renowned for miracles.”

This is referred to 16 September.

MOLAN. concerning Oswald, as BELIN.:

> “On the same day, Saint Anselm, bishop and confessor. At Rome, Saint Soter, pope, who sat in the episcopate for nine years and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He decreed,” etc.

> “In Africa, the commemoration of Maximinus the martyr, who in the time of Decius was crushed under stones after other tortures.”

Rabanus calls him thus, and Notker transcribes his eulogy. In the Acts, under the name Maximianus, he is referred to 30 April.

MOLAN continues, in smaller type:

> “From the book of anniversaries at Saint Lawrence: Lord Wolbodo, the most devout bishop of Liège, departed from this world. He gave sacred objects to this place and chose to be buried there.”

Thus far the first edition. In the others, concerning Anselm, as above. Then:

> “On the twenty-first day, Saint Januarius, hieromartyr, and his company, and the most holy martyr Theodore, who was at Perge.”

These two are discussed in the list of the *Omissions*, where it is asked whether the names are correct or perhaps reversed.

Again, in smaller type:

> “At Liège, in the church of Saint Lawrence, Lord Wolbodo,” etc., as above.]

At Persia: the feast of blessed Symeon, bishop and martyr. By order of Sapor, king of the Persians, he was arrested and loaded with chains; while he bore witness to the Lord with a free and utterly steadfast voice, he was first tortured in a prison dungeon with a hundred others—some bishops, some priests, and some clerics of various orders—and finally he was ordered to be beheaded together with them all. The most distinguished men Ustazades, Abdella, Ananias, and Pusitius also suffered with him, together with Pusitius’s daughter, who was a consecrated virgin. At Alexandria, Saints Arator the priest, Fortunus, Felix, Silvius, and Vitalis, who found rest in prison.

**The tenth day before the Kalends. April 22.**

[Note: [Col. 0959A]

Of all our codices I find none that I would dare to declare wholly pure in every respect. A comparison of the individual witnesses will provide a text as simple as it can be made. Grevenus and Molanus come closest to purity, since they insert only this concerning Melisius: “Distinguished for holiness and the glory of miracles.” I readily admit that these words are found in Ado; but that they are not Usuard’s is proved by the silence of absolutely all the other codices, both manuscript and printed. Something similar appears at first sight in the Tournai codex, where we read “Melisius, most acceptable to God”; in Rosweyd and Belin, “Melius, most acceptable.” But the copyist’s negligence is palpable, since *Acceptissimus* has been written in place of *Acepsimas*.

Now attend to why the remaining codices are excluded. The Pratensis, more deformed than usual, adds at the end: “At Sens, Saint Leo, bishop.” You will say that this belongs to Usuard. I do not think so: the otherwise wholly sound codices of Herinnes, Tournai, Muneratus, Grevenus, and Molanus stand against it; their combined authority, in my judgment, must be preferred to all the others [Col. 0959B]. Add Rosweyd and other not insignificant witnesses, though we do not rely upon them. If anyone thinks otherwise, I will readily yield to stronger arguments. [Col. 0960A]

I would also have experts in such matters observe that the exclusion of Leo is strongly supported by the fact that Grevenus and Molanus mention him neither in their first and purer edition nor in their *Auctaria*. The aforesaid Pratensis codex continues: “On the same day, the finding of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius.” But these words were, I believe, added in the margin, although by an ancient hand, as Castellanus testifies; they would do no harm to the purity of the text if the rest were sound. The Herinnes codex would be perfectly pure, were it not that it inserts in second place: “At Paris, the translation of the blessed martyrs Dionysius,” etc. The Tournai codex is not free from other blemishes; its capital defect is that it adds at the end: “On that same day, the finding of Saints Dionysius,” etc.

The Muneratus does exactly the same, though in words insufficiently corrected: “On that same day, the finding of the blessed bodies of Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, whose bodies [it would be better to say ‘which’] rest in the monastery of Saint Dionysius in France. On the same day, Saint Opportuna the virgin.” The Rosweyd codex, otherwise also pure, reads at the end: “The finding of the holy martyrs,” etc. [Col. 0960B]

[Note: [Col. 0959C]

From these considerations I believe it is demonstrated that the genuine and simple text is represented here by us, although on this day we could not draw it separately from any single codex. It is surely more than sufficient that most of the copies agree in it, and that they are of the highest quality, even though some have been sullied elsewhere by a little grime. If anyone thinks Grevenus and Molanus have been unjustly excluded, I will not object if their very brief encomium is attributed to Usuard. As for excluding all the others altogether, I think no one will deny that this must be done.

It remains for us, following our usual practice, to compare Usuard with the earlier witnesses. Caius is mentioned in the Hieronymian exemplars; for these one should consult Florentinius’s commentary. He also appears in the *Romanum parvum*. Bede adorns him with a brief encomium, which Ado somewhat expanded. In any case, the very words that they report here in the text are found verbatim in the aforementioned Bede and Ado, and likewise in Rabanus. Ado, however, has much more, and Notker adopted these additions both here and throughout his text.

We saw on the preceding day that Wandalbert celebrated Symeon the Persian there together with him [Col. 0959D]. Henschenius extracted his Life from the Acts of Saint Sebastian and Saint Susanna and illustrated it with notes, so that little is greatly lacking. What more recent critics think of it can more conveniently be examined in the larger work under August 11.

To yesterday’s company of Persians another large group of martyrs is added, as the *Romanum parvum* briefly indicates. Ado, if not more accurately, at least more distinctly, enumerates the names of some of them; from him Our Author derived all his material, with the phrasing slightly contracted [Col. 0960C]. The source of Ado’s encomium is the same as on the preceding day, namely Sozomen—or rather the *Tripartite History*. There it is expressly noted that the following year came after the killing of Symeon and the others, and that it was the very day on which the memory of Christ’s Passion is usually commemorated—not the day on which the martyrs suffered, but the day on which Sapor’s most cruel edict was issued throughout Persia.

For the enormous number of those martyrs and the kinds of torments inflicted on them, see Sozomen’s Acts, no. 7. The year must be determined from what was said on the preceding day, most probably 345. The day of each individual’s contest was doubtless very different; nevertheless, our martyrologists have all recorded them on this April 22. Meanwhile it is absolutely certain that the Friday of the Lord’s Passion could not have coincided with that date even throughout the entire fourth century. Thus it is again manifest that April 22 was selected merely at the discretion of the *Romanum parvum* and others; Henschenius is compelled to admit this. In him the spelling of the names is more accurate, and the separate Acts of some of the martyrs are reported and illustrated; Ruinart included some of them among his *Selecta*, beginning at page 639.

The next Persian company is attributed by Bede to Cordula, but wrongly by Rabanus and others to Corduba; we observed the same error above, under the fifteenth of this month, where the matter itself had to be discussed. The whole group appears to belong to Babylon, together with Polychronius on February 17. See more in the notes of Baronius, Florentinius, and Henschenius, and in our Observations under February 17, April 15, August 10, and other places where the Acts of Laurence are discussed.

That company’s encomium is found in Bede, Rabanus, and Ado; from the last of these Usuard took a few elements. Whether the Cordulian martyrs are clearly designated in the Hieronymian Martyrologies may be questioned. The *Romanum parvum* expressly mentions them. Wandalbert sings of the first three in his first two verses:

> Three priests crown the tenth day, and three palms—  
> Parmenius, Elimenes, and Chrysotelus—crown it.

In three other verses he plays upon the number three, on the occasion of the finding of Saints Dionysius, Eleutherius, and Rusticus; we showed above that this does not pertain to our text [Col. 0962A].

Epipodius is certainly recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, and Ado added Alexander as his companion, together with the eulogy of both. Our Author, however, extracted only what belonged specifically to Epipodius, omitting his companion Alexander, whom Ado places on April 24 as having suffered as though on the third day afterward; see there. Neither Usuard nor Notker remembered Julian, who is also listed in Ado, perhaps because he was not named in the older copies and was subsequently added, together with other names of holy bishops more closely connected with the city of Vienne.]

[Note: [Col. 0961A]

The principal codices of ours—PRATEN., HERINIEN., TORNACEN., ROSWEYD., MUNERAT., GREVEN., and MOLAN.—were discussed sufficiently in the preceding note, so that it would be entirely superfluous to describe their *Auctaria*, or rather their variants, separately here.

PULSANEN. is exceptionally defective on this day: [Col. 0961B] it deals only with Caius and the Cordulians.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. mutilate the text at Caius. In place of “in the passion of Blessed Laurence,” it has “Abdon and Sennis.” Finally: “At Sens, Saint Leo, bishop.”

ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC. begin as follows: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of Saint Soter, pope, who, after blessed Peter, was the eleventh, and, having ruled the Roman Church for eight years, was crowned with martyrdom and buried in the cemetery of Calixtus. At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of blessed Caius, pope, who was the twenty-ninth after blessed Peter and ruled the Church for eleven years,” etc. “On the same day, Saint Agapitus, pope. At Persia,” etc. At the end: “At Sens, Saint Leo, bishop.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., LEYDEN.-BELG., LOVANIEN., and the ULTRAJECT.-BELG. edition say nothing about Soter. Concerning Caius, as above. They are not pure in the Persian martyrs. At the end: “At Sens, Saint Leo, bishop.”

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Calixtus, Saint Caius, pope and martyr. In Persia, very many holy martyrs under the king of the Persians, among whom were Melisius, bishop; Acepsimas, bishop; Jacob, priest; Mareas and Bicor, bishops; two hundred and fifty of their clerics; and many monks and virgins, including also Zarbua, a virgin, sister of Saint Symeon, bishop and martyr. At Paris, the finding of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, martyrs. In the city of Corduba, Saints Parmenius and Helimena and Chrysotelus, priests, and Luke and Mucius, deacons, who suffered under Decius. At Lyons, Saint Epipodius, martyr. At Sens, Saint Leo, bishop.”

ANTUERPIEN.-MAJ. reproduces the text somewhat corruptly and in abbreviated form. At the end: “At Sens, the deposition of Saint Leo, bishop, whose life shone with miracles and whose precious death was likewise commended by miracles.”

BRUXELLEN. adds to Caius: “He established that no one should dare to accuse clerics before secular judges [Col. 0961D]. On the same day, Saint Agapitus, pope, who sat for eleven months. He established that processions should take place on Sundays. At Persia . . .” It continues the text quite purely. At the end: “At Sens, Saint Leo, bishop and confessor. Also, the finding of the bodies of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius.” See what was said in the note.

HAGENOYEN. begins with Soter, about whom enough has already been said. Then it treats of the Cordulians. Next comes Caius, where, after “Diocletian,” it adds: “his kinsman by marriage. He established the orders of clerics, namely doorkeeper, reader, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, and priest.” It is interpolated in the section on the Persian martyrs. After them comes: “Also at Camaria [he meant Canterbury], blessed Anselm, bishop and confessor, distinguished in life and doctrine [Col. 0962A].” It is pure in the section on Epipodius. At the end: “Also at Sens, Saint Leo, bishop and confessor.”

AQUICINCT., after “the emperor Diocletian,” adds from Ado: “He established that anyone worthy of becoming a bishop should first ascend through all the grades: doorkeeper, reader, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, [Col. 0962B] and priest. On the same day, Saint Agapitus, pope. When he entered Constantinople, he deposed Anthemium, bishop of that city, who denied the two natures in Christ, and consecrated the Catholic Mena in his place.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Caius, pope and martyr. Of very many martyrs at Persia. The translation of blessed Dionysius and his companions.”

BIGOTIAN., marked P 5: “At Enon [Sens], Saint Leo, bishop.” The same appears in the CLUNIACENSIS and UGHELLIAN codices.

REG. SUEC., marked no. 428: “At Paris, the finding of the bodies of the blessed martyrs of Christ, Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius. On the same day, Saint Opportuna, virgin.”

Codex D. DU CHEVAL, marked B: “At Liège, in the church of blessed Laurence, the burial of Saint Walbodo, bishop of that city.” Concerning him, see yesterday.

VATICAN., no. 5949: “At Rome, Saint Agapitus [Col. 0962C], pope, who sat at Rome for eleven months. On the same day, Saint John, martyr of Tete or Teate.” Until now he has been unknown.

ALTEMPS: “At Sens, Saint Leo, bishop. At Senlis, Saint Regulus, confessor of Christ. Also, Saint Opportuna, virgin. At Rome, Saint Soter, pope and martyr.”

STROZZIAN.: “At Sens, Saint Leo, bishop. Also in the monastery of Saint George Major at Venice, the translation of Saint Eustace, patriarch of Constantinople, in the year of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1246.” His Acts are given on April 6.

The LUBECO-COL. edition repeats what was said above, yesterday and today, concerning Soter, adding that he was crowned with martyrdom under Commodus Aurelius. Concerning Caius, beyond what was already stated, it says: “He established that pagans and heretics could not accuse Christians or bring a charge of infamy against them. He also decreed that no one should dare to accuse a bishop or other clerics before secular judges.” Concerning Agapitus, it says that he established that processions [Col. 0962D] should be held. It continues: “At Trier, Saint Abrunculus, bishop and confessor, who now rests in the monastery called Sprengersbach.” It is almost pure in the sections on the Cordulians and Epipodius. “At Sens, the feast of Saint Leo, bishop and confessor. At Vienne, Saint Julian, martyr. At Persia, the saints, etc., under Sapor, king of the Persians, on the day when the memory of the Lord’s Passion is celebrated.” The rest is pure.

BELIN., almost pure in the sections on Caius, the Persians, and the Cordulians, adds: “At Sens, Saint Leo, bishop. On that same day, Saint Soter, pope, by birth a Campanian.” Then concerning Epipodius, correctly. “Also in the monastery of Saint George,” etc., as above from STROZZ. In the second edition there is an additional entry: “At Paris, the holy martyrs Dionysius,” etc. “Near the city of Senlis, Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0963A]

GREVEN.: “Of Agapitus I, pope and confessor, who, as Ado says (in the edition published by Mosander), sat at Rome for eleven months. When he entered,” etc. “Of Philip, bishop, and his companions, martyrs.” See the *Praetermissi*, where he is assigned to October 22. “Of Leonidas, martyr, father of Origen. Of Pimolus, martyr.” Pimolus is Primolus or Primulus from the Cordulians. “Of Theodoric, priest and martyr.” See the *Praetermissi*. “At Vienne, Saint Julian, bishop and confessor. Abrunculus, archbishop of Trier and confessor, resting in the monastery called Sprengersbach. On that same day, the finding of the bodies of Saints Dionysius,” etc. “Of Alexandra, queen of the Persians and martyr, who is said to have believed through the confession of blessed George.” See again the *Praetermissi*. “Also Saint Opportuna, virgin.” It is better written *Opportuna*, whose Life is illustrated today.

MOLAN.: “Of Agapitus, pontiff, who sat at Rome for eleven months. When he entered Constantinople [Col. 0963B] to Justinian,” etc. “Also in the monastery of Saint George Major at Venice,” etc., as in STROZZ. and BELIN. It continues: “The finding of Saints Dionysius,” etc. Also: “Opportuna.” These entries are copied from MUNERATUS. In smaller letters it continues: “Of Leonidas, martyr, father of Origen. Abrunculus, archbishop of Trier and [Col. 0964A] confessor, resting in the monastery of Sprengersbach. On that same day, the feast of Saint Wulphhelm, abbot of Bruwiller. Saint Theodore of the Siceans, archimandrite, whose Life was written by George the priest, his disciple.”

In other editions it begins: “On the same day, Saint Opportuna, virgin. At Sens, Saint Leo, bishop and confessor. And elsewhere, the burial of Abrunculus, bishop. On the same day, Agapitus, pontiff, who sat,” etc. “On the twenty-second day, Saint Theodore of Sicea.” Above he is called “archimandrite of the Siceans,” but in our Acts his name and dignity are more accurately given, when he is called “Theodore of Sicea, bishop of Anastasiopolis, archimandrite of the monasteries in Galatia.” See there the Life, related at considerable length. “Also in the monastery of Saint George Major . . . On that same day, the finding of the blessed bodies of Dionysius . . .,” as in MUNERATUS. Then, in smaller type: “In Hainaut, in the monastery of Donon, the death of Saint Adalbert [Adelbert], count of Ostrevant and confessor, though not canonized. His body rests [Col. 0964B] on the high altar in a silver tomb.” In the Acts he is given the title “blessed,” and it is also noted that he had as wife blessed Regina and as daughter Saint Ragemfred, concerning whom elsewhere. “On the same day blessed Wulphhelm, abbot of Bruwiller, died.”]

[Col. 0957]

At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of blessed Caius, pope, who, after ruling the Church for eleven years, four months, and twelve days, was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Diocletian. At Persia, the holy martyrs who were slaughtered with the sword for the name of Christ under King Sapor. In this contest of faith suffered Melisius, bishop; also Bishop Acepsimas, with Jacob the priest; and Bishops Mareas and Bicor, together with nearly two hundred and fifty clerics, as well as very many monks and consecrated virgins. Among them was Tarbua, sister of Bishop Symeon, who was sawn apart with a saw, together with her maidservant. At Cordula, the feast of Parmenius, Helimena, and Chrysotelus, priests, and Luke and Mucius, deacons, whose triumph of martyrdom is contained in the Passion of blessed Laurence. At Lyons, Saint Epipodius, who, during the persecution of Antoninus Verus, after suffering severe tortures, completed his martyrdom by beheading.

[Added by Bouillart.: [Note: [Col. 0959B] There are few articles—if indeed there are any—for which Sollerius labored more intensely. He examined nearly eighty codices, and all were so defective that he dared to trust none of them absolutely; he therefore had to collate them all together in order to extract the text from each. “The comparison of the individual witnesses,” he says, “will provide a text as simple as it can be made.” Let others praise the labor; I greatly admire his discernment and judgment. For amid such corruption of the codices, who would not marvel that Sollerius knew Usuard’s meaning so well that he did not depart from it even by a hairsbreadth, rendering the autograph itself word for word? Someone will certainly suspect that, while working on this article, he had before his eyes the copy preserved by him and transcribed it at least as far as Sens. He ought to have copied the whole. This was not, however, the final mention of the Carolingian autograph, for the Dervensis codex lacks it. Yet even Sollerius does not deny that the same hand wrote it as the rest of the article. On this very day the Church of Sens celebrates the memory of Saint Leo; the older Martyrologies report him, and Saussay celebrates him in a more recent encomium. This is the same Saint Leo who nobly resisted King Childebert when he wished to appoint a bishop at Melun, where there had never been a bishop, writing him a letter published by Sirmondus in volume I of the Councils of Gaul. BOUILLART.] At Sens, Saint Leo, bishop. And in cursive type: “On the same day, the finding of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius.”]

**The ninth day before the Kalends. April 23.**

[Note: [Col. 0963]

The Herinnes, Tournai, Antwerp-Maximum-Lübeck, Grevenus, and Molanus codices are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0963C]

They scarcely deserve attention. *Persida* in Antwerp and Maximum-Lübeck, in place of *Perside*, is sufficiently common elsewhere. Most codices read *cujus gesta passionis*; but the Antwerp and Maximum-Lübeck codices have *cujus passio*, etc. *Apocrifas* in Herinnes and Tournai reflects the spelling of its period. The others come closer to the correct orthography by writing *apocriphas*, as we have left it in the text, although Molanus has the better form *apocryphas*. “The Church of God” must be read; in Antwerp and Maximum-Lübeck the final word is missing. *Equuleis*, in place of *equulei*, occurs in Herinnes; in the others, *eculei*. *Valencia*, *Faelicis*, and similar forms need not concern us.]

[Note: [Col. 0963D]

Whether, and on what day, the great martyr and trophy-bearer George was first recorded in the Hieronymian copies, Florentinius investigates at considerable length on this and the following days. The antiquity of this saint’s cult and of his uniquely widespread feast throughout the Church is clearly demonstrated by the Calendar edited by Fronto, pages 33 and 71, as well as by Gregory’s Sacramentary and many other arguments produced by Papebrochius in the Acts. The curious reader will find there, most fully and accurately excavated, everything concerning the universal Christian veneration of this most famous saint, both in the preliminary Commentary and in the appendices, from pages 100 to 163; Tillemont condensed these materials in volume V, beginning at page 185.

No more is needed here; let us return to our Martyrologies. As for Bede, the matter speaks for itself, for he expressly records George in the sacred registers: “The feast of Saint George, martyr,” rightly omitting those things drawn from apocryphal Acts that brought darkness rather than light [Col. 0964D]. The *Romanum parvum* supplied somewhat more, adding the very controversial location: “In Persia, in the city of Diospolis, George the martyr.” Ado follows in his footsteps; from him came the encomium of whatever quality it is, which Our Author copied word for word, while Notker mixed truth with falsehood by imprudently abandoning his usual guide and introducing the fables of Rabanus.

The passage in Notker under April 25 should be noted: relying on the Calendar of the most discerning Jerome, he argues that George should be celebrated on that day. For the true place of his martyrdom and other circumstances, one should also consult the commentary of the aforementioned Papebrochius.

Our two announcements are bound together in Wandalbert’s verse in such a way that one precedes the other. He writes:

> The ninth day tells of Felix, the holy one worthy of two ministers,  
> And of Fortunatus and Achilleus joined with him.  
> It also recounts for you, George, countless holy trophies—  
> You who despise the world by invincible blood.

[Col. 0965A] The martyrs of Valence are recorded in all the principal exemplars of Jerome, and therefore there is no doubt that they passed into Ado. From the Acts he set out the sequence of the martyrdom clearly, and Notker follows him word for word; Usuard is somewhat more concise. No one who has read both will deny that the whole entry belongs both to Ado and to Usuard.

The chief disagreement between Henschenius and more recent writers—such as Tillemont, volume III, page 97, and others—is that Henschenius considered the Acts to have been written by a contemporary, whereas they wholly deny this. They agree, however, in consistently and correctly asserting that the martyrs were crowned not at Valencia in Spain but at Valencia in the Dauphiné.

A third announcement concerning Saint Wulfrannus appears in Ado; we, with Usuard, placed him under March 20. Again, under March 30, following the agreement of our codices, we recorded Regulus of Senlis and observed there that he had been removed from the Pratensis with others and wrongly transferred here. It is therefore clear why the aforesaid Pratensis codex had to be excluded from the number of the pure codices even today.]

[Note: [Col. 0965]

PRATEN., as we have already said, adds at the end: “At the fortress of Senlis, Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor.”

PULSANEN., pure in the entry on George, completely cuts out the encomium of the Valentinian martyrs.

MUNERAT., pure in the text, wrongly inserts between the two announcements: “Near the city of Senlis, the burial of the holy Regulus, confessor of Christ and prelate. He was born at Mycenae in Greece and taught by blessed John the Evangelist. Later, coming with Saint Dionysius first to Rome and then to Arles, he was ordained bishop there. After Dionysius’s martyrdom, he came to the aforesaid city of Senlis, where he shines to this day, worthy of veneration, through the many signs of his virtues.” See what we said under March 30.

ROSWEYD., after the pure text: “At the fortress of Senlis, Saint Regulus, bishop. Also Saint Adalbert, bishop and martyr.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC., and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition add to the fairly pure text: “On that same day, in a village of Bohemia [DANIC. has ‘in Prague’], the feast of Saint Adalbert, bishop. When he preached the word of life to the Slavic people, he was pierced seven times and beheaded by pagans, and for three days was guarded by an eagle.”

[Col. 0965C] LOVANIEN., somewhat mutilated in the text, has only at the end: “On that same day, in a village of Bohemia, the feast of Adalbert, bishop.”

CENTULEN.: “The feast of blessed George, the famous and glorious martyr. In Gaul, in the city of Valencia, Saints Felix the priest, Fortunatus, and Achilleus, deacons, who were sent by blessed Herenaeus to preach and were brought to completion by the sword under the commander Cornelius.”

ANTUERP.-MAJ., usually purer, adds at the end: “At the fortress of Senlis, Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor.” See above under MUNERAT.

BRUXELLEN., with a moderate interpolation of the text, adds: “At Prague in Bohemia, the feast of blessed Adalbert,” etc., as above. “On that same day, the burial of Arnulf, patriarch of Jerusalem.” Concerning him, see the *Praetermissi*.

HAGENOYEN. stuffs George’s encomium with innumerable kinds of torture, a sample of which I reproduce here: “He was hung upon the rack by Dacian, emperor of the Persians, and afterward his body was torn limb from limb; torches were applied to his sides, so that his entrails could be seen. After this he was stretched out for scourging, covered with various wounds, salt was pressed into his wounds, and he was rubbed with the roughest haircloth; yet in all these things the martyr of God did not suffer. Then he was given poison, which did him no harm, and the poisoner was converted to the faith and beheaded; his name was Athanasius. After this George was placed on a wheel made of razors and swords, but he prayed, the wheel was shattered, and many of the pagan people perished beneath it. After this he was thrown into a frying pan full of molten lead,” etc. In the other announcement it presents the pure text.

AQUICINCTIN. has “In Palestine” in place of “In Persia.” At the end, concerning Regulus, it agrees with PRATEN. Observe here that this codex, as often also Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd, agrees with the Pratensis, as I note elsewhere too.

[Col. 0966A] VICTRORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked no. 130, have at the end: “At Rome, Saint Agapitus, pope.” Enough has already been said about him above.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Adalbert, bishop and martyr. Felix, Fortunatus, and Achilleus, martyrs.” Perhaps in the first place it should read Gorgonius rather than George, the martyr. [Col. 0966B] It is positioned in such a way that the location is uncertain.

CAMBERIEN., Convent of Saint Mary: “Near the city of Senlis, the holy Regulus,” etc., as in MUNERAT., but only as far as, and excluding, “after whose.”

The other REG. SUEC. codex, marked no. 428: “Near the fortress of Senlis, the translation of Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor.”

VATICAN., no. 5949, has at the end: “Saint Adalbert, bishop and martyr.”

STROZZIAN.: “On the same day at Prague, the feast of Saint Adalbert, bishop and confessor [rather, martyr].”

The LUGDUN. codex, in the section on the Valentinians, reads “by the judge Cornelius” instead of “by the commander Cornelius.”

LUXOVIEN.: “At Toul, the burial of Saint Gerard, bishop.” See below under GREVEN.

REMENS., of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “In the monastery of Fontenelle, Saint Wulfrannus, bishop [Col. 0966C] and confessor.” See what was said above in the Observations.

The LUBECO-COL. edition adds after the pure text at the end: “On that same day, at Prague in Bohemia, the feast of blessed Adelbert, bishop,” etc., as in the middle-grade codices. “On that same day, Saint Pusinna, virgin.”

Both editions of BELIN have at the end: “On the same day at Brucia [I think this is in place of Prague or Prussia], the feast of Saint Adalbert, bishop and martyr.” The second edition wrongly repeats today: “At Sens, Saint Leo, bishop and confessor.”

GREVEN.: “At Prague in Bohemia, the feast of blessed Adalbert, bishop. When he,” etc. “Also Saints Catulinus, Victor, and Ursus,” from the number of the Africans. “Germanus, abbot and martyr.” See among the *Praetermissi*. “In the monastery of Fontenelle, as Ado says, blessed Wulfrannus, bishop, a man distinguished in miracles and doctrine, whom Usuard records under the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April. Renobertus, bishop of Bayeux, who, renowned for life and miracles, completed forty years in the episcopate and rested in the Lord.” In the Acts he is referred to May 16. “At Toul, Saint Gerard, bishop and confessor. Born at Cologne, in the year of the Lord 963 he was ordained bishop of the aforesaid city; completing his course in holy deeds, he was enrolled in the catalogue of the saints by Pope Leo IX, who himself had also been bishop of Toul. Lugerius, tenth bishop of Utrecht and confessor.” He is omitted here. “Also, according to some, on this day the burial of Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor of Senlis. He, who was from Mycenae in Greece,” etc., almost as in MUNERAT. “Usuard has him under the third day before the Kalends of April. At Herford, Pusinna, virgin. Also Nigundis, virgin.” Is it *Nigunda*? Whichever way it is written, she has until now been unknown.

MOLAN.: “On the same day at Brutia [or in Prussia?], the feast of Saint Adalbert, bishop and martyr. At Sens, Saint Leo, bishop and confessor. On that same day, blessed Pusinna, virgin.” Then, in smaller letters: “At Toul, Saint Gerard,” etc., plainly taken from GREVEN. Other editions insert after George the martyr, in italic letters: “A glorious standard-bearer and renowned for miracles.” At the end: “On the same day in Prussia, the feast of Saint Adalbert, bishop and martyr. At Toul, [Col. 0967A] Saint Gerard, bishop and confessor. On that same day, blessed Pusinna, virgin, who was transferred to Herford in the time of Charlemagne.”]

[Col. 0963]

In the Persian city of Diospolis, the passion of Saint George, martyr. Although the account of his passion is numbered among the apocryphal writings, nevertheless the Church of God venerably honors his most illustrious martyrdom among the crowns of the martyrs. In the Gallic city of Valencia, the feast of Saints Felix the priest, Fortunatus, and Achilleus, deacons. After they had converted the greater part of the aforesaid city to the faith of Christ, they were thrust into prison by the commander Cornelius; afterward they were scourged for a very long time, their legs were broken, they were bound around the turning wheels, and they also endured smoke while suspended on the rack; finally they were brought to completion by the sword.

[Added by Bouillart.: [Note: [Col. 0963C] In the Carolingian autograph it was written: “Near the fortress of the Senonians, the burial of Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor.” Here it simply says “bishop and confessor.” Why did he omit “the burial”? There was certainly enough space to add it. Here I recognize Usuard’s acumen and discernment. He surely read the Acts of Saint Regulus, but, seeing them filled with fables and finding that no reliable trust could be placed in them, he consulted the Church, which ought to have preserved the deeds of Regulus and the day of his death more carefully in memory. Yet this agreed so little with the Carolingian autograph that it venerates his burial on this day and his translation on March 30. What was Usuard to do? He deleted what he had written on March 30. And lest he be deceived by marking the burial which the Acts commemorate on this day, he was content to record the day sacred to Saint Regulus. BOUILLART.] At the fortress of Senlis, Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor.]

**The eighth day before the Kalends. April 24.**

[Note: [Col. 0967]

Taken from PRATEN., TORNACEN., PULSANEN., MUNERAT., GREVEN., and MOLAN.]

[Note: [Col. 0967B]

In PULSANEN., *custodia* in place of *custodiam* is an error. Molanus likewise makes the sense incomplete: “first he was torn,” to which the particle found in all the codices must be added. All read *crate soluta*; Molanus tried to be too clever by substituting *carne*. Usuard followed Ado’s reading. Tournai and Pulsanen wrongly write *examinatus* for *exanimatus*. Tournai likewise transposed the word: “having examined the blessed [Col. 0968B] spirit, he gave it up.” Why Molanus had written *reddidit* instead of *emisit* is not particularly important to know. The ignorance of the copyists caused the sense in Pulsanen to end after “Bishop Mellitus,” and a new sentence to begin with a large red initial, as follows: “In Britain, in the city of Eliberi,” etc. I read *Heliberri*, with most witnesses, not *Heliberni* as in Tournai, nor *Heliberti* as in Muneratus. *Britania* may perhaps reflect the taste of the period.]

[Note: [Col. 0967B]

Those who remembered Epipodius on April 22 record Alexander today. Most of the Hieronymian codices add thirty-four companions and the dedication of the crypt where their bodies rest; Florentinius offers several noteworthy conjectures about them.

This, meanwhile, is certain: the Acts themselves—which all, even the most critical scholars, accept as weighty and trustworthy, as may be seen in Ruinart, beginning at page 63, and in Tillemont, volume III, beginning at page 30—mention no companions at all. The *Romanum parvum* is entirely silent; concerning it, the observations under February 28 could be repeated here.

Bede and Rabanus commemorate Mellitus alone. Florus, however, contrary to the sequence of the Acts, joined Alexander with Epipodius on this same day, composing an encomium in his own manner, which appears to have been drawn from those same Acts, although at the very beginning he inserts the thirty-four anonymous companions mentioned above. It is credible that they were customarily commemorated at Lyons with Epipodius and Alexander on the basis of some tradition, or that they were entered from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

Ado agrees, following the aforesaid Acts both on April 22 and here, but adds those thirty-four companions as well as the glorious contests of forty-eight martyrs, which he had placed before Epipodius’s Passion on April 22. Usuard, whom we saw there dealing with Epipodius alone, here copies almost everything from Ado word for word. Notker, wiser than his guide above, added certain things—or rather confused them—which are better removed [Col. 0967D].

Our Acts record both martyrs under April 22 because the Acts just praised are common to both, although Alexander completed his glorious contest only on the third day after Epipodius, that is, on this April 24. Let Wandalbert be heard, singing of Alexander alone and differing from the others by a single line in the number of companions:

> The martyr Alexander, rejoicing in thirty martyrs  
> And three, consecrates the walls of Lyons on the eighth day.
