Mellitus is first introduced by Bede; his Life was annotated by Henschenius and supplemented with several miracles from Capgrave. Ado adapted a very brief eulogy, whereas it was enough for Our Author to transcribe Bede’s very words. Perhaps Henschenius read the title “archbishop” in the Rosweyd manuscript. The text then proceeds to Gregory of Eliberis, concerning whom one should consult Papebrochius’s dissertation and Tillemont in various places of volumes VI and VII, especially volume VII, p. 767. There, together with Pagi, he considers the sanctity of this Gregory, commonly called Baeticus, at least doubtful, since it is not altogether established that he repented of the Luciferian schism before his death.

He is unknown to all martyrologists earlier than, or contemporary with, Usuard, and therefore must be considered to have been first entered by Usuard in the sacred calendars. This is demonstrated by our most ancient manuscripts, whatever may be absent from many manuscripts of secondary quality—probably omitted by an ignorant copyist in some manuscript from which these were subsequently copied. Such are the Antwerp manuscript, the Maxima, the first Lübeck edition, and other more recent manuscripts, to be listed among the Additions. For us, the genuine simplicity of Usuard’s calendar is in no way doubtful.

[Note: [Col. 0967D]]

HERINIENSIS, in a very pure text, adds a proper feast of Reims, as we have observed occasionally above. It reads: “At Reims, the city, of the holy virgins Bova and Doda.”

ANTWERP and MAXIMA-LÜBECK omit Gregory, as I said, substituting in his place: “On the same day, Sidrac, Misac, and Abdenago.” They are referred in the Acts to 16 December.

ROSWЕYD, at the end, reads: “In Babylon, Sidrac, Misac, and Abdenago.” They are taken from the Hieronymian Martyrology, where it is added: “under another name, namely Ananias, Azarias, and Misael; in the great city of Babylonia they were delivered from the furnace of blazing fire.” See Florentinius’s observation there.

GREVEN, interweaving and adding to an otherwise pure text, has: “In the territory of Blois, the anniversary of Deodatus, abbot and Levite.” We shall give his Addition below in its proper place; here it is included insofar as it concerns the text.

ANTWERP-MAXIMA, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, DANICUS, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition begin: “At Langres, Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago.” Gregory is omitted at the end.

ALBERGEN has the same addition together with the same omission. It also prefixes this beginning:

“At Werden, the deposition of Saint Ludger, first bishop and confessor of Münster. His most sacred body, preserved at Münster, in the church of blessed Mary, Mother of God, after his blessed passing, showed no trace of corruption until, at the command of Charlemagne, it was reverently buried at the aforesaid place on the thirtieth day. At his sacred tomb, miracles of God were very frequently performed.”

The days are counted from 26 March, on which Ludger was discussed above.

CENTULA: “At Lyon in Gaul, Saint Alexander, who, after suffering much, was finally crucified and commended his spirit to the Lord. On the same day, the deposition of blessed Mellitus, bishop and confessor, whom venerable Pope Gregory sent from Rome into Britain with Saint Augustine. In the city of Eliberis, Saint Gregory, bishop and confessor.”

ANTWERP-MAJOR, pure in the first announcement, continues as follows: “In the British city of Canterbury, the deposition of Saint Mellitus, archbishop and confessor, who, third after blessed Augustine, preached the word of God courageously to the English people. Also in the city of Eliberis,” and so forth. “On the same day, Saint Wilfrid, archbishop and confessor.”

BRUSSELS begins as follows: “At Langres, of the three boys Ananias, Misael, and Azarias, who, under changed names, were called Sydrac, Mysaac, and Abdenago. When they refused to worship the statue that Nebuchadnezzar had erected, they were thrown into a furnace of blazing fire at Babylon. In it they sang unharmed, with one voice, the hymn with which we bless the Lord at the Lauds of Matins on feast days.”

Concerning Alexander, it adds near the end from Ado: “And both of them, Epipodius and Alexander, were buried on either side of the altar, in a crypt built with beautiful and ancient workmanship on a hill below the city [or: above the city].” In the entry for Mellitus and Gregory it is pure.

HAGENOYEN, pure in the first announcement, adds: “On the same day, Saint Agapitus the martyr. Also in Britain, the deposition of Saint Mellitus, bishop and confessor. At Prague in Bohemia, the anniversary of Saint Adalbert.” This belongs to the preceding day. It then proceeds with Gregory, purely. Finally, at the end: “At Langres on the same day, Sydrat, Mysrath, and Abdenago.”

[Col. 0969C] AQUICINCT, at the end: “Also the anniversary of Saint Corona the virgin.” I think this is the Corona who is foremost among the Alexandrian saints, as you will find in the Acts.

VICTORIN and the REGISTRY OF SWEDEN, no. 130: “On that day, Saints Sidrac, Misac, and Abdenago. In Syracuse, Saints Evodius and Calixtus.” See the entries Omitted and the following day. “On the same day, Corona the virgin.” We have already spoken of her.

MATRICULA-CARTHUSIANA-UTRECHT: “Mellitus, bishop in England. Alexander the martyr with thirty-four companions.” See what was said above.

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, marked B, in first place: “At Langres, Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago.” The same entry is often repeated here.

In the VATICAN MANUSCRIPT, no. 5949, Gregory is omitted.

UGHELLIANUS also omits Gregory. It adds: “On the same day, Sidrac, Misac, and Abdenago.”

ALTEMPS: “The discovery of the body of Saint Yvo, archbishop and confessor.” This is referred to 10 June. “Also the translation of Saint Wilfrid, archbishop and confessor. Also Saint Corona the virgin. At Blois, Saint Deodatus.”

FLORENTINUS: “Also Saint Uldifrid, bishop and confessor.” Read Wilfrid.

[Col. 0970A] BURDIGALENSIS, after Mellitus and Gregory: “Also Saint Corona the virgin.”

DIVION, Saint Benignus: “In the territory of Auvergne, the deposition of Saint Robert, first abbot of La Chaise-Dieu.”

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION, in the entry for Alexander, agrees with the text. It adds:

“At Langres, the translation of the three boys Ananias, Azarias, and Misael. At Werden, the deposition and burial of Saint Ludger, first bishop and confessor of Münster. His most sacred body, preserved in the town of Münster, in the church of blessed Mary, Mother of God, remained unburied until the thirtieth day after his blessed passing and showed no trace of corruption; until, at the command of Charlemagne, it was reverently buried at the aforesaid place on the thirtieth day by his most devoted brother Hildegrin, as he had desired before his death, together with several other clerics, religious, and noblemen. During this burial, as the holy prelate had foretold, fresh blood flowed from his nostrils. At his sacred tomb also, miracles of God were very frequently performed. In Britain, the deposition of Saint Mellitus,” and so forth. Concerning Gregory, it is pure. “In the territory of Blois, the anniversary of Saint Deodatus, abbot and Levite. At Reims, the holy virgins Bova and Doda.” Read Bova.

The first edition of BELINUS inserts, in the penultimate place: “On the same day, Sydrach,” and so forth. The second edition, however, places before this announcement: “On the same day, the anniversary of Saint Corona the virgin.” At the end it has: “At Blois, Saint Deodatus the abbot.”

GREVEN: “At Langres, the translation,” and so forth. “In Africa, the anniversary of Saints Faustinus, Victorinus, and Valerius.” From the Hieronymian Martyrology. “Robert, the boy martyr. In Syria, Sarah the virgin and martyr. Benedict, the first pope and confessor.” See the entries Omitted concerning these three. “In Ireland, blessed Egbert, monk, priest, and confessor, concerning whom Bede, book III, testifies that he lived with great humility and in the perfection of gentleness, continence, simplicity, and justice. At Reims, Bova and Doda, virgins. At Werden, the deposition and burial of Saint Ludger, first bishop of Münster. Since his body had been kept unburied until the thirtieth day, until, at the command of Charlemagne, it might be buried at the aforesaid place as he himself had desired, it showed no trace of corruption.”

MOLANUS: “On the same day, Sidrac, Misac, and Abdenago. On the same day, the anniversary of Saint Corona the virgin. At Blois, Saint Deodatus, abbot and Levite. At Reims, the city, the holy virgins Bova and Doda.” In smaller type: “In Ireland, blessed Egbert, monk, priest, and confessor, concerning whom Bede,” and so forth. He is rightly called Egbert here; Greven calls him Egberechtus. He should probably not be confused with Hegberact or Hecheract, about whom Henschenius makes a careful investigation today in the Acts. Other editions have: “On the same day, the anniversary of Saint Corona the virgin.” Concerning Deodatus, Bova, and Doda, see above. “On the twenty-fourth day, Saint Sabas the martyr, commander of an army, and Saint Elizabeth the wonder-worker. In Ireland, blessed Egbert, monk, priest, and confessor. In the territory of Auvergne, the deposition of blessed Robert, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu and confessor.”

[Col. 0967]

At Lyon in Gaul, the anniversary of Saint Alexander the martyr, who, during the persecution of Antoninus Verus, after imprisonment, was first so mangled by the cruelty of those scourging him that, when the cage of his ribs was broken open, his entrails exposed, and the interior of his body laid bare, he was then fastened to the cross and, dying, gave up his blessed spirit. Thirty-four others suffered with him. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Mellitus, bishop, in Britain. Also in the city of Eliberis, Saint Gregory, bishop and confessor.

VII Kal. Day 25.

[Note: [Col. 0969]]

Thus read Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp, Maxima-Lübeck, Greven, and Molanus.

[Note: [Col. 0971A]]

There is little disagreement among the manuscripts today. Greven and Molanus incorrectly read “Here he was a disciple” and punctuate the sense differently. Muneratus likewise has scribit, “he writes,” instead of scripsit, “he wrote.” In the text it is Siracusa, as in the older witnesses; some have the better form Syracusa. Pratensis seems to read Enodius; we, with the others and correctly, read Evodius. Callista, their sister, ought to have been added to these two, but she was omitted by Usuard—I do not know for what reason—as we shall soon say.

[Note: [Col. 0971A]]

The Greater Litany to Saint Peter, known to no martyrologist before the author of the Little Roman Martyrology, is described from Ado, and from Ado by Usuard, in the same words, with no mention of its origin or the reason for its institution. More recent Usuardine manuscripts attribute it to Gregory the Great in the Additions that will be cited. Yet Fronto proves from Gregory’s own Register that it is older than Gregory the Great, in his note on the Calendar, p. 71.

I do not see what the account that Notker gives at length today concerning the beginnings of the Rogations has in common with the Greater Litany. Some call the Rogations the Lesser Litanies, although they ought to be older than the Greater Litany. It is clear that the aforesaid Litany was permanently established for the feast of Saint Mark, 25 April, whereas the Rogations, once the cause of many disagreements, like movable feasts, were customarily celebrated three days before the Lord’s Ascension, though not everywhere with the same rite.

The curious reader should consult Henschenius, under 11 May, concerning Saint Mamertus, the institutor of the Rogations, and Papebrochius, 27 June, concerning Saint Arialdus, chapter 5, and elsewhere. It is remarkable that in the Hieronymian copies the evangelist Mark is entered not on this day but on 23 September, and then differently by different witnesses, as may be seen in Florentinius and in the Acts. Most noteworthy, however, is Notker’s assertion that the feast of Mark on the preceding day was designated by Saint Jerome on the authority of Eusebius.

The Little Roman Martyrology places Mark on this day. He was preceded by Bede, whose eulogy Ado appears to have expanded, not in the Martyrology but in the feasts of the apostles. Our Author followed him and drew all his material from him. I consistently observe that the time of the martyrdom is given as the eighth year of Nero. If you desire more, see what we discussed concerning Mark’s apostolate and death in the Chronological Treatise on the Alexandrian Patriarchs, before volume V of June.

Tillemont does not agree with us on every point. His Life of Mark, composed in French, is nevertheless found in volume II, beginning at p. 89. The aforementioned Fronto observes, p. 72, that nothing concerning Saint Mark the evangelist is found either in Gregory the Great or in the most ancient books; therefore his earliest commemoration must be sought in our martyrologies, to which Wandalbertus adds his testimony:

“Soon blessed Mark thunders with evangelical voice,

[Col. 0972B] on the seventh day, girded with excellent radiance.”

Besides the Litany and Mark, the Little Roman Martyrology contains Erminus the confessor, entirely unknown to all the others. I suspect that Erminus, abbot and bishop of Lobbes, is indicated, inserted into the original text by someone, unless one thinks it corrupted from Evodius and Hermogenes—which is not probable, since we find nothing about him in Ado.

Evodius and Hermogenes, therefore, were separated from their sister Callista in the Hieronymian Martyrology and added by Our Author, whatever the fact that we observe them omitted in some Usuardine manuscripts. I think no one will call into doubt that the true Usuardine reading is given here.

As for why he omitted Clarentius, bishop of Vienne, whom Ado had included, no other conjecture occurs to me than that it may have been absent from the manuscript Usuard used, as we have suggested above more than once as probable concerning similar Viennese bishops—unless one prefers the alternative thought that Usuard paid no attention to the bishops of Vienne.

[Note: [Col. 0971C]]

PRATENSIS preserves the passage among the pure manuscripts, although in the margin, written by an ancient hand, it has the following words: “On that day, at Paris, the translation of the body of blessed Droctoveus, abbot, disciple of the most blessed Germanus the confessor, bishop and pontiff.” Either title could have sufficed.

ROSWЕYD and BELINUS are so little removed from purity that they ought scarcely to have been excluded. The former is defective because at the beginning it gives only these words: “The Greater Litany.” Belinus, more closely conforming to the text, gives the whole announcement but reads “the Greater Litanies” instead of “the Greater Litany.” Furthermore, concerning Mark, after the words “of the apostle Peter,” it inserts “and his son in baptism”; MOLANUS also has this in later editions, though in a typeface different from that of the text.

TORNACENSIS and PULSANENSIS are pure but entirely lack the final announcement.

ANTWERP-MAXIMA, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, DANICUS, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition place Mark first, as Belinus does. It follows with: “On the same day at Rome, the Greater Litany to Saint Peter, which blessed Pope Gregory instituted to bring an end to the pestilence of buboes that raged at Rome.” They are pure in the entries for Evodius and Hermogenes.

CENTULA: “At Alexandria, the passion of Saint Mark the evangelist, whom blessed Peter the apostle baptized and taught. When Peter had ordained him bishop, he also entrusted all Egypt and the neighboring regions to him, so that he might exalt them in the glory of Christ. At Rome, the Greater Litany to Saint Peter.”

BRUSSELS begins: “At Alexandria, the anniversary of blessed Mark the evangelist, of the tribe of Levi. He was a disciple and interpreter of blessed Peter the apostle, and his son in baptism. So that he might not be promoted to the priesthood, he cut off his thumb, and when he was asked by the brethren …” [Col. 0972C] It remains almost pure until the word “year,” where it adds: “On Easter Day itself he was dragged and torn to the places of the buffalo, and thus summoned to the heavenly kingdoms. Later merchants transported his body from Alexandria to Venice.”

Concerning the Litany, it agrees with Utrecht and the others. “In the city of Syracuse …” is pure. “At Venice, Saint Clarentius, bishop and confessor. At Lyon, Saint Rusticus, bishop. On that day in the district of Ponthieu, Saint Richarius, priest and confessor.” See the following day. “And the passing of Saint Erminus the confessor.” Erminus is the better reading.

HAGENOYEN: “At Rome, the Greater Litany to Saint Peter, which blessed Pope Gregory instituted because of the pestilence of buboes that was then especially severe at Rome. At Alexandria, the anniversary of Saint Mark the evangelist. He was the disciple and interpreter of the apostle Peter, and his son in baptism. At Rome, when asked by the brethren, he wrote the Gospel. He had previously been a companion of Paul and Barnabas, from whom he fled because of persecutions. Later, at Aquileia, he preached the Gospel that he had published at Rome. Then he appointed another bishop in his place, named Hermagoras. Taking the Gospel, he went to Egypt, and as the first to announce Christ at Alexandria, he established a church there.

“Afterward, when the pagans saw him growing strong in the word of the Lord and performing many miracles, on Easter Day, during the solemn celebration of Mass, they seized him, placed a rope around his neck, and dragged him over the rocks, so that his flesh fell upon the ground. That evening he was thrown into prison, where he was strengthened by an angel. Later Christ himself appeared to him and invited him to the heavenly kingdoms. In the morning, when he was again dragged, he gave thanks to God and, commending his spirit to Him, died happily, in the eighth year of Nero. In the city of Syracuse in Sicily, and so forth.” It is pure, as it appears in the text.

[Col. 0973A] AQUICINCT: “At Lobbes, the passing of Saint Erminus, bishop and confessor.” This entry recurs frequently here.

MATRICULA-CARTHUSIANA-UTRECHT: “Mark the evangelist. Floribert, bishop of Liège. Erminus, bishop and confessor.”

In the VATICAN MANUSCRIPT, no. 5949, the entry for Evodius and Hermogenes is absent. “Cletus the pope, and so forth,” has been added from the following day.

FLORENTINUS: “Saint Mark … then, in the year of the Lord 466 [or 467], the Venetians transported the body of the aforesaid Saint Mark from Alexandria to Venice by armed force, where a church of extraordinary beauty was built in honor of Saint Mark the evangelist.” That translation more probably belongs to the beginning of the ninth century, as is shown by its history in the Acts.

LUXOVIENSIS: “The translation of Saint Mansuetus, bishop and confessor.” His anniversary is 3 September.

REIMS: Saints Timothy and Apollinaris. “At Lyon, the deposition of Rusticus, bishop and confessor.”

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION has said enough about Mark and likewise about the Litany. “In the city of Syracuse …” is pure. [Col. 0974A] “At Liège, the anniversary of Saint Floribert, bishop and confessor of that place.”

GREVEN: “Alexander the martyr, Evodius, Fortunatus.” The usual confusion. “At Lyon, Saint Rusticus, bishop. At Vienne, Saint Clarentius, bishop and confessor. Floribert, bishop and confessor of Liège. Erminus, bishop and confessor. Also blessed Franca, virgin of the Cistercian order. Bede and Deodatus, confessors.” The first edition also adds Mark. See the entries Omitted.

MOLANUS: “At Binche, Erminus, bishop and abbot of Lobbes, successor of Saint Ursmar in the monastery of Lobbes.” Then in smaller letters: “His disciple, named Flacbert, testified about him, as did more fully the book of his deeds. He is transferred from Binche to the following day because of the feast of Mark. Also blessed Franca, virgin of the Cistercian order, at Piacenza. The anniversary of Saint Maris, bishop of Doliche. Tripartite History, book IX, chapter 3.” He is omitted in other editions and likewise in the Acts. In those editions, as I said, “and his son in baptism” is inserted, and at the end “and of the martyr Calixtus” appears instead of “Callista.” As an Addition there is: “At Lobbes, the passing of Saint Erminus, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0969]

At Rome, the Greater Litany to Saint Peter. At Alexandria, the anniversary of blessed Mark the evangelist. He was the disciple and interpreter of the apostle Peter. At Rome, when asked by the brethren, he wrote the Gospel; taking it with him, he went to Egypt, and as the first to announce Christ at Alexandria, he established the Church. Later, having been seized and severely afflicted for the faith of Christ, he was first strengthened by an angelic visitation, then, when the Lord himself appeared to him, summoned to the heavenly kingdoms. He died in the eighth year of Nero. In the city of Syracuse, Saints Evodius and Hermogenes.

[Bouillart, in the margin of the page: On that day, at Paris, the translation of the body of blessed Droctoveus, abbot, disciple of the most blessed Germanus the confessor and pontiff.]

VI Kal. Day 26.

[Note: [Col. 0973]]

The Heriniensis manuscript alone is pure in every respect.

[Note: [Col. 0973B]]

This matter chiefly comprises two points. First, we have printed not Cletus, as the most widely accepted and perhaps correct reading requires, but Anacletus. We consider this reading altogether Usuardine, on the evidence of Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Pulsanensis, Muneratus, and Antwerp-Major, to which several others must be added among the Additions to be listed. They write this consistently, although the first manuscript has the more corrupt form Anencletus, or perhaps preserves an older form, while the last displays the letters Ana almost erased.

You say that this reading is false because the context of the words plainly reveals a contradiction: “who was second after the apostle,” or, as Florus has it, “third” — either expression can be understood in different respects — statements that must refer only to Cletus and not to Anacletus, as the chronological succession of the Roman pontiffs clearly demonstrates.

You argue correctly, I think, according to the more common opinion, and I believe this was the reason why Cletus is found in later manuscripts after Anacletus was deleted, as we shall soon say Bede wrote. But this opposition and contradiction of whatever kind does not trouble us. We are not investigating the truth of the matter but Usuard’s reading, which he evidently took from Ado, and Ado from the Little Roman Martyrology. Therefore we had to preserve it as genuine and original, excluding those manuscripts that, for whatever reason or authority, judged Cletus should be restored in place of Anacletus. We shall cite these in the Additions.

The second point concerns the final announcement, which the Pratensis manuscript gives as follows: “In the district of Ponthieu, Saint Richarius,” and so forth, contrary to what almost all the others write, and what we read: “At the monastery of Centula,” and so forth.

Castellanus was consulted on this matter. He replied that nothing had been erased in that manuscript but, as he says in a letter dated 6 June 1709, a space of one line clearly appears to have been left blank between 26 and 27 April and subsequently filled, at another time, by the same hand but with more yellowish ink: “In the district of Ponthieu,” and so forth.

This is sufficient for us to exclude the aforesaid Pratensis, together with the Rosweyd and Antwerp-Major manuscripts, which are the only ones among so many manuscripts conforming to it. The same matter will often recur hereafter.

[Note: [Col. 0973C]]

Concerning Anacletus, or Cletus, and Marcellinus, the Hieronymian manuscripts say nothing on this day. Nor, as far as I know, does either Cletus or Anacletus appear anywhere else in that entire Martyrology with the title of bishop or pope.

Bede announces Cletus and joins Marcellus to him in place of Marcellinus—quite incorrectly, since he dealt with Marcellus most distinctly on 16 January. The Little Roman Martyrology, the source from which the present calendar sprang, expressly mentions Anacletus: “At Rome, Anacletus, pope and martyr.” Ado followed it and added a eulogy transcribed word for word by Our Author.

I admit that Mosander’s edition reads differently, but it is so contaminated by errors that it cannot be regarded as a genuine edition of Ado. Notker, although he did not adhere so closely to Ado’s words, likewise named Anacletus, not Cletus, on this day; but he himself deals with Cletus on 13 July.

Rabanus here abandons Bede and, disagreeing with all the other martyrologists, celebrates Cletus on 29 April and Anacletus on 11 June.

Henschenius has learnedly discussed on this day the confusion made by the Greeks between the names Cletus and Anacletus among the Roman pontiffs, defending the ancient opinion held in the Church for so many centuries. He follows Baronius’s prudent rule, by which Baronius judiciously determined that, in matters belonging to the Roman Church, greater trust should be placed in its own alumni than in others. By this rule, Anacletus must be entirely distinguished from Cletus.

Many more recent critics, however, followed by Tillemont in volume II, p. 555, and elsewhere, vigorously maintain that Cletus should be removed from the catalogues of pontiffs, or—what amounts to the same thing—that the two should be merged into one. Papebrochius attempted to explain their view by another route, as is briefly set out in the Responses to article 17, no. 20 onward.

I have read and weighed nearly all the arguments, including those most strongly urged by Pearson, yet I am not so far moved as to depart from Henschenius’s position or, with Pagi under the year 101, no. 4, to deny that in an uncertain matter it is safer not to depart from the common opinion. Nevertheless, if we attend to the martyrologists—especially Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Usuard—only one person is proposed for veneration in the sacred calendars, as Wandalbertus also holds in the passage to be quoted below.

For my part, I adopt neither opinion here. With God’s favor, I shall discuss the whole matter most carefully on 13 July, the day on which Anacletus is commemorated.

[Col. 0975B] The aforementioned Little Roman Martyrology likewise announces Marcellinus: “And Marcellinus, pope and martyr.” Bede also announces him with a eulogy. From Bede, Rabanus does the same—not Marcellus, as is incorrectly printed in our edition of Bede, but Marcellinus—while preserving the rest of the eulogy. This passed into Ado, Usuard, and Notker, though only the latter two, together with Ado, add the passage concerning the seventeen thousand martyrs crowned within one month.

The difficulty mentioned above recurs here concerning the confusion of the names of the Roman pontiffs, now also in the case of Marcellus and Marcellinus. Some of those who strive with all their might to abolish the distinction between Cletus and Anacletus likewise contend for their identity.

Among them was the distinguished Castellanus, as is clear from the note he appended to the Universal Martyrology on this day. Yet in his latest letters, given to me in another hand on 31 January 1711, he explicitly retracted what he had written concerning the alleged identity of Marcellus and Marcellinus both on this day and on 16 January, as he explains more fully there.

To say it once again: whatever Pearson may argue, Marcellus must be entirely separated from Marcellinus. If necessary, this can be demonstrated at greater length. Here I consider it sufficient that I have reproduced the pure and simple text of Usuard.

The accusations made by the Donatists against Marcellinus have been so thoroughly examined by scholars today that it would be pointless to turn the same stone here again. Whether his martyrdom is sufficiently certain, many doubt. See the Acts; Papebrochius’s Response to article 11, no. 48; Pagi under the year 304, no. 11; and Tillemont in volume V, beginning at p. 612. They also remove other matters wrongly attributed to Marcellinus.

We began above to discuss Richarius of Centula. It remains to note that Usuard correctly marks him with the sole title of priest, whereas Notker incorrectly calls him a bishop and gives no specific designation of place. I would not dare to say that he was taken from the Hieronymian copies, although he seems to have been added in some of them.

His Life was elucidated by Henschenius and also reported by Mabillon in volume II of the Benedictine century, beginning at p. 187. Let us hear Wandalbertus, celebrating him together with Cletus:

“The sixth day recalls the contests of Pontiff Cletus;

and shines with Richarius, cultivator of blessed life.”

[Note: [Col. 0975B]]

PRATENSIS. We have already noted that instead of “At the monastery of Centula,” it reads there: “In the district,” and so forth. This reading was followed by the ROSWEYD CODEX and ANTWERP-MAJOR.

TORNACENSIS. After the very pure text it adds: “On that day, Saint Autharius the confessor.” See what is said about him among the entries Omitted.

PULSANENSIS entirely lacks the final announcement. In all else it is sufficiently pure.

MUNERATUS, otherwise also pure, adds at the end: “At Paris, the dedication of the sacred royal chapel, magnificently endowed by blessed King Louis with the sacred insignia of our redemption.”

[Col. 0975C] ANTWERP, ROSWEYD, MAXIMA-LÜBECK, BELINUS, GREVEN, and MOLANUS, together with the more recent witnesses generally, read Cletus instead of Anacletus.

LOUVAIN, similar to the witnesses cited, writes concerning Cletus: “After he had governed the Church for seven years, he was crowned with martyrdom and buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican.” In the rest it is pure.

ANTWERP-MAXIMA, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, DANICUS, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition add to what has already been cited: “Eusebius of Caesarea and several others regard this Cletus and Anacletus as the same person. But Damasus, in the Chronicle of the Roman pontiffs, which he wrote to Jerome, presents them as two persons, saying that Cletus was a Roman, whereas Anacletus was Greek by nationality.” Otherwise they are pure, except that the first gives Richarius the title of bishop.

CENTULA celebrates the feast of its own patron first, as follows:

“In the district of Ponthieu, at the monastery of Centula, the anniversary of our most holy father Richarius, priest and founder of our house. A follower of remarkable abstinence and tireless preaching, he became renowned far and wide for miracles. Finally, when the Lord revealed it to him, he departed this life and ascended to the heavenly kingdoms. At Rome, Saint Cletus, pope and martyr, who was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Domitian. Also at Rome, Saint Marcellinus, pope, beheaded under Diocletian together with three clerics. At that time persecution became so savage that, according to the records, seventeen thousand martyrs suffered within one month.”

BRUSSELS: “At Rome, Saint Cletus, pope and martyr. [Col. 0976B] He governed the Church as second after blessed Peter, was crowned with martyrdom under the persecution of Domitian, and was buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican. He was the first who is found to have written in his letters, ‘Greetings and apostolic blessing,’ and he commended pilgrimages to the saints, especially to the threshold of Saint Peter; and he curses those who hinder or discourage them.”

It is easy today to judge these statements and those that follow. It continues:

“At Rome, Saint Marcellinus, pope. After governing the Church for nine years and four months, he was compelled by Diocletian to offer incense to idols. Later, when a synod had been held, he condemned himself and, going to Diocletian, confessed himself a Christian. For the faith of Christ he was beheaded together with Claudius, Cyrinus, and Antoninus. At that time the persecution was great, so that …” and so forth.

“Also at Troyes, Saint Exuperantia the virgin. At Rabas, Saints Aucharius and Alga, his wife, parents of Ado, Rado, and Odoen, archbishop of Rouen.” See the entries Omitted. At the end, in the margin, it also adds: “And the translation of Saint Modoald, archbishop of Trier.” His anniversary is 12 May.

HAGENOYEN: “At Rome, the anniversary of blessed Cletus, pope. After governing the Church for seven years, he suffered under the emperor Nero.” The error is obvious. “He established twenty-five priests in the city of Rome and commended pilgrimage to Saint Peter.”

It then attempts to reconcile the disagreement:

“Also at Rome, Saint Anacletus, pope and martyr. After governing the Church for nine years and two months, he suffered under the emperor Trajan. He established that at Mass bishops should say ‘Peace be with you,’ and ordinary priests ‘The Lord be with you’; and that both should receive the response, ‘And with your spirit,’ and ‘Amen.’

“On that day at Rome, Saint Marcellinus, pope and martyr. At first he became fearful because of the persecution and offered incense to idols; afterward he repented before 140 bishops and offered himself to Diocletian to be killed. Diocletian, together with Claudius, Cyrinus, and Antonius, subjected him to capital punishment. At that time there was …” and so forth.

Concerning Richarius, it is pure. “In Italy, Saint Tyta the virgin.” I think Zita of Lucca is indicated; she is discussed in the Acts on the following day. “In the Black Forest, Saint Trudpert the martyr.”

AQUICINCT reads Anacletus with us instead of Cletus, as the others have, and reads three months instead of four.

VICTORIN has twenty-seven thousand instead of seventeen thousand martyrs.

AMBIAN: “At the monastery of Centula, the anniversary of Saint Richarius the confessor.”

MATRICULA-CARTHUSIANA-UTRECHT: “Anacletus, pope and martyr, second after blessed Peter. Marcellinus, pope and martyr, with the others.”

AUGENSIS, at the monastery of Saint Lawrence: “On that day, Saint Autharius the confessor.”

In the VATICAN MANUSCRIPT, no. 5949, nothing is said about Richarius. It adds: “In Africa, Saints Victor, Siricius, and Honoratus.” They appear to have been taken from some Hieronymian manuscript.

UGHELLIANUS likewise reads Anacletus, not Cletus.

STROZZI: “At Rabas, Saints Aucharius and Agia his wife, and their sons Ado and Redo, among whom was born Augdonus [Audoenus], bishop of Rouen, from the same father and mother.” Some things are corrupt and distorted; concerning them, see the index of the entries Omitted.

The BELNEN CODEX OF SAINT MARY: “At the castle of Belno, the reception of Saints Flocellus and Hernaeus. Among them, the glorious athlete of Christ Flocellus, as his written Passion testifies, was honorably buried by faithful worshipers of the Christian religion in the village of Durrun, which lies in the district of Coutances, and was glorified by God with great powers. But when the fury of the pagans grew stronger and his holy limbs were deprived of the due honor of religious observance in that place, certain soldiers of the aforesaid castle transported them, together with blessed Hernaeus, most reverend abbot of Le Mans, to the village of Rufiana. There they became renowned for signs and miracles. Then, by the merciful providence of God, they were transferred to Belnenium in the time of Count Otho, and there, up to the present, they mercifully assist those who faithfully ask them in every kind of need.” See what is said about them in the index of the entries Omitted.

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION has Cletus, as do the manuscripts of middling quality mentioned above. It follows: “Also at Rome, on the Salarian Way, Saint Marcellinus,” and so forth, almost as in the text. Then: “At Troyes, Saint Exuperantia the virgin. In the district of Ponthieu, at the monastery of Centula, Saint Richarius, priest and confessor.”

GREVEN.: “In Africa, [the feast of] Saints Honoratus, Paul, Maximus, and Apollonius. Likewise, [that] of Saints Aurelius, Leonides, Virius, Cyricus, and Guideus.” Their names should be assigned to the martyrs who are listed in Jerome. “Likewise, [the feast of] blessed memory Frederick, bishop of Liège and martyr.” Referred back to May 27.

[Col. 0978B] MOLAN.: “On the same day, at Liège, [the feast of] Saint Floribert, bishop of that place and confessor.” He died on April 25. “At Paris, the dedication of the sacred chapel, etc., from MUNERATUS. At Vienne, [the feast of] Saint Clarentius, bishop and confessor.” Concerning him, see yesterday. It follows, in smaller type: “Saint Basil, bishop of Amasea, whose martyrdom is written by John, presbyter of Nicomedia.” In other editions: “On the same day, at Liège,” etc. Concerning Clarentius, the same. “At Troyes, [the feast of] Saint Exuperantia, virgin. On the twenty-sixth day, [the feast of] Saint Basil, martyr and bishop of Amasea. At Paris, the dedication,” etc. As we have already said, this was taken from MUNERATUS.]

[Col. 0973]

At Rome, the birthday of blessed Anacletus, pope, who, having governed the Church for twelve years, was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Domitian, being second after the Apostle Peter. Likewise at Rome, [the feast of] Saint Marcellinus, pontiff, who, after governing the Church for nine years and four months, was beheaded by Diocletian for the faith of Christ, together with Claudius, Cyrinus, and Antoninus. At that time there was a great persecution, so that within one month seventeen thousand were crowned.

[Note: [Col. 0973B] This unfortunate Pratensis codex could not obtain a place among the pure witnesses with Sollerius, and that because of its mention of Saint Richarius, which, although he does not deny that it was written by the same author, he was nevertheless informed had been made with another and more yellowish ink; such is the equity of that judge! BOUILLART.]

At the monastery of Centula [Bouillart.: in the district of Ponthieu], [the feast of] Saint Richarius, priest and confessor.

**V Kal. Day 27.** [Note: [Col. 0977]

The Pratensis, Herinien., Antwerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. witnesses alone are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0977C]

In Molanus, before Jerome, the designation “Saint” is missing. In the text the others have *Hieronimus*, as the Pratensis, Munerat., Greven., and others write it. Concerning *Iheronimus* or *Ieronymus*, and similar forms, it is not worth discussing at length; nor is it worth discussing *Nichomediam*, *hystoria*, *Antimi*, *Anthymi*, and so forth. More noteworthy is Muneratus’s error, when he writes “as it is read in the history,” instead of what we correctly placed in the marginal entry: “as it is described in ecclesiastical history.” Thus the Rosweyd codex corrupts the sense, reading “whom others” instead of “some of whom.” The Pratensis and Munerat. have *conflagrare*, and I think Usuard read this rather than *conflagrari*, as in Herinien. and Antwerp.-Maj., perhaps derived from Ado. Choose either form, as you please. But I think Rosweyd., Greven., and Molan. showed excessive ingenuity when they substituted *concremari* (“to be burned”). Muneratus again changes the construction, diverging from all the others and writing “he caused [him] to be drowned in the deep” instead of “he caused [him] to be plunged into the deep.” Some write *Tharso* with Muneratus and Molanus; the text has the better form, based on the others. The remarkable confusion in the Herinien. between the two words *Tarso Ciliciae* (“at Tarsus in Cilicia”) and *in Thessalonicae* (“at Thessalonica”) is, unless I am mistaken, the copyist’s carelessness: having confused or corrupted the words for nearly half their length, he left another an opportunity to supply the rest incorrectly in more recent ink.]

[Note: [Col. 0977C]

The author of the Roman Little Martyrology first introduced Pope Anastasius into the sacred Calendars: “Saint Anastasius, pope.” Ado followed him, but—strange to say—adorned him with no encomium, merely adding that he occupied the see for three years and ten days. Rabanus was more diligent; Notker here copied him word for word, as often elsewhere, inserting even the words quoted from Ado. Therefore, the brief but vigorous praise of Anastasius expressed in the text should be considered Usuard’s own. Henschenius has supplied more material in the Acts, carefully drawn from Jerome and others. Anthimus of Nicomedia is mentioned in the Hieronymian copies, but the Roman Little Martyrology announces him differently and joins to him an innumerable multitude of martyrs. Ado composed an elogium for Anthimus and his companions, from which Our author selected only the principal flowers, as will be clearly seen from a comparison of the two texts. It is most probable that Anthimus was taken by the author of the Roman Little Martyrology from Rufinus’s Eusebius, Book VIII, chapter 6, and that this day was assigned to him arbitrarily, as is said elsewhere more than once concerning others who were most cruelly killed in the same first fury of Diocletian. Eusebius’s words are cited in the Acts, which relate the triumph of a truly distinguished martyr and an innumerable number of companions. One may add what Lactantius wrote with great distinction; from him and other sources Tillemont sets out the historical sequence in volume V, beginning at page 23, without taking into account the particular Acts, edited by us in Latin and Greek, which more recent scholars do not value highly and which Ruinart did not admit, following Eusebius alone on page 320. Wandalbert’s metrical elogium mentions Anthimus together with Anastasius:

> On the fifth, Anastasius the pope we celebrate; with him  
> Anthimus the bishop is joined, worthy in virtue.

Castor of Tarsus occupies the first place in the cited Hieronymian copies, from which Usuard undoubtedly received him—and alone, as our most approved codices, together with Notker, plainly demonstrate. Codices of the second class, such as Antwerp. and Max.-Lubec., Belinus, and many others to be cited in the Appendices, join Stephen to Castor, both in place and in time; unless we are greatly mistaken, he is plainly distinct—namely, Castor at Tarsus and Stephen crowned at Nicomedia, exactly as the cited Hieronymian witnesses, preserved by Florentius, explicitly report. I am not unaware that Henschenius arranged the matter differently in the Acts, in order to conform himself to Baronius, perhaps following Belinus and Maurolycus. Yet Henschenius does not conceal there what seems more probable to him. I certainly judge the authority of the most ancient martyrologies and codices far preferable to that of Belinus and Maurolycus. Let this be said in passing, on the occasion of that connection, contrary to our text. Concerning the true and simple reading of Usuard, I do not see how there can be any doubt.]

[Note: [Col. 0979B]

TORNACEN. mutilates the text, deleting part of the elogium of Blessed Anthimus and beginning with “some of whom,” etc.; otherwise it is extremely pure.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC., ANTUERP.-MAX, LEYDEN.-BELG., and the ULTRAJECT.-BELG. edition add, after Castor: “and Saint Stephen the martyr.”

PULSANEN. is defective both in part of the elogium of Blessed Anthimus and in the final announcement.

LOVAN. is likewise mutilated in the elogium of Anthimus. It joins Stephen to Castor.

ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC. insert, after “be worthy to enjoy”: “He established that no one should rise to the clerical state without the permission of his own bishop, and that no one should sit while the holy Gospels are being recited in church.” At the end: “At Tarsus in Cilicia, [the feast of] Saints Castor and Stephen the martyr.”

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, [the feast of] Saint Anastasius, pope and confessor. At Nicomedia, [the feast of] Saint Anthimus, bishop and martyr, with whom many from the clergy and people were crowned. At Tarsus in Cilicia, [the feast of] Saint Castor.” In this announcement [Col. 0979C] it is purer than the codices cited immediately above.

BRUXELLEN. inserts the following concerning Anastasius, in other words: “He established that no one should sit, but should stand, while the holy Gospels are being recited in church.” In the entry for Anthimus, something has been interpolated from Ado. At the end: “At Tarsus in Cilicia, [the feast of] Saints Castor and Stephen, martyrs.”

HAGENOYEN. gives the entry for Anthimus first, quite purely. It follows: “At Tarsus in Cilicia, the passion of the holy martyrs Castor and Stephen. At Rome, the deposition of Saint Anastasius, pope, who was the fortieth after blessed Peter, concerning whom Saint Jerome,” etc., almost as above. “In the territory of Limoges [Lemovices], [the feast of] Saint Alpinian, confessor.” See the Acts.

AQUICINCT., after “to enjoy,” adds: “He established that whenever the holy Gospels were recited, the priests should not sit but stand bowed down. And he established that a man from overseas should not be received into the clerical state unless he were designated by the written attestations of five bishops. By these measures he condemned the orders of overseas men as illegitimate.” I think *inlegitimos* or *illegitimos* should be read. At the end, instead of Castor, it has Pastor, and adds: “and Stephen the martyr.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., no. 130, add at the end: “In Egypt, [the feast of] Saints Victor, Maximus, and Martin.” Rather, Marcian. In the Hieronymian Martyrology, Paul, Germanus, and six others are added to them.

MATRIC.-CARTH.-ULTRAJECT. has nearly the same entry for Anastasius as the text. Then: “Anthimus, bishop, with his companions, martyrs from his own flock.”

VATICAN., no. 5949, adds at the end Ursicinus, with a long narrative concerning Saint Vitalis. Concerning Ursicinus, see the Acts under Castor and Stephen. He and Vitalis are mentioned again on the following day.

UGHELLIAN. has at the end: “And Saint Stephen the martyr.” As above in ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., etc.

ALTEMPS. adds to Castor: “and Saint Stephen.”

STROZZ.: “Castor and Stephen. At the city of Foligno, [the feast of] Saints Heraclius, Justus, Maurus, and Vitalis, martyrs, who suffered martyrdom under the governor Dacian.” In the index of the Omitted, Vitalis is referred to the following day, and the other three from Foligno to May 4.

[Col. 0980C] The LUBECO-COL. edition, concerning Anastasius, adds after “to enjoy”: “He established that no one should rise to the clerical state without the permission of his own bishop. And no one who lacked any member could become a cleric. And that no one should sit while the holy Gospels are being recited in church.” The entry for Anthimus is fairly pure. At the end: “At Tarsus in Cilicia, Saints Castor and Stephen, martyrs.”

GREVEN.: “In Lydia, [the feast of] Saints Genesius, Sodalus, and Marinus. Likewise, [the feast of] Saints Hermes, Victor, and Germanus. At the city of Civiltana, [the feast of] Saint Pulio, lector and martyr.” You will find more precise information about these in the Acts. “At Tarsus in Cilicia, [the feast of] Saint Stephen the martyr. At Rome, [the feast of] Evellius the martyr.” Referred to May 11. “At the city of Altinum, [the feast of] Saint Liberalis, confessor.” See in the Acts the two summaries of his life.

MOLAN. In the first edition, immediately after Castor, in italic letters, adds: “And Saint Stephen the martyr.” Then, in smaller type: “At the city of Altinum, [the feast of] Saint Liberalis, confessor.” Later editions have the same concerning Stephen. Again, in smaller type: “At the city of Altinum, [the feast of] Saint Liberalis, confessor, brought up by Bishop Heliodorus, who, after the city of Altinum had been destroyed, was transferred to Treviso.”]

[Col. 0977]

At Rome, the deposition of blessed Anastasius, pope, concerning whom Saint Jerome bears witness in venerable language that, because of his long life, the undeserving world was permitted to enjoy him. At Nicomedia, the birthday of Saint Anthimus, bishop and martyr, who, for confessing Christ during the persecution of Diocletian, as it is described in ecclesiastical history, received the glory of martyrdom by decapitation. Almost the whole multitude of his flock followed him by the same path of martyrdom: the judge caused some to be beheaded with the sword, others to burn in the flames, and others, placed in small boats, to be plunged into the sea. At Tarsus in Cilicia, [the feast of] Saint Castor.

**IV Kal. Day 28.** [Note: [Col. 0979]

Taken from the Pratensis, Herinien., Antwerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. witnesses.]

[Note: [Col. 0979D]

*Ursicii*, instead of *Ursicini*, is an error in Muneratus; likewise, *cum honestate*. In the Pratensis and Belinus, the particle *et* is redundant after *equulei*. Greven. and Molan. construct the sentence as follows: “He WAS seized by the consul Paulinus and afterward,” etc. But this manner of writing conflicts with all the Usuardine codices and with Ado himself, although the construction is correctly arranged. The carelessness of the Herinien. copyist caused him to omit the word *profundam*. Belin. wrote *poni* instead of *deponi*; Munerat. has *demitti*. Greven. and Molan. read “he departed to Christ.” After Theodora the virgin, Molanus inserted, in italic letters: “Concerning whom blessed Ambrose [wrote].” He alone, and perhaps more correctly, wrote *Didymus*, as Ado also has it. We judged that the reading of all our codices [Col. 0982A] should be retained. Antwerp. and Max.-Lubec. omit two words, namely, “by the name of Didymus.” In our Pratensis copy *Aphrodisii* is read; the other codices have *Afrodisii*; Belin. and Greven. *Affrodisii*. I regard the rest as things to be corrected rather than noted: *equule in* for *eculei*, *contempnens*, *Karilippi* for *Caralippi*, *Agapiti* for *Agapeti*, *Apollonii* for *Apollionis*, *sanctae Apolionis*, and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0981A]

Vitalis the martyr of Ravenna, who is mentioned in the marginal entry, is either unknown to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, omitted by them, or deliberately joined to Gervasius and Protasius on June 19; for we have no concern here with another Vitalis, perhaps the Pannonian, who is indicated there. Bede omits the place of his deposition or martyrdom. The Roman Little Martyrology plainly announces: “At Ravenna, [the feast of] Saint Vitalis the martyr, father of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.” Florus added a longer narrative, Rabanus another, and Ado another; Notker copied Rabanus and Ado, while Our author selected a few things suited to his own style. It should be noted, however, that although those martyrologists do not entirely agree in their elogia, they all drew from the same source, namely, a passion which must have been older than the ninth century, though it was not composed in an age that would merit great confidence; certainly it seems to have been unknown to Bede. Nor is it supported by the celebrated letter which most people today admit to have been falsely attributed to Ambrose. Tillemont says little about Vitalis in volume II, page 75, and more in the notes on page 496. Yet the critics’ judgment concerning the Acts does not prevent the most certain monuments from proving that his cult is very ancient; among these are Fronton’s Calendar and other materials published by Papebrochius in the Acts. Wandalbert’s metrical encomium agrees with them:

> On the fourth, it commemorates Vitalis, slain for the name of Christ,  
> Who by death deserved life everlasting.

Why Christopher is read on this day in the cited Bede and Rabanus, and Eusicius in Florus and others, I do not know; in the index of the Omitted they are referred to their proper days. Theodora and Didymus were first introduced by the Roman Little Martyrology and adorned by Ado with a notable elogium abridged from the Acts; Notker again copied it in full, whereas Usuard treated the matter more briefly. Nevertheless, it is clear that in this elogium, as in the preceding one, he took everything of his own from Ado. Furthermore, Ado first composed the elogium in such a way that he must have seen the genuine and official ancient Acts themselves, and combined with them what Saint Ambrose related concerning the similar contest of an Antiochene virgin in Book II of *On Virgins*, chapter 4. Whether he did so correctly has not yet, as I find, been determined among scholars. Papebrochius agreed with Baronius in the Annals that the virgins were different, since different places and times are assigned to their contests; nor did he clearly determine whether this Theodora of ours shared in the crown of martyrdom, since the Acts do not state it. Tillemont does not disagree with Papebrochius’s opinion when he explains the history of the passion in French in volume V, beginning at page 244. Nevertheless, Ruinart, in *Sincera et Selecta*, prefaces the matter with a warning on page 425, in which he attempts to defend the opinion of those who think that Ambrose’s anonymous virgin should be identified with our Theodora of Alexandria, whatever Ambrose may have called his own virgin of Antioch. Certainly, I do not find in Ruinart solutions commensurate with the arguments, nor do I see why the same ardor of divine love could not have served to protect the chastity of several virgins, as the cited Papebrochius and Tillemont rightly demonstrate concerning others. Of the last two announcements, we can say only that, unknown to the Roman Little Martyrology, they were copied word for word from the aforementioned Ado, having originally been drawn from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, although the names appear variously altered and badly connected, as you will understand from the Acts. We are certain that the genuine reading of Usuard is represented in our text.]

[Note: [Col. 0981C]

TORNACEN. and PULSANEN. are again defective. In the former, the elogium of Theodora is absent. In the latter, both the elogium of Theodora and what follows are missing.

ROSWEYD., after the pure text, adds: “Likewise, [the feast of] Pamphilus, confessor and bishop.” Of Sulmona, etc.

ANTUERPIEN.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC., and the ULTRAJ.-BEL. edition are almost pure, but they insert the words of the Roman Little Martyrology: “Father of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.” After “he departed to Christ,” they insert: “On the same day, [the feast of] Saint Valeria, wife of Saint Vitalis.”

CENTULEN.: “At Ravenna, [the feast of] Saints Vitalis and Valeria, martyrs, whose sons, the blessed Gervasius and Protasius, became illustrious martyrs. At Alexandria, [the feast of] Saint Theodora, virgin, with whom a certain brother named Didymus suffered. On the same day, the translation of Saint Winwaloe, abbot. Likewise, [the feast of] Saints Aphrodisius, Caralippus, Agapitus, and Eusebius, martyrs. In Pannonia, [the feast of] Saint Pollio, martyr. On the same day at Milan, [the feast of] Saint Peter, martyr, crowned by heretics.” He is commemorated elsewhere on April 29.

ANTUERP.-MAJ. is pure in the text, but adds at the end: “On the same day, [the feast of] Saint Winwaloe, abbot.” We discussed him on March 3.

BRUXELLEN. is almost pure in the entry for Vitalis; in second place it has: “And Saint Ursicinus the physician, who suffered under the aforesaid judge. On the same day, [the feast of] Saint Valeria, wife of blessed Vitalis.” Then, in another hand and more recent ink, the following is inserted: “And the deposition of Saint Monica, mother of Saint Augustine.” Referred to May 4. In the entry for Theodora and the rest it is fairly pure. At the end it adds: “Likewise, the translation of Saint Lambert, bishop.” See his birthday on September 17.

HAGENOYEN. is moderately interpolated in the entry for Vitalis. Then: “On the same day, [the feast of] Saint Valeria, wife of Saint Vitalis the martyr. Because she refused to fast with the idolaters, saying that she was a Christian, she met the end of her life under blows.” In the entry for Theodora it adds some fairly familiar material. Finally: “On the same day, [the feast of] Saints Aphrodisius, Caralippus, Agapius, and Eusebius, martyrs.” The final announcement concerning Pollio is absent.

AQUICINCT. adds at the end: “And Saint Winwaloe, confessor.” We have already said that he was treated on March 3.

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., bearing no. 130, add at the end: “Likewise at Alexandria, [the feast of] Saint Euphrosyna, virgin.” See February 11.

DAVERON.: “Blessed Svingralocus, abbot.” It is quite clear that Winwaloe is indicated, concerning whom see above.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJ.: “Vitalis, martyr and soldier, who was the father of Saints Gervasius and Protasius; Theodora, virgin, and Didymus, who rescued her from danger and afterward died with her. Aphrodisius the martyr and others. The translation of Saint Lambert, bishop and confessor.”]

[Col. 0983A] CODEX BIGOTIAN., marked P 5: “In Pannonia, [the feast of] Saint Apollion, martyr.” Read *Pollion*.

REG. SUEC., marked no. 148: “At the monastery, [the feast of] Saint Winwaloe.” I think Blandinius is meant.

IN VATICAN., no. 5949, the following is corruptly added: “On the same day, Epius, Aphrodisius,” etc.

UGHELLIAN. writes *Apolionis* instead of *Pollionis*.

ALTEMPS.: “At the monastery of the church of Saint Ebrulf, the translation of Saint Wulsinus, bishop and confessor.” Is the younger Wilfrid of York indicated? Concerning him, see the Acts for April 29.

BIZUNTICEN.: “At Bellevaux, [the feast of] Saint Bernard, confessor.” So far he is unknown to us, at least as a saint. Perhaps someone will provide further information.

The LUBECO-COL. edition, after the interpolated text concerning Vitalis, adds further: “His body, however, after the translation, rests at Cologne, in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, on the Capitol. On the same day, [the feast of] Saint Valeria, wife of the aforementioned Saint Vitalis, who, refusing to sacrifice, was slaughtered [or: was slaughtered because she refused] even unto death.” The remainder of the text is fairly pure. It follows: “At Liège, the translation of Saint Lambert, bishop and martyr of that place. At Le Mans, the translation to Paderborn of Saint Liborius, bishop and confessor.” His birthday is July 23, on which day his feast is now celebrated by command.

GREVEN.: “Victorinus the martyr, Victor, Lucian, and others.” See the Acts. “Pamphilus, bishop of Corfinium.” He is the same person mentioned above, the Sulmonan. “Likewise, blessed Valeria, wife of the aforementioned Saint Vitalis. Refusing to sacrifice, she was slaughtered unto death and obtained the crown of martyrdom. At Liège, the translation of Saint Lambert, bishop and martyr of that place. At Paderborn, the translation of Saint Liborius, bishop of Le Mans and confessor.”

MOLAN.: “Likewise, the departure of Noah from the ark. At Liège, the translation of Saint Lambert the martyr. On the same day, [the feast of] Saint Valeria, wife of Saint Vitalis. On the same day, the elevation of Saint Amatus, bishop and confessor.” His life will be given on September 13. “At Laon-la-Fort, the translation of Saint Proba, virgin.” See the Acts. Other editions read: “On the same day, [the feast of] Saint Valeria,” etc. “In Spain, [the feast of] Saint Prudentius, bishop of Tarazona and confessor. At the city of Metz, [the feast of] Saint Adelphus, bishop and confessor. On the twenty-eighth day, [the feast of] Saints Dadas, Maximus, and Quintilian, martyrs.” Concerning these and Adelphus, see the index of the Omitted. “At Liège,” and “at Laon-la-Fort,” as above. “On the same day at Douai, the elevation of Saint Amatus, bishop and confessor. At this elevation of the sacred body, which they had lost, the Lord restored health to many—health to the sick, sight and hearing to the blind and the deaf;  then men whose limbs had previously been crippled returned, exulting and marveling at the traces of their feet. Likewise, the departure of Noah from the ark.” Then, in smaller letters: “On the same day, the martyrdom of Saint Paphnutius, abbot, and five hundred forty-six who suffered martyrdom together with him.” See the Omitted.]

[Col. 0979]

At Ravenna, the birthday of Saint Vitalis the martyr, who, after taking up the body of blessed Ursicinus and burying it honorably, was seized by the consul Paulinus. After being tortured on the rack, he was ordered to be thrown into a deep pit and crushed beneath earth and stones; by such a martyrdom he departed to Christ. At Alexandria, [the feast of] Saint Theodora, virgin, who, refusing to sacrifice and having been handed over to a brothel, was suddenly rescued by one of the brothers, named Didymus, through the marvelous favor of God; afterward, when he was struck down with her, he was crowned together with her. On the same day, [the feast of] Aphrodisius, Caralippus, Agapius, and Eusebius, martyrs. In Pannonia, [the feast of] Saint Pollio, martyr.

**III Kal. Day 29.** [Note: [Col. 0983]

Only the Pratensis, Herinien., Antwerp.-Maj., Greven., and Molan. witnesses are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0983C]

I wrote *Tychici* with the Pratensis and Molanus. No one can deny that this is the correct spelling, as though one were to say *Fortunatus*; but we are not undertaking to resolve grammatical questions here, and we have followed the cited codices as the more reliable witnesses. I admit, however, that in the Pratensis the writing leaves it uncertain whether the first letter is T or C. Herinien. and the others read *Tichici*; Greven. has the worse form *Titici*; Antwerp.-Maj. the worst, *Titi*. The same codex omitted the particle *in* before *Domino*; Molanus perhaps did so as well. Greven. and Antwerp.-Maj. have *Cirthensem*; Molan. [Col. 0984C] *Circensem*. I followed the Pratensis, Herinien., and others. *Secundii*, instead of *Secundini*, is an error in Antwerp.-Maj. There again it has *collegio* (“college”) instead of *sacerdotio* (“priesthood”). Herinien. also has *temptandam*. Greven. and Molan. read “glorious martyrs.” The former also has above “holy disciples of Paul.” All read *Emilianus*, except Molanus, who has *Aemilianus*, as he often arbitrarily corrects certain forms, especially diphthongs, and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0983C]

At Paphos, [the feast of] Tychicus, a disciple of the apostles. These are the words of the Roman Little Martyrology, from which both of today’s announcements derive, having been received by Our author through Ado. Why this saint is commemorated on this day rather than another, I think was determined by the author of the Roman Little Martyrology purely at will. What we have already cited from that work, scarcely altered by a single letter, was copied by Ado, and from him by Notker. Usuard, however, compiled a brief elogium from Paul’s Epistles, especially Colossians, chapter 4, as it appears in the marginal entry. Henschenius’s brief commentary on Tychicus gathers from other passages of Paul’s Epistles material which Tillemont inserted in its proper places in volume I, in the life of the Apostle. The Greeks relate more about him; this agrees with the observation of our Henschenius: namely, that the testimonies drawn from Sacred Scripture produced so elevated an impression concerning Tychicus that, since he seems to have benefited various cities by spreading the faith, many believed him to have been among their first bishops. But it is enough for us to explain the difficulties of our Latin martyrologists.

Agapius and Secundinus were likewise taken, as we have said, from the Roman Little Martyrology. Ado added an elogium distinguished by new circumstances, drawn from the Acts of Marianus and James, concerning whom on the following day; from Ado, Notker took it, with considerable ornament and elegance. Whatever Usuard has, however, he received from there word for word, so that it is surprising that he omitted only a few words. The entire group of martyrs is omitted from the Acts today because their deeds are connected with the triumph of Marianus and James, as can be read there on the thirtieth day. For us, the pure and simple text of Usuard is sufficient. Whoever wishes to view the whole cohort should consult Henschenius on the aforementioned day, on which the most distinguished Acts of all are elucidated; they were also published by Ruinart and explained with new observations on page 224. Tillemont discusses them in French in volume IV, beginning at page 215, where he rightly observes that their feast is more probably to be commemorated on May 6, on which James and Marinus, and another Marianus, are recorded in the Carthaginian Calendar, as we shall say on the following day. From this one may again infer that the author of the Roman Little Martyrology consecrated an arbitrary day to these martyrs also, separating them from the rest of the company. Meanwhile, Wandalbert sings of today’s bishops in verse:

> On the third, he venerates the bishops dedicated to the altar and to merit,  
> Agapus and likewise Secundinus.

] [Note: [Col. 0985A]

TORNACEN., here again more abbreviated, immediately after “of the bishops” adds: “Who, from distinguished priestly rank, omitting the intervening material, during the persecution of Valerian, after a long exile, at the aforesaid city,” etc.

PULSANEN., in the first announcement quite pure, has in second place: “At Alexandria, [the feast of] Saint Euphrosyna, virgin. It follows: In Numidia . . . .” through “of the bishops,” inclusive.

ANTUERP. adds after the text: “Likewise, the translation of Saint Robert, first abbot of the Cistercians.”

MAX.-LUBEC.: “In the territory of Langres, at Molesme [Molismum], [the feast of] blessed Robert, first abbot of Cîteaux.”

MUNERAT. also has at the end: “At Milan, [the feast of] Saint Peter the martyr, of the Order of Friars Preachers.” He is celebrated in many other recent codices, but nowhere more fully than in LEYDEN. and FLORENTINE codices.

ROSWEYD. likewise adds after the text: “In Tuscany, [the feast of] Torpetes the martyr, servant of Nero.” He is more solemnly commemorated on May 17.

LOVANIEN. is pure through “glorious martyrs.” It omits the rest and substitutes: “In the territory of Langres, at Molesme, [the feast of] blessed Robert, confessor, first abbot of Cîteaux. On the same day, in the territory of Milan, the passion of Saint Peter, of the Order of Preachers.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., LEYDEN., BELG., and the ULTBAJ.-BELG. edition, after a fairly pure text, append exactly the same Appendices as LOVAN.

[Col. 0985C] LEYDEN. adds to the pure text: “In the territory of Langres, at Molesme, [the feast of] blessed Robert, confessor, first abbot of Cîteaux. On the same day, in the territory of Milan, the passion of Saint Peter, of the Order of Preachers, who, after preaching the word of God far and wide throughout the regions of Italy against the men [or: poison] of heretical depravity, was finally killed by the sword of the heretics.”

ULTRAJECT., ALBERGEN., and DANIC. begin: “In the territory of Milan, etc.,” as we have just reported from LEYDEN. The text that follows is fairly pure. At the end, however: “In the territory of Langres,” etc.

CENTULEN.: “In Tuscany, [the feast of] Saint Torpetes the martyr. At Paphos, [the feast of] Tychicus, a disciple of the apostles. In Numidia, at the Circensian colony, [the feast of] Saints Agapius and Secundinus, bishops.”

BRUXELLEN., after a nearly pure text, adds: “In the territory of Langres, etc.” Then: “In the territory of Milan . . . . .” also as above. Finally: [Col. 0985D] “Elsewhere, [the feast of] Germanus, bishop.” [Could this be the Alexandrian or Nicomedian martyr?]

HAGENOYEN., in the fairly pure text, adds: “In the territory of Langres, in the monastery of Molesme, [the feast of] Saint Robert, abbot.” A long history of Peter the martyr follows, better read in the Acts. At the end: “Likewise, at the monastery of Cluny, [the feast of] Saint Hugh, abbot.”

AQUICINCT., after the twins, adds: “And Saint Germanus, bishop.” Then, in a more recent hand: “On the same day, in Burgundy, [the feast of] Saint Robert, abbot.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., no. 130: “At Cluny, the passing of Saint Hugh, abbot.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Peter the martyr. Hugh, abbot of Cluny. Robert, first abbot of Cîteaux. Tychicus, deacon, disciple of the apostles. Agapius and Secundinus, martyrs, with their companions.”

CLUNIACEN.: “On the same day, at Cluny, the birthday of most blessed Hugh, most devout father of monks, whose life was made illustrious by many virtues.”

VATICAN., no. 5949, first place: “The passing of Saint Euphrosyna, virgin.”

UGHELLIAN.: “On the same day, the deposition of most blessed Robert, first abbot of Cîteaux. At Milan, the passion of blessed Peter the martyr.” The latter was a rubric erased by the same scribe and written under the following day, as Papebrochius noted, having inspected and collated the codex himself.

[Col. 0986B] ALTEMPS.: “In Britain, the translation of Saint Edmund, king and martyr.” In the Acts it is referred to his birthday, November 20. “At Périgueux, [the feast of] Saint Frontasius, martyr.” In the Acts it is referred back to January 2. “And [the feast of] Torpetes the martyr.” Concerning him, see above.

FLORENTIN., first place: “At Rome, [the feast of] Saint Catherine of Siena, virgin, of the Order of Preachers, adorned with the ring of Jesus Christ and with great revelations. She died at Rome and was buried there in the church of Saint Mary sopra Minerva. Pope Pius II enrolled her in the catalogue of the saints. On the same day, at Milan, the passion of Saint Peter the martyr, a Veronese by birth, of the Order of Preachers, whose life was distinguished by steadfast preaching against heretics and by miracles. In the Tuscan city of Pisa, [the feast of] Saint Torpetes the martyr, whom Caesar Nero, after afflicting him with scourging, caused to be led outside the aforesaid city and beheaded; thus he departed to Christ. In the territory of Langres, in the monastery of Molesme, [the feast of] Saint Robert, abbot of Cîteaux. At Ravenna, [the feast of] Saint Liberius, archbishop; at the monastery of Cluny, [the feast of] Saint Hugh, abbot.” In these codices, when they are compared with one another and with GREVEN., various discrepancies sometimes occur. Since the copyist Henschenius did not record them very clearly, it can easily happen that we occasionally attribute one person’s words incorrectly, though harmlessly, to another; we gave warning of this also in the preface.

REMENS. SS. Thimothei and Apollinaris: “At Avenniacum, [the feast of] Saint Gumbert, king.” In the Acts he is more correctly called Gondebertus, not a king but a martyr.

The LUBECO-COL. edition begins: “At Cologne, the translation of Saint Anno, archbishop and confessor. This took place immediately after his death, from the city of Cologne to Mount Siegburg. But in the thirty-eighth year after the death of that most holy man, and in the year of the Lord 1083, by the venerable John, priest and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and Peter, bishop of the church of Luni, he was solemnly and reverently placed in a reliquary at the shrine.” Concerning Peter, nearly as in LEYDEN above. It follows: “At Rome, [the feast of] Saint Catherine, virgin. She was born in the city of Siena; in her youth she assumed the penitential habit of Saint Dominic, and, renowned for frequent miracles and teachings, rested at Rome in the thirty-third year of her age, buried in the church of Saint Mary above Minerva. Pope Pius II, who enrolled her in the catalogue of the saints, commanded that her feast be solemnly celebrated perpetually on the first Sunday of May.” See the Acts. A fairly pure text follows. Then, concerning Robert, etc.: “On the same day, [the feast of] blessed Ursio and Maurilius, confessors.” They are referred to their proper days in the Omitted. “In Britain, at the castle of Beatrice, the translation of Saint Edmund, king and martyr. In [Col. 0987A] Tuscany, [the feast of] Saint Torpetes the martyr.” These have been discussed fully above.

BELIN., at the end: “On the same day, at Milan, [the feast of] Saint Peter the martyr, of the Order of Friars Preachers. At the monastery of Cluny, most blessed Hugh, abbot [the second edition has: Hugh].”

GREVEN.: “In Tuscany, of Saint Torpes, martyr, who, at the command of Silvius, was led outside the city of Pisa and completed his martyrdom by decapitation. Nevertheless, his solemn feast is celebrated more festively on 21 May. In Africa, of Gratus with six others. In the territory of Milan, of Saint Peter, priest and martyr, of the Order of Preachers. Serving Christ in virginity, when through the regions of Italy, etc. In Alexandria, of Germanus, priest. At Nicomedia, of Prodocus, deacon. At Perugia, of Valens, Gratus, and Prodentius.” See the Acts. “Of Leo, bishop and confessor, who first rested on the island of Samos; then, when Venetians landed there, they were warned by a miracle and carried the saint’s body away with them. Of Maxentius, confessor. Of Vitus, confessor. Of Ursio and Maurilius, confessors.” See the saints omitted from the proper days. “Likewise of Urban. On the same day, of blessed Hugh, abbot of Cluny, a man of great holiness, who was educated by blessed Odilo and deserved to become his worthy successor in the government of the monastery. Likewise, of Saint Robert, abbot and confessor. When he was abbot in the monastery of Cluny, stirred by the divine Spirit and desiring to observe the Rule more strictly, he withdrew with several brothers who shared his zeal and began the monastery and Order of Cîteaux in the year of the Lord 1098; renowned for his life and miracles, he rested in peace. At Auxerre, of Saint Marianus, monk and confessor.” Is this the Marianus Scotus? I do not know who else could be indicated on this day. “At Rome, the deposition of Saint Catherine of Siena, virgin. She, in her youth, assumed the habit, etc.,” as above. “In Britain, at Castro Beatricis, etc. Likewise, of blessed memory, Peter Favre, of the Carthusian Order, prior of the house of the Holy Cross in the City. When he was suffering in his final illness and was almost cast into despair by the ancient adversary, he was freed by the glorious Mother of God, who appeared to him. Then he gave up his spirit to God while saying in the litany: ‘All you saints who are present here, pray for us.’ For he pointed out with great exultation and raised finger the very saints whom he himself saw present.” Nothing is said of him in the first edition. See the saints omitted from the proper days.

MOLAN.: “On the same day, at Milan,” etc., almost as in LEYDEN. “At the monastery of Cluny, of the most blessed Hugh, abbot. In the territory of Langres . . .” as there. “And the deposition of Saint Prudentius.” He is placed here without the title either of martyr or confessor; but, unless I am mistaken, no one other than that Prudentius can be indicated—the one who holds first place among the Nicomedian martyrs. From the same group, Prodocus is wrongly venerated, while Urban is correctly given by GREVENUS: see the Acts. In other editions, concerning Peter, as has already been said more than once. Concerning Catherine likewise, up to “above Minerva.” Then he adds: “Her feast, however, is deferred to the Sunday after the Invention of the Holy Cross.” It is very well known that, now that her cult is firmly established, her feast is celebrated on 30 April, while Peter the martyr is commemorated on this day. Concerning Robert and Hugh, as above. “On the twenty-ninth day, of the nine holy martyrs at Cyzicus.” See the individual names of each in our Acts, taken from the Greek Menologia, whose words Henschenius quotes in his brief Commentary. “And of Saint Memnon the wonderworker.” He too is drawn from Greek records, but is wrongly assigned to this day, since he belongs to 28 April, as you will find in the Acts. “On the same day, the feast of Saint Ava, virgin.” In smaller type: “Who rests at Donon, not canonized.” See what survives concerning her, collected by Henschenius, where he explains Molan’s observation concerning the anniversary prayers customarily offered for her at Donon. These prayers prejudice in no way the cult either of Ava or of the other saints whom we know to have been honored by a similar office. See volume I of June, p. 810, no. 4.]

[Col. 0983]

At Paphos, Saint Tychicus, deacon, disciple of blessed Paul. The same Apostle mentions him in his letters, declaring that he will be a most beloved brother and fellow servant in the Lord. In Numidia, near the colony of Cirta, the birthday of the holy martyrs Agapius and Secundinus, bishops, who, during the persecution of Valerian, after a long exile, at the aforesaid city—where at that time the fury of the pagans was especially eager to test the faith of the righteous—were made glorious martyrs from their distinguished priestly rank. In their company suffered Emilianus, a soldier, Tertulla and Antonia, sacred virgins, and a certain woman with her twin children.

The day before the Kalends. The 30th day.

[Note: [Col. 0987C]

The Pratensis, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, Muneratus, Belinus, Greven, and Molanus witnesses are pure. The Antwerp-Maximilian, Utrecht, Leyden, Louvain, Albergen, Danic, and Utrecht-Belgian editions are added.]

[Note: [Col. 0987D]

In Muneratus, the omission of the preceding word makes the meaning obscure. In Belinus, or in his printer, *infestationes* is an error, as is *Datianae*, which Muneratus also has. Some manuscripts write *clarissimo*, but the construction itself, unless I am mistaken, requires *carissimo*, as the Pratensis, Herinensis, Tornacensis, and other witnesses read, together with Ado. Likewise *allevati*, not *alleviati*, as many manuscripts have. In the most recent witness, however, it occurs only in Muneratus; it is sufficiently clear that *tamen* is redundant. Belinus wrote *Santone* instead of *Sanctonas*. These matters are quite clear. The greater question is whether *Euprobus* should be read, as we have retained it in the text, or rather *Eutropes*, as Ado has, or *Eutropii*, as the Acts and manuscripts commonly have. The oldest manuscripts, the Pratensis, Herinensis, and Tornacensis, support our reading; on their authority we rely above all, even when they are in error. Molanus reads wrongly *quem cum sanctus, alii pejus direxisset* for *direxit*, and these readings disturb the sense. Belinus has *Galliam*, omitting the preposition *in*, where *demum* is wrongly added. Greven and Molanus give *peracta diu*; the Pratensis, *peractamque praedicationem*. Belinus has *ceso capite*. Everything is correct in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0987D]

The Romanum parvum distinctly presents Marianus and Jacobus, beheaded with many others, today. Whether they are expressed so clearly in the Hieronymian copies is not entirely clear to me; nevertheless, it can be gathered from Florentinius and the Acts that they are indicated there with their companions. We sufficiently indicated yesterday that the older memory of both is recorded in the Carthaginian Calendar on the day before the Nones of May. Moreover, we explained yesterday the association of these martyrs with the Cirta martyrs of the preceding day. Henschenius gives fuller information concerning the place and time of the martyrdom of most of their companions.
